cards.title: Reversible simulation in polynomial time and linear space
cards.formal:
Does there exist one computable compiler \(\mathcal C\) that maps every deterministic multitape Turing machine \(M\) to a reversible multitape machine \(R=\mathcal C(M)\) with the following simultaneous guarantees? For every \(M\), there are a constant \(c_M\ge1\) and an integer \(d_M\ge1\) such that, on every input \(x\) on which \(M\) halts, \(R\) halts with exactly the output pair \((x,M(x))\), clears its auxiliary tapes, and satisfies
\[S_R(x)\le c_M S_M(x),\qquad T_R(x)\le c_M T_M(x)^{d_M}.\]
On every input on which \(M\) does not halt, \(R\) must also fail to halt. The same \(R\) must meet both bounds on every halting input. This is the previously selected polynomial-time, linear-space version of the source's broader simulation tradeoff question.
cards.definitions:
Each machine has a finite transition table, finitely many states, a finite tape alphabet containing 0, 1, a blank and delimiters, and a fixed finite number of two-way tapes with one head per tape. A transition reads the scanned symbols, writes symbols and moves each head by at most one cell. Tapes are indexed by integers, and all heads initially sit at a designated origin. The machine description lists these finite objects explicitly in a fixed effectively decodable binary syntax. Alphabet size, tape count and states may depend on the fixed machine but not on its input. There are no oracle, advice, random or external-storage tapes.

Initially the binary input \(x\), with fixed delimiters, occupies consecutive cells of one tape; all other cells are blank. A halting run has a finite designated binary output \(M(x)\), with delimiters on an output tape. A transition is a partial deterministic function on full configurations; a configuration with no next transition is terminal. The full configuration includes the state, every tape's contents and every head position. A simulator must implement the stated terminal-output convention on its intended input runs.

A machine is reversible if its partial one-step map is injective on its entire configuration space: whenever transitions from configurations \(u\) and \(v\) produce the same configuration, \(u=v\). Thus no step may merge two different predecessor configurations. This property concerns the finite machine's full transition semantics, not just the particular run from a blank workspace. Halting states have no outgoing step; injectivity does not require every configuration to have a predecessor. Reversibility is logical reversibility of a classical machine, not a physical energy model or a quantum operation.

For a halting run, \(S_M(x)\) is the number of distinct tape cells initially occupied or visited during the entire run, summed over all tapes, with a minimum of 1. A cell still counts if it is later erased. Input, output, delimiter, history and work cells all count. Let
\[T_M(x)=\max\{1,|x|,\text{number of transitions before halting}\}.\]
Define \(S_R,T_R\) in exactly the same way. This is a per-input resource comparison, not a comparison of unrelated worst-case inputs of a given length. Finite control is part of the fixed machine description, while every tape cell used at run time is included. No additional initially full catalytic tape is supplied for free.

At termination, the simulator has two designated output tracks or tapes containing the original \(x\) and \(M(x)\), with the fixed delimiters, and all auxiliary tape contents are blank. Retaining \(x\) is essential: different inputs can yield the same \(M(x)\), but a reversible computation cannot merge their histories into an identical final configuration. The output pair is required exactly; leaving a computation-history string as garbage is not accepted. The simulator need only preserve the partial function in this input-preserving sense, rather than reproduce each intermediate configuration of \(M\).

The compiler is a single total deterministic computable function on valid machine descriptions; its compilation time is unrestricted. It outputs a finite reversible machine description, with no dependence on the later input \(x\). Neither the compiler nor the simulator is given the eventual halting time or space use as an extra input. The constants \(c_M,d_M\) may depend on \(M\), but are fixed before quantifying over all \(x\). No halting-time or resource bound is required on divergent runs beyond preservation of nontermination. A simulator chosen separately for every individual input would not satisfy the compiler requirement.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof or refutation of the existence of this compiler. A positive answer must establish total computability of compilation, reversibility of every output machine on its full configuration space, preservation of the partial function and nontermination behavior, clean input-preserving output, and the two simultaneous per-input resource bounds. A negative answer must prove that no compiler can satisfy these requirements for all machines and inputs; failure of one known construction does not suffice. Separate simulators achieving the time and space bounds independently do not settle the conjunction. A lower bound only for reversible pebble games, an oracle-relative simulation model or circuits does not refute unrestricted reversible multitape simulation. The resource requirements are exact asymptotic claims, without additive numerical tolerance.
cards.why: Reversible computation avoids logical information erasure, but that advantage may require additional memory or time. This question asks whether a general computation can retain its asymptotic storage scale while paying only a polynomial time overhead.

importance.reason: A basic simultaneous-resource question about reversible computation, connecting time-space complexity with the informational cost of computation.

context_blocks.text: An irreversible computation may overwrite information that is no longer needed. A reversible machine must retain enough information elsewhere to make each transition invertible on its image. The question asks whether doing so can always preserve the original storage scale while incurring only polynomial time overhead.

Input preservation and clearing auxiliary tapes specify what counts as a completed simulation. They prevent two easy ambiguities: erasing distinct inputs that have the same answer, and treating a large retained execution history as an acceptable final result.

Bennett’s simulations establish polynomial-time reversible computation with space \(O(S\log(T+2))\), among other tradeoffs. The logarithmic multiplier is not bounded by one machine-dependent constant as the input grows, so this bound does not establish the card’s \(O(S)\) requirement.

Lange, McKenzie and Tapp show that deterministic space can be preserved by reversible computation. The general construction can take exponential time, so space preservation alone does not imply the required polynomial overhead in the original running time.

Buhrman, Tromp and Vitányi give intermediate time-space tradeoffs and discuss how to remove an advance bound on the simulated running time. Their result bridges the classical extremes but does not give the required simultaneous polynomial-time and constant-factor-space guarantee for every machine.

Reversible pebble games model a particular style of simulation, with memory snapshots represented by pebbles. A lower bound for that model need not apply to all reversible machines. The space-preserving theorem itself demonstrated that general simulation can escape restrictions of that particular model.

The 2026 catalytic-computation paper studies an additional tape initialized with arbitrary contents that must be restored. Its reversible-space lemma has no general polynomial-time-overhead guarantee. Both its separate catalytic resource and the missing time bound matter: it is related progress, not a solution to the total-storage target here.

Logical reversibility is relevant to the information erased during computation, but this card does not set an energy bound for hardware. Its mathematical success criterion is entirely the classical compiler, correctness, time and space statement.

cards.title: Closure of SZK under truth-table reductions
cards.formal:
Is statistical zero knowledge closed under deterministic polynomial-time truth-table reductions, using the promise-problem and three-valued circuit semantics of the source? In symbols,
\[\forall A,B,\qquad B\in\mathrm{SZK}\ \land\ A\le_{\mathrm{tt}}^{\mathrm P}B\quad\Longrightarrow\quad A\in\mathrm{SZK}.\]
The reduction writes all queries before obtaining their answers and combines those answers with an arbitrary polynomial-size Boolean circuit. Its circuit need not have logarithmic depth or be a polynomial-size formula. Queries outside the oracle’s promise are permitted under the explicit rules below.
cards.why: A positive answer would make statistical zero knowledge robust under a broad form of efficient nonadaptive composition. A negative answer would reveal a basic limitation on combining individually private verification tasks, despite the known strong formula closure.
cards.status_note: Source-open: the final ITCS 2023 paper explicitly poses the question after Theorem 20, under its Definition 19. The original JACM 2003 Definitions 4.6 and 4.12–4.13 and the formula-closure proof/Corollary 4.14 were read to recover the precise promise semantics. The accepted December 2024 manuscript of the 2025 TOCT paper was checked at §7/Definitions 7.1–7.2/Theorem 7.8 and the surrounding proof for the restricted later result. Bounded subsequent-work searches through 16 September 2026 found no matching general closure theorem or unconditional refutation; no exhaustive open-status certification or independent verification of every cited proof is claimed.

The reduction prepares all queries first and combines their answers with a polynomial-size Boolean circuit.
Promise-violating queries are handled by the source’s explicit gate-by-gate three-valued logic.

cards.definitions:
A promise problem is an ordered pair \(A=(A_Y,A_N)\) of disjoint subsets of \(\{0,1\}^{*}\). Correctness requires acceptance on \(A_Y\) and rejection on \(A_N\); inputs outside their union have no required answer. A polynomial-time many-one reduction \(h\) from \(A\) to \(B\) is one uniform deterministic algorithm with running time at most \(C(n+1)^d\), for fixed constants \(C,d\), such that \(h(A_Y)\subseteq B_Y\) and \(h(A_N)\subseteq B_N\). Its behavior outside the promise is unrestricted. All lengths and time bounds refer to full explicit binary encodings.

For a self-contained definition of SZK, use its standard complete promise problem Statistical Difference, SD. A well-formed SD instance is a pair of explicitly described Boolean sampling circuits \(C:\{0,1\}^{m}\to\{0,1\}^{\ell}\) and \(D:\{0,1\}^{r}\to\{0,1\}^{\ell}\). A circuit is a finite acyclic list of binary AND/OR gates, unary NOT gates and constants, with its input and output wires explicitly listed. The integers \(m,r,\ell\) and all wire indices are part of the description; each listed input wire receives an independent fair bit. Let \(X=C(U_m)\) and \(Y=D(U_r)\), with \(U_s\) uniform on all \(s\)-bit strings. Their statistical distance is
\[\Delta(X,Y)=\frac12\sum_{z\in\{0,1\}^{\ell}}\bigl|\Pr[X=z]-\Pr[Y=z]\bigr|.\]
Set \(\mathrm{SD}_Y=\{(C,D):\Delta(X,Y)>2/3\}\) and \(\mathrm{SD}_N=\{(C,D):\Delta(X,Y)<1/3\}\). Intermediate-distance pairs and malformed descriptions lie outside the promise. SZK is the class of all promise problems having a deterministic polynomial-time many-one reduction to SD. By the completeness theorem this is the usual classical statistical-zero-knowledge class; no additional choice of a protocol definition is needed for this formulation.

For any promise problem \(B\), define its partial characteristic value by \(\chi_B(z)=1\) on \(B_Y\), \(0\) on \(B_N\), and \(*\) outside the promise. The reduction \(A\le_{\mathrm{tt}}^{\mathrm P}B\) means that one uniform deterministic polynomial-time machine maps each input \(x\) to a finite list \(z_1,\ldots,z_k\) and a Boolean circuit \(F\) with those \(k\) answer variables, satisfying
\[x\in A_Y\Longrightarrow F(\chi_B(z_1),\ldots,\chi_B(z_k))=1,\]
\[x\in A_N\Longrightarrow F(\chi_B(z_1),\ldots,\chi_B(z_k))=0.\]
The number of queries, sum of their bit lengths and size of the explicitly written circuit are all polynomially bounded in \(|x|\). The generating machine does not query \(B\) while preparing them. \(F\) is an acyclic AND/OR/NOT circuit with constants and unrestricted reuse of intermediate wires; its depth is limited only by its polynomial size. The query count may be zero. No randomized, adaptive or nonuniform reduction is allowed.

Evaluate \(F\) gate by gate over \(\{0,1,*\}\). NOT exchanges 0 and 1 and leaves \(*\) unchanged. AND returns 0 if either input is 0, returns 1 if both are 1, and returns \(*\) otherwise. OR returns 1 if either input is 1, returns 0 if both are 0, and returns \(*\) otherwise. Constants retain their values. These rules are part of the source’s definition, including on queries outside the promise. A required final value 0 or 1 is stable under replacing unknown inputs by bits, but the converse fails: \(u\lor\neg u\) evaluates to \(*\) at \(u=*\), although it is 1 on both Boolean assignments. Thus mere agreement on all Boolean completions is not silently substituted for the specified circuit semantics. Requiring every query to satisfy the promise would also change the stated reduction notion.

A Boolean formula is a circuit presented as a tree, with repeated subcomputations written out separately. Closure for polynomial-size formulas or logarithmic-depth circuits is the known restricted case. The target permits arbitrary polynomial-size circuits, whose compact descriptions may reuse intermediate results many times. The quantifiers range over arbitrary promise problems and every valid reduction of the stated kind; the polynomial bounds and programs may depend on the fixed problems and reduction, but not on individual inputs.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof or refutation of the displayed universal closure statement. A positive answer must show that every promise problem reducing in the specified way to any SZK promise problem itself reduces to SD, or give an equivalent fully justified SZK protocol. A negative answer must establish promise problems \(A,B\), prove \(B\in\mathrm{SZK}\) and \(A\le_{\mathrm{tt}}^{\mathrm P}B\), and prove \(A\notin\mathrm{SZK}\). The reduction’s treatment of unknown answers and its uniform polynomial bounds must be included. Closure only for formulas, logarithmic-depth circuits, or a special oracle problem does not prove the full claim without an equivalence proof. An oracle-relative or conditional separation does not refute this unrelativized target. All class, promise and probability thresholds are exact; numerical acceptance tolerance is irrelevant.

source_formulation.text: After proving the Boolean-formula characterization of SZK, the source says that closure under general polynomial-time truth-table reductions remains open.
source_formulation.caption: Editorial paraphrase of the paragraph after Theorem 20, with Definition 19’s three-valued promise semantics retained

context_blocks.text: Statistical zero knowledge allows a verifier to be convinced of a statement without learning additional information, in the sense that the verifier’s view can be simulated with negligible statistical error. This card asks whether that property survives taking many nonadaptive questions and performing an arbitrary efficient Boolean computation on their answers.

The Statistical Difference complete problem makes the class concrete: distinguish two efficiently sampled distributions that are far apart from ones that are close. The middle range is deliberately left outside the promise. The card uses this characterization as its exact definition of SZK.

Sahai and Vadhan prove closure under polynomial-size Boolean formulas, and therefore under polynomial-size circuits of logarithmic depth. This is stronger than closure under a constant number of AND, OR and NOT operations, but still leaves general polynomial-depth circuit composition open.

The distinction is computational rather than a choice of logical connectives. Formulas must repeat each reused subcomputation, while circuits can share it. Replacing a circuit by its expanded expression tree need not preserve polynomial size.

The 2023 paper explicitly retains the general truth-table question while using the known formula closure in a characterization based on Kolmogorov complexity. That characterization does not claim general circuit closure.

The later space-bounded work proves a corresponding Boolean-formula closure for the logarithmic-space statistical-zero-knowledge class. Its Theorem 7.8 is a result about a restricted model and formula reductions; it does not establish the general circuit target here.

Handling queries outside the promise is essential: an SD oracle need not give meaningful information for distributions in the gap. The precise three-valued rules prevent such queries from being treated as reliable facts and preserve the formulation actually used by the source.

cards.context:
Statistical zero knowledge allows a verifier to be convinced of a statement without learning additional information, in the sense that the verifier’s view can be simulated with negligible statistical error. This card asks whether that property survives taking many nonadaptive questions and performing an arbitrary efficient Boolean computation on their answers.

The Statistical Difference complete problem makes the class concrete: distinguish two efficiently sampled distributions that are far apart from ones that are close. The middle range is deliberately left outside the promise. The card uses this characterization as its exact definition of SZK.

Sahai and Vadhan prove closure under polynomial-size Boolean formulas, and therefore under polynomial-size circuits of logarithmic depth. This is stronger than closure under a constant number of AND, OR and NOT operations, but still leaves general polynomial-depth circuit composition open.

The distinction is computational rather than a choice of logical connectives. Formulas must repeat each reused subcomputation, while circuits can share it. Replacing a circuit by its expanded expression tree need not preserve polynomial size.

The 2023 paper explicitly retains the general truth-table question while using the known formula closure in a characterization based on Kolmogorov complexity. That characterization does not claim general circuit closure.

The later space-bounded work proves a corresponding Boolean-formula closure for the logarithmic-space statistical-zero-knowledge class. Its Theorem 7.8 is a result about a restricted model and formula reductions; it does not establish the general circuit target here.

Handling queries outside the promise is essential: an SD oracle need not give meaningful information for distributions in the gap. The precise three-valued rules prevent such queries from being treated as reliable facts and preserve the formulation actually used by the source.

cards.title: \(\exists\!\cdot\!\mathrm{BPP}\) versus MA
cards.formal:
Do the following two classes of ordinary decision languages coincide?
\[\exists\!\cdot\!\mathrm{BPP}=\mathrm{MA}.\]
An \(\mathrm{MA}\) language has a polynomial-length classical witness and a polynomial-time randomized verifier: a yes-instance has some witness accepted with probability at least \(2/3\), and every witness to a no-instance is accepted with probability at most \(1/3\).

For \(\exists\!\cdot\!\mathrm{BPP}\), the witness predicate must additionally be an ordinary BPP language on pairs. Its acceptance probability is therefore always at most \(1/3\) or at least \(2/3\), including for every unsuccessful witness on a yes-instance. The equality asks whether every MA language admits some verifier with that stronger all-pairs gap, possibly with a different witness encoding and polynomial length bound.
cards.why: Existential witnesses and randomized verification interact differently depending on whether every witness must induce a valid bounded-error decision. Resolving this equality would determine whether the additional gap requirement changes computational power or only the presentation of a verifier. The distinction is fundamental when probabilistic predicates are nested beneath quantifiers in classical and quantum complexity hierarchies.

The source-open status does not certify an exhaustive literature search.

sentences: The question asks whether existential quantification over an ordinary BPP language has exactly the power of Merlin–Arthur verification.
Both settings use a polynomial-size witness chosen before a uniform randomized polynomial-time check.
Existential BPP additionally requires a bounded-error gap for every input-witness pair, even for unsuccessful witnesses on yes-instances.
Equality permits changing the verifier, so one verifier with intermediate probabilities is not a counterexample.
An oracle separation is known, while the ordinary class equality remains the source’s unresolved target.

cards.definitions:
A language is a subset of \(\{0,1\}^*\). Use uniform finite-program probabilistic multitape Turing machines, with independent fair random bits, binary input and an accept/reject output. Every random-bit sequence must lead to a halt in time polynomial in input length. Bit operations, random-bit generation and input and output handling count as work. No advice, oracle or quantum register is supplied.

For definiteness, encode a pair by \(\langle x,y\rangle=1^{|x|}0xy\). The initial unary field specifies exactly how many subsequent bits form \(x\), and the rest form \(y\). Strings without such a complete parse are malformed; a pair verifier rejects them deterministically. This is a uniquely decodable, polynomial-size encoding. On well-formed pairs, the time bound is at most \(C(|x|+|y|+2)^d\) for fixed positive integers \(C,d\), and the usual polynomial bound applies to all encoded inputs. Let \(a_V(x,y)=\Pr[V(\langle x,y\rangle)=1]\).

The class \(\mathrm{MA}\) consists of languages \(L\) for which there are a verifier \(V\) as above and fixed positive integers \(c,k\), giving a witness bound \(p(n)=c(n+1)^k\), such that
\[x\in L\ \Longrightarrow\ \exists y,\ |y|\le p(|x|)\ \text{and}\ a_V(x,y)\ge2/3,\]
\[x\notin L\ \Longrightarrow\ \forall y,\ |y|\le p(|x|)\ \Longrightarrow\ a_V(x,y)\le1/3.\]
The witness is chosen before the verifier's random bits are drawn, so it cannot depend on their realized values. When \(x\in L\), the probabilities for other witnesses may be anywhere in \([0,1]\). The language is total as a decision problem: every input is either in \(L\) or in its complement; this is not a promise-MA problem with unclassified inputs.

A language \(A\) is in \(\mathrm{BPP}\) if some uniform randomized polynomial-time machine accepts each \(z\in A\) with probability at least \(2/3\) and each \(z\notin A\) with probability at most \(1/3\). In particular, every input has the required gap. Define the existential operator by
\[L\in\exists\!\cdot\!\mathrm{BPP}\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad\exists A\in\mathrm{BPP}\ \exists c,k\ge1\ \forall x,\quad x\in L\ \Longleftrightarrow\ \exists y\ \bigl(|y|\le c(|x|+1)^k\ \land\ \langle x,y\rangle\in A\bigr).\]
Here \(c,k\) are integers. The set \(A\) may be assumed to reject malformed pair encodings. The witness bound is a polynomial size bound, not a bound on the cost of finding the witness.

Equivalently, \(L\) has an MA verifier \(W\) that also satisfies
\[\forall x,y\in\{0,1\}^*,\qquad a_W(x,y)\in[0,1/3]\cup[2/3,1].\]
This condition includes witnesses exceeding the chosen length bound; they may be rejected deterministically. It requires one uniform verifier for all \(x,y\), not a separately chosen randomized algorithm for each fixed witness. There is no requirement that a new \(W\) preserve the original verifier's probabilities or use its witness bound.

It follows from these definitions that \(\exists\!\cdot\!\mathrm{BPP}\subseteq\mathrm{MA}\). Thus the substantive equality direction is that every language in MA has some globally gapped witness predicate. A negative answer is a language in MA with no such predicate under any polynomial witness bound. Merely presenting one MA verifier with a probability in the gap does not establish that its language lacks a different globally gapped verifier.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct Lean-checked proof or refutation of the equality in the uniform, unrelativized language setting. A proof must establish a globally bounded-error witness predicate for every MA language, including exact polynomial runtime and witness-length guarantees. It may change the verifier and witness encoding and need not give an effective conversion between arbitrary machine descriptions. A refutation must prove that some MA language has no existential-BPP representation under any allowed verifier and polynomial bound. One verifier with intermediate acceptance probabilities, or an oracle separation, does not by itself refute the ordinary class equality.

context_blocks.text: Definition 16 applies the existential operator to ordinary languages. Remark 17 explains why fixing a witness in an MA verifier need not leave a BPP computation: a nonwinning witness on a yes-instance may lie inside the error gap. This does not itself prove that the language has no other suitable verifier.

The source encounters this distinction when bounding quantum hierarchies with classical witnesses. Its stronger-oracle simulations handle a different resource class; they do not establish the desired ordinary BPP predicate.

Fenner, Fortnow, Kurtz and Li construct an oracle relative to which MA is not contained even in nondeterministic polynomial time with access to a BPP oracle. Since existential BPP is contained in that latter class, the two target classes can differ relative to a common oracle. This is an obstruction to a proof valid under every oracle, not an unconditional separation.

cards.title: Effective enumeration of BPP
cards.formal:
Does there exist a total computable function \(E\) which, for every index \(i\in\mathbb N\), outputs the finite description of a randomized polynomial-time decision machine \(M_i\), such that
\[\forall i\ \forall x\in\{0,1\}^*,\quad\Pr[M_i(x)=1]\in[0,1/3]\cup[2/3,1],\]
and every language in \(\mathrm{BPP}\) is decided by at least one of these machines?

With \(L_i=\{x:\Pr[M_i(x)=1]\ge2/3\}\), the coverage condition is exactly
\[\{L_i:i\in\mathbb N\}=\mathrm{BPP}.\]
Repeated languages and repeated machine descriptions are allowed. The enumeration must include at least one suitable algorithm for each BPP language; it need not list every bounded-error program. There is no efficiency bound on computing \(E(i)\). Each \(M_i\) may have its own polynomial runtime bound, and the enumerator is not additionally required to output that bound.

source_formulation.text: The existence of an effective enumerable family of algorithms deciding all and only the problems in BPP is still an open question.
source_formulation.caption: Complete selected source sentence; PDF p. 2

cards.why: Polynomial running time can be guaranteed syntactically by a clock, but bounded error is a condition on every possible input. The question asks whether a computably generated family can still capture all feasible randomized decision problems while guaranteeing that condition. A resolution would clarify the relationship between semantic complexity classes, programming formalisms and what arithmetical theories can certify about randomized computation.

sentences: The problem asks for a computable list of randomized polynomial-time algorithms covering every language in BPP.
Each listed algorithm must have the required error gap on every input, but the list may repeat languages and omit alternative implementations.
The enumerator itself has no efficiency requirement, and the listed programs may have different polynomial time bounds that need not be supplied effectively.
Recognizing all bounded-error program codes is a different task from finding a representative family with complete language coverage.
Known arithmetical characterizations give useful enumerable subclasses, while a negative answer would separate BPP from deterministic polynomial time.

cards.definitions:
All languages are subsets of finite binary strings. A randomized decision machine is a finite-program probabilistic multitape Turing machine with read-only input, initially blank work tapes, a one-bit output and independent fair random bits. It has no oracle, advice or arbitrary real-number operations. Time counts ordinary tape operations, generation of random bits and output writing, in the worst case over random choices.

For each enumerated machine \(M_i\), there must exist positive integers \(C_i,d_i\) such that it halts with a decision bit within \(C_i(n+2)^{d_i}\) bit steps on every input of length \(n\) and every random-bit sequence. These constants may depend on \(i\), but not on the input or random choices. No common polynomial must bound the whole family. The time bounds are existential properties of the emitted programs; no computable method of finding their constants from \(i\), or proof certificate for those constants, is additionally required. An enumeration supplying explicit clocks would be a sufficient special case.

For every finite input, the runtime bound limits the number of coin tosses, so the acceptance probability is a well-defined dyadic rational from a finite probability space. Unused coin bits do not change an output. A machine has bounded error when its acceptance probability never lies strictly between \(1/3\) and \(2/3\). It then decides the unique language whose yes-instances have acceptance probability at least \(2/3\); every no-instance has acceptance probability at most \(1/3\). The gap must hold on every input, including the empty string.

The class \(\mathrm{BPP}\) consists of all languages decided by some randomized polynomial-time machine with this gap. Equivalently, \(L\in\mathrm{BPP}\) if some such machine satisfies \(\Pr[M(x)=\mathbf 1_L(x)]\ge2/3\) for every \(x\). The class \(\mathrm P\), used in the context, consists of languages decided by deterministic polynomial-time machines. Both classes use worst-case polynomial runtime.

Total computable means that one deterministic Turing machine, given the binary encoding of any nonnegative integer \(i\), halts and returns the finite transition-table code of \(M_i\). It may use arbitrarily large finite time and space as a function of \(i\). No finite or infinite advice sequence and no oracle are allowed. Codes use an ordinary effective finite encoding of machine states, tape symbols and transitions; standard such encodings can be effectively translated without changing the represented machine or its polynomial-time property.

Soundness requires every emitted machine to run in polynomial time and have the displayed gap on every input. Coverage requires that for each \(L\in\mathrm{BPP}\), some index \(i\) satisfies \(L=L_i\) on all strings. Neither an index for a given language nor a decision procedure for whether an arbitrary program has the gap is requested. In particular, \(E\) may omit a bounded-error program if it lists another program deciding the same language.

The negative answer excludes every total computable enumeration with these two properties. An inability to enumerate all codes of polynomial-time bounded-error programs is a different assertion: the target only needs an effectively chosen representative family that covers all the languages. No specific logical theory or proof system is prescribed for that family.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct Lean-checked proof or refutation of the existence of such an enumeration. A positive answer must specify a total computable enumerator and prove the polynomial-time and all-input error guarantees for every emitted machine, as well as coverage of every BPP language. The mathematical runtime proof may establish separately quantified constants for each index without providing an algorithm computing them. A negative answer must rule out every such representative-family enumeration, including families whose time bounds are not supplied effectively. Showing that the set of all valid machine codes is undecidable or not computably enumerable does not suffice. An enumeration covering only the languages whose correctness is proved in one selected theory also does not suffice without proving that it covers all of BPP.

context_blocks.text: Section 2 emphasizes the difference between listing all algorithms with a property and listing enough algorithms to cover the same languages. The former code sets can be recursion-theoretically difficult even for deterministic polynomial time, while the latter can have a simple effective enumeration.

The source gives characterizations of BPP in arithmetic and effectively enumerable subclasses based on error guarantees provable in a sound recursively enumerable theory. Its conclusion does not show that one such subclass contains every BPP language.

Proposition 20 shows that P equal to BPP would imply the desired kind of effective characterization. Thus a proof that no covering enumeration exists would in particular separate P from BPP. The reverse implication is not asserted.

The paper proves hardness of recognizing its all-input error condition and gives an enumerable sound-theory subclass containing polynomial identity testing. These results expose the certification issue and supply substantial examples, but neither code-recognition hardness nor one such subclass settles complete language coverage.

cards.title: Expected linear-time integer sorting for every word length
cards.formal: Does there exist a uniform Las Vegas word-RAM algorithm and a constant \(C\) such that, for every \(n\ge2\), every integer word length \(w\ge\lceil\log_2(n+1)\rceil\), and every list \(x_1,\ldots,x_n\in\{0,\ldots,2^w-1\}\), the algorithm outputs the list in nondecreasing order with expected running time at most \(Cn\)?
cards.definitions: The input occupies n words, with one unsigned w-bit key per word; repeated keys are allowed. The output must contain exactly the input multiset in nondecreasing numerical order, with no stability requirement. The machine is sequential and has w-bit data registers and random-access memory. Unit-cost operations are reads and writes, comparisons, branches, addition and subtraction modulo 2ʷ, multiplication of two words with the product returned in two words, quotient and remainder of two words with a nonzero divisor, bitwise Boolean operations, and left or right shifts by a word-specified amount. Shifted-out bits are discarded, and shifts by at least w return zero. Addresses may use a constant number of words to index polynomially many memory cells; all address computation is charged. An operation can generate one fresh independent uniform w-bit random word. These are the only primitive operations; arbitrary-length arithmetic, a built-in sorting operation and free tables are unavailable. All preprocessing, memory initialization performed by the algorithm, and output writes count. A fixed finite program receives n and w; it may select methods according to their values but has no advice depending on them. Las Vegas means every terminating computation is correct and the algorithm terminates with probability one. Expectation is over the internal random choices for each fixed input. C must be independent of both n and w, including when w grows with n.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove the existence of a single uniform, always-correct Las Vegas program whose expected running time is at most Cn on every admissible (n,w,input), for one C independent of n and w. A negative answer must show that every such sorting program has unbounded expected-time/n ratio over these inputs. A lower bound only for comparison sorting, deterministic programs, or a different word instruction set does not establish that negation.
cards.why: A basic limit on what word-level arithmetic can accomplish beyond comparisons. The challenge is a uniform bound across all word lengths, rather than the already solved polynomial-universe or sufficiently-large-word cases.

importance.reason: A foundational algorithmic primitive whose optimal complexity tests the computational power of the word RAM and would affect many tasks built on ordering integer keys.

cards.status_note: The checked primary bounds and the CMU Spring 2025 source leave expected linear-time sorting across all word lengths open. Searches through 11 September 2026 found no result settling this full target. Recent parallel sorting results for keys in \([n]\) concern a restricted universe and a different performance model.

context_blocks.text: Integer sorting asks how much of the cost of comparison sorting comes from treating keys as indivisible objects. If only comparisons are allowed, identifying one of n! possible orders needs \(\Omega (n \log  n)\) comparisons in the worst case. Word operations can inspect several bits at once, compute bucket addresses and manipulate packed fields. The comparison decision-tree lower bound therefore does not rule out a linear number of word operations.

The relevant input size is n words, not nw individual bits. Reading one entire word is a unit operation regardless of w, but reading a whole list is still n operations. Conversely, the machine cannot concatenate all n keys into an nw-bit integer and then treat that enormous object as one register. Fixing the register width and the permitted instructions is essential; unrestricted unit-cost arithmetic would answer a different question.

Simple radix sorting already handles \(w=O(\log  n)\). Divide each key into digits of about \(\log _{2}n\) bits, and sort stably by one digit at a time using counting arrays of size \(O(n)\). There are \(O(1+w/\log  n)\) passes, giving \(O(n(1+w/\log  n))\) time. For any fixed polynomial-size universe this is linear. If \(w=(\log  n)^{3/2}\), however, that same argument takes about \(\sqrt{\log  n}\) passes and does not prove the desired bound.

Surprisingly, very large words also admit linear expected time. Belazzougui, Brodal and Nielsen achieve this for \(w=\Omega ((\log  n)^{2} \log  \log  n)\), improving an earlier sufficiently-large-word regime. Their construction replaces full keys by shorter signatures and processes many packed fields with a single word operation. Larger keys bring more possible values, but the larger machine words simultaneously provide more internal parallelism. The difficult range sits between the easy radix regime and the proven large-word regime.

The best general expected upper bound retained in the sources is Han and Thorup’\(s O(n\sqrt{\log  \log  n})\), independent of word length. It is substantially below n log n, but the square-root iterated-log factor still grows without bound. The problem asks whether this remaining overhead can be removed completely. An upper bound with any unbounded overhead factor does not imply the stated linear bound.

Han also gives deterministic \(O(n \log  \log  n)\) sorting with linear space. This is a different guarantee: it bounds every computation without random choices. cards.context:
Integer sorting asks how much of the cost of comparison sorting comes from treating keys as indivisible objects. If only comparisons are allowed, identifying one of n! possible orders needs \(\Omega (n \log  n)\) comparisons in the worst case. Word operations can inspect several bits at once, compute bucket addresses and manipulate packed fields. The comparison decision-tree lower bound therefore does not rule out a linear number of word operations.

The relevant input size is n words, not nw individual bits. Reading one entire word is a unit operation regardless of w, but reading a whole list is still n operations. Conversely, the machine cannot concatenate all n keys into an nw-bit integer and then treat that enormous object as one register. Fixing the register width and the permitted instructions is essential; unrestricted unit-cost arithmetic would answer a different question.

Simple radix sorting already handles \(w=O(\log  n)\). Divide each key into digits of about \(\log _{2}n\) bits, and sort stably by one digit at a time using counting arrays of size \(O(n)\). There are \(O(1+w/\log  n)\) passes, giving \(O(n(1+w/\log  n))\) time. For any fixed polynomial-size universe this is linear. If \(w=(\log  n)^{3/2}\), however, that same argument takes about \(\sqrt{\log  n}\) passes and does not prove the desired bound.

Surprisingly, very large words also admit linear expected time. Belazzougui, Brodal and Nielsen achieve this for \(w=\Omega ((\log  n)^{2} \log  \log  n)\), improving an earlier sufficiently-large-word regime. Their construction replaces full keys by shorter signatures and processes many packed fields with a single word operation. Larger keys bring more possible values, but the larger machine words simultaneously provide more internal parallelism. The difficult range sits between the easy radix regime and the proven large-word regime.

cards.title: Sorting \(X + Y\)
cards.formal: Does there exist a uniform deterministic real-RAM algorithm A and a constant C such that, for every integer \(n\ge 2\) and every \(X=(x_{1},\ldots ,x_{n}), Y=(y_{1},\ldots ,y_{n})\in \mathbb{R} ^{n}, A\) outputs a permutation \(((i_{1},j_{1}),\ldots ,(i_{n^{2}},j_{n^{2}}))\) of \([n]\times [n]\) satisfying \(x_{i_{r}}+y_{j_{r}}\le x_{i_{r+1}}+y_{j_{r+1}}\) for \(1\le r<n^{2}\), in at most \(Cn^{2}\) unit-cost operations?
cards.why: This is a basic test of whether algebraic dependence among many sortable objects can be exploited with no overhead beyond writing them down. It also makes the distinction between short comparison decision trees and fast uniform algorithms unusually concrete.
cards.status_note: TOPP Problem 41, primary comparison and real-RAM sources, and subsequent-result searches were checked on 11 September 2026. No uniform quadratic-time algorithm or matching impossibility result for the stated real-valued problem was found. The \(2017/2018\) decision-tree result does not settle total time. This is a source review, not an independent proof audit.

cards.definitions: The input consists of n and the 2n exact real numbers in random-access arrays; no sortedness, distinctness, integrality or magnitude bound is promised. All \(n^{2}\) index pairs must occur once in the output, including pairs with equal sums. Ties may appear in any order. A real RAM has exact real registers and cells, supporting copy, addition, subtraction, multiplication, division by nonzero reals and comparisons at unit cost. A fixed finite program may use rational constants, with no advice depending on n. It also has integer registers and cells of \(b=d\lceil \log _{2}(n+2)\rceil\) bits for some fixed integer \(d\ge 3\) chosen with the algorithm. Integer instructions are copy, comparison, branching, addition, subtraction and multiplication modulo \(2^{b}\), quotient and remainder with nonzero divisor, bitwise Boolean operations, and logical shifts; shifts by at least b return zero. Integer addresses access individual real or integer cells, and each read or write costs one operation. Integer-to-real conversion is permitted, but real-to-integer conversion, floor on reals, extraction of their bits and arbitrary-precision integer operations are not primitives. Memory starts empty apart from the input and fixed program constants; all preprocessing, table construction, address computation and output writes are charged. The algorithm must halt correctly on every input and uses no randomness. Constants C and d are independent of n and of the real values. This is the quadratic-time real-RAM version explicitly asked in the cited necklace paper and identified as the main target in TOPP. Indexed multiset output resolves possible equal sums; allowing repeated input entries does not change the target, since repetitions can be grouped by \(O(n \log  n)\) comparison sorting and expanded within the output budget.
cards.answer_criterion: Give one uniform deterministic program with a proof of exact output correctness and the \(O(n^{2})\) worst-case total-time bound for every real input, or prove that no such program exists in the specified model. Equivalently, a negative answer shows that every correct program has unbounded worst-case running-time/\(n^{2}\) ratio. Neither a bound only on the number of comparisons nor an algorithm restricted to bounded integers resolves this claim.

context_blocks.text: The input is small compared with the output. For \(X=(0,3)\) and \(Y=(1,4)\), the four indexed sums are 1,4,4,7. Both occurrences of 4 remain in the sorted output because they come from different pairs. In general there are \(n^{2}\) output entries, but only 2n independent input numbers. This strong dependence is the reason ordinary sorting bounds for \(n^{2}\) unrelated numbers may be wasteful.

If the two input lists are already sorted, the matrix \(M_{ij}=x_{i}+y_{j}\) increases along every row and every column. That information alone does not determine the relative order of every two cells: a later row may contain an entry smaller than an entry in an earlier row. Moreover, sum matrices satisfy additional equalities such as \(M_{ij}+M_{kl}=M_{il}+M_{kj}\). The question concerns the full algebraic structure, not just arbitrary matrices with sorted rows and columns.

Explicitly generating and comparison-sorting all \(n^{2}\) sums takes \(O(n^{2} \log  n)\) time. Writing the required output already takes \(\Omega (n^{2})\) operations, so quadratic time would match the output-size lower bound. TOPP identifies removal of the logarithmic factor as the main question. The real-valued input convention avoids assuming a small integer universe, where different operations can change the complexity.

Fredman proved that \(O(n^{2})\) comparisons suffice. A decision tree specifies the next comparison after every possible history of answers and places the sorted order at its leaves. Its depth counts comparisons, but it does not charge for constructing the tree or determining the next comparison from a succinct program. Consequently, a short decision tree does not automatically become an equally fast uniform algorithm.

Lambert and Steiger–Streinu made the comparison savings algorithmic while retaining \(O(n^{2} \log  n)\) total running time. This is a concrete separation between counting tests and charging the bookkeeping that organizes them. The target includes both costs, as well as all preprocessing and output writes.

Kane, Lovett and Moran later obtained \(O(n \log ^{2} n)\) decision-tree depth by allowing tests involving differences of sums; each such linear test uses at most eight input coordinates. Those tests are more expressive than simply comparing two entries of \(X+Y\). The subquadratic depth does not conflict with the quadratic output-size lower bound, because decision-tree depth does not charge for writing the output.

Related convolution problems ask only for a minimum, maximum or median on each antidiagonal of the sum matrix. These requests can have subquadratic algorithms without supplying a complete sorted list of all entries. The necklace-alignment paper explicitly records this distinction and the unresolved quadratic-time real-RAM question.

The importance of the question extends beyond sorting. Pairwise sums describe many ordered geometric events, and TOPP records reductions from this sorting task to polygon-containment and arrangement-ordering problems. A resolution would clarify how much algorithmic work can be saved when a large output is generated from a much smaller collection of numerical parameters.

For bounded-integer inputs on a word RAM, a linear-time algorithm for sorting arbitrary word-sized integers would also sort the explicitly generated pairwise sums in quadratic time, allowing a constant-factor increase in word length for the sums. The present target instead allows arbitrary exact real inputs, without floor or bit extraction. An integer-sorting result therefore does not automatically answer this real-RAM question.

cards.definitions: For \(n\ge2\), write \(V=[n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}\). A weighted hypergraph \(H=(V,E,w)\) has a set \(E\subseteq\{e\subseteq V:|e|\ge2\}\) and finite nonnegative real weights \(w:E\to\mathbb R_{\ge0}\). For every \(S\subseteq V\), set \(\operatorname{cut}_H(S)=\sum_{\substack{e\in E:\ e\cap S\ne\varnothing,\\e\cap(V\setminus S)\ne\varnothing}}w(e)\). Thus each crossing hyperedge contributes its weight exactly once, regardless of the number of vertices on either side. Empty and singleton edges are omitted because they cross no cut; repeated edges can be merged by summing weights. The approximating hypergraph \(H'=(V,E',w')\) follows the same rules. Its edge set may contain any subsets of the original vertex set, not necessarily original edges; additional vertices are forbidden. Size is \(|E'|\), rather than the sum of edge cardinalities or a bit-encoding length. The same approximation must hold for all cuts simultaneously, and a zero-valued original cut must remain exactly zero. The empty edge set is allowed. This is an existence question with no construction-time, randomness or rational-weight restriction. The constant \(C\) is independent of dimension, accuracy, hyperedge count, maximum edge size and weights.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof of this universal existence theorem with one constant \(C\), or prove its logical negation in Lean: for every \(C>0\), some permitted \(n,H,\varepsilon\) has no same-vertex weighted hypergraph meeting both the size and all-cut guarantees. A refutation must allow arbitrary nonnegative replacement hyperedges, not just sampled original edges. A size bound retaining an unbounded logarithmic factor does not establish the stated theorem.

context_blocks.text: A sparsifier replaces a large interaction structure by a smaller one while preserving the values needed for later cut computations. The guarantee holds for every partition at once, including a partition chosen after seeing the sparsifier. A separate approximation for one predetermined cut would be much weaker. A hypergraph can contain exponentially many distinct hyperedges on n vertices, so reducing their number to near linear can be a large compression.

The cut convention is important for multiway interactions. A hyperedge \(\{1,2,3,4\}\) of weight one contributes one to both the partition \(\{1\}|\{2,3,4\}\) and the partition \(\{1,2\}|\{3,4\}\). Replacing it by a uniformly weighted clique gives contributions proportional to three and four respectively. Thus the ordinary graph representation does not automatically preserve the hypergraph’s cut function.

The formulation follows the broad source question: the approximating hypergraph may introduce different hyperedges on the same vertices. Requiring only reweighting and deleting original edges is an additional restriction. A construction satisfying that stronger condition also answers the stated existence question, but a lower bound restricted to that condition would not by itself refute it.

Ordinary graphs already admit \(O(n/\varepsilon ^{2})\)-edge sparsifiers. Batson, Spielman and Srivastava prove a spectral guarantee, which implies the required cut inequalities by substituting zero-one indicator vectors. This gives the benchmark without a logarithmic overhead. For hypergraphs, preserving an associated energy on all real vectors is also stronger than preserving cut indicators, and the particular energy definition must be specified before importing a spectral result.

The quadratic-in-n bound quoted in the 2018 problem entry is outdated. Chen, Khanna and Nagda give a randomized polynomial-time construction using \(O(n \log  n/\varepsilon ^{2})\) reweighted original hyperedges. Their result removes the extra dependence on maximum hyperedge size. The remaining log n is unbounded, so it cannot be absorbed into the universal C in this card.

Subsequent sketching and streaming results address how a sparsifier can be represented or maintained with limited memory. A rank-r hyperedge can require r vertex identifiers, so near-linear hyperedge count does not mean near-linear bit storage independent of r. The FOCS 2024 sketch bounds retain logarithmic factors in their near-linear output guarantee.
The ICLR 2026 insertion-only work further improves memory use, but its guarantees also retain logarithmic factors. Its space theorem does not establish the \(Cn/\varepsilon ^{2}\) hyperedge count.

Resolving the target would determine whether hypergraph cuts admit the same upper bound on the number of interactions as graph cuts at each accuracy. It would not automatically remove the cost of describing large hyperedges or reading the original input. Those separate costs explain why stronger data-access and streaming results can coexist with an unresolved existence question.

cards.context:
A sparsifier replaces a large interaction structure by a smaller one while preserving the values needed for later cut computations. The guarantee holds for every partition at once, including a partition chosen after seeing the sparsifier. A separate approximation for one predetermined cut would be much weaker. A hypergraph can contain exponentially many distinct hyperedges on n vertices, so reducing their number to near linear can be a large compression.

The cut convention is important for multiway interactions. A hyperedge \(\{1,2,3,4\}\) of weight one contributes one to both the partition \(\{1\}|\{2,3,4\}\) and the partition \(\{1,2\}|\{3,4\}\). Replacing it by a uniformly weighted clique gives contributions proportional to three and four respectively. Thus the ordinary graph representation does not automatically preserve the hypergraph’s cut function.

The formulation follows the broad source question: the approximating hypergraph may introduce different hyperedges on the same vertices. Requiring only reweighting and deleting original edges is an additional restriction. A construction satisfying that stronger condition also answers the stated existence question, but a lower bound restricted to that condition would not by itself refute it.

Ordinary graphs already admit \(O(n/\varepsilon ^{2})\)-edge sparsifiers. Batson, Spielman and Srivastava prove a spectral guarantee, which implies the required cut inequalities by substituting zero-one indicator vectors. This gives the benchmark without a logarithmic overhead. For hypergraphs, preserving an associated energy on all real vectors is also stronger than preserving cut indicators, and the particular energy definition must be specified before importing a spectral result.

The quadratic-in-n bound quoted in the 2018 problem entry is outdated. Chen, Khanna and Nagda give a randomized polynomial-time construction using \(O(n \log  n/\varepsilon ^{2})\) reweighted original hyperedges. Their result removes the extra dependence on maximum hyperedge size. The remaining log n is unbounded, so it cannot be absorbed into the universal C in this card.

Subsequent sketching and streaming results address how a sparsifier can be represented or maintained with limited memory. A rank-r hyperedge can require r vertex identifiers, so near-linear hyperedge count does not mean near-linear bit storage independent of r. The FOCS 2024 sketch bounds retain logarithmic factors in their near-linear output guarantee.

The ICLR 2026 insertion-only work further improves memory use, but its guarantees also retain logarithmic factors. Its space theorem does not establish the \(Cn/\varepsilon ^{2}\) hyperedge count.

Resolving the target would determine whether hypergraph cuts admit the same upper bound on the number of interactions as graph cuts at each accuracy. It would not automatically remove the cost of describing large hyperedges or reading the original input. Those separate costs explain why stronger data-access and streaming results can coexist with an unresolved existence question.

benchmark_focus.reason: A universal cut-preserving reduction of hypergraphs to few weighted hyperedges is a broad compression target supporting many downstream algorithms. Its focus is the size of a combinatorial sparsifier, with no query-interface guarantee.

cards.title: Near-linear-time approximation of reachability diameter
cards.formal:
Is there an integer constant \(C\ge1\) and a single uniform randomized word-RAM algorithm that, on every finite unweighted directed graph \(G\), returns an integer \(\widehat D\) satisfying
\[
\Pr\!\left[D(G)/C\le\widehat D\le D(G)\right]\ge 2/3
\]
and always halts in near-linear time? Here
\[
D(G)=\max\{d_G(u,v):u,v\in V(G),\ d_G(u,v)<\infty\}
\]
is the reachability diameter. The graph representation, machine and worst-case time bound are specified below. This retains the card's near-linear constant-factor specialization of the source's broader approximation-versus-time question; it does not ask to determine that entire tradeoff.
cards.why: This asks whether a basic distance statistic of an arbitrary directed network can be estimated without computing distances from every vertex. It captures information that conventional directed diameter loses when directions are disconnected, and appears in assessing diameter reduction by reachability-preserving shortcut edges. A resolution would establish a general algorithmic principle or limitation for directed reachability and distance estimation.
cards.definitions:
The input is a graph \(G=([n],E)\), where \(n\ge1\), \([n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}\), and \(E\subseteq[n]\times[n]\) is a set of directed edges. Loops are allowed, repeated edges are not, and every edge has length one. Write \(m=|E|\). A directed walk is a sequence \(v_0,\ldots,v_\ell\) with \((v_{j-1},v_j)\in E\) for \(1\le j\le\ell\), and has length \(\ell\). The distance \(d_G(u,v)\) is the minimum length of such a walk from \(u\) to \(v\), or \(\infty\) if no walk exists. Walks of length zero are permitted, so \(d_G(v,v)=0\), the displayed maximum is nonempty, and \(0\le D(G)\le n-1\). In particular, an edgeless graph has diameter zero. No connectivity, acyclicity or sparsity promise is imposed.

The input occupies \(O(n+m)\) read-only words: \(n,m\), an array of \(n+1\) offsets beginning with zero and ending with \(m\), and an array of \(m\) head labels. For each tail \(u\), the head labels between its two consecutive offsets list its outgoing neighbors without repetition, in arbitrary order. Correctness and cost bounds hold for every ordering of every valid list; there is no succinct encoding or separately supplied reachability information.

The algorithm is one finite program, independent of \(n,m,G\), with a fixed finite set of registers and random-access memory. For some fixed integer \(d\ge3\), a word has \(w=d\lceil\log_2(n+2)\rceil\) bits, represents an integer in \(\{0,\ldots,2^w-1\}\), and can hold a memory address. Work cells are initially zero; only addresses in that range can be used. The program has the word width available but no advice, oracle, input-dependent program or precomputed table. In one step it may read or write one addressed word, copy a word, compare two words, branch, or perform one of addition, subtraction, multiplication, integer quotient, remainder, Boolean bitwise operations or a shift. Arithmetic results other than comparison are reduced modulo \(2^w\); quotient and remainder on divisor zero return zero; shifts by at least \(w\) return zero. Each instruction has fixed bounded arity. Reading one fresh independent fair random bit also costs one step. Input access, memory operations, random bits, preprocessing and writing the output all count.

Near-linear worst-case time means that there are fixed integers \(K\ge1\) and \(k\ge0\) such that, on every valid input and every sequence of random bits, the program halts with an integer output in \(\{0,\ldots,n-1\}\) after at most
\[
K(n+m)\lceil\log_2(n+2)\rceil^k
\]
steps. The probability in the target is over these independent random bits for each fixed input. Both underestimates outside the allowed interval and overestimates count as failure; no correctness requirement is imposed on the failure event beyond the output range. The constants \(C,d,K,k\) and program are chosen once before the universal quantification over inputs. There is no separate input approximation parameter and no restriction to combinatorial algorithms.

progress.text: The first arXiv version introduces the approximation/time landscape and leaves the best tradeoff for general unweighted directed graphs open. It distinguishes that question from reducing general graphs to acyclic ones.

The ESA version states in Theorem 7 a randomized additive-\(k\) approximation and in Theorem 9 a randomized near-linear-time \(n^{1/2+o(1)}\)-approximation. Allowing logarithmic factors, the additive guarantee has time \(\widetilde O(nm/k)\) with high probability. The deterministic bound in Theorem 8 has an additional multiplicative factor and is restricted to acyclic graphs.

Corollary 5 conditionally rules out better-than-two approximation in time \(O(n^{\omega-\varepsilon})\), where \(\omega\) is the infimum exponent of arithmetic matrix multiplication and \(\varepsilon>0\) is fixed. Its separate combinatorial version rules out truly subcubic combinatorial algorithms. Theorem 6 gives a conditional better-than-\(3/2\) barrier on sparse instances. These results concern bounded approximation factors and do not settle existence of some absolute constant factor in near-linear time.

context_blocks.text: Reachability diameter measures the longest shortest route that actually exists. Unreachable ordered pairs are omitted, so a one-way path on five vertices has reachability diameter four. This differs both from ordinary directed diameter, which becomes infinite if any ordered pair is unreachable, and from min-diameter, which uses the smaller of the two directional distances.

The source studies general directed graphs and separately asks whether the reachability-diameter problem can be reduced to directed acyclic graphs. Its hardness instances can already be acyclic, but this does not make an algorithm for acyclic inputs a solution for arbitrary inputs. Strong connectivity makes reachability diameter coincide with ordinary directed diameter and removes an essential part of the general question.

The card retains the specialization recorded in September 2026: a constant approximation in time \(\widetilde O(n+m)\), where the tilde permits a fixed power of \(\log n\). Open Problem 1 asks more broadly for the best approximation/time tradeoff. The explicit word operations, finite program, \(2/3\) success convention, integer output and worst-case clock make the inherited algorithmic model precise; the source does not itself spell out this complete RAM instruction set.

Theorem 7 gives additive approximation, and Theorem 9 gives a randomized near-linear-time \(n^{1/2+o(1)}\)-approximation. Neither supplies a constant multiplicative factor on every input. Additive error can dominate the diameter on small-diameter graphs, even when it is useful on graphs with long routes. The source also gives conditional barriers for sufficiently small approximation factors; those barriers do not rule out all constant factors.

cards.answer_criterion: An accepted answer is a complete, mathematically correct Lean proof of the displayed existence statement or its negation. A positive answer must specify the finite uniform algorithm and constants \(C,d,K,k\), prove the stated time bound for every valid input and every random-bit sequence, and prove the approximation event has probability at least \(2/3\) for each such input. A negative answer must rule out every such choice of constants and program: for each candidate, either the required worst-case resource bound fails or some valid graph and encoding has approximation success probability less than \(2/3\). A conditional lower bound alone does not establish this unconditional negation. An algorithm only for acyclic, strongly connected, bounded-width or bounded-treewidth graphs does not establish the universal claim.

Root individually checked Theorems 7–9, Corollary 5, Theorem 6, and both open problems in the actual ESA text. The near-linear constant-factor yes/no question was already an explicit editorial specialization on this card, not the entire source tradeoff. Maintained that scope rather than silently changing to DAGs or the entire numerical tradeoff. The integer constant is without loss for the existence question by rounding a real constant upward. Integer-valued diameter supports an integral estimate convention; successful rational estimates can be rounded upward, preserving both bounds. Adding n to the usual tilde-m notation handles isolated vertices and explicit input representation.

Independent source audit by the parallel review agent confirmed the publisher date 25 August 2026 and checked actual arXiv v1 submitted 6 June 2026, with no later listed revision by 16 September. The conference PDF has 24 pages; the arXiv full version has 20. Table 1 is labelled for DAGs but Theorem 7 and Theorem 9 algorithms accept general directed graphs. Theorem 8 alone requires a DAG. The public card does not infer a general-to-DAG reduction from the table.

Runtime/probability caution from actual algorithm text: Theorem 7 states O(nm/k) and high probability, but Algorithm 3 on ESA page 21 samples O-tilde(n/k), whereas its proof mentions only 2n/k BFS runs. The latter constant sampling gives constant success for hitting a specified first k vertices. Public progress therefore uses the safe logarithm-suppressed bound at high probability and does not propagate a log-free high-probability assertion.

Theorem 9 does not explicitly say worst-case or expected time. Its argument on ESA page 22 invokes the shortcut construction of Jambulapati, Liu and Sidford. The independently read actual arXiv1905.08841v4 Lemma 4.3, PDF page 13/printed page 12, gives its near-linear runtime with probability at least 1-2n^{-10}. Public progress says randomized near-linear without attributing an always-worst-case clock to the literal published algorithm. A clocked Monte Carlo normalization can absorb rare slow executions into error, but that normalization is an editorial model choice, not a quoted theorem. The exact finite word-RAM convention makes the already-selected target reviewable.

Bounded later primary-source searches through 16 September 2026 included the paper title, reachability diameter, constant approximation, general directed graphs and shortcut sets, plus author publication lists. The ESA final version is itself only weeks old. The 2026 Structural parameterizations of Geodetic Set on directed (acyclic) graphs paper (arXiv2606.26414) concerns a different optimization task even when its instances have small reachability diameter. New parallel reachability and shortcut bounds do not by themselves approximate the original graph’s maximum finite distance. cards.title: Near-linear output-sensitive Subset Sum
cards.formal: Do there exist a uniform bounded-error randomized word-RAM algorithm and constants \(C>0\), \(b\ge0\) that, given \(n\ge1\) positive integers \(x_{1},\ldots,x_{n}\le t\) and an integer \(t\ge1\), output exactly the distinct values in \(S(X,t)=\{\sum_{i\in I}x_{i}:I\subseteq[n]\}\cap\{0,\ldots,t\}\) in at most \(C(n+|S(X,t)|)(\log(n+t+2))^{b}\) operations?
cards.definitions: The input is an explicitly listed multiset; repeated values are allowed and each index can be selected at most once. The empty subset contributes zero. Output every attainable value once, in any order, with no requirement to list subsets or witnesses. Inputs exceeding the threshold can be discarded when represented in the same word model. Use a uniform word RAM with word length \(w=d\lceil\log_{2}(n+t+2)\rceil\), for a fixed positive integer \(d\) chosen with the algorithm and large enough for its addresses and input values. Unit-cost instructions are word reads/writes, copying, comparisons, branching, Boolean operations, shifts, addition, subtraction and multiplication modulo \(2^{w}\), and integer quotient and remainder with nonzero divisor. Shifts by at least \(w\) return zero. Multiword computation is charged by its component instructions. The fixed finite program receives no advice or precomputed tables; all initialization, preprocessing and output writes count. Randomness consists of independent uniform random words, each generated at unit cost. On every input, the whole output must be correct with probability at least \(2/3\). The time bound holds for every random execution, including unsuccessful ones. The word-size constant and all time constants are independent of both \(n\) and \(t\). The target permits polylogarithmic dependence on the numerical threshold, but no linear scan of its universe unless covered by the stated output bound.

context_blocks.text: Subset Sum may have very few attainable values below the threshold even when the threshold is huge. Output-sensitive complexity measures the set that must actually be produced, together with reading the input.
Bringmann and Nakos explicitly ask for near-linear time in the number of attainable sums. Their algorithm gives a four-thirds power dependence on the output size.

Chan derandomizes pseudopolynomial Subset Sum in 2026 and also derandomizes the \(\widetilde O(|S|^{4/3})\) and \(\widetilde O(|S|\sqrt n)\) output-sensitive bounds. Those results do not attain the stated near-linear output-sensitive endpoint.

sentences: An adjacency labeling scheme assigns each vertex a short binary string from which adjacency can be determined using only two labels.
The conjecture asks for logarithmic labels in every hereditary class with at most a factorial times a fixed exponential number of labeled graphs.
Hereditary means closed under induced subgraphs, and is weaker than closure under all subgraphs.
The monotone case is known, and a 2025 follow-up proves logarithmic-cubed labels for all hereditary small classes.
The question isolates when low total information content permits efficient storage in locally decodable vertex descriptions.

cards.definitions: Graphs are finite, undirected and simple. A graph class \(\mathcal C\) is closed under isomorphism; it is hereditary when every induced subgraph of every member also belongs to it. Write \(\mathcal C_n\) for its members with labeled vertex set \([n]\). Small means that there is a constant \(c\geq1\) with \(|\mathcal C_n|\leq n!c^n\) for every \(n\geq1\). A labeling scheme consists of an encoder and a decoder, fixed for the class and all input lengths. The encoder, given an adjacency-matrix encoding of \(G\in\mathcal C_n\), assigns one finite binary label to each vertex. The decoder receives only two labels and returns whether the corresponding distinct vertices are adjacent; it receives no graph description, class-membership oracle, additional table or external value of \(n\). Any size information needed by the decoder must be encoded within the labels. Both are deterministic algorithms, with no imposed time bound; encoding must halt on every graph in the class and decoding must halt on every pair of finite labels. Outside-class encoder behavior is unrestricted. All answers for pairs of vertices of an input member must be exact and simultaneous. Label length is the sole resource being bounded. No polynomial-time recognition of the class is assumed. Monotone, which is a stronger condition, means closed under deletion of both vertices and edges; this question assumes only hereditary closure.

context_blocks.text: The saved source proves logarithmic adjacency labels for monotone small classes and explicitly conjectures the extension to hereditary small classes. Its Conjecture 9 is the Small Implicit Graph Conjecture. The earlier draft title incorrectly described the already-treated monotone case.

The broader conjecture for all hereditary classes of factorial growth is false. The sharper small-class bound limits the number of labeled graphs to a factorial times a fixed exponential, leaving a distinct question.

The 2025 follow-up proves \(O((\log n)^3)\)-bit labels for every hereditary small class and logarithmic labels for small weakly sparse classes. Weak sparsity means excluding some fixed complete bipartite graph as a subgraph; that additional restriction is absent in the general conjecture.

cards.answer_criterion: Provide a complete Lean-checked proof of a labeling scheme and a class-dependent logarithmic length constant for every hereditary small class, or exhibit such a class and prove that no scheme satisfying these conditions exists. No efficient encoding or decoding time is required beyond the source’s algorithmic definition. A result for monotone or weakly sparse classes alone does not settle the universal claim.

sentences: An additive spanner keeps original graph edges while limiting the increase in every pairwise distance.
This card fixes the increase to at most four and asks for the optimal worst-case number of edges.
The target is the complete asymptotic function up to universal constant factors.
The familiar candidate is \(n^{4/3}\), while recent constructions still have exponent \(7/5\) up to logarithmic factors.
This gap is a fundamental unresolved regime of distance compression, and the variable-error linear-size tradeoff has its own card.

cards.definitions: Each original edge has length one. \(d_{G}(u,v)\) is the minimum number of edges in a path, with \(d_{G}(u,u)=0\). A spanning subgraph H has the same vertex set and a subset of G’s edges, with unchanged unit lengths. If u,v are disconnected in H put \(d_{H}(u,v)=\infty\), so the requirement forces H to be connected. The lower inequality \(d_{H}(u,v)\ge d_{G}(u,v)\) follows from being a subgraph. Both extrema exist because there are finitely many graphs on a fixed labeled vertex set and \(H=G\) is feasible. The cost is number of retained edges; neither construction time nor weights, shortcuts, missing vertices, terminal subsets or faults are part of the model. New weighted edges would be an emulator and are not allowed. Restricting to connected inputs only removes disconnected bookkeeping; applying a universal bound componentwise recovers its usual all-graph form.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a positive function \(g(n)\), constants \(a,A>0\) and \(n_{0}\) such that a \(g(n)\le s_{4}(n)\le A g(n)\) for every integer \(n\ge n_{0}\). Prove a universal existence upper bound and a matching worst-case lower bound. Polynomial exponents alone do not settle this constant-factor target if a growing logarithmic gap remains. This is an asymptotic extremal-size question, not an additive 0.01 estimate of an integer function.

cards.title: Quasipolynomial dependence on vertices for hypergraph isomorphism
cards.formal: Is there a uniform deterministic algorithm that decides isomorphism of two explicitly represented hypergraphs in time \[2^{C(\log_2(n+2))^{a}}\,N^{b},\] for fixed constants \(C,a,b\geq1\), where \(n\) is the maximum number of underlying vertices and \(N\) is the combined input bit length?
cards.why: This asks whether symmetry testing can depend quasipolynomially only on the underlying universe, while remaining polynomial in the amount of set-system data. It matters for hypergraphs with many large edges and for algorithms that encode structural graph information as set systems.

sentences: Hypergraph isomorphism asks whether a relabeling of vertices makes two explicitly listed set systems identical.
The target running time is quasipolynomial in the number of vertices and polynomial in the full input size.

cards.definitions: A hypergraph is a finite pair \((V,\mathcal E)\) with \(V=[n]\) and \(\mathcal E\subseteq2^V\). Empty hyperedges and isolated vertices are allowed; edges have no colors, order, weights or repeated copies. The input lists the vertices and every hyperedge explicitly by its incidence bit vector; vertex counts and list lengths are included in the binary encoding. Input length \(N\) therefore includes all incidences and at least \(n\) symbols. An isomorphism from \((V_1,\mathcal E_1)\) to \((V_2,\mathcal E_2)\) is a bijection \(\pi:V_1\to V_2\) with \(\{\pi(e):e\in\mathcal E_1\}=\mathcal E_2\). The algorithm must decide whether one exists and must be correct on every well-formed input; unequal vertex counts imply rejection. Time is worst-case bit time on a deterministic multitape Turing machine with no advice or oracle. Neither the hyperedge size nor the number of hyperedges is bounded polynomially in \(n\). All constants and exponents are uniform over both parameters. Replacing incidence vectors by explicit incidence lists changes length by at most a polynomial and preserves the requested two-parameter bound.

context_blocks.text: The source distinguishes a quasipolynomial dependence on the number of vertices from a polynomial dependence on the possibly much larger collection of hyperedges. Encoding a hypergraph as a bipartite incidence graph does not automatically give that separation of dependencies.

Wiebking discusses a bound whose exponent on total hypergraph size depends polylogarithmically on the vertex count, and explicitly asks for the stronger bound in which the hyperedge-size exponent is constant. The same open question reappears in the outlook section.

cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof of an algorithm with fixed constants satisfying the displayed two-parameter bound, or prove that no such deterministic uniform algorithm exists. A quasipolynomial bound in the full incidence-graph size, or a polynomial exponent depending on the number of vertices or maximum hyperedge size, does not meet the target.

Defined explicit set-system encoding and worst-case deterministic bit time without a rank bound or polynomial bound on the edge count.
Kept ordinary isomorphism decision as the task; canonization and succinct hyperedge representations were not silently added.
