cards.title: Unconditional containment of unambiguous probabilistic automata
cards.formal: Is quantitative containment decidable when the left automaton \(A\) is unambiguous and the right automaton \(B\) is finitely ambiguous? In other words, does a single unconditional terminating algorithm decide \(\forall w\in\Sigma^{*},\ p_A(w)\leq p_B(w)\) for every promised pair of rational probabilistic automata as defined below? This selects the direction of bounded-ambiguity containment whose known decidability proof uses Schanuel’s conjecture; the reverse direction is already decidable unconditionally.
cards.why: This asks whether a basic exact comparison between small stochastic models can be decided from a finite bound on accepting behavior, without a conjecture in transcendental number theory. The asymmetry between one probability product and a bounded sum isolates the unresolved arithmetic obstacle in an otherwise effective verification setting.
cards.status_note: The 2021 primary journal theorem remains conditional for this direction, and the 2021 seminar question, published in 2022, specifically asks to remove that assumption. Bounded source and later-literature checks on 13 September 2026 found no unconditional decision theorem. This does not establish exhaustive present-day openness.

sentences: A probabilistic automaton assigns each finite word an acceptance probability.
The left automaton here has at most one positive accepting run per word, while the right one has a fixed finite bound on that number.
The task is to decide whether the left probability is at most the right probability for every word, with exact comparison and no numerical gap promise.
The known result for this direction assumes Schanuel’s conjecture; the reversed direction already has an unconditional algorithm.
An accepted answer proves decidability or undecidability in Lean without retaining the conjectural arithmetic assumption.

definitions: A probabilistic automaton is \(A=(\Sigma,Q,\delta,\iota,F)\), with a finite nonempty alphabet \(\Sigma\), a finite nonempty state set \(Q\), accepting states \(F\subseteq Q\), nonnegative rational initial weights \(\iota(q)\) satisfying \(\sum_q\iota(q)\leq1\), and nonnegative rational transition weights \(\delta(q,a,p)\) satisfying \(\sum_p\delta(q,a,p)\leq1\) for each state \(q\) and letter \(a\). Missing probability mass is lost to rejection. There are no epsilon transitions. The input lists the states, alphabet, initial weights, accepting states and all nonzero transitions; rational numerators and positive denominators use binary notation.

For \(w=a_1\cdots a_m\), a positive accepting run is a state sequence \(q_0,\ldots,q_m\) with \(q_m\in F\) and \(\iota(q_0)\prod_{i=1}^{m}\delta(q_{i-1},a_i,q_i)>0\). Its weight is this product. Let \(p_A(w)\) be the sum of these weights. In particular \(p_A(\varepsilon)=\sum_{q\in F}\iota(q)\). Zero-weight transitions do not create runs; identical state-and-letter transitions are represented by one weight.

Unambiguous means at most one positive accepting run for each word. Finitely ambiguous means that there exists one integer \(K\geq0\), depending on the automaton but independent of the word and its length, such that every word has at most \(K\) positive accepting runs. This bound need not be supplied. Every finite word has finitely many runs even without the promise; a uniform bound over all words is the essential restriction.

Quantitative containment means exact pointwise comparison \(p_A(w)\leq p_B(w)\) for every finite word \(w\in\Sigma^{*}\), including the empty word. There is no cutpoint, approximation tolerance, isolated-gap promise, or bounded word length.

Decidability asks for one deterministic Turing machine on the finite descriptions, halting on every input string and outputting a bit. On each pair satisfying the stated structural promises, the bit must be 1 precisely for quantitative containment; outside the promise either bit is permitted. There is no time bound, oracle or unproved mathematical assumption in the requested result.
cards.answer_criterion: A complete Lean-checked proof of an unconditional decision algorithm for the stated promise problem, or a Lean-checked proof that no such algorithm exists. A proof conditional on Schanuel’s conjecture or on the decidability of real exponentiation is not sufficient. A procedure that only terminates when a violating word exists is not a decider.

cards.title: Determinacy of Wadge games for Muller tree languages
cards.formal: Let \(D_{\mathrm{tree}}\) be the statement that, for every pair \(A,B\) of finite nondeterministic Muller automata on infinite full binary labeled trees, the Wadge game \(W(L(A),L(B))\) is determined. Is \(D_{\mathrm{tree}}\) provable in Zermelo–Fraenkel set theory with the axiom of choice, ZFC? The target is provability from these axioms, not an algorithm for finding the winning player.
cards.why: Asks how much set theory is needed to compare properties described by finite automata. A resolution would clarify whether the topological organization of all regular infinite-tree languages rests on ordinary ZFC or needs stronger foundations.
cards.status_note: Read the conference and full journal concluding questions, the tree-level game in the authors’ survey, and the scope of the 2016 hierarchy construction. Later-result searches through 12 September 2026 found no resolution of ZFC-provability for all Muller tree language pairs. Word-game independence, Borel determinacy and special hierarchy constructions were not treated as resolutions.

cards.definitions:
For a finite nonempty alphabet \(\Sigma\), a full binary labeled tree is a function \(t:\{0,1\}^*\to\Sigma\). The empty word is the root and the children of node \(u\) are \(u0,u1\). All branches are infinite.

A nondeterministic Muller tree automaton consists of a finite state set \(Q\), initial state \(q_0\), transition relation \(\Delta\subseteq Q\times\Sigma\times Q\times Q\), and an acceptance family \(\mathcal F\subseteq2^Q\). A run assigns a state to every node, starting with \(q_0\), and respects the transition relation at every node and its two children. It is accepting if, on each infinite branch, the set of states occurring infinitely often belongs to \(\mathcal F\). The language \(L(A)\) contains exactly the trees admitting at least one accepting run. No determinism, unambiguity or Borel-language promise is imposed.

In the Wadge game, Player I builds a tree over the alphabet of \(A\), and Player II builds one over the alphabet of \(B\). Both initially have empty finite trees. In each round I appends one or more complete levels, with all their labels, to I's own tree. II sees that move and appends finitely many complete levels to II's tree, or skips. Earlier labels cannot be changed. I therefore produces an infinite tree \(t\). II loses if II's output has only finitely many levels; otherwise it defines an infinite tree \(u\), and II wins exactly when
\[
t\in L(A)\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad u\in L(B).
\]
I wins in every other case. II may skip infinitely often, but must also extend the output infinitely often.

This is a perfect-information, length-\(\omega\), zero-sum game. A strategy specifies a legal move after every finite play history at which that player acts. A winning strategy succeeds against every legal opposing play. Strategies are arbitrary set-theoretic functions, with no computability, finite-memory or resource restriction. “Determined” means that one of the two players has a winning strategy.

The tree space has the product topology of discrete node labels: finitely many fixed levels specify basic neighborhoods. The tree-level version is the usual Wadge game; II has a winning strategy exactly when a continuous map \(F\) satisfies \(L(A)=F^{-1}(L(B))\). This equivalence explains the connection to language complexity, but does not assume determinacy.

The single sentence \(D_{\mathrm{tree}}\) universally quantifies over the finite automaton descriptions and asserts the existence of a winning strategy for each pair. The question asks whether ZFC proves that sentence. It does not assert that merely adding some stronger axiom is a negative resolution: such an axiom can prove statements already provable in ZFC.
cards.answer_criterion: A positive answer supplies a ZFC proof of determinacy for every pair in the specified class. A negative answer establishes nonprovability, for example by a relative-consistency or model construction yielding ZFC together with a failure of this universal determinacy statement; any metatheoretic consistency assumption must be stated explicitly. A theorem assuming a stronger determinacy principle without a nonprovability argument, or a proof for a restricted subclass, does not answer the ZFC-provability question.

cards.title: Positivity problem for linear recurrences
cards.formal: Does there exist a Turing machine that, on every input consisting of an integer \(d\ge 1\), integer initial values \(u_{0},\ldots ,u_{d- 1}\), and integer coefficients \(a_{0},\ldots ,a_{d- 1}\), halts and decides whether \(u_{n}\ge 0\) for every \(n\ge 0\), where \(u_{n+d}=\sum _{i=0}^{d- 1}a_{i} u_{n+i}\)? The order d is part of the input and has no fixed upper bound.
cards.definitions: All integers are given exactly in signed binary, and the coefficient and initial-value lists are explicit. The recurrence is homogeneous and its coefficients are constant in n. The requested property includes every term from \(u_{0}\) onward and allows zero terms. Coefficients may be zero, including \(a_{0}\); the decision procedure must accept these inputs as well. No promise of distinct characteristic roots, reversibility, eventual nonnegativity, or bounded order is imposed. The recurrence supplied need not be of minimal order. Computation uses the ordinary Turing model, with no real-number or number-theoretic oracle. No polynomial-time or other specified running-time bound is required, but the machine must halt for both possible answers. A simple sequence has a minimal characteristic polynomial with no repeated complex roots. In this statement, “explicitly given/encoded/listed” means the entire finite list, table or syntax tree described above is part of the input or output, with its full encoding counted; it does not mean a circuit, oracle or program generating a larger object.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove that nonnegativity of every term is decidable for integer linear recurrences of arbitrary input order, by a machine halting on both positive and negative instances, or prove that this decision problem is undecidable. The property is \(u_{n}\ge 0\) for all \(n\ge 0\), including the initial values.
cards.why: A basic infinite-time safety question for finite linear descriptions. Its resolution would establish a major decidability boundary connecting verification, discrete dynamical systems and effective number theory, and would also settle general Skolem decidability.

importance.reason: A longstanding foundational decision problem with an elementary input model, strong links to verification, and consequences for the separate Skolem problem; unrestricted decidability is unknown before any efficiency requirement is imposed.

progress.text: Ouaknine and Worrell establish positivity decidability through order five, and Diophantine consequences of extending it to order six.
For simple sequences, positivity is decidable through order nine.
Ultimate positivity is decidable for simple sequences of arbitrary order in PSPACE, and in polynomial time at each fixed order; this does not supply a general effective threshold.
Kenison, Nieuwveld, Ouaknine and Worrell establish positivity decidability for reversible sequences through order eleven, and simple reversible sequences through order seventeen.

The new survey retains general positivity as open and gives a concrete order-ten example whose positivity is unsettled. It also presents a reduction from order-five Skolem to positivity of simple order-ten sequences.

cards.status_note: The authors’ 2026 survey explicitly retains general Positivity and Skolem decidability as open. Rechecked on 11 September 2026 with a search for subsequent work. Low-order, simple-root, reversible and ultimate-positivity theorems have separate hypotheses and do not settle this arbitrary-order question.

context_blocks.text: A recurrence is a finite description of an infinite trajectory. One can compute any requested term exactly, but checking every term asks for a finite justification covering unbounded time. This makes positivity a basic test case for the limits of algorithmic verification. The July 2026 survey still lists its general decidability among the central unresolved problems. The word positivity is conventional here: the inequality is non-strict.

The connection to linear dynamics is direct. Store d consecutive values in a vector \(x_{n}\). A fixed integer companion matrix M then gives \(x_{n+1}=Mx_{n}\), and the first coordinate of \(M^{n} x_{0}\) is \(u_{n}\). The question is whether that coordinate ever enters the negative half-line. Even though the transition is linear and deterministic, the trajectory can combine growth, decay and oscillation through its characteristic roots.

No universal finite amount of simulation certifies the desired answer. For any chosen integer N, the sequence \(u_{n}=N- n\) satisfies \(u_{n+2}=2u_{n+1}- u_{n}\), is nonnegative through index N, and becomes negative afterward. Of course this particular family is easy to analyze. Its role is to distinguish sampling a long prefix from proving a bound that is computed from an arbitrary input and is sufficient for that input.

Ouaknine and Worrell decide positivity for all sequences of order at most five. Their analysis combines effective estimates from Diophantine approximation with decision procedures for real algebraic conditions. At order six, decidability would already imply that certain approximation constants associated with transcendental numbers are computable. This is a precise mathematical consequence, rather than a proof that no algorithm can exist.
Removing repeated characteristic roots improves the known frontier: positivity is decidable for simple sequences through order nine.

A separate theorem decides ultimate positivity for simple sequences of every order, in polynomial space. Ultimate positivity asks whether some finite prefix contains all negative terms. The algorithm need not provide an effective cutoff beyond which the terms are nonnegative. Without such a cutoff, the theorem cannot be turned into a positivity decider by checking the remaining prefix.

There are larger decidable orders under a different structural promise. An integer recurrence is reversible when its extension to all negative indices also has integer values. Kenison and coauthors decide positivity through order eleven for reversible sequences, and through order seventeen when they are also simple. The extra integrality in backward time matters; these bounds do not apply to arbitrary integer recurrences of those orders.

A general solution would also decide the Skolem problem, which asks whether an integer recurrence ever equals zero. Integer recurrence sequences are effectively closed under termwise products and subtraction of a constant. Thus \(w_{n}=u_{n}^{2}- 1\) is another such sequence, and it is nonnegative at every index exactly when u has no zero. Negating the answer to a positivity decider would decide Skolem. This reduction explains why positivity has consequences beyond sign analysis itself.

cards.context:
A recurrence is a finite description of an infinite trajectory. One can compute any requested term exactly, but checking every term asks for a finite justification covering unbounded time. This makes positivity a basic test case for the limits of algorithmic verification. The July 2026 survey still lists its general decidability among the central unresolved problems. The word positivity is conventional here: the inequality is non-strict.

The connection to linear dynamics is direct. Store d consecutive values in a vector \(x_{n}\). A fixed integer companion matrix M then gives \(x_{n+1}=Mx_{n}\), and the first coordinate of \(M^{n} x_{0}\) is \(u_{n}\). The question is whether that coordinate ever enters the negative half-line. Even though the transition is linear and deterministic, the trajectory can combine growth, decay and oscillation through its characteristic roots.

No universal finite amount of simulation certifies the desired answer. For any chosen integer N, the sequence \(u_{n}=N- n\) satisfies \(u_{n+2}=2u_{n+1}- u_{n}\), is nonnegative through index N, and becomes negative afterward. Of course this particular family is easy to analyze. Its role is to distinguish sampling a long prefix from proving a bound that is computed from an arbitrary input and is sufficient for that input.

Ouaknine and Worrell decide positivity for all sequences of order at most five. Their analysis combines effective estimates from Diophantine approximation with decision procedures for real algebraic conditions. At order six, decidability would already imply that certain approximation constants associated with transcendental numbers are computable. This is a precise mathematical consequence, rather than a proof that no algorithm can exist.

Removing repeated characteristic roots improves the known frontier: positivity is decidable for simple sequences through order nine.

A separate theorem decides ultimate positivity for simple sequences of every order, in polynomial space. Ultimate positivity asks whether some finite prefix contains all negative terms. The algorithm need not provide an effective cutoff beyond which the terms are nonnegative. Without such a cutoff, the theorem cannot be turned into a positivity decider by checking the remaining prefix.

There are larger decidable orders under a different structural promise. An integer recurrence is reversible when its extension to all negative indices also has integer values. Kenison and coauthors decide positivity through order eleven for reversible sequences, and through order seventeen when they are also simple. The extra integrality in backward time matters; these bounds do not apply to arbitrary integer recurrences of those orders.

A general solution would also decide the Skolem problem, which asks whether an integer recurrence ever equals zero. Integer recurrence sequences are effectively closed under termwise products and subtraction of a constant. Thus \(w_{n}=u_{n}^{2}- 1\) is another such sequence, and it is nonnegative at every index exactly when u has no zero. Negating the answer to a positivity decider would decide Skolem. This reduction explains why positivity has consequences beyond sign analysis itself.

cards.title: Simple stochastic games in polynomial time
cards.formal: Is the following decision problem in deterministic polynomial time? Given an explicitly represented finite simple stochastic game G, a start vertex s, and a binary rational threshold \(r\in [0,1]\), decide whether \(v_{G}(s)>r\), where \(v_{G}(s)=\sup _{\sigma} \inf _{\tau} \Pr _{s}^{\sigma ,\tau}\)[eventually reach the target sink 1]. The game and threshold follow the exact conventions below, and time is polynomial in their total bit length.
cards.definitions: The vertices are partitioned into Max, Min, random, and two distinct terminal sinks 0 and 1. Every nonterminal vertex has two listed successor slots; slots may have the same successor. At a Max or Min vertex its owner chooses a slot. At a random vertex each slot is chosen with probability \(1/2\), independently at each visit. Both players observe the complete finite history and the current vertex. Strategies may use history and private randomness; there is no bound on play length. Reaching 1 gives Max payoff one; reaching 0, or playing forever without reaching 1, gives payoff zero. Min minimizes the same expected payoff that Max maximizes. No promise of almost-sure termination is imposed. All vertices, ownership labels and successor indices are explicit; \(r=a/b\) is exact with binary integers \(0\le a\le b\) and \(b>0\). Equality \(v_{G}(s)=r\) is a NO instance. The algorithm is an ordinary uniform deterministic Turing algorithm; its polynomial bound has universal constants independent of the game and threshold. In this statement, “explicitly given/encoded/listed” means the entire finite list, table or syntax tree described above is part of the input or output, with its full encoding counted; it does not mean a circuit, oracle or program generating a larger object.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove that the exact threshold language \(\{(G,s,r):v_{G}(s)>r\}\) belongs to P, or prove that it does not. The polynomial-time algorithm must handle arbitrary finite games, including nonterminating plays, and reject equality to the threshold.
cards.why: A central test of efficient decision-making under both adversarial control and randomness. A polynomial algorithm would solve a canonical \(\mathrm{NP}\cap \mathrm{coNP}\) problem and carry through reductions to quantitative verification tasks with more expressive objectives.

importance.reason: An elementary game model with broad consequences for synthesis and stochastic verification; short optimal strategies and efficiently checkable certificates coexist with an unresolved polynomial-time search problem.

context_blocks.text: This game combines three elementary kinds of branching: a controller chooses, an adversary chooses, or a fair coin chooses. Removing one player gives a Markov decision process; fixing both players’ strategies leaves a Markov chain. The hard case is their interaction across cycles. Condon established that the threshold problem has polynomially checkable certificates on both sides, placing it in \(\mathrm{NP}\cap \mathrm{coNP}\). That classification has not yielded a deterministic polynomial-time algorithm.

Both players have optimal deterministic positional strategies: one successor choice per owned vertex suffices, even though the definition permits history and randomization. A candidate strategy is therefore short. Fixing one player leaves a one-player optimization problem that can be solved in polynomial time, which explains the certificates. The difficulty is finding a suitable strategy among the exponentially many combinations, rather than needing to represent an optimal strategy of enormous length.

The local equations look deceptively simple: a Max vertex takes the maximum successor value, a Min vertex the minimum, and a random vertex their average. In a nonterminating component these equations alone can have multiple solutions. For example, a random vertex whose two slots both lead back to itself satisfies \(x=(x+x)/2\) for every x, but its actual target-reaching probability is zero. A solver must identify the reachability values rather than accept an arbitrary fixed point.

Exact thresholds matter. A chain of k independent fair choices can reach the target with probability \(2^{- k}\), with any failed choice leading to 0. Its graph has only \(O(k)\) vertices. Thus an additive error suitable for many numerical applications may be too large to distinguish a positive value from zero or to decide a nearby rational threshold. Polynomially many bits of precision can still require very many iterations if convergence is slow.

Ludwig’s classical randomized algorithm uses an expected \(2^{O(\sqrt{n})}\) operations on n-vertex games. It demonstrates that straightforward enumeration is not the only way to search the strategy space. It still gives a subexponential bound rather than the polynomial deterministic bound requested here.

Recent progress develops both practical solvers and structural cases. Azeem, Kretinsky and Weininger extend sound value iteration to games with end components, maintaining lower and upper bounds while addressing probabilistic cycles.

Gärtner, Haslebacher and Hoang’s FUN 2026 paper solves stopping binary games on ladders: distance layers toward the sinks contain two vertices, except possibly the last layer. Their algorithm recovers an ordering of optimal values from this special geometry. This restricted-class theorem does not supply a polynomial-time solver for unrestricted games.

The consequences extend to more expressive objectives. Berthon, Katoen and Zhou give a direct polynomial reduction from quantitative stochastic parity games to simple stochastic games, using binary representations of transition probabilities. This strengthens the explanatory connection between recurring long-run conditions and a single reachability target. Their paper invokes the known polynomial equivalence of the usual probability encodings; the reduction does not itself remove the open algorithmic bottleneck.

Baldan, Gurke, König and Wittbold’s 2026 work extends convergent fixed-point iteration to simple stochastic games. Convergence of numerical approximations is a different guarantee from deciding every exact rational threshold using polynomially many bit operations. The iteration theorem does not establish the polynomial-time classification asked here.

cards.title: Internal semisimplicial types in ordinary HoTT
cards.formal: In the fixed ordinary HoTT theory T below, can one define a single internal family \(S:\mathbb{N} \to U_{1}\) and restriction maps \(r_{n}:S(n+1)\to S(n)\) whose finite stages are equivalent, compatibly with restriction, to the canonical finite semisimplicial telescopes \(D_{n}\)?
cards.definitions: Fix T to be intensional Martin–Löf type theory with dependent function and pair types \(\Pi ,\Sigma\), identity types with their J eliminator, empty and unit types, finite coproducts, natural numbers and W-types, a cumulative predicative sequence \(U_{0}:U_{1}:\cdots\) closed under these constructors, and univalence for these universes. Also allow propositional truncation and homotopy pushouts with their ordinary dependent eliminators and propositional computation rules for path constructors, as in the HoTT book. There is no equality reflection, axiom K/UIP, resizing, choice, excluded middle, second equality type, display modality, or additional primitive for semisimplicial types. The question concerns definability in this specified theory; a negative result would apply to this theory, not automatically to every possible extension called HoTT. Define an external, finite family of syntactic telescopes as follows. \(D_{0}\) is \(U_{0}\), with element \(A_{0}\). Given data \(d=(A_{0},\ldots ,A_{j- 1})\) in \(D_{j- 1}\), form \(B_{j}(d)\), the dependent type of labelled boundaries of a j-simplex: for every nonempty proper subset F of \(\{0,\ldots ,j\}\), in increasing cardinality and then lexicographic order, choose a label \(x_{F}\) in \(A_{|F|- 1}\) evaluated on the labels of all nonempty proper subfaces of F. Identify F with \(\{0,\ldots ,|F|- 1\}\) by its increasing enumeration when supplying these arguments. For singleton F this means \(x_{F}:A_{0}\). Set \(D_{j}=\Sigma (d:D_{j- 1})(B_{j}(d)\to U_{0})\), whose last field is \(A_{j}\), and let \(p_{j}:D_{j+1}\to D_{j}\) forget the last field. This describes an ordinary finite T-expression for each external integer j; it does not postulate an internal function \(j\mapsto D_{j}\). The required output is finite closed T-terms \(S:\mathbb{N} \to U_{1}\) and \(r:\Pi (n:\mathbb{N} )(S(n+1)\to S(n))\), together with a metatheoretic proof that for every external j there are T-terms \(e_{j}:S(j)\)≃\(D_{j}\) and homotopies \(e_{j}\circ r_{j} \sim  p_{j}\circ e_{j+1}\). Here j inside T denotes its numeral, ≃ is the usual type equivalence, and ~ is pointwise identity. No judgmental equality between \(S(j)\) and \(D_{j}\) is required. The equivalences classify the full type-valued telescopes, with arbitrary \(U_{0}\)-small simplex types and no fixed truncation bound.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove that the specified theory T admits finite closed terms S and r together with the external stagewise equivalences and compatibility homotopies required above, or prove that no such terms and witnesses exist in T. The positive conclusion must hold at every external finite stage and allow arbitrary \(U_{0}\)-small simplex types.
cards.why: Determine whether ordinary HoTT can express a fundamental unbounded coherent structure internally, a basic issue for higher categories and foundational proof languages.

importance.reason: A central expressiveness problem for homotopy type theory; precise internal construction would remove a major obstacle to formalizing higher structures without enriching the theory.

cards.status_note: The original question and the May 2026 two-level revision were rechecked on 11 September 2026. No construction in the specified theory T, or nondefinability theorem for T, was located. context_blocks.text: Homotopy type theory treats identity as mathematical data that can itself have nontrivial identities. This makes it a natural setting for spaces and higher structures, but it changes what it means to give a diagram. In set-level mathematics, equations between composites can be recorded once and used without further information. For general types, chosen identifications can have multiple distinct witnesses, and comparisons between those witnesses may matter in the next dimension.

A semisimplicial type begins with a type \(A_{0}\) of vertices. For every ordered pair of vertices, \(A_{1}\) gives a type of edges. For every triangle boundary—three vertices and three specified edges—\(A_{2}\) gives a type of fillers. At dimension three, a filler is indexed by four vertices, six edges and four triangular fillers sharing their appropriate faces. Nothing forces a filler to exist, and the type of fillers may itself have arbitrarily rich homotopy.

The finite telescope description records shared boundaries through dependent types. A triangle’s three edges are already assigned the required endpoints; one does not choose unrelated edges and then append a collection of endpoint equations. The same idea works at each externally fixed dimension. The difficulty is making the whole construction into one function that accepts an internal natural number, rather than a growing list of separately written definitions.

This is why the card distinguishes its externally specified \(D_{j}\) from the sought internal S. A script can generate the expression for \(D_{100}\) and a type checker can check it. That does not supply a HoTT term whose argument is an arbitrary \(n:\mathbb{N}\). The compatibility requirement also matters: a collection of unrelated types with the right apparent sizes would not tell us how to forget the highest-dimensional data.

The statement deliberately allows equivalence at each stage instead of demanding a particular syntactic normal form. Thus a clever alternative encoding can solve the problem if it represents all the prescribed data and respects truncation. Once the internal tower exists, dependent sums, products and identity types already express a compatible infinite sequence. The missing step is constructing the tower itself, not adding a primitive that merely asserts an infinite sequence exists.

Kraus’s TYPES 2018 discussion identifies uniform finite-dimensional semisimplicial types as a major open problem and explains their role in higher category theory. Adding suitable Segal and completeness conditions to such data provides a route toward internal higher categories. Those conditions are additional structure: this card asks first for unrestricted semisimplicial data, with no composition, identity or horn-filling axioms imposed.

Two-level type theory introduces an outer equality satisfying uniqueness of identity proofs, alongside the homotopical inner theory. It can formalize constructions indexed by outer natural numbers. Annenkov, Capriotti, Kraus and Sattler distinguish this from constructing an inner universe of infinite semisimplicial types; additional hypotheses relating the two natural-number objects support the latter. The May 2026 revision is labelled a typo and reference update, not a new solution in ordinary HoTT.

Displayed Type Theory takes another route. Kolomatskaia and Shulman introduce discrete and simplicial modes together with a primitive display operation, then use it for a coinductive construction of semisimplicial types. This is a substantive solution in their enriched system, with a detailed semantic correctness argument. It does not give a definition from the constructors of T alone, because those additional primitives are precisely what enable the construction.

Chen’s 2025 thesis studies internal models and Reedy-fibrant inverse diagrams directly. It explicitly retains the ordinary-HoTT semisimplicial problem as open. Section 6.1 labels its proposed classifier construction a sketch whose Agda formalization has unresolved termination and definitional-equality issues, and states that it is not intended to solve the unrestricted problem. This is useful progress toward articulating the required coherence, rather than a completed internal classifier.

A set-valued construction also does not suffice. If every simplex type is a set, identities between elements have no higher ambiguity, and ordinary categorical equations behave much more rigidly. The requirement that the simplex types range over \(U_{0}\) preserves the higher-dimensional content that motivates the problem. Likewise, having a satisfactory semantic construction in a model does not automatically produce a finite term definable in the specified syntax.

A positive answer would show that ordinary dependent types can organize this fundamental form of unbounded coherence without additional structure in the language. A negative answer would identify a precise expressive limitation and help explain why successful alternative foundations introduce new primitives. Either outcome would guide the design of proof assistants intended to support higher category theory and internal constructions of type-theoretic models.

Kolomatskaia and Shulman introduce discrete and simplicial modes together with a primitive display operation, then use it for a coinductive construction of semisimplicial types. This is a substantive solution in their enriched system, with a detailed semantic correctness argument. It does not give a definition from the constructors of T alone, because those additional primitives are precisely what enable the construction.

Chen’s 2025 thesis studies internal models and Reedy-fibrant inverse diagrams directly. It explicitly retains the ordinary-HoTT semisimplicial problem as open. Section 6.1 labels its proposed classifier construction a sketch whose Agda formalization has unresolved termination and definitional-equality issues, and states that it is not intended to solve the unrestricted problem. This is useful progress toward articulating the required coherence, rather than a completed internal classifier.

A set-valued construction also does not suffice. If every simplex type is a set, identities between elements have no higher ambiguity, and ordinary categorical equations behave much more rigidly. The requirement that the simplex types range over \(U_{0}\) preserves the higher-dimensional content that motivates the problem. Likewise, having a satisfactory semantic construction in a model does not automatically produce a finite term definable in the specified syntax.

A positive answer would show that ordinary dependent types can organize this fundamental form of unbounded coherence without additional structure in the language. A negative answer would identify a precise expressive limitation and help explain why successful alternative foundations introduce new primitives. Either outcome would guide the design of proof assistants intended to support higher category theory and internal constructions of type-theoretic models.

cards.formal: Does there exist a pointed directed-complete partial order D and Scott-continuous maps \(F:D\to [D\to D]\) and \(\mathrm{L}:[D\to D]\to D\) with \(F\circ \mathrm{L}=id\) such that, for every pair of finite untyped lambda terms M,N, equality of their interpretations for every environment in D holds if and only if M and N are beta-convertible?
cards.why: A foundational completeness question for denotational semantics: does the mathematical structure used to describe approximation and recursion inevitably identify programs beyond beta-conversion, or can it preserve every distinction made by that computation rule?

cards.definitions: Terms are generated by variables from a countably infinite set, application MN and abstraction \(\lambda x\).M, modulo renaming bound variables. Beta-convertibility is the least equivalence relation closed under application and abstraction containing (\(\lambda x\).M)\(N=M[N/x]\), with capture-avoiding substitution. A directed set is nonempty and every two of its elements have an upper bound in the set. D is a set with a partial order, a least element, and a supremum for every directed subset. Scott-continuous means monotone and preserving directed suprema. \([D\to D]\) consists of all Scott-continuous functions, ordered pointwise. An environment \(\rho\) assigns an element of D to each variable. Interpret x as \(\rho (x), MN\) as F(⟦M⟧\(\rho\))(⟦N⟧\(\rho\)), and \(\lambda x\).M as L(\(d\mapsto\)⟦M⟧\((\rho [x:=d])\)). The desired condition is \(\forall M,N\): (\(\forall \rho\), ⟦M⟧\(\rho\)=⟦N⟧\(\rho\)) ⇔ \(M=\beta N\). Models need not be countable, algebraic, effectively presented or extensional; in particular \(\mathrm{L}\circ F=id\) is not required. These are set-based directed-complete orders and all their continuous maps, without a restriction to graph models.

context_blocks.text: The untyped lambda calculus describes functions using variables, application and abstraction. Beta-reduction substitutes an argument into a function body. A denotational model assigns mathematical meanings to terms and makes every beta-conversion valid. The question asks whether continuity can coexist with complete precision: no two terms should become equal in the model unless beta-conversion already equates them.

In domain semantics, an order represents increasing information and a directed supremum combines compatible approximations. Scott continuity requires functions to preserve these suprema. The map L represents each continuous self-map by an element of D, and F turns an element back into its associated self-map. The equation \(F\circ \mathrm{L}=id\) ensures that interpreting function application recovers the represented function. This makes beta-reduction sound.

Representability is a semantic condition. The element representing a continuous function need not be denoted by any finite lambda term. Requiring every continuous function to have a finite program would change the question. The model need not have computable elements, a computable ordering or a computable interpretation algorithm.

Extensional equality makes an additional identification. If x is not free in f, eta-conversion equates \(\lambda x\).f x with f, although these terms need not be beta-convertible. Imposing \(\mathrm{L}\circ F=id\) would validate this extra equality. This card therefore requires only the retraction in the other direction and keeps the beta-eta version as a separate target.

Quotienting syntax by beta-conversion gives a term model with exactly the desired equality. It does not automatically provide a pointed dcpo representing all continuous self-maps. The issue is whether the exact syntactic theory can be realized in this particular semantic setting.

Berline, Manzonetto and Salibra prove that the effective models defined in their paper cannot have theory exactly \(\lambda \beta\) or \(\lambda \beta \eta\). They also prove non-enumerability of the order theory, which records inequalities between denotations. Equational theory records equalities instead. A theorem restricted to effective models, or to order rather than equality, cannot be generalized silently to arbitrary dcpos.

Divergent terms reveal another source of extra equations. A term is unsolvable when no finite reduction exposes a head normal form: an outer variable applied to arguments after any leading abstractions. A sensible model equates all unsolvable closed terms. This is stronger than beta-conversion, which distinguishes some of them. The 2025 filter-model paper studies when unsolvables receive nontrivial interpretations and which type-theoretic conditions govern that behavior.

Lambda Galore, published in 2026, constructs sensible filter models representing all continuous functions whose theories do not contain the full Böhm-tree theory. It separates two semantic properties and resolves a different question about models. Sensibility still identifies unsolvables, so these constructions do not realize exactly \(\lambda \beta\). Continuous representability alone does not make their equational theory the one requested here.

cards.title: Barendregt–Geuvers–Klop conjecture
cards.formal: For every pure type system \((S,A,R)\) defined below, does weak normalization of every typable term imply strong normalization of every typable term?
cards.why: Normalization connects computation with the metatheory of typed proofs. This conjecture asks whether the pure-type-system rules turn the existence of a terminating computation for every typable term into termination under every reduction order.
cards.status_note: The primary statement and Mull’s 2023 paper leave the unrestricted conjecture open. A later-result and author-publication search on 11 September 2026 found no general proof or counterexample. The positive theorems impose additional PTS structure.

cards.definitions: S is a set of sorts, \(A\subseteq S\times S\) is a set of axioms, and \(R\subseteq S\times S\times S\) is a set of product rules. Terms are finite expressions \(t ::= x | s | t u | \lambda x:B\).\(t | \Pi x:B\).C, with \(s\in S\) and variables from a countably infinite set, modulo renaming bound variables. A context is a finite sequence of declarations of distinct variables. Typing is the least relation \(\Gamma \vdash t:B\) generated by the following rules. Axiom: \(\varnothing \vdash s:t\) when \((s,t)\in A\). Start: \(\Gamma ,x:B\vdash x:B\) when \(\Gamma \vdash B:s\) and x is fresh. Weakening: \(\Gamma ,x:C\vdash t:B\) when \(\Gamma \vdash t:B, \Gamma \vdash C:s\) and x is fresh. Product: \(\Gamma \vdash \Pi x:B\).\(C:s_{3}\) when \(\Gamma \vdash B:s_{1}, \Gamma ,x:B\vdash C:s_{2}\) and \((s_{1},s_{2},s_{3})\in R\). Abstraction: \(\Gamma \vdash \lambda x:B\).\(t:\Pi x:B\).C when \(\Gamma ,x:B\vdash t:C\) and \(\Gamma \vdash \Pi x:B\).C:s for a sort s. Application: \(\Gamma \vdash t u:C[u/x]\) when \(\Gamma \vdash t:\Pi x:B\).C and \(\Gamma \vdash u:B\). Conversion: \(\Gamma \vdash t:C\) when \(\Gamma \vdash t:B, \Gamma \vdash C:s\) and \(B=\beta C\). All substitutions avoid capture. A beta step contracts (\(\lambda x:B\).t)u to \(t[u/x]\) at any subterm, including inside annotations and product types. =\(\beta\) is the reflexive, symmetric, transitive closure of those steps. A term is typable if \(\Gamma \vdash t:B\) for some finite \(\Gamma ,B\). Weak normalization means that each typable term has some finite beta-reduction sequence ending in a term with no beta redex. Strong normalization means that no typable term starts an infinite beta-reduction sequence. Both predicates quantify over open as well as closed terms and over all their reduction choices. The sets S,A,R need not be finite, decidable or functional.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove that every pure type system in which all typable terms are weakly beta-normalizing is strongly beta-normalizing, or exhibit a pure type system that is weakly normalizing for every typable term but has a typable term admitting an infinite beta-reduction sequence.

context_blocks.text: A term can contain several reducible applications, so computation involves choices. Weak normalization says that some sequence reaches a normal form. Strong normalization says that every sequence of beta-reductions terminates. The conjecture asks whether these two system-wide properties coincide for all pure type systems, a common framework for typed lambda calculi.

The distinction is real for untyped terms. Let \(\Omega\)=(\(\lambda z\).zz)(\(\lambda z\).zz). The term (\(\lambda x\).y)\(\Omega\) reduces to y in one step if the outer application is chosen, but it can also reduce \(\Omega\) forever. Thus it is weakly but not strongly normalizing. This only illustrates the distinction: a counterexample to the conjecture needs a pure type system whose entire collection of typable terms is weakly normalizing.

A pure type system specifies which sorts classify other sorts and which dependent function types may be formed, through its sets A and R. The common typing rules generate the resulting calculus. Familiar simply typed, polymorphic and dependent systems fit the framework, but the conjecture also covers unusual specifications, beyond established proof languages.

The global hypothesis concerns every typable term. Confluence cannot replace it: confluence says that two finite reductions can be joined, making normal forms unique when they exist. It does not prevent an infinite path from coexisting with a terminating path. The untyped example already separates these ideas.

Reduction here includes type annotations and components of dependent products. Termination of an implementation’s selected evaluation strategy therefore differs from strong normalization of the calculus. Results after erasing annotations, or for closed programs only, have a different scope from the property of every annotated typable term in every context.

Sørensen’s 1997 work proves the implication for specified classes of typed calculi. Barthe, Hatcliff and Sørensen extend it to a class of non-dependent pure type systems in 2001. Their structural hypotheses are substantive: the theorem does not claim to cover every non-dependent specification, let alone every dependent one. The TLCA list records these as partial results.

Mull’s TYPES 2022 paper, published in 2023, enlarges the known class using a translation preserving typability and infinite reduction paths while removing certain sorts and rules. The theorem includes some systems with dependent rules that earlier results did not cover. The author explicitly retains the unrestricted conjecture; the translation’s structural hypotheses cannot be omitted.

A universal implication would connect the existence of normal forms with complete freedom of reduction order throughout this family of type theories. A counterexample would identify a system in which every term can finish, yet some legal choices continue forever. Either outcome would sharpen normalization arguments in proof checking and the metatheory of dependent types.

cards.title: Parity games in polynomial time
cards.formal: Does there exist a deterministic Turing machine \(A\) and integers \(C,c\geq1\) such that, for every encoded finite parity game \(G\) and starting vertex \(s\), \(A\) decides whether Even has a winning strategy from \(s\) within \(C(L+1)^c\) steps, where \(L\) is the full input length defined below?
cards.definitions:
A parity game has vertices \(V=\{1,\ldots,n\}\), with \(n\geq1\), an edge relation \(E\subseteq V\times V\), an owner function \(o:V\to\{\mathrm{Even},\mathrm{Odd}\}\), and priorities \(p:V\to\mathbb N\), where \(\mathbb N=\{0,1,2,\ldots\}\). Each vertex has at least one outgoing edge; self-loops are allowed. The designated start is \(s\in V\). An infinite play is a sequence \((v_i)_{i\geq0}\) with \(v_0=s\) and \((v_i,v_{i+1})\in E\) for every \(i\). The owner of \(v_i\) chooses \(v_{i+1}\); ownership need not alternate along an edge. Both players see the entire finite history and there are no chance moves. Let \(I=\{d\in\mathbb N:p(v_i)=d\text{ for infinitely many }i\}\). This set is finite and nonempty. Even wins precisely when \(\min I\) is even, and Odd wins otherwise.

A strategy for a player assigns a legal successor to every finite valid history ending at a vertex owned by that player. A play is consistent with the strategy if it follows the prescribed successor at each such vertex. Even has a winning strategy from \(s\) if there exists a strategy for which every consistent infinite play starting at \(s\) is won by Even. Strategies and infinite plays are quantified mathematical objects; neither is supplied as input. A positional strategy depends only on the current vertex, but the target does not assume positionality in its definition.

For a nonnegative integer \(a\), let \(\operatorname{code}(a)=1^b0\operatorname{bin}(a+1)\), where \(b\) is the length of the binary expansion without leading zeroes. Encode a game by \(1^n0\), followed by its \(n^2\) adjacency bits in row order, \(n\) owner bits (0 for Even and 1 for Odd), then \(\operatorname{code}(p(1)),\ldots,\operatorname{code}(p(n)),\operatorname{code}(s)\), with no trailing bits. The input length \(L\) includes every priority bit. Invalid encodings are rejected within the same polynomial time bound. The machine is one uniform deterministic multitape Turing machine with a fixed finite program, finite tape alphabet and no oracle or advice; each transition costs one step. All arithmetic and input processing count toward time. The same \(A,C,c\) must work for every arena and all priority values, with no fixed bound on the number or magnitude of priorities.

context_blocks.text: The original source asks about computing winning regions: all vertices from which each player can force a win. A polynomial-time decider for one specified vertex computes these regions by making one call per vertex, and a region algorithm answers the single-vertex question immediately. Thus the present decision target preserves the original polynomial-time question.

Every vertex is winning for exactly one player, and each player has a positional strategy winning from every vertex in its region. Consequently the winner problem lies in \(\mathrm{NP}\cap\mathrm{coNP}\), and in fact in \(\mathrm{UP}\cap\mathrm{coUP}\). These inclusions do not supply a deterministic polynomial-time algorithm. The close connection to modal \(\mu\)-calculus model checking explains the problem’s role in verification.

The minimum-priority convention is equivalent to the maximum-priority convention used in some references: replace every priority \(p(v)\) by \(D-p(v)\), with an even integer \(D\geq\max_v p(v)\). This reverses order and preserves parity, using only polynomially many bit operations. Large numerical priorities can also be replaced, in sorted order, by increasing nonnegative priorities of the same respective parities, all at most \(2n-1\). This explains why binary priority values do not change the standard polynomial-time question.

Calude and coauthors established a deterministic quasipolynomial-time algorithm in 2017, meaning a bound of the form \(\exp((\log(L+2))^{O(1)})\). This was a major improvement, but such a bound need not be polynomial. Their paper also explicitly relates alternating-turn and vertex-owner conventions.

Czerwiński and coauthors prove quasipolynomial size lower bounds for the strong separating safety automata defined in their paper. This limits a broad collection of known constructions; it is not a lower bound against all deterministic parity-game algorithms.

Rick van der Heijden’s preprint of 4 November 2025 claims an algorithm taking \(O(n^2(n+m))\) time, with \(n\) vertices and \(m\) edges. Its Theorems 5, 7 and 8 assert correctness and the polynomial bound. The checked arXiv record still has only version 1. This review inspected the claim and theorem statements but did not establish their correctness or locate an authoritative primary-source resolution of the claim.

The 24 June 2026 revision of Suilen and Pérez’s paper, marked accepted at CONCUR 2026, continues to describe polynomial-time parity-game solving as open. Its Proposition 4.1 reduces parity games to a robust discounted-reward problem. That later treatment does not itself refute the 2025 algorithm claim; the current status remains explicitly unverified.

cards.why: Parity games are a central algorithmic component of model checking and reactive synthesis: they express recurring obligations in infinite executions by a finite arena. Their winner problem is polynomial-time equivalent to model checking the modal \(\mu\)-calculus. Determining whether general parity games admit polynomial time would resolve a basic complexity boundary for these verification tasks and for a natural problem in \(\mathrm{UP}\cap\mathrm{coUP}\).
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-verified proof of the stated existence proposition or its logical negation. A positive answer must specify a uniform algorithm and prove its termination, correctness for all valid games and polynomial bit-time bound, including rejection of malformed inputs. A negative answer must exclude every such polynomial-time decider for the full problem. A lower bound for a particular algorithm, automaton representation or restricted collection of methods does not prove that negation. Bounds whose polynomial exponent depends on the number of priorities, experimental performance, and conditional theorems do not settle the unconditional target.

importance.reason: A defining algorithmic question of verification and infinite-duration games, with direct modal-logic and synthesis connections and a major quasipolynomial breakthrough. cards.context:
The original source asks about computing winning regions: all vertices from which each player can force a win. A polynomial-time decider for one specified vertex computes these regions by making one call per vertex, and a region algorithm answers the single-vertex question immediately. Thus the present decision target preserves the original polynomial-time question.

Every vertex is winning for exactly one player, and each player has a positional strategy winning from every vertex in its region. Consequently the winner problem lies in \(\mathrm{NP}\cap\mathrm{coNP}\), and in fact in \(\mathrm{UP}\cap\mathrm{coUP}\). These inclusions do not supply a deterministic polynomial-time algorithm. The close connection to modal \(\mu\)-calculus model checking explains the problem’s role in verification.

The minimum-priority convention is equivalent to the maximum-priority convention used in some references: replace every priority \(p(v)\) by \(D-p(v)\), with an even integer \(D\geq\max_v p(v)\). This reverses order and preserves parity, using only polynomially many bit operations. Large numerical priorities can also be replaced, in sorted order, by increasing nonnegative priorities of the same respective parities, all at most \(2n-1\). This explains why binary priority values do not change the standard polynomial-time question.

Calude and coauthors established a deterministic quasipolynomial-time algorithm in 2017, meaning a bound of the form \(\exp((\log(L+2))^{O(1)})\). This was a major improvement, but such a bound need not be polynomial. Their paper also explicitly relates alternating-turn and vertex-owner conventions.

Czerwiński and coauthors prove quasipolynomial size lower bounds for the strong separating safety automata defined in their paper. This limits a broad collection of known constructions; it is not a lower bound against all deterministic parity-game algorithms.

Rick van der Heijden’s preprint of 4 November 2025 claims an algorithm taking \(O(n^2(n+m))\) time, with \(n\) vertices and \(m\) edges. Its Theorems 5, 7 and 8 assert correctness and the polynomial bound. The checked arXiv record still has only version 1. This review inspected the claim and theorem statements but did not establish their correctness or locate an authoritative primary-source resolution of the claim.

The 24 June 2026 revision of Suilen and Pérez’s paper, marked accepted at CONCUR 2026, continues to describe polynomial-time parity-game solving as open. Its Proposition 4.1 reduces parity games to a robust discounted-reward problem. That later treatment does not itself refute the 2025 algorithm claim; the current status remains explicitly unverified.

cards.title: Skolem problem
cards.formal: Is there a single deterministic Turing machine which, for every input consisting of an integer \(k\ge1\), integer coefficients \(c_0,\ldots,c_{k-1}\), and integer initial values \(u_0,\ldots,u_{k-1}\), halts and correctly decides whether \(u_t=0\) for some integer \(t\ge0\), where the infinite sequence is uniquely defined by \[u_{t+k}=\sum_{j=0}^{k-1}c_j u_{t+j}\qquad(t=0,1,2,\ldots)?\] The order \(k\) is part of the input and is unrestricted; no time or space bound is requested.
cards.definitions: Use input alphabet \(\{0,1,+,-,\#\}\). For a nonnegative integer \(a\), let \(\operatorname{bin}(a)\) be its ordinary base-two expansion without leading zeros, with \(\operatorname{bin}(0)=0\). Encode an integer \(z\) by a plus sign followed by \(\operatorname{bin}(z)\) if \(z\ge0\), and by a minus sign followed by \(\operatorname{bin}(-z)\) if \(z<0\); negative zero is invalid. A valid input is \(\operatorname{bin}(k)\), then exactly \(k\) signed coefficient fields in order, then exactly \(k\) signed initial-value fields in order, separated by one \(\#\) between consecutive fields, with no other symbols or trailing separator. The first field has \(k\ge1\). Output 1 means that a zero occurs at some nonnegative index, including among the initial values; output 0 means that every term at a nonnegative index is nonzero. The machine must halt with one of these two outputs on every valid input and reject every malformed input with output 0. This decidable syntax convention does not affect the underlying decidability question. A deterministic Turing machine has one finite transition table, a finite alphabet and finitely many work tapes; it has no randomness, external oracle, advice or input-dependent program. The sequence values are exact integers with no bound on their magnitude, and the same fixed coefficients apply at every index. The listed recurrence need not have the smallest possible order. Coefficients and initial values may vanish, all may be zero, and \(c_0=0\) is allowed; forward evolution is still uniquely defined. In particular, neither distinct characteristic roots nor a non-degeneracy assumption is promised. No upper bound on the index of a possible zero is supplied. This is a discrete-time existence-of-a-zero question, with indices \(0,1,2,\ldots\); negative or real-valued indices and nonnegativity of all terms are different targets.

context_blocks.text: Every individual term of the sequence is effectively computable from the finite input, and the existence of a zero is semidecidable: positive instances have a finite witnessing index. The unresolved demand is a procedure guaranteed to finish on zero-free inputs too. The problem concerns the whole class of input sequences; undecidability would not mean that the zero question for each particular named recurrence is unanswerable.

The same recurrence describes linear dynamics in \(k\)-dimensional integer space. With \(v_t=(u_t,\ldots,u_{t+k-1})^{\mathsf T}\), let \(B\) have ones just above the diagonal, zeros in the other entries of its first \(k-1\) rows, and last row \((c_0,\ldots,c_{k-1})\). Then \(v_{t+1}=Bv_t\), including when \(k=1\). The question is whether this orbit reaches the hyperplane where the first coordinate is zero. This makes the connection to exact reachability and termination guards in linear programs explicit.

The Skolem–Mahler–Lech theorem says that the zero indices form a finite union of arithmetic progressions, together with a finite exceptional set. Here a progression has the form \(\{a+br:r\ge0\}\), with integers \(a\ge0\) and \(b\ge1\). That qualitative structure does not itself provide an effective description of all exceptional zeros. The distinction between a structural existence theorem and an algorithm extracting its finite data is central to this problem.

Many sources assume that the coefficient of the oldest term is nonzero, which permits extending the sequence backward. The card retains arbitrary forward recurrences. A zero oldest-term coefficient can contribute a finite initial prefix before a recurrence of smaller order with nonzero oldest-term coefficient; the all-zero-coefficient case is eventually zero. Thus this input convention does not replace the classical decision problem with a different restriction. Rational coefficients and initial values also lead to the same zero-decision problem as integer data by an effective nonzero scaling, as explained in the 2026 survey.

For the recurrences considered in the cited number-theoretic results, the characteristic polynomial is the polynomial of a minimal-order recurrence. A sequence is simple when its characteristic roots are distinct, and non-degenerate when the ratio of no two distinct roots is a root of unity; a root of unity is a complex number whose positive integer power is one. These are different restrictions. Neither is imposed by the card. For nonzero non-degenerate sequences the zero set is finite, but no general effective bound on all those zeros is known in the inspected sources.

Bilu and coauthors’ MFCS 2022 Theorem 3 gives decidability for simple recurrences assuming both the Exponential Local-Global Principle, also called the Skolem Conjecture, and the weak p-adic Schanuel Conjecture. Their procedure produces an unconditional correctness certificate whenever it terminates; the universal termination assertion is conditional. The similarly named Skolem Conjecture is an additional arithmetic hypothesis, not the decision problem on this card.

Bacik, Ouaknine and Worrell’s SODA 2026 work, with a corrected arXiv revision of 17 July, places the order-at-most-four problem in coRP. For this zero-existence language, coRP means a randomized polynomial-time test accepting zero-containing inputs with probability one and rejecting zero-free inputs with probability at least one half. They also give such a bound for the bounded-index problem at each fixed order, where the upper index is supplied in binary. The latter remains restricted by that supplied bound; fixed-order complexity statements do not decide arbitrary unbounded-order recurrences.

Luca, Ouaknine and Worrell’s July 2026 Theorem 4.3 yields general decidability conditional on their Conjecture 4.2, which extends a Cramér–Granville prime-gap hypothesis to a specially defined density-one subset of primes. Ordinary prime-gap conjectures are not silently substituted for that stronger assumption. The same paper proves unconditionally the existence of a recursive index set \(S\) of natural density one on which zero existence is decidable for every recurrence. Density one means \(|S\cap\{0,\ldots,N\}|/(N+1)\to1\). Missing indices can still contain a recurrence’s only zero, so this does not decide existence over all nonnegative indices.

The joint survey dated 26 July 2026 continues to list both general Skolem and Positivity as open. Positivity asks whether all terms are nonnegative, while Bi-Skolem allows negative as well as nonnegative integer indices in a backward-extendible sequence. Continuous Skolem instead concerns zeros at real times in a linear differential equation. Results in these settings, or over rings of positive characteristic, have different input or index domains and are not resolutions of this integer recurrence target.

cards.why: Skolem asks whether exact reachability of zero is decidable for the simplest class of discrete linear recurrences with finite integer descriptions. The question connects arithmetic with verification of linear loops, matrix dynamics, automata and stochastic systems, and serves as a common unresolved decision problem to which other verification tasks are compared.
cards.answer_criterion: Supply a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean that such a total decision machine exists, with termination and correctness for every valid input and rejection of malformed strings, or a Lean-checked proof that no such machine exists. Equivalently, the language of valid encodings whose sequences contain a zero must be proved decidable or undecidable. A negative answer must rule out every total deterministic decider, not merely give an input on which one proposed program fails. A positive answer has to decide both the zero and zero-free cases uniformly over all orders; a semidecision procedure, a bounded-index algorithm, a theorem for a fixed order, or conditional termination under an unproved number-theoretic assumption does not settle the full target. A complexity lower bound such as NP-hardness does not prove undecidability. No polynomial bound, bound on the first zero, or enumeration of the entire zero set is required as the output.

importance.reason: A longstanding central decidability problem with an elementary finite input, substantial arithmetic content, and direct links to verification and automata. The 2026 work confirms current specialist attention; the importance is independent of the record’s previous incomplete wording.

cards.title: Mean-payoff games in polynomial time
cards.formal:
Is the exact mean-payoff winner language \(\mathrm{MPG}_{\ge0}\) defined below in deterministic polynomial time?

A valid instance is a finite directed graph \(G=(V,E)\) with \(V=[n]\), \(n\ge1\), at least one outgoing edge at every vertex, a partition \(V=V_{\mathrm{Max}}\sqcup V_{\mathrm{Min}}\), an integer weight function \(w:E\to\mathbb Z\), and a start vertex \(s\in V\). Its encoding is in \(\mathrm{MPG}_{\ge0}\) exactly when
\[\exists\sigma\in\Sigma_{\mathrm{Max}}\ \forall\tau\in\Sigma_{\mathrm{Min}},\qquad
\liminf_{T\to\infty}\frac1T\sum_{t=0}^{T-1}w(v_t,v_{t+1})\ge0,\]
where \(v_0=s\) and the unique infinite play \((v_t)_{t\ge0}\) follows the two strategies. Weights have the binary encoding specified below, and equality zero counts as winning for Max. Give a complete Lean proof of \(\mathrm{MPG}_{\ge0}\in\mathrm P\) or of \(\mathrm{MPG}_{\ge0}\notin\mathrm P\).
cards.definitions:
The edge set is a subset of \(V\times V\); self-loops are allowed and duplicate edges are not listed. Every listed edge has one arbitrary integer weight, possibly negative or zero. Either ownership set may be empty, and edges may connect vertices of the same owner. There are no chance vertices, additional agents, hidden information, simultaneous moves, fairness constraints, or extra payoff coordinates. Every vertex has a successor, so no finite-play convention is needed.

A finite history from \(s\) is a nonempty vertex sequence \(h=(s=v_0,v_1,\ldots,v_t)\) following edges of \(E\). A strategy of Max assigns to every such history ending in \(V_{\mathrm{Max}}\) a successor \(v\) with \((v_t,v)\in E\); define a strategy of Min analogously. The sets of these total deterministic history-dependent functions are \(\Sigma_{\mathrm{Max}}\) and \(\Sigma_{\mathrm{Min}}\). Neither player sees future choices. A strategy may depend on the complete known instance and entire finite history; the problem statement places no memory or computability restriction on strategies. For any pair, the play is uniquely determined by recursion. A positional strategy means that the selected successor depends only on the current vertex; positional optimality is an established theorem, not an additional promise on the instance.

For \(T\ge1\), set \(a_T=T^{-1}\sum_{t=0}^{T-1}w(v_t,v_{t+1})\). The lower limit means
\[\liminf_{T\to\infty}a_T=\sup_{N\ge1}\inf_{T\ge N}a_T.\]
It is a finite real number because \(|a_T|\le W\), where \(W=\max(1,\max_{e\in E}|w(e)|)\). The average need not converge for arbitrary history-dependent play. A negative finite prefix is allowed: this objective imposes no lower bound on the running cumulative sum and no prescribed initial energy budget. The payoff is not a discounted sum or a finite-window average.

For a concrete binary encoding, let \(b(u)\) be the binary expansion of a nonnegative integer \(u\), without leading zeros and with \(b(0)=0\). Define \(B(u)=1^{|b(u)|}0b(u)\). Encode an integer \(z\) by \(B(\zeta(z))\), where \(\zeta(z)=2z\) for \(z\ge0\) and \(\zeta(z)=-2z-1\) for \(z<0\). This is a signed binary representation with a uniquely recoverable sign and magnitude; it is not unary in \(|z|\).

The input is \(B(n)B(m)B(s)\), followed by the \(n\) ownership bits in vertex order, and then \(m=|E|\) triples \(B(u)B(v)B(\zeta(w(u,v)))\), listing edges in increasing lexicographic endpoint order. Ownership bit one denotes Max and zero denotes Min. The complete string must satisfy the stated graph and encoding conditions, with no trailing bits. All other binary strings are rejected and are outside \(\mathrm{MPG}_{\ge0}\). Let \(L\) denote the complete input length. Input validation and the translation to ordinary explicit adjacency-list signed-binary representations are polynomial-time operations; these representation conventions do not impose a graph or weight promise.

Membership in \(\mathrm P\) means that there are a finite deterministic multitape Turing-machine program \(A\) and fixed positive integers \(C,d\) such that for every binary string \(x\), \(A(x)\) halts within \(C(|x|+1)^d\) bit steps, outputting one exactly when \(x\in\mathrm{MPG}_{\ge0}\). The same program and constants must work for every size, graph, weight assignment and start vertex. Input reading, validation, arithmetic, storage access and output all count. There is no advice, randomization, game-solving oracle or unit-cost operation on arbitrarily large integers. The polynomial may depend on the fixed program but not on \(n,m,W\) or the instance. The output is only the exact winner bit; the task does not require printing an infinite strategy or play.

There is no bound on \(W\) in terms of \(n\) or \(m\). Its contribution to the input is logarithmic, so a bound polynomial in \(n,m,W\) is pseudopolynomial and need not be polynomial in \(L\). A rational threshold \(a/b\), with binary integers \(a\) and \(b>0\), gives an equivalent decision model: the weights \(bw(e)-a\) have polynomial encoding length and their nonnegative mean threshold expresses the original threshold. Thus fixing the threshold to zero retains the binary-weight complexity question.
cards.answer_criterion:
Give a complete, mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of either
\[\exists A\ \exists C,d\in\mathbb N_{\ge1}\ \forall x\in\{0,1\}^{*},\quad
 A(x)\text{ halts within }C(|x|+1)^d\text{ steps and outputs }\mathbf1_{\mathrm{MPG}_{\ge0}}(x),\]
or its logical negation, with the machine and language definitions above. A positive proof must establish the exact game semantics, correctness on every valid instance, rejection of invalid encodings, and the full polynomial bit bound. A negative proof must rule out every deterministic polynomial-time decider, rather than only a particular local-improvement rule, representation, certificate family or algorithmic framework.

A pseudopolynomial bound, a polynomial bound only after random perturbations, a randomized expected-time guarantee, or an algorithm for a restricted graph or weight family does not answer the full question. A polynomial number of arithmetic operations alone is insufficient if intermediate integers require superpolynomial bit length. A strongly polynomial algorithm with polynomially bounded bit representations would suffice but is more than required. There is no approximation tolerance or unproved complexity hypothesis in the target.
cards.why: Mean-payoff games model sustainable long-run rewards when an adversary controls part of a finite system. Their exact winner problem has short certificates for both answers, yet its unrestricted polynomial bit complexity remains an important question in quantitative verification and graph-game theory.

context_blocks.text: A finite initial loss disappears from a long-run average. For example, an eventual repetition of weights −5 and +7 has mean payoff one after any fixed finite prefix. Requiring every partial sum to stay nonnegative is a different objective. A play of weight zero forever is winning here because the threshold is nonnegative, not strictly positive.

Optimal positional strategies exist for both players. With both such strategies fixed, a finite graph produces an eventually repeated cycle, whose average determines the payoff. The resulting certificates place the winner language in \(\mathrm{NP}\cap\mathrm{coNP}\): yes and no instances each have polynomial-length certificates checkable in polynomial time. This does not provide a polynomial-time way to find them. Zwick and Paterson give the classical complexity analysis and a polynomial reduction to simple stochastic games, which add random transitions.

Brim and coauthors' Theorem 8 gives \(O(nmW)\) arithmetic-operation bounds for threshold decision and winning-strategy synthesis, where \(n=|V|\) and \(m=|E|\). A weight of magnitude \(2^b\) requires only \(b+1\) magnitude bits. Thus this dependence can be exponential in the encoding length even before charging for arithmetic. Their theorem is pseudopolynomial; it is not a uniform polynomial bit bound for arbitrary weights.

Fijalkow, Gawrychowski and Ohlmann establish size bounds for universal graphs, auxiliary weighted graphs that represent all bounded-size graphs satisfying the mean-payoff objective through weight-preserving maps. Their lower bounds constrain the resulting family of value-iteration algorithms. They do not exclude algorithms outside that framework, so they do not prove that the winner language is outside P.

The published ICALP 2024 theorem of Loff and Skomra assumes an ergodic game graph and independent random perturbations of rewards. Ergodic means that for every reward assignment the game value is independent of the starting vertex; ordinary strong connectivity does not imply this property. For example, Theorem 1 gives time polynomial in \(n\) and the inverse perturbation scale for normalized rewards perturbed by independent Gaussians, with high probability over those perturbations. Both the input restriction and probabilistic guarantee remain part of the theorem.

Maat’s September 2025 preprint identifies strategy improvement with simplex runs for a nondegenerate longest-shortest-path game formulation. Nondegeneracy excludes certain zero cycles and equal-weight competing paths. Section 5 explicitly warns that the constructed linear-program coefficients can have doubly exponential magnitudes, so writing them may require exponentially many bits. The existence of this linear program and its correspondence between iterations therefore do not supply a polynomial-bit-time solver.

Ohlmann’s March 2026 preprint gives a new deterministic recursive algorithm and a correctness argument. Its introduction and Section 7 explicitly leave a useful running-time analysis, including the hoped-for subexponential bound, unresolved. It does not claim a polynomial-time solution. Its presentation uses limsup and positional strategies; positional determinacy of these finite games preserves the game value, while the present definition retains its explicit liminf objective for arbitrary histories.

Adenwalla and coauthors’ July 2026 preprint relates mean-payoff games to tropical inequalities and graph classes defined by equality patterns among vertex labels. Tropical linear expressions replace ordinary addition and multiplication by maximum and addition. Section 7 gives a reduction using compact encodings of path clauses and functional constraints; it does not assume that an exponentially long clause is written out. This is a connection between decision problems, while Section 3.7.2 explicitly leaves polynomial-time mean-payoff solving open.
