cards.title: Tarski’s exponential function problem
cards.formal: Is the first-order theory of the standard real exponential field \(\mathbb R_{\exp}=(\mathbb R;0,1,+,-,\times,<,\exp)\) decidable? Precisely, does there exist one ordinary deterministic Turing machine \(D\) which halts on every encoded first-order sentence \(\varphi\) in this fixed language and outputs \(1\) exactly when \(\mathbb R_{\exp}\models\varphi\), and \(0\) otherwise? The exponential function is defined on all real numbers, and the required conclusion is unconditional.
cards.definitions: The domain is the standard field \(\mathbb R\), with its usual constants, addition, unary additive inverse, multiplication and strict order. Equality is a logical symbol. Here \(\exp(x)=\sum_{j=0}^{\infty}x^j/j!\), the standard real exponential, with \(0!=1\); it is not an input function or an oracle available to the machine. Terms are finite expressions formed from variables \(v_i\), \(i\in\mathbb N=\{0,1,\ldots\}\), the constants \(0,1\), unary negation and exponentiation, and binary addition and multiplication. Atomic formulas are term equalities or strict inequalities. Formulas are formed using negation, conjunction, disjunction and the quantifiers \(\exists v_i\) and \(\forall v_i\). Every quantifier ranges over all of \(\mathbb R\), regardless of the index \(i\); indices name variables, not integer-valued inputs. Binding has its usual nested scope, with the nearest enclosing quantifier on a given variable binding that occurrence. A sentence is a formula with no free variables, and truth uses the ordinary real operations and ordinary first-order semantics. Arbitrarily many variables, nested exponentials and arbitrary finite quantifier alternations are allowed. There are no names for arbitrary real parameters, integer predicates, trigonometric functions or additional input operations. For a fixed finite-alphabet encoding, write a variable as v[b], where b is the usual binary expansion of its nonnegative index, with no leading zero except for the index zero itself. Use literal strings 0 and 1 for constants, and the prefix term forms -(t), exp(t), +(t,u) and *(t,u). Formula forms are =(t,u), <(t,u), not(phi), and(phi,psi), or(phi,psi), exists(v[b],phi) and forall(v[b],phi), with the indicated parentheses and commas and no spaces; t,u stand for terms and phi,psi for formulas, not literal tokens. Thus all inputs are finite strings over a fixed finite alphabet of these characters. To make D total on all strings, malformed encodings and formulas with free variables must be rejected with output 0. D has finite control and finitely many ordinary work tapes, has no oracle, noncomputable real constant, advice or random choices, and is the same machine for every input length, number of variables and quantifier pattern. No running-time or space upper bound is imposed beyond halting.
cards.answer_criterion: Supply a complete, mathematically correct proof checked in Lean that such a single total deterministic Turing machine exists and has the stated exact truth behavior, or a complete Lean-checked proof that the language of true encoded sentences is undecidable by ordinary Turing machines. In the positive direction, termination and correctness must hold for every finite input, with the stated rejection convention on invalid strings. In the negative direction, the proof must rule out every candidate total decider, not merely refute one proposed algorithm or one recursively specified axiom system. A computably equivalent precise syntax may be used if its effective correspondence with the card’s encoding and sentence semantics is proved. A procedure that is correct whenever it terminates but lacks a universal termination proof does not meet the positive criterion. Deciding only a syntactic fragment qualifies only if the proof also establishes decidability of the full stated theory. Neither assuming Schanuel’s conjecture nor assuming another unresolved hypothesis is an unconditional resolution; the hypothesis would itself have to be proved in the accepted Lean development. Numerical evaluation with any fixed precision, bounded search for real solutions, or a time-complexity lower bound does not replace this exact decidability target.
cards.why: A central boundary in exact algorithmic reasoning over real numbers: polynomial real arithmetic is decidable, while adding one standard analytic function connects logical truth to unresolved transcendence questions. Its resolution would determine whether a uniform symbolic decision procedure can handle all finite first-order specifications involving real exponentiation, with consequences for verification problems already reducible to this theory.

context_blocks.text: Tarski’s decision theorem covers polynomial equations and inequalities over the reals with arbitrary first-order quantifiers. Adding the single function \(\exp\) asks whether that global decidability survives beyond polynomial arithmetic. The input remains a finite symbolic formula: a quantified real is part of the semantics, not a real number that must somehow be supplied as an infinite input string.

The target includes exact equalities and unrestricted quantifier alternation. For example, \(\forall x\,(x>0\Rightarrow\exists y\,\exp(y)=x)\) expresses surjectivity onto the positive reals; the implication here is an abbreviation for a disjunction in the specified syntax. Individual familiar identities are decidable, but they do not supply a machine for every sentence. Approximating an exponential value is also a different task: arbitrarily accurate approximations need not by themselves decide whether a given expression is exactly zero.

Wilkie proved model completeness of the real exponential theory in 1996: every formula is equivalent, in that theory, to an existential formula. The structure is also o-minimal, meaning that every definable subset of the real line is a finite union of points and intervals. These are strong finiteness properties, but neither statement alone certifies an algorithm for exact truth. cards.title: Continuous Skolem problem
cards.formal: Is there a Turing algorithm that, given any dimension \(d\ge 1\), rational matrix \(A\in \mathbb Q^{d\times d}\), and rational column vectors \(b,c\in \mathbb Q^{d}\), always halts and correctly decides whether \(c^{T}\exp (tA)b=0\) for some real \(t\ge 0\)?
cards.definitions: Every input rational is represented exactly by a signed binary integer numerator and a positive binary integer denominator. The dimension is part of the input and has no fixed upper bound. The matrix exponential is \(\exp (tA)=\sum_{j=0}^{\infty} t^{j} A^{j}/j!\), and \(x(t)=\exp (tA)b\) is the unique real solution of \(x' (t)=Ax(t), x(0)=b\). The target is the hyperplane \(\{x:c^{T}x=0\}; c=0\) is allowed and gives an immediate yes instance. Time ranges over all finite nonnegative real numbers, not just rational or integer times. Equality is exact. A zero at \(t=0\) counts, as does a trajectory that is identically in the hyperplane. If the scalar function approaches zero only in the limit \(t\to \infty\), the answer is no unless it also has a finite zero. No promise of diagonalizability, simple eigenvalues, bounded dimension, stability, spectral separation, transverse intersection, or robust distance from the hyperplane is supplied. The requested algorithm is an ordinary finite-input decision procedure without real-number or number-theoretic oracles; no complexity upper bound is prescribed. This card retains the rational-data version; some cited work treats the more general real-algebraic-data version.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof of an unconditional always-halting Turing decision algorithm for every finite rational input, or a complete Lean-checked proof that no such algorithm exists. A positive proof must specify a computable classifier and prove equivalence with \(\exists t\in\mathbb R_{\ge0},\ c^T\exp(tA)b=0\), including tangencies and the initial time. A negative proof must establish undecidability for this exact rational matrix/vector representation. The formalization must cover the analytic semantics and all effectiveness claims, rather than merely postulating an exact real-number test. A conditional procedure assuming Schanuel’s conjecture, a solver for a fixed low dimension, a procedure that may fail to halt, or a certificate requiring a nonzero-distance promise is partial progress. Hardness with arbitrary algebraic coefficients, nonlinear differential equations or a different target set needs a proved reduction into this rational linear model.
cards.why: A minimal exact reachability question for continuous linear systems whose decidability remains unresolved, linking algorithmic verification to real analysis, transcendence and effective number theory.

context_blocks.text: Linear differential equations have explicit matrix-exponential solutions, yet an explicit formula does not automatically decide whether a trajectory hits an exact target. The scalar output \(c^{T}x(t)\) may combine growth, decay, polynomial factors and oscillations. The matrix and vectors are finite rational data, while the possible hitting time is an unrestricted real number. This makes the question a basic test of what exact verification can decide even for linear continuous dynamics.

Numerical proximity is insufficient. The one-dimensional system \(x' =- x, x(0)=1\) has output \(e^{- t}\), which becomes arbitrarily small but never reaches zero. Conversely, a zero need not be accompanied by a sign change: the polynomial \((t- 1)^{2}\) touches zero and returns to positive values. Such a polynomial is itself an output of a rational nilpotent linear system. A grid search or a sign-change detector can therefore miss the distinction required by the card.

Simple degenerate cases can be removed exactly. The initial-time condition is \(c^{T}b=0\). By the Cayley–Hamilton theorem, the scalar function is identically zero precisely when \(c^{T}A^{j} b=0\) for \(j=0,\ldots ,d- 1\). These are finite rational calculations. Outside that case, analyticity ensures only finitely many zeros in each bounded interval, but neither a uniform numerical precision nor a final time beyond all zeros follows from that finiteness statement.

Spectral decomposition writes the output as a sum of polynomial multiples of exponentials, with conjugate terms combining into real sine and cosine expressions. The imaginary parts of eigenvalues give oscillation frequencies. Repeated eigenvalues can introduce polynomial factors. Competing terms can nearly cancel at very large times, so a proof that the long-term behaviour is simple enough to inspect is a substantive part of an unbounded decision procedure.

Chonev, Ouaknine and Worrell prove decidability of the bounded Continuous Skolem problem assuming Schanuel’s conjecture. That conjecture gives a transcendence-degree lower bound for complex numbers linearly independent over the rationals together with their exponentials. Their algorithm uses it to handle possible tangential zeros. The result does not supply an unconditional bounded-time procedure, and a bounded-time procedure alone does not supply a stopping criterion for checking all \(t\ge 0\).

The same paper reduces certain unbounded spectral cases to the bounded problem, including the case with at most one rationally independent frequency. A separate recurrent-reachability result decides whether a solution of differential order at most seven has infinitely many zeros and gives an effective last-zero bound when it has only finitely many. Combined with the conditional bounded solver, this yields conditional decisions in that low-order regime. Infinite recurrence and existence of even one zero are nevertheless different questions.

The broader algebraic-coefficient formulations reveal a connection with effective Diophantine approximation: handling multiple independent oscillations can entail computing quantities measuring unusually good rational approximations to algebraic numbers. Those implications are evidence of the mathematical obstacles, not undecidability proofs. Their precise dimension thresholds belong to the coefficient model of the cited theorem; this card does not automatically transfer them to the rational-matrix representation fixed above.

Platzer and Qian’s 2025 completeness theorem for compact initial-value problems concerns specified open safety and liveness properties. Its discussion explicitly identifies exact hyperplane reachability as an obstacle to replacing those topological conditions by arbitrary closed targets. A proof system that certifies entry into an open neighbourhood need not decide whether the trajectory touches its central hyperplane. This distinction matters when interpreting advances in numerical verification as progress on exact decision questions.

The July 2026 survey by Bacik and coauthors places the continuous problem alongside discrete recurrence questions, while emphasizing differences in technique. Sampling only integer times gives a sequence but changes the question: for example, a rational rotation system can have output cos t and reach zero at \(\pi /2\). The card asks whether any real hitting time exists, so discrete-time zero testing cannot simply replace the continuous analysis.

cards.title: Ultimate Positivity problem
cards.formal: Does there exist a single deterministic Turing machine which, for every finite description of a rational linear recurrence sequence \((u_n)_{n\ge0}\), halts and correctly decides whether \[\exists N\in\mathbb N\ \forall n\ge N,\qquad u_n\ge0?\] The input consists of \(k\ge1\), rational coefficients \(a_0,\ldots,a_{k-1}\), and rational initial terms \(u_0,\ldots,u_{k-1}\); subsequent terms satisfy \[u_{n+k}=\sum_{j=0}^{k-1}a_j u_{n+j}\qquad(n\ge0).\] The supplied recurrence length \(k\) is unrestricted, and repeated characteristic roots are allowed. “Positivity” in this problem's established name means nonnegativity.
cards.why: Ultimate Positivity asks whether finitely specified linear dynamics eventually remain on one side of a boundary. It connects recurrence sequences, eventual program behavior and precise approximation questions in number theory. A resolution would determine whether eventual sign stability is algorithmically recognizable even when repeated roots introduce polynomial factors and several oscillating contributions interact.
cards.status_note: Explicitly open in the termination survey version of 24 July 2026, p. 26. The checked positive results cover general recurrences through order five and simple recurrences at arbitrary order; the May 2026 preprint has a unique-dominant-root restriction. A bounded search on 16 September 2026 found no matching general resolution. This records the dated literature evidence and model checks, not an exhaustive status guarantee or independent formal verification of cited proofs.

Ultimate Positivity asks whether every sufficiently late term is nonnegative, allowing a finite negative prefix and infinitely many zero terms.

cards.definitions: Let \(\mathbb N=\{0,1,2,\ldots\}\). Each rational input is encoded exactly as a signed binary numerator and a positive binary denominator. The lists and their lengths are explicit finite input; the recurrence coefficients are constant in \(n\). These data uniquely determine every rational term. The supplied recurrence need not have minimum possible length. Its characteristic polynomial is \(p(X)=X^k-\sum_{j=0}^{k-1}a_jX^j\); no restriction is imposed on its roots, their multiplicities, ratios or moduli. In particular, zero coefficients and zero roots are allowed. A sequence is ultimately nonnegative exactly when the set \(\{n\in\mathbb N:u_n<0\}\) is finite. Infinitely many zeros are permitted, and the identically zero sequence is a yes-instance. A no-instance has \(\forall N\in\mathbb N\ \exists n\ge N:u_n<0\). The decision algorithm must be uniform in all recurrence lengths, coefficients and initial values, must use no oracle, and must always give the exact correct answer; there is no error probability, numerical tolerance, or time bound. Invalid encodings may be rejected. No threshold needs to be included with a yes-answer. Rational rather than integer data do not change this decidability target: for a positive integer \(D\) divisible by all input denominators, \(v_n=D^{n+1}u_n\) has integer initial terms, integer recurrence coefficients \(a_jD^{k-j}\), and exactly the same signs.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof of decidability or undecidability for the exact input language above. A positive answer must establish one total computable yes/no procedure correct for all finite recurrence descriptions. A negative answer must prove that no such procedure exists. Resolving an arbitrary fixed low order or the simple-root subclass positively is only partial; an undecidability theorem for any contained subclass would suffice negatively. A yes-answer is allowed without producing a threshold, because the target is the decision problem itself.

source_formulation.text: Given a rational linear recurrence sequence, decide whether all but finitely many of its terms are nonnegative, with no bound on the recurrence order.
source_formulation.caption: Editorial paraphrase of the source question

context_blocks.text: A finite recurrence description controls an infinite sequence. Eventual nonnegativity allows a finite exceptional prefix: \(u_n=n-5\) satisfies a constant-coefficient recurrence and is a yes-instance even though its first five terms are negative. In contrast, \(u_n=(-1)^n\) has arbitrarily late negative terms. The sequence need not converge or increase, and zeros can continue forever.

The question differs from requiring every term to be nonnegative, which is the Positivity problem, and from asking whether some term is zero, which is the Skolem problem. These problems share the same input format but have different quantifiers. The general Ultimate Positivity target includes repeated characteristic roots; it is not replaced by the already decidable simple-root subclass.

Ouaknine and Worrell prove a polynomial-time decision procedure for Ultimate Positivity when the recurrence has order at most five. At order six they prove a number-theoretic implication: decidability would make a specified family of Diophantine-approximation constants computable. This is a conditional consequence of a decision procedure, not a proof of undecidability.

For simple recurrences, whose minimal characteristic polynomial has distinct roots, Ultimate Positivity is decidable at every order. The known procedure can return yes without providing an index after which every term is nonnegative. Computing such an index is a separate effective-threshold problem, retained in the related card.

The July 2026 termination survey still identifies unrestricted Ultimate Positivity as open. Its algorithm for termination from all integer initial states does not decide the eventual sign behavior of one supplied sequence; those quantifiers lead to different questions. This is recent explicit source evidence, with the usual limit that a literature check is not a proof that no later result exists.

The May 2026 preprint on arbitrary-order polynomial-coefficient recurrences gives sufficient conditions with a unique dominant root. Arbitrary order alone does not supply a solution to this card: the present input permits repeated roots and multiple roots of maximal modulus and requires a total decision procedure for every instance.

cards.title: Termination of linear-constraint loops
cards.formal: Determine separately, for each state domain \(D\in\{\mathbb Z,\mathbb Q,\mathbb R\}\), whether termination of single-path linear-constraint loops over \(D\) is decidable. An input is \(d\ge1\) and an explicitly given system of rational linear inequalities \[A x+B y\le c,\qquad A,B\in\mathbb Q^{m\times d},\quad c\in\mathbb Q^m,\] defining allowed consecutive states \(x,y\in D^d\). Does there exist a deterministic Turing machine for that fixed domain which always halts and decides whether \[\neg\exists (x_n)_{n\in\mathbb N}\in(D^d)^{\mathbb N}\ \forall n\in\mathbb N,\qquad A x_n+B x_{n+1}\le c?\] Thus termination means that every execution from every initial state is finite, irrespective of the allowed successor choices. The three domain variants are retained separately, with no assumption that their decidability statuses coincide.
cards.why: This question asks how much nondeterminism can be introduced into elementary linear dynamics while preserving decidable universal termination. A single system of inequalities allows infinitely many possible successors but retains a strong convex structure over the reals. Resolving its domain-specific cases would locate a central boundary between complete verification algorithms for affine programs and undecidability in more expressive program models.
cards.status_note: Explicitly open over integers, rationals and reals in Carelli’s ICALP 2026 introduction and in Open Problem 2 of the survey revised 24 July 2026. The 2024 two-variable theorem is over real states; the 2026 one-variable integer theorem is conditional on a generalized Collatz conjecture. Neither resolves the unrestricted domain family. Bounded checking on 16 September 2026 found no matching later resolution, without independently verifying every cited proof.

cards.definitions: Here \(\mathbb N=\{0,1,2,\ldots\}\), \(m\ge0\), and all inequalities are non-strict and componentwise. The system describes one conjunction, equivalently one closed rational polyhedron in \(\mathbb R^{2d}\); no disjunction of different transition relations is permitted. Over integers or rationals, allowed transitions are the points of this same polyhedron in \(D^{2d}\). The state variables are unbounded, and all coordinates are chosen simultaneously. From \(x\), any \(y\) satisfying the conjunction may be the next state. If there is no such \(y\), the finite execution stops. There is no probabilistic or fairness condition; the existence of even one infinite sequence is nontermination. A guard involving only \(x\) is included as rows with zero \(y\)-coefficients. Equality is represented by two inequalities. If \(m=0\), every pair is allowed and the loop is nonterminating. All initial states in \(D^d\) are considered; no supplied initial-state region or fixed starting value is part of the input. Both \(d\) and the number of inequalities are unrestricted. Every rational coefficient is encoded as a signed binary numerator and positive binary denominator in explicit finite matrix lists. Multiplying each row by a positive common denominator gives an equivalent integer-coefficient input, over each domain separately. The machine receives only finite rational data, even for the real-state case; states themselves are not encoded as extra machine inputs. For each domain the required machine must be uniform in dimension and coefficients, with no oracle, random error or complexity bound. Termination does not require a common bound on the lengths of all finite executions.
cards.answer_criterion: Give complete Lean-checked decidability or undecidability results for all three stated domain variants, recording each outcome separately. For a positive result, provide a total computable classifier on the finite rational descriptions and prove equivalence with absence of an infinite execution over the selected domain. For a negative result, prove that no such decider exists for that domain. Positive results for affine assignments, restricted dimensions or restricted inequalities alone are partial. An undecidability result for a subclass with the same rational input and selected state domain suffices for that domain; a proof allowing irrational coefficients or disjunctions changes the problem. A ranking-function search that can fail to return an answer is insufficient.

source_formulation.text: Determine decidability of termination for loops whose body is a conjunction of linear constraints between the current and next state, beyond the affine-assignment case.
source_formulation.caption: Editorial paraphrase of the source question; domain variants made explicit

context_blocks.text: An affine assignment specifies one successor. A relational loop may admit a whole set of successors, and termination has to survive every permitted choice from every starting point. The finite description is still only a conjunction of linear inequalities; it does not contain a program with arbitrary branching or a supplied unbounded computation.

The original survey discusses termination across integer, rational and real state spaces before presenting the general relational question. The July 2026 survey makes the distinction explicit in Open Problem 2. The card therefore keeps the three cases as separate targets within the same family, rather than selecting one domain silently or assuming a transfer between them.

Universal termination permits arbitrarily long finite executions as the initial state varies. For example, the integer relation requiring a positive current value and decreasing it by one terminates from every start, although there is no bound valid for all positive starts. The displayed predicate instead rules out every infinite execution.

The affine subclass is decidable over all three domains. Allowing a finite disjunction of transition polyhedra leads to a different multipath model with undecidability results. The open single-path class lies between these settings: its choices arise from one conjunction, not an unrestricted union of branches.

Guilmant and coauthors decide the problem for at most two real-valued variables. This theorem fixes both a dimension bound and the real domain; it is not a theorem about two integer variables or arbitrary dimension. Distinguishing those hypotheses is essential when comparing nearby positive results.

Carelli’s ICALP 2026 paper retains the general question and investigates a single integer variable. Its polynomial-time termination result is conditional on a precisely stated generalized Collatz reachability conjecture. Deciding cycles is not enough by itself, because an infinite trace can keep visiting new states. Thus the paper does not supply an unconditional algorithm for the domain family here.

cards.title: Decidability of multiplicative-exponential linear logic
cards.formal: Does there exist one deterministic Turing machine that, for every finite propositional MELL sequent \(\Gamma\) in the calculus below, halts and answers yes exactly when \(\vdash \Gamma\) has a finite derivation? There is no promised bound on formula size or exponential nesting and no requested time bound beyond termination on every input.
cards.why: MELL combines resource-sensitive composition with controlled reuse. Its decision problem connects automated proof search to branching counter systems and tests a fundamental boundary of algorithmic reasoning about resources.

cards.definitions: Use atoms \(p_{i}\) and their distinct dual literals \(p_{i}^{\perp}\) for integers \(i\ge 0\). Formulas are finite syntax trees generated by \(A ::= p_{i} | p_{i}^{\perp} | 1 | \perp  | (A\otimes A) |\) (A⅋A) | !A | ?A. A sequent \(\Gamma\) is a finite multiset of formulas; commas denote multiset union, retaining multiplicity. The following rules, read from premises to conclusion, define derivations. Identity has no premises and concludes \(\vdash p_{i},p_{i}^{\perp}\). The unit rule has no premises and concludes \(\vdash 1\). Tensor takes \(\vdash \Gamma ,A\) and \(\vdash \Delta ,B\) to \(\vdash \Gamma ,\Delta ,A\otimes B\). Par takes \(\vdash \Gamma ,A,B\) to \(\vdash \Gamma ,A\)⅋B. The other unit rule takes \(\vdash \Gamma\) to \(\vdash \Gamma ,\perp\). Dereliction takes \(\vdash \Gamma ,A\) to \(\vdash \Gamma\),?A. Weakening takes \(\vdash \Gamma\) to \(\vdash \Gamma\),?A. Contraction takes \(\vdash \Gamma\),?A,?A to \(\vdash \Gamma\),?A. Promotion takes \(\vdash\)?\(\Gamma ,A\) to \(\vdash\)?\(\Gamma ,!A\), where every formula in ?\(\Gamma\) has outermost symbol ?. Contexts may be empty, and all displayed formula and context choices are arbitrary subject to these conditions. A derivation is a finite rooted tree whose leaves are the two nullary rules and whose internal nodes are instances of the other rules. There are no further rules; exchange is implicit in multisets. This is the cut-free presentation of classical commutative MELL, whose usual cut rule is admissible. Inputs explicitly list formula trees with constructor delimiters and binary atom indices; malformed strings are rejected. Formulas contain neither additives nor quantifiers, and there is just one pair of exponential modalities ! and ?.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove that the provable sequents of this calculus form a decidable language, or prove that no algorithm can decide that language. A procedure that terminates only on provable sequents does not establish decidability.

context_blocks.text: Linear logic treats assumptions as resources whose occurrences matter. An ordinary assumption cannot automatically be copied or discarded. For example, the resource-reading of \(p\to p\otimes p\) asks for two copies from one and is unavailable in general; marking the input !p permits reuse. MELL keeps multiplicative composition together with these reuse modalities.

The rules make each proposed finite proof checkable. That does not by itself make provability decidable: searching through larger proofs will eventually find a proof when one exists, but need not terminate when none exists. The question asks for a single procedure that also gives a terminating negative answer.

The restrictions on contraction and promotion are part of the problem. Allowing unrestricted contraction gives a different logic, and adding additive connectives or several interacting subexponential modalities changes the decidability boundary. A published 2015 decidability argument was challenged in Straßburger’s 2019 paper, which identifies gaps and separates MELL from its decidable relevant variant.

Branching vector addition systems describe trees of computations with nonnegative integer resources. Their general reachability problem is inter-reducible with MELL provability. The 2025 result in the original reference establishes decidability for two-dimensional systems, so its dimension restriction cannot be omitted.

Status update: the July 2026 preprint claims decidability of general branching vector addition systems and explicitly states that MELL provability follows. This reaches the full decision question, unlike the earlier low-dimensional result. This card records the claim with uncertain status because its proof has not been independently verified here.

cards.title: Effective ultimate-positivity thresholds for simple recurrences
cards.formal: Is there a single deterministic Turing machine that, given any simple rational linear recurrence sequence \((u_n)_{n\ge0}\), always halts and returns either \(\mathrm{NO}\), meaning that the sequence is not ultimately nonnegative, or a natural number \(N\) satisfying \[\forall n\ge N,\qquad u_n\ge0?\] It must return \(\mathrm{NO}\) exactly when \(\forall N\in\mathbb N\ \exists n\ge N:u_n<0\). A valid natural-number output may be any sufficient threshold; it need not be the smallest one. The input recurrence length is unrestricted. Equivalently, because Ultimate Positivity for simple recurrences is already decidable, ask for a procedure that halts and outputs such a threshold on every ultimately nonnegative simple input, with no condition on other inputs.
cards.why: This problem isolates a precise gap between deciding an eventual property and computing a point after which it holds. An effective bound would make the exceptional prefix finite and accessible and would decide all-time Positivity for simple recurrences. The difference matters whenever an eventual mathematical guarantee must become an exact finite certificate about a concrete linear dynamical system.
cards.status_note: The threshold-production gap is explicit in the 2014 primary theorem, the imported 2015 survey and Noubissie’s April 2025 manuscript. The checked growth theorem bounds the number of exceptional indices, and the May 2026 preprint imposes a unique-dominant-root hypothesis; neither provides the required total algorithm for arbitrary simple recurrences. A bounded search on 16 September 2026 found no matching resolution. This is dated source-open evidence with bounded current-status checking, not a proof of present openness or an independent verification of all cited arguments.

textbook_notes.caution: The nonnegativity convention is the formal one in the paper. Infinite occurrence of zero, real/rational universal termination and ultimate positivity of simple recurrences are already decidable here.
textbook_notes.status_note: Presented in the cited 2015 source version. The import does not verify present open status; this dated note does not override a later card review.

importance.reason: A substantial effectivity question tied to simple-recurrence Positivity and Skolem decidability, beyond merely improving a complexity bound. The known general ultimate-positivity decision procedure does not supply its witness, exposing a foundational algorithmic gap with verification consequences.

sentences: A simple rational linear recurrence has a characteristic polynomial with distinct roots and a finite exact description.
The question asks for an algorithm that produces an index beyond which every term is nonnegative whenever such an index exists.
Any sufficient index is accepted, with no requirement that it be minimal or small.
Ultimate Positivity itself is already decidable for this class, but the checked general algorithm does not compute the threshold and later cardinality bounds do not locate the final exception.
A general effective threshold would close a gap between eventual guarantees and finite witnesses and would decide all-time Positivity for simple recurrences.

cards.definitions: An input explicitly lists \(k\ge1\), rational coefficients \(a_0,\ldots,a_{k-1}\), and rational initial values \(u_0,\ldots,u_{k-1}\). For \(n\in\mathbb N=\{0,1,2,\ldots\}\), define \[u_{n+k}=\sum_{j=0}^{k-1}a_j u_{n+j},\qquad p(X)=X^k-\sum_{j=0}^{k-1}a_jX^j.\] The input is required to have a squarefree characteristic polynomial: \(p\) has no repeated complex roots, equivalently \(\gcd(p,p')=1\) over \(\mathbb Q[X]\). This effectively checkable representation covers every simple sequence via its minimal characteristic polynomial; minimum recurrence length is not itself an input requirement. A possible zero root contributes only a finite initial part and may be handled explicitly; allowing it does not extend the unresolved tail problem beyond the usual nonzero-root source convention. Every rational is given by a signed binary numerator and a positive binary denominator, and finite lists have explicit delimiters. Non-squarefree or malformed descriptions may be rejected as invalid inputs. Distinct roots may have equal moduli or root-of-unity ratios, and there is no promise of a unique dominant root. The recurrence coefficients are constant, not polynomials in the index. Nonnegative means \(u_n\ge0\), so zeros are allowed and the identically zero input admits \(N=0\). The output is a tagged \(\mathrm{NO}\) or an explicitly written binary natural number. The algorithm is uniform across all finite input lengths, uses no oracle or random error, and has no required time bound. Rational and integer presentations give the same target: multiplication by the positive factor \(D^{n+1}\), where \(D\) clears the input denominators, converts to integer initial values and integer coefficients while preserving signs, thresholds and distinctness of characteristic roots.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof that the specified total output procedure exists, or prove that no such computable procedure exists. A positive answer must provide an algorithm and prove that each natural-number output bounds every negative term of that input, and that NO is returned precisely when no threshold exists. An algorithm required to halt only on ultimately nonnegative simple inputs is equally sufficient, together with the already established simple-case decision theorem and a Lean-checked justification of the equivalence. Any valid threshold is acceptable; neither minimality nor a prescribed asymptotic size is required. A nonconstructive existence proof for each individual threshold, or an algorithm returning only a yes/no ultimate-positivity answer, does not meet the witness-output requirement.

source_formulation.text: For an ultimately nonnegative simple linear recurrence of arbitrary order, compute an index after which all terms are nonnegative; the general decision procedure in the source does not produce this threshold.
source_formulation.caption: Editorial paraphrase of the source question

context_blocks.text: Every yes-instance has at least one threshold by definition. The issue is whether one algorithm can obtain a valid threshold from each finite recurrence description. The target permits generous overestimates: there is no requirement to find the last negative term or an optimal bound. The requirement to compute a witness remains meaningful even with unlimited finite running time.

Simple recurrences have distinct characteristic roots, so the polynomial factors associated with repeated roots are absent. Nevertheless, multiple equally large oscillating contributions can nearly cancel at late indices. Restricting to a unique largest-modulus root would remove part of the source question.

The 2014 general simple-case theorem decides whether an eventual threshold exists, without computing it. Its proof uses noneffective Diophantine bounds; this explains a limit of that particular algorithm and does not prove that thresholds are uncomputable. The source explicitly identifies producing thresholds as the additional unresolved task.

The low-order result decides all-time Positivity for simple recurrences through order nine. The source distinguishes that effective result from the arbitrary-order decision theorem for Ultimate Positivity. A general threshold procedure would also decide all-time Positivity for the simple class, so completing this witness task would settle a significant associated decision problem.

Noubissie’s 2025 manuscript retains the threshold gap and gives an effective bound on how many indices violate a specified growth inequality. A bound on the number of exceptions does not locate the final exception: even a set with one element can place that element arbitrarily far out. The stated theorem therefore does not supply the threshold requested here.

The May 2026 preprint supplies sufficient conditions for polynomial-coefficient recurrences with a unique dominant root. Its unrestricted order parameter does not remove that root hypothesis or make its sufficient test a total procedure for every simple constant-coefficient recurrence. It is recorded as a restricted preprint result, not a resolution of this card.

cards.title: Constructive simplicial model with univalent universes
cards.formal: Does the constructive set theory \(\mathsf S\) specified below support a full simplicial interpretation of intensional Martin-Löf type theory with \(0,1,\mathbb N,\Pi,\Sigma,\mathsf{Id}\) and a cumulative sequence of univalent universes, in which every type former, term former and eliminator is strictly stable under substitution? The required universes classify the small Kan fibrations between cofibrant Kan complexes described below. Work in CZF with a sequence \((I_i)_{i\in\mathbb N}\) of constructive inaccessible sets, \(I_i\in I_{i+1}\), and the explicit small-subset principle \[\forall i\ \forall a,b\; (a\subseteq b\ \land\ b\in I_i\ \Rightarrow\ a\in I_i).\] Do not assume excluded middle or an axiom of choice. This is the full-model target selected by the user on 16 September2026; a univalent fibration with only weakly stable type operations is insufficient.

cards.why: Simplicial sets provide a standard geometric language for homotopy theory and classical univalent semantics. A constructive full model would connect that language with foundations that track how mathematical objects are built. The unresolved coherence and size issues determine whether partial semantic structures actually interpret dependent type-theoretic substitution and universes.

sentences: The question asks for a constructive simplicial interpretation of dependent type theory with univalent universes.
The selected metatheory is CZF with a sequence of constructive inaccessible sets and the explicit principle that every subset of a small set is small.
The model must interpret the stated dependent type formers and make all operations commute strictly with substitution.
Existing constructive simplicial work provides substantial weakly stable structure but leaves the strict coherence issue open in the checked sources.
A full construction would connect simplicial homotopy theory with constructive univalent foundations without importing excluded middle or choice.

cards.definitions:
The metatheory \(\mathsf S\) is intuitionistic first-order set theory CZF, together with the displayed sequence and small-subset axioms. CZF has Extensionality, Pairing, Union, Infinity, Set Induction, bounded Separation, Strong Collection and Subset Collection. Bounded Separation forms subsets using formulas whose quantifiers are all bounded by sets. Strong Collection says that if every \(x\in a\) has some \(y\) satisfying \(\varphi(x,y)\), there is a set \(b\) containing a witness for every such \(x\), with every element of \(b\) witnessing some \(x\in a\). Subset Collection can equivalently be given as Fullness: for sets \(a,b\), there is a set of total relations from \(a\) to \(b\) such that every total relation contains one in that set. A total relation from \(a\) to \(b\) is a subset of \(a\times b\) with a related element of \(b\) for each element of \(a\). Neither unrestricted Separation nor Power Set, excluded middle, countable choice or dependent choice is an additional axiom here. Ordinary consequences of the stated axioms remain available.

The word inaccessible uses the constructive set convention of Aczel–Rathjen. A set \(I\) is regular if it is inhabited and transitive, and whenever \(a\in I\) and \(R\subseteq a\times I\) is a total relation, there is a \(b\in I\) such that \[\forall x\in a\ \exists y\in b\ (xRy),\qquad\forall y\in b\ \exists x\in a\ (xRy).\] It is inaccessible if, in addition, \(\omega\in I\), it is closed under unions and under intersections of inhabited families that are elements of \(I\), and it satisfies internal Fullness: for every \(a,b\in I\), some \(C\in I\) is internally a full set of total relations from \(a\) to \(b\). Internally means that all quantifiers in this assertion are restricted to \(I\), using the inherited membership relation. Explicitly, its members are total subrelations of \(a\times b\), and each total relation \(R\in I\) contains one of them. This is a constructive inaccessible set, not a silently imported classical inaccessible cardinal. The whole sequence is supplied as one function on \(\omega\). A set is \(i\)-small if it belongs to \(I_i\). The small-subset principle quantifies over sets \(a\), not over arbitrary classes whose existence as sets is not given.

The simplex category \(\Delta\) has objects \([n]=\{0,\ldots,n\}\), \(n\ge0\), and order-preserving functions. A simplicial set is a functor \(\Delta^{\mathrm{op}}\to\mathsf{Set}\): sets \(X_n\) with restriction maps for every such function, satisfying identity and composition laws. Its morphisms are natural transformations. The standard simplex \(\Delta[n]\) has \(\Delta[n]_k=\operatorname{Hom}_{\Delta}([k],[n])\). The horn \(\Lambda^r[n]\subseteq\Delta[n]\), for \(n\ge1\) and \(0\le r\le n\), is the union of all codimension-one faces except the \(r\)-th. A Kan fibration \(p:E\to B\) has a specified diagonal filler for every commuting square with left map \(\Lambda^r[n]\hookrightarrow\Delta[n]\). A Kan complex is a simplicial set whose map to the one-point simplicial set has this structure. Existence of fillers cannot be converted to a chosen filler operation by unmentioned choice.

A simplex is degenerate if it is the image of a simplex in smaller dimension under a degeneracy map, corresponding to a nonidentity surjection in \(\Delta\). Cofibrant means that degeneracy of each simplex is decidable, the constructive Kan–Quillen cofibrancy condition for an object. A simplicial set is \(i\)-small if each \(X_n\in I_i\). A map is \(i\)-small if each degreewise fiber belongs to \(I_i\). These notions supply the universe sizes. Contexts are represented by cofibrant Kan complexes, substitutions by simplicial maps, dependent types by Kan fibrations with cofibrant total space, and terms by sections. Auxiliary data for chosen fillers, codes and coherent pullbacks are permitted; the underlying families must still be simplicial fibrations. The construction need not use one predetermined presentation of the partial model in the sources.

A full interpretation provides a category with families: for each context \(\Gamma\), types over \(\Gamma\), terms of those types, substitution actions, an empty context and context extension \(\Gamma.A\) with its projection and generic term. A section of \(\Gamma.A\to\Gamma\) represents a term. For every substitution \(\sigma:\Delta\to\Gamma\), the chosen interpretation of \(A[\sigma]\) and the associated square over \(\sigma\) realize pullback. Reindexing satisfies \(A[\mathrm{id}]=A\), \(A[\sigma][\tau]=A[\sigma\circ\tau]\), and the corresponding term equalities as equalities of chosen data, not merely through unspecified isomorphisms. Additional context-extension data may be used to achieve these equalities.

The object theory is intensional dependent type theory with empty and unit types, natural numbers, dependent functions \(\Pi\), dependent pairs \(\Sigma\) and identity types \(\mathsf{Id}_A(a,b)\). It has their formation, introduction and full dependent elimination rules, with judgmental beta computation for application, projections, natural-number recursion and identity elimination at reflexivity. The empty type has elimination into every type; the unit type has its usual dependent eliminator. Function and pair eta may be propositional; no judgmental eta rule is imposed as an extra target. There is no equality reflection or uniqueness-of-identity-proofs axiom. Empty, unit and natural-number types are interpreted by the corresponding discrete simplicial sets, with the usual distinct numerals and recursion. Identity types have the homotopy-theoretic path-object interpretation and the dependent identity eliminator; they are not interpreted using proof-irrelevant equality in the metatheory.

For each \(i\), a universe is a chosen fibration \(\widetilde U_i\to U_i\) with \(i\)-small fibers. It classifies \(i\)-small Kan fibrations between the specified cofibrant Kan complexes: each such family is, up to an isomorphism of families, a pullback along a code map into \(U_i\). Universes themselves have codes at the next level. Chosen inclusions of codes implement cumulativity and preserve their decoded families; there is no universe that contains itself. At every level, the universe contains codes for \(0,1,\mathbb N\) and is closed under the stated \(\Pi,\Sigma,\mathsf{Id}\) operations in arbitrary contexts, not just contexts made of small types.

Univalence requires that the canonical map from identity of two universe codes to equivalence of their decoded types is itself an equivalence. An equivalence is a function whose fibers are contractible; a type is contractible if it has a point and a path from that point to every other point. These are the internal type-theoretic notions, interpreted simplicially. All type constructors, terms, eliminators, universe codes, decoding operations and univalence witnesses must commute with substitution as equalities of the chosen interpretation. Their required judgmental computation rules must hold as equalities as well. Having operations that commute only up to isomorphism, homotopy or weak equivalence does not meet this strict stability condition.
cards.answer_criterion: Supply a complete Lean-checked construction and verification of this full simplicial interpretation using only the specified constructive metatheory and size axioms, or a complete Lean-checked impossibility theorem for that target. The formalization must make the metatheoretic assumptions explicit: either represent derivations in \(\mathsf S\), or give an interpretation parametrized by a model of \(\mathsf S\) whose construction uses exactly its permitted reasoning. Lean's ambient classical choice or excluded middle cannot silently prove a step required internally in \(\mathsf S\). A positive answer must verify all universe, substitution and computation conditions, including arbitrary-context dependent-product closure. A weakly stable comprehension category, an isolated univalent classifying fibration, a classical simplicial model or a constructive model solely in cubical sets is insufficient. A negative answer must concern the full allowed simplicial target, not merely show that one existing coherence construction fails. No additional higher inductive types or normalization theorem is requested.

context_blocks.text: The historical source asks broadly for a constructive simplicial model with univalent universes. On 16 September2026 the user selected CZF with a sequence of constructive inaccessible sets, the small-subset principle and a full strictly substitution-stable interpretation. This makes the metatheory and model requirements explicit; it does not replace the question by one theorem about a particular existing construction.

Gambino–Henry construct identity, sum, product and basic inductive type structure and a univalent universe in a comprehension category of cofibrant simplicial sets. Their Theorem8.1 labels the stability of these operations separately: some are pseudo-stable, products are weakly stable and identity elimination has a remaining stability qualification.

Remark8.5 leaves the passage to a strict model open. The standard cited coherence theorem has a hypothesis that fails in their constructive setting because cofibrant objects need not be closed under categorical dependent products. This is a limitation of that available coherence argument, not a theorem excluding every full constructive simplicial model.

The partial construction explicitly uses the additional principle that subsets of small sets are small when establishing universe closure under arbitrary dependent products. Remark8.3 gives weaker alternatives without it. The selected target allows this principle and therefore should not be described as the stronger no-resizing problem.

The 2026 equivariant cubical-model paper still describes the strictness gap in the constructive simplicial account. It separately discusses effective Kan fibrations, whose required universes and complete interpretation are not established in that comparison. Its own cubical construction has a different underlying category.

The 2025 presentation and May2026 higher-sheaf preprint describe constructive cubical developments and a base construction announced as forthcoming. They do not by themselves provide a checked strict interpretation with the specified simplicial families and size assumptions.

Constructive inaccessible sets are regular sets with additional closure and internal Fullness properties. Giving this definition matters because a classical inaccessible cardinal imports a different background theory. The separate small-subset axiom is recorded independently rather than being hidden inside the word inaccessible.

cards.title: Exponential witness bounds for three-dimensional VASS
cards.formal: Do there exist constants \(C,d\in\mathbb N\), with \(C,d\ge1\), such that every reachable instance \(I=(V,s,t)\) of a three-dimensional vector addition system with states has a legal run from \(s\) to \(t\) of length at most \[2^{C(L(I)+1)^d}?\] Here \(L(I)\) is the binary description size defined below, including the finite control graph, all transition updates, and both configurations. The constants must be independent of the instance. The target is the length of an actual sequence of transitions, not the size of a compressed representation of that sequence.

source_formulation.text: For binary three-dimensional vector addition systems with states, does every reachable source–target pair admit a run of at most exponential length in the input description?
source_formulation.caption: Editorial paraphrase; corrected VAS/VASS model from the source

cards.why: Exact reachability in counter systems is decidable, but the length of the necessary witness can be vastly larger than the finite description. Dimension three is the first unresolved step beyond the exponential-witness theorem for binary two-counter systems. A positive result would yield a PSPACE upper bound for three-dimensional reachability and expose a strong structural limit on how much counter behavior finite control can force.
cards.status_note: Source-open in CONCUR 2022, §3. The published ICALP 2025 theorem gives triply-exponential witnesses, and the 16 July 2026 preprint claims doubly-exponential witnesses; neither establishes or refutes the single-exponential bound. The August 2026 PSPACE result is for stateless VAS. Bounded later-work checking on 16 September 2026 found no matching resolution. Preprint proofs were not independently verified.

cards.definitions: Write \(\mathbb N=\{0,1,2,\ldots\}\). A three-dimensional VASS is \(V=(Q,T)\), where \(Q=\{0,\ldots,q-1\}\) for an input integer \(q\ge1\), and \(T\) is a finite explicitly listed set of transitions \((p,a,r)\in Q\times\mathbb Z^3\times Q\). A configuration is \((p,x)\in Q\times\mathbb N^3\). The transition \((p,a,r)\) sends \((p,x)\) to \((r,x+a)\) exactly when all three coordinates of \(x+a\) are nonnegative. Counters have no fixed upper bound and no extra zero tests. Input configurations \(s=(p_s,x_s)\) and \(t=(p_t,x_t)\) must be matched exactly, in both state and counter values. A legal run of length \(h\) is a sequence of \(h\) enabled transitions whose consecutive configurations all have nonnegative counters; \(h=0\) is allowed when \(s=t\). Reachable means that at least one finite such run exists. For a completely specified size measure let \(\ell(z)=1+\lceil\log_2(|z|+1)\rceil\) for \(z\in\mathbb Z\), and define \[L(I)=q+|T|+\ell(p_s)+\ell(p_t)+\sum_{j=1}^{3}\bigl(\ell((x_s)_j)+\ell((x_t)_j)\bigr)+\sum_{(p,a,r)\in T}\left(\ell(p)+\ell(r)+\sum_{j=1}^{3}\ell(a_j)\right).\] This counts an explicit state list and signed binary numerical data; separators change it by at most a constant factor. It is polynomially equivalent to ordinary explicit binary encodings. Exactly three counters are fixed, but the number of states and transitions and all numerical magnitudes are unrestricted. The question is a uniform combinatorial bound; it requests no randomized guarantee, average over inputs, approximate target, or construction-time bound.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof or refutation of the displayed uniform single-exponential bound. An affirmative proof must supply some fixed \(C,d\ge1\) and prove a sufficiently short actual run for every reachable instance. A refutation must prove \[\forall C,d\ge1\ \exists I\text{ reachable},\quad\text{every run from }s\text{ to }t\text{ has length }>2^{C(L(I)+1)^d}.\] One long instance only refutes a particular proposed bound. A decision procedure or succinct witness representation alone is insufficient unless its proof establishes the required bound on actual run length.

context_blocks.text: A transition adds a fixed integer vector, but it is enabled only if no counter becomes negative. The finite control graph determines which additions can follow which. Reaching a configuration with larger counters is not enough: the target includes exact counter values and a specified control state.

The source paragraph is explicitly about binary 3-VASS. The imported title abbreviated this as VAS, which would ordinarily remove the control states and change the fixed-dimensional problem. The revised title restores the model actually used by the source; it does not substitute the stateless variant.

For binary two-dimensional VASS, reachability is PSPACE-complete and every reachable pair has an exponentially bounded witness. The source asks whether this actual-run guarantee survives with three counters. It presents this as a witness-length question alongside, rather than identical to, the broader question of exact decision complexity.

The ICALP 2025 theorem provides the first elementary bound for three-dimensional VASS: reachable configurations have a run of at most triply-exponential length, yielding a doubly-exponential-space algorithm. This substantially improves the older non-elementary upper bounds but permits witnesses far larger than the single exponential asked for here.

The July 2026 preprint claims an EXPSPACE algorithm and a doubly-exponential bound on the shortest run. Its parameterized bound uses the number of strongly connected components and a numerical size convention, with the stated conclusion covering binary encoding as well. Even if all arguments are accepted, this remains a weaker upper bound than the present target.

The August 2026 preprint settles PSPACE-completeness for stateless three-dimensional VAS. A VAS lacks the arbitrary control graph allowed here; encoding that graph can require extra counters. Consequently the fixed-dimension result cannot be imported as a solution to this three-counter VASS question.

cards.title: Exact multi-objective LTL achievability in stochastic games
cards.formal: Is exact multi-objective probabilistic LTL achievability decidable for finite full-observation turn-based stochastic games? Given such a rational game \(G\) with initial state \(s_0\), a finite list of LTL formulas \(\varphi_1,\ldots,\varphi_m\), and rational thresholds \(p_i\in[0,1]\), decide whether \[\exists\sigma\ \forall\tau\ \forall i\in\{1,\ldots,m\}:\quad \Pr_{G,s_0}^{\sigma,\tau}(\varphi_i)\ge p_i.\] Both players may use arbitrary randomized strategies with unbounded history dependence. One deterministic algorithm must halt with the exact answer on every input. This is the decision target selected by the user on 16 September 2026 from the source's broader synthesis question.
cards.why: A controller often has several probabilistic requirements, such as reliability and eventual response, that must hold under the same policy against an adversarial environment. Exact achievability asks whether the stated requirements can all be guaranteed, including boundary thresholds that approximation alone may not decide. It is a central decision component of quantitative synthesis for stochastic systems.

The user selected the exact achievability decision subproblem on 16 September 2026, retaining arbitrary randomized history strategies. The checked AAMAS 2026 result handles qualitative reachability/safety fragments and does not resolve general rational-threshold LTL. No matching resolution was found in the bounded later-source check; source-open refers to the underlying dated programme, not independent certification of this explicitly selected variant.

cards.definitions:
The finite state set \(S\) is partitioned into controller states \(S_1\), adversary states \(S_2\), and chance states \(S_c\), with a designated \(s_0\in S\). At a player state \(s\), a nonempty finite set \(E(s)\subseteq S\) lists the legal next states. At a chance state \(s\), the table \(P(s,t)\in\mathbb Q_{\ge0}\) sums to one over \(t\in S\). A play starts at \(s_0\) and continues forever: its owner chooses a legal successor at a player state, and a successor is sampled from \(P(s,\cdot)\) at a chance state. Terminal behavior is represented by a self-loop. There is no stopping, acyclicity, finite-horizon, partial-observation or bounded-memory promise. A finite set \(AP\) of atomic propositions and a labelling \(\ell:S\to2^{AP}\) are supplied. All state partitions, edges, labels and rational probabilities are explicit finite tables; indices and rational numerators/positive denominators are binary encoded.

A controller strategy assigns to each finite legal state history ending in \(S_1\) a probability distribution on that last state's legal successors; adversary strategies are defined symmetrically for \(S_2\). Both players observe the complete state history. Distribution values may be arbitrary real numbers, and dependence on the entire finite history is unrestricted. Strategies are abstract mathematical functions: the quantifiers impose no rationality, computability or finite-memory requirement on them. The same controller strategy must meet all objectives against every adversary. The decision algorithm receives only the finite game, formulas and thresholds; a strategy is not an input or a required output. For a fixed pair of strategies, cylinder probabilities are the products of the corresponding transition probabilities along finite histories, defining the usual probability measure on infinite plays.

An LTL formula has finite syntax \(\varphi::=\top\mid a\mid\neg\varphi\mid(\varphi\land\varphi)\mid X\varphi\mid(\varphi U\varphi)\), for \(a\in AP\). It is interpreted on the infinite label sequence of the play, from position zero. An atom holds at position \(j\) if it belongs to \(\ell(s_j)\); Boolean connectives have their ordinary meaning; \(X\varphi\) holds at \(j\) if \(\varphi\) holds at \(j+1\); and \(\varphi U\psi\) holds at \(j\) if some finite \(k\ge j\) satisfies \(\psi\) and every position from \(j\) through \(k-1\) satisfies \(\varphi\). Thus until is strong, not weak. These events are measurable. Formula trees and the finite objective list are explicit input; their sizes are unbounded. The empty list, if supplied, is vacuously achievable.

Each displayed threshold is non-strict. An upper bound \(\Pr(\varphi)\le p\) can be represented as the lower bound \(\Pr(\neg\varphi)\ge1-p\), so these upper bounds require no separate semantic convention. Achievability means an actual strategy attaining all bounds, not membership in the closure of achievable vectors or existence of a different strategy for every positive tolerance. The sought machine is uniform, has no oracle or advice, uses ordinary exact finite computation and may take any finite running time. Its YES/NO output has no random error or numerical tolerance. A malformed encoding may be rejected.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean proof of a total computable exact decision procedure for the displayed predicate, or prove that no such procedure exists. The positive proof must formalize finite rational games, full-history real-valued strategy quantifiers, the induced play measure, LTL semantics, termination and both answer directions. A negative proof must preserve this complete-observation turn-based finite rational class and allow the stated randomized strategies. Deciding only pure or finite-memory strategies, qualitative thresholds, stopping games, approximate Pareto membership or limit-sure achievability does not settle the target. A decision answer is sufficient for the selected scope; computing an effective strategy witness is a separate synthesis requirement not selected here. This review supplies no Lean proof of a resolution.

Different requirements can conflict because the controller must use one policy. Solving each scalar objective using its own optimal strategy does not establish simultaneous achievability. The quantifier order puts that shared policy before the universally quantified adversary.

The 2016 overview separates verification, strategy synthesis and approximation. Approximation can identify vectors close to the achievable region while leaving exact boundary membership unresolved. The selected non-strict inequalities require actual attainment; replacing every threshold by a slightly easier one and using different strategies would answer a different question.

Graf–Lin–Majumdar establish PSPACE-completeness for conjunctions of almost-sure and nonzero reachability/safety requirements and other qualitative fragments. cards.title: Effective homotopy canonicity with propositional resizing
cards.formal: Does the fixed univalent De Morgan cubical type theory \(\mathsf T_R\) defined below, with individual propositional resizing between adjacent universe levels, satisfy both consistency and effective homotopy canonicity? For each \(i\ge0\), add the scheme \[R_i:\prod_{P:\mathcal U_{i+1}}\mathsf{isProp}(P)\to\sum_{Q:\mathcal U_i}(Q\simeq P).\] Require one ordinary computable algorithm which, from any finite derivation of a closed judgment \(\vdash t:\mathbb N\) in \(\mathsf T_R\), halts and returns a numeral \(\overline k\) and a checked object-theory derivation of \[\vdash e:\mathsf{Path}_{\mathbb N}(t,\overline k).\] Consistency here includes that there is no closed derivation of \(\mathsf{Path}_{\mathbb N}(0,\mathsf s0)\). The selected requirement is effective equality to a numeral, with no additional request for judgmental normalization of all terms.

sentences: The selected question adds individual propositional resizing to a fixed univalent De Morgan cubical calculus.
Each homotopy proposition in one universe must have an equivalent representative in the adjacent smaller universe.
The requested result combines consistency with an algorithm that turns every closed natural-number derivation into a numeral and an object-theory path proof.

cards.definitions:
The base is the Cohen–Coquand–Huber–Mörtberg (CCHM) De Morgan cubical calculus, fixing the core syntax and judgmental computation rules of the cited7 November2016 version, §§2–7 and AppendixA, stratified over universe levels \(i\in\mathbb N\). Optional higher inductive types from its §9 are not included. The following conventions identify the object theory and its size/computation choices explicitly. Contexts contain typed term variables, interval names and face restrictions. There are dependent function types \(\prod_{x:A}B(x)\), dependent pair types \(\sum_{x:A}B(x)\), natural numbers with zero, successor and dependent recursion, dependent path types, cubical composition, Glue types and a cumulative Russell universe tower \(\mathcal U_i:\mathcal U_{i+1}\). A term \(A:\mathcal U_i\) is itself a type, with inclusion into higher levels. Each constructor is formed at the maximum universe level of its type arguments; the constructors and their computation rules are the same at every level. No universe contains itself.

Interval expressions are the finite terms freely generated by interval names, endpoints \(0,1\), meet, join and involution \(r\mapsto1-r\), modulo the bounded distributive lattice and De Morgan identities. They are not Boolean: \(r\lor(1-r)=1\) and \(r\land(1-r)=0\) are not added. Face formulas form the distributive lattice generated by equations \((i=0)\), \((i=1)\), with \((i=0)\land(i=1)\) false. A system is a finite collection of terms on faces covering a context, agreeing where faces overlap; on each face it computes to its indicated term. Substitution acts on term variables and interval expressions and preserves the face restrictions.

For a type family \(i:\mathbb I\vdash A(i)\), a dependent path with endpoints \(a_0:A(0)\) and \(a_1:A(1)\) is represented by an interval abstraction \(\langle i\rangle u\) with those boundary values; it can be applied at any interval expression. Path abstraction/application obey beta and eta, and application at an endpoint gives that endpoint. Write \(\mathsf{Path}_A(a,b)\) for the constant-family case. Composition \(\mathsf{comp}^i A[\varphi\mapsto u]a_0\) takes a partial line \(u\) on a face \(\varphi\) and a compatible starting point \(a_0:A(0)\), and produces an endpoint in \(A(1)\) agreeing with \(u(1)\) on that face. The fixed CCHM computation rules for composition on functions, pairs, natural numbers, paths, Glue types and universes are part of the base theory; they are not a variable to choose in an answer. Functions and pairs have their ordinary beta/eta conversions, and natural-number recursion has its zero and successor equations. Conversion is generated by these rules and congruence, not by reflection of arbitrary path proofs.

A Glue type \(\mathsf{Glue}[\varphi\mapsto(T,f)]A\) identifies a type \(A\) with a type \(T\) on a face, using an equivalence \(f:T\simeq A\) there. It has the CCHM glue/unglue introduction and elimination operations and their boundary/composition equations. Univalence in the base theory is the theorem that the canonical map from paths between universe elements to equivalences of the corresponding types is an equivalence. Paths therefore represent homotopical identity, rather than proof-irrelevant or extensional equality. There is no equality reflection, uniqueness-of-identity-proofs axiom, excluded-middle axiom or choice axiom in the object calculus.

For any type \(P\), define \[\mathsf{isProp}(P)=\prod_{x:P}\prod_{y:P}\mathsf{Path}_P(x,y).\] Such a type has at most one point up to homotopical identity; it can also be empty. Define \[\mathsf{isContr}(A)=\sum_{a:A}\prod_{x:A}\mathsf{Path}_A(a,x).\] For \(f:A\to B\), its fiber over \(b:B\) is \(\sum_{a:A}\mathsf{Path}_B(f(a),b)\); the assertion that \(f\) is an equivalence says every such fiber is contractible. The type \(A\simeq B\) consists of a function with this equivalence witness. These definitions are internal to the object calculus and use its paths.

The extension \(\mathsf T_R\) adds exactly the displayed typed constants \(R_i\), one at every adjacent universe pair, with their ordinary substitution instances. Applying \(R_i\) to a proposition and a witness of \(\mathsf{isProp}\) returns a smaller type together with an equivalence. That smaller type is then a proposition as a consequence of the equivalence. No judgmental equation for \(R_i\) is postulated. Thus the selected theorem is about effective homotopy canonicity of this fixed axiomatic extension; it does not presuppose a particular reduction rule for resizing or strengthen the requirement to judgmental canonicity. The scheme applies in arbitrary contexts, not only to closed propositions, and can be iterated across finitely many universe levels. It does not add an axiom that \[\Omega_i=\sum_{P:\mathcal U_i}\mathsf{isProp}(P)\] itself has size \(\mathcal U_i\); that is the separate whole-universe impredicativity principle distinguished by the source.

Finite syntax, universe indices, binders, systems and derivation trees have an ordinary explicit finite encoding; alpha-renaming does not change the mathematical judgments. Closed means that no free term variable or interval name remains. The numeral \(\overline k\) is \(\mathsf s^k0\). The required algorithm is a deterministic Turing-computable procedure with no oracle or advice. It receives the entire term and a finite derivation of its closed natural-number type. It returns \(k\), a finite term \(e\) and a finite derivation of the displayed path judgment in this same \(\mathsf T_R\), including any permitted resizing constants it uses. Its guarantee is for every valid input derivation and every finite universe level used in it. There is no time or output-length bound beyond termination; malformed inputs have no required mathematical output. A semantic equality unaccompanied by the required object-theory certificate is not the requested output.

Consistency is a separate requirement because an inconsistent calculus could manufacture arbitrary equality certificates. Specifically there must be no closed term identifying zero with its successor in the natural-number type; this is the usual numeral-separation test for this dependent calculus. Native Lean propositions, proof irrelevance or classical choice must not be substituted for the represented object-theory propositions, path judgments or computational procedure. Lean serves to check the metatheorem and the algorithm's guarantees.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof that the specified extension is consistent and admits the stated terminating numeral-and-path-certificate algorithm, or a complete Lean-checked refutation of this conjunction. A positive answer must supply a computable procedure and prove its termination and correctness for all closed natural-number derivations, including those using resizing at arbitrary finite levels. Consistency alone, existence of a classical semantic model, an unevaluated resizing postulate, or a canonicity theorem only for the base calculus is insufficient. A refutation must concern this resizing scheme and this effective homotopy requirement; showing that a particular reduction strategy gets stuck or that judgmental canonicity fails does not by itself refute it. No normalization theorem for all terms and no smallness axiom for the entire \(\Omega_i\) is additionally required. This is an exact existence question, not a numerical-value benchmark.

cards.title: Decidability of weak bisimulation for normed BPA
cards.formal: Is there a deterministic Turing machine that, given any finite normed Basic Process Algebra system \(\Gamma\) and two finite process words \(\alpha,\beta\), always halts and decides whether \(\alpha\) and \(\beta\) are weakly bisimilar in the transition system generated by \(\Gamma\)? The equivalence is divergence-insensitive weak bisimilarity, with arbitrary finite sequences of silent transitions allowed before and after an observable transition, as defined below.

source_formulation.text: We do not know if the weak bisimilarity is decidable or not even for normed BPA.
source_formulation.caption: Complete selected source sentence; PDF p. 1

cards.why: Weak bisimilarity expresses that two recursive sequential systems can match every observable interaction while hiding internal computation. Normed BPA is a particularly small infinite-state model: a finite collection of rewrite rules acts on a sequential stack of variables, each able to terminate. Resolving this question would determine whether invisible computation alone defeats exact behavioral comparison in that model, beyond the related equivalences already known to be decidable.
cards.status_note: Source-open in CONCUR 2017 and explicitly retained in Jančar’s LMCS article published 28 November 2017. Fu’s positive theorem concerns branching bisimilarity; the 2007 tableau theorem concerns totally normed weak bisimilarity. A bounded later-work search on 16 September 2026 found no matching resolution for divergence-insensitive weak bisimilarity on arbitrary normed BPA. This is not an exhaustive current-status certification, and cited proofs were not independently formalized.

progress.text: Liu and Chen give a tableau decision result for totally normed context-free processes; the publisher abstract makes the narrower class explicit despite the title.

The CONCUR paper proves the EXPTIME-hardness of branching bisimilarity, completing its known EXPTIME classification, and records EXPTIME-hardness but unresolved decidability for weak bisimilarity.
Jančar’s LMCS article explicitly states that weak bisimilarity remains open for BPA and for normed BPA; its positive finite-transducer results concern branching bisimilarity.

importance.reason: A central longstanding decidability question for behavioral equivalence in infinite-state verification. Normed BPA removes parallelism and finite control while retaining recursive sequential behavior and arbitrary silent moves; the boundary with decidable branching equivalence is fundamental.
