sentences: Basic Process Algebra represents recursive sequential processes by finite words whose leftmost variable is rewritten using a finite rule system.
Normedness requires each variable to have some terminating execution and permits both silent termination and silent divergence.
The question asks whether weak bisimilarity of two such processes is decidable when finite silent paths may surround every matched visible action.
Known decision procedures for branching bisimilarity or totally normed subclasses do not cover the full weak equivalence defined here.
A resolution would locate the algorithmic limit of hiding internal computation during exact comparison of simple infinite-state processes.

cards.definitions:
A BPA system \(\Gamma=(V,A,\Delta)\) has a finite set \(V\) of process variables, a finite set \(A\) of action labels containing a distinguished silent label \(\tau\), and a finite set of rules \(X\xrightarrow{a}\gamma\), where \(X\in V\), \(a\in A\) and \(\gamma\in V^*\). A process is a finite word in \(V^*\); the empty word \(\varepsilon\) denotes termination. Only the leftmost variable acts: every rule gives \(X\delta\xrightarrow{a}\gamma\delta\) for every suffix \(\delta\in V^*\), and these are all transitions. In particular, \(\varepsilon\) has none. There is no additional finite control state or parallel composition. The system is normed when for every \(X\in V\) there exists a finite transition sequence \(X\xrightarrow{a_1}\cdots\xrightarrow{a_m}\varepsilon\), with the labels allowed to include \(\tau\). This is existence of a terminating execution, not termination of every execution. A variable may disappear using only silent actions and may also have infinite silent executions.

Write \(u\Rightarrow v\) if zero or more \(\tau\)-transitions take \(u\) to \(v\). For \(a\ne\tau\), write \(u\mathrel{\Rightarrow_a}v\) if there exist \(u',v'\) with \(u\Rightarrow u'\xrightarrow{a}v'\Rightarrow v\). Set \(\Rightarrow_\tau=\Rightarrow\). A symmetric relation \(R\subseteq V^*\times V^*\) is a weak bisimulation if \[uRv\ \land\ u\xrightarrow{a}u'\quad\Longrightarrow\quad \exists v'\in V^*,\quad v\mathrel{\Rightarrow_a}v'\ \land\ u'Rv'\] for every related pair and every transition. The symmetry imposes the same requirement for moves from either process. Define \(\alpha\approx\beta\) when some such \(R\) contains \((\alpha,\beta)\). Intermediate states in a matching weak transition need not stay related to the source state. No extra requirement preserves infinite silent divergence, and termination has no separate observable label. All rule right-hand sides and the two initial words are explicitly listed, using binary indices for variables and actions with delimiters; no compressed words or numeric repetition operators occur. The finite rule system is input, not fixed in advance. Normedness is an input promise that can itself be checked effectively; malformed or nonnormed inputs may be rejected. One machine must cover all valid inputs and give the exact Boolean answer, without approximation, random error or a prescribed time bound.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked decidability or undecidability proof for the specified recognition problem. A positive result must provide one effective total algorithm and prove it correct for arbitrary finite normed systems and initial words. A negative result must rule out every total computable decider on this normed input class. Decidability of branching or strong bisimilarity, or of weak bisimilarity only when variables cannot terminate silently, is insufficient. Undecidability after adding control states or parallel composition does not settle the BPA problem above.

context_blocks.text: A process word records tasks still to execute in order. Rewriting its leftmost variable can replace that task by several new ones, producing unbounded stack-like behavior from a finite rule set. Later variables cannot act until the prefix has disappeared. This sequential convention distinguishes BPA from the commutative or parallel model BPP.

Normedness is permissive about internal behavior. For example, rules \(X\xrightarrow{\tau}X\) and \(X\xrightarrow{\tau}\varepsilon\) make \(X\) normed, since termination is possible, even though it can silently loop forever. Under the divergence-insensitive definition above, this \(X\) is weakly bisimilar to \(\varepsilon\). A requirement to preserve silent divergence would ask a different equivalence question.

Weak bisimulation compares branching responses in both directions, rather than merely comparing the sets of complete action traces. However, it can hide internal states traversed while matching a visible move. Branching bisimulation adds a constraint that preserves the relevant branching point during such internal movement, so its decidability is not an algorithm for this coarser weak equivalence.

Fu’s 2013 theorem decides branching bisimilarity on normed BPA. Subsequent work gives an EXPTIME upper bound, and the source paper establishes the matching branching lower bound. The same source explicitly reports weak bisimilarity as undecided, with an EXPTIME-hardness lower bound but no decision procedure. The different equivalences must not be conflated.

The title of the 2007 tableau paper can look like a solution of this card, but its abstract states a result for totally normed processes. In that subclass no nonempty variable can disappear through silent transitions alone. The present normed input class permits exactly that behavior, and neither that earlier result nor the later branching theorem covers it.

Jančar’s journal paper, published after the source conference paper, again explicitly retains weak bisimilarity on normed BPA as open while developing branching-bisimilarity structure. The bounded later-work search performed for this review did not locate a matching resolution, and is recorded separately from the correctness of the finite input model.

cards.title: Unconditional decidability of exact time-bounded CTMDP reachability
cards.formal: Is there an unconditional terminating algorithm that, for every finite rational-rate continuous-time Markov decision process with an absorbing state \(\mathrm{good}\), rational deadline \(T>0\) and rational threshold vector \(r\), decides whether \[\forall s\in\{1,\ldots,n\},\quad \sup_{\pi\in\Pi_T}\Pr_s^\pi[\text{reach }\mathrm{good}\text{ by time }T]>r_s,\] where \(\Pi_T\) consists of the measurable timed positional policies defined below?
cards.definitions: The input lists a finite state set \(S=\{1,\ldots,n\}\sqcup\{\mathrm{good}\}\), with \(n\ge1\); a nonempty finite action set \(A_{s}\) for each state; nonnegative rational rates \(q(s,a,t)\) for \(t\ne s\); \(T\in\mathbb{Q}_{>0}\); and \(r\in([0,1]\cap\mathbb{Q})^{n}\). Integers and rational numerators/positive denominators are binary encoded. All rates out of good are zero, and the diagonal generator entry is \(q(s,a,s)=- \sum_{t\ne s}q(s,a,t)\). A decision vector d chooses one action \(d(s)\in A_{s}\) at each state. A policy is a Lebesgue-measurable map \(\pi :[0,T]\to \prod _{s} A_{s}\): at elapsed time u in state s the instantaneous generator row is \(q(s,\pi (u)(s),\cdot )\). Actions may change while the process remains in the same state, not only at jumps. Policies are deterministic and may depend on time and current state, with no computability restriction. For a fixed policy and initial state s, its probability law is the finite-state inhomogeneous Markov jump law with this bounded measurable generator. Equivalently its row distribution \(\rho _{s}(u)\) is the unique absolutely continuous solution of \(\rho _{s}(0)=e_{s}\) and \(\rho _{s}' (u)=\rho _{s}(u)Q^{\pi (u)}\) for almost every u. Bounded rates ensure nonexplosion. Since good is absorbing, the probability of reaching it at some time in \([0,T]\) equals \(\rho _{s}(T)_{\mathrm{good}}\). The supremum is taken over all such policies separately for each initial state. This defines the value without an attainment assumption; the source also proves existence of an optimal piecewise-constant timed positional policy. The decision uses strict > in every coordinate, so equality to any threshold requires NO. The algorithm is a deterministic Turing machine that halts with the correct YES/NO result on every valid encoding; there is no requested complexity bound and no number-theoretic oracle or unproved premise. Invalid encodings may be rejected.

context_blocks.text: A continuous-time decision process combines random event times with choices that can vary with elapsed time. The question concerns exact comparison of the best probability of reaching a target before a deadline.

Majumdar, Salamati and Soudjani define the strict vector-threshold question and prove its decidability assuming Schanuel’s conjecture. Their result does not give an unconditional decision procedure, and numerical approximation alone does not decide equality at the threshold.

cards.title: Inductive-inductive types from inductive types without UIP
cards.formal: In the intensional Martin-Löf type theory \(\mathsf T\) specified below, can every finitary inductive-inductive signature be implemented using the existing type formers, with its full dependent eliminator and propositional constructor computation equations? More precisely, is there a uniform effective derived-rule construction which, for every finite well-formed signature \(S\), every well-formed external parameter context and every permitted universe instance, produces the sorts and constructors of an \(S\)-algebra \(A_S\) and, for every displayed \(S\)-algebra \(D\) over \(A_S\), a section of \(D\) with a proof of each constructor equation? All these terms and proofs must be derivable in \(\mathsf T\). This is the user-selected intensional specialization, approved on 16 September 2026, of the source's broader question about a UIP-free setting; it does not ask to settle every possible UIP-free foundation.
cards.why: Inductive-inductive definitions express dependent syntax directly, including contexts and the types valid in each context. A generic reduction would identify which primitives a proof assistant needs to support such syntax while retaining identity types with higher structure. The issue concerns expressive power and dependent elimination, not merely implementation convenience: an encoding can supply all the apparent constructors yet lose the induction principle needed to use the data.

cards.definitions:
Base theory. \(\mathsf T\) is intensional Martin-Löf type theory with the cumulative predicative hierarchy \(\mathcal U_0:\mathcal U_1:\cdots\), dependent products \(\Pi\), dependent sums \(\Sigma\), the unit type, natural numbers, intensional identity types with reflexivity and the dependent identity eliminator \(J\), indexed W-types, and dependent function extensionality. The ordinary introductions, dependent eliminators and their judgmental beta rules are available; equality reflection and UIP are not rules or axioms. Function extensionality says that pointwise identity of dependent functions yields their identity. There is no additional univalence, cubical composition, quotient, higher inductive or inductive-inductive primitive. An indexed W-type is the well-founded tree family \(W:I\to\mathcal U_i\) for small data \(I\), shapes \(A(i)\), positions \(B(i,a)\) and child index \(s(i,a,b)\), with constructors \(\mathsf{sup}_i(a,f):W(i)\) for \(f:\prod_{b:B(i,a)}W(s(i,a,b))\), and its full dependent tree eliminator. Finite auxiliary universe increases in an encoding must be explicitly supplied and justified within this hierarchy; no resizing or impredicative universe is granted.

Signatures. A signature is a finite telescope of declarations in an external context. Its signature types are generated by a sort-code type \(U\), decoding \(\mathsf{El}(a)\) for a signature term \(a:U\), and dependent products \((x:\mathsf{El}(a))\to B\) and \((x:T)\to B\). In the first product, \(a\) is a sort code and \(B\) is again a signature type. In the second, \(T\) is a type of the external base theory, independent of the sorts being constructed; external types and families may depend on external parameters and are not assumed to have UIP. Terms of the signature language are declared variables, their well-typed applications and substitutions. The external expressions are finite base-theory expressions, with free parameters allowed. There is no signature identity-type former, equality constructor, lambda abstraction over inductive arguments, or function-valued recursive argument. Products bind individual recursive elements; each constructor has finitely many recursive arguments. A declaration ending in \(U\) introduces a sort or a family of sorts; one ending in \(\mathsf{El}(a)\) introduces a constructor. Later declarations may refer to earlier sort and constructor declarations. Universe levels are ordinary natural-number levels; all sorts, external types and motives are assigned levels admitted by the cumulative hierarchy. The construction is a derived-rule schema over all such level instances, with no requirement that its intermediate encoding live in the least available universe.

Algebras and dependent elimination. An algebra interprets each sort as a type or indexed family and each constructor as a term of its declared type. A displayed algebra supplies, over every interpreted sort element, a motive type; this type may also depend on the displayed elements of all earlier indices. For each constructor it supplies a method returning the corresponding motive, given the constructor arguments and displayed arguments for every recursive element. External arguments are passed unchanged. The displayed translation follows the telescope in order: duplicate each inductive argument by its motive inhabitant, substitute both components in later dependent declarations, and interpret a sort code as a family over its interpreted type. A section supplies an eliminator for every sort, into its motive, using the earlier eliminators for displayed indices; for each constructor, applying the eliminator to that constructor must equal its supplied method applied to the arguments and their recursive images. These equations are identity-type inhabitants in \(\mathsf T\), with the transports required by the dependent types. They need not hold by judgmental reduction.

For example, for \(\mathsf{Con}:\mathcal U_i\) and \(\mathsf{Ty}:\mathsf{Con}\to\mathcal U_i\), full motives have types \(P:\mathsf{Con}\to\mathcal U_j\) and \(Q:\prod_{\Gamma:\mathsf{Con}}P(\Gamma)\to\mathsf{Ty}(\Gamma)\to\mathcal U_j\). The required eliminators have types \(e_C:\prod_\Gamma P(\Gamma)\) and \(e_T:\prod_\Gamma\prod_{A:\mathsf{Ty}(\Gamma)}Q(\Gamma,e_C(\Gamma),A)\). Omitting the \(P(\Gamma)\) argument of \(Q\) gives a weaker principle. UIP would assert \(\prod_{X:\mathcal U_i}\prod_{x,y:X}\prod_{p,q:\mathsf{Id}_X(x,y)}\mathsf{Id}(p,q)\); it must not be smuggled in by requiring all external types to be sets.

Effectiveness means one terminating procedure on finite encodings of well-formed signature and base-theory derivations, producing finite terms and typing/equation derivations, uniformly in the open external context. Substitution of external parameters must yield valid instances of the construction. There is no time, space or output-size bound. This is an exact existence-of-construction question, not a numerical approximation problem.
cards.answer_criterion: An accepted answer is a complete Lean proof of the existence of the uniform derived-rule construction just specified, or of its negation. A positive answer must represent the object theory \(\mathsf T\), its signature syntax and permitted derivations, and verify the generated sort/constructor terms, full dependent eliminators, transports and propositional beta proofs for all signatures and universe instances. A suitably formalized semantic argument qualifies if it establishes that exact derived-rule conclusion; a construction in one stronger model alone does not. A negative answer must rule out the stated uniform construction; proving that one proposed encoding uses UIP is insufficient. A model of the stated base theory in which an allowed signature has no required implementation can establish a negative answer if the relevant soundness implication is proved. Lean's native equality lies in its proof-irrelevant proposition sort and cannot stand in for the object theory's possibly higher identity types: represent the latter as syntax or semantic type data, and check that neither UIP nor equality reflection enters the object derivations. This editorial completion does not itself provide a Lean formalization.

source_formulation.text: Can finitary inductive-inductive types, including their full dependent elimination principles, be reduced to inductive types in a foundation without UIP?
source_formulation.caption: Editorial paraphrase of the source question; the card selects the explicitly approved intensional MLTT variant

context_blocks.text: An inductive-inductive declaration defines several sorts together, allowing a later sort to be indexed by an earlier one. Contexts and context-indexed types are a basic example: a context constructor can consume a type over that context, so the two constructions are mutually dependent.

The source gives a generic reduction of finitary IITs to indexed W-types in an extensional setting. cards.title: One-dimensional piecewise-affine reachability
cards.formal: Is there a deterministic Turing machine that always halts and decides, given a one-dimensional rational piecewise-affine map \(f:[0,1]\to[0,1]\) and rational points \(s,t\in[0,1]\), whether \[\exists n\in\mathbb N,\qquad f^n(s)=t?\] The map is specified by finitely many rational linear guards and one rational affine expression on each guard, as defined below. The number of pieces is part of the input and is not bounded by a fixed constant. The question is exact point reachability after finitely many iterations, including zero iterations.

source_formulation.text: Yet, the decidability of the general one-dimensional reachability problem for PAMs remains open, even for maps defined with two pieces.
source_formulation.caption: Complete selected source sentence; PDF p. 2

cards.why: This is an elementary finite description of potentially complicated discrete dynamics: one rational number evolves by affine updates selected through interval tests. Exact reachability is the basic question behind checking whether such an iteration ever attains a specified state. A resolution would locate a decidability boundary between the tractable affine orbit problem and the already undecidable higher-dimensional piecewise-affine setting.
cards.status_note: Source-open in the MFCS paper published 20 August 2025, which explicitly includes the unresolved two-piece subcase. The checked March 2023 injective theorem and the MFCS Bellman-operator results impose additional restrictions. A bounded later-work search on 16 September 2026 found no matching resolution. This is a dated literature-status assessment, not independent proof that no later solution exists or verification of all cited proofs.

progress.text: Koiran, Cosnard and Garzon establish undecidability of piecewise-affine reachability already in dimension two. The checked MFCS introduction contrasts this with the unresolved dimension-one problem.

The revised injective-maps paper proves Theorem 1.1: exact reachability is decidable for injective one-dimensional maps with two half-open interval pieces. The general two-piece case remains outside that theorem.
The MFCS paper explicitly retains general one-dimensional reachability as open, even for two pieces. Its positive Bellman-operator theorems impose a different structural restriction.

The exact domain, rational point target and guard conventions were checked along with the injective subclass theorem. A bounded search located no matching later resolution for arbitrary one-dimensional rational piecewise-affine maps.

importance.reason: A longstanding and basic reachability problem at the boundary between elementary numerical dynamics and undecidable systems. Its unresolved two-piece subcase, exact rational arithmetic and connections to verification make the general one-dimensional problem broadly significant.
importance.basis: Individual assessment from the MFCS 2025 open statement and the 2023 injective two-piece result.

sentences: A one-dimensional rational piecewise-affine map repeatedly updates one number using the affine expression selected by its interval guards.
The question asks whether exact reachability of a rational target from a rational starting point is decidable for every finite description.
The number of pieces is unrestricted, all boundary choices are explicit, and any finite number of iterations including zero is allowed.
Injective two-piece maps and certain Bellman operators admit decision procedures, but the checked source retains the general question as open.
A resolution would locate a basic boundary between finite descriptions of numerical dynamics and algorithmic reachability analysis.

cards.definitions: The domain is the closed real unit interval \([0,1]=\{x\in\mathbb R:0\le x\le1\}\), following the source's unit-cube convention in dimension one. An input specifies an integer \(k\ge1\). For each \(i\le k\), a piece \(P_i\subseteq[0,1]\) is defined by a finite conjunction of inequalities \(\alpha x<\beta\) or \(\alpha x\le\beta\), with \(\alpha,\beta\in\mathbb Q\), and its affine expression is \(a_i x+b_i\), with \(a_i,b_i\in\mathbb Q\). Negative or zero slopes are allowed. The input must satisfy \[\bigcup_{i=1}^{k}P_i=[0,1],\qquad a_i x+b_i=a_jx+b_j\quad(x\in P_i\cap P_j),\qquad 0\le a_ix+b_i\le1\quad(x\in P_i).\] These conditions make \(f(x)=a_ix+b_i\) for \(x\in P_i\) a total single-valued self-map. Pieces are intervals, possibly empty or singletons; strict versus non-strict inequalities specify endpoint ownership exactly. When pieces overlap their formulas must agree, rather than using an implicit priority between guards. The map need not be continuous, injective, monotone or contractive. No Bellman-operator promise is imposed. Each rational is encoded by a signed binary numerator and a positive binary denominator, and the finite lists of guards and coefficients use explicit delimiters. The numbers \(s\) and \(t\) are encoded the same way. All input validity conditions are finite rational linear conditions; invalid descriptions may be rejected. Define \(f^0(s)=s\) and \(f^{n+1}(s)=f(f^n(s))\), with \(\mathbb N=\{0,1,2,\ldots\}\). Since the initial point and all affine coefficients are rational, every orbit point is rational, even though the map is defined on the real interval. Equality with \(t\) is exact rational equality. One uniform machine must answer all finite inputs, regardless of coefficient bit lengths and piece count, with no oracle, random error or prescribed time bound. The number of iterations is existentially quantified and has no input-supplied upper bound.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof of decidability or undecidability for the defined finite input language. An affirmative proof must provide a uniform terminating algorithm, correct for both reachable and unreachable rational targets. A negative proof must establish that no total computable decider exists. Decidability for two pieces or another restricted class is partial unless extended to arbitrary finite piece counts; undecidability within such a subclass would suffice for a negative answer. Approaching the target arbitrarily closely, reaching an interval around it, bounded-horizon simulation or a theorem for two-dimensional maps does not settle the displayed exact one-dimensional question.

context_blocks.text: With one piece, every iteration uses the same affine formula. With several pieces, the current value determines which update is applied next. The choice is deterministic, but the itinerary through the pieces may encode a long and complicated pattern. Rational coefficients do not make the state space finite: repeated division can produce infinitely many different denominators.

The target is a single rational point. For example, \(f(x)=x/2\) started at \(s=1\) converges to zero but never reaches \(t=0\) in finitely many iterations. Consequently a limiting value, an approximate numerical trajectory and exact reachability answer different questions. The zero-iteration convention means that every instance with \(s=t\) is immediately a yes-instance.

The source describes the general one-dimensional question and emphasizes that even two pieces remain unresolved. The card retains the full general target. A positive result limited to two pieces would be important progress without deciding all finite piece counts; a negative result for two pieces would also prove the general problem undecidable.

Ghahremani, Kelmendi and Ouaknine prove decidability when a two-piece map is injective, meaning distinct inputs have distinct images. Their precise convention uses a half-open unit interval partitioned into two half-open intervals. This is a restricted positive theorem; neither injectivity nor that endpoint convention is silently imposed on the present general closed-domain statement.

The MFCS source studies a different restriction: Bellman operators describing updates of reachability probabilities in finite Markov decision processes. Under its stated absence-of-end-components assumption, it obtains several arbitrary-dimensional decision results and a complete two-dimensional result for that subclass. These operators satisfy structural constraints absent from an arbitrary piecewise-affine map, so those theorems do not resolve the open one-dimensional class here.

A finite list of guards must define one function, including all boundary points. The source permits pieces described by strict and non-strict linear inequalities and requires the same function on overlaps. Recording those conventions prevents a rounding rule or an unstated branch priority from changing an orbit exactly at a breakpoint.

cards.title: Decidability and completeness of concurrent Kleene algebra with parallel iteration
cards.formal: Settle both parts of the source question for the full concurrent Kleene-algebra signature, including unbounded finite parallel iteration. For finite expressions \(e,f\), write \(e\preceq f\) when \(\downarrow\llbracket e\rrbracket\subseteq\downarrow\llbracket f\rrbracket\), using the pomset refinement semantics below. (1) Is there a total computable procedure deciding \(e\preceq f\) on every pair of such expressions? (2) Are the stated Kleene-algebra axioms for both products, together with weak interchange, complete for this semantics: \[\forall e,f,\quad e\preceq f\ \Longrightarrow\ \mathsf{CKA}\vdash e+f=f?\] The already settled fragment without parallel iteration is recorded in the context. The two remaining questions are separate: neither an algorithm alone nor an axiomatic completeness theorem alone is a complete answer to this paired target.

source_formulation.text: For expressions with sequential and parallel iteration, determine decidability of refinement by inclusion of downward-closed pomset languages and completeness of concurrent Kleene algebra with weak interchange.
source_formulation.caption: Editorial paraphrase of the full-signature questions; settled fragment identified in context

cards.why: The two questions ask whether unrestricted finite spawning of concurrent computations remains algorithmically comparable, and whether every valid refinement can be justified by a fixed algebraic calculus. Parallel iteration crosses the bounded-width boundary where existing decision and completeness results apply. Resolving the full signature would clarify the expressive and proof-theoretic cost of unbounded concurrency.
cards.status_note: The CONCUR 2017 source’s own EXPSPACE theorem and ESOP 2018 completeness theorem settle the signature without parallel star. The full signature’s completeness is explicitly retained in Kappé’s 2020 thesis, p. 132. Bounded later-work checking through 16 September 2026, including CONCUR 2026 Article 42, found no matching full-signature resolution of either target. This source-open assessment is not a proof that no later result exists, and generic continuous-model completeness is not identified with the stated finitary axiomatic completeness.

Retaining both decidability and completeness preserves the source’s distinct computational and proof-theoretic targets.

sentences: Concurrent Kleene algebra describes finite partially ordered executions using choice, sequential and parallel composition, and iteration.
The card asks both whether refinement is decidable and whether its valid inequalities follow from the stated axioms when both sequential and parallel iteration are allowed.
Refinement preserves events and labels while permitting extra ordering, and parallel iteration allows arbitrarily many concurrent copies.
Decision and completeness results for expressions without parallel iteration do not settle the full-signature questions retained here.
A resolution would establish the algorithmic and proof-theoretic limits of algebraic reasoning about unbounded finite concurrency.

cards.definitions:
An input supplies a finite alphabet \(\Sigma\) and two finite syntax trees generated by \[e ::= 0\mid1\mid a\ (a\in\Sigma)\mid e+e\mid e\cdot e\mid e\parallel e\mid e^*\mid e^\dagger.\] The alphabet and syntax trees have explicit finite encodings, with labels represented by binary indices; no succinctly shared circuits, numerical iteration counts or bound on nesting is imposed. A pomset is a finite partially ordered set of events labelled in \(\Sigma\), considered up to label-preserving order isomorphism. The empty pomset interprets \(1\), the singleton labelled \(a\) interprets \(a\), and \(0\) denotes the empty language. A sequential product \(P\cdot Q\) uses disjoint copies and places every event of \(P\) before every event of \(Q\); a parallel product \(P\parallel Q\) uses disjoint copies with no additional cross-order. Lift products to sets by taking every pair, and interpret \(+\) as union. The language of \(e^*\) is the union of all finite sequential products of members of \(\llbracket e\rrbracket\); \(e^\dagger\) is the analogous union of finite parallel products. Both include the empty product. These are finite executions of unbounded size, not infinite executions. A pomset \(P\) refines \(Q\), written \(P\sqsubseteq Q\), if there is a bijection from the events of \(Q\) to those of \(P\) preserving labels and every order comparison in \(Q\); \(P\) may add further comparisons. Put \(\downarrow L=\{P:\exists Q\in L,\ P\sqsubseteq Q\}\), ranging over all finite pomsets. Thus \(e\preceq f\) equivalently says every pomset of \(\llbracket e\rrbracket\) refines some pomset of \(\llbracket f\rrbracket\). For example, \(a\cdot b\preceq a\parallel b\).

The proof system \(\mathsf{CKA}\) uses ordinary finite equational reasoning (reflexivity, symmetry, transitivity, substitution and congruence) and the following axiom and inference schemas on arbitrary full-signature terms. Write \(x\le y\) as an abbreviation for \(x+y=y\). Addition is associative, commutative and idempotent, with identity \(0\). For each pair \((\circ,\star)\in\{(\cdot,*),(\parallel,\dagger)\}\), the product is associative, has identity \(1\), has absorbing element \(0\), distributes over addition on both sides, and satisfies \[1+x\circ x^\star=x^\star=1+x^\star\circ x.\] Its induction rules are \[x\circ y\le y\ \Longrightarrow\ x^\star\circ y\le y,\qquad y\circ x\le y\ \Longrightarrow\ y\circ x^\star\le y.\] Parallel product additionally commutes. Finally impose weak interchange \[(x\parallel z)\cdot(y\parallel w)\le(x\cdot y)\parallel(z\cdot w).\] Premises of induction rules must themselves be derived; no extra assumptions about the input letters are available. Soundness holds for the downward-closed pomset semantics. The decision question requires exact deterministic halting answers, with no error allowance, oracle or complexity bound.
cards.answer_criterion: Provide complete Lean-checked resolutions of both parts, with a separate conclusion for each. Decidability requires a total computable classifier for the displayed semantic preorder and a correctness proof; undecidability requires a proof that no such classifier exists. Completeness requires derivability of every valid refinement inequality from exactly the stated finite-proof schemas. Incompleteness requires a valid inequality and a proof of its nonderivability, for example through a fully verified algebraic countermodel to derivability. A proof for terms omitting \(\dagger\), or for plain language equality before refinement closure, is partial. A theorem about validity in all continuous models does not by itself prove completeness of the specified finitary axioms.

context_blocks.text: A pomset records which events must precede which other events. Refinement adds ordering constraints while preserving all events and labels. It can turn parallel behavior into more sequential behavior; it cannot delete an event or arbitrarily rename its action.

The operation \(e^\dagger\) permits any finite number of copies of \(e\) to run in parallel. Even the expression \(a^\dagger\) has executions with arbitrarily many mutually unordered events. Expressions without this operation have a width bound depending on their syntax, even when sequential star permits executions of unbounded length.

The source’s introductory paragraph recalls both the general question and its bounded-width fragment. Its own Theorem 26 then proves that refinement of series-rational expressions, without parallel star, is EXPSPACE-complete. The imported excerpt stopped before that result, so it was misleading to leave the whole historical paragraph marked unreviewed and open.

Laurence and Struth establish completeness and decidability for equality of full bi-Kleene pomset languages, before adding refinement closure. Their bounded-width refinement theorem and the ESOP 2018 result establish completeness in the smaller signature. None of these theorems removes the parallel-iteration qualification in the active question.

The ESOP 2018 paper explicitly omits parallel star. Its conclusion shows why its syntactic closure method cannot simply be reused: refinement closure of a parallel iteration can contain series-parallel pomsets with arbitrarily deep alternation of sequential and parallel composition, beyond any single plain series-parallel rational expression. This obstruction to one method is not a proof of undecidability or incompleteness.

The 2020 thesis retains the parallel-star completeness issue in its further-work section. Its extended correspondence between expressions and pomset automata is a different theorem: representing an expression by an automaton does not automatically decide refinement between the represented languages.

The August 2026 paper gives a broad semantics for continuous algebras with hypotheses and tools for particular axiomatic completeness proofs. It explicitly separates canonical model completeness from completeness of finitary axioms. The checked results do not supply a full parallel-star refinement decider or a proof of completeness of the exact calculus stated here.

cards.context:
A pomset records which events must precede which other events. Refinement adds ordering constraints while preserving all events and labels. It can turn parallel behavior into more sequential behavior; it cannot delete an event or arbitrarily rename its action.

The operation \(e^\dagger\) permits any finite number of copies of \(e\) to run in parallel. Even the expression \(a^\dagger\) has executions with arbitrarily many mutually unordered events. Expressions without this operation have a width bound depending on their syntax, even when sequential star permits executions of unbounded length.

The source’s introductory paragraph recalls both the general question and its bounded-width fragment. Its own Theorem 26 then proves that refinement of series-rational expressions, without parallel star, is EXPSPACE-complete. The imported excerpt stopped before that result, so it was misleading to leave the whole historical paragraph marked unreviewed and open.

Laurence and Struth establish completeness and decidability for equality of full bi-Kleene pomset languages, before adding refinement closure. Their bounded-width refinement theorem and the ESOP 2018 result establish completeness in the smaller signature. None of these theorems removes the parallel-iteration qualification in the active question.

The ESOP 2018 paper explicitly omits parallel star. Its conclusion shows why its syntactic closure method cannot simply be reused: refinement closure of a parallel iteration can contain series-parallel pomsets with arbitrarily deep alternation of sequential and parallel composition, beyond any single plain series-parallel rational expression. This obstruction to one method is not a proof of undecidability or incompleteness.

The 2020 thesis retains the parallel-star completeness issue in its further-work section. Its extended correspondence between expressions and pomset automata is a different theorem: representing an expression by an automaton does not automatically decide refinement between the represented languages.

The August 2026 paper gives a broad semantics for continuous algebras with hypotheses and tools for particular axiomatic completeness proofs. It explicitly separates canonical model completeness from completeness of finitary axioms. The checked results do not supply a full parallel-star refinement decider or a proof of completeness of the exact calculus stated here.

cards.title: Decidability of restricted elementary real functions
cards.formal: Is the joint first-order truth problem for \(\mathcal R_0\) and \(\mathcal R_1\) decidable, where \(\mathcal R_0=(\mathbb R;0,1,+,-,\times,<,\mathrm{rexp},\mathrm{rsin},\mathrm{rcos})\) and \(\mathcal R_1\) additionally includes the unrestricted real exponential \(\exp\)? The three restricted functions agree with exponential, sine and cosine on the closed interval \([0,1]\), and equal zero outside it. Precisely, does one ordinary deterministic Turing machine halt on every pair \((b,\varphi)\), with \(b\in\{0,1\}\) and \(\varphi\) a first-order sentence in the corresponding language, and correctly decide whether \(\mathcal R_b\models\varphi\), without any unproved number-theoretic hypothesis or oracle?

source_formulation.text: Similarly, it is an open question whether RRE and RRE exp are decidable, but they are also known to be decidable subject to Schanuel’s conjecture […]
source_formulation.caption: Truncated source excerpt (at most 25 words); PDF p. 4

cards.why: Real polynomial constraints admit exact decision procedures, while analytic functions can express descriptions needed for continuous-system verification. Determining whether the same kind of unconditional symbolic reasoning is possible for these restricted elementary operations would clarify the computational boundary of that extension. The problem concerns exact truth with arbitrary quantifier alternation, beyond numerical approximations to individual function values.
cards.status_note: The 2020 source poses both questions as open. The checked 2025 algorithmic survey continues to state decidability of the stronger theory conditionally on Schanuel’s conjecture, with an explicit caveat about the underlying unpublished argument. Later bounded searches through 2026-09-15 did not find a resolution of the unconditional joint truth problem. These checks do not independently verify the conditional proof or certify an exhaustive status review.

progress.text: Almagor et al. state the two open decidability questions in Section 2, page 107:4. Their Theorem 3.9 invokes the conditional theory for invariant existence; Section 4 treats semialgebraic error sets separately.
Karimov et al., Section 3.2, review the stronger exponential-plus-restricted-trigonometric theory and still make its decidability conditional on Schanuel’s conjecture over the complex numbers.

Jaoui and Kirby post a preprint on integration in finite terms and exponentially algebraic functions. The checked abstract concerns a different family of decision problems, not unrestricted first-order truth in the present finite languages.

sentences: The problem asks whether exact first-order truth is decidable over the real field with exponential, sine and cosine restricted to the unit interval.
It also includes the source’s extended language with unrestricted exponential, using a tag to make both signatures one decision problem.
Inputs are finite sentences with only fixed primitive constants, while all quantified variables range over the standard real numbers.
Known conditional results use Schanuel’s conjecture, and continuous-system invariant questions provide a computational motivation.
A solution must give an unconditional total decision procedure for the joint truth set or prove that none exists.

cards.definitions: The domain of each structure is the standard real field, and every quantifier ranges over all real numbers. The usual functions are \(\exp(x)=\sum_{j=0}^{\infty}x^j/j!\), \(\sin(x)=\sum_{j=0}^{\infty}(-1)^j x^{2j+1}/(2j+1)!\), and \(\cos(x)=\sum_{j=0}^{\infty}(-1)^j x^{2j}/(2j)!\). For \(h\in\{\exp,\sin,\cos\}\), its restricted symbol denotes the total function \(rh(x)=h(x)\) if \(0\le x\le1\), and \(rh(x)=0\) otherwise; endpoints are included and angles are in radians. Unrestricted sine and cosine are absent in both languages. For a concrete finite-string encoding, variables are v[q], where q is the binary expansion of a nonnegative integer without leading zero except for zero itself. Terms are the literal constants 0 and 1, variables, and prefix expressions neg(t), add(t,u), mul(t,u), rexp(t), rsin(t), rcos(t), with exp(t) also permitted when b is 1. Formulas are eq(t,u), lt(t,u), not(p), and(p,q), or(p,q), exists(v[j],p), and forall(v[j],p), with their usual first-order meanings and binding scopes; letters t,u,p,q here denote subexpressions. A sentence has no free variables. The input is the literal tag 0 or 1 followed by a colon and the sentence, using the indicated parentheses, commas and brackets, with no whitespace. Malformed strings, open formulas and use of exp in language 0 must be rejected. Formula length, nesting, variable count and quantifier alternation have no fixed upper bound. Only the constants 0 and 1 are primitive, so the input cannot carry arbitrary real constants or noncomputable information. A decision procedure is a single finite program with ordinary finite-alphabet work tapes, no real-operation oracle, no advice and no randomness; no time or space bound is required beyond termination on every input. Exact equality and strict inequality are interpreted in the real structure, with no perturbation promise. The joint problem is one set of finite strings. Because the first language is a sublanguage of the second with the same interpretations, its decidability is equivalent to decidability of the theory of \(\mathcal R_1\). This equivalence concerns deciding both source theories together; undecidability of the joint problem need not imply undecidability of \(\mathcal R_0\).
cards.answer_criterion: Provide a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean either that the joint truth set defined above is decidable or that it is not. A positive answer must specify a uniform Turing procedure and prove unconditional termination and exact correctness for every encoded sentence in both languages. A negative answer must prove that no such total correct procedure exists. Conditional decidability assuming Schanuel’s conjecture, a procedure for a restricted quantifier fragment, approximate satisfiability, or a numerical routine unable to decide exact zero does not meet the target. No running-time bound is requested.

context_blocks.text: The ICALP 2020 paper explicitly asks about both the restricted elementary real structure and its extension by unrestricted exponentiation. The card preserves those two signatures as one tagged truth problem. Since the larger signature contains the smaller, an algorithm for the larger one answers both, while a negative answer can leave the smaller theory’s separate status unsettled.

The source cites decidability conditional on Schanuel’s conjecture. The 2025 survey by Karimov and coauthors again describes the exponential-plus-restricted-trigonometric result as conditional, records its attribution to Macintyre and Wilkie, and points to Macintyre’s Theorem 3.1(4). It also states the zero-outside-domain convention used here.

The distinction between a tame description of definable sets and an effective truth procedure is essential. A structural theorem about the real sets definable in a language is not by itself an algorithm deciding every sentence in that language. Likewise, computability of the individual analytic functions does not by itself decide all exact equalities involving them.

For continuous linear systems, Almagor and coauthors use these theories in their conditional invariant-existence theorem for error sets described with elementary functions. They separately prove unconditional results for semialgebraic error sets. That restricted application does not establish unconditional decidability of the complete first-order theory.

Jaoui and Kirby’s October 2025 preprint studies exponential algebraicity of solutions to differential equations, using restricted elementary definability. Its stated decidability consequences concern the specified differential-algebraic problems; its abstract does not announce a decision procedure for the full first-order truth problem here.

cards.title: TOWER-hard reachability with seven nonnegative counters
cards.formal: Is reachability in unary-encoded seven-dimensional vector addition systems with states (7-VASS) \(\mathrm{TOWER}\)-hard under elementary-time many-one reductions?
cards.why: This seeks the dimension at which a small collection of nonnegative counters can already encode nonelementary computational difficulty. Reducing the eight-counter frontier would sharpen the low-dimensional boundary between tractable geometric behavior and extreme reachability complexity.

sentences: A VASS combines finite control with nonnegative integer counters updated by fixed transition vectors.
The question asks for TOWER-hard reachability using only seven counters and unary-encoded numbers.
Seven counters capture the source’s request for any improvement below the known eight-counter bound, by padding unused coordinates.

cards.definitions: A \(d\)-VASS has a finite nonempty control-state set \(Q\) and a finite transition set \(E\subseteq Q\times\mathbb Z^d\times Q\). A configuration is \((q,x)\in Q\times\mathbb N^d\), where \(\mathbb N\) includes zero. A transition \((q,a,q^{\prime})\) takes \((q,x)\) to \((q^{\prime},x+a)\) exactly when every coordinate of \(x+a\) is nonnegative. There are no zero tests, counter resets, unrestricted signed counters, stacks or fractional updates. An instance gives \(Q,E\) and source and target configurations; reachability asks for a finite transition sequence between them, possibly of length zero. For the target \(d=7\) is fixed, but the control graph, vectors and endpoint configurations are inputs. They are listed explicitly. Every integer magnitude in a displacement or endpoint is unary, with a separate sign where necessary; state identifiers use a finite binary encoding. Let \(e_0(n)=n\) and \(e_{j+1}(n)=2^{e_j(n)}\). An elementary time bound is bounded by \(e_k(n^c+c)\) for fixed nonnegative integer \(k\) and positive integer \(c\). Define \(T(0)=1\), \(T(h+1)=2^{T(h)}\). The class \(\mathrm{TOWER}\) consists of languages decidable by deterministic Turing machines in time \(O(T(f(n)))\) for some elementary-time computable nonnegative integer function \(f\). A many-one reduction from a binary language \(K\) to VASS reachability is a total computable function mapping each input string to a valid VASS instance, preserving yes and no answers. Elementary-time reductions must obey one elementary time bound for each fixed source language. TOWER-hardness quantifies over every language in TOWER; it does not additionally assert that the target problem belongs to TOWER.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof of TOWER-hardness in exactly the stated seven-counter, unary-encoded model and reduction convention. Alternatively prove in Lean that this problem is not TOWER-hard under those reductions. An elementary algorithm would imply a negative answer, but the target does not require that stronger conclusion. Results using eight counters or additional signed counters do not establish the required lower bound.

context_blocks.text: The original 2025 question asks whether the known eight-counter hardness can be attained in a lower dimension. This is exactly captured by testing seven counters: a lower-dimensional VASS can be padded with permanently zero counters, without changing reachability.

Czerwiński and Orlikowski prove TOWER-hardness already with eight counters and unary displacement encoding. Their result therefore cannot be explained solely by exponentially succinct binary counter values. The elementary reduction convention is significant for this nonelementary complexity class.

A fixed-height tower, such as a double or triple exponential, is an elementary bound. TOWER allows the tower height itself to grow with the input. Hardness for every fixed-height exponential class does not on its own supply the single TOWER-hardness statement.

The 2026 work on VASS extended with signed integer counters reports the ordinary three-counter reachability problem as elementary and the ordinary TOWER lower bound as known in dimension eight. Its new three-counter hardness counts only the nonnegative counters and permits additional unrestricted integer counters. Those extra counters are absent from the present model.

The number of counters stays fixed but the finite control graph can grow. This differs from fixing the entire VASS and varying only its endpoints. It also differs from requiring a long run in a particular example: a complexity lower bound must reduce every problem in the hardness class.

The source separately discusses geometric dimension, defined using the span of cycle effects. That structural parameter is not substituted for the seven actual nonnegative counters in this card; its associated question remains a distinct direction.

cards.title: Decidability of branching-VASS reachability
cards.formal: Is there an algorithm deciding reachability in branching vector addition systems with states when the dimension is part of the input? Given a finite system \(B\) as defined below and a target configuration \(q(x)\), decide whether \(q(x)\) is the root of a finite valid derivation tree of \(B\).
cards.why: Branching VASS extend the Petri-net style of counter computation to recursive combinations of resources. Settling exact reachability in arbitrary dimension would identify a central decidability boundary between path computations and branching derivations in infinite-state verification.
cards.status_note: Rechecked on 16 September 2026 against Bizière–Leroux–Sutre arXiv:2609.15869v1, the extended FOSSACS 2026 paper posted 14 September. Its introduction and conclusion explicitly retain arbitrary-dimensional BVASS reachability as open. Theorem 5.2 represents reachability sets as VASS sections without a general effective construction; Remark 5.4 and §6 distinguish existence of a structural bound from a computable bound. Theorem 7.3 handles two-dimensional BVASS and five-dimensional single-state BVAS, not five-dimensional arbitrary-state BVASS. No matching resolution is claimed by this new source. The formal target and the 2025 source conventions are retained; source theorem scopes were checked, not every proof independently certified.

sentences: A branching vector addition system combines finite control with nonnegative integer resources.
Rules can combine several already derived configurations by adding their resource vectors and a fixed displacement.
Reachability asks whether a finite valid derivation tree produces exactly a supplied target.
The dimension is part of the input, and every branch must be fully justified.
The September 2026 structural and low-dimensional results explicitly leave arbitrary-dimensional reachability open.

cards.definitions: The input dimension is an integer \(d\geq1\). A \(d\)-dimensional branching vector addition system with states (\(d\)-BVASS) has a finite nonempty state set \(Q\) and finite rules \((S,a,q)\), where \(S\subseteq Q\), \(a\in\mathbb Z^d\) and \(q\in Q\). A configuration \(q(x)\) consists of a state \(q\) and vector \(x\in\mathbb N^d\). A rule with \(S=\{q_1,\ldots,q_k\}\) combines one configuration \(q_i(x_i)\) for each input state into \(q(a+x_1+\cdots+x_k)\), provided all coordinates of this output are nonnegative. All child configurations must themselves have nonnegative coordinates. Input states in one rule are distinct, following the source’s set convention. When \(S\) is empty, the rule supplies the initial configuration \(q(a)\) if \(a\geq0\) coordinatewise. A derivation is a finite rooted tree: each node uses one rule, has exactly its rule’s specified children, and its label is obtained by the preceding sum. Leaves therefore use empty-input rules. A target is reachable if some such tree has that target as root. Derivations may use the same rule any finite number of times; there is no global stock of initial tokens shared between different branches. The number of children and the dimension are unbounded input parameters. States, rules, child-state sets and target are listed explicitly, with signed binary integers for displacement coordinates and binary nonnegative target coordinates. There are no equality or zero tests, resets, counter multiplication, probability or additional acceptance conditions. Decidability means one deterministic Turing machine that halts and answers correctly on every valid finite encoding, with no running-time bound requested.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof of a terminating algorithm for the stated arbitrary-dimensional finite-tree reachability problem, or prove in Lean that it is undecidable. A dimension-dependent result covering only some fixed dimensions, a coverability algorithm, or a procedure that terminates only on reachable targets does not decide this problem. Finite derivation trees must satisfy every branch and every exact target coordinate.

context_blocks.text: A unary rule follows one computation, while a branching rule combines completed subcomputations by adding their counter vectors. For example, in one dimension, initial rules yielding \(p(2)\) and \(q(3)\) together with a zero-displacement rule from \(\{p,q\}\) to \(r\) derive \(r(5)\). Both child computations are required.

Ordinary VASS are the fragment using only initial and unary rules. Their reachability is decidable. Branching changes paths into finite derivation trees, so ordinary reachability decidability does not automatically extend to the system in this card.

Bizière, Hilaire, Leroux and Sutre prove decidability in dimension two in 2025. They obtain an effectively computable semilinear description of the reachable set: a finite union, for each state, of sets consisting of a base vector plus arbitrary nonnegative integer combinations of finitely many period vectors.

The paper explicitly leaves reachability open in arbitrary dimension. It also cautions that its two-dimensional procedure does not provide a complexity upper bound. Decidability in every input dimension is therefore the main target here, rather than an optimization of the two-dimensional running time.

Reachability requires exactly the requested counter vector. Coverability would allow a vector above it coordinatewise and can discard information crucial to exact reachability. Similarly, a derivation that leaves a branch unresolved is not a valid witness.

Since every finite proposed tree can be checked, positive instances have finite verifiable witnesses. This alone gives no way to halt on every negative instance. The question is precisely whether an always-terminating decision procedure exists.

The extended FOSSACS 2026 paper proves that every BVASS reachability set is a section of a VASS reachability set: one intersects with specified semilinear constraints and projects selected counters. The theorem is a structural existence statement. The paper does not obtain a general effective construction that would turn it into a reachability decider, and Remark 5.4 explicitly explains this distinction.

Its low-dimensional result gives effectively semilinear reachability sets for two-dimensional BVASS and five-dimensional BVAS. A BVAS here is the single-control-state version, so the five-dimensional theorem must not be attributed to arbitrary-state BVASS. The conclusion again identifies arbitrary-dimensional exact reachability as open. The retained 2025 rule conventions and decision target are unchanged.

cards.context:
A unary rule follows one computation, while a branching rule combines completed subcomputations by adding their counter vectors. For example, in one dimension, initial rules yielding \(p(2)\) and \(q(3)\) together with a zero-displacement rule from \(\{p,q\}\) to \(r\) derive \(r(5)\). Both child computations are required.

Ordinary VASS are the fragment using only initial and unary rules. Their reachability is decidable. Branching changes paths into finite derivation trees, so ordinary reachability decidability does not automatically extend to the system in this card.

Bizière, Hilaire, Leroux and Sutre prove decidability in dimension two in 2025. They obtain an effectively computable semilinear description of the reachable set: a finite union, for each state, of sets consisting of a base vector plus arbitrary nonnegative integer combinations of finitely many period vectors.

The paper explicitly leaves reachability open in arbitrary dimension. It also cautions that its two-dimensional procedure does not provide a complexity upper bound. Decidability in every input dimension is therefore the main target here, rather than an optimization of the two-dimensional running time.

Reachability requires exactly the requested counter vector. Coverability would allow a vector above it coordinatewise and can discard information crucial to exact reachability. Similarly, a derivation that leaves a branch unresolved is not a valid witness.

Since every finite proposed tree can be checked, positive instances have finite verifiable witnesses. This alone gives no way to halt on every negative instance. The question is precisely whether an always-terminating decision procedure exists.

The extended FOSSACS 2026 paper proves that every BVASS reachability set is a section of a VASS reachability set: one intersects with specified semilinear constraints and projects selected counters. The theorem is a structural existence statement. The paper does not obtain a general effective construction that would turn it into a reachability decider, and Remark 5.4 explicitly explains this distinction.

Its low-dimensional result gives effectively semilinear reachability sets for two-dimensional BVASS and five-dimensional BVAS. A BVAS here is the single-control-state version, so the five-dimensional theorem must not be attributed to arbitrary-state BVASS. The conclusion again identifies arbitrary-dimensional exact reachability as open. The retained 2025 rule conventions and decision target are unchanged.

cards.title: Decisiveness of static probabilistic Petri nets for finite targets
cards.formal: Is there a deterministic Turing machine that always halts and decides the following problem? The input is a finite Petri net with positive constant integer transition weights, an initial marking \(m_0\), and a finite explicitly listed set \(A\) of target markings. In the induced discrete-time Markov chain, let \(U_A\) consist of markings from which no marking in \(A\) is reachable by a finite sequence of enabled transitions. Decide whether \[\Pr_{m_0}\bigl[\exists n\in\mathbb N:\ M_n\in A\cup U_A\bigr]=1.\] This property is decisiveness from \(m_0\) with respect to \(A\). We retain the source's static-weight, finite-target question; its other, dynamic-weight variant is already resolved negatively and is described in the context.

source_formulation.text: For probabilistic Petri nets with constant transition weights, is decisiveness with respect to a supplied initial marking and a finite target set decidable?
source_formulation.caption: Editorial paraphrase of the source’s remaining static-weight question

cards.why: Decisiveness says that unresolved probability mass almost surely disappears: a run eventually either succeeds or enters a state from which success is impossible. This supports certified approximation of reachability probabilities in infinite-state systems. Deciding the property for ordinary constant-weight Petri nets would identify exactly when this general verification guarantee can be recognized from a finite concurrent-system description.
cards.status_note: The retained static-weight finite-target question is explicit in CONCUR 2023 and in the 2025 follow-up author presentation. The QEST+FORMATS 2025 paper’s conclusion retains constant-weight Petri nets; its undecidability theorem permits affine marking-dependent weights. A bounded later-work search on 16 September 2026 found no matching resolution for the defined static class. This source-open assessment does not independently certify all cited proofs or exhaust later literature.

sentences: A static probabilistic Petri net randomly chooses an enabled transition according to its fixed positive weight.
Decisiveness for a finite target means that almost every run eventually reaches either the target or a marking from which the target is unreachable.
The question asks whether this property is decidable from the net, one initial marking and an explicit finite target set.
Known upward-closed-target guarantees and undecidability with marking-dependent weights do not settle this constant-weight finite-target case.
A resolution would clarify when a general guarantee supporting certified probability approximation can be recognized in an ordinary probabilistic counter model.

cards.definitions: Let \(\mathbb N=\{0,1,2,\ldots\}\). The net consists of a finite set of places \(P\), a finite set of transitions \(T\), input and output vectors \(\mathrm{Pre}(t),\mathrm{Post}(t)\in\mathbb N^P\), and weights \(w(t)\in\mathbb N\setminus\{0\}\). A marking \(m\in\mathbb N^P\) records the number of tokens in each place. Transition \(t\) is enabled exactly when \(m\ge\mathrm{Pre}(t)\) componentwise; firing it gives \(m-\mathrm{Pre}(t)+\mathrm{Post}(t)\). There are no inhibitor, reset or transfer arcs and no extra zero tests. Write \(E(m)\) for the set of enabled transitions. If it is nonempty, select each \(t\in E(m)\) with probability \(w(t)/\sum_{r\in E(m)}w(r)\), and fire it once. If several transitions yield the same successor, their probabilities add. Each listed transition receives its one weight regardless of how many token subsets could enable it. If \(E(m)\) is empty, the chain stays at \(m\) with probability one. The weight of a transition never changes with the marking. All weights, token counts and finite incidence tables are explicitly encoded in binary; the numbers of places, transitions and target markings are unrestricted. The chain \((M_n)_{n\ge0}\) starts at \(M_0=m_0\) and uses the probability measure on infinite paths whose finite-prefix probabilities are the products of the corresponding transition probabilities. Reachability is reflexive, so a target is reached at time zero and \(A\cap U_A=\varnothing\). The empty target set is allowed and makes \(U_A\) the entire state space. The machine must make the exact yes/no decision on every finite input, with no oracle, random error, time limit or probability tolerance. The initial marking is part of the input; the question does not quantify over all initial markings at once.
cards.answer_criterion: Provide a complete Lean-checked proof of decidability or undecidability for precisely these constant-weight nets, supplied initial markings and arbitrary finite targets. A positive answer must specify one uniform total computable algorithm and prove its equivalence with the displayed probability-one predicate. A negative answer must prove that no such algorithm exists in this model. Nondecisiveness of some example is not an undecidability proof. A result for weights depending on the current marking, or for targets given only as upward-closed sets, does not settle the retained static finite-target problem.

context_blocks.text: Decisiveness does not require reaching the target with probability one. It also permits reaching the avoid set, where the target is no longer reachable at all. The obstruction is positive probability of continuing forever outside the target while retaining some finite path to it at every visited state.

Constant transition weights still produce state-dependent probabilities: which transitions are enabled changes with the current marking. The model makes this dependence only through enabling and normalization. Assigning a weight that grows with a token count is a different, dynamic model.

A one-place net illustrates why static weights do not automatically ensure finite-target decisiveness. Give the increment transition weight two and the decrement transition weight one, with decrement enabled only above zero. Starting at one and targeting zero gives an upward-biased random walk: zero remains reachable everywhere, yet the probability of never hitting it is positive. This defeats decisiveness, while a universal recognition algorithm could still in principle classify the instance.

For constant-weight nets, upward-closed targets are known to be decisive. An upward-closed set contains every marking obtained by adding tokens to one of its elements. A finite exact target set generally lacks this closure, so the established theorem does not apply to the question here.

The same 2023 source resolves its dynamic-weight question: polynomial marking-dependent weights make decisiveness undecidable even for finite or upward-closed targets. Its Theorem 22 also identifies a positive subclass with a regular firing language. The active question retained here is the separately stated constant-weight finite-target case; the resolved dynamic variant is not presented as still open.

The 2025 paper strengthens the dynamic-weight negative theorem to affine functions of one place marking. Its conclusion and the authors’ presentation retain static Petri nets with finite targets as a further question. Dependence on even one place remains genuine dependence, so the improved negative theorem does not reach the constant-weight class.

cards.title: Linear-length witnesses for reachability in each fixed vector addition system
cards.formal: For every integer \(d\geq1\) and finite set \(V\subseteq\mathbb Z^d\), does there exist a constant \(C_V\geq1\) such that every reachable pair \(s,t\in\mathbb N^d\) has a run of length at most \(C_V(\|s\|_1+\|t\|_1)\)?
cards.why: The conjecture isolates whether unbounded shortest-run growth is caused by changing the transition system or can already occur within one fixed system. This structural distinction is fundamental for understanding the complexity of reachability when only numerical configurations vary.
cards.status_note: The 2022 source and 2024 fixed-VASS paper retain the linear shortest-run conjecture. A bounded later-work check on 13 September 2026 did not locate a proof or a fixed-system counterexample. The zero-endpoint inequality convention is an explicit editorial repair of the literal strict source wording, not a claimed research resolution.

sentences: A fixed vector addition system supplies a finite collection of updates on nonnegative integer vectors.
The conjecture asks whether every reachable pair has a run linear in the numerical sizes of its endpoints.
The multiplicative constant may depend on the entire fixed system, while the endpoints vary freely.
The non-strict bound includes the zero-length run from zero to itself.
This structural witness bound would have complexity consequences, but it is not a linear-time algorithm in binary input length.

cards.definitions: A vector addition system (VAS) is the finite set \(V\) of allowed displacement vectors; there is no control-state graph. Its configurations are vectors in \(\mathbb N^d\), where zero coordinates are allowed. A run from \(s\) to \(t\) is a finite sequence \(c_0=s,c_1,\ldots,c_m=t\) with \(c_i\in\mathbb N^d\) and \(c_i-c_{i-1}\in V\) for all \(1\leq i\leq m\). Its length is the number \(m\) of transitions, not the magnitude of its largest counter. Empty runs of length zero are permitted, so every configuration reaches itself. The norm is \(\|x\|_1=\sum_{j=1}^d |x_j|\). The whole system, including its dimension, number of updates and their integer magnitudes, is fixed before \(C_V\) is chosen. The constant must then work for all source and target vectors in that system. There are no tests except the requirement that updated coordinates remain nonnegative. No algorithm for computing \(C_V\), finding a short run or deciding reachability in a specified time is required. The bound measures numerical endpoint magnitudes, not their binary encoding lengths. Choosing another fixed norm would change only the system-dependent constant. The non-strict inequality includes the zero-to-zero empty run; the source’s strict wording otherwise has an artificial zero-endpoint exception. For positive endpoint norm sums, strict and non-strict versions are equivalent after enlarging \(C_V\).
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof of the universal system-dependent linear witness bound. Alternatively give one explicit finite VAS \(V\) and prove in Lean that for every \(C\geq1\) there are reachable endpoints \(s,t\) for which every run has length greater than \(C(\|s\|_1+\|t\|_1)\). Letting the update system vary with \(C\), using binary bit length instead of endpoint magnitudes, or merely displaying one unnecessarily long run does not refute the proposition.

context_blocks.text: For a one-counter system allowing increments and decrements by one, the shortest run has length \(|s-t|\), which meets the desired bound. The conjecture says that more involved interactions among a fixed finite collection of counters never force a superlinear shortest detour as the endpoints grow.

Jecker’s source formulates a short-witness conjecture, despite the entry’s broad complexity title. The present title and criterion expose that actual mathematical claim. The choice of a non-strict bound simply handles the permitted empty run at zero rather than turning a wording defect into a counterexample.

A fixed system can contain very large displacement constants, and the allowed multiplicative constant may be correspondingly large. Exhibiting a family of larger and larger systems with hard instances would not disprove this conjecture: a counterexample must keep one finite update set for every endpoint pair.

The 2024 fixed-VASS paper discusses Jecker’s conjecture and reports that its lower-bound constructions give no evidence against it. It proves PSPACE-hardness for a fixed five-counter VASS when initial counter values are binary and explains the PSPACE upper-bound implication of the proposed short-path property.

There is no conflict between a path linear in endpoint magnitudes and a high complexity measured in binary digits. A counter value with a short binary encoding can be exponentially larger than that encoding, so writing out such a path may already take exponentially many steps.

A positive answer would constrain how much of the infinite configuration graph is needed to witness each reachable pair once the system is fixed. It would not make all VAS reachability uniformly linear-time, since the constant carries the entire fixed system and the target is existential.

cards.title: Elementary-time reachability for one-dimensional grammar-controlled VAS
cards.formal: Can reachability for one-dimensional grammar-controlled vector addition systems be decided in elementary deterministic time? More explicitly, do there exist fixed integers \(h\geq0\), \(c\geq1\) and one deterministic Turing machine deciding every instance of bit length \(n\) within \(O(e_h(n^c+c))\) steps, where \(e_0(z)=z\) and \(e_{j+1}(z)=2^{e_j(z)}\)?
cards.why: This asks whether one nonnegative counter interacting with context-free control can still be analyzed within a fixed-height exponential time bound. It separates existence of a decision algorithm from a meaningful complexity boundary and tests whether enormous reachable sets force equally enormous decision time.
cards.status_note: Rechecked on 13 September 2026. General 1-GVAS decidability is established by the later Bizière–Czerwiński paper, superseding the survey’s provisional wording. The selected elementary-time question is explicitly left open there and remains distinguished from the 2026 index-dependent thin-grammar bound. These proof texts were checked for statements and scope, not independently formalized in Lean.

cards.definitions: A one-dimensional grammar-controlled vector addition system (1-GVAS) is a finite context-free grammar with nonterminal set \(N\), distinguished start nonterminal \(S\), and finitely many productions \(X\to\alpha\) with \(X\in N\) and \(\alpha\) a finite sequence of nonterminals and integer terminals. There is no restriction on recursion or on the number of nonterminals occurring in a sentential form. The empty right-hand side is allowed. A terminal word \(a_1\cdots a_m\), with \(a_i\in\mathbb Z\), is generated when a finite sequence of production applications transforms \(S\) into that word. Given starting and target counters \(s,t\in\mathbb N\), the word witnesses reachability if \(s+\sum_{i=1}^j a_i\geq0\) for every \(0\leq j\leq m\), and \(s+\sum_{i=1}^m a_i=t\). The terminal order is the left-to-right order in the generated word, not the order in which productions were expanded. An empty terminal word witnesses exactly \(s=t\), if generated. There is one nonnegative counter, no test for zero except through inability to take a negative update, and no restriction on stack depth implicit in the grammar. The whole grammar, both counters and all production sequences are explicit inputs. Integer terminals use signed binary encodings, and \(s,t\) use binary nonnegative encodings; their digits and every symbol occurrence contribute to input length. The tower height \(h\), polynomial exponent \(c\), hidden multiplicative constant and program must be independent of the grammar and both counters. Correctness concerns exact reachability, not coverability or an approximation of the reachable set.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof of a deterministic decision algorithm with one fixed elementary time bound for all instances, or prove in Lean that no elementary-time decider exists. A bound whose tower height depends on the input grammar or a theorem only for structurally restricted grammars does not establish the positive answer. The output need only decide reachability; it need not print a potentially enormous derivation.

context_blocks.text: The 2024 survey asks broadly for the complexity of 1-GVAS reachability and at that time describes an unconfirmed decidability argument. Editorial specialization: this card selects the elementary-time boundary, explicitly conjectured in the subsequent complete decidability paper. It does not claim that answering this boundary alone determines the exact complexity class.

The counter constrains prefixes, not just the final sum. A generated word \((-1),1\) has total effect zero but is invalid from counter zero. A word \(1,(-1)\) with the same total effect is valid from zero. A grammar’s ordering constraints and counter nonnegativity therefore interact.

Bizière and Czerwiński’s November 2024 paper proves reachability decidable for general 1-GVAS. It constructs a thin grammar with the same reachability relation. A nonterminal is thin if no derivation from it can produce a sentential form containing two copies of that same nonterminal; a grammar is thin when all its nonterminals are thin.

Theorem 2 and Corollary 3 show that an elementary algorithm for thin grammars would imply an elementary algorithm for all 1-GVAS. Thin grammars are already a subclass, so the elementary-time question has the same yes/no answer in the two settings. This is a preservation theorem for the complexity boundary, not an existing elementary bound.

The February 2026 thin-GVAS preprint improves an upper bound parameterized by its structural index and continues to leave an elementary upper bound open. Since that index can grow with the grammar, its stated fast-growing bound does not supply a fixed-height exponential tower for every input.

The survey illustrates small grammars with extremely large finite reachable sets. Such cardinality alone does not prove a matching lower bound for deciding whether one supplied counter value is reachable. Conversely, merely finding short derivations in a collection of examples does not give a uniform decision algorithm.
