cards.context:
The 2024 survey asks broadly for the complexity of 1-GVAS reachability and at that time describes an unconfirmed decidability argument. Editorial specialization: this card selects the elementary-time boundary, explicitly conjectured in the subsequent complete decidability paper. It does not claim that answering this boundary alone determines the exact complexity class.

The counter constrains prefixes, not just the final sum. A generated word \((-1),1\) has total effect zero but is invalid from counter zero. A word \(1,(-1)\) with the same total effect is valid from zero. A grammar’s ordering constraints and counter nonnegativity therefore interact.

Bizière and Czerwiński’s November 2024 paper proves reachability decidable for general 1-GVAS. It constructs a thin grammar with the same reachability relation. A nonterminal is thin if no derivation from it can produce a sentential form containing two copies of that same nonterminal; a grammar is thin when all its nonterminals are thin.

Theorem 2 and Corollary 3 show that an elementary algorithm for thin grammars would imply an elementary algorithm for all 1-GVAS. Thin grammars are already a subclass, so the elementary-time question has the same yes/no answer in the two settings. This is a preservation theorem for the complexity boundary, not an existing elementary bound.

The February 2026 thin-GVAS preprint improves an upper bound parameterized by its structural index and continues to leave an elementary upper bound open. Since that index can grow with the grammar, its stated fast-growing bound does not supply a fixed-height exponential tower for every input.

The survey illustrates small grammars with extremely large finite reachable sets. Such cardinality alone does not prove a matching lower bound for deciding whether one supplied counter value is reachable. Conversely, merely finding short derivations in a collection of examples does not give a uniform decision algorithm.

cards.title: Consistency of excluded middle and Church’s thesis in Coq
cards.formal:
Is \(\mathcal T+\mathrm{LEM}+\mathrm{CT}\) logically consistent, where \(\mathcal T\) is Coq's ordinary cumulative inductive core calculus specified below, and the two added propositional axioms are
\[\mathrm{LEM}:\quad\forall P:\mathrm{Prop},\ P\lor\neg P,\]
\[\mathrm{CT}:\quad\forall f:\mathbb N\to\mathbb N,\ \exists e:\mathbb N,\ \forall x:\mathbb N,\ \exists s:\mathbb N,\ T(e,x,s)=\mathrm{Some}(f(x))?\]
Here \(T\) is the fixed bounded evaluator for ordinary register-machine programs defined below. Consistency means that there is no finite well-typed closed proof term of \(\mathrm{False}\) in the extended calculus. The existence quantifiers in CT are in Prop; they are not computational dependent pairs.
cards.why: This would clarify whether classical reasoning about propositions can coexist with the claim that every internal numerical function is computable, while retaining a rich dependent type theory. The distinction matters for synthetic computability developments that use Church’s thesis as an axiom and for the foundational role of separating propositions from computational data.
cards.status_note: Forster’s Section 7 conjecture, the Coq 8.11 calculus documentation and Putrle’s 2023 consistency theorem were checked on 2026-09-14. The latter explicitly covers a fragment without general inductive types. A bounded later-work search did not identify a consistency model or contradiction for the full ordinary core with exactly the selected two axioms.

cards.definitions:
The base \(\mathcal T\) is the Prop/Set/Type calculus of inductive constructions in the Coq 8.11 reference manual, with predicative Set and cumulative predicative universes \(\mathrm{Type}_i\) above it. This fixes the source's full inductive-calculus setting rather than only the arithmetic fragment used in some consistency models. The optional separate SProp sort and the impredicative-Set extension are outside this selected core. Terms include variables, universe sorts, dependent products \(\Pi x:A.B(x)\), abstractions, applications, local definitions, inductive constructors, pattern matching and guarded recursive or co-recursive definitions. Definitions and conversion follow the cited calculus: function application reduces by substitution, pattern matching computes on constructors, local definitions unfold, and recursive/co-recursive unfolding obeys the guardedness rules. Universe constraints must have a well-founded assignment to levels. Arbitrary mutual inductive and coinductive declarations satisfying its positivity and universe conditions are permitted; not just a fixed list of natural-number and list types.

Prop is the impredicative universe of propositions: a proposition may quantify over a type at any universe level and remain in Prop. Ordinary data live in Set or Type. Propositional disjunction and existential quantification are inductive propositions. Their proofs generally cannot be pattern-matched to produce arbitrary computational data. The standard exceptions for empty and singleton inductive propositions remain allowed, including elimination of False into any type. Singleton elimination is the calculus's syntactic constructor rule, not a new assumption that every inhabited proposition has one proof. Identity is the usual inductive equality with reflexivity and its permitted elimination rule. Equality reflection, functional or propositional extensionality, univalence, unrestricted choice and proof irrelevance are not added as axioms.

Natural numbers have constructors zero and successor. Fix a computable, effectively decodable Gödel numbering of finite deterministic register-machine programs. Registers hold natural numbers. A program consists of labelled increment-and-jump instructions, decrement-with-zero-test-and-jump instructions, and halt instructions. It starts with register zero containing \(x\), all other registers zero, and its initial program counter at the first instruction; on halting it outputs register zero. The selected model is Turing complete. The total, structurally recursive function \(T(e,x,s)\) simulates the program coded by \(e\) for at most \(s\) transitions, returning \(\mathrm{Some}(y)\) if it has halted with output \(y\), and \(\mathrm{None}\) otherwise. Invalid codes are interpreted as nonhalting programs. The numbering and evaluator are fixed before adding either axiom; CT does not assert the existence of an unspecified oracle evaluator. Standard effectively intertranslatable program codings yield equivalent CT assertions.

The symbol \(\neg P\) means \(P\to\mathrm{False}\), where False is the proposition with no constructors. Add opaque proof constants of the displayed LEM and CT types and no computational reduction equations for them. The quantifier over \(f\) ranges internally over all functions of the extended theory, not merely functions in a chosen list of already written programs. A contradiction would be a closed derivation of False using finitely many permitted declarations and these constants. The question concerns the mathematical inference rules, not bugs in a proof-assistant executable.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct Lean-checked proof that the extended formal calculus has no closed proof of False, or exhibit such a proof and verify its typing. A semantic construction must include soundness for the selected universes, general permitted inductive/coinductive declarations and elimination rules; modeling only a restricted arithmetic fragment is insufficient. A proof of consistency for CT alone, for a different type theory, or after replacing propositional existentials by a different assertion does not settle this joint-consistency target.

context_blocks.text: Classical set-theoretic reasoning commonly turns an existence statement into a function by choice. Combining such a choice principle with excluded middle produces noncomputable numerical functions and contradicts CT. The source explains that the corresponding choice principle is not derivable merely from Coq’s Prop-level excluded middle.

CT asserts that a program index exists propositionally. It does not provide an operation that extracts an index from an arbitrary function. Likewise, LEM is a propositional disjunction, not a Boolean decision procedure for every proposition. These distinctions are essential to the conjecture.

Forster explicitly conjectures joint consistency at the end of Section 7. Earlier consistency results for Church’s thesis in other constructive type theories do not automatically establish this particular combination of classical logic, impredicative propositions and Coq’s elimination rules.

Putrle’s 2023 thesis proves consistency of the fCIC fragment used for a synthetic computability development, with stronger synthetic computability assumptions and selected large-elimination rules. Its Definition 6.4 and following text explicitly restrict general inductive types. This is substantial partial progress but does not by itself model the full core selected here.

cards.title: Univalence, impredicativity and propositional resizing
cards.formal: Does there exist a nondegenerate model of ordinary dependent type theory, with the type formers and computation rules specified below, containing a univalent impredicative universe \(U\) of data types into which every homotopy proposition can be resized?

source_formulation.text: There is a natural question: can we construct a model of type theory with a univalent and impredicative universe satisfying the propositional resizing axiom?
source_formulation.caption: Complete selected source sentence; PDF p. 16

cards.why: Determine compatibility of univalence, impredicative data-type universes and propositional resizing under ordinary dependent computation rules, clarifying a substantive boundary in foundations for proof assistants.

Their semantic qualifications are retained; this is not an exhaustive current-openness certificate.

sentences: An impredicative universe supports quantification over types without the usual increase in universe size, while univalence connects equivalence with equality.
Propositional resizing adds the requirement that large propositions have equivalent small representatives.
The source asks for a model of type theory supporting all three features together.

Constructing a model with the intended ordinary type-theoretic rules would clarify whether these attractive foundational principles can coexist without sacrificing essential forms of dependent reasoning.

cards.definitions: A model is a set-based category with families: it has contexts and substitutions forming a category with an empty terminal context, types over each context, terms of each type, and context extension \(\Gamma.A\) classifying a substitution into \(\Gamma\) together with a term of its reindexed type \(A\). Reindexing of types and terms obeys identity and composition strictly. Type-forming operations, constructors and eliminators commute strictly with reindexing. Require dependent products \(\prod_{x:A}B(x)\), dependent sums \(\sum_{x:A}B(x)\), intensional identity types \(\operatorname{Id}_A(a,b)\), empty and unit types, binary coproducts, and natural numbers. Products have abstraction and application with the usual judgmental beta and eta equations; sums have pairing, projections and dependent elimination with their usual computation equations. Identity types have reflexivity and the unrestricted dependent eliminator \(J\), whose reflexivity computation equation holds judgmentally. Empty, unit, coproduct and natural-number types have their usual dependent eliminators and judgmental constructor equations. Also require function extensionality: the canonical map from an identity of dependent functions to their pointwise identities is an equivalence. Judgmental equations are equalities of the interpreted operations, rather than merely inhabited identity types. Nondegenerate means that the interpreted empty type has no closed term. A Tarski universe is an ambient type \(U\) with a decoding family \(\operatorname{El}:U\to\mathrm{Type}\). It has codes for empty, unit, binary coproduct and natural-number types and is closed under dependent sums and identity types of decoded small types. It is impredicative when, for every ambient type \(A\) and family \(b:A\to U\), the dependent product \(\prod_{x:A}\operatorname{El}(b(x))\) has a code in \(U\). These coding operations and their decoding identifications must be specified and stable under substitution; decoded closure may hold up to specified isomorphism. The domain \(A\) need not itself have a code in \(U\). There is no requirement that \(U\) code itself. Write \(\operatorname{isProp}(P)=\prod_{x,y:P}\operatorname{Id}_P(x,y)\). A type is contractible if it has a point identified with every point; a map is an equivalence if every fiber \(\sum_x\operatorname{Id}(f(x),y)\) is contractible. Univalence means that, for all \(a,b:U\), the canonical transport map \(\operatorname{Id}_U(a,b)\to\operatorname{Equiv}(\operatorname{El}(a),\operatorname{El}(b))\) is an equivalence. Propositional resizing means that for every ambient type \(P\), in every context with a term of \(\operatorname{isProp}(P)\), there is a small proposition code \(p:U\) and an equivalence \(P\simeq\operatorname{El}(p)\), uniformly under substitution. These are internal structures of the model; external equivalence of isolated fibers is insufficient. No particular assembly, cubical or path-category presentation, no Church’s thesis and no higher inductive types are required.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean that such a model exists, specifying its semantic structures and verifying all rules, closure, univalence, resizing and nondegeneracy; or prove in Lean that no such model exists. A merely postulated model, a model with only propositional universes, or a model validating only weaker identity or dependent-product computation rules does not satisfy this formulation. A failure of resizing in one candidate model is not a universal nonexistence proof.

context_blocks.text: A universe is a type whose elements name other types. Ordinary predicative universes generally move to a larger level when one quantifies over a larger domain. Impredicativity instead keeps a product small whenever its values are small, even if the domain is large. Here the universe includes natural numbers and other data types; it is not only a collection of propositions.

Univalence says that equivalent small types are identified in the universe, with the appropriate higher identity structure. Resizing asks a different question: whether every ambient proposition already has a small representative. A proposition is a type whose any two inhabitants are identified, which does not require it to have an inhabitant.

Uemura constructs a cubical assembly model with a univalent impredicative universe and proves that resizing into that universe fails. His concluding question asks for compatibility of the three principles in another model, rather than for a proof of resizing in the displayed countermodel.

This card spells out the ordinary-type-theory reading of that question. The data-type codes and nondegeneracy prevent a vacuous or proposition-only interpretation; strict substitution and the stated computation rules specify the coherence demanded of a model. It does not add a requirement for a particular semantic construction.

Van den Berg gives related positive path-category constructions, including an impredicative univalent universe of sets with resizing. Uemura explicitly distinguishes their weaker identity and dependent-product structure from a model of ordinary homotopy type theory. Those positive results therefore need their semantic qualification when compared with this target.

Speight’s later groupoidal realizability work constructs an impredicative universe of 1-types, but the model does not validate function extensionality in general. Its concluding questions still distinguish univalent universes and resizing. The presence of an impredicative universe alone does not supply the full structure requested here.

A resolution would clarify whether a universe supporting ordinary data, equivalence-based identity and quantification over larger domains can coexist with small representatives for all propositions. This affects the foundations of dependent reasoning and proof-assistant universe systems, rather than the runtime of a program.

cards.title: Shortest runs in 3-D VASS
cards.formal: Is there no single-exponential bound on shortest runs in binary-encoded three-dimensional vector addition systems with states? Precisely, is it true that for every integer \(k\ge 1\), every real \(C>0\) and every \(N_{0}\ge 1\), there is a reachable instance I of encoding length \(N\ge N_{0}\) whose shortest source-to-target run has more than \(2^{C N^{k}}\) transitions?
cards.why: Isolates how much witness complexity three unbounded counters can force. Resolving the single-exponential threshold would clarify the gap between low-dimensional reachability and the much more expensive behavior possible when the number of counters grows.
cards.status_note: Original question and the 2025 explicit binary formulation checked, with subsequent-work searches through 11 September 2026. The July 2026 preprint improves the upper bound but does not resolve whether single-exponential shortest runs always suffice. No resolution of that threshold was located; proofs were not independently verified.

progress.text: Czerwiński asks for a three-counter shortest-run lower bound beyond the exponential scale; the upper-bound discussion is historical.
The ICALP paper obtains a triple-exponential shortest-run upper bound and 2-EXPSPACE membership. Section 7 retains the question whether single-exponential runs suffice for binary 3-VASS.

Chen and coauthors state a doubly-exponential shortest-run upper bound and EXPSPACE membership in a new preprint. This review checked the model and theorem statements, not the full proof; the result does not supply the requested super-single-exponential lower bound.

cards.definitions: A three-dimensional vector addition system with states (3-VASS) is a finite set Q of control states and a finite transition set \(T\subseteq Q\times \mathbb{Z} ^{3}\times Q\). A configuration is \((q,u)\) with \(q\in Q\) and \(u\in \mathbb{N} ^{3}\), where \(\mathbb{N}\) includes zero. A transition \((q,a,q' )\) sends \((q,u)\) to \((q' ,u+a)\) only when every coordinate of \(u+a\) is nonnegative. There are no zero tests or counter bounds. A reachability instance I consists of Q,T and two configurations s,t. It is reachable if some finite sequence of enabled transitions sends s to t. Its shortest-run length \(\ell\)\((I)\) is the minimum number of transitions in such a sequence; the empty run is allowed, and \(\ell\)\((I)=0\) when \(s=t\). Unreachable instances are excluded from the quantified claim. N is the bit length of an explicit description: states are numbered, the transition list and the source and target are given explicitly, and all integer coordinates are written in signed binary (nonnegative binary for configurations), with delimiters and state indices included. Usual explicit binary-list encodings differ by polynomial factors, which do not affect existence of a \(2^{N^{O}(1)}\) bound. The dimension is always exactly three, while the number of states, transitions and counter magnitudes may grow. No finite-reachability-set promise or effective construction of the hard instances is required. The single-exponential convention and binary encoding follow the explicit later formulation in Section 7 of the 2025 source.

cards.formal: Is every equation valid in binary relations with union, intersection, composition, converse, constants \(0,1,\top\), and reflexive-transitive closure derivable from all valid closure-free equations in these operations together with the Kleene algebra axioms and induction rules specified below?
cards.why: This asks whether standard induction for iteration remains complete when programs can also be intersected and reversed as binary relations. sentences: Expressions denote binary relations using positive operations, converse and finite-path closure.
The target asks whether every relationally valid equation follows from a specified proof system.

cards.definitions: Expressions are finite terms over countably many relation variables using binary operations \(+\) (union), \(\cap\) (intersection), \(\cdot\) (composition), unary converse \((-)^{\circ}\), unary closure \((-)^*\), and constants \(0,1,\top\). On any set \(X\), variables denote arbitrary subsets of \(X\times X\). The constants denote the empty relation, the identity relation and \(X\times X\). Composition is \(R\cdot S=\{(x,z):\exists y\in X,\ (x,y)\in R\text{ and }(y,z)\in S\}\). Converse reverses each ordered pair. Closure is \(R^*=\bigcup_{n\geq0}R^n\), with \(R^0=1\) and \(R^{n+1}=R\cdot R^n\); it contains paths of every finite length, including zero. Complements and tests are absent. An equation is valid if it holds for every set \(X\), finite or infinite, and every assignment of its relation variables. Define \(u\leq v\) as the equation \(u+v=v\). The base axiom scheme consists of every valid equation whose expressions have no occurrence of \((-)^*\); it includes the interactions between union, intersection, converse and the constants. The Kleene algebra axioms make \((+,\cdot,0,1)\) an idempotent semiring: addition is associative, commutative and idempotent with identity zero; multiplication is associative with identity one, distributes over addition on both sides and has absorbing zero. The closure axioms are \(1+xx^*\leq x^*\) and \(1+x^*x\leq x^*\). The left induction rule infers \(x^*y\leq z\) from \(y+xz\leq z\); the right rule infers \(yx^*\leq z\) from \(y+zx\leq z\). Proofs are finite derivations using these schemes and rules, equality reflexivity, symmetry and transitivity, congruence for every operation, and uniform substitution of arbitrary expressions for variables. In particular, closure-bearing expressions may be substituted into closure-free axiom schemes. No other closure axiom, infinitary rule, relational-validity oracle for closure-bearing expressions or auxiliary operation is permitted.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof that this specified derivation system proves every relationally valid equation. Alternatively exhibit a valid equation and prove in Lean that it is not derivable in this system, for example using a model of all the axioms that refutes it. Decidability of relational validity alone, or a complete axiomatization of a proper signature fragment, does not establish completeness of these particular rules.

context_blocks.text: The source asks for axiomatizations and suggests adding Kleene algebra axioms to a complete closure-free relational calculus. Editorial specification: this card uses all valid closure-free laws in the full positive signature as the base. This explicitly includes interactions between union and intersection rather than leaving the interface between separate axiom systems ambiguous.

Without the specified base and rules, asking for an axiomatization would be too loose: declaring every valid equation an axiom gives no structural explanation. The target instead asks whether ordinary finitary Kleene induction accounts for all additional identities created by closure once the closure-free theory is available.

Intersection requires the same pair of endpoints to satisfy two relational conditions. It cannot generally be pushed through composition: \(R\cdot(S\cap T)\subseteq (R\cdot S)\cap(R\cdot T)\), but the reverse inclusion can fail because the two right-hand paths may use different intermediate points. Such interactions make relational closure more subtle than independent word-language iteration.

The 2018 paper records complete axiomatizations for important smaller signatures and explains why finite axiomatization of representable allegories is already delicate without closure. The target here deliberately permits an infinite closure-free axiom scheme and asks for relative completeness, rather than promising a finite list of all relational axioms.

Nakamura’s December 2025 journal article proves EXPSPACE-completeness of validity for the full positive signature, including identity, top, converse and closure. Its final discussion still distinguishes axiomatizability from the decision procedure. Thus an effective validity test does not by itself verify the relative proof system specified here.

The same later article cites a finite axiomatization for identity-free Kleene lattices. That result omits operations present in this card. It is retained as a boundary of known completeness results, not generalized to the full signature.

cards.title: Word problem for the S-combinator
cards.formal: Is convertibility of closed S-combinator terms decidable? Let \(\mathcal{T}\) be the least set with \(S\in\mathcal{T}\) and \((uv)\in\mathcal{T}\) whenever \(u,v\in\mathcal{T}\). The sole rewrite rule, applicable inside any term context, is \[(((Sx)y)z)\longrightarrow ((xz)(yz)),\qquad x,y,z\in\mathcal{T}.\] Does there exist a deterministic algorithm that halts on every pair \(p,q\in\mathcal{T}\) and decides whether they are connected by a finite sequence of forward or backward applications of this rule?
cards.why: The S-only fragment retains duplication and nonterminating behavior with just one combinator. Its word problem tests whether symbolic equality becomes decidable after removing the other primitives of combinatory logic, beyond the already-known ability to recognize normalizing terms.
cards.status_note: The original RTA list and the 2023 primary Satellite account leave this convertibility problem open. A bounded later-literature check on 13 September 2026 did not find a decision or undecidability theorem. Normalization results do not resolve this target; no exhaustive present-day certification is claimed.

definitions: A term is a finite ordered binary application tree whose leaves are all the one constant \(S\). Application is not associative; by convention \(uvw\) abbreviates \(((uv)w)\). There are no object-language variables, other combinator constants, lambda abstractions, types or infinitary terms. The letters \(x,y,z\) in the rule range over entire closed terms.

A one-hole context is built from a hole \(\square\) by repeatedly forming \((Ct)\) or \((tC)\), where \(t\in\mathcal{T}\) and \(C\) is a one-hole context. Write \(C[t]\) for replacing its hole by \(t\). A forward step is exactly \(C[(((Sx)y)z)]\to C[((xz)(yz))]\). Both appearances of \(z\) on the right are copies of the same finite tree.

Terms \(p,q\) are convertible when there exist \(m\geq0\) and closed terms \(t_0=p,\ldots,t_m=q\) such that, for each \(i<m\), either \(t_i\to t_{i+1}\) or \(t_{i+1}\to t_i\). This is the reflexive, symmetric and transitive closure of the contextual rewrite relation. No extensionality, eta law or identification merely by an infinitary semantic tree is added.

The two input trees are written explicitly, for example using prefix encodings \(\operatorname{enc}(S)=0\) and \(\operatorname{enc}(uv)=1\operatorname{enc}(u)\operatorname{enc}(v)\) with a delimiter between the two trees. A decider is one deterministic Turing machine halting on all valid pairs and outputting yes exactly on convertible pairs; malformed descriptions can be rejected. No time bound and no normalization promise are imposed.
cards.answer_criterion: A complete Lean-checked proof of decidability for all pairs of closed S-terms under this conversion relation, or a Lean-checked proof of undecidability. Deciding whether individual terms have normal forms, deciding only pairs of normalizing terms, or comparing a coarser semantic invariant is insufficient.

cards.title: Exact finite-iteration reachability for Bellman operators
cards.formal: Is there an algorithm that, given a finite rational Markov decision process with no end components, its reachability Bellman operator \(\Phi:[0,1]^d\to[0,1]^d\), and rational vectors \(s,t\in[0,1]^d\), decides whether \(\Phi^n(s)=t\) for some integer \(n\geq0\)? cards.why: Exact attainment is a sharper verification property than convergence of value iteration. Resolving it for Bellman operators would locate how much decidability survives the structured maxima of affine probability updates, beyond the already solved two-dimensional and single-policy cases.

cards.definitions: A Markov decision process (MDP) has finitely many states, a designated target sink \(g\), and a finite set of available actions at each other state. Sinks have no actions. Each available action \(a\) at state \(i\) has rational probabilities \(p(i,a,j)\geq0\), summing to one over all states \(j\). An end component consists of a nonempty state subset \(U\) and a nonempty choice of available actions at each state in \(U\), such that all their positive-probability successors stay in \(U\), and the directed graph of these chosen positive-probability transitions is strongly connected. The input promise excludes all such end components. Let \(Q=\{1,\ldots,d\}\) consist of the non-target states from which a path of positive-probability transitions to \(g\) exists. Other non-target states have reachability value zero and are omitted from the vector coordinates. For every \(i\in Q\), define \(L_{i,a}(x)=p(i,a,g)+\sum_{j\in Q}p(i,a,j)x_j\) and \(\Phi(x)_i=\max_{a\in\mathrm{Act}(i)}L_{i,a}(x)\). Each such action set is nonempty. The maximum is coordinatewise: different coordinates may attain it at different actions. All probabilities, the explicit transition tables and the vectors \(s,t\) are inputs with binary rational encodings; \(d\) is the number of retained coordinates. Iteration is \(\Phi^0(s)=s\) and \(\Phi^{n+1}(s)=\Phi(\Phi^n(s))\). Equality means equality of every rational coordinate at one finite iteration, without a numerical tolerance. An action is tight at a fixed point \(u\) when \(L_{i,a}(u)=u_i\). The no-end-component promise gives a unique fixed point and convergence of all iterations to it; no uniqueness of tight actions is assumed. A decision procedure is one deterministic Turing machine halting on every valid input; no time bound or bound on the witnessing \(n\) is imposed.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof of a terminating exact reachability algorithm on this entire promised class, or prove in Lean that the decision problem on this class is undecidable. Merely computing or approximating the fixed point, deciding whether a limit equals the target, or solving unrestricted matrix-semigroup reachability does not decide finite-iteration reachability of the specified Bellman operator.

context_blocks.text: Convergence does not imply that an iteration ever attains its limit. For \(\Phi(x)=(x+1)/2\), starting at zero produces \(1-2^{-n}\); the fixed point one is approached forever and never reached at a finite step. This scalar map is a valid reachability Bellman operator for a state that either repeats or reaches the target, each with probability one half.

The source proves decidability in arbitrary dimension when the requested vector differs from the unique fixed point. It also handles a fixed-point target when the starting vector is comparable to it coordinatewise, meaning all coordinates lie on the same side of their respective target values.

In dimension two, the paper resolves the remaining incomparable case as well. Thus the outstanding general question permits higher-dimensional starts with some coordinates above and others below their target values, and permits several tight actions.

If every coordinate has a unique tight action, the local fixed-point dynamics reduce to powers of one rational matrix. Proposition 27 gives a finite bound for testing whether these powers send a difference vector to zero. With multiple tight actions, the maximizing matrix can change during the iteration.

The associated matrices have nonnegative entries and row sums at most one. Their available rows can be chosen independently at each coordinate, forming the source’s product family. The resulting map takes coordinatewise maxima; it does not permit an arbitrary favorable sequence of matrices irrespective of those maxima.

The exclusion of end components is part of the target, not an incidental computational convenience. An MDP transformation preserving the least fixed point need not preserve the exact sequence of iterates from a supplied vector. General piecewise-affine undecidability results therefore require an actual reduction into this promised Bellman class before they could answer the question.

cards.formal: Does every finite, full, confluent first-order term-rewriting system \(R\) have a total computable one-step strategy \(F_R\) that reaches a normal form from every term having a normal form? sentences: The system has finitely many first-order rewrite rules and admits every term over its finite signature.
Confluence makes normal forms unique when they exist.
The question asks for a computable strategy that chooses exactly one available contraction from the current term.
The next-step computation must halt even on terms that never reach a normal form, without retaining an external history.
The strategy must nevertheless normalize every term for which some terminating reduction exists.

cards.definitions: A finite ranked signature \(\Sigma\) is a finite collection of function symbols with specified nonnegative integer arities. Terms are all finite ordered trees built from these symbols and a countably infinite set of variables; a variable is a leaf. “Full” means this entire term set is admitted, without a type, language or reachability restriction. A rule \(\ell\to r\) consists of terms, with \(\ell\) not a variable and every variable of \(r\) occurring in \(\ell\). The system \(R\) has finitely many rules. A substitution replaces variables by finite terms; a context is a term with one designated hole. One step \(C[\ell\sigma]\to_R C[r\sigma]\) contracts a single occurrence of a rule instance at any position. No simultaneous contractions, equations modulo which to match, or variable binding are included. Write \(\to_R^*\) for zero or more steps. Confluence means that whenever \(u\to_R^*v\) and \(u\to_R^*w\), there is \(z\) with \(v\to_R^*z\) and \(w\to_R^*z\); this is equivalent to the Church–Rosser property in the source. A normal form has no outgoing rewrite step. A term has a normal form if it reaches one by finitely many steps. The strategy \(F_R\) is a function on all terms, computable by an ordinary Turing machine from a finite tree encoding with numbered variables. It fixes every normal form and satisfies \(u\to_R F_R(u)\) for every other term, even when a permitted rewrite has identical input and output. It is total: computing the next step halts for every finite term. Normalization requires that for every term \(u\) having a normal form there is \(n\geq0\) such that \(F_R^n(u)\) is a normal form. There is no persistent history input or extra state carried between successive applications of \(F_R\). No time bound is required. The quantifiers are \(\forall R\,\exists F_R\,\forall u\); an algorithm synthesizing \(F_R\) uniformly from \(R\) is not additionally required.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof that every system satisfying the hypotheses admits such a total computable strategy. Alternatively exhibit a finite full confluent first-order system and prove in Lean that every total computable valid one-step strategy fails to normalize at least one term that has a normal form. A partial procedure that waits indefinitely on non-normalizable terms, a strategy with external memory, or a strategy allowed several contractions per output does not meet the stated conditions.

context_blocks.text: Confluence ensures that a term cannot have two different normal forms, but an arbitrary choice of reductions can still run forever. For example, the rules \(f(x)\to a\) and \(b\to b\) form a confluent system; \(f(b)\) has normal form \(a\), while repeatedly contracting its occurrence of \(b\) never reaches it.

A search can eventually discover a reduction to a normal form when one exists. That observation does not immediately produce the required total next-step function: on a term without a normal form, the strategy must still choose and return an available step in finite time.

Kennaway’s question combines finite generation, fullness and Church–Rosser confluence. The source reports counterexamples when these restrictions are dropped. This card selects its first-order term-rewriting formulation; the parenthetical extension to calculi with bound variables is not silently included.

The source records a positive result for weakly orthogonal systems: rules are left-linear, and nonvariable overlaps of rule instances give the same immediate reduct. The general question permits nontrivial overlaps, so that result does not establish the full proposition.

One-step and dependence only on the current term are substantive conditions. A procedure that remembers previously explored branches has a larger input state, while outputting a whole discovered reduction sequence changes the required interface. The question asks whether confluence always suffices under the more restrictive interface.

The RTALooP entry cites the later 1996 work on sequential reduction strategies. The source does not mark the general problem solved. Its historical dates identify the provenance of the question rather than certify the entire subsequent literature.

cards.title: Decidability of termination for one left- and right-linear term rule
cards.formal: Is there an algorithm that, given one first-order rewrite rule \(\ell\to r\) over a finite ranked signature, with both \(\ell\) and \(r\) linear, decides whether its unrestricted rewrite relation terminates on every finite term?
cards.why: The problem asks whether simultaneous linearity of the two sides imposes enough structure to make global termination decidable for a single rule. It probes how little rewrite syntax can already encode unbounded computation, beyond the established left-linear and string-only boundaries.
cards.status_note: The original source retains the left-and-right-linear one-rule termination question. The checked 2024 undecidability paper concerns existence of linear interpretation proofs, not the variable-linear termination property itself. No resolution of the exact latter question was located in the bounded 13 September 2026 later-work check.

importance.reason: A precise minimal-syntax decidability boundary for rewriting, retaining the existing score while distinguishing variable-linearity from restrictions on termination proof methods.

sentences: The input is one first-order rewrite rule whose left and right sides each use every variable at most once.
The rule may be applied at any position in any finite term, with ordinary syntactic substitutions.
The question asks whether an algorithm can decide absence of every infinite reduction sequence.
Left-linearity alone and the smaller string-rewriting subclass have different known boundaries.
Recent undecidability for linear-interpretation proof methods must not be confused with linearity of the rule itself.

cards.definitions: A ranked signature \(\Sigma\) consists of finitely many function symbols with specified nonnegative integer arities. Terms are finite ordered trees over \(\Sigma\) and a countably infinite set of variables. A term is linear if each variable occurs at most once in that term; occurrences are counted separately on the two sides of a rule. The left side \(\ell\) must not be a variable and every variable of \(r\) must occur in \(\ell\); variables may be erased, but may not be duplicated on either side or newly introduced on the right. A substitution maps variables to finite terms. A one-step rewrite replaces one occurrence of \(\ell\sigma\) by \(r\sigma\) inside an arbitrary term context, for some substitution \(\sigma\). The same single rule may be used at any position and any number of times. Matching is syntactic; no equations, types, binding operations or restrictions such as innermost-only rewriting are present. Termination means there is no infinite chain \(u_0\to u_1\to u_2\to\cdots\) starting from any finite term, including terms with variables. It is not only existence of one terminating reduction, termination from one designated input, or absence of short cycles. If a rewrite returns the same term, it is still a step and can witness nontermination by repetition. The finite signature, symbol arities, variables and both finite term trees are explicitly encoded and form the algorithm’s input. A decision algorithm is one deterministic Turing machine that halts on every valid input rule and answers the global termination question exactly; no complexity bound is required.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof of a terminating decision algorithm for every valid rule linear on both sides, or prove in Lean that this restricted global termination problem is undecidable. A single nonterminating example does not prove undecidability. A decision procedure for string rules, a bounded search for loops, or a test for whether one specific interpretation proves termination does not settle the full proposition.

context_blocks.text: Linearity controls variable repetition, not the number of function symbols. Both \(f(x)\to x\) and \(f(x)\to f(f(x))\) are linear on each side. The first decreases term size at every step and terminates; the second can grow forever. Thus the input class includes both possible answers even with unary function symbols.

Dauchet’s 1991 question explicitly requires both left and right linearity. The source cites undecidability for one rule with only left linearity, so omitting the right-side restriction would replace the open question by a known harder model.

One-rule string rewriting is a special case, represented by unary function symbols with a shared tail variable. Its unresolved termination question is therefore related but does not cover the branching first-order terms admitted here. The source separately discusses confluence, which is another property and is not part of the present target.

The 2024 paper Linear Termination is Undecidable studies whether termination can be certified by linear polynomial interpretations. Here “linear” describes the proof interpretation, whereas this card uses it for occurrence of variables in a rule. The paper’s undecidability result is not a resolution of the question merely because the titles share the word linear.

Indeed, that paper can make the interpretation-existence question undecidable even within systems already known to terminate by another polynomial interpretation. This emphasizes the difference between deciding actual termination and deciding whether a particular proof method succeeds.

Global termination quantifies over every finite term and every choice of redex. A collection of successful test reductions or the absence of a repeated term in bounded exploration does not establish it. Likewise, a rule may fail to terminate by unbounded growth without ever repeating a term.

cards.title: A coanalytic upper bound for fair almost-sure termination
cards.formal: Does fair almost-sure termination for finitely branching probabilistic nondeterministic Turing machines admit a computable many-one reduction to well-foundedness of primitive-recursive trees on \(\mathbb N\)? That is, is there one total computable map sending each machine/input pair \((M,w)\) to such a tree \(T_{M,w}\) with \(M\) terminating with probability one under every fair scheduler exactly when \(T_{M,w}\) has no infinite branch?
cards.why: The target locates how much logical complexity fairness adds to probabilistic termination. A reduction to well-founded trees would connect general FAST reasoning to the established coanalytic framework; a negative answer would show that those certificates cannot cover this model through any computable translation.
cards.status_note: The July 2025 source leaves the complexity of its strong-fairness FAST model unspecified. The card explicitly selects the coanalytic upper-bound variant, rather than attributing it verbatim to the source author. The checked PAST classification and 2026 weak-fairness rules do not establish it; no matching general reduction or impossibility theorem was located in the bounded September 2026 check.

category_assignment.reason: The question concerns program termination under fair probabilistic scheduling and complete proof methods.

importance.reason: The existing specialist score is retained for this precise strong-fairness model; its specific significance is the logical complexity of probability-one termination under unrestricted history-dependent schedulers.

sentences: The machine combines finite nondeterministic choices with rational probabilistic choices and unbounded tape memory.
Schedulers may use arbitrary histories, but must satisfy strong fairness on every supported infinite execution.
FAST requires probability-one termination under each such fair scheduler, without an expected-runtime bound.
This card selects the precise question of a computable reduction to well-foundedness of primitive-recursive trees.
Known results for positive almost-sure termination and weakly fair distributed protocols have different hypotheses.

cards.definitions: A machine has a finite control, a finite tape alphabet with a blank symbol, one unbounded tape initially containing the finite input \(w\), and a head position. Nonhalting control states are probabilistic or nondeterministic. Each has a fixed finite nonempty set of actions. An action is a total finite table indexed by the currently scanned symbol, prescribing a symbol to write, a head move by at most one cell and the next control state. Thus an available action is enabled whenever its origin control state is visited. A probabilistic state also has a fixed rational distribution of strictly positive probabilities over its actions; these choices are sampled independently conditional on the execution history. Deterministic behavior is represented by a single action of probability one. Halting states have no actions. A scheduler is any function from finite execution histories ending at a nondeterministic state to an available action. Histories include the configurations and actions taken. Schedulers are deterministic but need not be computable and may use the entire history. A scheduler is fair from the given initial configuration if, on every infinite execution consistent with it and the probabilistic action supports, every nondeterministic action whose origin state occurs infinitely often is itself taken infinitely often. This is pathwise strong fairness, including individual infinite paths of probability zero. The scheduler induces the usual probability measure on executions, with finite-prefix probabilities given by products of the rational choices. Fair almost-sure termination (FAST) means that every fair scheduler gives probability one to reaching a halting state. It imposes no bound on expected running time. Machine tables, rational probabilities and input words have finite binary encodings. A tree on \(\mathbb N\) is a prefix-closed subset of finite sequences of natural numbers. It is presented by a primitive-recursive membership predicate: a finite expression built from zero, successor and projections using composition and primitive recursion, with a fixed effective encoding of sequences. An infinite branch is a function \(b:\mathbb N\to\mathbb N\) whose every finite prefix belongs to the tree. Well-foundedness means no such branch exists. Branching is not restricted to two children or any fixed finite bound. The reduction must halt on every valid machine/input pair and output a valid predicate for a prefix-closed tree; no resource bound on the reduction is required.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof of a total computable reduction satisfying the displayed equivalence for all machine/input pairs, or prove in Lean that no such reduction exists. Requiring computable schedulers, fairness only with probability one, weak fairness, finite expected time, or finitely branching witness trees changes the problem. Sound proof rules for selected program classes alone do not establish this universal reduction.

context_blocks.text: The source asks both for the recursion-theoretic complexity of FAST and for sound complete reasoning techniques. Editorial specialization: this card selects the coanalytic upper-bound question, expressed concretely as a reduction to tree well-foundedness. It does not present a conjectured upper bound as a theorem or claim that this choice already supplies a Hoare-style proof system.

Fairness rules out indefinitely ignoring an action at a control state revisited infinitely often. It still permits arbitrarily long finite postponements. Requiring this property on every supported infinite execution is stronger than requiring that unfair executions merely have probability zero.

The source reports \(\Pi^1_1\)-completeness for the corresponding non-probabilistic fair-termination problem. Well-foundedness of recursive, arbitrarily branching trees is the standard complete problem at that coanalytic level; the reduction target makes the prospective upper-bound question precise.

Probability-one termination permits exceptional nonterminating executions of probability zero. It is therefore weaker than termination on every path, even though the scheduler’s fairness requirement in this card quantifies over every supported infinite path. These two uses of quantification must not be conflated.

The 2023 positive-almost-sure-termination work proves a \(\Pi^1_1\)-complete classification for a different property: finite expected runtime for each scheduler, without the same fair-scheduler restriction. That theorem does not automatically classify FAST.

The 2026 distributed-algorithm verification paper supplies sound rules combining probabilistic reasoning with weak fairness and applies them to consensus protocols. Those applications are important evidence of useful techniques, but its stated soundness and fairness convention do not prove the universal strong-fairness reduction requested here.

cards.title: P versus NC
cards.formal: Is \(\mathrm{P}=\mathrm{NC}\), where NC consists of decision languages recognized by logspace-uniform Boolean circuit families of polynomial size and polylogarithmic depth? Equivalently, does the Circuit Value Problem have such a circuit family?
cards.definitions: P is deterministic polynomial time on ordinary Turing machines. For \(\mathrm{L}\in \mathrm{NC}\) there must be fixed constants c,k,C and a family \((C_{n})_{n}\ge 0\) such that \(C_{n}\) decides membership in L correctly on every n-bit input, has at most \(C(n+2)^{c}\) gates, and has depth at most \(C(\log _{2}(n+2))^{k}\). Gates are two-input AND and OR and one-input NOT; fan-out is unrestricted and one output bit is designated. Depth is the longest input-to-output gate path. A deterministic \(O(\log (n+2))\)-space transducer given \(1^{n}\) must output the description of \(C_{n}\); its polynomial output bound is part of the size requirement. Constants and the generator may depend on L but not on n. Circuit Value receives an explicit topologically ordered Boolean gate DAG, its input-bit values, and an output-gate index; it asks whether that gate evaluates to 1. Its input length n is the entire binary encoding length, and malformed encodings are rejected. No randomization, advice, oracle, or restriction to monotone gates is permitted. In this statement, “explicitly given/encoded/listed” means the entire finite list, table or syntax tree described above is part of the input or output, with its full encoding counted; it does not mean a circuit, oracle or program generating a larger object.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove that every language in P has a logspace-uniform family of polynomial-size, polylogarithmic-depth circuits, or prove that some language in P has no such family. By the stated completeness result, the affirmative answer is equivalent to Circuit Value belonging to NC, and the negative answer to Circuit Value not belonging to NC. Excluding only one fixed depth exponent, nonuniform monotone circuits, or one evaluation procedure does not establish \(\mathrm{P}\ne \mathrm{NC}\).
cards.why: This asks whether a feasible computation can require intrinsically many sequential stages even when polynomially many processors are available. It is the central unresolved premise behind P-completeness as an explanation for resistance to parallelization, spanning graph algorithms, simulation, optimization, and language processing.

importance.reason: The foundational tractability question for parallel computation: whether every polynomial-time task admits polylogarithmic dependency depth with polynomial work.

progress.text: Ladner establishes that Circuit Value is logspace complete for P, giving a concrete universal target for efficient parallelization.
Greenlaw, Hoover, and Ruzzo organize the theory of P-completeness and its open P-versus-NC question, including uniform circuit and parallel-machine formulations.
Raz and McKenzie prove monotone \(\mathrm{NC}\ne\)monotone P and a strict monotone NC hierarchy. These results restrict the gates used by the computing circuits.

Cavalar and coauthors prove perfect matching requires monotone circuit size \(2^{n^{\Omega (1)}}\), improving Razborov’s quasipolynomial lower bound. The November 2025 revision appears in STOC 2026; general Boolean circuits are not covered.

cards.status_note: The primary P-completeness monograph and subsequent-result searches were checked on 11 September 2026. No unrestricted resolution of P versus logspace-uniform NC was found. The \(2025/2026\) matching lower bound concerns monotone circuits and therefore does not resolve the stated \(\mathrm{AND}/\mathrm{OR}/\mathrm{NOT}\) model.

context_blocks.text: Circuit evaluation makes the apparent obstacle concrete. A sequential algorithm visits the gates in their supplied topological order and computes every value in polynomial time. The question is whether the Boolean function described by an arbitrary such circuit always has an efficiently constructible, much shallower evaluation circuit. Depth of the supplied circuit and depth of an algorithm that evaluates it are different quantities.

For example, a long chain that successively ANDs input bits can be replaced by a balanced tree of AND gates with logarithmic depth. Thus a long chain in the input is not by itself a lower bound on the time needed to evaluate it. Circuit Value allows arbitrary sharing and combinations of gate types, rather than promising this particular associative form.

Ladner proved Circuit Value complete for P under logarithmic-space reductions. These reductions themselves admit NC computation, and NC is closed under their composition. An NC algorithm for this one problem would therefore parallelize every problem in P. P-completeness supplies this conditional consequence; it does not already prove the absence of a parallel algorithm.

The resource tradeoff is polynomial total circuit size against polylogarithmic dependency depth. The exponent of the polynomial work budget may be large, so a positive answer would not automatically provide nearly linear work or useful speedups on a small machine. Logspace uniformity prevents the circuit descriptions from supplying arbitrary nonuniform information. The union over all fixed depth exponents also makes this broader than asking whether P equals \(\mathrm{NC}^{1}\).

Restricted circuit models reveal real obstructions. Raz and McKenzie separate monotone NC from monotone P, and separate consecutive levels of the monotone NC hierarchy. Their lower bounds restrict the computing circuit to AND and OR. cards.context:
Circuit evaluation makes the apparent obstacle concrete. A sequential algorithm visits the gates in their supplied topological order and computes every value in polynomial time. The question is whether the Boolean function described by an arbitrary such circuit always has an efficiently constructible, much shallower evaluation circuit. Depth of the supplied circuit and depth of an algorithm that evaluates it are different quantities.

For example, a long chain that successively ANDs input bits can be replaced by a balanced tree of AND gates with logarithmic depth. Thus a long chain in the input is not by itself a lower bound on the time needed to evaluate it. Circuit Value allows arbitrary sharing and combinations of gate types, rather than promising this particular associative form.

Ladner proved Circuit Value complete for P under logarithmic-space reductions. These reductions themselves admit NC computation, and NC is closed under their composition. An NC algorithm for this one problem would therefore parallelize every problem in P. P-completeness supplies this conditional consequence; it does not already prove the absence of a parallel algorithm.

The resource tradeoff is polynomial total circuit size against polylogarithmic dependency depth. The exponent of the polynomial work budget may be large, so a positive answer would not automatically provide nearly linear work or useful speedups on a small machine. Logspace uniformity prevents the circuit descriptions from supplying arbitrary nonuniform information. The union over all fixed depth exponents also makes this broader than asking whether P equals \(\mathrm{NC}^{1}\).

Restricted circuit models reveal real obstructions. Raz and McKenzie separate monotone NC from monotone P, and separate consecutive levels of the monotone NC hierarchy. Their lower bounds restrict the computing circuit to AND and OR. A monotone function can still have a substantially more powerful circuit when NOT gates are allowed, so the restriction cannot be removed from the conclusion.

Recent matching lower bounds sharpen this caution. Cavalar and coauthors prove a stretched-exponential monotone circuit-size lower bound for perfect matching, a problem with polynomial-time general algorithms. cards.title: Directed reachability with nearly linear memory and polylogarithmic passes
cards.formal: Do there exist constants a,b,C and a uniform randomized streaming algorithm that decides directed s–t reachability on every n-vertex graph using at most \(Cn(\log (n+2))^{a}\) bits of memory and \(C(\log (n+2))^{b}\) passes, with success probability at least \(2/3\) for every adversarially ordered edge stream?
cards.definitions: The input is a finite simple directed graph on the labelled vertex set \([n], n\ge 2\), with distinct designated vertices s,t. The algorithm knows n,s,t before reading the edges. Each directed edge occurs once in an insertion-only stream, in an arbitrary order fixed independently of the algorithm’s random bits. Each pass scans this same stream in the same forward order. The input is read-only: there are no adjacency queries, random-access reads, sorting operations on external storage, or writable auxiliary streams. All mutable working storage counts toward the bit bound; fresh independent random bits may be read from a one-way random source. The memory and pass bounds hold on every execution. Computation between successive input items is unrestricted but must terminate; no running-time bound beyond termination is imposed. A yes answer means that there is a directed path from s to t in the input graph. The constants and algorithm are independent of n, the graph, and the edge order.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove that one uniform randomized decision algorithm has simultaneous \(O(n \log ^{a}(n+2))\)-bit space and \(O(\log ^{b}(n+2))\)-pass bounds for fixed constants a,b on every execution, and success probability at least \(2/3\) on every fixed graph and edge order. Alternatively, prove that no such algorithm and constants exist. Ruling out a fixed pass count, requiring the output of a path, or restricting computation between stream items does not establish the stated negation.
cards.why: Determine whether global directed reachability can be recovered from repeated sequential scans with only nearly linear memory, a central unresolved graph-streaming tradeoff.

importance.reason: A basic directed-graph primitive with a polynomial-versus-polylogarithmic pass gap, connections to communication lower bounds and consequences for other streaming tasks.

context_blocks.text: Directed reachability asks an elementary question: can one vertex eventually lead to another by following arrows? With the whole graph in memory, a search answers it in linear time. In a graph stream, the difficulty is that the next useful edge may already have gone past before the algorithm learns that its tail is reachable. Repeated scans provide another opportunity to use the edge, but every scan revisits the entire input.

Nearly linear memory means linear in the number of vertices, up to powers of a logarithm. It can store labels, several values per vertex and a sparse auxiliary graph, but a dense input may have quadratically many edges. The card allows every fixed polylogarithmic memory overhead: it does not ask for an especially restrictive exact n-bit implementation. Conversely, allowing storage proportional to all the edges would erase the intended obstacle.

A simple baseline maintains the set of vertices already reached from s. Whenever an edge leaves this set, its head is marked reachable. After at most \(n- 1\) scans every reachable vertex has been found, using a bit per vertex and counters. A path whose edges appear in reverse path order makes this particular algorithm advance slowly. That example is not a lower bound for all algorithms: a path has only linearly many edges and fits entirely in the permitted memory.

The undirected analogue has a much stronger one-pass solution: maintain connected components with union–find. Direction removes the equivalence-relation structure that makes this summary sufficient. Strongly connected components can still be contracted in a digraph, but their directed reachability relation is another graph rather than just a partition. A small summary must somehow preserve the information needed for the specified source and target.

Jambulapati, Liu and Sidford give a randomized parallel reachability algorithm using nearly linear work and \(n^{1/2+o(1)}\) depth. Their shortcut construction can also be implemented in the streaming model. Assadi and coauthors explicitly state the resulting \(n^{1/2+o(1)}\)-pass semi-streaming path-finding algorithm as Proposition 4. This supplies the relevant upper bound through a concrete simulation, rather than through an assumption that every shallow parallel computation automatically yields a streaming algorithm.

A reachability-preserving shortcut is an extra arc \((u,v)\) added only when the original graph already contains a directed path from u to v. Such arcs can reduce the number of edges in a path without changing which vertices are reachable. The cited streaming upper bound constructs and uses a sparse collection within its memory budget; its pass guarantee is part of that implementation, not a consequence of the existence of shortcuts alone.

On the lower-bound side, Guruswami and Onak extend earlier path-output barriers to the decision problem itself. Their multipass space bound implies that semi-streaming reachability requires \(\Omega (\log  n/\log  \log  n)\) passes. The exact theorem includes polynomial factors in the pass count and logarithmic factors in n; these should not be dropped when comparing parameters. The conclusion rules out constant passes but leaves the polylogarithmic target available.

Chen, Kol, Paramonov, Saxena, Song and Yu prove that \(o(\sqrt{\log  n})\) passes require \(n^{2- o(1)}\) space. This is a striking strengthening of how much memory is necessary when the pass budget is very small. It is not a larger asymptotic lower bound on the number of passes with nearly linear memory than the \(\Omega (\log  n/\log  \log  n)\) statement above. The two results describe different parts of the tradeoff.

Azarmehr and coauthors’ September 9, 2026 revision still identifies \(n^{1/2+o(1)}\) as the fastest known semi-streaming reachability pass bound. Their Theorem 9 links an improved streaming approximation for distance to monotonicity to an improved reachability algorithm. This is evidence that the question controls progress beyond reachability itself, and gives a recent explicit check of the benchmark used on this card.

A positive answer would show that repeated sequential access with a compact memory can recover global directed information surprisingly quickly. A negative answer would establish a fundamental barrier to that access pattern, even without restricting local computation time. Either result would help explain the difference between graph problems admitting compact summaries and those that require many rounds of discovering dependencies.

cards.title: Perfect matching in NC
cards.formal: Do there exist constants \(C,a,b>0\) and a logspace-uniform family of Boolean circuits which, on the adjacency matrix of every n-vertex simple undirected graph, output a perfect matching or correctly report that none exists, with at most \(C(n+2)^{a}\) gates and depth at most \(C(\log _{2}(n+2))^{b}\)?
cards.why: I include this because perfect matching is a basic polynomial-time graph problem for which randomization and parallelism interact in a particularly sharp way. The question asks whether randomness is needed to find globally compatible choices quickly, and whether the structural tools for odd cycles can be made as parallel as the algebraic ones.
cards.definitions: The input is the \(n\times n\) binary adjacency matrix of a graph on \([n]\), with symmetry and zero diagonal promised. A perfect matching is a set of edges with exactly one edge incident to each vertex. Output is a flag and an \(n\times n\) binary incidence matrix for the chosen matching; when the flag reports nonexistence the remaining output bits are ignored. The empty graph has the empty perfect matching. Circuits use fan-in-two \(\mathrm{AND}/\mathrm{OR}\), fan-in-one NOT, constants 0,1 and unrestricted fan-out. Depth counts gates on the longest input-output path and size counts gates; the \(n^{2}\) output positions are specified as part of the description. A deterministic Turing transducer on unary input \(1^{n}\) writes the description using \(O(\log _{2}(n+2))\) work bits, with read-only input and write-only output. Constants and generator are fixed across n; every valid input must receive an exact answer. No randomness, oracle, advice, bipartiteness or other structural graph promise is supplied.

progress.text: The randomized parallel approach of Mulmuley, Vazirani, and Vazirani uses isolation to single out a matching. Svensson and Tarnawski review this starting point and the need to derandomize it.

Svensson and Tarnawski give a deterministic general-graph algorithm in $O(\log^3 n)$ parallel time with $n^{O(\log^2 n)}$ processors. It achieves quasi-NC, leaving a quasipolynomial-versus-polynomial resource gap.
Chakraborty and coauthors’ revision constructs maximum matchings in general graphs in polynomial-time catalytic logspace. The restored auxiliary-memory model does not by itself yield ordinary NC.
The bipartite NC preprint reaches revision 2, covering weighted and search versions and extending to linear matroid intersection. General-graph matching is outside the stated theorem.

cards.status_note: The general quasi-NC result, the bipartite preprint’s revision 2 of 15 July 2026, and the catalytic-logspace revision of 1 June 2026 were checked on 11 September 2026. Subsequent-result searches found no deterministic NC search algorithm for arbitrary graphs. The newly cited preprint proofs have not been independently audited.

context_blocks.text: A polynomial-time sequential algorithm is known, so the issue is how many dependent stages remain when the work is spread across many processors. Polynomial total size is essential: evaluating exponentially many candidate matchings in parallel is outside NC. The output requirement is also explicit. The circuit must select a set of edges forming one matching, or certify nonexistence with its output flag.

Choosing matching edges independently can give incompatible decisions. On a four-cycle, deleting any one edge leaves a perfect matching. Deleting all four edges at once leaves none. This small example distinguishes a collection of individually valid existence statements from the coordinated selection required for a search output.

General graphs also need more structure than the bipartite case. Two disjoint triangles have an even total number of vertices and admit a fractional assignment of one half to every edge, giving total incident weight one at each vertex. They have no perfect matching. This example shows why degree constraints alone do not describe the general matching polytope; odd vertex sets impose additional conditions.

The June 2026 bipartite preprint, updated on 15 July, gives NC algorithms for bipartite matching and extends the results to search and weighted variants and to linear matroid intersection. Its scope restriction matters: an arbitrary graph need not be bipartite. The July revision does not state the general-graph theorem asked here.

A separate June 2026 revision places maximum-matching construction in general graphs in polynomial-time catalytic logspace. Catalytic space means a larger auxiliary memory tape may begin in an arbitrary state and must be restored on termination. This additional resource is different from ordinary logarithmic workspace, and the result does not establish an NC circuit family. It is a nearby complexity improvement whose model must remain attached to its conclusion.

The 2017 quasi-NC result already obtains polylogarithmic parallel time, but permits \(n^{O(\log ^{2} n)}\) processors. Such a quantity eventually exceeds every fixed polynomial. The open gap is therefore the total resource bound for arbitrary graphs, not simply finding any parallel algorithm with a short dependency chain.

cards.title: Distributed Lovász Local Lemma in \(O(\log  \log  n)\) rounds
cards.formal: Does there exist an integer \(c\ge 2\) such that, for every fixed integer \(d\ge 2, a\) uniform randomized LOCAL algorithm \(A_{d}\) and a constant \(K_{d}\) solve every n-event variable Lovász Local Lemma instance of dependency degree at most d and maximum bad-event probability p with \(p\cdot d^{c}<1/2\), within \(K_{d}(1+\log _{2}\log _{2}(n+2))\) rounds, with probability at least \(1- n^{- 3}\) of avoiding all bad events simultaneously?
cards.why: The question asks whether sparse dependencies can always be resolved within a log-logarithmic communication radius under fixed polynomial slack. This would determine the complexity of a widely used distributed primitive and clarify a central scale in the LOCAL complexity hierarchy.
cards.status_note: The original conjecture, primary distributed bounds, the 2025 locality result and the August 2026 resilient-LLL paper were checked on 11 September 2026. No result settling the exact bounded-degree \(O(\log  \log  n)\) worst-case target was found. The fixed factor \(1/2\) and order of slack/degree quantifiers preserve the saved precise interpretation. Node averages and results for stronger communication models are not substituted for this guarantee.

cards.definitions: There are \(n\ge 2\) bad events, each a predicate on a specified finite subset of finitely many mutually independent variables. Each variable has a finite nonempty alphabet and a rational probability distribution; event predicates and distributions are given by finite tables. Variables occurring in no event can be omitted. Two distinct event nodes are adjacent exactly when their variable sets intersect; this graph is the communication network. Its maximum degree is at most d. The number p is the largest probability of an event under the product of the specified distributions. Each node initially knows n,d, its own event table, its variables and their distributions, its neighbours and their identifiers. Node identifiers are distinct integers in \([n^{2}]\); shared variables have consistent names. LOCAL means synchronous rounds with arbitrarily long finite messages in each direction on each edge, and unrestricted terminating local computation. Nodes have private independent fair random bits. A single finite program is used at all nodes, independently of n and the instance. Each node outputs one value for each of its variables. Success requires agreement on shared variables and falsity of every event. The round bound holds on every random tape; the success probability is over all node coins for each fixed instance and identifier assignment. Constants and the algorithm may depend on d; the slack exponent c is chosen before d. No preprocessing using the full instance is supplied. The factor \(1/2\) removes the low-degree ambiguity recorded in the source conjecture.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove that some fixed integer \(c\ge 2\) admits, for every fixed \(d\ge 2\), algorithms \(A_{d}\) and constants \(K_{d}\) with the stated round and global-success bounds on all eligible instances. Alternatively, prove that for every candidate c there is a fixed d for which no such algorithm and constant exist. An obstruction at one slack exponent alone does not refute the existential choice of c. Bounds averaged over nodes, expected round bounds, or a higher fixed power of log log n do not meet the stated guarantee.

context_blocks.text: The Lovász Local Lemma concerns many individually unlikely failures that share only limited dependencies. In a variable instance, a bad event is a condition on some independent random variables. The goal is to choose the variables so that none of these conditions holds. The distributed question asks how quickly processors located at the events can agree on such choices when communication follows the dependency graph.

For an illustrative instance, independently color the vertices of a hypergraph red or blue, and let each hyperedge define the bad event that all its vertices receive the same color. A hyperedge containing k vertices is monochromatic with probability \(2^{1- k}\). Events are adjacent when their hyperedges share a vertex. A successful assignment is a two-coloring with no monochromatic hyperedge. This example explains the objects; the card allows arbitrary finite event tables, rather than only coloring events.

Small individual probabilities do not mean that one simultaneous random assignment succeeds with high probability globally. Even n mutually independent events of probability p are all avoided with probability \((1- p)^{n}\), which can be tiny. The LLL guarantees existence in a suitable probability-and-dependency regime. A distributed algorithm must obtain a globally valid assignment with the much stronger success guarantee stated on the card.

The slack condition \(p\cdot d^{c}<1/2\) is deliberately stronger than the usual existence threshold. One universal constant c must work before the degree bound d is chosen; choosing an exponent that grows with n would answer a different question. Each d is fixed while n grows, so constants in the round bound may depend on d. This bounded-degree convention is essential to interpreting the conjecture.

In LOCAL, messages have no bandwidth limit, but information still crosses only one dependency edge per round. After r rounds a node can depend only on information and random choices within its r-hop neighborhood. Shared variables also require agreement: two neighboring event processors cannot assign different colors to the same underlying variable and count that as a solution.

Fischer and Ghaffari gave a sublogarithmic algorithm under polynomially strengthened criteria. Subsequent derandomization tools and Davies’s algorithm yield bounds of the form \(O(d/\log  d + (\log  \log  n)^{O(1)})\) in the relevant regime. For fixed d this is polynomial in log log n, but it does not give a bound linear in log log n. The conjecture targets that remaining distinction.

The 2025 locality paper gives an \(O(\log  \log _{1/p} n)\) node-averaged guarantee while retaining a larger worst-case round bound. The average measures how long a typical node remains active; it can be small while a few nodes keep working. This card requires every node to finish within the same \(O(\log  \log  n)\) budget. Results for local-computation queries, MPC or the congested clique also have different access and communication rules.

The 2026 resilient-LLL paper broadens the coloring applications with polynomial-log-log round algorithms. It also distinguishes those applications from unrestricted dependency degree. Its broader general-LLL question must not erase the bounded-degree upper bounds already known here. Lower bounds from sinkless orientation explain why log log n is a central scale, with the precise LLL criterion relevant when transferring such a bound.

The question has broad consequences because distributed conflict-resolution tasks can be expressed as avoiding overlapping bad events. Chang and Pettie’s connection to locally checkable labeling problems gives the LLL a structural role in distributed complexity, beyond its use in any one coloring algorithm.
