cards.title: Optimal exact single-source shortest paths in CONGEST
cards.formal: For every fixed integer \(b\ge 1\), do there exist constants \(K,c>0\) and a uniform randomized CONGEST algorithm which, on every connected simple undirected graph with \(n\ge 2\) vertices, integer edge weights in \([0,n^{b}]\) and a designated source s, makes every vertex output its exact weighted distance from s in at most \(K(\sqrt{n}+D)(\log _{2}(n+2))^{c}\) rounds on every execution, with simultaneous correctness probability at least \(1- n^{- 3}\)? Here D is the diameter of the unweighted graph.
cards.why: This asks whether exact weighted shortest distances can be computed as quickly as the general communication lower bound permits, up to logarithmic factors. It separates the cost of exact optimization from the costs of network diameter and limited link bandwidth.
cards.status_note: Primary exact CONGEST bounds, randomized distance lower bounds, the approximation result and later-result searches were checked on 11 September 2026. No algorithm or impossibility theorem settling the full stated polylogarithmic-overhead target was found. The inherited 2026 paper is retained as related-work provenance, rather than used alone as evidence of the current best bound.
cards.review_note: User-approved research proposal, imported as a short draft. Its importance was assessed editorially; the full research-card standard has not yet been completed.

progress.text: Das Sarma and coauthors establish randomized communication lower bounds for exact and approximate distance problems, giving the \(\tilde\{\Omega\}(\sqrt{n}+D)\) lower-bound benchmark.
Chechik–Mukhtar obtain \(\tilde\{O\}(\sqrt{n} D^{1/4}+D)\) rounds for exact weighted SSSP.
Rozhoň and coauthors give near-optimal deterministic distributed algorithms for \((1+\varepsilon )\)-approximate undirected distances, with accuracy-dependent complexity.
Cao–Fineman give \(\tilde\{O\}(n^{2/5+o(1)}D^{2/5}+\sqrt{n}+D)\) rounds for polynomially bounded weights, including an improvement in the intermediate-diameter comparison.
The programmable-matter article retains a CONGEST gap in related work. Its own communication model and theorems are different, and that summary does not include the 2023 bound above.

cards.definitions: A path length is the sum of its edge weights; the distance is the minimum path length, and the source distance is zero. D is the maximum over vertex pairs of the minimum number of edges on a path between them. The graph itself is the network. In each synchronous round, each endpoint of each edge can send at most \(B\lceil \log _{2}(n+2)\rceil\) bits to the other endpoint, for a constant B depending only on b. Nodes initially know n,b, the source identifier, their own identifiers, and the identifiers and weights of incident neighbours. Identifiers are distinct integers in \([n^{2}]\). Local computation and memory are unrestricted, but each local computation between rounds terminates. Nodes use independent private fair random bits. One finite program, allowed to depend on b, runs at all nodes; no global graph description, advice, routing tables or preprocessing is supplied. The graph, weights, source and identifiers are fixed before randomness is drawn. Output at v is an ordinary binary integer for \(\operatorname{dist}(s,v)\), stored locally. The guarantee concerns all vertices together, over all coins. All communication, including finding termination and any preprocessing, counts in the round bound. K,c,B are independent of n,D and the instance; no value of D is initially supplied.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove that for every fixed weight exponent b there is a single uniform algorithm meeting the stated \(O((\sqrt{n}+D)\operatorname{polylog} n)\) round bound on every execution and the simultaneous \(1- n^{- 3}\) correctness probability on every eligible network. Alternatively, prove that this is impossible for at least one fixed b, for every choice of algorithm and fixed constants K,c,B. An approximation guarantee, an \(n^{o(1)}\) overhead not bounded by a fixed power of log n, or a result for only one diameter regime is not the stated affirmative answer.

context_blocks.text: Every vertex must learn its distance from one designated source, measured by the sum of edge weights. The processors sit at the vertices and can communicate only along the graph’s edges. The question is about the number of synchronous communication rounds, rather than the time a single processor would spend on an adjacency-list representation.

There are two different notions of distance. If s is joined directly to v by an edge of weight 10, but a two-edge route has weights 2 and 2, the weighted distance is 4 even though v is one communication hop from s. The parameter D ignores weights and measures the largest hop distance between vertices. A minimum-weight path can contain many more edges than a minimum-hop path.

Each edge transports only \(O(\log  n)\) bits per direction in one round, while different edges can communicate simultaneously. A distance fits in \(O(\log  n)\) bits because weights are polynomially bounded, but many different pieces of information may need the same link. The \(\sqrt{n}\) term in the benchmark reflects a bandwidth obstacle in worst-case networks; the D term reflects how far information has to travel.

The requested output is distributed: vertex v stores \(\operatorname{dist}(s,v)\). Collecting all distances at s, printing full paths, or making every vertex learn the whole distance table would impose additional communication requirements. Conversely, a local estimate that is merely close to the shortest distance is not the exact output required here.

Chechik and Mukhtar give an exact randomized bound \(\tilde\{O\}(\sqrt{n} D^{1/4}+D)\), where the tilde hides factors polynomial in log n. Their theorem also handles directed weighted graph inputs over an undirected communication network, so it covers the undirected case retained on this card. The extra \(D^{1/4}\) factor is not absorbed by the logarithmic allowance when D grows polynomially with n.

Cao and Fineman’s 2023 theorem supplies another bound, \(\tilde\{O\}(n^{2/5+o(1)}D^{2/5}+\sqrt{n}+D)\), for polynomially bounded weights. This improves the comparison in part of the diameter range. For \(D\approx n^{1/2}\), its displayed terms give \(n^{3/5+o(1)}\), while the target is \(\tilde\{O\}(n^{1/2})\). This comparison of proven bounds displays a remaining gap; it does not prove that any particular graph requires \(n^{3/5}\) rounds.

The notation \(n^{o(1)}\) allows factors larger than every fixed power of log n. Such a factor cannot automatically be treated as the polylogarithmic overhead specified in the statement. Similarly, a theorem for one fixed diameter regime does not supply the single bound required for all connected networks.

Near-optimal algorithms for \((1+\varepsilon )\)-approximate undirected distances provide an important contrast. For fixed \(\varepsilon\) they may return a nonzero relative error. Since integer distances can be as large as \(n^{b+1}\), forcing exactness by taking \(\varepsilon\) extremely small can increase the algorithm’s complexity through its \(\varepsilon\) dependence. A fixed-accuracy approximation theorem therefore does not imply this exact result.

The inherited 2026 reference studies programmable matter with reconfigurable circuits that transmit signals in a different way. Its related-work section is useful background for CONGEST, but its own polylogarithmic algorithm is not a solution in the present model. The card now cites the original CONGEST results as well, including the 2023 bound missing from that summary.

Resolving the question would determine whether exact numerical optimization has an additional distributed cost beyond the familiar bandwidth-and-diameter benchmark. Shortest distances are also a primitive in other distributed constructions, so a faster exact computation would affect more than routing from one source.

cards.title: Explicit superconstant lower bounds in the congested clique
cards.formal: Does there exist a Boolean predicate P of finite simple undirected graphs on \([n]\), decidable from the full adjacency matrix by one deterministic polynomial-time algorithm, such that every uniform deterministic unicast congested-clique algorithm computing P has worst-case round complexity \(R_{A}(n)=\omega (1)\)? Only node 1 is required to output the decision bit, and the input, bandwidth and limiting convention are fixed below.
cards.why: A central unbroken barrier in unconditional lower bounds for a powerful distributed model.
cards.status_note: The checked primary literature leaves explicit superconstant unicast bounds as a central challenge. Searches through 11 September 2026 found no established resolution of this polynomial-time, one-bit target. The latest checked revision of the one-round MST result is January 2024; it is not presented as a new 2026 status theorem.
cards.review_note: Preserved the proposal’s centralized polynomial-time restriction and strict \(\omega (1)\) notation. Specified labeled graph inputs, uniform deterministic algorithms, logarithmic per-link messages, unrestricted local computation and designated-node output. cards.definitions: For each \(n\ge 2\), the communication network is the complete graph on processors \(1,\ldots ,n\). The input is a separate simple undirected graph G on the same labeled vertex set. Initially processor v knows n, its identifier v and the \(n- 1\) adjacency bits for edges incident to v in G. No other input or certificate is supplied. In a synchronous round every processor performs a finite, otherwise unrestricted amount of local deterministic computation and sends a separate message of at most \(\operatorname{ceil}(\log _{2} n)\) bits to each other processor; all messages arrive before the next round. Local memory is unrestricted. All processors execute one fixed finite algorithm with their identifiers and n as inputs; no nonuniform advice, randomness, oracle or free communication is allowed. The cost counts communication rounds only, not local computation. Node 1 must halt with \(\mathrm{P}(G)\) on every input; requiring all nodes to receive this one bit changes the cost by at most one round. \(R_{A}(n)\) is the maximum number of rounds until node 1 outputs, over all n-vertex input graphs. The statement \(R_{A}(n)=\omega (1)\) means that for every integer \(B\ge 1\) there is N such that \(R_{A}(n)>B\) for every \(n\ge N\); it is stronger than a lower bound at only infinitely many sizes. The chosen predicate may depend on vertex labels, as in Korhonen–Suomela’s graph-language model. “Explicit” is fixed by the source proposal’s centralized polynomial-time condition: one deterministic Turing machine computes P on every adjacency matrix within \(C(n+1)^{k}\) steps for constants C,k independent of n. There is no polynomial bound imposed on processors’ local work. A constant multiple of log n message bits can be simulated by a constant factor more rounds and does not change the \(\omega (1)\) target.
cards.answer_criterion: A positive resolution gives a single graph predicate with a proved centralized polynomial-time decision procedure and proves the displayed \(\omega (1)\) lower bound against every correct uniform deterministic protocol in the specified model. A negative resolution proves the logical negation of that existence statement. A two-round lower bound, a lower bound for broadcast messages or restricted local computation, or a hard predicate without the centralized polynomial-time guarantee does not settle the target.

context_blocks.title: The network and the input graph differ
context_blocks.text: Even if the input graph is a long path, the processors can communicate directly with every other processor. The path’s large diameter therefore does not force a long wait for information to travel from one endpoint to the other. The obstacle, if any, must arise from the amount and arrangement of the information needed for the decision, while each individual communication link carries only logarithmically many bits.

context_blocks.title: One bit can be much easier than collecting the input
context_blocks.text: For example, deciding whether G has an edge takes two rounds: every processor sends node 1 one bit saying whether it has an incident edge, and node 1 can broadcast the answer. Computing the decision at node 1 itself takes just the first round. Although the whole input contains quadratically many potential edge bits, this predicate does not need those bits collected individually. Input size alone is not a lower bound for an arbitrary one-bit output.

context_blocks.title: Why unicast is essential
context_blocks.text: In the unicast model, a processor may send different pieces of information to different recipients in the same round. Broadcast restricts it to one common message. The latter can admit bottleneck arguments that do not remain valid once a sender uses all its links separately. Drucker, Kuhn and Oshman study both versions and explicitly distinguish their lower bounds. A theorem for the broadcast version cannot be silently transferred here.

context_blocks.title: The explicitness requirement
context_blocks.text: Counting arguments show that some Boolean functions require many rounds. Korhonen and Suomela also establish a uniform time hierarchy by selecting hard functions through exhaustive enumeration. Such a selection supplies computability, but not the polynomial-time centralized algorithm demanded by this card. The desired separation concerns a task that is computationally manageable once its entire graph is available, while still resisting distributed communication with unrestricted local computation.

context_blocks.title: Connections and known limitations
context_blocks.text: The 2014 circuit simulations relate distributed lower bounds to difficult circuit lower bounds, with important bandwidth and depth qualifications. In particular, the introduction distinguishes a superconstant bound with one-bit links from an \(\Omega (\log  \log  n)\) bound with logarithmic links. These are not interchangeable claims for the weaker \(\omega (1)\) target here. Robinson’s PODC 2023 result rules out one-round MST computation at logarithmic bandwidth under its edge-output convention. It proves a genuine limitation, but two rounds are still a constant, and outputting a spanning tree differs from computing one decision bit.

cards.title: Almost-linear-work parallel exact maximum flow
cards.formal: For every fixed integer \(a\ge1\), is there a uniform bounded-error randomized parallel algorithm that computes an exact maximum flow in any directed graph with integer capacities in \(\{0,\ldots,n^{a}\}\), using \((m+n)^{1+o(1)}\) work and \((m+n)^{o(1)}\) depth?
cards.definitions: The graph is given by its vertex set \([n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}\), with \(n\ge2\), and an explicit list of \(m\) arcs. It has no loops and at most one arc per ordered pair; opposite arcs are allowed. A feasible flow assigns a value \(f_{e}\) to every arc with \(0\le f_{e}\le u_{e}\) and equal incoming and outgoing total flow at each vertex except the distinct specified source \(s\) and sink \(t\). Its value is outgoing minus incoming flow at \(s\). The required output is a feasible flow attaining the largest possible value, including every arc value. Output integral arc flows. Use a synchronous priority CRCW PRAM: concurrent reads are allowed; if several processors write one cell in a round, the lowest-index writer succeeds. Each active processor executes one word-RAM instruction per round, with the instructions and word length specified below. Work is the total number of executed processor instructions, including activation, input access and output; depth is the number of rounds. Processor IDs and addresses fit in words. All processors run a fixed finite program with their IDs; there is no advice or free preprocessing. Independent uniform random words cost one instruction each. The entire output is correct with probability at least \(2/3\). Both resource bounds hold on every execution. Use a uniform word RAM with word length \(w=d\lceil\log_{2}(n+2)\rceil\), for a fixed positive integer \(d\) chosen with the algorithm and large enough for its addresses and input values. Unit-cost instructions are word reads/writes, copying, comparisons, branching, Boolean operations, shifts, addition, subtraction and multiplication modulo \(2^{w}\), and integer quotient and remainder with nonzero divisor. Shifts by at least \(w\) return zero. Multiword computation is charged by its component instructions. The fixed finite program receives no advice or precomputed tables; all initialization, preprocessing and output writes count. With \(N=m+n\), require a function \(h_{a}:\mathbb{N}\to[1,\infty)\) satisfying \(\lim_{N\to\infty}\log h_{a}(N)/\log N=0\), such that work is at most \(C_{a}Nh_{a}(N)\) and depth at most \(C_{a}h_{a}(N)\). The program, \(d\), \(C_{a}\) and \(h_{a}\) may depend on \(a\), but not on the graph. Initially the explicit input is in shared memory; all subsequent computation is charged.

context_blocks.text: Sequential almost-linear time does not imply that the same computation can be completed with very few dependent stages. This target asks for both near-optimal total work and subpolynomial parallel depth.

Haeupler, Jiang and Saranurak explicitly identify almost-optimal parallel exact maximum flow as a major open problem. Their DAG Projections paper gives efficient reductions between exact directed flow and approximation problems on directed acyclic graphs.

The reductions classify the difficulty of several parallel tasks; they do not establish the requested work and depth. The capacity restriction makes each numerical input occupy logarithmically many bits.

cards.why: This is a central unresolved parallelization problem for exact network optimization, asking whether near-optimal sequential work can coexist with subpolynomial dependence depth.

cards.title: Work-efficient parallel directed reachability
cards.formal:
Does directed single-source reachability admit nearly linear work and polylogarithmic depth simultaneously in the uniform randomized CREW PRAM model specified below? Precisely, is the following statement true?
\[
\forall c\in\mathbb N_{\ge1}\ \exists A_c,K_c,a_c,b_c,q_c\ \forall n\ge2\ \forall G\ \forall s\in V(G),
\]
\[
\Pr\!\left[\begin{array}{l}
A_c(G,s)\text{ terminates with the exact reachability indicator,}\\
W\le K_c(n+m)L^{a_c}\ \text{and}\ D\le K_cL^{b_c}
\end{array}\right]\ge1-n^{-c},
\]
where \(G\) ranges over every directed graph on the labeled vertex set \(\{1,\ldots,n\}\), \(m=|E(G)|\), and \(L=\lceil\log_2(n+2)\rceil\)? Here \(K_c\ge1\), \(a_c,b_c\ge0\) and \(q_c\ge3\) are integers independent of \(n,G,s\); \(A_c\) is one finite program independent of input size. The word length is \(q_cL\). The required event jointly bounds total work \(W\), depth \(D\), and correctness of the entire output on each fixed input. The confidence exponent is requested as a fixed constant before choosing the program. The one-vertex case has the prescribed output consisting of a single 1 and is omitted only to avoid a vacuous probability bound.
cards.why: Directed reachability is a basic graph operation with a linear-work sequential solution. The unresolved issue is whether its dependencies can be processed in polylogarithmic parallel time while retaining nearly that work bound on every input. A resolution would determine whether a fundamental sequential graph task admits efficient use of many processors, rather than a speedup purchased with polynomially more computation.
cards.definitions:
Graphs are unweighted and directed. Their edge sets satisfy \(E\subseteq\{1,\ldots,n\}^{2}\); loops are allowed and repeated copies of an edge are absent. A vertex is reachable from \(s\) when there is a finite directed path from \(s\) to it, including the length-zero path. No assumption of strong connectivity, acyclicity, bounded diameter or a lower bound on \(m\) is imposed.

The input is an outgoing adjacency-array representation in shared read-only word memory. Cells 0, 1 and 2 contain \(n,m,s\). The next \(n+1\) cells contain offsets \(o_0,\ldots,o_n\), with \(0=o_0\le\cdots\le o_n=m\). The next \(m\) cells contain target labels \(t_0,\ldots,t_{m-1}\). The outgoing neighbors of vertex \(v\) are exactly the distinct labels \(t_j\) for \(o_{v-1}\le j<o_v\). Neighbor order is arbitrary. The output occupies the next \(n\) cells, one word for each vertex in label order: its value must be 1 for a reachable vertex and 0 otherwise. Thus the answer is the entire exact set, represented by \(n\) Boolean values, and does not include distances or a transitive closure.

For the chosen program, words are unsigned \(w=q_cL\)-bit integers. Shared cells and processor identifiers are numbered from 0 to \(2^w-1\). Every processor has a fixed finite number of word registers and runs the same finite program, with its identifier available in a designated register. These register counts and the program may depend on \(c\), but not on the graph or its size. Noninput cells and all other registers initially contain zero. There is no advice, oracle, precomputed graph index or uncharged preprocessing. The polynomial address space is the only imposed working-space limit.

Execution is synchronous. One active processor executes one primitive instruction per round. Instructions read or write one shared cell by its word address; copy words; add, subtract or multiply modulo \(2^w\); perform bitwise AND, OR, XOR or complement; shift a word left or logically right by an integer between 0 and \(w-1\); compare unsigned words; branch; or obtain one fresh unbiased random bit. A shift by at least \(w\) returns zero. Instructions use a constant number of registers. Reads observe the memory at the beginning of the round, and writes commit at its end. Several processors may read one cell, but at most one processor may write a given cell in a round, even if competing writes would contain the same value. Input cells cannot be written. Programs must obey these CREW access rules on every execution.

To account explicitly for activation, only processor 0 starts active. A unit-cost fork instruction activates one previously unused processor with a specified identifier, a program entry label and a constant number of copied registers; it starts in the next round. Two simultaneous forks may not name the same processor. Halting a processor costs one instruction; halted or not-yet-activated processors do no work. All input-independent setup, processor activation, data movement, auxiliary graph construction and output writes count toward work. Work is the total number of executed primitive instructions, and depth is the number of synchronous rounds until all activated processors halt. Nontermination gives infinite depth and does not satisfy the success event. The fork convention makes processor initialization explicit and allows ordinary parallel scheduling with polylogarithmic overhead.

All random-bit instructions draw mutually independent fair bits; the probability is over these bits for each fixed input representation. The required probability concerns correct output and both resource bounds together, not three expectations or an average over graphs. On the exceptional event, the program may return an incorrect answer, exceed a resource bound or fail to terminate. The notation \(\widetilde O(n+m)\) and polylogarithmic depth in the motivating question is replaced by the explicit logarithmic powers and constants in the statement.

progress.text: Jambulapati, Liu and Sidford give directed single-source reachability with \(\widetilde O(n+m)\) work and \(n^{1/2+o(1)}\) depth with high probability. This entry uses the corrected fourth arXiv version of their FOCS 2019 paper.

Ashvinkumar, Bernstein, Probst Gutenberg and Saranurak give \(\widetilde O(m)\) work and \((n^{\omega+o(1)}/m)^{1/(2\omega-2)}\) span for \(m\ge n\). Here \(\omega\) is the exponent used for parallel matrix multiplication. Their dense-graph bound is \(n^{0.136}\); this is not a polylogarithmic bound on arbitrary inputs.

Kogan and Parter claim polylogarithmic-depth single-source reachability with \(\widetilde O(T^{\omega/2})\) work, where \(T\) is the number of ordered pairs in the reflexive transitive closure. The arXiv record reports FOCS 2026 acceptance. The claim concerns work in terms of \(T\), which need not be nearly linear in \(n+m\).

context_blocks.text: The target concerns arbitrary directed inputs and the full reachable set from one source. Near-linear work and polylogarithmic depth must be achieved in the same execution. Neither a low-work algorithm with polynomial depth nor a fast parallel algorithm with polynomially excessive work meets that requirement.

The input parameter is \(n+m\), including isolated vertices. The cited papers sometimes assume \(m\ge n\) or absorb one implicit self-loop per vertex into \(m\). This card makes the additive vertex term explicit. For a directed path, \(m=n-1\), whereas the reflexive transitive closure contains \(n(n+1)/2\) ordered pairs; a bound in closure size can therefore be much larger than a bound in input size.

The sources use the standard work/depth terminology but do not fully specify shared-memory write conflicts, word instructions or input layout. This card retains its previously selected CREW convention and makes word size, adjacency arrays, exact output, processor activation and the joint high-probability event explicit editorial model choices. It permits a program selected for each fixed confidence exponent; the program is uniform over input sizes. These details are not quotations of a particular source model.

The May 2026 full version explicitly identifies improving the sparse-graph regime as open. The August result gives polylogarithmic depth with work parameterized by \(T=|TC(G)|\), where \(TC(G)=\{(u,v):v\text{ is reachable from }u\}\). Since \(T\) may be quadratic on a sparse graph, that theorem does not provide the nearly linear input-work guarantee asked for here.

cards.answer_criterion:
Give a complete, mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of the quantified algorithm-existence statement or its negation in the specified model. A positive answer must provide the uniform program witnesses and prove the joint correctness, work and depth guarantee on every admissible graph, source and adjacency-array ordering for every fixed confidence exponent. A negative answer must refute that entire existence statement without an additional unproved complexity assumption. A result restricted to a class of graphs, a particular representation of auxiliary information, or work measured by transitive-closure size does not establish either answer unless it entails the full statement.

Explicitly, a negative answer establishes an integer \(c\ge1\) such that for every legal finite program and every proposed integer constants \(K\ge1\), \(a,b\ge0\), \(q\ge3\), there are \(n\ge2\), a valid graph, source and adjacency-array ordering for which the joint probability in the formal statement is strictly below \(1-n^{-c}\). A legal program obeys the stated word and CREW rules on all executions. The failing instance may depend on the candidate program and constants.

cards.title: Depth-first search in NC
cards.formal: Does there exist a logspace-uniform family of deterministic Boolean circuits of polynomial size and polylogarithmic depth that, on the adjacency matrix of every finite simple undirected graph, outputs a valid depth-first-search forest? The roots and the order of visiting neighbors may be chosen freely for each input.
cards.why: DFS is a basic graph structure whose standard construction has a long chain of sequential choices. Resolving this question would determine whether randomness can always be removed from its efficient parallel construction while retaining polynomial total resources.

progress.text: Aggarwal and Anderson give a randomized NC algorithm for undirected DFS, as documented in the 2025 paper’s introduction. This permits randomness.

cards.definitions: For \(n\ge 1\) the input is the \(n\times n\) symmetric zero-diagonal adjacency matrix of a graph G on \(V=\{1,\ldots ,n\}\). The output is a parent array \(p\in \{0,\ldots ,n\}^{n}\), with 0 denoting a root. If \(p(v)\ne 0\), require \(\{v,p(v)\}\in E(G)\); repeatedly taking parents must reach 0 from every vertex. These parent edges define a rooted forest, and each connected component of G must be spanned by one of its trees. A vertex u is an ancestor of v if u lies on the tree path from v to its root. The forest is a DFS forest if, for every edge \(\{u,v\}\in E(G)\), one endpoint is an ancestor of the other. For undirected graphs this is exactly the class of forests produced by recursive depth-first search under some choices of roots and neighbor orders. Encode each parent entry in \(\lceil \log _{2}(n+1)\rceil\) bits. Each circuit \(C_{n}\) has \(n^{2}\) input bits and \(n\lceil \log _{2}(n+1)\rceil\) output bits, uses AND and OR gates with at most two inputs and NOT gates with one input, and has size at most \(O(n^{c})\) and depth at most \(O((\log _{2}(n+2))^{k})\), for fixed constants c,k independent of n and G. Logspace uniformity means that one deterministic Turing machine, given \(1^{n}\), writes the description of \(C_{n}\) while using \(O(\log (n+2))\) working space, excluding its read-only input and write-only output tapes. Correctness is required on every valid adjacency matrix; behavior on other bit strings is unrestricted. The empty graph has the empty output. No randomness or input-length-specific advice is supplied. NC here refers to computing a valid encoded output, rather than deciding a Boolean language.
cards.answer_criterion: Construct one circuit family satisfying all the stated correctness, uniformity, size and depth requirements, or prove that no such family exists. The output may be any valid DFS forest. A randomized algorithm, a quasipolynomial-size circuit family, an algorithm only for a restricted graph class, or a lower bound for one prescribed traversal order does not settle this question.

context_blocks.text: Depth-first search explores an unvisited neighbor, completes the recursive exploration from that neighbor, and only then tries another neighbor of the current vertex. The resulting parent pointers form a spanning forest. The question asks whether that structure can always be assembled in a small number of parallel stages, even though the familiar sequential procedure follows one exploration at a time.

Being a spanning tree is not enough. In a triangle with vertices 1, 2 and 3, a tree rooted at 1 with children 2 and 3 fails: edge \(\{2,3\}\) joins different branches. The path with parent pointers \(p(1)=0, p(2)=1\) and \(p(3)=2\) is a valid DFS tree. The ancestor condition makes this distinction explicit without prescribing a traversal order.

The height of the output tree is not the running time being bounded. A path graph may require a DFS tree of height \(n- 1\), yet its n parent entries may be computed in parallel. Conversely, a sequential algorithm with linear running time need not have polylogarithmic parallel depth.

The freedom to choose a valid output matters. Reproducing the lexicographically first DFS order under fixed choices is P-complete according to the cited source. That hardness result does not exclude efficient parallel computation of a different valid DFS forest.

The general undirected problem has a randomized NC algorithm, and a deterministic parallel algorithm with quasipolynomially many processors is known. The latter exceeds the polynomial resource bound in this question. Deterministic NC algorithms are also known for several restricted graph families. The 2025 source still leaves general deterministic NC open.

There is a separate goal of keeping total work close to the input size. The 2023 algorithm obtains work \(\widetilde{O}\)\((m+n)\) and depth \(\widetilde{O}\)\((\sqrt{n})\), where m is the number of edges and \(\widetilde{O}\) suppresses factors polynomial in logarithms. Its depth bound is sublinear but does not establish the polylogarithmic depth required here.

Uniformity requires one small-space procedure to describe the circuits for every input length. The circuits cannot be unrelated choices supplied separately for each n. Both this requirement and the polynomial size bound belong to the target; merely showing that suitable circuits exist with larger resources leaves a different question.

sentences: A depth-first-search forest records the parent choices of recursive graph exploration.
For an undirected graph, it is a rooted spanning forest in which every graph edge joins a vertex to one of its ancestors.
The problem asks for a deterministic, uniformly specified parallel computation that constructs any such forest with polynomial resources and polylogarithmic depth.
Randomized NC algorithms and deterministic results for restricted graph classes are known, but those guarantees do not settle the general target.
A solution would show whether this basic search structure can always be built efficiently in parallel without random choices.

cards.title: Quantum 3-coloring of cycles in \(o(\log^{*}n)\) rounds
cards.formal:
Does there exist one uniform quantum-LOCAL protocol \(A\) and a function \(T:\mathbb N_{\ge3}\to\mathbb N\) such that, for every integer \(n\ge3\) and every injective identifier assignment \(\lambda:V(C_n)\to\{1,\ldots,n^2\}\), all nodes of the consistently oriented cycle \(C_n\) finish within \(T(n)\) communication rounds on every possible execution branch, and their classical outputs \(c_v\in\{1,2,3\}\) satisfy
\[
\Pr\bigl[\forall\{u,v\}\in E(C_n),\ c_u\ne c_v\bigr]\ge1-\frac1n,
\qquad
\lim_{n\to\infty}\frac{T(n)}{1+\log^{*}_2n}=0?
\]
The probability is over the protocol's quantum measurement outcomes. Initially the quantum state is a product of local zero states. Each node knows \(n\), its own identifier and the predecessor/successor ports, and communication in both directions is permitted.
cards.definitions:
For specification only, \(C_n\) has vertices \(v_0,\ldots,v_{n-1}\) and edges \(\{v_i,v_{(i+1)\bmod n}\}\). Its consistent orientation tells each node which port leads to its successor and which to its predecessor. The indices \(i\) are not inputs to the protocol. Identifiers are distinct integers in \(\{1,\ldots,n^2\}\), represented in binary. Nodes receive no distinguished leader, numerical position, neighbor identifiers, list of all identifiers, or other global information beyond \(n\). The identifier assignment is fixed before quantum randomness; the success bound holds for every such assignment.

All nodes execute the same fixed finite classical control program. Its initial classical input consists only of \(n\), the node's identifier and its two port labels. Classical computation manipulates finite binary strings by ordinary Turing-machine operations and may determine which local qubits to use next. There is no bound on local computation time, local storage or message length, but every local phase and every message must be finite on every possible branch. No advice depending on \(n\), the identifiers or the graph is supplied.

Local quantum storage is a finite tensor product of qubits. A node may append a fresh qubit in state \(\lvert0\rangle\), discard a local qubit, apply \(H\) or \(T\) to one local qubit, apply CNOT to an ordered pair of distinct local qubits, or measure a local qubit in the computational basis, with subsequent classical control depending on the outcome. The gates are
\[
H=\frac1{\sqrt2}\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\1&-1\end{pmatrix},
\qquad
T=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&e^{\mathrm i\pi/4}\end{pmatrix},
\qquad
\mathrm{CNOT}\lvert x,y\rangle=\lvert x,x\mathbin{\oplus}y\rangle
\quad(x,y\in\{0,1\}).
\]
Here \(\mathrm i^2=-1\) and \(\oplus\) denotes addition modulo two. On a global density operator \(\rho\), a local gate acts by unitary conjugation on its chosen registers; discarding a register takes its partial trace. A computational-basis measurement with outcome \(b\in\{0,1\}\) has probability \(\operatorname{tr}(P_b\rho)\) and, when that probability is nonzero, leaves normalized state \(P_b\rho P_b/\operatorname{tr}(P_b\rho)\), where \(P_b\) projects the measured qubit onto \(\lvert b\rangle\). Classical random choices may be obtained by such measurements. There is no postselection that discards unsuccessful outcomes from the success probability.

A communication round consists of finite local processing followed by simultaneous noiseless transmission of finite quantum registers along the cycle edges. Each node may send registers to both neighbors and receives their sent registers before the next local phase. Sending transfers ownership of the qubits; it does not copy unknown states. Classical messages can be encoded as computational-basis registers. A final finite local phase may produce the node's color without another round. There is no communication between nonneighbors, no information conveyed by elapsed local computation time, and no additional inter-node channel. The initial global quantum state is the tensor product of all freshly initialized local \(\lvert0\rangle\) registers; there is no shared randomness or preshared entanglement. Entanglement created by the protocol through counted communication is allowed.

Every node must output one color and halt, including on branches where the resulting coloring is improper. A possible branch is one whose finite measurement outcomes have nonzero Born probability. The round bound holds on every such branch and uniformly over all identifier assignments of the same size, rather than merely in expectation or with high probability. Local operations, message lengths and numbers of qubits are not charged to round complexity. The program has no real-number oracle or arbitrary exact unitary as an extra primitive; the gate set above retains the card's existing concrete uniform interpretation.

For real \(x\ge1\), \(\log^{*}_2x\) is the least nonnegative integer \(r\) for which applying \(\log_2\) repeatedly \(r\) times reaches a value at most \(1\), stopping as soon as that occurs. The displayed limit means that for every real \(\varepsilon>0\) there is \(N\) such that \(T(n)\le\varepsilon(1+\log^{*}_2n)\) for every integer \(n\ge N\). The probability target is global correctness of all edges simultaneously, not separate correctness probabilities for individual nodes.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct Lean proof of the existence of a uniform protocol and a worst-case round-bound function satisfying every stated input, quantum-operation, termination and global-success condition, or a complete Lean proof of the logical negation of that existence statement. A conditional lower bound alone does not prove nonexistence. A lower bound limited to anonymous probability-one protocols, to one-way one-round communication, to two-coloring, or to growing-degree trees does not settle the stated protocol class.
cards.why: Cycle coloring is a basic distributed symmetry-breaking problem with a sharp classical locality threshold. Settling whether quantum communication beats that threshold would establish a concrete capability or limitation for coordinating neighboring processors with classical outputs.

importance.reason: A central concrete benchmark for quantum distributed computation, with an elementary output condition and a sharp classical threshold. The recent zero-error breakthrough leaves the practically standard high-probability regime unresolved.

context_blocks.text: The primary problem list asks whether cycles can be 3-colored in \(o(\log^{*}n)\) quantum rounds and separately asks about a constant-round algorithm. This card retains the first question with its already chosen orientation, identifiers, known size, finite gate set and global error bound.

Classical deterministic and high-probability randomized cycle coloring both have \(\Theta(\log^{*}n)\) round complexity. The August 2026 paper summarizes those classical bounds and distinguishes them from the unknown quantum-LOCAL complexity.

Finitely dependent proper color distributions exist on finite cycles: collections of colors on vertex sets at sufficiently large graph distance are independent. This is a statement about distributions, not an implementation by the local quantum protocol specified here. The finite-cycle result is due to Holroyd, Hutchcroft and Levy, following the earlier integer-line construction.

The July 2026 preprint proves quantum lower bounds for 3-coloring rooted trees using growing degree, and for 2-coloring even cycles. It explicitly distinguishes the bounded-degree case; neither result resolves three-coloring cycles.

The August 2026 preprint proves a linear-round lower bound for anonymous finite-qubit protocols that color cycles with probability exactly one. Its Section 1.4 leaves high-probability correctness open. The identified, nonzero-error model here is retained.

The September 2026 preprint rules out high-probability four-coloring in the restricted one-way one-round quantum model. Section 1.4 explicitly leaves bidirectional communication and additional rounds as further questions; this does not resolve the sub-log-star target.

The cited quantum papers allow general finite-dimensional local operations in their mathematical models. This card preserves its pre-existing uniform finite-gate formulation; the review does not claim an exact compilation equivalence for probability-one results.

cards.title: Sublogarithmic distributed MIS
cards.formal:
In the randomized LOCAL model, does there exist an algorithm that finds a maximal independent set in $o(\log n)$ rounds on every $n$-vertex simple graph? Its output $I\subseteq V$ must satisfy $(u,v)\in E\Rightarrow\{u,v\}
subseteq I$ and $v
otin I\Rightarrow N(v)\cap I
e\varnothing$. Require success probability at least $1-n^{-c}$ for each fixed constant $c>0$, allowing the constant in the running time to depend on $c$. The bound must hold uniformly over all maximum degrees $\Delta\le n-1$.
cards.why: This isolates the communication needed for a basic symmetry-breaking task whose feasibility is easy to check locally. I include it because either outcome would change the benchmark for distributed graph algorithms: a faster algorithm would supply a stronger primitive, while a logarithmic lower bound would expose a substantial limitation of local coordination.
cards.definitions:
The network is the input graph. Rounds are synchronous; each edge can carry an arbitrarily large message in each direction. Vertices may have distinct $O(\log n)$-bit identifiers and private random bits. Every vertex outputs its own membership bit. The measured time is the number of elapsed rounds until all outputs are available, not the number of rounds in which an individual processor stays awake.

Nodes may know n and the maximum degree. Both the algorithm and the asymptotic time bound are uniform over input graphs and valid identifier assignments.

progress.text: Ghaffari gives the degree-sensitive MIS algorithm. With subsequent deterministic finishing routines, the standard bound is $O(\log\Delta+\operatorname{poly}(\log\log n))$.

Khoury and Schild give a randomized lower bound $\Omega(\min\{\log\Delta,\sqrt{\log n}\})$ for maximal matching and, by reduction, MIS on general graphs. This implies an $\Omega(\sqrt{\log n})$ worst-case barrier, not an $\Omega(\log n)$ barrier.

Their separate degree-reduction paper obtains $O(\log\Delta/\log(\log^{*}\Delta)+\operatorname{poly}(\log\log n))$ rounds for girth at least seven. Its Open Question 1 asks for the general-graph improvement.

context_blocks.text: A sequential greedy algorithm can scan vertices and select each vertex whose neighbors have not been selected. The difficulty here is distributing those decisions: a processor sits at each vertex and initially sees only local information. After r communication rounds, it cannot have learned anything beyond distance r. Message size and local computation are free in LOCAL, so a lower bound measures the reach of coordination itself.

Maximal means that no further vertex can be added. It does not require the largest possible independent set. For example, on a star, either the center alone or all leaves is a valid answer. The challenge is to choose consistently across a general network, rather than to optimize the number of selected vertices.

Degree-sensitive algorithms achieve $O(\log\Delta+\operatorname{poly}(\log\log n))$ rounds. This is already sublogarithmic when the degree is sufficiently small; the unresolved target includes polynomial-degree graphs. Repeatedly making only constant-factor progress leaves a logarithmic running time.

Recent work breaks that pattern on graphs with no cycles of length at most six. It does not extend to arbitrary graphs. Together with stronger lower bounds, this leaves a concrete question: can local choices still make sufficiently rapid progress when short cycles create dependencies between nearby decisions?

cards.context:
A sequential greedy algorithm can scan vertices and select each vertex whose neighbors have not been selected. The difficulty here is distributing those decisions: a processor sits at each vertex and initially sees only local information. After r communication rounds, it cannot have learned anything beyond distance r. Message size and local computation are free in LOCAL, so a lower bound measures the reach of coordination itself.

cards.title: One-cycle versus two-cycles conjecture
cards.formal: For every fixed $0<\delta<1$, must every randomized MPC algorithm distinguishing one n-cycle from two vertex-disjoint \((n/2)\)-cycles use $\Omega(\log n)$ rounds in the worst case over even n and input placement? Each machine has $O(n^\delta)$ words and total memory is \(O(n)\) words. Require success probability at least $1-n^{-c}$ for each requested fixed $c>0$. An $o(\log n)$-round algorithm for one fixed $\delta<1$ would refute this lower-bound conjecture.
cards.why: I include this because the input removes most graph-theoretic complications and leaves the cost of assembling global connectivity information. It is a standard conditional-hardness benchmark for massively parallel algorithms, and a resolution would clarify whether limited memory creates an inherent logarithmic coordination cost even on degree-two graphs.
cards.definitions: Words have $O(\log n)$ bits. The input edge list is distributed across machines without exceeding their local memory. Each synchronous round allows arbitrary local computation followed by sending and receiving at most $O(n^{\delta})$ words per machine. The desired success probability is $1-n^{-c}$ for fixed $c>0$. This card fixes linear total memory; variants allowing more total space must be stated separately.

progress.text: Nanongkai and Scquizzato develop equivalence classes and conditional-hardness connections around this cycle problem and logarithmic-space computation. Their reductions have explicit global-memory requirements; those should be checked before transferring them to the linear-total-memory variant here.

Gan, Wirth, and Zhang explicitly state the linear-total-memory 2-CYCLE conjecture while giving a constant-round algorithm for embedded grid graphs. The promised arbitrary-cycle problem is left unresolved.

context_blocks.text: Both promised inputs have exactly n vertices and n edges, and every vertex has degree two. Counting vertices, counting edges, and checking degrees therefore gives the same answer. The difference is how those edges join into components. Vertex identifiers are arbitrary, so the labels do not reveal where a cycle begins or whether two pieces belong together.

A sequential scan with graph traversal solves the problem in linear time. With the edge list spread across machines, no one machine can store the whole instance. Repeatedly joining path fragments or doubling the length represented by a pointer gives a natural logarithmic-round approach. The conjecture says that general distributed computation cannot compress this process into asymptotically fewer communication rounds under the stated memory limits.

It is tempting to justify the conjecture by saying that information travels only one graph edge per round. That would be incorrect here. Any machine may send to any other machine, and local computation between exchanges is unrestricted. The restriction is how much information a machine can store, send, and receive at once. A valid lower bound must cope with arbitrary encodings and nonlocal communication.

Extra geometric structure can change the answer. The 2025 grid-connectivity algorithm uses an embedding with bounded edge lengths to obtain constant rounds in its parameter regime. An arbitrarily labelled cycle does not provide that embedding, so the geometric result does not refute this promise-problem conjecture.

cards.title: Deterministic LOCAL MIS in \(O(\log  n)\) rounds
cards.formal: Is there a deterministic LOCAL algorithm that outputs a maximal independent set on every $n$-vertex simple graph in $O(\log n)$ synchronous communication rounds? Each vertex has a distinct $O(\log n)$-bit identifier, and the guarantee must hold for every valid identifier assignment and every maximum degree. The output must be independent, and every vertex outside it must have a neighbor inside it. No random bits are available.
cards.why: This measures the quantitative cost of removing randomness from a basic distributed task. I include it separately from randomized sublogarithmic MIS because the algorithm must work against every identifier assignment with no failure probability. An \(O(\log  n)\) result would match the familiar randomized worst-case benchmark and propagate through reductions to other symmetry-breaking problems.
cards.definitions:
LOCAL allows unbounded messages along input edges and unrestricted local computation. A vertex’s r-round view contains only its radius-r neighborhood and the identifiers and input data revealed there. The complexity is elapsed communication rounds until all vertices output. The target is uniform over arbitrary graphs, not restricted to bounded degree, planar graphs, or trees.

Nodes may know n and the maximum degree; the time guarantee must still be \(O(\log  n)\) uniformly over degrees.

progress.text: Balliu and coauthors prove a deterministic lower bound $\Omega(\min\{\Delta,\log n/\log\log n\})$. In particular, the general worst-case complexity cannot be substantially below logarithmic up to a log-log factor.
Rozhoň and Ghaffari obtain polylogarithmic deterministic network decomposition and consequently polylogarithmic deterministic MIS.
Ghaffari and Grunau improve MIS to $\widetilde O(\log^{5/3}n)$ rounds, where the hidden factors are polylogarithmic in $\log n$.
Bourreau, Brandt, and Nolin use the same deterministic MIS benchmark to improve \(\Delta\)-coloring; their result does not give an \(O(\log  n) \mathrm{MIS}\) algorithm.

context_blocks.text: Identifiers make deterministic symmetry breaking possible, but they do not automatically make it fast. Consider the rule that selects every vertex whose identifier is smaller than those of all its remaining neighbors, then removes the selected vertices and their neighbors. On a path with identifiers increasing from one endpoint to the other, each phase selects just the smallest remaining endpoint. This rule takes linearly many phases, even though much faster algorithms exist for paths.

Randomized MIS algorithms avoid adversarial identifier patterns by making new random choices. A deterministic algorithm has to arrange useful progress from the graph and identifiers alone. The existence of a good assignment of random choices is insufficient: processors must find suitable choices while paying for the communication that coordinates them.

Network decomposition supplied a general way to organize that work into small-diameter clusters that can be processed in groups. It settled the old question of whether polylogarithmic deterministic MIS is possible. The present target concerns the finer exponent and cannot be recorded as the already-solved polylogarithmic-time question.

The 2024 improvement reaches approximately $\log^{5/3}n$ rounds and avoids the log-squared cost of the standard decomposition-based route. Closing the remaining gap requires more than optimizing the constants of that route. The 2026 coloring reduction still uses this improved MIS bound as its benchmark.

cards.title: Subquadratic metric TSP cost estimation below factor two
cards.formal:
Do there exist an absolute constant \(\delta\in(0,1)\) and a classical randomized distance-query algorithm that estimates the minimum traveling-salesperson tour cost of every \(n\)-point metric within a factor \(2-\delta\), using \(o(n^2)\) distance queries?

For a metric \(d\) on \([n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}\), with \(n\ge3\), define
\[\operatorname{TSP}(d)=\min_{\pi\in\mathfrak S_n}\sum_{j=1}^{n}d\bigl(\pi(j),\pi(j+1)\bigr),\qquad \pi(n+1)=\pi(1).\]
The algorithm knows \(n\) and can request \(d(i,j)\) for any chosen pair of labels. Its output \(Z\) must satisfy
\[\Pr\!\left[\operatorname{TSP}(d)\le Z\le(2-\delta)\operatorname{TSP}(d)\right]\ge\frac23\]
for every input metric. Only the number of oracle calls is bounded; the output is a cost estimate and need not describe a tour.
cards.why: This is a central test of how well a global optimization value can be estimated from incomplete metric information. Resolving it would determine whether the factor-two barrier is inherent to sparse distance access or reflects limitations of current estimators, with a sharp separation between learning a value and constructing a tour.
cards.status_note: Source-open in Onak’s Sublinear.info Problem 71 (Baltimore 2016) and explicitly retained as open for arbitrary metrics by Chen, Khanna and Tan, ICALP 2023, abstract and §1.1. On 16 September 2026, this review checked the arbitrary-metric oracle model in Czumaj–Sohler, the 2020 lower-bound scope and the exact promises of the 2023 algorithms. Bounded subsequent searches found no unrestricted subquadratic-query below-two estimator or impossibility theorem for the target. The 2023 paper’s positive results assume positive integral distances and either supplied MST information or a unit-tree promise; these are recorded as limited progress. This review did not independently audit every proof deferred from the conference papers to full versions and does not claim an exhaustive current-status certification.

The fixed improvement below two exposes a general information barrier rather than a small adjustment to a known approximation ratio.

sentences: A metric TSP cost query algorithm asks for distances between selected pairs of labeled points.
The question asks whether some fixed approximation factor below two is achievable with a subquadratic number of queries on every metric.
The algorithm is randomized and only needs to output a cost estimate, with success probability at least two thirds.
Nearly linear MST-weight estimation gives the factor-two baseline, while stronger TSP estimates are known for special metrics or with extra spanning-tree information.
The target separates sparse access to a global optimum value from the information needed to construct an explicit tour.

cards.definitions:
The input consists of a known integer \(n\ge3\), the labels \([n]\), and an oracle for a function \(d:[n]\times[n]\to\mathbb R_{\ge0}\). It is promised that \(d(i,j)=0\) exactly when \(i=j\), that \(d(i,j)=d(j,i)\), and that
\[d(i,k)\le d(i,j)+d(j,k)\quad\text{for all }i,j,k\in[n].\]
Thus all off-diagonal distances are finite positive real numbers. The triangle inequality and symmetry are input promises, not properties that the algorithm must verify. Metrics are arbitrary: no Euclidean embedding, dimension bound, integer-distance restriction, bounded aspect ratio or distribution on inputs is supplied.

One query consists of specifying labels \(i,j\in[n]\) and receiving the exact real distance \(d(i,j)\). It costs one oracle call. Queries may depend on earlier replies and on the algorithm’s private randomness. Repeated calls are charged again. Diagonal values are known to be zero; allowing a paid diagonal call gives no additional information. The metric remains fixed throughout the execution and is chosen independently of the random bits.

The algorithm is uniform: a single finite program works for every \(n\). To specify computation with exact real oracle replies, use a classical real-register machine with rational program constants, ordinary finite control, integer counters, and exact real arithmetic and comparisons. Allowed real operations are addition, subtraction, multiplication and division by a nonzero value; registers may store queried distances and calculated real values. Randomness consists of independent fair bits, which may be used to select labels. Integer computation, local arithmetic, storage and random-bit generation are not charged to the query budget. They must define an algorithm that halts with probability one on each input. No advice depending on the metric or on \(n\), quantum queries, further metric oracle, precomputed spanning tree or access to unqueried matrix entries is available.

This is a query-complexity question, so there is no polynomial-time or subquadratic-time requirement on the computation between calls. In particular, the original source’s suggestion of subquadratic total time is a stronger aspiration, not an additional condition for answering its primary query question. A positive solution with such a time bound would also solve this card, provided it meets all the stated guarantees.

The output \(Z\) is one real value. On a successful execution it is an upper estimate at most \(2-\delta\) times the optimum. An equivalent lower-estimate convention would require \(\operatorname{TSP}(d)/(2-\delta)\le Z'\le\operatorname{TSP}(d)\); multiplication by the fixed approximation factor converts between the conventions without oracle calls. The algorithm may fail to meet the interval on at most one third of its random executions. Success is required for each metric individually, not merely on average over an input distribution.

The query bound is worst case over inputs and random executions, apart from null-probability exceptional executions. Formally, there must exist \(q:\mathbb N\to\mathbb N\) such that every \(n\)-point input uses at most \(q(n)\) oracle calls with probability one, and
\[\lim_{n\to\infty}\frac{q(n)}{n^2}=0.\]
The constant \(\delta\), the program and this bound are independent of all distance values. There is no hidden dependence on the ratio of the largest to the smallest positive distance. For finitely many small \(n\), all pair distances may be queried without affecting the limit. The little-o condition is weaker than demanding \(O(n^{2-\gamma})\) for some fixed \(\gamma>0\); both a fixed polynomial saving and a genuine slower asymptotic saving would qualify.

The quantifier order is \(\exists\delta\;\exists A\;\exists q\;\forall n\ge3\;\forall d\), followed by probability over the execution of \(A\). The improvement \(\delta\) must be a positive constant; an approximation factor approaching two from below as \(n\) grows is insufficient. The card asks whether any such constant improvement exists, not for the largest possible improvement or a full approximation-query tradeoff.

A tour is a cyclic ordering of all labels, using each exactly once before returning to the start. The cost includes that closing edge. The oracle describes the complete metric, so each tour edge costs the queried distance itself; no separate underlying graph path needs to be output. \(\mathfrak S_n\) is the set of all permutations of \([n]\). The finite minimum in the definition of \(\operatorname{TSP}(d)\) is attained and is strictly positive.

For background, a spanning tree is a connected acyclic graph on all labels, and \(\operatorname{MST}(d)\) is the minimum sum of its edge distances. The familiar inequalities \(\operatorname{MST}(d)\le\operatorname{TSP}(d)\le2\operatorname{MST}(d)\) explain the factor-two threshold. Estimating the weight of an MST does not give its edges. A graphic metric is the shortest-path distance metric of a connected unweighted undirected graph. A \((1,2)\)-metric has every off-diagonal distance equal to one or two. Both are special classes of the general metric inputs here.

This is not a streaming task: a stream reveals entries in an imposed order, whereas the algorithm here chooses each pair it queries. A result that is given a minimum spanning tree as additional input, or promises a spanning tree of unit-distance edges, concerns additional information or structure absent from the target. Full-input approximation algorithms may also use quadratically many distance entries, regardless of their approximation ratio.
cards.answer_criterion: Supply a complete Lean-checked proof or refutation of the existence of an absolute \(\delta>0\), a uniform classical randomized algorithm and a worst-case query bound \(q(n)=o(n^2)\) with the stated success probability for every metric. A positive answer must prove the cost guarantee, the uniform little-o bound independent of the metric’s scale and aspect ratio, and almost-sure halting in the specified oracle model. It need not output a tour or run in subquadratic total time. A negative answer must refute this quantified existence statement for randomized adaptive algorithms; a lower bound only for deterministic algorithms, near-exact approximation, or a specific algorithm is insufficient. Positive results restricted to graphic or \((1,2)\)-metrics, or assuming an MST is supplied, do not resolve the arbitrary-metric target. Experimental success rates, conditional computational hardness and an improvement that vanishes with \(n\) do not establish the required result.

source_formulation.text: Sublinear.info Problem 71 asks whether some positive constant improvement below approximation factor two is possible for metric TSP cost with fewer than quadratically many pair-distance queries. It presents a subquadratic total running time as an even stronger goal. This card retains the primary query-complexity question and makes the randomness and cost-estimation convention explicit.
source_formulation.caption: Editorial paraphrase of Sublinear.info Problem 71; the primary distance-query target is retained

context_blocks.text: A distance matrix contains quadratically many entries. Estimating a global optimum after reading a vanishing fraction of these entries asks how much information about a metric is needed to recover a useful numerical summary, rather than an explicit combinatorial solution.

Czumaj and Sohler estimate metric MST weight within a factor \(1+\varepsilon\) using nearly linear oracle access for fixed \(\varepsilon\). The resulting TSP estimate approaches factor two. Their arbitrary-metric model does not assume a given geometric embedding or a bounded ratio of distances.

Classical tour algorithms can rely on an actual spanning tree and further global structure. The source emphasizes that obtaining the tree itself can require quadratically many distance queries even though estimating its total weight is much easier. This is an information-access distinction between value estimation and producing a witness.

Chen, Kannan and Khanna obtain below-two estimation for graphic and two-valued metrics. They also prove that sufficiently accurate approximation already requires quadratic query complexity on these special classes. That obstruction near factor one does not rule out every fixed improvement below two.

Chen, Khanna and Tan extend below-two estimation to positive integral metrics that either have a promised unit-edge spanning tree or are supplied with an MST. The query cost is \(\widetilde O(n^{3/2})\). Their paper explicitly leaves the unrestricted general-metric query question open.

The 2023 paper also gives streaming algorithms and lower bounds. Those theorems have different access rules and cannot be substituted for a pair-distance query theorem. In particular, a result with an extra pass over every matrix entry need not inspect only a subquadratic number of distances.

The requested estimate need not correspond to a tour produced by the algorithm. A positive answer would establish that useful information about tour cost is accessible with strictly fewer than all pairwise measurements, even where recovering the usual intermediate structures is expensive.

cards.title: Fast merging of summaries for symmetric streaming computations
cards.formal: Does every total, order-invariant Boolean stream function computable deterministically in polylogarithmic space and polylogarithmic time per item also admit a deterministic summary scheme with polylogarithmic message size, working space, and time per merge, correct for every binary merge tree? The uniform families, input lengths and costs in this question are specified below.

cards.definitions: For each integer \(N\geq2\), let \(f_N\) map every nonempty sequence over \([N]=\{1,\ldots,N\}\) of length at most \(N\) to one bit. Totality means every such sequence is in its domain. Order invariance means permuting any sequence leaves its value unchanged; it is stronger than merely swapping two players. A streaming algorithm is one fixed deterministic program given \(N\) in binary, which starts with an initialized state, reads one item at a time, and produces \(f_N(x)\) when the stream ends. There must be constants \(B,c\), depending on the family but not \(N\), for which initialization, each update and final output take at most \(B\log^c(N+2)\) steps, and the stored state and temporary workspace use that many bits. A merge scheme consists of three fixed deterministic programs: a map \(\Phi_N\) from one item to a summary, a map \(\mu_N\) from two summaries to a summary, and a decoder \(\eta_N\) from a summary to a bit. Summaries may include their represented length. For every valid sequence and every rooted binary tree whose leaves are its items in any order, apply \(\Phi_N\) at the leaves, \(\mu_N\) at internal nodes and \(\eta_N\) at the root. The resulting bit must equal \(f_N(x)\). Intermediate summaries may depend on the tree; only the decoded answer must be invariant. Each message, workspace and invocation time is bounded by \(B_1\log^{c_1}(N+2)\), for constants depending on the family. Time means steps of a standard deterministic multitape Turing machine on binary representations; input and output tapes have the usual sequential access. The programs receive \(N\) and their local arguments, with no advice or precomputed data depending on \(N\). Both models are exact and deterministic. The conclusion is existence of a merge scheme for each streaming-computable family, not a promised efficient compiler from arbitrary program descriptions.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof of the universal simulation, including the time, memory and arbitrary-tree guarantees. Alternatively give a total symmetric family with a qualifying streaming algorithm and prove that no qualifying merge scheme exists. A slow merge procedure with short messages, a separation using a promise, or a private-randomness separation does not decide this specified question.

context_blocks.text: The workshop page asks broadly whether good streaming algorithms yield good sketches and compares one-way with simultaneous communication. Editorial specialization: this card selects the deterministic, total-function question with efficient merging. This is the time-sensitive refinement motivated by the paper cited on that page, rather than a claim that the already established space-only simulation remains unknown.

Feldman, Muthukrishnan, Sidiropoulos, Stein and Svitkina show that symmetric deterministic streaming computation can be distributed through a binary aggregation tree with comparable message size and polynomially related space. Their simulation uses reachability search and can take superpolynomial time. The retained target asks whether that time cost can always be avoided.

A sequential chain of merges is itself a streaming computation. The converse must support balanced trees and every other arrangement, even when the stream algorithm’s intermediate states record order-dependent information that disappears from the final answer.

The cited paper also gives failures of analogous comparisons for promises, multiple permissible outputs and private randomness. This card removes those routes to a separation by requiring a total Boolean function and deterministic exact computation. The malformed final sentence on the workshop page is not used as a theorem statement.

Associativity of the summary representation is not required: two different trees can leave different internal summaries provided both decode correctly. Demanding identical summaries would strengthen the problem beyond the aggregation model used here.

Recent turnstile-to-linear-sketch simulations address algebraic update streams and space preservation. Their hypotheses and conclusions do not provide this uniform polylogarithmic-time merging theorem for arbitrary insertion streams and arbitrary total symmetric functions.

cards.title: Common2 membership of FIFO queues
cards.formal:
Is the following proposition true?
\[
\forall n\in\mathbb N,\ n\ge3\quad
\exists A_n:\quad A_n\text{ implements a linearizable wait-free FIFO queue for }n\text{ processes}
\]
using only the atomic read/write registers and one-shot test-and-set bits defined below? The queue is initially empty and has no capacity bound. Every process may perform arbitrarily many operations of either kind, with arbitrary finite binary strings as enqueued values. Each \(A_n\) is deterministic and has finite code; it may depend on \(n\). The quantifiers do not additionally require one compiler producing all \(A_n\).
cards.definitions:
Fix \(n\ge3\). There are \(n\) named sequential processes with identifiers \(1,\ldots,n\), each knowing \(n\) and its own identifier. A process has unbounded private storage, initially containing only its identifier, \(n\), and its fixed program data. Its local computation is given by a deterministic finite Turing program on finite strings. Shared communication is confined to two countable arrays with natural-number addresses: registers \(R_0,R_1,\ldots\), initially containing the empty binary string, and bits \(B_0,B_1,\ldots\), initially zero. A register read atomically returns its whole current finite string; a write atomically replaces that string and returns an acknowledgement. The primitive \(\operatorname{TAS}(j)\) atomically returns the old value of \(B_j\) and changes it to one. A bit is never reset, and every later test-and-set on that bit returns one. Any process can access any address; using a previously unused address does not require an allocation oracle. There is no fixed bound on addresses used, register bit lengths, private storage or total operations over a whole execution. A finite execution prefix uses only finite data and finitely many primitive calls.

The scheduler interleaves individual local computation steps and atomic primitive calls. Each scheduled process chooses its next action from its private state, its current invocation and previous primitive responses. Processes receive no randomness, clock, failure detector, schedule information or noncomputable oracle. They can be delayed arbitrarily and can stop forever at any point. No fairness assumption constrains other processes. Local Turing steps, primitive invocations and operation responses count as that process's own steps; no bounded step complexity is demanded.

The sequential queue state is a finite sequence of finite binary strings, initially empty. \(\operatorname{Enqueue}(v)\) appends one occurrence of \(v\) at the end and returns a distinguished acknowledgement. \(\operatorname{Dequeue}()\) removes and returns the first occurrence if the sequence is nonempty; otherwise it returns a distinguished \(\mathsf{Empty}\) value without changing the state. Empty, acknowledgement and string-valued responses have separate tags, so the empty binary string is an ordinary possible item. Repeated equal values represent separate occurrences. Each process can invoke either operation whenever its previous invocation has returned, so it has at most one pending invocation. Clients may choose later invocations from earlier responses; there are no designated enqueuer or dequeuer roles, no bound on the number of calls and no promise that a dequeue finds an item.

Linearizability is required for every finite execution prefix. Take its history of queue invocations and responses. Append responses to any chosen subset of pending invocations and discard the other pending invocations. There must be a total order of the resulting completed operations that preserves each process's order, respects every real-time precedence in the completed history, and gives exactly their responses under the sequential queue specification. Here real-time precedence means that one operation's response occurs before the other's invocation. The choice of this total order may differ between different execution prefixes; it is not required to preserve earlier choices when a history is extended. Infinite executions must satisfy this safety condition at every finite prefix.

Wait-freedom is the following per-process termination property: from any reachable configuration with a pending operation of process \(p\), every continuation in which \(p\) takes infinitely many of its own steps contains a response to that operation after finitely many such steps, regardless of all other processes' delays, crashes or continuing operations. Thus an infinite execution in which one process's pending operation never finishes despite that process continuing to take steps is forbidden, even if other operations keep completing. These definitions specify ordinary linearizability and wait-freedom, with unlimited resource capacity; they impose neither strong linearizability nor a resource bound uniform over all histories.
cards.why: A queue orders work shared by concurrent processes. This question asks whether very weak synchronization suffices to guarantee that each continuing process finishes, even while others stop or interfere. It tests the distinction between consensus power and the ability to implement a reusable data type.

context_blocks.text: The OPODIS 2015 paper, published in 2016, explicitly asks whether an \(n\)-process ordinary linearizable wait-free queue can be built from test-and-set and registers for every \(n\ge3\). This card retains that quantifier order and the unrestricted repeated-operation interface, with finite-string values and explicit deterministic computation conventions.

The consensus number of an object type is the largest number of processes for which copies of that type together with registers can solve wait-free consensus: every continuing process decides one proposed input value and all decisions agree. Test-and-set and queues have consensus number two. That agreement capability by itself does not supply a many-process queue implementation. Common2 is the historical class of types implementable in a wait-free manner from any object type of consensus number two.

Stacks admit Common2 implementations. This result concerns last-in-first-out removal and does not supply the first-in-first-out semantics of the target. The source also studies unbounded numbers of participating processes; the present question allows a separate implementation for each fixed finite process count.

Eisenstat gives a Common2 queue for at most two enqueuing processes and any number of dequeuing processes. The stated restriction on who can enqueue leaves the unrestricted interface in this card unanswered.

The OPODIS 2022 article, published in February 2023, explicitly repeats the open Common2 queue question. Its efficient exact queue uses compare-and-swap, which atomically checks an expected value and conditionally writes a replacement; that primitive is unavailable here. Its separate multiplicity variant relaxes removal semantics.

Strong linearizability requires one choice of linearizations that preserves prefixes across histories. The 2025 paper proves an impossibility for strongly linearizable queues from the relevant weak primitives. Its progress condition is lock-freedom, meaning that infinitely many steps yield infinitely many completed operations somewhere in the system. The stronger correctness requirement prevents this result from being an impossibility for ordinary linearizability.

The PODC 2026 paper extends impossibility results for strongly linearizable queues, including settings with additional primitives and at least four processes. Those results continue to assume strong linearizability. The checked full version therefore does not refute the ordinary wait-free target.
