cards.title: Deterministic volume gap
cards.formal: For every locally checkable labeling problem \(\Pi\) on all finite graphs of some fixed maximum degree \(\Delta\), does the existence of a deterministic VOLUME algorithm A with \(V_{A}(n)=o(n)\) imply the existence of a deterministic VOLUME algorithm B with \(V_{B}(n)=O(1+\log * n)\)? Algorithms know the exact size of their input graph, and node identifiers are distinct integers in \(\{1,\ldots ,|V(G)|^{2}\}\). Here \(V_{A}(n)\) is the maximum number of distinct vertices visited to determine one vertex’s output, over all allowed instances with at most n vertices and all requested vertices.
cards.definitions: An LCL is specified by fixed \(\Delta \ge 2, a\) fixed verification radius \(r\ge 1\), finite nonempty input/output alphabets, and a finite set of permitted rooted radius-r labeled neighborhoods. Rules may inspect degrees and local ports, but not n or IDs. Instances include every finite nonempty simple undirected graph of maximum degree \(\Delta\), possibly disconnected, every input labeling and every port numbering. A labeling is valid exactly when all neighborhoods satisfy the rules. A deterministic VOLUME computation for a requested vertex v starts with v’s ID, degree, input, ports, \(\Pi\) and the exact |\(V(G)|\), and visited set \(\{v\}\). It may adaptively choose a visited vertex w and one of its incident ports, learning the neighbor u, its ID, degree, input and incident port names, then add u to the visited set. Arbitrary jumps to unseen IDs are forbidden. Only the number of distinct visited vertices, including v, is charged; local computation must terminate but its time and temporary space are unrestricted. Queries at different vertices run independently with no preprocessing or shared mutable state. Their outputs must jointly form a valid labeling for every input and ID assignment. Each algorithm is one finite computable program for all graph sizes. \(\log * n\) is the number of iterated base-2 logarithms needed to reach at most 1; the added 1 handles small n.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove the universal implication, or specify one fixed LCL with a sublinear-volume deterministic algorithm and prove it has no \(O(\log * n)\)-volume deterministic algorithm. Precisely, the latter lower bound means that for every correct B, every \(C>0\) and every \(n_{0}\), some \(n\ge n_{0}\) satisfies \(V_{B}(n)>C(1+\log * n)\). This gap formulation fixes the asymptotic quantifiers without assuming an optimal algorithm or an arbitrary symbolic complexity function exists.
cards.why: This tests whether deterministic access to local solutions has only a tiny-information regime and an essentially global regime. Either outcome would substantially constrain the design and possible complexity classes of deterministic local computation algorithms.

importance.reason: A proposed collapse of an entire deterministic complexity interval, rather than a bound for one task. It clarifies the power of adaptive exploration and the role of randomness in local computation.

progress.text: Rosenbaum and Suomela introduce the distance-versus-volume framework and pose the deterministic intermediate-volume question as Question 7.1. Their examples establish several randomized intermediate scales while retaining linear deterministic volume.

Brandt, Grunau, and Rozhoň show that randomized local computation below \(o(\sqrt{\log  n})\) can be sped up to deterministic \(O(\log * n)\). Their results also give linear deterministic volume lower bounds for fixed-color tree-coloring tasks in the relevant bounded-degree setting. These do not cover every LCL.
Grunau, Rozhoň, and Brandt close the gap between constant and iterated-logarithmic VOLUME complexity. The much larger interval above \(\log * n\) remains the issue here.
Suomela’s updated problem list retains the question of deterministic volume strictly between iterated logarithmic and linear.

Peng gives randomized VOLUME and LCA constructions of complexity \(\Theta (\log ^{k} n)\) for positive integers k and polynomial scales up to logarithmic factors. Section 1.1 explicitly leaves the deterministic gap unresolved.

cards.status_note: The July 2026 primary paper explicitly retains the deterministic gap as open. The new constructions are randomized; no deterministic resolution located through 10 September 2026.

context_blocks.text: A processor that sees far through a narrow part of a graph can inspect much less information than one that explores an entire ball of the same radius. The VOLUME model measures that inspected information. Its adaptive exploration captures a central feature of answering a query about a huge graph without first constructing an entire solution.

Correctness still couples the answers. Independently determining the color or matching status of one vertex must agree with the answers obtained for every other vertex. The algorithm cannot save previous answers and use their accumulated state as a growing global solution. This makes a low-volume construction substantially stronger than an arbitrary sequential greedy algorithm.

Rosenbaum and Suomela ask whether there is any deterministic volume complexity strictly between iterated logarithmic and linear, and conjecture there is none. Their model supplies exact graph size and polynomially bounded identifiers. Removing these conventions changes the indistinguishability arguments, so the card keeps them explicit.

The known small-complexity gaps leave the central interval unresolved. Randomized examples inhabit many intermediate scales, but an algorithm that follows a favorable random exploration does not automatically give a deterministic procedure that succeeds on every labeled graph. A deterministic counterexample to the proposed collapse would establish a new basic behavior.

July 2026 work constructs additional randomized polylogarithmic and polynomial volume complexities. Its introduction explicitly separates those results from the still-open deterministic question. The increased richness on the randomized side makes the contrast sharper while supplying no deterministic intermediate example.

It concerns fixed bounded-degree graph families with exact size information and polynomially bounded identifiers.
Proving the collapse would eliminate an entire intermediate range of deterministic local information complexity, despite the richer range available to randomized algorithms.

cards.context:
A processor that sees far through a narrow part of a graph can inspect much less information than one that explores an entire ball of the same radius. The VOLUME model measures that inspected information. Its adaptive exploration captures a central feature of answering a query about a huge graph without first constructing an entire solution.

Correctness still couples the answers. Independently determining the color or matching status of one vertex must agree with the answers obtained for every other vertex. The algorithm cannot save previous answers and use their accumulated state as a growing global solution. This makes a low-volume construction substantially stronger than an arbitrary sequential greedy algorithm.

Rosenbaum and Suomela ask whether there is any deterministic volume complexity strictly between iterated logarithmic and linear, and conjecture there is none. Their model supplies exact graph size and polynomially bounded identifiers. Removing these conventions changes the indistinguishability arguments, so the card keeps them explicit.

The known small-complexity gaps leave the central interval unresolved. Randomized examples inhabit many intermediate scales, but an algorithm that follows a favorable random exploration does not automatically give a deterministic procedure that succeeds on every labeled graph. A deterministic counterexample to the proposed collapse would establish a new basic behavior.

July 2026 work constructs additional randomized polylogarithmic and polynomial volume complexities. Its introduction explicitly separates those results from the still-open deterministic question. The increased richness on the randomized side makes the contrast sharper while supplying no deterministic intermediate example.

cards.title: Linear-sketch complexity of the nuclear norm
cards.formal:
Determine the optimal number \(m_\varepsilon(n)\) of exact real linear measurements required to estimate the nuclear norm of an arbitrary real \(n\times n\) matrix with relative error at most \(\varepsilon\) and success probability at least \(2/3\), up to matching constant factors in \(n\), for every fixed \(0<\varepsilon<1\).

The sketch is randomized and chosen independently of the input matrix. It must satisfy, for every fixed \(A\in\mathbb R^{n\times n}\),
\[\Pr_\omega\!\left[(1-\varepsilon)\|A\|_*\le d_\omega(S_\omega A)\le(1+\varepsilon)\|A\|_*\right]\ge\frac23,\]
where \(S_\omega:\mathbb R^{n\times n}\to\mathbb R^m\) is linear and \(d_\omega\) is a decoder that receives only the sketch and the input-independent random choices. The quantity \(m_\varepsilon(n)\) is the smallest possible dimension \(m\).

Give an explicit asymptotic description \(g(n,\varepsilon)\) and prove that for every fixed \(\varepsilon\in(0,1)\) there exist \(0<c_\varepsilon\le C_\varepsilon<\infty\) and \(N_\varepsilon\) such that
\[c_\varepsilon g(n,\varepsilon)\le m_\varepsilon(n)\le C_\varepsilon g(n,\varepsilon)\qquad(n\ge N_\varepsilon).\]
The constants may depend on the fixed accuracy, but not on \(n\). Logarithmic factors in \(n\) must be resolved; determining only a polynomial exponent does not meet this target.
cards.why: Determining this complexity would explain whether summing singular values permits a materially smaller linear summary than storing a general matrix, and exactly how much compression is possible. It would also locate a central matrix norm within the sharply differing sketching behavior of the Schatten family.
cards.status_note: The exact asymptotic order up to constant factors remains source-open in the checked material. The original question is Woodruff’s 2014 survey Open Question 4. The 2019 journal article’s model and linear lower bound were checked. A bounded search on 16 September 2026 found Yang’s arXiv:2608.22247v3, revised 27 August 2026: its stated near-quadratic lower and upper bounds leave logarithmic factors unresolved, as explicitly discussed in §6. This review inspected its model, theorem statement and remaining-gap discussion, not a full independent verification of its 94-page proof; no verified journal acceptance is asserted. The recent bounds are therefore identified as preprint claims, and even as stated they do not complete this card’s matching-constant-factor criterion.

sentences: The nuclear norm of a matrix is the sum of its singular values.
The question asks for the smallest number of randomized exact real linear measurements that suffice to approximate this norm for every fixed input matrix.
The requested answer must give matching upper and lower bounds up to constant factors for each fixed relative accuracy.
Published results separate this matrix problem from ordinary vector norms, bilinear sketches and finite-bit streaming complexity.
An August 2026 preprint claims near-quadratic bounds but leaves logarithmic factors unresolved, and its proof is not independently verified by this review.

cards.definitions:
Let \(n\) be any positive integer. For a real square matrix \(A\), its singular values \(\sigma_1(A),\ldots,\sigma_n(A)\) are the nonnegative square roots of the eigenvalues of \(A^{\mathsf T}A\), with multiplicities and zeros included. Its nuclear norm, also called the trace norm or Schatten-1 norm, is
\[\|A\|_*=\sum_{i=1}^{n}\sigma_i(A).\]
No symmetry, positive-semidefiniteness, rank, sparsity, integrality or bounded-entry promise is imposed. In particular, this is not the entrywise sum of absolute values. A symmetric positive semidefinite matrix has nonnegative eigenvalues, and for that restricted class the nuclear norm equals the trace; the target covers all real matrices.

An \(m\)-measurement randomized linear sketch for given \(n,\varepsilon\) is specified by an input-independent probability space of random seeds \(\omega\), a real linear map \(S_\omega\), and a decoding function \(d_\omega:\mathbb R^m\to\mathbb R\). Equivalently, each measurement has the form
\[(S_\omega A)_t=\sum_{i=1}^n\sum_{j=1}^n B_{tij}(\omega)A_{ij},\qquad1\le t\le m,\]
where all coefficients are fixed once the seed is sampled, before inspecting any entry of \(A\). The map may depend on \(n\) and \(\varepsilon\), but not on \(A\). The seed may also specify independent decoder randomness. The coefficient functions and the combined decoding map \((\omega,y)\mapsto d_\omega(y)\) are measurable with respect to their probability space and the usual Borel sigma-algebra on finite-dimensional real spaces, so every displayed success probability is defined.

All randomness is over the seed. The matrix is fixed before that seed is chosen, with the quantifier order \(\exists\text{ sketch distribution}\;\forall A\;\Pr_\omega[\text{success on }A]\ge2/3\). The same seed need not work simultaneously for all matrices. Conversely, a guarantee only for a random input matrix is insufficient. For \(A=0\), success requires the output to be exactly zero. For nonzero inputs the error bound is multiplicative, equivalently \(|d_\omega(S_\omega A)-\|A\|_*|\le\varepsilon\|A\|_*\).

The cost is the fixed number \(m\) of data-dependent real scalars retained. Coefficients, measurements and arithmetic are exact real objects. Their bit lengths, the description of the seed, evaluation time, and the decoder's auxiliary working space are not counted. No finite-precision or efficient-sampling requirement is added. The decoder can be nonlinear and have unbounded computational cost. This is an information measure for general linear sketches, not a claim of a Turing-machine implementation. Separate choices of distribution and decoder for each \(n,\varepsilon\) are allowed; an algorithm constructing them uniformly in polynomial time is not part of the target.

Define
\[m_\varepsilon(n)=\min\{m\in\mathbb N_0:\text{ an admissible }m\text{-measurement sketch satisfies the stated guarantee}\}.\]
This minimum is finite and attained as a minimum over integers: retaining all \(n^2\) entries is a linear sketch from which the norm is defined exactly. The target seeks a noncircular asymptotic description of this optimization, with upper bounds witnessed by admissible sketch distributions and lower bounds applying to every such distribution and decoder.

A restricted bilinear sketch retains a matrix \(UAV\) for input-independent matrices \(U\) and \(V\); its scalar entry count is one possible general linear-sketch dimension. General sketches are not restricted to this form. Lower bounds for one selected architecture do not automatically extend to all real linear maps. Likewise, bits of streaming memory and real measurement dimension are different resources. An entry update can be reflected linearly in the sketch, but this does not identify the number of exact counters with their finite binary storage cost.

The source asks for a constant-factor approximation without fixing the constant. This review spells out the family of fixed relative accuracies \(0<\varepsilon<1\), with constant success probability \(2/3\), in the standard model made explicit in the subsequent literature. Each accuracy is held constant while \(n\to\infty\); the answer need not optimize a joint regime where \(\varepsilon\) tends to zero with \(n\). The requested precision for the optimal dimension is equality of asymptotic order up to multiplicative constants, including every unbounded logarithmic factor.
cards.answer_criterion: Supply a noncircular asymptotic description of \(m_\varepsilon(n)\) and a complete Lean-checked proof of matching upper and lower bounds for every fixed \(\varepsilon\in(0,1)\), with the quantifiers and input domain above. An upper bound must give a valid input-independent sketch and decoder with the per-matrix success guarantee. A lower bound must apply to arbitrary measurable decoders and all general randomized real linear maps. Bounds matching only up to polylogarithmic factors, only the exponent in \(n^{\alpha+o(1)}\), a result confined to positive semidefinite matrices, or a finite-bit streaming bound alone do not determine the requested order. The parameter \(\varepsilon\) is the sketch's relative error; the benchmark's default additive numerical tolerance does not replace the required asymptotic precision.

source_formulation.text: Woodruff asks for the optimal dimension of a linear sketch that approximates the Schatten-1, or nuclear, norm within a constant factor. The question contrasts it with the much better understood Frobenius and spectral norms.
source_formulation.caption: Editorial paraphrase of Open Question 4, with the general real linear-sketch model and constant-factor precision made explicit below

context_blocks.text: The nuclear norm sums the strengths of all singular directions of a matrix. It is a standard matrix norm with uses in low-rank modeling, and its sketching complexity asks how much linear information must be retained to estimate that total without retaining the full matrix.

The neighboring Schatten norms behave very differently: for fixed approximation accuracy, the Frobenius norm admits a constant-dimensional sketch, whereas spectral-norm approximation requires \(\Theta(n^2)\) dimensions. The nuclear norm has long occupied an unresolved position between these extremes.

For real matrices, changing an entry changes the singular values indirectly. Ordinary vector norm sketches therefore do not automatically estimate a Schatten norm. The 2019 paper makes this distinction and connects nuclear-norm sketching to the possibility of small summaries for matrix nearest-neighbor search.

Theorem 4.1 of the 2019 paper gives an \(\Omega(n)\) general-sketch lower bound for nuclear-norm approximation at a sufficiently small fixed relative error. Its stated error probability can be converted to the convention here by constant repetition. The theorem does not by itself identify the optimum or assert the same threshold for every coarse approximation factor.

The August 2026 preprint claims, for each fixed \(0<\varepsilon<1\), constants \(A_\varepsilon,C_\varepsilon\) with
\[\frac{n^2}{(\log n)^{A_\varepsilon}}\le m_\varepsilon(n)\le C_\varepsilon\frac{n^2\{\log\log(e^e n)\}^2}{\log(en)}\]
for sufficiently large \(n\). These are the claims of its Theorem 1.1, whose full proof has not been independently verified in this review. The paper explicitly retains a logarithmic gap, so the displayed bounds would still fall short of the card’s constant-factor target.

The short description of a “sketch” can hide several inequivalent costs. This card fixes the number of exact real measurements and a guarantee for each fixed matrix. Finite-bit streaming, input-dependent measurements, and recovery of the matrix itself have different requirements.

cards.title: One-pass semi-streaming depth-first search
cards.formal:
Does there exist one uniform randomized one-pass streaming algorithm and fixed constants \(C\ge1\), \(k\ge0\) that, for every connected simple undirected graph \(G\) on \(n\ge1\) vertices, outputs a depth-first-search spanning tree using at most
\[C n\bigl(\log_2(n+2)\bigr)^k\]
bits of working memory, with probability at least \(2/3\) for every ordering of its edge stream?

The stream lists each edge once, contains no deletions, and can only be scanned from beginning to end. The algorithm may choose the root and neighbor order of the DFS tree. The question concerns the memory and pass bounds, with no additional polynomial-time requirement.

source_formulation.text: The 2020 paper explicitly asks whether DFS-tree computation needs more than one pass with semi-streaming memory. It treats connected simple undirected graphs and distinguishes insertion-only lower bounds from stronger insertion-deletion upper bounds.
source_formulation.caption: Editorial paraphrase of the abstract and introduction, with the source model from p.34:3; replaces the truncated extraction

cards.why: DFS is a basic graph decomposition tool whose required ancestor structure is stronger than connectivity or an arbitrary spanning tree. Resolving its one-pass feasibility would explain whether near-linear memory can retain enough information for this globally constrained traversal without revisiting edges.
cards.status_note: The exact one-pass question is explicitly open in the checked STACS 2020 source, and the 2024 engineering paper records the existing many-pass bounds rather than a general one-pass algorithm. Current status is uncertain: the introduction of Konrad–Trehan, ESA 2025 p.22:2 (also arXiv:2508.16022v1), states that subquadratic-space BFS/DFS algorithms do not exist, citing Cormode–Dark–Konrad 2019 and Assadi–Chen–Khanna 2019. On 16 September 2026 this review followed both citations; their inspected statements establish maximal-independent-set lower bounds, and text searches and relevant theorem readings did not locate a DFS lower bound or a reduction supporting the assertion. The 2025 statement is not used as a verified resolution, but the conflict prevents a confident current-open certification. Bounded additional searches located no matching theorem. This is a completed formulation and evidence review with its status limit retained.

The long-path paper contains a conflicting introductory DFS lower-bound assertion. Following its two citations located maximal-independent-set results, without identifying a theorem resolving this DFS question. This review does not certify that assertion.

sentences: The input is an arbitrary-order stream of edges of a connected undirected graph.
The task is to output any DFS spanning tree in one pass using nearly linear bit memory.
The tree must place the endpoints of every graph edge in an ancestor relationship, beyond ordinary connectivity.

cards.definitions:
The graph has labelled vertex set \(V=\{1,\ldots,n\}\), is connected and undirected, and has no self-loops or parallel edges. The algorithm is given \(n\) in advance. Its input stream is an arbitrary permutation of the edges \(\{u,v\}\in E\), represented by the two binary vertex labels, followed by an end marker. No adjacency lists, neighbor-query oracle, random access to the graph or second scan are available. The empty stream for \(n=1\) is valid. The requirement is a promise on these well-formed connected graph streams; recognition of the promise is not an additional task.

A rooted spanning tree \(T\) consists of a root \(r\in V\) and one parent in \(V\) for each other vertex, with every parent edge belonging to \(E\). Following parents must reach \(r\) and visit no cycle. A vertex \(u\) is an ancestor of \(v\) when it lies on the tree path from \(r\) to \(v\). The required DFS condition is
\[\forall\{u,v\}\in E:\quad u\text{ is an ancestor of }v\ \text{or}\ v\text{ is an ancestor of }u.\]
For undirected graphs this characterizes a spanning tree obtainable by depth-first search: start at the root, recursively finish exploring a newly discovered neighbor before exploring another, and retain the edges used for first discovery. The root and each vertex's order of neighbors may be chosen by the algorithm. No prescribed or lexicographic traversal must be reproduced, and the neighbor order need not equal edge-arrival order. An arbitrary spanning tree need not satisfy the ancestor condition.

The output is an explicit root and parent table on all \(n\) labels; for \(n=1\), the sole vertex is the root. It has \(O(n\log(n+2))\) bits. The output may be produced after the stream ends using only retained memory and fresh randomness. A write-only output tape cannot be reread as extra storage. Deferring the output to the end does not change semi-streaming feasibility: an earlier root/parent output of this size could instead be retained within the same asymptotic memory regime.

The algorithm has a single finite description, independent of \(n\) and of the graph. It processes the input in one left-to-right pass and may keep at most \(C n(\log_2(n+2))^k\) bits at any time, including retained edges, summaries, counters, random seeds, temporary computation and postprocessing. The bound is worst case over valid streams and random choices. No advice or external writable storage is allowed. Fresh fair random bits are independent of the graph and edge order; old random bits can be accessed again only if retained within the memory bound. The algorithm must finish processing and produce an output with probability one, but no numerical bound on its processing time is imposed. In particular, the question does not silently add efficient offline computation to the streaming space restriction.

For every fixed \(G\) and every fixed edge permutation chosen before the random bits, the probability that the entire root/parent table is a valid DFS tree must be at least \(2/3\). An invalid tree or failure symbol counts as failure. Deterministic algorithms are allowed as a special case. This is a guarantee on arbitrary graphs and orders, not on random graphs or random-order streams.

Semi-streaming space here means \(O(n\,\operatorname{polylog} n)\) bits with one fixed exponent. A word of \(O(\log n)\) bits changes only that exponent, but arbitrary-precision words do not have unit storage cost. The source studies both insertion-only and insertion-deletion streams and states its lower-bound convention for insertion-only streams. This card retains the one-pass question in that basic insertion-only setting. A result only for streams with deletions would not refute it, while an algorithm handling deletions would be a stronger positive result.

A negative answer means that no pair of constants \(C,k\) and no such randomized algorithm works on every promised stream. It need not establish a full quadratic-space lower bound: any lower bound excluding \(n(\log n)^k\) for every fixed \(k\) would suffice. Extra passes, a restriction to sparse graphs with \(O(n\,\operatorname{polylog} n)\) edges, or a prescribed traversal order change the problem.
cards.answer_criterion: Provide a complete proof checked in Lean of the existence proposition or its logical negation in the stated insertion-only streaming model. A positive answer must prove that one algorithm makes one pass, respects its worst-case bit-space bound including postprocessing, terminates with probability one, and outputs some valid DFS tree with probability at least \(2/3\) on every valid graph and edge order. A negative answer must exclude all fixed polylogarithmic exponents and all allowed randomized algorithms, without relying on a processing-time limitation absent from the model. A lower bound only for a prescribed traversal, directed graphs, streams with deletions or deterministic algorithms does not suffice. Experiments, random-graph guarantees, and a many-pass algorithm do not settle the target. The output is exact; numerical tolerance does not apply.

context_blocks.text: Ordinary depth-first search takes linear time when the entire graph is available in memory. The challenge here is that edges needed later in the traversal may have already passed by, and the full dense graph cannot be retained.

Finding some spanning tree is possible with near-linear memory in one pass. A DFS tree has the additional global ancestor condition: every edge must connect comparable vertices in the rooted tree. On a triangle, a star rooted at its center is a spanning tree but is not a DFS tree, because the two leaves are adjacent.

The source’s Theorem 4 gives a deterministic insertion-only algorithm with \(p\) passes and \(\widetilde O(n^2/p^2)\) bits, for \(1\le p\le\sqrt n\). At \(p\) of order \(\sqrt n\), this yields semi-streaming space, while at one pass its bound is quadratic. The quoted draft missed this improvement from the very paper containing the question.

For insertion-deletion streams the same theorem gives a randomized \(\widetilde O(n^3/p^4)\)-space tradeoff. That is a different input model. Neither tradeoff establishes a one-pass semi-streaming algorithm or a matching impossibility theorem for the target here.

The 2024 engineering paper evaluates practical versions and heuristics, often observing only one or a few passes, and discusses special random-graph behavior. These observations help explain practical relevance but do not give a one-pass worst-case guarantee on arbitrary edge orders.

Current-status evidence has a specific unresolved conflict: the 2025 long-path paper’s introduction asserts a quadratic-space obstruction for BFS/DFS, while the two papers cited there establish maximal-independent-set lower bounds in the inspected statements. No DFS lower-bound theorem or reduction supporting that assertion was located in those references. The card therefore records uncertainty rather than treating that sentence as a verified resolution.

For insertion-deletion streams the same theorem gives a randomized \(\widetilde O(n^3/p^4)\)-space tradeoff. That is a different input model. Neither tradeoff establishes a one-pass semi-streaming algorithm or a matching impossibility theorem for the target here.

The 2024 engineering paper evaluates practical versions and heuristics, often observing only one or a few passes, and discusses special random-graph behavior. These observations help explain practical relevance but do not give a one-pass worst-case guarantee on arbitrary edge orders.

Current-status evidence has a specific unresolved conflict: the 2025 long-path paper’s introduction asserts a quadratic-space obstruction for BFS/DFS, while the two papers cited there establish maximal-independent-set lower bounds in the inspected statements. No DFS lower-bound theorem or reduction supporting that assertion was located in those references. The card therefore records uncertainty rather than treating that sentence as a verified resolution.

cards.title: Local certificate size versus verification radius
cards.formal: Determine the worst-case certificate-size function \[F(s,d)=\max\{c_d(P):P\text{ is a graph property and }c_1(P)\le s\},\qquad s\in\mathbb Z_{\ge0},\ d\in\mathbb Z_{\ge1},\] in the anonymous local-verification model defined below. Here \(c_d(P)\) is the minimum number of certificate bits per vertex permitting sound and complete verification of \(P\) at radius \(d\), uniformly over all finite graphs. This asks for the whole numerical tradeoff, with pointwise absolute accuracy \(1/100\), rather than only a yes-or-no answer to the source’s proposed inverse-radius scaling.

cards.definitions:
Graphs are finite, nonempty, simple and undirected; they may be disconnected and have arbitrary degree. A graph property \(P\) is a set of these graphs invariant under graph isomorphism. Vertices have no identifiers, port numbers, input labels, advice or knowledge of the graph order. Graph distance is the minimum number of edges in a path; vertices in different components have infinite distance.

Fix integers \(d\ge1\) and \(b\ge0\). A certificate assignment is any function \(z:V(G)\to\{0,1\}^{b}\); for \(b=0\) there is one empty certificate. At a root \(v\), the radius-\(d\) view consists of the root, all vertices at distance at most \(d\), their certificates, and precisely the graph edges with at least one endpoint at distance at most \(d-1\) from \(v\). Edges between two vertices at distance exactly \(d\) are not visible. Neither edges leading beyond the view nor the degrees of its boundary vertices outside the view are additional input.

A verifier is one finite deterministic Turing-machine program accepting or rejecting a view. A view is encoded by its finite adjacency matrix, root index and certificate strings; the decision must be invariant under all renumberings of that encoding. Thus encoding indices convey no persistent identifiers. The program halts on every finite view. Its running time and memory are unrestricted, and it may depend on \(P,d,b\), but it is the same program for every graph order and every vertex. It has no oracle, random bits or additional input.

Such a verifier certifies \(P\) with \(b\) bits when, for every allowed graph \(G\),
\[
G\in P\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
\exists z:V(G)\to\{0,1\}^{b}\ \ \forall v\in V(G),\
A(\operatorname{view}_d(G,z,v))=\operatorname{accept}.
\]
The existential certificate assignment is unrestricted and may depend on the entire graph. On a graph outside \(P\), every assignment must cause at least one vertex to reject. There is no error probability. The cost is the common maximum number \(b\) of certificate bits stored at a vertex, not the total number of bits in the graph or view. Using a subset of the \(2^b\) strings is allowed.

Define \(c_d(P)\) as the least such integer \(b\), with value \(+\infty\) if no such verifier exists. The domain of the maximum in \(F(s,d)\) consists only of properties with a certificate bound \(s\) independent of graph order. Different properties and different values of \(d\) may use different verifiers; no algorithm receiving a description of \(P\) is required. The set of possible values is a nonempty subset of \(\{0,\ldots,s\}\): the property containing every graph has cost zero, and a radius-\(d\) verifier can restrict its input to radius one. Hence this maximum is finite and attained as a numerical value. All graphs, graph orders, properties and degrees in its definition are quantified; neither \(s\) nor \(d\) is hidden in an unspecified constant.
cards.answer_criterion: Supply a mathematically specified function \(g:\mathbb Z_{\ge0}\times\mathbb Z_{\ge1}\to\mathbb R\) and a complete mathematically correct Lean proof that \(\lvert g(s,d)-F(s,d)\rvert\le1/100\) for every \(s\ge0,d\ge1\). The approximation need not be integer-valued. An unambiguous expression or certified rule can specify \(g\); merely repeating the defining maximum, giving sampled values, or proving only asymptotic upper or lower bounds does not determine this function to the required precision.

cards.title: Two-dimensional sandpile prediction in NC
cards.formal: Is the language \(\mathrm{SP}_2\) defined below in logspace-uniform \(\mathrm{NC}\)? An instance explicitly supplies a finite stable rectangular array of sand grains and cells \(p,q\) inside that rectangle. Extend the array by zero to all of \(\mathbb Z^2\), add one grain at \(p\), and accept exactly when \(q\) eventually topples under the simultaneous four-neighbor rule. The question concerns one uniform circuit family with polynomial size and polylogarithmic depth for all input lengths.
cards.definitions:
Let \(W,H\ge1\), let \(B=\{0,\ldots,W-1\}\times\{0,\ldots,H-1\}\), let \(c:B\to\{0,1,2,3\}\), and let \(p=(p_x,p_y),q=(q_x,q_y)\in B\). Define \(\bar c(v)=c(v)\) on \(B\) and \(\bar c(v)=0\) elsewhere in \(\mathbb Z^2\). Set \(c_0(v)=\bar c(v)+\mathbf1_{\{v=p\}}\). With
\[
E=\{(1,0),(-1,0),(0,1),(0,-1)\},
\]
define, for every integer \(t\ge0\) and every \(v\in\mathbb Z^2\),
\[
c_{t+1}(v)=c_t(v)-4\mathbf1_{\{c_t(v)\ge4\}}+
\sum_{e\in E}\mathbf1_{\{c_t(v-e)\ge4\}}.
\]
Here \(\mathbf1_A\) is \(1\) when assertion \(A\) holds and \(0\) otherwise. Every unstable cell topples once per simultaneous round; its threshold and the number of grains sent to each neighbor are fixed. The required output is \(1\) exactly when \(\exists t\ge0:\ c_t(q)\ge4\). All cells outside the supplied rectangle participate in the same dynamics. There is no absorbing boundary, periodic identification, missing neighbor or cell-dependent weight.

For a nonnegative integer \(z\), let \(s(z)\) be its ordinary binary expansion without leading zeros, using \(s(0)=0\), and let \(b(z)=|s(z)|\). Encode \(z\) as \(1^{b(z)}0s(z)\). A valid binary input is the concatenation of these codes for \(W,H,p_x,p_y,q_x,q_y\), followed by exactly \(2WH\) bits encoding the entries of \(c\): list rows in increasing \(y\), and within each row increasing \(x\), using \(00,01,10,11\) for \(0,1,2,3\). Dimensions must be positive and the encoded coordinates must belong to \(B\). Strings not meeting these conditions are rejected. Let \(N\) be the complete binary string length, including all array entries. Extra zero rows or columns are permitted, but their entries still count; this is not a sparse or succinct configuration encoding.

Membership in logspace-uniform \(\mathrm{NC}\) means that there exist fixed integers \(a,k\ge1\), a fixed real \(K\ge1\), and a deterministic finite Turing-machine program generating a Boolean circuit \(C_N\) from the unary input \(1^N\), for every \(N\ge0\). It must halt, use at most \(K\log_2(N+2)\) work-tape cells, and write an explicit gate-and-wire description to a write-only output tape. Its input tape is read-only. The circuit has \(N\) input bits and one output, uses AND and OR gates of fan-in two, NOT gates of fan-in one and constants \(0,1\), has at most \(K(N+2)^a\) gates and depth at most \(K(\log_2(N+2))^k\), and decides \(\mathrm{SP}_2\) exactly on all length-\(N\) strings. Gate descriptions use binary indices in topological order and specify the output gate. There is no advice or oracle. The constants, circuit generator and gate basis are independent of the instance. Randomized error is not allowed; no time \(t\) is supplied as part of the instance.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct Lean proof of membership of this language in the specified uniform circuit class, or a complete Lean proof that no such circuit family and generator exist. Polynomial sequential simulation alone is insufficient. A proof of P-completeness under logspace reductions would imply nonmembership only with the additional assumption that P differs from NC; it is not an unconditional negative answer.
cards.why: One extra grain can trigger a long deterministic cascade. Whether its eventual effect can always be computed in polylogarithmic parallel time is a canonical test of how much sequential dependence a simple physical process can express.

importance.reason: A canonical unresolved parallel-complexity question for a simple two-dimensional dynamical system, connecting computational prediction with statistical physics.

cards.title: Characterizing separable distances approximable in small streaming space
cards.formal: Characterize the functions \(\phi:\mathbb N_0^2\to\mathbb Q_{\geq0}\) in the domain below for which the separable dissimilarities \[d_\phi(f,g)=\sum_{i=1}^n\phi(f_i,g_i)\] admit arbitrarily accurate relative approximation by one-pass algorithms using space polynomial in \(\log(n+M+2)\) and \(1/\varepsilon\), under deletions that preserve nonnegative frequencies. Equivalently, determine the classification function \(\chi(\phi)\in\{0,1\}\), equal to one exactly for functions with such algorithms.
cards.why: A full classification would explain which local comparisons of large frequency vectors retain enough structure for accurate compression under deletions. It would connect individual distance estimators and impossibility results through a general mathematical criterion, including dissimilarities that are not norms or even metrics.
cards.status_note: The source asks for a broad characterization. This card explicitly fixes an effective separable streaming variant rather than attributing every resource convention to the source. The 2016 one-variable result is only a partial classification, and the later metric counterexample concerns another model. No full characterization for the specified domain was located in the bounded September 2026 check.

sentences: A local nonnegative cost φ defines a dissimilarity by summing over corresponding frequency coordinates.
The stream may insert and delete frequencies while keeping both vectors nonnegative.
The selected task classifies exactly which effectively evaluable costs admit polylogarithmic-space relative approximations.
The criterion must cover the entire specified domain and include both algorithms and impossibility proofs.

cards.definitions: The domain consists of all fixed total functions \(\phi\) with \(\phi(t,t)=0\) for every \(t\geq0\), whose rational value on binary integers \(a,b\) can be computed in time polynomial in \(\log(a+b+2)\). Numerators and positive denominators are output in binary; the polynomial may depend on \(\phi\). Symmetry, the triangle inequality, homogeneity and dependence only on \(a-b\) are not assumed. A stream starts with \(f=g=0\) in \(\mathbb N_0^n\). Each item selects one vector, a coordinate \(i\in[n]\), and a change \(+1\) or \(-1\); no intermediate coordinate may become negative. The total number of updates is at most a given bound \(M\geq1\), so all coordinates are at most \(M\). Inputs \(n,M\) and a rational accuracy \(0<\varepsilon\leq1/2\) are known in advance. The algorithm reads each update once, in an arbitrary order independent of its coins, and at the end outputs a nonnegative rational \(D\). For every valid stream it must satisfy \((1-\varepsilon)d_\phi(f,g)\leq D\leq(1+\varepsilon)d_\phi(f,g)\) with probability at least \(2/3\); zero dissimilarity must therefore produce zero on a successful execution. The algorithm is a uniform randomized Turing machine that may depend on the fixed function \(\phi\). It may read fresh independent random bits, but remembered randomness, counters, work tapes and evaluation of \(\phi\) all count toward its working space. The read-once input and final write-only output are separate tapes and cannot serve as auxiliary storage. No running-time bound is required beyond termination on every run. Define \(\chi(\phi)=1\) if there are such an algorithm and constants \(B,a,b\), depending only on \(\phi\), using at most \(B\varepsilon^{-b}\log^a(n+M+2)\) working bits on every input and every coin outcome; otherwise define \(\chi(\phi)=0\). This definition ranges over all \(n,M,\varepsilon\). It does not require that a single decision program classify arbitrary descriptions of \(\phi\).
cards.answer_criterion: Give a noncircular necessary-and-sufficient condition on the numerical function \(\phi\), expressed without quantifying over streaming algorithms or communication protocols, and prove the classification completely in Lean. The positive direction must establish the specified approximation scheme; the negative direction must rule out every space bound of the stated form. As a function-valued benchmark answer, a supplied real-valued classification \(h\) must satisfy \(|h(\phi)-\chi(\phi)|\leq1/100\) throughout the domain. An exact zero-one characterization satisfies this tolerance. Repeating the definition of \(\chi\), covering only a proper subclass, or giving an uncertified list of examples is insufficient.

context_blocks.text: The source asks broadly which distances and dissimilarities can be compressed, especially when updates can delete items. Editorial specialization: this card fixes the separable, effectively evaluable rational-valued family, one-pass nonnegative-frequency deletion model and polylogarithmic-space approximation regime. The classification function makes the domain and acceptance precision explicit without requiring an algorithm to decide the classification from source code.

The source gives a linear-space obstruction when the cost of the same coordinate difference varies too much with its offset. This explains why dependence on the vector difference is a natural candidate property, but a necessary obstruction alone does not classify all admissible functions or provide matching algorithms.

The admissible family includes \(\phi(a,b)=|a-b|\), \(\phi(a,b)=(a-b)^2\), and coordinate disagreement \(\phi(a,b)=1\) when \(a\ne b\), zero otherwise. The last is not homogeneous. Thus “must be a norm” cannot be used literally as the characterization of every dissimilarity covered by the question.

Braverman, Chestnut, Woodruff and Yang characterize a large class of sums \(\sum_i h(|f_i-g_i|)\), including nonmonotone functions, with a specific exceptional class. Their work explicitly describes this as a partial answer to the Guha–Indyk question. It does not cover arbitrary two-argument \(\phi\).

The source’s norm-sketching update concerns a geometric characterization for normed spaces and a different constant-size communication formulation. Khot and Naor subsequently show that the corresponding norm characterization fails for general metric spaces. Neither statement is a characterization of the whole streaming class defined here.

An additive error proportional to the total frequency would be much weaker when two large vectors are very close. Relative error and exact treatment of zero are therefore central to the lower bounds and must be retained. Insertion-only algorithms or summaries of normalized probability distributions have different guarantees and input models.

cards.title: Linear-round weighted APSP in CONGEST
cards.formal:
For every fixed integer \(b\ge1\), does there exist a uniform randomized CONGEST algorithm and a constant \(C_b\) that, on every connected simple undirected \(n\)-vertex graph with integer edge weights in \(\{0,\ldots,n^b\}\), outputs all exact weighted distances at their respective vertices within \(C_b n\) communication rounds, with probability at least \(2/3\) that all outputs are correct simultaneously?

The bound must hold on every execution, for all \(n\ge2\). “Linear” means \(O(n)\) with no factor growing with \(n\); a bound \(\widetilde O(n)=O(n\,\operatorname{polylog} n)\) does not meet the target.

source_formulation.text: The source asks whether exact weighted all-pairs shortest paths can be computed in linear CONGEST time, after proving a linear lower bound and a limitation of the standard two-party lower-bound framework.
source_formulation.caption: Editorial paraphrase of §5, p.10:12, preserving the literal linear-round question; the explicit probability convention is recorded in the definitions

cards.why: Exact APSP is a central global task in bandwidth-limited networks. Closing the remaining logarithmic gap would identify whether transmitting the necessary information is the only asymptotic obstacle, while respecting the established near-linear breakthrough rather than treating its older polynomial gap as open.
cards.status_note: Source-open for the literal O(n)-round question in the 2017 paper. The April 2025 message-complexity preprint still records that near-linear round result; its own improvement concerns message count. Bounded later-result searches did not locate an O(n) protocol or a superlinear lower bound for the specified randomized model. The newer paper is evidence about the known near-linear bound, not an explicit exhaustive certification that the literal O(n) question remains open.

cards.definitions:
The communication network is the input graph \(G=(V,E,w)\). It has \(n\ge2\) vertices, no loops or parallel edges, is connected, and has nonnegative integer edge weights. For a fixed \(b\), each weight lies between 0 and \(n^b\) inclusive and is represented in binary. A vertex is a processor with a unique identifier in \(\{1,\ldots,n\}\). It initially knows \(n\), \(b\), its own identifier, the identifiers of its neighbors and the weights of its incident edges, but no other part of the topology or other edge weights. The requirement holds for all labelled graphs and therefore all assignments of these identifiers. The usual polynomial-size identifier range is equivalent for this target because identifiers can be renamed in \(O(n)\) rounds.

Computation is synchronous. In each round each endpoint of each edge can send the other endpoint a message of at most \(B_b\lceil\log_2(n+1)\rceil\) bits, for a fixed constant \(B_b\). Both directions operate independently and different neighbors may receive different messages. All messages sent in a round arrive before the next round. Communication is allowed only along edges of \(G\); there are no additional links between non-neighbors. Edge weights affect shortest-path lengths, not message latency or bandwidth. Local storage and finite local computation are unrestricted and uncharged; only the number of communication rounds is counted. The local rules form one finite, computable program, fixed for all \(n\) and inputs, with no topology-dependent advice or preprocessing.

Randomized processors use independent private fair random bits. For every fixed graph, weights and identifier assignment, probability is over these bits. By the prescribed worst-case round deadline every processor must halt and produce its output; an invalid or incomplete output counts as failure. The success event requires all vertices' entire distance tables to be correct in the same execution, with probability at least \(2/3\). Deterministic algorithms are included as a special case. No average over graphs or identifier assignments is used.

For vertices \(u,v\), define
\[d_G(u,v)=\min_{P:u\leadsto v}\sum_{e\in P}w(e),\qquad d_G(u,u)=0.\]
The minimum may be taken over simple paths, since weights are nonnegative. Each vertex \(v\) must output the labelled table \(\{(u,d_G(u,v)):u\in V\}\). Distances are finite integers of at most \((n-1)n^b\); zero-weight edges and equal-length alternative paths are allowed. The output is the exact distance table, without a requirement to list every path. Output and retained local tables are local memory, not extra communication channels.

The constants, bandwidth bound and program may depend on \(b\), but not on \(n\), graph density, diameter, individual weights or the random choices. At most \(C_b n\) rounds are allowed on every execution. There is no message-count bound beyond the per-edge per-round bandwidth. The source's linear-time question is retained literally. The explicit bounded-error convention uses one fixed constant global success probability; it does not impose an additional failure probability tending to zero with \(n\). The source's nonnegative polynomially bounded integer-weight setting includes the zero-weight edges used in its lower-bound example.

The proposition's negation says that for some fixed \(b\), no such uniform bounded-error algorithm has a linear worst-case round bound on all instances. It does not demand an \(\Omega(n^{1+\delta})\) lower bound for a fixed positive \(\delta\); a rigorously unavoidable unbounded logarithmic or slower factor could already refute linear time. The notation \(\widetilde O(n)\) suppresses polylogarithmic factors and therefore must not be read as \(O(n)\).
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof or refutation of the stated linear-round existence proposition. A positive answer must give, for every fixed weight exponent \(b\), a uniform protocol with the stated bandwidth, worst-case \(C_b n\) deadline and simultaneous exact correctness probability at least \(2/3\) on every input. A negative answer must rule out every such protocol for at least one fixed \(b\), preserving the communication and randomness conventions. A near-linear bound with an unbounded factor, approximate distances, a result only for unweighted graphs, a deterministic-only lower bound, or an algorithm with communication links outside the input graph is insufficient. Neither an expected-time bound alone nor a per-vertex success probability alone supplies the stated guarantee. The target is exact asymptotic linearity; numerical error tolerance does not apply.

context_blocks.text: Every node needs an entire row of the distance matrix, yet communication occurs only through the original network. The task therefore combines many shortest-path computations that compete for the same bounded-capacity links.

The 2017 source proves an \(\Omega(n)\) lower bound even on a weighted graph with a constant hop diameter. Its example encodes many edge weights that must pass through one communication link. Thus dependence on the network diameter alone cannot describe the cost of this problem.

The same source shows that its standard two-party reduction with a fixed partition of the vertices cannot yield a superlinear weighted-APSP lower bound. This is a theorem about the scope of that reduction framework, not an \(O(n)\) algorithm or a general impossibility of stronger lower bounds.

Bernstein and Nanongkai subsequently obtain a randomized Las Vegas \(\widetilde O(n)\)-round algorithm for exact weighted APSP, with additional generality including directed inputs. Their analysis retains polylogarithmic overhead, so it resolves the near-linear question without establishing the literal linear bound of this card.

The 2025 message-complexity paper still cites that \(\widetilde O(n)\) randomized round bound. Its own weighted-APSP result uses \(\widetilde O(n^2)\) messages and \(\widetilde O(n^2)\) rounds. Minimizing total messages and eliminating the logarithmic overhead in rounds are different objectives.

A resolution would determine whether the information-transfer lower bound fully captures exact weighted distance computation, or whether coordinating distance information imposes an additional asymptotic cost. The remaining gap concerns factors suppressed by near-linear notation, rather than the large polynomial gap present in 2017.

cards.title: Maximum independent set in the congested clique
cards.formal: Determine, up to constant factors as \(n\to\infty\), the minimum worst-case round complexity \(T_{\mathrm{MaxIS}}(n)\) for computing an exact maximum independent set of an arbitrary simple undirected graph on \(n\) labelled vertices in the deterministic unicast congested clique defined below. The output is distributed: each processor outputs the membership bit of its own vertex in one common maximum independent set. Local computation and storage have no resource bound, but each local computation must terminate. Only synchronous communication rounds are charged.
cards.definitions: For every integer \(n\ge2\), the vertices and processors have identifiers \([n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}\). An input is a simple undirected graph \(G=([n],E)\), represented at processor \(v\) by its \(n\)-bit incident-edge row. Initially each processor knows only this row, its own identifier, \(n\), all identifiers and the common protocol; it has no information about edges not incident to it. The communication network is complete, independently of \(E\). Let \(b(n)=\lceil\log_2 n\rceil\). In each round and for each ordered pair of distinct processors, the sender supplies one \(b(n)\)-bit string; shorter payloads must use a fixed padded encoding within that string. Different recipients may receive different strings. All messages for a round depend only on the initial state and messages from earlier rounds, and arrive simultaneously at its end. Local computations are deterministic, with finite descriptions and arbitrary finite local memory; no random coins, advice depending on the input graph, or additional communication channel are available. For fixed \(n\), a protocol may depend on \(n\), but it must work for every labelled graph of that size. All processors must produce their final bits after at most its round bound; their set \(S\) must satisfy both independence, \(\{u,v\}\notin E\) for all distinct \(u,v\in S\), and optimality, \(|S|\ge |I|\) for every independent \(I\subseteq[n]\). Ties between maximum sets are unrestricted, provided the output bits describe one such set. Define \(T_{\mathrm{MaxIS}}(n)\) as the least integer round bound of any such protocol, taking the worst case over all input graphs. There is no promise on density or graph structure. This retains the earlier card’s deterministic, logarithmic-bandwidth specialization of the source’s broader question with bandwidth \(b\).
cards.answer_criterion: Supply an unambiguous nonnegative asymptotic function \(f(n)\), a computably specified family of correct deterministic protocols, and a complete Lean-checked proof of constants \(c,C>0\) and \(n_0\ge2\) such that, for every integer \(n\ge n_0\), the supplied protocol uses at most \(Cf(n)\) rounds on every input graph, while every correct protocol for that size needs at least \(cf(n)\) rounds on some graph. Thus \(T_{\mathrm{MaxIS}}(n)=\Theta(f(n))\) in precisely the stated model. The upper-bound family must be described by one finite procedure taking \(n\), whose local computation is uncharged. Logarithmically separated bounds, a conditional lower bound alone, approximate solutions, or maximal rather than maximum independent sets are insufficient. This is an asymptotic communication-complexity target; the numerical absolute-error convention does not apply to its big-Theta bounds.
cards.why: Exact independent set separates the cost of learning a global optimum from the cost of computing it once the input is known. The complete communication network removes distances and narrow cuts, yet each link still carries only logarithmically many bits. A tight characterization would identify whether this canonical optimization problem intrinsically requires substantially more information exchange than easier graph tasks in the same network. The circuit connections also make it a meaningful test of the limits of current distributed lower-bound methods.

importance.reason: A canonical exact optimization task testing the communication power of the congested clique. Its relevance extends beyond symmetry breaking, although the chosen deterministic model is one specific frontier.

cards.title: Bipartite maximal matching with polynomial-in-degree volume
cards.formal: Do there exist universal constants \(C>0\), \(k\in\mathbb N\) and one uniform deterministic local-query algorithm which, on every finite simple bipartite graph of maximum degree at most \(\Delta\), answers each vertex query after visiting at most \(C(\Delta+1)^k\) distinct vertices, such that all answers together specify one maximal matching? A proper two-coloring of the input graph is supplied. The bound has no dependence on the number \(n\) of graph vertices.
cards.definitions: The input is a finite simple undirected graph \(G=(V,E)\) with \(n=|V|\ge1\), an integer bound \(\Delta\ge1\) with \(\deg(v)\le\Delta\) for all vertices, an injective identifier map \(V\to[n^2]\), and a proper coloring \(\chi:V\to\{0,1\}\) satisfying \(\chi(u)\ne\chi(v)\) on every edge. At each vertex \(v\), the incident edges have an arbitrary fixed bijective port numbering by \(\{1,\ldots,\deg(v)\}\); the two endpoints’ port numbers need not agree. A query rooted at \(v\) initially knows only \(n,\Delta\), the identifier, degree and color of \(v\), and its port index set. Its visited set starts as \(\{v\}\). It can adaptively probe port \(j\) of any visited vertex \(w\), thereby learning the corresponding neighbor \(u\), its identifier, degree, color and the reciprocal port of that edge at \(u\). This adds \(u\) to the visited set. Revisited vertices are recognized by their identifiers and counted only once. A probe does not reveal unvisited vertices behind other ports. The explored vertices form a connected set; direct probes of arbitrary identifiers are forbidden. The volume is the number of distinct visited vertices, including the root, at termination. Temporary memory and local computation are unrestricted but finite. Each rooted query starts afresh, with no preprocessing, shared mutable state or information retained from earlier queries. One finite deterministic program must work for all sizes, degree bounds, graphs, identifier assignments, port orders and supplied proper colorings. It receives no advice or randomness. It outputs either an unmatched symbol \(\bot\) or one local port at its root. For the outputs to describe a matching, whenever \(v\) selects its port leading to \(u\), the separate query at \(u\) must select the reciprocal port leading to \(v\). Let \(M\) be the selected undirected edges. Maximality requires that every edge in \(E\) has an endpoint incident to an edge of \(M\). Equivalently, no further edge can be added to \(M\) while keeping all selected edges vertex-disjoint. Maximum cardinality is not required. The same matching must result for every order of queries, and repeating a query must give the same answer. The constants \(C,k\) are independent of all input parameters, including \(\Delta\).
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct Lean-checked construction and correctness/volume proof for the quantified algorithm, or a complete Lean-checked proof of its logical negation. A negative result must rule out every universal polynomial degree bound for every correct uniform deterministic algorithm in this connected, stateless model. An algorithm with a factor depending on \(n\), randomized or expected volume guarantees, an oracle allowing arbitrary jumps, a method requiring preprocessing, or an approximation to maximum matching that need not be maximal does not establish the positive statement. A linear-in-degree lower bound alone does not establish the negative statement.
cards.why: This asks how much graph information is needed to answer a single matching query while remaining consistent with all other answers. A polynomial degree bound would give a deterministic local oracle for a basic graph primitive with cost independent of graph size. A superpolynomial lower bound would separate this information requirement from the known linear dependence on degree in communication rounds.

importance.reason: A fundamental maximal-matching oracle question that isolates degree dependence and the difference between distance and volume. It asks for a qualitative polynomial-versus-superpolynomial classification with no network-size term.

progress.text: As reviewed in the checked 2020 paper, Balliu and coauthors establish the deterministic LOCAL lower bound \(\Omega(\min\{\Delta,\log n/\log\log n\})\) for bipartite maximal matching. This yields a degree-linear obstruction for degree-only volume bounds.

Rosenbaum and Suomela formalize connected adaptive volume, and Brandt and Olivetti refine degree-dependent bipartite matching bounds in the round model. Their exact round constants are not asserted as exact volume constants.
Suomela’s updated list retains the explicit polynomial-in-degree volume question and states an exponential-degree conjecture.

context_blocks.text: Suomela’s problem list, updated 23 February 2026, explicitly asks whether maximal matching in bipartite graphs admits volume polynomial in the maximum degree. The supplied coloring and deterministic connected exploration are part of the model used here.

The list records a degree-only lower bound \(\Omega(\Delta)\) and an upper bound \((\Delta+1)^{O(\Delta)}\) for volume. These bounds leave open whether some fixed polynomial in \(\Delta\) is sufficient.

Rosenbaum and Suomela define volume by the number of distinct vertices seen through adaptive connected queries. This can differ substantially from the largest graph distance reached. The output of every rooted execution must still fit the same globally valid solution.
Suomela conjectures a \(2^{\Theta(\Delta)}\) dependence. This is a conjecture about the full degree dependence, and the cited page does not present it as a proved superpolynomial lower bound.
The degree parameter grows in this question. A bound that is constant in graph size for each separately fixed degree does not necessarily give one universal polynomial in the degree.

cards.title: Superlinear local certificates for hereditary graph classes
cards.formal:
Does there exist an isomorphism-invariant hereditary class \(\mathcal C\) of finite simple undirected graphs, with connected members of arbitrarily large order, and a fixed real exponent \(c>1\), such that every correct one-round proof-labeling scheme for membership in \(\mathcal C\) has worst-case certificate size \(\Omega(n^c)\) bits per vertex on connected \(n\)-vertex inputs?

More explicitly, for the optimal accepting-certificate size \(s_A(n)\) of a fixed correct local verifier \(A\), as defined below, require
\[\exists\mathcal C\;\exists c>1\;\forall A\text{ correct for }\mathcal C\;\exists a_A>0\;\exists N_A\;\forall n\ge N_A:\ s_A(n)\ge a_A n^c.\]
The exponent and graph class are common to all verifiers. This asks for a polynomial gap above linear certificate size, not merely for a bound that grows faster than \(n\).
cards.why: The question asks whether vertex-deletion stability imposes a fundamental information limit on distributed proofs. A polynomially superlinear example or a general obstruction would clarify how far local verification of structural graph properties can depart from the linear examples now known.
cards.status_note: Explicitly source-open in MFCS 2024 and still explicitly asked in the full arXiv v5 revision of 24 February 2026. On 16 September 2026 the review checked both versions’ local-verifier definitions, Theorem 3.1 and the exact final superlinear question, with the current arXiv revision history confirmed. Bounded subsequent-result searches found no matching hereditary-class resolution. This is current source evidence through the checked revision, not an exhaustive certification of all later literature.

progress.text: The MFCS paper proves linear lower bounds for hereditary and monotone geometric classes and asks whether \(\Omega(n^c)\) is possible for any fixed \(c>1\).

sentences: A prover gives each vertex a binary certificate, and each vertex checks only its immediate certified neighborhood.
The question asks for a hereditary graph class requiring a fixed polynomial factor more than linear certificate length at some vertex.

cards.definitions:
A graph class is a set of finite simple undirected graphs invariant under relabelling of vertices. It is hereditary if \(G\in\mathcal C\) implies \(G[U]\in\mathcal C\) for every subset \(U\subseteq V(G)\), where \(G[U]\) retains exactly the edges of \(G\) with both endpoints in \(U\). The class is fixed independently of input size. Membership is certified only on nonempty connected input graphs, as in the source. Closure under induced subgraphs is a property of the full class, including disconnected graphs; it does not require certifying disconnected networks. Requiring arbitrarily large connected members excludes vacuous lower bounds. Such a hereditary class has connected members of every positive order, by taking connected induced subgraphs of larger connected members.

On an \(n\)-vertex input graph, each vertex has a distinct positive integer identifier from \(\{1,\ldots,n^2\}\), in binary. These are arbitrary identifiers, not part of the graph property. This fixes the source's polynomial-size identifier convention. Every completeness and soundness condition holds for every permitted identifier assignment. The prover knows the entire labelled graph and assigns a finite binary string \(\sigma(v)\in\{0,1\}^{*}\) to every vertex. Certificates may depend on the graph and its identifiers. Their cost is the maximum length at a vertex, \(\max_v|\sigma(v)|\), not the sum of all certificate lengths.

The same deterministic local verifier \(A\) is used at every vertex, on every input size and every certificate assignment. At a vertex \(v\), it sees its own identifier and certificate, and the identifiers and certificates of its immediate neighbors, with the center distinguished. It has no information about edges among neighbors, about more distant vertices, or about a geometric representation of the graph. It outputs either accept or reject. This is the one-round proof-labeling model: certificates are assigned once and examined locally, without further interaction with the prover. The graph order is not supplied as extra global information. There is no randomization or acceptance error.

As in the source's definition, a verifier and prover are mathematical functions with no computational resource bound. The quantity measures the amount of local information, not the running time of deciding a local predicate; no separate computability or recognition-time requirement is imposed on the graph class or those functions. This convention is what makes the source's universal quadratic upper bound applicable to arbitrary graph classes. A scheme must still satisfy both exact logical requirements:
\[G\in\mathcal C\ \Longrightarrow\ \exists\sigma\;\forall v\in V(G):\ A(v,\sigma)=\mathrm{accept},\]
\[G\notin\mathcal C\ \Longrightarrow\ \forall\sigma\;\exists v\in V(G):\ A(v,\sigma)=\mathrm{reject}.\]
These quantify over every connected input and every valid identifier assignment. In the second condition the adversarial strings may be of any finite length; soundness is not restricted to certificates obeying an advertised short length. The prover is untrusted, and acceptance means that every vertex accepts.

For a fixed correct verifier \(A\) and a connected yes-instance \((G,\mathrm{id})\), let
\[\ell_A(G,\mathrm{id})=\min_{\sigma:\ \forall v\ A(v,\sigma)=\mathrm{accept}}\ \max_{v\in V(G)}|\sigma(v)|.\]
Completeness makes this a finite nonnegative integer. Define
\[s_A(n)=\max_{\substack{|V(G)|=n,\ G\in\mathcal C,\ G\text{ connected}\\ \mathrm{id}:V(G)\hookrightarrow\{1,\ldots,n^2\}}}\ell_A(G,\mathrm{id}).\]
Only finitely many labelled graphs and identifier assignments occur at a fixed \(n\), so the maximum is well-defined; if the set is empty it is defined as zero. The target's \(\Omega(n^c)\) means the displayed eventual bound for every sufficiently large integer \(n\). The verifier is fixed before taking the asymptotic limit; a different verifier for each size is not allowed. Since the prover may choose the shortest accepting certificates, this rules out cheap schemes rather than merely identifying inefficient choices of proof.

The source also asks whether the witnessing class can be monotone, meaning closed under all subgraphs obtained by deleting edges as well as vertices. Monotone classes are hereditary, so such an example would satisfy this card's main target, but edge-deletion closure is not required. The source's hereditary question is the main proposition; its stronger parenthetical variant remains context. The stronger locally-checkable-proof model additionally lets a vertex inspect the entire induced graph on its closed neighborhood. The known lower bounds in the paper hold even in that model, but the target here uses its stated proof-labeling model.

To refute the proposition, one must rule out a common positive polynomial gap for every hereditary class in the stated domain. Formally, for each such \(\mathcal C\) and each \(c>1\), there must be a correct verifier \(A\) for which \(s_A(n)\) is not \(\Omega(n^c)\): for every \(a>0\) and \(N\), some \(n\ge N\) has \(s_A(n)<a n^c\). A universal near-linear upper bound would suffice, but the logical negation does not require that particular stronger result.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof or refutation of the quantified existence statement. A positive answer must specify a hereditary class and one exponent \(c>1\), verify the closure and unbounded connected-member conditions, and prove the per-vertex lower bound against every correct verifier in the stated model, even when the prover chooses its best certificates. A negative answer must prove the logical negation for every admissible hereditary class and exponent. A linear lower bound, a bound such as \(n\log n\), a total-certificate lower bound spread over many vertices, or a lower bound for one selected verifier is insufficient. Computational hardness of centralized recognition alone is not a local certificate-size lower bound in this unrestricted-computation model. The target is an exact asymptotic proposition; numerical tolerance does not apply.

source_formulation.text: After proving the first linear local-certificate lower bounds for nontrivial hereditary and monotone graph classes, the authors ask whether some hereditary class has a lower bound with a fixed exponent strictly greater than one, and ask additionally whether it can be monotone.
source_formulation.caption: Editorial paraphrase of the final question in MFCS 2024 §8, retained in the February 2026 full revision; the main hereditary variant is preserved

context_blocks.text: A short global proof can be difficult to verify when its readers only see neighboring pieces. Local certification asks how much evidence must be copied or distributed to individual vertices so that all honest instances are accepted and every false instance is rejected somewhere.

Hereditary properties survive deleting vertices. Many geometric intersection classes have this stability: deleting objects leaves a representation of the induced subgraph. The closure condition distinguishes this question from large lower bounds for properties that depend on a particular global size or symmetry.

The source proves linear lower bounds for several geometric classes, including penny graphs, graphs that are subgraphs of the square grid, and 1-planar graphs. These supply substantial examples at the linear threshold but do not establish a fixed exponent \(c>1\).

Theorem 3.1 bounds the local complexity of a connected graph class by \(\log_2|\mathcal C_n|+O(\log n)\), where \(\mathcal C_n\) is its set of isomorphism types with \(n\) vertices. Thus the number of possible graphs in a class gives a general information bound, and every class has an \(O(n^2)\) upper bound. The question concerns where hereditary classes can lie inside this range.

The known examples illustrate how sensitive local evidence can be to the graph property: planar graphs have logarithmic-size certificates, whereas the source proves a linear bound for 1-planar graphs. A 1-planar graph admits a drawing with at most one crossing on each edge. This comparison concerns certificate size even though local computation is unrestricted.

The full February 2026 revision retains the superlinear question. It also keeps the stronger neighborhood-inspection model separate from ordinary proof labeling. This review fixes the latter and records the stronger known lower-bound scope without changing the target.

cards.title: Linear CONGEST lower bound with logarithmic LOCAL complexity
cards.formal: Do there exist a fixed maximum degree \(\Delta\), a locally checkable labeling problem \(\Pi\) on all connected simple graphs of maximum degree at most \(\Delta\), and a deterministic LOCAL algorithm solving \(\Pi\) in \(O(\log N)\) rounds, such that every randomized CONGEST algorithm solving \(\Pi\) with global failure probability at most \(1/N\) requires \(\Omega(N)\) worst-case rounds? The common size parameter \(N\ge2\) is known to every vertex, and each algorithm must meet its guarantee on every input with at most \(N\) vertices. Use the models and quantifiers below; no additional promise on the graph or input labels is allowed.

source_formulation.text: More concretely, it is an open question whether there exists an LCL problem that is solvable in \(O(\log  n)\) rounds in the LOCAL model but […]
source_formulation.caption: Truncated source excerpt (at most 25 words); PDF p. 4

cards.why: Local verifiability limits what a problem can demand of a global solution, but it need not make that solution easy to construct with short messages. A logarithmic-versus-linear separation would show that bandwidth can cause a near-global delay even when graph distances and local verification permit a much faster solution. The requirement of one total bounded-degree LCL rules out explanations based on an arbitrary promise or an output whose size grows with the network.
cards.status_note: Explicitly posed in DISC 2021. Bounded primary-source checks through 2026-09-15 found the existing sublinear CONGEST lower bound and 2026 results on LCL formalisms, but no resolution of the logarithmic deterministic LOCAL versus linear randomized CONGEST target. This is an individual model review, not an exhaustive certification of current openness.
