importance.reason: A fundamental bandwidth-versus-locality separation question for the broad and precisely defined LCL framework. Closing the logarithmic-to-linear gap would identify an extreme resource separation even when solutions are locally checkable and degrees and labels are constant.

sentences: An LCL specifies legal output labels by a finite list of constant-radius neighborhoods.
The question asks for one problem that is solvable in logarithmic deterministic LOCAL time but needs linear randomized CONGEST time.
Both models communicate along the same bounded-degree graph, while CONGEST restricts each message to logarithmically many bits.
Such a result would isolate an extreme cost of bandwidth despite local verifiability of solutions.
The card requires all connected inputs without additional promises and states the identifiers, private randomness and global error convention explicitly.

cards.definitions: An LCL specification consists of an integer \(\Delta\ge1\), a radius \(r\ge1\), finite nonempty input and output alphabets \(\Sigma_{\mathrm{in}},\Sigma_{\mathrm{out}}\), and a finite list \(\mathcal C\) of permitted rooted radius-\(r\) neighborhoods with both input and output labels on every incidence \((v,e)\) where vertex \(v\) is an endpoint of edge \(e\). A radius-\(r\) neighborhood is the subgraph induced by vertices at graph distance at most \(r\) from its root; labels on incidences of its included edges are retained. An output is legal if every such rooted neighborhood is isomorphic to one in \(\mathcal C\), preserving roots and input/output labels. Identifiers, the parameter \(N\), and communication-port numbers are not part of this legality test. The problem must have a legal output for every connected simple graph of degree at most \(\Delta\) with every assignment of input incidence labels. All parts of the specification are fixed independently of the input size. Each vertex is a processor; each incident edge has a distinct local port number in \(\{1,\ldots,\deg(v)\}\), chosen arbitrarily. Initially a vertex knows only \(N\), its degree, its ports and its own incidence input labels, together with its identifier in the deterministic model. Communication uses only graph edges. In one synchronous round each vertex sends a separate message to each neighbor using only its state before the round; messages arrive at its end. LOCAL permits any finite message length. A CONGEST algorithm has a fixed integer bandwidth constant \(\beta\ge1\) and sends one padded string of at most \(\lceil\beta\log_2(N+2)\rceil\) bits per directed edge per round; the bound includes all protocol data. Local computation and memory are uncharged but finite and terminating, and each algorithm has one finite program independent of \(N\). The deterministic LOCAL algorithm must work for every injective assignment of identifiers from \(\{1,\ldots,N^3\}\). The randomized CONGEST algorithm receives no identifiers and uses mutually independent fair private random bits at the vertices, with some finite computable bound \(h_B(N)\) on the number used per vertex. It must finish within a deterministic round bound on every coin sequence, and for each graph, port assignment and input labeling, the probability that all output neighborhoods are legal is at least \(1-1/N\). Outputs are labels on the processor’s own incidences. Let \(t_B(N)\) be the maximum rounds until all vertices output, over all such inputs of size at most \(N\) and all coins. The claimed separation means there is one LOCAL algorithm and constant \(C\) with round bound \(C\log_2(N+2)\) for every \(N\), and, for every correct randomized CONGEST algorithm \(B\) with any fixed \(\beta\), there exist \(c_B>0,N_B\) such that \(t_B(N)\ge c_BN\) for all integers \(N\ge N_B\). The constants in the lower bound may depend on \(B\) and its bandwidth, but \(\Pi,\Delta,r\) and the alphabets are fixed first.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean either establishing this existence statement or proving its negation. An affirmative answer must provide the complete finite LCL specification, prove total solvability, give the deterministic logarithmic-round LOCAL algorithm, and prove the linear worst-case CONGEST lower bound against every randomized algorithm in the stated error and bandwidth model. A lower bound only for deterministic algorithms, a lower bound on a promised subfamily without a total LCL on all bounded-degree inputs, or an \(\Omega(N/\log N)\) bound does not meet the target. A negative answer must exclude every qualifying LCL, not merely the existing construction. No numerical tolerance replaces the required asymptotic bounds.

context_blocks.text: The 2021 paper establishes equality between LOCAL and CONGEST complexities for LCLs on trees, and a separation on general bounded-degree graphs. Its explicit open question asks whether the gap can extend from logarithmic LOCAL time to linear CONGEST time. The statement here retains that stronger endpoint rather than counting any superpolylogarithmic gap as success.

The authors’ known example has an \(O(\log N)\) deterministic LOCAL algorithm and an \(\Omega(\sqrt N/\log^2 N)\) randomized CONGEST lower bound. It establishes a genuine bandwidth effect but falls short of the linear lower bound requested here.

Arbitrary input labels and every connected graph up to the degree bound are part of the problem domain. Restricting the network to a specially chosen family would remove a central part of the LCL requirement. The graph size, identifiers and random bits also cannot be encoded into a growing output alphabet, since the specification must be finite and fixed.

The source defines randomized algorithms without identifiers and deterministic algorithms with polynomially bounded identifiers. It also requires a deterministic round bound and high global success probability. The card fixes those conventions explicitly; the paper’s discussion explains that randomized identifier generation can bridge the common identifier conventions, with a change in failure probability.

Cruciani, Das, Raevskaya and Suomela’s 2026 work studies robustness of LCL definitions under local reductions. Its stated translation results concern formalism and local simulation overhead, rather than a logarithmic-versus-linear LOCAL–CONGEST theorem. They do not resolve this target.

cards.context:
The 2021 paper establishes equality between LOCAL and CONGEST complexities for LCLs on trees, and a separation on general bounded-degree graphs. Its explicit open question asks whether the gap can extend from logarithmic LOCAL time to linear CONGEST time. The statement here retains that stronger endpoint rather than counting any superpolylogarithmic gap as success.

The authors’ known example has an \(O(\log N)\) deterministic LOCAL algorithm and an \(\Omega(\sqrt N/\log^2 N)\) randomized CONGEST lower bound. It establishes a genuine bandwidth effect but falls short of the linear lower bound requested here.

Arbitrary input labels and every connected graph up to the degree bound are part of the problem domain. Restricting the network to a specially chosen family would remove a central part of the LCL requirement. The graph size, identifiers and random bits also cannot be encoded into a growing output alphabet, since the specification must be finite and fixed.

The source defines randomized algorithms without identifiers and deterministic algorithms with polynomially bounded identifiers. It also requires a deterministic round bound and high global success probability. The card fixes those conventions explicitly; the paper’s discussion explains that randomized identifier generation can bridge the common identifier conventions, with a change in failure probability.

Cruciani, Das, Raevskaya and Suomela’s 2026 work studies robustness of LCL definitions under local reductions. Its stated translation results concern formalism and local simulation overhead, rather than a logarithmic-versus-linear LOCAL–CONGEST theorem. They do not resolve this target.

cards.title: Lifting CSP sketching resistance to sublinear streaming resistance
cards.formal: For every finite family \(\Pi\) of Boolean predicates of a fixed arity, does the following implication hold? If no \(o(\sqrt n)\)-bit sketching algorithm nontrivially approximates Max-CSP(\(\Pi\)), then no \(o(n)\)-bit single-pass streaming algorithm nontrivially approximates it. Nontrivial approximation, sketching and the polynomial stream-length convention are defined below.
cards.why: A universal implication would upgrade a broad sketching classification to a fundamental limitation on all small-memory streaming algorithms. A counterexample would show that some CSPs admit an informative sequential summary even though every substantially smaller mergeable summary is approximation resistant.
cards.status_note: The 2025 source states this as a conjecture. A substantial April 2026 theorem now gives LP-gap-based linear-space lower bounds, but the checked text does not explicitly establish or refute Conjecture 8 for every sketching-resistant family. Status remains uncertain rather than certifying that the 2025 question survives that theorem. The card’s mathematical statement is complete, and its polynomial-length convention is identified explicitly.

Singer, Tulsiani and Velusamy establish LP-gap-based linear-space lower bounds, creating a stronger framework that must be compared with the conjecture’s premise.

sentences: Each fixed predicate family defines a maximum constraint-satisfaction problem.
A nontrivial approximation beats the best constant lower bound on the optimum by a fixed amount.
The conjecture lifts resistance to small mergeable sketches into resistance to all sublinear-space streaming algorithms.
Both the algorithm model and the space threshold change in the implication.

cards.definitions: Fix an integer \(k\geq1\) and a nonempty finite family \(\Pi\subseteq\{\pi:\{0,1\}^k\to\{0,1\}\}\). A constraint on \(n\geq k\) variables consists of a predicate \(\pi\in\Pi\) and an ordered tuple of \(k\) distinct indices in \([n]\). An instance \(\Phi\) is a nonempty list of such constraints; repetitions are allowed and every occurrence has unit weight. For an assignment \(x\in\{0,1\}^n\), its value is the fraction of constraint occurrences it satisfies, and \(\operatorname{OPT}(\Phi)\) is the maximum over assignments. Let \(\rho(\Pi)=\inf_{n\geq k,\Phi}\operatorname{OPT}(\Phi)\). Padding with unused variables makes this the limiting trivial approximation threshold. A nontrivial approximation has a fixed \(\delta>0\), with \(\rho(\Pi)+\delta\leq1\), and outputs a value \(v\) satisfying \((\rho(\Pi)+\delta)\operatorname{OPT}(\Phi)\leq v\leq\operatorname{OPT}(\Phi)\) with probability at least \(2/3\) on every instance and order. The algorithm need not output an assignment. A deterministic streaming algorithm has a finite state represented by \(s\) bits, a fixed initial state, an update map taking the current state and next constraint, and a final output map. It reads the constraint list once in an adversarial order. A randomized algorithm is a distribution over deterministic algorithms, chosen independently of the list. Local computation and the choice of this distribution are unrestricted; this is the nonuniform randomness model used for the source’s lower bounds. A sketching algorithm additionally has a state map \(K\) on lists and a binary combination map \(H\), with \(K(\sigma\tau)=H(K(\sigma),K(\tau))\) for every pair of lists whose concatenation is allowed; its updates append a singleton through this map, and its output depends only on the sketch. Randomized sketches are distributions over such deterministic schemes. Commutativity and linearity of the sketches are not separately required. Editorial length convention: an algorithmic space regime must handle every fixed polynomial length bound. Precisely, to admit nontrivial approximation in \(o(b(n))\) space means that there is one fixed \(\delta>0\) such that, for every fixed integer \(d\geq2\), there is an algorithm family for all lists of length at most \(n^d\), with worst-case state size \(s_d(n)\) satisfying \(s_d(n)/b(n)\to0\). The algorithm may depend on \(\Pi,d,\delta,n\), but not on the input list; the ratio improvement \(\delta\) does not depend on \(n\) or \(d\). The two occurrences of “no” in the conjecture negate this full definition.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof of the implication for every predicate family in the stated model, or give a fixed family that is resistant to nontrivial o(√n)-space sketching and a nontrivial o(n)-space streaming approximation for that family. Both parts of a counterexample need proofs. A faster approximation for a family already admitting nontrivial small sketches, or a lower bound under an additional condition not proved for all families in the premise, is insufficient.

context_blocks.text: This is Conjecture 8 of Singer’s column. It simultaneously enlarges the algorithm class and the permitted memory, while asking only whether any fixed improvement over the trivial ratio is possible. It does not claim that every approximation threshold of every CSP stays unchanged as space increases.

The sketching dichotomy gives polylogarithmic-space algorithms or square-root-space lower bounds, with a small slack in the approximation thresholds. Its definition of a sketch permits general mergeable summaries; restricting the premise to linear sketches would be a different statement.

Max-DiCut illustrates why the premise matters. Its trivial ratio is one quarter, while small sketches already give a ratio approaching four ninths. Better streaming approximations using more memory therefore do not by themselves refute the resistance implication in this card.

Singer, Tulsiani and Velusamy’s April 2026 manuscript proves linear-space lower bounds from integrality gaps of the basic linear programming relaxation. That relaxation assigns a distribution of local assignments to each constraint and requires consistent one-variable marginals on shared variables. Its ratio is not defined by the sketching premise in this card.

The same manuscript gives a tight classification for bounded-degree instances and explicitly continues to distinguish general sketching lower bounds from streaming lower bounds. Applying its theorem to Conjecture 8 requires a theorem connecting every resistant predicate family to the needed LP gap. This review does not claim that such a connection has been proved or disproved.

cards.title: Register space of obstruction-free set agreement
cards.formal: For every integer pair \(n>k\ge1\), determine \(R(n,k)\), the minimum number of shared atomic read/write registers sufficient for deterministic obstruction-free one-shot \(k\)-set agreement among \(n\) named processes with input domain \([n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}\), in the model below. Supply a real-valued function approximating \(R\) with pointwise absolute error at most \(1/100\) registers throughout this domain.
cards.definitions:
Fix \(n>k\ge1\). There are \(n\) processes with distinct known identifiers \(1,\ldots,n\); each knows \(n,k\) and initially knows only its own input in \([n]\), not other processes' inputs. A protocol may depend on \(n,k\), and is given by finite deterministic programs with unbounded private storage and no bound on finite local computation. No uniform procedure generating protocols for different \(n,k\) is required. A process may invoke the task at most once; it participates when it invokes, and may decide at most once, after which it stops. Any subset may participate.

The only communication is through a fixed array of \(r\ge0\) shared multiwriter/multireader registers with common names \(1,\ldots,r\). Every process can read and write every register. A register stores a finite binary string of unrestricted length; one atomic read returns its entire current string, and one atomic write replaces that string. Initial shared contents may depend on \(n,k\) and the protocol but are fixed independently of the input assignment and participation. All shared storage is in these counted registers. A scheduled process takes a local computation step, including invocation or decision, or performs one atomic read or write with a finite local update; no stronger shared primitive, random choice, clock, or failure detector is supplied.

An execution is any finite or infinite interleaving of such steps; a process may stop forever at any point, representing a crash, with no fairness or timing assumption. In every finite execution prefix, each decided value must be the input proposed by a process that has already invoked, and at most \(k\) distinct values may have been decided.

Obstruction-freedom requires that, from every reachable configuration, every participating undecided process \(p\) decides after finitely many further own steps if only \(p\) is scheduled thereafter. Other processes may subsequently resume, so safety must also hold under every extension. Register widths, private storage and running time are uncharged.

Define \(R(n,k)\) as the least integer \(r\) for which a protocol satisfies these requirements for every assignment of inputs and every schedule. A finite sufficient \(r\) is known, so this minimum exists.
cards.why: This measures how much shared memory is intrinsically needed for synchronization when processes may disagree on a bounded number of proposed values. Resolving the gap would connect the solvability of agreement tasks to their exact memory requirements, even under the weak guarantee of eventual progress in isolation.

context_blocks.text: The known bounds are \(\lceil n/k\rceil\le R(n,k)\le n-k+1\). The lower bound applies to named processes; the upper bound is achieved even by anonymous processes, so it also applies here. Both ends of the parameter range are determined: \(R(n,1)=n\) and \(R(n,n-1)=2\). In the interior, the general bounds can leave a substantial gap.

The upper-bound algorithm uses exactly \(n-k+1\) physical read/write registers, including the implementation of the snapshots appearing in its presentation. The resource is the number of arbitrarily large registers, not their combined bit capacity. The repeated version, in which processes solve a sequence of agreement instances, already has the exact bound \(n-k+1\); this card concerns one invocation per process.

Ellen, Gelashvili and Zhu conjecture in the preprint that the exact register requirement for \(x\)-obstruction-free \(k\)-set agreement is \(n-k+x\), for \(1\le x\le k<n\). Here \(x\)-obstruction-freedom means that all sufficiently active processes finish whenever at most \(x\) processes continue taking steps. The present question fixes \(x=1\) and asks for the full optimal function, an editorial broadening of the resulting conjecture \(R(n,k)=n-k+1\). It also accepts a determination that refutes that conjecture.

The OPODIS 2025 paper published in January 2026 still lists the same lower and upper bounds for the n-valued problem. Its results about different wait-free tasks do not close this gap. Bounds for swap or other stronger shared objects concern different computational models.

A second paper published in January 2026 continues to state the same register-space bounds while studying limitations of particular classes of impossibility proofs. It does not determine the register-space function.

cards.answer_criterion: Supply an unambiguously specified real-valued function \(g\) on all integer pairs \(n>k\ge1\), and a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean that \(|g(n,k)-R(n,k)|\le1/100\) throughout the domain, with error measured in registers and \(R\) defined by the stated model. The approximation need not be integer-valued. A certified interval of width at most \(1/50\) qualifies through its midpoint. Exact determination also qualifies. A finite table, an asymptotic estimate, or unmatched bounds outside this precision do not meet the criterion; merely restating the defining minimization does not specify a determination.
cards.status_note: The 2024 journal abstract explicitly describes determining register space as open. Two primary papers published on 7 January 2026 retain the same general bounds. A bounded primary-source and subsequent-result review through 16 September 2026 found no verified determination for all \(n>k\ge1\); this is not exhaustive certification of current openness. The 1/100 tolerance is the atlas acceptance rule, not a tolerance proposed by these papers.

Ellen, Gelashvili and Zhu conjecture in the preprint that the exact register requirement for \(x\)-obstruction-free \(k\)-set agreement is \(n-k+x\), for \(1\le x\le k<n\). Here \(x\)-obstruction-freedom means that all sufficiently active processes finish whenever at most \(x\) processes continue taking steps. The present question fixes \(x=1\) and asks for the full optimal function, an editorial broadening of the resulting conjecture \(R(n,k)=n-k+1\). It also accepts a determination that refutes that conjecture.

The OPODIS 2025 paper published in January 2026 still lists the same lower and upper bounds for the n-valued problem. Its results about different wait-free tasks do not close this gap. Bounds for swap or other stronger shared objects concern different computational models.

A second paper published in January 2026 continues to state the same register-space bounds while studying limitations of particular classes of impossibility proofs. It does not determine the register-space function.

cards.title: Triangle detection in CONGEST
cards.formal: For arbitrary simple undirected n-vertex networks, determine the optimal worst-case randomized round complexity of triangle detection in CONGEST, up to constant factors. Each vertex initially knows its distinct \(O(\log  n)\)-bit identifier and its neighbors, and may send a separate \(O(\log  n)\)-bit message in each direction of every incident edge per synchronous round. On a triangle-free graph all vertices must output NO; otherwise at least one must output YES. The joint answer must be correct with probability at least \(2/3\) on every input and identifier assignment. The algorithm is uniform, has private random bits, and may know n. The currently established bounds are $\Omega(\log\log n)$ and $\widetilde O(n^{1/3})$.
cards.why: I include this because it isolates the cost of learning one local pattern under network bandwidth constraints. A sharp answer would distinguish the communication needed for deciding existence from the communication needed for distributing all witnesses, and would test how far current lower-bound methods reach.
cards.definitions: $\widetilde O$ suppresses polylogarithmic factors. Local computation is unrestricted, vertex identifiers have $O(\log n)$ bits, and the communication graph is exactly $G$, not an all-to-all overlay. Nodes may know $n$. The output convention avoids charging the graph diameter merely to inform every vertex of a remote triangle. The triangle is a subgraph on three distinct mutually adjacent vertices.

progress.text: Chang, Pettie, Saranurak, and Zhang give $\widetilde O(n^{1/3})$-round algorithms for triangle enumeration, counting, and detection. The matching enumeration lower bound does not establish the same detection lower bound.
Assadi and Sundaresan prove an $\Omega(\log\log n)$ lower bound for deterministic and randomized detection, providing the first lower bound beyond a single round.
Censor-Hillel’s ADGA survey explicitly retains the round complexity of CONGEST triangle detection as an open problem after incorporating that lower bound.

context_blocks.text: Every vertex knows two of the three edges of a triangle containing it. The missing information is whether two of its neighbors are adjacent. If messages had unlimited length, neighbors could exchange their complete adjacency lists in one round. The difficulty comes from fitting the relevant information through bounded-capacity edges.

For example, a vertex with many neighbors cannot simply send its entire neighborhood to every neighbor in one short message. On the other hand, most pairs of its neighbors may be irrelevant, so transmitting every adjacency list can be wasteful. An algorithm must exploit the topology to decide which information needs to move and where it can be combined.

Detection asks for one bit of global evidence, whereas listing requires the network collectively to output every triangle. A graph can contain a cubic number of triangles. Consequently, a lower bound driven by the volume of listed output does not automatically apply to detection. The near-optimal listing algorithm supplies a detection upper bound, but leaves this distinction unresolved.

The 2025 lower bound rules out every fixed number of rounds, including randomized protocols. It changes the old question of whether even two rounds are necessary into a quantitative gap. Conventional two-party communication reductions encounter barriers here, making stronger lower bounds a problem about proof techniques as well as about graph algorithms.

cards.title: Polylogarithmic-space streaming Euclidean MST estimation
cards.formal:
Does there exist a uniform randomized one-pass insertion-only streaming algorithm A and absolute constants \(C\ge1\), \(K\ge1\) and integer \(k\ge1\) such that, for every \(n\ge2\), \(d\ge1\), \(\Delta\ge2\), and every stream of n distinct points in \(\{0,\ldots,\Delta\}^{d}\), A uses at most
\[K\bigl(d\lceil\log_2(n+2)\rceil\lceil\log_2(\Delta+2)\rceil\bigr)^k\]
bits of working memory and returns a rational estimate Z satisfying
\[\Pr[\operatorname{MST}(X)\le Z\le C\operatorname{MST}(X)]\ge 2/3?\]
The stream order is arbitrary and fixed independently of the algorithm’s private random bits. The output estimates total Euclidean MST cost; it need not describe a tree. For polynomially bounded integer coordinates, the required space is \(\mathrm{poly}(d\log n)\), as in the community proposal.
cards.definitions:
The point set X consists of the n distinct inserted vectors. Coordinates are nonnegative integers given in binary, and the parameters n,d and the bound \(\Delta\) are supplied before the stream. The graph is complete on X; an edge between x and y has weight \(\|x-y\|_2=(\sum_{j=1}^{d}(x_j-y_j)^2)^{1/2}\). The quantity \(\operatorname{MST}(X)\) is the minimum sum of edge weights over all spanning trees of this graph. It is a real number even though the input coordinates are integers.

The algorithm is one fixed finite probabilistic Turing-machine program with a read-once input stream, private independent fair random bits, working tapes, and an output tape used only for the final rational estimate. An input record may be buffered, with those bits charged to memory. All retained state, counters, random seeds and postprocessing workspace count toward the space bound, on every input and every random tape. Consumed input cannot be revisited, and there are no deletions, extra passes, random-order promise, external storage, nonuniform advice or real-number registers. The machine must halt on every random tape; no separate update-time or total-time bound is imposed. The probability is over its coins for each fixed stream. The constants and exponent do not depend on n,d or the coordinate bound.

Dependence polynomial in the bit length of coordinates makes the finite-input convention explicit. In particular, for each fixed integer b and \(\Delta\le n^b\), the bound has the proposal’s \(\mathrm{poly}(d\log n)\) form. The logarithmic coordinate factor is recorded rather than silently treating arbitrary reals as constant-size words. The target allows d to grow, including \(d=\Theta(\log n)\); a bound exponential in d does not qualify. The approximation constant can be any fixed finite C. Requiring the estimate to lie above the true cost is a normalization: a two-sided constant-factor estimate can be rescaled at the cost of changing C. Neither an explicit tree nor a \(1+\varepsilon\) approximation is required.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof of existence of an algorithm satisfying the stated memory, pass and probability bounds for some absolute finite approximation constant, or prove the negation for every such algorithm and constants. An \(n^{\varepsilon}\)-space algorithm for a fixed positive \(\varepsilon\), a factor growing with n, a multiple-pass algorithm, or a lower bound excluding only constants near 1 does not settle this target.
cards.why: An MST measures the cost of connecting an entire geometric data set. A small summary that estimates this global quantity within a constant factor would clarify how much connectivity information survives a single streaming pass as dimension grows.

context_blocks.text: Pavel Veselý proposed the insertion-only, one-pass, constant-factor question through the Atlas website. The requested output is the cost of the Euclidean minimum spanning tree, with memory polynomial in dimension and logarithmic in the number of points. This card adds the finite-coordinate, randomness and output conventions needed to make that request precise.

The STOC 2023 paper obtains constant-factor estimation using \(n^{O(\varepsilon)}\) space for a fixed positive parameter \(\varepsilon\). Its sketches support insertions and deletions. This leaves a gap to polylogarithmic memory even in the insertion-only model selected here.

The same paper rules out one-pass space \(o(\sqrt n)\) for approximation better than 1.1035 in sufficiently high dimension. This near-one barrier does not exclude every absolute approximation constant. Its multiple-pass improvements also do not settle the one-pass target.

cards.title: Optimal measurements and near-linear decoding for universal ℓ₂/ℓ₁ sparse recovery
cards.formal: Do there exist absolute constants \(C,B>0\), \(a\geq0\), and a deterministic recovery scheme such that, for every \(n\geq1\) and \(1\leq k\leq n\), one fixed matrix \(A_{n,k}\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}\) with \(m\leq Bk\log_2(en/k)\) permits recovery from \(A_{n,k}x\) in at most \(Bn\log_2^a(n+2)\) operations, with \[\|x-\widehat x\|_2\leq \frac{C}{\sqrt{k}}\min_{z:\,|\operatorname{supp}(z)|\leq k}\|x-z\|_1\] simultaneously for every \(x\in\mathbb R^n\)?
cards.why: The target combines information-efficient sensing with fast, uniformly reliable reconstruction for arbitrary signals. Resolving it would show whether the strongest standard universal mixed-norm guarantee can be obtained without sacrificing near-optimal compression or practical asymptotic decoding time.
cards.status_note: The 2009 source poses this universal mixed-norm tradeoff, and the checked later for-all recovery paper still distinguishes it from its ℓ₁/ℓ₁ result. importance.reason: A central universal compressed-sensing tradeoff between measurement count, robust mixed-norm error and decoding time; explicit matrix generation is a separate issue.

sentences: A fixed matrix compresses every real signal to a short vector of linear measurements.
The decoder must work for all signals with error controlled by the best k-sparse ℓ₁ tail divided by √k.
The conjecture combines O(k log(en/k)) measurements with near-linear deterministic decoding.
The arithmetic model permits input-independent polynomial preprocessing but charges decoding accesses.
Faster results with an ℓ₁ reconstruction error or only per-input randomized success do not meet this target.

cards.definitions: The support of a vector is the set of its nonzero coordinates; a vector is \(k\)-sparse if its support has size at most \(k\). The norms are \(\|v\|_1=\sum_i|v_i|\) and \(\|v\|_2=(\sum_i v_i^2)^{1/2}\). The minimum in the statement is the sum of absolute values outside the \(k\) largest-magnitude coordinates of \(x\); ties may be broken arbitrarily. The decoder receives \(n,k\), the exact real measurement vector \(y=A_{n,k}x\), and read-only access to the fixed description of the scheme. It receives neither \(x\) nor its support, and must output all \(n\) coordinates of \(\widehat x\). The output need not itself be sparse. Measurements are linear and selected independently of the unknown signal. We use the real-arithmetic model: real addition, subtraction, multiplication, division by a nonzero number, square root of a nonnegative number, comparison, and access to an addressed stored entry each cost one operation; ordinary integer index operations cost one as well. The decoder is one fixed algorithm, with polynomial-size read-only advice depending only on \(n,k\), including the matrix and any preprocessing data. Reading advice is charged. Advice generation and forming the original measurement vector are outside the requested decoding bound. No polynomial-time explicit matrix construction is required. Once the scheme is fixed its decoder is deterministic and the guarantee holds for all real signals; a matrix chosen by the probabilistic method is admissible only if a single fixed choice works for all signals. Constants, the polynomial advice exponent and the decoding exponent are independent of \(n,k,x\). Measurements are noiseless; no additional post-measurement perturbation is included.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked construction or existence proof of a scheme meeting both resource bounds and the universal mixed-norm error guarantee in the specified arithmetic model, or prove that no such scheme exists. A guarantee holding with high probability separately for each input, an ℓ₁/ℓ₁ error bound, or optimal row count with slower decoding is insufficient.

context_blocks.text: The source’s “deterministic” target is universal recovery from one matrix: the same measurements must work for every signal. Editorial model convention: this card makes the arithmetic-operation and preprocessing conventions explicit, without adding the separate challenge of efficient deterministic matrix generation. It also uses \(\log(en/k)\) and \(k\geq1\) to remove the source formula’s undefined or zero endpoint expressions.

For exactly \(k\)-sparse signals the right-hand side is zero, so the scheme must recover them exactly. For nonsparse signals, recovery quality depends on the entire tail and gains a factor \(1/\sqrt{k}\). Merely outputting a plausible support does not establish this robust guarantee.

The original question emphasizes achieving optimal measurement count and fast reconstruction together. Classical constructions achieve the two features separately for this error criterion, whereas some fast optimal-measurement schemes use a different norm on the reconstruction error.

The later for-all sparse-recovery work of Gilbert, Li, Porat and Strauss improves measurements and decoding for the ℓ₁/ℓ₁ formulation, and explicitly lists mixed-norm recovery as a remaining direction. Its use of a matrix fixed for all signals is compatible with a nonconstructive probabilistic existence proof.

The inequality \(\|v\|_2\leq\|v\|_1\) does not convert an \(\ell_1/\ell_1\) theorem into the requested result: it loses the essential \(1/\sqrt{k}\) factor. Likewise, an input-dependent success probability does not imply that one random seed works simultaneously over the uncountable set of all real inputs.

When \(k\) is comparable to \(n\), storing the full vector is consistent with the measurement bound. The compression challenge lies in the sparse regime. Counting the output cost explains why near-linear decoding remains a meaningful target even when the number of measurements is much smaller than \(n\).

cards.title: Constant-round MIS in the congested clique
cards.formal: Does randomized maximal independent set admit a constant-round algorithm in the unicast Congested Clique? Precisely, for every fixed integer \(c\ge1\), do there exist a uniform randomized distributed algorithm \(A_c\) and positive constants \(R_c,B_c\) such that, on every simple undirected graph \(G\) with vertex set \([n]\), \(n\ge2\), the algorithm always terminates within \(R_c\) rounds, uses at most \(B_c\lceil\log_2 n\rceil\) bits per directed communication link per round, and outputs a maximal independent set with probability at least \(1-n^{-c}\)? Constants and program may depend on \(c\), but not on \(n\), the graph or its maximum degree.
cards.why: The question measures how much communication exact distributed symmetry breaking needs when every processor can directly contact every other processor. A constant-round solution would establish a sharp capability of this widely studied model. A general lower bound would expose a bandwidth limitation that survives unrestricted local computation and arbitrary global coordination.
cards.definitions: There is one processor for each vertex \(v\in[n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}\). Initially it knows \(n\), its own identifier \(v\), the common identifier set, and exactly the identifiers of its neighbors in the input graph. The physical communication network is complete: in each synchronous round every processor may send a separate message to every other processor, even when the corresponding input edge is absent. Messages sent in a round arrive by its end. Each directed link has the stated bit limit independently; processors may send different messages to different recipients. No extra processors or initially centralized graph description are provided. All processors run the same finite program, with their identifier and local input as parameters. Local computation and local storage have no asymptotic bound, but each local computation terminates and reads only finitely many independent private fair random bits on every execution. All communication, including initialization and distribution of any shared randomness, counts toward the round bound. No graph-dependent or size-dependent advice is supplied. At termination each processor outputs one bit, defining \(S=\{v:\text{processor }v\text{ outputs }1\}\). Correctness means both \(\forall\{u,v\}\in E(G):\{u,v\}\nsubseteq S\) and \(\forall v\notin S:\exists u\in S:\{u,v\}\in E(G)\). Thus maximality means that no additional vertex can be inserted while preserving independence; maximum cardinality is not required. The probability refers to the single global event that all output bits together define a valid set. The round and message bounds hold on every random execution, including unsuccessful ones. Restricting the requested fixed failure exponent to positive integers is equivalent to allowing every fixed positive real exponent.

cards.formal: For every fixed rational \(\varepsilon\in(0,1)\) and fixed integer \(c\geq1\), is there a randomized insertion-only streaming algorithm that, on every \(n\)-vertex simple undirected graph with integer edge weights in \([1,n^c]\), outputs a matching of weight at least \((1-\varepsilon)\operatorname{OPT}\) with probability at least \(2/3\), using at most \(p_{\varepsilon,c}\) passes and \(B_{\varepsilon,c}n\log_2(n+2)\) bits of memory, where \(p_{\varepsilon,c},B_{\varepsilon,c}\) do not depend on \(n\)?

sentences: The input is an arbitrary-order insertion stream of a positively weighted general graph.
The algorithm must output a nearly maximum-weight matching after a number of passes independent of graph size.
The retained space target is O(n log n) bits with polynomially bounded integer weights.
Linear-time RAM approximation and broader constant-pass semi-streaming results are already known.
The card distinguishes those achievements from the exact bit-space endpoint it asks to settle.

cards.definitions: The vertex set is \([n]\). A matching is a subset of edges with no shared endpoint, its weight is the sum of its edge weights, and \(\operatorname{OPT}\) is the largest such sum over all matchings of the graph. The input is a list of distinct edges, each represented by two binary vertex identifiers and its positive binary integer weight. The algorithm knows \(n,\varepsilon,c\). It reads the list sequentially in an arbitrary order selected independently of its random choices. A pass reads the same complete list in that same order; no deletions, changes of order, random access to earlier items, or requests for selected edges are allowed. The algorithm may stop after any number of passes up to the stated bound. At the end it must output the actual edges of a matching, not merely an estimate of its value. The empty graph has optimum zero and admits the empty output. All stored bits, including edge identifiers, weights, random seeds retained for reuse, counters and temporary working memory, count toward space. A final write-only output tape is permitted, but cannot be used as storage during the passes. The bound is worst case over inputs and random choices; success is required for each input and order. Local computation time is unrestricted, and the finite algorithm may depend on the fixed accuracy and weight exponent. Equivalently the space target is O(n) words of O(log n) bits for each fixed pair of parameters. No polynomial dependence on \(1/\varepsilon\) is required for the pass count or space constant.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked algorithm and proof of the approximation, actual matching output, pass and bit-space guarantees for every fixed accuracy and weight exponent. Alternatively prove that this family of guarantees is impossible, for some fixed parameters. A constant-pass algorithm with extra logarithmic factors in bits, an algorithm for bipartite graphs only, or a RAM approximation algorithm does not establish the displayed statement.

context_blocks.text: The 2006 page contains two questions: a constant-pass streaming approximation with O(n log n) space, and a linear-time RAM approximation scheme. This card keeps the streaming question as its single target. Editorial convention: space is measured explicitly in bits and weights have polynomially bounded integer encodings, removing an ambiguity in the historical page.

Duan and Pettie resolved the RAM direction with running time \(O(m\varepsilon^{-1}\log\varepsilon^{-1})\) for maximum-weight matching. That algorithm can access and store the graph in ways unavailable to the streaming model. The old RAM question is therefore recorded as solved context rather than repeated as an open demand.

Gamlath, Kale, Mitrović and Svensson obtained arbitrarily accurate weighted matching in a number of passes depending only on accuracy, using memory linear in n up to polylogarithmic factors. This settles the broader constant-pass semi-streaming objective, but the stated space guarantee alone does not supply the exact bit bound retained here.

Huang and Su improve the number of passes to a polynomial in \(1/\varepsilon\). Their Theorem 1.2 states \(O(n\log W\,\operatorname{poly}(1/\varepsilon))\) words, where \(W\) is the weight ratio. Under the present weight encoding this can be \(O_{\varepsilon,c}(n\log^2 n)\) bits. One must account for word size before comparing it with the target.

The 2025 overview distinguishes general weighted graphs from bipartite and unweighted cases and tabulates their different pass-space guarantees. Strong bounds for one of those restrictions cannot be silently substituted for the graph class here.

For weighted matchings, improving the objective can involve both alternating paths and alternating cycles. Retaining enough information to coordinate such improvements while storing only a linear number of words is the specific resource issue in this formulation.

cards.title: LOCAL coloring below square-root degree dependence
cards.formal: Is there one deterministic LOCAL algorithm that properly colors every simple n-vertex graph of maximum degree $\Delta\ge2$ with colors in $\{1,\ldots,\Delta+1\}$ in $O(\Delta^{0.499}+\log^* n)$ synchronous rounds? Vertices have arbitrary distinct \(O(\log  n)\)-bit identifiers and know n and Delta. Messages along input edges and local computation are unbounded. The constant in the round bound must be independent of both n and Delta.
cards.answer_criterion: Construct an algorithm with the specified uniform round bound, or prove that no deterministic LOCAL algorithm attains it. Improving a logarithmic factor while retaining degree exponent one-half does not meet the target.
cards.why: I include this because the familiar greedy palette bound hides a distinct distributed coordination problem. A fixed improvement in the degree exponent would reveal new ways to resolve local conflicts, while an impossibility result would explain why the square-root dependence persists across different coloring methods.
cards.definitions: Proper coloring means adjacent vertices receive different output colors. Delta denotes a supplied upper bound on degree, and the guarantee holds for every such valid bound. The algorithm is uniform over n, Delta, and identifier assignments. Log-star n is the number of repeated base-two logarithms needed to reach at most one. Elapsed synchronous rounds are measured; this is not a sequential running-time or message-count target.

progress.text: Maus and Tonoyan obtain $O(\sqrt{\Delta\log\Delta}+\log^*n)$ deterministic rounds for the more general degree-plus-one list-coloring task. Ordinary coloring follows by using a common palette.
Suomela’s updated open-problem list explicitly asks whether the exponent 0.499 is attainable with Delta+1 colors and only an additive log-star n dependence.

The SODA 2026 discussion records a separate deterministic $\widetilde O(\log^{5/3}n)$ upper bound for Delta+1 coloring. That bound is independent of degree but does not provide the two-parameter guarantee asked here.

context_blocks.text: A sequential greedy algorithm needs only one more color than the maximum degree: when processing a vertex, at most Delta colors have already been used by its neighbors. In a distributed algorithm many adjacent vertices act simultaneously, so they can choose conflicting colors unless their decisions are coordinated.

Unique identifiers break perfect symmetry, but treating every identifier as a color starts with far too many colors. Color reduction has to compress this large palette while preserving a distinction across every edge. The degree controls how many simultaneous conflicts a vertex may need to avoid.

The two parameters in the target play different roles. Even when degree is fixed, the network can have arbitrarily many vertices, and iterated logarithmic time captures the unavoidable symmetry-breaking dependence on that size. An algorithm taking a power of log n cannot simply replace this term: for sufficiently large n, it exceeds every bound depending only on Delta plus log-star n.

The target chooses a specific exponent strictly below one-half, as in Suomela’s list. The numerical improvement is small; its purpose is to cross the apparent degree barrier while keeping the optimal-size palette. Allowing more colors, randomness, or a larger n-dependent term gives separate questions.

cards.title: Randomized parity sketches versus one-way communication for XOR functions
cards.formal: Are there universal constants \(C>0\) and \(a\geq0\) such that, for every \(n\geq1\) and every Boolean function \(f:\mathbb F_2^n\to\{0,1\}\), \[R^{\mathrm{lin}}_{1/3}(f)\leq C\bigl(1+R^{\rightarrow}_{1/3}(f^+)\bigr)\log^a(n+2),\qquad f^+(x,y)=f(x+y)?\] Here the two complexities use worst-input error and shared randomness as defined below. This fixes the polylogarithmic-loss convention in the source’s conjecture.
cards.why: A positive result would justify proving lower bounds for arbitrary one-way XOR protocols by analyzing linear summaries, a much more structured class. A separation would identify Boolean information that a short nonlinear message preserves more effectively than nonadaptive random parities.
cards.status_note: The primary CCC 2018 paper leaves the worst-input randomized comparison open. The checked April 2026 simulation is for a different streaming model and does not claim this one-way communication theorem. legacy.year_basis: workshop year listed on problem page

importance.reason: A broad structural comparison between randomized communication and parity measurements, with consequences for transferring sketching lower bounds to unrestricted one-way protocols.

sentences: The input is an arbitrary Boolean function on a binary vector space.
A parity sketch measures a fixed random collection of linear forms and then decodes their bits.
A one-way protocol may instead send any randomized message about Alice’s vector to Bob.
The conjecture asks whether parity sketches lose only a universal polylogarithmic factor for the associated XOR function.
Known deterministic and uniform-input comparisons do not establish the required worst-input randomized bound.

cards.definitions: The field \(\mathbb F_2\) has elements zero and one, with addition modulo two; vector addition is bitwise XOR. A randomized parity sketch of length \(k\) consists of a jointly sampled matrix \(A\in\mathbb F_2^{k\times n}\) and a decoder \(g\). Their joint distribution is fixed in advance, independently of the input \(z\). The sketch is the \(k\)-bit vector \(Az\); the decoder knows the sampled matrix and all shared coins, and may depend on \(f\) and \(n\). For each fixed \(z\), its probability of outputting \(f(z)\) must be at least \(2/3\). The minimum possible \(k\), including zero, is \(R^{\mathrm{lin}}_{1/3}(f)\). Each row of \(A\) specifies a subset of input coordinates whose parity is measured. Rows are chosen before seeing any measurement outcome: adaptive parity queries are not allowed. In the communication model Alice knows \(x\in\mathbb F_2^n\), Bob knows \(y\in\mathbb F_2^n\), and both know \(f,n\) and a public random string independent of their inputs. Alice sends one message; Bob must output \(f(x+y)\). For every fixed pair \((x,y)\), success probability is at least \(2/3\). The cost is the largest message length over inputs and coin outcomes; variable-length messages can be padded. Its minimum is \(R^{\rightarrow}_{1/3}(f^+)\). Local computation, the description of \(f\), and shared randomness are free in both models. No uniform polynomial-time construction of optimal protocols is required. Logarithms are base two. The constants in the proposed inequality are independent of the truth table of \(f\), the dimension and its communication complexity. The additive one handles zero-cost constant functions without imposing a convention for logarithms of zero.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof of the displayed inequality with fixed universal constants, or prove its negation: for every proposed constants there is a dimension and Boolean function violating the bound. A superpolylogarithmic separation family suffices for a negative answer. Equality for deterministic protocols, average error under the uniform input distribution, or a polynomial rather than polylogarithmic loss does not settle this target.

context_blocks.text: The source asks whether randomized linear sketching and randomized one-way communication of the associated XOR function agree up to polylogarithmic factors. The card spells out the usual dimension-based interpretation at error one third; it does not request exact equality of the two integer complexities.

The easy comparison is \(R^{\rightarrow}_{1/3}(f^+)\leq R^{\mathrm{lin}}_{1/3}(f)\): Alice sends \(Ax\), and Bob forms \(Ax+Ay=A(x+y)\) before using the decoder. The question is whether an arbitrary message can always be replaced, with the stated loss, by information of this linear form.

For deterministic exact computation the complexities agree. The randomized case allows a different error set for each choice of coins, so the deterministic statement does not give the desired simulation by simply fixing a seed.

Kannan, Mossel, Sanyal and Yaroslavtsev prove an analogue under uniformly distributed inputs, with an adjustment of the error constant, and analyze several function classes. Worst-input correctness is stronger: a protocol cannot ignore even a very small exceptional set of pairs.

The 2026 turnstile simulation paper concerns streams of integer-coordinate insertions and deletions. Its discussion treats modular and XOR updates as a separate line of work. A simulation for algorithms that already process long streams does not itself convert a single arbitrary Alice-to-Bob message into a parity sketch.

cards.title: Two-stage group testing with arithmetic progressions
cards.formal:
Do there exist absolute constants \(C,D>0\) such that, for every pair of integers \(n\ge2\) and \(1\le k\le n\), an unknown set \(S\subseteq[n]\) with \(|S|\le k\) can be identified exactly by the following deterministic two-stage scheme?

The first stage uses at most \(Ck\log_2 n\) tests. Each test asks whether \(S\) meets a finite arithmetic progression contained in \([n]\), and every first-stage test is fixed before any answers are received. After seeing all first-stage answers, the second stage chooses at most \(Dk\) individual indices and learns their membership in \(S\). All second-stage indices must be chosen before receiving any second-stage answer. The final output must equal \(S\) for every admissible hidden set.

The constants must work simultaneously for all \(n,k,S\). The resource being bounded is the number of tests in each stage; neither constructing the scheme nor decoding the answers is subject to a running-time bound.
cards.why: This question tests how much measurement restrictions can cost in sparse identification even when one follow-up round is available. A resolution would distinguish what arbitrary pooling achieves from what regularly spaced queries can support, a distinction motivated by pattern matching rather than by a new statistical noise model.

cards.definitions:
Write \([n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}\). The input parameters \(n\) and \(k\) are known; only the subset \(S\) is hidden. The promise is an upper bound \(|S|\le k\), not knowledge of its exact size. In particular \(S=\varnothing\) is allowed. The elements have their fixed integer positions, and the arithmetic-progression constraint refers to these positions. There is no ability to permute the hidden input and then declare arbitrary pools to be progressions.

An admissible first-stage pool has the form
\[T=\{a,a+d,\ldots,a+(\ell-1)d\},\qquad a,d,\ell\in\mathbb N_{>0},\quad a+(\ell-1)d\le n.\]
Each pool may have its own start, step and length. Singletons are allowed. There is no wraparound modulo \(n\), no repeated item within a pool, and no requirement that the progression be extended to the ends of \([n]\). The answer is the noiseless bit \(b(T,S)=1\) if \(T\cap S\ne\varnothing\), and zero otherwise. It does not reveal the number or positions of the elements in the intersection.

For given \(n,k\), a scheme consists of a nonnegative integer \(m\), a list of admissible pools \(T_1,\ldots,T_m\), a selection function \(J\), and a final decoding function \(F\). The list depends only on \(n,k\); it is identical for every possible hidden set of the promised size. Write
\[y(S)=(b(T_1,S),\ldots,b(T_m,S))\in\{0,1\}^m.\]
The selection function takes any first-stage answer vector \(y\) to a set \(J(y)\subseteq[n]\) of indices with \(|J(y)|\le Dk\). Every selected index is queried separately, giving the function \(z_S:J(y(S))\to\{0,1\}\) defined by \(z_S(j)=1\) exactly when \(j\in S\). The final decoder knows the parameters, the entire first-stage design, \(y(S)\), the selected indices and their individual answers. Correctness means
\[\forall S\subseteq[n]\text{ with }|S|\le k:\quad F\bigl(y(S),z_S\bigr)=S.\]
The decoder may infer membership of unqueried indices from the complete transcript. It is not required to query every element that it finally reports. Queries in the second stage are individual membership tests only; no additional pooled tests or third stage are allowed. Unrealizable first-stage answer vectors can have arbitrary decoding behavior, subject to the same advertised second-stage query cap.

One test is one oracle answer, independent of the pool's cardinality. First-stage pools may be represented by their integer triples \((a,d,\ell)\), and individual indices and parameters in binary, but description length and computational time are not the costs asked about. No noise, random hidden-set distribution, random design, or probability of error is part of this formulation. This records the source's exact identification problem for an arbitrary set, as opposed to average-case recovery. An existence proof for the finite designs and functions suffices; a polynomial-time construction is not an extra requirement. Since all choices for fixed finite parameters can be enumerated and their correctness checked, this convention does not allow an undecidable query operation.

The quantifier order is \(\exists C,D>0\;\forall n,k\;\exists(T_1,\ldots,T_m,J,F)\;\forall S\), with the stated size restrictions. In particular a separate design tailored to the unknown \(S\) is inadmissible. The upper bound uses \(\log_2 n\), not \(\log_2(n/k)\). The source's \(O(k\log n)\) and \(O(k)\) mean absolute constant factors independent of both parameters. Using \(n\ge2\) avoids the irrelevant zero logarithm at one item.

A negative answer is the logical negation: for every proposed pair of constants \(C,D>0\), there are admissible \(n,k\) for which every scheme satisfying both test caps fails on some hidden set. It need not establish a particular alternative asymptotic lower-bound formula. A lower bound for a single family of progressions, a chosen decoder, or a nonadaptive one-stage scheme would not by itself disprove the target.
cards.answer_criterion: Provide a complete Lean-checked proof or refutation of the existence of absolute constants and two-stage schemes with the stated bounds. A positive answer must prove the arithmetic-progression restriction, first-stage independence from answers, the \(O(k)\) cap on individual second-stage queries, and exact recovery for every hidden set of size at most \(k\), uniformly over the full parameter domain. A negative answer must rule out all allowed designs and decoders with every proposed pair of constant factors. Results allowing arbitrary first-stage pools, more rounds, non-individual second-stage tests, or error on some hidden sets do not settle this proposition. This is an asymptotic existence question, so additive numerical tolerance is inapplicable.

sentences: The output is a single estimate of the largest absolute coordinate of a streamed frequency vector.
The allowed additive error is one over k times the final L1 or L2 norm.
Insertion-only streams and signed differences of two streams are distinct modes of the same resource question.

cards.definitions: Parameters \(n,M,k\) are integers supplied in binary before the stream, together with the two flags. The frequency vector starts at \(f=0\in\mathbb Z^n\). There are at most \(M\) updates \((i,\Delta)\), where \(1\le i\le n\). In insert mode every \(\Delta=1\); in difference mode \(\Delta\in\{-1,1\}\), and update \((i,\Delta)\) replaces \(f_i\) by \(f_i+\Delta\). Negative intermediate and final frequencies are allowed in difference mode. Equivalently, positively and negatively tagged insertions describe the difference of two streams, with their combined length bounded by \(M\). Only this bound, not the actual stream length, is known in advance. Set \(\|f\|_1=\sum_i|f_i|\), \(\|f\|_2=(\sum_i f_i^2)^{1/2}\), and \(\|f\|_\infty=\max_i|f_i|\). The additive tolerance is scaled by the final vector, not by the total number of updates; cancellation therefore matters. At the end, output one rational number \(z\) as a signed binary numerator and positive binary denominator. No coordinate identity or list of heavy items is requested. On \(f=0\), the success event requires exactly \(z=0\). The fixed stream is chosen independently of the algorithm’s private independent fair random bits. There is one terminal query, with success at least \(2/3\) separately on every valid stream; there is no requirement of simultaneous success at all prefixes. Use a uniform randomized multitape streaming machine with one fixed finite program for all parameters, no advice, no public random table and no oracle. The parameter header is read-only. An update is available in a read-only buffer until the machine advances to the next update, after which earlier updates cannot be revisited. Every work-tape bit, stored random bit or seed, counter, index, table and input-dependent retained state counts toward space, including all scratch space used during processing and final decoding. Input and write-only output cells do not count; copies do. Address and head-position information accessible to the algorithm that can carry input-dependent state is charged. The unreadable physical position of the one-way stream is not work memory; the number of updates already consumed is not supplied as a free clock. Random bits cannot be reread unless retained. The machine must halt on every valid finite stream and every random tape; computation time is unrestricted. Space is the maximum number of charged bits over all such streams and random tapes for the given parameters, not its expectation. Bounds may be piecewise over parameter regimes and must use ordinary asymptotic notation with all logarithmic factors exposed. The reciprocal-integer accuracy convention \(\epsilon=1/k\), finite update budget, private randomness and bit accounting make the source’s qualitative space question precise.
cards.answer_criterion: Supply a tight asymptotic space characterization across the complete parameter domain and a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean. It must include uniform algorithms attaining the stated upper bounds, their terminal-error and worst-case-space guarantees, and matching lower bounds for every algorithm in the same model, up to constants independent of all parameters and flags. A one-sided bound, a bound only for identifying heavy items, a word count hiding bit costs, or a result for only one norm or update mode does not determine the whole characterization. This is an asymptotic resource target: the benchmark does not apply an additive 1/100 tolerance to big-O or big-Theta bounds.

context_blocks.text: The largest absolute frequency is a scalar statistic. Identifying which item attains it can require additional information about a large item domain. The source asks whether that distinction can reduce memory when an additive error measured against the full frequency vector is allowed.

The two norms specify different accuracy requirements. For \(f=(3,-2,0)\), the target value is three, while the error scale is either \(5/k\) or \(\sqrt{13}/k\). For a difference stream, many updates can cancel, so an error proportional to the number of processed updates can be much larger than the permitted error.

This card retains both error scales and both update settings from the source as flags in one space-complexity characterization. It asks for their full dependence on the domain, stream budget and accuracy, rather than for a new yes/no claim that every historical bound remains unimproved. The exact finite-input and randomness conventions are editorial specifications.

Bhattacharyya, Dey and Woodruff explicitly report answering the insertion-only \(L_1\)-error part of the 2006 question. For maximum-frequency estimation they report \(O(\epsilon^{-1}\log\epsilon^{-1}+\log n+\log\log t)\) bits, where \(t\) is the stream length, and describe optimality in their stated regimes. Their result is recorded as existing progress, not as an unsolved insertion-only endpoint.

That result does not by itself supply the \(L_2\)-relative or signed-difference cases. In particular, insertion-only \(\|f\|_1\) equals the number of updates, whereas cancellation destroys that equality in a difference stream. A theorem’s norm, update promise, scalar versus item output, and parameter restrictions must all match before it can be counted toward the full target.

The original page explicitly distinguishes bit space from a count of machine words: random-function descriptions and counters also consume memory. The reviewed card preserves that distinction. The requested comparison is therefore about complete memory usage, not only the number of stored counters.

A full characterization would identify which memory costs arise from maintaining frequency magnitudes and which arise from recovering item names. It would clarify the value of scalar summaries for comparing streams over large domains and the cost of allowing deletions or cancellation.

cards.title: Breaking the quadratic color bound for bounded outdegree
cards.formal: Do there exist a constant \(\varepsilon \in\)(0,1], constants \(C_{1},C_{2}>0, a\) computable function \(f:\mathbb{N} _{+}\to \mathbb{N} _{+}\) and one deterministic LOCAL algorithm that, for every n-vertex graph supplied with an orientation of maximum outdegree at most \(\beta \ge 1\), computes a proper vertex coloring using at most \(\lceil C_{1}\beta ^{2- \varepsilon}\rceil\) colors within \(f(\beta )+C_{2}\log * n\) rounds?

cards.definitions: The communication network is a finite undirected simple graph \(G=(V,E), |V|=n\ge 2\). Every edge has a supplied direction, known to its endpoints; no acyclicity is promised. A vertex’s outdegree is its number of outgoing edges, and every vertex has outdegree at most the supplied bound \(\beta\). Its indegree and total degree may be arbitrarily large. A proper coloring assigns each vertex a label from one common palette so that endpoints of every edge have different labels, regardless of the edge direction. Vertices execute the same deterministic algorithm in synchronous rounds, have unique identifiers of \(O(\log  n)\) bits, know their incident ports and edge directions, and may know n and \(\beta\). Each round allows a separate message of unbounded size to each neighbor in either direction and unrestricted finite local computation. Cost is worst-case round count over graphs, orientations and identifiers. No precomputed coloring or graph decomposition is supplied. The function f may grow arbitrarily fast with \(\beta\), but cannot depend on n, total degree or the orientation’s path lengths. Both the exponent improvement \(\varepsilon\) and the coefficient of \(\log * n\) must be uniform over \(\beta\) and n. Here \(\log * n\) is the number of repeated base-two logarithms needed to reach a value at most one. Edgeless graphs, including the \(\beta =0\) case, can be assigned one color separately.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove the existence of the uniform deterministic algorithm with the stated palette and additive round bound, or establish that no such \(\varepsilon\), constants, computable f and algorithm exist. A palette reduction by only logarithmic factors, a runtime depending on total degree, or a multiplicative log n term does not establish this claim.

sentences: Strong Byzantine agreement requires correct processes to agree while preserving the strong validity condition even when some participants behave arbitrarily.
Here adaptivity refers to communication that scales with the actual number f of faulty processes, rather than only the tolerated maximum t.
The source asks for a fully adaptive strong-agreement algorithm with optimal resilience \(n = 2t + 1\).
Its constructions achieve \(O(n(f+1))\) communication for broadcast and weak agreement, but the strong version becomes quadratic once failures occur.
Closing that gap would retain optimal fault tolerance while making communication economical in executions with only a few faults.

cards.title: Strongly polynomial linear programming
cards.formal:
Does there exist one deterministic algorithm and fixed positive integers \(C,d,C',e\) with the following guarantee for every \(m,n\ge1\), \(A\in\mathbb Q^{m\times n}\), \(b\in\mathbb Q^m\) and \(c\in\mathbb Q^n\)? For the linear program
\[\min\{c^{\mathsf T}x: x\in\mathbb R^n,\ Ax=b,\ x\ge0\},\]
the algorithm returns an exact rational optimal vector, or correctly reports infeasibility or an objective unbounded below. It uses at most \(C(m+n+1)^d\) elementary operations in the rational arithmetic model below, and every numerical value during the computation has binary encoding length at most \(C'(N+1)^e\), where \(N\) is the full input bit length. The same program and constants must work for all dimensions and coefficient values.
cards.definitions:
The input contains the dimensions and the complete dense lists of entries of \(A,b,c\), including zeros. Each rational is supplied as a signed binary integer numerator and a positive binary integer denominator. Their lengths, the dimensions and the delimiters all contribute to \(N\). No rank, nondegeneracy, strict-feasibility, boundedness, coefficient-size or conditioning promise is imposed. The variables range over the real numbers; rational input guarantees that a finite optimum, when the feasible set is nonempty and the objective bounded below, has a rational optimal vector.

Computation uses one fixed finite arithmetic-RAM program with rational registers, integer addresses and finite control. One scalar addition, subtraction, multiplication, division by a nonzero rational, exact comparison, register read/write or copy costs one operation. Conditional branches, elementary integer index arithmetic and comparisons, and data transfers also count. Index operations are integer addition and subtraction; indirect addressing accesses one location at a time. Indices start from dimensions or fixed integer constants and are manipulated by these index operations. A rational coefficient or computed rational cannot be reinterpreted as an address. Each scalar entry of a vector or matrix operation must be charged separately. All preprocessing, memory access, feasibility testing and production of the output count. A scalar rational input read or output write counts once at this arithmetic level; transferring its individual binary digits is accounted for by the bit implementation.

The program may contain finitely many fixed rational constants. It has no oracle, advice, randomness, floor or integer-part primitive, square-root primitive, or instruction inspecting the binary digits, numerator, denominator or encoding length of a rational register. Comparisons and arithmetic act on exact rational values, not floating-point approximations. Here the binary size of a rational is the combined length of its signed numerator and positive denominator in lowest terms. The bound also covers integer indices and the output. Reduction to lowest terms specifies representation and exact bit simulation; it supplies no additional operation with which the arithmetic program can extract numerator or denominator data. The elementary rational operations must admit an exact implementation on a binary multitape Turing machine in time polynomial in their operand lengths. Thus the dimension-only operation bound together with the polynomial numerical-size bound yields total bit time polynomial in \(N\); the bit-time bound is not required to be independent of \(N\).

Let \(F=\{x\in\mathbb R^n:Ax=b,\ x\ge0\}\). An infeasibility answer is correct exactly when \(F=\varnothing\). An unbounded-below answer is correct exactly when \(F\ne\varnothing\) and
\[\forall M\in\mathbb R\ \exists x\in F,\qquad c^{\mathsf T}x<M.\]
Otherwise the algorithm must return \(x^*\in F\cap\mathbb Q^n\) with
\[\forall y\in F,\qquad c^{\mathsf T}x^*\le c^{\mathsf T}y.\]
Any optimal vector is allowed when several exist; an optimal basis is not required. An unbounded feasible region can still have a finite minimum, and must then receive an optimal-vector output. Infeasibility and unboundedness outputs are distinct tags, not an approximate numerical infinity. The operation bound depends only on \(m+n\); neither coefficient magnitudes, their bit lengths, numerical conditioning nor a requested accuracy may enter it.
cards.answer_criterion:
Give a complete, mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of this algorithm-existence statement or of its logical negation. A positive answer must specify a finite deterministic program, prove its correct exact output in all three cases for every rational input, and prove both a single dimension-only polynomial operation bound and a single polynomial bound on numerical encoding lengths, with an exact polynomial-time bit implementation.

A negative answer must prove that no program with any fixed constants \(C,d,C',e\) satisfies all these requirements on every input. An exponential example for one pivot rule or a restricted class of interior-point methods does not exclude every algorithm in the specified model. A guarantee restricted to special matrices, fixed dimension, well-conditioned or strictly feasible inputs, or an approximate optimum does not settle the question. This is a yes/no existence target; the benchmark's numerical approximation tolerance does not replace exact optimization or either complexity bound.
cards.why: Linear programming is a basic language for optimization across combinatorics, algorithms and applications. The question asks whether exact optimization needs a number of arithmetic decisions that grows with numerical precision, or whether the dimensions alone suffice. A positive answer would extend a central efficiency property of several combinatorial optimization problems to every rational linear program.

importance.reason: A leading open question in optimization, separating ordinary polynomial-time solvability from a dimension-only arithmetic bound. Its reach includes general linear programming and many combinatorial optimization problems.

progress.text: Tardos establishes arithmetic bounds independent of the right-hand side and objective magnitudes, with remaining dependence on the constraint matrix.
Exponential iteration lower bounds apply to the stated central-path neighborhood framework, not to all LP algorithms.
The STOC theorem gives a deterministic strongly polynomial algorithm for minimum-cost generalized flow and the two-nonzero-per-row-or-column classes, with a Turing-model implementation.
The STOC 2026 trust-region work improves path-following bounds relative to neighborhood straight-line complexity; it does not assert a dimension-only bound for arbitrary LP.
Awoniyi’s version 10 retains a general solution claim; its proof has not been independently certified by this review.
Truffet’s version 4 states a general solution claim and describes a correction to earlier versions. Its source PDF is internally dated 1 September 2026.

context_blocks.text: Linear programming already has algorithms polynomial in the full binary input length. That length can increase while the numbers of variables and constraints stay fixed. Strong polynomiality asks for a dimension-only arithmetic operation count while retaining polynomially bounded numerical representations. It does not promise that writing an arbitrarily long exact output takes a constant number of bit operations.

The three output cases refer to the objective as well as the feasible set. For example, \(x_1=1\), \(x_2\ge0\), with objective \(x_1\), has an unbounded feasible region and finite minimum \(1\). The algorithm must return an optimal vector in this case. Failure to find a feasible point is not by itself a certificate that none exists.

Tardos’s 1986 theorem removes the dependence of the arithmetic operation count on the right-hand side and objective coefficients, while retaining dependence on the constraint matrix. This gives strong polynomiality for important small-coefficient matrix classes. Dadush, Koh, Natura, Olver and Végh’s STOC 2024 theorem covers minimum-cost generalized flow and linear programs with at most two nonzero entries per row or per column, including controlled bit complexity. An unrestricted dense matrix need not belong to these classes.

Allamigeon, Gaubert and Vandame prove exponential iteration lower bounds for interior-point trajectories confined to the specified neighborhoods of self-concordant-barrier central paths. A central path is the curve of minimizers of the barrier-penalized objective as its parameter varies. Their theorem restricts which trajectories the method follows; it is not a lower bound for every arithmetic algorithm for linear programming.

The STOC 2026 trust-region paper gives guarantees relative to the straight-line complexity of an appropriate central-path neighborhood: the number of line segments needed to traverse it. Instance optimality within this path-following framework does not supply a dimension-only polynomial bound on that quantity for every LP. The paper also distinguishes its real-RAM running times from the additional work needed to control bit complexity. Its approximate trust-region subproblems retain accuracy parameters and are not exact general LP solvers.

A separate paper entitled Validation is by the same author, so its title does not establish independent confirmation.
