importance.reason: A central runtime frontier in randomized numerical linear algebra, separating worst-direction compression guarantees from aggregate-error guarantees for arbitrary sparse matrices.

sentences: Spectral low-rank approximation seeks a rank-k representation whose largest directional error is near the best possible.
The source asks for a relative-error guarantee in time equal to reading the nonzero matrix entries plus a term linear in n and polynomial in k over epsilon.
That speed is available in the cited comparison for Frobenius error, which aggregates squared errors instead of controlling the worst direction.
The spectral target is therefore substantially stronger.
A solution would make sparse-matrix compression fast while protecting against a large error concentrated in one singular direction.

cards.definitions: The matrix is given as a list of its nonzero entries, each with its row index, column index and real value; unspecified entries are zero and index pairs do not repeat. The integer \(\operatorname{nnz}(A)\) is the length of this list. The spectral norm is \(\|D\|_2=\sup_{\|x\|_2=1}\|Dx\|_2\). For singular values \(\sigma_1(A)\geq\cdots\geq\sigma_n(A)\geq0\), the optimum on the right is \(\sigma_{k+1}(A)\). Orthonormality means \(Z^{\mathsf T}Z=I_k\), so \(ZZ^{\mathsf T}\) is an orthogonal projection of rank \(k\). The output is the explicit matrix \(Z\); forming the generally dense product \(ZZ^{\mathsf T}A\) is not required. All real input matrices are included, with no gap, conditioning, spectral-decay, positivity or distributional promise. If \(\operatorname{rank}(A)\leq k\), the required residual is exactly zero on a successful run. The selected arithmetic model is a uniform real RAM with unit-cost addition, subtraction, multiplication, division by nonzero values, square root of a nonnegative value, real comparison, and indexed memory access. Registers store exact reals or integer indices; integer indexing arithmetic is charged, and no real-to-integer floor or bit extraction is a free primitive. Independent fair random bits and independent standard normal real samples are available at unit cost. This explicitly adopts the ideal arithmetic and sampling convention used in randomized numerical linear algebra; bit complexity is not the target. The operation bound includes reading the input, all preprocessing, random sampling and writing the output, and must hold on every random run. Only correctness may fail with probability at most one third, separately for each fixed input. A single algorithm and the same constants work for all parameters; \(n\geq2\).
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked algorithm and proofs of its probability guarantee and stated arithmetic running time, or prove that no such algorithm exists in this model. The coefficient of the nonzero-entry term must be an absolute constant: multiplying that term by k, inverse accuracy or logarithms of n misses the target. Frobenius-norm error, additive spectral error, extra output rank, or a bound conditional on a singular-value gap does not establish the displayed claim.

context_blocks.text: Woodruff’s Open Question 1 asks whether the input-sparsity bound for relative Frobenius approximation can also give the relative spectral projection guarantee in Equation (65). The card makes the arithmetic model, success probability and output representation explicit; it retains the square-matrix target.

The Frobenius norm sums squared errors over all entries, whereas the spectral norm controls the largest error in a unit direction. A relative Frobenius guarantee therefore need not provide a relative spectral guarantee when many small singular values contribute to the total tail energy.

The survey presents a spectral approximation based on repeated matrix products, but its dependence on repeated passes and the target rank does not have the requested additive input-sparsity form. Its Frobenius result already achieves that form.

Bakshi, Bhattacharyya, Kannan, Woodruff and Zhou’s 2021 latent-simplex algorithm obtains input-sparsity time under a spectral-mass assumption. Their paper connects removal of that assumption to a breakthrough for spectral low-rank approximation, rather than claiming to solve the unrestricted matrix problem.

A bound of the form input size plus a polynomial in rank and accuracy times n matters especially when a large sparse matrix can be read once but cannot cheaply be multiplied by many vectors. The additive second term also accommodates the n-by-k output. No explicit n-by-n projection is requested.

cards.title: Superlinear randomized query lower bounds for submodular minimization
cards.formal: Let \(R(n)\) be the minimum worst-case number of value-oracle queries needed by a randomized algorithm to find an exact minimizer of every real-valued submodular function on \(n\) elements, with success probability at least \(2/3\). Is \(R(n)=\omega(n)\), meaning \(R(n)/n\to\infty\) as \(n\to\infty\)?

source_formulation.text: We leave proving a super-linear lower bound on the query complexity of randomized algorithms for SFM as an open question.
source_formulation.caption: Complete selected source sentence; PDF p. 5

cards.why: Submodular minimization is a central tractable optimization problem, yet its information requirements remain far from its best general algorithms. A superlinear randomized lower bound would establish that even unlimited computation and adaptive random querying cannot reduce exact minimization to a linear amount of oracle information.
cards.status_note: The 2022 source explicitly leaves superlinear randomized query lower bounds open and explains why its deterministic argument does not transfer. No matching resolution for the bounded-query exact-minimization model was located in the bounded September 2026 check.

importance.reason: A fundamental information lower-bound gap for general submodular minimization, separating randomization from the first known superlinear deterministic obstruction.

sentences: A value oracle answers exact evaluations of an unknown submodular set function.
The randomized algorithm must find a true global minimizer on every input with constant success probability.
The question asks whether the worst-case query requirement grows faster than every constant multiple of the ground-set size.
Neither numeric evaluation cost nor local computation is charged.
Known deterministic and parallel-round lower bounds do not settle this randomized total-query question.

cards.definitions: The ground set is \([n]\), and a function \(F:2^{[n]}\to\mathbb R\) is submodular if \(F(A)+F(B)\geq F(A\cup B)+F(A\cap B)\) for all subsets \(A,B\). No monotonicity, nonnegativity, symmetry or normalization is promised. A query specifies any subset \(S\) and receives its exact real value \(F(S)\). The algorithm may adapt later queries to all previous values and its own random choices. Its final answer is a subset \(S_*\) satisfying \(F(S_*)\leq F(S)\) for every \(S\subseteq[n]\); any minimizer is acceptable, including the empty or full set. For every fixed valid oracle \(F\), the probability of a correct output is at least \(2/3\). In the definition of \(R(n)\), a cost bound \(q\) requires at most \(q\) oracle calls on every input and every outcome of the random choices, not just in expectation. Arbitrary finite local computation and exact operations on the oracle answers are free. The algorithm has no direct access to a formula, table or circuit for \(F\). We use classical randomized query complexity: for each dimension, random coins select a deterministic adaptive query procedure, independently of \(F\); the maps and distributions must define measurable success events. An algorithm may depend on \(n\), so lower bounds also apply to nonuniform choices. The value magnitudes and their bit encodings do not enter the query cost. Exhaustively querying all \(2^n\) subsets shows that \(R(n)\) is finite. A superlinear lower bound means that for each real constant \(C>0\), all sufficiently large \(n\) satisfy \(R(n)>Cn\).
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked superlinear lower bound in the specified randomized bounded-query model. Alternatively prove the negation of that growth statement: a fixed constant C and infinitely many dimensions admit correct algorithms using at most Cn queries. An O(n)-query algorithm for all dimensions would suffice for a negative answer but is stronger than the logical negation. A deterministic lower bound, a lower bound on parallel rounds, or hardness only for finding a nonempty proper minimizer does not establish the target.

context_blocks.text: The source proves an Ω(n log n) deterministic query lower bound and explicitly asks for a superlinear randomized one. The selected target is any unbounded multiplicative improvement over n, rather than a demand for the same n log n expression.

In the deterministic construction, an adversary can exploit the algorithm’s fixed queries to delay discovery of a hidden set. The paper explains why random subsets can defeat the local obstruction used for that logarithmic factor. Transferring the deterministic proof without a new randomized argument is therefore insufficient.

The paper also proves a nearly linear lower bound on the number of adaptive parallel rounds when each round permits polynomially many queries. This measures how often answers must be used to choose the next batch. It does not imply a superlinear lower bound on the total number of sequentially adaptive queries.

Earlier lower bounds include a linear bound for general minimization and stronger statements for nontrivial minimizers of certain function classes. The requirement to exclude the empty and full sets changes the optimization problem; this card allows both and asks for the usual unconstrained minimum.

Exact oracle values can reveal more than comparisons between candidate subsets. A lower bound in this model must survive that extra information and cannot assume a bounded numeric range unless it constructs hard functions within that range. Conversely, bit complexity of evaluating an oracle is outside the target.

Strongly polynomial query upper bounds do not depend on the range of function values. The source compares algorithms with different amounts of local computation, including exponential local time; the lower-bound target here deliberately imposes no polynomial-time restriction.

cards.title: Limited-memory convex optimization
cards.formal: Determine, up to universal constant factors, the deterministic first-order oracle complexity \(T(d,M,\varepsilon)\) of minimizing a globally convex, Euclidean \(1\)-Lipschitz function with a global minimizer in the unit ball, when only \(M\) bits can be retained between queries. The target is the entire tradeoff for integers \(d\geq1\), \(M\geq0\) and real \(0<\varepsilon\leq1/4\), including the parameters for which \(T(d,M,\varepsilon)=\infty\).
cards.why: The tradeoff separates acquiring information about a convex objective from retaining that information for later decisions. A full answer would quantify when nearly linear storage can preserve fast convergence and when the geometry needed for a small number of queries forces substantially larger memory.
cards.status_note: The full tradeoff is open in the 2019 source. A review on 13 September 2026 found substantial later endpoint and partial-tradeoff results, but no complete characterization in the precise source model. The bounded later-work check is not an exhaustive certification of current openness.

sentences: First-order convex optimization learns about an objective through queries returning its value and a subgradient.
The source asks how the number of queries needed for a prescribed accuracy changes when the algorithm has limited working memory.
It highlights methods with strong oracle complexity whose stored geometric information can require quadratic space in dimension.
The question is whether that memory cost is inherent or can be traded away without losing the optimal query rate.
A sharp tradeoff would distinguish information acquired from the oracle from information that must remain available between optimization steps.

cards.definitions: Let \(\mathcal F_d\) contain all convex functions \(f:\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R\) such that \(|f(x)-f(y)|\leq\|x-y\|_2\) for every \(x,y\), and such that some global minimizer \(x_*\) satisfies \(\|x_*\|_2\leq1\). A subgradient at \(x\) is a vector \(g\) with \(f(y)\geq f(x)+\langle g,y-x\rangle\) for every \(y\in\mathbb R^d\). A query at any \(x\in\mathbb R^d\) returns the exact pair \((f(x),g)\) for any valid subgradient; correctness is required for every sequence of such choices. An \(M\)-bit, \(t\)-query algorithm consists of deterministic maps \(\phi_i:\{0,1\}^M\to\mathbb R^d\), \(\psi_i:\{0,1\}^M\times\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^d\to\{0,1\}^M\) for \(1\leq i\leq t\), and \(\zeta:\{0,1\}^M\to\mathbb R^d\). Starting with \(s_0=0^M\), it queries \(x_i=\phi_i(s_{i-1})\), receives \((f(x_i),g_i)\), and sets \(s_i=\psi_i(s_{i-1},f(x_i),g_i)\). Its final output is \(\zeta(s_t)\); for \(t=0\) it is \(\zeta(s_0)\). All maps may depend on \(d,M,t,\varepsilon\), but not on the unknown function. They are unrestricted mathematical maps: computing an update can use arbitrary real operations and temporary memory. Only the retained state is limited; there is no runtime, uniformity or computability requirement on these maps. The iteration index is implicit in the maps and is not charged to memory. Define \(R(d,M,t)=\inf_A\sup_{f\in\mathcal F_d,\,(g_i)}[f(\zeta(s_t))-\min_x f(x)]\), and \(T(d,M,\varepsilon)=\min\{t\in\mathbb N_0:R(d,M,t)\leq\varepsilon\}\), with the minimum of the empty set equal to infinity. The infimum over algorithms need not be attained: \(R\leq\varepsilon\) means that for every \(\eta>0\) some algorithm has worst-case error at most \(\varepsilon+\eta\). Queries and outputs are not restricted to the unit ball.
cards.answer_criterion: Supply a noncircular characterization \(G(d,M,\varepsilon)\in[0,\infty]\) and a complete Lean-checked proof of \(cG\leq T\leq CG\) throughout the stated domain, for fixed \(c,C>0\). Prove exactly which parameters have infinite complexity. The memory argument and requested accuracy must be those stated, without an unstated constant enlargement of memory or accuracy. Upper bounds must respect the infimum convention. Resolving only optimal-query memory requirements or one accuracy regime is not a characterization of the full tradeoff.

context_blocks.text: This is Question 1 of Woodworth and Srebro’s 2019 contribution, with its preferred constant-factor accuracy selected explicitly. The source also permits a weaker polylogarithmic characterization and poses several subsidiary endpoint questions; those alternatives are not the acceptance criterion here.

The normalization loses no scale parameter: a Lipschitz constant \(L>0\) and a known minimizer radius \(B>0\) replace the accuracy by \(\varepsilon/(LB)\). The formal target retains the source’s global-function model and its bottleneck-memory convention, rather than total machine space.

The source exhibits gradient descent with \(O(\varepsilon^{-2})\) queries and \(O(d\log(1/\varepsilon))\) retained bits, and a discretized center-of-mass method with \(O(d\log(1/\varepsilon))\) queries and \(O(d^2\log^2(1/\varepsilon))\) bits. These are achievable resource pairs; neither states the optimal query rate in every dimension and accuracy regime.

Blanchard, Zhang and Jaillet’s 2023 work establishes a nearly quadratic memory barrier for optimal query complexity in convex minimization over the unit ball. This addresses a source endpoint question, not the complete three-parameter tradeoff. Their separate recursive cutting-plane work gives additional memory-query upper bounds, including a high-accuracy regime.

Menart, Nikolov and Shamir’s July 2026 preprint strengthens deterministic and randomized lower bounds and reports a sharp transition near quadratic memory. Its stated model restricts queries to the feasible unit ball. No transfer of its numerical bounds to the global, unrestricted-query model above is assumed by this card.

A real-valued oracle answer can carry unlimited precision, but retaining it requires encoding it in the next finite state. Conversely, restricting temporary arithmetic would create a different problem. These distinctions are central to what a memory lower bound establishes.

cards.title: Smooth convex optimization with different domain and smoothness norms
cards.formal: For each fixed \(1\leq p<q\leq\infty\) and \(1<\kappa\leq2\), determine the optimal worst-case error \(\mathcal R_{p,q,\kappa}(n,T)\), up to constant factors, of deterministic algorithms making \(T\) exact first-order queries to minimize a convex function whose gradient is Hölder continuous in the \(\ell_q\) geometry over the unit \(\ell_p\) ball. The target covers every integer \(n\geq2\) and \(1\leq T\leq n\).
cards.why: The problem isolates whether the geometry of a constrained model can improve the fundamental convergence rate when smoothness is measured differently. Matching bounds would explain which gains in sparse and structured regression follow from geometry alone and which require access to additional problem structure.
cards.status_note: The selected cross-norm problem is open in the 2015 source. Later-work checks on 13 September 2026 did not identify matching rates for the full first-order family; the 2026 proximal-oracle result uses different access. This is a dated source-backed status, not an exhaustive proof of current openness.

sentences: Smooth convex optimization is often analyzed when the objective's regularity and the feasible region use compatible norms.
The source instead studies settings where these geometries differ, including vector norms and their matrix counterparts.
It asks for the optimal oracle complexity of minimizing such functions using black-box first-order information.
The stated gaps concern how smoothness, domain geometry, dimension, and target accuracy interact.
Matching algorithms and lower bounds would show whether sparse and low-rank optimization models permit faster convergence than methods designed around a single common norm suggest.

cards.definitions:
For \(1\leq s<\infty\), put \(\|x\|_s=(\sum_{i=1}^n|x_i|^s)^{1/s}\), and put \(\|x\|_\infty=\max_i|x_i|\). Write \(B_p^n=\{x:\|x\|_p\leq1\}\). The conjugate exponent \(q_*\) is defined by \(1/q+1/q_*=1\), with \(1/\infty=0\). Let \(\mathcal F_{q,\kappa}^n\) be the class of all continuously differentiable convex functions \(f:\mathbb R^n	o\mathbb R\) such that \[\|
abla f(x)-
abla f(y)\|_{q_*}\leq\|x-y\|_q^{\kappa-1}\qquad(x,y\in\mathbb R^n).\] There is no bound on the affine part of \(f\), no strong-convexity assumption and no promise of a sparse minimizer. One oracle query at any \(x\in\mathbb R^n\) returns the exact pair \((f(x),
abla f(x))\). A deterministic algorithm chooses each query as a function of the parameters and previous answers, and after at most \(T\) queries outputs \(\widehat x\in B_p^n\). It receives no explicit formula, data matrix, decomposition, proximal oracle or higher derivative. All computation between queries is free and unrestricted; arbitrary deterministic decision maps depending on \(n,T,p,q,\kappa\) are allowed, with no uniformity or bit-precision restriction. Its error is \(f(\widehat x)-\min_{x\in B_p^n}f(x)\). Define \(\mathcal R_{p,q,\kappa}(n,T)=\inf_A\sup_{f\in\mathcal F_{q,\kappa}^n}[f(\widehat x_A(f))-\min_{B_p^n}f]\). Allowing an output outside the ball with error infinity gives the same definition. The minimum of each function exists because the ball is compact. The infimum over algorithms need not be attained. A Hölder bound with constant \(L>0\) and a feasible ball of radius \(R>0\) scales this risk by \(LR^\kappa\).
cards.answer_criterion: Give a noncircular rate \(G_{p,q,\kappa}(n,T)\) and a complete Lean-checked proof of \(c_{p,q,\kappa}G\leq\mathcal R\leq C_{p,q,\kappa}G\) over the entire stated domain, with positive constants independent of \(n,T\). The upper bound may be approached arbitrarily closely if the minimax infimum is not attained. Both the query and dimension dependence, including any logarithmic factors needed for constant-factor matching, must be established. A result for one pair of norms or for a stronger oracle alone does not characterize this family.

context_blocks.text: Guzmán’s 2015 Open Problem 1 asks for large-scale minimax rates when the feasible ball and the smoothness norm differ. This card explicitly selects the vector case \(p<q\), where the reported gaps are substantial, and exact value-and-gradient access. The source also discusses matrix Schatten norms and a more general class of local oracles; those are related extensions rather than additional requirements.

When \(p<q\), the unit \(\ell_p\) ball is contained in the unit \(\ell_q\) ball. The source asks whether algorithms can exploit this smaller feasible geometry more effectively than methods analyzed only in the smoothness norm.

For \(p=1,q=2,\kappa=2\), the source compares an accelerated \(O(T^{-2})\) upper bound with a lower bound of order \(T^{-3}\), up to logarithmic factors, in its large-scale regime. These are dated nonmatching bounds, not a claimed present-day formula for the minimax risk.

Convex regression over a norm-constrained predictor class motivates the problem. Access to the complete regression data can supply structure unavailable to a first-order black box, so a faster algorithm for one explicit regression loss does not automatically determine this oracle complexity.

Adil, Bullins, Jambulapati and Sidford’s 2026 work studies stronger norm-dependent proximal oracles that solve a regularized minimization problem in one call. Its accelerated rates and matching span-restricted lower bounds concern that different information model.

The precision requested here concerns asymptotic error rates as the query budget and dimension vary. It is not an additive numerical tolerance on the risk. Constants may depend on the fixed norm and smoothness exponents; dependence on dimension cannot be hidden there.

cards.title: Deterministic near-linear-query approximation schemes for matroid intersection
cards.formal: Is there a deterministic algorithm and absolute constants \(C,a,b>0\) that, given independence-oracle access to any two matroids on a common \(n\)-element ground set and any rational \(0<\varepsilon<1\), finds a common independent set of size at least \((1-\varepsilon)r\) using at most \(Cn\log^a(n+2)\varepsilon^{-b}\) oracle queries, where \(r\) is the maximum size of a common independent set?

cards.why: The question asks whether random sampling is essential for information-efficient approximate intersection of arbitrary matroids. importance.reason: A broad derandomization and oracle-efficiency question for a central combinatorial optimization primitive, covering all common ranks and arbitrary matroids.

sentences: Two unknown matroids are accessed only by tests of whether a proposed subset is independent.
The algorithm must output a large set independent in both matroids.
The target is deterministic approximation arbitrarily close to optimum with near-linear query complexity.
The guarantee must cover every common rank, without stronger rank queries or matrix representations.
Randomized near-linear schemes and a deterministic two-thirds approximation are known.

cards.definitions: A matroid on \(V=[n]\) is a family \(\mathcal I\subseteq2^V\) containing the empty set, closed under taking subsets, and satisfying augmentation: if \(X,Y\in\mathcal I\) and \(|X|<|Y|\), some \(e\in Y\setminus X\) has \(X\cup\{e\}\in\mathcal I\). The two unknown families \(\mathcal I_1,\mathcal I_2\) are supplied through separate exact independence oracles. A query specifies an index \(j\in\{1,2\}\) and a subset \(S\subseteq[n]\), and returns one bit indicating whether \(S\in\mathcal I_j\). The total number of calls to both oracles is charged, including repeated calls. Queries may depend on all previous answers. The algorithm knows \(n\) and \(\varepsilon\), but need not be told \(r=\max\{|S|:S\in\mathcal I_1\cap\mathcal I_2\}\), and receives no representation, rank oracle or additional promise. It must output the elements of a feasible common independent set, not merely estimate \(r\). The guarantee must hold for every pair of matroids and every attainable \(0\leq r\leq n\); loops, parallel elements, unequal matroid ranks and rank zero are allowed. Computation between queries is unrestricted but finite, and the algorithm is deterministic and uniform over \(n\) and the binary accuracy parameter. The target measures query complexity rather than arithmetic or bit running time. The constants and exponents in the displayed bound are independent of the matroids, \(n,r\) and \(\varepsilon\).
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked algorithm with the stated feasibility, approximation and query bounds, or prove that no such deterministic approximation scheme exists in this oracle model. A randomized scheme, a nearly linear scheme only when the common rank is a constant fraction of n, or a scheme that uses stronger rank queries does not decide the target.

context_blocks.text: Terao’s 2025 paper explicitly asks whether deterministic near-linear-query approximation can approach one throughout the rank range. Its soft-O convention permits polynomial factors in inverse accuracy and logarithms of n; the displayed bound makes those factors explicit.

For two partition matroids representing the endpoints of a bipartite graph, common independent sets are matchings. General matroids can hide much more information behind each membership bit, so algorithms for explicitly represented graphs alone do not answer the oracle question.

A greedy maximal common independent set gives a one-half approximation with a linear number of independence queries. Terao improves the ratio to two thirds minus an accuracy term with O(n/ε+r log r) queries. This is a fixed approximation threshold, not an arbitrarily accurate scheme.

Blikstad and Tu achieve a near-linear-query randomized approximation scheme. Their work also provides a deterministic strictly linear-query guarantee in the large-common-rank regime for fixed accuracy. These results show why neither randomization nor the quantifier over all ranks can be omitted.

Terao’s 2026 algorithm for linear matroid intersection accesses two explicit matrices and exploits linear-algebraic structure. Its input-sparsity running time is a different resource guarantee and does not yield a deterministic near-linear membership-query algorithm for arbitrary matroids.

Taking ε very small eventually forces an exact answer because the output size is integral. This causes no contradiction with exact-intersection lower bounds: the allowed polynomial dependence on 1/ε may then be large. The interesting approximation regime fixes accuracy while n and the optimum rank vary.

cards.title: Polynomial-time linear convergence for geodesically convex optimization
cards.formal: In the geometric arithmetic model below, is there a deterministic first-order algorithm and absolute constants \(C,a,b>0\) that minimize every Lipschitz geodesically convex function on a strongly geodesically convex ball in a complete Riemannian manifold, using at most \(C(d+\zeta)^a\lceil\log(2/\varepsilon)\rceil\) objective-oracle queries and at most \(C(d+\zeta)^b\) additional operations between consecutive queries? Here \(d\) is the manifold dimension, \(\zeta=r\sqrt K/\tanh(r\sqrt K)\), with value one at \(K=0\), and the required additive objective error is \(\varepsilon Lr\). The same polynomial overhead bound applies before the first query and after the last.
cards.why: Euclidean cutting-plane methods show that high accuracy need not require a polynomial number of inverse-accuracy steps. Extending that efficiency to geodesic convexity would provide a general computational foundation for optimization on curved spaces, including matrix geometries used in scaling and statistical models.
cards.status_note: The joint query-and-computation question is open in the 2023 source. A bounded review on 13 September 2026 did not find a resolution for the full geodesically convex class. The computational oracle convention is an explicit editorial specification, not a claim that all manifolds admit efficient finite-precision geometric implementations.

sentences: Geodesically convex optimization replaces straight segments with shortest paths on a Riemannian manifold.
The question asks for a deterministic first-order algorithm with query complexity polynomial in dimension and logarithmic in inverse accuracy.
It also requires polynomial arithmetic work per query, so a powerful but computationally intractable geometric oracle would not suffice.
The source develops an ellipsoid-like approach for constant-curvature spaces and identifies obstacles on more general manifolds.
A solution would extend the efficient precision dependence of Euclidean convex optimization to curved spaces while respecting the cost of manipulating their geometry.

cards.definitions: The input consists of a complete connected smooth \(d\)-dimensional Riemannian manifold \(\mathcal M\), \(d\geq1\), a reference point \(x_0\), a radius \(r>0\), a Lipschitz bound \(L>0\), a sectional-curvature bound \(K\geq0\), and real \(0<\varepsilon\leq1/2\). All sectional curvatures lie in \([-K,K]\). The distance \(\operatorname{dist}\) is the infimum of lengths of connecting curves in the given Riemannian metric. The closed ball \(D=\{x:\operatorname{dist}(x_0,x)\leq r\}\) is promised strongly geodesically convex: every two points of \(D\) have a unique minimizing geodesic in \(\mathcal M\), and its whole segment lies in \(D\). If \(\gamma\) is such a segment parametrized on \([0,1]\) at constant speed, the unknown function \(f:D\to\mathbb R\) satisfies \(f(\gamma(t))\leq(1-t)f(\gamma(0))+tf(\gamma(1))\), and \(|f(x)-f(y)|\leq L\operatorname{dist}(x,y)\). A function query at \(x\in D\) returns \(f(x)\) exactly and any tangent vector \(g\in T_x\mathcal M\) satisfying \(f(y)\geq f(x)+\langle g,\operatorname{Log}_x(y)\rangle_x\) for every \(y\in D\); correctness is required for every valid sequence of returned subgradients. Here \(\operatorname{Log}_x(y)\) is the initial velocity at time zero of the unit-time minimizing geodesic from \(x\) to \(y\). Only functions and subgradient oracles meeting these conditions are inputs. The output must be a point \(\widehat x\in D\) with \(f(\widehat x)-\min_D f\leq\varepsilon Lr\). Completeness makes the closed bounded ball compact, so this minimum exists. The algorithm has no access to a formula for \(f\). For computational access to geometry, points and tangent vectors are exact typed objects supplied by a geometric oracle; the input includes an orthonormal basis of \(T_{x_0}\mathcal M\). The available geometric operations are: distance between points; inner product of two vectors in one tangent space; linear combination of such vectors; \(\operatorname{Exp}_x(v)\), the time-one point of the geodesic with initial velocity \(v\); \(\operatorname{Log}_x(y)\) for \(x,y\in D\); and parallel transport of a tangent vector along the explicitly specified geodesic \(t\mapsto\operatorname{Exp}_x(tv)\), \(0\leq t\leq1\). Each such operation is charged \((d+1)^3\) units, irrespective of point or vector magnitude. Object storage and access cost one unit; objects cannot be inspected except by these operations. Exact real scalar addition, subtraction, multiplication, division by nonzero values, square root on nonnegative arguments, exponential, logarithm on positive arguments, comparisons and integer indexing operations each cost one unit. There is no floor or extraction of bits from a real register. All computation, including geometric operations, is charged apart from the separately counted function queries. One uniform finite program must work for every admissible manifold, basis, oracle and parameter tuple. There is no randomization, integral oracle, convex-hull oracle or free optimization subroutine.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked algorithm with the required uniform objective accuracy, logarithmic query dependence on inverse accuracy, and polynomial overhead independent of inverse accuracy, or prove that no such algorithm exists in the stated access model. A query bound with an uncomputable geometric step, a theorem only for a particular manifold, or an additional logarithmic factor in the query count does not meet the target. A negative result must allow the full list of geometric primitives provided here.

context_blocks.text: This retains the manifold, curvature, ball and objective quantifiers of the source’s Open Question 1. The source leaves the computational representation of a general manifold implicit. The listed exact geometric primitives and their costs are an explicit editorial choice making its arithmetic-overhead requirement testable. A result in this model is not automatically a polynomial bit-complexity result for an arbitrary encoded metric.

The parameter \(\zeta\) is comparable within universal constants to \(1+r\sqrt K\). It allows dependence on the curvature scale and radius. The source explains that curvature dependence cannot generally be removed, even though logarithmic dependence on inverse accuracy remains the requested target.

The source distinguishes methods with good query complexity but expensive geometric work from subgradient methods with cheap steps but slower precision dependence. Thus proving either resource guarantee separately does not settle the joint question.

For constant-curvature spaces the source gives an ellipsoid-like method with \(O(\zeta d^2\log^2(1/\varepsilon))\) queries and polynomial per-query work. This is a substantial partial result, but its extra logarithm and restricted geometry are both relevant to the full statement.

Positive definite matrices with the affine-invariant Riemannian metric are an important nonconstant-curvature example discussed by the source. Boumal’s textbook gives explicit distance, exponential and logarithmic maps for that geometry. These differ from the log-Euclidean metric, under which a coordinate logarithm makes convexity Euclidean.

Criscitiello and Kim’s 2025 work develops algorithms for horospherical convexity, a stronger geometric notion with additional structure. It does not by itself supply the required method for every geodesically convex objective in this question.

cards.title: Gap-entropy conjecture
cards.formal: Are there absolute constants \(0<c\leq C<\infty\) such that, for every Gaussian best-arm instance \(I\) defined below and every \(0<\delta<1/10\), \[cH(I)\bigl(\log(1/\delta)+\operatorname{Ent}(I)\bigr)\leq L(I,\delta)\leq CH(I)\bigl(\log(1/\delta)+\operatorname{Ent}(I)\bigr)?\] Here \(L\) is the order-oblivious instance-wise optimum over globally correct sampling algorithms, not the performance of one algorithm required to attain the bound on every instance.
cards.why: The conjecture predicts the full instance-sensitive cost of identifying the best alternative, including the cost of learning which gap scales matter. Its entropy term would explain why instances with the same total inverse-square gap can have different exploration costs at fixed confidence.
cards.status_note: A preprint submitted on 9 September 2026 explicitly claims a positive resolution of this exact Gaussian instance-wise conjecture. Its Theorem 1.1 matches the target and its separate uniform-algorithm theorem addresses the related conjecture. This 13 September review has not independently checked the entire proof or located an established validation, so the status is uncertain, not source-open and not certified resolved.

sentences: The arms have independent Gaussian rewards with unit variance and a unique best mean.
The benchmark averages expected sample cost over arm relabelings and takes an infimum over globally correct algorithms.
The conjecture predicts that cost from the total inverse-square gaps and the entropy of their scale distribution.
It differs from asking one algorithm to attain the benchmark on all instances without an adaptation cost.
A 9 September 2026 preprint claims the precise formula; its proof has not been independently certified in this review.

cards.definitions: An instance has \(n\geq2\) independent arms with distributions \(\mathcal N(\mu_i,1)\), unknown means \(\mu_i\in[0,1]\), and a unique largest mean \(\mu_*\) at index \(*\). Each pull of arm \(i\) reveals a fresh independent sample from its distribution. An adaptive sampling algorithm knows \(n\) and \(\delta\), chooses pulls using earlier samples and independent internal randomness, and eventually outputs an arm index. It is \(\delta\)-correct if on every valid instance it stops almost surely and outputs its unique best arm with probability at least \(1-\delta\). Local computation is unrestricted; the resource is total number of pulls, and expectations include sampling noise and algorithmic randomness. Algorithms are measurable so that these probabilities and expectations are defined. Let \(T_A(I)\in[0,\infty]\) be the expected number of pulls. If \(S_n\) is the set of all permutations of arm labels and \(\pi I\) is the corresponding relabeled instance, define \(L(I,\delta)=\inf_A (1/n!)\sum_{\pi\in S_n}T_A(\pi I)\), where the infimum ranges over algorithms correct on every instance of the same Gaussian model. The infimum is taken separately for each \(I,\delta\): an algorithm selected for favorable performance at I must nevertheless remain correct on all other instances. It need not attain the infimum. For each suboptimal arm, set \(\Delta_i=\mu_*-\mu_i\in(0,1]\), and \(H(I)=\sum_{i\ne *}\Delta_i^{-2}\). For integers \(r\geq0\), set \(G_r=\{i\ne *:2^{-(r+1)}<\Delta_i\leq2^{-r}\}\), \(H_r=\sum_{i\in G_r}\Delta_i^{-2}\), and \(p_r=H_r/H(I)\). The gap entropy is \(\operatorname{Ent}(I)=\sum_{r:p_r>0}p_r\log(1/p_r)\), with natural logarithms. Only finitely many groups are nonempty. The constants in the conjecture are independent of n, all means, the number of gap scales and δ.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof of both uniform constant-factor bounds, or prove that no such universal pair of constants exists. A result only as δ tends to zero with the instance fixed, only for dyadic gaps or monotone algorithms, or an algorithm with an extra closest-gap term does not by itself prove the displayed claim about L. The recent claimed proof must meet the same mathematical and Lean-checking requirement.

context_blocks.text: This card selects Chen and Li’s Conjecture 3.5, which gives an explicit formula for the instance-wise optimum. Their separate Conjecture 3.2 asks for one algorithm attaining that optimum up to an additive two-arm adaptation term. The two statements are related but are not interchangeable.

Averaging over relabelings prevents an algorithm from gaining an artificial advantage because the best arm was placed at a preferred index. Taking an infimum over globally correct algorithms still permits a different favored sampling schedule for each target instance; it does not allow an algorithm to simply output a known best label without verifying correctness elsewhere.

Gap entropy weights a scale by its share of the inverse-square sampling burden, not by its fraction of arms. It vanishes when all gaps fall in one group and can grow when many scales carry comparable burden. The specified dyadic endpoint convention includes gaps equal to one; changing boundary conventions affects the full proposed complexity by at most constant factors.

Chen, Li and Qiao’s 2017 progress gives a nearly matching algorithmic bound and a lower bound for dyadic-gap instances under a monotonicity condition on algorithms. These restrictions and extra factors are relevant because the conjecture quantifies over all Gaussian instances and all correct algorithms.

A preprint submitted on 9 September 2026 by Aronow, Kallus and Lopatto states the displayed two-sided result as Theorem 1.1. It also states a separate uniform-algorithm theorem with the closest-gap adaptation term. The present review matched their definitions and theorem statements, but has not independently certified the complete proof.

Asymptotic confidence-optimal algorithms study δ tending to zero for a fixed instance, when log(1/δ) eventually dominates its fixed entropy. Such a limit does not determine the uniform cost when gap scales and confidence vary together. This is why the nonasymptotic quantifiers matter.

cards.title: Second-order cone lift dimension of semialgebraic convex hulls
cards.formal: Determine the function \(a(S)\) giving the minimum number of auxiliary real scalar variables in an exact second-order cone representation of \(\operatorname{conv}(S)\), for every semialgebraic set \(S\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) and every integer \(n\geq1\). Set \(a(S)=\infty\) when no finite such representation exists. For finite values, the benchmark accepts a real approximation within absolute error \(1/100\); infinite values require proof of nonrepresentability.
cards.why: Second-order cone lifts expose nonlinear convex structure through a class of conic constraints with effective optimization methods. Understanding both representability and the minimum added dimension would distinguish intrinsic geometric obstacles from the overhead of particular reformulations, while keeping those questions separate from numerical relaxation quality.
cards.status_note: The general characterization and auxiliary-dimension questions are open directions in the 2018 source. The individual review on 13 September 2026 checked major obstruction and positive-family results through 2025 but found no complete determination of the selected function. No exhaustive present-day openness certification is claimed.

importance.reason: A broad structural question about exact conic formulations, connecting real algebraic geometry with the extra dimension needed to represent convex optimization models.
importance.basis: Individual formulation and primary-source review.

sentences: A semialgebraic set is described by polynomial equalities and inequalities, while its convex hull collects all convex combinations of its points.
The source asks when that convex hull can be represented using second-order cone constraints and auxiliary variables.
It also asks how many additional variables such a representation requires.
Representability is stronger than having a useful numerical relaxation, because the projected feasible region must agree exactly with the desired hull.
A structural answer would identify nonlinear models that can be converted into a tractable conic formulation and quantify the cost of that conversion.

cards.definitions: A semialgebraic set is one defined by a finite Boolean combination of polynomial equalities and strict or non-strict polynomial inequalities with real coefficients. Its convex hull is the set of all finite convex combinations of its points: \(\sum_{i=1}^t\lambda_i s_i\), where \(t\geq1\), \(s_i\in S\), \(\lambda_i\geq0\) and \(\sum_i\lambda_i=1\). The convex hull of the empty set is empty. No closure is taken, and neither compactness nor closedness is assumed. For \(d\geq2\), the Lorentz cone is \(\mathcal L_d=\{(t,z)\in\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^{d-1}:t\geq\|z\|_2\}\); also let \(\mathcal L_1=\mathbb R_{\geq0}\). An admissible representation with \(r\in\mathbb N_0\) auxiliary variables has the form \[\operatorname{conv}(S)=\{x\in\mathbb R^n:\exists y\in\mathbb R^r,\ E(x,y)=e,\ F_j(x,y)\in\mathcal L_{d_j}\ (1\leq j\leq N)\},\] where \(N\geq0\), all cone dimensions \(d_j\geq1\) are finite, \(E\) is a real linear map with finitely many rows, \(e\) is a real vector, and each \(F_j\) is a real affine map into \(\mathbb R^{d_j}\). There is no bound on the number or dimensions of the cones, the number of affine equations or coefficient sizes. The number \(r\) counts only the scalar coordinates of \(y\), not the original coordinates of \(x\), the number of constraints or their output dimensions. Let \(a(S)\) be the least such \(r\), or infinity if the set of admissible integers is empty. In particular, zero auxiliary variables are allowed. The domain consists of mathematical sets with their ambient dimension, not particular defining formulas; equivalent descriptions of the same set must give the same answer. Coefficients of both the input descriptions and the lifts may be arbitrary real numbers. This is a characterization problem, not a claim that arbitrary real coefficients have finite machine encodings.
cards.answer_criterion: Supply a noncircular mathematical description or certified rule for \(a\), together with a complete Lean-checked proof identifying its infinite-value domain and giving a real-valued function \(g\) with \(|g(S)-a(S)|\leq1/100\) whenever \(a(S)<\infty\). A proved interval of width at most \(1/50\) may specify a finite answer through its midpoint. The approximation need not be integer-valued. Upper-bound constructions without matching minimality information, isolated representable families, or merely repeating the defining optimization over lifts are insufficient.

context_blocks.text: Section 5.1 of the 2018 Dagstuhl report asks both when a semialgebraic convex hull has a second-order cone representation and how many extra variables are necessary. The minimum-auxiliary-dimension function combines these into one target. The displayed model is an explicit editorial convention for “extra variables”; it permits all finite Lorentz-cone dimensions and real affine coefficients.

Allowing auxiliary variables can express convex sets that are not intersections of second-order cone constraints in their original coordinates. The number of auxiliary variables differs from conic extension complexity measured by the number of cones, their total dimension, or a semidefinite matrix block size. Those measures cannot silently replace a(S).

Fawzi proves that the cone of positive semidefinite real symmetric three-by-three matrices has no second-order cone representation. Thus even a semialgebraic convex set with a direct semidefinite description can have an infinite value here.

Scheiderer proves that every closed convex semialgebraic subset of the plane is second-order cone representable. This establishes finiteness for that class, but does not on its own give the minimum number of auxiliary variables for each member.

Scheiderer’s 2025 preprint proves representability for compact convex semialgebraic sets with Nash-smooth boundary of strictly positive curvature and for Nash-smooth hyperbolicity cones. These are substantial additional sufficient conditions, not a characterization of every set or its minimum auxiliary dimension.

Exact equality matters even for nonclosed hulls: linear projections of closed conic feasible sets need not be closed. Replacing a convex hull by its closure can therefore change the problem. Since this target leaves constraint counts unrestricted, a small auxiliary dimension alone is not a polynomial runtime guarantee.

cards.title: Deterministic competitive ratio for matching with delays
cards.formal: Determine, up to universal constant factors as \(n\to\infty\), the optimal deterministic competitive ratio \(\rho(n)\) for online minimum-cost perfect matching with linear waiting costs on a known \(n\)-point metric. The ratio must depend only on \(n\), uniformly over the number and timing of requests and all distances in the metric.
cards.why: This question measures the unavoidable cost of making irrevocable pairings while deciding how long to wait for future demand. A sharp deterministic ratio would separate the value of randomization from the difficulty of balancing spatial matching cost and elapsed waiting time in general metric spaces.
cards.status_note: The n-parameter deterministic gap is open in the 2020 source. Checks through 13 September 2026 found the major new polylogarithmic m-bound and results for other delay models, but no matching characterization of the stated n-only function. This bounded review does not exhaustively certify current openness.

sentences: Matching with delays pairs arriving requests while charging both the distance between partners and the time each request waits.
The selected question asks for the optimal deterministic competitive ratio as a function of the number of points in a known metric.
The guarantee must hold for any finite even request sequence, with no bound on its length or advance notice of its end.
A SODA 2026 algorithm gives a polylogarithmic ratio in the number of requests, which does not alone determine the ratio uniformly in metric size.
Matching bounds in the metric-size parameter would clarify the value of randomization in balancing spatial cost against waiting.

cards.definitions: A metric on \([n]\) is a symmetric map \(d:[n]^2\to\mathbb R_{\geq0}\) that vanishes exactly on equal points and satisfies the triangle inequality. The algorithm knows the whole metric before requests arrive. An input is any finite sequence of \(m\geq2\) distinctly identified requests, with \(m\) even, locations \(v_i\in[n]\), and arrival times \(0\leq a_1\leq\cdots\leq a_m<\infty\). Repeated locations and simultaneous arrivals are allowed; all requests at a given time are revealed before decisions made at that time. The algorithm does not know \(m\), future arrivals or an end-of-input time. It can irrevocably match two currently unmatched requests \(i,j\) at any real time \(t\geq\max(a_i,a_j)\), paying \(d(v_i,v_j)+(t-a_i)+(t-a_j)\). Every request must eventually be matched at a finite time on every finite even input. There are no colors, capacities or restrictions on the pairs. A deterministic online algorithm is a causal rule: its decisions through time \(t\) depend only on the known metric and requests revealed through \(t\). Computation and memory are unrestricted and uncharged, and decisions may be scheduled between arrivals. The total cost is the sum of all pair costs. The offline optimum, knowing the entire sequence, is \[\operatorname{OPT}(d,\sigma)=\min_{\text{perfect matchings }P}\sum_{\{i,j\}\in P}\bigl(d(v_i,v_j)+|a_i-a_j|\bigr),\] since an offline pair can be matched when its later request arrives. Define \(r(d)=\inf\{C\geq1:\exists A\ \forall\sigma,\ \operatorname{cost}_A(d,\sigma)\leq C\operatorname{OPT}(d,\sigma)\}\), with infinity if no finite ratio is possible, and \(\rho(n)=\sup_{d\text{ on }[n]}r(d)\), for \(n\geq2\). The algorithm in the infimum may depend on the entire metric. This is pure multiplicative competitiveness, with no additive constant; an input of optimum zero must incur zero cost. Infima over algorithms and suprema over metrics need not be attained. For deterministic rules, allowing an adaptive adversary does not change the requirement over all inputs.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a noncircular rate \(G(n)\) and a complete Lean-checked proof of \(cG(n)\leq\rho(n)\leq CG(n)\) for universal positive constants and all sufficiently large \(n\). Upper bounds must hold for every metric and all finite even request sequences; lower bounds must apply to every deterministic online algorithm in the specified model. Use approaching bounds if an extremum is not attained. A ratio depending on the request count, a randomized expected guarantee, or a theorem only for the line or uniform metrics does not determine this function.

context_blocks.text: Azar’s 2020 problem statement asks to close the deterministic competitiveness gap, expressed either through the metric size or through the number of requests. This card explicitly selects the known finite metric and metric-size parameter. Its separately mentioned red-blue matching variant is not part of the target.

The source reports an \(O(n)\) deterministic upper bound and a lower bound of order \(\log n/\log\log n\), the latter holding even against randomized algorithms. It also reports an \(O(\log n)\) randomized upper bound. These are dated source bounds and should not be conflated with a deterministic logarithmic theorem.

Dufay and Wattenhofer’s SODA 2026 result gives a deterministic \(O(\log^5 m)\)-competitive algorithm even when the metric and request count are unknown. It substantially improves the source’s request-count comparison. However, \(m\) can be arbitrarily large at fixed \(n\), so that displayed bound alone gives no uniform polylogarithmic bound in \(n\).

Gan, Sun and Umboh’s September 2026 paper studies general size-dependent delay rates and nonlinear convex waiting costs. Its tight deterministic result for the broader size-dependent model is not a matching lower bound for this fixed linear-per-request delay objective. Its uniform-metric results also have a narrower geometric scope.

Waiting may expose a nearby future partner, but it also accumulates cost on every unmatched request. The metric can have arbitrary scale and aspect ratio, making the information available from future arrivals essential even when computation of a present-day best matching is free.

cards.title: First-order convergence to local minimax optima
cards.formal:
Consider sequential minimax optimization \(\min_{x\in\mathbb R^p}\max_{y\in\mathbb R^q} f(x,y)\), with \(p,q\ge1\), \(f\in C^2(\mathbb R^{p+q},\mathbb R)\), and a supplied constant \(L>0\) satisfying
\[\|\nabla f(z)-\nabla f(w)\|_2\le L\|z-w\|_2\qquad\text{for all }z,w\in\mathbb R^{p+q}.\]
Does there exist one uniform deterministic first-order oracle method, in the model below, that produces iterates \(z_k=(x_k,y_k)\) from every initial point and has both of these properties for every such \(p,q,f,L\)?

First, for Lebesgue-almost every initial point \(z_0\), whenever the complete sequence \((z_k)_{k\ge0}\) converges to a finite point \(z^*\), that point is a local minimax point in the neighborhood definition below. Second, every strict local minimax point has an open neighborhood of initial points from which the method converges to that point. The second requirement excludes a method that satisfies the first merely by never converging.
cards.why: Sequential adversarial optimization needs the minimization and maximization roles to be respected at the limiting solution. Reaching a stationary point alone can select the wrong kind of equilibrium. A first-order selection theorem that remains valid with degeneracy would clarify what gradient information can guarantee beyond the curvature-restricted cases already analyzed.

sentences: In sequential minimax optimization, one player minimizes a smooth function of x while a second player maximizes it in y.
A local minimax point respects this order using shrinking neighborhoods whose radii may differ for the two players.
The selected variant asks for one deterministic method with exact function-value and gradient queries whose finite limits are local minimax points for almost every initialization.
The same method must converge locally to every strict local minimax point, so avoiding convergence everywhere is not a valid answer.
Existing convergence theorems retain extra hypotheses or weaker derivative-based targets, and the exact variant and limits of the current source review are explicitly recorded.

cards.definitions:
The order of play is fixed: \(x\) is the minimization variable and \(y\) is the maximization variable. All norms are Euclidean. A point \(z^*=(x^*,y^*)\) is a local minimax point if there exist \(\delta_0>0\) and a function \(h:(0,\delta_0]\to[0,\infty)\), with \(\lim_{\delta\downarrow0}h(\delta)=0\), such that for every \(0<\delta\le\delta_0\) and all \(x,y\) with \(\|x-x^*\|_2\le\delta\) and \(\|y-y^*\|_2\le\delta\),
\[f(x^*,y)\le f(x^*,y^*)\le
 \max_{\|y'-y^*\|_2\le h(\delta)} f(x,y').\]
The closed maximization ball is nonempty and compact, so the maximum exists. The radius function may depend on \(f,z^*\). There is no additional bound on \(h(\delta)/\delta\), no restriction to a Hessian range, and no assumption of concavity in \(y\). In particular, local minimax does not mean a simultaneous local Nash equilibrium or a global minimax solution.

A stationary point satisfies \(\nabla f(z^*)=0\). Define its Hessian blocks
\[A=\nabla^2_{xx}f(z^*)\in\mathbb R^{p\times p},\quad
 B=\nabla^2_{yy}f(z^*)\in\mathbb R^{q\times q},\quad
 C=\nabla^2_{xy}f(z^*)\in\mathbb R^{p\times q}.\]
A strict local minimax point here means a stationary point satisfying
\[B\prec0,\qquad A-CB^{-1}C^{\mathsf T}\succ0.\]
For a symmetric matrix, positive definiteness means that its quadratic form is positive on every nonzero vector; negative definiteness is defined with a negative sign. These sufficient conditions imply the neighborhood definition above. They define the points at which attraction is required, not a promise on every stationary point or every local minimax point of the input. Degenerate and non-strict points remain subject to the first, limit-selection requirement.

A first-order oracle queried at \(z\in\mathbb R^{p+q}\) returns the exact pair \((f(z),\nabla f(z))\). The function is available only through this oracle, not through its formula, a Hessian oracle, a maximization oracle or a best-response oracle. A method is one fixed finite real-arithmetic program supplied with \(p,q,L,z_0\), initialized with empty history and fixed rational constants. It uses scalar addition, subtraction, multiplication, division by nonzero numbers, exact comparisons, branching, copying, and integer loop/address operations. Real registers cannot be inspected digit by digit. Oracle calls may be adaptive, at points computed from the supplied data and earlier replies. Finite differences or other numerical quantities computed from finitely many permitted replies are allowed; direct derivative queries above first order are not.

The program may retain finite history and use iteration-dependent or adaptively chosen parameters. On every permitted input and after every finite iteration count it must finish the finite work needed to produce the next iterate, using finitely many elementary operations, stored values and oracle calls. No infinite inner loop, exact limit operation, uncharged auxiliary oracle, function-dependent advice or external randomization is allowed. Auxiliary storage is finite at each finite stage but need not have a fixed bound over the infinite run. This is an asymptotic convergence question: no polynomial iteration bound, oracle-complexity rate or bit-complexity bound is requested. The real oracle and exact arithmetic are part of the model, not claims about finite-precision implementation.

For precision, let \(z_k^{f,L}(u)\) be the sequence produced from initial point \(u\), with dimensions understood and \(z_0^{f,L}(u)=u\). The first guarantee means that, for each \(p,q,f,L\), there exists a set \(E_{f,L}\subseteq\mathbb R^{p+q}\) of Lebesgue outer measure zero such that
\[\forall u\notin E_{f,L}\ \forall z^*,\quad
 \lim_{k\to\infty}z_k^{f,L}(u)=z^*
 \ \Longrightarrow\ z^*\text{ is a local minimax point of }f.\]
The one exceptional set must cover all possible bad limits, not a separate uncountable union of exceptions for individual points. Equivalently, the same implication must hold almost surely for every initialization distribution with a density with respect to Lebesgue measure. The algorithm itself is deterministic.

The second guarantee means that for every strict local minimax point \(z^*\), there exists \(r>0\), depending on \(f,L,z^*\), such that
\[\forall u\in\mathbb R^{p+q},\quad
 \|u-z^*\|_2<r\ \Longrightarrow\ \lim_{k\to\infty}z_k^{f,L}(u)=z^*.\]
Every start uses the same program initialization; no target point or attracting radius is supplied to it. The requirements permit divergent or nonconvergent runs outside these local basins. They concern limits of the full sequence, not every subsequential accumulation point, and do not require global convergence or attraction to every non-strict local minimax point.
cards.answer_criterion:
Give a complete, mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of the existence of a method meeting both guarantees, or of its logical negation. A positive proof must specify one finite oracle program, establish that it produces every next iterate after finite work, prove the common measure-zero exception statement for every permitted objective and every valid supplied \(L\), and prove local attraction at every point satisfying the strict Hessian conditions.

A negative proof must exclude every method in this specified oracle model from satisfying the conjunction. Counterexamples only to gradient descent-ascent, extragradient or another named update do not exclude every method. A method that never converges, convergence only to stationary points or second-order necessary-condition points, local linear stability without the stated limit guarantees, or a theorem assuming additional curvature or neighborhood-radius restrictions does not meet this target. No finite iteration rate is demanded, and the benchmark's numerical tolerance does not replace exact convergence or exact local minimaxity.

source_formulation.text: Editorial choice of a concrete benchmark variant, as authorized for source questions that leave the target unspecified. The COLT 2023 contribution poses a broad first-order convergence question and discusses both local stability and alternative notions of local optimality; it does not specify one complete oracle model or every convergence quantifier. This card keeps its original Jin–Netrapalli–Jordan neighborhood definition, includes degenerate objectives, and fixes deterministic exact first-order oracle access. The chosen target is almost-everywhere correctness of finite limits, together with local attraction at every strict local minimax point to prevent vacuous nonconvergence. This is stronger than a statement only about linearly stable fixed points and is not asserted to be a verbatim or proved-equivalent formulation of the source title. Global convergence, attraction to all non-strict points, fixed-step restrictions, and a different restricted-minimax definition are not part of this selected variant.

context_blocks.text: Both \(f(x,y)=x^2-y^2\) and \(g(x,y)=-x^2+y^2\) have zero gradient at the origin. For the prescribed minimization in \(x\) and maximization in \(y\), the first has a strict local minimax point there, while the second fails even the required local maximization in \(y\). Thus stationarity does not identify the intended local solution.

The local minimax definition allows the maximizing player’s response neighborhood to shrink at a different rate from the minimizing player’s neighborhood. It describes the sequential order of play. Requiring the minimizing player to keep the maximizer’s action fixed instead gives the stronger local Nash notion; reversing the players gives a different local optimization question.

The original convergence literature distinguishes sufficient strict curvature conditions from necessary second-order conditions. With degeneracy, satisfying the latter need not certify a local minimax point. A guarantee stated only for strict linearly unstable points also does not automatically exclude convergence to every other undesirable stationary point.

The ICLR 2024 two-timescale extragradient paper extends analysis beyond an invertible maximizing-player Hessian. Its theorems still retain conditions on the restricted Schur complement, the full saddle-gradient Jacobian or spectral thresholds. Its stable points are characterized using necessary second-order conditions in the relevant regimes; this is not the unrestricted true-minimax limit guarantee selected here.

The ICML 2024 double-step alternating extragradient work improves local stability for further non-strict cases and studies increasing timescale separation. Its local results retain nondegeneracy conditions on specified Hessian-derived matrices; the increasing-timescale stability theorem additionally assumes a third derivative. The paper’s separate global-convergence result assumes star-convex–star-concave structure. Those hypotheses are absent from this card’s objective class.

Follow-the-Ridge gives a related local fixed-point theorem using second-order information and an invertible maximizing-player Hessian. Its distinction between strict linear stability and weak spectral stability also matters. This is a useful comparison with the first-order question, but its Hessian-assisted theorem is not a solution for every objective in the model here.

Lu and Wang’s August 2026 constrained minimax paper proves complexity bounds for approximate stationary points under a local Kurdyka–Łojasiewicz condition on a lifted inner problem. That condition restricts the relation between objective residuals and generalized gradients. The assumptions and approximate-stationarity target differ from exact local-minimax limit selection for arbitrary smooth objectives.

The probability qualifier concerns the initial point. It allows, for example, an exceptional initialization exactly at an undesirable stationary point when such starts form a null set. The local-attraction condition supplies a positive guarantee near strict solutions. No convergence assertion is being made for every trajectory of a nonconvex–nonconcave game.

cards.title: Kannan–Lovász–Simonovits conjecture
cards.formal: Does there exist a real constant \(C>0\) such that, for every integer \(n\ge1\), every isotropic log-concave probability measure \(\mu\) on \(\mathbb R^n\), and every locally Lipschitz function \(f:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R\) with \(\int f^2\,d\mu<\infty\) and \(\int\|\nabla f\|_2^2\,d\mu<\infty\), \[\operatorname{Var}_{\mu}(f)\le C\int_{\mathbb R^n}\|\nabla f(x)\|_2^2\,d\mu(x)?\] The same constant must work for all dimensions, measures and admissible functions. This is the Poincaré formulation of the Kannan–Lovász–Simonovits conjecture.
cards.definitions: All norms and derivatives are Euclidean, with \(\|x\|_2=(\sum_{i=1}^n x_i^2)^{1/2}\). Here a log-concave probability measure has a Lebesgue density \(\rho(x)=e^{-V(x)}\) of integral one, where \(V:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R\cup\{+\infty\}\) is measurable and convex; \(e^{-\infty}=0\). Convexity means \(V((1-s)x+sy)\le(1-s)V(x)+sV(y)\) for all \(x,y\) and \(0<s<1\), using the extended-real convention on the right. Thus \(d\mu(x)=\rho(x)\,dx\). Isotropy means finite second moments and \(\int x_i\,d\mu=0\), \(\int x_i x_j\,d\mu=\delta_{ij}\) for every \(i,j\), where \(\delta_{ij}=1\) if \(i=j\) and zero otherwise. Equivalently, the mean vector is zero and the covariance matrix is the identity. Isotropy excludes measures supported on a proper affine subspace, so no lower-dimensional singular case is omitted by using a density. Locally Lipschitz means that every point has a neighborhood on which \(|f(y)-f(z)|\le L\|y-z\|_2\) for some finite \(L\); the neighborhood and constant may depend on the point. Such a function has a Euclidean derivative outside a Lebesgue-null set, and \(\nabla f\) is the vector of its partial derivatives there; set it to zero where the derivative does not exist. This choice on the null set does not affect integration against \(\mu\). Write \(\bar f=\int f\,d\mu\), which is finite by the second-moment assumption, and \(\operatorname{Var}_{\mu}(f)=\int(f-\bar f)^2\,d\mu\). The gradient energy is the integral of \(\|\nabla f\|_2^2\). Define \(C_{\mathrm P}(\mu)\) as the infimum of all \(a\ge0\) for which the displayed inequality holds with \(a\) for every admissible function, with infimum of the empty set interpreted as \(+\infty\). The question asks whether these constants are uniformly bounded; it does not ask for their optimal universal value. No symmetry, product structure, differentiability of \(V\), bounded support or positive lower bound on its curvature is assumed. Uniform laws on full-dimensional convex bodies are included after isotropic normalization; a convex body is a compact convex set with nonempty interior. The problem is an analytic existence statement, with no oracle, encoding or algorithmic-time requirement.
cards.answer_criterion: Supply a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of the universal Poincaré inequality with some finite real \(C>0\), or a Lean-checked proof of its logical negation: for every real \(C>0\), there exist an integer \(n\ge1\), a measure \(\mu\) satisfying all stated log-concavity and isotropy conditions, and an admissible locally Lipschitz \(f\) of finite second moment and finite gradient energy such that \(\operatorname{Var}_{\mu}(f)>C\int\|\nabla f\|_2^2\,d\mu\). The dimension, measure and function may depend on \(C\). A single violation for one proposed numerical constant does not refute existence of some larger universal constant. A dimension-dependent bound, or a theorem restricted to linear, radial or quadratic functions or a narrower class of measures, is insufficient unless the proof also establishes the entire stated target. No optimal value of \(C\) is required. An equivalent geometric statement can qualify only with a Lean-checked implication proving this proposition or its negation; cited but unproved conjectural dependencies do not complete acceptance.

context_blocks.text: Isotropy fixes scale in every linear direction. For a unit vector \(\theta\), the function \(f(x)=\sum_i\theta_i x_i\) has variance one and gradient energy one, so every admissible universal constant is at least one. The conjecture asks whether nonlinear observables can have an arbitrarily greater variance relative to their average squared local change. Log-concavity is much weaker than independence of coordinates or a uniformly curved smooth potential.

The geometric formulation compares the boundary size of a set with the probability mass it separates. For a Borel set \(S\), let \(S_\varepsilon=\{x:\operatorname{dist}(x,S)<\varepsilon\}\), where distance is the infimum of \(\|x-y\|_2\) over \(y\in S\), and define \(\mu^+(S)=\liminf_{\varepsilon\downarrow0}(\mu(S_\varepsilon)-\mu(S))/\varepsilon\). The Cheeger expansion constant is \(h_\mu=\inf_{0<\mu(S)<1}\mu^+(S)/\min\{\mu(S),1-\mu(S)\}\). KLS asserts a positive universal lower bound on this expansion after isotropic normalization. A small value describes a separator with little boundary relative to the masses on its sides.

Notation changes across sources: Lee and Vempala’s survey uses its isoperimetric symbol for expansion itself, while Klartag and Letwin use \(\psi_\mu=1/h_\mu\), the reciprocal. With the latter convention, \(\psi_\mu^2\) and \(C_{\mathrm P}(\mu)\) differ by at most universal factors for log-concave measures, as recalled in Klartag’s equation (1.4). Thus an upper bound \(O((\log n)^{1/4})\) on the reciprocal expansion means an upper bound \(O(\sqrt{\log n})\) on the Poincaré constant, rather than the same exponent.

The original algorithmic motivation was sampling by random walks: poor expansion can slow movement between substantial parts of a convex body. The Lee–Vempala survey explains how sampling supports volume estimation, integration and optimization. These algorithmic consequences also depend on access to the input body or density, initialization and the chosen walk; the analytic inequality alone is not a complete computational-cost statement.

Klartag and Lehec’s 2022 Theorem 1.1 gives a polylogarithmic upper bound on reciprocal expansion, with exponent five in that paper. This broke the earlier subpolynomial dimension dependence. It is a historical bound, not a dimension-free resolution.

Klartag’s 2023 Theorem 1.2 improves reciprocal expansion to \(O(\sqrt{\log n})\), hence \(C_{\mathrm P}(\mu)=O(\log n)\). These logarithmic estimates are stated for \(n\ge2\); no formula involving \(\log1=0\) is asserted for the one-dimensional case.

Klartag and Lehec’s thin-shell paper, first posted in 2025 and revised in February 2026, proves \(\operatorname{Var}(\|X\|_2^2)\le a n\) and consequently \(\mathbb E(\|X\|_2-\sqrt n)^2\le a\) for a universal \(a\) and isotropic log-concave \(X\). These results control particular radial observables. Their relation to the now resolved slicing problem does not turn them into the full inequality for every locally Lipschitz function.

Chen and Klartag’s July 2026 preprint states the sharp radial bound \(\operatorname{Var}(\|X\|_2^2)\le8n\), with equality for independent centered exponential coordinates. The statement of Theorem 1.1 was inspected, but its complete new proof was not independently verified here. This optimizes the thin-shell constant, not the universal Poincaré constant over all test functions.

Letwin’s preprint of 27 July 2026 states \(\operatorname{Var}(X^{\mathsf T}MX)\le2\mathbb E\|\nabla(X^{\mathsf T}MX)\|_2^2\) for every real symmetric matrix \(M\), where \(X\) is isotropic and log-concave. It derives \(\psi_n=O((\log n)^{1/4})\) for \(n\ge2\), where \(\psi_n=\sup_\mu\psi_\mu\) over the measures in dimension \(n\). Its general-function consequence is \(C_{\mathrm P}(\mu)=O(\sqrt{\log n})\), which still grows. The paper’s new proof was not independently verified in this review.

Zhang’s sampling preprint, revised on 5 September 2026, still explicitly calls KLS open. It claims an improved mixing theorem for hit-and-run, the walk that chooses a random line through its current point and then a uniform point on the chord inside the body. The result requires a warm initial distribution, whose density is bounded by a finite multiple of the uniform target density, and retains dependence on the KLS constant. Resolving that mixing-time question is therefore distinct from proving a universal Poincaré bound.

cards.title: Gupta–Newman–Rabinovich–Sinclair conjecture
cards.formal: For every fixed finite simple graph H, is there a finite constant \(C_{H}\ge 1\) such that, for every finite connected simple undirected H-minor-free graph G with strictly positive real edge lengths, its shortest-path metric \(d_{G}\) admits a map \(f:V(G)\to \mathbb{R} ^{m}\) into some finite-dimensional \(\ell\)\(_{1}\) space satisfying \(d_{G}(u,v)\le \Vert f(u)- f(v)\Vert _{1}\le C_{H} d_{G}(u,v)\) for all vertices u,v?
cards.definitions: H-minor-free means that deleting vertices and edges and contracting edges of G cannot produce a graph isomorphic to H, after removing loops and duplicate edges. The length of a path is the sum of its edge lengths, and \(d_{G}(u,v)\) is the minimum path length. In \(\mathbb{R} ^{m}, \Vert x- y\Vert _{1}=\sum_{j=1}^{m} |x_{j}- y_{j}|\). The displayed inequalities normalize the embedding to be noncontracting; permitting a common scaling factor gives the same distortion notion. The constant \(C_{H}\) may depend on the excluded graph H, but must be independent of |\(V(G)|\), the edge lengths and their ratio. The target dimension m and the map f may depend on the entire weighted graph and have no computational or dimension bound. This is an existence question for all vertex pairs simultaneously. It concerns undirected shortest-path distances themselves, without a snowflake transformation, average-pair guarantee or restriction to selected terminals.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove the proposition in the problem statement or prove its logical negation, using exactly the definitions, hypotheses and quantifier order stated here. The proof must cover the complete target.
cards.why: Determine whether excluded graph minors exactly prevent unbounded \(\ell\)\(_{1}\) distortion and multicommodity flow–cut gaps in proper minor-closed graph families.

importance.reason: A central link between graph minor structure, metric embeddings and the quality of the basic sparsest-cut relaxation, already open in the planar case.
