cards.definitions: The ambient dimension is \(n\), the subspace dimension is \(d\), and the reduced dimension is \(m\). All logarithms are natural logarithms; changing the base changes only the universal constant. For \(x\in\mathbb R^n\), \(\|x\|_2=(\sum_{j=1}^n x_j^2)^{1/2}\). A linear subspace \(W\) is closed under real linear combinations and has a basis of exactly \(d\) linearly independent vectors. Its embedding is the linear map \(x\mapsto\Pi x\). The distribution is a Borel probability measure on the finite-dimensional real matrix space and is supported on matrices satisfying the per-column sparsity bound. Different matrix entries need not be independent; neither a particular sparsity pattern nor a particular distribution of nonzero values is prescribed. The same \(\mathcal D\), chosen from \(n,d,\varepsilon,\delta\) alone, must satisfy the probability guarantee for every fixed \(W\). It cannot depend on a basis or other information about \(W\). The order of quantifiers is \(\forall(n,d,\varepsilon,\delta)\ \exists(m,\mathcal D)\ \forall W\); this does not require one sampled matrix to succeed simultaneously for all subspaces. Inside the success event, however, the inequalities must hold simultaneously for every vector of the chosen subspace, rather than separately with fresh randomness for each vector. The failure probability is \(\delta\) for the entire subspace. The statement is distributional existence, with one universal dimension/sparsity constant, and does not require a finite-bit sampling algorithm or bit-complexity bound for arbitrary real entries. This is the explicit dimension-and-sparsity conjecture underlying the source’s input-sparsity application-time discussion. The accuracy and confidence regime \(0<\varepsilon,\delta\le1/3\) is fixed explicitly; neither parameter is assumed to be inverse polynomial in \(d\). There is no restriction relating \(n\) to the desired row bound, and \(m\) is permitted to exceed \(n\) when the parameter bound does. For an \(n\times d\) input matrix \(A\), \(\operatorname{nnz}(A)\) denotes the number of its nonzero entries. Column sparsity controls the number of scalar contributions needed to form \(\Pi A\); this motivates the running-time terminology but is not an extra end-to-end bit-time requirement.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct Lean-checked proof of the quantified existence statement, or of its logical negation. A positive proof must give the simultaneous row and column-sparsity bounds for all stated parameter values and a distribution independent of the target subspace. Constants may not depend on \(n,d,\varepsilon,\delta\). Bounds with extra logarithmic or sub-polylogarithmic factors, only inverse-polynomial failure probabilities, or only inverse-polynomial accuracy do not establish this exact target. A construction chosen after examining the subspace, a guarantee for a finite list of vectors, or a failure example for a single proposed distribution does not settle the general conjecture.

context_blocks.text: Woodruff’s survey, in the discussion after Theorem 10, records the proposed row bound \(O((d+\log(1/\delta))/\varepsilon^2)\) and input-sparsity application cost involving \(\log(d/\delta)/\varepsilon\). The original title-level card omitted the concrete parameters.

Conjecture 2 of the 2025 ICALP paper states the underlying distributional question explicitly in terms of row dimension and nonzeros per column. This supplies the precise formulation used here, without imposing a particular embedding construction.

The 2025 result reaches optimal row dimension with sparsity \(\widetilde O(1/\varepsilon)\) in its stated parameter regime, where that notation hides growing polylogarithmic factors. It therefore does not give the exact logarithmic sparsity bound required here.

The SODA 2026 paper improves the remaining losses to sub-polylogarithmic factors in \(d\) for inverse-polynomially bounded \(\varepsilon\), with a polynomially small failure probability in its headline theorem. Its more detailed Theorem 2.1 gives explicit dimension/sparsity tradeoffs. Neither statement removes all extra factors in the full parameter range of this card.

The preserved norm guarantee concerns one entire fixed subspace. An embedding for selected vectors alone or one constructed using the particular matrix is a different object from an oblivious subspace embedding.

cards.definitions: The input gives \(n\ge 0, V=\{1,\ldots ,n\}\), and two symmetric zero-diagonal \(n\times n\) binary adjacency matrices, with total bit length N; each graph is promised planar. No drawing, vertex coordinates or embedding is supplied. The common graph is \(H=(V,E_{1}\cap E_{2})\), which may be disconnected and have isolated vertices. A drawing assigns distinct points \(p(v)\in \mathbb{R} ^{2}\) to vertices and to each edge uv a simple continuous arc with endpoints \(p(u),p(v)\), whose interior contains no vertex point. Planarity means that arcs for distinct edges of the same graph meet only at a common endpoint, if there is one. A simultaneous drawing uses the same \(p(v)\) in both graphs and exactly the same arc image for every edge in \(E_{1}\cap E_{2}\). Edges exclusive to different graphs may cross each other. Arcs may bend freely; no grid, edge-length, area or bend bound is imposed. The requested output is only YES or NO. Polynomial time means one always-correct deterministic Turing machine and constants \(C,c\ge 1\) with at most \(C(N+1)^{c}\) bit steps on every promised input, with no oracle or advice. “Fixed edges” means shared drawings agree on their common edges, not that any geometry is fixed in the input.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove that a polynomial-time decider exists for all promised pairs, or prove that none exists. A positive answer must cover arbitrary disconnected common graphs and freely chosen embeddings. A nonembeddable pair is a NO instance, not a refutation of polynomial decidability. Hardness for three input graphs, straight-line drawings or an additional optimization objective does not answer this question.

context_blocks.title: Two compatible views of the same objects
context_blocks.text: Think of two network diagrams whose vertices denote the same objects and whose edges describe two relations. Each view must be crossing-free on its own. Shared edges must stay in place when switching views. This is why drawing each graph independently can fail to meet the simultaneous requirement.

context_blocks.title: The union need not be planar
context_blocks.text: Take \(G_{1}\) to be \(K_{5}\) with one edge deleted and \(G_{2}\) to contain just that missing edge on the same five vertices. \(G_{1}\) is planar, and \(G_{2}\) can use the same vertex positions with its edge crossing edges exclusive to \(G_{1}\). This is a valid simultaneous drawing, even though the union is the nonplanar graph \(K_{5}\). Testing the union’s planarity would therefore reject valid instances.

context_blocks.title: The connected common case is solved
context_blocks.text: The checked 2025 papers report polynomial-time algorithms when H is connected. This is connectivity of the shared edges and vertices, not merely connectivity of each input graph. Allowing H to have multiple components introduces compatibility of their positions as well as choices of embeddings, and the unrestricted two-graph question remains open in those sources.

context_blocks.title: Which nearby results apply
context_blocks.text: Three-graph SEFE is NP-complete, but the number two is essential here. The March 2026 work on two paths studies straight-line grid drawings and optimizes geometric quantities. Its hardness result for edge length does not imply hardness of deciding whether unrestricted curved-edge drawings exist.

cards.title: Euclidean minimum spanning tree complexity
cards.formal: For each fixed integer \(d\geq3\), determine up to constant factors the optimal deterministic worst-case time for computing an exact Euclidean minimum spanning tree of \(n\geq2\) distinct points in \(\mathbb R^d\). The input is the array of coordinates of the points \(p_1,\ldots,p_n\); the output is a list of \(n-1\) pairs of indices forming a connected acyclic graph \(T\) that minimizes \(\sum_{\{i,j\}\in T}\|p_i-p_j\|_2\) over all spanning trees on these labels. Include logarithmic factors in the requested complexity, and use the real-arithmetic model below.
cards.why: The problem asks how effectively fixed-dimensional geometry can accelerate one of the most basic graph optimization tasks. Sharp complexity bounds would clarify the algorithmic cost of exact geometric connectivity and its relation to proximity searching.
cards.status_note: The original exact-complexity gap is source-backed. The bounded later-work review through 14 September 2026 did not find matching bounds for the specified deterministic fixed-dimensional family. The 1991 randomized results are dated partial progress, not asserted to be current deterministic records.

The input gives coordinates, while the complete graph of candidate edges is implicit.

cards.definitions: The Euclidean distance is \(\|p-q\|_2=(\sum_{j=1}^d(p_j-q_j)^2)^{1/2}\). Coordinates are arbitrary exact reals; there is no general-position, bounded-spread or unique-optimum promise. Any minimum tree is a correct output. The complete graph and its edge weights are implicit, so reading every possible edge is not a required part of the input. For each fixed \(d\), the algorithm is one finite deterministic program for all \(n\) and all coordinates, with rational constants, exact real registers and indexed memory. Each operation \(+,-,\times,/\) on its domain, nonnegative square root, comparison, copy, indexed read or write costs one step. Addresses and counters are integers of \(O_d(\log(n+t+2))\) bits after \(t\) steps, with ordinary arithmetic and comparisons charged per word operation. There is no floor or bit extraction from real registers, advice depending on the input size, or geometric oracle. All input access and output steps count. Worst-case time is the supremum over all valid size-\(n\) inputs. Constants and programs may depend on fixed \(d\), but not on \(n\) or the coordinates; no simultaneous polynomial dependence on variable dimension is requested.
cards.answer_criterion: Supply a noncircular positive rate \(g_d(n)\) for every fixed \(d\geq3\), together with a complete Lean-checked proof of matching uniform upper and lower bounds. For each \(d\), one correct deterministic program must have worst-case time at most \(C_dg_d(n)\) for all sufficiently large \(n\). Every correct program must have worst-case time at least \(c_{A,d}g_d(n)\) for all sufficiently large \(n\), with \(c_{A,d}>0\). The constants and thresholds may depend on \(d\) and, for the lower bound, on the program. An approximation scheme, an expected-time bound alone, or the polynomial exponent without matching logarithmic factors does not determine this target.

context_blocks.text: The original entry asks whether exact Euclidean MST computation can approach the sorting-scale \(\Omega(n\log n)\) lower bound. This card makes its resource question concrete by requesting optimal deterministic arithmetic complexity in every fixed dimension at least three. This is an editorial sharpening of the source’s informal word “close,” not an assertion that the source prescribed a particular logarithmic overhead.

An MST has only a linear number of edges. Nevertheless, applying a graph algorithm after explicitly creating the complete graph already processes quadratically many candidate edges. The unresolved issue is the cost of identifying the optimum from the much smaller coordinate description.

Agarwal, Edelsbrunner, Schwarzkopf and Welzl relate Euclidean MST computation to bichromatic closest pairs: given red and blue points, find a shortest pair with opposite colors. Their 1991 results include subquadratic expected-time algorithms in fixed dimensions. Those randomized guarantees are not silently assigned to the deterministic model used here.

The plane admits a sorting-scale exact MST algorithm, whereas higher fixed dimensions are the subject of the source question. Large-dimensional distance problems, approximate spanning trees and dynamic maintenance ask for different guarantees.

Cabello, Chan and Giannopoulos study Delaunay triangulations and related MST tasks with predictions in 2026. Their stated setting is planar and includes additional prediction data, so it does not resolve this arbitrary-input higher-dimensional complexity question.

Exactness here refers to the combinatorial tree. In particular, edge ordering can use squared distances because squaring preserves the order of individual nonnegative lengths. This does not require replacing the objective by an approximation or outputting the total length as a decimal number.

Cabello, Chan and Giannopoulos study Delaunay triangulations and related MST tasks with predictions in 2026. Their stated setting is planar and includes additional prediction data, so it does not resolve this arbitrary-input higher-dimensional complexity question.

Exactness here refers to the combinatorial tree. In particular, edge ordering can use squared distances because squaring preserves the order of individual nonnegative lengths. This does not require replacing the objective by an approximation or outputting the total length as a decimal number.

cards.title: Exact planar Euclidean matching
cards.formal: Determine, up to constant factors including logarithmic factors, the optimal deterministic worst-case running time for computing a minimum-length perfect matching of \(2n\) distinct points in \(\mathbb R^2\), for all integers \(n\geq1\), in the exact real-arithmetic model below. The output is a list of \(n\) unordered pairs of input indices, every index occurring exactly once, minimizing \(\sum_{\{i,j\}\in M}\sqrt{(x_i-x_j)^2+(y_i-y_j)^2}\) among all perfect matchings. The input consists only of the point coordinates; the complete graph is implicit.
cards.why: Exact Euclidean matching is a basic geometric optimization primitive. Its unresolved complexity tests how far geometric structure can reduce the cost of optimization over an implicit complete graph, beyond the easier approximation guarantees.
cards.status_note: The exact complexity gap is explicitly present in the checked April 2026 article. The bounded later-work search on 13 September 2026 found no matching resolution. The real-arithmetic model is an explicit editorial specification of the geometric task; bit complexity and approximation are separate targets.

sentences: Given an even number of planar points, a perfect matching pairs every point with exactly one other point.
The Euclidean objective minimizes the sum of the lengths of all chosen segments.
The question is the optimal complexity of computing that minimum exactly, with bipartite matching as a related restricted variant.
Approximation algorithms can exploit geometry differently and do not by themselves settle the exact problem.
Sharper algorithms would improve a central geometric pairing primitive whose implicit complete graph contains quadratically many candidate edges.

cards.definitions: The coordinates are arbitrary real numbers supplied in an indexed array. No general-position, bounded-spread, coordinate-precision or unique-optimum promise is made; any minimizing matching is acceptable. An algorithm is one finite deterministic program, valid for every input size, with rational program constants, no advice and no oracle. It has exact real registers and an indexed memory. A real arithmetic operation \(+,-,\times,/\) on its domain, a nonnegative square root, a comparison, a register copy, or an indexed read or write costs one step. Integer addresses and loop counters use ordinary arithmetic and comparisons on \(O(\log(n+t+2))\)-bit words after \(t\) steps, with a program-dependent constant in this word bound; there is no floor, bit extraction from reals, or operation that solves an entire optimization problem. Input access, memory operations and output are charged. Running time is the supremum of the number of steps over all valid inputs of the given size. All programs must halt and be correct on every valid input. This fixes the conventional geometric arithmetic interpretation of the source; it is not a bit-complexity question about sums of square roots. The main problem is unrestricted perfect matching: no red/blue partition is supplied.
cards.answer_criterion: Supply a noncircular rate \(g:\mathbb N_{\geq1}\to\mathbb R_{>0}\) and a complete Lean-checked proof of matching bounds in the stated model. The upper bound must give one uniform deterministic algorithm with worst-case time at most \(C g(n)\) for all sufficiently large \(n\). The lower bound must show that every correct uniform algorithm has worst-case time at least \(c_A g(n)\) for all sufficiently large \(n\), where \(c_A>0\) and the threshold may depend on the algorithm. Constants are independent of the point configuration and \(n\). Approximate matchings, a bound only for bipartite matching, or a polynomial exponent with unresolved logarithmic factors do not meet this criterion.

context_blocks.text: The Open Problems Project asks for the optimal complexity of exact Euclidean matching in the plane and mentions the bipartite problem separately. This card retains the unrestricted objective and makes the deterministic arithmetic and worst-case conventions explicit.

A matching contains only a linear number of edges, but the coordinate input describes quadratically many possible pairs. Its objective is the sum of their Euclidean lengths; replacing lengths by squared lengths can change the minimizing matching.

Varadarajan proves an \(O(n^{3/2}\log^5 n)\) exact algorithm. The separator subroutine in the author manuscript has a deterministic implementation, so this is an upper bound for the deterministic target rather than merely an expected randomized bound.

Hougardy and Tammemaa’s April 2026 journal article still identifies Varadarajan’s bound as the fastest known exact algorithm. Their new results improve fast approximation guarantees and do not compute the exact optimum.

The same article recalls an \(\Omega(n\log n)\) lower bound for deterministic geometric approximation algorithms with approximation ratio depending only on input size. Thus the exact task has a substantial known gap even before finer logarithmic factors are considered.

The arithmetic convention matters because the objective involves square roots and comparisons between sums of lengths. Counting each such arithmetic step is different from bounding the number of bit operations needed to certify every comparison for rationally encoded points. The requested output here is an optimal pairing, not a decimal expansion of its total length.

cards.title: Flip graph connectivity in three dimensions
cards.formal:
For every finite point set \(P\subset\mathbb R^3\) with \(|P|\ge4\) and no four points coplanar, is the graph of all geometric tetrahedralizations of \(P\) connected under \(2\leftrightarrow3\) bistellar flips?

A tetrahedralization must use exactly the vertices \(P\), consist of straight, nondegenerate tetrahedra meeting along common faces, and cover \(\operatorname{conv}(P)\). A legal flip replaces two tetrahedra filling a convex triangular bipyramid by the three tetrahedra with the same five vertices and the same union, or performs the reverse replacement. Every intermediate tetrahedralization must retain all points of \(P\) as vertices.

Equivalently, for every such \(P\) and every pair \(T,T'\) of its tetrahedralizations, must there exist a finite sequence \(T=T_0,T_1,\ldots,T_m=T'\) in which each consecutive pair differs by one legal flip?
cards.why: This is a basic reachability question for three-dimensional meshes: can local bistellar moves explore every tetrahedralization without changing the underlying points? A resolution would identify a fundamental difference, or an essential commonality, between planar triangulation algorithms and their three-dimensional counterparts.
cards.status_note: Source-open in TOPP Problem 28 (entry history through 22 December 2008) and explicitly retained as open in the introduction of Wagner–Welzl, Discrete & Computational Geometry 68 (2022). On 16 September 2026 the source’s fixed-vertex move restriction, the 2007 regular-triangulation consequence and the 2022 discussion were checked. Bounded subsequent searches found no proof or geometric counterexample for this precise target. The regular result was checked through its publisher abstract and the TOPP statement, not by independent verification of its full proof. This records dated explicit openness and limited later review, not an exhaustive current-status certification.

Pournin and Liebling establish the fixed-vertex connectivity result for regular triangulations, leaving arbitrary tetrahedralizations outside this theorem.

importance.reason: A longstanding central problem in computational geometry and triangulation theory, with direct relevance to local mesh transformations and a sharp distinction between geometric and abstract complexes. The simple local moves conceal a global connectivity question that remains unsettled beyond regular triangulations.

sentences: A tetrahedralization divides the convex hull of a fixed three-dimensional point set into tetrahedra.
A local flip replaces two tetrahedra by three, or reverses that replacement, while retaining the same five vertices.
The question asks whether every pair of tetrahedralizations can be joined by such moves when no four input points are coplanar.
All intermediate meshes must keep every original point as a vertex at its original coordinates.
Regular tetrahedralizations are known to be connected, but the unrestricted geometric question remains open in the checked sources.

cards.definitions:
The set \(P\) is finite and consists of distinct points with arbitrary real coordinates in ordinary three-dimensional Euclidean space. General position here means that every four distinct points are affinely independent, equivalently that no four lie in a common plane. Together with \(|P|\ge4\), this ensures a three-dimensional convex hull and nonzero volume for every tetrahedron with four vertices in \(P\). Points may lie in the interior of \(\operatorname{conv}(P)\); they are not assumed to be in convex position. No additional condition on cospherical points is imposed.

For a finite set of points \(A\), its convex hull \(\operatorname{conv}(A)\) is the set of all convex combinations of points of \(A\), with \(\operatorname{conv}(\varnothing)=\varnothing\). A geometric tetrahedron with vertex set \(A\subset P\), \(|A|=4\), is the closed set \(\operatorname{conv}(A)\). Its faces are the convex hulls of subsets of its vertices, including vertices, edges, triangles, the tetrahedron itself and the empty face.

A tetrahedralization is a collection \(T\) of four-element subsets of \(P\) satisfying all of the following conditions. Every point of \(P\) belongs to some member of \(T\). The union of the corresponding closed tetrahedra is \(\operatorname{conv}(P)\). For every \(A,B\in T\),
\[\operatorname{conv}(A)\cap\operatorname{conv}(B)=\operatorname{conv}(A\cap B).\]
Thus different tetrahedra have disjoint interiors and any intersection is their common face; overlaps, crossing faces and hanging vertices inside another tetrahedron are excluded. All faces of the tetrahedra are understood to belong to the resulting simplicial complex. This is a full geometric triangulation, not merely an abstract complex homeomorphic to a ball. No extra vertices, curved faces or gaps in the convex hull are allowed.

The local replacement can be specified by five distinct points \(a,b,c,d,e\in P\). They must all be vertices of their convex hull, and that hull must be the convex triangular bipyramid formed by the two tetrahedra \(\{a,b,c,d\}\) and \(\{a,b,c,e\}\) sharing triangle \(abc\). In particular, \(d\) and \(e\) are on opposite sides of the plane of \(a,b,c\). Write
\[U_2=\bigl\{\{a,b,c,d\},\{a,b,c,e\}\bigr\},\qquad U_3=\bigl\{\{a,b,d,e\},\{b,c,d,e\},\{c,a,d,e\}\bigr\}.\]
These are the two tetrahedralizations of this bipyramid: \(U_2\) uses the interior triangle \(abc\), while \(U_3\) uses the interior edge \(de\). A \(2\)-to-\(3\) flip is allowed when \(U_2\subseteq T\) and
\[T'=(T\setminus U_2)\cup U_3\]
is a tetrahedralization of the same \(P\), with the replaced tetrahedra and the new tetrahedra having exactly the same geometric union. A \(3\)-to-\(2\) flip is the inverse operation under the same conditions. Requiring both configurations to be valid tetrahedralizations makes the local move compatible with all tetrahedra outside the replaced region.

The flip graph \(\mathcal F(P)\) is the finite undirected graph whose vertices are these tetrahedralizations and whose edges join pairs related by one such flip. Reversing a legal move is legal. Connectivity means that every pair of graph vertices can be joined by a finite path. The path may have length zero when the two tetrahedralizations coincide. No polynomial bound, sharp diameter, monotonicity condition or prescribed target triangulation is part of the proposition.

Only \(2\)-to-\(3\) and \(3\)-to-\(2\) moves are permitted. A \(1\)-to-\(4\) move inserts an interior vertex into a tetrahedron, and a \(4\)-to-\(1\) move removes a vertex; neither is allowed, even if the point is restored later. Points cannot be moved or perturbed along a path. Allowing such operations changes the graph under study.

The quantifier order is \(\forall P\;\forall T,T'\;\exists m\ge0\;\exists(T_i)_{i=0}^m\). All tetrahedralizations and all intermediate coordinates refer to the same fixed geometric point set. A negative answer consists of a set meeting the general-position hypothesis and two valid tetrahedralizations in different components, with a proof that no finite legal path joins them. Merely showing that one particular greedy rule gets stuck, or displaying an abstract nonrealizable tetrahedral complex, is insufficient.

Regular tetrahedralizations are a special class mentioned in the known results. A tetrahedralization \(T\) is regular if there is a height assignment \(w:P\to\mathbb R\) such that, for each \(A\in T\), an affine function \(\ell_A:\mathbb R^3\to\mathbb R\) equals \(w\) on the four points of \(A\) and is strictly below \(w\) at every point of \(P\setminus A\). These are the tetrahedralizations obtained by projecting the simplicial lower hull of the lifted points. The target includes nonregular tetrahedralizations as well. It is an exact geometric existence question; there is no coordinate encoding, running-time or approximation tolerance to optimize.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof or refutation of connectivity for every finite point set in the stated general position. A positive proof must establish a finite legal \(2\leftrightarrow3\) path between every pair of full geometric tetrahedralizations, with all intermediate complexes using the same point coordinates and vertex set. No efficient path-finding algorithm or polynomial path length is required. A negative proof must establish the general position and geometric validity of a counterexample and prove that two tetrahedralizations lie in different components of its full flip graph. A result only for regular triangulations, higher-dimensional point sets, abstract complexes, or paths that remove or add vertices does not settle the target. Numerical experiments and approximate coordinate pictures alone are insufficient.

source_formulation.text: TOPP Problem 28 asks whether tetrahedralizations of a general-position point set in three-dimensional space form a connected graph when adjacency is restricted to replacing two tetrahedra by three, or three by two. The source specifies general position as having no four coplanar points and distinguishes results that permit vertex insertion or deletion.
source_formulation.caption: Editorial paraphrase of TOPP Problem 28; the fixed geometric vertex set and the allowed two-to-three moves are retained

context_blocks.text: A tetrahedral mesh can be changed locally while leaving its boundary and vertex coordinates fixed. Connectivity asks whether these basic local changes can in principle reach every mesh of the same point set, or whether the space of meshes splits into inaccessible regions.

For planar point sets, diagonal flips connect all triangulations. This is an important structural basis for local triangulation algorithms. The analogous conclusion in three dimensions does not follow just from the existence of tetrahedralizations or from the planar argument.

For regular triangulations with a fixed vertex set, Pournin and Liebling prove connectivity by paths that preserve faces common to the two endpoints. TOPP explicitly notes that in the three-dimensional general-position setting this uses the required two-to-three and three-to-two moves. The unrestricted question is whether nonregular tetrahedralizations can also be connected within the full graph.

There are disconnected triangulation spaces in higher dimensions, and TOPP records nonrealizable abstract tetrahedral complexes with no allowed flips. These show why dimensional and geometric-realizability hypotheses matter, but neither gives a counterexample for the three-dimensional point sets in this question.

Wagner and Welzl’s 2022 paper proves stronger connectivity results in the plane and explicitly says in its introduction that connectivity remains open in dimensions three and four. It also carefully distinguishes full triangulations, which retain all points, from partial triangulations that may omit interior points.

A positive answer would establish reachability by the permitted local moves, rather than a running-time guarantee for a mesh optimization heuristic. Even a connected graph can have long routes, and connectivity does not ensure that an objective improves on every move.

cards.title: NP certificates for homeomorphism of three-manifolds
cards.formal: Does homeomorphism of connected compact triangulated 3-manifolds, allowing boundary and nonorientable manifolds, have polynomially bounded certificates verifiable in polynomial time? Precisely, do there exist a polynomial \(p\) and a uniform deterministic polynomial-time verifier \(V\) such that for every promised pair \((T,U)\in\mathcal D\) of total encoded length \(N\), \[H(T,U)\iff\exists w\in\{0,1\}^{\leq p(N)}\;V(T,U,w)=1?\] This is the NP-certificate question for the promised homeomorphism problem below.
cards.why: Short certificates would separate the cost of discovering topological equivalence from the cost of checking it. An NP upper bound would place a fundamental classification problem within the standard theory of efficient verification.
cards.status_note: The NP question is explicit in the 2024 report and Jackson’s 2024/2025 article. The bounded later-work review through 14 September 2026 found no general certificate theorem. The stated target retains the source’s broad compact connected domain; closed-oriented and Seifert results are limited to their published hypotheses.

sentences: Two triangulations can describe the same three-dimensional manifold while looking combinatorially unrelated.
This question asks whether every homeomorphic pair has a certificate whose size and verification time are polynomial in the input.
Such a certificate need not be found efficiently by the verifier itself.
The challenge is to encode the necessary topological equivalence without an excessively long sequence of transformations.
An NP upper bound would distinguish the difficulty of discovering a homeomorphism from the difficulty of checking convincing evidence that one exists.

cards.definitions: A triangulation consists of \(t\geq1\) labelled copies of \(\Delta^3=\{x\in\mathbb R^4:x_i\geq0,\ \sum_{i=0}^3x_i=1\}\), with some triangular faces paired by affine bijections specified by permutations of their three vertices. Each face is unpaired or paired with one other face; a pairing to the identical face slot is forbidden, pairings are reciprocal, and different faces of the same tetrahedron may be paired. The realization \(|T|\) is the disjoint union of the tetrahedra modulo the stated identifications, with the quotient topology. The input promise is that each realization is a nonempty connected compact 3-manifold, possibly with boundary: every point has a neighborhood homeomorphic to an open subset of \(\mathbb R^3\) or of \(\mathbb R^2\times[0,\infty)\). Orientability is not promised and no orientation, boundary marking or distinguished submanifold is supplied. Homeomorphism means a continuous bijection with continuous inverse, with no orientation-preserving or boundary-label requirement. In dimension three this agrees with equivalence of PL triangulations; combinatorial isomorphism of the supplied tetrahedron lists is not required. For a concrete binary encoding, write \(t\) in unary followed by the \(4t\) face slots in label order, each recording an unpaired flag or a partner tetrahedron index, a two-bit face index and one of the six vertex permutations; tetrahedron indices use \(\lceil\log_2(t+1)\rceil\) bits. The two encodings are concatenated and their total bit length is \(N\). Let \(\mathcal D\) be the promised domain of such pairs and \(H(T,U)\) the assertion \(|T|\cong|U|\). Algorithms and verifiers are uniform deterministic multitape Turing machines with bit-operation cost, no advice, oracles or randomness. The certificate statements concern this promised domain: verifiers must halt in their polynomial time bound on all bit strings, but acceptance outside \(\mathcal D\) has no specified topological meaning.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove or refute the displayed existence of \(p,V\) with a complete Lean-checked proof. A positive answer needs completeness for every homeomorphic promised pair and soundness against every candidate witness for every nonhomeomorphic promised pair, with polynomial worst-case verification time in \(N+|w|\). The verifier need not find the witness. A negative answer must exclude all polynomially bounded certificate systems in this model, not merely certificates made from a particular type of topological transformation. A result restricted to a fixed manifold, orientable closed manifolds, or one geometric class does not settle the full domain.

context_blocks.text: Schleimer’s Question 3 asks whether Homeo(3) lies in NP. His standing domain is compact connected manifolds supplied by triangulations. The boundary, orientation and binary-verifier conventions above make that domain explicit.

Two very different tetrahedron lists can describe the same space. A positive certificate must establish equality of the represented topological types, rather than just exhibit a relabelling of the supplied pieces. Its form is unrestricted; the polynomial bound concerns the entire witness and its verification.

Kuperberg proves an elementary-recursive decision algorithm for closed oriented 3-manifolds: the running time has a fixed-height exponential-tower bound. This establishes a quantitative decidability result in that setting, not polynomial certificates for the broader domain.

Jackson proves NP recognition for compact orientable Seifert fibered spaces with nonempty boundary, together with NP and coNP certification for their naming problem. The paper explicitly asks about general homeomorphism, which its special-class results do not decide.

NP verification concerns yes instances. It does not imply a polynomial-time method for constructing a homeomorphism, nor provide short certificates when the manifolds differ. The latter is the separate coNP question.

The 2025 seminar report asks a related fixed-parameter tractability question measured by the treewidth of the input triangulations. A parameter-dependent algorithm with no global polynomial bound would not by itself resolve this certificate question.

cards.definitions: The input lists \(n\ge 0\) distinct points \((x_{i},y_{i})\), and B, with every rational written as a signed binary integer numerator and a positive binary integer denominator. Let N be the total bit length. A triangulation is a maximal plane straight-line graph with vertex set exactly S: edges are segments joining pairs of distinct input points, no edge interior contains another input point, and two edges meet only at a shared endpoint. Maximal means that no further admissible segment can be added while preserving these conditions. This definition permits collinear points; in the entirely collinear case the graph is the path through consecutive points, and with fewer than two points it has no edges. No new vertices are permitted. Hull-boundary edges are included in the weight \(\mathrm{W}(T)=\sum _{\{i,j\}\in E(T)}\sqrt{(x_{i}- x_{j})^{2}+(y_{i}- y_{j})^{2}}\). Lengths are exact nonnegative square roots, with no rounding or tolerance, and equality \(\mathrm{W}(T)=B\) is accepted. Malformed encodings and lists with duplicate points are rejected. Membership in NP means that there are a polynomial q and one deterministic Turing-machine verifier V, running in time polynomial in |x|+|y|, such that for every encoded instance x, x is a yes instance if and only if \(V(x,y)\) accepts for some binary certificate y of length at most q(|x|). Certificates may include auxiliary information beyond a list of edges; no exact-real arithmetic primitive has unit cost.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove NP membership by establishing a polynomial-length, polynomial-bit-time-verifiable certificate system for precisely these yes instances, or prove that this language is not in NP. Showing that one proposed verifier fails does not prove nonmembership. The certificate need only establish some triangulation below the threshold, not optimality of that triangulation.

context_blocks.title: The geometry is small; the lengths need not be rational
context_blocks.text: A triangulation can be described by listing its edges. Even with integer coordinates, their lengths can be irrational: the three points \((0,0), (1,0), (0,1)\) have a single triangular boundary of total length \(2+\sqrt{2}\). A rational threshold must be compared with that exact value. With many edges, many different radicals appear in the sum.

context_blocks.title: What a certificate would have to establish
context_blocks.text: The edge list and its geometric validity have polynomial-size descriptions and can be checked using rational-coordinate operations. The remaining numerical comparison is why merely saying “guess the triangulation” does not establish an NP upper bound. The definition of NP also permits other short auxiliary certificates, so difficulty with direct numerical evaluation is not a proof that membership is impossible.

context_blocks.title: Hardness is already known
context_blocks.text: Mulzer and Rote prove strong NP-hardness of minimum-weight triangulation. Their paper explicitly distinguishes this lower bound from NP membership for exact Euclidean costs. Its rounded-cost variant is NP-complete, but replacing lengths by rounded values changes the language and the thresholds.

context_blocks.title: The related arithmetic frontier
context_blocks.text: An edge-length sum is a sum of square roots of rational numbers. After a common rational scaling, the threshold comparison is an instance of square-root sum with integer data. A polynomial-time method, or suitable NP certificates, for that general arithmetic comparison would supply the missing numerical verification. The 2025 ICALP paper still identifies an unresolved NP bound for square-root sum; the reverse implication from this triangulation question is not asserted.

context_blocks.title: Large solved instances and worst-case guarantees
context_blocks.text: Haas reports practical methods that solve very large triangulation instances to optimality. This is useful computational progress, but it does not establish a polynomial bound on verification resources for every possible binary-encoded input. The card asks for that uniform complexity guarantee.

cards.title: Output-sensitive convex hull complexity
cards.formal: For every fixed integer \(d\geq4\), determine up to constant factors the optimal deterministic output-sensitive running time for constructing the convex hull of \(n\geq d+1\) points in \(\mathbb R^d\) in general position, as a function of \(n\) and the actual number \(f\) of hull facets. The coordinate array is the input. Output the complete facial structure of the hull, as specified below. The required complexity must cover every realizable pair \((n,f)\), including small hulls, and retain logarithmic factors.
cards.why: Sharp output-sensitive hull bounds would connect the work of discovering a geometric boundary to its actual combinatorial size. This matters for hull construction, polyhedral representations and geometric computations whose input contains many nonextreme points.

cards.definitions: General position means every subset of at most \(d+1\) input points is affinely independent. The convex hull is \(H=\{\sum_{i=1}^n\lambda_i p_i:\lambda_i\geq0,\ \sum_i\lambda_i=1\}\). Its proper nonempty faces are intersections with supporting hyperplanes; a facet has dimension \(d-1\). The promise makes \(H\) full-dimensional and simplicial, with exactly \(d\) vertices per facet. Output each proper nonempty face by its set of input-vertex indices and list every containment incidence between faces of consecutive dimensions; also identify the facets. The total output size is \(O_d(f)\). Interior input points need not be output. Let \(\mathcal D_d\) be the pairs \((n,f)\) realized by a valid input, and let \(T_A(n,f)\) be the supremum of algorithm \(A\)’s steps over all such inputs with exactly these parameters. One finite deterministic program per fixed \(d\) must work for all \(n\); it is given neither \(f\) nor advice. The model has exact real registers with rational program constants and indexed memory; \(+,-,\times,/\), comparisons, copies and memory accesses cost one each. Integer indices and counters have \(O_d(\log(n+t+2))\) bits at time \(t\), with ordinary word arithmetic and comparisons charged. No floor, extraction of real digits, or free geometric query is available. Reading input and reporting faces are charged. Coordinates have no bounded-precision promise, and no randomization or input distribution is used.
cards.answer_criterion: Provide a noncircular positive rate \(g_d(n,f)\) on each domain \(\mathcal D_d\) and a complete Lean-checked proof of matching bounds. For each fixed \(d\geq4\), give one uniform algorithm \(A_d\) with \(T_{A_d}(n,f)\leq C_dg_d(n,f)\) on all feasible pairs with sufficiently large \(n\). For every correct algorithm \(A\), prove \(T_A(n,f)\geq c_{A,d}g_d(n,f)\) on all feasible pairs with sufficiently large \(n\). Positive constants and thresholds may depend on \(d\), and in the lower bound on \(A\), but not on the feasible pair. A worst-case bound in \(n\) alone, listing only extreme vertices, or resolving only dimensions two and three is insufficient.

context_blocks.text: The Open Problems Project asks for the best output-sensitive hull algorithm. The general-position convention used here is explicit in Chan’s cited primary paper. Without it, a facet can contain many vertices, and the number of facets alone need not measure the amount of output.

Output sensitivity accounts for what the particular input produces. Many points may lie inside a hull with few facets, so a bound based solely on the largest possible hull of an equally large point set can greatly exceed the size of the actual result.

Chan’s 1996 theorem gives \(O_d(n\log f+(nf)^{1-1/(\lfloor d/2\rfloor+1)}\log^{O_d(1)}n)\) time. The paper contrasts this with the \(\Omega_d(n\log f+f)\) lower bound and explains the range of small outputs where its upper bound is optimal. These are dated results, not a claim that every intervening bound has been exhaustively surveyed.

The same paper distinguishes the hull’s full facial structure from the task of finding only its extreme points, and records optimal \(O(n\log f)\) algorithms in dimensions two and three. In dimension four there are also stronger specialized bounds than a literal use of the general-dimensional expression.

The ESA 2025 work on universal optimality concerns planar hulls and additionally reports certificates for interior points. It addresses a refined form of input sensitivity but does not settle the higher-dimensional two-parameter target here.

The fixed dimension is allowed to affect constants; the input size and output size are not. General position is a substantive source assumption, not a license to perturb a degenerate input while pretending its output size remains unchanged.

cards.title: Earth mover distance sketching complexity
cards.formal: Determine, up to universal constant factors, the minimum sketch length \(s(n,c)\) for approximating planar earth mover distance for every integer \(n\geq2\) and real approximation factor \(c\geq1\). Inputs are subsets \(A,B\subseteq[n]^2\) of equal cardinality, with unit mass at each occupied grid point, and \[\operatorname{EMD}(A,B)=\min_{\pi:A\to B\ \mathrm{bijection}}\sum_{a\in A}\|a-\pi(a)\|_1.\] Each set must be encoded independently using the same public randomness. From the two \(s\)-bit encodings the decoder must return \(\widehat d\) satisfying \(\operatorname{EMD}(A,B)\leq\widehat d\leq c\operatorname{EMD}(A,B)\) with probability at least \(2/3\) for every fixed pair.
cards.why: EMD sketching asks how much information must be retained to compare geometric mass distributions without keeping the original data. Sharp tradeoffs would clarify the limits of metric compression and the distinction between embeddings, sketches and full-input transport algorithms.
cards.status_note: The full tradeoff and highlighted constant-approximation/polylogarithmic-size question are open in the 2011 source. The bounded later-work search through 14 September 2026 found no matching characterization for this exact subset and public-coin model. Full transportation-norm and L₁-distortion results have been checked separately and do not by themselves certify a resolution.

sentences: Each planar grid subset must be compressed independently before the other input is available.
The decoder uses the two bit strings to estimate the minimum Manhattan-cost matching of equal-size sets.
The target is the optimal tradeoff between sketch length and multiplicative approximation, with constant success probability for every fixed pair.
Known embedding and full transportation-norm results do not automatically characterize arbitrary decoders for these subset sketches.
Sharp bounds would establish how much information optimal-transport comparisons must retain.

cards.definitions: Here \([n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}\) and \(\|(x,y)-(u,v)\|_1=|x-u|+|y-v|\); grid spacing and point mass are both one. Empty sets are allowed and their distance is zero. There are no repeated points, arbitrary real weights or bounds on cardinality beyond \(|A|=|B|\leq n^2\). A length-\(s\) scheme for parameters \((n,c)\) is a probability space of public seeds \(R\), encoders \(L_R:2^{[n]^2}\to\{0,1\}^s\), and decoders \(D_R:\{0,1\}^s\times\{0,1\}^s\to\mathbb R_{\geq0}\), with all relevant events measurable. The estimate is \(D_R(L_R(A),L_R(B))\). The seed is independent of the inputs and available to both encoders and the decoder. Seed length and local computation are unrestricted and not charged; this is information-theoretic sketch length in bits, not streaming update time or the dimension of a real vector. The decoder knows \(n,c,R\), but receives no input-dependent information beyond the two sketches; any stored cardinality is charged. The same encoder works for both inputs. Success is required for each fixed pair chosen independently of \(R\), not simultaneously for all pairs under one seed or against adaptive exposure of the seed. When \(A=B\), success requires estimate zero. Define \(s(n,c)\) as the least integer \(s\geq0\) admitting such a scheme; it is finite because the entire \(n^2\)-bit incidence vector can be stored. The displayed interval fixes the usual one-sided multiplicative convention explicitly; it is not an additive-error guarantee.
cards.answer_criterion: Provide a noncircular positive rate \(g(n,c)\) and a complete Lean-checked proof that universal constants \(a,b>0\) and \(n_0\) satisfy \(a g(n,c)\leq s(n,c)\leq b g(n,c)\) for every \(n\geq n_0\) and every \(c\geq1\). The upper bound must supply schemes with the stated probability and bit length; the lower bound must cover all allowed, possibly nonlinear, public-coin schemes. Constants and \(n_0\) cannot depend on \(c\), so varying approximation regimes and logarithmic factors must be accounted for. A single upper bound, a linear-embedding lower bound alone, or the answer for only one fixed approximation factor does not determine the requested tradeoff.

context_blocks.text: Indyk’s 2011 question asks for the sketch-length/approximation tradeoff and highlights the possibility of constant \(c\) with \(s=\operatorname{polylog}n\). The card retains that full tradeoff and specifies the grid, masses, randomness and approximation convention.

A sketch must be computed without seeing the other set. The decoder then estimates one transport cost from two compressed descriptions. A fast algorithm that reads both complete inputs can exploit information that the sketch decoder does not have.

Andoni, Do Ba, Indyk and Woodruff prove that, for any fixed \(0<\varepsilon<1\), a sketch of polynomially sublinear grid-size dependence can obtain approximation \(O(1/\varepsilon)\). Their Theorem 1.1 uses \(O(n^\varepsilon)\) integer coordinates of polynomial magnitude; for sets this converts to \(O(n^\varepsilon\log n)\) bits. Thus constant-factor approximation is possible with more than polylogarithmic space in the stated construction.

Andoni, Krauthgamer and Razenshteyn prove that the full planar transportation norm cannot have both constant approximation and constant-size distance-threshold sketches. That norm allows general signed real mass vectors; the theorem neither identifies this subset-only bit tradeoff nor rules out polylogarithmic sketches.

The published STOC 2026 lower bound of Gartland and Ostrovskii closes the planar \(L_1\)-distortion gap for transportation cost spaces at order \(\log n\). An embedding theorem is not a theorem about every arbitrary decoder of two finite sketches, so this result does not automatically resolve the present question.

The number of grid locations and the number of occupied points are different parameters. Here the grid side length is the parameter and every equal-size pair is covered. Likewise, replacing the one-unit point masses by arbitrary weighted distributions would enlarge the input family.

Their Theorem 1.1 uses \(O(n^\varepsilon)\) integer coordinates of polynomial magnitude; for sets this converts to \(O(n^\varepsilon\log n)\) bits. Thus constant-factor approximation is possible with more than polylogarithmic space in the stated construction.

Andoni, Krauthgamer and Razenshteyn prove that the full planar transportation norm cannot have both constant approximation and constant-size distance-threshold sketches. That norm allows general signed real mass vectors; the theorem neither identifies this subset-only bit tradeoff nor rules out polylogarithmic sketches.

The published STOC 2026 lower bound of Gartland and Ostrovskii closes the planar \(L_1\)-distortion gap for transportation cost spaces at order \(\log n\). An embedding theorem is not a theorem about every arbitrary decoder of two finite sketches, so this result does not automatically resolve the present question.

The number of grid locations and the number of occupied points are different parameters. Here the grid side length is the parameter and every equal-size pair is covered. Likewise, replacing the one-unit point masses by arbitrary weighted distributions would enlarge the input family.

cards.title: Counting simple polygonalizations
cards.formal:
Is there a deterministic polynomial-time algorithm that, given a finite planar point set \(S\subset\mathbb Q^2\) in binary rational coordinates, outputs the exact number \(\operatorname{poly}(S)\) of simple polygonalizations of \(S\)?

A simple polygonalization is a non-self-intersecting closed polygonal curve that visits every point of \(S\) exactly once and joins consecutive points by straight segments. Two cyclic orders count as the same polygonalization precisely when one is obtained from the other by changing the starting point or reversing the traversal. Collinear points are allowed, but crossings, overlapping edges and contacts between nonadjacent edges are forbidden.

The running time must be polynomial in the total binary input length, including the coordinate encodings, and the output count is written in binary.
cards.why: This is a basic exact-counting question for a geometric family of Hamiltonian cycles. A resolution would clarify whether planarity of the drawing and freedom to choose its edges make counting fundamentally easier than familiar hard graph-counting problems, and would separate compact numerical output from exhaustive geometric enumeration.

Bounded 2025–2026 searches found no polynomial exact-counting algorithm or unconditional impossibility theorem for this target. This records dated explicit openness and limited later review, not an exhaustive current-status certification; the omitted full-version proofs behind the 2016 extended abstract were not independently audited.

sentences: A simple polygonalization connects all points of a planar set into one noncrossing closed polygon.
The question asks whether its exact number can be computed in deterministic polynomial time from binary rational coordinates.
Starting-point changes and reverse traversals count as the same polygon, and collinear input points are allowed.
Subexponential counting in general position and output-polynomial enumeration are known, but neither gives a polynomial-time exact count for every input.

cards.definitions:
The input is a finite list \(S=(p_1,\ldots,p_n)\) of pairwise distinct points \(p_i=(x_i,y_i)\in\mathbb Q^2\). Each rational coordinate is represented by a signed integer numerator and a positive integer denominator in binary, in lowest terms, using a fixed self-delimiting encoding. Let \(N\) be the total length in bits of the encoded list, including the coordinates, signs, delimiters and list length. Input order supplies labels for describing cyclic orders; it does not change the answer. The exact bit model makes the source’s polynomial-time question explicit rather than treating arbitrary-precision arithmetic as a unit-cost operation.

For \(n\ge3\), choose a permutation \((i_0,\ldots,i_{n-1})\) of \(\{1,\ldots,n\}\). Its edges are the closed segments
\[e_j=[p_{i_j},p_{i_{j+1}}],\qquad j=0,\ldots,n-1,\]
where indices are read modulo \(n\). Each edge must have no point of \(S\) in its relative interior. Two adjacent edges must intersect in exactly their common endpoint. Two nonadjacent edges must be disjoint. These conditions say that the cyclic polygonal curve is simple: it is an embedded circle made of line segments. In particular, edges cannot cross, overlap along a segment, or touch a nonincident vertex.

Three successive vertices may be collinear if the path proceeds straight through the middle vertex. Such an input point is still counted as a vertex even though its interior angle is \(\pi\). Reversing direction along an already traversed segment is forbidden by the intersection conditions. No general-position promise is imposed, and an arbitrary perturbation that changes collinearities would change the input counting problem.

A polygonalization uses every point and no additional vertices. Its region need not be convex, and its boundary need not be monotone in any direction. There is no prescribed graph of allowed edges, no obstacle polygon, no additional forbidden region and no weight or length objective. Admissibility depends only on the geometry of the given points and the straight segments selected between them.

Cyclic permutations of a valid order and reversal of that order describe one unoriented polygonalization. Distinct geometric edge sets on the fixed point set are counted separately, even if a symmetry of the point set maps one to another. For example, one can count each polygon exactly once using the representative with \(i_0=1\) and \(i_1<i_{n-1}\). These conventions remove the \(2n\)-fold starting-point and orientation multiplicity; they do not quotient by translations, rotations or reflections of the input configuration.

Define \(\operatorname{poly}(S)\) as the number of valid equivalence classes of cyclic orders. For \(n<3\), set \(\operatorname{poly}(S)=0\). A set with all points on one line also has count zero. For \(n\ge3\), the elementary bound
\[0\le\operatorname{poly}(S)\le (n-1)!/2\]
shows that the binary count has \(O(n\log(n+1))\) bits, despite potentially having many polygonalizations. The target is the count for each input set, not the maximum or minimum number over all \(n\)-point sets.

The computational model is a uniform deterministic multitape Turing machine with a fixed finite description, ordinary bit operations and no oracle or advice. All input parsing, exact geometric predicates, integer arithmetic and output writing are charged to the running time. The requested quantifiers are
\[\exists A\;\exists a\ge1\;\exists k\in\mathbb N\;\forall S:\quad A(S)=\operatorname{poly}(S),\qquad \operatorname{time}_A(S)\le a(N+1)^k.\]
The constants and exponent are independent of the number, positions and encoding lengths of the points. The machine may return zero on malformed inputs; it can check the encoding and pairwise distinctness in polynomial time. There is no restriction on workspace beyond that implied by the time bound.

The task requires the exact integer count in binary. An estimate with bounded relative error, an approximation to the logarithm of the count, or a random polygon is a different computational task. This card asks a yes-or-no question about existence of an exact-counting algorithm, rather than asking the solver for a numerical value of a single instance or an unrestricted approximation to a function.

Writing down every polygonalization may require exponentially many symbols. An enumeration algorithm whose time is polynomial in that whole output length therefore need not run in time polynomial in \(N\), even though the binary count is short. Likewise, generating one simple polygon or listing only a particular geometric subclass does not compute the required count.

For complexity context, \(\#\mathrm P\) consists of integer-valued functions counting accepting branches of polynomial-time nondeterministic machines. A canonical cyclic order is a polynomial-size witness here, and its segment-intersection conditions can be verified exactly in polynomial bit time, placing the count in this class. \(\mathrm{FP}\) denotes functions computable by a deterministic polynomial-time machine. A conditional hardness theorem would describe consequences of a polynomial algorithm; it would not by itself refute the algorithm’s existence without proving the relevant separation.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof or refutation of the existence of the stated uniform deterministic polynomial-bit-time exact-counting algorithm. A positive answer must establish correctness for every encoded finite rational point set, including collinearities and zero-count cases, and a single polynomial bound that includes arithmetic and output costs. A negative answer must prove that no such machine and polynomial bound exist. A #P-hardness result conditional on an unproved complexity separation is progress but does not by itself supply that unconditional refutation. A polynomial-time approximation, output-polynomial enumeration, a result only for general-position or convex-position sets, or a lower bound for one particular counting algorithm does not satisfy the full target.

source_formulation.text: TOPP Problem 16 asks whether the number of simple polygonalizations of a planar point set can be computed in polynomial time, defining a polygonalization as a simple polygon with exactly the given vertices. The card retains that exact-counting existence question and spells out binary rational input, collinearities and the removal of cyclic-order multiplicities.
source_formulation.caption: Editorial paraphrase of TOPP Problem 16; computational encoding and counting conventions are explicit

context_blocks.text: Finding one noncrossing polygon through a point set and counting all such polygons are different tasks. The latter asks whether a geometric restriction on Hamiltonian cycles permits efficient exact counting despite the large number of possible cyclic orders.

Marx and Miltzow give a subexponential algorithm for counting noncrossing Hamilton cycles on point sets in general position. Their Theorem 6 states a running time of \(n^{O(\sqrt{n})}\). This is substantial progress but is not a polynomial-time bound, and their stated general-position hypothesis must be retained.

The same paper gives a sharper constant in the exponent for counting triangulations. The TOPP progress paragraph compresses these statements too aggressively: this card does not attribute the triangulation constant to every graph family, nor does it treat a triangulation count as a polygonalization count.

Eppstein proves that all polygonalizations can be listed in time polynomial in the input size and the total output size, even when the input has collinearities. An exponential number of polygons still permits an exponential running time under that guarantee.

Eppstein’s polynomial-time estimates concern the logarithm of the number of polygonalizations. Such an estimate can allow a large multiplicative uncertainty in the count itself. The paper’s conclusion retains both stronger approximate counting and the #P-completeness question as open.

For points in convex position there is only one polygonalization, while other configurations have exponentially many. The difficulty lies in determining the exact count for arbitrary inputs, not in the bit length needed to write the resulting integer.

Uniform random generation on a fixed point set is a closely related theme in the source. Heuristic generation or a distribution that favors some polygons is not a counting algorithm, and no unconditional equivalence with the exact counting target is asserted here.

cards.definitions: A line is the set \(\ell_i=\{p_i+tv_i:t\in\mathbb R\}\), where \(p_i,v_i\in\mathbb R^3\) and \(v_i\ne0\). Distances are ordinary Euclidean point-to-line distances. For every nonempty \(I\subseteq\{1,\ldots,n\}\), define \(V_I\) to be the set of points whose set of nearest lines is exactly \(\{\ell_i:i\in I\}\). Regular means that \(V_I\) is empty for \(|I|>4\), and for \(1\le|I|\le4\) each nonempty \(V_I\) is a smooth embedded manifold of dimension \(4-|I|\). The cells counted are the connected components of every nonempty \(V_I\), including unbounded components and zero-dimensional components. Let \(b_0(V_I)\) be the number of such components, with \(b_0(\varnothing)=0\); total complexity is \(\sum_{\varnothing\ne I\subseteq[n]}b_0(V_I)\). These semialgebraic sets have finitely many connected components. The statement is an extremal mathematical bound; no bit encoding or construction algorithm for real coordinates is required. The constants depend only on \(\varepsilon\), not on the lines or their coordinates.

context_blocks.text: At each point of space, the nearest-line set describes which sites compete to be closest. Regions with one nearest line, interfaces with two, curves with three, and isolated points with four form the strata counted here. A stratum can have several connected components, and unbounded components count as well. Counting just the input lines would omit this geometric arrangement.

The question concerns Euclidean distance to complete affine lines in three dimensions. The source records a quadratic lower bound and an upper bound of \(O(n^{3+\varepsilon})\) for every fixed \(\varepsilon>0\), leaving a full exponent gap. A nearest-point diagram, a planar diagram, or a polyhedral distance function is a different object.

The conjectured guarantee is \(n^{2+\varepsilon}\) for every fixed positive \(\varepsilon\), with a constant allowed to depend on that exponent slack. It does not require a single \(Cn^2\) bound. Conversely, a bound with one fixed exponent strictly above two does not meet the universal quantifier over \(\varepsilon\).

The source also distinguishes the full diagram from a fixed-distance level set, describable through a union of cylinders. Complexity controlled at one distance does not automatically count all strata of the nearest-site partition throughout space.

The March 2026 four-line classification describes a base case with zero through eight Voronoi vertices under general-position assumptions. The result clarifies local configurations, but fixes the number of sites and supplies no asymptotic bound for arbitrary input size.

The August 2026 regulus preprint claims quadratic total complexity when all lines lie in one ruling of a smooth doubly ruled quadric: one of the two line families covering that surface. Its hypotheses strongly restrict the line configuration. It explicitly retains the broader quadratic-to-cubic gap for arbitrary Euclidean line sites. The present card spells out its own regular-stratum convention rather than leaving “general position” undefined.

cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof of the stated bound for every \(\varepsilon>0\) on all diagrams in the defined regular class, or prove its logical negation in Lean: some \(\varepsilon_0>0\) has unbounded total complexity divided by \(n^{2+\varepsilon_0}\) over that class. The count must include connected components in all four dimensions, including unbounded ones. A bound only for four sites, one ruled-surface family, vertices alone, or a different metric does not establish the full statement.

cards.title: coNP certificates for three-manifold homeomorphism
cards.formal: Does nonhomeomorphism of connected compact triangulated 3-manifolds have polynomially bounded certificates verifiable in polynomial time? Allow boundary and nonorientable manifolds. Precisely, do there exist a polynomial \(p\) and a uniform deterministic polynomial-time verifier \(W\) such that for every promised pair \((T,U)\in\mathcal D\) with total input length \(N\), \[\neg H(T,U)\iff\exists w\in\{0,1\}^{\leq p(N)}\;W(T,U,w)=1?\] This is the coNP-certificate question for the promised homeomorphism problem.
cards.why: The question asks whether topological difference always has efficiently checkable finite evidence. Its reduction from graph isomorphism ties the difficulty of distinguishing 3-manifolds to a central unresolved certificate problem in complexity theory.
cards.status_note: The general coNP question is explicitly open in the 2024 report. The bounded search through 14 September 2026 found no general result meeting these unconditional quantifiers. Special Seifert naming certificates do not establish the full target.

This card asks for short certificates precisely when those spaces are not homeomorphic.

cards.definitions: A triangulation consists of \(t\geq1\) labelled copies of \(\Delta^3=\{x\in\mathbb R^4:x_i\geq0,\ \sum_{i=0}^3x_i=1\}\), with some triangular faces paired by affine bijections specified by permutations of their three vertices. Each face is unpaired or paired with one other face; a pairing to the identical face slot is forbidden, pairings are reciprocal, and different faces of the same tetrahedron may be paired. The realization \(|T|\) is the disjoint union of the tetrahedra modulo the stated identifications, with the quotient topology. The input promise is that each realization is a nonempty connected compact 3-manifold, possibly with boundary: every point has a neighborhood homeomorphic to an open subset of \(\mathbb R^3\) or of \(\mathbb R^2\times[0,\infty)\). Orientability is not promised and no orientation, boundary marking or distinguished submanifold is supplied. Homeomorphism means a continuous bijection with continuous inverse, with no orientation-preserving or boundary-label requirement. In dimension three this agrees with equivalence of PL triangulations; combinatorial isomorphism of the supplied tetrahedron lists is not required. For a concrete binary encoding, write \(t\) in unary followed by the \(4t\) face slots in label order, each recording an unpaired flag or a partner tetrahedron index, a two-bit face index and one of the six vertex permutations; tetrahedron indices use \(\lceil\log_2(t+1)\rceil\) bits. The two encodings are concatenated and their total bit length is \(N\). Let \(\mathcal D\) be the promised domain of such pairs and \(H(T,U)\) the assertion \(|T|\cong|U|\). Algorithms and verifiers are uniform deterministic multitape Turing machines with bit-operation cost, no advice, oracles or randomness. The certificate statements concern this promised domain: verifiers must halt in their polynomial time bound on all bit strings, but acceptance outside \(\mathcal D\) has no specified topological meaning.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof that such \(p,W\) exist, or that none exist. A positive answer needs a short accepted witness for every nonhomeomorphic promised pair and rejection of every candidate witness for every homeomorphic promised pair. Verification time must be polynomial in \(N+|w|\) on every binary input. A particular invariant that distinguishes only some pairs is insufficient. A negative answer must rule out all polynomial certificate systems, rather than showing the inadequacy of one invariant or representation. Conditional upper bounds qualify only if the additional hypothesis is also proved.

context_blocks.text: Schleimer states this as Question 4, separately from NP membership and NP-hardness. Its quantifiers run over nonhomeomorphic pairs; changing the sign of the target changes which instances need certificates.

Different triangulations can share many familiar invariants without being homeomorphic. The card does not prescribe an invariant: an accepted certificate system may use any finite evidence, but it must be complete for every pair in the full domain.

Lackenby gives a polynomial-time many-one reduction from graph isomorphism to closed 3-manifold homeomorphism. Consequently a coNP certificate system for the domain here would also provide polynomial certificates for graph nonisomorphism. The implication runs from a manifold upper bound to a graph upper bound.

Jackson’s naming theorem provides both NP and coNP certificates within the compact orientable Seifert setting with nonempty boundary. These two-sided certificates apply to the specified naming problem, not arbitrary pairs of triangulated 3-manifolds.

A decidability theorem guarantees that a search eventually terminates. It does not bound the size of evidence for a negative answer by a polynomial. Similarly, an NP system for homeomorphic pairs supplies no general witness for the opposite answer.

If homeomorphism were both NP-hard under the valid-output reductions defined in the related hardness card and in coNP, then \(\mathrm{NP}=\mathrm{coNP}\). This is a logical consequence of the two prospective results, not a proof that either is false.

cards.title: Point location in three-dimensional subdivisions
cards.formal: Do there exist uniform deterministic preprocessing and query algorithms that, for every explicitly represented polyhedral subdivision of a three-dimensional box of total boundary complexity \(n\), store \(O(n)\) words and answer every point-location query in \(O(\log(n+2))\) worst-case time? A query gives an arbitrary point \(q\in\mathbb R^3\) and must return the label of a subdivision region whose closure contains \(q\), or the exterior label for points outside the box. Constants are universal, the guarantee is exact, and the subdivision may have nonconvex regions.
cards.why: Point location is a basic spatial-search operation. Resolving the simultaneous storage and query bounds would establish whether arbitrary three-dimensional partitions admit the same asymptotic search economy as planar subdivisions.
cards.status_note: The checked 2017 handbook explicitly retains the joint bound as open. The bounded later-work review through 14 September 2026 found no resolution for the general subdivision model. The triangulated total-complexity representation and deterministic arithmetic conventions are explicit editorial specifications, rather than hidden assumptions about arbitrary face sizes.

sentences: A three-dimensional subdivision divides space into labelled polyhedral regions.
After preprocessing the boundary representation, a query asks for the region containing an arbitrary supplied point.

cards.definitions: The input includes a bounded axis-aligned box \(B\) with nonempty interior, real coordinates of vertices, an embedded finite triangle mesh containing \(\partial B\), and the labels of the two incident regions of every triangle (one label is the exterior on \(\partial B\)). Nondegenerate closed triangles meet only in a common whole edge, a common vertex, or not at all. The input is promised to describe the boundaries of a partition: bounded regions are closures of the connected components of \(\operatorname{int}(B)\) minus the mesh, with disjoint interiors and no unrepresented boundary; the exterior region is \(\mathbb R^3\setminus\operatorname{int}(B)\). Arbitrary topology and collinear or coplanar incidences consistent with these conditions are allowed. Bounded regions have distinct labels \(1,\ldots,r\), with \(r\leq n\), and the exterior has label zero. All vertex coordinates, triangle vertex-index triples and incident labels are explicitly listed. Define \(n\) as their total number of real-coordinate and integer-index entries, including the box. Thus complicated polygon boundaries are charged through their triangulated representation. Any incident region is acceptable for a query on a shared face, edge or vertex, including the exterior on \(\partial B\). The algorithms are finite deterministic programs independent of the input, with rational constants, exact real registers and indexed memory. Each real \(+,-,\times,/\) operation on its domain, comparison, copy or memory access costs one step. Each stored word contains one real or one integer; query-stage integer words have \(O(\log(n+2))\) bits, with ordinary arithmetic and comparisons charged. Floor and digit extraction from reals, size-dependent advice and free geometric oracles are excluded. Storage includes the input retained for queries and temporary query workspace. Preprocessing must halt on every valid input but has no prescribed time or temporary-space bound; only the final stored structure and each query have the stated bounds.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove the existence of such algorithms, or refute it, with a complete Lean-checked proof. Existence requires constants \(C_s,C_q\) and one pair of uniform algorithms such that every valid subdivision yields a structure of at most \(C_s n\) words and every query is answered correctly within \(C_q\log_2(n+2)\) steps. Refutation must exclude all such pairs in the defined model. Expected performance, a query-distribution promise, linear storage with slower queries, or logarithmic queries with superlinear storage do not establish the positive statement.

context_blocks.text: The Open Problems Project asks for linear space and logarithmic point-location queries in a three-dimensional subdivision. Snoeyink’s 2017 handbook version states the question for a subdivision with a linear number of faces and vertices. This card makes the total boundary representation explicit; it does not count an arbitrarily complicated polygonal face as a constant-size input.

The source asks for a data structure: one preprocessing stage must support arbitrary later queries without knowing them in advance. Checking membership in every region can save storage but loses the logarithmic query requirement.

The 2017 handbook reports \(O(n\log n)\) space and \(O(\log^2 n)\) query time for general three-dimensional subdivisions, with \(O(n\log n)\) preprocessing. Its Section 38.6 then explicitly lists achieving both target bounds as open.

The same section distinguishes point membership in a single convex polyhedron and subdivisions into axis-aligned boxes, where stronger bounds are known. An algorithm restricted to those objects does not handle the arbitrary oblique subdivision boundaries in this card.

A boundary convention is necessary for exact inputs: a query may fall on a face shared by several regions. Returning any incident label avoids making the answer undefined while preserving the search task. No average over query positions or perturbation promise is used.

The target measures words and exact arithmetic operations. The finite representation and word operations prevent treating a real constant as a free oracle encoding answers to all queries; no claim about bounded coordinate bit lengths is implicit in the statement.

cards.title: NP-hardness of three-manifold homeomorphism
cards.formal: Is homeomorphism of connected compact triangulated 3-manifolds NP-hard under deterministic polynomial-time many-one reductions? Use the domain \(\mathcal D\) below, allowing boundary and nonorientable manifolds. Equivalently, is there one uniform polynomial-time Turing machine \(R\) which, on every binary string \(x\), outputs a valid pair \((T_x,U_x)\in\mathcal D\), such that \[x\in\mathrm{3SAT}\iff H(T_x,U_x)?\] Outputs must satisfy the manifold promise on both satisfiable and unsatisfiable inputs.
cards.why: NP-hardness would locate a central topological classification task relative to general combinatorial search. It would supply a stronger complexity obstruction than the currently known reduction from graph isomorphism.
cards.status_note: The NP-hardness question is open in the checked 2024 report, and the 2025 discussion retains graph-isomorphism hardness as the known comparison. The bounded search through 14 September 2026 found no valid-output NP-hardness resolution for the stated target.
