cards.title: Polynomial-time distribution-free PAC learning of DNF
cards.formal:
Does there exist one uniform classical randomized learner \(A\) and absolute positive integers \(a,d\) such that the following holds for every pair of integers \(n,s\ge1\), every Boolean function \(f:\{0,1\}^n\to\{0,1\}\) representable by a DNF with at most \(s\) terms, every probability distribution \(D\) on \(\{0,1\}^n\), and every pair of integers \(t,b\ge2\)? Given only \((n,s,t,b)\) and access to independent labeled examples \((x,f(x))\) with \(x\sim D\), the learner halts within
\[a(n+s+t+b+1)^d\]
steps on every run and outputs an explicitly encoded deterministic Boolean circuit \(h\) on \(n\) inputs such that
\[\Pr\!\left[\sum_{x\in\{0,1\}^n}D(x)\,\mathbf 1[h(x)\ne f(x)]\le\frac1t\right]\ge1-2^{-b}?\]
The outer probability includes the learner’s coins and sampled examples. Membership queries, equivalence queries and descriptions of \(f\) or \(D\) are not supplied. The output need not be a DNF; it must be an efficiently evaluable circuit as defined below.
cards.definitions:
A literal is a variable \(x_i\) or its negation, \(1\le i\le n\). A term is the conjunction of a subset of literals with at most one sign for each variable; the empty conjunction equals \(1\). A disjunctive normal form (DNF) is the disjunction of finitely many terms; the disjunction with no terms equals \(0\). Contradictory terms may be removed and repeated literals or terms ignored without increasing size. The size bound \(s\) counts terms, each of arbitrary width at most \(n\). The learner receives an upper bound \(s\), not a representation or a promise that the minimum DNF has exactly \(s\) terms. Both negated and unnegated literals are allowed.

The learner is a probabilistic multitape Turing machine with a fixed finite program and unit-cost transitions. The integer parameters are in canonical binary notation with separators. The runtime is polynomial in their displayed values, not merely their encoding lengths. Apart from the example oracle, it has no oracle or advice and performs no quantum operations. Reading parameters, processing samples, generating random bits, storing data, arithmetic and writing the entire hypothesis all count toward the same worst-case time bound. Internal random bits are independent unbiased coins, independent of the example stream.

Each example-oracle request returns a fresh independent pair \((x,f(x))\) from the same fixed \(D\) and target \(f\). The learner can choose when to request or reuse an obtained example, but cannot choose or condition the next sampled point. Transferring its \(n+1\) bits costs \(n+1\) steps, and subsequent processing is also charged. One may equivalently supply an infinite independent example stream and charge for each read example. All answers are noiseless. The algorithm receives neither point probabilities nor a sampling program for \(D\). The distribution is an arbitrary assignment of nonnegative real masses summing to one on the finite Boolean cube; no product structure, uniformity, smoothness or efficient samplability is promised. Thus finite exact sampling is an idealized access model, and the cost of implementing a sampler for \(D\) is not part of the learning task.

A hypothesis is a finite acyclic Boolean circuit with input wires \(x_1,\ldots,x_n\), constants \(0,1\), binary AND/OR gates, unary NOT gates and one designated output wire. It is encoded by its full topologically ordered gate list, gate types and binary indices of preceding wires, with separators, followed by the output index. The output is always valid circuit syntax. The number of written bits is bounded by the learner’s runtime; evaluation on any new \(n\)-bit input uses ordinary deterministic circuit evaluation, with time polynomial in \(n\) and the written circuit length. It uses no example oracle, target oracle or new randomness. A circuit that only describes a procedure for generating a much larger circuit is not an explicit output in this convention. No abstention output is allowed at prediction time.

The inner sum is the prediction error on a fresh point drawn from \(D\). The outer probability is over the finite sample/coin experiment bounded by the clock. The guarantee is required separately for every fixed \(f,D,n,s,t,b\); the same program and constants must work for all of them. No worst-case correctness on every point is required. With \(\varepsilon=1/t\) and \(\delta=2^{-b}\), the requirement is the usual polynomial dependence on \(n,s,1/\varepsilon,\log(1/\delta)\). Other \(0<\varepsilon,\delta<1\) are covered by rounding to reciprocal-integer accuracy and dyadic confidence at least as strong as requested. These encodings retain the original PAC target without an input representation for arbitrary real numbers.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of the existence proposition or its full logical negation. An affirmative proof must specify one learner and universal polynomial bound, establish valid explicit circuit output and the all-run time bound, and prove the stated error/confidence inequality for every target, distribution and parameter choice. A negative proof must rule out every uniform learner and every fixed polynomial bound in this model. It must cover arbitrary circuit hypotheses, not only proper learners that return DNFs or a restricted algorithm class. A conditional lower bound whose computational assumption is left unproved, an algorithm with membership queries, a guarantee only for a special distribution or constant number of terms, and a superpolynomial runtime do not establish either full answer.

context_blocks.text: A DNF accepts a point when at least one conjunction of feature conditions holds. Learning predicts these labels from observations without receiving the rules. The unknown distribution can concentrate its probability on any subset of the Boolean cube, so uniform-input arguments do not automatically extend to this task.

The obstacle is computational rather than a shortage of samples: the finite DNF class admits sample complexity \(O((ns+\log(1/\delta))/\varepsilon)\). This statistical guarantee does not give a polynomial-time learner. The 2025 survey explicitly separates sample complexity from the cost of producing an evaluable hypothesis.

For each fixed term bound \(s\), a runtime \(n^{O(s)}\) is polynomial in \(n\), but the required single polynomial in both \(n\) and \(s\) is stronger. Servedio’s Theorem 8 records the general upper bound \(2^{\widetilde O(n^{1/3}\log s)}\), with accuracy and confidence dependence suppressed as specified in that survey; the tilde hides polylogarithmic factors. This remains superpolynomial for polynomially many terms.

Improper learning allows hypotheses outside the DNF class. A lower bound for outputting a small DNF can therefore leave this question open. Daniely–Shalev-Shwartz give an improper-learning hardness result under their random-K-SAT refutation assumption, including polynomially growing term bounds. That assumption is not an established unconditional lower bound.

Daniely–Vardi’s Theorem 3 rules out efficient learning of DNFs with a superconstant number of terms under their Assumption 1 on local pseudorandom generators. Their learning definition permits efficiently evaluable hypotheses outside the target class. The local-generator hypothesis is a specific average-case assumption, not merely \(\mathrm P\ne\mathrm{NP}\) or an unconditional theorem.

The 2025 faster exact learner of Alman and coauthors has access to membership and equivalence queries. A membership query obtains the target value at a chosen point; an equivalence query can provide a counterexample to a proposed hypothesis. Those access guarantees differ from an independent random-example stream, even when the question still concerns small DNFs.

The May 2026 Iterative Chow Filtering result obtains quasipolynomial-time DNF learning in the PQ distribution-shift framework under a uniform training distribution. Its predictor may use a selector to abstain, and training labels and unlabeled test data have distinct roles. Those distribution, runtime and output guarantees do not supply the polynomial-time distribution-free predictor required here.

The January 2026 relative-error DNF result is a property tester: it distinguishes membership in the class from the specified notion of distance using function-query access. Testing whether an unknown function is a DNF is a different output task from learning an accurate predictive circuit from random examples.

Every \(k\)-junta, a Boolean function depending on at most \(k\) coordinates, has a DNF representation with at most \(2^k\) terms. Consequently, a learner meeting this target would give a learner polynomial in \(n,2^k,1/\varepsilon,\log(1/\delta)\) for juntas, including under the uniform distribution. This implication does not assert that learning juntas alone suffices for general DNF learning.

cards.why: DNF learning is a central question about whether compact Boolean rules can be inferred efficiently from observations. Polynomial sample complexity is available, but achieving polynomial computation for arbitrary input distributions remains the difficulty. A positive answer would also cover important target classes such as decision trees and juntas through their DNF representations.

cards.context:
A DNF accepts a point when at least one conjunction of feature conditions holds. Learning predicts these labels from observations without receiving the rules. The unknown distribution can concentrate its probability on any subset of the Boolean cube, so uniform-input arguments do not automatically extend to this task.

The obstacle is computational rather than a shortage of samples: the finite DNF class admits sample complexity \(O((ns+\log(1/\delta))/\varepsilon)\). This statistical guarantee does not give a polynomial-time learner. The 2025 survey explicitly separates sample complexity from the cost of producing an evaluable hypothesis.

For each fixed term bound \(s\), a runtime \(n^{O(s)}\) is polynomial in \(n\), but the required single polynomial in both \(n\) and \(s\) is stronger. Servedio’s Theorem 8 records the general upper bound \(2^{\widetilde O(n^{1/3}\log s)}\), with accuracy and confidence dependence suppressed as specified in that survey; the tilde hides polylogarithmic factors. This remains superpolynomial for polynomially many terms.

Improper learning allows hypotheses outside the DNF class. A lower bound for outputting a small DNF can therefore leave this question open. Daniely–Shalev-Shwartz give an improper-learning hardness result under their random-K-SAT refutation assumption, including polynomially growing term bounds. That assumption is not an established unconditional lower bound.

Daniely–Vardi’s Theorem 3 rules out efficient learning of DNFs with a superconstant number of terms under their Assumption 1 on local pseudorandom generators. Their learning definition permits efficiently evaluable hypotheses outside the target class. The local-generator hypothesis is a specific average-case assumption, not merely \(\mathrm P\ne\mathrm{NP}\) or an unconditional theorem.

The 2025 faster exact learner of Alman and coauthors has access to membership and equivalence queries. A membership query obtains the target value at a chosen point; an equivalence query can provide a counterexample to a proposed hypothesis. Those access guarantees differ from an independent random-example stream, even when the question still concerns small DNFs.

The May 2026 Iterative Chow Filtering result obtains quasipolynomial-time DNF learning in the PQ distribution-shift framework under a uniform training distribution. Its predictor may use a selector to abstain, and training labels and unlabeled test data have distinct roles. Those distribution, runtime and output guarantees do not supply the polynomial-time distribution-free predictor required here.

The January 2026 relative-error DNF result is a property tester: it distinguishes membership in the class from the specified notion of distance using function-query access. Testing whether an unknown function is a DNF is a different output task from learning an accurate predictive circuit from random examples.

Every \(k\)-junta, a Boolean function depending on at most \(k\) coordinates, has a DNF representation with at most \(2^k\) terms. Consequently, a learner meeting this target would give a learner polynomial in \(n,2^k,1/\varepsilon,\log(1/\delta)\) for juntas, including under the uniform distribution. This implication does not assert that learning juntas alone suffices for general DNF learning.

cards.title: Efficient learning of well-separated Gaussian mixtures
cards.formal: Is there an end-to-end polynomial-time, polynomial-sample algorithm for learning the parameters of well-separated spherical Gaussian mixtures at the source’s square-root-logarithmic separation scale? More precisely, do there exist one uniform randomized learner \(A\) and universal constants \(C_{\rm sep},B,a\ge1\) such that the following holds for every integer \(k\ge3\), \(d\ge1\), \(s\ge k\), \(R\ge1\), \(t\ge3\)? For every mixture \[P=\sum_{i=1}^{k}\pi_i N(\mu_i,\sigma_i^2 I_d),\qquad \pi_i\ge1/s,\quad \frac{\max_i\sigma_i}{\min_i\sigma_i}\le R,\] whose means satisfy \[\|\mu_i-\mu_j\|_2\ge C_{\rm sep}\max\{\sigma_i,\sigma_j\}\sqrt{\log(sR)}\quad(i\ne j),\] the learner, given only \(d,k,s,R,t\) and independent unlabeled samples from \(P\), returns \(k\) estimated component parameters with probability at least \(2/3\) for which some permutation \(\tau\) of \([k]\) satisfies, for every \(i\), \[\frac{|\widehat\pi_{\tau(i)}-\pi_i|}{\pi_i}\le\frac1t,\qquad \frac{\|\widehat\mu_{\tau(i)}-\mu_i\|_2}{\sigma_i}\le\frac1t,\qquad \frac{|\widehat\sigma_{\tau(i)}-\sigma_i|}{\sigma_i}\le\frac1{t\sqrt d}.\] Require at most \(B(d+k+s+R+t)^a\) samples and total arithmetic operations, including output. The learner receives no initial estimates of the means, weights or variances. It need not attain the source’s sharper near-linear sample bound; the selected question asks for polynomial sample complexity and polynomial time simultaneously.
cards.why: Identifiable clusters need not be easy to locate. This problem asks whether the separation that makes parameter recovery statistically feasible also permits an efficient global algorithm. It is a basic test of the computational cost of fitting latent-variable models when the number of components grows.
cards.status_note: The source’s selected §4.3 question concerns a global polynomial-time algorithm at square-root-logarithmic separation, while Theorem9 supplies the parameter metric and a statistically efficient but potentially inefficient procedure. The strongest directly checked later polynomial-time identity-covariance result uses log^{1/2+c}(k) separation with fixed c>0. Low-dimensional Fourier results, the 2026 slow-characteristic-function family excluding Gaussians, and newer nonspherical clustering bounds do not match the full target. No matching resolution was found in this bounded review through 16 September 2026; current status remains uncertain rather than a proved assertion of openness. The public bound parameters and exact-real arithmetic convention are explicit and are not claimed equivalent to a finite-bit interface.

The weights, centers and unequal component scales are hidden, and all must be recovered to the source’s stated relative accuracy up to one permutation.
The source’s efficient local refinement requires initialization that its sample-efficient procedure does not find in polynomial time.

cards.definitions:
Here \(\pi_1,\ldots,\pi_k>0\) sum to one, \(\mu_i\in\mathbb R^d\), and \(\sigma_i>0\). The covariance matrix of component \(i\) is \(\sigma_i^2 I_d\), so \(\sigma_i\) is a standard deviation, not a variance. To draw an observation, select an index with probabilities \(\pi_i\) and then draw from that component; the index is never revealed. Different observations and learner coins are independent. Each component’s coordinates have independent variance \(\sigma_i^2\), but both its center and scale are unknown. Weights need not be equal and scales need not coincide. There is no bound on the absolute centers or on the common absolute scale, no general-position or linear-independence assumption on centers, and no target-specific advice.

\([k]=\{1,\ldots,k\}\), \(I_d\) is the identity matrix and \(\|v\|_2=(\sum_j v_j^2)^{1/2}\). The logarithm is natural. The same constant \(C_{\rm sep}\) applies to every instance and is independent of requested accuracy. In the balanced equal-scale special case \(s=k,R=1\), the separation is a constant times \(\sqrt{\log k}\) standard deviations. For general mixtures, the source’s separation (14) uses \(\sqrt{\log(\rho_\sigma/\pi_{\min})}\), where \(\rho_\sigma=\max_i\sigma_i/\min_i\sigma_i\) and \(\pi_{\min}=\min_i\pi_i\). The public integers \(s,R\) are conservative bounds on \(1/\pi_{\min}\) and \(\rho_\sigma\); the displayed separation is imposed with those supplied bounds. Rounding each true quantity upward increases it by at most a factor of two, absorbed by the universal separation constant. This is an explicit public-parameter convention for the source’s polynomial-resource question, not a restriction to balanced or known-variance mixtures.

All five integer parameters are supplied in unary. Accuracy is \(\varepsilon=1/t\); these reciprocal tolerances express arbitrary precision within a constant factor. The output is a finite list \((\widehat\pi_i,\widehat\mu_i,\widehat\sigma_i)_{i=1}^k\) with positive estimated scales, nonnegative weights summing to one, and real mean vectors. Its component order is immaterial: the same permutation must match all three parameter types. The loss is parameter recovery in the displayed relative/scaled units. Merely producing a distribution close in total variation, a good partition for some observations, or a sampler with a different representation does not by itself meet this output requirement.

Use a finite uniform exact-real register program, with rational constants in its fixed code. Copy, addition, subtraction, multiplication, division guarded at zero, comparison, branching, square root of a nonnegative number, and each random fair bit cost one operation. Integer control, input reading, register access and writing each output real are counted. Loading a \(d\)-coordinate observation costs \(d\) operations. The program has no component-label oracle, chosen-input density oracle, exact-moment oracle, free optimization procedure, floor/digit extraction or arbitrary real advice. Its single polynomial bound must hold for every target, sample history and coin history; the success guarantee accounts for the randomness. Constants, program and polynomial exponent are common to all parameters. The source does not specify coordinate-bit precision; this declared real-arithmetic convention does not assert an equivalent finite-bit algorithm. Any finite-precision version needs its own sample representation and justified rounding/error analysis.

The time bound explicitly allows polynomial dependence on the weight and scale-ratio bounds, while the separation depends on their logarithm. It is not polynomial time if the exponent on dimension or component count grows with \(k\), \(t\), or a separation parameter. A family of algorithms at separation \(\log^{1/2+c}k\) with constants or exponents depending on a fixed \(c>0\) does not imply a single algorithm at \(c=0\).
cards.answer_criterion: Give a Lean proof of the uniform existence proposition or its negation. A positive proof must include global initialization from unlabeled samples, every component’s mean/weight/scale guarantee under one permutation, the stated success probability, and a universal polynomial bound for samples and all arithmetic/output costs. A local convergence theorem with accurate starting parameters is not enough. A negative result must rule out every learner and universal constants for some allowed parameters and mixture, rather than merely a particular iterative method. A computational assumption must remain a hypothesis unless proved. Larger asymptotic separation, fixed component count, equal variances only, or a weaker distribution-learning output is not a complete answer. The requested parameter accuracy is explicitly \(1/t\), with the dimension factor in the standard-deviation error retained.

source_formulation.text: At the well-separated spherical-Gaussian regime of the paper, can parameter learning from unlabeled samples use both polynomial time and polynomial sample complexity?
source_formulation.caption: Editorial paraphrase

context_blocks.text: Expectation maximization alternates between estimating component membership probabilities and updating parameters. The source proves strong local refinement guarantees and an information-theoretically sample-efficient initialization. The latter can be computationally expensive, which is why its final initialization discussion still asks for an end-to-end polynomial algorithm.

The source permits unknown unequal spherical variances and unequal weights. Its Theorem 9 measures mean error in units of each component’s standard deviation and asks for a smaller relative scale error as dimension grows. The completed statement preserves those parameter guarantees, rather than replacing them with a total-variation approximation or clustering-only task.

Li–Liu obtain polynomial-time learning for identity-covariance mixtures when separation is \(\Omega(\log^{1/2+c}k)\) for any fixed \(c>0\). Their parameter-estimation guarantee is a major improvement over earlier polynomial separation requirements. The theorem does not set \(c=0\), and its common known covariance differs from the full unequal-scale formulation.

Qiao and coauthors give a Fourier-based algorithm with stronger separation guarantees in the low-dimensional regime \(d=O(\log k/\log\log k)\). Their general runtime is polynomial in \(k\) multiplied by a function of dimension, separation and accuracy. This does not provide one polynomial bound over the full high-dimensional parameter range.

The 2026 sparse-Fourier method efficiently learns mixtures whose component characteristic functions decay sufficiently slowly. The main theorem explicitly excludes Gaussians. Its combined treatment of slow- and fast-decaying components retains separate separation and runtime dependencies for the latter, so it does not establish the present Gaussian threshold.

COLT 2026 gives substantial improvements for nonspherical centered mixtures and mixtures with identical unknown covariance. The centered result retains a nonpolynomial function of inverse minimum weight, and the equal-covariance result retains a weight-dependent exponent. Neither theorem supplies the fully polynomial growing-component guarantee specified here.

cards.title: Fully polynomial learning of halfspace intersections under Gaussian and uniform inputs
cards.formal: Resolve the following two distribution-specific questions, separately. For \(D_n=\gamma_n=N(0,I_n)\) on \(\mathbb R^n\), and for \(D_n=U_n\), the uniform measure on \(\{-1,+1\}^n\), does there exist a uniform randomized learner \(A_D\) and constants \(B_D,C_D\ge1\) such that, for all integers \(n,k\ge1\), \(t\ge3\), and all intersections \(f\) of at most \(k\) affine halfspaces, \(A_D(n,k,t)\), using only independent examples \((x,f(x))\) with \(x\sim D_n\), outputs a predictor \(h\) satisfying \[\Pr\!\left[\Pr_{x\sim D_n}[h(x)\ne f(x)]\le\frac1t\right]\ge\frac23\] in total training, output-writing and evaluation cost at most \(B_D(n+k+t)^{C_D}\)? The Gaussian branch uses the explicit real-arithmetic convention below; the Boolean-cube branch uses bit computation. The learner may be improper. Both the number of halfspaces and inverse accuracy are variable parameters: a polynomial whose exponent depends on \(k\) or \(t\) does not answer either branch affirmatively. A full resolution reports an answer to each branch, rather than treating failure of one as a classification of both.

source_formulation.text: Can intersections of a variable number of halfspaces be learned in time polynomial in dimension, number of halfspaces and inverse accuracy under Gaussian inputs or uniform Boolean-cube inputs?

cards.why: Simple independent input coordinates do not identify which inequality caused a negative label. The question asks whether that ambiguity creates a computational barrier even when the distribution is completely known. Its uniform dependence on the number of inequalities and desired accuracy separates practical polynomial learning from algorithms efficient only for fixed parameters.

Through 16 September 2026, the checked primary results include Alman–Patel–Servedio’s subexponential distribution-free learner (v2, July), bounded-geometric-width Gaussian learning applications, and a proper agnostic Gaussian learner with nonconstant parameter-dependent exponents. cards.definitions:
An affine halfspace has Boolean value \(+1\) when \(\sum_{i=1}^n w_i x_i+b\ge0\), and value \(-1\) otherwise, for arbitrary real \(w_1,\ldots,w_n,b\). Its boundary is included in the positive side. An intersection has value \(+1\) exactly when all its component inequalities hold; otherwise it has value \(-1\). The intersection with no components is the constant positive function. All coefficients and the number of nonredundant inequalities are hidden; only the upper bound \(k\) is supplied. No coefficient-size, margin, balance or homogeneity promise is added. On the cube, the function is simply the restriction of those inequalities to the finite domain; their real coefficients are not input strings whose sizes the learner must read.

\(\gamma_n\) has independent standard normal coordinates, with joint density \((2\pi)^{-n/2}\exp(-\|x\|_2^2/2)\). Under \(U_n\), each of the \(2^n\) sign vectors has mass \(2^{-n}\). The appropriate distribution is known to its learner, but the target is unknown. Each example is an independent draw with the exact noiseless target label. The learner cannot ask for labels at chosen points, inspect the target description, or query conditional distributions. The inner probability is disagreement on a fresh example; the outer probability includes training examples and the learner’s random coins. The error tolerance is \(\varepsilon=1/t\), with integer \(t\) supplied in unary together with \(n,k\). These reciprocal tolerances define arbitrary requested accuracy up to a constant factor without introducing an uncounted rational encoding length. Confidence is fixed at \(2/3\); neither branch promises perfect recovery of coefficients.

For the cube, \(A_U\) is one probabilistic multitape Turing machine with a source of independent fair bits and an example tape. Writing a labeled example costs \(n+1\) bit operations. The output is an ordinary finite acyclic Boolean circuit, using AND, OR and NOT gates and constants, evaluated on the input signs encoded as bits. Training, reading, output length, and worst-case output evaluation time are all counted. The polynomial bound must hold on every sample and coin history. The same program and constants must work for every \(n,k,t,f\), with no advice depending on input length.

For the Gaussian branch, use one finite real-register program whose fixed constants are rational. Copying, addition, subtraction, multiplication, division with an explicit zero-denominator guard, comparison, branching, and generating a fair bit have unit cost; discrete control, register access and output writing are also charged. Loading one exact labeled Gaussian vector costs \(n+1\) units. Integer control and the unary public parameters do not supply any infinite advice. There is no floor or digit extraction, optimization oracle, expectation oracle or oracle deciding general real-number properties. The output is a finite acyclic arithmetic-and-comparison circuit with constants computed during training and a total Boolean sign output. Every division must be guarded so evaluation is defined on every input. Its stored constants, instructions and worst-case evaluation operations are counted in the same polynomial bound; it requires no further target access. This permits any such efficiently evaluable predictor, including ones outside the intersection class. All these predictors are Borel measurable.

The real-arithmetic convention explicitly fills the source’s unspecified continuous-input cost interface. Exact Gaussian coordinates need not have finite binary representations, so this branch does not silently claim an equivalent finite-bit learning theorem. Conversely the discrete branch uses actual bit costs and Boolean outputs. A result stated in a different computational model must justify the transfer before it resolves the corresponding branch. Independent programs and constants for the two branches are allowed; each program must be uniform over its own parameters.
cards.answer_criterion: Give Lean proofs deciding the displayed uniform-existence proposition for each of \(D=\gamma\) and \(D=U\). A positive proof supplies one learner, universal polynomial constants, termination/resource bounds, a valid finite predictor and the learning guarantee for every parameter and target. A negative proof negates that full existence statement: for every candidate learner and polynomial constants, show a violating parameter/target or resource requirement. A conditional lower bound proves only the corresponding implication unless its assumption is also established. A restriction to statistical-query learners, proper hypotheses, fixed \(k\), a positive margin or a different sample source does not by itself resolve these propositions. State the model transfer for any invoked bound. The answer is a pair of exact truth values; no numerical approximation or unspecified asymptotic exponent counts as a resolution.

context_blocks.text: The selected question is in the related-work discussion of the 2025 paper. Its antecedent distributions are Gaussian inputs and the uniform Boolean cube. The original card title mentioned factorizable distributions, which describe the surrounding paper’s main two-halfspace margin theorem; that title did not describe the selected question. The revised title restores the source scope.

An individual linear inequality is a simple classifier. An intersection accepts only points satisfying every inequality, while a rejected example does not say which condition failed. The desired learner receives labeled examples and may output any efficient predictor, rather than having to reconstruct the hidden inequalities.

The 2025 paper’s main result assumes two component halfspaces, a positive data margin, and a factorization relative to the subspace of relevant directions. Those are additional promises. Its theorem therefore does not resolve the separate question about a variable number of arbitrary affine halfspaces under the two known distributions.

Alman–Patel–Servedio’s 2026 Theorem 1 learns arbitrary Boolean functions of \(k\) halfspaces from random examples under any distribution in time \(\operatorname{poly}(2^{\sqrt n(\log n)^{O(k)}},1/\varepsilon,\log(1/\delta))\). The paper specifically notes the previously missing subexponential bound for two halfspaces on the uniform cube at \(\varepsilon=1/n\). This is substantial progress, but the displayed bound is not polynomial in \(n,k,1/\varepsilon\).

The STOC 2026 Gaussian sparsification theorem has learning applications for intersections with bounded geometric width, meaning the defining hyperplanes have a bounded distance from the origin in its stated representation. Its constants depend on width and accuracy. That result does not supply a single polynomial bound for arbitrary thresholds and arbitrary accuracy in the current question.

The May 2026 proper agnostic learner for Gaussian functions of halfspaces also includes realizable labels as a special case. However its dimension exponent depends on the number of halfspaces and inverse error, and it has an additional parameter-dependent term. The output restriction is stronger than needed here, but the running-time guarantee does not meet the fully polynomial target.

cards.title: Distribution-free learning of two margin halfspaces
cards.formal: Does there exist one uniform randomized learner and one polynomial \(p\) with the following guarantee? For every dimension \(d\geq 1\), every \(0<\gamma,\varepsilon<1\), and every distribution \(D\) satisfying the realizability and margin promises below, the learner receives independent labeled examples from \(D\) and, within \(p(d,\lceil1/\gamma\rceil,\lceil1/\varepsilon\rceil)\) operations, outputs a hypothesis \(h\) such that \[\Pr_{\text{samples, learner}}\!\left[\Pr_{(x,y)\sim D}[h(x)\ne y]\leq\varepsilon\right]\geq 2/3.\] The hypothesis may be improper, but its evaluation on a new point must also take polynomial time in these parameters. No factorization or other restriction on the example distribution is imposed beyond the stated promises.
cards.why: This asks whether the simplest intersection of linear classification rules remains efficiently learnable from ordinary examples under arbitrary distributions. A positive answer would remove a distributional assumption from a central margin-learning model; a negative answer would establish a computational obstruction even when the learner may use any efficiently evaluable representation.
cards.status_note: The 2025 source explicitly describes the general margin-learning question as open. On 13 September 2026, a targeted small-text search and the July revisions of two 2026 abstracts did not supply a resolution of the fixed-two polynomial-time target. The 2026 proofs and their complete lower-bound parameter regimes were not independently checked; status remains source_open.

sentences: The intersection of two halfspaces labels a point positively when both linear inequalities hold.
This question asks whether such labels can be learned in polynomial time from independent examples under any distribution with a margin from both boundaries.
The learner may output a different kind of hypothesis, provided that predictions remain efficient.
The 2025 source proves efficient learning under an extra factorization assumption, while two 2026 preprints report broader bounds that do not by themselves meet this polynomial target.
A resolution would determine whether two linear rules can be learned efficiently without favorable structure in the example distribution.

cards.definitions: The instance distribution is a Borel probability distribution on \(\mathbb R^{d}\times\{-1,+1\}\). There exist unknown unit vectors \(u,v\in\mathbb R^{d}\) and thresholds \(a,b\in\mathbb R\) such that, almost surely, \(\|x\|_{2}\leq1\), \(|\langle u,x\rangle+a|\geq\gamma\), \(|\langle v,x\rangle+b|\geq\gamma\), and \(y=+1\) precisely when both \(\langle u,x\rangle+a\geq0\) and \(\langle v,x\rangle+b\geq0\). In particular the margin promise applies to both defining hyperplanes, including on negatively labeled examples. The learner receives \(d,\gamma,\varepsilon\) and a sample oracle for independent draws from \(D\); it does not receive the unknown vectors, thresholds, a description of \(D\), membership queries or statistical-query oracles. Time is measured in the real-arithmetic model for the continuous-example formulation: a finite uniform program, with rational constants, exact real registers, integer indexing, arithmetic \(+, -, \times, /\) (division only by nonzero values), comparisons and independent fair random bits. Each arithmetic operation, comparison, register access and random bit costs one step; obtaining and reading a sample costs \(d+1\) steps. No operation extracts arbitrarily many bits of a real number in one step. The learner outputs a finite description of a deterministic prediction program together with finitely many stored real parameters; description length, storage, sample count, training time and evaluation time must obey fixed polynomial bounds. All bounds are worst-case over samples and internal randomness; only the accuracy guarantee is probabilistic. This explicitly fixes the arithmetic-cost convention for the source model, rather than asserting a finite-bit running-time theorem for arbitrary-precision real inputs.

context_blocks.text: A single separating hyperplane with a margin is a basic tractable classification model. Intersecting two such regions is already a substantial test of distribution-independent learning: allowing an arbitrary output hypothesis removes the requirement to recover two separating hyperplanes themselves.

Diakonikolas, Ma, Ren and Tzamos obtain an efficient learner when the distribution factors between the span of the two normal vectors and its orthogonal complement. Their general-model discussion on printed page 1473 leaves the distribution-free margin problem unresolved. The factorization promise is an additional assumption, not a consequence of a geometric margin.

A July 2026 revision by Alman, Patel and Servedio reports subexponential-time distribution-free learning for Boolean functions of a fixed number of halfspaces. That running time does not meet the polynomial bound asked here.

A separate July 2026 revision by Patel and Vempala reports a margin-sensitive algorithm for intersections of a variable number of halfspaces. Its abstract does not establish a polynomial-time learner for two halfspaces; its discussion of matching lower bounds cannot be transferred to the fixed-two case without checking their parameter range.

A negative answer must be unconditional for this model; hardness restricted to proper learners, statistical-query learners, a growing number of halfspaces, or an additional complexity assumption does not refute the statement.

cards.title: One-way functions from hardness of learning P/poly
cards.formal: Does worst-case computational hardness of distribution-free PAC learning of polynomial-size Boolean circuits from random labeled examples imply the existence of one-way functions? Precisely, let \(\mathsf{Learn}_{\mathrm{circ}}\) be the size-parameterized uniform learning assertion below, and let \(\mathsf{OWF}\) mean the existence of an ordinary uniformly computable one-way function secure against every uniform probabilistic polynomial-time inverter. The target is \[\neg\mathsf{Learn}_{\mathrm{circ}}\ \Longrightarrow\ \mathsf{OWF}.\] Equivalently, would the nonexistence of all such one-way functions guarantee an efficient learner for every target circuit and every example distribution? Hardness here is the failure of efficient learning in the worst case over targets and distributions; no efficiently samplable distribution of hard target descriptions, depth promise on those descriptions, or hardness reduction from SAT is assumed.

source_formulation.text: Does worst-case hardness of efficiently learning polynomial-size circuits from random examples imply the existence of one-way functions?
source_formulation.caption: Editorial paraphrase

cards.why: One-way functions provide the basic computational ingredient for much of classical private-key cryptography. The question asks whether failure of a general-purpose circuit learner is already enough to supply that ingredient, without assuming that hard target functions can be efficiently generated at random.

The 2025 journal metadata/abstract were checked, but subscription full text was unavailable. Bounded checks through 16 September 2026 found no matching resolution, so current status remains uncertain. Ordinary uniform strong OWF security and all learning parameters are explicit in the formulation.

cards.definitions:
Fix ordinary acyclic one-output Boolean circuits with two-input AND/OR gates, one-input NOT gates and constants, together with a standard effective binary encoding. For integers \(n\ge1\), \(s\ge n+1\), let \(\mathcal C(n,s)\) be all functions \(f:\{0,1\}^n\to\{0,1\}\) represented by such a circuit with at most \(s\) input nodes and gates in total. Polynomial-size circuit families, with no uniform construction requirement across lengths, form \(\mathrm{P/poly}\). The public bound \(s\) exposes the source’s usual polynomial-in-target-size learning convention; the hidden target description is not an input to the learner.

\(\mathsf{Learn}_{\mathrm{circ}}\) means that there exist one randomized classical Turing machine \(A\) and one polynomial \(p\) such that, for all \(n,s\) as above, all integers \(a,b\ge3\), all \(f\in\mathcal C(n,s)\), and all probability distributions \(D\) on \(\{0,1\}^n\), the following holds. Given \(1^n,1^s,1^a,1^b\) and access only to independent examples \((x,f(x))\), \(x\sim D\), the machine runs for at most \(p(n+s+a+b)\) steps on every execution and outputs a deterministic ordinary Boolean circuit \(h\) with \[\Pr_{A,\,\text{examples}}\left[\Pr_{x\sim D}[h(x)\ne f(x)]\le1/a\right]\ge1-1/b.\] The outer randomness consists of the training draws and independent fair machine coins; the inner draw is fresh. Example requests, reading their bits, all computation and output bits count toward the bound. The hypothesis may have size larger than \(s\), but its description and evaluation remain polynomially bounded by the learning time. It needs no further samples or access to \(f\) when evaluated. It is not required to reconstruct the target circuit, identify a unique representation, or be a member of the size-\(s\) class. This avoids imposing proper learning at the prescribed size. The learner has no membership queries, equivalence queries, nonuniform advice or code for sampling \(D\). The example source supplies independent draws even for distributions with no short sampling program. Labels are noiseless values of one fixed target. Arbitrarily large inverse-error and inverse-failure parameters \(a,b\) express ordinary PAC accuracy/confidence. Worst-case hardness is the logical negation of this uniform guarantee, not a lower bound against one particular learner or one restricted type of output.

\(\mathsf{OWF}\) means that there exist a polynomial-time computable length function \(\ell\) and one deterministic polynomial-time machine \(F\) giving maps \(F_n:\{0,1\}^n\to\{0,1\}^{\ell(n)}\), such that for every uniform randomized polynomial-time machine \(I\) and every integer \(k\ge1\), there is \(N_{I,k}\) for which, for all \(n\ge N_{I,k}\), \[\Pr_{x\sim U_n,\,I}\big[I(1^n,F_n(x))\in\{0,1\}^n\ \land\ F_n(I(1^n,F_n(x)))=F_n(x)\big]\le n^{-k}.\] In this display the inverter is run once and its returned string is reused in both tests. \(U_n\) is the uniform distribution on \(n\)-bit strings, independent of inverter coins. Equivalently the event says that the one returned string is any length-\(n\) preimage of \(F_n(x)\), not necessarily \(x\) itself. Invalid output is failure. Evaluation of the family is uniform in \(n\), with no secret key, trapdoor or advice; \(1^n\) tells the inverter the input length. Its running time is polynomial in \(n\). The probability bound is negligible: it is eventually below every inverse power. This is the ordinary all-sufficiently-large-lengths strong one-way notion, not only security on infinitely many lengths. These uniformity and length conventions are made explicit because later learning characterizations use several different variants. No efficient transformation with a specified runtime overhead between witnesses is additionally requested; the target is the existential implication itself.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove the displayed implication in Lean, or prove its logical negation \(\neg\mathsf{Learn}_{\mathrm{circ}}\land\neg\mathsf{OWF}\). A positive result must derive a single uniform one-way family with negligible inversion probability at all sufficiently large lengths from the stated unrestricted worst-case learning failure. It may equivalently prove a distribution-free learner from nonexistence of such families, but the learner must handle every target and distribution, not merely a samplable average or a special low-description-complexity promise. A result giving only an auxiliary-input primitive or infinitely-often security is a different conclusion unless its upgrade to the stated notion is proved. An oracle-relative separation or a limitation on a specified reduction method alone does not refute the ordinary implication. This is an existence question with exact logical quantifiers, not a numerical approximation problem.

context_blocks.text: The forward evaluation of a hidden target circuit is easy when its description is known. Learning is different: from observed input-output examples the learner must build a predictor that works on future draws. The challenge is computational, since a polynomial-size description and enough noiseless examples already give a finite statistical learning problem.

One-way functions are known to yield pseudorandom functions and thereby hard circuit-learning tasks. The reverse direction in this card starts with only failure of a worst-case learner. The source contrasts that question with classical equivalences based on average-case learning hardness, where an efficient process chooses the hidden target from a distribution.

The source proves a worst-case/average-case robustness theorem for learning the stronger concept classes EXP/poly and PSPACE/poly. The corresponding decision-complexity consequences concern those stronger classes. They do not establish that every worst-case obstruction for ordinary polynomial-size circuits contains cryptographic average-case hardness.

FOCS 2023 Hirahara–Nanashima extends learning under nonexistence of one-way functions to richer agnostic and distribution-learning models. Its average-case guarantees sample the hidden advice or target distribution. Its worst-case guarantees have runtime exponential in the computational depth of the hidden description, where depth compares a time-bounded shortest description with an unbounded shortest description. That depth need not be logarithmic for arbitrary target descriptions.

ITCS 2025 Liu–Mazor–Pass Theorem 6 gives a worst-case characterization using black-box PAC learning under an explicit computational-shallowness promise on the joint sampler and predictor description. It also uses failure of infinitely-often polynomial-time learning for ordinary one-way functions. The theorem is stronger than an average-case-only analogy, but its promise and length quantifiers do not supply the unrestricted antecedent of this card.

STOC 2026 Hirahara–Nanashima studies approximation of the minimum program description needed for agnostic learning. Its Theorem 1.5 connects average-case hardness of the GapLearn decision problem to infinitely-often one-way functions, with an approximation factor governed by advice complexity of sampling. A minimum-description decision problem, average-case input choice and infinitely-often security are each distinct from this card’s exact implication.

The 2021 full source expressly retains the question. The 2025 journal version’s metadata and abstract were checked, but its subscription full text was not available. The checked 2023–2026 theorems clarify important partial connections without a matching resolution; the card therefore records uncertain current status rather than treating a bounded literature search as proof of openness.

The forward evaluation of a hidden target circuit is easy when its description is known. Learning is different: from observed input-output examples the learner must build a predictor that works on future draws. The challenge is computational, since a polynomial-size description and enough noiseless examples already give a finite statistical learning problem.

One-way functions are known to yield pseudorandom functions and thereby hard circuit-learning tasks. The reverse direction in this card starts with only failure of a worst-case learner. The source contrasts that question with classical equivalences based on average-case learning hardness, where an efficient process chooses the hidden target from a distribution.

The source proves a worst-case/average-case robustness theorem for learning the stronger concept classes EXP/poly and PSPACE/poly. The corresponding decision-complexity consequences concern those stronger classes. They do not establish that every worst-case obstruction for ordinary polynomial-size circuits contains cryptographic average-case hardness.

FOCS 2023 Hirahara–Nanashima extends learning under nonexistence of one-way functions to richer agnostic and distribution-learning models. Its average-case guarantees sample the hidden advice or target distribution. Its worst-case guarantees have runtime exponential in the computational depth of the hidden description, where depth compares a time-bounded shortest description with an unbounded shortest description. That depth need not be logarithmic for arbitrary target descriptions.

ITCS 2025 Liu–Mazor–Pass Theorem 6 gives a worst-case characterization using black-box PAC learning under an explicit computational-shallowness promise on the joint sampler and predictor description. It also uses failure of infinitely-often polynomial-time learning for ordinary one-way functions. The theorem is stronger than an average-case-only analogy, but its promise and length quantifiers do not supply the unrestricted antecedent of this card.

STOC 2026 Hirahara–Nanashima studies approximation of the minimum program description needed for agnostic learning. Its Theorem 1.5 connects average-case hardness of the GapLearn decision problem to infinitely-often one-way functions, with an approximation factor governed by advice complexity of sampling. A minimum-description decision problem, average-case input choice and infinitely-often security are each distinct from this card’s exact implication.

The 2021 full source expressly retains the question. The 2025 journal version’s metadata and abstract were checked, but its subscription full text was not available. The checked 2023–2026 theorems clarify important partial connections without a matching resolution; the card therefore records uncertain current status rather than treating a bounded literature search as proof of openness.

cards.title: Nontrivial agnostic membership-query learning of \(\mathrm{ACC}^{0}\)
cards.formal: Can polynomial-size constant-depth modular circuits be agnostically learned under uniform inputs using membership queries in time \(2^n/n^{\omega(1)}\)? Precisely, for every fixed depth bound \(d\ge1\), fixed modulus \(m\ge2\), and fixed integer size exponent \(k\ge1\), do there exist one uniform randomized oracle Turing machine \(A_{d,m,k}\), an integer \(n_0\), and a saving function \(\sigma:\mathbb N_{\ge2}\to[0,\infty)\) such that \(\sigma(n)/\log_2 n\to\infty\) and the following holds? For every \(n\ge n_0\) and every joint distribution \(D\) on \(\{0,1\}^n\times\{-1,+1\}\) whose first marginal is uniform, \(A_{d,m,k}\), given \(1^n\) and the conditional-label oracle described below, runs in worst-case time at most \(2^{n-\sigma(n)}\) and outputs a hypothesis \(h\) satisfying \[\Pr\left[\operatorname{corr}_D(h)\ge \max_{c\in\operatorname{ACC}_{d,m,k}(n)}\operatorname{corr}_D(c)-2^{-n^{99/100}}\right]\ge\frac13,\qquad \operatorname{corr}_D(g):=\mathbb E_{(x,y)\sim D}[g(x)y].\] All machine coins and oracle responses are included in this probability. The success constant \(1/3\) is the literal consequence of the source’s full-learning convention \(1-\delta\) and its assignment \(\delta=2/3\); it is recorded explicitly rather than silently exchanged with the separate weak-learning convention.

cards.definitions:
An \(\operatorname{ACC}_{d,m,k}(n)\) circuit is a finite acyclic circuit with \(n\) input bits, constants, unbounded-fan-in AND and OR gates, one-input NOT gates, and unbounded-fan-in \(\mathrm{MOD}_m\) gates. A \(\mathrm{MOD}_m\) gate returns one exactly when the number of its one-valued inputs is divisible by \(m\). There are at most \(d\) gates along each input-to-output path and at most \(n^k\) internal gates and wires in total. Its output bit is converted to \(-1,+1\) by \(b\mapsto2b-1\). Fix an effective binary encoding of gates and their ordered incoming wires. These fixed-depth, fixed-modulus, polynomial-size classes give the usual \(\mathrm{ACC}^0\) target when the fixed parameters vary. Gate-count versus wire-count conventions change polynomial size exponents only; the question quantifies over every exponent. The parameters are fixed before input length and may determine the learner and its saving; neither depth nor modulus grows with \(n\). Hidden comparator circuits may be chosen independently at different lengths and need not form a uniformly constructible family. No target circuit description is given to the learner.

The joint distribution \(D\) is otherwise arbitrary. For each chosen query \(z\in\{0,1\}^n\), the oracle returns one fresh label sampled from \(D(Y\mid X=z)\), independently of its earlier samples conditional on the submitted queries. Queries may adapt to previous answers, and repeated queries need not agree. The uniform marginal gives every \(z\) positive probability, so all conditional label distributions are defined. Labels may be deterministic, stochastic, noisy, or inconsistent with every comparator circuit; no realizability promise is made. The learner knows the uniform marginal and can itself draw uniform inputs. It has no sampler description for the label probabilities, equivalence oracle, circuit advice, or oracle access to an optimal comparator. Correlation lies in \([-1,1]\), and the maximum exists because the comparator set is finite and nonempty. For \(\{-1,+1\}\)-valued functions, zero-one error equals \((1-\operatorname{corr})/2\); thus the displayed correlation slack is excess prediction error at most \(2^{-n^{99/100}}/2\), rather than a multiplicative approximation to optimum error.

The output is a finite description of an ordinary Boolean circuit with AND, OR and NOT gates, interpreted as \(h:\{0,1\}^n\to\{-1,+1\}\). The hypothesis need not be an ACC circuit, have depth \(d\), or have size \(n^k\); this is improper learning. Its description is counted in the learner’s running time, and it is evaluated without further training queries. Using ordinary finite circuits makes the usual effectively evaluable hypothesis convention explicit. All query writing and reading, fair random bits, bit computation and output writing count toward worst-case running time; one submitted label is one oracle response, and the oracle’s internal generation cost is not charged. Consequently the number of queries is bounded by the same time. There is no real-arithmetic unit-cost computation in the learner. The exponential accuracy threshold is a mathematical success condition fixed by \(n\), not an exact irrational input that must be encoded or compared by the machine.

The expression \(2^n/n^{\omega(1)}\) means that a single learner for each fixed \((d,m,k)\) has a saving \(\sigma(n)\) whose ratio to \(\log_2 n\) tends to infinity: for every real \(B>0\), eventually \(\sigma(n)\ge B\log_2 n\). The saving is a runtime-bound witness, not an additional oracle or input. Finite exceptional lengths are allowed. A fixed-factor improvement or division by one fixed power of \(n\) is insufficient. Polynomial factors in an otherwise qualifying time can be absorbed into a smaller saving with the same limit. No efficient procedure for constructing the learner uniformly from the fixed depth, modulus and size exponent is additionally requested.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a Lean-checked proof of the displayed existence statement, or of its full logical negation: some fixed \((d,m,k)\) admits no uniform learner with the stated eventual superlogarithmic saving and correlation guarantee simultaneously for all uniform-marginal label distributions. A positive answer must meet the specified shrinking accuracy, the literal full-learning success constant, the conditional-query interface and worst-case total time, including a finite evaluable output. Constant-error learning, realizable-only learning, a fixed polynomial-factor saving or a multiplicative optimum-error factor does not meet this agnostic target. A lower bound against a restricted query method or a conditional cryptographic obstruction is not the unconditional negation unless the additional assumption is also proved. This is an exact asymptotic yes/no statement, not a request to approximate a numerical quantity.

context_blocks.text: Agnostic learning compares the returned predictor with the best member of a chosen circuit class, while allowing the observed labels to be generated by an arbitrary process. Membership queries let the learner choose which input is labeled; they do not reveal a target circuit or guarantee that an exact circuit representation exists. The original paper fixes both the extremely small correlation slack and the confidence parameter when defining its nontrivial-time problem.

The source explicitly states that the ACC⁰ problem is open even with uniform inputs and even without the agnostic requirement. This card retains the agnostic question selected in its title and records the source’s uniform-input version. It does not replace the comparator by only prime-modulus circuits or by a restricted family of symmetric-polynomial gates.

Carmosino–Impagliazzo–Kabanets–Kolokolova obtain quasipolynomial-time query learning for prime-modulus AC⁰[q] with a polylogarithmic multiplicative factor on optimum error. That is a meaningful earlier result, but both the restricted modulus and the multiplicative error criterion differ from full ACC⁰ agnostic learning with the additive slack specified here.

Karchmer’s positive results treat several circuit classes built from restricted low-degree threshold or symmetric-polynomial functions. Those classes include functions outside earlier families, but the published statement does not contain all polynomial-size ACC⁰ circuits. The paper separately identifies that missing full class as a frontier question.

The full-learning definition gives success at least 1−δ and then sets δ to 2/3. The separate weak-learner definition uses success at least 2/3. These are distinct displays in the source. This record preserves the literal full-learning guarantee 1/3 and marks the convention explicitly; it does not assume a typographical correction or silently use the weak definition as the target.

The original arXiv record still lists only its November 2023 version, and the checked published ALT 2024 text contains the question. Bounded later-work searches through September 2026 found no matching theorem, but that search is not a proof of continued openness. Current status is therefore recorded as uncertain.

cards.title: Learning decision trees from uniform random examples in polynomial time
cards.formal: Does there exist one uniform classical randomized learner \(A\) and universal positive integers \(B,C\) such that, for every \(n,s\ge1\), \(t\ge3\), and every Boolean function \(f:\{0,1\}^n\to\{0,1\}\) represented by a decision tree with at most \(s\) nodes, \(A\), given \(1^n,1^s,1^t\) and independent uniform examples labeled by \(f\), runs on every execution for at most \(B(n+s+t)^C\) steps and outputs a Boolean circuit \(h\) satisfying \[\Pr_{A,\,\mathrm{examples}}\left[\Pr_{x\sim U_n}[h(x)\ne f(x)]\le\frac1t\right]\ge\frac23?\] The hypothesis may be an arbitrary efficiently evaluable circuit. The target remains the previously selected polynomial-time sample-only uniform-PAC question; reciprocal-integer error \(\varepsilon=1/t\) makes the accuracy encoding explicit.
cards.definitions:
A Boolean decision tree is a finite rooted binary tree. Each internal node is labeled by a coordinate index in \([n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}\) and has two children, with outgoing edges labeled zero and one; each leaf is labeled by an output bit. On input \(x\), evaluation follows the edge specified by the queried bit at each internal node until it reaches a leaf, whose bit is the output. Coordinates may occur repeatedly and there is no depth, monotonicity, balance, or randomness promise on the hidden tree. Size counts all nodes, as in the existing card. A full branching binary tree with \(\ell\) leaves has \(2\ell-1\) nodes, so the leaf-count convention used by the backdoor-defense source changes this polynomial-size question only by a constant factor. The size bound and input dimension are public; the target tree, its structure and its node labels are not supplied.

\(U_n\) is uniform on \(\{0,1\}^n\). Each example request yields a fresh independent \((x,f(x))\), \(x\sim U_n\), under one fixed target. Labels are exact and noiseless. Requests may be scheduled adaptively, but the learner cannot choose the input to be labeled or require correlations between successive inputs. In particular, there is no membership oracle, equivalence oracle or free access to the tree representation. The learner uses independent fair random bits and no length-dependent advice. Its guarantee is required for every target tree, rather than for a random tree or a randomly perturbed input distribution. The outer probability is confidence over the training draws and internal coins; the inner error probability concerns a fresh independent uniform input.

An output hypothesis is a finite acyclic circuit on the same \(n\) bits, using two-input AND/OR, one-input NOT and constant gates in a fixed effective binary encoding. It need not be a tree or have size at most \(s\). The output is evaluated without further samples, the hidden target or any unreported target-dependent state. This is improper predictive learning, not exact tree identification or minimum-size reconstruction. The learner is a probabilistic multitape Turing machine with unary public parameters; every bit operation, request, example read, stored-data access, random bit and output bit is counted. One fixed worst-case bound applies across all parameters and sample histories; the same bound also limits sample count and output length. Circuit evaluation takes polynomial time in the written circuit size. The example source’s internal sampling cost is not charged. Unlimited computation on polynomially many examples does not meet the requirement.

The error parameter ranges over \(1/t\), \(t\ge3\). For any desired real \(\varepsilon\in(0,1)\), choosing \(t=\max\{3,\lceil1/\varepsilon\rceil\}\) yields error at most \(\varepsilon\) with only polynomial dependence on \(1/\varepsilon\). Thus this encoding retains the ordinary arbitrary-accuracy learning target without treating an arbitrarily long rational spelling as a constant-cost input. Fixed confidence \(2/3\) is retained. The universal polynomial has no degree depending on \(s\), tree depth, the particular target or the accuracy parameter. The problem is a yes/no existence statement; there is no unspecified numerical optimization precision.

context_blocks.text: Decision trees describe classification through simple successive tests of individual input bits. A small tree may nevertheless hide complicated interactions among the variables. The question asks whether uniform random observations suffice for efficient prediction, even when the learner is free to return a representation different from a tree.

At a fixed node bound, the number of tree descriptions is at most exponential in a polynomial in the size and logarithm of the input dimension. Consequently the realizable information-theoretic sample requirement is polynomial in size, dimension and inverse error. The desired theorem concerns computation as well as data, rather than mere statistical identifiability.

A tree with at most \(s\) nodes has at most \(s\) leaves and can be expressed as a DNF with at most \(s\) terms. Known uniform-example DNF learners therefore provide quasipolynomial algorithms in the polynomial-size regime, as summarized by Servedio’s Theorem 13. That is a useful general upper bound, but a dimension exponent growing logarithmically with size or inverse error is not the requested one fixed polynomial.

Kalai–Teng’s Theorem 1 learns every target tree efficiently for most product distributions obtained by randomly perturbing their coordinate means by a fixed positive amount. Its probability is over both the perturbation and the training examples. The exact vector of uniform means is a particular unperturbed point, so success for almost all perturbed means does not imply the guarantee at that point. The theorem is explicitly improper and outputs a polynomial threshold function.

The ITCS 2025 source again states that efficient uniform-PAC learning of polynomial-size trees is unknown in the sample-only model. Its positive backdoor-defense theorem gives the defender the represented tree, which allows direct examination and evaluation. That observation model differs from receiving only labeled examples of a hidden tree. A fast detector with the representation supplied is not a PAC learner for this card.

Membership queries make uniform decision-tree learning easier because they provide labels at chosen inputs. Proper-learning problems impose a different restriction by requiring a tree output. This target has the passive observation interface and permits arbitrary Boolean circuit output; hardness for a restricted output class cannot be transferred just by matching the words “decision tree learning.”

The checked May 2026 paper on product spaces explicitly allows label queries at arbitrary inputs in §3. Its main size bound also depends on the optimal tree’s maximum and average depths and can be quasipolynomial even for logarithmic-depth trees. These are useful guarantees for the studied greedy procedure, but neither the interface nor the bound supplies the full polynomial sample-only learner.

Every \(k\)-junta has a decision tree with at most \(2^{k+1}-1\) nodes. Thus the desired learner would give time polynomial in \(n,2^k,1/\varepsilon\) for arbitrary juntas from uniform examples. The 2025 survey describes that junta problem as a continuing obstacle. This is a consequence of the tree-learning target, not an added promise that the tree must depend on few variables.

cards.why: Settle the sample-only computational learnability of a canonical interpretable Boolean model.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove in Lean that the stated uniform learner and universal polynomial bound exist, or prove their logical negation: every proposed machine and constants fail for some allowed dimension, size, accuracy and target, in either the worst-case resource guarantee or the PAC success condition. A positive answer must use only independent uniform labeled examples and cover every target tree. Proper-learning hardness, minimum-consistent-tree hardness, or a lower bound for one greedy heuristic does not rule out the allowed arbitrary circuit output. A result under an unproved computational assumption proves only the corresponding conditional negation. Membership-query learning, random-tree learning, smoothed-distribution learning and correlated-example algorithms have different access or target promises and are not accepted as a resolution of the displayed statement.

Every \(k\)-junta has a decision tree with at most \(2^{k+1}-1\) nodes. Thus the desired learner would give time polynomial in \(n,2^k,1/\varepsilon\) for arbitrary juntas from uniform examples. The 2025 survey describes that junta problem as a continuing obstacle. This is a consequence of the tree-learning target, not an added promise that the tree must depend on few variables.

cards.title: Sample-optimal Gaussian graphical model learning in polynomial time
cards.formal: Can general Gaussian conditional-independence graphs be learned in uniform polynomial time using, up to a universal constant factor, the information-theoretically optimal number of independent observations? For integers \(p\ge2\), \(1\le d\le p-1\), \(r\ge2\), and rational \(0<\kappa<1\), let \(\mathcal G(p,d,\kappa)\) be the Gaussian family defined below and let \(m^*(p,d,\kappa,r)\) be its minimax sample count for exact graph recovery with failure probability at most \(2^{-r}\), allowing unrestricted measurable estimators. Is there one uniform randomized algorithm \(A\) and constants \(C,B,a\ge1\) such that, for every parameter choice and every \(P\in\mathcal G(p,d,\kappa)\), \(A(p,d,\kappa,r)\) returns its exact graph with probability at least \(1-2^{-r}\), draws at most \(\lceil C m^*(p,d,\kappa,r)\rceil\) independent samples, and uses at most \[B\bigl(p+d+\lceil\kappa^{-1}\rceil+r+L\bigr)^a\] real-arithmetic operations, including sample loading and output, where \(L\) is the binary encoding length of \(\kappa\)? The exponent and constants must be independent of every parameter and of the unknown distribution. This retains the general sample-optimal computational question from the source’s conclusion; bounded-degree recovery is already treated there. The minimax definition does not presume that the commonly quoted \(d\log p/\kappa^2\) sample scale is sharp in all joint parameter regimes.

source_formulation.text: Can the information-theoretically optimal independent-sample count for general Gaussian graph recovery be attained by a polynomial-time algorithm?
source_formulation.caption: Editorial paraphrase

cards.why: Sparse conditional dependence can be statistically identifiable even when variables are extremely correlated. Recovering that graph from few observations is useful only if the necessary search is computationally affordable. The problem asks whether uniformly efficient computation must pay an extra sample cost without regularity assumptions on the covariance.
cards.status_note: The source already gives sample-efficient polynomial-time recovery for bounded degree, but with a degree-dependent runtime exponent. COLT 2024 Remark 43 gives a conditional statistical-computational gap under Conjecture 33; that assumption is not asserted true. A 2026 primary paper still distinguishes the independent-sample difficulty while solving a different Glauber-trajectory problem. No unconditional resolution of the displayed uniform arithmetic-time target was checked through 16 September 2026. Numerical precision and cross-model hardness transfers are explicitly not certified.

sentences: The problem asks whether sparse Gaussian conditional-independence graphs can be recovered in polynomial time with an information-theoretically optimal number of independent samples.
The statement allows arbitrary means and condition numbers and requires every edge and nonedge to be identified correctly.
Sample optimality is defined by a minimax benchmark that retains degree, normalized edge strength and confidence without assuming a universally sharp formula.
Known degree-dependent algorithms, structural-subclass results, conditional hardness and trajectory-based algorithms each address a different part of the question.
A Lean resolution must establish or refute one uniform algorithm with both a universal sample factor and a fixed polynomial arithmetic-time bound.

cards.definitions:
A member \(P\) of \(\mathcal G(p,d,\kappa)\) is \(N(\mu,\Sigma)\), where \(\mu\in\mathbb R^p\) is arbitrary, \(\Sigma\) is a real symmetric positive definite \(p\times p\) covariance matrix, and \(\Theta=\Sigma^{-1}\) is its precision matrix. Its undirected graph has vertices \([p]=\{1,\ldots,p\}\) and an edge \(\{i,j\}\), for \(i\ne j\), exactly when \(\Theta_{ij}\ne0\). Every vertex has at most \(d\) neighbors, and every edge satisfies \[\frac{|\Theta_{ij}|}{\sqrt{\Theta_{ii}\Theta_{jj}}}\ge\kappa.\] This normalized precision entry is the magnitude of the corresponding partial correlation. For an empty graph the edge condition holds vacuously. The parameters are upper and lower promises, not assertions that degree equals \(d\) or minimum strength equals \(\kappa\). No eigenvalue, condition-number, variance, sign-pattern, incoherence, faithfulness, treewidth or walk-summability restriction is imposed. The learner is not given \(\mu,\Sigma,\Theta\), or a graph representation.

An observation is an entire vector \(X\in\mathbb R^p\) drawn from \(P\); observations are independent and identically distributed. The graph-recovery loss is zero exactly when all off-diagonal zero/nonzero decisions are correct, and one otherwise. Estimating covariance entries to a numerical tolerance is a different task. The probability in the guarantee includes the observations and internal randomness. The public failure tolerance is \(2^{-r}\); allowing all integers \(r\ge2\) keeps confidence variable. The graph output is its \(p\times p\) symmetric binary adjacency matrix with zero diagonal.

For a fixed \((p,d,\kappa,r)\), define \(m^*\) as the least nonnegative integer \(m\) for which some Borel-measurable randomized estimator from \((\mathbb R^p)^m\) to the finite set of labeled undirected graphs satisfies \[\inf_{P\in\mathcal G(p,d,\kappa)}\Pr_{X_1,\ldots,X_m\sim P}[\widehat G(X_1,\ldots,X_m)=G(P)]\ge1-2^{-r}.\] Randomization is an independent infinite fair-bit sequence, and the estimator must be measurable jointly in data and that sequence. It may depend arbitrarily on the four public parameters and has no computation bound; this defines an information benchmark, not a computational oracle. If the set of such sample counts were empty, set \(m^*=+\infty\); known finite sample upper bounds exclude that case for this family. The target algorithm receives neither \(m^*\) nor an optimal estimator. Its sample limit must hold on every possible observation and coin history, even if it adaptively decides when to stop. Padding an early stop with unused observations makes comparison with fixed-size estimators unambiguous.

Computation uses an explicitly chosen standard exact-real arithmetic convention. One finite uniform register program has rational constants in its code, discrete control and fair random bits. Copying, \(+,-,\times,\div\), comparison, branching and each control or output operation cost one unit; any division must be guarded at a zero denominator. Loading one observed vector costs \(p\) units. The algorithm outputs only finite bits for the adjacency matrix. It has no access to conditional samples, a Markov transition trajectory, matrix entries of the unknown distribution, exact expectations, optimization oracles, arbitrary real advice, floor/digit extraction, or an oracle deciding general real-number properties. The positive integers \(p,d,r\) are public unary inputs and \(\kappa\) is supplied by positive coprime binary numerator and denominator, with total bit length \(L\). Reading and translating these inputs are counted. The displayed worst-case operation bound applies to all sample and random-bit histories, not just in expectation.

This convention makes the source’s continuous-observation computational question precise without asserting equivalence to finite-bit Gaussian data. Exact Gaussian coordinates are generally not finite binary strings; the source does not prescribe a rounding budget. In particular, allowing arbitrary condition numbers in the distribution is material to numerical implementation. Any finite-precision result, or computational hardness assumption in another machine model, needs a justified relation to this arithmetic convention before it resolves the displayed proposition. Polynomial time means a single fixed exponent for variable \(d\); \(p^{O(d)}\) is insufficient. Sample optimality means a universal multiplicative factor, with no suppressed dependence on \(d,\kappa,r\) or logarithmic loss.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a Lean proof of the existence proposition or its full negation. An affirmative result must supply one uniform algorithm and constants, prove exact graph recovery over the entire promised Gaussian family, prove the universal constant-factor comparison with the defined information-theoretic minimum, and verify worst-case sample and arithmetic-time bounds. A negative result must rule out every such learner and constants on some allowed parameters or distribution. A conditional computational obstruction remains conditional unless its hypothesis is also proved. A \(p^{O(d)}\) method, a result only for a fixed degree, a polynomial-time method using more than a universal-factor sample overhead, or a theorem with extra spectral/sign assumptions does not suffice. Neither does learning from a Glauber trajectory establish the independent-observation guarantee. A closed form for \(m^*\) is useful but is not assumed in advance; any claimed closed form must be proved uniformly in its stated regime. The answer is an exact yes/no theorem, not a numerical estimate of a covariance matrix.

context_blocks.text: The graph records conditional dependence, not merely pairwise correlation: an edge is determined by a nonzero entry of the inverse covariance matrix. Strong correlations and poor conditioning are allowed. This explains why guarantees depending only on dimension, sparsity and normalized edge strength are stronger than many familiar covariance-estimation results.

The source’s DICE theorem gives exact recovery when \(m>2d+192\kappa^{-2}d\log p+64\kappa^{-2}\log(4d/\delta)\). Its neighborhood-search cost is \(O(p^{2d+1})\). Thus fixed-degree graphs have a polynomial-time guarantee, but the exponent is not uniform over growing degree.

The source explicitly qualifies statistical tightness when degree grows while minimum edge strength shrinks. Therefore its motivating abstract sentence cannot be read as an unresolved bounded-degree theorem, or its sample bound as a universally matching minimax formula. The current question retains the general computational issue using an explicit minimax benchmark.

Kelner–Koehler–Meka–Moitra provide fixed polynomial-time algorithms without condition-number bounds for attractive and walk-summable Gaussian models. These are genuine positive results for additional structural subclasses. Their assumptions do not cover every signed precision matrix in the present family.

COLT 2024 Kelner–Koehler–Meka–Rohatgi, Remark 43, gives conditional evidence of a sample-computation gap. Under its Conjecture 33 relating low-degree likelihood tests to polynomial-time detection for a spiked Wishart model, efficient general recovery would need nearly quadratic rather than linear dependence on sparsity in the relevant regime, even at constant normalized edge strength. The conjecture is not a proved theorem about arbitrary algorithms.

The hard family in that remark has covariance equal to identity plus a negative rank-one perturbation supported on a hidden sparse set. Exact graph recovery would distinguish it from the independent-coordinate null model. This is a stated reduction under a specific detection-hardness conjecture, not an unconditional archive-worthy impossibility. Its computational convention must also match any use against the real-arithmetic target.

The 2026 Shen–Wu–Majid–Moitra paper gives a polynomial-time method observing one Glauber trajectory, where coordinates are successively resampled conditional on the others. Its introduction still identifies efficient recovery from few independent samples as unresolved. A trajectory exposes update information that independent observations do not provide, so the newer theorem does not automatically answer the present question.
