cards.title: Distribution-free improper learning of two unrestricted halfspaces
cards.formal: Is there a single randomized learner that, for every distribution \(D\) on \(\{0,1\}^n\), every target \(f\) expressible as the intersection of two integer-weight halfspaces of total description length at most a supplied bound \(B\), and every rational \(0<\varepsilon<1/2\), uses only independent labeled examples from \(D\) to output a Boolean circuit \(H\) with \(\Pr_{x\sim D}[H(x)\ne f(x)]\le\varepsilon\) with probability at least \(2/3\), in time polynomial in \(n+B+\lceil1/\varepsilon\rceil+\operatorname{len}(\varepsilon)\)?
cards.definitions: A halfspace is \(h(x)=1\) exactly when \(\sum_{i} w_{i} x_{i}\ge \theta\), with \(w_i,\theta\in\mathbb{Z}\) in signed binary; equality is positive. The target f is the conjunction of two such predicates. Its description length is the bit length of a list of both weight vectors and thresholds, using self-delimiting binary integers. The learner receives n and B in unary and a rational \(\varepsilon\) with \(0<\varepsilon <1/2\) in binary. It is promised that f has at least one such description of length at most B, but receives neither that description nor its weights. An example oracle returns independent pairs \((x,f(x))\) with x sampled from an arbitrary fixed distribution D on \(\{0,1\}^{n}\). The learner receives only these labeled examples and its own independent fair coins. Each oracle call costs at least \(n+1\) steps to receive its bits; all further work is charged in Turing-machine bit steps. Membership queries, advice and descriptions or probability evaluations of D are absent. There must be a fixed polynomial P such that on every random tape the running time, and hence sample count and output length, are bounded by \(P(n+B+\lceil1/\varepsilon\rceil+\operatorname{len}(\varepsilon))\). Output a deterministic Boolean circuit \(H:\{0,1\}^{n}\to \{0,1\}\) in the explicit \(\mathrm{AND}/\mathrm{OR}/\mathrm{NOT}\) basis. The success condition is \(\Pr_{\mathrm{samples,coins}}[\Pr_{x\sim D}[H(x)\ne f(x)]\le\varepsilon]\ge2/3\), uniformly over \(n,B,\varepsilon ,D\) and every promised f. Circuit evaluation costs polynomial time in its output encoding. The hypothesis need not be an intersection of halfspaces. Encoding an arbitrary deterministic polynomial-time evaluator by its Boolean circuit preserves this unrestricted efficient-output convention.

context_blocks.text: A single halfspace is efficiently learnable, but combining only two thresholds introduces a longstanding computational obstacle. Allowing an arbitrary output representation avoids the known hardness of proper learning.

The existing TCS-6544 explicitly assumes a positive margin and polynomial dependence on its reciprocal. This candidate instead concerns unrestricted integer-weight thresholds on the Boolean cube. The distinction affects the running time and cannot be hidden behind their similar titles.

cards.title: PAC learning of finite automata under the uniform distribution
cards.formal: Are deterministic finite automata efficiently PAC learnable from independent uniformly distributed words and their acceptance bits? Use the ordinary finite-word, fixed-length uniform model. Does there exist one randomized classical Turing machine \(L\) and one polynomial \(p\) such that, for every alphabet size \(q\ge2\), word length \(n\ge1\), state bound \(s\ge1\), integers \(a,b\ge3\), and deterministic finite automaton \(M\) with at most \(s\) states over \(\Sigma_q=\{0,\ldots,q-1\}\), the following holds? Given \(1^q,1^n,1^s,1^a,1^b\) and access only to independent examples \((w,M(w))\) with \(w\sim U_{q,n}\), \(L\) runs in worst-case time at most \(p(q+n+s+a+b)\), and outputs a finite predictor \(h\) satisfying \[\Pr_{L,\,\mathrm{examples}}\left[\Pr_{w\sim U_{q,n}}[h(w)\ne M(w)]\le\frac1a\right]\ge1-\frac1b?\] The predictor may use any efficiently evaluable representation; it need not be an automaton. A 2021 theorem rules out this guarantee under a specified local-pseudorandom-generator assumption, already for binary alphabets. This card retains the unconditional algorithm-existence question, while recording that published conditional negative answer explicitly.

cards.definitions:
A deterministic finite automaton is a tuple \(M=(\Sigma_q,Q,q_0,F,\tau)\) with a nonempty finite state set \(Q\), \(|Q|\le s\), initial state \(q_0\in Q\), accepting states \(F\subseteq Q\), and a total transition function \(\tau:Q\times\Sigma_q\to Q\). Starting at \(q_0\), it reads the letters of a finite word from left to right and updates its current state by \(\tau\); \(M(w)=1\) exactly when its final state lies in \(F\), and otherwise \(M(w)=0\). The target transition table, states and accepting set are hidden. The public value \(s\) is an upper bound on the number of states, not the full target description. The source’s size convention is state count. A complete transition-table encoding has length polynomial in \(s\) and \(q\), so the explicit polynomial dependence on both parameters accounts for that representation.

\(U_{q,n}\) assigns probability \(q^{-n}\) to every word in \(\Sigma_q^n\); equivalently its \(n\) letters are independent and uniform in \(\Sigma_q\). Each oracle request supplies a fresh independent word and its deterministic acceptance bit under the same fixed \(M\). The learner may request more independent examples adaptively but cannot select the word to be labeled. It sees neither the final state nor the sequence of intermediate states. There are no membership queries, equivalence queries, counterexamples, nonuniform advice or random-target assumption. The guarantee must hold for every automaton, including arbitrarily chosen transition graphs and accepting sets. Randomness in the outer probability comes only from examples and the learner’s independent fair coins; the inner probability is error on a fresh uniform word. This is the realizable PAC model with noiseless labels. Parameters \(1/a\) and \(1/b\) range over inverse integers, which suffice to express every desired positive accuracy and failure tolerance by rounding downward.

For a concrete hypothesis interface, encode each letter in \(\lceil\log_2 q\rceil\) bits and let the output be an ordinary Boolean circuit on the resulting \(n\lceil\log_2 q\rceil\) bits. Its output on valid word encodings is \(h(w)\); values on unused letter codes are irrelevant. The circuit may use two-input AND/OR, one-input NOT and constant gates with a fixed effective binary encoding. Its description is written within the learning-time bound and is evaluated without examples or access to the target. This expresses unrestricted improper efficient prediction: the output is not constrained to at most \(s\) states or to a minimal consistent automaton. Uniformly polynomial-time evaluable finite predictors have ordinary polynomial-size circuit representations under the usual bit-computation convention. All bit operations, reading examples, fair random bits and output writing count toward the one polynomial bound, as does the number of example requests. The example oracle supplies the promised distribution; its own sampling computation is not charged. The same machine and polynomial work for all displayed parameters, lengths and targets.

Uniformity refers to words of the specified length, not to an impossible probability measure assigning equal mass to all of \(\Sigma_q^*\). The learner may depend on the public \(n\), and its guarantee is only over words of that length. Exact identification of the complete infinite regular language, prediction simultaneously at every length by one output, geometric length mixtures, and real-valued limit-average behavior on infinite words are different tasks. The arbitrary-finite-alphabet convention follows the source’s DFA and \(U^n\) definitions; the later hardness theorem applies already when \(q=2\). Computational efficiency is essential: the question does not merely ask for a finite or polynomial information-theoretic sample bound.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove the existence of \(L,p\) with the complete uniform guarantee in Lean, or prove its logical negation: for every proposed machine and polynomial, some allowed parameters and target violate the runtime, finite-output or PAC condition. A positive answer must allow every target automaton and observe only independent acceptance-labeled uniform words. A result for random transition graphs, additional state labels, membership queries or only a fixed bounded state count does not meet the statement. A negative answer under the local-PRG assumption is a conditional theorem and must retain that premise; it does not by itself prove the unconditional negation. Hardness of finding a smallest consistent DFA also does not exclude an arbitrary efficient predictor. The yes/no assertion has exact logical quantifiers and rational error/confidence tolerances; no numerical optimum is being approximated.

context_blocks.text: The 2019 source studies weighted limit-average automata, but its related-work paragraph cites Pitt’s older question about ordinary deterministic automata. The imported card refers to that ordinary Boolean acceptance problem. The paper’s own infinite-word impossibility and minimization results concern a different model and do not answer the selected question.

Knowing that every finite automaton has a finite transition table does not imply a polynomial learning algorithm. There are only finitely many targets at a fixed state bound, but computationally finding a useful predictor is a stronger requirement than having enough examples to identify one statistically. The target permits improper prediction and therefore does not ask for minimum-state reconstruction.

Daniely–Vardi Theorem 12 proves a conditional obstruction substantially stronger than failure of high-accuracy PAC learning: for every constants c, η>0, no efficient learner achieves error at most 1/2−1/n^c for all n^η-state DFAs under the uniform distribution on n-bit words, under their Assumption 1. The learning model allows arbitrary efficiently evaluable hypotheses. Consequently the obstruction is not merely a lower bound for proper automaton reconstruction.

Assumption 1 is the existence of Goldreich-style local pseudorandom generators with every constant polynomial stretch: for each constant \(t>1\), some constant locality \(k\) and Boolean predicate \(P\) make the length-\(N^t\) output formed by applying \(P\) to independent random ordered \(k\)-tuples of distinct seed positions computationally indistinguishable from uniform with advantage at most \(1/3\). The chosen tuples are public to the polynomial-time distinguisher. This is an unproved computational assumption, not a consequence of merely defining a finite automaton or a uniform distribution. The exact security convention is the named Assumption 1 of the cited paper; it is not added as a premise of this card’s unconditional target.

The official ALT 2026 paper on learning regular expressions explicitly lists uniform-distribution DFA PAC hardness under its local-PRG Assumption C and attributes that result to Daniely–Vardi. Its additional regular-expression results concern a different succinct representation: equivalent languages can require exponentially different description sizes. Thus the 2026 table corroborates the conditional status rather than proving the cryptographic premise.

Angluin–Chen’s 2015 positive result assumes a random transition graph and access to information about the terminal state reached by a sampled word. The acceptance bit does not identify that state. Likewise, the known polynomial algorithms with membership and equivalence queries use more information than the sampling-only oracle in this card. These distinctions prevent positive results in richer observation models from being substituted for the target.

The historical source described the question as open in 2019; that summary is incomplete after the 2021 conditional hardness theorem. The present record makes this development prominent and keeps current unconditional status uncertain. It does not claim that an unproved local-PRG assumption has been established or that a bounded literature check proves continued unconditional openness.

cards.title: Optimal multiclass regret versus Littlestone dimension
cards.formal: Determine, up to universal constant factors, the function \[R(d,T)=\sup\bigl\{R_T(H):\ X,Y\text{ nonempty sets},\ \varnothing\ne H\subseteq Y^X,\ \mathrm L(H)\le d\bigr\}\] for all integers \(T\ge d\ge1\). The supremum permits infinite instance sets, infinite label sets and arbitrary hypothesis classes. For the prediction game defined below, \[R_T(H)=\inf_A\ \sup_{(x_1,y_1),\ldots,(x_T,y_T)\in X\times Y}\left\{\sum_{t=1}^T(1-p_t(y_t))-\min_{h\in H}\sum_{t=1}^T\mathbf1\{h(x_t)\ne y_t\}\right\}.\] Here \(p_t=A_t((x_1,y_1),\ldots,(x_{t-1},y_{t-1}),x_t)\) is a probability distribution on labels. The infimum ranges over all causal prediction rules, without computational restrictions. Retain all logarithmic factors. This is the previously authorized quantitative reformulation of the source conjecture, which predicts \(R(d,T)=\Theta(\sqrt{dT})\).
cards.why: Would determine whether Littlestone dimension alone controls the exact minimax cost of multiclass sequential prediction, beyond the already known learnability characterization.
cards.status_note: The source’s 2023 universal multiclass conjecture is retained as context for the previously authorized full minimax-rate target. The sharper finite-label theorem is qualified by its explicitly stated minimax condition; Raman’s 2025 thesis retains the unrestricted binary issue. The checked May 2026 binary oracle result retains logarithmic factors, and no matching unrestricted multiclass resolution was found in the bounded search through 16 September 2026.

cards.definitions: A hypothesis \(h\in H\) assigns a label from \(Y\) to each instance in \(X\). A depth-\(r\) Littlestone tree is a complete binary tree with an instance at each internal node and two distinct labels from \(Y\) on that node's outgoing edges; the pair of labels may vary by node. The tree is shattered if every root-to-leaf path has one fixed hypothesis agreeing with all its edge labels on its instance points. The dimension \(\mathrm L(H)\) is the largest shattered depth, or infinity if depths are unbounded. On each round the adversary presents \(x_t\), the learner supplies \(p_t\), and the adversary then reveals \(y_t\). The learner observes the actual label before the next round and is charged expected zero-one loss \(1-p_t(y_t)\). It does not observe future instances. The adversary may react to \(p_t\); loss is the displayed expectation, not a reaction to a sampled label. The sequence need not be realizable by any hypothesis. The comparator is one fixed hypothesis chosen in hindsight, whose minimum loss exists since the possible losses are integers from zero to \(T\). A distribution here is a function \(p:Y\to[0,1]\) satisfying \(\sum_{y\in Y}p(y)=1\), with this sum defined as the supremum of sums over finite subsets. It automatically has at most countable positive support. This atomic convention does not increase the best possible regret relative to arbitrary probability measures with measurable singletons: any missing atom mass can be assigned to one fixed label, increasing no zero-one loss. All histories and rules are arbitrary set functions, so no topology or measurability structure on \(X,H\) is required. Rules may know \(H\) and \(T\), need not be proper, and have no runtime, memory, computability or finite-description bound. Infima and suprema need not be attained. Dimension zero means all hypotheses agree pointwise and zero regret is attainable. The range \(T\ge d\) avoids the separate saturation regime because cumulative regret cannot exceed \(T\). All requested comparison constants must be independent of the instance and label spaces, class, dimension and horizon.
cards.answer_criterion: Supply an explicit positive rate function \(g(d,T)\) of the two integer parameters and universal constants \(a,A>0\), and prove in Lean that \[a\,g(d,T)\le R(d,T)\le A\,g(d,T)\qquad(T\ge d\ge1).\] The rate must describe the parameter dependence, rather than merely rename the original game optimization. An upper bound must hold for every class in the supremum; a lower bound may choose a class separately for each parameter pair. If an extremum is not attained, approaching rules or classes suffice. The criterion allows a different sharp rate if the source's square-root conjecture fails. A bound conditional on class regularity, a constant depending on the label-space size, or a remaining logarithmic gap does not determine this unrestricted function. This requests constant-factor asymptotic precision in cumulative expected regret, not additive numerical error.

context_blocks.text: The learner sees the current instance and then receives the correct label after predicting. It can distribute its prediction among labels, and is scored by expected mistakes relative to the best fixed hypothesis. Labels can contradict every member of the class. The regret target is therefore different from a realizable mistake bound.

The 2023 paper proves that finite Littlestone dimension characterizes agnostic multiclass online learnability even for unbounded label spaces. This general learnability theorem does not require the separate minimax regularity assumption used in its sharper finite-label result. The remaining rate question asks how far a learner must fall behind the best fixed concept.

The unrestricted argument in §3 gives regret at most \(\mathrm L(H)+\sqrt{(T/2)\mathrm L(H)\ln(eT/\mathrm L(H))}\) for positive dimension. In the stated horizon range this yields \(R(d,T)=O(\sqrt{dT\log(eT/d)})\). A universal lower scale is \(\Omega(\sqrt{dT})\). The logarithm is part of the unresolved gap and cannot be suppressed when asking for constant factors.

For a finite label set, Theorem 9 gives \(O(\sqrt{\mathrm L(H)T\log|Y|})\) under the additional minimax regularity condition explicitly stated in p. 9 footnote 4 for those results. Under that condition a fixed label count yields the square-root scale, but the coefficient grows with the count. Even for two labels, removing the condition for unrestricted classes is a separate open issue recorded by the source and by the 2025 thesis.

The previously approved quantitative target takes the worst minimax regret over classes of dimension at most d. It asks for the complete function, allowing a rate different from the source conjecture if necessary. This change of answer form remains explicit; no equivalence between an arbitrary sharp-rate answer and proving the conjectured square-root bound is asserted.

The checked May 2026 oracle-complexity paper concerns binary classification and retains logarithmic factors in its dimension-dependent regret statement. It improves resource use within an online algorithm and does not resolve the unrestricted multiclass constant-factor rate.

cards.title: Time complexity of Gaussian agnostic halfspace learning
cards.formal: Determine the optimal joint running-time dependence on dimension \(n\) and inverse excess error \(t=1/\varepsilon\) for agnostically learning affine halfspaces from Gaussian examples. Retain the source’s deterministic Boolean target-function model: for every measurable \(f:\mathbb R^n\to\{-1,+1\}\), a learner sees independent \((x,f(x))\) with \(x\sim\gamma_n=N(0,I_n)\), and must output a predictor \(h\) such that \[\Pr\left[\operatorname{err}_f(h)\le\operatorname{OPT}_n(f)+\frac1t\right]\ge\frac23,\qquad \operatorname{err}_f(h)=\Pr_{x\sim\gamma_n}[h(x)\ne f(x)],\] where \[\operatorname{OPT}_n(f)=\inf_{w\in\mathbb R^n,\ b\in\mathbb R}\Pr_{x\sim\gamma_n}[\operatorname{sgn}(\langle w,x\rangle+b)\ne f(x)].\] The parameters range over \(n\ge2\), \(t\ge3\). More precisely, characterize the asymptotically attainable uniform time bounds \(T(n,t)\) defined below, with matching algorithmic upper and general lower bounds in each stated parameter regime. The source’s subsidiary question about \(n^{O(\log t)}\) is recorded in context; it does not replace the broader optimal-time target. The real-arithmetic convention and its distinction from a finite-bit implementation are explicit parts of this formulation.
cards.why: Gaussian inputs remove many distributional complications, yet arbitrary labels can still make even the best linear predictor difficult to match. The question asks for the precise computational cost of decreasing excess error, allowing any output representation. It separates the number of examples needed for learning from the much larger time used by current algorithms.
cards.status_note: The broad optimal-time question remains without a checked matching resolution under the exact formulation given here. The 2014 Definition 4 uses a fixed target function and leaves real-input precision implicit; affine halfspaces are stated in its introduction. The completed record explicitly selects an exact-real arithmetic convention and preserves deterministic Boolean labels. COLT 2021 gives SQ optimality in a larger joint-label model. ICML 2023 gives conditional LWE hardness with stochastic labels, a sqrt(log n) exponent loss and a stated error range; a deterministic-label and exact-real lower-bound transfer was not established in this review. The 2026 proper and homogeneous results have their own output/runtime qualifications. These known theorems are substantive related progress, not a claimed constant-factor classification or unconditional resolution. Current status is uncertain after checks through 16 September 2026.

cards.definitions:
\(\gamma_n\) is the Borel probability measure on \(\mathbb R^n\) with density \((2\pi)^{-n/2}\exp(-\|x\|_2^2/2)\) with respect to Lebesgue measure; its coordinates are independent standard normal random variables. A halfspace predictor has the form \(x\mapsto\operatorname{sgn}(\sum_i w_i x_i+b)\), with real coefficients and threshold and \(\operatorname{sgn}(z)=+1\) for \(z\ge0\), otherwise \(-1\). Constant predictors are allowed by \(w=0\). Affine halfspaces follow the source’s introductory definition, which includes a constant term; its later notation sometimes suppresses that term. No margin, bounded coefficient encoding, sparsity or homogeneity assumption is added. The infimum in \(\operatorname{OPT}_n(f)\) does not presume an available optimum or supply its value to the learner.

The unknown target \(f\) is any Borel-measurable Boolean function, fixed before the examples and learner coins are drawn. It need not itself be a halfspace. Each oracle request returns an independent Gaussian vector with its exact value under the same \(f\); the learner cannot choose the sampled point, inspect code for \(f\), ask for a label at a selected point, or query the optimum. There is no independent stochastic label distribution conditional on \(x\) in this literal target-function formulation. The outer success probability includes all sample draws and internal randomness; error is measured on a fresh Gaussian input. The learner may output an improper predictor. The source uses \(L^1\) notation: for \(\{-1,+1\}\)-valued \(h,f\), \(\mathbb E|h-f|=2\operatorname{err}_f(h)\). Thus excess disagreement \(1/t\) is excess \(L^1\) loss \(2/t\), not \(1/t\). This exact factor is kept separate from asymptotic runtime notation.

Computational convention: use one finite uniform real-arithmetic register program, with rational constants in its fixed code, integer control and rational public parameters \(n,t\). It can copy real registers, apply \(+,-,\times,\div\) to a constant number of registers, compare their values, branch and generate a fair random bit, each at unit arithmetic cost. Division by zero must be handled by a comparison before division. Discrete control, register access and writing an output instruction each cost one step. Sampling and loading an \(n\)-coordinate labeled example costs \(n+1\) units. The oracle supplies exact real coordinates; no cost for internally generating a Gaussian real is attributed to the learner. There is no floor, digit-extraction primitive, arbitrary real advice, optimization oracle, expectation oracle or decision oracle for general properties of real numbers. Uniformity means the same finite program works for all \(n,t,f\), with no length-dependent constants or advice.

The output is a finite acyclic arithmetic-and-comparison circuit on \(n\) real inputs, built from the same operations, Boolean choices and sign tests. Constants may be stored real values computed during training. It must define a total \(\{-1,+1\}\)-valued predictor on every real input, with each division guarded when its denominator vanishes. Output writing and each stored real coefficient are charged one unit per written item. Evaluation cost is the number of circuit operations; it is included in the resource measure. Such circuits give measurable predictors and need no further examples or target access after training. There is no requirement that the output be a halfspace, and no fixed polynomial degree or circuit-size restriction beyond the stated time bound.

For a learner \(A\), let \(\tau_A(n,t)\) be the supremum over every allowed target, sample history and coin history of its training cost plus the evaluation cost of its output circuit, with nontermination or invalid output charged infinite cost. A computable nondecreasing positive integer function \(T(n,t)\) is an attainable asymptotic time bound if there are one such uniform learner \(A\) and a constant \(K\ge1\), independent of \(n,t,f\), such that the PAC guarantee holds for every \(n,t,f\) and \(\tau_A(n,t)\le K T(n,t)\) for every \(n\ge2,t\ge3\). Characterizing optimal complexity means an explicit description of which rates are attainable, up to constant factors, rather than a pointwise infimum over a different hard-coded algorithm for each parameter pair. The dependence on both parameters must remain visible; any restriction such as \(t\le n^c\) must be stated for that bound. No single asymptotically fastest uniform algorithm is assumed to exist in advance.

This exact-real arithmetic model is an explicitly stated convention completing the source’s continuous-example interface. It does not assert a theorem translating arbitrary real computations to the bit model. Exact Gaussian examples have no finite binary representation in general, and the 2014 question specifies neither a rounding oracle nor a coordinate-bit budget. A separate bit-complexity variant would need those definitions and a proof that rounding preserves the learning guarantee for arbitrary measurable targets. Numerical rounding is therefore not silently included as a free primitive in the present arithmetic target.
cards.answer_criterion: Provide a Lean-checked asymptotic classification of the attainable bounds just defined: explicit noncircular conditions on \(T(n,t)\), together with proofs of attainability for the asserted upper rates and impossibility for the excluded lower rates. An optimal-rate expression must have matching bounds with the same dimension/error regimes and cost convention. If a fastest uniform rate is not attained, describe and prove the resulting attainable-rate structure instead of assuming a pointwise optimum corresponds to one algorithm. An upper bound alone, a conditional obstruction alone, or a matching result only for statistical-query algorithms does not determine the unrestricted optimum. Computational assumptions must remain hypotheses of the relevant partial result. A lower bound with stochastic labels or a restricted proper output must establish its applicability to the deterministic-target, improper-output interface before being used here. A proof about finite-bit computation must likewise establish a relation to the specified real-arithmetic model. The requested precision is matching asymptotic rates up to constants, not an additive approximation to a numerical value.

source_formulation.text: What is the optimal time complexity of Gaussian agnostic halfspace learning; in particular, can the dimension exponent be only logarithmic in inverse excess error?
source_formulation.caption: Editorial paraphrase

context_blocks.text: A halfspace classifies points by which side of a hyperplane they occupy. In an agnostic task, the labels need not be linearly separable: the benchmark is the least disagreement achievable by a halfspace, plus a requested excess error. A regular Gaussian input marginal does not itself constrain the complexity of the labeling rule.

The 2014 paper contrasts the known \(n^{O(1/\varepsilon^2)}\) algorithmic scale with a sparse-noisy-parity-based conditional \(n^{\Omega(\log(1/\varepsilon))}\) obstruction. Its Question 3 asks for the optimal time and explicitly proposes \(n^{O(\log(1/\varepsilon))}\) as a possibility. The quoted lower scale comes from a reduction and a hardness premise; it is not an unconditional time lower bound.

Definition 4 of the source labels examples by a deterministic target function and states an L¹ approximation guarantee; its halfspace discussion also uses Boolean classification language. Later papers often start directly from an arbitrary joint distribution on features and labels. An upper guarantee for all such joint distributions includes deterministic labels as a special case. A lower bound for the larger family does not automatically apply to the deterministic subfamily.

COLT 2021 Diakonikolas–Kane–Pittas–Zarifis proves essentially matching \(n^{\Omega(1/\varepsilon^2)}\)-scale statistical-query hardness for halfspaces in its general joint-distribution model. Statistical queries return approximate expectations of bounded test functions instead of the actual independent examples. This is an important optimality theorem for that restricted access model, not a lower bound for every sample-based learner in the present formulation.

ICML 2023 Diakonikolas–Kane–Ren gives a stronger related cryptographic obstruction. Its Corollary 3.2, under Assumption 2.3 on subexponential LWE hardness, excludes time \(n^{O((1/(\varepsilon\sqrt{\log n}))^\alpha)}\) for every fixed \(0<\alpha<2\), in its stated range \(c/(\sqrt n\log n)\le\varepsilon\le1/(\log n)^\gamma\), with \(\gamma>1/2\) and the specified sufficiently large constant \(c\). Both the logarithmic loss in the exponent and the error range are material. The theorem uses arbitrary joint labels and a computational cryptographic reduction; it is not an unconditional constant-factor characterization of this real-arithmetic deterministic-label problem.

The 2023 hard-instance construction contains residual random noise in the labels even after conditioning on the Gaussian feature vector, and its null case has independent fair labels. This review has not established a conversion of that construction into a fixed deterministic target with the same computational costs. Nor does a finite-bit cryptographic assumption by itself give a lower bound against unit-cost exact-real programs. Those interface gaps are stated explicitly rather than hidden by a claim that the original question is fully resolved.

Tikhonov–Vasilyan’s May 2026 Theorem 3.14 outputs an affine halfspace with error \(\operatorname{OPT}+\varepsilon\) and time \(n^{O(1/\varepsilon^2)}+(1/\varepsilon)^{O(1/\varepsilon^{2.5})}\) at constant confidence. Its general joint-label guarantee includes fixed deterministic targets, and proper output is allowed by an improper-learning task. The theorem advances proper learning and matches the known dimension exponent; its additional accuracy-only term and continuous computational conventions must remain visible in a joint optimal-time comparison. No finite-bit equivalence is claimed here.

The April 2026 Huang–Juba paper studies a further related problem with homogeneous halfspace output and general joint labels. Its LWE-based hardness is stated with those restrictions. Homogeneous proper learning is not substituted for unrestricted improper affine learning, and the computational assumption is not asserted true.

The original source does not fix coordinate precision or a universal elementary cost model for real samples. This card states a real-arithmetic convention so the resource question can be read precisely. Its current-status review remains uncertain: the inspected recent results explain substantial progress but do not certify a matching resolution with all the displayed label, computation and parameter conventions.

cards.title: Memory–sample tradeoffs for noisy parity learning
cards.formal: Do there exist absolute constants \(c_{1},c_{2}>0\) and \(n_{0}\) such that, for every integer \(n\ge n_{0}\), every \(0<\varepsilon <1/2\) and every one-pass learner recovering a uniformly random \(x\in \{0,1\}^{n}\) with probability at least \(2/3\) from the noisy parity samples defined below, its worst-case memory S and maximum sample count T satisfy \(S\ge c_{1}n^{2}/\varepsilon ^{2}\) or \(T\ge 2^{c_{2}n}\)? Constants are independent of \(n, \varepsilon\) and the learner, and \(\varepsilon\) may tend to zero with n. This states the bounded-error recovery interpretation of Conjecture 1; it does not additionally require a lower bound at exponentially small success probability.
cards.why: Would quantify how observation noise increases the storage needed for a central learning problem, strengthening unconditional limits relevant to streaming learning and bounded-storage cryptography.

cards.definitions: Arithmetic in 𝔽\(_{2}=\{0,1\}\) uses addition and multiplication modulo two; \(\langle a,x\rangle =\sum_{i=1}^{n}a_{i}x_{i}\) mod 2. First choose x uniformly from \(\{0,1\}^{n}\) and hold it fixed. Independently for each t, choose \(a_{t}\) uniformly from \(\{0,1\}^{n}\) and a noise bit \(Z_{t}\) with \(\Pr [Z_{t}=1]=1/2- \varepsilon\); observe \((a_{t},b_{t})\) with \(b_{t}=\langle a_{t},x\rangle +Z_{t}\) mod 2. Noise bits, query vectors and internal learner coins are mutually independent. The learner outputs one estimate x̂; success means \(\hat\{x\}=x\), and its probability averages over x, all observations and internal coins. The learner sees each sample once in order, cannot choose \(a_{t}\) or revisit discarded observations, and has no computational-time restriction. Formally use a branching program with \(T+1\) layers and width at most \(2^{S}\), one start vertex and one outgoing edge for each possible sample at each nonterminal vertex, all going to the next layer. Leaves, possibly in earlier layers, are labelled by estimates in \(\{0,1\}^{n}\). Randomized learners may use fresh coins to choose state updates; retained coins are part of the state. Equivalently, the lower bound may be checked on deterministic nonuniform programs, since a random tape can be fixed to achieve at least the average success under this fixed input distribution without increasing width or length. The program may depend on n and \(\varepsilon\); its transition description, current layer and input sample are not charged as stored data. Memory counts persistent state bits, \(S=\lceil \log _{2}(\operatorname{width})\rceil\), and T is the maximum number of consumed samples, not its expectation. No hypothesis is made about the hardness of LPN in unrestricted computation.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove the universal bounded-error memory/sample tradeoff with constants uniform in \(\varepsilon\), or refute that asymptotic claim by showing that no such constants can work. A bound \(\Omega (n^{2}/\varepsilon ), a\) result only for constant \(\varepsilon\), or a lower bound in a restricted statistical-query model does not settle the proposed dependence on noise.

cards.title: Learning PH/poly from learning NP/poly
cards.formal: Does efficient distribution-free PAC learnability of \(\mathrm{NP/poly}\) from random labeled examples imply the same learnability for every fixed level of \(\mathrm{PH/poly}\)? In the size-parameterized model below, write \(\mathsf{Learn}_r\) for efficient learning of Boolean concepts represented by circuits with \(r\) alternating witness blocks, starting existentially. The target is the single implication \[\mathsf{Learn}_1\ \Longrightarrow\ \forall r\in\mathbb N_{\ge1},\ \mathsf{Learn}_r.\] The learner for each fixed \(r\) may be different and have a different polynomial running-time bound. This does not request one polynomial uniform over arbitrarily many alternations. Both sides use ordinary Boolean circuits as output hypotheses and only independent random examples of the unknown target.
cards.why: The question asks whether solving one level of a powerful prediction task automatically solves every fixed level above it. An affirmative answer would give a structural collapse for efficient learning, beyond the familiar collapses for deciding languages or merely representing them by small circuits.

cards.definitions:
Fix the ordinary Boolean circuit basis consisting of two-input AND and OR gates, one-input NOT gates, and constants; circuits are acyclic and have one output bit. Fix a standard effective binary encoding. For \(n\ge1\), \(s\ge n+1\), and fixed \(r\ge1\), let \(\mathcal C_r(n,s)\) contain every function on \(\{0,1\}^n\) of the form \[f(x)=\mathbf1\{\exists u_1\ \forall u_2\ \exists u_3\ \cdots Q_r u_r:\ C(x,u_1,\ldots,u_r)=1\},\] where \(Q_i\) alternates with \(i\), each \(u_i\) ranges over a specified finite Boolean cube, and the total number of input nodes, witness bits and gates of the deterministic matrix circuit \(C\) is at most \(s\). Zero-length witness blocks are allowed. The size is a combinatorial circuit-size bound; encoding such a circuit takes a polynomial number of bits in \(s\). At \(r=1\), these are nondeterministic circuits. Allowing size polynomial in \(n\) gives the usual nonuniform class \(\mathrm{NP/poly}\). The union over every fixed alternation depth gives \(\mathrm{PH/poly}\), the polynomial hierarchy with polynomial-length advice. Equivalently, advice can be included in the matrix circuit; it is not given to the learner. There is no requirement that the target descriptions at different input lengths be produced by one algorithm.

Precisely, \(\mathsf{Learn}_r\) says that there exist one randomized classical Turing machine \(A_r\) and one polynomial \(p_r\) such that the following holds for every \(n,s\) as above, every pair of integers \(a,b\ge3\), every \(f\in\mathcal C_r(n,s)\), and every probability distribution \(D\) on \(\{0,1\}^n\). Given the public unary parameters \(1^n,1^s,1^a,1^b\) and independent examples \((x,f(x))\) with \(x\sim D\), the learner halts on every execution in at most \(p_r(n+s+a+b)\) steps and outputs a deterministic ordinary Boolean circuit \(h:\{0,1\}^n\to\{0,1\}\) such that \[\Pr_{A_r,\,\text{examples}}\left[\Pr_{x\sim D}[h(x)\ne f(x)]\le 1/a\right]\ge1-1/b.\] The outer probability includes the random training draws and the machine’s independent fair random bits. The inner probability uses a fresh test draw. Each requested example is an independent draw; requests count toward the time bound and reading its \(n+1\) bits is charged. The bound therefore also limits the number of examples, random bits and output bits. The predictor is evaluated without access to the example source, target or learner state. Its gates have no nondeterministic or higher-hierarchy oracle. It need not use the target’s representation or respect its size bound, but its printed description must fit the learner’s polynomial time.

The learner knows the size bound, not the unknown circuit, its advice, witness assignments, or the distribution. There are no membership queries asking for labels at chosen points, and no equivalence queries. All distributions are admitted; efficient sampling code is not required because the example source is part of the PAC interface. Labels are noiseless values of one fixed concept, so this is realizable rather than agnostic learning. Integer inverse-error and inverse-failure parameters specify the usual arbitrary accuracy and confidence guarantees without numerical-encoding ambiguity. Supplying \(s\) makes explicit the source’s standard polynomial-in-target-size convention: combining all polynomial-size representations at one \(n\) without any size bound would erase the intended computational restriction.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove the displayed implication in Lean, with a polynomial-time learner for every fixed alternation depth under the hypothesis \(\mathsf{Learn}_1\), or prove its negation \(\mathsf{Learn}_1\land\exists r\ge1,\neg\mathsf{Learn}_r\). All distribution, target-size, accuracy and confidence quantifiers must be preserved. The requested result is a qualitative implication about uniform learning algorithms; it does not ask for a particular optimal exponent. An oracle-relative separation by itself is evidence about relativizing arguments, not a refutation of the unrelativized implication. A theorem about average-case decision algorithms, membership-query learners, or existence of nonuniform hypothesis circuits alone does not establish this random-example learning implication.

source_formulation.text: Does polynomial-time learnability of NP/poly imply polynomial-time learnability of PH/poly?
source_formulation.caption: Editorial paraphrase

context_blocks.text: An NP/poly concept labels an input by whether some short witness makes a small verification circuit accept. Higher levels alternate existential and universal witness tests. The learner never performs those tests on the hidden target description; it sees only random correctly labeled examples and must produce an efficiently evaluatable prediction circuit.

The classical Karp–Lipton theorem concerns small circuit representations for NP and a resulting collapse of decision complexity. The question here is about finding useful predictors from limited observed data. A guarantee that some small circuit exists is weaker than a learning algorithm that discovers one under every distribution.

Uniformity applies to the learner: for a fixed level, one Turing algorithm must handle every input length, size bound and target circuit. The target class is nonuniform because its hidden descriptions may vary arbitrarily with input length. Neither target advice nor a circuit solving a higher-level decision problem is supplied as free advice to the learner.

The 2021 paper proves stronger equivalences for EXP/poly and PSPACE/poly. In those classes it relates worst-case and average-case learning and shows that restricting the example distribution to uniform or allowing membership queries does not alter the qualitative polynomial-time learnability conclusion. These results concern stronger classes and do not prove the NP-to-PH implication.

The source separately studies restricted reductions from SAT to learning NP/poly. Its hierarchy-collapse consequence for such a reduction concerns a hardness proof with additional structural properties. The existence of that kind of reduction is not part of the premise of this card. The source’s additional question about an oracle-relative obstacle is also separate from the unrelativized implication.

The December 2021 full manuscript explicitly retains the hierarchy question. The January 2025 journal publication is confirmed by the publisher, whose accessible abstract states the paper’s stronger-class and reduction results. Its subscription-only full text was not available in this review. Bounded later-work searches found no checked theorem answering this exact implication, so current status remains qualified rather than certified from publication metadata.

cards.title: Proper decision-tree learning in polynomial time
cards.formal: Is there a uniform randomized membership-query algorithm that properly learns Boolean decision trees under the uniform distribution in polynomial time? For every \(n,s\geq1\), every integer \(m\geq2\), and every \(f:\{0,1\}^n\to\{0,1\}\) representable by a decision tree with at most \(s\) leaves, the learner is given \(n,s,m\) and oracle access to \(f\). It must output an explicitly represented decision tree \(h\), with probability at least \(2/3\), such that \[2^{-n}|\{x\in\{0,1\}^n:h(x)\ne f(x)\}|\leq1/m.\] Its worst-case running time must be polynomial in \(n,s,m\).
cards.why: The question tests whether efficient prediction can be achieved while retaining a decision-tree representation in a basic, well-specified query model. Its resolution would clarify the computational cost of proper learning beyond sample complexity alone.
cards.status_note: The exact uniform-distribution proper query question is explicit in the 2022 source. Checked later hardness results do not cover this distributional setting. The bounded review through 14 September 2026 found no polynomial-time learner or unconditional impossibility theorem for the stated model.

cards.definitions: A Boolean decision tree is a finite rooted binary tree. Each internal node queries one coordinate \(x_i\), \(i\in\{1,\ldots,n\}\), and its two outgoing edges correspond to values zero and one. Leaves are labelled zero or one; following the input’s path defines the output bit. Size means the number of leaves. Repeated coordinate tests are allowed. The unknown target need only admit a tree with at most \(s\) leaves; that tree is not supplied. A membership query may be any chosen bit string \(x\in\{0,1\}^n\) and returns the exact noiseless bit \(f(x)\). The learner is one finite probabilistic multitape Turing program with independent fair random bits, no advice, and no other oracle. Writing the \(n\)-bit query costs ordinary bit steps; reading its returned label costs one. All random-bit generation, computation and output are charged. Its time is bounded by \(K(n+s+m+1)^a\) on every target and every random execution, for constants \(K,a\) independent of parameters. Integers are supplied in binary. The accuracy convention \(\varepsilon=1/m\) specifies the usual inverse-accuracy parameter without an arbitrary real input encoding; existence for these accuracies is equivalent to existence for arbitrary requested positive accuracy by rounding to a smaller reciprocal accuracy. Properness is weak properness: the output must be a decision tree, but need not have at most \(s\) leaves. Its full explicit description, with variable indices, children and leaf bits, must fit the polynomial time bound. The success probability concerns the learner’s randomness; prediction error is measured over a fresh uniform point and the guarantee holds for every promised target.
cards.answer_criterion: Provide a complete Lean-checked proof that a learner satisfying all these quantifiers exists, or that no such learner exists. The positive direction requires polynomial bit time, a proper explicit tree output and the uniform-distribution error bound with probability at least \(2/3\). A negative result must rule out all randomized learners of this kind, including those allowed polynomial-size trees larger than the target. An improper hypothesis, a random-examples-only result, distribution-free hardness alone, or a conditional obstruction whose assumption is unproved does not settle the stated existence question.

context_blocks.text: Open Problem 1 asks for polynomial time in the number of variables, target size and inverse accuracy. The source explicitly distinguishes strict properness, which preserves the target size bound, from weak properness, which merely returns a tree; its question is open even for the latter.

The representation constraint matters: an efficient predictor need not come with a comparably small tree representation. Membership queries also matter because they let the learner choose inputs instead of relying only on the examples that a distribution happens to provide.

The source’s Theorem 2 reports an almost-polynomial proper query learner, with time \(\widetilde O(n^2)(s/\varepsilon)^{O(\log((\log s)/\varepsilon))}\). In the usual polynomial-size, constant-error regime this yields \(n^{O(\log\log n)}\), which still exceeds a fixed polynomial.

Koch, Strassle and Tan prove NP-hardness for distribution-free proper learning with queries in FOCS 2023. Their paper explicitly contrasts that result with the easier uniform-distribution setting. A lower bound obtained from a specially chosen distribution does not rule out this card’s learner.

Their FOCS 2024 coding-theoretic work gives further hardness connections for decision-tree learning. Its discussion distinguishes the remaining uniform-distribution problem from the distributions used in its reductions.

An empirical tree-fitting procedure and its success on a finite collection of datasets are not the universal learning guarantee. The error bound must hold for every small-tree target, even when the target’s structure is unknown and the output tree has a different topology.

cards.title: NP-hardness of improper learning of \(\mathrm{P}/\mathrm{poly}\)
cards.formal: Is there an integer \(a\ge1\) such that, for every integer \(b\ge a\), there are an integer \(r\ge1\) and a uniform randomized polynomial-time oracle reduction \(R_b\) which decides SAT with success probability at least \(2/3\) using the following agnostic circuit-learning oracle? A query is a Boolean sampling circuit producing a distribution \(D\) on \(\{0,1\}^{m}\times\{0,1\}\). Every oracle reply must be a circuit \(h\) of size at most \((m+1)^{b}\) satisfying \[L_D(h)\le\min_{g\in\operatorname{SIZE}_{m}((m+1)^{a})}L_D(g)+(m+1)^{-r}.\] The reduction must succeed for every sequence of valid replies. The exponent \(r\), reduction and its running-time polynomial may depend on \(b\), but not on the SAT instance. No cryptographic or unproved complexity assumption is part of the target. This selects the source's agnostic, efficiently samplable-distribution reduction formulation.
cards.why: This asks whether learning general small circuits remains hard when the learner is free to use a different and polynomially larger representation. Establishing such hardness from SAT would connect worst-case NP difficulty with a central general learning task, while the known links to witness encryption expose consequences beyond learning itself.
cards.status_note: Open in the CCC 2025 source. The subsequent ECCC TR26-091 checked on 2026-09-14 establishes related conditional hardness under cryptographic and proof-complexity assumptions, not the unconditional claim here. The selected formal oracle-reduction variant and its quantifier order are explicit; this bounded check is not an exhaustive literature or proof verification.

cards.definitions:
A Boolean circuit is an explicitly listed directed acyclic graph with named input wires, constant zero and one wires, fan-in-two AND and OR gates, fan-in-one NOT gates, and named output wires. Its size is its number of noninput gates, including constant gates. Gate types and predecessor indices are encoded in binary in topological order; all input and output counts are explicit. Write \(\operatorname{SIZE}_{m}(s)\) for the binary functions on \(m\) input bits computed by one-output circuits with at most \(s\) gates. A language is in \(\mathrm{P}/\mathrm{poly}\) if its restriction to each input length is computed by a circuit family with polynomial size; those circuits need not be generated uniformly.

A sampling-circuit query has some number \(q\ge0\) of random input bits and \(m+1\) output bits, with \(m\ge1\). Uniform independent bits in \(\{0,1\}^{q}\) induce the joint distribution \(D\); the first \(m\) outputs are the example and the last is its label. Labels may be noisy and need not be realizable by a small circuit. The risk is \(L_D(h)=\Pr_{(x,y)\sim D}[h(x)\ne y]\). The oracle returns the full description of a predictor satisfying the displayed excess-risk guarantee. An answer always exists because the smaller comparator family is finite, contains constant functions, and is included in the allowed output family. The oracle itself has no computational restriction. It may select different valid circuits based on the query history; the reduction must work for all such selections, not only for a favorable learning rule.

The reduction is a randomized multitape Turing machine using independent fair bits. For each fixed \(b\), one polynomial in the SAT input bit length bounds its running time on every random tape and response history, counting construction of all sampling circuits and reading all reply descriptions; oracle computation is uncharged. Queries may be adaptive and may have different \(m,q\). In particular, the entire sampling circuit and every reply must have polynomial encoding length in the reduction's input length. The reduction may inspect hypothesis descriptions and evaluate them; it has no additional oracle or advice. SAT uses an explicit syntax-tree encoding of AND, OR and NOT formulas, with malformed encodings rejected. Probability of a correct SAT answer is over the reduction's coins, for each fixed input and each valid response policy.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct Lean-checked proof that such an exponent \(a\) and reductions exist, or a proof of the negation. A positive answer must cover every polynomial output-size exponent \(b\ge a\), allowing the stated dependence of the reduction on \(b\). Hardness only when the predictor is restricted to the target size, or only under an additional cryptographic assumption, does not suffice. A negative answer must rule out the displayed family of reductions, not merely one restricted reduction technique.

context_blocks.text: An improper learner may return a larger circuit than any circuit in the comparator class. Showing hardness only for size-preserving output can therefore leave an efficient improper learner possible. The quantification over every fixed polynomial output-size bound makes this distinction explicit.

The source defines learning reductions by giving the oracle a sampling circuit for a distribution and receiving a sufficiently accurate hypothesis. This card retains that oracle interface. Sampling distributions are generated by the reduction; the task does not give a practical learner arbitrary target membership queries.

The polynomial target-size exponent is fixed before the allowed output exponent. For each allowed output exponent the reduction may be different. Adaptive randomized Turing reductions are allowed; the card does not impose the additional deterministic, nonadaptive, witness-mapping or honesty conditions used in some of the source’s cryptographic consequences.

The June 2026 paper proves conditional hardness for a related full-support learning problem. It assumes a strong indistinguishability obfuscator and a lower-bound hypothesis for propositional proof systems. These are substantive assumptions, so the result does not by itself give the unconditional reduction asked for here.

cards.title: Polynomial-time robust spectral estimation
cards.formal: For every fixed \(q\in[2,\infty]\), is there a polynomial-time algorithm that always recovers a robust low-rank representation of an unknown clean matrix from bounded perturbations to every data point, with the spectral-error guarantee available information-theoretically in Proposition 27? Specifically, do there exist, for each fixed \(q\), a uniform algorithm \(\mathcal A_q\) and constants \(b_q,C_q,B_q,a_q\ge1\) such that the following holds for all integers \(n,m\ge1\), \(0\le r\le n\), real \(\kappa,\delta\ge0\), and matrices \(A,\widetilde A\in\mathbb R^{n\times m}\) satisfying \(\|\widetilde A_j-A_j\|_q\le\delta\) for every column \(j\)? Given only \((\widetilde A,r,\kappa,\delta)\), the algorithm must output an orthogonal projection \(\widehat\Pi\) with \[\operatorname{rank}(\widehat\Pi)\le r,\qquad \|\widehat\Pi\|_{q\to2}\le b_q\kappa,\] and, for every \(\eta>0\), \[\|(I_n-\widehat\Pi)A\|_{2\to2}\le C_q(1+\eta^{-1})\left(\operatorname{OPT}_{q,r,\kappa}(A)+\sqrt m\,\delta\kappa\right)+\sqrt{2\eta}\,\|A\|_{2\to2}.\] The same output must satisfy every \(\eta\); \(\eta\) is an analysis parameter, not an extra source of clean-data information. Require at most \(B_q(n+m+1)^{a_q}\) operations in the explicit fixed-\(q\) real-arithmetic model below. The output must be a projection, even when the observed matrix has large spectral distortion; reporting only that the input was poisoned is insufficient.

source_formulation.text: Can a polynomial-time estimator always return a robust low-rank projection with the spectral-error guarantee available information-theoretically under bounded perturbations to every training point?
source_formulation.caption: Editorial paraphrase

cards.why: A representation can be stable against future perturbations and still be difficult to learn from already corrupted data. This question asks whether worst-case robust spectral reconstruction is computationally attainable whenever it is information-theoretically possible. It isolates a gap that is hidden if an algorithm may simply report severe corruption.
cards.status_note: The 2021 source’s Proposition 27 gives the information-theoretic spectral recovery guarantee, while its efficient Theorem 25 may return a poisoning certificate. The exact always-return-a-projection target, rank bound, robustness factor and eta tradeoff are retained. Related Gaussian principal-subspace results have extra distributional structure. The live original manuscript history and bounded later-work checks through 16 September 2026 did not yield a verified theorem resolving this full worst-case question. Status is uncertain, not a proof of openness. Polynomial time is explicitly interpreted in a fixed-q exact-real arithmetic model with unit-cost q-powers; neither finite-bit equivalence nor an unrestricted norm/optimization oracle is asserted.

A Lean resolution must prove or refute guaranteed recovery with the stated approximation and computational costs, without extra distributional assumptions.

cards.definitions:
Columns \(A_j\in\mathbb R^n\) are the clean data points and columns \(\widetilde A_j\) are the supplied observations. An adversary may change every column, in any correlated way, subject only to the displayed per-column constraint. There is no distributional assumption, random design, fraction of uncontaminated points, spectral gap, incoherence or sparsity promise. For finite \(q\), \(\|v\|_q=(\sum_i|v_i|^q)^{1/q}\); for \(q=\infty\), \(\|v\|_\infty=\max_i|v_i|\). Thus the infinite-norm version permits a change of magnitude at most \(\delta\) to every entry.

For a matrix \(M\), \(\|M\|_{u\to v}=\sup_{\|x\|_u\le1}\|Mx\|_v\), with input and output dimensions determined by \(M\). The spectral norm \(\|M\|_{2\to2}\) is its largest singular value; it measures maximum Euclidean amplification, not the sum of squared entry errors. A real \(n\times n\) matrix \(\Pi\) is an orthogonal projection when \(\Pi^T=\Pi\) and \(\Pi^2=\Pi\). Its rank is the dimension of its range. The condition \(\|\Pi\|_{q\to2}\le\kappa\) means every input perturbation of \(q\)-norm at most \(\delta\) moves the projected point by at most \(\kappa\delta\) in Euclidean norm.

Define the clean benchmark by \[\operatorname{OPT}_{q,r,\kappa}(A)=\min\{\|(I_n-\Pi)A\|_{2\to2}:\Pi^T=\Pi=\Pi^2,\ \operatorname{rank}(\Pi)\le r,\ \|\Pi\|_{q\to2}\le\kappa\}.\] The zero projection is feasible, so the class is nonempty; it is a closed bounded subset of the finite-dimensional matrix space and the minimum exists. The rank constraint is an upper bound, as in the source’s robust approximation framework and Theorem 25. The algorithm is not given the optimizer, its value, the clean matrix, its norm or the perturbation matrix. Only \(n,m\), the observed entries, rank budget and two corruption/robustness bounds are available. The output is the complete \(n\times n\) projection matrix. No extra data access is available at evaluation.

The constants \(b_q,C_q,B_q,a_q\) may depend on the fixed norm exponent, consistently with the source’s \(q\)-dependent approximation constants, but not on dimensions, rank, matrix entries, \(\kappa,\delta\) or \(\eta\). For a fixed \(q\), the same finite algorithm works on all sizes. The recovery inequality is the source’s constant-factor spectral guarantee with its additive corruption term and \(\eta\)-tradeoff, not an exact recovery or squared-Frobenius guarantee. It is valid for every compatible clean matrix \(A\): the algorithm sees only \(\widetilde A\). In particular, \(\eta\) is universally quantified after the output; a different projection for each value is not silently substituted.

Computational convention: the observed matrix and real bounds are held in exact real registers. Copying, \(+,-,\times,\div\) with a zero-denominator guard, comparisons, branching, square roots of nonnegative reals, discrete control and register access each cost one unit. For finite fixed \(q\), the primitives \(x\mapsto x^q\) and \(x\mapsto x^{1/q}\) on \(x\ge0\) also have unit cost, with \(0^q=0\). For \(q=\infty\), maxima and absolute values use comparisons instead. These are explicit elementary-power conventions for each fixed real \(q\), including exponents that are not rational; no algorithm uniform in an encoded variable exponent is requested. Program constants otherwise are rational. Reading each observed entry and writing each output entry costs one unit. The stated bound is a worst-case arithmetic-operation bound on every input, and the algorithm must always return a valid output satisfying the guarantees. It has no optimization oracle, spectral-decomposition oracle, induced-norm oracle, digit-extraction operation, clean-data oracle or general-real decision oracle. The norms used in the target are mathematical definitions, not free computational queries.

The source formulates its algorithms on real matrices and does not fix an entry-bit or approximation budget. The displayed model is an explicit real-arithmetic interpretation of polynomial time; it does not assert equivalence to a bit-complexity formulation. In particular, exact real output and the special fixed-\(q\) power operations must not be imported into a finite-bit claim without a separate numerical analysis. The full range of fixed exponents, including infinity, is preserved rather than restricting the question to the illustrative entrywise case.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a Lean proof of the displayed existence statement for every fixed \(q\), or of its negation. An affirmative answer must construct the uniform algorithms, prove their polynomial arithmetic costs, exact projection/rank properties, constant-factor robustness and clean spectral-error bounds for every adversarially compatible input and every \(\eta>0\). A negative answer must exhibit an exponent for which no algorithm and constants with these guarantees exist; a lower bound for one heuristic is insufficient. A conditional complexity assumption must remain a hypothesis unless established. Returning a corruption certificate, controlling Frobenius error alone, allowing a larger rank, assuming Gaussian/spiked input, or giving an inefficient estimator does not meet the stated goal. The objective is the explicit approximation inequality, so a numerical eigenvector estimate without a proved error and robustness bound does not constitute a resolution.

context_blocks.text: Ordinary principal component analysis minimizes reconstruction error without a robustness constraint. Here the projection must also limit how much a small change to one point can move its representation. Training data may already be corrupted, so the reconstruction guarantee concerns an unknown matrix rather than the observed matrix alone.

The source proves efficient recovery with Frobenius error and gives a different spectral algorithm that may return a certificate of substantial poisoning. Proposition 27 establishes that a robust projection satisfying the stronger spectral guarantee exists information-theoretically. The selected open question asks for efficient recovery with that guarantee, without the certification-only alternative.

The rank bound and robustness factor are separate requirements. The source’s worst-case spectral approximation theorem also has a variant trading increased rank for improved approximation, but that enlarged-rank variant does not by itself give the rank-at-most-r recovery requested here.

The additive term involving column count, corruption size and robustness is essential to the target. Small changes to all coordinates can collectively create a large matrix perturbation, so controlling each point is different from assuming the whole perturbation has small spectral norm.

The related COLT 2020 work studies principal-subspace estimation for Gaussian covariance models under per-sample adversarial perturbations. Its statistical assumptions supply structure absent from an arbitrary clean matrix. The 2021 source explicitly distinguishes that setting from its worst-case recovery question.

cards.title: Proper unlabeled compression of ample classes
cards.formal: Does every nonempty ample concept class \(C\subseteq \{0,1\}\)ᵁ on a finite domain U admit a proper unlabeled sample compression scheme of size at most \(d=\operatorname{VC}(C)\)? Precisely, do there exist maps \(\kappa :RS(C)\to \{A\subseteq U:|A|\le d\}\) and \(\rho :\{A\subseteq U:|A|\le d\}\to C\) such that, for every realizable labeled partial sample \(s, \kappa (s)\subseteq dom(s)\) and \(\rho (\kappa (s))\) agrees with every label in s? The stored object is only an unordered subset of the sample’s input points. The bound is d, not an unspecified multiple of d.
cards.why: Would extend sharp label-free sample compression from maximum classes to the larger class characterized by equality of shattering and strong shattering, clarifying how far the VC dimension controls lossless reconstruction of consistent samples.

Searches through 12 September 2026 found no resolution for every finite ample class; searches are not exhaustive.

cards.definitions: A concept \(c\in C\) is a function \(c:U\to \{0,1\}\). A set \(A\subseteq U\) is shattered by C if \(\{c|_{A}:c\in C\}=\{0,1\}^{A}\). It is strongly shattered if some \(b:U\setminus A\to \{0,1\}\) has the property that, for every \(a:A\to \{0,1\}\), the combined labeling \(a\cup b\) belongs to C. Thus strong shattering requires a full cube of concepts with identical labels outside A. The class is ample when every shattered set is strongly shattered; ample classes are also called lopsided or shattering-extremal. Its VC dimension d is the maximum size of a shattered set. A labeled partial sample is a function \(s:A\to \{0,1\}\) on some \(A\subseteq U\), equivalently a set of pairs \((x,s(x))\) with distinct x. It is realizable if \(s=c|_{A}\) for some \(c\in C; RS(C)\) contains every such sample, including the empty sample. The compressor \(\kappa\) sees the entire labeled sample and may use its labels to choose a subset \(\kappa (s)\) of its domain, of size at most d. It sends only that subset. The reconstructor \(\rho\) receives no labels, ordering, multiplicities, sample size, omitted sample points or auxiliary bits; \(U,C,\kappa\) and \(\rho\) are fixed and shared beforehand. It returns a total concept belonging to C, which must agree with the original entire sample, including omitted labels. This is the proper convention explicitly used in the full source. Requiring \(\rho\) on all subsets of size at most d is equivalent to defining it only on \(Im(\kappa )\), because C is nonempty and unused inputs can be assigned any fixed concept. The existence of \(\kappa ,\rho\) is quantified separately for each finite C; no running-time bound for constructing or evaluating them, distributional assumption or probability of error is part of the statement. For \(d=0 a\) nonempty class has a single concept and the empty compressed set suffices. A maximum class of dimension d has cardinality \(\sum_{j=0}^{d} binomial(|U|,j)\); every maximum class is ample, but the converse need not hold.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove existence of the two maps with the stated d-point bound for every finite nonempty ample class, or give an ample class with a proof that no such pair of maps exists. A scheme retaining labels, returning a hypothesis outside C, storing extra information, or exceeding d points does not meet the target. A scheme that handles only full concepts rather than every realizable partial sample is also insufficient. Failure of a proposed corner-peeling construction alone does not refute existence of a compression scheme.

cards.title: Multiclass sample compression from binary compression
cards.formal: Is the following implication valid for every function \(f:\mathbb N_0\to\mathbb N_0\)? Suppose every nonempty binary concept class \(B\subseteq\{0,1\}^{U}\) on every nonempty domain \(U\), with finite VC dimension \(v\), admits an exact realizable sample compression scheme of size at most \(f(v)\). Must there exist an integer \(A_f\ge1\) such that every nonempty multiclass concept class \(H\subseteq Y^X\), on arbitrary nonempty sets \(X,Y\) and with finite graph dimension \(d\), admits such a scheme of size at most \[A_f f(d)?\] The constant may depend on the chosen binary bound \(f\), but not on \(X,Y,H,d\), the sample size or the labels occurring in a sample. Label sets may be infinite. No properness, majority-vote form, stability, effectiveness or computational efficiency of the compression schemes is assumed. This restores the hypothesis omitted from the imported source sentence: the question concerns transfer of an arbitrary universal binary compression bound, not just existence of some graph-dimension bound.

source_formulation.text: If every binary class admits compression of size f of its VC dimension, must every multiclass class admit compression of size O(f of its graph dimension)?
source_formulation.caption: Editorial paraphrase

cards.why: A general transfer theorem would carry any improvement in binary sample compression to multiclass prediction without a penalty for the number of labels. It would separate the combinatorial difficulty of binary compression from additional requirements imposed by multiclass reconstruction. This matters even though bounded compression at an exponential graph-dimension scale is already known.

Nearby impossibility results concern another dimension. No matching unrestricted transfer theorem or counterexample was found in the bounded search through 16 September 2026; this is not a proof of current openness.

sentences: A compression scheme stores labeled examples and auxiliary bits so a fixed decoder can reproduce all labels of a realizable sample.
The question assumes a universal binary compression bound f in terms of VC dimension.

cards.definitions: \(\mathbb N_0=\{0,1,2,\ldots\}\). A concept is a function assigning a label to every instance. A finite labeled sample is a sequence \(S=((x_1,y_1),\ldots,(x_n,y_n))\); repetitions and the empty sample are allowed. It is realizable by \(H\) if a single \(h\in H\) satisfies \(h(x_i)=y_i\) for every \(i\). A compression scheme for the fixed class is a pair of deterministic set functions \[\kappa:(X\times Y)^*\to(X\times Y)^*\times\{0,1\}^*,\qquad \rho:(X\times Y)^*\times\{0,1\}^*\to Y^X.\] Writing \(\kappa(S)=(S',b)\), every labeled record in \(S'\) must occur in \(S\). Following the source’s explicit convention that subset notation for sequences means inclusion of their underlying sets, the retained list may be reordered and may repeat a retained record. Every occurrence counts toward its length. No new or relabeled record may be introduced. The bit string \(b\) is auxiliary information. Size at most \(s\) means \(|S'|+|b|\le s\) on every finite input sample. The reconstruction receives only \(S',b\), not the original sample, its length, or the original positions of retained records. One retained labeled record costs one unit; one auxiliary bit costs one unit. Domain points and labels are mathematical objects, not charged by bit length. Exact realizable consistency means \(\rho(\kappa(S))(x_i)=y_i\) for every record of every realizable \(S\). The reconstructed function need not belong to \(H\), and no accuracy requirement is imposed on unrealizable samples. Both functions may depend on the complete class, but the same pair must work at all sample sizes. There is no randomness or failure probability. A binary class has VC dimension \(v\) when \(v\) is the largest size of a set of distinct domain points on which all binary label patterns occur. A multiclass class graph-shatters distinct points \(x_1,\ldots,x_r\) if there are reference labels \(a_1,\ldots,a_r\in Y\) such that every subset \(I\subseteq[r]\) has a hypothesis with \(h(x_i)=a_i\) exactly for \(i\in I\). The graph dimension is the largest such \(r\). Only classes of finite dimension enter the implication; dimension zero permits a size-zero scheme because all hypotheses agree pointwise. No monotonicity or computability assumption is placed on \(f\).
cards.answer_criterion: Prove the universal implication in Lean, or prove its logical negation. A positive answer must show that every binary bound satisfying the premise transfers with a constant \(A_f\) uniform over all multiclass classes and all sample sizes; an effective black-box procedure is not required. A negative answer must exhibit one function \(f\) that really bounds compression for every binary class as stated, and prove that for every integer \(A\ge1\) some finite-graph-dimension multiclass class admits no compression scheme of size at most \(Af(d)\). Merely showing failure of a particular reduction does not refute the implication. A result with an extra label-count factor, an added structural requirement on the binary reconstruction, or a substituted dimension does not settle this question. The assertion concerns exact consistency and constant-factor size transfer; there is no numerical error tolerance.

context_blocks.text: Sample compression retains a few labeled examples and a few auxiliary bits, from which a fixed reconstruction rule must recover a predictor agreeing with the entire original realizable sample. It compresses the information needed for consistency, not the literal binary encoding of all discarded data. The size bound must hold regardless of the original sample length.

VC dimension records which binary patterns a class can realize on a finite set. Graph dimension asks which agreement and disagreement patterns with chosen reference labels a multiclass class can realize. These dimensions coincide for binary classes. The target uses graph dimension, not the different dimension characterizing general multiclass learnability.

Theorem 4 of the proceedings paper transfers any binary bound \(f(d)\) to a finite-label multiclass bound \(O(f(d)\log|Y|)\). The question asks whether that extra label-count cost can be removed without assumptions on the binary compression scheme. In the April 2025 revision the same open question is numbered 3.3.

The source removes the extra factor if the available binary reconstruction is proper or is a finite majority vote of class members; that result also covers infinite label sets. Proper means that the reconstructed binary predictor belongs to the class, and majority vote means pointwise voting among finitely many members, with ties assigned zero. The existence of an unrestricted binary compression scheme does not supply either property.

A separate result removes the extra factor for finite label spaces if the binary compressor is stable: removing records outside its retained set leaves its compressed message unchanged. The source treats infinite labels in that direction using a stronger extension of compression to infinite samples. Those are extra premises, so none is silently inserted into this card’s general finite-sample question.

Finite graph dimension already guarantees bounded compression of size \(2^{O(d)}\), and the source also gives size one for graph dimension one. These results do not establish transfer of every potentially smaller binary bound. In particular, proving a new binary bound would answer this card only if its multiclass consequence preserved the requested order.

Pabbaraju’s counterexample concerns multiclass learnability with a different dimension and an infinite label space. The paper explicitly distinguishes finite graph dimension, where bounded compression is available. Thus the broad slogan that multiclass learnability does not imply compression does not refute this finite-graph-dimension reduction.
