cards.title: Oblivious transfer from public-key encryption
cards.formal:
In the classical plain model, does the existence of public-key encryption secure against chosen-plaintext attacks imply the existence of 1-out-of-2 bit oblivious transfer secure against static semi-honest corruption of either party?

Let \(E\) assert the existence of the bit-encryption scheme defined below, and let \(T\) assert the existence of the two-party protocol and simulators defined below. The target is the unrelativized implication
\[E\ \Longrightarrow\ T.\]
All honest algorithms and simulators are uniform probabilistic polynomial-time classical machines; security is against arbitrary nonuniform polynomial-size classical circuit families. The implication may use the full code of the encryption algorithms, non-black-box reasoning and polynomially many messages. It must not assume an additional property of encryption unless that property is proved to follow from the stated premise.
cards.definitions:
Common conventions. The security parameter \(\lambda\ge1\) is provided as the unary string \(1^\lambda\). A nonnegative function \(\mu\) is negligible if for every positive integer \(c\), some \(\lambda_0\) satisfies \(\mu(\lambda)\le\lambda^{-c}\) for all \(\lambda\ge\lambda_0\). An algorithm is uniform probabilistic polynomial time if it has one fixed finite multitape Turing-machine program and a bound \(K(L+1)^d\) on its bit steps for every input of total length \(L\) and every sequence of independent fair random bits, for some fixed positive integers \(K,d\). Reading, arithmetic, coin generation and all output bits are charged. Malformed inputs may be rejected but must satisfy the clock. There is no advice, ideal oracle, quantum resource or uncharged preprocessing.

For polynomial-length random bit strings \(X_\lambda,Y_\lambda\), write \(X_\lambda\approx_c Y_\lambda\) when for every Boolean circuit family \((D_\lambda)\) of polynomially bounded description length,
\[\left|\Pr[D_\lambda(X_\lambda)=1]-\Pr[D_\lambda(Y_\lambda)=1]\right|\]
is negligible in \(\lambda\). Such a family need not be uniformly generated. It may hardwire polynomial-length auxiliary information, including the input sequence under consideration. Deterministic circuits with binary AND/OR gates, unary NOT gates and constants suffice; private random coins could equivalently be allowed. Encodings expose actual string lengths, with zero padding to a common polynomial bound for the distinguisher. Tuples and messages are encoded by their number of components and each component's length followed by its bits. Nonnegative lengths use \(U(t)=1^\ell0s\), where \(s\) is the canonical binary expansion of \(t\), \(\ell=|s|\), and zero uses \(s=0\).

Public-key encryption. A scheme consists of three uniform probabilistic polynomial-time algorithms, with public code:
\[(pk,sk)\leftarrow\mathrm{KeyGen}(1^\lambda),\quad z\leftarrow\mathrm{Enc}(1^\lambda,pk,m),\quad \widehat m\leftarrow\mathrm{Dec}(1^\lambda,sk,z).\]
Keys and ciphertexts are ordinary finite bit strings; \(m\in\{0,1\}\), and decryption returns a bit or a failure symbol \(\bot\). All invocations use fresh independent coins. Keys generated at parameter \(\lambda\), honest ciphertexts and their encodings have polynomial length in \(\lambda\). Correctness requires one negligible function \(\mu_E\) such that for every \(\lambda\) and both message bits,
\[\Pr[\mathrm{Dec}(1^\lambda,sk,\mathrm{Enc}(1^\lambda,pk,m))\ne m]\le\mu_E(\lambda),\]
where the probability includes fresh key-generation, encryption and any decryption randomness.

IND-CPA security for bits means
\[(pk,\mathrm{Enc}(1^\lambda,pk,0))\ \approx_c\ (pk,\mathrm{Enc}(1^\lambda,pk,1)),\]
with fresh keys and encryption coins in each experiment. The secret key is not given to the distinguisher. The encryption algorithm is public, so polynomially many encryptions chosen by an attacker can be computed locally. No decryption oracle is available. For this bit-message case the two displayed challenge distributions specify the chosen-plaintext confidentiality requirement. The assertion \(E\) is existence of any scheme satisfying this correctness and security, without algebraic, rerandomization, key-sampling or ciphertext-sampling promises.

Oblivious transfer. The sender \(S\) receives private bits \((m_0,m_1)\), and the receiver \(R\) receives a private choice bit \(c\). Both receive \(1^\lambda\), have independent private fair coins, and exchange a finite ordered sequence of classical messages directly. There is one fixed protocol, with polynomially many bit steps per party, messages and communicated bits on every honest execution and every random-tape choice. Equivalently, all these quantities are bounded by some \(B(\lambda)=K(\lambda+1)^d\) independent of the inputs. The receiver outputs \(y\in\{0,1,\bot\}\); the sender has no output. Correctness requires a negligible \(\mu_T\) such that
\[\forall\lambda\ \forall(m_0,m_1,c)\in\{0,1\}^3:\quad\Pr[y=m_c]\ge1-\mu_T(\lambda).\]
The failure symbol counts as an error. There is no requirement of two rounds or constant rounds.

Static semi-honest corruption means that at most one party is designated corrupted before execution, then follows the prescribed algorithm with the prescribed coin distribution while retaining all information it sees. It may afterwards apply any polynomial-size computation to this information. It does not modify messages, bias its randomness, change its input during the protocol or erase data to satisfy a security condition. The real view \(\operatorname{View}_S\) includes the sender's input, its complete random tape and all sent/received messages. The real view \(\operatorname{View}_R\) includes the receiver's input, its complete random tape, all messages and its final output. A fixed polynomial number of fair bits may be sampled at the start and unused bits retained. Internal computation is determined by the input, coins and messages and is thus recoverable from the view.

Privacy requires two fixed uniform probabilistic polynomial-time simulators \(\operatorname{Sim}_S,\operatorname{Sim}_R\). For every sequence of input triples \((m_{0,\lambda},m_{1,\lambda},c_\lambda)\), the following ensemble pairs must be computationally indistinguishable:
\[\operatorname{View}_S(1^\lambda,m_{0,\lambda},m_{1,\lambda},c_\lambda)\ \approx_c\ \operatorname{Sim}_S(1^\lambda,m_{0,\lambda},m_{1,\lambda}),\]
\[\operatorname{View}_R(1^\lambda,m_{0,\lambda},m_{1,\lambda},c_\lambda)\ \approx_c\ \operatorname{Sim}_R(1^\lambda,c_\lambda,m_{c_\lambda,\lambda}).\]
The source of randomness on the left is an honest interaction of both parties; each right-hand experiment uses the simulator's own fresh coins. Input sequences need not be efficiently computable. The sender simulator receives no choice bit; the receiver simulator receives no unchosen message. The simulators precede the quantifiers over sequences and distinguishers, and have worst-case polynomial clocks rather than merely expected polynomial time. The assertion \(T\) is existence of a protocol and simulators satisfying these requirements.

The plain model supplies no common reference string, random oracle, trusted third party or hardware, and no pre-shared correlated randomness or secret. It permits only the independent randomness and communication just described. The security task is one standalone execution with static passive corruption; malicious deviation, adaptive corruption, fairness, guaranteed delivery against abort and universal composability are not additional requirements.
cards.answer_criterion: Provide a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of \(E\Rightarrow T\) or its full logical negation. A positive proof must obtain the specified uniform protocol and simulators, establish all polynomial clocks and communication bounds, and prove correctness and both privacy ensembles from the encryption premise alone. Non-black-box use of encryption code and non-black-box security arguments are permitted. The literal negative answer is \(E\land\neg T\) in the ordinary, unrelativized model. An oracle world with encryption but no OT, a lower bound on black-box reductions, an attack on one protocol or a failure at a prescribed round count does not prove that negation. Any extra sampling or rerandomization property used by a proposed construction must also be derived from the premise.
cards.why: Public-key encryption protects a message from someone without its decryption key. Oblivious transfer must also protect a sender from a receiver who is entitled to learn one selected message, while hiding that selection from the sender. Determining whether the first capability already implies the second would clarify a basic boundary between secure communication and general private computation.

importance.reason: A foundational comparison between ordinary public-key confidentiality and a primitive complete for secure computation; resolving it would change which assumptions suffice for a broad range of protocols.

cards.status_note: Checked on 16 September 2026. No unrestricted implication from arbitrary classical IND-CPA public-key encryption to the specified static semi-honest standalone OT was found in the inspected literature. The original oracle separation explicitly uses uniform adversaries, and does not refute this ordinary-world nonuniform-security formulation. Structured rerandomizable/updatable-encryption results retain extra properties. context_blocks.text: The two privacy obligations are different. The sender must not learn the receiver’s choice, and the receiver must not learn anything about the unselected message beyond what its allowed input and output already imply. Simulation expresses both requirements without assuming the messages themselves are random or secret from all prior information. Correctness is separate: a protocol that exchanges nothing may reveal nothing, but it does not deliver the selected bit.

Gertner and coauthors ask directly whether public-key encryption implies OT. Their positive results require additional oblivious-sampling properties of public keys or ciphertexts. Their negative result constructs an oracle relative to which encryption exists but even semi-honest OT does not. That theorem is a substantial restriction on relativizing construction methods; it is not an ordinary-world separation of the two existence statements.

The historical oracle theorem also has an explicit uniformity qualification. Its authors prove security and separation for probabilistic polynomial-time adversaries and state that extension to nonuniform circuit adversaries would require further work. The present card fixes nonuniform distinguishers, so the original theorem should not be presented as an exact separation for every quantifier in its definitions.

Allowing non-black-box techniques means a proof may use the actual finite descriptions of encryption algorithms. Replacing those algorithms by a freely chosen oracle can remove information that such a proof uses. An oracle barrier therefore cannot simply be reinterpreted as the negation of the unrestricted implication. The target also allows polynomially many rounds, so a barrier at a fixed small round count is insufficient.

Even passive-security OT is a powerful goal. Haitner and coauthors give a fully black-box transformation from semi-honest OT to maliciously secure OT and then to general secure computation. Their formulation uses static corruption, standalone security and, for the stronger malicious task, simulators that may run in expected polynomial time. It does not promise fairness or delivery despite malicious abort. These are consequences in a specified model, not extra requirements silently added to this card.

Li, Zhang and Lin replace earlier oblivious-sampling conditions by public rerandomizability: given a public key, an algorithm can turn a ciphertext into a fresh one with the same plaintext. Their abstract gives OT constructions under this property. IND-CPA confidentiality by itself does not include such an algorithm, so the result covers an enriched encryption primitive.

The March 2026 updatable-encryption article likewise retains precise extra properties. Its two-round OT implication uses oblivious samplability of original ciphertexts and update tokens; its three-round implication uses oblivious samplability of updated ciphertexts. Updatable encryption is a structured symmetric encryption primitive with tokens for transforming ciphertexts across keys. The inspected theorem summaries do not start from an arbitrary IND-CPA public-key scheme.

The January 2026 Minicrypt preprint gives a particularly relevant distinction between a non-black-box implication and an oracle construction. Its abstract claims OT from a standard-model oblivious interactive hash function, and separately constructs that hash primitive in a random-oracle model. It explicitly says that these two statements cannot be composed into OT from a random oracle: the non-black-box step applies only to an ordinary finite implementation. No generic construction of that implementation from arbitrary PKE is claimed in the checked abstract.

The March 2026 stabilizer-decoding preprint gives another kind of progress: a new average-case hardness premise supports both PKE and OT. Having a common sufficient assumption does not show that either primitive follows from every implementation of the other. The additional algebraic structure of that decoding problem remains part of its construction’s foundation.

Fair coin tossing provides a related comparison. Maji and Wang prove limits on protocols that use PKE or key agreement as black boxes, whereas an OT resource supports the optimal fairness scale considered there. That result concerns a different functionality and a restricted construction model. It adds evidence about the hierarchy without resolving the unrestricted semi-honest OT implication.

cards.title: Collision-resistant hashing from one-way functions
cards.formal:
In the ordinary classical computational model, is the following existence implication true?
\[\bigl(\exists f\;\operatorname{OWF}(f)\bigr)\ \Longrightarrow\ \bigl(\exists\operatorname{Gen},H\;\operatorname{CRH}(\operatorname{Gen},H)\bigr).\]
The predicates are defined below. The honest functions and algorithms are uniform and polynomial-time, and security is against every nonuniform family of polynomial-size classical Boolean circuits. The hash family has a freshly sampled public key \(k\) and maps \(H_k:\{0,1\}^{2\lambda}\to\{0,1\}^{\lambda}\) for every positive integer security parameter \(\lambda\). Both members of a proposed collision may be chosen after the key is known. The implication permits unrestricted constructions and proof techniques, including use of a one-way function's implementation.
cards.definitions:
Parameters and computation. All strings are finite binary strings. The security parameters \(n,\lambda\) range over the positive integers, and \(1^n\) denotes the unary string of \(n\) ones. Honest algorithms are ordinary Turing machines with one fixed finite program, no advice and no oracles. Deterministic algorithms have polynomial bit running time in the total input length. A probabilistic polynomial-time algorithm additionally uses independent fair random bits and has a polynomial running-time bound on every random tape; it therefore uses at most polynomially many random bits. The polynomial and its degree are fixed for each program, independent of the parameter and sampled inputs.

Adversaries. A nonuniform polynomial-size circuit family \((A_n)_{n\ge1}\) consists of finite acyclic Boolean circuits over AND, OR, NOT and constant gates, with fan-in at most two and unrestricted fan-out. Size counts all gates and input and output wires, including random input wires. There are constants \(C,d\in\mathbb N_{>0}\) such that each size is at most \(C(n+1)^d\). A randomized circuit receives independent uniform bits on its random wires. Circuit descriptions may be arbitrary functions of the parameter and the fixed public honest programs; no algorithm generating the family is required. They are fixed before the fresh challenge or hash key is sampled. Each family has its own polynomial bound.

Finite-string encoding. To supply a string \(z\) of length at most an integer bound \(P\) to a fixed-width circuit, use \(\operatorname{enc}_P(z)\): the binary representation of \(|z|\), padded to exactly \(\lceil\log_2(P+1)\rceil\) bits, followed by \(z\) and enough zero bits to fill a \(P\)-bit data field. Bounds used below are positive integer-valued polynomials. This encoding reveals the string and its length and adds only polynomial overhead. In particular, variable-length function outputs and public keys are not supplied as a length-regularity promise.

Negligibility. A function \(\mu:\mathbb N_{>0}\to[0,1]\) is negligible if
\[\forall c\in\mathbb N_{>0}\ \exists N_c\in\mathbb N_{>0}\ \forall n\ge N_c:\quad\mu(n)\le n^{-c}.\]
The threshold may depend on the exponent and the adversary, as well as on the fixed primitive. Security must hold eventually for every parameter, not merely on an infinite subsequence. No fixed inverse-polynomial or constant error is allowed.

One-way function. A candidate \(f:\{0,1\}^{*}\to\{0,1\}^{*}\) is total and uniformly deterministic polynomial-time computable. Fix a positive integer-valued polynomial \(p\) bounding \(|f(x)|\) whenever \(|x|=n\). In its inversion experiment, sample \(X\) uniformly from \(\{0,1\}^n\), independently sample the circuit's random wires \(R\), and compute exactly once
\[Y=A_n(1^n,\operatorname{enc}_{p(n)}(f(X));R)\in\{0,1\}^n.\]
Define \(\operatorname{Inv}_{f,A}(n)=\Pr[f(Y)=f(X)]\). Then \(\operatorname{OWF}(f)\) means this probability is negligible for every permitted family \(A\). Any preimage of the challenge of length \(n\) is accepted; recovery of the original \(X\) is not required. Restricting the circuit output to \(n\) bits only removes invalid answers, which could always be replaced by a fixed \(n\)-bit candidate. The choice of the polynomial padding bound does not change security because valid encodings with different bounds can be converted in polynomial time.

Publicly keyed hash family. A candidate consists of a uniform probabilistic polynomial-time generator \(\operatorname{Gen}(1^\lambda)\) and a uniform deterministic polynomial-time evaluator \(H(1^\lambda,k,x)\). There is a fixed positive integer-valued polynomial \(q\) such that every generated key has length at most \(q(\lambda)\). For every key in the support of the generator and every \(x\in\{0,1\}^{2\lambda}\), the evaluator outputs exactly \(\lambda\) bits. Write \(H_k(x)=H(1^\lambda,k,x)\) when the parameter is understood. No evaluator property is required for keys outside that support. The key need not be uniform over all strings; its actual distribution is the output of the generator. It is fully public, and evaluation needs no secret.

Collision experiment. Independently sample the generator's random tape \(S\) and the adversary's random wires \(R\), set \(k=\operatorname{Gen}(1^\lambda;S)\), and compute exactly once
\[(x,x')=B_\lambda(1^\lambda,\operatorname{enc}_{q(\lambda)}(k);R)\in\{0,1\}^{2\lambda}\times\{0,1\}^{2\lambda}.\]
Define
\[\operatorname{Coll}_{\operatorname{Gen},H,B}(\lambda)=\Pr[x\ne x'\ \land\ H(1^\lambda,k,x)=H(1^\lambda,k,x')].\]
The predicate \(\operatorname{CRH}(\operatorname{Gen},H)\) means this probability is negligible for every permitted circuit family \(B\). The adversary can compute the public evaluator within its circuit budget and select both inputs as functions of the key. It does not receive the generator's private random tape. Fixed-width candidate outputs again lose no successful attacks.

Scope of the implication. Existence of any one-way function in this model is the only cryptographic hypothesis. The conclusion is existence of some secure hash family; it need not be a particular proposed transformation applied to every one-way function. There is no requirement that a single algorithm transform arbitrary program descriptions into hash-family descriptions. No random oracle, trusted setup, quantum computation, extra hardness assumption or stronger exponential-security requirement is supplied. The all-parameter, nonuniform security and exact factor-two compression conventions are retained from the inherited card.
cards.answer_criterion:
Give a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of the stated implication or its logical negation. A positive proof must establish the existence of the specified public-key generator and evaluator from the one-way-function hypothesis alone, including uniform polynomial-time computability, exact compression for every generated key, and negligible collision success against every nonuniform polynomial-size circuit family. All transformations of parameters and security guarantees used in that proof must be justified. A proof may use function implementations and need not be black-box.

The logical negation requires proving both that a one-way function exists and that no hash family satisfying this model exists. For the latter assertion, every pair of uniform polynomial-time programs meeting the hash syntax must admit a permitted circuit family with nonnegligible collision probability. Equivalently, for each such pair there must be an adversary and a fixed \(c\in\mathbb N_{>0}\) whose success exceeds \(\lambda^{-c}\) for infinitely many \(\lambda\). Merely proving that a chosen construction fails, even for one secure one-way function, is insufficient.

An oracle world separating these primitives or an impossibility theorem restricted to black-box reductions establishes a barrier, not this ordinary-model negation. Target-collision resistance, resistance only to finding three or more colliding inputs, injective noncompressing functions, security only for uniform adversaries or only infinitely often, and constructions assuming quantitative product hardness do not meet the full conclusion. This is an exact yes-or-no implication, with no additive numerical tolerance on the security requirement.
cards.why: Determines whether a fundamental compressing cryptographic primitive needs assumptions beyond ordinary one-wayness, while exposing the gap between known black-box barriers and unrestricted constructions.

importance.reason: A central unresolved implication among cryptographic primitives, with consequences for authentication, data commitments and succinct verification.

progress.text: Rompel obtains universal one-way hashing and secure signatures from arbitrary one-way functions; this uses the weaker target-before-key collision game.
Simon proves an oracle separation from one-way permutations, establishing the classical black-box obstacle.
Holmgren–Lombardi construct collision-resistant hashing from quantitatively strong one-way product functions, an additional assumption.
Folwarczný and coauthors extend total-search barriers to specified single-query semi-black-box reductions; the preprint appears at ITCS 2024.

Mao–Zhang report a fully black-box separation between successive constant-multiplicity collision-resistance notions, including pair resistance from triple resistance. The unrestricted one-way-function implication remains open.
Rothblum constructs bounded-space interactive arguments from one-way functions, without resolving the hashing implication.

cards.status_note: Checked through 16 September 2026. The March/April 2026 primary multicollision paper explicitly leaves construction from general one-way functions open. It adds a fully black-box hierarchy, while the July interactive-argument result bypasses full collision resistance in a specific application. No unrestricted implication or ordinary-model refutation was found in the bounded primary-source search. Uniform honest programs, nonuniform classical adversaries, all-parameter negligible security and fresh public factor-two-compressing hashes remain the selected model; external proofs were not independently certified.

context_blocks.text: A collision-resistant hash compresses its input while making it computationally difficult to find two distinct messages with the same digest. Collisions must exist by the pigeonhole principle: there are \(2^{2\lambda}\) possible inputs and only \(2^{\lambda}\) outputs. Security is therefore not a claim that collisions never occur, or that a digest uniquely identifies a message. It is a claim about what an efficient adversary can construct after learning the hash key.

A one-way function poses a different challenge. The attacker receives the image of a random input and must find any preimage. An injective one-way function can have no collisions at all, yet it is not a compressing hash. Conversely, a compressing map may have easily found collisions even if some inversion tasks look difficult. The question asks whether the minimal assumption of computationally hard inversion can always supply the more structured difficulty of finding collisions.

The public key matters to the asymptotic definition. If a single compressing function were fixed at each security parameter and security were required against nonuniform circuits, an attacker could hard-code one collision for each parameter. A fresh polynomial-length key prevents that pair from being selected in advance for the actual function used. The key is not secret: the adversary sees it before choosing either colliding message.

Target-collision resistance changes the order of moves. An attacker first commits to one message, then sees a random key and seeks a second message colliding with its committed target. Rompel constructs universal one-way hash functions of this kind from arbitrary one-way functions, as part of the route to secure signatures. That theorem does not give the present game, where both messages are chosen after the key is known. The order difference is small syntactically but central to the unresolved assumption gap.

Simon constructs an oracle setting with one-way permutations but no collision-resistant hash functions in the relevant relativized sense. It rules out building and proving the desired primitive by treating the assumed function purely as an oracle in the separated framework. The theorem does not rule out exploiting a function’s implementation or a proof that fails to relativize. The ordinary mathematical implication in this card therefore remains stronger than the black-box construction question already answered negatively.

Holmgren and Lombardi construct collision-resistant hashing under stronger assumptions on simultaneously inverting independently sampled challenges. Their Theorem I.5 uses symmetric injective two-product functions whose batch inversion probability is at most \(2^{-n-\omega(\log n)}\) for polynomial-time attackers; a separate theorem treats noninjective functions under stronger quantitative hardness. Ordinary one-wayness only requires a negligible single-challenge inversion probability. The product assumption is therefore additional structure and security, not an established consequence of the hypothesis on this card.

Collision finding is also a total search problem: an explicitly represented shrinking circuit always has two distinct inputs with the same output, and a proposed pair can be checked efficiently. The published ITCS 2024 paper of Folwarczný and coauthors extends separation results to a restricted class of reductions for total NP search. Its main condition permits a single call to a total-search solver and no query to the one-way function before that call. The result includes semi-black-box reductions, but is still a limitation on a specified reduction model.

Mao and Zhang's March 2026 manuscript, published on ECCC in April, reports a further black-box hierarchy: for every fixed \(K\ge2\), \(K\)-collision resistance cannot be constructed fully black-box from \((K+1)\)-collision resistance in their model. Here an attacker seeks \(K\) distinct inputs with one common hash value. In particular, hardness of finding a triple does not give a black-box construction of hardness of finding a pair. The paper also separates distributional collision resistance from three-collision resistance. These are barriers among weaker primitives; the ordinary unrestricted implication from one-way functions remains open in the introduction.

Rothblum's July 2026 manuscript reports interactive arguments for deterministic computations taking time \(T\) and space \(S\), assuming one-way functions. The communication is \(S\operatorname{poly}(\log T,\kappa)\), the verifier time is \((S+n)\operatorname{poly}(\log T,\kappa)\), and the number of rounds is polylogarithmic in \(T\). Soundness loses a factor polynomial in \(T\) in the adversary-size bound. This weakens assumptions for an interactive application; its use of target-collision-resistant hashing does not supply full public-key collision resistance.

A resolution would clarify the foundations of many protocols that use short commitments to large data. It would either place full collision resistance on the same assumption level as ordinary one-wayness, or demonstrate a separation that survives beyond black-box barriers. The card asks for polynomial security only; requiring near-optimal exponential security or resistance to quantum attacks would introduce additional questions.

cards.title: One-way permutations from one-way functions
cards.formal: Does the existence of classical one-way functions secure against nonuniform polynomial-size adversaries imply the existence of a classical, efficiently generated family of full-domain one-way permutations with the same security convention?
cards.definitions: A one-way function is a uniformly polynomial-time computable family \(f_{n}:\{0,1\}^{n}\to \{0,1\}^{\ell (n)}\), for a polynomially bounded, computable output length \(\ell\), such that for every randomized polynomial-size circuit family \(A_{n}, \Pr [f_{n}(A_{n}(1^{n},f_{n}(X)))=f_{n}(X)]\) is negligible in n for uniform \(X\in \{0,1\}^{n}\); outputs outside \(\{0,1\}^{n}\) fail. A function \(\mu\) is negligible if for every \(c>0, \mu (n)\le n^{-c}\) for all sufficiently large n. A permutation family consists of a uniform probabilistic polynomial-time key generator \(Gen(1^{n})\) and deterministic polynomial-time evaluation \(Eval(1^{n},pk,x)\), with a fixed polynomially bounded, polynomial-time computable integer \(m(n)\ge n\). For every pk in the support of \(Gen(1^{n})\), Eval defines a bijection \(\pi _{pk}:\{0,1\}^{m(n)}\to \{0,1\}^{m(n)}\). For every randomized polynomial-size adversary \(A_{n}, \Pr [\pi _{pk}(A_{n}(1^{n},pk,\pi _{pk}(X)))=\pi _{pk}(X)]\) must be negligible, with \(pk\leftarrow Gen(1^{n})\), independent uniform X and independent adversary coins. Malformed outputs fail. The public key is available to the attacker; no trapdoor is required or given. All security is classical. “Full-domain” fixes the input set to the whole Boolean cube; the valid public-key set need not be all bit strings of its length. The implication is an ordinary existence implication, without restrictions to black-box constructions and without extra assumptions such as obfuscation or subexponential security.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove the stated existence implication, allowing any mathematical construction or proof technique, or refute that implication in the ordinary computational model. Proving that one-way functions do not exist would make the implication vacuously true. An oracle separation or a theorem excluding a restricted class of reductions is a construction barrier, not a refutation of the unrestricted implication. A permutation family on special sparse domains does not meet the full-domain convention fixed here; an additional trapdoor property would be a stronger positive result.
cards.why: Determine whether basic average-case inversion hardness necessarily supports efficient bijections, a rigid primitive at the foundation of cryptographic constructions.

importance.reason: A longstanding question about the structure obtainable from minimal cryptographic assumptions, with strong construction barriers and a recent full-domain breakthrough under additional assumptions.

progress.text: Rudich develops oracle barriers; the thesis’s one-way-function-to-permutation argument is conditional on a combinatorial conjecture.
Håstad–Impagliazzo–Levin–Luby establish pseudorandom generators from arbitrary one-way functions, without obtaining a permutation guarantee.
Matsuda–Matsuura exclude fully black-box constructions from even one-bit-expanding injective one-way functions with adaptive one-wayness.
Asharov–Segev handle domains depending on the primitives in their OWF-only barrier, and separately study domain-invariant constructions using obfuscation.
Shmueli–Zhandry obtain full-domain trapdoor permutations from subexponentially secure iO and OWFs; Section 1.4 distinguishes input-domain from key-domain invariance.

The 2025 full-domain trapdoor construction requires subexponential iO and OWF assumptions. Existing oracle and black-box barriers do not settle the unrestricted question. This card explicitly fixes the full-domain keyed convention.

context_blocks.text: A one-way function is easy to evaluate but hard to invert on a random input. It may identify many different inputs and need not cover its output space. A one-way permutation has exactly one preimage for every output in its domain. The extra requirement is structural: nothing is lost mathematically, yet efficiently recovering the uniquely determined input must remain infeasible.

This card fixes the full-domain, public-key family version because the original phrase “one-way permutation” leaves several conventions unspecified. A public key chooses a permutation of an entire Boolean cube; all input strings of that length are valid. A stronger unkeyed formulation asks for a single length-preserving permutation on all bit strings. A more permissive formulation allows key-dependent sparse domains. Results in those settings must be compared with their domain and sampling requirements visible.

Making a computation reversible is not enough. The map \((x,z)\mapsto (x,z \mathrm{XOR} f(x))\) is a bijection for any efficiently computable length-compatible f, but its inverse is obtained by applying exactly the same map. Likewise, simply attaching x to \(f(x)\) makes the output injective while revealing the desired preimage. The construction has to preserve computational difficulty while removing collisions and covering the domain, without publishing the information needed for inversion.

Many other forms of cryptographic structure can be derived from bare one-wayness. Håstad, Impagliazzo, Levin and Luby show that every one-way function yields a pseudorandom generator. That success does not enforce bijectivity. The permutation question tests whether computational hardness can always be reorganized into a particularly rigid, uniquely invertible mathematical object.

Rudich’s 1988 thesis developed the oracle-separation approach and gave a barrier for this implication conditional on a combinatorial conjecture. The thesis abstract states that qualification explicitly. It is misleading to describe the original thesis alone as an unconditional separation of the ordinary existence assumptions. An oracle world changes what algorithms can access, so it diagnoses limitations of proof techniques rather than settling the actual implication.

Matsuda and Matsuura subsequently prove a fully black-box barrier even when the starting function is injective, increases length by only one bit, and satisfies their stronger adaptive one-wayness condition. Thus an apparently tiny departure from a permutation already defeats a broad class of generic constructions. Their result concerns constructions that treat the supplied primitive and adversary through specified interfaces; it does not exclude exploiting the code or other structure of a concrete function.

Asharov and Segev address another subtlety: earlier negative arguments could fail when the construction’s domains depended on the underlying primitives. They exclude black-box constructions from one-way functions even without that domain-invariance requirement. They also give a separate barrier for constructions using oracle-aided indistinguishability obfuscation, under domain-invariance conditions. The two statements have different assumptions and should not be merged into an unrestricted impossibility theorem.

There is significant progress with stronger assumptions. Shmueli and Zhandry’s July 2025 paper constructs full-domain trapdoor one-way permutations assuming subexponentially secure indistinguishability obfuscation and subexponentially secure one-way functions. It uses a new kind of pseudorandom permutation that supports controlled permutation of its outputs. The trapdoor guarantee is stronger than this card requests, but both the extra primitive and the stronger hardness assumptions prevent this from proving the target implication.

The same paper explains why its full-domain result is compatible with the earlier obfuscation barrier. Its input domain is the whole cube, but its public keys are obfuscated programs. The valid-key domain therefore depends on the building blocks. The older formal domain-invariance condition constrains both input and key domains. Keeping these two notions separate prevents an erroneous claim that a published barrier has been contradicted.

A positive answer would show that unique, length-preserving inversion hardness is available whenever basic cryptographic hardness exists. A negative answer would reveal a structural separation inside foundational cryptographic assumptions. Existing barriers make the problem especially informative: a successful construction from ordinary one-way functions would need to escape the established generic approaches, rather than merely improve their efficiency.

cards.title: Chosen-ciphertext security from ordinary public-key encryption
cards.formal: Does the existence of IND-CPA-secure public-key encryption imply the existence of IND-CCA2-secure public-key encryption in the plain model, with classical security against all nonuniform polynomial-size adversaries and no additional computational assumption?
cards.definitions: A public-key encryption scheme has uniform probabilistic polynomial-time algorithms \(Gen(1^{n})\to (pk,sk)\) and \(Enc(pk,m)\to c\) and a deterministic polynomial-time algorithm \(Dec(sk,c)\to m\) or ⊥. It supports bit-string messages of any polynomially bounded length. For every polynomial p, the maximum decryption-error probability over messages |\(m|\le p(n)\) is negligible in n, with probability over key generation and honest encryption. In the IND-CPA game an adversary receives pk, chooses equal-length messages \(m_{0},m_{1}\) and state, receives \(c*=Enc(pk,m_{b})\) for an independent uniform bit b, and guesses b. Its advantage is |Pr[guess=b]−\(1/2|\). In the IND-CCA2 game it also has adaptive access to \(Dec(sk,\cdot )\), both before and after choosing the challenge messages and receiving c*. After the challenge, the oracle rejects the exact bit string c*; all other ciphertext queries are allowed. Security requires negligible advantage for every nonuniform probabilistic polynomial-time adversary, allowing any polynomial number of oracle queries. Negligible means eventually smaller than \(n^{-a}\) for every \(a>0\). Each adversary has its own polynomial resource bound, but the scheme is fixed independently of that bound. The plain model has no ideal random oracle, externally supplied common reference string, hardware or trusted setup beyond the recipient generating its own key pair. This is an unrestricted existence implication, not a requirement that a compiler treat the original scheme as a black box.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove that an IND-CCA2 scheme with these guarantees exists whenever an IND-CPA scheme exists, or refute that implication in the ordinary computational model. A conversion assuming additional trapdoor functions, suitable proof systems, special pseudorandom generators or ideal random oracles does not by itself suffice. A theorem excluding a restricted class of black-box conversions is a barrier, not a negative answer to the unrestricted implication. Fixed-query bounded CCA2, pre-challenge-only CCA1 and non-malleability without adaptive decryption access are weaker targets.
cards.why: Determine whether public-key confidentiality alone can always be strengthened to resist adaptive decryption attacks, without importing another cryptographic assumption.

importance.reason: A central question about the minimal assumptions for robust public-key encryption, connecting encryption, proof systems, trapdoor structure and generic security transformations.

The revised threshold-encryption work retains additional-model or stronger-security requirements in its CPA-to-CCA transformations.

context_blocks.text: Public-key encryption already allows anyone, including the attacker, to create ciphertexts. Ordinary chosen-plaintext security protects the contents of an honestly generated challenge ciphertext. Chosen-ciphertext security additionally protects it while the attacker submits other ciphertexts for decryption and uses the responses to decide what to ask next. The only forbidden query is the challenge itself, because returning its plaintext would make confidentiality impossible by definition.

A simple modification illustrates the gap between definitions. Start with a secure ordinary scheme, append an unused bit to every ciphertext, and make decryption ignore that bit. The modification preserves chosen-plaintext security. A chosen-ciphertext attacker flips the challenge’s unused bit and submits the resulting different string to the oracle, which returns the challenge plaintext. This proves that a particular CPA scheme need not itself be CCA-secure; it does not rule out building another scheme from its existence.

This is why the question concerns a construction or existence implication. A successful transformation may change the ciphertext format, use many public keys, encode messages, and inspect the original algorithms’ descriptions. It must arrange that responses to every other ciphertext remain harmless. A proof faces the corresponding simulation problem: how can it answer decryption queries while relying only on a challenge from the weaker security game?

The source proposal points to Trevisan’s cryptography project list, which explicitly asks whether CCA security can be derived from CPA security by black-box techniques or by any techniques. Its bibliography juxtaposes partial negative results with positive results for non-malleability. That distinction remains important: an advance for one attack model should not silently be reported as a solution for another.

Gertner, Malkin and Myers give a black-box separation for constructions whose new decryption algorithm never calls the original encryption algorithm. This covers a substantial class of natural attempts. It still leaves constructions that re-encrypt during decryption, and does not cover arbitrary use of the source code. The scope of that restriction is central to the theorem, rather than a technical detail that can be omitted.

Choi, Dachman-Soled, Malkin and Wee construct non-malleable encryption from any semantically secure scheme and extend their approach to bounded chosen-ciphertext attacks. In the bounded version, the permitted number q of decryption queries is fixed before constructing the scheme. Full CCA2 instead asks for one scheme that withstands every polynomial-time attacker, whose query polynomial can be larger than any particular bound built into that scheme.

Another productive route adds a primitive that helps enforce ciphertext validity. Hohenberger, Koppula and Waters prove in CRYPTO 2020 that injective trapdoor functions suffice for CCA-secure public-key encryption, without requiring lossiness or correlated-product security. This removes significant earlier restrictions. An arbitrary encryption scheme is not automatically such a trapdoor function: its decryption need only recover the message, not a unique full input including encryption randomness.

Koppula and Waters obtain generic upgrades using a hinting pseudorandom generator, whose security survives a special kind of auxiliary information. Ordinary pseudorandomness does not state that guarantee. Their construction offers another way to organize the decryption proof, but applying it to arbitrary public-key encryption still requires establishing the additional hinting property from the original assumption.

Matsuda’s PKC 2025 work shows that a publicly verifiable noninteractive batch argument for NP can supply the additional ingredient. The May 2025 revision weakens the required proof-length savings: they need not be strong enough for currently known constructions of noninteractive zero knowledge. This is progress in reducing the extra structure needed for the upgrade. The paper still assumes the batch argument; it does not construct it from arbitrary CPA encryption.

A PKC 2026 paper by Brzuska, Klooß and Woo gives CPA-to-CCA transformations for threshold encryption, where several parties jointly decrypt. Its generic transform from arbitrary CPA-secure threshold encryption uses a random oracle. Its other route has additional requirements, including a stronger semi-malicious CPA notion. The July 2026 revision therefore does not establish the plain-model implication in this card.

Resolving the implication would clarify whether protection against active ciphertext manipulation is an additional foundational assumption or a consequence of ordinary public-key confidentiality. It would also explain why existing general approaches repeatedly need structure beyond the weak starting primitive. The target is a foundational security theorem; it does not ask that the resulting construction be practical or preserve the original scheme’s efficiency.

cards.title: Noninteractive zero knowledge from one-way functions
cards.formal: Does the existence of classical one-way functions imply reusable, adaptively secure noninteractive zero-knowledge arguments for circuit satisfiability in the honestly generated common-reference-string model, with computational soundness and computational zero knowledge against nonuniform polynomial-size adversaries?
cards.definitions: A one-way function is a uniformly polynomial-time computable family \(f_{n}\) on uniform n-bit inputs with polynomial-length outputs, such that every nonuniform randomized polynomial-size adversary given \(1^{n}\) and \(f_{n}(X)\) finds any n-bit preimage with negligible probability. Circuit satisfiability has statements x encoding Boolean circuits and witnesses w assigning their inputs, with \(R(x,w)=1\) exactly when the circuit outputs 1. A proposed argument consists of uniform algorithms \(Setup(1^{\lambda},1^{B})\to\)crs, Prove(crs,x,w)→\(\pi\), and Verify(crs,\(x,\pi\))→\(\{0,1\}\); their time and output length are polynomial in \(\lambda +B\), where B bounds statement and witness lengths. Setup is independent of the later statements; its private coins are not published. For every polynomial \(B=B(\lambda )\), completeness error is negligible uniformly over valid \((x,w)\) of length at most B. Adaptive computational soundness means that every nonuniform polynomial-time adversary given crs has negligible probability of outputting an unsatisfiable x and an accepted \(\pi\). Reusable computational zero knowledge means there exist uniform polynomial-time SimSetup and SimProve such that no nonuniform polynomial-time distinguisher separates these experiments: \((i)\) it receives honest crs and can adaptively request Prove(crs,x,w) for polynomially many valid pairs; \((ii)\) it receives simulated crs from SimSetup, and each valid query is answered by SimProve using the simulation trapdoor and x, without receiving w. Both experiments reject invalid queries, and the distinguisher retains arbitrary polynomial-size auxiliary information. All negligible bounds are in \(\lambda\): for each \(a>0\) the error is eventually below \(\lambda ^{-a}\). Only crs is public in the real system, and one proof message is sent for each statement. No random oracle, extra cryptographic assumption, online verifier challenge, proof of knowledge or succinctness requirement is included. Circuit satisfiability covers every NP language through witness-preserving polynomial reductions.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove the stated existence implication, or refute it in the ordinary computational model. The result may use the code of the one-way function and need not be black-box. A construction adding LWE, an appropriate batch argument, trapdoor hashing, or strong extra complexity assumptions does not suffice unless those ingredients are themselves derived from the same ordinary OWF premise. An interactive proof, a witness-indistinguishable argument, or a single-theorem result without a justified reusable upgrade is not the specified conclusion.
cards.why: Determine whether the minimal assumption supporting basic cryptography is sufficient for reusable, publicly verifiable proofs that reveal no witness and require no online interaction.

importance.reason: A fundamental boundary between interactive and noninteractive zero knowledge, with implications for the assumptions behind privacy-preserving proof systems and cryptographic transformations.

The cited BARG, trapdoor-hash and derandomization constructions retain extra assumptions; recent OWF-only succinct proofs are interactive, and high-error characterizations run in the reverse direction.

context_blocks.text: An NP witness can be easy to check and sensitive to reveal. For circuit satisfiability, publishing a satisfying assignment gives a verifier complete evidence, but also exposes every bit of that assignment. Zero knowledge asks for convincing evidence whose visible distribution can instead be simulated without the assignment. It formalizes the requirement that verification disclose no additional information beyond the statement’s truth.

The common reference string is an explicit resource. An honest setup algorithm produces public parameters before any statements are selected. After that setup, a prover sends one message that anyone can verify. The setup may retain randomness while generating the string, but that randomness is not handed to users. The simulation trapdoor exists only in the security experiment. This model differs from asking for a noninteractive system with no setup at all.

The card allows computational soundness: a computationally unbounded attacker might find a false accepted proof, but efficient attackers must not. Such a system is called an argument. It also asks for a reusable reference string, with statements chosen after seeing the string and earlier proofs. These choices make the target precise without requiring short proofs or a way to extract a witness from a successful prover.

The classical Goldreich–Micali–Wigderson theorem already supplies interactive zero-knowledge proofs for NP from one-way functions. Interaction gives the verifier a role in challenging what the prover has prepared. The inherited Damgård–Nielsen survey explicitly asks whether one-way functions suffice in the noninteractive setting. That survey discusses a proof-system version with stronger soundness; the argument target here asks for protection only against efficient cheating.

Known positive constructions use more structure. Peikert and Shiehian construct NIZK for NP from ordinary LWE in 2019. Their method builds hash families whose correlation-intractability property supports a sound Fiat–Shamir transformation. The point is a proved property of a specially constructed family, not simply substituting an arbitrary hash function for a verifier’s random challenge. LWE is a sufficient assumption, but it has not thereby been derived from arbitrary one-way functions.

Bradley, Waters and Wu show that an adaptively sound noninteractive batch argument for NP, together with a one-way function, yields NIZK. Their TCC 2024 result also studies how to obtain the needed adaptive soundness from other batch-argument guarantees. The title “Batch Arguments to NIZKs from One-Way Functions” must be read with its starting resource intact: the batch argument is an additional primitive, rather than something their theorem constructs from a bare one-way function.

Branco and coauthors develop a vector-trapdoor-hash approach, with an updated version in March 2026. Their constructions use either LWE or a combination of DDH and LPN assumptions. The initial black-box constructions provide single-theorem zero knowledge, and their multi-theorem upgrade uses cryptography in a non-black-box way. Chen, Rothblum and Tell pursue a different route through derandomization and strong computational hardness. Recent results in the reverse direction should not be read as a construction. Chakraborty, Hulett, Khurana and Tomer show in February 2026 that nontrivial NIZK arguments imply one-way functions under the hypothesis that NP is not contained in ioP/poly, even in a broad high-error regime. Another 2026 result gives succinct zero-knowledge proofs using one-way functions as black boxes. Florentz–Konopnicki and Rothblum’s protocol is interactive: its theorem explicitly bounds a number of public-coin rounds that depends on the relation’s parameters. Its noninteractive commitment component does not make the whole protocol noninteractive. A resolution of this card would isolate exactly how much cryptographic structure is needed to remove that interaction after a single reusable setup.

cards.context:
An NP witness can be easy to check and sensitive to reveal. For circuit satisfiability, publishing a satisfying assignment gives a verifier complete evidence, but also exposes every bit of that assignment. Zero knowledge asks for convincing evidence whose visible distribution can instead be simulated without the assignment. It formalizes the requirement that verification disclose no additional information beyond the statement’s truth.

The common reference string is an explicit resource. An honest setup algorithm produces public parameters before any statements are selected. After that setup, a prover sends one message that anyone can verify. The setup may retain randomness while generating the string, but that randomness is not handed to users. The simulation trapdoor exists only in the security experiment. This model differs from asking for a noninteractive system with no setup at all.

The card allows computational soundness: a computationally unbounded attacker might find a false accepted proof, but efficient attackers must not. Such a system is called an argument. It also asks for a reusable reference string, with statements chosen after seeing the string and earlier proofs. These choices make the target precise without requiring short proofs or a way to extract a witness from a successful prover.

The classical Goldreich–Micali–Wigderson theorem already supplies interactive zero-knowledge proofs for NP from one-way functions. Interaction gives the verifier a role in challenging what the prover has prepared. The inherited Damgård–Nielsen survey explicitly asks whether one-way functions suffice in the noninteractive setting. That survey discusses a proof-system version with stronger soundness; the argument target here asks for protection only against efficient cheating.

Known positive constructions use more structure. Peikert and Shiehian construct NIZK for NP from ordinary LWE in 2019. Their method builds hash families whose correlation-intractability property supports a sound Fiat–Shamir transformation. The point is a proved property of a specially constructed family, not simply substituting an arbitrary hash function for a verifier’s random challenge. LWE is a sufficient assumption, but it has not thereby been derived from arbitrary one-way functions.

Bradley, Waters and Wu show that an adaptively sound noninteractive batch argument for NP, together with a one-way function, yields NIZK. Their TCC 2024 result also studies how to obtain the needed adaptive soundness from other batch-argument guarantees. cards.title: One-way functions from errorless average-case NP hardness
cards.formal: Is the following implication true? \[(\mathrm{NP},\mathrm{PSamp})\not\subseteq\mathrm{AvgP}\quad\Longrightarrow\quad\text{there exists a classical one-way function}.\] Here the antecedent means that some fixed NP language, under some fixed polynomial-time samplable distribution ensemble, has no deterministic exact decider with average polynomial running time in the moment sense below. The conclusion asks for a total polynomial-time computable function \(f:\{0,1\}^{*}\to\{0,1\}^{*}\) such that, for every uniform probabilistic polynomial-time inverter \(I\) and every integer \(c\ge1\), there exists \(n_0\) for which, for every \(n\ge n_0\), \[\Pr_{x\sim U_n,\ I}\bigl[|z|=n\ \land\ f(z)=f(x)\bigr]\le n^{-c},\qquad z\leftarrow I(1^n,f(x)).\] The statement is unrelativized and has no additional hardness, derandomization or cryptographic assumption.
cards.why: A problem can be difficult to decide on typical efficiently generated inputs without obviously providing an efficiently computed map that is hard to invert. Connecting these two kinds of difficulty would clarify the minimum computational assumptions needed for classical cryptography. The precise decision-error and security-length conventions are essential to that comparison.

sentences: This card selects the average-case-to-one-way-function branch of a broader question in Wigderson’s book.
The hardness assumption concerns exact deterministic decision under an efficiently samplable distribution, with average polynomial time defined by a runtime moment.
The conclusion requires a polynomial-time function that every uniform probabilistic inverter fails to invert with more than negligible probability at all sufficiently large lengths.
Recent heuristic-hardness characterizations, infinitely-often security results and oracle separations use different guarantees.
A resolution would clarify whether broad distributional hardness already forces the computational structure underlying classical one-wayness.

cards.definitions: A language \(L\subseteq\{0,1\}^{*}\) is in NP if there are a fixed deterministic polynomial-time predicate \(R\) and a polynomial \(p\) such that \(x\in L\) exactly when some \(u\in\{0,1\}^{p(|x|)}\) satisfies \(R(x,u)=1\). A sampler is one probabilistic Turing machine \(S\) that, on the unary size parameter \(1^n\), uses independent unbiased random bits and halts within \(q(n)\) bit steps on every random tape, for a fixed polynomial \(q\). Its exact output distribution is \(D_n\), over finite strings of length at most \(q(n)\). The ensemble parameter \(n\) need not equal the output length. PSamp is the class of these ensembles. A deterministic exact decider \(A\), given \((1^n,x)\), must halt and return the membership bit of \(L\) correctly for every \(n\ge1\) and every finite \(x\), including inputs outside the support of \(D_n\). Let \(T_A(1^n,x)\) be its number of bit steps. The pair \((L,D)\) belongs to AvgP if there exist \(A\), constants \(\alpha>0,C>0\), and an integer \(k\ge1\) such that \(\mathbb E_{x\sim D_n}[T_A(1^n,x)^\alpha]\le C(n+1)^k\) for every \(n\ge1\). These choices may depend on \(L,S\), but not on \(n\). This is an exact, deterministic moment-based notion, not merely a polynomial first moment or a heuristic allowed to misclassify a small fraction of inputs. The antecedent asserts the existence of one pair \((L,D)\) in the stated class failing this condition. In the conclusion, \(U_n\) is uniform on all \(n\)-bit strings, and the probability also includes the inverter’s independent unbiased coin flips. An inverter is a fixed finite probabilistic Turing program whose running time is polynomial in its input length on every random tape; all reading, writing and arithmetic are charged. It receives both \(1^n\) and \(f(x)\). It may output any preimage of \(f(x)\) of length exactly \(n\), not necessarily the original \(x\); malformed or wrong-length outputs fail. The function \(f\) is computed by one fixed finite deterministic polynomial-time program on all input strings, so output length is automatically polynomially bounded. All programs are uniform and have no advice or oracle. Security is required for all sufficiently large \(n\) for each inverter and exponent; security on only infinitely many lengths is a different guarantee.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of the implication or its logical negation. A positive answer must derive the existence of a function with the full uniform, all-sufficiently-large-length inversion guarantee from the stated distributional hardness alone. The implication does not require an efficient black-box transformation from a description of the hard pair. A negative answer must establish the antecedent together with nonexistence of every such function in the unrelativized model; an oracle world, a barrier to one type of reduction or failure of one candidate construction is insufficient. A result assuming randomized heuristic hardness instead of the specified deterministic exact hardness, or yielding only infinitely-often security or a fixed polynomial security gap, does not alone settle this formulation.

cards.title: Public-key quantum money from LWE alone
cards.formal: Does quantum hardness of decisional Learning with Errors with the fixed polynomial parameters below imply reusable, unforgeable public-key quantum money in the standard model?
cards.definitions: For each integer \(\lambda\ge2\), let \(q(\lambda)\) be the least prime at least \(\lambda^4\), and let \(\chi_\lambda\) give integer z probability proportional to \(\exp(-\pi z^2/\lambda^2)\). The assumption states that, for every polynomially bounded sample count m, the distributions \((A,As+e\bmod q)\) and \((A,u)\) are computationally indistinguishable: A is uniform in \(\mathbb Z_q^{m\times\lambda}\), s is independently uniform in \(\mathbb Z_q^\lambda\), the coordinates of e are independent samples from \(\chi_\lambda\), and u is independent uniform in \(\mathbb Z_q^m\). Indistinguishability is against all nonuniform polynomial-size quantum circuit families with classical advice. Advantage is the absolute difference of acceptance probabilities and must be negligible in lambda, meaning eventually less than \(\lambda^{-c}\) for every constant c>0. Quantum circuits use a fixed universal Clifford-plus-T gate set, zero-state ancillas and computational-basis measurements; polynomial-size classical control is allowed. A money scheme consists of uniform quantum polynomial-time algorithms Gen, Mint and Verify. Gen on unary lambda outputs classical keys (pk,sk). Mint(sk) outputs a classical serial string s and a quantum register rho; their lengths are polynomial in lambda. Verify(pk,s,rho) returns an accept/reject bit and a residual note register, without secret information. For every polynomial t, an honestly generated note survives t successive verifications, all accepting, with probability at least one minus a negligible function, over key generation, minting and verification. For every polynomially bounded integer-valued k and every nonuniform polynomial-size quantum adversary with classical advice, give the adversary pk and k independently minted notes under the same key. The probability that it produces k+1 serial/register pairs all accepted by fresh local applications of Verify is negligible; its output registers may be jointly entangled and serials need not be distinct. This also applies to k=0. The construction has no ideal oracle, externally supplied setup, obfuscation assumption, leakage assumption, or additional hardness assumption. The target is the implication from the explicitly stated LWE assumption; a construction with an arbitrary computational reduction qualifies.

Known constructions with stronger assumptions and restricted impossibility results leave a gap. iO-based schemes and schemes founded on group-action assumptions do not establish the LWE-only implication specified here.
The 2025 obfuscation barrier applies to a particular black-box interface. It is evidence about a restricted class of constructions, not a refutation of this unrestricted implication.

cards.title: Average-case RSA inversion versus factoring for exponent 65537
cards.formal: For the fixed exponent \(e=65537\) and the balanced-prime ensemble below, does the existence of a uniform randomized polynomial-time RSA inverter with inverse-polynomial average success imply the existence of a uniform randomized polynomial-time factoring algorithm with inverse-polynomial average success?
cards.definitions: For each integer \(n\ge 3\) let \(\mathrm{P}_{n}\) be the finite set of primes p with \(2^{n- 1}\le p<2^{n}\) and \(\gcd (e,p- 1)=1\). Choose an ordered pair \((p,q)\) uniformly from \(\{(p,q)\in \mathrm{P}_{n}^{2}:p\ne q\}\), and set \(N=pq\). All assertions are for sufficiently large n with at least two such primes. Conditional on N, choose x uniformly from \(\mathbb{Z}_{N}^{*}=\{a\in \{0,\ldots ,N- 1\}:\gcd (a,N)=1\}\), independently of algorithm coins, and set \(y=x^{e}\) mod N. The inverter I receives \((1^{n},N,y)\), in binary except for \(1^{n}\), and must output the unique \(x\in\mathbb{Z}_{N}^{*}\) with that image. Nonnegligible success here means that some integer \(a\ge 1\) and \(n_{0}\) exist such that \(\Pr [I(1^{n},N,y)=x]\ge n^{- a}\) for every \(n\ge n_{0}\). The factoring algorithm F receives \((1^{n},N)\) and succeeds by outputting p or q; require some \(b\ge 1\) and \(n_{1}\) such that \(\Pr [F(1^{n},N)\in \{p,q\}]\ge n^{- b}\) for every \(n\ge n_{1}\). Both machines use independent fair random bits and have worst-case running time bounded by their own fixed polynomials in their input lengths on every random tape. The probabilities average over the stated modulus ensemble as well as x and the coins, with no promise of success separately on each modulus. The assertion is the ordinary existence implication \((\exists I,a,n_{0})\Rightarrow (\exists F,b,n_{1})\). It does not restrict a proof to black-box reductions: a construction of F may use the fixed code of I and count all calls to it in F’s polynomial running time. No independent oracle or advice is supplied.

cards.title: Noninteractive SZK versus SZK
cards.formal: Does NISZK equal SZK? Equivalently, does there exist a uniform deterministic polynomial-time reduction that maps every promised pair of sampling circuits X,Y to a sampling circuit Z, preserving the near/far promises specified below?
cards.definitions: A sampling circuit is a finite acyclic Boolean circuit with AND and OR gates of fan-in two, NOT gates, constants, a specified list of random input bits and an ordered list of output bits. Its description explicitly lists gates and wires in binary. Fresh independent uniform bits are supplied to all random inputs; the output distribution is the resulting distribution on bit strings. X and Y may have different numbers of random inputs but have the same output length. For finite distributions P,Q on the same set, \(d_{\mathrm{TV}}(P,Q)=\tfrac12\sum_z|P(z)-Q(z)|\). The source convention for Statistical Difference has YES instances with \(d_{\mathrm{TV}}(X,Y)<1/3\) and NO instances with \(d_{\mathrm{TV}}(X,Y)>2/3\). Inputs between these promises impose no correctness obligation. The reduction outputs one circuit Z with \(m\ge 3\) output bits. On every YES input require \(d_{\mathrm{TV}}(Z,U_{m})<1/m\); on every NO input require \(d_{\mathrm{TV}}(Z,U_{m})>1- 1/m\), where \(U_{m}\) is uniform on \(\{0,1\}^{m}\). The reduction runs in a fixed polynomial of the combined encoded input length on every syntactically valid input, including inputs outside the promise; writing Z and all its input/output nodes counts in that time. It receives no advice or sampling oracle. These are the source’s Statistical Difference and Statistical Difference from Uniform promise problems. Their completeness under deterministic polynomial-time many-one reductions makes existence of this reduction equivalent to the original class equality. Thus the complete-problem formulation fixes the question without having to choose a new auxiliary-input or setup convention for protocols.

The same question can be stated entirely in terms of finite sampling circuits. Statistical Difference is complete for SZK, while Statistical Difference from Uniform is complete for NISZK. cards.title: Fully homomorphic encryption from public-key encryption
cards.formal: Does the existence of IND-CPA-secure public-key bit encryption imply the existence of an IND-CPA-secure, compact, unleveled fully homomorphic bit-encryption scheme for every polynomial-size Boolean circuit, with the algorithms and security convention below?
cards.definitions:
All algorithms are uniform probabilistic Turing machines with worst-case polynomial bit running time in their explicit input lengths; decryption is deterministic. The security parameter \(\lambda\) is supplied in unary. An adversary is a nonuniform family of randomized Boolean circuits of size polynomial in \(\lambda\), including its advice and random-input nodes. All random bits are independent and fair. A function \(
u:\mathbb{N}	o [0,1]\) is negligible when for every positive integer a there exists \(\lambda _{0}\) such that \(
u (\lambda )\le \lambda ^{- a}\) for all \(\lambda \ge \lambda _{0}\). Security is quantified separately over every such adversary family, with a negligible bound allowed to depend on the family. A public-key bit-encryption scheme consists of \(Gen(1^{\lambda})=(pk,sk), Enc(pk,b)=c\) for \(b\in \{0,1\}\), and \(Dec(sk,c)\in \{0,1,\perp\}\). There is one negligible \(
u\) such that for every \(\lambda\) and b, \(\Pr[\operatorname{Dec}(sk,\operatorname{Enc}(pk,b))
e b]\le
u(\lambda)\), over key generation and encryption. In the IND-CPA experiment Gen is run, the adversary receives pk and selects bits \(b_{0},b_{1}\) and a state, an independent uniform \( eta \in \{0,1\}\) is chosen, \(c=Enc(pk,b_{ eta})\) is returned, and the adversary outputs \( eta '\). Require \(|\Pr[ eta\prime= eta]-1/2|\) to be negligible. The adversary may perform any polynomial number of public encryptions on its own before and after the challenge. There is no decryption oracle. Bit encryption suffices; longer messages are represented by bit lists. For FHE, Gen outputs (pk,evk,sk); the evaluation key evk is public and is included with pk in the IND-CPA experiment. Gen receives no circuit size or depth bound. Eval(evk,\(C,c_{1},\ldots ,c_{t}\)) outputs one ciphertext for a circuit \(C:\{0,1\}^{t}	o \{0,1\}\), encoded as an acyclic \(\mathrm{AND}/\mathrm{OR}/\mathrm{NOT}\) circuit with listed wires. For every polynomial s there is a negligible \(
u _{s}\) such that for every \(\lambda\), every such C of description length and input count at most \(s(\lambda )\), and every \(m\in \{0,1\}^{t}\), independently of the generated keys, \(\Pr[\operatorname{Dec}(sk,\operatorname{Eval}(evk,C,\operatorname{Enc}(pk,m_1),\ldots,\operatorname{Enc}(pk,m_t)))
e C(m)]\le
u_s(\lambda)\). The probability includes key generation, fresh encryption coins for each bit, and evaluation coins. Eval’s time is polynomial in the entire supplied circuit and ciphertext encoding, with one algorithm for all C. There is one polynomial q, independent of C,t and s, bounding every evaluated ciphertext length and its decryption time by \(q(\lambda )\); keys also have polynomial length. The scheme must also correctly decrypt fresh encryptions. Multiple output bits mean separate output ciphertexts, so compactness scales linearly with output length. Only the usual one-evaluation correctness contract is required; no circuit privacy or additional guarantee for arbitrary malformed or previously evaluated ciphertexts is imposed. The assertion is an existence implication between these two primitives in the classical standard model; it permits non-black-box constructions and supplies no extra setup, ideal oracle, circular-security or number-theoretic assumption.

It therefore supplies a barrier and motivation, not a negative answer to an arbitrary non-black-box implication. The existing LWE-to-FHE card starts from a specific stronger assumption.

cards.title: PZK versus SZK
cards.formal: Does PZK=SZK for classical single-prover interactive proofs of promise problems, with polynomial-time verifiers and simulators, negligible proof error, and zero knowledge against every polynomial-time verifier?
cards.definitions: A promise problem is a pair \((Y,N)\) of disjoint sets of finite binary strings. An interactive proof consists of a computationally unbounded prover P and a uniform probabilistic polynomial-time verifier V exchanging polynomially many bits on common input x. There is a negligible function \(\varepsilon\) such that on \(x\in Y\) the honest interaction accepts with probability at least \(1- \varepsilon (|x|)\), and on \(x\in N\) every prover strategy is accepted with probability at most \(\varepsilon (|x|)\). Negligible means smaller than |\(x|^{- d}\) for every fixed \(d>0\) at all sufficiently large lengths. No condition is imposed outside \(Y\cup N\). The view of a verifier consists of its random bits and exchanged messages. SZK requires that for every uniform probabilistic polynomial-time verifier V* there is a uniform probabilistic polynomial-time simulator S* which, on x alone, produces a distribution within negligible total variation distance of the view of \((\mathrm{P},V*)(x)\), for every \(x\in Y\). Total variation distance is one half of the sum of absolute probability differences over possible views. PZK instead permits S* to output a failure symbol ⊥ with probability at most \(1/2\); conditioned on nonfailure, its output distribution must equal that view exactly. Every runtime bound is a strict polynomial bound over all random outcomes, with a polynomial allowed to depend on the fixed verifier or simulator. This is the ordinary input-only simulation convention of the cited definitions, without a shared random string, an oracle, a setup assumption, or a restriction to honest verifiers.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove that every promise problem admitting the stated statistical proof also admits a perfect one in this model, or exhibit a promise problem in SZK and prove that it has no PZK proof. The protocol may change completely in a positive result. An oracle separation, a failure of one proposed compiler, a perfect-zero-knowledge PCP, or an honest-verifier-only theorem does not resolve this unrelativized class equality.

context_blocks.text: Zero knowledge formalizes the idea that a verifier can reproduce what it sees without receiving help from the prover. Statistical simulation permits a negligible discrepancy between distributions. Perfect simulation requires exact agreement after the allowed failure event. Goldreich’s textbook asks whether this difference changes which statements can be proved.

The failure convention is part of the model. A strict polynomial-time perfect simulator that never fails is a different requirement, often called super-perfect zero knowledge. Allowing an expected polynomial runtime is also a separate definitional issue discussed in the source. Neither convention is silently substituted here.

PZK is contained in SZK: repeat the bounded-failure perfect simulator polynomially many times until it succeeds, and use an arbitrary output if every attempt fails. The remaining probability of failure is negligible, while successful outputs retain the exact distribution. The open direction asks whether negligible simulation error can always be eliminated by some proof system.

Bouland, Chen, Holden, Thaler and Vasudevan construct an oracle relative to which SZK is not contained in PZK. This supplies evidence against equality and rules out a proof that relativizes in the corresponding way. It does not separate the classes in the ordinary model specified here.

Gur, O’Connor and Spooner explicitly retain PZK versus SZK as open in their 2024 paper. Their perfect-zero-knowledge construction is for probabilistically checkable proofs, where a verifier queries a proof oracle. That achievement concerns a different access model from ordinary interactive proofs and leaves this equality unresolved.

The target asks for a class equality, not a quantitative improvement in a particular cryptographic protocol. Its resolution would determine whether exact distributional privacy has an intrinsic expressive cost. TCS-1929 instead concerns zero knowledge for streaming interactive proofs with a memory restriction.

cards.title: Low-noise LPN hardness from Nearest Codeword hardness
cards.formal: Does the following implication hold? If binary Nearest Codeword is not in BPP, then no uniform probabilistic polynomial-time distinguisher D has advantage at least $n^{-c}$, for any fixed $c>0$ and all sufficiently large square n, between $(A,As+e)$ and $(A,u)$. Here $A\in\mathbb F_2^{n^2\times n}$, $s\in\mathbb F_2^n$, and $u\in\mathbb F_2^{n^2}$ are independent uniform random variables, and the coordinates of e are independent Bernoulli variables with rate $1/\sqrt n$. Advantage is the absolute difference of D’s acceptance probabilities in the two experiments.
cards.why: A basic security assumption would obtain an explanation through independently studied hardness. The extra assumption in the new reduction makes the remaining target concrete.

progress.text: The revision gives a reduction for $\eta=n^{-\alpha}$, any constant $\alpha<1$, from simultaneous worst-case hardness of two tasks on a code and its dual. This advances beyond earlier near-half-noise reductions; the single-assumption target remains stronger.
