On 16 September 2026 the full 2D frustration-free introduction and theorem, official February 2026 article introduction and approximate-projector definition, April 2026 thermodynamic introduction and frustration-free section, primary historical abstracts and bounded later-work searches were checked. The newer area-law consequences retain extra assumptions; no proof or counterexample for the stated uniformly globally gapped, unique-ground-state two-dimensional family was identified. Entanglement-spread and area-law computational-hardness results address different claims. No cited proof was independently verified or formalized in Lean.

context_blocks.text: A region containing \(m\) sites has entropy at most \(m\log_2q\). For a square block with side length \(\ell\), this volume bound is quadratic in \(\ell\), while the conjecture permits only a constant times its boundary length. Fixing both interaction norms and the gap prevents rescaling an increasingly gapless family from appearing uniformly gapped.

Hastings proves the corresponding entropy bound for gapped one-dimensional local systems. An interval has only a constant number of boundary edges, so its entropy stays bounded as the chain grows. Grouping columns of a two-dimensional lattice into single one-dimensional sites does not give a constant independent of width: each grouped site has dimension \(q^L\).

Anshu, Arad, and Gosset make major progress for frustration-free systems with a local gap. Frustration freeness means one state minimizes every local term; the local-gap assumption controls Hamiltonians obtained from subsets of terms, and is stronger than the global gap here. Their cited version proves a vertical-cut entropy bound \(n^{1+O((\log  n)^{- 1/5})}\) for cut length n. It is asymptotically almost linear, but the remaining factor is not a constant and neither extra assumption follows from the statement in this card.

Anshu, Harrow, and Soleimanifar prove an area law for entanglement spread, a measure of variation among the Schmidt coefficients after an appropriate smoothing. This controls a different feature of entanglement from its entropy. For intuition, a maximally entangled state can have arbitrarily many equal Schmidt coefficients: its spread is zero while its entropy is the logarithm of their number. A spread bound therefore does not by itself answer the entropy question.

Arad, Firanko, and Jain’s February 2026 theorem treats mutual information of the maximally mixed ground state. It assumes a sufficiently accurate approximation to the ground-space projector whose operator Schmidt rank is suitably small. Constructing such an approximation for general gapped two-dimensional Hamiltonians remains a missing ingredient; the general wording of the title does not remove this hypothesis.

Garratt and Abanin’s April 2026 preprint provides thermodynamic upper bounds and proves area laws for frustration-free systems when ground-space degeneracies of the relevant subsystem Hamiltonians have suitable boundary scaling. A unique ground state for the full system does not impose that condition on each subsystem. These results retain additional assumptions.

The computational significance also needs care. Huang proves that two-dimensional local Hamiltonian instances whose ground states satisfy area laws can still be QMA-complete. Those instances are not claimed to have the uniform gap fixed here. The result nevertheless shows why an entropy bound alone should not be advertised as a general efficient classical algorithm for finding or manipulating two-dimensional ground states.

cards.title: Information-theoretic classical verification of quantum computation
cards.formal:
Can a completely classical verifier check arbitrary efficient quantum computation by interacting with one efficient quantum prover, with soundness against every computationally unbounded cheating prover?

The common input is an explicitly encoded quantum circuit \(C\) over \(\{H,T,\mathrm{CNOT}\}\), with all qubits initially zero and a designated output qubit. Write \(N\) for its description length and \(p(C)\) for the probability that measuring that output in the computational basis gives one. The promise is
\[C\in\mathrm{YES}\iff p(C)\ge 2/3,\qquad C\in\mathrm{NO}\iff p(C)\le 1/3.\]
Does there exist one uniform interactive protocol \((P,V)\) and positive integer constants \(a,d\) with the following properties? The verifier \(V\) is a classical probabilistic machine; the honest prover \(P\) is a quantum machine with classical control. They exchange only classical messages with no setup or extra prover. Both honest computations, the verifier against every cheating strategy, the number of messages and total communication have the polynomial bounds specified below. For every promised circuit,
\[C\in\mathrm{YES}\ \Longrightarrow\ \Pr[V\text{ accepts in interaction with }P\text{ on }C]\ge2/3,\]
\[C\in\mathrm{NO}\ \Longrightarrow\ \forall P^*\quad\Pr[V\text{ accepts in interaction with }P^*\text{ on }C]\le1/3.\]
Here \(P^*\) ranges over all adaptive response strategies, without any computational bound. The protocol and the constants precede the quantifiers over inputs and cheating strategies.
cards.definitions:
A circuit consists of \(q\ge1\) labelled qubits, an ordered list \(g_1,\ldots,g_m\) of gates with \(m\ge0\), and an output index \(o\in\{1,\ldots,q\}\). The one-qubit matrices and two-qubit action are
\[H=\frac1{\sqrt2}\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\1&-1\end{pmatrix},\qquad T=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&e^{i\pi/4}\end{pmatrix},\qquad \mathrm{CNOT}|x,y\rangle=|x,x\mathbin\oplus y\rangle.\]
Here \(x,y\in\{0,1\}\) and \(\oplus\) is addition modulo two. Each gate acts on its indicated qubit or ordered pair of distinct qubits and as the identity on the rest. Let \(U_C=g_m\cdots g_1\), with identity for an empty list. In the vector space \((\mathbb C^2)^{\otimes q}\), set
\[p(C)=\sum_{\substack{z\in\{0,1\}^q\\z_o=1}}|\langle z|U_C|0^q\rangle|^2.\]
These gate entries and probabilities are exact mathematical quantities, not floating-point input data. No correctness condition is imposed when \(1/3<p(C)<2/3\).

For a concrete bit encoding, write \(q\) as \(1^q0\), followed by \(U(m),U(o)\) and every gate in sequence. The length-delimited integer code is \(U(b)=1^\ell0s\), where \(s\) is the canonical binary expansion of \(b\ge0\), \(\ell=|s|\), and zero has expansion 0. A gate uses a two-bit tag for H, T or CNOT, followed by the \(U\)-encoded target indices; the fourth tag is invalid. All indices must be within the declared range and CNOT indices must be distinct. No trailing bits are allowed. Thus \(q\le N\) and all gates are explicitly listed. Both parties receive the same classical description; neither receives an additional quantum input or witness. Malformed descriptions are rejected by the verifier.

The two algorithms have fixed finite classical control programs, independent of \(N\) and \(C\). The verifier has ordinary classical work tapes, private independent fair random bits, and a classical message interface. It has no quantum register, quantum channel or ability to prepare, transform or measure qubits. The honest prover starts with zero qubits, may create zero ancillas, apply H, T and CNOT gates, measure qubits in the computational basis, and use outcomes in subsequent classical computation. Measurements follow the squared-amplitude rule; a measured qubit may be discarded. Its classical controller may also toss fair coins. Gate addresses, classical arithmetic and generation of the next instruction are computed and charged. There is no input-dependent or length-dependent advice, precomputed advice state or uncharged oracle for either honest party.

Put \(R(N)=a(N+1)^d\). On every input and every branch of its private randomness, the verifier uses at most \(R(N)\) classical bit steps, reads at most that many received bits, and halts with accept or reject. This clock holds against every possible sequence of replies. In an honest execution, the prover uses at most \(R(N)\) classical bit steps and elementary quantum operations in total, on every randomness and measurement branch. One elementary quantum operation acts on at most two addressed qubits; all classical bit operations and all written or read message bits are charged. The honest prover holds at most \(R(N)\) qubits. These bounds also apply to well-formed circuits outside the promise. The protocol allows at most \(R(N)\) messages and \(R(N)\) communicated bits in total; the verifier enforces the declared message lengths and aborts on a violation. A missing reply or an explicit abort is rejection. There is no constant-round requirement or uncharged preprocessing phase.

For soundness, an arbitrary prover strategy can be described by a conditional distribution on its next classical reply for each input and history of messages it has seen. It can have unlimited private memory and arbitrary input-dependent information, but cannot see the verifier's private coins except through sent messages. This description includes the observable behaviour of any quantum cheating prover through the classical interface; no bound on its computation, circuit size or internal state is assumed. Acceptance probabilities include all private randomness and measurement outcomes. There is no initial shared secret, correlated setup state, trusted third party, random oracle or enforced separation inside the single prover.

Completeness concerns the one fixed honest algorithm on all YES instances. Soundness concerns every strategy on each NO instance. The task is verification of this decision promise problem; it imposes no separate blindness, sampling-output or witness-preservation requirement. Fixed error constants are part of the specification, rather than a numerical approximation tolerance for the final answer.
cards.answer_criterion: Provide a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of the existence of such a protocol or its full logical negation. A positive answer must give uniform algorithms and universal polynomial resource bounds, prove completeness on every YES circuit, and prove the stated bound against all unbounded response strategies on every NO circuit. A negative answer must rule out every protocol in this model: for each resource-bounded pair, some YES input violates completeness or some NO input and cheating strategy violate soundness. A cryptographic argument sound only against efficient attackers, a quantum verifier, extra isolated provers, an inefficient honest prover or an impossibility theorem restricted to particular protocols does not settle this proposition.
cards.why: The question isolates the resources needed for a classical user to trust a quantum answer. Known protocols obtain trust by giving the verifier some quantum capability, separating several devices, or assuming that particular computations are hard for an attacker. Resolving the stated conjunction would determine whether any of those additional resources is necessary when the honest server itself remains efficient.

cards.status_note: Checked on 16 September 2026. The inspected April 2026 primary source explicitly leaves efficient, unconditional single-prover verification by a classical verifier open. Its relativizing MIP theorem does not supply one efficient honest prover. The February witness-preserving protocol retains LWE; the February non-interactive barrier concerns a restricted QMA model; and the May trusted-gate article retains quantum client operations. None meets or rules out the full conjunction specified here. No matching later resolution was found in the bounded search; individual cited proofs were not independently certified.

context_blocks.text: The honest-prover condition matters as much as the classical-verifier condition. The standard containments of quantum polynomial time in polynomial space, and IP=PSPACE, provide classical interactive proofs with an unrestricted prover. They do not establish that the auxiliary answers needed by that prover can be generated by a quantum polynomial-time machine. A verification protocol that demands a substantially more powerful server would not meet this card.

Aharonov, Ben-Or, Eban and Mahadev supply information-theoretically sound verification with an efficient quantum prover when the verifier retains a small quantum register. For a fixed error gap, a constant number of qubits suffices in their result. Although their class definition first restricts dishonest provers, they explicitly state that the protocol proof protects against unbounded provers. Eliminating the verifier’s remaining quantum capability is the open question highlighted in their §1.8.

Reichardt, Unger and Vazirani use separated entangled quantum subsystems. Their classical verifier can certify and control quantum operations under the noncommunication constraints of that model. A single freely communicating prover is allowed to coordinate its replies across all of its internal components, so combining the devices loses a condition used by the multiprover theorem.

Mahadev’s protocol achieves the classical verifier and single efficient quantum prover by using a computational assumption. The inspected version bases its construction on quantum hardness of Learning With Errors with the specified superpolynomial noise ratio. Its soundness quantifies over efficient quantum cheating algorithms. An unbounded strategy is outside that guarantee, even if the protocol is otherwise fully classical at the interface.

The February 2026 quantum-cat preprint addresses preservation of a quantum witness: the prover can reuse one copy while obtaining negligible errors. Its abstract retains the post-quantum LWE assumption. A QMA witness is an additional quantum input that is not present in the all-zero BQP computation here, and preserving it does not remove the computational soundness assumption.

Another February 2026 preprint gives a conditional barrier to quantum black-box reductions for non-interactive QMA verification from falsifiable assumptions. Its model has one message after instance-independent setup, and its premise is a QMA–QCMA gap problem. Both the task and the restrictions differ from this card’s arbitrary polynomial interaction for BQP. The checked abstract therefore supplies no general impossibility answer here.

cards.title: NPT bound entanglement
cards.formal: Does there exist a negative-partial-transpose state that is undistillable for every finite number of copies? Precisely, are there integers \(a,b\ge2\) and a density matrix \(\rho\) on \(\mathbb C^a\otimes\mathbb C^b\) such that \(\rho^{\Gamma_B}\) has a strictly negative eigenvalue and \[\langle\psi,(\rho^{\Gamma_B})^{\otimes k}\psi\rangle\ge0\] for every integer \(k\ge1\) and every unit vector \(\psi\in(\mathbb C^a)^{\otimes k}\otimes(\mathbb C^b)^{\otimes k}\) of Schmidt rank at most two across the displayed bipartition? The same dimensions and the same state must satisfy the condition for all \(k\).
cards.definitions:
All vector spaces are finite-dimensional over \(\mathbb C\). The inner product is \(\langle u,v\rangle=\sum_j\overline{u_j}v_j\), and a unit vector has \(\langle u,u\rangle=1\). A density matrix \(\rho\) is Hermitian, positive semidefinite and of trace one: \(\rho=\rho^\dagger\), \(\langle v,\rho v\rangle\ge0\) for every vector \(v\), and the sum of its diagonal entries is one. Dagger denotes conjugate transpose. In the fixed standard product basis, with indices \(i,r\in\{1,\ldots,a\}\) and \(j,s\in\{1,\ldots,b\}\), its partial transpose on the second party is \[(\rho^{\Gamma_B})_{(i,j),(r,s)}=\rho_{(i,s),(r,j)}.\] This matrix is Hermitian but need not be positive semidefinite. Negative partial transpose, abbreviated NPT, means it has an eigenvalue strictly less than zero. Positive partial transpose, abbreviated PPT, means all its eigenvalues are nonnegative; zero eigenvalues do not make a state NPT. The \(k\)-fold tensor power is the Kronecker product of \(k\) copies of the same matrix. When evaluating the displayed expectation, regroup the tensor factors from \((A_1B_1)\cdots(A_kB_k)\) into \((A_1\cdots A_k)(B_1\cdots B_k)\), where \(A_j=\mathbb C^a\) and \(B_j=\mathbb C^b\). The corresponding permutation of basis vectors is part of this identification. Schmidt rank of \(\psi\) across these two groups is the least integer \(r\) such that \(\psi=\sum_{j=1}^r u_j\otimes v_j\), with \(u_j\in(\mathbb C^a)^{\otimes k}\) and \(v_j\in(\mathbb C^b)^{\otimes k}\). No independence or product condition is imposed between copies within either party.

A bipartite state is separable if it is a finite convex combination \(\sum_j p_j\sigma_j\otimes\tau_j\) of local density matrices, with \(p_j\ge0\) and \(\sum_jp_j=1\); otherwise it is entangled. Every NPT state is entangled. The exact criterion used in this question defines \(k\)-copy distillability as existence of a Schmidt-rank-at-most-two unit vector with strictly negative displayed expectation. A state is distillable if such a vector exists for at least one finite \(k\); undistillable means none exists at any finite \(k\). This finite-matrix definition is the formal target. It agrees with the standard operational notion of obtaining entangled two-qubit states with positive probability from finitely many copies using local operations and classical communication, and hence of distilling Bell pairs at positive asymptotic rate. That interpretation allows two-way classical communication and local ancillary systems, but no quantum communication or extra shared entanglement. The card asks for mathematical existence, not efficient preparation or an algorithm acting on a finite encoding of \(\rho\); arbitrary complex matrix entries are allowed.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof of existence of a single finite-dimensional state satisfying the NPT condition and every quantified rank-two inequality, or a complete Lean-checked proof of the logical negation: for every finite \(a,b\) and every NPT density matrix \(\rho\), some finite \(k\) and eligible unit vector \(\psi\) give a strictly negative expectation. In the second outcome, \(k\) and the vector may depend on \(\rho\), and no universal copy bound is requested. Numerical checks, one fixed copy count, a restricted set of test vectors, or a sequence of different states depending on \(k\) do not establish the existential all-copy statement. Positivity and negativity are exact; this yes/no problem has no numerical approximation substitute.
cards.why: A defining question about whether partial-transpose negativity completely captures the possibility of converting bipartite entanglement into useful Bell pairs. Its precise all-copy quantifier connects quantum resource theory to tensor-stable matrix inequalities.

importance.reason: A central structural boundary in entanglement theory, with canonical finite-dimensional candidates and consequences for what quantum correlations can accomplish under local operations.

context_blocks.text: Entanglement is a property of a state, whereas distillation is an operational ability to turn many noisy shared states into nearly perfect Bell pairs. These pairs are useful because a pair, together with classical communication, can transfer an unknown qubit by teleportation. The question asks whether there is a form of entanglement that passes the necessary negative-partial-transpose test for distillation but is nevertheless permanently unusable for this particular conversion.

The Horodeckis established that entangled states with positive partial transpose can be bound entangled. Their obstruction survives every tensor power: a positive semidefinite partial transpose remains positive semidefinite after tensoring, so no test vector can have negative expectation. This card concerns the complementary regime, where some negative eigenvector exists already, but its Schmidt rank may be too large to provide the rank-two witness needed for a distillation protocol.

In local dimension two, every bipartite vector has Schmidt rank at most two, so an NPT state is already one-copy distillable. The open problem therefore concerns larger local spaces. The formal statement still quantifies over all finite dimensions, with no promise that the state has a rational description, a symmetry, or an efficient preparation circuit.

DiVincenzo, Shor, Smolin, Terhal and Thapliyal investigated NPT states whose one-copy behavior differs from their spectral negativity. Their evidence did not establish one fixed NPT state undistillable for every finite number of copies. The present question retains that full order of quantifiers.

The Werner family is \(\rho_{\mathrm W}(d,\alpha)=(I+\alpha F)/(d^2+\alpha d)\), for \(d\ge2\) and \(-1\le\alpha\le1\), where \(F(u\otimes v)=v\otimes u\) swaps the two local systems and \(I\) is identity. Its members are NPT exactly for \(\alpha<-1/d\), and one-copy distillable exactly for \(\alpha<-1/2\). Thus \(-1/2\le\alpha<-1/d\) is the NPT one-copy-undistillable interval when \(d\ge3\). This is a known subclass; the target is not restricted to Werner states.

Several July 2026 papers prove that the one-copy and two-copy thresholds for Werner states coincide. Fraser and coauthors obtain this from a rank-constrained partial-trace inequality, with no Hermiticity or positivity assumption on the coefficient matrix. These results include the formerly open two-ququart example \(\rho _{\mathrm{W}}(4,- 1/2)\). They remove a major finite-copy obstacle, but do not prove that any particular NPT Werner state is undistillable for every number of copies.

Bharti, Gajjala and Haug also obtain the two-copy threshold and several restricted finite-copy extensions, while explicitly leaving the general all-copy assertion open. A family of states indexed by the allowed number of copies does not give the single fixed state required by the existential target.

Wu and Zou prove three-copy endpoint nonnegativity for specified sectors, including normal rank-two coefficient operators. A coefficient operator is the matrix of a bipartite test vector in product bases; normal means that the matrix commutes with its conjugate transpose. Other rank-two matrices are allowed in the full criterion, so these sector results do not settle unrestricted three-copy distillability or the all-copy question.

cards.title: Asymptotically good quantum locally testable stabilizer codes
cards.formal: Do there exist real constants \(r,\delta,s>0\) and positive integers \(w,b\) such that, for every integer \(N\ge1\), some stabilizer code on \(n\ge N\) qubits has an admissible list of checks as defined below and satisfies \[k\ge rn,\qquad d\ge\delta n,\qquad H\succeq\frac{s}{n}D_Q?\] Here \(k\) is its number of logical qubits, \(d\) its code distance, each listed check acts on at most \(w\) qubits, and each qubit occurs in at most \(b\) listed checks. All five constants are fixed for the unbounded family. This is the bounded-degree stabilizer version of asymptotically good quantum local testability.
cards.definitions:
The physical Hilbert space is \(\mathcal H_n=(\mathbb C^2)^{\otimes n}\). In the standard one-qubit basis, \(X|0\rangle=|1\rangle\), \(X|1\rangle=|0\rangle\), \(Z|0\rangle=|0\rangle\), \(Z|1\rangle=-|1\rangle\), and \(Y=iXZ\), where \(i^2=-1\). The Pauli group consists of tensor products of \(I,X,Y,Z\), multiplied by phases from \(\{1,-1,i,-i\}\). A Pauli's support is the set of positions with a nonidentity tensor factor, and its weight is the cardinality of that set; the scalar phase does not affect support.

An admissible stabilizer presentation is a finite nonempty list \(S_1,\ldots,S_m\) of Hermitian Pauli checks of positive weight. Hermitian means \(S_j=S_j^\dagger\), with dagger denoting conjugate transpose. The checks commute pairwise, and the group they generate does not contain \(-I\). Its code space is \[Q=\{\psi\in\mathcal H_n:S_j\psi=\psi\text{ for every }j\}.\] This nonzero space has dimension \(2^k\); the target requires \(k\ge1\). The distance \(d\) is the minimum weight of a Pauli \(P\) that preserves \(Q\), meaning \(P(Q)=Q\), but whose restriction to \(Q\) is not a scalar multiple of identity. For a stabilizer code with \(k\ge1\), such logical Paulis exist. This distance concerns undetectable changes to encoded information. The rate is \(k/n\) and the relative distance is \(d/n\).

The checks need not be independent, and a list may contain repetitions. The bounds refer to that actual list: \(\operatorname{wt}(S_j)\le w\) for every \(j\), and each qubit belongs to the supports of at most \(b\) checks, counting repetitions separately. Both are maximum bounds, not average bounds. Define the normalized check Hamiltonian \[H=\frac1m\sum_{j=1}^m\frac{I-S_j}{2}.\] Each summand is the orthogonal projection onto the failing eigenspace of one check. If a check is selected uniformly, the rejection probability on a unit vector \(\phi\) is \(\langle\phi,H\phi\rangle\); on a density matrix \(\rho\) it is \(\operatorname{Tr}(H\rho)\). A density matrix is Hermitian, positive semidefinite and of trace one.

For \(0\le t\le n\), let \(Q_t\) be the complex linear span of vectors \(E\psi\), where \(\psi\in Q\) and \(E\) ranges over Pauli errors of weight at most \(t\). Let \(\Pi_t\) be the orthogonal projection onto \(Q_t\). These spaces are nested, with \(Q_0=Q\) and \(Q_n=\mathcal H_n\). Define \[D_Q=\sum_{t=0}^{n-1}(I-\Pi_t)=\sum_{t=1}^n t(\Pi_t-\Pi_{t-1}).\] The two expressions agree by telescoping. The eigenvalue \(t\) measures the error radius of the corresponding orthogonal layer. Using Pauli errors in the span is equivalent to using arbitrary operators supported on at most \(t\) qubits, since local Pauli products span all such operators. This is not trace distance between density matrices.

The inequality \(H\succeq(s/n)D_Q\) means its difference is positive semidefinite: \(\langle\phi,[H-(s/n)D_Q]\phi\rangle\ge0\) for every vector \(\phi\in\mathcal H_n\), where \(\langle u,v\rangle=u^\dagger v\). Equivalently it holds in expectation for every density matrix. The number \(s\) is normalized soundness. The family may use an arbitrary unbounded sequence of lengths rather than every integer length. Checks may connect any qubits, without geometric locality. No CSS restriction, efficient construction, decoding algorithm or transversal-gate property is required.
cards.answer_criterion: Provide a complete Lean-checked proof that fixed constants and an unbounded family satisfying all conditions exist, or a complete Lean-checked proof of the logical negation: for every \(r,\delta,s>0\) and positive integers \(w,b\), there is a finite length bound beyond which no admissible presentation satisfies all the conditions simultaneously. An existence proof need not provide a polynomial-time construction. A failure for one proposed family, one subclass such as CSS codes, or one geometry does not prove nonexistence. Inverse-polylogarithmic soundness or relative distance, a growing maximum check weight or incidence, and a soundness guarantee confined to selected error weights do not meet the target. The operator inequality must cover the entire physical Hilbert space. This is an exact existence question, not a numerical approximation task.
cards.why: A central missing object connecting quantum error correction to robust verification. It asks whether sparse quantum constraints can simultaneously protect a linear amount of information and detect global corruption with constant normalized soundness.

importance.reason: A defining construction problem beyond good quantum LDPC codes, with direct links to local testing, Hamiltonian complexity, fault tolerance and the quantum PCP program.

context_blocks.text: A quantum code is the common accepting space of many checks. Measuring a uniformly selected check rejects a state with probability equal to its expected normalized energy under H. Local testability asks for a robust version of exact membership: a state that requires many local changes to reach the code must violate a noticeable fraction of checks. Constant check weight then makes this a test involving only a constant number of qubits.

The distance operator measures distance from the entire code space, not the written weight of one chosen Pauli error. A stabilizer leaves every codeword unchanged, while a logical Pauli can change the encoded information and still stay inside the code space. Both therefore remain at distance zero from the code as a subspace. The nested spaces \(Q_t\) account for these identifications. The operator inequality also controls superpositions and mixed states, not only individual Pauli-corrupted codewords.

A simple classical analogy illustrates the missing property. Consider a chain of equality checks requiring adjacent bits to agree. A string consisting of a long zero block followed by a long one block can be far from either valid repetition-code word while violating only one check. Local constraints and even a large code distance therefore do not by themselves imply robust local testing. The quantum target additionally requires storing a linear number of logical qubits.

Panteleev and Kalachev resolved the existence of asymptotically good quantum LDPC codes: constant check size can coexist with constant rate and linear distance. Their work also establishes good locally testable classical codes. These are two different conclusions. Quantum local testability with constant soundness does not follow by combining the words in the paper’s title; it is the extra property sought here.

Cross and coauthors obtain constant-soundness qLTC constructions with other parameter compromises. One approach has distance growing with check locality; another has constant average locality while some checks and qubit incidences grow. Wills, Lin and Hsieh analyze distance balancing with more general classical ingredients, quantifying the accompanying soundness loss. Such tradeoffs make it important to track the maximum locality, normalized soundness, rate and distance simultaneously.

Dinur, Lin and Vidick’s construction comes much closer: it has \(k=\Omega (n)\), distance \(\Omega (n/\log ^{3}n)\), soundness \(\Omega (1/\log ^{3}n)\), and constant check size. Its September 2025 revision corrects the rate analysis by shifting the chain complex. The paper also describes ways to obtain constant soundness, and then linear distance, at the cost of polylogarithmic check size. These variants do not provide all the constants required by this card at once.

The NLTS theorem is another nearby achievement with a distinct conclusion. Anshu, Breuckmann and Nirkhe show that certain good quantum codes yield Hamiltonians whose low-energy states require nontrivial circuit depth to prepare. That theorem resolves a major quantum-complexity conjecture without establishing constant-soundness local testability. A qLTC would give a stronger relation between energy and distance from a code, and could support further work toward quantum PCP; it would not by itself prove the full quantum PCP conjecture.

Li, Li and Liu’s July 2026 revision adds transversal non-Clifford operations to almost-good constructions. For example, their three-qubit controlled-controlled-Z case retains logarithmic losses in distance and soundness. The revision replaces an invalid cap-product argument from April with a substantially different proof using product-expanding local codes. This adds computational functionality while leaving the constant-parameter qLTC question open.

Sun and Vidick’s June 2026 work uses qLTCs in interactive oracle proofs for QMA, with polynomial communication and polylogarithmically many queried qubits. It illustrates the value of the available approximate parameters. Interaction and a polylogarithmic query budget remain part of that result; it is not a constant-query static quantum PCP or a construction meeting the stronger code parameters here.

Garg and Sengupta obtain a further constant-soundness result using algebraic-geometry codes. Their stated application has locality growing as the square root of code length. This still misses the maximum constant check weight required here.

cards.title: Passive quantum memory in three dimensions
cards.formal: Do there exist constants \(B,R>0\), a fixed finite inverse temperature \(\beta>0\), strictly increasing qubit counts \(n_j\to\infty\), local three-dimensional stabilizer Hamiltonians \(H_{n_j}\), and fixed encoding maps \(\operatorname{Enc}_{n_j}\), all satisfying the definitions below, for which \[\tau_{n_j}(\beta)\longrightarrow\infty?\] The dynamics couple every single-qubit Pauli error to the same specified positive-temperature bath, with no intervention during storage. This card retains a claimed affirmative resolution from May2026; the complete preprint proof has not been independently verified here.
cards.definitions:
Place the \(n\) qubits at points in \(\mathbb R^3\), with at most \(B\) qubits in every closed unit ball. Each Hamiltonian is \[H_n=\sum_{a=1}^{M_n}\frac{I-S_a}{2}.\] The operators \(S_a\) are commuting, nonidentity Hermitian Pauli checks. Each has support contained in a ball of radius \(R\), and each qubit belongs to at most \(B\) checks. Support is the set of wires where a tensor factor is not identity. The common \(+1\) eigenspace of all checks must have dimension exactly two, so the Hamiltonian has a single encoded ground-space qubit. A check is a signed tensor product of \[I=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&1\end{pmatrix},\quad X=\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\1&0\end{pmatrix},\quad Y=\begin{pmatrix}0&-i\\i&0\end{pmatrix},\quad Z=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&-1\end{pmatrix},\] with overall sign \(+1\) or \(-1\). The coefficient of each term is fixed as displayed, so local energy penalties cannot grow with \(n\). The geometry need not be translation invariant, a regular lattice, or connected. The constants \(B,R\) work for the entire sequence. No efficient construction of the sequence is required.

All states live in finite-dimensional complex Hilbert spaces. A density matrix \(\rho\) is Hermitian, positive semidefinite and of trace one: \(\rho=\rho^\dagger\), \(v^\dagger\rho v\ge0\) for every vector \(v\), and \(\operatorname{Tr}\rho=1\). A quantum channel is a complex-linear map on matrices that preserves trace and is completely positive, meaning that its tensor product with the identity on every auxiliary register preserves positive semidefiniteness. Such channels model encoding, noise and recovery. Use units \(\hbar=k_B=1\), so physical temperature is \(1/\beta\). The same finite positive \(\beta\) is used for all sizes.

Here is the complete bath convention. Let \(\Pi_E\) denote the spectral projector of \(H_n\) at energy \(E\). For every site \(u\), every \(P\in\{X,Y,Z\}\), and every energy difference \(\omega\) for which the following operator is nonzero, define \[A_{u,P,\omega}=\sum_{E'-E=\omega}\Pi_{E'}P_u\Pi_E,\qquad g_\beta(\omega)=\min\{1,e^{-\beta\omega}\}.\] Thus positive \(\omega\) means an increase in system energy; its rate is suppressed by the Boltzmann factor. The generator on density matrices is \[\mathcal L_{n,\beta}(\rho)=-i[H_n,\rho]+\sum_{u,P,\omega}g_\beta(\omega)\left(A_{u,P,\omega}\rho A_{u,P,\omega}^\dagger-\frac{A_{u,P,\omega}^\dagger A_{u,P,\omega}\rho+\rho A_{u,P,\omega}^\dagger A_{u,P,\omega}}2\right).\] The commutator is \([H,\rho]=H\rho-\rho H\). The evolution for real \(t\ge0\) is the channel \(\Phi_{n,\beta,t}=\exp(t\mathcal L_{n,\beta})\), the finite-dimensional linear-map exponential. All single-site \(X,Y,Z\) couplings are included; no symmetry forbids one of them. Rates for allowed transitions are positive, and their attempt-rate normalization does not depend on size. The opposite-frequency ratio ensures the Gibbs state \(e^{-\beta H_n}/\operatorname{Tr}(e^{-\beta H_n})\) is stationary. Although the spectral formula uses global energy projectors, commuting finite-range checks make these frequency components local: only checks meeting the site can affect its energy change. With the fixed range and density bounds, their support and possible energy changes are bounded independently of \(n\).

For each size choose one completely positive trace-preserving encoding \(\operatorname{Enc}_n\) from one qubit to the \(n\)-qubit system. It must have a completely positive trace-preserving left inverse \(D_{n,0}\), so \(D_{n,0}\circ\operatorname{Enc}_n\) is exactly the identity channel. This encoding may depend on the chosen temperature, and may initialize a thermal auxiliary state; it need not map entirely into the ground space or be efficiently preparable. It is chosen once for the device, independently of storage time and the unknown logical input. This retains the previous card’s thermal-encoding convention rather than adding a ground-state-only initialization requirement.

Let \(\|A\|_1=\operatorname{Tr}\sqrt{A^\dagger A}\) be the trace norm. For this fixed encoding define \[\varepsilon_{n,\beta}(t)=\inf_{D}\ \sup_{\rho}\left\|D\circ\Phi_{n,\beta,t}\circ\operatorname{Enc}_n(\rho)-\rho\right\|_1.\] The supremum ranges over every one-qubit density matrix; the infimum ranges over recovery channels \(D\) from \(n\) qubits to one. One recovery channel must work for every logical input at the given time. It may depend on \(n,\beta,t\), but cannot depend on the unknown input \(\rho\). Recovery is not required to be efficient. Define \[\tau_n(\beta)=\inf\{t\ge0:\varepsilon_{n,\beta}(t)>1/10\},\qquad \inf\varnothing=+\infty.\] The trace norm here has no factor of one half. Encoding occurs before storage and recovery only at readout; no syndrome measurements, feedback, cooling procedure or active corrections are allowed during the evolution. Divergence means that for every finite \(T>0\) there is an index \(j_0\) such that \(\tau_{n_j}(\beta)>T\) for all \(j\ge j_0\), at the same fixed temperature and local parameter bounds.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof of existence of the family, fixed temperature and encoding maps in the displayed statement, including the lifetime bound for this generator, or a complete Lean-checked proof of its logical negation. The affirmative side need only prove divergence; a lower bound \(\exp(c n^\eta)\) for fixed \(c,\eta>0\) is stronger than required. The negative side must cover every admissible sequence and encoding, including thermal encodings, rather than a particular candidate geometry. The May2026 preprint claims a stronger affirmative bound, but this review has not independently verified its full construction or supplied its Lean formalization. A finite-size numerical trend or lifetime growth only up to a temperature-dependent crossover does not establish the fixed-temperature limit. Changing the bath with size, increasing local energy scales, forbidding local errors, adding corrections during storage, or demanding ground-state-only initialization changes the target.
cards.why: A foundational question about whether quantum information can enjoy passive thermal protection in physical three-dimensional space. The recent claimed solution makes careful separation of storage, initialization, bath restrictions and stability especially important.

importance.reason: A defining problem at the intersection of quantum information and many-body physics; retained with an explicit claimed-resolution flag to preserve its history and prevent misleading open-status selection.

context_blocks.text: This record now has a claimed affirmative resolution. Balasubramanian, Davydova and Lin’s May 2026 preprint presents local three-dimensional stabilizer Hamiltonians with lifetime \(\exp (\Omega (n^{\eta}))\) at sufficiently low fixed temperature, for some \(\eta >0\). Its initialization is a thermal encoding. The catalogue flags this as a recent proof claim whose complete argument has not been independently verified here, rather than continuing to present the broad existence problem as confidently open.

A passive memory asks the Hamiltonian and its thermal environment to preserve information between an initial encoding and a final recovery. No repeated syndrome measurements or corrections are performed during storage. Quantum information requires preserving arbitrary superpositions, not only two distinguishable classical states. A material can preserve whether it is mostly magnetized up or down while rapidly losing the phase between those two possibilities; such a material is a classical memory, not a qubit memory.

The bath must be part of the mathematical specification. If errors that change the logical information are simply forbidden, a long lifetime may reflect that restriction. If every local transition is slowed as the device grows, a divergent lifetime can be manufactured by changing the clock. The generator above fixes the time scale and includes all single-qubit Pauli couplings, with ordinary positive-temperature suppression of energy-raising transitions.

An energy barrier is informative but does not alone determine memory time. A logical error may require crossing a high-energy configuration, yet the number of routes and intermediate configurations can be so large that entropy offsets the energetic suppression. Thermodynamic stability criteria therefore use both the bath dynamics and the thermal probability of configurations on which a recovery rule becomes unstable. A recovery map used to analyze the information is compatible with passive storage when it is applied only at readout.

The order of limits matters. Williamson’s layer-code result, published in August 2026, proves a regime in which lifetime grows exponentially with linear system size, but only up to a length scale exponential in inverse temperature. The lifetime at that crossover is very large as temperature falls. For the present question, however, temperature is fixed while system size goes to infinity, so an improvement restricted to a finite crossover regime is partial self-correction.

Roberts, Koh, Tan and Yao’s cored product codes take a different route using disordered geometry. Their January 2026 revision reports finite-temperature simulations of a pinwheel-based three-dimensional memory with up to 60,000 qubits, finding evidence that lifetime increases with size below a critical temperature. Those numerical results motivate a candidate construction but cannot by themselves establish the infinite-family limit required here.

Stahl and Nandkishore obtain protection in three dimensions by enforcing a one-form symmetry on the dynamics, even when enforcement is confined to a subvolume of vanishing relative size. This is a meaningful mechanism, but it restricts which local errors the environment may produce. The present model permits every single-qubit X, Y and Z coupling, so symmetry-protected results must be distinguished from this target.

The May construction’s proven version uses a randomized geometric embedding; its separate explicit variant lacks a complete lifetime proof. Efficient passive preparation and stability under arbitrary local Hamiltonian perturbations are also left for further work. These are additional requirements, beyond the fixed-Hamiltonian storage question formulated here.

The status distinction is useful for selecting research projects: the original existence target now requires assessment of the new theorem, while initialization, perturbation stability and alternative constructions remain separate directions. They should receive their own precise statements if added to the catalogue, rather than silently replacing the question under this identifier.

The current preprint’s Equation(5) prints a first-threshold condition with error at most \(1/10\), which already holds at time zero. The card instead defines lifetime by the first time the recovery error exceeds the threshold. The source’s substantive claim is the trace-norm estimate in Equation(3), supported by its stated stability theorem and §5.4; that estimate would imply the intended lower bound with this corrected convention.

For the present question, however, temperature is fixed while system size goes to infinity, so an improvement restricted to a finite crossover regime is partial self-correction.

Roberts, Koh, Tan and Yao’s cored product codes take a different route using disordered geometry. Their January 2026 revision reports finite-temperature simulations of a pinwheel-based three-dimensional memory with up to 60,000 qubits, finding evidence that lifetime increases with size below a critical temperature. Those numerical results motivate a candidate construction but cannot by themselves establish the infinite-family limit required here.

Stahl and Nandkishore obtain protection in three dimensions by enforcing a one-form symmetry on the dynamics, even when enforcement is confined to a subvolume of vanishing relative size. This is a meaningful mechanism, but it restricts which local errors the environment may produce. The present model permits every single-qubit X, Y and Z coupling, so symmetry-protected results must be distinguished from this target.

The May construction’s proven version uses a randomized geometric embedding; its separate explicit variant lacks a complete lifetime proof. Efficient passive preparation and stability under arbitrary local Hamiltonian perturbations are also left for further work. These are additional requirements, beyond the fixed-Hamiltonian storage question formulated here.

The status distinction is useful for selecting research projects: the original existence target now requires assessment of the new theorem, while initialization, perturbation stability and alternative constructions remain separate directions. They should receive their own precise statements if added to the catalogue, rather than silently replacing the question under this identifier.

The current preprint’s Equation(5) prints a first-threshold condition with error at most \(1/10\), which already holds at time zero. The card instead defines lifetime by the first time the recovery error exceeds the threshold. The source’s substantive claim is the trace-norm estimate in Equation(3), supported by its stated stability theorem and §5.4; that estimate would imply the intended lower bound with this corrected convention.

cards.title: Quantum capacity of the qubit depolarizing channel
cards.formal: Determine the unassisted quantum-capacity function \(Q(q)=Q(\mathcal D_q)\) for every real \(q\in[0,1]\), where the qubit depolarizing channel is \[\mathcal D_q(\rho)=(1-q)\rho+\frac q3(X\rho X+Y\rho Y+Z\rho Z).\] The parameter \(q\) is the total probability of a nonidentity Pauli error. Capacity uses the operational definition below and is measured in qubits per independent channel use. The quantitative benchmark accepts a function with absolute error at most \(1/100\) throughout the whole domain.
cards.definitions:
For the standard basis \(|0\rangle,|1\rangle\) of \(\mathbb C^2\), define \(X|0\rangle=|1\rangle\), \(X|1\rangle=|0\rangle\), \(Z|0\rangle=|0\rangle\), \(Z|1\rangle=-|1\rangle\), and \(Y=iXZ\), where \(i^2=-1\). Each of the three nonidentity errors has probability \(q/3\), and identity has probability \(1-q\). The formula therefore defines a channel for every real \(q\in[0,1]\). On general matrices it extends complex-linearly. In the coding definition, take \(A=B=\mathbb C^2\) and \(\Phi=\mathcal D_q\). The parameter is fixed across a code block and across the sequence of block lengths; a different parameter may have a different code sequence.

A density matrix on \(\mathbb C^d\) is a Hermitian matrix \(\rho=\rho^\dagger\) satisfying \(v^\dagger\rho v\ge0\) for every vector \(v\) and \(\operatorname{Tr}\rho=1\). Dagger denotes conjugate transpose and trace is the sum of diagonal entries. A quantum channel from \(\mathbb C^a\) to \(\mathbb C^b\) is a complex-linear map on matrices of the form \(\Psi(X)=\sum_j K_jXK_j^\dagger\), with finitely many \(b\)-by-\(a\) matrices obeying \(\sum_j K_j^\dagger K_j=I_a\). These are precisely the completely positive trace-preserving maps, abbreviated CPTP. Matrices in coding operations may have arbitrary complex entries. Memorylessness means that \(n\) uses of a fixed channel \(\Phi:A\to B\) act as the tensor power \(\Phi^{\otimes n}\), with independent noise and the same channel on every use.

For each integer \(n\ge1\), a code consists of a nonnegative integer \(k_n\), a CPTP encoder \(E_n\) from \(k_n\) qubits to \(A^{\otimes n}\), and a CPTP decoder \(D_n\) from \(B^{\otimes n}\) to \(k_n\) qubits. A qubit is a copy of \(\mathbb C^2\), so the message space has dimension \(2^{k_n}\). Let \[|\Omega_k\rangle=2^{-k/2}\sum_{x\in\{0,1\}^k}|x\rangle_R\otimes|x\rangle_M\] be a maximally entangled unit vector between an untouched reference register \(R\) and a message register \(M\), each of dimension \(2^k\). For \(k=0\), both spaces are one-dimensional and the sum has one term. The entanglement fidelity of a code is \[F_n=\langle\Omega_{k_n}|\bigl[\operatorname{id}_R\otimes(D_n\circ\Phi^{\otimes n}\circ E_n)\bigr](|\Omega_{k_n}\rangle\langle\Omega_{k_n}|)|\Omega_{k_n}\rangle.\] The identity map leaves the reference unchanged, and \(\circ\) denotes composition, with the rightmost operation applied first. This tests preservation of quantum information and its correlations, rather than only classical basis labels.

A real rate \(r\ge0\) is achievable if there is a sequence of these codes, one for every \(n\ge1\), such that \(F_n\to1\) and \(\liminf_{n\to\infty}k_n/n\ge r\). Define \(Q(\Phi)\) as the supremum of achievable rates, in qubits per channel use. Rate zero is always achievable. The encoder and decoder may jointly process their entire blocks, use local ancillary systems and discard local systems. There is no bound on their computation or circuit sizes and no uniformity requirement on the sequence of codes. They depend on the channel but not on the unknown input message state. No preshared entanglement, additional classical communication, feedback or auxiliary quantum channel is supplied. The reference in the fidelity test is a mathematical test system, not a communication resource. The whole coding map is trace preserving: postselecting a successful event for free is not allowed. This is asymptotic, vanishing-error, unassisted quantum transmission capacity.
cards.answer_criterion: Give an unambiguous real-valued function \(g:[0,1]\to\mathbb R\), together with a complete Lean-checked proof that \[|g(q)-Q(q)|\le\frac1{100}\qquad\text{for every real }q\in[0,1].\] The proof must establish both the lower and upper sides of this absolute error bound in qubits per channel use. Exact equality with \(Q\) also qualifies. A finite table, uncertified numerical plot, or restatement of the defining optimization or supremum does not determine the requested curve. There is no prescribed formula grammar, finite representation for the argument \(q\), or polynomial evaluation-time requirement. The inherited numerical acceptance is weaker than the source's exact-capacity question; a solution at this tolerance need not settle the exact positive-capacity threshold.
cards.why: The unresolved communication limit of a canonical quantum-noise model. It tests whether quantum coding theory can turn regularized existence formulas into sharp quantitative limits despite degeneracy and multi-copy advantages.

context_blocks.text: Depolarizing noise treats the three Pauli errors symmetrically. Despite this short channel description, its quantum transmission limit allows arbitrary collective encodings over arbitrarily long blocks. The entanglement-fidelity criterion keeps the distinction between transmitting an unknown quantum state and sending only classical data.

Parameter conventions matter: the probabilities \((1-3p,p,p,p)\) correspond to \(p=q/3\). The expression \((1-\lambda)\rho+\lambda I/2\) has \(\lambda=4q/3\), with the usual convex-mixture interpretation only for \(q\le3/4\). Thus \(q=3/4\) is the completely depolarizing channel; \(q=1\) still specifies a valid channel, but is a different map. All thresholds here use total Pauli error \(q\).

The quantum coding theorem identifies the operational capacity with \(\sup_{n\ge1} n^{-1}\max_\rho I_c(\rho,\Phi^{\otimes n})\). Here \(\rho\) ranges over all input density matrices on \(A^{\otimes n}\). If \(|\psi\rangle\) is a purification of \(\rho\), meaning a unit vector on a reference and the input with input marginal \(\rho\), and \(\omega=(\operatorname{id}\otimes\Phi^{\otimes n})(|\psi\rangle\langle\psi|)\), then \(I_c=S(\omega_{B^{\otimes n}})-S(\omega)\). The marginal is obtained by tracing out the reference. For eigenvalues \(\lambda_j\) of a density matrix, \(S=-\sum_j\lambda_j\log_2\lambda_j\), with \(0\log_2 0=0\). The result is independent of the chosen purification. This exact regularized expression includes every block length; it is not an evaluation of the capacity curve or a finite stopping rule.

A known lower bound is \(\max\{0,1-h_2(q)-q\log_2 3\}\), where \(h_2(q)=-q\log_2q-(1-q)\log_2(1-q)\), with the endpoint convention \(0\log_2 0=0\). Its positive part vanishes near \(q=0.1893\). Multicopy results surpass this bound, so the one-use expression is not the capacity curve throughout the noise range.

Agarwal and coauthors report positive coherent information for a 45-copy symmetric rank-two input up to a numerically evaluated per-Pauli value \(p=0.064657\), corresponding to \(q=0.193971\). This is a lower bound from particular inputs, not optimality over all block lengths.

Krohn-Grimberghe supplies an exact-arithmetic certificate for a 45-copy state with positive coherent information at \(q=48717/250000=0.194868\). The paper also gives positivity below this point and distinguishes its certified witness from stronger numerical states in the earlier authors' repository. This review checked the statement, conventions and limitations; it did not rerun the supplied verification artifact.

The endpoints and a whole zero-capacity range are known: \(Q(0)=1\) and \(Q(q)=0\) for every \(q\ge1/4\). In that range the channel is antidegradable, meaning that a channel applied to the environment output can simulate the receiver's output. The certificate paper explicitly does not determine the true positivity threshold. Knowing that threshold alone would still not determine the positive-rate curve.
Leditzky, Leung and Smith determine low-noise capacities to leading orders. This controls an asymptotic regime near the noiseless channel and does not evaluate the whole parameter interval.

Zhu and coauthors give improved upper bounds for depolarizing channels. Their §3.4 retains a gap between achievable rates and upper bounds; a numerical comparison of bounds does not by itself certify the benchmark error throughout the domain.

The August 2026 strong-converse paper establishes fidelity decay above capacity for degradable and antidegradable channels and additional upper bounds. It explicitly distinguishes those bounds from an exact capacity value. A strong converse therefore does not supply the missing depolarizing curve.

The source literature retains the exact-capacity question. The absolute 0.01 acceptance rule was already adopted by the atlas before this review. Openness of the exact question does not alone imply that approximation to this tolerance is open; the status records that distinction.

cards.title: NP outside BQP
cards.formal:
Is \(\mathrm{NP}\not\subseteq\mathrm{BQP}\)? That is, does there exist a total decision language
\[L\subseteq\{0,1\}^{*}\quad\text{with}\quad L\in\mathrm{NP}\ \text{and}\ L\notin\mathrm{BQP}?\]
Equivalently, is the total language \(3\text{-}\mathrm{SAT}\) defined below outside \(\mathrm{BQP}\)? The negation is that every language with polynomially bounded classical certificates and a polynomial-time classical verifier has a uniform bounded-error quantum polynomial-time decider. This is noncontainment, not merely inequality of two classes.
cards.definitions:
A language is a set of finite binary strings. Put \(n=|x|\) and write \(\mathbf1_L(x)\) for its membership bit, allowing \(n=0\). The condition \(L\in\mathrm{NP}\) means that there exist a finite deterministic classical multitape Turing-machine verifier \(V\) and fixed positive integers \(C,d,K,e\) such that
\[x\in L\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
\exists y\in\{0,1\}^{*},\quad |y|\le C(n+1)^d\ \land\ V(x,y)=1.\]
For every pair of binary strings \((x,y)\), the verifier halts with a bit output within \(K(|x|+|y|+1)^e\) ordinary tape steps. The existentially quantified certificate is classical. It defines membership but is not supplied to the quantum decider, which receives only \(x\). All programs and exponents are fixed independently of the input length.

The condition \(L\in\mathrm{BQP}\) is defined using circuits over the fixed gates \(H,T,\mathrm{CNOT}\). In the ordered one-qubit basis \((|0\rangle,|1\rangle)\),
\[H=\frac{1}{\sqrt2}\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\1&-1\end{pmatrix},\qquad
T=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&(1+i)/\sqrt2\end{pmatrix},\qquad i^2=-1.\]
On two distinct addressed qubits, \(\mathrm{CNOT}|a,b\rangle=|a,a\mathbin{\oplus}b\rangle\) for bits \(a,b\), where \(\oplus\) is addition modulo two. Gates act as the identity on all other qubits. They may address any qubits; there is no geometric locality restriction.

There must exist one deterministic classical multitape Turing machine \(G\) and fixed positive integers \(K,e\) such that, on unary input \(1^n\), including the empty unary string at \(n=0\), \(G\) prints within \(K(n+1)^e\) bit steps a complete circuit description. The description specifies a register size \(q(n)\ge n+1\), an ordered list of \(m(n)\) gates with binary qubit addresses, and one designated output qubit \(j(n)\). Both \(q(n)\) and \(m(n)\) are at most \(K(n+1)^e\). Every listed address must be valid, and the list depends only on \(n\), not on the particular \(x\). The circuit may have unrestricted depth subject to this polynomial gate bound.

For \(x\in\{0,1\}^n\), initialize the register to the computational basis state \(|x\rangle\otimes|0^{q(n)-n}\rangle\). A computational basis state \(|y\rangle\) is the unit coordinate vector indexed by \(y\in\{0,1\}^{q(n)}\) in \(\mathbb C^{2^{q(n)}}\). Apply the listed unitary matrices in order, obtaining
\[|\psi_x\rangle=\sum_{y\in\{0,1\}^{q(n)}}\alpha_y|y\rangle,
\qquad \sum_y|\alpha_y|^2=1.\]
Measure only qubit \(j(n)\) at the end. The probability of output \(b\in\{0,1\}\) is exactly \(\sum_{y:y_{j(n)}=b}|\alpha_y|^2\). For every \(x\), this probability must be at least \(2/3\) when \(b=\mathbf1_L(x)\). These equations specify the mathematical semantics; the machine is not asked to write down the exponentially long state vector or its amplitudes.

There is no advice, oracle gate, postselection, supplied quantum state or freely chosen real parameter. All auxiliary qubits start at zero. Only the stated finite gate set is primitive; gate descriptions and uniform generation are finite classical data. Quantum computation is ideal; hardware noise is outside the model. Constants and exponents may depend on the fixed language's algorithms, but not on \(n\) or \(x\).

For a concrete satisfiability language, a formula has variables \(z_1,\ldots,z_N\) and \(M\) explicitly listed clauses. Each clause has zero to three literals, each a variable or its negation. A truth assignment is a vector in \(\{0,1\}^{N}\); it satisfies a clause when at least one literal is true and satisfies the formula when every clause is satisfied. The empty conjunction is true and an empty clause is false; repeated variables, repeated clauses and tautologies are allowed.

Here is one explicit binary representation. For an integer \(u\ge0\), let \(b(u)\) be its binary expansion without leading zeros, with \(b(0)=0\), and put \(B(u)=1^{|b(u)|}0b(u)\). Begin with \(1^N0B(M)\). For each of the \(M\) clauses, write \(B(k)\) for its length \(0\le k\le3\), followed by its \(k\) literals. A literal is a sign bit and \(B(j)\) for \(1\le j\le N\); sign zero denotes \(z_j\), sign one denotes \(\neg z_j\). There are no trailing bits. The language \(3\text{-}\mathrm{SAT}\) consists of the valid encodings with a satisfying assignment. Every malformed string is a no-instance. Input length counts every encoding bit, rather than only \(N\), and the unary variable-count field ensures that the full assignment has polynomial length in the encoding.

This encoding is polynomially equivalent to the usual explicit 3-CNF satisfiability problem, with variables relabeled consecutively when necessary. By NP-completeness and closure of BQP under deterministic polynomial-time many-one reductions, \(3\text{-}\mathrm{SAT}\in\mathrm{BQP}\) is equivalent to \(\mathrm{NP}\subseteq\mathrm{BQP}\). A many-one reduction here is one deterministic polynomial-time map \(f\) with \(x\in L\) exactly when \(f(x)\) is a satisfiable valid encoding. This equivalence concerns total languages, with the required bounded error on every yes- and no-instance.
cards.answer_criterion:
Give a complete, mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of either
\[\exists L\subseteq\{0,1\}^{*},\quad L\in\mathrm{NP}\land L\notin\mathrm{BQP},\]
or its full negation \(\mathrm{NP}\subseteq\mathrm{BQP}\).

A separation must establish the classical verifier and polynomial certificate bound for one fixed language and exclude every polynomial-time-uniform quantum circuit family with any fixed polynomial size/register bounds in the stated finite-gate model. Equivalently, it may prove that the full encoded 3-SAT language is outside BQP. A containment proof may instead give a uniform quantum decider for this 3-SAT language, including rejection of malformed encodings, and establish its complete resource and pointwise success guarantees together with the NP-completeness implication.

An oracle or unstructured-search lower bound does not exclude algorithms that inspect the explicit input. Neither a restriction to selected formula families nor a lower bound for one quantum architecture answers the full question. Merely proving \(\mathrm{NP}\ne\mathrm{BQP}\) is insufficient if the argument only places a language in BQP outside NP. A proposed SAT algorithm must count all elementary operations and qubits, including state preparation and any subroutine implementation. Nonlinear dynamics, postselection, supplied witnesses or uncharged exponential resources are outside this BQP definition. There is no unproved hardness assumption or numerical approximation tolerance in the target.
cards.why: This asks whether efficient classical verification always permits efficient quantum decision. Noncontainment would identify a limit even for ideal scalable quantum computers and would also imply P differs from NP. Containment would place all classically verifiable decision problems within quantum polynomial time.

importance.reason: A foundational relation between quantum algorithms and NP-completeness; a noncontainment proof would also separate P from NP.

progress.text: Quantum factoring and discrete-logarithm algorithms establish important polynomial-time upper bounds for structured function problems.
Grover establishes \(O(\sqrt M)\) query search, a quadratic improvement in the number of candidates rather than a general polynomial-time SAT result.
Bennett–Bernstein–Brassard–Vazirani give quantum lower bounds relative to random oracles and explicitly distinguish them from ordinary NP noncontainment.
The inspected book edition records \(\mathrm{NP}\not\subseteq\mathrm{BQP}\) as Conjecture 11.4.
The large-Pauli-coefficient reduction transfers NP noncontainment to a promised quantum-state task as a hardness assumption.
A revised Valiant–Vazirani paper discusses a nonlinear coprocessor model; that extra operation is outside ordinary BQP.

cards.status_note: Source-open evidence checked through 16 September 2026. The inspected 2019 source states NP noncontainment in BQP as Conjecture 11.4, and the June 2026 Pauli-coefficient paper uses it as an unproved hardness assumption. The checked oracle lower bounds, formula-oracle synthesis and nonlinear-coprocessor results do not settle the stated total-language comparison in the standard finite-gate model. Bounded current searches located neither a matching unconditional noncontainment proof nor a general BQP SAT algorithm. This review does not independently certify every cited proof or exhaust all later literature.

context_blocks.text: For a satisfiable formula, one assignment certifies a yes answer; for an unsatisfiable formula, every assignment fails. The quantum decider receives the formula without a certificate and must answer both cases reliably. Its input is the entire explicit syntax, so shared variables and clause structure are available to every algorithm being quantified over.

Since deterministic polynomial-time computation is contained in BQP, \(\mathrm{NP}\not\subseteq\mathrm{BQP}\) implies \(\mathrm P\ne\mathrm{NP}\). A proof merely that classical deterministic computation is weaker than NP would not by itself establish this stronger noncontainment. The statement also differs from BPP versus BQP: quantum algorithms could be more powerful than classical randomization while still failing on some NP languages.

Shor’s factoring and discrete-logarithm algorithms are polynomial in the input bit length. These structured function tasks do not provide a general quantum decider for every NP language, and their quantum upper bounds do not prove any unrestricted classical lower bound. They are major algorithmic successes whose scope remains distinct from the NP-complete decision target.

For unstructured search over \(M\) candidates with one marked candidate, Grover’s bound is \(O(\sqrt M)\) oracle queries. With \(N\) binary assignment coordinates, the square-root search scale \(\sqrt{2^N}=2^{N/2}\) is still exponential in \(N\); evaluating a candidate also has a cost. This resource comparison does not establish a lower bound for all algorithms on an explicitly supplied formula.

Bennett, Bernstein, Brassard and Vazirani prove that relative to a randomly chosen length-preserving oracle, with probability one NP is not contained in bounded-error quantum time \(o(2^{n/2})\). Both the quantum algorithm and the NP verifier receive the oracle. The source expressly warns that its oracle theorem does not rule out unrelativized \(\mathrm{NP}\subseteq\mathrm{BQP}\). Black-box evaluations reveal less structure than a full formula description.

Cifuentes’ June 2026 preprint studies whether a circuit-prepared state has a nonidentity Pauli observable with expectation magnitude at least \(\varepsilon\), promised against all such magnitudes being at most \(\varepsilon/2\). Pauli observables are tensor products of the standard one-qubit identity and Pauli matrices. Its reduction shows that an efficient quantum solver for this promise task would imply \(\mathrm{NP}\subseteq\mathrm{BQP}\), even for pure states and thresholds bounded below by a positive constant. The resulting hardness is conditional on this card’s conjecture; it does not prove the conjecture.

Kelly and coauthors’ June 2026 revision discusses efficient SAT solving with an added nonlinear quantum coprocessor. Its first section explicitly distinguishes those dynamics from the usual linear unitary circuit model and notes the exponential space cost of the discussed large-system simulation. Consequently, its proposed computational power is not a BQP algorithm under the gate and qubit bounds specified here.

cards.title: QMA versus QCMA
cards.formal: Is \(\mathrm{QMA}=\mathrm{QCMA}\) for ordinary promise problems without an oracle? Equivalently, does every promise problem that has a uniform polynomial-time quantum verifier with polynomially many quantum witness qubits also have such a verifier with only polynomially many classical witness bits, with completeness at least \(2/3\) and soundness at most \(1/3\)? The converse inclusion is available by measuring a purported classical witness in the computational basis, so the requested equality is exactly the inclusion \(\mathrm{QMA}\subseteq\mathrm{QCMA}\).
cards.why: This asks whether an untrusted quantum state can certify something that no short classical message can certify, even when the recipient already has a quantum computer. It isolates the power of the evidence itself from the power of the verifier and is a basic boundary in quantum complexity.

progress.text: Aaronson–Kuperberg separate quantum and classical witnesses relative to a quantum oracle.
Bostanci–Haferkamp–Nirkhe–Zhandry post an unconditional separation relative to a standard classical oracle; the revised manuscript is dated 17 January 2026 and appears at STOC 2026.

Bostanci–Huang–Vaikuntanathan give a simpler classical-oracle proof using good codes; the checked ECCC revision is dated 12 April and also separates quantum from classical advice in that oracle setting.

context_blocks.text: Both sides allow quantum computation. A classical certificate may tell the verifier which quantum experiment to perform; it need not describe a quantum witness state. Consequently, showing that some state needs many classical bits to describe does not establish a separation of the verification classes.

Soundness is essential: a verifier must reject a no-instance for every permitted witness. A proof that works only when the prover follows the intended preparation is not a QMA or QCMA verification guarantee. The mathematical model makes this universal quantifier explicit.

Aaronson–Kuperberg gave a separation after both verifiers are granted access to the same quantum black box. This supplied evidence about black-box methods while leaving the ordinary classes without that extra resource unresolved.

The November 2025 manuscript, published at STOC 2026, strengthens the oracle type to a standard classical function. Classical here describes the function encoded by the oracle, not a requirement to ask only classical queries: the quantum verifiers can query it in superposition. The result remains relative to an oracle.

The 2026 good-code construction gives a simpler classical-oracle separation and extends to quantum versus classical advice. Advice is trusted information that depends only on input length; a witness is untrusted information tailored to the individual input. The advice theorem is therefore recorded as related work, not as a replacement of this card’s witness question.

An ordinary separation would require an explicit promise problem and a lower bound against every uniform classical-witness quantum verifier. The checked oracle theorems do not remove their black box, so they do not justify marking the original class comparison resolved.

cards.answer_criterion: Provide a complete Lean-checked proof of \(\mathrm{QMA}\subseteq\mathrm{QCMA}\), or a complete Lean-checked proof of its negation: there exists a disjoint promise pair in QMA for which no uniform polynomial-time QCMA verifier meets both guarantees. The affirmative direction must cover every QMA promise problem, with a possibly different verifier and polynomial witness bound. A negative proof must quantify over all eligible classical-witness verifiers. An oracle separation, a gap between two particular verifiers, or a quantum state's large classical description length does not alone settle the target. The output is a proof of class equality or strict containment, not an approximation to an acceptance probability.
cards.definitions:
A promise problem is an ordered pair \(L=(L_{\mathrm{yes}},L_{\mathrm{no}})\) of disjoint subsets of \(\{0,1\}^*\). There is no requirement on inputs outside their union. A verifier is specified by one deterministic classical Turing machine that, on a string \(x\) of length \(n\), outputs in time polynomial in \(n\) the description of a quantum circuit \(V_x\), its witness-register lengths and a designated output qubit. All register lengths and the number of gates are bounded by a polynomial depending on the verifier, not on \(x\). Apart from its witness registers, the circuit starts with ancillary qubits in state \(|0\rangle\). It uses the fixed gate set \(\{H,T,\mathrm{CNOT}\}\), acting on specified qubits, where \[H=\frac1{\sqrt2}\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\1&-1\end{pmatrix},\qquad T=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&e^{i\pi/4}\end{pmatrix},\] and \(\mathrm{CNOT}|a,b\rangle=|a,a\mathbin\oplus b\rangle\) for bits \(a,b\); \(\oplus\) is addition modulo two. The circuit accepts when its final computational-basis measurement of the output qubit is 1. Qubits are two-dimensional complex systems; an \(m\)-qubit pure state is a unit vector in \(\mathbb C^{2^m}\), with computational basis \(\{|z\rangle:z\in\{0,1\}^m\}\). A mixed state is a positive semidefinite, trace-one complex matrix on this space. For witness density matrix \(\rho\), acceptance probability is \[\operatorname{Tr}\!\left[\Pi_1V_x\bigl(\rho\otimes |0\rangle\langle0|^{\otimes a}\bigr)V_x^\dagger\right],\] where \(a\) is the number of ancillary qubits, \(V_x^\dagger\) is the conjugate transpose, and \(\Pi_1\) projects onto output-qubit value 1 and acts as identity on the other qubits. Positive semidefinite means \(v^\dagger\rho v\ge0\) for every vector \(v\); \(\operatorname{Tr}\) is the sum of diagonal entries. Witnesses may depend arbitrarily on the whole input and need not be efficiently preparable. Circuit uniformity forbids advice depending only on input length, and neither model receives an oracle. The witness is sent once, before verification, with no further interaction. The stated finite universal gate set fixes an encoding; bounded-error classes permit the usual polynomial-overhead approximations of other effective universal gate sets. A different verifier and polynomial bound may be used for each promise problem.

The class \(\mathrm{QMA}\), quantum Merlin–Arthur, consists of the promise problems with such a verifier and one polynomial-length quantum witness register for which both conditions hold: for every \(x\in L_{\mathrm{yes}}\), some witness state is accepted with probability at least \(2/3\); for every \(x\in L_{\mathrm{no}}\), every witness state is accepted with probability at most \(1/3\). The quantifiers apply to arbitrary mixed states, not merely the honestly intended state. Pure witnesses suffice for completeness by linearity of acceptance probability.

The class \(\mathrm{QCMA}\), quantum classical Merlin–Arthur, uses the same uniform quantum verifier model, but its witness is a binary string \(w\in\{0,1\}^{m(n)}\), loaded in the computational-basis state \(|w\rangle\). For every yes-input some such string must be accepted with probability at least \(2/3\); for every no-input every such string must be accepted with probability at most \(1/3\). Lengths can be padded to a polynomial bound. Classical witnesses are untrusted and may depend on the individual input. They are not trusted advice shared by all inputs of a given length. A QCMA verifier may perform general quantum computation after receiving the classical witness. Equality means equality of the sets of promise problems under these definitions, not equality of the two witness representations for a particular circuit.

importance.reason: Separates quantum from classical witnesses and therefore addresses a basic source of quantum computational power.
