cards.title: Computability of quantum channel capacity
cards.formal: Does there exist a single deterministic classical Turing algorithm that, for every valid finite description of a memoryless finite-dimensional quantum channel \(\Phi\) specified below and every positive rational \(\varepsilon\), halts and outputs a rational \(r\) satisfying \(|r-Q(\Phi)|\le\varepsilon\)? Here \(Q\) is unassisted, vanishing-error quantum capacity in qubits per channel use. The algorithm must work for all valid descriptions and all positive requested accuracies; there is no time or space bound beyond eventual halting.
cards.definitions:
The input consists of positive integers \(d_A,d_B\), a finite program \(P\) for an ordinary deterministic Turing machine, and a positive rational \(\varepsilon\). Integers use binary notation and a rational uses a signed binary numerator and a positive binary denominator. Programs use one fixed effective encoding over a finite alphabet; choosing a different standard encoding only changes effective translations. Write \(A=\mathbb C^{d_A}\), \(B=\mathbb C^{d_B}\). The program \(P\), on every positive integer input \(m\), is promised to halt and output a complex matrix \(J_m\) of order \(d_Ad_B\), with rational real and imaginary entries in this encoding. There is a matrix \(J\) such that, for every entry, both its real and imaginary parts differ from those of \(J_m\) by at most \(2^{-m}\). No additional time bound on \(P\) is promised. The approximating matrices themselves need not be positive or trace preserving.

Index matrix entries by pairs \((i,u)\), with \(1\le i\le d_A\) and \(1\le u\le d_B\). The limiting matrix is promised to be positive semidefinite and to satisfy \[\sum_{u=1}^{d_B}J_{(i,u),(j,u)}=\delta_{ij}\qquad(1\le i,j\le d_A),\] where \(\delta_{ij}\) is one if \(i=j\) and zero otherwise. These conditions say \(\operatorname{Tr}_B J=I_A\). They make \(J\) the unnormalized Choi matrix of the unique CPTP channel defined on matrix units by \([\Phi(|i\rangle\langle j|)]_{u,v}=J_{(i,u),(j,v)}\) and extended complex-linearly. Equivalently, \(J=\sum_{i,j}|i\rangle\langle j|\otimes\Phi(|i\rangle\langle j|)\). The guarantee supplies effective approximation of arbitrary computable complex entries; algebraic-entry channels and ordinary finite circuits over computable gates are included. The algorithm receives the program's finite code and may execute it. It receives no oracle deciding equality, positivity or ordering of arbitrary computable real numbers.

All guarantees for the requested capacity algorithm apply only to inputs satisfying these promises. It need not recognize validity and has no prescribed behavior on invalid descriptions. Every valid program describing the same channel must yield an approximation to that channel's same capacity, though the output rational and running time may differ between programs. The description specifies the channel, not a particular encoder or decoder.

A density matrix on \(\mathbb C^d\) is a Hermitian matrix \(\rho=\rho^\dagger\) satisfying \(v^\dagger\rho v\ge0\) for every vector \(v\) and \(\operatorname{Tr}\rho=1\). Dagger denotes conjugate transpose and trace is the sum of diagonal entries. A quantum channel from \(\mathbb C^a\) to \(\mathbb C^b\) is a complex-linear map on matrices of the form \(\Psi(X)=\sum_j K_jXK_j^\dagger\), with finitely many \(b\)-by-\(a\) matrices obeying \(\sum_j K_j^\dagger K_j=I_a\). These are precisely the completely positive trace-preserving maps, abbreviated CPTP. Matrices in coding operations may have arbitrary complex entries. Memorylessness means that \(n\) uses of a fixed channel \(\Phi:A\to B\) act as the tensor power \(\Phi^{\otimes n}\), with independent noise and the same channel on every use.

For each integer \(n\ge1\), a code consists of a nonnegative integer \(k_n\), a CPTP encoder \(E_n\) from \(k_n\) qubits to \(A^{\otimes n}\), and a CPTP decoder \(D_n\) from \(B^{\otimes n}\) to \(k_n\) qubits. A qubit is a copy of \(\mathbb C^2\), so the message space has dimension \(2^{k_n}\). Let \[|\Omega_k\rangle=2^{-k/2}\sum_{x\in\{0,1\}^k}|x\rangle_R\otimes|x\rangle_M\] be a maximally entangled unit vector between an untouched reference register \(R\) and a message register \(M\), each of dimension \(2^k\). For \(k=0\), both spaces are one-dimensional and the sum has one term. The entanglement fidelity of a code is \[F_n=\langle\Omega_{k_n}|\bigl[\operatorname{id}_R\otimes(D_n\circ\Phi^{\otimes n}\circ E_n)\bigr](|\Omega_{k_n}\rangle\langle\Omega_{k_n}|)|\Omega_{k_n}\rangle.\] The identity map leaves the reference unchanged, and \(\circ\) denotes composition, with the rightmost operation applied first. This tests preservation of quantum information and its correlations, rather than only classical basis labels.

A real rate \(r\ge0\) is achievable if there is a sequence of these codes, one for every \(n\ge1\), such that \(F_n\to1\) and \(\liminf_{n\to\infty}k_n/n\ge r\). Define \(Q(\Phi)\) as the supremum of achievable rates, in qubits per channel use. Rate zero is always achievable. The encoder and decoder may jointly process their entire blocks, use local ancillary systems and discard local systems. There is no bound on their computation or circuit sizes and no uniformity requirement on the sequence of codes. They depend on the channel but not on the unknown input message state. No preshared entanglement, additional classical communication, feedback or auxiliary quantum channel is supplied. The reference in the fidelity test is a mathematical test system, not a communication resource. The whole coding map is trace preserving: postselecting a successful event for free is not allowed. This is asymptotic, vanishing-error, unassisted quantum transmission capacity.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof of the existence of such an algorithm, including its termination and additive error guarantee for every valid description and every positive rational \(\varepsilon\), or a complete Lean-checked proof that no such single algorithm exists in the specified input representation. The negative alternative means that every candidate algorithm fails termination or the error guarantee on at least one promised input and requested accuracy. The yes/no assertion quantifies over all requested accuracies; a fixed \(1/100\) error guarantee is not a replacement for it. A regularized formula without a finite stopping guarantee, polynomial-time hardness, or undecidability for an assisted, zero-error or memoryful capacity does not answer this question. Nor would undecidability of the exact predicate \(Q(\Phi)=0\) alone rule out additive approximation.

context_blocks.text: Capacity is the best rate at which a noisy channel can transmit information reliably after coding over many uses. For quantum transmission, the object being preserved is an arbitrary quantum state, including its entanglement with a reference system. A channel may badly corrupt each individual input and still support a positive asymptotic rate through suitable coding. This card asks whether that optimal rate can always be computed to requested precision at all.

The quantum coding theorem identifies the operational capacity with \(\sup_{n\ge1} n^{-1}\max_\rho I_c(\rho,\Phi^{\otimes n})\). Here \(\rho\) ranges over all input density matrices on \(A^{\otimes n}\). If \(|\psi\rangle\) is a purification of \(\rho\), meaning a unit vector on a reference and the input with input marginal \(\rho\), and \(\omega=(\operatorname{id}\otimes\Phi^{\otimes n})(|\psi\rangle\langle\psi|)\), then \(I_c=S(\omega_{B^{\otimes n}})-S(\omega)\). The marginal is obtained by tracing out the reference. For eigenvalues \(\lambda_j\) of a density matrix, \(S=-\sum_j\lambda_j\log_2\lambda_j\), with \(0\log_2 0=0\). The result is independent of the chosen purification. This exact regularized expression includes every block length; it is not an evaluation of the capacity curve or a finite stopping rule.

The regularized formula gives approximable finite-dimensional objectives at every fixed block length. This yields lower semicomputability: certified rational lower bounds can approach capacity. Such a sequence alone need not tell an algorithm when its distance from the limit is below a requested tolerance.

Cubitt and coauthors prove that no fixed number of channel uses suffices uniformly over all channels even to detect positive coherent information. For every chosen block length, they construct a channel whose optimized coherent information is zero there but whose capacity is positive. The channel can change with the chosen length. This does not rule out an algorithm with stopping time depending on the channel description and requested accuracy.

The input convention is important because a quantum channel is described by real and complex numbers. A finite program that supplies certified rational approximations gives an algorithm meaningful access to those numbers without granting exact tests of arbitrary computable-real equality. It also includes ordinary finite circuit descriptions over computable gates. The validity of the channel and approximation program is promised; solving the separate problem of recognizing all valid descriptions is not required.

Leung and Smith prove continuity of unassisted quantum capacity in finite output dimension, with an explicit bound in terms of channel distance and dimension. Thus small errors in specifying a fixed-dimensional channel change its capacity by a controlled amount. This prevents a simple discontinuity argument from settling this approximation question. Continuity controls perturbations of the channel, while the missing stopping rule concerns convergence over code block lengths.

The 2025 review Undecidability in Physics distinguishes this question from established undecidability results for other information-theoretic quantities. Channels with memory can carry an evolving hidden state across uses; that is different from repeating \(\Phi\) independently. Zero-error capacities demand perfect distinguishability at finite stages, unlike an error that tends to zero under asymptotic coding. Neither change can be imported silently into the present problem.

Bhattacharyya, Mehta and Zhao prove in 2026 that approximating quantum capacity is QMA-hard for channels specified succinctly by circuits. Their promise distinguishes capacity at least \(3/4\) from capacity at most \(1/4\), even for degradable channels. This is strong evidence against efficient computation, but it leaves unrestricted computability untouched: a QMA-hard problem can still have an exhaustive terminating algorithm. Circuit size also differs substantially from the length of a fully expanded channel matrix.

Their corrected March 2026 version proves undecidability for a separate restricted capacity: one-shot, entanglement-assisted, zero-error classical communication through a classical-to-quantum channel, with maximally entangled assistance and projective decoding measurements. Those restrictions are part of the theorem. The paper explicitly says it does not resolve general quantum-capacity computability. Its revision history records a correction to the earlier treatment of the assisted zero-error result.

It is also necessary to separate approximation from deciding whether the answer is exactly zero. Even when a nonnegative real quantity is computable to arbitrary error, every finite approximation can leave open whether it is zero or merely very small. Conversely, identifying some zero-capacity families does not provide approximations for every channel. The requested output and tolerance make this card an unambiguous uniform approximation problem.

A positive resolution would supply a general certification procedure for quantum communication rates, however slow. A negative resolution would show that no universal procedure can always certify the optimal rate to a chosen tolerance, despite finite input and output dimensions and independent repeated noise. Either outcome would clarify whether regularized formulas describe quantities that are algorithmically accessible or can exceed the reach of computation.

cards.title: Quantum query-to-communication lifting
cards.formal: Do there exist constants \(C\ge1\) and an integer \(k\ge0\) such that, for every \(n\ge2\), there is a total nonconstant Boolean communication gadget \(g_n:\{0,1\}^{a_n}\times\{0,1\}^{b_n}\to\{0,1\}\), with finite positive integers \(a_n,b_n\), for which every partial Boolean function \(f:D\to\{0,1\}\), \(D\subseteq\{0,1\}^n\), satisfies \[\frac{Q_{1/3}(f)}{C(\log_2n)^k}\ \le\ Q^*_{1/3}(f\circ g_n^n)\ \le\ C(\log_2n)^k Q_{1/3}(f)?\] Here \(Q_{1/3}\) is quantum query complexity and \(Q^*_{1/3}\) is two-party quantum communication complexity with unrestricted prior entanglement. Both have worst-case error at most \(1/3\). The gadget depends on \(n\), but not on \(D\) or \(f\), and the constants are common to the entire family.
cards.why: Quantum query complexity captures information obtainable from an oracle, while communication complexity measures information exchanged between separated parties. A universal lifting theorem would tightly connect these two models across all Boolean promise problems. The demand for only polylogarithmic loss is substantially stronger than transferring a weaker lower-bound measure or obtaining an arbitrary polynomial relation.
cards.status_note: The original question remains explicitly open in the checked ICALP 2026 primary discussion. The CCC 2021 and ICALP 2026 positive results have weaker lower-bound measures, additional hypotheses or model restrictions. Bounded checks through 2026-09-16 did not verify a full resolution; this is not an exhaustive survey of all subsequent work.

sentences: A lifting theorem would turn the quantum query complexity of a Boolean promise problem into the communication complexity of a composed two-party problem.
The question asks for one gadget per input length that works for every partial outer function.
Both complexity measures should agree up to common polylogarithmic factors.
The communication model allows arbitrary prior entanglement and an unrestricted number of rounds.
Known bounded-round, adversary and hybrid lifting results leave this general bounded-error transfer open in the checked 2026 source.

cards.definitions: For \(z\in D\subseteq\{0,1\}^n\), a query applies \(O_z:|i,b,w\rangle\mapsto|i,b\mathbin{\oplus}z_i,w\rangle\), where \(i\in[n]\), \(b\in\{0,1\}\), and \(w\) denotes an arbitrary finite workspace. A quantum query algorithm starts in an input-independent state, uses arbitrary input-independent local quantum operations and measurements between queries, and produces \(f(z)\) with probability at least \(2/3\) on every promised \(z\). \(Q_{1/3}(f)\) is the minimum worst-case number of calls to \(O_z\), counting all branches. Computation between queries is free; there is no uniformity or finite-gate-set restriction. A function constant on its promise, including an empty promise, has query complexity zero. For the composed communication problem Alice receives \(x=(x_1,\ldots,x_n)\) with \(x_i\in\{0,1\}^{a_n}\), Bob receives \(y=(y_1,\ldots,y_n)\) with \(y_i\in\{0,1\}^{b_n}\), and the promise is that \(z=(g_n(x_i,y_i))_{i=1}^n\) belongs to \(D\). Bob must output \(f(z)\). A protocol has arbitrary finite-dimensional local registers and any finite-dimensional shared initial state independent of the inputs, with no bound on its entanglement. It may exchange messages in both directions, perform arbitrary local quantum operations and measurements depending on its own input and local history, and use shared or private randomness. All communicated qubits in both directions count; a classical bit sent as a message costs one qubit. Local computation, local memory, and the shared initial state are free. \(Q^*_{1/3}\) is the minimum worst-case total communication over protocols whose error probability is at most \(1/3\) for every promised input pair. The number of rounds is unrestricted, subject to finite protocol length; communication cost includes every branch. Query algorithms and protocols may depend on the particular finite function and promise and need not be uniformly constructible. The gadget family is existential: no efficient method to print its truth table, input-length bound on \(a_n,b_n\), or fixed gadget independent of \(n\) is required. Its communication cost is nevertheless constrained by the universal two-sided inequality, which includes coordinate functions \(f(z)=z_i\). All logarithms in the inequality are base two.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct Lean proof of the existence of this gadget family and common constants with both inequalities for all \(n,D,f\), or a complete Lean proof that no such family and constants exist. A theorem for a restricted class of outer functions, a fixed round bound, approximate polynomial degree instead of quantum query complexity, or a polynomial rather than polylogarithmic loss does not meet the stated affirmative target. The target is bounded-error lifting; a separate zero-error theorem is not also required.

context_blocks.text: The source asks about both bounded-error and zero-error quantum lifting. This card selects its bounded-error branch, retaining partial outer functions and polylogarithmic losses. The source’s reductions between lifting statements are conditional implications, not a proof of the missing lifting theorem.

Ben-David’s lecture notes state a gadget-family conjecture in which the gadget may depend on the outer input length and has only polylogarithmic communication cost. This card does not add a constant-size, logarithmic-input-length or efficient-construction requirement.

The communication convention is made explicit as the entanglement-assisted model used in the later quantum lifting literature. This is a documented choice within the original general question, whose short extraction did not specify the shared-state convention. The quantification over partial functions follows the original paper’s Section 7.

The CCC 2021 work proves an unconditional bounded-round lifting result for a classical adversary measure and a conditional result for a simplified positive-weight quantum adversary bound. Neither is a general, unconditional lifting theorem for full quantum query complexity with unrestricted rounds.

The ICALP 2026 hybrid theorem lifts approximate degree within a model that begins with classical communication and then uses quantum messages. Its Introduction explicitly retains general quantum query-to-communication lifting as a major open problem. Approximate degree and full quantum query complexity are distinct targets.

cards.title: QMA versus \(\mathrm{QMA}_1\) over Clifford+T
cards.formal: Is \(\mathrm{QMA}=\mathrm{QMA}_1^{\mathcal G}\) for the exact gate set \(\mathcal G=\{H,\mathrm{CNOT},T\}\) defined below? Both classes concern promise problems on finite binary strings and use polynomial-size, uniformly generated verification circuits with polynomially many witness qubits. In \(\mathrm{QMA}\), every yes-instance has a witness accepted with probability at least \(2/3\); in \(\mathrm{QMA}_1^{\mathcal G}\), it has a witness accepted with probability exactly \(1\). In both classes, every witness for a no-instance is accepted with probability at most \(1/3\). The one-sided class in this question is explicitly the Clifford+T version.

Two September 2026 preprints now claim finite-register perfect completeness with fixed gates that cover this card’s exact Clifford+T model.
Their stated results match the target, whose status is uncertain pending independent proof verification.

cards.definitions:
A promise problem is a pair \(L=(L_{\mathrm{yes}},L_{\mathrm{no}})\) of disjoint subsets of \(\{0,1\}^*\). The input length is \(n=|x|\). No acceptance condition is imposed on strings outside the promise. For a fixed problem, a deterministic classical algorithm, on input \(x\), produces a quantum verification circuit \(V_x\) in time polynomial in \(n\). Its witness register \(W\) has \(m(n)\) qubits and its private ancillary register \(A\) has \(a(n)\ge1\) qubits, where \(m,a\) are polynomially bounded integer functions. Circuit size is also polynomially bounded. All bounds and the generating algorithm are fixed for the problem, independently of the particular input.

A qubit is \(\mathbb C^2\) with basis \(|0\rangle,|1\rangle\). A witness is any density matrix \(\rho\) on \(W=(\mathbb C^2)^{\otimes m(n)}\): it is Hermitian, positive semidefinite and has trace one. Hermitian means \(\rho=\rho^\dagger\), with dagger denoting conjugate transpose, and positive semidefinite means \(v^\dagger\rho v\ge0\) for every vector \(v\). Its entries may be arbitrary complex numbers; no efficient preparation or finite classical description of the witness is required. All private ancillas start in \(|0\rangle^{\otimes a(n)}\), uncorrelated with the witness. There is one witness message and no interaction, oracle, preshared resource or nonuniform advice.

The allowed unitary gates, applied to specified wires, are \[H=\frac1{\sqrt2}\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\1&-1\end{pmatrix},\qquad T=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&e^{i\pi/4}\end{pmatrix},\qquad \mathrm{CNOT}|b,c\rangle=|b,c\oplus b\rangle,\] where \(b,c\in\{0,1\}\), \(\oplus\) is addition modulo two, and \(i^2=-1\). These exact matrices define the finite gate set; arbitrary real rotations are not allowed as single gates. A circuit is a finite product of these gates, tensored with identity on all other wires. One designated output qubit is measured in the displayed basis, with outcome one meaning accept. Equivalently, with \(\Pi_{\mathrm{acc}}\) the orthogonal projector onto output value one, its acceptance probability is \[p_x(\rho)=\operatorname{Tr}\!\left[\Pi_{\mathrm{acc}}V_x\bigl(\rho\otimes|0^{a(n)}\rangle\langle0^{a(n)}|\bigr)V_x^\dagger\right].\]

The verifier is a QMA verifier if \(\forall x\in L_{\mathrm{yes}}\ \exists\rho:\ p_x(\rho)\ge2/3\) and \(\forall x\in L_{\mathrm{no}}\ \forall\rho:\ p_x(\rho)\le1/3\). Using this fixed universal gate set gives the usual bounded-error class QMA. The class \(\mathrm{QMA}_1^{\mathcal G}\) changes only the first acceptance requirement to \(p_x(\rho)=1\), retaining all other resources and the same exact gate set. The accepting witness can depend on the yes-input. It need not be accepted by the original QMA verifier with probability one; equality of classes permits a different verifier and polynomial witness length. All registers remain finite and polynomial in input length. Acceptance approaching one through a sequence of circuits is not perfect completeness unless one admissible circuit family attains one exactly.
cards.answer_criterion: Provide a complete Lean-checked proof that every QMA promise problem has a verifier in \(\mathrm{QMA}_1^{\mathcal G}\) under these exact conventions, or a complete Lean-checked proof that some QMA promise problem has no such verifier. The reverse inclusion \(\mathrm{QMA}_1^{\mathcal G}\subseteq\mathrm{QMA}\) is immediate from the acceptance bounds, so the issue is the stated containment or its failure. A negative proof must rule out every eligible one-sided verifier for the separating promise problem, not only one attempted amplification procedure. Exponentially or doubly exponentially small completeness error still differs from zero. Perfect completeness using an infinite register, extra interaction, a different exact gate set without a suitable equivalence proof, or an added oracle does not establish the target. Numerical approximation to the acceptance probability cannot replace this exact yes/no assertion.

context_blocks.text: Editorial gate-set choice: the source treats a family of exact-gate versions of QMA with perfect completeness. This card now fixes Hadamard, CNOT and T, as explicitly selected on 16 September 2026. It does not assert that every other exact-gate version defines the same one-sided class.

A quantum witness can make a yes-instance convincing without being efficiently preparable. Perfect completeness asks whether at least one witness can be accepted with certainty, while keeping every no-instance resistant to all witnesses. The question is about the power of proof systems, not reliability of an experimental device.

Approximate gate synthesis preserves a bounded acceptance gap after allowing sufficiently small error. It does not automatically preserve an acceptance probability equal to one. This is why the source attaches an explicit exact gate set to the one-sided class.

The source proves containment and completeness results for finite gate sets with entries in specified cyclotomic fields, which are fields generated by selected roots of unity. These results clarify exact-gate conventions and quantum satisfiability, but explicitly leave equality with bounded-error QMA open in that earlier source; the September preprints make matching new claims.

Aaronson constructs a quantum oracle relative to which QMA and its perfectly complete version differ. An oracle supplies an additional unitary operation; that theorem does not separate the ordinary classes with only the gates in this card.

Jeffery and Witteveen obtain perfect completeness when the witness system includes an infinite counter register with shift access. Their finite-dimensional truncation instead yields exceptionally small positive completeness error. Neither conclusion gives exact acceptance one with polynomially many ordinary qubits in the selected model.

The source also recalls perfect-completeness results for classical-witness quantum verification and for interactive quantum proofs. A restriction to classical witnesses or the addition of verifier-prover messages changes the model, so those equalities do not settle this single-message quantum-witness question.

Grewal and Rudolph's preprint of 11 September 2026 claims \(\mathrm{QMA}=\mathrm{QMA}_1^{\mathcal G_2}\) for \(\mathcal G_2=\{X,\mathrm{CNOT},\mathrm{Toffoli},H\otimes H\}\). Corollary 1.2 transfers the claimed equality to any gate set implementing these gates exactly with clean ancillas, and the text explicitly includes Clifford+T. Thus this is a matching claim for the exact gate set in the card, not only an equality using arbitrary rotations or an infinite counter. The proof is not independently certified in this review.

Liu and Vidick's preprint of 14 September 2026 separately claims perfect completeness for QMA over \(\{H,X,\mathrm{Toffoli},S\}\), where \(S=\operatorname{diag}(1,i)\), in Theorem 1.3. The model uses finite polynomial resources. Its gates have exact Clifford+T implementations, preserving acceptance probability one; the claimed constant soundness gap permits the usual exact Boolean error reduction. The same paper treats two-message proof systems in separate theorems. Those stronger interaction claims should not be confused with, or substituted for, its one-message QMA theorem.

cards.title: Quantum–classical communication gaps for total functions
cards.formal:
Do there exist real constants \(a\ge1\), \(\delta>0\), an integer \(b\ge1\), and an infinite set \(\mathcal N\subseteq\{2,3,\ldots\}\) such that, for every \(n\in\mathcal N\), some total Boolean function
\[f_n:\{0,1\}^n\times\{0,1\}^n\longrightarrow\{0,1\}\]
has bounded-error communication complexities satisfying
\[Q^*_{1/3}(f_n)\le a(\log_2 n)^b,
\qquad R_{1/3}(f_n)\ge a^{-1}n^\delta?\]
Here \(R_{1/3}\) permits classical public randomness and unrestricted interaction, and \(Q^*_{1/3}\) permits quantum communication and arbitrary finite prior entanglement. Only communication is charged. The constants are fixed independently of the input length and the function chosen at that length.

source_formulation.text: The imported passage is the background question on ITCS 2021 page 54:2 asking for exponential quantum advantage on total functions. This card makes its quantitative scale explicit as polylogarithmic quantum versus polynomial classical communication on an infinite family, matching the scale used in that source and in the new preprints. The source paper’s own main theorem additionally concerns efficient local players and partial functions; those extra restrictions are not part of the imported total-function question. Prior entanglement is permitted on the quantum side, and all classical interaction is allowed.

cards.why: This asks whether the large quantum savings known for promise problems can persist for a Boolean function defined on every input pair. A positive family would refute any universal polynomial simulation of quantum communication by randomized classical communication, even when local computation is unrestricted.
cards.status_note: Checked on 16 September 2026. Gavinsky arXiv:2608.18784v1 and Le Gall arXiv:2609.16726v1 claim total Boolean families with the displayed polylogarithmic quantum and polynomial randomized-classical costs. Their stated protocols/lower bounds match the free-entanglement, unrestricted-classical-interaction, per-input-error and worst-case-cost conventions here, allowing a final answer bit to Bob. The full PDFs and relevant scope were inspected, but the complete proofs have not been independently certified or Lean-checked. Status remains uncertain pending verification; the 2021 source-open statement is historical.

cards.definitions:
For a fixed function \(f:\{0,1\}^n\times\{0,1\}^n\to\{0,1\}\), Alice receives \(x\) and Bob receives \(y\). A protocol is fixed for the entire function before these inputs are chosen. Bob must output the bit \(f(x,y)\) with probability at least \(2/3\) for every pair \((x,y)\). Total means all \(2^{2n}\) pairs are included; no joint promise or relation with several acceptable outputs is allowed.

In a classical protocol the parties exchange bits and may use a shared random seed and private random bits, independent of the inputs. They have no shared entanglement. Each message and the final output depend only on the sender's own input, random information and received history. In a quantum protocol the parties exchange finite-dimensional registers consisting of qubits, may use arbitrary finite-dimensional local quantum operations and measurements, and may initially share any finite-dimensional entangled state independent of \((x,y)\). Local operations are completely positive trace-preserving maps, and the final output is a two-outcome measurement at Bob. Measurements may have classical outcomes stored locally. Transmitting a classical bit within a quantum protocol costs one qubit; communication is not hidden in a message's timing or length. Shared randomness and entanglement are not supplied as input-dependent advice, and postselection is not available.

Local computation, memory and preparation of input-independent shared resources are free. There is no bound on their complexity or on the finite dimension of prior entanglement. A protocol may depend nonuniformly on the full function \(f\). It uses a finite predetermined alternating schedule of transmissions, padding unused messages if needed, so a choice of schedule cannot convey information for free. Arbitrarily many rounds are permitted, subject to finite termination. The cost is the maximum total number of transmitted bits or qubits, over all input pairs and all random or measurement branches. \(R_{1/3}(f)\) and \(Q^*_{1/3}(f)\) are the least costs of protocols with the stated per-input error bound. These costs are finite because transmitting an entire input gives a finite deterministic protocol.

The family need exist only for infinitely many, hence arbitrarily large, input lengths. The constants \(a,b,\delta\) are common to all of them; the functions and their protocols may vary with \(n\). The display defines the precise polylogarithmic-versus-polynomial meaning of the exponential-advantage question used here. It does not require efficient local players, a uniform generator for the functions, one-way communication or a fixed number of messages. A stronger construction with any of these properties is allowed but not required.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of the displayed family-existence proposition, or of its logical negation. A positive answer must specify admissible constants and an unambiguous infinite family, establish the quantum upper guarantee and prove the classical lower bound against every public-coin protocol in the stated model. A negative answer must establish that for every choice of the constants, only finitely many lengths admit a function satisfying both bounds. A separation only on promised input pairs, for relations, or against restricted-round classical protocols does not meet this target. A preprint theorem statement alone is not a checked proof.

context_blocks.text: Communication complexity studies two parties who can process their own inputs without charge but must pay for information exchanged. Thus an advantage measures transmitted information, not execution time. Total Boolean functions require one specified answer for every input pair; partial functions can exclude some pairs, and relations can permit several valid outputs. These distinctions are essential to interpreting a separation.

Girish, Raz and Tal’s ITCS 2021 work supplies a partial-function separation with efficient quantum players given oracle access to their inputs. Its introduction separately states that exponential advantage for total functions is open. The paper’s efficient-player theorem is a different statement from this card: importing its title as an extra runtime requirement would change the background question.

The chosen scale requires a classical cost growing as a positive power of \(n\), while quantum cost grows as a fixed power of \(\log n\). A fixed polynomial relation between the two communication costs is incompatible with such a family. The converse implication is not automatic: disproving every universal polynomial relation need not, by itself, yield this particular input-length scale.

Gavinsky's preliminary August 2026 preprint states an explicit total family with quantum cost \(O(\log^3 N\log\log N)\) and classical cost \(\Omega(N^{1/6}/\log^{7/3}N)\), where \(N\) is the per-party input length. These stated bounds fit the displayed scale after absorbing logarithmic factors into a fixed power and a slightly smaller positive exponent. The claimed quantum protocol has two messages and needs no prior entanglement; its classical lower bound permits unrestricted rounds.

Le Gall's September 2026 preprint claims a larger two-message separation, with \(\operatorname{polylog}(n)\) quantum cost and \(\widetilde\Omega(\sqrt n)\) randomized classical cost. It further states a classical lower bound \(\widetilde\Omega(n^{1-1/j})\) for every fixed integer \(j\ge2\), with a larger constant number of quantum messages. Its definitions explicitly allow public classical randomness and require worst-case communication and error at most \(1/3\) on each input.

A protocol without prior entanglement is admissible in the entanglement-assisted model, so that stronger resource restriction does not obstruct the claimed upper bound here. If the protocol outputs at Alice, sending the final answer bit to Bob adds only one unit of communication. These convention checks establish that the fresh claims match the target; they do not independently validate the new lower-bound proofs.

The matching claims are recorded with uncertain status. The original source, new full PDFs, theorem statements and relevant model conventions were inspected, but no complete independent proof certification or Lean verification was performed. The question has not been replaced by a stronger optimal exponent or an efficient-player variant merely because the new papers claim to answer it.

cards.title: Entanglement without distillable secret key
cards.formal: Do there exist finite integers \(a,b\ge2\) and an entangled density matrix \(\rho\) on \(\mathbb C^a\otimes\mathbb C^b\) with zero distillable secret-key rate, \(K_D(\rho)=0\), under arbitrary local quantum operations and two-way public classical communication? The rate is the standard asymptotic, vanishing-error rate defined below. There is no restriction to one-way communication, perfect finite-block output, a chosen measurement, or efficient protocols.

source_formulation.text: So far, it is known that separable, i.e., disentangled states, are useless [43], while it remains open if entangled but key-undistillable states exist.
source_formulation.caption: Complete selected source sentence; PDF p. 3

cards.why: This question determines whether every entangled bipartite state has some usable private correlation when arbitrary collective quantum processing is allowed. An entangled zero-key state would establish an additional form of irreversibility beyond ordinary bound entanglement; a universal positivity theorem would identify entanglement itself as the exact boundary for asymptotic key usefulness.
cards.status_note: Source-open. On 16 September 2026 the full official May 2026 source and March one-way no-go paper, primary historical key abstract, July classical bound-information abstract and bounded later-work searches were checked. The source explicitly assumes the negative answer rather than proving it. One-way exact key obstructions and classical bound information do not establish an entangled zero-key state under the retained two-way vanishing-error model. No verified resolution was found; cited proofs were not independently verified or formalized in Lean.

cards.definitions:
A state on a finite-dimensional complex vector space is a positive semidefinite Hermitian matrix of trace one. Hermitian means \(X=X^\dagger\), with dagger denoting conjugate transpose; positive semidefinite means \(v^\dagger Xv\ge0\) for every vector \(v\); trace is the sum of diagonal entries. The state \(\rho\) is separable if \(\rho=\sum_jp_j\sigma_j\otimes\tau_j\) for some finite list of local states \(\sigma_j,\tau_j\) and real weights \(p_j\ge0\), \(\sum_jp_j=1\). It is entangled if no such decomposition exists. All matrix entries may be arbitrary complex numbers.

A local quantum instrument has finitely many outcomes \(t\). Outcome \(t\) sends a local matrix \(X\) to \(\mathcal E_t(X)=\sum_jA_{t,j}XA_{t,j}^\dagger\), where the rectangular matrices \(A_{t,j}\) obey \(\sum_{t,j}A_{t,j}^\dagger A_{t,j}=I\). On a normalized input, \(\operatorname{Tr}\mathcal E_t(X)\) is the outcome probability and division by this probability gives the conditional state. An LOCC protocol is a finite adaptive sequence of these instruments performed alternately in the two laboratories. An outcome may be sent as a classical message to the other party; later instruments may depend on the messages and local outcomes already available. Classical communication is public and can proceed in both directions. Local ancillary states, local randomness, public shared randomness and discarding local systems are allowed. No extra shared entangled state, preshared secret key or quantum communication is supplied. The resulting map \(\Lambda\), including all outcomes rather than conditioning for free on a success branch, is trace preserving. Each protocol may have arbitrarily many finite rounds and finite-dimensional ancillary systems; their sizes may grow with the number of input copies. There is no bound on local computation, no finite gate-set restriction and no uniformity requirement on the sequence of protocols. Finite-round approximations suffice for the vanishing-error rate, so allowing limits of LOCC maps on fixed finite systems does not change the target.

For an integer \(M\ge1\), a private state with key dimension \(M\) has the form \[\gamma=\frac1M\sum_{i,j=0}^{M-1}|i\rangle\langle j|_{K_A}\otimes|i\rangle\langle j|_{K_B}\otimes U_i\sigma U_j^\dagger.\] Here \(K_A,K_B\cong\mathbb C^M\) are the local key registers, \(\sigma\) is an arbitrary state on finite local shield systems \(S_A\otimes S_B\), and each \(U_i\) is a unitary matrix on the joint shield space. This is a mathematical description of the target state; applying these joint unitaries is not a free operation available to the two parties. The physical output partition is \((K_AS_A):(K_BS_B)\). Measuring both key registers in the displayed basis gives the same uniform symbol, independent of any purifying external system, hence \(\log_2M\) bits of secret key. The shields remain local output systems. For matrices on the same space, trace distance is \(D(X,Y)=\tfrac12\|X-Y\|_1\), where \(\|Z\|_1=\operatorname{Tr}\sqrt{Z^\dagger Z}\).

A real rate \(R\ge0\) is achievable from \(\rho\) if there are, for every integer \(n\ge1\), a protocol \(\Lambda_n\) acting on \(n\) independent copies \(\rho^{\otimes n}\), an integer \(M_n\ge1\), and a private state \(\gamma_n\) of key dimension \(M_n\) on the protocol's output systems, such that \[D\bigl(\Lambda_n(\rho^{\otimes n}),\gamma_n\bigr)\longrightarrow0,\qquad \liminf_{n\to\infty}\frac{\log_2M_n}{n}\ge R.\] The private states, shields and protocols can depend on \(n\) and \(\rho\). Define \(K_D(\rho)\) as the supremum of achievable rates. The zero rate is always available. Thus zero distillable key means no strictly positive rate with error tending to zero, not merely inability to produce one exact secret bit at a particular block size. The private-state formulation is equivalent to local quantum operations and public communication that produce classical keys secure against an eavesdropper holding a purification of the input state.
cards.answer_criterion: Provide a complete Lean-checked proof that some finite-dimensional entangled state has \(K_D=0\), or a complete Lean-checked proof that every such entangled state has \(K_D>0\). The same chosen state must defeat every allowed protocol sequence in an affirmative existence proof. Refuting existence may use a state-dependent strictly positive rate, with no rate uniform over all entangled states. Failure of one-way protocols, an exact-output no-go theorem, or zero key after one chosen local measurement is insufficient. Conversely, proving arbitrarily small positive rates for a sequence of different states does not exhibit a state of zero rate. The target is an exact yes/no assertion about positivity; an additive estimate of the rate cannot replace it.

context_blocks.text: Secret-key distillation asks two parties to turn a noisy shared quantum resource into matching random data unavailable to an eavesdropper. Entanglement is necessary, but the open issue is whether it is always sufficient for some positive asymptotic rate.

The source develops a theory of the cost of creating quantum secret key under the explicit assumption that entangled states with zero distillable key do not exist. Its conditional theorems therefore do not answer this existence question.

Bound entanglement obstructs producing maximally entangled pairs. Horodecki and coauthors nevertheless show that certain bound-entangled states yield secret key, so zero distillable entanglement cannot be substituted for zero distillable key.

The March 2026 no-go theorem concerns heralded exact key and one-way classical communication. It explicitly exhibits a gap from approximate key distillation. The present target permits vanishing error and two-way messages, so that no-go theorem is not a counterexample here.

The July 2026 classical bound-information preprint concerns three classical random variables supplied to the parties and an eavesdropper. The abstract also distinguishes particular measurements of quantum states from the original states. Such a fixed classical distribution does not rule out all collective local quantum operations on an entangled input state.

cards.title: Dihedral hidden subgroup problem in BQP
cards.formal: Does there exist one uniform quantum algorithm and integers \(C,c\ge1\) such that, for every integer \(N\ge2\), every integer \(\ell\ge1\), every subgroup \(H\le D_N\), and every function \(f:D_N\to\{0,1\}^{\ell}\) hiding \(H\) as defined below, the algorithm outputs a finite list generating exactly \(H\) with probability at least \(2/3\), using at most \(C(\lceil\log_2N\rceil+\ell+2)^c\) total operations? The only external quantum oracle is the reversible evaluation of \(f\). The bound is uniform over subgroup and hiding-function choices and includes both oracle calls and all other computation.
cards.definitions:
Let \(\mathbb Z_N=\{0,1,\ldots,N-1\}\) with addition modulo \(N\). The dihedral group \(D_N=\mathbb Z_N\times\{0,1\}\) has multiplication \[(x,b)(y,d)=\bigl((x+(-1)^by)\bmod N,\ (b+d)\bmod2\bigr).\] Its identity is \((0,0)\). A subgroup is a subset containing the identity and closed under products and inverses. For \(g\in D_N\), the left coset \(gH\) is \(\{gh:h\in H\}\). The hiding promise is \[f(g)=f(g')\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad gH=g'H.\] Thus each coset has one label and distinct cosets have different labels; no structure in the label bits is promised. The classical input is \(N\) in binary and the register width \(\ell\) in unary, fixing input size at the parameter scale \(\log N+\ell\) used in the inherited bound. With \(m=\lceil\log_2N\rceil\), an element is encoded by \(m\) bits for \(x\), followed by one bit for \(b\). Bit strings with \(x\ge N\) are invalid element encodings. The oracle acts on a group register and an \(\ell\)-bit register by \[U_f|g,z\rangle=|g,z\mathbin\oplus f(g)\rangle\] for valid \(g\), extended linearly to superpositions, and acts as identity on invalid group encodings. Here the XOR acts coordinatewise. Each invocation costs one operation; it is self-inverse. The algorithm has no classical truth table of \(f\), subgroup description, coset-state preparation oracle, subset-sum oracle or uncharged random-access-memory service. It may implement additional operations using the allowed gates and controller, with their full cost charged. Output is a classical finite list of valid encoded elements; success means that the smallest subgroup containing all listed elements is \(H\). The empty list generates the identity subgroup. Writing the list is charged, so its length is automatically bounded by the running time. The algorithm may fail with probability at most \(1/3\), but its running-time guarantee holds on every execution. Probability is over its measurements and internal randomness for each fixed legal \(N,\ell,H,f\). When \(\ell\) is polynomial in \(\log N\), as in the usual succinct oracle setting, the requested time is polynomial in \(\log N\).

The allowed elementary gates are \(H,T,\mathrm{CNOT}\), where \[H=\tfrac1{\sqrt2}\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\1&-1\end{pmatrix},\qquad T=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&e^{i\pi/4}\end{pmatrix},\qquad \mathrm{CNOT}|a,b\rangle=|a,a\mathbin\oplus b\rangle.\] Here \(a,b\) are bits and \(\oplus\) is addition modulo two. A quantum register of \(r\) qubits has computational basis \(\{|z\rangle:z\in\{0,1\}^r\}\); its pure state is a unit vector \(\sum_z\alpha_z|z\rangle\) with complex coefficients. Gates act by their specified unitary matrices on selected qubits and as identity elsewhere. A computational-basis measurement of a register has outcome probabilities given by the squared norms of its corresponding state components. All working qubits start at zero. Classical control is performed by one finite Turing program with no advice; each classical bit step, each elementary gate, and each measured or initialized qubit is charged. Fair random bits, if used, cost one step each. All executions halt within the displayed worst-case bound. This uniform circuit-and-control model charges total work, including input parsing, data preparation, classical postprocessing and output, rather than only circuit depth.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof of existence of an algorithm with all stated guarantees, or of the logical negation ruling out every eligible uniform algorithm and polynomial total-work bound. An affirmative proof must establish exact subgroup-generation correctness with the specified probability for every legal hiding function. A negative proof must apply to the full model, not merely a particular sieve, measurement family or recently proposed procedure. Polynomial query complexity with superpolynomial postprocessing, a method requiring an additional oracle, or uncounted parallel work is insufficient. The target is a yes/no algorithm-existence statement; subgroup generators on each input must be exact, and numerical approximation of a group element is not an alternative answer.
cards.why: A central test for quantum algorithms beyond abelian Fourier sampling. The information can be acquired with few queries, but extracting the subgroup efficiently remains a fundamental computational challenge with lattice-related consequences under the appropriate reductions.

importance.reason: A basic nonabelian hidden-structure problem with a long-standing gap between polynomial information requirements and subexponential known algorithms.

context_blocks.text: Hidden subgroup problems ask a quantum algorithm to recover symmetry from equality patterns in a function. In an abelian group, Fourier sampling can turn those patterns into usable constraints, providing the framework for familiar quantum period-finding algorithms. The dihedral group adds a reflection to a cyclic rotation group and is among the simplest noncommutative settings in which the general polynomial-time method remains unresolved.

A representative hard case has \(H=H_{s}=\{(0,0),(s,1)\}\), with an unknown \(s\in \mathbb{Z} /N\mathbb{Z}\). The hiding promise says \(f(x,0)=f(x+s,1)\), and each restriction to \(b=0\) or \(b=1\) is injective. Recovering the subgroup is therefore recovering a cyclic hidden shift. The unrestricted subgroup problem reduces to this reflection case after handling its rotational part; the inherited Kuperberg paper uses the hidden-shift formulation for its main algorithm.

In the reflection case, a coset sample is a state \((|0,x\rangle+|1,x+s\rangle)/\sqrt2\) with an unknown random \(x\). Its Fourier representation includes a known random label \(k\) and a qubit with relative phase \(e^{2\pi i ks/N}\), for a chosen Fourier-sign convention. This phase encodes information about \(s\); it is not a classical register containing \(ks\). The sample interface and the hiding-function oracle interface are distinct.

This is already enough information in a statistical sense: polynomially many queries suffice if computationally expensive processing is allowed. The main obstacle is implementing an effective collective extraction of the hidden shift with polynomial total work. A bound on oracle calls therefore cannot be substituted for a bound on running time. The card deliberately counts both quantum gates and classical postprocessing.

Kuperberg’s first sieve gives time and query complexity \(2^{O(\sqrt{\log  N})}\). It repeatedly combines phase states so that their labels become more useful for recovering the shift. This is a substantial speedup over generic classical approaches, yet it is superpolynomial in the input length \(n\approx \log  N\): the target here is \(n^{O(1)}\), not \(2^{O(\sqrt{n})}\).
Regev’s separate polynomial-space algorithm uses time \(\exp(O(\sqrt{\log N\log\log N}))\). Improving quantum memory alone and obtaining polynomial total running time are different achievements.

Kuperberg’s later collimation algorithm attains \(\exp(O(\sqrt{\log N}))\) time with logarithmic quantum space and subexponential classical storage. The paper explicitly separates quantum-addressable classical memory from ordinary memory: Proposition 4.2 analyzes the former, while Corollary 4.3 gives an implementation without quantum memory access, with its additional work counted. No free memory-access primitive is included in this card’s target.

The lattice connection is important but needs its access-model qualification. Regev reduces a unique-shortest-vector problem to solving dihedral coset samples. Thus a polynomial algorithm that works from those samples would have consequences for lattice algorithms. An arbitrary hiding-function oracle provides a different interface, so one should not silently claim that every conceivable oracle-HSP algorithm automatically implements the coset solver required by that reduction.

An older positive claim remains visible in search results. Moore and Young’s February 2022 preprint claimed polynomial time for dihedral groups of power-of-two size, but was withdrawn on February 23. The withdrawal states that Lemma 4.3 is wrong and that the main algorithm needs the states asserted by that lemma. It is retained here as a documented withdrawn attempt, not a known algorithm.

A much more recent claim requires a separate status entry. Daniel Simon’s August 2026 preprint claims a polynomial-time dihedral coset algorithm, replacing a subset-sum step with a different erasure procedure. Its latest listed revision is August 17 and acknowledges a correction to the analysis as well as a new critical response. A valid coset algorithm of the claimed generality would settle the reflection case, making this directly relevant to the present question.

Gupte, Ragavan and Zhandry’s response, revised September 1, gives an information-theoretic obstruction to the proposed algorithm. They show that its use of only a truncated portion of the classical Fourier labels leaves negligible advantage in guessing the secret’s least-significant bit. Their theorem covers a broader template containing the proposed procedure; it does not exclude all algorithms for the dihedral problem. The authors also supply a Lean formalization. This catalogue review checked the primary statements and repository description, but did not independently rerun that formalization.

Guo and Yang independently analyze the supporting lemmas. Their August 17 paper proves corrected statements while identifying a remaining independence assumption that the proposed choice of a partition does not supply. They explicitly conclude that establishing those lemmas does not establish correctness of the algorithm. The card therefore flags the recent claim as disputed rather than presenting polynomial time as established.

Positive results elsewhere among nonabelian groups continue to refine the boundary. Morales’ August 2026 algorithm handles certain scalar-action semidirect products with bounded generator rank and exponent-to-prime ratio polylogarithmic in group size, and another family with modular subgroup structure. For the ordinary dihedral family, the relevant ratio would be \(N/2\), which does not meet that condition as N grows. These structural advances leave the unrestricted dihedral target intact.

A solution would identify a new way to convert nonabelian quantum information into efficiently recoverable classical structure. A negative result would be equally consequential because polynomial query complexity is already available: it would isolate a genuine computational obstruction in processing the information. The significance comes from that algorithmic boundary, alongside the precise reductions to coset and lattice problems.

cards.title: Graph isomorphism in BQP
cards.formal: Does the ordinary graph-isomorphism decision problem belong to \(\mathrm{BQP}\), bounded-error quantum polynomial time? That is, do there exist one uniform quantum algorithm and integers \(C,c\ge1\) such that, for every pair of finite simple graphs given by their complete binary adjacency matrices, the algorithm decides whether a vertex bijection preserves adjacency, with error at most \(1/3\), using at most \(C(n+2)^c\) total elementary operations, where \(n\) is the larger vertex count? No distributional or structural promise is imposed on the graphs.
cards.definitions:
For an integer \(r\ge0\), write \([r]=\{1,\ldots,r\}\), with \([0]=\varnothing\). A finite simple graph on \([r]\) is an undirected graph with no loops or parallel edges. Its adjacency matrix \(A\in\{0,1\}^{r\times r}\) is symmetric with zero diagonal. Each input graph is encoded by its binary order with a self-delimiting length prefix, followed by all adjacency entries in row-major order; the two graph encodings are concatenated. A prefix can be encoded as \(1^t0\) followed by a \(t\)-bit binary order, using \(t\ge1\) and the usual minimal binary representation. Invalid encodings are rejected. Graphs of different orders are not isomorphic. If both have order \(r\), an isomorphism is a bijection \(\pi:[r]\to[r]\) such that \[A_{uv}=B_{\pi(u),\pi(v)}\qquad\text{for every }u,v\in[r].\] The two order-zero graphs are isomorphic. A yes-instance has at least one such bijection; a no-instance has none. The algorithm must accept every yes-instance with probability at least \(2/3\) and every no-instance with probability at most \(1/3\). Its probability is over its quantum measurement outcomes and any internal random bits, separately for each fixed input. It receives only the explicit classical input, with no witness, nonuniform advice, graph-orbit state, isomorphism oracle, promised rigidity, degree bound or typical-input assumption. Here GI denotes this ordinary permutation-based relation, not the distinct relation called quantum graph isomorphism in nonlocal-game theory. The running time is polynomial in the graph order and hence in the explicit input length; malformed encodings must be rejected in time polynomial in their actual length.

The allowed elementary gates are \(H,T,\mathrm{CNOT}\), where \[H=\tfrac1{\sqrt2}\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\1&-1\end{pmatrix},\qquad T=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&e^{i\pi/4}\end{pmatrix},\qquad \mathrm{CNOT}|a,b\rangle=|a,a\mathbin\oplus b\rangle.\] Here \(a,b\) are bits and \(\oplus\) is addition modulo two. A quantum register of \(r\) qubits has computational basis \(\{|z\rangle:z\in\{0,1\}^r\}\); its pure state is a unit vector \(\sum_z\alpha_z|z\rangle\) with complex coefficients. Gates act by their specified unitary matrices on selected qubits and as identity elsewhere. A computational-basis measurement of a register has outcome probabilities given by the squared norms of its corresponding state components. All working qubits start at zero. Classical control is performed by one finite Turing program with no advice; each classical bit step, each elementary gate, and each measured or initialized qubit is charged. Fair random bits, if used, cost one step each. All executions halt within the displayed worst-case bound. This uniform circuit-and-control model charges total work, including input parsing, data preparation, classical postprocessing and output, rather than only circuit depth.
cards.answer_criterion: Provide a complete Lean-checked proof that the specified language lies in BQP, including uniformity, bounded error on every input and polynomial total work, or a complete Lean-checked proof that it does not lie in BQP. A classical polynomial-time algorithm is a valid affirmative solution because it can be implemented within the quantum model with polynomial overhead. A negative proof must exclude all uniform bounded-error polynomial-time quantum algorithms, rather than only coset-state, Fourier-sampling or photonic-sampling methods. A necessary invariant that distinguishes only some nonisomorphic graphs, an efficient fixed relaxation, or uncharged preparation of a helpful state does not establish membership. The output is a proof of the yes/no complexity statement, not an approximate isomorphism score.

context_blocks.text: Graph isomorphism asks whether two descriptions encode the same finite relational structure after renaming the vertices. It is an exact equivalence problem, rather than a search for approximately similar networks. A proposed permutation is easy to verify by comparing all adjacency entries, but finding a successful permutation or ruling out every permutation can require reasoning about highly symmetric graphs.

Elementary invariants help without settling the problem. For instance, a six-cycle and two disjoint triangles both have six vertices, six edges and degree two at every vertex, but cannot be isomorphic because one is connected and the other is not. More elaborate invariants must likewise be assessed by whether they distinguish every required pair, not just by how well they perform on a test set.

Aaronson’s 2005 challenge list identifies graph isomorphism among the natural targets for quantum algorithms beyond Shor and Grover. The formulation on this card turns that broad research motivation into one exact complexity-class membership question. It imposes no particular algorithmic approach and permits a classical algorithm as a special case of a quantum one.

Babai’s classical breakthrough gives a quasipolynomial-time algorithm, with bound \(\exp ((\log  n)^{O(1)})\). The original argument required a correction in January 2017, after which the quasipolynomial claim was restored. This is the relevant general classical benchmark, rather than brute-force examination of n! permutations. Quasipolynomial time is still larger than the polynomial bound asked for here.

A classical adjacency matrix is the entire input resource. Preparing a special quantum representation of its relabelings is additional computation and must be charged. Distinguishability of hypothetical states therefore cannot substitute for a complete uniform algorithm that prepares and processes its data within the required running time.

The established hidden-subgroup approach makes this difficulty precise in another form. Graph isomorphism can be reduced to finding hidden symmetry in permutation groups, and the standard procedure generates quantum coset states. Hallgren, Roetteler and Sen, independently of Moore and Russell and later in joint work, prove that measurements on too few such states reveal insufficient information in the relevant hard cases. Their bound requires joint access to \(\Omega (n \log  n)\) states to obtain useful information.

That lower bound is a restriction on information extraction in a particular representation. The number of required states is itself polynomial. It does not say that every measurement on that many states needs superpolynomial computation, and it does not forbid an algorithm that uses the explicit input graphs in a different way. A negative solution to \(GI\in \mathrm{BQP}\) would have to rule out those broader possibilities as well.

The inherited quantum-inspired reference has a substantive June 2026 revision. Maxwell, van den Hoven and Renema analyze correlations in Gaussian boson samplers and derive a classical test for a necessary condition of graph isomorphism. At restricted correlation order it can certify that some graph pairs are different. At the maximum order their condition becomes sufficient, but their method is no longer efficient. The authors explicitly separate these two regimes.

This illustrates why a photonic sampling procedure is not automatically a polynomial-time decision algorithm for all graphs. One must account for how many samples or correlations are required to distinguish a worst-case pair, how accurately they must be estimated, and the classical work used to interpret them. Efficiently generating individual samples does not by itself establish a uniform bound for the complete decision task.

May 2026 work by Gheorghiu, Jacobs, Mehraban and Motamedi studies isomorphism of quantum states under group actions. They show, among other results, that a Clifford-group state problem is at least as hard as ordinary graph isomorphism, while a Pauli-group variant is BQP-complete. The direction and the group matter: the BQP algorithm for the Pauli problem is not thereby an algorithm for the GI-hard Clifford problem.

The 2026 paper by Kar, Roberson, Seppelt and Zeman concerns the different relation called quantum graph isomorphism. It gives randomized polynomial-time algorithms for exact feasibility at each fixed level of a hierarchy of noncommutative semidefinite relaxations. Neither the relation nor a fixed relaxation is the ordinary vertex-bijection decision problem posed here.

A positive answer would enlarge the collection of important exact structure problems known to admit efficient quantum algorithms, unless a classical polynomial algorithm arrived at the same time. A negative answer would be exceptionally strong: GI has efficiently verifiable permutation witnesses and hence belongs to NP, so \(GI\notin \mathrm{BQP}\) would in particular imply \(\mathrm{P}\ne \mathrm{NP}\). The question is fundamental on both sides, independently of any particular physical implementation.

cards.title: Classical hardness of approximate Boson Sampling
cards.formal: Is the following classical sampling impossibility statement true? There is no single probabilistic classical Turing machine \(M\) and polynomial \(p\) such that, for every valid ideal Boson Sampling input \(B\) defined below and every integer \(k\ge2\), the machine \(M(B,1^k)\) outputs an occupation vector with law \(Q_{B,k}\), always halts in at most \(p(|B|+k)\) steps, and satisfies \[d_{\mathrm{TV}}(Q_{B,k},D_B)=\frac12\sum_{s\in\Omega_{m,n}}|Q_{B,k}(s)-D_B(s)|\le\frac1k?\] The target distribution is \[D_B(s)=\frac{|\operatorname{Per}(A_s)|^2}{\prod_{j=1}^{m}s_j!},\qquad A=\operatorname{GS}(B),\qquad \Omega_{m,n}=\{s\in\mathbb N_0^m:\sum_js_j=n\}.\] Thus the approximation must meet every requested error tolerance, in time polynomial in the explicit network description and the inverse tolerance. The claim is unconditional and concerns all valid inputs, rather than only typical random optical networks.
cards.why: This asks for an unconditional boundary between classical sampling and a concrete, restricted quantum optical experiment. It would clarify whether reproducing an entire physically defined distribution can require superpolynomial classical resources even when universal quantum computation is not part of the device model.

No unconditional resolution of the selected all-input arbitrary-total-variation-accuracy question was identified. The current hardness results retain stated assumptions or stronger error conventions; their proofs were not independently verified or formalized in Lean.

cards.definitions:
There are \(n\ge1\) indistinguishable photons and \(m\ge n\) modes. A mode is one orthogonal single-particle state. Initially each of the first \(n\) modes contains one photon and every other mode is empty. The network is ideal passive linear optics: it preserves photon number and acts on the single-particle mode space by an \(m\times m\) unitary matrix \(U\). It has no loss, noise, distinguishability of photons, intermediate measurements, adaptive feed-forward or postselection. The output records the photon count in every mode. Collisions, meaning two or more photons in a mode, are included.

Only the first \(n\) columns of \(U\) matter for this input. Write these columns as \(A\in\mathbb C^{m\times n}\), so \(A^\dagger A=I_n\), where \(\dagger\) denotes conjugate transpose. Any such column isometry can be completed to a unitary, and the distribution below is independent of that completion. The input therefore specifies this part of the optical network rather than an exponentially large many-photon transition matrix.

Here is an explicit finite encoding of the matrix convention in the source's footnote19. The input \(B\) contains \(m,n\) and every entry of an \(m\times n\) complex matrix. Real and imaginary parts are signed dyadic rationals, each stored as an integer numerator and a nonnegative denominator exponent in unary: \(a/2^b\). All numerator bits, signs, exponents and matrix entries count toward \(|B|\). Dimensions and lists are explicitly delimited. A valid input satisfies \[\|B^\dagger B-I_n\|_{\mathrm{op}}\le\frac12,\] where the operator norm is \(\|C\|_{\mathrm{op}}=\sup_{\|v\|_2=1}\|Cv\|_2\). This promise ensures that the columns are linearly independent. It is a convenient fixed conditioning threshold for the finite encoding, not a physical noise parameter. Define the represented ideal isometry by exact ordered Gram–Schmidt orthonormalization: for the columns \(b_j\) of \(B\), set \[v_j=b_j-\sum_{i<j}a_i(a_i^\dagger b_j),\qquad a_j=v_j/\sqrt{v_j^\dagger v_j},\] using the positive square root, and let \(A=(a_1,\ldots,a_n)\). These equations define the ideal mathematical distribution exactly; they do not give the classical sampler a real-arithmetic oracle or make numerical computation free. Finer explicit dyadic approximations can represent arbitrary optical isometries to arbitrary precision. The encoding spells out the source's correction of a finite-precision matrix to an isometry; its chosen threshold does not impose a restriction on the number of photons or on network depth.

For \(s=(s_1,\ldots,s_m)\in\Omega_{m,n}\), form the square \(n\times n\) matrix \(A_s\) by repeating row \(j\) of \(A\) exactly \(s_j\) times, in increasing row order. For an \(n\times n\) matrix \(C\), its permanent is \[\operatorname{Per}(C)=\sum_{\pi\in S_n}\prod_{i=1}^n C_{i,\pi(i)},\] where \(S_n\) is the set of permutations of \(\{1,\ldots,n\}\). The factorial convention is \(0!=1\). The bosonic transition rule gives the displayed \(D_B\); because \(A\) is an isometry, these nonnegative probabilities sum to one. The output lists all \(m\) occupation numbers in binary. No requirement to enumerate the whole distribution or to estimate each exponentially small probability is imposed.

The classical machine is a uniform multitape Turing machine with independent fair random bits. It receives the complete explicit finite input, has no advice, quantum operations or oracle, and its polynomial runtime bound holds for every input and every random tape. Correctness is required only on valid matrices. For each such input, its output must lie in \(\Omega_{m,n}\). The law \(Q_{B,k}\) averages over all its random bits; there is no separate high-probability event certifying closeness. Total variation compares this full output law with the target distribution. The polynomial and machine are fixed independently of \(m,n,B,k\).

The unary accuracy input \(1^k\) requests error at most \(1/k\). This gives the arbitrary-error convention \(\varepsilon>0\) with runtime polynomial in input length and \(1/\varepsilon\): choose \(k=\max\{2,\lceil1/\varepsilon\rceil\}\). It does not require polynomial dependence on \(\log(1/\varepsilon)\). Every \(m\ge n\) is allowed, with its full matrix encoding charged; in particular the class includes the dilute, polynomially many-mode families used in the original hardness results. It does not claim that every individual network is hard. Easy subfamilies are compatible with the universal-sampler impossibility statement.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof of the impossibility statement, or a complete Lean-checked refutation by a uniform classical probabilistic machine with one polynomial bound satisfying all input, output and accuracy quantifiers above. A positive answer must rule out every such machine without assuming a separation of complexity classes or an unproved permanent conjecture. A conditional polynomial-hierarchy consequence, hardness of computing an individual probability, an exact-sampling lower bound, a multiplicative-error result, a fixed numerical error guarantee, or experiments on finitely many networks do not settle this total-variation question. This is an exact yes/no question about arbitrarily requested sampling accuracy; the benchmark's numerical-value tolerance does not replace its quantified error requirement.

context_blocks.text: The overview presents Boson Sampling as a restricted quantum experiment whose output distribution is conjectured to be difficult to reproduce classically. Its source paragraph does not choose an error model. On 16 September2026 the user selected approximate sampling to every requested total-variation error with polynomial inverse-error cost; this card records that specialization explicitly. The exact version remains distinct source context, not an asserted equivalent formulation.

Passive optics acts linearly on the single-photon modes, but the output probabilities for several indistinguishable photons involve squared permanents and factorial collision factors. Sampling asks for one random occupation pattern with the right distribution, rather than a list of all probabilities. The two computational tasks cannot be identified merely from that formula.

The 2013 paper proves that an efficient exact classical sampler would entail a collapse of the polynomial hierarchy. Its route to a corresponding total-variation statement additionally uses conjectures about average-case Gaussian permanents and anticoncentration. These are conditional consequences; neither the noncollapse of the hierarchy nor all the required permanent statements are unconditional theorems.

The 2025 work substantially strengthens average-case probability-estimation hardness and proves a conditional multiplicative-error sampling theorem. Its Theorem1 still has an accuracy gap relative to the permanent conjecture, while Theorem3 assumes noncollapse of the polynomial hierarchy and an anticoncentration conjecture. Multiplicative control of individual probabilities is stronger than the total-variation guarantee selected here.

The present claim concerns ideal indistinguishable photons and a sampler that works on every explicitly represented network. Typical-network hardness, constant-error hardness, loss-tolerant experiments and Gaussian Boson Sampling are separate variants. No measured experimental advantage or special family of classically simulable networks decides the stated universal-sampler question.

The present claim concerns ideal indistinguishable photons and a sampler that works on every explicitly represented network. Typical-network hardness, constant-error hardness, loss-tolerant experiments and Gaussian Boson Sampling are separate variants. No measured experimental advantage or special family of classically simulable networks decides the stated universal-sampler question.

cards.title: QMA versus \(\mathrm{QMA}(2)\)
cards.formal: Is \(\mathrm{QMA}(2)=\mathrm{QMA}\) for ordinary uniform promise problems without an oracle? A QMA(2) verifier receives two polynomial-length quantum witnesses that are promised to be unentangled across the two witness registers, even on a no-instance. A QMA verifier receives one arbitrary polynomial-length quantum witness. The easy inclusion \(\mathrm{QMA}\subseteq\mathrm{QMA}(2)\) follows by ignoring a second witness; the question is whether every QMA(2) promise problem is also in QMA under the definitions below.
cards.why: This asks whether a promise of independence between two untrusted quantum messages can increase what an efficient quantum computer can verify. It connects computational verification with the geometry of entanglement and separates the value of unentanglement from simply supplying more qubits.
