context_blocks.text: Advice is fixed before the particular input is seen and is trusted to be the chosen length-specific information. It must support every input of that length. A witness, by contrast, may be selected for one instance and must be checked against dishonest alternatives. Neither comparison is obtained simply by changing the name of the auxiliary register.

Quantum advice is supplied as a fresh copy on each run. The definition does not assume the algorithm can clone an unknown state or preserve it for unlimited reuse. Classical advice can be copied, but the class comparison allows either algorithm to consume the supplied resource during its computation.

The advice families can be uncomputable in both models. The question concerns what polynomial-size information makes possible for the uniform computation, not how to construct that information. Allowing input-specific advice would remove the crucial requirement that one message works for all strings of a given length.

Aaronson proved \(\mathrm{BQP/qpoly}\subseteq\mathrm{PP/poly}\). PP permits polynomial-time classical randomized computation with acceptance probability strictly greater than one half on yes-inputs and at most one half on no-inputs, without an inverse-polynomial margin; poly again permits length-specific classical advice. This upper bound uses a different computation model from bounded-error BQP, so it is not the desired simulation in BQP/poly.

The 2007 quantum-oracle separation demonstrated an advice advantage when both computations share a quantum black box. This supplies evidence in that augmented computation model and retains the oracle as an essential part of its statement.

The 2024 result separates the advice classes with an oracle encoding a classical function, but restricts even quantum algorithms to classical queries. This is a genuine precursor to the later standard classical-oracle theorem. Permitting superposition queries gives the classical-advice algorithm more power, so the access conventions must not be conflated.

The February 2026 construction, checked in its April revision, separates the advice classes using a standard classical oracle that both quantum algorithms may query in superposition. It resolves that oracle question while leaving the ordinary language equality asked here unresolved.

cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof of \(\mathrm{BQP/qpoly}\subseteq\mathrm{BQP/poly}\), or a complete Lean-checked proof that some language has quantum advice as defined but no eligible classical-advice algorithm and family. An affirmative proof need not produce the classical advice efficiently, but must establish one length-indexed family and a uniform algorithm that work for all inputs. A negative proof must rule out every polynomial advice length, every classical advice family and every uniform quantum algorithm. A separation of promise problems alone does not automatically meet this card’s retained total-language target. Oracle separations, a difficult-to-describe state, or an advantage for advice selected after seeing the input do not suffice.
cards.definitions: A language is a set \(L\subseteq\{0,1\}^*\); here every binary string must be decided, with no promise excluding some inputs. For each \(n\ge0\), let \(m(n),a(n)\) be nonnegative integers bounded by a fixed polynomial. A single deterministic classical Turing machine, given an input string \(x\) of length \(n\), generates in polynomial time a quantum circuit \(U_x\) with an \(m(n)\)-qubit advice register, \(a(n)\) ancillary qubits initialized to \(|0\rangle\), polynomially many gates, and one designated output qubit. The generating machine has no advice and no oracle. It uses the fixed exact gates \(H,T,\mathrm{CNOT}\), with \[H=\frac1{\sqrt2}\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\1&-1\end{pmatrix},\qquad T=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&e^{i\pi/4}\end{pmatrix},\qquad \mathrm{CNOT}|b,c\rangle=|b,b\mathbin\oplus c\rangle,\] where \(b,c\in\{0,1\}\) and \(\oplus\) is addition modulo two. The circuit outputs the computational-basis measurement of its output qubit. The quantum advice family is a sequence \((\rho_n)_{n\ge0}\) of density matrices on \(\mathbb C^{2^{m(n)}}\). A density matrix is positive semidefinite with trace one; positive semidefinite means \(v^\dagger\rho_nv\ge0\) for all vectors \(v\), and trace is the sum of diagonal entries. The probability of output 1 is \[\operatorname{Tr}\!\left[\Pi_1U_x\bigl(\rho_n\otimes|0\rangle\langle0|^{\otimes a(n)}\bigr)U_x^\dagger\right],\] where \(\Pi_1\) projects onto output 1 and is identity on the remaining qubits, and dagger denotes conjugate transpose. The language belongs to \(\mathrm{BQP/qpoly}\) if some such generating machine, polynomial bounds and advice family satisfy output-1 probability at least \(2/3\) for every \(x\in L\) and at most \(1/3\) for every \(x\notin L\). The same fixed \(\rho_n\) must work for all \(2^n\) strings of length \(n\). A fresh copy of that state is supplied for each independent computation; no cloning or repeated reuse of a consumed copy is promised. Advice is trusted: the requirement concerns the selected family, not all possible advice states. There is no computability or efficient-preparation requirement on the family, and its preparation cost is not charged. The language belongs to \(\mathrm{BQP/poly}\) if the advice can instead be a binary string \(b_n\in\{0,1\}^{m(n)}\), supplied as the basis state \(|b_n\rangle\). Its length may have a different polynomial bound and the circuit may be different, but \(b_n\) still depends only on \(n\), need not be computable, and must work for every length-\(n\) input. Both classes use uniform quantum computation in addition to the explicitly allowed nonuniform advice. BQP abbreviates bounded-error quantum polynomial time; poly and qpoly indicate classical-bit and quantum-qubit advice of polynomial length.

cards.title: Quantum query complexity versus bounded approximate degree
cards.formal: Determine, up to universal multiplicative constants, the extremal function \[M(n,d)=\max\bigl\{Q(f):\varnothing\ne D\subseteq\{0,1\}^n,\ f:D\to\{0,1\},\ \operatorname{bdeg}_{1/3}(f)\le d\bigr\}\] for all integers \(n\ge1\) and \(1\le d\le n\). The bounded approximate degree \(\operatorname{bdeg}_{1/3}(f)\) is the least total degree of a real polynomial \(p\) satisfying \[|p(x)-f(x)|\le1/3\quad(x\in D),\qquad 0\le p(x)\le1\quad(x\in\{0,1\}^n).\] The query measure \(Q\) has worst-case error at most \(1/3\). This makes the source's largest-gap question a two-parameter extremal query bound. The source's additional question of whether an exponential gap exists was answered affirmatively in 2023.
cards.why: Bounded approximate degree is the main numerical object behind the polynomial method for quantum query lower bounds. Determining its worst possible discrepancy from actual quantum query complexity would quantify how much algorithmic difficulty this method can miss under promises.
cards.status_note: The exponential-separation part of the 2021 question was resolved by Ambainis and Belovs at CCC 2023. The card retains the broader maximum-gap target as the explicit extremal curve M(n,d). The source, published separation and 2024 follow-up were checked on 2026-09-14; their checked theorems do not determine this curve, and a bounded later-work search found no complete characterization.

progress.text: Aaronson asks for the largest bounded-degree-versus-quantum-query gap for partial Boolean functions and whether it can be exponential.
Ambainis and Belovs prove an exponential separation, with full-cube boundedness retained after encoding the alphabet into Boolean bits.
Ben-David and Kundu reprove the partial-function exponential separation and establish related separations for stronger measures and total search problems.

importance.reason: Relates quantum query algorithms to polynomial approximation, connecting two core tools for quantum upper and lower bounds.

sentences: The question compares quantum query complexity with polynomials that approximate a promised Boolean function.
The polynomial must remain between zero and one even on inputs outside the promise.
The target is the largest quantum query complexity possible at each input length and bounded-degree budget.
A 2023 theorem already proves that the gap can be exponential, so that subquestion is no longer open.
The remaining task is to determine the full extremal bound up to universal multiplicative constants.

cards.definitions:
A partial Boolean function has a nonempty promise domain \(D\) of valid inputs, with one prescribed output bit for each valid input. An algorithm knows the function and promise but receives the actual input only through its bit oracle. Correctness is required on \(D\). Its fixed query budget applies on every input, including inputs outside the promise, where the output bit may be arbitrary.

For an input \(x\in\{0,1\}^n\), a quantum bit query is the unitary \(O_x|i,b,z\rangle=|i,b\mathbin{\oplus}x_i,z\rangle\), where \(i\in\{0,\ldots,n\}\), \(b\in\{0,1\}\), \(z\) is a work register, \(\oplus\) denotes addition modulo two, and the dummy coordinate has \(x_0=0\). A \(T\)-query algorithm starts in a fixed state, alternates at most \(T\) calls to this oracle with input-independent unitary operations on a finite-dimensional workspace, and finally measures a designated output bit. Arbitrary finite workspace and unitary matrices are allowed. Only oracle calls are charged; all other computation is free. Intermediate measurements and classical random choices can equivalently be included by storing their outcomes coherently. Algorithms may depend on the function and input length, but their operations cannot depend on the unknown input except through oracle calls. No uniform circuit-generation or time bound is imposed. Write \(Q(f)\) for the least integer \(T\) that achieves error at most \(1/3\) on every input in the domain of \(f\). The query bound is a worst-case bound, not an expected number of calls.

A real polynomial is a finite linear combination of monomials in \(n\) real variables; its total degree is the largest sum of variable exponents in a monomial with nonzero coefficient. Multilinear polynomials suffice because \(x_i^j=x_i\) on Boolean inputs for \(j\ge1\). Their real coefficients have no bit-length or computability restriction. Boundedness is imposed only on the entire Boolean cube, not on all of \(\mathbb R^n\), and includes inputs outside the promise. Every partial Boolean function has a bounded exact representing polynomial of degree at most \(n\): extend its values to a total Boolean function and interpolate.

There are finitely many partial Boolean functions on a fixed cube, so the displayed maximum is over a finite set. It is nonempty and satisfies \(1\le M(n,d)\le n\) on the stated domain, using a single input-bit function for the lower bound and reading all bits for the upper bound. The parameter \(n\) counts individual Boolean oracle bits. A symbol from a larger alphabet is not available in one query. Neither the promise nor the polynomial is supplied as an additional input-dependent oracle.
cards.answer_criterion: Supply a specified positive function \(H(n,d)\), universal constants \(0<c\le C<\infty\), and a complete mathematically correct Lean-checked proof of \(cH(n,d)\le M(n,d)\le CH(n,d)\) throughout the stated integer domain. The answer must identify the asymptotic dependence on \(n,d\), not merely rename the defining optimization over functions or algorithms. Both a universal upper bound and matching worst-case examples are required. Exponential separation alone is already known and does not settle this full extremal target.

context_blocks.text: A \(T\)-query quantum algorithm has an acceptance probability that is a polynomial of degree at most \(2T\), bounded between zero and one on every Boolean input. Hence bounded approximate degree is always at most twice quantum query complexity. The question asks how far the converse can fail.

The promise does not remove the full-cube boundedness condition. Omitting that condition changes the measure and permits simple examples with artificially low degree. For total Boolean functions the two measures are polynomially related, but promises permit much larger separations.

Ambainis and Belovs give Boolean promise functions on \(n\) bits with bounded exact polynomial degree \(O(\log n)\) and quantum query complexity at least \(n^{1/3}\) up to logarithmic losses along their family. Bounded exact degree also upper-bounds bounded approximate degree, so this answers the exponential-gap subquestion.

The 2024 paper reproves such a partial-function separation through total search problems and strengthens the polynomial measure in additional results. These results establish large gaps, but the checked theorems do not determine the full extremal dependence on the input length and degree budget.

sentences: QAOA is a widely studied quantum optimization ansatz using alternating objective and mixing operations.
The SK model provides a canonical random quadratic objective with a known limiting optimum.
The question asks for the best limiting energy reachable by finite-depth QAOA when depth is subsequently allowed to grow.
Angles are optimized only after taking the infinite-size ensemble limit.
The source conjectures that this limiting value reaches the Parisi optimum, and the card now accepts a proved numerical determination within 0.01.

cards.definitions: For \(n\ge 2\) let \(J_{ij}, 1\le i<j\le n\), be independent real normal random variables of mean 0 and variance 1. On \((\mathbb{C} ^{2})^{\otimes n}\), let \(Z_{i}\) and \(X_{i}\) act on the i-th qubit by the Pauli matrices \(Z=diag(1,- 1)\) and X with off-diagonal entries 1 and diagonal entries 0. Put \(H_{J}=n^{- 1/2}\sum_{i<j}J_{ij}Z_{i} Z_{j}\) and \(B_{n}=\sum_{i} X_{i}\). Let |+⟩=\((|0\rangle +|1\rangle )/\sqrt{2}\). For integer depth \(p\ge 1\) and fixed real angle vectors \(\gamma ,\beta \in \mathbb{R} ^{p}\), define |\(\psi _{p,J}\rangle =e^{- i\beta _{p} B_{n}}e^{- i\gamma _{p} H_{J}}\cdots e^{- i\beta _{1} B_{n}}e^{- i\gamma _{1} H_{J}}|+\rangle ^{\otimes n}\). Matrix exponentials have their usual convergent-series meaning; states have unit norm. Expectation is over J. The n limit exists for each fixed p and angles as established for this model in the source. Angles may depend on p but are fixed independently of n and J. First take the infinite-n ensemble limit for fixed angles, then optimize those angles, then take the supremum over finite depths. Supremum need not be attained. Identity layers imply that the optimized depth values are nondecreasing. They are bounded by \(\Pi *=\lim _{n\to \infty} E_{J}[\max _{z\in \{- 1,1\}^{n}} n^{- 1/2}\sum_{i<j}J_{ij}z_{i} z_{j}]/n\), the finite Parisi ground-state value in this normalization. Maximization, rather than minimization, fixes the sign convention.
cards.answer_criterion: Supply an unambiguous value a and a Lean proof that |\(a- A|\le 1/100\), or certified lower and upper bounds of width at most \(1/50\) with the midpoint as answer. Exact determination also qualifies. Merely restating the defining supremum, reporting floating-point optimization at finitely many depths, or interchanging depth and instance-size limits is insufficient. Equality with \(\Pi\)* is a stronger possible answer, not assumed by the target.

cards.title: Optimal quantum query complexity of uniformity testing

Access is to an arbitrary distribution synthesizer with the precise oracle convention below.

cards.definitions: Write \([d]=\{1,\ldots ,d\}, u_{d}(i)=1/d\) and \(d_{\mathrm{TV}}(p,u_{d})=(1/2)\sum_{i}|p_{i}- 1/d|\). The algorithm receives d and \(\varepsilon\) and oracle access to a unitary \(U_{p}\) satisfying \(U_{p}|0^{k}\rangle =\sum_{i}\sqrt{p_{i}}|i\rangle |\psi _{i}\rangle\), where each garbage state |\(\psi _{i}\rangle\) is normalized. The extension of \(U_{p}\) away from |\(0^{k}\rangle\) and its garbage states are arbitrary; the tester must work for every valid oracle satisfying the promise. A query is one application of \(U_{p}, U_{p}\dagger\) or controlled-\(U_{p}\); intervening quantum operations, ancillas and measurements are unrestricted and do not count toward query complexity. The code is used as a black box: the tester does not get a classical description to inspect for free. Let \(Q(d,\varepsilon )\) be the minimum worst-case number of such queries among testers whose probability of the correct yes/no output is at least 0.99 for every oracle with \(p=u_{d}\) or \(d_{\mathrm{TV}}(p,u_{d})>\varepsilon\), taking the worst case over allowed oracle-register sizes. No guarantee is required in the intermediate gap.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a positive function \(g(d,\varepsilon )\) and absolute constants \(a,A>0\) such that a \(g(d,\varepsilon )\le Q(d,\varepsilon )\le A g(d,\varepsilon )\) throughout the stated domain. Prove both bounds uniformly over its two parameters and all valid oracle implementations. A formula or certified evaluation rule may specify g; merely renaming Q is insufficient. This is an asymptotic query bound up to multiplicative constants, not pointwise additive 0.01 accuracy.

cards.title: \(\mathrm{QMA}(2)\) versus \(\mathrm{BQEXP}\)
cards.formal: Is \(\mathrm{QMA}(2)\subseteq\mathrm{BQEXP}\)? In promise-problem terms, does every pair \(\Pi=(Y,N)\) of disjoint sets of binary strings that has a polynomial-time quantum verifier with two unentangled polynomial-size proofs also admit a uniform quantum algorithm running in time \(2^{p(n)}\), for some polynomial \(p\), with error at most \(1/3\) on every promised input? The algorithm receives no proofs. The polynomial may depend on \(\Pi\) and its verifier, but not on the individual input of length \(n\).
cards.why: Unentangled quantum proofs add a nonconvex constraint to quantum verification. An exponential-time quantum simulation would place a meaningful algorithmic limit on this model and clarify whether its power can be explained without nondeterministic exponential-time witness search.
cards.status_note: The source explicitly asks this inclusion in January 2026. Primary definitions and the NEXP upper bound were checked together with July 2026 hierarchy and stoquastic results on 2026-09-14. None of those checked results supplies a BQEXP simulation for general QMA(2); this is a bounded literature check.

sentences: The question asks whether every problem with two unentangled quantum proofs can be decided in quantum exponential time without proofs.
The verifier is polynomial-time and may process both proofs jointly, but the proofs must initially be a product state.
The deciding algorithm must be uniform and have bounded error on every promised input.
The standard upper bound uses nondeterministic exponential time, which does not give the requested algorithm.
Recent quantified and stoquastic results concern different upper-bound models and leave this inclusion unresolved.

cards.definitions:
A promise problem specifies yes-inputs \(Y\) and no-inputs \(N\); on inputs outside \(Y\cup N\), a deciding algorithm has no correctness requirement but must still obey its resource bound. A qubit has state space \(\mathbb C^2\). A pure state on \(w\) qubits is a unit vector in \(\mathbb C^{2^w}\). Two unentangled proofs have the tensor-product form \(|\psi\rangle\otimes|\phi\rangle\), where each vector describes at most \(w(n)\) qubits for some polynomial \(w\). Arbitrary entanglement within either proof is allowed, but entanglement between the proofs is excluded.

Membership in \(\mathrm{QMA}(2)\) means that one deterministic polynomial-time Turing machine, on input \(x\), generates a quantum circuit \(V_x\) of polynomial size. The circuit takes the two proof registers and zero-initialized work qubits, and finally measures an output bit. Write \(a_x(\psi,\phi)\) for its acceptance probability. Its guarantees are \[x\in Y\ \Longrightarrow\ \exists\psi,\phi:\ a_x(\psi,\phi)\ge2/3,\qquad x\in N\ \Longrightarrow\ \forall\psi,\phi:\ a_x(\psi,\phi)\le1/3.\] The two proofs are sent once; there is no later interaction. The same definition results if mixed product states or convex mixtures of product states are permitted, by linearity of acceptance probability. The verifier need not certify that an arbitrarily supplied entangled pair is a product: unentanglement is the proof model's assumption.

Use the fixed finite gate set consisting of Hadamard \(H=2^{-1/2}\left(\begin{smallmatrix}1&1\\1&-1\end{smallmatrix}\right)\), \(T=\operatorname{diag}(1,e^{i\pi/4})\), its inverse, and controlled NOT, acting on named wires. Circuit size counts every gate; every initialized or proof qubit counts toward the relevant qubit bound. Uniform generation outputs the full gate and wire list.

Membership in \(\mathrm{BQEXP}\) means that one deterministic circuit generator, on input \(x\) of length \(n\), runs in at most \(2^{p(n)}\) steps and outputs a circuit with at most \(2^{p(n)}\) gates and qubits, using the same finite gate set. The circuit begins with zero-initialized qubits, receives no proof or advice, and accepts yes-inputs with probability at least \(2/3\) and no-inputs with probability at most \(1/3\). Classical dependence on \(x\) is through the generator. Polynomial overheads in the generator and circuit can be absorbed into \(p\). No oracle or postselection is available. Probability in both models is ordinary quantum measurement probability.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct Lean-checked proof of the inclusion, or of its negation. Inclusion requires a bounded-error, uniform exponential-time quantum decision procedure for every problem satisfying the stated two-proof verification definition. Separation requires a promise problem in \(\mathrm{QMA}(2)\) with no such decision procedure. Simulations only for restricted verifiers, shorter proofs, or a different completeness-soundness gap do not suffice.

context_blocks.text: Classically, two existential witnesses can simply be concatenated. In this quantum model, allowing an arbitrary joint state would remove the product restriction and give the ordinary single-proof model. That restriction is therefore part of the computational resource, rather than an incidental communication detail.

A known upper bound is \(\mathrm{QMA}(2)\subseteq\mathrm{NEXP}\), where \(\mathrm{NEXP}\) allows nondeterministic time \(2^{\mathrm{poly}(n)}\). Guessing sufficiently accurate classical descriptions of the two states and verifying them explains this bound. Enumerating all such descriptions is much more expensive, so this does not give a deterministic or quantum exponential-time algorithm.

The 2026 hierarchy result gives a structural upper bound using competing quantifiers over pure quantum states. Its stated containments still end at nondeterministic exponential time. An existential/universal characterization does not itself implement a bounded-error quantum decision procedure.

The July 2026 work obtains exponential-time algorithms for a stoquastic restriction, designed to remove destructive interference. Its verifier restrictions are substantive, so those algorithms do not yield the requested simulation for general quantum verifiers.

cards.title: Succinct entangled proofs with efficient provers
cards.formal: Does quantum circuit acceptance admit a uniform two-prover, one-round proof with a classical polynomial-time verifier, total classical communication \(O((\log(N+2))^k)\) for some fixed \(k\), completeness at least \(2/3\), and soundness at most \(1/3\) against arbitrary entangled provers, such that the honest provers can prepare and execute their strategy in quantum polynomial time given polynomially many copies of an accepting witness? Here \(N\) is the explicit circuit-instance length, and the instance, efficiency and soundness requirements are defined below.

source_formulation.text: The best of both worlds The essential reason that two-prover succinct verification remains an open problem is that nonlocal answer reduction is hard.
source_formulation.caption: Complete selected source sentence; PDF p. 3

cards.why: This asks whether a classical verifier can check general quantumly provable claims using very little communication while keeping the honest quantum resources polynomial. It joins three substantial demands—two separated provers, unconditional soundness and succinct communication—and would clarify the practical content of entangled proof systems beyond their unconstrained complexity-class power.

importance.reason: A broad quantum verification question for a canonical QMA-complete promise problem, joining information-theoretic soundness, two-prover separation, short communication and polynomial honest resources. The tension between succinctness and witness-dependent prover efficiency connects quantum complexity with feasible verification, beyond a single protocol’s parameter optimization.

sentences: The question asks a classical verifier to check a quantum circuit’s acceptance using two separated quantum provers.
Both the questions and answers together must use only polylogarithmically many bits in the circuit description length.
Honest provers must prepare and execute their shared strategy efficiently from polynomially many copies of a valid quantum witness.
Cheating provers may use arbitrary finite-dimensional entanglement and unlimited computation, but cannot communicate while answering.
Known succinct computational arguments and entangled proofs without efficient honest preparation do not supply all of these requirements.

cards.definitions: An instance is an explicitly listed quantum circuit \(U\) with \(w\) witness qubits, \(a\) auxiliary qubits initially in \(|0\rangle^{\otimes a}\), and a designated output qubit. The wire counts are included in unary and each gate and its wire indices are explicitly encoded in binary, so the total bit length \(N\) bounds the numbers of gates and wires. Use the fixed universal gate set \(H,T,\mathrm{CNOT}\), where \(H|b\rangle=(|0\rangle+(-1)^b|1\rangle)/\sqrt2\), \(T=\operatorname{diag}(1,e^{i\pi/4})\), and \(\mathrm{CNOT}|b,c\rangle=|b,b\mathbin\oplus c\rangle\), for bits \(b,c\). Acceptance means measuring output one in the computational basis. A YES instance has a normalized witness \(|\psi\rangle\) for which acceptance is at least \(2/3\); a NO instance has acceptance at most \(1/3\) for every witness density matrix, meaning every positive semidefinite trace-one matrix on the witness register. The input is promised to satisfy one of these cases. All parties know the circuit. The verifier uses private independent random bits, sends one classical question to each of two separated provers, receives one classical answer from each, and accepts or rejects in worst-case polynomial time in \(N\). Each prover sees only its own question. The worst-case sum of both question lengths and both answer lengths is at most \(C(\log_2(N+2))^k\), for constants \(C>0\) and integer \(k\ge1\) independent of the instance and strategy. The verifier rejects overlong messages, and no uncharged timing or message-length channel is permitted. For completeness there must be fixed uniform quantum algorithms for setup and for each prover, and a fixed polynomial \(p\). For every YES instance some accepting witness \(|\psi\rangle\) enables the setup algorithm, given at most \(p(N)\) independent copies of \(|\psi\rangle\) and clean auxiliary qubits, to prepare the provers’ joint state using at most \(p(N)\) gates and qubits. Setup occurs before the verifier samples its questions and distributes the two shares of this state. Each local response then takes at most \(p(N)\) gates, qubits and classical computation steps. Uniform means that circuit descriptions and classical control are generated from the public instance and available local messages by fixed polynomial-time algorithms; arbitrary input-dependent advice is not supplied in addition to the witness copies. These algorithms may use the stated universal gates, computational-basis measurements and classical randomness and control. The resulting acceptance probability must be at least \(2/3\). For soundness, on every NO instance, acceptance must be at most \(1/3\) for every finite-dimensional shared state and every pair of local quantum measurement strategies, regardless of dimension or computational cost. In particular, a cheating strategy need not obey the honest resource bound. Its initial entanglement may depend on the instance but not on the verifier’s private questions. Neither honest nor cheating provers communicate after setup. All probabilities include the verifier’s randomness and measurement outcomes. This is an information-theoretically sound proof; no computational hardness assumption or security parameter is part of the target.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean that such a verifier and uniform honest algorithms exist with some universal constants and polynomial bounds, or prove that no such protocol exists for the stated circuit promise problem. A positive answer must establish both efficient witness-dependent setup and local execution as well as soundness against unrestricted entangled cheating. Short questions with polynomial-length answers, a protocol with more than two provers or more rounds, an inefficient honest strategy, or a single-prover computational argument does not meet this particular target. The negation rules out every choice of the verifier, honest algorithms and fixed bounds; a limitation of one construction alone is insufficient.

context_blocks.text: The circuit asks whether some quantum witness makes a known computation accept. The verifier sees the circuit description but receives only a very short classical exchange with two quantum devices. The witness itself need not have an efficiently computable classical description.

Entangled provers may share a joint quantum state before the test, even though they cannot exchange information while answering. Soundness must hold for every such cheating strategy. This is a stronger security demand than an argument whose guarantee assumes that cheating computations are efficient.

The honest side has a different resource requirement. Copies of a valid witness are allowed as input, but a vast precomputed state or an exponential computation hidden in setup is not. Natarajan and Nirkhe explicitly distinguish efficient setup from efficient responses, and explain why membership in a larger complexity class does not supply a witness-preserving efficient strategy.

Metger, Natarajan and Zhang identify succinct two-prover verification with efficient honest provers as unresolved. Their discussion distinguishes protocols with short questions from those with short total communication and distinguishes efficient honest strategies from general entangled proofs.

This card fixes the one-round nonlocal-game interpretation and ordinary polynomial verifier time. It expresses the quantum claim as an explicit circuit-acceptance promise problem and requires preparation from copies of an accepting circuit witness. It asks only for polylogarithmic total communication; it does not add the sharper logarithmic-question, constant-answer target of a quantum games PCP.

Fu, Mastel and Zhang’s 2025 paper gives two-prover, one-round succinct perfect-zero-knowledge proofs for every recursively enumerable language, a class that includes undecidable problems. Its main theorem does not supply polynomial-time honest preparation from QMA witness copies. An efficient simulator for zero knowledge is also not a pair of separated efficient provers.

Bartusek, Liu and Malavolta’s 2026 result broadens the assumptions under which succinct classical-verifier arguments for QMA exist: it assumes oblivious state preparation and collapsing hash functions. It remains a computational argument system. Its small communication therefore does not establish the unconditional two-prover proof requested here.

cards.title: Strong quantum IOPs with polynomial communication
cards.formal: Does every QMA promise problem have a strong quantum interactive oracle proof with polynomial communication, constantly many messages and a constant total number of queried message qubits? More precisely, for every \(L\in\mathrm{QMA}\), do there exist a polynomial \(p\), constants \(r,q\in\mathbb N\), and one uniform verifier under the strong access rules below such that, on every input \(x\) of length \(n\), its running time and total incoming prover-message length are at most \(p(n)\), the total number of messages is at most \(r\), the total query cost is at most \(q\), and \[x\in L_{\mathrm{yes}}\Rightarrow\sup_P\Pr[V_x\leftrightarrow P\text{ accepts}]\ge2/3,\] \[x\in L_{\mathrm{no}}\Rightarrow\sup_P\Pr[V_x\leftrightarrow P\text{ accepts}]\le1/3?\] Here \(P\) ranges over all allowed prover strategies, with no computational bound. Strong means that the verifier returns each incoming quantum register in full and sends no additional quantum register of its own.
cards.why: This asks whether very local interactive verification of quantum evidence can avoid enormous communication while obeying the strong return rules. Resolving it would clarify the joint limits of proof length, local access and interaction for QMA.

progress.text: The source proves polynomial communication in the general model and exponential communication in the strong model, both with constant query and message bounds; Question1.9 asks for polynomial communication in the strong model.

The later construction achieves polynomial communication with polylogarithmic queries and rounds in a model retaining parts of the initial witness. These bounds do not settle the stated strong constant-query question.

cards.definitions:
A promise problem \(L=(L_{\mathrm{yes}},L_{\mathrm{no}})\) is a pair of disjoint subsets of finite binary strings; inputs outside these sets have no correctness requirement. QMA is the class of such pairs with a uniform polynomial-time quantum verifier receiving one polynomial-size quantum witness. For every yes-input there is a witness accepted with probability at least \(2/3\); on a no-input every witness is accepted with probability at most \(1/3\). Uniform means that a single deterministic classical algorithm generates the input-dependent circuit in polynomial time. Its private ancillas start in zero. Gate count, number of qubits and witness length are polynomial in the classical input length. The witness can be any density matrix and need not be efficiently preparable.

A qubit has state space \(\mathbb C^2\). A density matrix is Hermitian, positive semidefinite and of trace one: \(\rho=\rho^\dagger\), \(v^\dagger\rho v\ge0\) for all vectors \(v\), and \(\operatorname{Tr}\rho=1\). A quantum channel is a complex-linear map on matrices that preserves trace and remains positive when tensored with the identity on an arbitrary auxiliary register. Verifier operations are uniformly described polynomial-size circuits of fixed elementary gates, zero-state preparations and computational-basis measurements with classical control. For a concrete universal gate convention take \[H=2^{-1/2}\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\1&-1\end{pmatrix},\quad T=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&e^{i\pi/4}\end{pmatrix},\quad\mathrm{CNOT}|b,c\rangle=|b,b\oplus c\rangle.\] Here \(b,c\in\{0,1\}\), \(\oplus\) means addition modulo two, and \(i^2=-1\). No arbitrary numerical matrix is a free gate. Channel descriptions include their finite circuit realization; all uniform classical computation and elementary gate operations count toward running time.

An interactive proof has one verifier and one prover, exchanging a bounded sequence of registers and classical messages. They begin with no shared entanglement. The verifier has private workspace \(R\) initialized in zero, containing both its quantum memory and classical records. The prover has an unrestricted private register and may apply any quantum channel to its own memory and the messages it receives; its strategy can depend on \(x\) and the prior interaction. It may entangle different messages with its private memory and with returned registers. Soundness must hold against every such strategy, even computationally unbounded ones. The honest prover is also allowed to be unbounded, as in the source's formal Definitions5.14–5.15. Neither efficient preparation of an honest quantum witness nor a bound on the honest prover's computation is part of this question.

In one verifier turn, let the incoming prover register be \(W=(W_1,\ldots,W_\ell)\). It can contain quantum data or classical data encoded in the computational basis; reading a bit in such a message is still a query. The verifier first applies a channel only to its private register \(R\), then measures an address register in \(R\) to obtain a classical list specifying a set \(S\subseteq\{1,\ldots,\ell\}\) of at most \(q_i\) positions. Conditioned on these addresses, it applies a circuit channel only to \(R\) and the qubits \(W_S\). Its operation is identity on the other incoming wires. This is the query-channel structure of Definitions5.1–5.2: the addresses may depend on private randomness and earlier rounds, but are classical measurement outcomes before the current message is touched. Coherent querying in a superposition of addresses, or choosing a second set adaptively after inspecting the same message within this turn, is not this one-batch query operation. Repeated local gate operations on the already selected qubits affect running time but do not add new positions to that turn's query set.

After its turn the verifier returns the entire \(W\) register to the prover and retains only its own private register. It may also send polynomially many classical bits, but no additional quantum register. The returned qubits may have changed through the allowed interaction; their original state need not be restored. Keeping information acquired in private workspace is allowed, including quantum information transferred through the queried-qubit channel. The restriction forbids keeping incoming message wires between turns, not all changes to private memory. The verifier's own quantum workspace may be polynomial: the formal strong model does not impose a constant bound on all its private qubits. Merely forwarding the unqueried wires counts as communication, but is not counted as inspecting them. At its final turn the verifier produces an accept/reject bit, returning the message if a return is needed to respect the same convention; a final unused return changes the constant message bound only by one.

The incoming message lengths \(\ell_i\), the query budgets \(q_i\), and the protocol's uniform circuit descriptions are fixed by the input and protocol; branchwise budgets may be bounded by fixed worst-case values. Total prover-message length is \(\sum_i\ell_i\), including every incoming copy or retransmission of a register. Total query cost is \(\sum_iq_i\), counting access again if a position is queried in a later message. All resource bounds hold on every branch, not only in expectation or for the honest prover. Returning the full registers adds at most the same quantum communication again. Classical messages generated by the polynomial-time verifier are also polynomially bounded. The constants \(r,q\), the polynomial \(p\) and the verifier may depend on the promise problem but not on \(n\) or the individual input. A polynomial bound on communication does not permit polynomially many queried qubits: the latter must remain a constant.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof of the stated inclusion of QMA in the constant-message, constant-query strong class with polynomial communication, or a complete Lean-checked proof that some QMA promise problem admits no such verifier. An affirmative construction must prove uniform resource bounds, completeness and soundness against arbitrary entangled adaptive prover strategies. A negative result must quantify over all eligible verifiers and all constants and polynomials in the definition. Exponential communication, polylogarithmic queries or messages, retaining part of an incoming register between rounds, or sending extra verifier-generated quantum registers does not meet the target. No computational hardness assumption can replace the required unconditional soundness. A protocol with constant private quantum space would suffice, but that extra condition is not necessary in the selected formal model. This is an exact class-inclusion question, not a numerical approximation target.

cards.title: Oracle separation of BQP from IP
cards.formal: Does there exist a classical Boolean oracle A and a language \(\mathrm{L}\subseteq \{0,1\}\)* such that \(\mathrm{L}\in \mathrm{BQP}^{A}\) but \(\mathrm{L}\notin \mathrm{IP}^{A}\)?
cards.why: Determines whether classical single-prover verification of efficient quantum computations survives arbitrary oracle access. The distinction is sharper than a quantum speedup over direct classical computation: even an unrestricted interactive helper must fail in the separating world.
cards.status_note: Source Problems 7–8 and the April 2026 paper checked; subsequent-work searches through 11 September 2026 located no resolution of the stated oracle question. cards.definitions: An oracle is an arbitrary fixed Boolean function \(A:\{0,1\}*\to \{0,1\}\); it need not be computable. All languages are subsets of \(\{0,1\}\)*, and n is the input length. A classical oracle call supplies one string z and returns \(A(z)\). Quantum access uses the unitary |\(z,b\rangle \mapsto |z,b\oplus A(z)\rangle\), extended linearly to superpositions of strings of a given length. Query registers and the work required to prepare them count toward the computation bound. No quantum-valued oracle, advice string or promise on inputs is supplied. \(\mathrm{BQP}^{A}\) consists of languages decided by one uniform quantum algorithm with polynomial total running time, oracle calls and qubits. On every yes input it accepts with probability at least \(2/3\), and on every no input with probability at most \(1/3\). One standard machine convention uses Hadamard \(H=(1/\sqrt{2})[[1,1],[1,- 1]], T=diag(1,e^{i\pi /4})\) and CNOT |\(a,b\rangle \mapsto |a,a\oplus b\rangle\) gates, zero-initialized auxiliary qubits, computational-basis measurements and polynomial-time classical control. Circuit descriptions are generated uniformly in polynomial time; there is no nonuniform advice. Probabilities are over measurements and any internal random bits. An \(\mathrm{IP}^{A}\) protocol has one classical probabilistic polynomial-time verifier and one prover, exchanging only classical bit strings. The verifier has private fair random bits and classical access to A. Its total computation, random bits, communication and number of rounds are bounded by a polynomial in n, with no predetermined universal degree. Completeness requires one honest prover strategy that makes the verifier accept with probability at least \(2/3\) on every yes input. Soundness requires acceptance probability at most \(1/3\) on every no input against every prover strategy, including computationally unbounded strategies. The prover knows the common input and oracle but not the verifier’s unrevealed private coins; its messages can depend on its conversation history. There is no trusted setup or shared entanglement. Prover efficiency is unrestricted in \(\mathrm{IP}^{A}\). Probabilities include verifier randomness and any randomness or measurements of the prover.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove the existence of one oracle A and language L with the stated separation, ruling out every polynomial-time classical interactive proof for L relative to A. Alternatively, prove \(\mathrm{BQP}^{A}\subseteq \mathrm{IP}^{A}\) for every classical Boolean oracle A. A lower bound for a fixed round limit does not by itself exclude all polynomial-round protocols.

context_blocks.title: Can a classical verifier trust a quantum computation?
context_blocks.text: A quantum computer might efficiently decide a language while a classical computer cannot directly reproduce its calculation. An interactive proof lets the verifier ask questions and test the answers. This card asks whether even an all-powerful helper can always make the quantum answer classically checkable when both sides must use a supplied oracle through its query interface.

context_blocks.title: The same function, different query access
context_blocks.text: The quantum computation may query a superposition, whereas the verifier queries one ordinary string at a time. The oracle function itself is identical for both. Some oracle languages are easy for both: for \(\mathrm{L}=\{x:A(x)=1\}\), the verifier simply queries x. The question requires a language whose quantum computation cannot be certified by the stated interaction.

context_blocks.title: Two distinct single-prover questions
context_blocks.text: For every oracle, \(\mathrm{IP}_{\mathrm{BQP}}^{A}\subseteq \mathrm{BQP}^{A}\) and \(\mathrm{IP}_{\mathrm{BQP}}^{A}\subseteq \mathrm{IP}^{A}\) by definition. An oracle separation of BQP from unrestricted-prover IP therefore also separates BQP from \(\mathrm{IP}_{\mathrm{BQP}}\). The efficient-honest-prover separation is a weaker demand: an unrestricted prover might still verify that language. The two cards record this implication without identifying the targets.

context_blocks.title: Unbounded cheating is part of the guarantee
context_blocks.text: The prover can lie in any computationally possible way, even with unlimited computation. Restricting only a dishonest prover to efficient strategies would instead describe a computationally sound argument. Cryptographic verification protocols with that guarantee do not establish the information-theoretic IP containment requested here.

context_blocks.title: What the 2026 multiple-prover result changes
context_blocks.text: Aaronson, Natarajan, Tal and Villányi state \(\mathrm{BQP}^{A}\subseteq MIP^{A}\) for every classical oracle. MIP permits several separated provers who cannot communicate during the protocol; the stated result uses classical provers without shared entanglement. The source still identifies the single-prover oracle question as open and does not supply a polynomial-time quantum honest prover for its MIP result.

cards.title: Quantum query–space tradeoffs for collisions and distinctness
cards.formal: Determine, up to universal multiplicative constants, the functions \(T_b(n,m,S)\) for \(b\in\{\mathrm{collision},\mathrm{distinctness}\}\): the minimum worst-case number of quantum queries needed by an algorithm with at most \(S\) qubits of total retained memory to solve the specified decision problem with error at most \(1/3\). The input is an oracle for \(f:[n]\to[m]\). In the collision problem, \(n\) is even and \(f\) is promised to be either injective or exactly two-to-one; distinguish these cases. In element distinctness there is no promise; decide whether \(f\) is injective. The full parameter domain is \(m\ge n\ge2\) and \(S\ge4(\lceil\log_2(n+1)\rceil+\lceil\log_2(m+1)\rceil)+10\), with integer parameters. This card selects the source's total-memory tradeoff, allowing all retained memory to be quantum; separating classical and quantum memory budgets is a further variant.
cards.why: Quantum collision and distinctness algorithms gain speed while retaining substantial information about queried values. Their optimal time/space tradeoffs would quantify how much memory is necessary for those advantages and develop lower-bound methods for problems whose output contains only one bit.

cards.definitions:
The notation \([r]\) means \(\{1,\ldots,r\}\). Injective means that distinct inputs have distinct outputs. Exactly two-to-one means that every value in the image has exactly two preimages; unused output values have none. The required output is one bit, not a pair of colliding indices.

Let \(a=\lceil\log_2(n+1)\rceil\) and \(v=\lceil\log_2(m+1)\rceil\). A query maps \(|i,y,z\rangle\) to \(|i,y\mathbin{\oplus}\operatorname{enc}(f(i)),z\rangle\), with \(a\) address qubits, \(v\) answer qubits and a remaining work register. Here \(\operatorname{enc}\) is the length-\(v\) binary encoding and \(\oplus\) is bitwise addition modulo two. For address zero or an address larger than \(n\), use the all-zero answer. One call returns one entire output symbol and costs one query. The address and answer registers are included in \(S\).

An algorithm begins with an input-independent state on at most \(S\) qubits, alternates a fixed finite sequence of input-independent quantum channels with oracle calls, and ends with a two-outcome measurement. A density matrix describes its state. An allowed intervening channel has the form \(\rho\mapsto\sum_j K_j\rho K_j^\dagger\), where the finitely many matrices satisfy \(\sum_j K_j^\dagger K_j=I\); it maps the retained memory back into the same bounded space. This allows measurement, randomization and resetting memory. Discarded information cannot be retrieved later. Any measurement outcomes, classical work bits, or tables that remain accessible must occupy the counted memory. Input-dependent classical control is therefore also stored in that memory. There is no external input-dependent advice, second oracle, or uncounted read/write storage.

The channels and measurement may depend on \(b,n,m,S\), but not on \(f\). Their descriptions and the input-independent instruction index are not workspace, and no uniformity, gate-count or computation-time restriction is imposed between queries. Arbitrary computation on the stored memory, including coherent access to stored tables, is free. All oracle calls count, including preprocessing and calls on branches later discarded. The finite query budget is worst-case, and correctness must hold on every valid oracle, with probability at least \(2/3\). The stated space floor allows elementary repeated scans, so both minima are finite; no upper limit on \(S\) is imposed.
cards.answer_criterion: Supply positive functions \(H_b(n,m,S)\), universal constants \(0<c\le C<\infty\), and a complete mathematically correct Lean-checked proof that \(cH_b(n,m,S)\le T_b(n,m,S)\le CH_b(n,m,S)\) for both tasks throughout their parameter domains. Both algorithms and matching lower bounds must respect the stated memory budget; an unrecorded increase in space is not allowed. The functions must describe the asymptotic dependence on the parameters, not simply repeat the optimization defining \(T_b\). Bounds for collision search, random inputs, or label-symmetric algorithms alone do not establish the required worst-case decision tradeoffs.

context_blocks.text: Without a restrictive memory budget, the familiar quantum query scales are \(n^{1/3}\) for the collision promise and \(n^{2/3}\) for element distinctness in their standard parameter regimes. Their optimality as query bounds does not determine the memory needed to attain them.

A classical table that can be queried coherently still occupies memory in this formulation. Counting its bits prevents a large external table from making a small-qubit algorithm appear to use little total storage. The separate question of which part of the storage must preserve quantum coherence is not resolved by a total-space bound.

The February 2026 work establishes memory lower bounds for a nested collision task with short output. Its input uses an additional oracle and a different success condition, so its lower bounds are not automatically the tradeoffs for either decision problem defined here.

The September 2026 preprint claims tight bounds for collision search and element-distinctness search under a label-symmetry restriction. Its Section 1.4 explicitly leaves removal of that restriction open. Permuting labels to symmetrize an arbitrary algorithm may require additional memory, which prevents treating symmetry as free.

cards.context:
Without a restrictive memory budget, the familiar quantum query scales are \(n^{1/3}\) for the collision promise and \(n^{2/3}\) for element distinctness in their standard parameter regimes. Their optimality as query bounds does not determine the memory needed to attain them.

A classical table that can be queried coherently still occupies memory in this formulation. Counting its bits prevents a large external table from making a small-qubit algorithm appear to use little total storage. The separate question of which part of the storage must preserve quantum coherence is not resolved by a total-space bound.

The February 2026 work establishes memory lower bounds for a nested collision task with short output. Its input uses an additional oracle and a different success condition, so its lower bounds are not automatically the tradeoffs for either decision problem defined here.

The September 2026 preprint claims tight bounds for collision search and element-distinctness search under a label-symmetry restriction. Its Section 1.4 explicitly leaves removal of that restriction open. Permuting labels to symmetrize an arbitrary algorithm may require additional memory, which prevents treating symmetry as free.

cards.title: Sequential randomness certification against non-signaling adversaries
cards.formal: Is the randomness certifiable from a single pure entangled pair of qubits universally bounded against time-ordered no-signaling adversaries, even when Bob measures his qubit arbitrarily many times? Precisely, does a real constant \(B\ge0\) exist such that \[H_{\mathrm{NS}}(P,\mathbf y^0)=-\log_2 G_{\mathrm{NS}}(P,\mathbf y^0)\le B\] for every finite sequence length, every experiment in the single-pair model below, and every fixed generation input string \(\mathbf y^0\)?
cards.why: The question tests how much repeated randomness certification depends on quantum theory beyond no-signaling. It separates the physical resource available to the honest experiment—a single pair of qubits—from assumptions about an adversary. A universal bound or unbounded family would clarify whether recycling one entangled system can retain its qualitative advantage under this stronger adversarial model.
cards.status_note: Checked on 14 September 2026. The source explicitly conjectures boundedness against no-signaling adversaries. The 2024 quantum-security result and 2025 no-signaling accumulation preprint do not establish a resolution with this single-pair resource and measurement model. No matching proof or counterexample was found in the bounded search; the new proofs were not independently verified.

progress.text: The source proves unbounded certification against quantum adversaries and conjectures boundedness against post-quantum no-signaling adversaries for its sequential setting.

importance.reason: A substantial foundational question about the relation between finite entanglement resources, sequential measurements and device-independent randomness. The difference between quantum and post-quantum no-signaling adversaries tests the assumptions behind an unbounded resource claim, with consequences for the conceptual limits of randomness certification.

sentences: A single entangled pair of qubits is measured once by Alice and repeatedly by Bob.
The question asks whether the certified unpredictability of Bob’s entire outcome string has a universal finite bound against an adversary constrained only by no-signaling and causal order.
The honest experiment uses just one qubit per wing, but the adversary is not assumed to be quantum or dimension-limited.
Alice may have more possible measurement choices as the sequence grows, and the full observed correlations are assumed known.
Unbounded randomness against quantum adversaries and general repeated Bell-test accumulation do not by themselves settle this fixed-resource post-quantum question.

cards.definitions: Fix an integer \(N\ge1\) and a nonempty finite set \(X\) of Alice’s measurement choices. Initially Alice and Bob share one normalized pure entangled state \(|\psi\rangle\in\mathbb C^2\otimes\mathbb C^2\), and no other shared quantum resource. Alice receives \(x\in X\), performs one binary measurement and outputs \(a\in\{-1,+1\}\). Its effects are positive semidefinite matrices \(A_a^x\) on \(\mathbb C^2\) with \(A_{-1}^x+A_{+1}^x=I\). Bob performs \(N\) binary instruments successively on his same qubit. At step \(i\), he receives \(y_i\in\{0,1\}\) and produces \(b_i\in\{-1,+1\}\). His instrument may depend on all his earlier inputs and outputs. It consists of maps \(\mathcal M^{h,y_i}_{i,b_i}\) from two-by-two matrices to two-by-two matrices, where \(h=(y_1,b_1,\ldots,y_{i-1},b_{i-1})\). Each map is completely positive and trace-nonincreasing, and their sum over \(b_i\) is trace-preserving. Completely positive means that tensoring with the identity map on matrices of any finite size preserves positive semidefiniteness. The output quantum register passed to the next step is only the same two-dimensional system. Local auxiliary systems may implement an instrument but are discarded within that step; no extra persistent quantum register or fresh shared entanglement is supplied. The recorded classical history is available to later Bob steps. There is no communication between Alice and Bob during the experiment. Inputs are chosen independently of the preparation and of any adversarial side information. Let \(\mathbf b=(b_1,\ldots,b_N)\), \(\mathbf y=(y_1,\ldots,y_N)\), and let \(\mathcal M_{\mathbf b}^{\mathbf y}\) denote the composition of the corresponding history-dependent Bob maps. The exactly known observed distribution is \[P(a,\mathbf b\mid x,\mathbf y)=\operatorname{Tr}\!\left[(A_a^x\otimes I)(\operatorname{id}\otimes\mathcal M_{\mathbf b}^{\mathbf y})(|\psi\rangle\langle\psi|)\right].\] The size of \(X\), the state and the instruments may vary with \(N\); in particular Alice’s input set is not fixed to two settings. Define \(\mathsf{NS}_N(X)\) to be all nonnegative conditional arrays \(Q(a,\mathbf b\mid x,\mathbf y)\), normalized for each input, with the following marginal constraints. The sum over \(\mathbf b\) is independent of \(\mathbf y\); the sum over \(a\) is independent of \(x\); and, for every \(0\le j<N\), \(\sum_{b_{j+1},\ldots,b_N}Q(a,\mathbf b\mid x,\mathbf y)\) is independent of \(y_{j+1},\ldots,y_N\). The last condition includes the joint Alice outcome and Bob prefix and forbids signaling from later Bob inputs to earlier outputs. Forward dependence on earlier Bob inputs and outputs is permitted. Members of this set need not be quantum correlations or admit any qubit realization. For a fixed publicly known \(\mathbf y^0\in\{0,1\}^N\), set \[G_{\mathrm{NS}}(P,\mathbf y^0)=\sup_{P=\sum_e q_e Q_e}\ \sum_e q_e\max_{\mathbf b\in\{-1,+1\}^N}\sum_a Q_e(a,\mathbf b\mid x,\mathbf y^0),\] where the supremum runs over all finite convex decompositions with \(q_e\ge0\), \(\sum_e q_e=1\), and \(Q_e\in\mathsf{NS}_N(X)\). The mixture identity holds at every input and output, and the weights are independent of inputs. The expression is independent of \(x\) by no-signaling. Eve knows the label \(e\), may choose a decomposition for the fixed generation input, and guesses the entire Bob string. Alice’s outcome is not revealed or conditioned upon. The certified randomness here is this raw conditional min-entropy, without smoothing, postselection or an extractor; all \(N\) Bob outcomes belong to the string. The two-qubit restriction constrains which observed distributions the honest experiment can generate, not the adversary’s decomposition. Exact correlations are assumed; finite sampling and a noise tolerance uniform in \(N\) are not additional requirements.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of a universal finite bound \(B\), or prove that the certified min-entropy is unbounded in this model. A negative answer to the boundedness question must establish that for every real \(M\ge0\) there exist a finite \(N\), finite \(X\), one entangled qubit pair, allowed measurements and instruments, and \(\mathbf y^0\) with \(H_{\mathrm{NS}}(P,\mathbf y^0)>M\). Different experimental designs may be used for different \(M\). Equivalently, a positive answer requires a uniform constant \(c>0\) with \(G_{\mathrm{NS}}\ge c\). The optimal numerical value of a finite bound is not requested. Security only against quantum adversaries, a bound depending on the sequence length, or accumulation using an increasing supply of entangled systems does not resolve this fixed-single-pair question.

context_blocks.text: A quantum measurement can produce an unpredictable outcome while leaving a state that can be measured again. The question is how much unpredictability can be certified from the observed input-output statistics of this repeated experiment, when only one entangled pair was initially supplied.

An ordinary random-looking output is not enough: Eve may know which hidden component of the observed distribution occurred. The guessing probability maximizes her success over all allowed decompositions, and min-entropy measures the resulting unpredictability of the whole Bob string.

Curchod and coauthors show that one pure entangled qubit pair can certify any finite amount of randomness against quantum adversaries using a sufficiently long sequence. Their concluding question asks whether a finite upper limit returns when the adversary is constrained only by no-signaling.

Their sequential construction increases Alice’s number of possible measurement settings as the sequence grows. Fixing Alice to two settings would impose an extra restriction absent from that result. The present card permits every finite input set while keeping Alice’s output binary and her quantum system a single qubit.

The adversary model is made explicit here by replacing the source’s quantum decomposition with the full time-ordered no-signaling set. Each component preserves separation of Alice and Bob and the causal order within Bob’s sequence. Its dimension and physical realization are unrestricted: the honest qubit promise is not trusted as a constraint on Eve.

Padovan and coauthors’ 2024 work studies one Alice and two sequential Bobs, with a quantum correlation boundary and improved robustness of randomness certification. Its quantum-adversary guarantee does not answer the post-quantum boundedness question.

Ramanathan, Liu and Wu’s 2025 preprint reports linear min-entropy accumulation against time-ordered no-signaling adversaries when Alice and Bob run a Bell test repeatedly with a prescribed nonlocal value in each round. That theorem does not impose this card’s single-qubit-per-wing resource and single Alice output. General sequential Bell-test accumulation therefore cannot by itself be treated as a resolution of the single-pair question.

Unboundedness would mean that experiments can be designed to certify any chosen finite amount. It does not demand infinitely many outputs in one finite experiment, nor a fixed noise tolerance as the target amount grows.

cards.title: Constant-round quantum refereed games versus \(\mathrm{PSPACE}\)
cards.formal: Does \(\mathrm{QRG}_{\mathrm{const}}\subseteq\mathrm{PSPACE}\)? For every promise problem \(\Pi=(Y,N)\) admitting a quantum refereed game with a uniform polynomial-time verifier, two competing provers and some fixed constant \(k\) of interaction cycles, must there be a deterministic algorithm deciding \(\Pi\) using polynomial space? For \(x\in Y\), a yes-prover must have a strategy that makes the verifier accept with probability at least \(2/3\) against every no-prover strategy. For \(x\in N\), a no-prover must have a strategy that makes it reject with probability at least \(2/3\) against every yes-prover strategy. The constant \(k\) and the polynomial bounds may depend on the problem and verifier, but not on input length.
cards.why: These games combine efficient quantum verification with competition between two powerful provers who have different information. Locating constant-length games would clarify whether repeated alternation of private interaction can increase computational power beyond polynomial space, even when only a few exchanges are allowed.
cards.status_note: The July 2026 source asks the general constant-round question. The primary game definitions, polynomial-length EXP characterization and bounded-turn PSPACE results were checked on 2026-09-14, with a bounded later-work search. The one-switch/DQIP result does not settle arbitrary constant interleaving, and no full resolution was identified.

sentences: A quantum refereed game has two competing provers trying to make an efficient verifier accept or reject.
The provers exchange private quantum messages with the verifier and may keep private memory.
The question asks whether every game with a constant number of interaction cycles can be simulated in deterministic polynomial space.
Polynomial-space simulations are known for specific patterns in which interaction switches from one prover to the other only once.
Polynomially many general rounds capture exponential time, leaving the full constant-round boundary open.

cards.definitions:
A promise problem is a pair of disjoint sets \(Y,N\subseteq\{0,1\}^{*}\); no answer is prescribed outside their union. Both provers know the classical input \(x\) and the verifier's complete specification. The yes-prover seeks acceptance and the no-prover seeks rejection. They cannot communicate directly and do not initially share an entangled state or correlated private randomness. Each may retain private quantum memory throughout the interaction, use randomness, and perform arbitrary finite-dimensional quantum operations without a time or memory bound.

The verifier is generated from \(x\), of length \(n\), by one deterministic polynomial-time Turing machine. Its total gate count, workspace, and total communicated qubits are polynomial in \(n\). It starts with zero-initialized registers. In each of at most \(k\) cycles, it applies a quantum circuit, sends one message register privately to each prover, and receives both response registers. Each prover acts only on its current message and its own retained private memory. The verifier then proceeds to the next cycle or its final two-outcome measurement. Messages to the two provers may be entangled through the verifier's preparation; this is part of the specified protocol. Empty messages are allowed. Sequential exchanges can be scheduled in separate cycles, so allowing every fixed \(k\) includes any constant-length message pattern. The verifier never gives a prover access to the other prover's private channel unless its own prescribed operations deliberately convey information from it.

Use a fixed universal finite gate set: Hadamard maps \(|0\rangle\) to \((|0\rangle+|1\rangle)/\sqrt2\) and \(|1\rangle\) to \((|0\rangle-|1\rangle)/\sqrt2\); \(T\) multiplies \(|1\rangle\) by \(e^{i\pi/4}\) and fixes \(|0\rangle\); include \(T^{-1}\) and controlled NOT. The verifier's measurements, randomness and adaptive choices may be implemented coherently with polynomially many ancillary qubits. Prover operations are unrestricted quantum channels, expressible as \(\rho\mapsto\sum_j K_j\rho K_j^\dagger\) with \(\sum_j K_j^\dagger K_j=I\), on their message and private registers. Initial private states can be prepared by those channels. All winning probabilities are over the resulting quantum measurement outcomes and private randomization. Each winning strategy may depend on \(x\), but must work against every opposing strategy on that input.

The class \(\mathrm{PSPACE}\) consists here of promise problems decided by a deterministic multitape Turing machine with a read-only input tape and at most \(C(n+1)^r\) work-tape cells for fixed constants \(C,r\). It must halt on all inputs and give the correct answer on \(Y\cup N\). It has no oracle or advice. The simulator need only decide which side can force a win; it need not output either prover's strategy.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct Lean-checked proof of the inclusion, or of its negation. An inclusion proof must cover every fixed constant number of interaction cycles and every polynomial-time uniform verifier in the stated private-message model. A negative proof must exhibit a promise problem in this class with no deterministic polynomial-space decision algorithm. An exponential-time simulation, or a polynomial-space simulation only for one exchange pattern, does not suffice.

context_blocks.text: The winning-strategy requirements contain opposite quantifier orders on yes- and no-inputs. A prover must force its preferred outcome against all opposing strategies. This is different from two cooperating proof providers or a verifier receiving two unentangled existential witnesses.

Gutoski and Wu prove a polynomial-space simulation when all interaction with one prover is completed before interaction with the other begins. This includes their class QRG(2). Their result does not cover arbitrary repeated interleaving of the two private conversations.

Different papers count individual messages, turns and full send/receive rounds differently. This card fixes a complete interaction cycle explicitly. Since it asks about every constant cycle count, a constant change of counting convention does not change its scope.

With polynomially many messages, quantum refereed games capture \(\mathrm{EXP}\), deterministic time \(2^{\mathrm{poly}(n)}\). This gives an upper bound for constant-length games, but it does not supply a polynomial-space simulation. The constant-length question remains meaningful even for classical messages.

cards.title: Black-box unitary synthesis
cards.formal: Is there one polynomial-time uniform family of polynomial-size quantum oracle circuits \(\{A_n\}_{n\ge1}\) such that, for every \(n\)-qubit unitary matrix \(U\), some Boolean function \(f_U:\{0,1\}^{m(n)}\to\{0,1\}\) makes the channel implemented by \(A_n^{f_U}\) approximate \(\rho\mapsto U\rho U^\dagger\) within diamond distance \(1/10\)? The oracle input length \(m(n)\), total number of qubits, number of ordinary gates, and number of oracle calls must all be bounded by one fixed polynomial in \(n\). The circuit family is chosen before \(U\); only the Boolean oracle may depend on \(U\). This is the fixed-constant-error version of black-box unitary synthesis.
cards.why: The question asks whether implementing arbitrary quantum transformations can be reduced efficiently to evaluating Boolean functions. A negative answer would establish a black-box obstruction to explaining all quantum transformation complexity through classical function computation, a central issue for unitary complexity and quantum cryptography.
cards.status_note: The source question is retained in Rosenthal’s May 2026 revision and the July 2026 Dong–Lombardi–Ma paper. Checked on 2026-09-14. Their bounds concern exponential-time upper bounds or restricted-query lower bounds, not a resolution of the displayed general polynomial-time, constant-diamond-error formulation.

cards.definitions:
An \(n\)-qubit system has state space \(\mathbb C^{2^n}\). A unitary matrix satisfies \(U^\dagger U=UU^\dagger=I\), where \(\dagger\) denotes conjugate transpose. A density matrix is a positive semidefinite matrix with trace one and describes a possibly mixed quantum state.

Each circuit receives an arbitrary \(n\)-qubit input, initializes all additional qubits to zero, and outputs a specified \(n\)-qubit register. Other registers are discarded, inducing a quantum channel \(\Phi_{A_n^{f_U}}\). The ordinary gate set is Hadamard \(H=2^{-1/2}\left(\begin{smallmatrix}1&1\\1&-1\end{smallmatrix}\right)\), the phase gate \(T=\operatorname{diag}(1,e^{i\pi/4})\), its inverse, and controlled NOT. Gates may act on any named wires. One oracle call applies \(|z,b\rangle\mapsto|z,b\mathbin{\oplus}f_U(z)\rangle\) to the address and answer registers, including on superpositions; \(\oplus\) is addition modulo two. All calls use the same fixed Boolean function. Oracle inputs and answer registers count toward the qubit bound. The oracle's own computation is uncharged, but every ordinary gate and each oracle call counts toward circuit size. General adaptive quantum computation is allowed through its equivalent coherent circuit representation with polynomially many ancillas.

Uniformity means that a single deterministic Turing machine, on input \(1^n\), outputs the complete gate and wire list in time polynomial in \(n\). It receives no description of \(U\). The oracle function may be arbitrary, and no efficient procedure for computing it or deriving it from \(U\) is required. No additional quantum advice, input-dependent initial ancilla, postselection, or other oracle is available.

For channels with \(n\)-qubit input and output, define their diamond distance by \[D_\diamond(\Phi,\Psi)=\tfrac12\sup_{\rho}\|((\Phi-\Psi)\otimes\operatorname{id}_R)(\rho)\|_1,\] where \(R\) is an untouched \(n\)-qubit reference register and the supremum ranges over density matrices on input and reference together. The trace norm is \(\|M\|_1=\operatorname{Tr}\sqrt{M^\dagger M}\). The desired inequality holds for every input, including one entangled with the reference. The constant \(1/10\) is the allowed channel-approximation error, not an acceptance-probability or heralded-success condition. Global phases of \(U\) are irrelevant to its channel.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct Lean-checked proof that such a universal efficient oracle-circuit family exists, or a proof of its negation. A positive proof must supply the uniform circuit family and show the existence of a suitable Boolean oracle for every unitary while meeting all resource and diamond-distance bounds. A negative proof must rule out polynomially many sequential oracle calls with polynomial total computation. A lower bound restricted to one query, parallel queries, or a prescribed oracle encoding does not suffice.

context_blocks.text: Preparing a chosen state starts from a known blank input. Unitary synthesis must act correctly on an unknown state and preserve its coherent relationships with any external system. Preparing each output column of a matrix separately does not by itself implement the unitary on an arbitrary superposition.

The Boolean oracle is allowed to encode the desired transformation without a computational restriction. The difficulty lies in extracting and using that information through short coherent queries within polynomial total computation. Counting the number of possible ordinary circuits therefore does not alone refute this model.

Rosenthal gives an oracle implementation using time \(\widetilde O(2^{n/2})\), with exponentially small approximation error. This improves a more direct exponential construction but remains far above polynomial time. His matching lower bound is for a particular column-construction interface, not every possible Boolean oracle.

Lombardi, Ma and Wright rule out general one-query synthesis and the corresponding polynomial parallel-query setting with efficient resources. The July 2026 follow-up studies one-query separations for more structured unitary families. These results leave unrestricted polynomially many sequential queries as a different question.

cards.title: Complement of quantum approximate counting in \(\mathrm{QMA}(2)\)
cards.formal: Is the following complementary quantum approximate-counting promise problem in \(\mathrm{QMA}(2)\)? The input is a finite quantum verification circuit \(V\) with \(w\) witness qubits, together with a binary integer \(1\le K\le2^w\). Let \(A_V\) be its acceptance operator on the witness space and let \(D_a(V)\) count its eigenvalues at least \(a\), with multiplicity. Distinguish \[\text{YES: }D_{1/3}(V)\le K/2\qquad\text{from}\qquad\text{NO: }D_{2/3}(V)\ge K,\] promised that one of these conditions holds. Membership asks for one uniform polynomial-time quantum verifier using two polynomial-size, mutually unentangled witnesses, with completeness at least \(2/3\) and soundness at most \(1/3\). The two spectral thresholds deliberately leave a buffer; the selected target is the complement of this buffered counting problem.
cards.why: This asks whether two unentangled quantum certificates can verify that a quantum verifier has only a small accepting space. It connects the power of independent quantum witnesses to approximate counting and distinguishes proving scarcity from merely proving existence.

The authorized spectral buffer is recorded as a repair of the source’s brief definition, not asserted to be identical to a sharp single-threshold problem. No cited proof was independently verified or formalized in Lean.
