cards.definitions:
Use a conventional explicit binary circuit encoding. It specifies the ordered list of gates and their wire indices, which wires hold the \(w\) input witness qubits, which \(a\ge1\) ancillary qubits start in \(|0\rangle\), and one measured output wire. Wire counts are written in unary, so both \(w\) and \(a\) are bounded by the input length. The allowed gates are the fixed exact unitary matrices \[H=\frac1{\sqrt2}\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\1&-1\end{pmatrix},\quad T=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&e^{i\pi/4}\end{pmatrix},\quad \mathrm{CNOT}|b,c\rangle=|b,b\oplus c\rangle,\] acting as identity on the other wires. Here \(b,c\in\{0,1\}\), \(\oplus\) is addition modulo two, and \(i^2=-1\). The sole measurement of \(V\) is its final computational-basis output, with value one interpreted as acceptance. The input includes the complete gate list, not an oracle or a succinct generator of an exponentially long circuit. Let \(N\) be the total bit length of the circuit description and the binary encoding of \(K\). Malformed inputs and inputs outside the promise have no correctness requirement. The bound \(K\) varies with the input and may be exponential in \(w\); it is not a universal constant.

A state of the witness register is a density matrix \(\rho\) on \(\mathbb C^{2^w}\): a Hermitian positive semidefinite matrix of trace one. Hermitian means \(\rho=\rho^\dagger\), and positive semidefinite means \(v^\dagger\rho v\ge0\) for every complex vector \(v\). With \(\Pi_1\) the projector onto output one, define \[A_V=(I\otimes\langle0^a|)V^\dagger\Pi_1V(I\otimes|0^a\rangle).\] It satisfies \(0\preceq A_V\preceq I\) and \(\Pr[V\text{ accepts }\rho]=\operatorname{Tr}(A_V\rho)\). Its \(2^w\) eigenvalues lie in \([0,1]\). For \(a\in[0,1]\), \(D_a(V)=\operatorname{rank}\mathbf1_{[a,1]}(A_V)\): the dimension of the span of eigenvectors with eigenvalue at least \(a\). Eigenvalues are counted with multiplicity, including equality at the threshold. This is neither the number of individual normalized states nor the dimension of an arbitrarily chosen accepting basis. There are continuously many possible witnesses, but the spectral count is a finite integer.

Since \(D_{1/3}\ge D_{2/3}\) and \(K>0\), the two promised cases are disjoint. The YES bound means \(D_{1/3}\le\lfloor K/2\rfloor\). Eigenvalues strictly between \(1/3\) and \(2/3\) are allowed; the promise does not say the entire spectrum avoids this interval. They contribute to the larger count, but not the smaller one. The uncomplemented buffered counting problem labels \(D_{2/3}\ge K\) as YES and \(D_{1/3}\le K/2\) as NO. Complementation swaps these two sets and retains the promise; it does not replace \(A_V\) by \(I-A_V\) or count all eigenvalues below a single threshold.

For \(\mathrm{QMA}(2)\), there must exist one deterministic classical polynomial-time circuit generator and a fixed polynomial \(p\) such that, on every input \(x=(V,K)\) of length \(N\), it produces a circuit \(W_x\) with at most \(p(N)\) gates and private zero-initialized ancilla qubits. Two additional witness registers \(R_1,R_2\) each have at most \(p(N)\) qubits. Their supplied joint state must have the form \(\rho_1\otimes\rho_2\); each factor may itself be mixed and internally entangled, with arbitrary complex entries and no efficient-preparation requirement. The verifier may act jointly on the two registers and its ancillas, using the gate convention above, and measures a final output bit. Write its acceptance probability as \(p_x(\rho_1,\rho_2)\). The requirements are \[x\in L_{\mathrm{yes}}\Rightarrow\exists\rho_1,\rho_2:\ p_x(\rho_1,\rho_2)\ge2/3,\] \[x\in L_{\mathrm{no}}\Rightarrow\forall\rho_1,\rho_2:\ p_x(\rho_1,\rho_2)\le1/3.\] Product witnesses suffice to specify soundness; by linearity the same bound then holds for every separable mixture of products. Soundness is not required against arbitrary entangled states across the two supplied registers. There are no additional messages, advice or oracle calls. Polynomial running time is measured in \(N\), including the length of \(K\), not in its numerical value or in \(2^w\). The spectral count describes the problem; no eigenbasis is supplied to the verifier.
cards.answer_criterion: Provide a complete Lean-checked proof that this exact promise pair belongs to \(\mathrm{QMA}(2)\), or a complete Lean-checked proof that it does not. An affirmative answer must supply a uniform verifier with polynomial resources and prove both quantified acceptance conditions for all promised circuit inputs and all allowed witnesses. A negative answer must rule out every such verifier, rather than one proposed protocol. A result for a single spectral threshold, a verifier given an eigenbasis, exponentially large witnesses, entangled witnesses without the stated product restriction, or a model with interaction or an oracle does not establish the claim. Quantum-oracle separations alone do not give an unrelativized nonmembership theorem. This is an exact class-membership question; the fixed counting promise and verifier error are part of the model, not a request to estimate a number to additive precision.

context_blocks.text: The imported card broadly asked for the complexity of quantum approximate counting. The source separately asks whether its complement is in QMA(2). On 16 September 2026 the user selected that narrower target and authorized repairing the brief single-threshold description to the standard version with two separated spectral thresholds. This scope change is explicit; the broad classification programme is not claimed complete.

An ordinary quantum witness can demonstrate the existence of a state that a verifier accepts. Approximate counting asks how large the accepting eigenspace is. The selected complement instead asks for efficient verification that even the lower-threshold accepting space is small.

Definition 17 of the ITCS 2026 paper uses two thresholds \(b<a\) separated by at least an inverse polynomial, and allows a returned estimate between \((1-\varepsilon)D_a\) and \((1+\varepsilon)D_b\). The present decision formulation fixes the spectral thresholds to \(2/3\) and \(1/3\) and keeps the original source's factor-two count gap. It does not assume an absence of eigenvalues between the thresholds.

The two witnesses in QMA(2) are separate resources. They may be compared by a joint quantum verifier, but cannot arrive entangled with one another. The requested membership is therefore different from supplying one larger arbitrary witness, and from asking two provers to participate in an interactive protocol.

The ITCS 2026 authors prove a quantum-oracle separation between quantum approximate counting and quantum verification with a QMA oracle, ruling out a black-box analogue of the classical approximate-counting algorithm in that setting. Their statement concerns an additional oracle and a different verification model. It does not settle this ordinary two-witness complement question.

The phrase quantum approximate counting also occurs for counting marked inputs of a classical Boolean oracle using quantum queries, or for estimating the acceptance probability of a computation with no witness. The cited paper explicitly distinguishes those tasks from counting the accepting eigenspace of a quantum verifier.

cards.title: Oracle separation of BQP from efficient-prover interactive proofs
cards.formal: Does there exist a classical Boolean oracle A and a language \(\mathrm{L}\subseteq \{0,1\}\)* such that \(\mathrm{L}\in \mathrm{BQP}^{A}\) but \(\mathrm{L}\notin \mathrm{IP}_{\mathrm{BQP}}^{A}\), where \(\mathrm{IP}_{\mathrm{BQP}}^{A}\) requires a polynomial-time quantum honest prover and classical interaction with a polynomial-time classical verifier?
cards.why: Distinguishes the existence of a classical interactive proof from the ability of an efficient quantum device to carry out its honest strategy. It tests whether verification can match the computational resources of the device while retaining soundness against all cheating provers.
cards.status_note: Source Problems 7–8 and the April 2026 paper checked; subsequent-work searches through 11 September 2026 located no resolution of the stated oracle question. The MIP containment changes the prover model and is recorded as preprint progress. This is a formulation and source review, not an exhaustive literature or proof audit.

cards.definitions: An oracle is an arbitrary fixed Boolean function \(A:\{0,1\}*\to \{0,1\}\); it need not be computable. All languages are subsets of \(\{0,1\}\)*, and n is the input length. A classical oracle call supplies one string z and returns \(A(z)\). Quantum access uses the unitary |\(z,b\rangle \mapsto |z,b\oplus A(z)\rangle\), extended linearly to superpositions of strings of a given length. Query registers and the work required to prepare them count toward the computation bound. No quantum-valued oracle, advice string or promise on inputs is supplied. \(\mathrm{BQP}^{A}\) consists of languages decided by one uniform quantum algorithm with polynomial total running time, oracle calls and qubits. On every yes input it accepts with probability at least \(2/3\), and on every no input with probability at most \(1/3\). One standard machine convention uses Hadamard \(H=(1/\sqrt{2})[[1,1],[1,- 1]], T=diag(1,e^{i\pi /4})\) and CNOT |\(a,b\rangle \mapsto |a,a\oplus b\rangle\) gates, zero-initialized auxiliary qubits, computational-basis measurements and polynomial-time classical control. Circuit descriptions are generated uniformly in polynomial time; there is no nonuniform advice. Probabilities are over measurements and any internal random bits. An \(\mathrm{IP}^{A}\) protocol has one classical probabilistic polynomial-time verifier and one prover, exchanging only classical bit strings. The verifier has private fair random bits and classical access to A. Its total computation, random bits, communication and number of rounds are bounded by a polynomial in n, with no predetermined universal degree. Completeness requires one honest prover strategy that makes the verifier accept with probability at least \(2/3\) on every yes input. Soundness requires acceptance probability at most \(1/3\) on every no input against every prover strategy, including computationally unbounded strategies. The prover knows the common input and oracle but not the verifier’s unrevealed private coins; its messages can depend on its conversation history. There is no trusted setup or shared entanglement. Prover efficiency is unrestricted in \(\mathrm{IP}^{A}\). Probabilities include verifier randomness and any randomness or measurements of the prover. \(\mathrm{IP}_{\mathrm{BQP}}^{A}\) is the subclass of \(\mathrm{BQP}^{A}\) whose languages admit such an \(\mathrm{IP}^{A}\) protocol with one uniform quantum polynomial-time oracle algorithm as the honest prover. Its total local work and oracle queries across all rounds are polynomial in n, under the same quantum access convention as \(\mathrm{BQP}^{A}\). Only the honest prover is restricted: soundness still quantifies over all computationally unbounded cheating strategies. Polynomial bounds and machines may depend on A and the language, but must work for all input lengths; they cannot depend on the particular input through advice.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove the existence of one oracle A and \(\mathrm{BQP}^{A}\) language L for which no classical interactive proof has an honest quantum polynomial-time oracle prover. Alternatively, prove \(\mathrm{BQP}^{A}=\mathrm{IP}_{\mathrm{BQP}}^{A}\) for every classical Boolean oracle A. All negative instances must rule out arbitrary polynomial bounds on rounds and honest-prover work, and the positive alternative must retain soundness against unbounded cheating provers.

context_blocks.title: Can a classical verifier trust a quantum computation?
context_blocks.text: A proof of a quantum answer is useful for verification by a classical computer only if the honest quantum device can actually provide it. An interactive proof with an unrestricted prover does not guarantee this. This card asks whether some oracle world separates efficient quantum computation from verification with an efficient quantum honest prover.

context_blocks.title: The same function, different query access
context_blocks.text: The quantum computation may query a superposition, whereas the verifier queries one ordinary string at a time. The oracle function itself is identical for both. Some oracle languages are easy for both: for \(\mathrm{L}=\{x:A(x)=1\}\), the verifier simply queries x. The question requires a language whose quantum computation cannot be certified by the stated interaction.

context_blocks.title: Two distinct single-prover questions
context_blocks.text: For every oracle, \(\mathrm{IP}_{\mathrm{BQP}}^{A}\subseteq \mathrm{BQP}^{A}\) and \(\mathrm{IP}_{\mathrm{BQP}}^{A}\subseteq \mathrm{IP}^{A}\) by definition. An oracle separation of BQP from unrestricted-prover IP therefore also separates BQP from \(\mathrm{IP}_{\mathrm{BQP}}\). The efficient-honest-prover separation is a weaker demand: an unrestricted prover might still verify that language. The two cards record this implication without identifying the targets.

context_blocks.title: Unbounded cheating is part of the guarantee
context_blocks.text: The prover can lie in any computationally possible way, even with unlimited computation. Restricting only a dishonest prover to efficient strategies would instead describe a computationally sound argument. Cryptographic verification protocols with that guarantee do not establish the information-theoretic IP containment requested here.

cards.definitions: For bits \(s,x_{1},\ldots ,x_{n}\in \{0,1\}\), FANOUT\(_{n}|s,x_{1},\ldots ,x_{n}\rangle =|s,s\oplus x_{1},\ldots ,s\oplus x_{n}\rangle\), extended linearly to all states; ⊕ is addition modulo two. A permitted circuit acts on \(n+1+a(n)\) qubits for some finite \(a(n)\ge 0\). Its gates are arbitrary one-qubit unitary matrices over \(\mathbb{C}\) and generalized Toffoli gates: for any \(k\ge 1\) distinct controls and a distinct target, |\(z_{1},\ldots ,z_{k},t\rangle\) maps to |\(z_{1},\ldots ,z_{k},t\oplus (z_{1}\cdots z_{k})\rangle\). Each layer contains gates on disjoint sets of qubits, and depth is the number of layers. Gates may connect any qubits; fanout gates, measurements, postselection and classical feed-forward are not additional primitives. Exact implementation means that for some global phase \(e^{i\varphi _{n}}\), independent of the input state \(\psi , C_{n}(|\psi \rangle \otimes |0\rangle ^{\otimes}a(n))=e^{i\varphi _{n}}\)(FANOUT\(_{n}|\psi \rangle\))⊗|\(0\rangle ^{\otimes}a(n)\) for every unit vector \(\psi\) in \((\mathbb{C} ^{2})^{\otimes}(n+1)\). The ancillas must return to zero, as in the source’s implementation definition. Gate count, ancilla count and gate arities may grow arbitrarily with n but must be finite at each n. The family is nonuniform: there is no required circuit-generation algorithm or finite gate alphabet. The one depth bound d must work for all n. QAC0 usually adds a polynomial-size bound; this question explicitly drops it.
cards.answer_criterion: Construct an exact clean-ancilla implementation with a depth bound independent of n, or prove that no such bound exists even when size, ancilla count and Toffoli arity are unrestricted. An approximation with arbitrarily small nonzero error, a lower bound only for polynomial-size circuits, or a bound for one fixed small depth does not settle this formulation.

context_blocks.title: Fanout is a coherent controlled operation
context_blocks.text: On a basis input, the control flips every target when it is one and leaves them unchanged when it is zero. The same circuit must act correctly on superpositions, including inputs entangled with other systems. Agreement only on measured classical outputs would be weaker.

context_blocks.title: This operation does not clone an arbitrary quantum state
context_blocks.text: For example, applying two-target fanout to |+⟩|\(00\rangle\) yields \((|000\rangle +|111\rangle )/\sqrt{2}\). It does not yield three independent copies of |+⟩. The target is therefore compatible with the distinction between coherent basis fanout and cloning.

context_blocks.title: Only depth is restricted

The question permits enormous circuits and arbitrarily many zero-initialized ancillas. A negative answer would therefore be a structural limitation of constant depth, beyond ordinary polynomial-size lower bounds.

cards.definitions: Write \(n=|x|\). QMA consists of promise problems whose YES instances have polynomial-qubit quantum witnesses accepted by a uniform polynomial-time quantum verifier with probability at least \(2/3\), while every witness on a NO instance is accepted with probability at most \(1/3\). In the requested game, a classical verifier samples correlated questions, sends one to each of r noncommunicating provers, receives one classical answer from each, and decides acceptance in polynomial time. The provers may share entanglement prepared before the questions arrive. For each L, r and an exponent a are fixed independently of n, and every individual message has at most \(O((\log (n+2))^{a})\) bits. Honest efficiency includes a uniform quantum polynomial-time setup algorithm which, given x and polynomially many copies of a polynomial-qubit state \(\psi _{x}\), prepares the shared state, followed by uniform quantum polynomial-time local response algorithms. The state \(\psi _{x}\) is an existential witness depending on x, not a supplied circuit for preparing it. Soundness quantifies over arbitrary local quantum strategies with arbitrary finite-dimensional shared entanglement; only communication after separation is forbidden. There is no promise on inputs outside \(\mathrm{L}_{\mathrm{yes}}\cup \mathrm{L}_{no}\). The fixed gap can be amplified by a constant number of repetitions without changing the polylogarithmic communication scale. The question imposes no logarithmic bound on the verifier’s total random bits and no additional cryptographic assumption.
cards.answer_criterion: Construct the stated protocol for every QMA promise problem, proving both witness-assisted honest efficiency and soundness against unrestricted entangled provers; or prove that at least one QMA promise problem has no such protocol. A protocol with polynomial-length answers, or one whose honest entanglement cannot be prepared efficiently from a polynomial witness, does not meet this target.

cards.definitions: A promise problem is a pair \((\mathrm{L}_{\mathrm{yes}},\mathrm{L}_{no})\) of disjoint sets of finite binary strings, with no required answer outside their union. Membership in \(StoqMA(a,b)\) means there is a deterministic polynomial-time procedure which, given x of length n, produces a verification circuit \(V_{x}\) on \(m(n)+r(n)+s(n)\) qubits, all counts polynomially bounded in n. Its initial state is |\(w\rangle \otimes |0\rangle ^{\otimes r}\otimes |+\rangle ^{\otimes s}\), where |+⟩=\((|0\rangle +|1\rangle )/\sqrt{2}\) and the m-qubit witness has norm one. The circuit uses only classical reversible gates: NOT flips a bit, CNOT flips its target if its control is one, and Toffoli flips its target if both controls are one. These gates act linearly on computational-basis states. There are no intermediate measurements or arbitrary quantum gates. At the end a designated output qubit is measured in the \(\{|+\rangle ,|- \rangle\}\) basis, with |−⟩=\((|0\rangle - |1\rangle )/\sqrt{2}\), and outcome + means acceptance. Its acceptance probability is the squared norm after projection onto |+⟩ on that qubit. If \(x\in \mathrm{L}_{\mathrm{yes}}\), some witness with real nonnegative computational-basis amplitudes must be accepted with probability at least \(a(n)\). If \(x\in \mathrm{L}_{no}\), every normalized witness, including arbitrary complex amplitudes, must be accepted with probability at most \(b(n)\). The source proves that a maximizing witness can be chosen nonnegative. Efficient threshold computability is understood in the standard precision sense: their values can be approximated within \(2^{- t}\) in time polynomial in \(n+t\). The inverse-polynomial gap permits this conventional representation. Class containment quantifies over promise problems and asserts existence of new uniform verifiers; it does not demand a blackbox compiler acting on an arbitrary verifier description. Polynomial bounds of the new verifier may depend on the original verifier, q and \(\ell\). Soundness approaches \(1/2\) from above, not zero; the requested improvement is relative to the stoquastic acceptance baseline.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove the containment for every admissible a,b and \(\ell\), or refute this universally quantified amplification statement. A positive answer must achieve both exponentially small completeness error and exponentially small excess soundness above \(1/2\) while retaining the allowed gates, initial ancillas and final measurement. Soundness-only repetition, perfect-completeness special cases, extra destructive-interference gates, or additional unentangled provers do not establish the claim.

cards.definitions: The matrix \(H=H^*\) is fixed, not part of a circuit input. Its entries are algebraic complex numbers, specified by finite integer-polynomial and isolating-region descriptions that may be hardcoded into an algorithm depending on \(H\). A circuit has \(N\ge1\) qubits initialized to an explicitly supplied computational-basis string \(b\in\{0,1\}^N\). Each gate chooses an ordered pair of distinct qubits and applies \(\exp(-itH)\) on that pair for a signed rational time \(t\); negative times give exact inverse evolution. There are no free single-qubit gates or intermediate measurements. At the end all qubits are measured in the computational basis, defining a probability distribution \(p_C\) on \(\{0,1\}^N\). The input explicitly lists the initial bits, gate sequence, ordered wire indices and rational numerators and positive denominators in binary. It also includes a unary integer \(B\ge1\) with \(|t|\le B\) for every gate. Let \(L\) be the full bit encoding length. This charges enough description length for polynomial physical evolution time, as required by the source model. The simulation branch requires a single uniform randomized Turing machine for this fixed \(H\), taking \(C\) and a binary rational \(0<\varepsilon<1\), that halts on every random tape within a fixed polynomial in \(L+\lceil1/\varepsilon\rceil+\operatorname{len}(\varepsilon)\) and outputs a string with distribution \(s_C\) satisfying \(\tfrac12\sum_z|s_C(z)-p_C(z)|\le\varepsilon\). It uses independent fair coins and no oracle or advice. Define \(\operatorname{Post}(H)\) as follows. For a language \(K\subseteq\{0,1\}^*\), a uniform deterministic polynomial-time compiler maps each input \(x\) to such a circuit \(C_x\), a designated output bit, and a disjoint list of postselection bits with prescribed values. There is a polynomial \(p\) such that the prescribed event has probability at least \(2^{-p(|x|)}\) on every input. Conditional on it, the output is 1 with probability at least \(2/3\) for \(x\in K\) and at most \(1/3\) otherwise. Circuit descriptions, including the unary time bound, have polynomial length in \(|x|\). The postselection list and values may depend on the input through the compiler. PP consists of languages for which a uniform polynomial-time fair-coin Turing machine accepts with probability strictly greater than \(1/2\) on members and at most \(1/2\) on nonmembers. The second branch is the source’s postselected-computation criterion expressed via PP; the algebraic-entry, accuracy and exponentially bounded postselection conventions are explicit editorial choices. The alternatives need not be disjoint. No commutativity promise is imposed on \(H\).
cards.answer_criterion: Provide a Lean proof of the disjunction for every allowed fixed interaction, or a Lean counterexample interaction for which both branches fail. The proof must use the supplied finite-precision sampling and uniform postselection conventions. A classification with free local gates, arbitrary analog reductions, a commutativity promise or a different sampling error does not automatically settle this variant.

cards.title: Martin’s conjecture
cards.formal: Assume \(\mathsf{ZF}+\mathsf{DC}+\mathsf{AD}\). Is the following conjunction true for all total Turing-invariant functions \(f:2^{\omega}\to2^{\omega}\)? Part I: every such \(f\) is constant in Turing degree on a cone or computes its input on a cone. Part II: the relation \(\leq_M\) of Turing reducibility on a cone prewellorders the set \(\mathcal F\) of all such functions above the identity on a cone, and for every \(f\in\mathcal F\), its pointwise Turing jump \(f'\) has rank exactly \(\operatorname{rank}_M(f)+1\) in that same prewellorder. All functions, cones, ordinals and quantifiers are interpreted within the stated set-theoretic universe.
cards.definitions:
Write \(\omega=\{0,1,2,\ldots\}\) and \(2^{\omega}=\{x:\omega\to\{0,1\}\}\). Such a real is identified with the subset \(\{n:x(n)=1\}\) of \(\omega\). Fix an acceptable effective enumeration \((\Phi_e)_{e\in\omega}\) of ordinary oracle Turing programs with natural-number inputs and outputs. The oracle answers membership queries in a real. Define \(x\leq_T y\) to mean that some index \(e\) satisfies \(\Phi_e^y(n)\downarrow=x(n)\) for every \(n\in\omega\), with no time bound. The single index computes the entire real, and may depend on \(x,y\). Define \(x\equiv_T y\) by mutual reducibility. A Turing degree is an equivalence class for \(\equiv_T\). The jump \(y'\) is the characteristic real of \(\{e:\Phi_e^y(e)\text{ halts}\}\). Any acceptable effective numbering gives the same induced operation on degrees.

A total function \(f:2^{\omega}\to2^{\omega}\) is Turing-invariant when \(\forall x,y:\ x\equiv_T y\Rightarrow f(x)\equiv_T f(y)\). No computability, measurability, Borel definability, order preservation or uniform production of reduction indices is required. The quantifiers concern functions on reals with this invariance property; no choice of a representative from every Turing degree is assumed.

For \(a\in2^{\omega}\), the cone with base \(a\) is \(C_a=\{x\in2^{\omega}:a\leq_T x\}\). Being constant in degree on a cone means
\[\exists a,b\in2^{\omega}\;\forall x\in C_a:\ f(x)\equiv_T b.\]
Being above the identity on a cone means
\[\exists a\in2^{\omega}\;\forall x\in C_a:\ x\leq_T f(x).\]
The base may depend on \(f\). Constancy is equality of degrees, not literal equality of output reals. A cone requirement holds for every real in that cone, not merely infinitely many reals or a set of full ordinary Lebesgue measure.

For invariant \(f,g\), define
\[f\leq_M g\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad\exists a\in2^{\omega}\;\forall x\in C_a:\ f(x)\leq_T g(x).\]
The base may depend on both functions; no single base must work for all comparisons. Set \(f\equiv_M g\) when both \(f\leq_M g\) and \(g\leq_M f\). Let \(\mathrm{id}(x)=x\) and \(\mathcal F=\{f:2^{\omega}\to2^{\omega}: f\text{ is Turing-invariant and }\mathrm{id}\leq_M f\}\). The prewellorder clause means that \(\leq_M\) is reflexive, transitive and total on \(\mathcal F\), and that the induced order on the set \(\mathcal F/{\equiv_M}\) is a well-order: every nonempty subset of that quotient has a least member. Its strict order is \([g]<[f]\) when \(g\leq_M f\) and \(f\not\leq_M g\). When this clause holds, \(\operatorname{rank}_M(f)\) is the ordinal order type of the quotient classes strictly below \([f]\), with its least class having rank zero. The pointwise jump is \(f'(x)=(f(x))'\). The \(+1\) in Part II is ordinal successor, and the rank is computed in the full quotient above the identity, not a selected definable subclass.

The background \(\mathsf{ZF}\) is Zermelo–Fraenkel set theory without the axiom of choice. Full dependent choice \(\mathsf{DC}\) asserts that for every nonempty set \(S\), every relation \(R\subseteq S\times S\) with \(\forall s\in S\;\exists t\in S:\ sRt\), and every \(s_0\in S\), there is a sequence \((s_n)_{n\in\omega}\) starting at \(s_0\) with \(s_nRs_{n+1}\) for all \(n\). The axiom of determinacy \(\mathsf{AD}\) asserts that for every set \(W\subseteq\omega^{\omega}\), the following perfect-information game is determined. Players I and II alternate choosing natural numbers, with I moving at even-numbered stages starting at zero; I wins exactly when the resulting sequence belongs to \(W\). A strategy assigns a next move to every finite history at that player’s turn, and is winning if every infinite play compatible with it is won by that player. Determined means that one player has such a winning strategy. No regularity condition is imposed on \(W\). These are internal set-theoretic axioms; the full axiom of choice is not added to them.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete, mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of both parts of the conjunction under \(\mathsf{ZF}+\mathsf{DC}+\mathsf{AD}\), or a refutation of at least one part under that same background. A refutation of Part I must establish the existence of an invariant function that is neither constant in degree on any cone nor above the identity on any cone. A refutation of Part II must establish failure of the stated full prewellorder or, when that prewellorder exists, failure of the exact jump-successor clause. A result only for uniformly invariant, Borel, regressive or order-preserving functions does not prove the full conjunction. Counterexamples obtained with the full axiom of choice do not refute the stated determinacy version. The Lean formalization must represent the set-theoretic background faithfully, for example through an internal set universe and its satisfaction relation, with all reals and functions interpreted there; importing ambient choice into that universe and deriving a contradiction with determinacy is not a proof of this target. No unproved classification or uniformity principle may be substituted for a required part.
cards.why: Turing degrees encode relative computational power and have a highly non-linear structure. Martin’s conjecture asks whether invariance under mutual computability nevertheless forces every nontrivial operation into an ordered hierarchy once behaviour is compared on cones under determinacy. It gives a precise structural target behind the observed regularity of many degree operators, and connects computability with descriptive set theory and analogous hierarchies of logical strength.

importance.reason: A flagship conjecture about the global structure of Turing degrees and the classification of invariant computational operations.

context_blocks.text: A function can assign different output reals to equivalent inputs while still inducing a well-defined operation on degrees. This is the invariance required here. The operation itself need not be computable: the Turing jump is a central example. The conjecture concerns the organization of such operations rather than an algorithm for listing or calculating their values.

The two parts have separate content. Part I is a dichotomy for all invariant functions. Part II concerns the full collection already above the identity and asserts both a well-order after identifying cone-equivalent functions and an exact successor rule. In particular, strict increase under the jump alone is weaker than the assertion that its rank is the next ordinal. No continuity rule at limit ordinals is included in that successor clause.

Determinacy gives a zero-one law for invariant sets: each contains a cone or its complement contains one. Martin measure assigns these cases values one and zero. Thus the phrase almost everywhere in the cited formulation means on a Turing cone. It does not refer to the usual probability measure from independent bits, and a comparison base need not work for unrelated functions.

Uniform invariance requires one map \(u:\omega^2\to\omega^2\) that converts any pair of indices witnessing \(x\equiv_T y\) into a pair witnessing \(f(x)\equiv_T f(y)\), independently of the reals. Even this index map is not required to be computable in the survey’s definition. Steel and Slaman–Steel establish the two parts for the uniform subclass. Ordinary invariance does not supply such a map.

The regressive case is already settled: if invariant \(f\) satisfies \(f(x)\leq_T x\) on a cone, then on a cone it is constant in degree or equivalent to the identity. Order preservation is a different restriction, namely \(x\leq_T y\Rightarrow f(x)\leq_T f(y)\). The saved full target includes neither restriction. Earlier extraction of only a regressive subcase was corrected before this audit; this review preserves the full conjecture.

Lutz and Siskind prove Part I for all order-preserving functions and for all measure-preserving invariant functions. Here the latter means \(\forall a\;\exists b\;\forall x\geq_T b:\ a\leq_T f(x)\), with the base allowed to depend on the fixed target degree. Their Theorem 3.7 and Theorem 4.8 use determinacy and dependent choice for reals, which follow from this card’s stronger fixed background. The older Part II theorem for order-preserving functions retains a Borel restriction; Borel means inverse images of open sets belong to the sigma algebra generated by the finite-prefix open sets of Cantor space.

The background cannot be replaced by \(\mathsf{ZFC}\). Lutz and Siskind’s §6.4 supplies choice-based counterexamples, including an invariant order-preserving function that is neither constant nor above the identity on a cone. These do not satisfy the determinacy setting. A faithful proof-assistant treatment must keep that internal set universe distinct from any ambient use of choice.

The author erratum to the Marks–Slaman–Steel survey withdraws Theorem 1.8, an asserted equivalence whose argument fails at limit ordinals. This audit therefore uses the actual two-part conjecture and checked restricted theorems, without importing the withdrawn equivalence as a fact about arbitrary invariant Borel functions.

cards.title: Kolmogorov–Loveland randomness versus Martin-Löf randomness
cards.formal:
Is every Kolmogorov–Loveland random infinite binary sequence Martin-Löf random for the fair-coin product measure? In the precise model below, determine whether
\[\forall X\in\{0,1\}^{\mathbb N},\qquad
\operatorname{KLR}(X)\Longrightarrow\operatorname{MLR}(X).\]
The reverse implication is known, so this is equivalently equality of the two randomness classes. Betting strategies may choose fresh coordinates adaptively, need not visit every coordinate, and are ordinary partial computable procedures without an oracle.
cards.definitions:
Space and measure. Let \(\mathbb N=\{0,1,2,\ldots\}\). Cantor space \(2^{\mathbb N}=\{0,1\}^{\mathbb N}\) consists of all functions \(X:\mathbb N\to\{0,1\}\), including noncomputable ones. Let \(2^{<\mathbb N}\) be the finite binary strings. For a string \(\sigma\), its length is \(|\sigma|\), and its cylinder is
\[[\sigma]=\{X:\ X(i)=\sigma(i)\text{ for all }i<|\sigma|\}.\]
The fair-coin product probability measure \(\mu\) makes coordinates independent and assigns \(\mu([\sigma])=2^{-|\sigma|}\). No bias, alternative measure or oracle relativization is involved.

Martin-Löf tests. A uniformly effectively open family is specified by one ordinary Turing program enumerating a set \(W\subseteq\mathbb N_{\ge1}\times2^{<\mathbb N}\). Put
\[U_k=\bigcup_{(k,\sigma)\in W}[\sigma].\]
It is a Martin-Löf test when \(\mu(U_k)\le2^{-k}\) for every \(k\ge1\). This condition concerns the measure of the union, not the sum of cylinder measures when cylinders overlap. Repetitions in an enumeration are harmless, no disjointness or prefix-free presentation is required, and levels need not be nested. The measure bound is a mathematical condition on a test; the enumerating program is not required to certify it or compute the exact measure. Define
\[\operatorname{MLR}(X)\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
\text{for every Martin-Löf test }(U_k)_{k\ge1},\quad X\notin\bigcap_{k\ge1}U_k.\]
Uniform enumeration across all levels is mandatory.

Histories and betting procedures. A history is a finite ordered list
\[h=((j_0,a_0),\ldots,(j_{s-1},a_{s-1}))\]
with distinct \(j_i\in\mathbb N\) and \(a_i\in\{0,1\}\). It records precisely the coordinates already queried and their observed values, in query order. A strategy is a deterministic partial computable function \(S\) which, on such a history, either fails to return an action or returns
\[S(h)=(j,q),\qquad j\notin\{j_0,\ldots,j_{s-1}\},\quad q\in\mathbb Q\cap[0,2].\]
Every returned action on a valid history must meet these conditions. Computability means a finite Turing-machine program operating on an effective finite encoding of this list, natural coordinates, and rational numerator/positive-denominator pairs. These encodings carry no resource bound. The program receives only the history; it cannot inspect any further bit of \(X\) before choosing its action, use an oracle, or use an uncomputable real parameter. Internal deterministic work and previously computed data can be recovered from the history and program. The equivalent history of observed bit values alone suffices when the query coordinates are reconstructed by rerunning that same strategy.

Run and capital. Start at empty history with capital \(C_0^S(X)=1\). If \(S(h_s)=(j_s,q_s)\) returns, reveal \(a_s=X(j_s)\), append \((j_s,a_s)\), and update
\[C_{s+1}^S(X)=\begin{cases}
C_s^S(X)q_s,&a_s=0,\\
C_s^S(X)(2-q_s),&a_s=1.
\end{cases}\]
The two possible multipliers average to one, so the bet is fair on a fresh unbiased bit. Capital is always nonnegative, with no borrowing or outside deposits; zero capital remains zero. The choice \(q_s=1\) reads a bit without risking capital. Coordinates may be arbitrarily large and need not increase. They cannot repeat, including after a zero wager. There is no requirement to query every coordinate even on an infinite run.

If the next computation diverges or returns no action, the run has no further completed bets and earns no further capital. Computation time itself does not increase capital. There are no time or space bounds. Let \(D_S(X)\subseteq\mathbb N\) be the finite or infinite initial segment of completed-bet counts, including zero. The strategy succeeds precisely when
\[\forall K\in\mathbb N\ \exists s\in D_S(X):\quad C_s^S(X)>K.\]
This is unbounded supremum of capital, not a requirement that capital converge to infinity, grow at a computable rate, or exceed a single fixed threshold.

Kolmogorov–Loveland randomness. Let \(\mathcal S\) be the class of all strategies just specified. Define
\[\operatorname{KLR}(X)\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
\forall S\in\mathcal S\ \exists K\in\mathbb N\ \forall s\in D_S(X):\quad C_s^S(X)\le K.\]
The bound may depend on both \(S\) and \(X\), and no algorithm producing those bounds is required. Rational stakes and unit initial capital give the standard notion. Replacing partial computability by total computability gives the same randomness class, but requiring every coordinate to be visited is a separate condition and is not imposed here.
cards.answer_criterion:
Give a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of the stated implication or its negation, with these exact measure, effectiveness and betting conventions.

A positive answer must hold for every infinite binary sequence and every uniformly effective Martin-Löf test. Equivalently, prove that for each \(X\) failing some Martin-Löf test there exists an admissible computable strategy with unbounded capital on \(X\). That existential strategy may depend on \(X\); it must still be a finite oracle-free program. A uniform conversion of tests to a finite universal family of strategies is not an additional requirement.

A negative answer must prove the existence of one sequence \(X\) and one Martin-Löf test \((U_k)_{k\ge1}\) such that
\[X\in\bigcap_{k\ge1}U_k\qquad\text{and}\qquad
\forall S\in\mathcal S\ \exists K\in\mathbb N\ \forall s\in D_S(X):\ C_s^S(X)\le K.\]
The same sequence must satisfy every test level and defeat every allowed strategy. A nonconstructive existence proof qualifies; an algorithm computing the bits of \(X\) is not required. Different sequences for different levels or strategies, a separation for fixed query orders, a generalized betting game, or a frequency-only stochasticity result does not settle the full target. Finite simulations or a one-sided known implication are insufficient.
cards.why: Determines whether adaptive computable fair betting detects every effective measure-theoretic failure of randomness in an individual infinite sequence. Equality or separation would connect two foundational ways to formalize unpredictability.

context_blocks.text: Martin-Löf randomness and betting randomness concern individual infinite objects. Effective tests describe events of arbitrarily small fair-coin probability, while a gambler uses observed bits to determine future bets. Neither definition is a confidence score for a finite sample. Every finite binary string can occur at the start of a Martin-Löf random sequence, so a finite unusual-looking prefix alone cannot settle membership in either class.

Adaptivity changes the information available to a strategy. It may inspect coordinate 100, then choose between coordinates 3 and 7 based on that value. Reading a bit with no money at risk still reveals it and makes it unavailable for later betting. The strategy must choose its next fresh position and wager using only its current history; otherwise it could exploit information it has not legitimately obtained.

The established implications are \(\operatorname{MLR}\subseteq\operatorname{KLR}\subseteq\operatorname{CR}\), where computable randomness \(\operatorname{CR}\) rules out successful total computable fair gamblers that read bits in their original order. The first inclusion is the known direction; the card asks whether it is equality. Kolmogorov–Loveland stochasticity instead controls limiting frequencies of adaptively selected bits and is a different, weaker requirement than defeating all fair betting strategies.

Partiality must be separated from which bits are eventually visited. The standard theory permits partial computations, and using total nonmonotonic procedures yields the same randomness class. However, a total procedure can still leave infinitely many coordinates unseen. Requiring a total strategy to visit every coordinate changes its power: the classical source shows that such a strategy can be matched by a monotonic gambler on every sequence where it succeeds.

Kastermans and Lempp separate Martin-Löf randomness from randomness against predetermined computable permutation orders, and against the more general predetermined computable injective orders. A permutation visits every position; an injection may omit positions. In both cases the query order is fixed independently of revealed bit values. These separations therefore do not decide what fully adaptive strategies can detect.

Merkle, Miller, Nies, Reimann and Stephan show that a Kolmogorov–Loveland random sequence has Martin-Löf random subsequences on computable sets of coordinates with densities arbitrarily close to one. Their Theorem 12 says that splitting at any infinite co-infinite computable set leaves at least one Martin-Löf random part. These are substantial proximity results, but randomness of a subsequence does not establish randomness of the whole interleaving.

Petrović’s universal-pair result concerns a generalized half-betting game. Such games allow richer computable partitions of the remaining possible sequences than asking for the value of one fresh coordinate. A pair of generalized strategies can cover all failures of Martin-Löf randomness, but this theorem does not turn them into strategies in the more restricted query model of the card.

The 2025 open-set theorem is stronger than merely a statement about one finite family: it assigns bounds to all Kolmogorov–Loveland strategies and finds arbitrarily small effective open sets, each containing a sequence staying below every strategy’s bound. The witnessing sequence can depend on the open-set level. The result does not give one such sequence in every level of a single Martin-Löf test, and the paper leaves equality open.

The decisive quantifiers concern one infinite sequence at a time. For a negative answer, that sequence must fail an effective test and simultaneously evade every permitted computable gambler. For a positive answer, a successful gambler may be different for different nonrandom sequences. The mathematical question does not require one fixed gambler, a fixed finite family, or uniform speed of winning.

The 2025 open-set theorem is stronger than merely a statement about one finite family: it assigns bounds to all Kolmogorov–Loveland strategies and finds arbitrarily small effective open sets, each containing a sequence staying below every strategy’s bound. The witnessing sequence can depend on the open-set level. The result does not give one such sequence in every level of a single Martin-Löf test, and the paper leaves equality open.

The decisive quantifiers concern one infinite sequence at a time. For a negative answer, that sequence must fail an effective test and simultaneously evade every permitted computable gambler. For a positive answer, a successful gambler may be different for different nonrandom sequences. The mathematical question does not require one fixed gambler, a fixed finite family, or uniform speed of winning.

benchmark_focus.reason: A defining open question linking computability, adaptive information access, fair betting and effective null tests; a resolution would settle the relationship between two foundational randomness notions.

cards.title: Rigidity of the Turing degrees
cards.formal:
Let \(D_T=\mathcal P(\mathbb N)/{\equiv_T}\) be the set of all Turing degrees, ordered by Turing reducibility. Is this order rigid? The exact assertion is
\[\forall\pi:D_T\to D_T,\quad \Bigl[\pi\text{ is bijective}\ \land\ \forall a,b\in D_T\,\bigl(a\le_T b\iff\pi(a)\le_T\pi(b)\bigr)\Bigr]\ \Longrightarrow\ \forall a\in D_T\,\pi(a)=a.\]
The domain is the full quotient of all subsets of the standard natural numbers. The quantifier over \(\pi\) ranges over arbitrary functions on this quotient in ordinary classical set theory, with ZFC as the set-theoretic background.
cards.definitions:
Write \(\mathbb N=\{0,1,2,\ldots\}\), \(\mathcal P(\mathbb N)\) for its full power set, and \(\chi_A:\mathbb N\to\{0,1\}\) for a set's characteristic function. A deterministic oracle Turing machine is a finite program with ordinary unbounded work tapes and an additional operation that receives \(\chi_B(k)\) when it asks whether \(k\) belongs to the oracle set \(B\). Each terminating computation takes finitely many steps and makes finitely many queries; no uniform bound on their number, time or space is imposed. Natural inputs and queries have the usual finite binary encodings. Any fixed effective enumeration \((\Phi_e)_{e\in\mathbb N}\) of all such programs gives
\[A\le_T B\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad\exists e\in\mathbb N\ \forall n\in\mathbb N,\ \Phi_e^B(n)\text{ halts with output }\chi_A(n).\]
The same index must work on every input, but may depend on \(A,B\). Programs contain no additional oracle, infinite advice or noncomputable constants. All subsets are eligible oracle sets, including noncomputable ones.

Define \(A\equiv_T B\) by \(A\le_T B\) and \(B\le_T A\). A degree \([A]\) is the equivalence class of \(A\), and \([A]\le_T[B]\) means \(A\le_T B\); this is independent of the representatives. Equality of degrees is mutual reducibility, not equality of their representatives. The set \(D_T\) includes every degree, not just degrees containing computably enumerable sets, arithmetical degrees, or degrees below a selected bound. A set is computably enumerable if a program with no oracle lists exactly its members, with arbitrary repetition and delay allowed.

An order automorphism is a total injective and surjective map \(\pi:D_T\to D_T\) that preserves and reflects every reducibility comparison. It need not be computable, definable, continuous or induced by a prescribed operation on sets. A representation \(F:\mathcal P(\mathbb N)\to\mathcal P(\mathbb N)\), if used to specify it, must satisfy \([F(A)]=\pi([A])\) for every \(A\); the representation itself need not be bijective. The order language has only equality and \(\le_T\). Jump preservation is a known consequence of this order structure, not an extra assumption in the target.

For the dated context, \(\mathbf 0=[\varnothing]\). The join \([A]\vee[B]\) is \([A\oplus B]\), where \(A\oplus B=\{2n:n\in A\}\cup\{2n+1:n\in B\}\). Set \(A'=\{e:\Phi_e^A(e)\text{ halts}\}\); the Turing jump is \([A]'=[A']\), and \(\mathbf 0''=(\mathbf 0')'\). These degrees are independent of the chosen effective machine enumeration. The upper cone with base \(b\) is \(\{a:b\le_T a\}\). Its complement includes both degrees below \(b\) and degrees incomparable with \(b\).

The assertion concerns the degree order built from the full power set in the ambient universe, not a selected countable model's internally computed degrees. The continuum hypothesis and determinacy are not hypotheses of the target. There are no finite input sizes, efficiency bounds or numerical approximation parameters in this structural question.
cards.answer_criterion:
Give a complete, mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of the displayed universal assertion or its exact negation. A positive answer must apply to every set-theoretic order automorphism of the entire \(D_T\). A negative answer must prove
\[\exists\pi:D_T\to D_T\ \exists a\in D_T,\quad\pi\text{ is bijective},\quad \forall b,c\in D_T\,\bigl(b\le_Tc\iff\pi(b)\le_T\pi(c)\bigr),\quad\pi(a)\ne a.\]
An existence proof is sufficient; no computable formula for the automorphism is required. A construction on representatives must establish that it descends to this full quotient and has all the stated properties. Proving rigidity only on a proper substructure or for a restricted family of maps does not meet the criterion. Nor does a non-surjective order embedding or a permutation of representatives that fixes every degree. Both answer directions retain the stated classical background without an unproved extra hypothesis; relative consistency or independence alone does not assert either of these two mathematical conclusions. All supporting formalized definitions and theorems needed for the chosen direction must be included or supplied by verified Lean libraries.
cards.why: Rigidity asks whether the entire ordering of relative computational power has any nontrivial global symmetry. Its connection with intrinsic definability and second-order arithmetic makes it a central structural question in computability, beyond the classification of individual computable problems.

importance.reason: A defining open problem of degree theory, closely tied to the intrinsic definability of computational structure and constrained by deep but incomplete rigidity theorems.

progress.text: Nerode and Shore proved that each automorphism is the identity on some upper cone. Kjos-Hanssen’s introduction distinguishes this from the later common \(\mathbf 0''\) cone bound.
Shore and Slaman proved order-theoretic definability of the Turing jump; the inspected author manuscript states the conclusion as Theorem 1.15.
Cooper announced a nontrivial automorphism of the full degree order. The later survey reports its construction as not independently verified; this review does not certify the claim.

Slaman’s published survey states rigidity on the cone above \(\mathbf 0''\), countability of the automorphism group and equivalence between full rigidity and its bi-interpretability conjecture. It retains the global question as open.
Slaman and Soskova’s journal article gives finite automorphism bases and related definability results for \(D_T(\le_T\mathbf 0')\), without proving local or global rigidity.

Kjos-Hanssen’s preprint and later journal publication exclude nontrivial automorphisms induced by coordinate permutations or by homeomorphisms preserving all Bernoulli measures. The preprint record remains version 1.

Ongay-Valverde’s version 1 gives a conditional restriction on genericity of degrees and their images; Theorem 7.4 and its Section 8 consequences assume the continuum hypothesis. The complete proof was not independently certified in this review.

context_blocks.text: Two oracle decision problems represent the same Turing degree precisely when each can compute the other. Their degree records computational power without committing to a particular set of integers as its encoding. This question asks whether all degrees can be consistently relabeled, changing at least one point while preserving every reducibility comparison. A nontrivial symmetry must work simultaneously across the whole structure.

The computable degree \(\mathbf 0\) and the join operation are fixed by every order automorphism. Shore and Slaman proved the stronger fact that the graph of the Turing jump is first-order definable using the degree order alone. Thus \(\pi(a')=\pi(a)'\) for every degree \(a\), and all finite jumps of \(\mathbf 0\) are fixed. Preservation of the jump is an established restriction, not a proof of full rigidity.

Slaman and Woodin proved that every automorphism fixes every degree at least \(\mathbf 0''\); their automorphism group is also at most countable. These are statements about restrictions of global automorphisms. They do not assert that an arbitrary automorphism of the upper cone extends to the full structure, and they do not cover degrees incomparable with its base. The underlying set of all degrees has cardinality \(2^{\aleph_0}\).

The same structural analysis connects rigidity with the Slaman–Woodin bi-interpretability conjecture: the degree structure and full second-order arithmetic would recover one another through logical interpretations, with the correspondence to degrees definable without parameters. The survey states equivalence with rigidity in its precise sense of bi-interpretability. This concerns the expressive power of the whole order.

Rigidity does not mean that every degree has its own parameter-free first-order definition. There are only countably many finite formulas in this language and uncountably many degrees. Most degrees therefore cannot be individually defined that way, even if the entire order is rigid.

Kjos-Hanssen proves that a coordinate permutation \(p:\mathbb N\to\mathbb N\), acting on characteristic sequences by \(F_p(A)(n)=A(p(n))\), can induce an automorphism of all Turing degrees only when that automorphism is the identity; in fact \(p\) must be computable. He also excludes nontrivial automorphisms induced by homeomorphisms of \(\{0,1\}^{\mathbb N}\) preserving every Bernoulli product measure. Here the topology is generated by finite initial segments, and the measure with parameter \(t\in[0,1]\) makes coordinates independent bits with probability \(t\) of being one. These representation and measure restrictions are absent from the main question.

Slaman and Soskova study the separate structure of degrees at most \(\mathbf 0'\), equivalently the \(\Delta^0_2\) degrees. They prove that this local structure has a finite automorphism base: agreement on a fixed finite tuple determines an automorphism. They obtain a countable automorphism group and an equivalence between local rigidity and bi-interpretability with first-order arithmetic. None of these conclusions states that the group is trivial. Their local arithmetic comparison is distinct from the full structure’s second-order comparison.

Ongay-Valverde’s 2021 preprint gives restrictions on the action of a hypothetical automorphism on generic degrees under the continuum hypothesis \(2^{\aleph_0}=\aleph_1\). Theorem 7.4 additionally concerns families meeting a relative genericity condition above every degree, with jointly generic representatives for each degree and its image. Its Section 8 explicitly keeps the continuum-hypothesis assumption. This conditional restriction neither constructs a nontrivial automorphism nor proves that all automorphisms are trivial, even under that hypothesis.

Cooper’s 1999 Theorem 1.1 claims a nonidentity global automorphism fixing every degree at least \(\mathbf 0'\). This is a claim of a full negative answer, rather than merely a local example. The present review checked the statement in the author-uploaded text but did not verify its long construction.

Slaman’s later survey explicitly reports that Cooper’s construction had not been independently verified and treats the general problem as unresolved. The subsequent permutation paper also states the full question as open. The card therefore keeps the historical full-solution claim visible and uses uncertain status; it does not infer either correctness or a proved error from the announcement alone.

cards.title: Busy Beaver \(\mathrm{BB}(6)\)
cards.formal:
Determine the exact six-state binary Busy Beaver runtime \(\mathrm{BB}(6)=S(6)\) by giving a concrete machine \(M_*\in\mathcal M_6\) and proving
\[M_*\text{ halts on the blank tape},\qquad
\forall M\in\mathcal M_6:\ M\text{ halts on the blank tape}\ \Longrightarrow\ T(M)\le T(M_*).\]
Here \(\mathcal M_6\) is the finite class of deterministic six-nonhalting-state, two-symbol Turing machines defined below, and \(T(M)\) is the number of transitions through the first entry into the separate halting state. The complete transition table of \(M_*\), together with proofs of its halting and universal maximality, specifies the answer exactly as \(S(6)=T(M_*)\).
cards.definitions:
Machine. Fix the nonhalting states \(Q=\{A,B,C,D,E,F\}\), one additional halting state \(Z\notin Q\), and the tape alphabet \(\{0,1\}\). A machine is a total transition function
\[\delta:Q\times\{0,1\}\longrightarrow\{0,1\}\times\{-1,+1\}\times(Q\cup\{Z\}).\]
Thus its description has exactly twelve entries. The three outputs specify the symbol to write, a move of exactly one cell left or right, and the next state, respectively. There are no stationary moves, extra tapes or transitions out of \(Z\). Unreachable states and entries are allowed. Different tables need not have different behavior; no symmetry reduction is imposed on the quantified class \(\mathcal M_6\).

Execution. The tape is indexed by all integers. A configuration consists of a state \(q\), a head position \(h\in\mathbb Z\), and a tape function \(\tau:\mathbb Z\to\{0,1\}\). At time zero, \(q=A\), \(h=0\), and \(\tau(i)=0\) for every integer \(i\). If \(q\ne Z\) and \(\delta(q,\tau(h))=(b,d,q')\), one transition replaces \(\tau(h)\) by \(b\), leaves every other tape cell unchanged, replaces the head position by \(h+d\), and enters \(q'\). Execution stops immediately on entering \(Z\); that final write-and-move transition is included in the count. Each transition costs one step, irrespective of head position or time elapsed. There is no external input, randomness or resource limit.

Halting time and maximum. A machine halts if its unique execution first enters \(Z\) at some positive integer time. Only for such a machine, \(T(M)\) denotes this least time. Let \(\mathcal H_6\subseteq\mathcal M_6\) be the halting machines. Define
\[S(6)=\max\{T(M):M\in\mathcal H_6\}.\]
There are \(28^{12}\) tables in \(\mathcal M_6\), since each entry has \(2\cdot2\cdot7\) choices. The halting subset is nonempty, since a table can send \((A,0)\) directly to \(Z\). Hence the maximum exists as a finite positive integer. No value of \(T\) on a nonhalting machine is used in the statement or the submitted certificate.

Answer representation. The runtime of a specified, proved-halting table defines an exact integer through a terminating step-counting computation, even when actually evaluating it is infeasible. The accepted answer need not separately evaluate that computation. In this card, \(\mathrm{BB}\) always means the runtime maximum \(S\), not the distinct extremal function \(\Sigma\) that maximizes the number of ones on the final tape.

Notation in the context. For positive integer \(k\), \(2\uparrow\uparrow k\) is a tower of \(k\) twos, equivalently \(2\uparrow\uparrow1=2\) and \(2\uparrow\uparrow(k+1)=2^{(2\uparrow\uparrow k)}\). Three arrows mean iteration of this tower operation: \(2\uparrow\uparrow\uparrow1=2\) and \(2\uparrow\uparrow\uparrow(k+1)=2\uparrow\uparrow(2\uparrow\uparrow\uparrow k)\).
cards.answer_criterion:
Supply the complete twelve-entry transition table of a particular \(M_*\in\mathcal M_6\), with complete mathematically correct proofs checked in Lean that it halts from the stated blank initial configuration and that every halting \(M\in\mathcal M_6\) has \(T(M)\le T(M_*)\). These two proofs must establish the exact equality \(\mathrm{BB}(6)=T(M_*)\). This is the user-approved exact witness criterion, superseding the default numerical tolerance for this card only.

The witness runtime is an accepted exact finite description of the integer. A simple closed form, decimal expansion, separately evaluated integer literal or full execution trace is not required. A candidate machine without both proofs, an estimated runtime, a one-sided bound, a list of undecided machines or a restatement of the defining maximum is insufficient. Any reduction to representative transition tables must itself be justified as covering the full stated class. A result for a different alphabet, state count, tape convention or final-tape score does not settle this target.
cards.why: The halting behavior of a finite set of exceptionally short programs is still beyond complete classification. This problem makes the boundary of current computability knowledge concrete: one additional nonhalting state separates the established five-state maximum from an unresolved maximum with enormous certified examples and difficult residual halting questions. A solution would give a universal exact upper bound for every halting program in this precisely fixed class.

context_blocks.text: Radó introduced Busy Beaver functions in 1962 as concrete examples of noncomputability. The runtime function takes a maximum over finitely many halting programs at each state count, but there is no algorithm computing all its values. That statement about the entire sequence does not make every individual value unknowable. The first five binary runtime values have now been determined.

Finiteness alone does not supply an effective stopping rule for the search: a machine still running may halt much later or may run forever. Conversely, a proved value of \(S(6)\) would decide blank-tape halting for every table in this finite class in principle, by checking whether it halts within that many steps. The enormous possible duration makes this a mathematical consequence, not a practical promise.

The collaboration proves \(S(5)=47{,}176{,}870\) in Coq, now called Rocq. Its 2026 revised paper proves coverage of the relevant five-state machines as well as their halting classifications. The total number of representatives examined by that proof is \(181{,}385{,}789\); it is not a count of six-state holdouts or of all syntactically distinct tables in this card.

The formal paper presents halting entries as undefined transitions. Its convention counts the final attempt to execute such an entry, so even an immediately halting machine takes one step. Replacing an undefined entry by a write/move transition into the separate state Z preserves its runtime exactly. The card retains total twelve-entry tables to make a submitted witness fully explicit.

For six states, the paper records the lower bound \(S(6)>2\uparrow\uparrow\uparrow5\). Appendix B carefully separates two kinds of evidence: the champion’s halting is proved in Coq, while the stated enormous step lower bound is estimated mathematically from its verified abstract evolution rules. The paper does not claim a formally verified exact runtime for that champion or a proof of universal six-state maximality.

Runtime and final output are different objectives. The function \(\Sigma(n)\) maximizes the number of ones present when a machine halts; \(S(n)\) maximizes the duration. Even their maximizing machines need not coincide: the paper records this already for three states. cards.title: Reversal of Hindman’s theorem to the \(\omega\)-jump
cards.formal: Over RCA\(_{0}\), does Hindman’s finite-sums theorem imply ACA\(_{0}^{+}\)? Equivalently, does RCA\(_{0}+HT\) prove that every set X has an \(\omega -th\) Turing jump?
cards.definitions: Work in classical two-sorted second-order arithmetic, with number variables and variables for sets of natural numbers. RCA\(_{0}\) has the usual elementary arithmetic axioms, \(\Sigma ^{0}_{1}\) induction and \(\Delta ^{0}_{1}\) comprehension, allowing set parameters. HT is the assertion that for every integer \(k\ge 1\) and every coloring c of the positive integers into \(\{0,\ldots ,k- 1\}\), there exist an infinite set H of positive integers and a color i such that \(c(\sum_{h\in F}h)=i\) for every nonempty finite subset F of H. Terms in a sum are distinct; there is no fixed upper bound on their number and no additional sparsity requirement on H. For a set X, its Turing jump \(X'\) is {e: the e-th oracle Turing machine with oracle X halts on input e}, using one fixed effective enumeration. The \(\omega\)-jump existence axiom says \(\forall X\exists Y\) [\(Y_{0}=X\) and \(\forall j(Y_{j+1}=Y_{j}' )\)], where \(Y_{j}=\{e:\langle j,e\rangle \in Y\}\) and \(\langle \cdot ,\cdot \rangle\) is a fixed primitive recursive pairing. ACA\(_{0}^{+}\) is RCA\(_{0}\) plus that axiom. The question is formal provability of this implication over the stated base, not truth of Hindman’s theorem in ordinary set theory and not a single-instance computability claim.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove the \(\omega\)-jump existence axiom in RCA\(_{0}+HT\), or prove nonimplication by constructing a model of RCA\(_{0}+HT\) in which some set has no coded \(\omega\)-jump. A standard-natural-number model is sufficient for a separation but is not required. A lower bound of ACA\(_{0}\) alone, an upper bound of ACA\(_{0}^{+}\), or a theorem about only bounded-length sums does not decide this implication. A negative answer need not show that HT is equivalent to ACA\(_{0}\); an intermediate strength would also refute the implication.
cards.why: A longstanding gap in the computational and axiomatic strength of a central infinite combinatorial theorem, with a precise target at the \(\omega -th\) Turing jump.

importance.reason: A landmark reverse-mathematical calibration problem connecting finite-sums combinatorics, oracle computation and the hierarchy of set-existence axioms.

progress.text: Blass–Hirst–Simpson establish ACA\(_{0}^{+}\Rightarrow HT\Rightarrow\)ACA\(_{0}\) over RCA\(_{0}\), leaving the reversal in this card open.
Carlucci–Zdanowski characterize ACA\(_{0}^{+}\) using Ramsey’s theorem for exactly large sets; this supplies a comparison principle rather than an HT reversal.
Carlucci–Kołodziejczyk–Lepore–Zdanowski reach the ACA\(_{0}\) lower bound already for sums of at most two elements with four colors; conference precursor 2017, journal version 2020.
Csima and coauthors prove nontrivial computability and reverse-mathematical lower bounds for sums of exactly two elements, a weaker principle than full HT.
Liu–Patey prove new upper bounds and separations for variable-word and unordered Carlson–Simpson principles, without claiming a resolution of HT’s strength.
Le Houérou–Patey obtain a conservation theorem for a one-variable, two-color Carlson–Simpson principle.

cards.status_note: Reviewed through 11 September 2026. No proof or separation for RCA\(_{0}+HT\Rightarrow\)ACA\(_{0}^{+}\) was found in the checked primary literature. The recent variable-word and Carlson–Simpson results have different formulations and do not establish this reversal.

context_blocks.text: Hindman’s theorem says that a finite coloring contains an infinite set whose entire collection of finite sums has one color. This is much more than finding an infinite monochromatic subset: the same color must work for single elements, pairs, triples and every larger finite selection. For parity coloring, the positive even numbers give an immediate example. The theorem must also handle colorings with no such simple arithmetic description.

The combinatorial statement is a theorem, not the unresolved claim on this card. Reverse mathematics asks which set-existence axioms are needed to prove it. One works over a deliberately weak base theory and compares stronger principles by implication. The inherited paper records the classical bounds ACA\(_{0}^{+}\Rightarrow HT\Rightarrow\)ACA\(_{0}\) and identifies closing this gap as a major open problem. This card asks specifically whether the upper implication reverses.

ACA\(_{0}\) allows arithmetic comprehension; equivalently over the base theory, every set has its Turing jump. An individual jump supplies answers to halting questions relative to the given set. Repeating that operation a fixed finite number of times yields increasingly strong information. The \(\omega\)-jump places every finite iterate into the sections of one set. Being able to discuss each fixed finite stage is not the same as having this whole sequence available as a single object.

The distinction is visible in the model consisting of the standard natural numbers together with all arithmetical sets. It is closed under the ordinary Turing jump, since jumping an arithmetical set still yields an arithmetical set. It does not contain the join of all finite jumps of the empty set. Thus ACA\(_{0}^{+}\) demands more set existence than ACA\(_{0}\). Whether Hindman’s theorem already forces that additional existence is the precise issue here.

The computability bounds show why ordinary computable colorings already matter. The account by Csima and coauthors recalls a computable coloring for which every finite-sums solution computes the halting set, and an upper bound placing a solution in the \((\omega +1)-st\) jump of the coloring. These are bounds on information in solutions. Neither identifies the exact reverse-mathematical strength, and noncomputability alone falls far short of an \(\omega\)-jump reversal.

Restricted sum lengths have provided substantial progress without closing the full gap. Carlucci–Kołodziejczyk–Lepore–Zdanowski prove that the version requiring monochromatic singletons and pairs already implies ACA\(_{0}\); four colors suffice without an additional sparsity condition. Their results for sums of exactly \(n\ge 3\) terms use an apartness condition on the binary supports of the chosen integers. These carefully specified variants should not be merged with unrestricted HT.

Even replacing “at most two” by “exactly two” changes the logical picture. Csima and coauthors construct a computable two-color instance of the exactly-two version with no \(\Sigma ^{0}_{2}\) solution and prove a lower bound through diagonally noncomputable functions relative to the halting set. Yet exactly-two sums follow from Ramsey’s theorem for pairs, placing that principle strictly below full HT over the base. This is a useful warning that small wording changes can alter the problem.

There is a separate combinatorial principle known to capture the desired upper level exactly. Carlucci–Zdanowski prove that Ramsey’s theorem for exactly large finite sets is equivalent to ACA\(_{0}^{+}\). A finite set F is exactly large when |\(F|=\min (F)+1\), so its dimension varies with its elements. This yields a potential comparison target: an implication from HT to this precisely defined Ramsey principle would suffice. Its equivalence does not itself supply that missing implication.

Recent results in the neighboring theory of variable words require the same care. Liu–Patey’s June 2026 preprint, revised in July, gives low\(_{2}\) solutions to the Ordered Variable Word theorem for colorings of ordinary words and proves each fixed-dimensional unordered Carlson–Simpson lemma in ACA\(_{0}\). The paper distinguishes these principles from ordered higher-dimensional counterparts and still describes ACA\(_{0}^{+}\) as the weakest known system proving HT. Its new upper bounds should not be transferred to Hindman’s theorem.

Le Houérou–Patey’s July 2026 preprint obtains a conservation result for a one-variable Carlson–Simpson principle with two colors. It controls which arithmetical consequences that particular principle adds to a weak theory. This is a different assertion from constructing the \(\omega\)-jump out of unrestricted finite-sums homogeneity. Together the recent papers sharpen nearby boundaries without answering the implication stated here.

A positive answer would make a concrete additive-combinatorial theorem a characterization of closure under all finite Turing jumps at once. A negative answer would show that known proofs use more set existence than the theorem itself entails. Either outcome would clarify the information content of an infinite combinatorial search principle, which is the reason for its place in the computability part of this catalogue.

cards.title: Universality of Turing equivalence
cards.formal: For every countable Borel equivalence relation E on a standard Borel space X, does there exist a Borel function \(f:X\to 2^{\mathbb{N}}\) such that x E y if and only if \(f(x)\equiv _{T} f(y)\), for all \(x,y\in X\)?
cards.definitions: The space \(2^{\mathbb{N}}\) consists of all infinite binary sequences, identified with subsets of \(\mathbb{N}\). For \(a,b\in 2^{\mathbb{N}}, a\le _{T} b\) means that some oracle Turing machine with oracle b computes every bit of a and halts on every input coordinate; \(a\equiv _{T} b\) means both \(a\le _{T} b\) and \(b\le _{T} a\). There is no time or space restriction on these computations. A standard Borel space is a set with the Borel \(\sigma\)-algebra of some Polish topology. The relation E must be a Borel subset of \(X\times X\) and each equivalence class must be at most countable; X itself may be uncountable. The function f is Borel measurable: inverse images of Borel sets are Borel. It need not be computable, continuous, injective on points, or uniform on indices witnessing equivalence. It must preserve both equivalence and inequivalence on every input pair, not merely almost everywhere for a chosen measure. The quantifiers ask for a separate Borel reduction for each E, without requiring an algorithm that takes a code for E and outputs f. This is the ordinary ZFC formulation of Borel universality.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove that Turing equivalence is universal by producing the requisite Borel reductions, or prove it is not by identifying one countable Borel relation that does not reduce to it. Equivalently, settle whether \(E_{\infty}\le _{B}\equiv _{T}\) for a fixed standard universal countable Borel relation \(E_{\infty}\). A negative theorem conditional on a form of Martin’s conjecture must be labeled conditional. Failure of reductions with an additional uniformity or computability requirement is not a negative solution to the unrestricted Borel question.
