context_blocks.text: Two infinite binary sequences have the same Turing degree when each can compute the other. This partitions all possible oracles by their computational power. The universality question asks how complicated that partition is as a classification problem: can every countable Borel pattern of equivalence be represented exactly by equality of Turing degrees? The objects being classified are infinite sequences, not finite machine descriptions.

There are countably many oracle programs. Consequently, for a fixed oracle b, only countably many sequences can be computed from b, and its Turing-equivalence class is countable. The relation is Borel because a claim that an oracle program computes a given sequence can be written using countably many conditions about finite computations. Thus Turing equivalence itself belongs to the class of relations compared on this card.

A Borel reduction is a structured assignment of invariants. If f reduces E to Turing equivalence, the Turing degree of \(f(x)\) is a complete invariant for the E-class of x: equivalent objects receive the same degree, and inequivalent objects receive different degrees. Distinct representatives of one E-class may receive different binary sequences, provided those sequences have the same degree. Injectivity on equivalence classes is essential; injectivity on individual points is not.

It suffices to study a single standard benchmark \(E_{\infty}\). One realization is the orbit relation for the shift action of the free group \(F_{2}\) on \(\{0,1\}^{F_{2}}\): two labelings x,y are equivalent when \(y(h)=x(g^{- 1}h)\) for some group element g and every \(h\in F_{2}\). This countable Borel relation is universal. A reduction of that one relation to Turing equivalence would therefore answer the full universally quantified question.

The inherited Caicedo–Löwe survey records the question as Question 6 in its discussion of Martin’s conjecture. It traces the universality problem to Kechris and distinguishes it from nearby statements about arithmetic equivalence and uniform coding. The source is a 2019 preprint; the later published chapter updates the year in its title. The card retains the exact inherited version and locator.

There are strong positive results for neighboring relations. Slaman and Steel proved that arithmetic equivalence is universal; Marks, Slaman and Steel provide a published proof and discussion. Arithmetic equivalence allows each sequence to be computed from some finite Turing jump of the other, with the finite jump levels depending on the pair. That extra allowance changes which sequences become equivalent.

In the other direction, Marks proved universality of polynomial-time Turing equivalence, as well as polynomial-time many-one equivalence. These compare arbitrary languages over finite strings by resource-bounded oracle reductions. The theorem concerns the entire space of languages, not only decidable languages or languages inside a familiar complexity class. It establishes universality for a finer relation than unrestricted Turing equivalence.

Finer and coarser relations do not give an automatic transfer here. A coding that keeps two outputs inequivalent under polynomial-time reductions may still make them equivalent under unrestricted oracle computation. Once that happens, the reverse implication required of a Borel reduction fails. Preserving the encoding under all additional computations is the missing task; simply reusing the polynomial-time result does not complete it.

There is also a structural obstruction to familiar coding approaches. With Turing equivalence generated in its usual way by oracle-program reductions, it is not uniformly universal. Roughly, uniformity would require indices for computations between encoded outputs to be chosen solely from the indices witnessing the original equivalence, independently of the particular objects. Marks develops this distinction and shows why the choice of generating maps must be specified.

The present problem permits arbitrary Borel reductions, so that uniform obstruction is not the desired nonuniversality theorem. Whether ordinary universality must entail appropriate stronger uniformity properties is itself part of the surrounding theory. A proof that rules out one common coding pattern therefore reveals a methodological barrier without exhausting all Borel encodings.

Martin’s conjecture supplies a competing prediction. Its Borel form implies that Turing equivalence is not universal; in particular, it obstructs reducing two disjoint copies of Turing equivalence into one copy. Conversely, a universality proof would contradict that prediction. The point is a genuine conditional connection between two major structural questions, not an unconditional settlement in either direction.

Day and Marks’ February 2026 revision investigates an older question about writing Turing equivalence as an increasing union whose stages omit certain uniformly computable infinite sequences. A positive answer would imply nonuniform invariant functions and universality of ordinary many-one equivalence. Their consequences remain conditional on that decomposition question, and concern distinctions among degree relations that must not be collapsed into a proof of Turing universality.

Settling the card would tell us whether mutual computability provides a universal language for countable Borel classification, or has a structural limitation absent from some nearby degree notions. Either outcome would matter beyond computability: it would constrain the ways orbit equivalence relations, invariants and definable encodings can interact. The answer criterion is a precise existence theorem for reductions, with no algorithmic-efficiency requirement hidden inside the word “Borel.”

cards.definitions: The input explicitly gives \(m\ge 0\) and all four entries of each \(A_{i}\) as signed binary integers. Entries have no magnitude or sign restriction, and m is part of the input, not a fixed constant. Products use ordinary exact integer matrix multiplication: \((AB)_{r,s}=\sum _{t=1}^{2} A_{r,t}B_{t,s}\). The target \(0_{2}\) is the matrix with all four entries zero. The product length \(\ell\) is finite but unbounded, and generator indices may repeat in any order. Only listed generators can be used; inverses are not supplied automatically. The empty product is excluded, and an empty list is a NO instance. The semigroup generated by the list is the set of all such nonempty products, so mortality means membership of \(0_{2}\) in that set. The machine must return YES exactly for mortal lists and NO otherwise, terminating on both kinds. No running-time or memory bound is imposed beyond finite termination; there is no oracle, numerical tolerance or real-arithmetic primitive.
cards.answer_criterion: A positive answer gives a uniform decision algorithm with proofs of correctness and termination on every finite input list. A negative answer proves that the stated decision problem is undecidable. A procedure that only certifies particular zero products, a bounded-length decision algorithm, or a lower bound against polynomial time does not settle the target.

context_blocks.title: Can a sequence erase every vector?
context_blocks.text: A product equal to the zero matrix sends every two-dimensional vector to zero at once. The question is whether some finite sequence of the allowed transformations has this effect. It is stronger than sending one specified vector to zero: a matrix can kill that vector while acting nontrivially on others.

context_blocks.title: Two small examples
context_blocks.text: Let \(A=[[1,0],[0,0]]\) and \(B=[[0,0],[1,0]]\). Neither is the zero matrix, but \(AB=0_{2}\), so the list \((A,B)\) is mortal. Reversing the order gives \(BA=B\), showing that order matters. The list containing only A is not mortal, since every positive power of A equals A. Thus the presence of a singular generator by itself does not answer the question.

context_blocks.title: Hardness and undecidability are different claims
context_blocks.text: Bell, Hirvensalo and Potapov established NP-hardness in 2012; their 2024 paper still identifies unrestricted two-dimensional mortality as an open decidability problem. NP-hardness leaves open the possibility of a terminating algorithm with very large running time. Mortality is already undecidable for general finite lists of three-dimensional integer matrices, placing dimension two at a basic boundary.

context_blocks.title: Restricted matrix classes have stronger results
context_blocks.text: Jaax and Kiefer prove NP-completeness when each determinant is either 0 or +1. This gives a decision procedure for that promise and does not cover arbitrary determinants. The 2024 membership theorem concerns generators in \(GL_{2}(\mathbb{Z} )\), whose determinants are ±1; their products are invertible and cannot equal zero. Neither theorem decides mortality when unrestricted singular and nonsingular generators are mixed.

context_blocks.title: Relation to other matrix questions
context_blocks.text: General semigroup membership, discussed in TCS-5921, allows a target matrix supplied as input; mortality fixes that target to zero. A solution of general membership would therefore decide mortality. The April 2026 work on complex matrix embeddings studies different algebraic representation questions and supplies no general resolution of the present integer-matrix target.

cards.title: Scaling joint Kolmogorov-complexity profiles
cards.formal: For every fixed integer \(k\ge 1\) and real \(\lambda >0\), does there exist a constant \(c>0\) such that, for every integer \(n\ge 2\) and every tuple of binary strings \(a_{1},\ldots ,a_{k}\) of length at most n, there are finite binary strings \(b_{1},\ldots ,b_{k}\) satisfying |\(C(b_{S})- \lambda  C(a_{S})|\le c \log _{2} n\) for every nonempty \(S\subseteq \{1,\ldots ,k\}\)? cards.definitions: Fix one optimal plain Kolmogorov machine U: an optimal partial computable map from finite binary programs to finite binary strings. \(C(x)\) is the minimum program length with U(program)=x. Only joint unconditional complexities of all nonempty subtuples are required. The constants may depend on \(k, \lambda\) and U but not on n, the input strings or S. The additive slack is measured in bits. This uses the original length normalization \(O(\log  n)\); it does not silently replace it by the potentially smaller \(O(\log  C(a_{1},\ldots ,a_{k}))\).
cards.answer_criterion: Prove the displayed universal statement, or its logical negation with the same quantifier order. Failure of one algorithm for producing b, or failure of obtaining the scaling by conditioning the original strings on an auxiliary string, is not a refutation. cards.title: Shannon feasibility from algorithmic network coding
cards.formal: For every fixed finite acyclic directed network with correlated finite-alphabet sources and specified source-reconstruction demands, does high-probability algorithmic feasibility on independent source blocks imply Shannon achievability at the same edge rates? The algorithmic model permits sample-dependent local programs of length \(O(\log N)\) and \(O(\log N)\) extra bits on each edge for a block of \(N\) samples. The Shannon model requires fixed local encoding and decoding maps for each block length, with vanishing error and arbitrarily small rate slack, as defined below.
cards.why: The question compares information transmission for random sources with transmission of their individual realized strings. A positive answer would show that logarithmic sample-dependent algorithmic descriptions cannot create new asymptotic network rates. A negative answer would expose a concrete operational distinction between Shannon and Kolmogorov descriptions of distributed information.

cards.definitions: Fix a finite directed acyclic graph \(G=(V,E)\), an integer \(m\ge1\), nonempty finite alphabets \(\mathcal X_1,\ldots,\mathcal X_m\), and any joint probability law \(P\) for \(X=(X_1,\ldots,X_m)\) on their product. The law is fixed as block length varies; its coordinates may be arbitrarily correlated, and no computability assumption is imposed on its probabilities. Each vertex \(v\) has fixed sets \(S_v,T_v\subseteq\{1,\ldots,m\}\): it initially receives the source coordinates in \(S_v\) and must reproduce the coordinates in \(T_v\). Require \(\bigcup_v S_v=\{1,\ldots,m\}\). Several vertices may know or demand the same source, and a vertex may both receive sources and relay messages. Each edge \(e\) has a fixed finite real rate \(r_e\ge0\), measured in bits per joint source sample. For \(N\ge1\), take \(N\) independent copies of the entire vector \(X\); write \(X_j^N\) for the resulting length-\(N\) word of coordinate \(j\). The block law is \(P^{\otimes N}\), not independence between different coordinates. All finite words, integers and tuples use fixed computable binary encodings; tuple components and incident edges are ordered once with the network. Let \(C(u\mid v)\) be plain conditional Kolmogorov complexity: the least length of a binary program for a fixed optimal interpreter that halts with output \(u\) on auxiliary input \(v\). There is no time bound. Optimal means that this interpreter simulates every other partial computable interpreter with an additive program-length overhead independent of \(u,v\). Let \(L_N=\lceil\log_2(N+2)\rceil\). For a realized source block and an integer \(K\ge1\), algorithmic feasibility means that there exist edge-message strings \(M_e\) with \(|M_e|\le\lfloor Nr_e\rfloor+K L_N\), such that at every vertex \(v\), \[C\bigl(( (M_e)_{e\in\operatorname{out}(v)}, (X_j^N)_{j\in T_v})\mid N,(X_j^N)_{j\in S_v},(M_e)_{e\in\operatorname{in}(v)}\bigr)\le K L_N.\] The demanded outputs in this formula are the true source words, so reconstruction is exact on a feasible realization. Messages and witnessing programs may depend on the whole realized source block; only their lengths and the displayed local conditional complexities are constrained. They need not arise from one choice of encoding functions used for every realization. Call the rate vector algorithmically feasible with high probability if there exists one \(K\) such that, for every \(\eta\in(0,1)\), some \(N_0\) makes the probability of this feasibility event at least \(1-\eta\) for all \(N\ge N_0\). The same \(K\) works for every block length, realization and error threshold. Shannon achievability means that for every rate slack \(\delta>0\) and every error tolerance \(\eta\in(0,1)\), there is \(N_0\) such that for every \(N\ge N_0\) there exist deterministic local encoding and decoding maps with the following properties. In a topological order, each vertex computes its outgoing edge messages from only its local source words and incoming messages; each demand is decoded from the same local information. Each edge message belongs to the finite set of binary strings of length at most \(\lfloor N(r_e+\delta)\rfloor\). For each edge this bounded-string alphabet is shared by the parties and the receiver observes the whole message, including its length; the same convention is used for algorithmic messages. The probability, under \(P^{\otimes N}\), that every demanded word is reconstructed correctly is at least \(1-\eta\). The local maps are fixed before observing the source realization; they may depend on the network, law, rates, block length and tolerances, and have no computational time or description-size bound. There is no feedback, extra channel, shared sample-dependent advice or communication other than the edge messages. This is an asymptotic rate-region converse. It does not assert equivalence with logarithmic finite-block overhead in the Shannon model.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of the implication for every network, source law, demand pattern and finite rate vector just defined, or refute it. A refutation requires a fixed admissible network, joint law and rate vector for which algorithmic feasibility holds with one logarithmic-overhead constant and probability tending to one, but Shannon achievability fails. In particular, failure at a single block length or at a rate boundary without accounting for arbitrarily small positive rate slack is insufficient. Results for only one source, independent sources, one terminal, particular network shapes, or only information-cut inequalities do not settle the general converse. An inefficient Shannon code is allowed; the target is coding feasibility, not efficient construction.

context_blocks.text: A network code chooses how each relay transforms its received messages and local source data. The same code must handle many possible source realizations. Several correlated sources and several destinations can make compatibility between these local choices a substantial constraint.

The algorithmic version instead asks whether a particular tuple of strings admits suitable edge messages. A short program may certify each local transformation, and a different realized tuple may use different programs. Their permitted logarithmic length is small compared with the transmitted source block, but this nonuniform freedom is exactly what the converse must address.

Shen’s 2006 framework defines algorithmic requests on finite acyclic directed graphs, with message-length capacities and logarithmic conditional-complexity allowances. The graph, local-information and program conventions in this card make that model explicit.

The 2021 problem list compares the two settings by taking independent repeated samples of a joint source law. Question 13 asks whether algorithmic feasibility with high probability can occur even when the corresponding Shannon transmission is impossible. The earlier direction from Shannon codes to algorithmic requests is discussed with an explicit warning that logarithmic precision may be lost.

Accordingly, the main target here is the converse actually asked in Question 13. It fixes logarithmic algorithmic overhead and the standard Shannon closure under vanishing error and positive rate slack. It does not claim a two-way finite-block equivalence, and it keeps arbitrary correlation within each source sample.

The source surveys networks where both theories have strong positive coding theorems, including transmission with side information and the two-sender Slepian–Wolf problem. It also discusses networks where elementary cut constraints do not suffice. Agreement in these special cases does not supply a general translation between the models.

The distinction is operational rather than a change of terminology for entropy. The conclusion requires one collection of local maps that succeeds on almost all realizations, while the premise only asserts the existence of compatible short local descriptions separately for those realizations.

cards.title: Strong extractors for infinite sequences
cards.formal:
Does there exist one deterministic oracle Turing machine \(F\) such that for every pair of infinite binary sequences \(x,y\) with
\[\dim(x)=\dim(y)=\tfrac12\]
and global algorithmic independence as defined below, all computations \(F^{x\oplus y}(i)\), \(i\ge0\), halt with a bit, and the resulting sequence \(z(i)=F^{x\oplus y}(i)\) satisfies
\[\dim^x(z)=\dim^y(z)=1?\]
Here \(\dim^a\) is effective Hausdorff dimension measured with the entire sequence \(a\) available as an oracle. The same machine must work for all promised pairs; it receives no description of their independence constants.

This card takes the explicit dimension-one-half instance in the 2012 question and uses “independent” in the global oracle sense of Calude–Zimand's Definition 2.1. The weaker finitary prefix-independence notion is distinguished below; it is not silently substituted for this premise.
cards.why: The question asks whether two imperfectly random infinite sources can yield information of full asymptotic density that remains incompressible even after either entire source is disclosed. It tests how far the strong-extraction principle from finite information extends to arbitrary individual sequences. The distinction matters because an infinite oracle can expose information beyond any fixed pair of input prefixes.
cards.status_note: Checked on 2026-09-14: the full 2012 question, the 2007 ordinary extraction theorem, and Calude–Zimand’s global/finitary independence definitions and restricted positive result. The published finite-string abstract and July 2026 finite-state extraction abstract were checked for their scope. A bounded search found no matching strong global-oracle extractor or general impossibility for the fixed half-dimensional promise. The independence interpretation is explicit; source-open does not claim exhaustive present-status certification.

sentences: The question asks for one computable transformation of two independent infinite binary sequences of effective dimension one half.
Its output must have effective dimension one even when either entire input is available as an oracle.
Independence is the global oracle condition, which is stronger than comparing only finite input prefixes.
The transformation may use unbounded computation but must produce every output bit on every promised input pair.
Known ordinary extraction, finite-string strong extraction and finite-state impossibility results do not settle this stated target.

cards.definitions:
An infinite binary sequence is a function \(a:\mathbb N\to\{0,1\}\), with positions starting at zero. Its length-\(n\) prefix is \(a{\upharpoonright}n=a(0)\cdots a(n-1)\). The join is the interleaving \((x\oplus y)(2i)=x(i)\), \((x\oplus y)(2i+1)=y(i)\).

Fix an optimal plain universal Turing machine and an optimal plain universal oracle Turing machine. For a finite binary string \(u\), let \(C(u)\) be the minimum number of program bits required by the first machine to halt with exactly \(u\) as output. Let \(C^a(u)\) be the corresponding minimum for the oracle machine with access to the entire sequence \(a\): a query at index \(i\) returns \(a(i)\). No time, space or oracle-use bound is imposed. Programs are finite binary strings and are not required to form a prefix-free set. Optimality means simulation of every fixed machine of the same type with an additive constant in program length, uniformly in the oracle for the oracle version. Changing the chosen optimal machines changes the complexities only by constants and does not change the dimensions or independence condition here.

Define
\[\dim(a)=\liminf_{n\to\infty}\frac{C(a{\upharpoonright}n)}n,\qquad
\dim^b(a)=\liminf_{n\to\infty}\frac{C^b(a{\upharpoonright}n)}n,\]
where \(n\) ranges over positive integers. Both dimensions lie in \([0,1]\). The input requirement is equality to one half, not a uniform finite-prefix lower bound with a supplied deficiency. In particular the point at which a lower estimate begins to hold may depend on the sequence and on the estimate's accuracy.

Global algorithmic independence means that there exists a finite constant \(c\ge0\), depending on the pair but not on prefix length, such that for every integer \(n\ge1\),
\[C^y(x{\upharpoonright}n)\ge C(x{\upharpoonright}n)-c\log_2(n+2),\qquad
C^x(y{\upharpoonright}n)\ge C(y{\upharpoonright}n)-c\log_2(n+2).\]
An additive constant can be absorbed into \(c\), so this fixes the logarithmic-loss convention also at small lengths. These are requirements about individual infinite sequences; there is no probability distribution from which inputs must be sampled.

For comparison only, finitary independence requires a constant \(d\ge0\) such that for every \(n,m\ge1\),
\[C((x{\upharpoonright}n)(y{\upharpoonright}m))\ge C(x{\upharpoonright}n)+C(y{\upharpoonright}m)-d\bigl(\log_2(n+2)+\log_2(m+2)\bigr).\]
Juxtaposition here is finite-string concatenation. Global independence implies this condition, but the converse fails; the finitary condition alone is not this card's input promise. The 2007 extraction paper uses “independent” for that weaker condition, whereas the 2010 paper explicitly distinguishes both.

The machine \(F\) has a finite program and input the binary representation of the output position \(i\). It may adaptively query either sequence through the join and use arbitrarily much finite time and space on each halting computation. Each output bit must halt for every promised pair. The machine may diverge on pairs outside the promise, and no computable uniform bound on oracle positions queried is required. There is no additional oracle, random seed or input-dependent advice. A truth-table reduction, which halts on all oracles, would qualify, but that stronger requirement is not imposed.

The output condition means that for each \(\varepsilon>0\) there is an onset \(N\), allowed to depend on \(x,y,\varepsilon\), such that for every \(n\ge N\), both \(C^x(z{\upharpoonright}n)\) and \(C^y(z{\upharpoonright}n)\) are at least \((1-\varepsilon)n\). The two conditionings are separate: the output need not retain dimension one relative to the join, from which it is computable. Ordinary dimension one alone is insufficient, as is a high limsup ratio achieved only along selected prefix lengths. The word “strong” refers here to resistance to either input oracle, not to the distinct limsup notion called effective strong dimension.
cards.answer_criterion: Provide a complete mathematically correct Lean-checked proof or refutation of the displayed uniform extraction claim. A positive answer must supply one finite oracle-machine program, prove termination for every output bit on every promised pair, and prove both relative liminf-dimension guarantees for its full infinite output. A negative answer must show that every candidate machine has a promised pair on which some bit fails to halt with a bit or one required relative dimension is less than one. Failure of one proposed construction, or an impossibility restricted to finite-state or truth-table transformations, does not by itself refute existence of the general Turing reduction. A finite-string conditional extraction theorem does not meet the infinite-oracle target.

context_blocks.text: The 2012 report explicitly asks for dimension one relative to either source after recalling ordinary two-source dimension amplification. The card preserves its concrete half-dimensional case and makes the oracle meaning of both conditioning and independence explicit.

The 2007 theorem supplies one transformation whose output has every randomness rate below one, hence effective dimension one. Its stated conclusion is ordinary output complexity, without either entire input supplied as side information. It therefore establishes the baseline rather than the strong conclusion.

Calude and Zimand distinguish global and finitary independence, prove that the notions differ, and give a positive independence-production result when the two sources are already fully random. That restricted source class does not cover the half-dimensional inputs required here.
The finite-string result permits high-complexity output even conditional on either finite input. Such finite conditioning does not give free access to all future bits of an infinite input oracle.

The July 2026 finite-state impossibility concerns a different computational model and a different dimension. It is recorded as related later work, not as a resolution of the unrestricted Turing question.

cards.formal: Is there a constant \(a>0\) such that, for every integer \(n\ge 2\) and all finite binary strings x,y,z with \(C(x,y)\le n\), some finite binary string \(z'\) satisfies \(C(z' |x,y)\le a \log _{2} n\) and |\(C(w|z)- C(w|z' )|\le a \log _{2} n\) for each \(w\in \{x,y,\langle x,y\rangle\}\)?
cards.why: Tests how far a central information-theoretic replacement principle extends to individual strings, including highly non-stochastic data. Preserving the whole two-string conditional profile would clarify which information relationships can be represented by side information determined almost entirely by the data itself.

cards.definitions: Fix an optimal plain conditional universal machine U. Define \(C(u|v)=\min\){|\(p|:U(p,v)\) halts with output u}; there is no prefix-free restriction or time bound on programs p. Set \(C(u)=C(u|\varepsilon )\), where \(\varepsilon\) is the empty string. Use the computable, uniquely decodable pairing \(\langle x,y\rangle =1^{|}x|0xy\), and write \(C(x,y)=C(\langle x,y\rangle )\) and \(C(u|x,y)=C(u|\langle x,y\rangle )\). The integer n bounds joint description length, not the bit lengths of x or y; z has no length or complexity bound. The single constant a may depend on U and the fixed encoding, but not on n,x,y,z. Choosing a larger constant absorbs the additive effects of different fixed optimal machines or computable tuple encodings. The auxiliary string \(z'\) may depend on all three strings. No bound on \(C(z' |z)\), and no efficient procedure for finding \(z'\), is required.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove the uniformly logarithmic bounds for every permitted triple, or refute them by showing that every constant a fails for some n,x,y,z with \(C(x,y)\le n\). An example that only violates a particular small constant does not refute the asymptotic assertion.

cards.title: Superpolynomial Extended Frege lower bounds
cards.formal: Is classical Extended Frege not polynomially bounded? Precisely, for every pair of integers \(C\ge1,c\ge1\), does there exist a propositional tautology \(\varphi\) such that every Extended Frege proof \(\pi\) of \(\varphi\) has binary encoding length \(|\pi|>C(|\varphi|+2)^c\)? The formula and proof encodings and the fixed proof rules are specified below.
cards.definitions:
A propositional formula is a finite syntax tree built from variables \(v_i\), indexed by \(i\in\mathbb N\), unary negation and binary material implication. Its Boolean value under an assignment \(v_i\mapsto\{0,1\}\) is defined recursively, with \(A	o B\) false exactly when A is true and B is false. A tautology is true under every assignment to its variables. Let code(a), for \(a\ge0\), be \(1^b0\) followed by the b-bit binary expansion of a+1, with \(b=\lfloor\log_2(a+1)floor+1\). Encode \(v_i\) as 00 followed by code(i), \(
eg A\) as 01 followed by the encoding of A, and \(A	o B\) as 10 followed by the encodings of A and B. This prefix syntax contains the whole formula tree, not a circuit or a program generating it; \(|\varphi|\) is its bit length. Fix the three classical Frege axiom schemes \(A	o(B	o A)\), \((A	o(B	o C))	o((A	o B)	o(A	o C))\), and \((
eg B	o
eg A)	o(A	o B)\). An instance substitutes arbitrary formulas for A, B and C consistently. Modus ponens infers B from two earlier lines A and \(A	o B\). An extension introduction adds two consecutive lines \(e	o	heta\) and \(	heta	o e\), where e is a variable absent from the target formula, theta and every line before this pair. The defining formula theta may use variables of the target and previously introduced extension variables, so definitions are acyclic. Freshness is checked before the pair, not between its two lines. There are no unproved hypotheses. A proof is a finite nonempty list of lines justified by these axiom schemes, modus ponens or such an extension pair; its last line is exactly the target formula and contains no extension variables. Earlier lines can be cited any number of times. There is no depth bound, tree-like proof restriction or restriction on the sizes of intermediate formulas. For a complete proof encoding, first write code(m) for its number of lines, and then encode each line with a two-bit tag, its metadata and its entire formula in the prefix syntax above. Tag 00 stores the axiom-scheme number 1, 2 or 3 with code; tag 01 stores with code the two earlier, one-based line indices for modus ponens, in the order A then A implies B; tag 10 stores with code the index of the fresh extension variable and must be followed immediately by a tag-11 line giving the reverse implication for the same definition. Tag 11 has no metadata and is valid only as that second line of an extension pair. The first extension formula uniquely determines theta, and both implication formulas are fully written and counted. Missing or trailing bits and invalid justifications are rejected. The proof length counts all bits, including the line count, formulas, variable indices, rule tags and inference references. This is a fixed polynomial-time checkable presentation of classical EF, polynomially equivalent to the usual finite Frege bases with extension. EF is complete, so every tautology has some finite proof; the issue is a common polynomial bound. The chosen binary encoding and paired extension rule fix presentation details without changing polynomial boundedness. The hard formula may depend on C and c; no polynomial-time procedure generating a hard family is imposed.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof of the displayed lower-bound assertion or its logical negation. The affirmative answer must, for every polynomial bound \(C(n+2)^c\), establish a tautology whose every valid EF proof exceeds that bound. The negative answer must establish fixed integers C,c for which every tautology has some valid EF proof of length at most \(C(|\varphi|+2)^c\); it need not give a polynomial-time proof-search algorithm. A bound for one search procedure, for bounded-depth or ordinary Frege, for a different logic, or for an algebraic encoding without a valid polynomial-size propositional translation does not settle this target.
cards.why: Extended Frege captures a powerful form of efficient propositional reasoning with reusable definitions. A superpolynomial lower bound would cross one of the central barriers in proof complexity and clarify whether a standard, highly expressive certificate language necessarily fails on some short true statements.

importance.reason: A defining open lower-bound problem for strong propositional reasoning, closely connected to bounded arithmetic, circuit complexity, and the limits of efficiently checkable certificates.

progress.text: Cook and Reckhow define propositional proof-system efficiency and formalize the extension rule. Their equivalence theorems make EF polynomial boundedness independent of standard presentations; Cook’s posted correction to Corollary 4.7 keeps the coNP-versus-NP premise explicit.

Wigderson’s book lists superpolynomial unrestricted Frege lower bounds as open and distinguishes the additional sharing available in Extended Frege. Lower bounds for the weaker system would not automatically apply to EF.

Pich and Santhanam give implications from EF lower bounds to \(\mathrm P\ne\mathrm{NP}\) with additional formal provability hypotheses. The checked preprint does not give an unconditional EF lower bound.

Hsieh, Jain, Li and Mathialagan construct succinct non-interactive arguments for NP under promise derandomization, LWE, SXDH and a bounded-arithmetic hardness-certification assumption. The formal unprovability premise differs from the unconditional proof-size target.

Alekseev’s journal paper proves an exponential bit-size lower bound for algebraic Binary Value Principle refutations and explicitly explains why it does not give a Frege or EF lower bound for propositional tautologies.

Akbar Tabatabai reports exponential separations between EF systems for intuitionistic substructural and linear logics. The preprint’s stated scope differs from this classical system; its proof was not independently verified.

context_blocks.text: Extension variables let a proof name a formula once and reuse its name. This can represent shared computations economically, as a Boolean circuit shares intermediate gates. Expanding all abbreviations into formula trees can cause an exponential increase in length, so a lower bound that counts only ordinary Frege proofs does not automatically survive the extension rule.

The question concerns the existence of short certificates, not the time required to discover them. A particular proof search method might take exponential time even though another method could find a short proof; conversely, a proof-size lower bound would constrain every method that outputs an EF derivation. The input length is the final tautology’s actual encoding length, so a lower bound exponential in a smaller hidden parameter may still be only polynomial in the input.

If \(\mathrm{NP}\ne \mathrm{coNP}\), every polynomial-time verifiable propositional proof system has hard tautologies, including EF. The converse for this particular system is unknown: showing that EF is inefficient does not rule out a different proof system that gives short certificates for all tautologies. This is why an EF lower bound would be a major advance without automatically constituting a proof of \(\mathrm{NP}\ne \mathrm{coNP}\). Cook’s author page corrects the premise of Corollary 4.7 in the original paper to coNP differing from NP; a P-versus-NP separation alone is not the stated premise.

Recent algebraic lower bounds illustrate an encoding issue. Alekseev proves exponential bit-size lower bounds for an extension of polynomial calculus that can simulate EF on suitable propositional translations. The hard Binary Value Principle instance is not the corresponding translation of a polynomial-size CNF. The paper explicitly explains that its result therefore does not yield a Frege or EF lower bound.

Pich and Santhanam give implications from EF lower bounds to \(\mathrm{P}\ne \mathrm{NP}\) under additional bounded-arithmetic assumptions. This explores the consequences of proof-complexity hypotheses without proving an unconditional EF lower bound.

Hsieh and coauthors construct succinct arguments under derandomization, cryptographic, and formal unprovability assumptions. Their result connects the difficulty of certifying hard tautologies to cryptography; it does not establish the unconditional size lower bound asked for here.

The use of classical implication matters. Recent lower bounds for Extended Frege systems of intuitionistic or linear logics concern different rules and valid formulas. The August 2026 preprint on those systems therefore cannot be read as a solution of the unrestricted classical problem fixed here.

cards.title: Frege versus Extended Frege
cards.formal:
Does ordinary Frege polynomially simulate Extended Frege in proof size? For the two fixed systems and binary size convention below, determine whether
\[\exists C,k\in\mathbb{N}_{\ge1}\ \forall\varphi\ \forall\pi\;\bigl(\operatorname{EFProof}(\pi,\varphi)\Rightarrow\exists\rho\,[\operatorname{FProof}(\rho,\varphi)\land |\rho|\le C(|\pi|+2)^{k}]\bigr).\]
Here \(\varphi\) ranges over all finite propositional formulas in the ordinary variables, and \(\pi,\rho\) range over finite binary strings. The constants are independent of the formula and of both proofs. This asks for existence of short Frege proofs of the same conclusions; it does not require a polynomial-time algorithm that finds them. Equivalently, for every tautology \(\varphi\), is its minimum Frege proof size \(s_{\mathrm F}(\varphi)\) bounded by one fixed polynomial in its minimum Extended Frege proof size \(s_{\mathrm{EF}}(\varphi)\)?
cards.definitions:
Formulas are finite ordered syntax trees generated by ordinary variables \(x_i\), temporary extension variables \(e_i\), negation \(\neg A\), and material implication \(A\to B\), with \(i\in\mathbb{N}=\{0,1,\ldots\}\). Ordinary formulas contain no \(e_i\). A Boolean assignment gives each variable a value in \(\{0,1\}\); negation reverses this value and implication is false exactly when its antecedent is true and consequent false. A tautology is an ordinary formula true under every assignment to its ordinary variables. Every syntactic occurrence is written separately: a formula is a tree, not a circuit with shared subformulas.

The fixed Frege calculus has precisely these three axiom schemes:
\[A\to(B\to A),\qquad (A\to(B\to C))\to((A\to B)\to(A\to C)),\qquad (\neg B\to\neg A)\to(A\to B).\]
Each occurrence of a scheme uses a consistent substitution of formulas for its metavariables \(A,B,C\). The only inference rule is modus ponens, deriving \(B\) from earlier lines \(A\) and \(A\to B\). A Frege proof is a nonempty finite sequence of ordinary formulas, each justified by an axiom instance or modus ponens, with the last formula its conclusion. There are no hypotheses, extension axioms or separate rules that substitute into an already derived line. Any earlier line may be reused arbitrarily often. Auxiliary ordinary variables not occurring in the conclusion are permitted.

Extended Frege uses the same schemes and modus ponens, and additionally permits a consecutive pair of extension lines \(e_i\to\theta\) and \(\theta\to e_i\). At this introduction, \(e_i\) has not occurred in any earlier line and does not occur in \(\theta\) or in the final conclusion. The formula \(\theta\) may contain any ordinary variables and extension variables from completed earlier pairs, but no other extension variables. Both lines are written explicitly. After the pair, \(e_i\) may occur in later axiom instances, modus-ponens lines and definitions. Every extension variable in any line must be introduced this way; the final conclusion contains none. Definitions are thus acyclic, and cannot assert arbitrary assumptions about the ordinary variables. There is no bound on formula depth, proof depth, number of extensions, or reuse of earlier lines. No tree-like restriction is imposed on the proof sequence.

Use the following fixed prefix-free binary encoding. For an integer \(t\ge0\), let \(b(t)\) be its binary expansion without leading zeros, with \(b(0)=0\), and put \(E(t)=1^{|b(t)|}0b(t)\), where concatenation is intended. A formula uses tag 00 followed by \(E(i)\) for \(x_i\), tag 01 followed by \(E(i)\) for \(e_i\), tag 10 followed by the child encoding for negation, and tag 11 followed by the antecedent and consequent encodings for implication. A proof of \(m\ge1\) lines starts with \(E(m)\). Each line then consists of a three-bit justification tag and its entire formula encoding. Tags 000, 001 and 010 specify the first, second and third axiom schemes, respectively; the written formula must be an instance of the specified scheme. Tag 011 specifies modus ponens and is followed, after the formula, by \(E(a)E(b)\): for line number \(j\), the indices satisfy \(1\le a,b<j\), line \(a\) is \(A\), and line \(b\) is exactly \(A\to B\) where the current formula is \(B\). Tags 100 and 101 specify the first and second lines of an extension pair. They must occur consecutively with exactly the two formulas and freshness conditions above; no additional data are implicit. The other tags and all malformed encodings are invalid. Frege permits only the first four tags and no extension variables. The size \(|\pi|\) is the bit length of this entire string, including every formula occurrence, variable index, line count and inference reference.

The predicates in the question mean validity under these syntactic rules with the specified final formula, not mere semantic validity of an unverified proof string. The displayed finite calculus is a standard complete classical Frege presentation; the explicit pair convention, auxiliary-variable convention and binary annotations fix ordinary polynomially equivalent presentations of the source systems. In particular, the bit cost is not merely the number of inference steps. The minimum sizes are defined for tautologies, all of which have finite Frege proofs. A size simulation alone is the target; the stronger notion of p-simulation additionally requires a polynomial-time proof translation.
cards.answer_criterion:
Supply a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of the displayed proposition or its logical negation for the fixed systems and encoding. A positive answer must establish one pair of constants \(C,k\ge1\) that works for every valid Extended Frege proof and supplies the existence of a Frege proof of exactly the same ordinary conclusion with the required size. A negative answer must establish
\[\forall C,k\in\mathbb{N}_{\ge1}\ \exists\varphi,\pi\;\bigl(\operatorname{EFProof}(\pi,\varphi)\land\forall\rho\,[\operatorname{FProof}(\rho,\varphi)\Rightarrow |\rho|>C(|\pi|+2)^k]\bigr).\]
The formula and Extended Frege proof may depend on \(C,k\); no additional uniform construction of a separating family is imposed. All validity, size and quantifier claims must be justified in Lean. Conditional comparisons, a particular expensive expansion, restricted proof systems, a quasipolynomial simulation, or a polynomial-time proof-search lower bound alone do not meet this criterion. This is a binary asymptotic proof-size comparison, so the numerical 1/100 tolerance does not replace its polynomial bound.
cards.why: This asks whether naming and reusing intermediate formulas can shorten rigorous propositional proofs by more than every polynomial factor. It is a central comparison between strong proof systems and between reasoning with formula trees and shared circuit representations. A separation would yield superpolynomial lower bounds for unrestricted Frege; an equivalence would show that the extension rule changes shortest-proof lengths by at most polynomial factors.

progress.text: Cook and Reckhow formalize Frege rules, fresh extension definitions and polynomial robustness of standard presentations. Their size accounting distinguishes total proof length from the number of lines.

Buss characterizes Frege size simulation of EF through polynomial-size partial EF consistency proofs in Frege, and proves polynomial-size partial Frege self-consistency proofs. The 2002 date on the downloadable typescript is not a new publication.
The Stanford mini-tutorial explicitly presents Frege versus Extended Frege as an open comparison between strong propositional systems.
Aisenberg and coauthors establish polynomial EF and quasipolynomial Frege upper bounds for the Kneser–Lovász principles for each fixed \(k\); no lower-bound separation follows.

Krajíček states a polynomial-size local circuit-rewriting characterization of EF reasoning. The intermediate representations remain circuits; the concluding discussion does not assert a polynomial-time construction by the displayed argument.

ECCC TR26-166, submitted 4 September and published 5 September, reports quasipolynomial Frege simulation of two-group partially commutative formula IPS over \(\mathrm{GF}(2)\), under its explicit placeholder and axiom conventions.

Bounded primary-source checks through 15 September 2026 did not identify a polynomial-size Frege simulation of unrestricted EF or a superpolynomial separation. The checked June circuit-rewriting and September restricted formula-IPS results have different representations or overhead. context_blocks.text: Frege proofs model a finite list of ordinary propositional deductions. Extended Frege adds named definitions, allowing a long expression to be referenced by a variable after paying for its definition. Chains of these definitions describe shared Boolean circuits. Every assignment to the ordinary variables extends uniquely through an acyclic sequence of definitions, so the extension rule preserves truth of conclusions that contain no extension variables. This explains the systems' common set of theorems while leaving their proof lengths potentially different.

Proof reuse and subformula sharing are different resources. Both systems may cite an earlier proof line many times; ordinary Frege still pays for every occurrence inside each newly written formula. Extended Frege also has names for intermediate expressions. This representational distinction does not itself show that any tautology lacks a short Frege proof. The question compares the best proofs available in the two systems, irrespective of how those proofs were discovered.

The usual robustness theorem compares finite sound and complete Frege presentations with polynomial overhead. Cook and Reckhow also define fresh extension variables and establish the analogous robustness of Extended Frege. The card preserves the saved size-simulation target while making its syntax and bit accounting explicit. It restores the source convention allowing auxiliary ordinary variables; restricting such variables to those of the conclusion gives a polynomially equivalent convention. A bounded-depth, tree-like or otherwise restricted Frege system would be a different question.

A polynomial bound on the existence of translated proofs is distinct from a polynomial-time translator. Buss's work separates these notions and relates size simulation to short finite consistency proofs. His 1991 result characterizes Frege simulation of Extended Frege by polynomial-size Frege proofs of the corresponding partial EF consistency statements: finite propositional assertions that a contradiction has no proof up to a specified length. Frege already has polynomial-size partial self-consistency proofs. This comparison is a stated theorem about the systems, not a resolution of Frege versus EF. The current review checked the author and publisher abstracts; the author's downloadable copy is headed 11 July 2002, although the journal publication is from 1991.

Buss's Stanford tutorial of 27 February 2014 explicitly presents the formula-versus-circuit proof comparison as a longstanding open question. Its discussion of proposed separating principles is historical context, not a current lower-bound theorem. Quasipolynomial upper bounds for particular families must remain distinct both from polynomial upper bounds and from a separation of the unrestricted systems.

A concrete example is the Kneser–Lovász coloring principle. The graph has the \(k\)-element subsets of \(\{1,\ldots,n\}\) as vertices and joins disjoint subsets; for \(n\ge2k\), its propositional principle rules out a proper coloring with \(n-2k+1\) colors. Aisenberg and coauthors give polynomial-size EF proofs and quasipolynomial-size Frege proofs for each fixed \(k\). Constants and exponents may depend on that fixed parameter. Their 2015 conference version states these as Theorems 4 and 5; the 2018 expanded journal abstract retains the fixed-parameter condition. These are upper bounds for particular tautologies, not a superpolynomial Frege lower bound or a uniform bound with both parameters growing.

Krajíček's 11 June 2026 preprint describes circuit-equivalence reasoning by local circuit rewrites. Its relation is polynomial-time recognizable, and each rewrite may delete gates and add at most seven; a short EF proof yields a polynomially bounded chain. The intermediate objects retain circuit sharing. The concluding discussion also distinguishes existence of a small chain from a polynomial-time construction of it by the presented proof. This normal-form statement therefore supplies neither the polynomial-size formula proof nor the polynomial-time translator that could be mistakenly inferred from the abstract.

The September 2026 report by Chatterjee, Chatterjee, Ghosal and Mukhopadhyay states a quasipolynomial Frege simulation of a restricted Ideal Proof System over \(\mathrm{GF}(2)\), the field with two elements. Certificates are algebraic formulas. The original variables are divided into two groups, noncommuting within a group and commuting across groups; Definition 1.1 separately specifies the noncommuting placeholder variables and included Boolean and commutator axioms. Theorem 1.2 concerns refutations of unsatisfiable CNFs in that model. Its certificate restrictions and quasipolynomial overhead both prevent it from answering the unrestricted EF question. The report and theorem scope were checked; its complete new proof was not independently verified.

An EF proof includes its final formula, so a superpolynomial separation from Frege would imply superpolynomial Frege proof-size lower bounds as a function of formula length. The converse need not follow: a family hard for Frege might also require long EF proofs. Likewise, the separate question whether EF is polynomially bounded asks whether every tautology has a short EF proof, rather than whether Frege can match EF's shortest proofs. The present card makes no assumption that \(\mathrm{NP}\ne\mathrm{coNP}\) and does not identify a computation-class separation with this proof-system comparison.

benchmark_focus.reason: A canonical strong-system simulation problem, directly tied to Frege lower bounds, finite consistency and circuit-based reasoning.

cards.title: Superpolynomial \(\mathrm{AC}^{0}[p]\)-Frege lower bounds
cards.formal:
For every prime integer \(p\), does there exist a single polynomial-time constructible family of DNF tautologies \((\tau_{p,n})_{n\ge1}\) of length polynomially related to \(n\), such that its proofs in the fixed modular Frege calculus below exceed every polynomial size bound at every fixed line depth? Precisely, require for each \(p\) a finite deterministic machine \(M_p\) and integers \(C_p,k_p\ge1\) such that, for every \(n\ge1\), on input \(1^n\) the machine outputs a DNF \(\tau_{p,n}\) within \(C_p(n+2)^{k_p}\) bit steps, this formula is a tautology, and
\[n\le |\tau_{p,n}|\le C_p(n+2)^{k_p}.\]
The required lower bound is
\[\forall d,r,N\in\mathbb{N}_{\ge1}\ \exists n\ge N\ \forall\pi\;\bigl(\operatorname{Proof}_{p,d}(\pi,\tau_{p,n})\Rightarrow |\pi|>n^r\bigr).\]
The machine and the family may depend on \(p\) but not on \(d,r,N\); the witness \(n\) may depend on all three. No effective procedure producing \(M_p\) from \(p\) is required. The family consists of genuine tautologies, not formulas whose lack of short proofs might be due to falsity. The lower bound is infinitely often, not necessarily eventually for every \(n\).
cards.definitions:
Fix a prime \(p\ge2\). Formulas are finite ordered syntax trees built from constants \(0,1\), variables \(x_i\) for \(i\in\mathbb{N}=\{0,1,\ldots\}\), unary \(\neg\), binary \(\land,\lor\), and gates \(\operatorname{MOD}_{p,j}(A_1,\ldots,A_t)\) for \(0\le j<p\) and any finite arity \(t\ge0\). Under an assignment of Boolean values to the variables, the usual connectives have their ordinary truth tables, and a modular gate is true exactly when the number of its true arguments is congruent to \(j\) modulo \(p\). A tautology is true under every assignment. A literal is a variable or its negation. A DNF is a finite disjunction of finite conjunctions of literals, written as a binary formula with any parenthesization; an empty conjunction is \(1\), an empty disjunction is \(0\), and a singleton conjunction or disjunction is its sole member. Target DNFs contain no modular gates.

The notation \(A\Rightarrow B\) is an abbreviation for \(\neg A\lor B\), and \(A\Leftrightarrow B\) abbreviates \((A\Rightarrow B)\land(B\Rightarrow A)\). Both are expanded fully before checking syntax, depth or size. Fix the following finite ordinary Frege axiom schemes, in the order displayed:
\[\begin{gathered}
 A\Rightarrow(B\Rightarrow A),\\
 (A\Rightarrow(B\Rightarrow C))\Rightarrow((A\Rightarrow B)\Rightarrow(A\Rightarrow C)),\\
 (\neg B\Rightarrow\neg A)\Rightarrow(A\Rightarrow B),\\
 (A\land B)\Rightarrow A,\qquad (A\land B)\Rightarrow B,\\
 A\Rightarrow(B\Rightarrow(A\land B)),\\
 A\Rightarrow(A\lor B),\qquad B\Rightarrow(A\lor B),\\
 (A\Rightarrow C)\Rightarrow((B\Rightarrow C)\Rightarrow((A\lor B)\Rightarrow C)),\\
 1,\qquad \neg0.
\end{gathered}\]
The metavariables \(A,B,C\) may be replaced consistently by arbitrary formulas of the full modular language. The sole inference rule is modus ponens: from earlier lines \(A\) and \(A\Rightarrow B\), infer \(B\). There are no hypotheses. Besides these eleven schemes, allow the modular axioms
\[\operatorname{MOD}_{p,0}(),\qquad \neg\operatorname{MOD}_{p,j}()\quad(1\le j<p),\]
and every instance of
\[\operatorname{MOD}_{p,j}(\Gamma,A)\Leftrightarrow
 \bigl((\operatorname{MOD}_{p,j}(\Gamma)\land\neg A)\lor
 (\operatorname{MOD}_{p,j-1}(\Gamma)\land A)\bigr),\]
where \(\Gamma\) is any finite ordered list of formulas, including the empty list, and \(j-1\) is reduced modulo \(p\) to \(\{0,\ldots,p-1\}\). These are the modular schemes of the cited source, attached to the specified finite complete classical Frege basis. An axiom line must match its indicated scheme syntactically after expansion, using the same substituted formula at each occurrence of a metavariable. A proof is a nonempty finite sequence of axiom or modus-ponens lines ending with the claimed formula. Earlier lines may be reused without restriction. There are no extension-variable definition axioms, no separate substitution rule for previously derived lines, and no restrictions of regularity or tree shape.

Define the logical depth \(\delta\) of constants and variables to be zero. Negation has depth \(1+\delta(A)\), and a modular gate has depth \(1+\max(0,\delta(A_1),\ldots,\delta(A_t))\). For a conjunction, flatten its maximal connected subtree of conjunction nodes and collect the boundary subformulas whose roots are not conjunctions; its depth is one plus the maximum depth of those subformulas. Use the same rule for disjunctions. Flattening does not cross a negation, modular gate or different Boolean connective. It defines the depth measure only: the actual binary syntax tree is still written and counted in full. A depth-at-most-\(d\) proof must have \(\delta\le d\) for every line, including instantiated axioms and the conclusion. This bounds individual formulas, not the length of an inference path in the proof graph. Such paths and the total number of lines are unrestricted.

All sizes are bits in a fixed prefix encoding. For \(t\ge0\), let \(b(t)\) be its binary expansion without leading zeros, with \(b(0)=0\), and let \(E(t)=1^{|b(t)|}0b(t)\), using concatenation. Formula tags 000 and 001 encode constants \(0\) and \(1\); 010 followed by \(E(i)\) encodes \(x_i\); 011 followed by the child encodes negation; 100 and 101 followed by both child encodings encode conjunction and disjunction. Tag 110 followed by \(E(j)E(t)\) and all \(t\) ordered child encodings represents \(\operatorname{MOD}_{p,j}\). Tag 111 is invalid. The prime is fixed by the system, not supplied as an oracle. A proof starts with \(E(m)\), its positive number of lines. Each line contains \(E(q)\) followed by its complete formula encoding. Rule labels \(q=1,\ldots,11\) refer to the ordinary schemes in their displayed order; labels 12, 13 and 14 refer respectively to the empty-zero-residue, empty-nonzero-residue and recursive modular schemes. Label 15 denotes modus ponens and is followed, after the formula, by \(E(a)E(b)\): on line \(j\), require \(1\le a,b<j\), line \(a=A\) and line \(b=A\Rightarrow B\), with the current line exactly \(B\). Other rule labels and malformed strings are invalid. The length \(|\pi|\) includes every variable index, gate, repeated formula occurrence, line count and inference reference. Formula length uses the same formula encoding. Nothing is given by a compressed circuit, advice or a program for generating a larger proof.

The predicate \(\operatorname{Proof}_{p,d}(\pi,\tau)\) means validity under all these rules, conclusion \(\tau\), and line depth at most \(d\). Construction time for the target family is measured on a standard deterministic Turing machine with a fixed finite number of tapes and a finite alphabet containing input/output bits and blank. A transition reads and writes at most one cell per tape and moves each head by at most one cell; all transitions and output writes count. Each \(M_p\) is one finite program, with no oracle or length-dependent advice. Its constants \(C_p,k_p\) may depend on that program and the fixed prime. The formula-size lower bound \(|\tau_{p,n}|\ge n\) and polynomial upper bound make size in \(n\) polynomially comparable with size in the conclusion. Quantifying over positive integer exponents \(r\) is equivalent to exceeding every polynomial bound, including bounds with arbitrary fixed multiplicative constants.
cards.answer_criterion: Supply the stated families, their construction machines and bounds, together with a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean that all outputs are DNF tautologies and that the displayed lower-bound quantifiers hold for every prime and every fixed line depth. Alternatively, give a complete Lean proof of the logical negation: some prime \(p\) has no family satisfying all the stated requirements. Equivalently, for that prime, every polynomial-time constructible DNF tautology family of the prescribed length scale has some fixed depth \(d\), exponent \(r\) and threshold \(N\) for which every \(n\ge N\) admits a valid depth-\(d\) proof of size at most \(n^r\). A negative answer does not require an efficient proof-finding algorithm. Unproved tautologicity, one fixed polynomial lower bound, a bound only at restricted derivation depth, or a result for only one prime does not establish the full positive claim. All assumptions, construction bounds, depth and size conventions must match the card. This binary asymptotic claim retains its polynomial precision; the numerical 1/100 tolerance is not a replacement for a proof-size lower bound.
cards.why: This is a central unresolved comparison between the expressive power of shallow formulas and the length of rigorous deductions. Ordinary bounded-depth Frege lower bounds are known, but modular gates permit compact reasoning about arithmetic counts, including parity. Proving the stated lower bounds would move a major proof-complexity frontier beyond shallow reasoning without modular counting.

importance.reason: A classical next step beyond the strongest broadly established bounded-depth Frege lower bounds, with direct connections to algebraic proof systems and a persistent gap between circuit and proof complexity.

progress.text: Ajtai establishes superpolynomial ordinary bounded-depth Frege lower bounds for pigeonhole formulas; Pitassi, Beame and Impagliazzo publish exponential-type improvements in 1993. These systems do not contain modular gates.

Krajíček gives the explicit modular Frege schemes and flattened logical-depth convention in §5 of the preprint, revised 27 September 2023 and published in November 2024. The modular lower-bound frontier remains open there.
Efremenko and Itsykson publish tree-like lifting and stronger size-versus-derivation-depth tradeoffs for resolution over parities. Derivation depth is not the logical depth of each line.
Lu, Santhanam and Tzameret publish an unconditional no-short-proof result for explicit candidate DNFs while leaving their tautologicity unresolved. The full arXiv version is v1 of 20 September 2025.
Itsykson, Podolskii and Shekhovtsov report near-quadratic derivation-depth lifting and an unconditional quadratic size lower bound for parity resolution, under their stated lifting conditions.

Hakoniemi, Limaye and Tzameret publish ECCC TR26-070, submitted 5 May, reporting hard Boolean CNF instances for the restricted linear-certificate roABP fragment of IPS, for all variable orders and fields.

context_blocks.text: A modular gate states that a count has a particular residue. The case \(p=2\) includes parity, while other primes give other fixed modular tests. A bounded-depth proof may make arbitrarily many deductions, each of which uses only a bounded number of logical layers. Krajíček's §5 explicitly defines the modular recurrence axioms and the depth convention that flattens consecutive conjunctions or disjunctions. The card fixes a finite ordinary basis and a complete binary encoding within that presentation.

The saved benchmark asks for one efficiently generated DNF family for each prime that defeats all fixed line depths, with the same family at every exponent. This explicit construction and quantifier order are retained as the card's chosen formulation of the broad modular-Frege frontier; they are not silently replaced by a family chosen separately for each depth. A method for selecting the program uniformly from the prime is not an additional requirement. Hard instances may occur on different infinite subsequences at different depths and exponents.

Without modular gates, the bounded-depth comparison has established lower bounds. Ajtai's 1988 work proves superpolynomial bounds for propositional pigeonhole formulas, and Pitassi, Beame and Impagliazzo's 1993 paper strengthens them to exponential-type size bounds at each fixed depth. These are statements about ordinary bounded-depth Frege. Adding all modular axiom instances enlarges the set of possible proofs, so an ordinary-Frege lower bound does not itself establish the present one.

Circuit lower bounds and proof lower bounds measure different things. Prime-modulus circuit lower bounds concern nonconstant Boolean functions that cannot be computed by small circuits. Every tautology in this card instead computes the constant true function. The object required to be large is a syntactically verified deduction of that tautology in a fixed calculus. The February 2026 source explicitly retains modular Frege lower bounds as open while distinguishing the circuit results.

Resolution over parities permits disjunctions of linear equations modulo two as proof lines. It is a restricted proof system within the modular-Frege setting. Efremenko and Itsykson's CCC 2025 Theorems 3 and 4 give a tree-like lifting statement and a size-versus-derivation-depth tradeoff, respectively. For their lifted Tseitin family with \(m\) variables, the latter requires either size \(2^{\Omega(m/\log m)}\) or derivation depth \(\Omega(m\log m)\). The depth tradeoff and quadratic bound each fall short of a superpolynomial bound on unrestricted derivation size.

cards.title: Superpolynomial lower bounds for unrestricted Frege proofs
cards.formal:
Is ordinary Frege not polynomially bounded? For the fixed calculus and complete binary encoding below, determine whether
\[\forall C,k\in\mathbb{N}_{\ge1}\ \exists\varphi\;\bigl(\operatorname{Taut}(\varphi)\land\forall\pi\,[\operatorname{FProof}(\pi,\varphi)\Rightarrow |\pi|>C(|\varphi|+2)^k]\bigr).\]
Here \(\varphi\) ranges over finite propositional formulas, and \(\pi\) over finite binary strings. Equivalently, for every fixed polynomial bound, some tautology has minimum Frege proof size \(s_{\mathrm F}(\varphi)\) exceeding that bound in its own encoded length. Neither a polynomial-time construction of hard tautologies nor any algorithm for finding their shortest proofs is required. The depth and length of intermediate formulas and the reuse of previous lines are unrestricted.
cards.definitions:
Ordinary propositional formulas are finite ordered syntax trees generated by variables \(x_i\), where \(i\in\mathbb{N}=\{0,1,\ldots\}\), unary negation \(\neg A\), and binary material implication \(A\to B\). A Boolean assignment gives every variable a value in \(\{0,1\}\); negation reverses it, and implication is false exactly when its antecedent is true and its consequent false. The predicate \(\operatorname{Taut}(\varphi)\) means that \(\varphi\) evaluates to true under every assignment to its variables. Formulas are fully written trees: repeated occurrences of a subformula are counted separately.

Fix exactly three axiom schemes:
\[A\to(B\to A),\qquad (A\to(B\to C))\to((A\to B)\to(A\to C)),\qquad (\neg B\to\neg A)\to(A\to B).\]
Each instance consistently replaces the metavariables \(A,B,C\) by arbitrary formulas. The only inference rule is modus ponens: from earlier lines \(A\) and \(A\to B\), infer \(B\). A proof is a nonempty finite sequence of axiom instances and such inferences, with its last formula the conclusion. There are no hypotheses, no extension axioms naming other formulas, and no separate rule substituting into a previously derived line. Variables absent from the final formula may appear in ordinary intermediate formulas. Earlier lines may be reused arbitrarily often, so the dependency graph need not be a tree. There is no cap on line size, logical depth, dependency-path length or number of lines.

Use the following explicit prefix encoding. For an integer \(t\ge0\), let \(b(t)\) be its binary expansion without leading zeros, with \(b(0)=0\), and put \(E(t)=1^{|b(t)|}0b(t)\), using concatenation. The formula \(x_i\) is encoded by tag 00 followed by \(E(i)\); a negation by tag 01 followed by the child formula; an implication by tag 10 followed by the antecedent and consequent formulas in order. Formula tag 11 is invalid. A proof of \(m\ge1\) lines starts with \(E(m)\). Each line then has a two-bit justification tag followed by its complete formula encoding. Tags 00, 01 and 10 identify the first, second and third axiom schemes, respectively; the written formula must be a syntactic instance of the indicated scheme. Tag 11 denotes modus ponens and is followed, after the formula, by \(E(a)E(b)\). On line \(j\), require \(1\le a,b<j\), line \(a\) to be some \(A\), and line \(b\) to be exactly \(A\to B\), where the current line is \(B\). Malformed strings are not proofs. This makes \(\operatorname{FProof}(\pi,\varphi)\) a specific syntactic validity predicate with final formula \(\varphi\), rather than a claim that unspecified inference rules are sound.

The lengths \(|\varphi|\) and \(|\pi|\) are their entire binary encoding lengths. Every connective, variable index, repeated subformula, line count and inference reference is included. A huge formula is not a constant-cost proof line; proof-size bounds are measured against the full conclusion length, not just its number of distinct variables. This finite Hilbert calculus is sound and complete for classical propositional tautologies. Therefore every tautology has some finite proof, and \(s_{\mathrm F}(\varphi)\) is the minimum bit length among its valid proof strings. Standard finite Frege presentations are polynomially equivalent, so this explicit convention fixes the meaning without changing polynomial boundedness. Restricting the coefficients and exponents of candidate polynomial bounds to positive integers also does not change the question.
cards.answer_criterion: Provide a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of the displayed proposition or its logical negation. For an affirmative answer, prove that for every pair \(C,k\ge1\) there exists a genuine tautology for which every valid proof exceeds the specified size; an efficiently generated hard family is welcome but is not required. A negative answer must establish one fixed pair \(C,k\ge1\) such that every tautology has some valid Frege proof of size at most \(C(|\varphi|+2)^k\). It need not supply a polynomial-time proof-search algorithm. All formula semantics, syntactic verification and size claims must match the given model and be justified in Lean. A fixed-degree lower bound, an independent cap on line size or depth, a bound for a subsystem, or hardness of finding proofs does not answer the full question. The numerical 1/100 convention does not replace this binary asymptotic comparison.
cards.why: This asks whether a standard, robust language of propositional deduction must sometimes use certificates larger than every polynomial in the statement proved. It is a central unresolved lower-bound question for formal reasoning, beyond the restricted proof systems for which strong size lower bounds are known. It concerns the size of the best possible proof, independently of the resources used to discover it.

importance.reason: A central unresolved step in the Cook–Reckhow program, beyond the systems for which current general lower-bound methods succeed.

cards.status_note: Open in Wigderson’s checked 6 August 2019 draft and reiterated in the September 2026 primary literature. Bounded checks through 15 September 2026 identified no unconditional superpolynomial bit-size lower bound for unrestricted Frege and no universal polynomial upper bound. The April tree-like result has a separate line cap, the refutation-principle result has bounded-depth/line parameters and quasipolynomial overhead, and the June algebraic theorem does not transfer its hard instance to the required propositional setting. New proofs were not independently verified.

context_blocks.text: Frege systems formalize ordinary propositional deduction with finitely many rule patterns. A proof can derive intermediate lemmas, combine them and cite them again. Checking a proposed step is a syntactic task with polynomial cost in its written size. The question asks whether some short true statements inevitably require much larger certificates in this particular language, even when no restrictions are placed on intermediate formulas.

The distinction between statement length and variable count matters. A formula on \(n\) variables can itself have exponential length in \(n\), so an exponential bound expressed only in the variable count need not be large compared with the actual input. This card compares total proof bits directly with \(|\varphi|\). It also distinguishes the number of proof lines from their combined size: a single enormous intermediate assertion is fully charged.

Cook and Reckhow show that some polynomially bounded propositional proof system exists if and only if \(\mathrm{NP}=\mathrm{coNP}\). Thus \(\mathrm{NP}\ne\mathrm{coNP}\) would imply a positive answer here, and polynomial boundedness of Frege would imply \(\mathrm{NP}=\mathrm{coNP}\). A lower bound for this one fixed proof language does not by itself establish that no other proof language is polynomially bounded. The card asks for an unconditional answer and does not assume a complexity-class separation.

Short proofs and efficient proof discovery are separate resources. The positive statement quantifies over all candidate polynomial size bounds, then permits a different hard tautology for each bound. It does not impose a construction algorithm for those tautologies. Conversely, a universal polynomial upper bound would assert that short certificates exist, without by itself giving a polynomial-time algorithm that finds them.

The propositional pigeonhole principle asserts that \(n+1\) pigeons cannot be injected into \(n\) holes. Its familiar CNF encoding requires exponential-size resolution refutations, while Buss proved polynomial-size Frege proofs in 1987. This is a concrete separation between a weaker clause-based system and Frege. It also explains why a hard family for one proof system cannot automatically be treated as hard for every stronger system. The original author abstract and theorem statements were checked, together with Wigderson's textbook account.

Wigderson states the unrestricted question as Open Problem 6.10 in the author draft of 6 August 2019, on printed page 66, following the pigeonhole upper bound in Theorem 6.9. The older cached March 2018 draft has different pagination; the 2019 file was checked separately in this review. Arbitrary intermediate formulas are part of this problem even when the final tautology is shallow. A theorem limiting only bounded-depth proofs does not cover deductions using deeper formulas.

De Rezende, Engström, Ghannane and Risse's April 2026 preprint states average-case superpolynomial refutation-length bounds for tree-like semantic Frege with a separate line-size cap. Corollary 1.6 considers \(n^{2-\varepsilon}\le s(n)\le2^{n^{1-\varepsilon}}\), with source-prescribed fixed \(\varepsilon>0\), and an explicit family of CNFs of size at most \(s(n)^{1+\varepsilon}\); a uniformly sampled member is hard with probability tending to one for tree-like proofs whose individual lines have size at most \(s(n)\). The conclusion concerns that capped system and the stated distribution, not every member or every unrestricted Frege proof. The arXiv submission is dated 30 April; the downloaded typescript is headed 1 May.

The line cap is material. Without a separate line-size cap, ordinary tree-like Frege polynomially simulates general Frege. The cited paper explains that the known conversion increases individual formula sizes, so it does not preserve the capped model used by its lower bound. In the stronger semantic setting, allowing a line large enough to represent the entire inconsistent input even permits an immediate semantic contradiction. None of this supplies a lower bound for unrestricted syntactic Frege.

Davis and Robere's 10 April 2026 report concerns proofs of statements about proof lengths. Its refutation-principle formula asserts that a specified pigeonhole CNF has a depth-\(d\) Frege refutation with a prescribed number of lines, each of polynomially bounded size. Theorem 1.3 gives refutations of those assertions in \(\operatorname{Res}(\log)\), where lines are DNFs with logarithmically bounded conjunction width. The bound is quasipolynomial in the length of the encoded refutation-principle assertion; it is not a polynomial upper bound in the original pigeonhole parameter. The depth and line-size restrictions on the asserted proofs remain essential.

Alekseev's journal paper, published 21 June 2026 after a CCC 2021 precursor, proves an exponential bit-size lower bound over \(\mathbb Q\) for Polynomial Calculus with extension and square-root rules. Its Binary Value Principle instance consists of \(1+\sum_{i=1}^{n}2^{i-1}x_i=0\) and \(x_i^2-x_i=0\). The paper explicitly notes that this algebraic input is not the relevant polynomial-size propositional CNF translation, so the theorem does not yield Frege or EF lower bounds. This is a limit on transferring that specific lower bound, not a claim that no Boolean encoding of the arithmetic condition can exist.

Extended Frege additionally permits variables naming intermediate formulas. A lower bound for EF would imply one for Frege, while a Frege lower bound need not persist in the presence of those definitions. Separating Frege from EF is also a different question: Frege could have hard tautologies that are equally hard for EF. The present target requires only failure of a universal polynomial bound for Frege itself.

The September 2026 report on partially commutative Ideal Proof Systems again records that unrestricted Frege has no known superpolynomial lower bound. Its own theorem is an upper bound: a quasipolynomial Frege simulation of a restricted algebraic formula system over \(\mathrm{GF}(2)\). This fresh source supplies dated context, not a proof of the present conjecture. The model restrictions and complete new proof have not been independently validated beyond the source-scope review.
