cards.context:
Frege systems formalize ordinary propositional deduction with finitely many rule patterns. A proof can derive intermediate lemmas, combine them and cite them again. Checking a proposed step is a syntactic task with polynomial cost in its written size. The question asks whether some short true statements inevitably require much larger certificates in this particular language, even when no restrictions are placed on intermediate formulas.

The distinction between statement length and variable count matters. A formula on \(n\) variables can itself have exponential length in \(n\), so an exponential bound expressed only in the variable count need not be large compared with the actual input. This card compares total proof bits directly with \(|\varphi|\). It also distinguishes the number of proof lines from their combined size: a single enormous intermediate assertion is fully charged.

Cook and Reckhow show that some polynomially bounded propositional proof system exists if and only if \(\mathrm{NP}=\mathrm{coNP}\). Thus \(\mathrm{NP}\ne\mathrm{coNP}\) would imply a positive answer here, and polynomial boundedness of Frege would imply \(\mathrm{NP}=\mathrm{coNP}\). A lower bound for this one fixed proof language does not by itself establish that no other proof language is polynomially bounded. The card asks for an unconditional answer and does not assume a complexity-class separation.

Short proofs and efficient proof discovery are separate resources. The positive statement quantifies over all candidate polynomial size bounds, then permits a different hard tautology for each bound. It does not impose a construction algorithm for those tautologies. Conversely, a universal polynomial upper bound would assert that short certificates exist, without by itself giving a polynomial-time algorithm that finds them.

The propositional pigeonhole principle asserts that \(n+1\) pigeons cannot be injected into \(n\) holes. Its familiar CNF encoding requires exponential-size resolution refutations, while Buss proved polynomial-size Frege proofs in 1987. This is a concrete separation between a weaker clause-based system and Frege. It also explains why a hard family for one proof system cannot automatically be treated as hard for every stronger system. The original author abstract and theorem statements were checked, together with Wigderson's textbook account.

Wigderson states the unrestricted question as Open Problem 6.10 in the author draft of 6 August 2019, on printed page 66, following the pigeonhole upper bound in Theorem 6.9. The older cached March 2018 draft has different pagination; the 2019 file was checked separately in this review. Arbitrary intermediate formulas are part of this problem even when the final tautology is shallow. A theorem limiting only bounded-depth proofs does not cover deductions using deeper formulas.

De Rezende, Engström, Ghannane and Risse's April 2026 preprint states average-case superpolynomial refutation-length bounds for tree-like semantic Frege with a separate line-size cap. Corollary 1.6 considers \(n^{2-\varepsilon}\le s(n)\le2^{n^{1-\varepsilon}}\), with source-prescribed fixed \(\varepsilon>0\), and an explicit family of CNFs of size at most \(s(n)^{1+\varepsilon}\); a uniformly sampled member is hard with probability tending to one for tree-like proofs whose individual lines have size at most \(s(n)\). The conclusion concerns that capped system and the stated distribution, not every member or every unrestricted Frege proof. The arXiv submission is dated 30 April; the downloaded typescript is headed 1 May.

The line cap is material. Without a separate line-size cap, ordinary tree-like Frege polynomially simulates general Frege. The cited paper explains that the known conversion increases individual formula sizes, so it does not preserve the capped model used by its lower bound. In the stronger semantic setting, allowing a line large enough to represent the entire inconsistent input even permits an immediate semantic contradiction. None of this supplies a lower bound for unrestricted syntactic Frege.

Davis and Robere's 10 April 2026 report concerns proofs of statements about proof lengths. Its refutation-principle formula asserts that a specified pigeonhole CNF has a depth-\(d\) Frege refutation with a prescribed number of lines, each of polynomially bounded size. Theorem 1.3 gives refutations of those assertions in \(\operatorname{Res}(\log)\), where lines are DNFs with logarithmically bounded conjunction width. The bound is quasipolynomial in the length of the encoded refutation-principle assertion; it is not a polynomial upper bound in the original pigeonhole parameter. The depth and line-size restrictions on the asserted proofs remain essential.

Alekseev's journal paper, published 21 June 2026 after a CCC 2021 precursor, proves an exponential bit-size lower bound over \(\mathbb Q\) for Polynomial Calculus with extension and square-root rules. Its Binary Value Principle instance consists of \(1+\sum_{i=1}^{n}2^{i-1}x_i=0\) and \(x_i^2-x_i=0\). The paper explicitly notes that this algebraic input is not the relevant polynomial-size propositional CNF translation, so the theorem does not yield Frege or EF lower bounds. This is a limit on transferring that specific lower bound, not a claim that no Boolean encoding of the arithmetic condition can exist.

Extended Frege additionally permits variables naming intermediate formulas. A lower bound for EF would imply one for Frege, while a Frege lower bound need not persist in the presence of those definitions. Separating Frege from EF is also a different question: Frege could have hard tautologies that are equally hard for EF. The present target requires only failure of a universal polynomial bound for Frege itself.

The September 2026 report on partially commutative Ideal Proof Systems again records that unrestricted Frege has no known superpolynomial lower bound. Its own theorem is an upper bound: a quasipolynomial Frege simulation of a restricted algebraic formula system over \(\mathrm{GF}(2)\). This fresh source supplies dated context, not a proof of the present conjecture. The model restrictions and complete new proof have not been independently validated beyond the source-scope review.

cards.title: Existence of p-optimal proof systems
cards.formal: Does there exist a Cook–Reckhow proof system P for propositional tautologies such that, for every Cook–Reckhow proof system Q for the same tautologies, there is a deterministic polynomial-time translation \(t_{Q}\) satisfying \(\mathrm{P}(t_{Q}(\pi ))=Q(\pi )\) for every finite binary proof string \(\pi\)?

cards.definitions: Fix an explicit binary syntax for Boolean formulas built from indexed variables, AND, OR and NOT. A tautology evaluates to true under every assignment to its variables; TAUT is the set of encodings of such formulas. A Cook–Reckhow proof system is a total function \(\mathrm{P}:\{0,1\}*\to\)TAUT, computed by one uniform deterministic multitape Turing machine in time polynomial in its input length, whose range is all of TAUT. A string \(\pi\) proves formula F when \(\mathrm{P}(\pi )=F\). Soundness requires every output to be a tautology; completeness requires every tautology to occur as an output. There is no polynomial upper bound on the shortest proof of every formula. In this total-function presentation, strings that would be malformed proofs in a conventional calculus may instead produce a fixed tautology such as \(x_{1}\lor \neg x_{1}\). A simulation translation is total and satisfies the equality on all strings, preserving the exact output formula. Its program, polynomial exponent and constants may depend on Q and P, but not on \(\pi\). The order is \(\exists \mathrm{P} \forall Q \exists t_{Q} \forall \pi\). No algorithm taking an arbitrary program for Q and producing its translator is required. Neither advice, randomization nor an oracle is allowed in the systems or translations. Polynomial translation time also bounds the translated proof length polynomially in |\(\pi |\).
cards.answer_criterion: Prove that one sound and complete polynomial-time proof system admits the required polynomial-time translations from every other such system, or prove that for every candidate P some sound and complete Q has no such translation. A proof-length comparison without an efficient translation proves only ordinary optimality. Refuting a particular named proof system’s p-optimality does not exclude all systems.

context_blocks.title: One common format for efficiently checked proofs
context_blocks.text: Different proof calculi can establish the same tautology with very different amounts of work. The question asks whether one format can accept a polynomial-time translation of any already-given proof in any other efficiently checkable format. The translator receives the proof; it is not being asked to discover a proof from the formula alone.

context_blocks.title: A simple simulation
context_blocks.text: Suppose Q is a proof system and another system merely adds a leading marker to each Q-proof. Removing the marker translates those proofs back with linear overhead. More generally, any fixed finite collection of sound systems can be combined using a system tag. The question quantifies over every sound polynomial-time system, so combining a predetermined finite list does not finish it.

context_blocks.title: Three distinct notions
context_blocks.text: Ordinary optimality asks only that comparably short proofs exist in the common system. P-optimality additionally asks for efficient translations of the given proofs. Polynomial boundedness instead asks that every tautology have a proof polynomial in the formula’s own length. A p-optimal system could still have very long proofs of some tautologies, so this target does not by itself say \(\mathrm{NP}=\mathrm{coNP}\).

context_blocks.title: Known connections and current limits
context_blocks.text: Krajíček and Pudlák connect p-optimality with a tautology recognizer that is optimal up to polynomial overhead on positive inputs, compared with each other correct recognizer. Their theorem also gives the conditional implication from \(\mathrm{P}=\mathrm{NP}\). Egidy’s February 2026 paper retains the question as open and proves limitations of relativizing arguments; the oracle supplied to those machines is extra computational power, absent from this card.

context_blocks.title: Later work on improving proof systems
context_blocks.text: The ICALP 2026 paper studies when the absence of an ordinary optimal system entails an effective procedure producing stronger systems. Its oracle and other-language results leave p-optimal propositional proof systems unresolved. Ordinary optimality, a procedure for improving systems, and efficient proof translation are related but separately quantified properties.

sentences: Does one propositional proof system efficiently translate proofs from every other efficiently checkable system?
The translation must preserve the proved formula and run in time polynomial in the given proof length.
Each simulated system may have its own translator and polynomial.
This is stronger than comparing proof lengths alone, and different from requiring short proofs of every tautology.
The 2026 oracle and jump-operator results leave the ordinary, oracle-free existence question open.

cards.title: Complete disjoint NP pairs
cards.formal:
Let \(\Sigma=\{0,1\}\), and let
\[
\mathcal D=\{(A,B):A,B\subseteq\Sigma^{*},\ A,B\in\mathrm{NP},\ A\cap B=\varnothing\}.
\]
Does there exist a disjoint NP pair that is complete under deterministic polynomial-time many-one reductions of pairs? Precisely, is
\[
\exists(A,B)\in\mathcal D\ \forall(C,D)\in\mathcal D\ \exists f\in\mathrm{FP}\
\forall x\in\Sigma^{*}\
\bigl[(x\in C\Rightarrow f(x)\in A)\land(x\in D\Rightarrow f(x)\in B)\bigr]
\]
true? Here \(\mathrm{FP}\) consists of total polynomial-time functions \(\Sigma^{*}\to\Sigma^{*}\), as specified below. The target pair is fixed before the source pair is chosen; the reduction and its polynomial running-time bound may depend on the source pair.
cards.definitions:
\(\Sigma^{*}\) is the set of all finite binary strings, including the empty string, and \(|x|\) denotes the number of bits of \(x\). A language is an arbitrary subset of \(\Sigma^{*}\). The pairs are ordered, and disjointness means that no string belongs to both components. Empty component languages are permitted. The quantifiers range over all pairs that are actually disjoint, without requiring their disjointness to be provable in any particular theory.

Computations use uniform deterministic multitape Turing machines with finite control, a fixed finite number of tapes per machine, and tape alphabet \(\{0,1,\#,\square\}\), where \(\square\) is blank. Each tape has cells indexed by nonnegative integers and one head, initially at cell zero; a left move at cell zero leaves the head there. There is one read-only input tape and finitely many initially blank work tapes. One transition reads the symbols under the heads, changes the finite state, writes at most one symbol on each work tape, and moves each head by at most one cell. A transducer additionally has an initially empty output string and may append at most one output bit per transition. Each transition costs one step. Verifiers halt in an accept or reject state; transducers halt with their accumulated binary output. The finite program and tape count are independent of input length. There is no advice, random input or oracle access.

A language \(L\) belongs to \(\mathrm{NP}\) if there exist such a verifier \(V\), integers \(a,b\ge1\) and \(k,\ell\ge0\), with the following properties. For every \(x,y\in\Sigma^{*}\), the verifier on input \(x\#y\) halts within \(b(|x|+|y|+2)^{\ell}\) steps, and for every \(x\in\Sigma^{*}\),
\[
x\in L\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
\exists y\in\Sigma^{*}\ \bigl(|y|\le a(|x|+1)^{k}\ \land\ V(x\#y)\text{ accepts}\bigr).
\]
The string \(y\) is a certificate. These verifier and polynomial constants may depend on \(L\), but not on \(x\) or \(y\).

A function \(f:\Sigma^{*}\to\Sigma^{*}\) belongs to \(\mathrm{FP}\) if there exist one deterministic transducer \(M\), an integer \(c\ge1\) and an integer \(d\ge0\) such that, for every \(x\in\Sigma^{*}\), \(M\) on input \(x\) halts within \(c(|x|+1)^{d}\) steps and outputs \(f(x)\). Thus \(f\) is defined and polynomial-time computable on every binary input, including strings outside the source promise. Its output length is charged through bit writing and is consequently polynomially bounded.

A reduction from \((C,D)\) to \((A,B)\) is one such function \(f\) satisfying both displayed implications. The same function handles both sides. For \(x\notin C\cup D\), its output may lie anywhere in \(\Sigma^{*}\), including inside \(A\cup B\), but the same totality and time bound still apply. Neither surjectivity nor reverse membership implications are required. For a fixed source pair the transducer, coefficient and degree must work for every input length; they need not be shared by different source pairs. The target does not require a computable procedure that takes descriptions of source pairs and produces their reductions.

The mathematical target concerns the ordinary, unrelativized classes \(\mathrm{NP}\) and \(\mathrm{FP}\). Completeness for a restricted family of pairs, or completeness or noncompleteness after supplying machines with an oracle, is a different assertion.

context_blocks.text: Pudlák's 2017 revision defines precisely these pair reductions and conjectures that no complete disjoint NP pair exists. The card preserves its yes-or-no existence question, so proving that conjecture gives a negative answer.

A propositional proof system is a polynomial-time map whose range is exactly the Boolean tautologies. A p-optimal system can translate proofs from every such system in polynomial time; its existence would imply a complete disjoint NP pair. Pudlák's Proposition 5.2 in fact obtains this implication from the weaker requirement that one system polynomially bounds the shortest proof lengths of every other system. No converse implication is asserted.

Dose's 2019 result constructs an oracle relative to which no complete disjoint NP pairs exist even though every NP language has a p-optimal proof system. The proof systems in that result concern NP languages, whereas the propositional implication concerns tautologies; the results do not contradict one another.

Egidy's ICALP 2026 paper constructs an oracle relative to which disjoint NP pairs have no complete pair and the polynomial-time hierarchy remains infinite. An oracle supplies membership answers for a fixed auxiliary language to the machines defining both the classes and reductions. This result concerns those modified classes and does not establish nonexistence for the ordinary classes on this card.

cards.why: A complete pair would be a universal promise problem for two disjoint cases that each have efficiently checkable certificates. The question links the structure of promise problems to the possible existence of a strongest propositional proof system and to feasible versions of incompleteness.
cards.answer_criterion:
Give a complete mathematically correct Lean proof of the displayed existence proposition, including the target languages' NP membership and disjointness and the total polynomial-time reductions for every source pair, or a complete Lean proof of its full logical negation:
\[
\forall(A,B)\in\mathcal D\ \exists(C,D)\in\mathcal D\ \forall f\in\mathrm{FP}\
\exists x\in\Sigma^{*}\
\bigl[(x\in C\land f(x)\notin A)\lor(x\in D\land f(x)\notin B)\bigr].
\]
In the negative statement the witness source pair may depend on the candidate target pair but must defeat every eligible reduction; the witness string may depend on the reduction. All computational classes and reductions must have the definitions above. A conditional implication, an oracle construction, or failure of one candidate pair does not alone decide this unconditional target.

cards.context:
Pudlák's 2017 revision defines precisely these pair reductions and conjectures that no complete disjoint NP pair exists. The card preserves its yes-or-no existence question, so proving that conjecture gives a negative answer.

A propositional proof system is a polynomial-time map whose range is exactly the Boolean tautologies. A p-optimal system can translate proofs from every such system in polynomial time; its existence would imply a complete disjoint NP pair. Pudlák's Proposition 5.2 in fact obtains this implication from the weaker requirement that one system polynomially bounds the shortest proof lengths of every other system. No converse implication is asserted.

Dose's 2019 result constructs an oracle relative to which no complete disjoint NP pairs exist even though every NP language has a p-optimal proof system. The proof systems in that result concern NP languages, whereas the propositional implication concerns tautologies; the results do not contradict one another.

Egidy's ICALP 2026 paper constructs an oracle relative to which disjoint NP pairs have no complete pair and the polynomial-time hierarchy remains infinite. An oracle supplies membership answers for a fixed auxiliary language to the machines defining both the classes and reductions. This result concerns those modified classes and does not establish nonexistence for the ordinary classes on this card.

cards.title: Linear versus general resolution
cards.formal:
Is linear resolution strictly weaker than general resolution in polynomial refutation size, for the same input CNF formula? Here linear resolution has no restarts, and the size \(\ell\) is one plus the number of resolution inferences. More precisely, is the following assertion true?
\[
\forall c,k\in\mathbb N_{\ge1}\ \exists n\in\mathbb N_0\
\exists F\in\operatorname{CNF}_n\ \exists\pi\
\left[
\operatorname{GRef}(F,\pi)\ \land\
\forall\lambda\
\left(\operatorname{LRef}(F,\lambda)\Longrightarrow
\ell(\lambda)>c\,\ell(\pi)^{k}\right)
\right].
\]
The classes of formulas and the two syntactic refutation predicates are defined below. This asserts failure of every polynomial bound on the extra proof length needed by linear resolution. The constants \(c,k\) range independently over positive integers; \(n,F,\pi\) may depend on them. The comparison concerns existence of proofs, with no requirement that a conversion between proofs be computable in polynomial time. It does not prescribe an exponential separation or an effectively generated family of formulas.
cards.why: This compares two longstanding, complete refinements of a foundational propositional proof system. It isolates the effect of how deductions are organized and reused, with the inference rule and input formula held fixed. A separation would identify an intrinsic proof-length cost of the linear discipline; a polynomial simulation would show that arbitrary resolution structure can always be reproduced within polynomial length. The result would clarify the strength hierarchy of resolution refinements, independently of how efficiently a solver can discover the proofs.
cards.status_note: Open in the inspected 2013 source, the Buss–Johannsen author preprint and Johannsen's 2018 Dagstuhl Open Problem 11. The card explicitly repairs the 2013 survey's restart-permitting definition using the later no-restarts definition. cards.definitions:
For \(n\in\mathbb N_0\), put \([n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}\), with \([0]=\varnothing\). A literal is \(x_i\) or \(\neg x_i\), for \(i\in[n]\). A clause is a finite set of literals containing at most one of \(x_i,\neg x_i\) for each \(i\); thus all clauses are non-tautological and repeated literals are identified. A formula \(F\in\operatorname{CNF}_n\) is a finite set of clauses, interpreted as their conjunction. A valuation \(v:[n]\to\{0,1\}\) makes \(x_i\) true when \(v(i)=1\) and makes \(\neg x_i\) true when \(v(i)=0\). A clause is true if it contains a true literal. The empty clause \(\varnothing\) is false, while the empty conjunction is true. A formula is unsatisfiable if no valuation makes all its clauses true.

The sole inference rule is resolution. If \(i\in[n]\), neither \(x_i\) nor \(\neg x_i\) occurs in clauses \(A,B\), and \(A\cup B\) is non-tautological, the rule is
\[
\frac{A\cup\{x_i\}\qquad B\cup\{\neg x_i\}}{A\cup B}.
\]
The two premises may be interchanged. The variable \(x_i\) is the pivot. Every input and derived clause uses variables in \([n]\). There is no weakening rule, additional axiom, introduction of a new variable, or permission to add tautological clauses. Equality of clauses is equality of their literal sets.

A general resolution refutation \(\pi\) of \(F\) is a finite nonempty directed acyclic graph of clause occurrences with one sink, labelled \(\varnothing\). Every vertex reaches that sink. Each source vertex is labelled by a clause of \(F\); every other vertex has exactly two parent vertices and is labelled by the resolvent of their labels under the displayed rule. Each such vertex records its pivot and premise orientation. A clause occurrence may be used as a parent arbitrarily many times. Distinct vertices may have equal labels. This defines \(\operatorname{GRef}(F,\pi)\). A single vertex labelled \(\varnothing\) is allowed exactly when \(\varnothing\in F\).

A linear resolution refutation \(\lambda\) of \(F\) is a finite main sequence
\[
C_0,C_1,\ldots,C_t,\qquad
t\in\mathbb N_0,\quad C_0\in F,\quad C_t=\varnothing,
\]
together with the following annotations. For every integer \(j\) with \(0\le j<t\), the next clause \(C_{j+1}\) is the resolvent of \(C_j\) and a side clause \(D_j\). The side clause is either an input clause \(D_j\in F\), or an earlier main clause \(D_j=C_i\) for a specified integer \(i\) with \(0\le i<j\). The annotation records which alternative is used, its clause or index, and the pivot and premise orientation. This defines \(\operatorname{LRef}(F,\lambda)\).

Every step after the first main clause must therefore use the immediately preceding main clause as a premise. One cannot insert a new input clause as the next main clause without deriving it by that rule: such an insertion would be a restart. An input clause can nevertheless be used as a side clause whenever needed, whether or not it appeared previously in the main sequence. Earlier main clauses can be reused as side clauses without a limit on the number of uses. All such earlier main clauses are ancestors of the current main clause along the main sequence; no further ancestor test is imposed. Side clauses are not restricted to input clauses. There is no regularity requirement forbidding repeated use of a pivot along a proof path, and no subsumption requirement that a conclusion be contained in its preceding main clause.

For either type of refutation, define
\[
\ell(\Pi)=1+\text{the number of resolution inferences in }\Pi.
\]
Thus \(\ell(\pi)\) for a general refutation is one plus its number of non-source vertices, and \(\ell(\lambda)=t+1\) for the displayed linear refutation. Reusing a parent is not a new inference; deriving a new occurrence is. Input clauses used as side premises do not themselves count as resolution inferences. The additive one includes a refutation with no inference. This is a count of deductions, not the binary length of the whole formula or of its serialized proof.

For a finite representation, label variables by their integer indices, store clauses as sorted lists of signed indices without repetitions, and store formulas as sorted lists of distinct clauses. In a general proof, index vertices in a topological order and store their clause labels and source or two-parent annotations; in a linear proof store the main sequence and its side-clause annotations. All integer indices have ordinary finite binary encodings. These representations specify finite proof objects; the cost remains \(\ell\), without charging literal, index or annotation bits. The same \(F\) must be used in both proof systems. No formula transformation, additional input clause, width bound, clause bound, or proof-search time bound is part of the comparison.

In this card, polynomial simulation means that there are single constants \(c,k\ge1\) such that every general refutation of every \(F\) has some linear refutation of that same \(F\) of size at most \(c\,\ell(\pi)^k\). This is ordinary proof-size simulation. Requiring a polynomial-time algorithm producing the latter proof would be the stronger notion of \(p\)-simulation and is not required here. Every linear refutation is a particular general refutation when its main and input occurrences are represented as a graph, so only the converse simulation is at issue.
cards.answer_criterion:
Give a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of the assertion in the formal statement or of its full negation, using exactly the formulas, inference rule, proof predicates and size measure above.

A positive answer must show that for every pair \(c,k\in\mathbb N_{\ge1}\), there is a finite formula with a general refutation \(\pi\) for which every linear refutation has size greater than \(c\,\ell(\pi)^k\), with all the quantifiers of the displayed assertion. No particular exponential rate or uniformly generated counterexample family is required.

A negative answer must prove the polynomial simulation statement
\[
\exists c,k\in\mathbb N_{\ge1}\ \forall n\in\mathbb N_0\
\forall F\in\operatorname{CNF}_n\ \forall\pi\
\left[
\operatorname{GRef}(F,\pi)\Longrightarrow
\exists\lambda\
\left(\operatorname{LRef}(F,\lambda)\land
\ell(\lambda)\le c\,\ell(\pi)^k\right)
\right].
\]
The same \(c,k\) must work for every formula and every general refutation; the linear refutation may depend on the formula and proof. An efficient proof-conversion algorithm would suffice if its size guarantee meets this statement, but is not an additional obligation. Comparisons allowing restarts, changing the input formula, using resolution over linear equations, or imposing extra regularity or input-only restrictions do not answer the stated question. A separation at one fixed polynomial degree also does not prove the universal separation assertion. This is a yes/no comparison of asymptotic proof lengths, so numerical \(1/100\) tolerance does not alter the quantifiers or polynomial bounds.

Buss and Johannsen distinguish the two systems: allowing restarts gives a polynomial-time simulation of general resolution, whereas the strength of linear resolution without restarts remains open in their account. They also prove that regular resolution does not simulate linear resolution; that different comparison does not settle the question here.

cards.title: Linear-space Cutting Planes refutations
cards.formal:
Does there exist one constant \(C\in\mathbb N_{\ge1}\) such that every unsatisfiable CNF formula on \(n\) Boolean variables has a Cutting Planes refutation using total space at most \(C(n+1)\), with the exact rules and space measure below?
\[
\exists C\in\mathbb N_{\ge1}\ \forall n\in\mathbb N_0\
\forall F\in\operatorname{CNF}_n\
\left(\operatorname{Unsat}(F)\ \Longrightarrow\
\exists\Pi\
\left[\operatorname{Ref}_{\mathrm{CP}}(F,\Pi)
\land\operatorname{TotSp}(\Pi)\le C(n+1)\right]\right).
\]
Here \(n\) counts variables, rather than clauses, literal occurrences or the binary length of the whole input. There is no restriction on the number of clauses, proof length or coefficient magnitudes. The same constant \(C\) must work for every \(n\) and \(F\); the finite refutation \(\Pi\) may depend on \(F\). The \(n+1\) convention includes formulas with no variables and is equivalent to the source's asymptotic linear bound.

source_formulation.text: Can every unsatisfiable CNF be refuted in CP in linear total space?
source_formulation.caption: Complete selected source sentence; PDF p. 14

cards.why: The question tests a basic memory limit of a central arithmetic proof system used to study pseudo-Boolean reasoning. Counting only inequalities hides the cost of large coefficients, whereas total space records that cost. A resolution would determine whether the known constant-line-space phenomenon extends to a linear numerical representation budget, or whether some Boolean contradictions force additional simultaneous information even when arbitrarily long proofs are permitted. This is a universal structural question about the proof system, with a separate meaning from lower bounds on proof length.
cards.status_note: Open as stated in CCC 2015, Section 7, Problem 2. A bounded later-source review through 16 September 2026 found no verified resolution. The 2021 handbook account still describes a linear-versus-quadratic total-space gap; inspected 2020/2021 length-space and coefficient tradeoffs, the November 2024 size-depth result, and the July 2026 clique proof-length result do not settle the unrestricted-length total-space target. This is not an exhaustive literature review, an independent verification of the cited proofs, or a Lean verification. The apparent linear-space claim in Corollary 6 of an older 29 October 2014 author draft conflicts with its own introduction and is corrected to quadratic space in the final 2015 proceedings; it is not treated as a resolution.

cards.definitions:
Put \([n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}\), with \([0]=\varnothing\), and let the variables be \(x_1,\ldots,x_n\). A clause is a pair of subsets \(P,N\subseteq[n]\), representing the disjunction of the positive literals \(x_i\), \(i\in P\), and negative literals \(\neg x_i\), \(i\in N\). Repeated occurrences of a literal are removed. A CNF \(F\in\operatorname{CNF}_n\) is a finite set of such clauses, interpreted as their conjunction; tautological clauses are allowed. A valuation is a map \(v:[n]\to\{0,1\}\). It satisfies \((P,N)\) exactly when some \(i\in P\) has \(v(i)=1\), or some \(i\in N\) has \(v(i)=0\). Thus
\[
\operatorname{Unsat}(F)\ \Longleftrightarrow\
\forall v:[n]\to\{0,1\}\ \exists(P,N)\in F\
\left[(\forall i\in P,\ v(i)=0)\land
(\forall i\in N,\ v(i)=1)\right].
\]
The empty clause is false and the empty conjunction is true. Allowing unused variables in \([n]\) does not change the universal assertion, since one can also take \(n\) to be the number of variables that occur and rename them.

A line is a pair \(J=(a,b)\), where \(a\in\mathbb Z^n\) and \(b\in\mathbb Z\), denoting \(\sum_{i=1}^n a_i x_i\ge b\). Terms are collected, zero coefficients are omitted, and the constant is on the right. Equality of lines means equality of these integer data, not logical equivalence. There are no extension variables, semantic inference rules or implicit rescaling operations.

The input line for clause \((P,N)\) is
\[
\sum_{i\in P}x_i-\sum_{i\in N}x_i\ge 1-|N|.
\]
Let \(A(F)\) be the set of these lines after collecting coefficients. Besides downloading a line in \(A(F)\), the permitted rules are exactly the following.

1. For each \(i\in[n]\), introduce either Boolean axiom \(x_i\ge0\) or \(-x_i\ge-1\).
2. Choose any integer \(k\ge1\), currently stored lines \((a^{(1)},b_1),\ldots,(a^{(k)},b_k)\), and positive integers \(s_1,\ldots,s_k\), and derive
\[
\left(\sum_{j=1}^k s_j a^{(j)},\ \sum_{j=1}^k s_j b_j\right).
\]
There is no fixed upper bound on the number \(k\) of premises. A premise may be selected more than once, equivalently by increasing its multiplier.
3. From a currently stored line \((a,b)\), choose an integer \(d\ge1\) dividing every \(a_i\), and derive
\[
\left(a/d,\ \left\lceil b/d\right\rceil\right).
\]
Division of \(a\) is coordinatewise. The ceiling is the least integer greater than or equal to the rational number \(b/d\), also when \(b\) is negative.

A memory configuration \(M\) is a finite set of lines. A refutation \(\Pi=(M_0,\ldots,M_T)\) is a finite sequence, with \(T\in\mathbb N_0\), starting with \(M_0=\varnothing\) and ending with \((0,1)\in M_T\), the contradiction \(0\ge1\). At each step, either \(M_{t+1}=M_t\cup\{J\}\), where \(J\in A(F)\), \(J\) is a Boolean axiom, or \(J\) follows by one permitted rule using premises in \(M_t\); or \(M_{t+1}\subsetneq M_t\), an erasure. This defines \(\operatorname{Ref}_{\mathrm{CP}}(F,\Pi)\). In particular, premises and a new conclusion coexist before a later erasure; overwriting a premise is not a free operation. An erased input line may be downloaded again. The full input need never be present simultaneously.

For \(z\in\mathbb Z\), let its unsigned binary length be
\[
\beta(z)=
\begin{cases}
1,&z=0,\\
1+\lfloor\log_2|z|\rfloor,&z\ne0.
\end{cases}
\]
This uses the one-digit representation of zero and omits leading zeroes. Define
\[
\operatorname{size}(a,b)=\beta(b)+
\sum_{\substack{i\in[n]\\a_i\ne0}}\beta(a_i),\qquad
\operatorname{sp}(M)=\sum_{J\in M}\operatorname{size}(J),\qquad
\operatorname{TotSp}(\Pi)=\max_{0\le t\le T}\operatorname{sp}(M_t).
\]
This is the source's numerical-symbol measure: count binary digits of nonzero coefficients and the right-hand constant, ignoring signs, variable names or indices, punctuation and arithmetic symbols. It is not the bit length of a fully serialized proof or machine memory. The conceptual vector \(a\) does not charge for its zero entries. Each distinct stored line is counted once. Input lines count while stored; the separate input, previous erased lines, proof history and rule annotations or multipliers do not count. There is no running-time, randomization or effective proof-search requirement: the target concerns existence of finite syntactically valid refutations.
cards.answer_criterion:
Give a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of the displayed assertion or of its full negation, using exactly the CNF encoding, inference rules, configurations and total-space measure above.

A positive answer must establish a single universal constant \(C\ge1\) and a finite refutation meeting \(C(n+1)\) for every unsatisfiable \(F\in\operatorname{CNF}_n\). No uniform polynomial-time procedure for finding the refutations is required.

A negative answer must prove
\[
\forall C\in\mathbb N_{\ge1}\ \exists n\in\mathbb N_0\
\exists F\in\operatorname{CNF}_n\
\left(\operatorname{Unsat}(F)\land
\forall\Pi\
\left[\operatorname{Ref}_{\mathrm{CP}}(F,\Pi)
\Longrightarrow
\operatorname{TotSp}(\Pi)>C(n+1)\right]\right).
\]
The final universal quantifier includes proofs of every finite length and every integer coefficient magnitude. The counterexample formula may depend on \(C\); a fixed power-law lower bound is not required. A bound only for short proofs, bounded coefficients, a restricted inference system or a different space measure does not establish this negation. This is an asymptotic existence question with a constant-factor linear bound, so the numerical \(1/100\) tolerance does not replace its quantifiers or inequalities.

context_blocks.text: Galesi, Pudlák and Thapen's 2015 Problem 2 asks precisely whether every unsatisfiable CNF has a Cutting Planes refutation in linear total space. Their parameter is the number of variables, and their Section 2 ignores variable-name length while charging coefficient magnitudes in binary.

The same paper proves that five simultaneously stored inequalities suffice without coefficient restrictions, and gives an \(O(n^2)\) total-space upper bound. The former result counts lines, so it does not already give the linear total-space conclusion.

Buss and Nordström's 2021 handbook chapter records a linear lower bound and a quadratic general upper bound for total space, with no known superlinear lower bound at the time of that account. These are dated statements, not a claim that all later literature has been exhausted.

The later papers checked here establish length-space tradeoffs, a bounded-coefficient length-space separation, size-depth tradeoffs, and a 2026 proof-length lower bound. Their resource restrictions differ from this card's unrestricted-length total-space question, and none of their inspected statements settles it.

cards.title: Effective polynomial simulation of Extended Frege by Resolution
cards.formal: Do there exist a deterministic transformation R and fixed polynomials p,q such that, for every propositional formula F and every integer \(s\ge 1, R\)(F,1ˢ) outputs a CNF formula in at most p(|F|+s) bit operations, F is a tautology if and only if R(F,1ˢ) is unsatisfiable, and whenever F has an Extended Frege proof of length at most s, R(F,1ˢ) has a Resolution refutation of length at most q(|F|+s)?
cards.why: Determines whether allowing efficient preprocessing fundamentally changes the apparent gap between elementary clause reasoning and proof systems that can name arbitrary intermediate Boolean computations. This affects what proof-size separations say about algorithms for finding proofs.

cards.definitions:
A propositional formula uses Boolean variables, negation \(
eg\) and implication →, with the usual truth tables; other connectives are fixed abbreviations. A tautology is true under every Boolean assignment. A literal is a variable or its negation, a clause is a disjunction of literals, and a CNF formula is a conjunction of clauses. The empty clause is false. A Resolution refutation is a finite sequence ending in the empty clause, each line being an input clause or the resolvent \(C\lor D\) of earlier clauses \(C\lor x\) and \(D\lor 
eg x\). Lines can be reused, so the proof is a directed acyclic derivation, not necessarily a tree. Fix Extended Frege as follows: ordinary Frege lines are substitution instances of \(A	o (B	o A), (A	o (B	o C))	o ((A	o B)	o (A	o C))\), and \((
eg B	o 
eg A)	o (A	o B)\), or follow by modus ponens from A and \(A	o B\). One may also introduce an extension axiom \(z\leftrightarrow B\), where z is fresh, does not occur in the target F, and B uses only original variables and previously introduced extension variables. Here \(z\leftrightarrow B\) abbreviates \((z	o B)\land (B	o z)\). The final line is F, containing no extension variables. Formulas, proofs and line references have explicit finite binary encodings; length counts the whole encoding. Standard alternative Frege bases and symbol-count conventions are polynomially equivalent. The input 1ˢ is a unary string, so the permitted time is polynomial in s, not log s. The transformation receives F and s but no EF proof. It must preserve the tautology/unsatisfiability equivalence for every F and every s, even if s is smaller than the shortest proof or F is not a tautology. Only the short-Resolution-refutation guarantee is conditional on an EF proof of length at most s. Resolution is represented by refuting a CNF, while Frege proves a tautology; this explicitly implements the source’s comparison of proof systems over their natural encodings.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove or refute the existence of R,p,q satisfying all these conditions. The requested notion is effective polynomial simulation as in Definition 2.5 of the source. A polynomial procedure that converts a supplied EF proof is an additional, stronger guarantee and is not required. A lower bound on Resolution proofs of the original untransformed formula alone does not refute this claim.

context_blocks.title: Can preprocessing change the proof-size comparison?
context_blocks.text: Resolution is a basic way to certify that a set of clauses is inconsistent. Extended Frege additionally uses named intermediate formulas, allowing compact reuse of complicated expressions. The question asks whether a uniformly efficient transformation of the statement can make Resolution proofs as short, up to a polynomial, as EF proofs.

context_blocks.title: A Resolution step
context_blocks.text: From \(x\lor y\) and \(\neg x\), Resolution derives y. Together with the clause \(\neg y\), it then derives the empty clause and certifies inconsistency. Larger derivations reuse earlier clauses. An extension variable, by contrast, can name a compound formula and be reused wherever that formula is needed.

context_blocks.title: Why the extra input matters
context_blocks.text: The transformation is given a proposed proof-size allowance s. It may spend polynomial time in that allowance, even if the statement itself is short. It must preserve correctness for all allowances, but it needs to guarantee a short output refutation only when an EF proof fits within the allowance. The actual proof is never supplied to it.

context_blocks.title: The known separation answers a different comparison
context_blocks.text: Ordinary polynomial simulation compares proofs of the same statement. Known Resolution lower bounds rule out ordinary simulation of Extended Frege. Effective simulation allows the statement to change through a correctness-preserving transformation, so those lower bounds do not automatically answer this question.

context_blocks.title: A later example of the distinction
context_blocks.text: Buss and Yolcu show that regular Resolution effectively simulates unrestricted Resolution, despite known exponential separations when both systems must use the same formula. Regular Resolution forbids resolving a variable twice along a derivation path. Their result demonstrates that the distinction has mathematical force, but does not provide an effective simulation of EF.

The question asks whether a uniformly efficient transformation of the statement can make Resolution proofs as short, up to a polynomial, as EF proofs.

cards.title: Polynomial resolution length from logarithmic clause space
cards.formal:
Does logarithmic clause space imply polynomial refutation length for every fixed input clause width in general resolution?

Precisely, for every fixed integer \(k\ge1\) and real constant \(a>0\), do there exist constants \(B>0\) and \(d\ge1\), depending only on \(k,a\), such that every unsatisfiable \(k\)-CNF formula \(F\) satisfies
\[\operatorname{Sp}(F)\le a\log_2 N(F)\quad\Longrightarrow\quad L(F)\le B\,N(F)^d?\]
Here \(N(F)=2+|F|+\sum_{C\in F}|C|\) is formula size, \(\operatorname{Sp}(F)\) is the minimum number of clauses simultaneously retained in a resolution refutation, and \(L(F)\) is its minimum number of axiom downloads and inference steps. These two minima are taken independently over all general resolution refutations. The short refutation whose existence is requested has no space restriction.
cards.why: The question asks whether a resolution proof that can be checked with only logarithmically many retained clauses necessarily has a short certificate somewhere in the same proof system. Resolving it would sharpen the relation between proof memory and proof length beyond the known constant-space case, without conflating proof existence with an efficient search algorithm.

cards.definitions:
A Boolean variable takes values in \(\{0,1\}\). A literal is a variable or its negation, and a clause is a finite set of literals interpreted as their disjunction. Clauses contain no repeated literal and no complementary pair \(x,\neg x\). The empty clause \(\bot\) is false. A CNF formula is a finite set of clauses interpreted as their conjunction; it is unsatisfiable if no assignment to its variables makes every clause true. A \(k\)-CNF has at most \(k\) literals in every input clause. The fixed input-width parameter \(k\) does not bound clauses derived during a proof.

The variable universe for a proof is the finite set of variables occurring in \(F\). Renaming these variables has no cost. The size \(N(F)\) counts input clauses and literal occurrences, with the added constant two ensuring that its logarithm is positive. Input clauses are a set, so padding by duplicate clauses does not change the formula or its size. If a concrete binary encoding is needed, number the occurring variables consecutively, encode each literal by its index and sign, and list clauses with delimiters. For fixed \(k\), this encoding and the stated combinatorial size are polynomially related; the logarithmic-space versus polynomial-length question is invariant under this choice of size convention.

A resolution refutation is a finite sequence of configurations \(\mathcal D_0,\ldots,\mathcal D_T\), each a set of clauses over the input variables. Initially \(\mathcal D_0=\varnothing\), and the final configuration contains \(\bot\). Each step performs exactly one of the following operations. It may download one input clause \(C\in F\) into memory, adding it to the current set. It may erase one currently retained clause. It may add a resolvent \(C\cup D\) from two currently retained premises \(C\cup\{x\}\) and \(D\cup\{\neg x\}\), where neither \(C\) nor \(D\) contains the pivot variable and the resolvent is non-tautological. It may also weaken a retained clause by adding literals, provided the result is a clause over the same variables. These are the ordinary syntactic resolution and weakening rules. Arbitrary semantic consequence is not an additional inference rule.

Premises must be present before an inference, and they remain present after it unless erased in subsequent steps. An inference adds its conclusion before any such erasure, so the temporary memory needed to hold the conclusion is counted. An erased clause must be downloaded or derived again before reuse. The input formula itself is available for downloads without occupying working memory. Resolution proofs may share intermediate results arbitrarily; neither the tree-like restriction nor the regularity restriction forbidding repeated pivots on a proof path is imposed. No extension variables, stronger proof rules, randomization or error are allowed.

For a refutation \(\pi\), define
\[\operatorname{Sp}(\pi)=\max_{0\le t\le T}|\mathcal D_t|,\]
and let \(L(\pi)\) be its number of axiom-download and inference steps, with repetitions counted. Erasures are not counted in length. One can instead count all steps without changing polynomial-length bounds, because useful erasures can be bounded by the number of additions. Clause space counts each stored clause as one object regardless of its width. It is different from total literal space \(\max_t\sum_{C\in\mathcal D_t}|C|\), from the number of distinct variables in memory, and from the number of stored bits.

For an unsatisfiable formula, resolution completeness guarantees that the following finite integer minima exist:
\[\operatorname{Sp}(F)=\min_{\pi:F\vdash\bot}\operatorname{Sp}(\pi),\qquad L(F)=\min_{\pi:F\vdash\bot}L(\pi).\]
The refutation attaining the first minimum may have very large length. The question is whether a possibly different refutation of polynomial length must nevertheless exist whenever that minimum space is logarithmic.

The full quantifier order is \(\forall k\ge1\;\forall a>0\;\exists B>0,d\ge1\;\forall F\). The exponent \(d\) may depend on the input-width bound and the constant multiplying the logarithm, but not on the individual formula or its size. The proposition does not demand one exponent uniform in all \(k,a\), a procedure finding the short proof, or a transformation that keeps the original space bound.

A negative answer means that for some fixed \(k\) and \(a>0\), no polynomial bounds the minimum length throughout this class: for every \(B>0\) and \(d\ge1\), some unsatisfiable \(k\)-CNF \(F\) has \(\operatorname{Sp}(F)\le a\log_2 N(F)\) but \(L(F)>B N(F)^d\). Thus it must establish genuinely superpolynomial unrestricted resolution length despite the small-space refutation. Merely proving that all proofs which retain small space are long does not refute the proposition.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof or refutation of the quantified implication. A positive answer must establish a polynomial length bound for all promised formulas, with its dependence on fixed \(k,a\) explicit or provably existent. A negative answer must prove the stated logical negation against all polynomial length bounds, including unrestricted-space refutations. A quasipolynomial upper bound, a theorem for constant clause space only, a result for tree-like resolution only, or a simultaneous length–space tradeoff does not settle the target. The statement is an exact asymptotic proposition; additive numerical tolerance is inapplicable.

source_formulation.text: Nordström records Esteban and Torán’s question whether an unsatisfiable CNF with a fixed bound on input-clause width and a resolution refutation in logarithmic clause space must also have a polynomial-length resolution refutation.
source_formulation.caption: Editorial paraphrase of Open Problem 13; the two minimum resources are independent, and input size and constant dependencies are explicit

context_blocks.text: Resolution combines clauses to certify that a Boolean formula is inconsistent. Its proof length is a basic lower bound on the work needed by resolution-based proof search, while clause space records how many learned facts must be retained together.

The memory measure here treats a clause as one object even when it is long. This makes logarithmic clause space fundamentally different from logarithmic bit space of an ordinary machine computation; a small number of clauses may encode many bits.

For constant-width input CNFs, the known space-to-width relation and the width counting bound imply \(L(F)\le N(F)^{O(\operatorname{Sp}(F)+k)}\). In particular, constant clause space implies polynomial length, whereas logarithmic clause space gives only a quasipolynomial bound \(N(F)^{O(\log N(F))}\). The question asks whether that remaining gap can always be removed.

The reverse implication behaves differently: the survey documents families with short refutations but large minimum clause space. Those examples do not decide whether small clause space forces short refutations.

A simultaneous-resource question asks whether a single proof can be both short and economical in memory. This card asks only whether a short proof exists at all. A tradeoff forcing a memory-limited proof to be long is compatible with a polynomial proof that uses more memory.

The 2023 work organizes connections among clause space, other space measures and tree-like proof size, and leaves major simultaneous-resource questions open in its concluding section. Those developments supply recent structural context but are not a solution or a newly restated confirmation of the precise logarithmic-space implication in this card.

cards.title: Frege lower bounds from circuit hardness
cards.formal:
Does the following implication hold?
\[\mathrm{NP}\not\subseteq\mathrm{P/poly}\quad\Longrightarrow\quad\text{Frege is not polynomially bounded}.\]
Precisely, assuming that some NP language has no polynomial-size Boolean circuit family, must it be true that for every integer \(k\ge1\) and every constant \(C\ge1\), there is a propositional tautology \(\varphi\) such that every Frege proof \(\pi\) of \(\varphi\), in the fixed system below, has
\[|\pi|>C(|\varphi|+1)^k?\]
This asks for a conditional connection between two lower-bound statements. It does not separately require proving the circuit-hardness premise.
cards.why: General Boolean circuit lower bounds and Frege proof lower bounds are two major barriers in complexity theory. A positive implication would make progress on the former sufficient for the latter, even without an explicit hard-tautology construction. It would clarify whether these difficulties are formally linked or whether proof complexity requires an additional source of hardness.

cards.definitions:
A language \(L\subseteq\{0,1\}^{*}\) is in NP if there are a deterministic polynomial-time Turing machine \(V\) and a polynomial \(p\) such that \(x\in L\) exactly when some binary string \(y\), with \(|y|\le p(|x|)\), satisfies \(V(x,y)=1\). A Boolean circuit has input bits, constants zero and one, fan-in-two AND/OR gates, NOT gates, and one output. Its size is its number of gates, and its depth and fan-out are unrestricted. The class P/poly consists of languages decided at each input length \(n\) by a circuit \(D_n\) of size at most \(C(n+1)^k\), for fixed \(C,k\). These circuits need not be produced by an algorithm: they may be chosen nonuniformly. Thus NP not contained in P/poly asserts that at least one NP language has no such circuit family.

Fix the following classical Hilbert presentation of Frege. Formulas are finite trees built from propositional variables \(p_0,p_1,\ldots\), negation \(\neg\), and implication \(\to\). Under a Boolean assignment, negation reverses the truth value and \(A\to B\) is false exactly when \(A\) is true and \(B\) false. A tautology evaluates to true under every assignment to its finitely many variables. The axiom schemes, allowing arbitrary formulas \(A,B,D\), are
\[A\to(B\to A),\]
\[(A\to(B\to D))\to((A\to B)\to(A\to D)),\]
\[(\neg A\to\neg B)\to(B\to A).\]
The only inference rule is modus ponens: from earlier lines \(A\) and \(A\to B\), infer \(B\). A proof is a finite sequence of formulas, each an instance of an axiom scheme or obtained by this rule; its last formula is the theorem proved. No extension axioms introducing a new variable as an abbreviation for a formula are allowed.

Choose a fixed uniquely parsable binary tree encoding with constant-length tags for connectives and binary, self-delimited variable indices. Let \(|\varphi|\) be its bit length. Encode a proof by its full sequence of formula strings, with line delimiters; let \(|\pi|\) be that total bit length. Identical subformulas are written out each time they occur, not stored as a shared circuit. Earlier proof lines may be reused in multiple inferences. Including explicit rule tags and premise indices changes these sizes by at most polynomial factors and does not affect polynomial boundedness. The source recalls that standard finite complete Frege presentations polynomially simulate one another, so fixing this presentation does not change its lower-bound question.

Frege is polynomially bounded if there exist \(C,k\) such that every tautology has at least one proof of size at most \(C(|\varphi|+1)^k\). Its negation does not require a polynomial-time generator for the hard tautologies or a single explicit family: existence of arbitrarily hard tautologies with the displayed quantifiers suffices. Formula size, proof size and circuit-input length are different parameters and are not silently identified.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct Lean-checked proof of the displayed implication or of its negation. A positive proof may use exactly the circuit-hardness premise, without assuming additional cryptographic hardness, a feasible-interpolation property of Frege, or a lower bound for another system. A proof of the negation must establish both NP not contained in P/poly and polynomial boundedness of the fixed Frege system. An oracle separation or an obstruction to one reduction technique is not itself a negation of the stated unrelativized implication.

The source asks about ordinary Frege, with unrestricted formula depth. Lower bounds for bounded-depth Frege do not settle it. Extended Frege permits abbreviation variables and is a stronger system; the names should not be interchanged.

cards.title: Simultaneous polynomial-length constant-space refutations
cards.formal: Is the following statement true? For every fixed integer \(k\ge1\) and every family \((F_n)_{n\ge1}\) of unsatisfiable \(k\)-CNF formulas of size polynomial in \(n\), if there is a constant \(s\) such that every \(F_n\) has a resolution refutation using at most \(s\) clauses simultaneously, then there are constants \(S\ge1\), \(C>0\), \(d\in\mathbb N\) such that every \(F_n\) has a single resolution refutation \(\pi_n\) with \[\operatorname{Sp}(\pi_n)\le S\qquad\text{and}\qquad L(\pi_n)\le C(n+1)^d.\] The constants may depend on the family and on \(k,s\), but not on \(n\). In particular, the conclusion may use a larger constant space bound \(S\) than the original bound \(s\).
cards.why: Proof length measures how many lines a refutation generates, and clause space measures how many it must retain at once. The question asks whether a formula that is easy in each measure separately can be hard when both restrictions apply to the same proof. Its constant-space regime makes it a sharp structural question about resolution and the interpretation of proof-memory bounds.

cards.definitions: Variables are drawn from a countable set. A literal is a variable or its negation. A clause is a finite set of literals, interpreted as their disjunction, and a CNF formula is a finite set of clauses, interpreted as their conjunction. A \(k\)-CNF has at most \(k\) literals per input clause; derived clauses have no width bound. Define the size of \(F\) to be \(\sum_{A\in F}(1+|A|)\). Polynomial size means that some \(a>0,b\in\mathbb N\), fixed for the family, satisfy this size bound \(\le a(n+1)^b\) for every \(n\). The parameter \(n\) indexes the family; it need not equal the number of variables. There is no computability or uniform generation requirement on the family. A proof is a finite sequence of configurations \(\mathcal C_0,\ldots,\mathcal C_t\), each a finite set of clauses, starting at \(\mathcal C_0=\varnothing\). One step may add an input clause from \(F\); add the resolvent \(A\cup B\) when \(A\cup\{x\}\) and \(B\cup\{\neg x\}\) are both currently present, with \(x\) absent from \(A\) and \(\neg x\) absent from \(B\); add a weakening \(A\cup B\) when \(A\) is present and \(B\) is any finite clause; or erase one currently present clause. An inference adds its conclusion before any separate erasure, so premises and conclusion coexist in that configuration. The proof ends with the empty clause present. The clause space is \(\operatorname{Sp}(\pi)=\max_j|\mathcal C_j|\), counting input clauses only while they have been downloaded and retained. The length \(L(\pi)\) is the number of input-clause downloads and inference steps, including weakenings and rederivations, but excluding erasures. Erased clauses may be downloaded or derived again; their reappearance is charged again. There is no read-once, tree-like, regularity or restriction on reuse. Space counts clauses regardless of how many literals they contain: it is not total literal space, variable space, bit memory or width. Length counts proof lines as specified, not the bit cost of manipulating a long clause. The target concerns existence of proofs with the two simultaneous bounds, not an efficient algorithm that finds them.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of the stated implication for every fixed width and every polynomial-size family, or prove its negation. A positive answer must produce or establish existence of refutations satisfying both resource bounds at once. Separate witnesses for polynomial length and constant clause space do not suffice. A negative answer must exhibit a fixed \(k\) and a polynomial-size family with a common constant-space refutation bound, but such that for every \(S\ge1,C>0,d\in\mathbb N\) some member has no refutation satisfying both \(\operatorname{Sp}(\pi)\le S\) and \(L(\pi)\le C(n+1)^d\). A polynomial length lower bound, a lower bound only for tree-like proofs, or a trade-off that disappears after increasing space by a fixed constant does not refute this statement.

context_blocks.text: Nordström’s Open Problem 16 asks this simultaneous length–clause-space question for polynomial-size fixed-width CNF families. It is distinct from the neighboring question about trade-offs when space is at least linear in formula size, whose later resolution is already noted in the survey.

The survey records that a constant clause-space bound guarantees some polynomial-length refutation, but that conclusion does not bound the clause space of the short refutation. The missing simultaneous guarantee is precisely the present target.

With total literal space in place of clause space, the corresponding simultaneous constant-space and polynomial-length statement is already known. A constant number of clauses may nevertheless contain many literals, so that result does not apply to this measure.

Papamakarios and Razborov’s ICALP 2022 paper revisits the same constant-clause-space question explicitly in Section 5. Theorem 4.7 gives formulas of linear size with clause-space-four tree-like refutations for which all tree-like refutations have a nearly quadratic length lower bound. A polynomial lower bound in that restricted proof system does not contradict the present unrestricted polynomial-length conclusion.

Their broader equivalences relate proof-space measures to tree-like proof size and identify stronger separation questions. The checked journal metadata places the expanded publication in November 2023; the theorem numbering quoted here is from the fully read ICALP version.

cards.title: Separating levels of bounded arithmetic
cards.formal:
Are there integers \(i>j\ge1\) and a closed first-order arithmetic sentence \(\theta\) such that
\[T_2^i\vdash\theta\qquad\text{and}\qquad T_2^j\nvdash\theta?\]
The theory \(T_2^r\) is BASIC together with induction for every \(\Sigma_r^b\) formula in the language defined below. The question asks for a separation as sets of provable sentences, with no assumed separation of computational complexity classes and no additional oracle symbols. One pair of levels is enough; it need not be fixed in advance, and proving strictness at every pair is not required.
cards.why: These theories organize arithmetic reasoning by the logical complexity permitted in induction hypotheses. Showing that even two positive levels prove different sentences would establish an unconditional difference in the strength of those reasoning principles. It would clarify how computational complexity is reflected in provability, beyond the known conditional connections.

Ježil–Tsintsilidas, arXiv:2602.19934v1 (February 2026), explicitly retain removal of assumptions in their hierarchy separations as an open problem. A bounded subsequent search found no matching unconditional separation or proof that all positive levels coincide. This records the checked sources and search limits, not exhaustive certification of present openness.

cards.definitions:
Use classical first-order logic with equality and the one-sorted language \(L=\{0,1,+,\cdot,H,\ell,\#,\le\}\). Here \(H\) and \(\ell\) are unary, \(+\), \(\cdot\), \(\#\) are binary, and \(\le\) is a binary predicate. Terms are the finite expressions formed from variables, these constants and these function symbols. Atomic formulas are equalities or inequalities between terms. The logical operations are negation, conjunction, disjunction and first-order universal/existential quantification; implication and equivalence abbreviate their usual Boolean expansions. The successor notation \(Sx\) abbreviates \(x+1\), \(2\) abbreviates \(1+1\), and \(2x\) means \(2\cdot x\).

The intended standard structure has domain \(\mathbb N=\{0,1,\ldots\}\), its usual addition, multiplication and order, \(H(x)=\lfloor x/2\rfloor\), \(\ell(0)=0\), \(\ell(x)=\lfloor\log_2 x\rfloor+1\) for \(x>0\), and \(x\#y=2^{\ell(x)\ell(y)}\). This interpretation explains the symbols; the theory's nonlogical axioms are exactly the following finite BASIC list and the specified induction scheme, rather than all sentences true in this standard structure. Every free variable in the following displays is universally quantified.

The order and successor axioms are
\[\begin{gathered}
a\le b\ \to\ a\le b+1,\qquad a\ne a+1,\qquad 0\le a,\\
(a\le b\land a\ne b)\ \to\ a+1\le b,\qquad a\ne0\ \to\ 2a\ne0,\\
a\le b\lor b\le a,\qquad (a\le b\land b\le a)\ \to\ a=b,\\
(a\le b\land b\le c)\ \to\ a\le c,\qquad a\le a+b,\\
(a\le b\land a\ne b)\ \to\ (2a+1\le2b\land 2a+1\ne2b).
\end{gathered}\]
The addition and multiplication axioms are
\[\begin{gathered}
a+b=b+a,\qquad a+0=a,\qquad a+(b+1)=(a+b)+1,\\
(a+b)+c=a+(b+c),\qquad a+b\le a+c\ \to\ b\le c,\\
a\cdot0=0,\qquad a\cdot(b+1)=a\cdot b+a,\qquad a\cdot b=b\cdot a,\\
a\cdot(b+c)=(a\cdot b)+(a\cdot c),\\
1\le a\ \to\ ((a\cdot b\le a\cdot c)\leftrightarrow(b\le c)).
\end{gathered}\]
The length, halving and smash axioms are
\[\begin{gathered}
\ell(0)=0,\qquad \ell(1)=1,\qquad a\le b\ \to\ \ell(a)\le\ell(b),\\
a\ne0\ \to\ (\ell(2a)=\ell(a)+1\land\ell(2a+1)=\ell(a)+1),\\
\ell(a\#b)=\ell(a)\cdot\ell(b)+1,\qquad 0\#a=1,\\
a\ne0\ \to\ (1\#(2a)=2(1\#a)\land1\#(2a+1)=2(1\#a)),\\
a\#b=b\#a,\qquad \ell(a)=\ell(b)\ \to\ a\#c=b\#c,\\
\ell(a)=\ell(b)+\ell(c)\ \to\ a\#d=(b\#d)\cdot(c\#d),\\
a\ne0\ \to\ \ell(a)=\ell(H(a))+1,\\
a=H(b)\ \leftrightarrow\ (2a=b\lor2a+1=b).
\end{gathered}\]
These are the 32 axioms in Krajíček's Definition 5.2.1, regrouped by operation, with \(H\) and \(\ell\) replacing the printed halving and length notation. No sequence function or oracle predicate is added.

For a term \(t\) not containing \(y\), write \(\exists y\le t\,\psi\) for \(\exists y(y\le t\land\psi)\), and \(\forall y\le t\,\psi\) for \(\forall y(y\le t\to\psi)\). These are bounded quantifiers. They are sharply bounded when the bound is explicitly \(\ell(t)\). The bound may contain other free variables. Let \(\Sigma_0^b=\Pi_0^b\) be all formulas built from atomic formulas using Boolean operations and only sharply bounded quantifiers. Recursively, \(\Sigma_{r+1}^b,\Pi_{r+1}^b\) are the smallest pair of classes satisfying: both contain \(\Sigma_r^b\cup\Pi_r^b\); both are closed under conjunction, disjunction and both sharply bounded quantifiers; \(\Sigma_{r+1}^b\) is closed under bounded existential quantification; \(\Pi_{r+1}^b\) is closed under bounded universal quantification; and negation sends either class into the other. These are the full formula classes, allowing sharply bounded quantifiers inside as well as outside the other quantifiers, rather than only a strict prenex fragment.

For a set \(T\) of closed axioms, \(T\vdash\theta\) means that the closed sentence \(\theta\) has a finite proof in classical first-order logic with equality from those axioms. Equivalently, every nonempty \(L\)-structure satisfying all axioms of \(T\) satisfies \(\theta\). This equivalence is first-order completeness; structures in this characterization are not restricted to the standard natural numbers. There is no bound on proof length. Equality of theories here means equality of their deductive closures in the same language.

For each integer \(r\ge1\), \(T_2^r\) has the displayed BASIC axioms and, for each \(\varphi(x,\vec a)\in\Sigma_r^b\), the universal closure over all parameter variables \(\vec a\) of
\[\bigl(\varphi(0,\vec a)\land\forall x(\varphi(x,\vec a)\to\varphi(x+1,\vec a))\bigr)\ \to\ \forall x\,\varphi(x,\vec a).\]
Parameters are allowed and are not required to be numerals. There are no induction axioms for formulas outside the specified class unless they are consequences of these axioms. Since the formula classes are nested, \(T_2^j\subseteq T_2^i\) in deductive strength when \(j<i\). A positive answer therefore gives a strict inclusion. The separating sentence may have unrestricted first-order quantifiers; no complexity or syntactic bound on that witness sentence is part of the target.

The indices, finite formulas and finite proofs in the question range over ordinary standard mathematical objects. The nonprovability claim is external: it means that no finite proof from the weaker theory exists, rather than asking the weaker theory itself to prove its inability. A countermodel for the weaker theory and the sentence is an equivalent way to certify that nonprovability. A positive answer must be unconditional in the usual mathematical metatheory; adding an unproved complexity assumption changes the requested statement.
cards.answer_criterion: Supply a complete mathematically correct Lean-checked proof or refutation of the displayed existential separation. A positive answer must establish one pair of standard integers \(i>j\ge1\), a closed sentence provable in \(T_2^i\), and its nonprovability in \(T_2^j\); the latter can equivalently be proved by a model of \(T_2^j\) falsifying the sentence. A negative answer must establish equality of the deductive closures for every pair \(i>j\ge1\). A difference between axiom lists, a lower bound on the shortest proof of a still-provable sentence, a relativized separation, or a separation conditional on an unproved complexity conjecture does not settle this target.

cards.title: Unprovability of polynomial circuit upper bounds in \(S_2^1\)
cards.formal:
Is the following unconditional unprovability statement true?
\[\forall k\in\mathbb Z_{\ge1}\ \exists\eta\ \forall c\in\mathbb Z_{\ge1}:\qquad S_2^1\nvdash\operatorname{UB}_{c,k}[\eta].\]
Here \(\eta(x,y)\) must be a \(\Sigma_1^b\) formula for which \(S_2^1\) proves that every \(x\) has exactly one output \(y\). It therefore represents a polynomial-time function. The sentence \(\operatorname{UB}_{c,k}[\eta]\), defined below with explicit coding, asserts that the predicate “the output is nonzero” has exact Boolean circuits of description size at most \(c n^k\) on every positive input length \(n\).

For each fixed exponent, the same represented function must resist provability for every fixed coefficient. The question concerns what this formal theory can prove; it does not ask directly for a circuit lower bound in the standard natural numbers or for unprovability of all possible upper bounds for one fixed function.
cards.why: Circuit upper bounds assert that small nonuniform computations exist, even when no efficient method for finding them is supplied. This question asks whether a theory designed to formalize polynomial-time reasoning can certify fixed-polynomial circuit bounds for every polynomial-time predicate. A positive result would expose an unconditional limitation on the power of such proofs without requiring the corresponding unconditional circuit separation.

for every \(\Sigma_1^b\) formula \(\varphi\). This is polynomial induction, with halving in the hypothesis; it is not unrestricted successor induction for these formulas.

To specify the polynomial-time predicate without leaving its formal representation implicit, let \(\eta(x,y)\) range over \(\Sigma_1^b\) formulas whose only free variables are among \(x,y\) and for which
\[S_2^1\vdash\forall x\,\exists y\bigl(\eta(x,y)\land\forall z(\eta(x,z)\to z=y)\bigr).\]
Thus the theory proves that \(\eta\) defines one total number-valued function. The associated language consists of numbers whose unique output is nonzero. By the definability/witnessing characterization of \(S_2^1\), these provably total \(\Sigma_1^b\) graphs represent polynomial-time functions. This is a base-language presentation of the source's polynomial-time function symbols in a conservative definitional extension. The formula \(\eta\), rather than just its extension in the standard natural numbers, is part of the witness being quantified over.

Here is an explicit arithmetic encoding of the circuits used in the upper-bound sentence. An \(n\)-input circuit has constants at nodes zero and one, inputs at nodes \(2,\ldots,n+1\), and \(g\ge0\) computational nodes \(n+2,\ldots,n+g+1\) in evaluation order. Each computational node has a two-bit operation tag: zero is AND, one OR, two NOT of the first predecessor, and three a copy of the first predecessor. It also has two predecessor indices, both less than its own index; the second is ignored for the last two tags. The output is any node. Shared values and unrestricted depth are allowed, with exact correctness on all inputs. Copy gates are only a serialization convenience and can be removed; this is an ordinary bounded-fan-in Boolean model.

Let \(w=\ell(n+g+2)\), \(q=2+2w\), and \(d=gq+w\). The circuit number \(C\) has binary length \(d+1\); its highest bit is a delimiter. In the lower bits, counted from position zero at the least significant bit, gate \(i\in\{0,\ldots,g-1\}\) has its tag at positions \(iq,iq+1\), first predecessor in the next \(w\) bits, and second predecessor in the next \(w\) bits. The output index occupies the \(w\) bits starting at \(gq\). A valid encoding has both predecessors below \(n+2+i\) and output below \(n+g+2\). Denote these conditions by \(\operatorname{Valid}(n,g,C)\). The description size charged in the sentence is \(\ell(C)+\ell(g)\); the input length is supplied separately. Thus the measure is a binary description length, not an unannounced change to an exact gate-count bound.

All bit and field operations in this description have the following fixed bounded-arithmetic expansion. For \(X\ge1\), define \(\operatorname{Field}(X,a,b,v)\) by the existence of \(z,t,u,r,s\), all at most \(X+(1\#X)+1\), such that
\[\begin{gathered}
z=1\#H(z),\quad \ell(z)=a+1,\quad t=1\#H(t),\quad \ell(t)=b+1,\\
X=uz+r,\quad r<z,\quad u=st+v,\quad v<t.
\end{gathered}\]
Here \(a\) is the starting position, \(b\ge1\) is field width, and \(u< v\) abbreviates \(u\le v\land u\ne v\). The equations select \(z=2^a\) and \(t=2^b\). Define \(\operatorname{Bit}(X,a,e)\), for \(e\in\{0,1\}\), as
\[(\ell(X)\le a\land e=0)\ \lor\ (a<\ell(X)\land\operatorname{Field}(X,a,1,e)).\]
This also defines the padded zero bits of \(X=0\). In \(\operatorname{Valid}\), each extracted tag or index is a bounded existential variable at most \(n+g+4\); gate checks are quantified over \(i<g\). These conventions expand validity into one definite arithmetic formula.

Define \(\operatorname{Eval}(N,n,g,C,x)\) to assert that the encoded circuit outputs one on the \(n\)-bit, zero-padded representation of \(x\). Its arithmetic expansion is: validity holds and there exists an integer
\[V\le (N\#N)\cdot(C\#C)\]
whose bits at node indices give a correct evaluation, with output bit one. Bits zero and one of \(V\) equal zero and one respectively; for each \(r<n\), bit \(r+2\) of \(V\) equals bit \(r\) of \(x\); and for each \(i<g\), the bit at \(n+2+i\) is the Boolean operation indicated by the tag applied to the predecessor bits. All field and bit occurrences use the preceding formulas, with Boolean auxiliary variables bounded by one and extracted indices bounded by \(n+g+4\). The four Boolean operations are specified by their truth tables. The output index is extracted from its field and its \(V\)-bit must be one. The quantifiers over nodes and gates are bounded by \(n\) and \(g\). Since validity implies \(g\le\ell(C)\) and \(n=\ell(N)\ge1\), the displayed bound is ample for the finite evaluation vector. This description fixes the formula through bounded quantifiers and Boolean combinations, and introduces no extra axioms about an opaque evaluator.

For fixed positive integers \(c,k\), let \(\operatorname{UB}_{c,k}[\eta]\) be the following closed \(L\)-sentence, with the defined predicates expanded:
\[\begin{split}
\forall N\ge1\ \exists g\ \exists C\ \bigl(&\operatorname{Valid}(n,g,C)\land\ell(C)+\ell(g)\le c\,n^k\\
&\land\forall x\ \forall y\bigl((\ell(x)\le n\land\eta(x,y))\to
(\operatorname{Eval}(N,n,g,C,x)\leftrightarrow y\ne0)\bigr)\bigr),
\end{split}\]
where every \(n\) abbreviates \(\ell(N)\). The fixed numeral \(c\) and fixed power \(n^k\) are expanded using multiplication. This is the source's Log convention: lengths come from the length of an arbitrarily quantified number, instead of treating their unary encodings as separately available objects. Zero input length is omitted. The quantifier \(\ell(x)\le n\) permits leading-zero padding; the represented function is a function of the number \(x\), exactly as in the source's unary function-symbol formulation.

The choices of \(k\), \(\eta\) and \(c\) in the main question are external standard integers/formulas. For each fixed exponent, one formula must work against every coefficient. The required conclusion is absence of any finite proof of each displayed upper-bound sentence, not that the theory proves its negation. The description encoding above makes a routine circuit serialization explicit; it is not a claim that the source printed this exact bit layout. Polynomially related standard circuit encodings yield the same all-exponents unprovability target after a fixed change of exponent and coefficient. No single EXP language or unproved complexity assumption substitutes for a provably total polynomial-time graph.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct Lean-checked proof or refutation of the displayed metamathematical statement. A positive answer must, for every standard exponent \(k\ge1\), establish a permitted formula \(\eta\) with its \(S_2^1\)-provable totality and uniqueness and prove that no finite \(S_2^1\) proof of \(\operatorname{UB}_{c,k}[\eta]\) exists for any standard coefficient \(c\ge1\). A negative answer must establish an exponent \(k\) such that every permitted \(\eta\) has some coefficient \(c\) for which the corresponding upper-bound sentence is provable. The coefficient and proof may depend on \(\eta\). Nonprovability for a weaker theory, an EXP computation, one proposed proof, or one coefficient alone is insufficient. No unproved complexity hypothesis is part of the target.

cards.formal: Is it true that, for every unary function symbol \(g\) in the syntactically generated language \(L_{PV}\) below, \[PV_1\not\vdash\Phi_g,\qquad \Phi_g=\forall F\,\forall a\bigl(\operatorname{Sat}(F,a)\to\operatorname{Sat}(F,g(F))\bigr)?\] The theory, admissible symbols and arithmetic formula \(\operatorname{Sat}\) are fixed in the definitions.
