The standard BPTIME model is explicitly sourced separately from the survey’s RAM convention, and recent fixed-width SAT improvements do not settle the hypothesis.

cards.definitions:
Fix an integer \(k\ge3\). A \(k\)-CNF formula \(F\) is a finite list of clauses, each a finite list of at most \(k\) literals. A literal is a variable \(x_i\) or its negation \(\neg x_i\). The distinct variables occurring in the entire formula are exactly \(x_1,\ldots,x_n\), so \(n\) counts variables, not clauses or encoding bits. Repeated literals, repeated clauses and clauses containing both signs of a variable are allowed. A Boolean assignment is a map \(\{1,\ldots,n\}\to\{0,1\}\); it satisfies \(F\) when every clause has at least one true literal. The empty clause is false, the empty conjunction is true, and the empty conjunction has \(n=0\). Define \(\operatorname{SAT}(F)=1\) if some assignment satisfies \(F\), and \(0\) otherwise.

Use the following explicit binary encoding. For each integer \(a\ge0\), let \(\operatorname{bin}(a+1)\) be the binary expansion of \(a+1\) with no leading zeros, let \(b\) be its length, and put \(\operatorname{code}(a)=1^b0\operatorname{bin}(a+1)\). Encode the number \(n\) of variables and the number \(m\) of clauses using this code. Then encode each clause by its coded length, followed by its literals in their listed order. Encode a literal by one sign bit, \(0\) for positive and \(1\) for negated, followed by \(\operatorname{code}(i)\) for its variable index. Require \(1\le i\le n\), all declared lists to be fully present, every declared variable to occur, no trailing bits, and every clause length to be at most \(k\). Let \(L=|\operatorname{enc}(F)|\).

The inputs range over all such formulas. There is no promise of linearly many clauses, bounded variable occurrences, a unique satisfying assignment, a gap in the optimum number of satisfied clauses, or a random input distribution. The clause width is a fixed constant for each language \(k\)-SAT; it does not grow with the input length. The model allows arbitrarily many explicitly listed clauses, including duplicates, and the displayed polynomial factor in \(L\) includes their processing.

A machine has one finite program, finitely many tapes and finite tape alphabets, with these choices fixed independently of input length. Its tapes have cells indexed by the nonnegative integers, all heads start at cell zero, and an attempted left move from cell zero leaves that head there. The read-only input tape contains the encoding starting in cell zero, followed by an end marker and blanks; work tapes are initially blank. The finite control starts in a fixed initial state and has halting states labelled by the decision bits \(0\) and \(1\). At each transition the machine reads or writes only the symbols under its heads and moves each head by at most one cell. It may request one fresh fair random bit during a transition. The random source \(r\) is an infinite sequence of independent unbiased bits; a run reads a finite prefix before halting. All transitions, including input access, random-bit generation and internal computation, count toward \(t_M\). There is no unit-cost random access, unbounded-integer arithmetic, quantum operation, oracle or advice depending on input length.

A \(k\)-SAT algorithm in the quantified class halts with output \(0\) or \(1\) on every input and every random sequence. It rejects malformed encodings in polynomial time in their bit length, with a fixed polynomial for that machine. On each valid formula its answer is correct with probability at least \(2/3\), independently of whether the formula is satisfiable. Thus errors on both yes-instances and no-instances are permitted. The runtime bound is required for every random sequence, not only in expectation or with high probability. There is no additional space bound.

The constants \(C,d\) and the program may depend on the fixed width \(k\) and on a proposed saving \(\varepsilon\), but cannot depend on \(F\), \(n\), \(L\) or the realized random bits. Any finite exceptional set of input lengths can be covered by increasing \(C\). Every algorithm is uniform across input lengths. A different algorithm may be considered for each width; no computable procedure selecting those algorithms from \(k\) is built into the hypothesis.

The quantifier over \(\varepsilon\) asks about every fixed positive saving in the exponent. It does not assert a \(2^{n-o(n)}\) lower bound for a single fixed width, and it does not preclude a width-dependent saving tending to zero as \(k\) increases. The claim also does not replace bounded-width satisfiability by arbitrary-width CNF-SAT. The randomness belongs to the algorithm while correctness and time are worst-case over formulas.
cards.answer_criterion:
Provide a complete, mathematically correct Lean proof of the displayed hypothesis or of its full negation in the stated machine and input model.

A positive answer must establish that, for every real \(\varepsilon\in(0,1)\), some fixed integer \(k\ge3\) excludes all machines and constants satisfying both the correctness and runtime conditions. It must cover all uniform bounded-error randomized algorithms, not only a selected algorithm or a restricted family.

A negative answer must establish the quantifier order
\[
\exists\varepsilon_0\in(0,1)\ \forall k\ge3\
\exists M_k,\ C_k\ge1,\ d_k\ge0\
\forall F\in k\text{-CNF}:
\]
\[
\Pr_r[M_k(\operatorname{enc}(F);r)=\operatorname{SAT}(F)]\ge\frac23
\quad\text{and}\quad
\forall r:\ 
t_{M_k}(\operatorname{enc}(F);r)
\le C_k\,2^{(1-\varepsilon_0)n(F)}(L(F)+1)^{d_k}.
\]
Here \(C_k,d_k\) are integers and each \(M_k\) meets all machine, termination and malformed-input requirements above. The same positive \(\varepsilon_0\) must work for every fixed width; programs and polynomial factors may vary with the width. Proving these existential witnesses for every width suffices without an additional requirement of one algorithm that accepts the width as input.

An improvement only for one width, a saving that vanishes as the width grows, average-case performance, or a result under an additional unproved hypothesis does not settle this statement. A proof only about deterministic algorithms establishes a different claim unless it also yields the required randomized statement. Numerical evidence about running-time bases and a Lean definition of the hypothesis alone are insufficient.

context_blocks.text: The 2018 survey explicitly extends the Strong Exponential Time Hypothesis to randomized algorithms in Hypothesis 1. The later definition by Ron-Zewi and Rothblum names the hypothesis RSETH and states it using bounded-error probabilistic time. This card adopts that standard Turing-machine formulation and records the original survey’s different global RAM convention rather than silently identifying the two models.

Exhaustive search examines \(2^n\) assignments. For any particular fixed clause width, randomized algorithms can improve its exponential base. The hypothesis concerns whether the savings can be kept bounded away from zero across every fixed width, so improvements for \(3\)-SAT are compatible with it.

Cygan and coauthors formulate the randomized growth rate with error probability at most \(1/3\) and a polynomial factor in the complete input size. They distinguish the hypothesis for all fixed widths from the weaker assertion that unrestricted-width CNF-SAT has no fixed improvement over exhaustive search. Their work also connects the bounded-width hypothesis to corresponding exponential-time barriers for Hitting Set, Set Splitting and Not-All-Equal SAT.

The randomized claim excludes a larger class of algorithms than deterministic SETH in the same bit model, so it implies that deterministic hypothesis. Randomized ETH asks instead for a positive exponential-time barrier already for \(3\)-SAT; it does not demand that the optimal exponent approach one with increasing width. Nondeterministic SETH, parity hypotheses and assumptions about randomly sampled formulas concern other algorithmic or input models.

The July 2026 preprint on PPSZ reports improved randomized bounds for Unique-\(3\)-SAT and general \(3\)-SAT. Its theorems address that fixed width and do not supply the common positive exponent saving for every width that would negate rSETH. This bounded literature check records the preprint’s scope without treating it as a verified resolution of the hypothesis.

Polynomial input-factor normalization is substantive and sourced, rather than permitting a vacuous input-reading lower bound on arbitrarily padded formulas. For a fixed width k, removing repeated literals, tautological clauses and duplicate clauses yields at most sum_{j=0}^k 2^j binomial(n,j) distinct non-tautological clauses. The resulting length is polynomial in n for fixed k. Preprocessing arbitrary explicit input costs poly(L); the polynomial length factors on reduced instances can be absorbed by any fixed smaller exponent saving. Thus the full every-epsilon assertion uses the customary polynomial-input-factor normalization without a hidden linear-clause promise. The audit does not assert pointwise equality of exact runtime bounds at a fixed epsilon.

The chosen bounded-error constant is directly supported by Cygan et al. Definition 2.1. The statement permits both false positives and false negatives. For this satisfiability hypothesis the conventional one-sided and two-sided exclusion formulations can also be related with polynomial overhead: amplify a decider to inverse-polynomial error, make at most n adaptive restricted-formula queries to recover a candidate assignment, then verify it. Width does not increase and the number of actual variables does not increase; verification eliminates false positives. This explanatory normalization remains in the audit, not as a public solution hint.

Worst-case time over all fair-coin runs is the BPTIME convention. An expected-time bounded-error speedup with a uniform bound on each input can be amplified by constant repetitions and truncated at a constant multiple of its expected-time bound; the added error can be kept below 1/3. If necessary, choose a smaller rational exponent saving to make the cutoff explicit. Conversely worst-case bounds imply expected bounds. This justifies treating the overall hypothesis as robust to the usual expected-time convention after changing constants or slightly shrinking the saving, not equating every individual machine guarantee. No conversion from arbitrary real/quantum randomness is asserted.

The negation is some one positive epsilon_0 followed by every fixed width and then an algorithm and constants for that width. The program need not be the same for different widths, but is finite and uniform in input size for each width. A particular small-width speedup, a width-dependent saving tending to zero, or a mere sparse/random/unique-input result cannot refute this quantified statement. Positive lower-bound proofs must also address two-sided randomized machines. No conjectural premise is built into either answer.

Bounded later searches through 16 September 2026 checked exact randomized-strong-ETH/BPTIME formulations, recent k-SAT/PPSZ work and apparent SETH-refutation titles. Downloaded arXiv:2607.10697v1 and read pp. 1–3, Theorem 1.1 and Corollary 1.2. Its claimed numerical improvement is exclusively for Unique-3-SAT and general 3-SAT. The preprint is not promoted to an independently verified best-known theorem; the card uses only its checked scope. No verified proof or refutation of the full rSETH statement was recovered in this bounded check.

Checked primary abstract and metadata of Kulikov–Mihajlin, If Edge Coloring is Hard under SETH, then SETH is False, arXiv:2607.21276v1 (23 July 2026; notes the SOSA 2024 publication). It is a conditional barrier to certain edge-coloring hardness reductions, not an unconditional SAT speedup or proof that SETH is false. It is not needed in the public card. Average-case random-k-SAT and stronger quantitative SSETH leads were kept distinct from worst-case randomized SETH.

cards.context:
The 2018 survey explicitly extends the Strong Exponential Time Hypothesis to randomized algorithms in Hypothesis 1. The later definition by Ron-Zewi and Rothblum names the hypothesis RSETH and states it using bounded-error probabilistic time. This card adopts that standard Turing-machine formulation and records the original survey’s different global RAM convention rather than silently identifying the two models.

Exhaustive search examines \(2^n\) assignments. For any particular fixed clause width, randomized algorithms can improve its exponential base. The hypothesis concerns whether the savings can be kept bounded away from zero across every fixed width, so improvements for \(3\)-SAT are compatible with it.

Cygan and coauthors formulate the randomized growth rate with error probability at most \(1/3\) and a polynomial factor in the complete input size. They distinguish the hypothesis for all fixed widths from the weaker assertion that unrestricted-width CNF-SAT has no fixed improvement over exhaustive search. Their work also connects the bounded-width hypothesis to corresponding exponential-time barriers for Hitting Set, Set Splitting and Not-All-Equal SAT.

The randomized claim excludes a larger class of algorithms than deterministic SETH in the same bit model, so it implies that deterministic hypothesis. Randomized ETH asks instead for a positive exponential-time barrier already for \(3\)-SAT; it does not demand that the optimal exponent approach one with increasing width. Nondeterministic SETH, parity hypotheses and assumptions about randomly sampled formulas concern other algorithmic or input models.

The July 2026 preprint on PPSZ reports improved randomized bounds for Unique-\(3\)-SAT and general \(3\)-SAT. Its theorems address that fixed width and do not supply the common positive exponent saving for every width that would negate rSETH. This bounded literature check records the preprint’s scope without treating it as a verified resolution of the hypothesis.

cards.title: Randomized APSP hypothesis for polynomial integer weights
cards.formal: Is the following hypothesis true? \[\forall\varepsilon\in\mathbb Q\cap(0,1]\ \exists c\in\mathbb N_{\ge1}:\ \neg\mathrm{FastAPSP}(c,\varepsilon).\] Here \(\mathrm{FastAPSP}(c,\varepsilon)\) means that a uniform randomized word-RAM algorithm computes the entire exact distance matrix of every directed \(n\)-vertex graph with integer edge weights in \([-n^c,n^c]\) and no negative-weight cycle, succeeds with probability at least \(2/3\) on each input, and has worst-case time \(O(n^{3-\varepsilon})\) over all inputs and coin sequences. The word model and the quantifiers hidden in this definition are specified below. The weight exponent \(c\) may depend on \(\varepsilon\). This makes explicit the weaker quantifier order stated in the 2026 source; the 2018 source's phrase about sufficiently large \(c\) did not specify that dependence.
cards.why: The randomized APSP hypothesis is a principal foundation of fine-grained complexity. Resolving it would determine whether exact distances in general integer-weighted graphs admit a fixed polynomial improvement over cubic time, and would affect a large network of conditional bounds for graph, matrix, sequence and dynamic problems.
cards.status_note: The original 2018 source states the randomized polynomial-integer-weight hypothesis. Fischer's 29 March 2026 full preprint explicitly states the modern forall-epsilon/exists-c formulation adopted here as Hypothesis 1.1, describes truly subcubic APSP as a major open question, and fixes the randomized word-RAM model. A bounded primary-source review through 16 September 2026, including the 2025 few-weight results, the conditional 2026 universe reduction, July 2026 node-weighted-triangle work and the August 2026 reduction barrier, found no verified resolution of this exact statement. This does not exhaustively certify current openness. The stronger quantifier order with one absolute c for every epsilon is not silently substituted for this target.

importance.reason: A core fine-grained hardness hypothesis for a basic graph problem, including randomized algorithms and polynomial integer weights. Its extensive graph and matrix equivalences and consequences for other algorithmic problems make a resolution foundational. This individual assessment is based on that breadth and the precise target, not the inherited provisional score or the existence of a survey entry.

sentences: All-pairs shortest paths asks for the exact distance between every ordered pair of vertices in a directed graph.
The graph has polynomially bounded signed integer edge weights and no negative-weight cycle.
The hypothesis says that for every fixed improvement over the cubic exponent, some polynomial weight bound rules out every randomized algorithm with that running time.
Computation uses logarithmic-size machine words, and the whole distance matrix must be correct with probability at least two thirds on every input.
Known general algorithms save a subpolynomial factor, while recent restricted algorithms and conditional equivalences do not settle this hypothesis.

cards.definitions:
For fixed integers \(n\ge2\) and \(c\ge1\), the vertex set is \([n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}\). The input is \(n\) and an \(n\times n\) adjacency matrix in vertex order, with a presence flag for each ordered pair and, for each present edge, a signed integer weight \(w(u,v)\) satisfying \(|w(u,v)|\le n^c\). There is at most one edge per ordered pair; self-loops are allowed. Missing edges are indicated by their flags. The graph is promised to have no directed cycle with negative total weight. Negative edges, zero-weight cycles and ties between shortest paths are allowed. For vertices \(u,v\), let \(d_G(u,v)\) be the minimum total weight of a finite directed walk from \(u\) to \(v\), or a separate unreachable symbol \(+\infty\) if there is no such walk. The empty walk has weight zero. Under the promise every reachable minimum is attained, \(d_G(u,u)=0\), and each finite distance has absolute value at most \((n-1)n^c\). The output consists of these \(n^2\) exact integers or unreachable flags in vertex-pair order; listing all path vertices is not required.

The machine is a word RAM with one fixed finite program. For a fixed integer \(a\ge c+4\), its word length on \(n\)-vertex inputs is \(b(n)=\lceil a\log_2(n+1)\rceil\) bits. Each memory address and memory cell is one word. The input is one word for n followed in row-major order by two words for each matrix entry: its zero-or-one presence flag and its signed weight, with zero in the weight word when the flag is zero. The output uses the same row-major order and two words per entry: a zero-or-one finite-distance flag and its signed distance, with zero in the second word for unreachable pairs. Signed integers use two's-complement encoding; distances fit in a constant number of words. Word load, store, copy, comparison, conditional branch, bitwise Boolean operations, shifts, and addition, subtraction and multiplication modulo \(2^{b(n)}\) each cost one step. Unsigned quotient and remainder by a nonzero word also cost one step. Division by zero is invalid; shifts by at least \(b(n)\) positions return zero. Algorithms may use several words for larger quantities, charging all operations. All accessed addresses must fit in a word. Work memory initially contains zero, and no input-dependent precomputed tables, advice or oracle are supplied. All preprocessing, table construction, memory operations and output writing count toward the time bound. One random instruction yields one fresh independent fair bit in one step. The input graph is fixed before the coins are drawn. Deterministic programs are included by ignoring random bits.

Precisely, \(\mathrm{FastAPSP}(c,\varepsilon)\) asserts the existence of a finite program \(A\), an integer word-size factor \(a\ge c+4\), and an integer constant \(C\ge1\), such that for every integer \(n\ge2\) and every promised graph, every run halts within \(Cn^{3-\varepsilon}\) steps, and with probability at least \(2/3\) its entire output matrix equals \((d_G(u,v))_{u,v\in[n]}\). Correctness is joint for the matrix, rather than a separate bound for each entry. The program, \(a\) and \(C\) may depend on the fixed \(c\) and \(\varepsilon\), but not on \(n\) or the input graph. There is no requirement to classify or detect inputs that violate the promise. The exponent in the time bound concerns the number \(n\) of vertices; the input has \(\Theta(n^2)\) words and \(O(n^2\log n)\) bits for each fixed \(c,a\). Rational \(\varepsilon\in(0,1]\) capture every possible fixed positive exponent saving.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete, mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of the displayed hypothesis, or of its full logical negation \[\exists\varepsilon\in\mathbb Q\cap(0,1]\ \forall c\in\mathbb N_{\ge1}:\ \mathrm{FastAPSP}(c,\varepsilon).\] A refutation must therefore establish one common positive exponent saving for every fixed polynomial weight bound; programs and runtime constants may depend on \(c\). A proof of the hypothesis must rule out all uniform randomized algorithms in the specified model for a suitable \(c\) at each saving \(\varepsilon\). A deterministic-only lower bound, a barrier for a particular algorithm or reduction technique, or a truly subcubic algorithm only for one restricted weight regime does not settle the statement. Neither do approximate distances, random input distributions, single-source bounds, distributed round bounds or extra accurate predictions. A subpolynomial-factor improvement over cubic time alone is insufficient. This yes/no target concerns exact APSP algorithms; an unproved APSP hypothesis cannot be assumed as the proof of itself.

context_blocks.text: The 2018 survey treats APSP as one of the central hypotheses used to explain polynomial-time barriers. Its model permits randomization and logarithmic machine words, and its graph weights are polynomially bounded signed integers with no negative cycle.

Fischer's 2026 formulation explicitly places the requested exponent saving before the weight exponent: for every saving there is a polynomial weight range that remains hard. Its footnote distinguishes the stronger hypothesis with one absolute weight exponent for all savings. The paper uses nonnegative weights and explicitly states equivalence with the signed, no-negative-cycle convention retained here.

Williams gives a randomized word-RAM algorithm for nonnegative integer weights bounded by \(M\) in time \(n^3/2^{\Omega(\sqrt{\log n})}+n^{2+o(1)}\log M\). For polynomial \(M\), this achieves a substantial improvement over cubic time while the saving remains subpolynomial in \(n\), so it does not provide a fixed exponent improvement.

The 2025 few-weights algorithms exploit a bound on the number of distinct edge weights associated with each vertex. Their truly subcubic results concern those restricted instances, whereas this hypothesis imposes no such bound.

The 2026 universe-reduction paper connects APSP to stronger hypotheses for small-weight and unweighted graphs. Its full equivalence is conditional on the matrix-multiplication exponent being two and on an additional algorithmic assumption from additive combinatorics; it proves neither the APSP hypothesis nor its negation.

The August 2026 lower bound concerns a class of black-box triangle reductions. It limits those reductions' ability to preserve precise running-time exponents, and does not establish a general lower bound for APSP algorithms.

checked_sources: Retain as an active source-open yes/no hypothesis in the signed-integer word-RAM model. Do not archive as solved or automatically merge with the real-weight APSP card. This inert draft contains no canonical, queue, selection, comment, commit or publication mutation. Preserve the existing category and original notes/comments.

Recovered source exactly: author survey eccentri.pdf, PDF p. 5 defines polynomially bounded integer edge weights and excludes negative cycles; Hypothesis 3 on PDF p. 6 excludes randomized O(n^{3-epsilon}) algorithms for sufficiently large c; pp. 3–4 specify logarithmic-word RAM. The source does not explicitly quantify c relative to epsilon or enumerate its RAM instruction set and success probability. The draft makes those conventions visible rather than claiming they were literally written there.

The key later source is Fischer 2026, arXiv:2603.27736v1, Hypothesis 1.1 and footnote 3 on printed p. 1/PDF p. 3. It explicitly adopts forall epsilon > 0 exists c, and distinguishes the stronger exists c forall epsilon > 0 formulation. Parent approved using the weaker explicitly sourced formulation and publicly disclosing the ambiguity of the 2018 wording. No equivalence between these two quantifier orders is asserted. Taking c to be a positive integer is harmless by rounding a finite real exponent upward and monotonicity of the input family. Similarly, sufficiently large c can be expressed by existence because hardness persists upon enlarging the admissible weight range.

Negation audit: the target is forall epsilon exists c not Fast(c,epsilon), so its full negation is exists epsilon forall c Fast(c,epsilon). Each c may have its own finite algorithm, word-size constant and runtime constant, while the same positive saving epsilon must work for every c. Merely giving different positive savings epsilon_c tending to zero with c does not refute this formulation. The card does not strengthen the negation by requiring a compiler that takes c as input and produces algorithms.

The directed model is explicit in Fischer footnote 1; original APSP permits directed graphs. The signed weights and no-negative-cycle promise are preserved from 2018 rather than silently changed to nonnegative or unit weights. Fischer footnote 2 states the equivalence of its nonnegative convention to signed weights via a potential reweighting and a sufficiently fast single-source computation. Such normalization may enlarge the polynomial weight exponent, which is allowed by the chosen quantifiers. No equivalence to the fixed-small-weight Strong APSP hypothesis is assumed.

Definitions include a dense explicit matrix, at most one directed edge per ordered pair, possible self-loops, missing-edge flags, zero-weight ties/cycles, unreachable pairs, empty paths, all n^2 exact outputs, and the lack of any requirement to detect a violated negative-cycle promise. Distances of reachable distinct vertices have a simple-path witness with at most n-1 edges, so they fit in O(log n) bits for fixed c. They are not real-valued inputs or approximate outputs. The 1/100 numerical benchmark rule does not change the computational problem inside this yes/no hypothesis.

The finite-program word-RAM convention is a concrete editorial completion of the source's standard logarithmic-word RAM. Word-size factors may depend on fixed c and the algorithm, keeping every word O(log n) bits and permitting all weights and addresses in O(1) words. The explicit instruction set has only conventional word operations; multiword arithmetic, preprocessing, generated tables, random bits and output are charged. It supplies no unbounded-precision real primitive, arbitrary-real advice, nonuniform lookup table or cryptographic/quantum oracle. Using fair words rather than fair bits or simulating word multiplication/division with simpler bit operations changes costs by at most polylogarithmic factors; with a possible smaller epsilon, this preserves whether a fixed truly subcubic saving exists.

Probability/time normalization: Fischer Section 2.5 (printed p. 15/PDF p. 17) allows randomized algorithms succeeding with probability 1-n^{-d} for arbitrarily large constant d. The draft chooses joint matrix success 2/3 and a worst-case bound for every coin sequence. Repeating independently and taking a coordinatewise majority increases whole-matrix success: whenever a majority of complete runs are correct, every coordinate majority is correct. O(log n) repetitions give high probability, adding O(n^2 log n) output-comparison cost and preserving truly subcubic existence after shrinking epsilon. Conversely high probability implies constant success, after harmless treatment of finitely many sizes. These equivalences concern the existence of some positive saving, not equality of one fixed epsilon predicate.

Expected-time variants also do not change the full no-truly-subcubic hypothesis under conventional bounded error: first amplify success to at least 5/6 by a constant number of repetitions, then abort after a sufficiently large constant multiple of the worst-case-over-input expected runtime. Markov's inequality bounds abort probability by at most 1/6, giving joint success at least 2/3 and a worst-case runtime bound. Conversely a worst-case bound implies the same expected bound. The draft itself fixes worst-case time explicitly; it does not confuse average input distributions with per-input randomization. This normalization is an audit explanation, not a proposed APSP solution technique.

Verified Williams' exact Theorem 1.1 in arXiv:1312.6680v2, PDF p. 3: Monte Carlo word-RAM time n^3/2^{Omega(sqrt(log n))}+n^{2+o(1)} log M for nonnegative weights. For M=n^c with fixed c, the second term is lower order and the saving is n^{o(1)}, not a fixed n^epsilon. The theorem's expanded 2018 journal proof was not separately audited. The 2026 universe paper still identifies this as the best known general bound at its date.

Bounded later review checked the actual 2025 few-weight paper's input definition and main results, rather than inferring a full solution from the title. Checked Fischer's actual 2026 Theorem 1.13 and critical remarks: its full APSP/Strong APSP/unweighted equivalence assumes both omega=2 and a sum-order-preserving hashing hypothesis with polynomial bounds. It does not settle APSP. Also read the July 2026 ICALP node-weighted-triangle introduction/Theorem 1/Corollary 2, DOI 10.4230/LIPIcs.ICALP.2026.10: vertex weights are a restriction and the result is not arbitrary edge-weighted APSP. Finally, the actual August 2026 black-box reduction paper's Definition 1 and Theorem 1 restrict a class of reductions for arbitrary relations; it cannot be called an unconditional APSP lower bound. Cached sources have prefix apsp-hyp-.

Duplication audit read the current TCS-6510 formal statement, definitions, answer criterion and sources. Despite the request's deterministic-versus-randomized concern, that card currently itself permits randomization; its real distinction is arbitrary real weights in a comparison-addition real RAM. It is not just this integer word-RAM hypothesis with opposite polarity. Here integer digits and word operations on weights are accessible; there the representation of real values cannot be inspected. Conversely an unrestricted real-addition computation can create intermediate values whose bit lengths preclude an automatic constant-time word simulation. No exact equivalence of these fully specified models was verified, so automatic merging or an unqualified implication is unsupported. TCS-7347 asks a different threshold for directed unweighted APSP, while TCS-0478 is dynamic. Existing related IDs TCS-3123 and TCS-6940 had no corresponding current data/cards JSON file when checked; the draft leaves related IDs to the parent's repository-level validation rather than mutating them.

Importance was previously unassessed at 50. Recommend 97 independently: this is a central randomized fine-grained assumption for general integer-weighted graphs, with widespread consequences and source-documented equivalences. Its conceptual scope is not a minor parameter refinement. Preserve category. Source-open status is qualified to the exact modern quantifier formulation and bounded literature review, not an exhaustive proof that no solution exists.

Root independently read Fischer actual PDF pages 3 and 17: Hypothesis 1.1, footnotes 1–3 and Section 2.5 explicitly confirm the adopted order, the signed-weight normalization and randomized logarithmic-word RAM. Fixed a literal two-word row-major input/output record and integral clock constant to remove remaining representation choices; no change in asymptotic resource target. Preserved the categorical distinction from real comparison-addition APSP. Converted the progress bound into explicit LaTeX delimiters.

cards.title: Orthogonal Vectors Hypothesis
cards.formal:
Is it true that
\[\forall\varepsilon\in(0,1)\ \exists c\in\mathbb N_{>0}:\ \text{no allowed algorithm solves bichromatic Orthogonal Vectors in }O(n^{2-\varepsilon})\text{ time}\]
for all integers \(n\ge2\) on two lists of \(n\) vectors in \(\{0,1\}^{d}\), where \(d=\lceil c\log_2n\rceil\)? An allowed algorithm is a uniform randomized classical word-RAM program in the model below. Its running-time bound is worst-case over both inputs and random choices, and its answer must be correct with probability at least \(2/3\) on every input. The dimension constant \(c\) may depend on the proposed exponent saving \(\varepsilon\), but is fixed as \(n\) grows.
cards.definitions:
Decision problem. For \(n\ge2\), the input consists of ordered lists \(A=(a^{(1)},\ldots,a^{(n)})\) and \(B=(b^{(1)},\ldots,b^{(n)})\) of binary vectors of common dimension \(d=\lceil c\log_2n\rceil\). Repeated vectors, zero vectors and overlap between the lists are allowed. Output YES exactly when
\[\exists r,s\in\{1,\ldots,n\}:\quad\sum_{j=1}^{d}a^{(r)}_j b^{(s)}_j=0.\]
The sum is an ordinary nonnegative integer sum. Equivalently, the two supports are disjoint. Orthogonality modulo two is a different predicate. The selected pair must come from opposite lists, but the task only asks for a decision bit, not for a witness. There is no promise on Hamming weights, intersections, number of solutions or input distribution.

Words and encoding. A machine fixes an integer \(\lambda\ge2\) and uses unsigned words of
\[w=\lambda\lceil\log_2(n+d+2)\rceil\]
bits. Input headers supply \(n,d\), followed by the two lists in order. Each vector occupies \(\lceil d/w\rceil\) consecutive words, with its coordinates packed from least to most significant bit and unused final bits zero. Thus for fixed \(c\) one vector occupies a constant number of words as \(n\) grows. The input is explicit, not supplied by a membership or inner-product oracle. Changing between ordinary explicit bit arrays and this packing costs at most a logarithmic factor; the stated acceptance bound itself uses the packed model.

Instruction set and cost. The program is finite and independent of \(n\). It has word registers and random-access memory addressed by single words. One step may read or write a constant number of addressed words; perform addition, subtraction or multiplication modulo \(2^w\); perform unsigned integer quotient or remainder with a nonzero divisor; apply bitwise AND, OR, XOR or NOT; shift logically left or right; compare words; or branch using a comparison. Shifts discard overflow and give zero when their shift count is at least \(w\). A fresh uniform random \(w\)-bit word costs one step and is independent of all previous random words. A compound operation on several words must be built from these instructions and charged accordingly. There is no unit-cost arbitrary-precision arithmetic, real arithmetic, vector instruction of input-dependent width, or additional oracle.

Uniformity, memory and preprocessing. Outside the explicit input, memory initially contains only zeros. Programs may contain fixed finite constants, but receive no advice, precomputed tables or extra data depending on \(n\). Any such tables must be produced during the charged computation. The program and \(\lambda\) may depend on the fixed \(c\) and \(\varepsilon\), as may constants in the running-time bound; none may vary with \(n\). Single-word addressing bounds available memory by \(2^w\) words. Reading input, constructing tables, preprocessing either list, generating randomness and producing the answer are all charged. There is no separate free preprocessing phase.

Time and error. To solve the problem, the program must halt with a decision bit on every allowed input and random execution. For each fixed input, over its independent internal random words, the bit must equal the predicate above with probability at least \(2/3\). Either type of error is allowed within this bound. The claim \(O(n^{2-\varepsilon})\) means that there exist a real \(K>0\) and an integer \(n_0\ge2\) such that every input of every size \(n\ge n_0\), and every sequence of random choices, takes at most \(K n^{2-\varepsilon}\) steps. An expected-time or average-input bound is not itself this worst-case guarantee. Deterministic programs are included by ignoring the random instruction.
cards.answer_criterion:
Give a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of this lower-bound proposition or its logical negation. A positive answer must cover every allowed uniform randomized program in the specified instruction model, with the quantifier order \(\forall\varepsilon\,\exists c\) and the per-input success requirement. A proof conditional on an unproved version of the Strong Exponential Time Hypothesis is evidence for the conjecture, not an unconditional resolution.

A refutation must establish
\[\exists\varepsilon\in(0,1)\ \forall c\in\mathbb N_{>0}\ \exists A_c,\lambda_c,K_c,n_{0,c}:\quad A_c\text{ meets the stated time and correctness conditions}.\]
The same positive saving \(\varepsilon\) must work for every fixed \(c\). The programs, word-size constants, multiplicative constants and asymptotic thresholds may depend on \(c\). Each \(A_c\) must be uniform in \(n\); no additional uniform algorithm taking \(c\) as input is demanded. A deterministic family would also refute the randomized hypothesis.

An exponent saving \(\varepsilon_c>0\) that shrinks with \(c\), a bound for a fixed small dimension, logarithmic improvements over quadratic time, success only on random instances, or a lower bound restricted to monotone circuits, formulas or branching programs does not settle the full proposition. A fast online query bound with separate preprocessing must satisfy the total charged offline time before it qualifies. This is an asymptotic yes-or-no claim, with no additive numerical approximation tolerance.

July 2026 Conjecture 1 explicitly retains the unrestricted randomized OV hypothesis while proving circuit, formula and branching-program restrictions. Deterministic and randomized dimension-dependent algorithms remain compatible with its quantifier order. context_blocks.text: Each vector can be viewed as a subset of a universe of d coordinates. The task is to find a disjoint pair across two collections. Although checking one pair is easy, there are \(n^{2}\) possible pairs. For logarithmic dimension, packed coordinates make a single check take only a constant number of machine operations when c is fixed. The hypothesis asks whether there is an unavoidable exponent arbitrarily close to two as that fixed dimension constant grows.

The dependence on \(c\) is the main subtlety. Abboud, Williams and Yu’s SODA 2015 algorithm runs in \(n^{2-1/O(\log c)}\) time in the relevant large-\(c\) regime. Thus a positive exponent saving is already known for every fixed dimension constant, but the saving decreases as that constant increases. This is compatible with the hypothesis, which excludes one positive saving shared by all constants. The conference year is 2015, even though some later bibliographies label the paper 2014.

Randomness is not necessary for the existing dimension-dependent saving. Chan and Williams’s SODA 2016 result obtains deterministic \(n^{2-1/O(\log c)}\) time, including counting orthogonal pairs and batched bichromatic detection. It still allows the saving to decrease with \(c\). The hypothesis therefore does not assert that randomization is the only obstacle to a universal subquadratic algorithm.

The ICALP 2026 algorithm has a one-sided-error running-time bound \(\widetilde O(1.25^d n)\), with a reported computer-aided improvement to \(O(1.16^d n)\). Here the tilde suppresses logarithmic factors in the input size, including polynomial factors in \(d\) in the stated logarithmic regime. The finite parameter evaluation was not independently rerun in this review. Exponential dependence on dimension becomes a power of \(n\) after substituting \(d=\lceil c\log_2n\rceil\), so this bound does not give the uniform exponent saving excluded by the hypothesis.

For example, substituting \(c=2\) into \(1.25^{d} n\) gives, up to constant and logarithmic factors, \(n^{1+2 \log _{2} 1.25}\), whose exponent is about 1.644. Increasing c increases this exponent. Thus an impressive subquadratic algorithm for one small logarithmic dimension does not supply one exponent saving for all logarithmic dimensions. This numerical example illustrates the quantifiers; it is not an additional algorithmic theorem.

The corresponding randomized Strong Exponential Time Hypothesis implies this randomized OV hypothesis through the standard satisfiability reduction and sparsification. That supplies a conditional explanation for the proposed barrier, not an unconditional lower bound. A deterministic-only satisfiability assumption cannot by itself rule out randomized OV algorithms. The current primary literature continues to separate these assumptions from the restricted-model theorems it proves.

Reductions then transfer the conjectured time barrier to problems that look quite different. Rohatgi’s Earth Mover Distance paper, the inherited source for this record, develops one such geometric application. The significance of OV is its role as a common intermediate problem: a new algorithm can overturn a collection of conditional barriers, while an unconditional proof would establish a strong lower bound for a concrete problem already known to be in polynomial time.

Restricted-model lower bounds provide evidence without establishing that unrestricted conclusion. Choudhury and coauthors prove near-quadratic monotone-circuit lower bounds for the negation of OV at logarithmic dimension. This negated predicate says every cross-pair intersects and is monotone in the input bits. Their July 2026 paper also strengthens formula and branching-program bounds. General RAM programs can use operations and intermediate representations beyond those restrictions, so these theorems do not prove the hypothesis as formulated here.

Distributional improvements are a separate frontier. Alman, Andoni and Zhang obtain faster algorithms when vector coordinates are independently sampled with a specified Bernoulli bias, including difficult parameter ranges. Such a result can explain why random instances are easier while leaving adversarial instances unresolved. The card deliberately requires correctness and the stated running time on every input rather than only on a random input distribution.

The May 2026 online-OV paper deterministically refutes a different conjecture about preprocessing space and later query time. Its logarithmic-dimensional query saving depends on \(c\), and preprocessing has its own stated cost. The offline decision problem here is charged for both lists and every preprocessing step. The word “refutation” in that paper consequently does not mean the present OV hypothesis was refuted.

cards.title: Algebraic k-Clique Hypothesis
cards.formal: Let \(\tau (k)\) be the infimum of worst-case time exponents of randomized algorithms deciding k-Clique, as specified below, and let \(\omega\) be the arithmetic matrix-multiplication exponent over C. Is \(\liminf _{k\to \infty} \tau (k)/k=\omega /3\)?
cards.definitions: For each fixed integer \(k\ge 3\), the input is the adjacency matrix of a simple undirected graph on \(n\ge k\) labeled vertices; accept iff some k distinct vertices are pairwise adjacent. A uniform randomized word-RAM algorithm must be correct with probability at least \(2/3\) on every input, and its time bound must hold for every random tape. Set \(\tau (k)=\inf\){\(a\ge 0\): such an algorithm runs in \(O(n^{a})\) time as \(n\to \infty\)}. The program and hidden constants may depend on k, but not on n. Words have \(C_{k}\lceil \log _{2}(n+2)\rceil\) bits for some fixed constant \(C_{k}\); arithmetic modulo the word range, division with remainder, comparisons, Boolean operations, shifts and indirect memory access cost one step, and a fresh random word costs one step. Initial memory apart from the input is zero; preprocessing counts; there is no nonuniform advice, giant-word operation or free oracle. For \(\omega\), let \(M(N)\) be the smallest number of binary +,−,× gates in a circuit over C that computes all entries of the product of two formal \(N\times N\) matrices. Arbitrary complex constants and sharing are allowed, but division and branching are not. Define \(\omega =\inf \{a:M(N)=O(N^{a})\}\). This fixes the characteristic-zero arithmetic convention, separately from the bit-based graph algorithm. The question concerns the coefficient of k in the exponent; it does not fix k proportional to n or treat the latest published numerical upper bound on \(\omega\) as its exact value.
cards.answer_criterion: The matrix-multiplication reduction gives the upper asymptotic benchmark \(\omega /3\). An affirmative answer therefore proves that, for every \(\delta >0\), there is K such that \(\tau (k)\ge (\omega /3- \delta )k\) for every fixed \(k\ge K\). A negative answer proves a strict saving in this coefficient, for example via algorithms with \(\tau (k)\le (\omega /3- \delta )k\) for arbitrarily large k and one \(\delta >0\). Saving logarithmic time factors or an additive \(o(k)\) in the exponent does not refute this leading-exponent formulation.
cards.why: A basic quantitative hardness hypothesis for graph patterns and many reductions in fine-grained complexity, precisely testing whether the matrix-multiplication exponent gives the optimal leading coefficient.

importance.reason: A principal fine-grained benchmark connecting clique detection, matrix multiplication, dynamic data structures, and constraint optimization.

Fischer–Künnemann–Redzic obtain conditional optimality results for maximum coverage and partial domination using clique and hyperclique assumptions.
Dupont and coauthors report \(\omega <2.371177\), improving the available clique upper bound through the existing reduction without settling optimality.

cards.status_note: Open in the stated unrestricted randomized leading-exponent form, following the inherited hypothesis and later primary sources checked through 11 September 2026. The liminf and machine conventions make the asymptotic claim explicit. Logarithmic speedups, matrix-exponent improvements and conditional lower bounds do not settle it.

context_blocks.text: For each fixed k, clique detection is already a polynomial-time problem: one can inspect every k-element subset. The issue is which polynomial is necessary. An exponent near k and an exponent near 0.79k differ dramatically as the fixed pattern size increases. This is why ordinary NP-hardness, which allows k to vary with the input, leaves the main quantitative question unanswered.

The arithmetic reduction groups the vertices of a candidate clique into three parts. For \(k=3r\), create auxiliary vertices representing r-cliques and join two auxiliary vertices when their represented sets are disjoint and their union is a clique. A triangle in this auxiliary graph represents a 3r-clique in the original graph. There are \(O(n^{r})\) auxiliary vertices, so matrix-based triangle detection gives the familiar leading time exponent \(\omega k/3\).

When k is not divisible by three, the groups have unequal sizes. Rectangular matrix multiplication gives more refined bounds for individual k; padding to the next multiple of three already changes the exponent by only a constant. Because this card asks for the leading coefficient as k grows, those residue-class effects do not alter the target. They would matter in a card asking for the exact exponent at a particular small k.

The inherited source states the hypothesis in the \(n^{\omega k/3- o(k)}\) form and allows both randomized and deterministic algorithms. The explicit liminf formulation records the order of limits: first study \(n\to \infty\) for each fixed k, then ask about large k. The model definitions make time, error and machine operations explicit. This avoids relying on an informal distinction between which graph algorithms count as combinatorial.

The word algebraic names the benchmark supplied by matrix multiplication. It does not restrict the algorithms against which the conjecture asserts hardness. A refuting algorithm could use arithmetic, combinatorial structure, randomization, or a combination. Likewise, \(\omega\) is an unknown mathematical constant defined by the best possible arithmetic circuits, rather than a decimal frozen at the date of an old reduction.

A better upper bound on \(\omega\) immediately improves the matrix-based clique algorithm without disproving this hypothesis. Conversely, an algorithm whose exponent beats an old numerical estimate may still be slower than the conjectured benchmark using the true \(\omega\). The distinction becomes especially relevant after small improvements in matrix multiplication: Dupont and coauthors’ August 2026 note reports \(\omega <2.371177\), improving the preceding 2.371339 bound. Its numerical certificate has not been replayed for this catalogue.

Abboud–Fischer–Shechter improve the algorithms usually called combinatorial by logarithmic factors. At fixed k, their displayed detection bound is \(n^{k}(\log  n)^{- (k+1)}(\log  \log  n)^{k+3}\). Such progress is useful, but the logarithmic factor changes an exponent by \(o(1)\) as n grows and does not establish a new leading coefficient below \(\omega /3\). Their separate hypergraph and listing results have different outputs or incidence structures.

The hypothesis supports lower bounds for tasks that do not look like clique detection. Das–Lincoln–Lynch–Munro use clique reductions for dynamic Boolean-formula evaluation and counting. A faster data structure with the relevant preprocessing and update guarantees could therefore force faster clique algorithms. This explains the inclusion of an apparently indirect dynamic-data-structure paper as the inherited reference: its computational-hypothesis section states this exact leading-exponent assumption.

Recent work strengthens the network of reductions rather than proving the hypothesis. Fischer–Künnemann–Redžić–Stieß show that suitable regularity restrictions on partite graphs and hypergraphs preserve the relevant detection exponent, with parameter-dependent factors. This helps transfer conditional hardness to Boolean constraint optimization. Their result cannot be read as an unconditional lower bound for all word-RAM algorithms.

Fischer–Künnemann–Redzic’s January 2026 coverage and partial-domination results similarly give algorithms and matching bounds conditional on clique and hyperclique hypotheses. The 3-uniform hyperclique assumption concerns triples as constraints and has a different exhaustive-search benchmark; it is not the graph hypothesis in this card. Keeping the two separate prevents a strong conditional statement for one problem from being mistaken for a resolution of the other.

The fundamental question is whether all-pairs algebra can capture the optimal leading cost of enforcing every pairwise adjacency in a growing fixed pattern. An affirmative answer would justify a widely used quantitative barrier. A negative answer would identify a way to exploit the clique decision task beyond the matrix-multiplication benchmark, potentially changing many currently conditional optimality claims.

When k is not divisible by three, the groups have unequal sizes. Rectangular matrix multiplication gives more refined bounds for individual k; padding to the next multiple of three already changes the exponent by only a constant. Because this card asks for the leading coefficient as k grows, those residue-class effects do not alter the target. They would matter in a card asking for the exact exponent at a particular small k.

The inherited source states the hypothesis in the \(n^{\omega k/3- o(k)}\) form and allows both randomized and deterministic algorithms. The explicit liminf formulation records the order of limits: first study \(n\to \infty\) for each fixed k, then ask about large k. The model definitions make time, error and machine operations explicit. This avoids relying on an informal distinction between which graph algorithms count as combinatorial.

The word algebraic names the benchmark supplied by matrix multiplication. It does not restrict the algorithms against which the conjecture asserts hardness. A refuting algorithm could use arithmetic, combinatorial structure, randomization, or a combination. Likewise, \(\omega\) is an unknown mathematical constant defined by the best possible arithmetic circuits, rather than a decimal frozen at the date of an old reduction.

A better upper bound on \(\omega\) immediately improves the matrix-based clique algorithm without disproving this hypothesis. Conversely, an algorithm whose exponent beats an old numerical estimate may still be slower than the conjectured benchmark using the true \(\omega\). The distinction becomes especially relevant after small improvements in matrix multiplication: Dupont and coauthors’ August 2026 note reports \(\omega <2.371177\), improving the preceding 2.371339 bound. Its numerical certificate has not been replayed for this catalogue.

Abboud–Fischer–Shechter improve the algorithms usually called combinatorial by logarithmic factors. At fixed k, their displayed detection bound is \(n^{k}(\log  n)^{- (k+1)}(\log  \log  n)^{k+3}\). Such progress is useful, but the logarithmic factor changes an exponent by \(o(1)\) as n grows and does not establish a new leading coefficient below \(\omega /3\). Their separate hypergraph and listing results have different outputs or incidence structures.

The hypothesis supports lower bounds for tasks that do not look like clique detection. Das–Lincoln–Lynch–Munro use clique reductions for dynamic Boolean-formula evaluation and counting. A faster data structure with the relevant preprocessing and update guarantees could therefore force faster clique algorithms. This explains the inclusion of an apparently indirect dynamic-data-structure paper as the inherited reference: its computational-hypothesis section states this exact leading-exponent assumption.

Recent work strengthens the network of reductions rather than proving the hypothesis. Fischer–Künnemann–Redžić–Stieß show that suitable regularity restrictions on partite graphs and hypergraphs preserve the relevant detection exponent, with parameter-dependent factors. This helps transfer conditional hardness to Boolean constraint optimization. Their result cannot be read as an unconditional lower bound for all word-RAM algorithms.

Fischer–Künnemann–Redzic’s January 2026 coverage and partial-domination results similarly give algorithms and matching bounds conditional on clique and hyperclique hypotheses. The 3-uniform hyperclique assumption concerns triples as constraints and has a different exhaustive-search benchmark; it is not the graph hypothesis in this card. Keeping the two separate prevents a strong conditional statement for one problem from being mistaken for a resolution of the other.

The fundamental question is whether all-pairs algebra can capture the optimal leading cost of enforcing every pairwise adjacency in a growing fixed pattern. An affirmative answer would justify a widely used quantitative barrier. A negative answer would identify a way to exploit the clique decision task beyond the matrix-multiplication benchmark, potentially changing many currently conditional optimality claims.

cards.title: Hyperclique Hypothesis
cards.formal: For every fixed pair of integers \(h\ge 3\) and \(k>h\) and every constant \(\varepsilon >0\), is there no classical randomized \(O(n^{k- \varepsilon})\)-time algorithm deciding whether an n-vertex h-uniform hypergraph contains a k-clique, with error at most \(1/3\) on each input?
cards.definitions: The input hypergraph \(H=([n],E)\) is simple and unweighted, with E a subset of the h-element subsets of \([n]\). It is given by a dense table containing one Boolean membership entry for each h-element subset, in a fixed computable order. A k-clique is a set \(S\subseteq [n]\) of k distinct vertices such that every h-element subset of S belongs to E. The task outputs one yes/no bit and requires neither counting nor listing cliques. Fix the classical word-RAM with \(O(\log (n+2))\)-bit words, constant-time arithmetic, bitwise operations and random access on words; the word-length constant and runtime constants may depend on the fixed \(h,k,\varepsilon\). Random bits are allowed, but quantum operations, nonuniform advice and precomputed input-dependent tables are not. All processing of the input and construction of auxiliary data are charged. The excluded algorithm must run in \(O(n^{k- \varepsilon})\) steps on every execution and answer correctly with probability at least \(2/3\) for every input. The quantifiers concern each fixed pair h,k separately, not only a limit as k tends to infinity. The card explicitly uses the bounded-error randomized version of the classical hypothesis.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove the stated exclusion of all such algorithms, or refute it by giving one fixed pair \(h\ge 3,k>h\), one fixed \(\varepsilon >0\) and a correct algorithm with the required worst-case time and per-input success probability. A conditional confirmation must name the stronger assumption. A logarithmic-factor speedup, an algorithm for a sparse or promised subclass, or a circuit-size bound in a restricted algebraic model is not a resolution of the full claim.
cards.why: A principal fine-grained hypothesis for higher-order combinatorial interactions, supporting conditional lower bounds beyond ordinary graph clique and shortest paths.

importance.reason: A foundational unresolved exponent question with consequences for Max-CSP optimization, algebraic identity checking and sparse graph/hypergraph algorithms.

cards.status_note: Reviewed through 11 September 2026. No classical bounded-error algorithm with a fixed positive exponent saving for a covered h,k pair was found in the checked sources. The 2025 regularization and 2026 reductions use or relate the hypothesis; they do not prove it unconditionally.

context_blocks.text: A graph records pairwise compatibility. An h-uniform hypergraph records compatibility of h vertices at a time. For \(h=3\) and \(k=4, a\) positive instance contains four vertices whose four triples are all hyperedges. Knowing that every pair participates in some hyperedge is insufficient: the compatible triples must be exactly those supported on the same four vertices. This is the smallest parameter pair covered by the hypothesis.

For fixed h and k, exhaustive search takes \(O(n^{k})\) time: enumerate all k-element vertex sets and check the fixed number of required hyperedges. The problem is therefore already polynomial-time for every individual card parameter pair. The conjecture asks whether that polynomial exponent can be reduced by a positive constant. Ordinary NP-hardness when k varies would not establish such a fine-grained statement.

The graph case \(h=2\) behaves differently. Matrix multiplication gives algorithms beating the direct k-tuple search for many clique sizes. Lincoln–Vassilevska Williams–Williams explain why the corresponding higher-order operation for hypergraphs is a separate obstacle and formulate hyperclique-based lower bounds. This distinction is the reason the present hypothesis starts at \(h=3\), instead of extending a graph-clique bound mechanically to all uniformities.

Their connections to satisfiability concern optimization problems such as Max-h-SAT: find an assignment satisfying as many clauses as possible. A suitable hyperclique speedup would also improve exhaustive-search algorithms for these problems. This must be distinguished from deciding whether every clause of a fixed-width SAT instance is simultaneously satisfiable, for which exponential improvements are already known. The Max-h-SAT hypothesis is an additional assumption, not an unconditional proof.

The fixed exponent saving is essential. A running time \(n^{k}\) divided by any fixed power of log n would not contradict the card. Nor would an improvement available only when k grows with n. Conversely, an \(O(n^{3.99})\) algorithm for 4-cliques in 3-uniform hypergraphs would be enough to refute the universally quantified statement, without resolving every other h,k pair.

The dense encoding prevents an implicit promise about sparsity. Its size is \(\Theta (n^{h})\) table entries, which is below the exhaustive-search exponent because \(k>h\). Any refuting exponent saving can be reduced to a smaller positive saving so that reading this table still fits the claimed time. Thus routine conversions between explicit dense representations do not provide an artificial refutation.

The inherited paper works with k-partite hypergraphs. This is essentially equivalent for fixed k: make k copies of the vertex set and place an edge between copies in distinct parts whenever their distinct original vertices form an input hyperedge. Selecting one vertex from each part then tests the original clique condition. The vertex blowup depends only on k, preserving a positive polynomial exponent saving.

Fischer–Künnemann–Redžić–Stieß go further in their ICALP 2025 regularization theorem. They transfer algorithms between general k-partite hypergraphs and a strongly regular class in which each transversal \((h- 1)\)-tuple has the same number of extensions to a hyperedge. Controlling these overlapping incidences without introducing false cliques is the substantive part of the construction. The result shows that this regularity promise does not remove the conjectured difficulty.

The same work uses regularization to classify optimization of Boolean CSPs over assignments with exactly k nonzero variables. The degree of the constraint functions separates easy linear cases, graph-clique cases and higher-degree cases with exhaustive-search lower bounds under a 3-uniform hyperclique assumption. This supplies a reason to study the hypothesis beyond the clique problem itself.

Dudek and coauthors’ STOC 2026 work gives another connection: a refutation for the 3-uniform, 4-clique case would yield a truly subquadratic algorithm for detecting four-term arithmetic progressions in an integer universe. Their paper studies verification of algebraic identities and uses this relationship for conditional lower bounds. It supplies a new consequence or conditional foundation, rather than establishing the hyperclique lower bound outright.

Fritsch–Künnemann–Redžić–Stieß’s ICALP 2026 paper studies when sparsity helps for small independent sets in hypergraphs and Boolean CSPs. Its algorithms have separate vertex-count and edge-count terms, with matching bounds under clique hypotheses. Improved running time on sparse forbidden-hyperedge inputs is compatible with the dense worst-case statement here; taking a complement can turn a sparse instance into a dense one.

The hypothesis expresses a possible computational divide between pairwise and higher-order interactions. Its value is that precise reductions turn it into concrete runtime barriers for other tasks. The proper status is a conjectural foundation for those barriers. Repeated applications and increasingly robust reductions strengthen its usefulness, while a proof or one genuine exponent-saving algorithm would be a qualitatively different result.

cards.title: Truly subquadratic exact edit distance
cards.formal: For the binary alphabet \(\Sigma =\{0,1\}\), do there exist a constant \(\varepsilon \in\)(0,1], a constant \(C>0\) and one uniform deterministic word-RAM algorithm A such that, for every \(n\ge 1\) and every pair \(x,y\in \Sigma ^{n}, A\) outputs the exact unit-cost edit distance \(ED(x,y)\) in at most \(C(n+1)^{2- \varepsilon}\) operations?
cards.why: A fundamental quadratic barrier for string comparison and a principal example in fine-grained complexity.

A randomized approximation scheme obtains a quasi-polynomial speedup; it does not compute exact distances.

cards.definitions: An edit inserts one symbol, deletes one symbol, or substitutes one symbol by the other; each operation costs 1. \(ED(x,y)\) is the minimum total number of edits transforming the entire string x into the entire string y. Equal symbols can be retained at cost 0. The output is this integer, not necessarily a sequence of edits. Both strings have length n and are provided explicitly, one symbol per word. The word-RAM has \(w=\operatorname{ceil}(4 \log _{2}(n+2))\) bits per word, zero-initialized addressable memory of w-bit words, and a fixed finite program independent of n. One operation reads or writes one addressed word, branches or compares words, or applies unsigned addition, subtraction or multiplication modulo \(2^{w}\), integer division by a nonzero word with rounding down, a bitwise Boolean operation, or a logical shift by fewer than w positions. Constants are fixed by the program, and words cannot hold arbitrarily large integers in one step. The running time includes every memory access and arithmetic operation; no oracle, advice or input-dependent precomputed table is supplied. All preprocessing is charged. The time guarantee is worst-case over inputs, with no random coins or probability of error. The constant exponent saving \(\varepsilon\) cannot tend to zero with n. The chosen binary alphabet is an explicit specialization of the imported phrase “a fixed finite alphabet”, supported by Bringmann–Künnemann’s binary-alphabet formulation; a unary alphabet would make the equal-length problem trivial.
cards.answer_criterion: A positive resolution supplies one algorithm with a proof of exact correctness for every binary input pair and a worst-case \(O(n^{2- \varepsilon})\) bound for some fixed \(\varepsilon >0\) in the specified model. A negative resolution rules out every such deterministic algorithm and every fixed positive exponent saving. A lower bound conditional on an unproved hypothesis is not an unconditional negative resolution. Faster approximation, special-case performance and logarithmic-factor savings do not meet the target.

context_blocks.title: Edits can shift an entire alignment
context_blocks.text: The strings 0101 and 1010 disagree at all four positions, but their edit distance is 2: delete the first 0 and append a 0. One edit cannot suffice, because the lengths are equal and a single substitution would leave other disagreements. Edit distance therefore measures more than the number of mismatched positions. Insertions and deletions let long portions of the two strings line up at different offsets.

context_blocks.title: What the quadratic barrier means
context_blocks.text: The classical dynamic-programming computation compares prefixes of the two strings and takes \(O(n^{2})\) time. The question concerns the best possible algorithm, not the necessity of evaluating every entry in that particular computation. A bound such as \(n^{2}/\log  n\) is smaller than \(n^{2}\) but does not give a fixed positive saving in the exponent. The target asks for \(n^{2- \varepsilon}\) with one \(\varepsilon >0\) that remains valid for arbitrarily long strings.

context_blocks.title: A precise conditional obstacle
context_blocks.text: The Strong Exponential Time Hypothesis, SETH, states that for every \(\delta >0\) there is a clause width k for which Boolean k-SAT on N variables cannot be decided deterministically in \(O(2^{(1- \delta )N} \operatorname{poly}(\mathrm{L}))\) time, where L is the formula length. Backurs and Indyk relate a truly subquadratic exact edit-distance algorithm to a faster satisfiability algorithm. Bringmann and Künnemann establish the conditional obstruction even for binary strings. This is strong evidence for a barrier, but SETH is an assumption. The reduction does not prove unconditionally that the requested algorithm is impossible.

context_blocks.title: Why recent approximation is different
context_blocks.text: Mao and Rubinstein’s March 2026 result gives a randomized \((1+\eta )\)-approximation for each fixed \(\eta >0\), with running time \(n^{2}/2^{\log ^{\Omega}(1) n}\). A multiplicative approximation can return a nearby value rather than the exact minimum. Its error guarantee and its dependence on \(\eta\) cannot simply be replaced by exact correctness at no cost. Thus this progress does not supply the deterministic exact algorithm requested here.

context_blocks.title: Scope of the benchmark
context_blocks.text: The alphabet is explicitly binary, the edit costs are all one, and the guarantee is for every input pair. Results for typical strings, a bounded number of edits, weighted substitution schemes, or a supplied good alignment may have different complexity. Computing the distance is already a polynomial-time task. The unresolved issue is the finer rate within polynomial time and its connection to the exponential-time cost of satisfiability.

cards.title: Online matrix–vector multiplication conjecture
cards.formal: Given a Boolean matrix $M\in\{0,1\}^{n\times n}$, receive vectors $v_1,\ldots,v_n\in\{0,1\}^n$ one at a time. Output each Boolean product $(Mv_t)_i=\bigvee_{j=1}^{n}(M_{ij}\wedge(v_t)_j)$ before receiving $v_{t+1}$. Is there any constant $\varepsilon>0$ and randomized algorithm with total running time $O(n^{3-\varepsilon})$ and error probability at most $1/3$? The OMv conjecture asserts that there is no such algorithm. In this formulation the total includes preprocessing of $M$.
cards.why: I include this because it is one of the central assumptions used to explain why many dynamic data structures resist fast updates and queries simultaneously. Refuting it would invalidate a large collection of conditional barriers; proving it would give a major unconditional lower bound for an explicit polynomial-time problem.
cards.definitions: The product uses OR and AND, not addition modulo two. The matrix remains fixed throughout the sequence. The word-RAM has logarithmic-size words. Success concerns the complete online computation. This is distinct from multiplying over a field, updating the matrix itself, or answering one query after an uncharged preprocessing phase.

progress.text: Henzinger, Krinninger, Nanongkai, and Saranurak formulate OMv and derive conditional lower bounds for dynamic problems, including reachability and variants of connectivity.
Larsen and Williams give randomized online multiplication in total time $n^3/2^{\Omega(\sqrt{\log n})}$. This improves the algorithmic baseline without refuting the conjecture.

Hu and Polak show fine-grained equivalences between Boolean OMv and several online non-Boolean products, including min-max, dominance, and equality. These broaden the supporting connections; they do not prove the conjecture.

context_blocks.text: If all vectors were available together, they would form another matrix and fast matrix multiplication could batch the work. The online requirement forbids waiting for future columns. A data structure can learn and preprocess the fixed matrix, but it must answer a sequence of queries whose later values have not yet arrived.

A small graph construction explains the relevance to dynamic algorithms. Make one vertex for each matrix column and one for each row; put a directed edge from column j to row i exactly when the matrix entry is one. Add a source with edges to the columns activated by the current query vector. The rows reachable from the source are exactly the one-entries of the answer vector. Changing the active columns turns each matrix query into a sequence of graph updates followed by reachability questions.

The conjecture is about a polynomial saving in the exponent. An improvement from $n^3$ to $n^3/\log n$ is significant but compatible with it. Even the stronger documented saving $2^{\Omega(\sqrt{\log n})}$ is only $n^{o(1)}$, so it leaves the total time in the $n^{3-o(1)}$ range.

The graph reduction gives intuition, not a universal update-time theorem by itself. To derive a particular data-structure lower bound, one must account for preprocessing, the number of updates and queries, and how the graph size relates to the matrix dimension. These are precisely the parameters handled in the original reductions.

cards.title: Min-Plus Convolution Hypothesis
cards.formal: Does there exist a constant \(\varepsilon\in(0,1)\) such that, for every fixed integer \(a\ge1\), a uniform bounded-error randomized word-RAM algorithm computes the min-plus convolution of any two length-\(n\) integer arrays with entries in \([-n^{a},n^{a}]\) in \(O(n^{2-\varepsilon})\) worst-case time?
cards.why: A central fine-grained hypothesis supporting quadratic barriers in knapsack and dynamic programming.

No fixed-saving algorithm or unconditional impossibility proof for this explicit integer formulation was located. Source proofs were not independently audited.

references.authors: David Bremner; Timothy M. Chan; Erik D. Demaine; Jeff Erickson; Ferran Hurtado; John Iacono; Stefan Langerman; Mihai Pătraşcu; Perouz Taslakian

importance.reason: A central fine-grained hypothesis supporting quadratic barriers in knapsack and dynamic programming.

category_assignment.reason: The fixed polynomial exponent improvement is a fine-grained complexity target.

cards.definitions: For \(n\ge2\), input arrays \(A=(a_{0},\ldots,a_{n-1})\) and \(B=(b_{0},\ldots,b_{n-1})\) are explicitly listed. Output all \(2n-1\) integers \(c_{k}=\min\{a_{i}+b_{j}:0\le i,j<n,\ i+j=k\}\), for \(0\le k\le2n-2\). Inputs need not be sorted or monotone. Use a uniform word RAM with word length \(w=d\lceil\log_{2}(n+2)\rceil\), for a fixed positive integer \(d\) chosen with the algorithm and large enough for its addresses and input values. Unit-cost instructions are word reads/writes, copying, comparisons, branching, Boolean operations, shifts, addition, subtraction and multiplication modulo \(2^{w}\), and integer quotient and remainder with nonzero divisor. Shifts by at least \(w\) return zero. Multiword computation is charged by its component instructions. The fixed finite program receives no advice or precomputed tables; all initialization, preprocessing and output writes count. Randomness consists of independent uniform random words, each generated at unit cost. On every input, the whole output must be correct with probability at least \(2/3\). The time bound holds for every random execution, including unsuccessful ones. The exponent saving \(\varepsilon\) is common to all fixed magnitude exponents \(a\); the program, word-size constant and hidden time constant may depend on \(a\). Signed entries and exact output sums use a constant number of words.

context_blocks.text: Min-plus convolution combines two cost profiles: entry \(c_k\) is the cheapest way to split the total index \(k\) between them. For \(A=(3,1)\) and \(B=(4,2)\), the output is \((7,5,3)\). The middle entry compares two different splits, while an endpoint has only one. All output positions are required simultaneously.

The direct computation checks every pair of input entries, producing a quadratic amount of work for a linear-size output. Unlike ordinary convolution, replacing sums of products by minima of sums changes the algebraic operation. The hypothesis is a computational barrier for this exact cost-combination primitive.

The 2026 paper records an unrestricted upper bound \(n^2/2^{\Theta(\sqrt{\log n})}\), obtained from earlier results. This is an improvement over quadratic time, but its exponent saving tends to zero with input length. The requested algorithm must save a fixed positive exponent, not merely a growing subpolynomial factor.

The same paper gives \(n^{1.5+o(1)}\) deterministic time when the arrays are monotone and their values obey the specified bounded-range condition. Neither monotonicity nor that special linear range is assumed by this card. Structured convolution is therefore a restricted positive result rather than an unrestricted resolution.

The established hypothesis name predicts a negative answer to the displayed algorithm-existence question. The card fixes a precise polynomially bounded integer formulation: one exponent saving works for every fixed magnitude exponent \(a\), while the implementation and constants may depend on \(a\). There is no claim about arbitrary real-number inputs or bit lengths growing faster than \(O(\log n)\).

The probability guarantee is for the entire output on each fixed input. A small error probability for each entry separately would not automatically give that guarantee for the full array. Likewise, average performance over an input distribution is different from the worst-case time and per-input correctness requirements.

cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof that some fixed \(\varepsilon\in(0,1)\) permits the stated family of uniform algorithms for every fixed magnitude exponent \(a\), with worst-case time and whole-output success guarantees, or prove the logical negation in Lean. In the negation, every proposed saving \(\varepsilon\) fails for at least one fixed \(a\), allowing all permitted algorithms and their constants. Neither a conditional hardness implication nor a theorem for monotone inputs proves that negation.

cards.title: Truly subquadratic algorithms for 3SUM
cards.formal:
Is there a constant \(\varepsilon\in(0,1)\) such that, for every fixed integer \(B\ge1\), a uniform randomized Las Vegas algorithm solves integer 3SUM with worst-case expected time \(O(n^{2-\varepsilon})\) on the word RAM defined below? An input consists of three lists \(A,B',C\), each containing at most \(n\) integers in \([-n^B,n^B]\), and the task is to decide whether
\[\exists a\in A\ \exists b\in B'\ \exists c\in C:\quad a+b=c.\]
The algorithm and hidden constant may depend on the fixed universe exponent \(B\); the saving \(\varepsilon\) must be independent of \(B\). This selects the polynomial-universe integer version of the source's question, with the expected-time convention used by Kopelowitz–Pettie–Porat.
cards.why: 3SUM is a central test of whether apparently quadratic search over pairs can admit a fixed polynomial improvement. Its conjectured hardness supports fine-grained lower bounds for many geometric, graph and data-structure problems. The exact model matters: removing a logarithmic factor, changing integer size or omitting preprocessing costs can make a result look stronger than the improvement asked for here.
cards.status_note: The source problem list and Kopelowitz–Pettie–Porat’s modern expected-time formulation were checked on 2026-09-14, together with 2026 preprocessed-3SUM work. A bounded later search found no from-scratch Las Vegas algorithm or general lower bound resolving the explicitly selected polynomial-universe variant.

Kopelowitz, Pettie and Porat develop reductions from the modern expected-time 3SUM conjecture to set-intersection, graph and data-structure tasks.
ICALP work obtains improved subquadratic-space tradeoffs for preprocessed 3SUM; the model retains a preprocessing phase and does not establish a truly subquadratic from-scratch algorithm.
