sentences: 3SUM asks whether a value in one integer list is the sum of values from two other lists.
The target is a fixed polynomial improvement over quadratic running time on a precisely specified word RAM.
The selected variant allows every fixed polynomial integer universe and requires a common exponent saving.
Randomization may change the running time but must never produce an incorrect answer.
Known logarithmic savings and faster queries after preprocessing do not meet the from-scratch target.

cards.definitions:
The size parameter \(n\ge2\) bounds the length of each of the three lists. Repeated values are allowed and do not affect the answer; each chosen value comes from its prescribed list. A triple may contain equal numerical values from different lists. There is no single-list distinctness condition. Integers are supplied explicitly in signed binary and fit in one word of
\[w=\left\lceil(B+3)\log_2(n+1)\right\rceil\]
bits. The target equation is equality of ordinary integers, not congruence modulo the word size.

For each fixed \(B\), a uniform word-RAM algorithm has a finite program independent of \(n\) and of all list contents. Its memory cells contain \(w\)-bit words and are addressed by words. Initially only the input and its lengths are present; other cells are zero. Unit-cost instructions are reading or writing a word, copying, comparing, branching, addition, subtraction and multiplication modulo \(2^w\), integer quotient and remainder for a nonzero divisor, bitwise Boolean operations, and shifts by a word-specified amount; a shift by at least \(w\) yields zero. Division by zero can be defined to return zero. The program may obtain an independent uniformly random \(w\)-bit word at unit cost. There is no arbitrary-precision unit-cost arithmetic, real-number operation, oracle or nonuniform lookup table. Any table construction, sorting and preprocessing count toward the runtime. Arithmetic on more than one word must be implemented by these instructions.

Las Vegas means that the program halts with probability one and every output produced is correct; randomization affects its runtime, not its answer. The required bound means that for each \(B\) there are \(K_B,n_B\) such that the expected number of instructions is at most \(K_B n^{2-\varepsilon}\) on every valid instance with \(n\ge n_B\). Expectation is over the program's random words, followed by a worst case over the input lists. All smaller valid instances must also be decided correctly with finite expected time. No average-case input distribution or reusable preprocessing is supplied.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct Lean-checked proof of the existence claim, including one positive exponent saving uniform over every fixed \(B\), correctness, almost-sure termination and the expected instruction bound; or prove its negation. Negation means that for every \(\varepsilon>0\) some fixed polynomial universe admits no algorithm meeting that saving. An improvement by logarithmic factors alone, a fast data-structure query after expensive preprocessing, a restricted comparison-tree lower bound, or a Monte Carlo algorithm without the stipulated zero-error guarantee does not settle this selected target.

context_blocks.text: Known algorithms beat \(n^2\) by logarithmic factors. Such bounds are \(o(n^2)\), but they do not give \(O(n^{2-\varepsilon})\) for a fixed positive \(\varepsilon\). The modern conjecture concerns this latter, truly subquadratic improvement.

The three-set input convention follows the source. The integer word-RAM and polynomial-universe choices distinguish this target from real-RAM variants and from decision trees that charge only selected comparisons. The lower-bound claim is not restricted to a comparison-only instruction set.

Kopelowitz, Pettie and Porat formulate the modern conjecture even for expected running time and use Las Vegas complexities in their reductions. The zero-error convention here follows that formulation; it is made explicit rather than silently identifying different randomized models.

Recent work improves time–space tradeoffs after sets have been preprocessed. This is useful progress for data structures, but the present input arrives from scratch, so the entire preprocessing time must be included in its complexity.

cards.title: Hitting Set conjecture
cards.formal:
Is the randomized Hitting Set conjecture true? For every \(\varepsilon\in(0,1)\), does there exist an integer \(c\ge1\) such that no uniform bounded-error randomized word-RAM algorithm decides the following problem in worst-case time \(O(n^{2-\varepsilon})\)? The input is two lists \(A,B\), each of \(n\) subsets of \([d]\), where \(n\ge2\) and \(d=\lceil c\log_2 n\rceil\). Decide whether
\[\exists a\in A\ \forall b\in B:\quad a\cap b\ne\varnothing.\]
The chosen set must be one of the supplied sets in \(A\). This is the source's fine-grained two-list problem, not the general optimization problem of selecting a small hitting set from the universe.
cards.why: This hypothesis captures a quadratic barrier with an existential choice followed by a universal test. It supports fine-grained lower bounds for graph radius, centers and quantified geometric problems where the more familiar two-existential-quantifier orthogonal-vectors hypothesis does not directly match the task. Settling it would clarify the role of quantifier order in fine-grained complexity.
cards.status_note: The original 2016 conjecture and the 2021 logarithmic-dimension formulation were checked on 2026-09-14. A bounded later search, including 2026 graph-center work, found continuing conditional applications and no resolution of the selected randomized bounded-error hypothesis.

sentences: Two lists contain subsets of a logarithmic-size universe.
The task is to find whether one supplied set in the first list intersects every set in the second.
The conjecture rules out a single fixed polynomial improvement over quadratic time across all constant multiples of logarithmic dimension.
The selected model permits randomization with bounded error and counts all word-RAM computation.

cards.definitions:
Write \([d]=\{1,\ldots,d\}\). Sets are supplied explicitly as \(d\)-bit incidence vectors; lists may contain repetitions and empty sets. Equivalently, the answer is yes if some vector \(a\in A\) has integer inner product \(\sum_{j=1}^d a_j b_j>0\) with every \(b\in B\). The coordinate sum is over integers, not modulo two. The dimension constant \(c\) is fixed independently of input size.

Use a word RAM with word length \(w=\lceil4\log_2(n+2)\rceil\). Incidence vectors are packed into consecutive words, with unused bits zero. A machine has a finite program independent of \(n\), word-addressed memory, and unit-cost word reads/writes, copies, comparisons, branches, arithmetic addition/subtraction/multiplication modulo \(2^w\), quotient and remainder for a nonzero divisor, bitwise Boolean operations and shifts. Shifts by at least \(w\) return zero; division by zero may return zero. A uniformly random independent \(w\)-bit word is available at unit cost. Memory initially contains only the instance; any further preprocessing or lookup-table construction is charged. There are no oracles, advice or unit-cost operations on arbitrarily long integers.

A bounded-error algorithm must output the correct yes/no answer with probability at least \(2/3\) on every valid input. Its runtime bound applies to every random tape and every input, not only in expectation. For fixed \(\varepsilon,c\), a forbidden algorithm would have constants \(K,n_0\) such that it takes at most \(Kn^{2-\varepsilon}\) instructions for every \(n\ge n_0\); the constants and program may depend on \(c,\varepsilon\). Finite smaller instances must also be decided correctly within finite time.

The order \(\forall\varepsilon\,\exists c\) is essential. Refutation requires one \(\varepsilon>0\) such that for every fixed \(c\) there is an algorithm with that same exponent saving; it does not require the same program or multiplicative constant for all \(c\). Conversely, a faster algorithm at one small dimension constant does not refute the conjecture. Choosing integral \(c\) is harmless because extra zero coordinates pad smaller dimensions.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct Lean-checked proof of the conjecture or its negation in the stated bounded-error word-RAM model. A refutation must supply a common positive exponent saving across all fixed dimension constants. A proof conditional on another unproved hypothesis is not a proof of this conjecture. A lower bound only for deterministic algorithms, a restricted instruction set, or an isolated value of \(c\) does not suffice.

context_blocks.text: For fixed \(c\), comparing every pair of packed vectors gives an \(O(cn^2)\)-time baseline. The conjecture permits savings that vanish as dimension grows; it rules out one fixed polynomial saving valid across all dimension constants.

Orthogonal Vectors asks whether some pair has zero inner product. Here one supplied vector must have nonzero inner product with every vector on the other side. Exchanging these quantifiers changes the question, just as finding a graph center differs from finding a distant pair of vertices.

The 2021 source transfers this hypothesis to model checking with an existential–universal–existential quantifier pattern. Such reductions establish consequences of the conjecture, not an unconditional lower bound for Hitting Set.

The card retains the randomized bounded-error convention of the saved formulation and specifies its machine model. Restricted-dimensional algorithms and expected-time-only guarantees should be compared against these exact quantifiers and resources.

cards.title: ETH versus Gap-ETH
cards.formal: Does the deterministic Exponential Time Hypothesis imply the deterministic Gap Exponential Time Hypothesis for sparse 3-CNF formulas?
cards.definitions: For a 3-CNF formula F with n variables, let \(\operatorname{val}(F)\) be the maximum fraction of clauses simultaneously satisfiable. The ETH convention here asserts that there is \(c>0\) for which no deterministic algorithm decides satisfiability of all 3-CNF formulas in time \(O(2^{cn} \operatorname{poly}(\mathrm{L}))\), where L is the binary encoding length. Gap-ETH asserts that there exist constants \(B\ge 1, \delta \in (0,1)\) and \(c' >0\) for which no deterministic algorithm in time \(O(2^{c' n} \operatorname{poly}(\mathrm{L}))\) distinguishes \(\operatorname{val}(F)=1\) from \(\operatorname{val}(F)\le 1- \delta\) on formulas with at most Bn clauses. Its inputs are promised to satisfy one of those two alternatives. Empty formulas are satisfiable. All constants are fixed independently of F; randomized versions are not asserted.

context_blocks.text: ETH concerns exact satisfiability, while Gap-ETH postulates comparable exponential hardness even when unsatisfiable inputs violate a fixed fraction of clauses. Their equivalence would unify many exact and approximation lower-bound assumptions.

Bitansky and coauthors distinguish ETH from the stronger gap hypothesis while obtaining exponential hardness for particular approximation tasks. Hardness for those tasks does not imply a gap-preserving sparse 3-CNF statement. This implication is distinct from asking whether either hypothesis is true.

cards.title: Min-Weight k-Clique hypothesis
cards.formal: Is the following hypothesis true? For every fixed integer \(k\ge3\) and every real \(\varepsilon>0\), there is no uniform randomized word-RAM algorithm that, on every simple undirected \(n\)-vertex graph with integer edge weights in \([-n^{100k},n^{100k}]\), outputs a minimum-total-edge-weight \(k\)-clique, or correctly reports that no \(k\)-clique exists, with probability at least \(2/3\), and has worst-case running time \(O(n^{k-\varepsilon})\). The time bound is over both input graphs and all random choices, with \(k\) fixed and \(n\to\infty\). This is the fixed weight-range version of Hypothesis 7 in the cited survey.
cards.why: Weighted clique optimization is a basic way to express interactions among several selected objects. Its conjectured exponent underlies exact-time lower bounds for problems far beyond clique detection. A polynomial exponent improvement would change those conditional barriers, while a proof would establish strong unconditional limits for a family of explicit polynomial-time tasks. The question also separates the difficulty of arbitrary edge costs from that of merely requiring all pairwise adjacencies.
cards.status_note: The survey explicitly poses this fixed-range randomized hypothesis in 2018. Related min-weight clique assumptions continue to be used in ITCS 2026, with different weight-constant quantifiers. A bounded later-work search through 14 September 2026 did not identify a resolution of this exact formulation; conditional reductions and continuing use are not an independent proof of openness.

cards.definitions: An instance has an integer \(n\ge k\), labelled vertices \([n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}\), a set \(E\subseteq\binom{[n]}2\), and weights \(w:E\to\mathbb Z\) satisfying \(|w(e)|\le n^{100k}\). A feasible answer is a set \(S\in\binom{[n]}k\) with \(\binom S2\subseteq E\); its weight is \(\sum_{e\in\binom S2}w(e)\). Any minimizing set is acceptable, and a special failure symbol is correct exactly when no feasible set exists. The input is a read-only array consisting of \(n\) and, in lexicographic order for all unordered vertex pairs, an adjacency bit, sign bit and unsigned weight magnitude, each in its own word; absent edges use zero sign and magnitude. The output is the sorted list of \(k\) vertex labels or the failure symbol. For each fixed \(k\), an algorithm is one finite program independent of \(n\), using words of \(W=\lceil d\log_2(n+2)\rceil\) bits for some fixed integer \(d\ge100k+4\). The constant \(d\) may depend on the program and \(k\), but not on \(n\) or the input graph. One operation reads or writes a constant number of addressed words, branches or compares, performs a word-level Boolean operation or shift, adds, subtracts or multiplies modulo \(2^W\), divides unsigned words with quotient and remainder when the divisor is nonzero, or obtains one fresh uniform random \(W\)-bit word. Shifts by at least \(W\) produce zero. All work memory initially contains zero, and arbitrary precomputed tables depending on \(n\) are not supplied. A fixed number of registers, addressing, input reads, all preprocessing and output writes are charged. Random words are mutually independent. There is no real arithmetic, oracle, quantum operation or nonuniform advice. Uniformity is with respect to \(n\); a different finite program is allowed for each fixed \(k\). Formally, the prohibited bound would give constants \(C,n_0\), depending on the program, \(k\) and \(\varepsilon\), such that every run on every valid instance with \(n\ge n_0\) uses at most \(Cn^{k-\varepsilon}\) operations, while the full output is correct with probability at least \(2/3\) on each instance.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of the hypothesis with all its quantifiers, or of its negation. A refutation must supply some fixed \(k\ge3\), some \(\varepsilon>0\), and a finite algorithm with a proved \(O(n^{k-\varepsilon})\) worst-case time bound and the stated per-instance success probability for the full weight range. A proof of the hypothesis must exclude every such algorithm for every fixed \(k\ge3\). A conditional reduction from another unproved hypothesis does not prove it unconditionally. Polylogarithmic or other \(n^{o(1)}\) savings, algorithms only for smaller weights or vertex weights, and approximations to the optimum do not refute it. The integer weights and exact combinatorial output define the algorithmic task; this yes/no hypothesis is not a numerical estimation problem with additive tolerance.

context_blocks.text: The source fixes the weight range \([-n^{100k},n^{100k}]\) and asks whether the exponent \(k\) can be decreased by any positive constant. For fixed \(k\), these are polynomially bounded integers with logarithmic bit length, not unbounded-precision real costs. The constant \(100\) is retained from the source rather than replaced by an unspecified polynomial.

The elementary \(O(n^k)\) bound gives a reference scale for fixed \(k\). The hypothesis permits smaller factors such as powers of logarithms: it only excludes a fixed positive saving in the exponent. Consequently, an \(n^{k-o(1)}\) algorithm can coexist with the claim.

Edge weights are essential. The survey distinguishes unweighted clique detection and vertex-weighted clique optimization, whose algorithmic bounds need not match the edge-weighted problem. It also separates minimum weight from the requirement that a clique have total weight exactly zero. These related tasks must not be substituted in the formal statement.

The three-vertex case is closely connected to all-pairs shortest paths through subcubic reductions. Higher clique sizes provide additional hardness assumptions used for sequence alignment, geometric optimization and graph problems across density ranges. This makes the family useful beyond a single graph-search task.

Abboud, Bringmann, Dell and Nederlof establish implications connecting weighted clique hardness to the Orthogonal Vectors conjecture. Such conditional connections strengthen the network of evidence but do not prove the hypothesis. Hu, Nogler and Saha still use a min-weight clique conjecture in ITCS 2026; their nonnegative weight range has a differently quantified exponent constant, so it is recorded as a related formulation rather than asserted to be identical to the fixed range here.

cards.title: Directed unweighted APSP below \(n^{5/2}\)
cards.formal: Do there exist a constant \(\varepsilon\in(0,1/2)\) and a uniform bounded-error randomized word-RAM algorithm computing the full exact all-pairs distance matrix of every unweighted directed graph on \(n\) vertices in \(O(n^{5/2-\varepsilon})\) worst-case time?
cards.definitions: The graph is given by its vertex set \([n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}\), with \(n\ge2\), and an explicit list of \(m\) arcs. It has no loops and at most one arc per ordered pair; opposite arcs are allowed. Every arc has length one. For each ordered pair \((u,v)\in V\times V\), output the minimum number of arcs on a directed path from \(u\) to \(v\), or infinity if no path exists; diagonal entries are zero. The output is an explicit \(n\times n\) array. Use a uniform word RAM with word length \(w=d\lceil\log_{2}(n+2)\rceil\), for a fixed positive integer \(d\) chosen with the algorithm and large enough for its addresses and input values. Unit-cost instructions are word reads/writes, copying, comparisons, branching, Boolean operations, shifts, addition, subtraction and multiplication modulo \(2^{w}\), and integer quotient and remainder with nonzero divisor. Shifts by at least \(w\) return zero. Multiword computation is charged by its component instructions. The fixed finite program receives no advice or precomputed tables; all initialization, preprocessing and output writes count. Randomness consists of independent uniform random words, each generated at unit cost. On every input, the whole output must be correct with probability at least \(2/3\). The time bound holds for every random execution, including unsuccessful ones. The constant \(\varepsilon\) and all other constants are independent of the graph. No assumption about the matrix multiplication exponent \(\omega\), or about additive combinatorics, is included in the claim.

context_blocks.text: Even without numerical weights, directed all-pairs distances have resisted the exponent improvements available for undirected graphs. Direction alone preserves a substantial fine-grained bottleneck.

Chan, Vassilevska Williams and Xu explain why the established directed bounds still encounter \(n^{5/2}\) when \(\omega=2\), and develop reductions relating this problem to small-integer min-plus products.
Fischer gives conditional equivalences among APSP hypotheses in 2026, assuming \(\omega=2\) and an additive-combinatorics assumption. Those equivalences do not supply the algorithm requested here.

cards.title: Balanced dense NFA Acceptance Hypothesis
cards.formal: For the balanced dense binary NFA acceptance problem and word-RAM model below, is it true that for every constant \(\varepsilon\in(0,1)\) no uniform randomized algorithm has worst-case running time \(O(n^{3-\varepsilon})\) and error at most \(1/3\) on every input?
cards.definitions:
An instance supplies \(n\ge2\), states \(Q=\{0,\ldots,n-1\}\), a start state \(q_0\in Q\), accepting states \(F\subseteq Q\), transitions \(\Delta\subseteq Q\times\{0,1\}\times Q\), and an explicit binary word \(x=x_1\cdots x_n\) of length exactly \(n\). There are no empty-word transitions and no repeated copies of a transition. Require \(n^2\le|\Delta|\le2n^2\). The transition relation is given as two \(n\times n\) Boolean matrices, with entry \((a,b)\) for symbol \(s\) indicating whether \((a,s,b)\in\Delta\). The accepting set is an \(n\)-bit indicator vector. The word is accepted exactly when \[ \exists q_1,\ldots,q_n\in Q:\quad q_n\in F\ \text{ and }\ \forall j\in\{1,\ldots,n\},\ (q_{j-1},x_j,q_j)\in\Delta.\]

The matrices are stored in row-major order, one Boolean entry per word; \(n,q_0\), the indicator entries and the input characters likewise occupy one word each in a fixed layout. Use a uniform sequential word RAM with word length \(w=d\lceil\log_2(n+2)\rceil\), where the fixed integer \(d\ge8\) is chosen with the algorithm. The input is read-only, random-access memory; auxiliary memory initially contains zeros. Its addresses and individual values fit in one word. The algorithm is a fixed finite program with no advice or precomputed input-dependent data.

Unit-cost instructions are word reads and writes, copying, comparisons, branching, Boolean operations, logical shifts, addition, subtraction and multiplication modulo \(2^w\), and unsigned integer quotient and remainder for a nonzero divisor. Shifts by at least \(w\) return zero. Multiword computations pay for their constituent instructions. Each random instruction returns an independent uniform \(w\)-bit word. All initialization, preprocessing, table construction and final output are charged. Arbitrary algebraic algorithms in this instruction model are allowed; no combinatorial restriction is imposed.

Correctness means that for every valid fixed input, the output equals its acceptance bit with probability at least \(2/3\). Running time is a worst-case bound over valid inputs and all random choices, not an expected bound. For a fixed \(\varepsilon\), a putative algorithm, \(d\), and constants \(C,n_0\) may depend on \(\varepsilon\), but not on \(n\) or the input. The excluded guarantee is that all valid instances with \(n\ge n_0\) terminate within \(C n^{3-\varepsilon}\) instructions while every valid instance, including smaller ones, is correctly decided with the stated error.

context_blocks.text: The automaton records possible state changes under each symbol. Acceptance asks whether one possible trajectory follows the entire supplied word and ends in an accepting state. Here both the number of states and the word length grow together, and the transition relation has quadratic size.

The 2024 source formulates a broader hypothesis with transition count \(\Theta(n^\alpha)\), word length \(\Theta(n^\beta)\), and a subpolynomial alphabet. It identifies \(\alpha=2,\beta=1\) as a core regime. This card retains its previously selected specialization to a binary alphabet, exactly \(n\) symbols, and the explicit density interval \([n^2,2n^2]\). It does not identify that one proposition with every parameter regime of the broader hypothesis.

The elementary bound in this balanced regime is \(O(n^3)\). The source reports subpolynomial-factor improvements for dense automata, which are compatible with excluding every fixed power saving. Its sparse-automaton bounds use SETH, and its combinatorial lower bounds have a restricted algorithm model. Neither type constitutes the unconditional all-algorithm lower bound requested here.

The broader framework connects automaton acceptance to context-free language reachability, Word Break and the online matrix-vector multiplication hypothesis. These are consequences of the source’s stated hypothesis and reductions; they should not be attributed without qualification to every editorially restricted variant.

Bille and Gørtz study the amount of nondeterministic activity during a particular regular-expression simulation. That density differs from the number of transitions in a general dense NFA. Their work explains the researcher connection recorded at import, rather than authorship of the NFA Acceptance hypothesis.

cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of the universal lower-bound proposition or its logical negation. A refutation supplies some fixed \(\varepsilon\in(0,1)\), a uniform algorithm in the stated RAM model, and proofs of its worst-case time and per-input correctness guarantees on all promised instances. A positive answer excludes all such algorithms without an unproved complexity assumption. The negation of this asymptotic statement is not a single hard or easy finite instance. A bound restricted to combinatorial or deterministic algorithms, or a subpolynomial improvement of cubic time, does not meet the target.

cards.title: Consequences of linear-time Orthogonal Vectors
cards.formal:
Does essentially-linear deterministic time for Orthogonal Vectors in every fixed polylogarithmic dimension regime imply failure of the Exponential Time Hypothesis? With \(\mathsf{EL}_{\mathrm{OV}}\) and \(\mathsf{ETH}\) defined below, the proposition is
\[
\mathsf{EL}_{\mathrm{OV}}\ \Longrightarrow\ \neg\mathsf{ETH}.
\]
Equivalently, does \(\mathsf{ETH}\) imply that some such dimension regime lacks deterministic \(O(N^{1+\varepsilon})\)-time algorithms for at least one \(\varepsilon>0\)? Here \(N\) is the complete binary input length. The target is a logical implication about algorithm existence, not a request to assume that the premise already holds. The explicit dimension quantifiers and binary encodings below complete the source's informal polylogarithmic-dimension formulation, while retaining its deterministic multitape Turing-machine model.

source_formulation.text: Furthermore, we do not know if the existence of an essentially-linear time algorithm for OVP would imply that ETH is false.
source_formulation.caption: Complete selected source sentence; PDF p. 3

cards.why: A proof would base some polynomial-time hardness on ETH rather than the stronger SETH assumption, clarifying how much exponential hardness is needed for a widely used fine-grained benchmark. A refutation would expose a substantive separation between these algorithmic barriers. The importance lies in the relationship between two major hypotheses, beyond an improvement to one OV algorithm.
cards.status_note: The STACS 2022 source explicitly asks this OV-to-ETH implication in Remark 1. A bounded primary-source review through 16 September 2026 checked the source’s latest recorded preprint version, the authors’ subsequent guessing paper and selected 2024–2026 OV/circuit and low-dimensional algorithm results, finding no verified resolution. Source-open status is dated and qualified, not an exhaustive present-day certificate. The exact polylogarithmic promise family, encodings and finite-alphabet details are disclosed editorial completions of the source’s deterministic Turing-machine setting.

progress.text: The STACS source explicitly leaves the OV-to-ETH implication open in Remark 1 while proving an analogous implication for log-CircuitSAT in Theorem 22.

The authors’ later journal work studies deterministic-to-nondeterministic speedups and SAT in nondeterministic linear time. Its main implications do not establish the OV-to-deterministic-ETH statement.
Williams relates OV algorithms and hardness to nonuniform circuit lower bounds and SETH. These are distinct consequences from falsifying ETH.
Alman and Li state a deterministic \(\widetilde O(n\,1.155^{d})\)-time OV algorithm in Theorem 1.3, improving the exponential dependence on dimension.

The ICALP paper of Dürr, Kipouridis, Lampis and Węgrzycki gives further low-dimensional and multi-list OV results; its introductory hardness statements concern SETH and Set Cover, not the target ETH implication.

Individual review recovered the source’s time and machine conventions, made the implication and its full negation explicit, and checked selected later primary papers without finding a resolution of this precise implication.

sentences: Orthogonal Vectors asks whether two lists of Boolean vectors contain a pair with no coordinate equal to one in both vectors.
The premise asks for deterministic essentially-linear algorithms in every fixed polylogarithmic dimension regime.
The question is whether that premise forces the Exponential Time Hypothesis to fail.
Known implications to the stronger SETH assumption and recent low-dimensional algorithms do not settle this precise target.
A complete answer must prove the implication or establish both its algorithmic premise and ETH as the full negation.

cards.definitions:
All logarithms have base two. An Orthogonal Vectors instance consists of integers \(n\ge2\), \(d\ge1\), and two ordered lists \(A=(a_1,\ldots,a_n)\), \(B=(b_1,\ldots,b_n)\) with \(a_i,b_j\in\{0,1\}^{d}\). Repeated vectors and zero vectors are allowed. The answer is yes exactly when
\[
\exists i,j\in\{1,\ldots,n\}:\quad
\sum_{h=1}^{d}a_{i,h}b_{j,h}=0.
\]
The sum is over the integers, not modulo two. Thus no coordinate may be one in both selected vectors. Both lists are explicitly present; there is no succinct input, preprocessing phase, online sequence of queries, or promise on vector weights.

For a nonnegative integer \(r\), let \(\operatorname{bin}(r+1)\) be its usual binary representation without leading zeroes, put \(\ell(r)=|\operatorname{bin}(r+1)|\), and encode it by \(\operatorname{code}(r)=1^{\ell(r)}0\operatorname{bin}(r+1)\). An OV encoding is \(\operatorname{code}(n)\operatorname{code}(d)\), followed by the \(nd\) coordinate bits of \(A\) in list order and then those of \(B\). There is no padding or trailing data. Its length is denoted by \(N\).

For each fixed integer \(b\ge1\), the promised domain \(\mathcal I_b\) consists of these valid encodings satisfying
\[
d\le\bigl\lceil\log_2(n+2)\bigr\rceil^{b}.
\]
This specifies the family of polylogarithmic regimes, rather than selecting a single low-dimensional constant or allowing arbitrary polynomial dimension. The essentially-linear premise means
\[
\mathsf{EL}_{\mathrm{OV}}:\quad
\forall b\in\mathbb Z_{\ge1}\ \forall\varepsilon\in\mathbb Q_{>0}\
\exists M\ \exists C\in\mathbb Z_{\ge1}\
\forall z\in\mathcal I_b:\quad
M(z)\text{ returns the correct OV answer in at most }
C(|z|+1)^{1+\varepsilon}\text{ steps}.
\]
The program and constant may depend on \(b,\varepsilon\), but not on the input. No correctness or time requirement is imposed outside the promised domain. Every positive rational overhead exponent is required; one fixed \(1+\varepsilon\) bound does not establish the premise. Nor is one algorithm with a single subpolynomial overhead demanded. For each fixed \(b\), the explicit length is \(n\) times a polylogarithmic factor, so using \(n\) instead of \(N\) gives the same family of essentially-linear bounds after changing \(\varepsilon\).

A 3-CNF instance consists of \(v\ge0\) named Boolean variables \(x_1,\ldots,x_v\) and an ordered list of \(m\ge0\) clauses, each an ordered list of at most three literals. A literal is \(x_i\) or \(\neg x_i\) for \(1\le i\le v\); repeated literals and clauses are allowed. A formula is satisfied when each clause has a true literal. The empty conjunction is true and an empty clause is false. An assignment gives a bit to each of the \(v\) variables. Its binary encoding is \(\operatorname{code}(v)\operatorname{code}(m)\), followed for each clause by its encoded length and then its literals, each represented by a sign bit followed by \(\operatorname{code}(i)\); sign zero denotes a positive literal. There are no extra bits. Write \(L\) for this encoding length and \(v(F)\) for its declared number of variables, including unused ones.

For \(\delta\in\mathbb Q_{>0}\), define \(\mathsf{SATFast}(\delta)\) to mean that there exist a deterministic machine \(S\) and integers \(C\ge1\), \(k\ge0\), such that on every valid encoded 3-CNF formula \(F\), \(S\) decides satisfiability correctly and halts within
\[
C(L+1)^k\,2^{\delta v(F)}
\]
steps. The clock is worst case, and the constants and program may depend on \(\delta\). Invalid formula encodings are outside this domain. The Exponential Time Hypothesis used here is precisely
\[
\mathsf{ETH}:\quad
\exists\delta\in\mathbb Q_{>0}\;\neg\mathsf{SATFast}(\delta).
\]
Its failure is \(\forall\delta\in\mathbb Q_{>0}\;\mathsf{SATFast}(\delta)\). This definition does not silently exchange the order of the algorithm and exponent quantifiers, or replace ETH by its stronger variant concerning every clause width.

All machines in both definitions are ordinary deterministic multitape Turing machines with finitely many states and a fixed finite positive number of two-way infinite tapes. The alphabet is \(\{0,1,\#,\square\}\), with \(\square\) blank. The binary input occupies consecutive cells of the first tape beginning at zero; every other cell starts blank, and every head starts at zero. All tapes, including the input tape, are writable. In one transition the machine reads one symbol per tape, writes one per tape, moves each head by at most one cell, and changes state. An accepting or rejecting halting state returns the answer. Every transition costs one step. There is no randomness, advice, oracle, random-access instruction or parallel primitive. Each program is uniform over its input lengths, even though different fixed exponents may have different programs. These are standard finite-alphabet refinements of the model in Section 3.1 of the source.
cards.answer_criterion:
Supply a complete, mathematically correct Lean proof of \(\mathsf{EL}_{\mathrm{OV}}\Rightarrow\neg\mathsf{ETH}\), or of its full logical negation
\[
\mathsf{EL}_{\mathrm{OV}}\ \land\ \mathsf{ETH}.
\]
A positive proof must respect all input, dimension, machine and exponent quantifiers in the two definitions. It may establish the implication by any valid mathematical argument; no particular reduction format or uniform compiler between algorithms is imposed. For a negative answer it is necessary to prove both essentially-linear OV algorithms in every specified regime and an ETH lower bound: a faster OV algorithm alone, a failure of one proposed reduction, or an oracle-relative separation is insufficient. Likewise, merely deriving failure of SETH or a \(2^{c v}\) SAT algorithm for one fixed \(c>0\) does not prove failure of ETH. A randomized algorithm, an algorithm only for a fixed small multiple of logarithmic dimension, or a fixed truly subquadratic OV bound does not meet the full premise. No Lean formalization is claimed by this review.

context_blocks.text: The question compares two central sources of conditional lower bounds. Orthogonal Vectors is a polynomial-time problem used to transfer fine-grained hardness to many algorithmic tasks. ETH instead asserts an exponential-time obstruction for 3-CNF satisfiability.

The source defines essentially-linear time by having \(O(N^{1+\varepsilon})\) decision algorithms for every fixed positive \(\varepsilon\). This includes a family of algorithms with different exponents; it does not mean exact linear time or only linear time times a fixed power of a logarithm.

Its main ETH implication concerns log-CircuitSAT, a restricted circuit-satisfiability problem. Remark 1 separately asks the OV implication. The log-CircuitSAT theorem cannot be reported as already resolving this different target.

Later work continues to connect faster OV algorithms to SETH and to nonuniform circuit lower bounds. Those conclusions address other assumptions or resources and do not by themselves establish the ETH implication.

Recent low-dimensional algorithms improve the dependence on dimension in their respective source models, including a deterministic \(\widetilde O(n\,1.155^{d})\) bound. An exponential factor in \(d\) does not supply the required essentially-linear algorithm throughout every fixed polylogarithmic dimension regime.

The exact list representation, dimension-exponent family and finite-alphabet conventions are explicit editorial completions. The original question does not spell them out, and its separate discussion of random-access machines makes it especially important to retain the chosen Turing-machine setting.

checked_sources: Read the full canonical record and actual STACS2022 article55 PDF, pp2–3 for the source question, p6 for DTIME’s writable-input multitape model, and pp12–13 for Theorem22 and Question26. Publisher metadata gives 9March2022, not the conference’s 15March opening date or misleading recent crawler timestamps. arXiv2008.06805 history lists v1 August2020 through v5 23January2022 and no later version.

The source defines essentially-linear as membership in O(N^(1+epsilon)) for every positive epsilon, not a single O(N polylogN) algorithm. The card therefore quantifies separately over algorithms for each rational epsilon and fixed dimension exponent b. Rational exponents suffice by monotonicity. All polynomial-logarithmic dimension bounds with fixed multiplicative constants are covered by a higher integer b beyond finitely many small n; n+2 avoids boundary issues. Exact promise-family encoding is an explicitly disclosed editorial completion, not a verbatim source theorem.

Used the standard two-list, integer-inner-product-zero OV definition, confirmed directly in ICALP2026 Definition1.1 and Alman–Li Section1.6. Repetitions do not affect decision existence. For fixed b the binary length N=2nd+O(logn+logd), so switching n versus full input length preserves the for-every-positive-exponent notion. Did not substitute arbitrary polynomial dimension, online indexing, parity orthogonality, randomized success or a single fixed d=c logn regime.

ETH is copied in its precise source quantifier sense: some positive delta precludes all deterministic 3SAT algorithms with poly(L)2^(delta v) running time. Failure gives an algorithm for each delta, with its polynomial exponent allowed to depend on delta. The card does not silently infer one uniform 2^o(v) algorithm. The implication’s full negation requires both EL_OV and ETH, not merely proving the antecedent or showing one reduction fails.

cards.title: Linear-size Circuit-SAT below exhaustive search
cards.formal: For every fixed integer \(c\ge 1\), do \(\varepsilon _{c}>0\) and a deterministic algorithm exist deciding satisfiability of every Boolean circuit with n inputs and at most cn gates in time \(O((2- \varepsilon _{c})^{n}\cdot n^{O(1)})\)?
cards.definitions: Use uniform classical deterministic Turing computation, with no advice or oracle. Integers and rational numerators and denominators are encoded in binary; L denotes the total input bit length. A polynomial bound has constants independent of the input. Circuits are finite acyclic directed graphs with input bits and one output, binary AND and OR gates and unary NOT gates; gates have unrestricted fan-out. Size counts non-input gates. The input lists every gate and predecessor index. Satisfiability means that some assignment to the n input bits makes the output one. The algorithm and the constants in its polynomial factor may depend on c, but \(\varepsilon _{c}\) must be positive and independent of n. There is no depth restriction.

context_blocks.text: Exhaustive assignment search works in roughly \(2^{n}\) time regardless of circuit structure. Linear-size circuits restrict the amount of computation performed on each assignment while retaining arbitrary depth and sharing.

Obtaining a fixed exponential saving for every fixed size density would establish a general algorithmic benefit of that restriction. The question is part of the algorithms-to-lower-bounds landscape described by Wigderson. Algorithms for bounded-depth or threshold-restricted circuits do not settle the stated general model.

cards.why: A broad satisfiability-speedup question connecting fine-grained algorithms with unrestricted circuit lower bounds.

cards.title: P versus BPP
cards.formal:
Does \(\mathrm P=\mathrm{BPP}\)? Equivalently, is the following statement true?
\[\forall L\subseteq\{0,1\}^{*},\qquad L\in\mathrm{BPP}\ \Longrightarrow\ L\in\mathrm P.\]
Here \(\mathrm{BPP}\) requires one randomized polynomial-time machine whose probability of a correct answer is at least \(2/3\) separately on every input, including both members and nonmembers of \(L\). The proposed deterministic machine must decide the same total language correctly on every input in polynomial time.
cards.definitions:
A language \(L\) is a set of finite binary strings; its membership bit is \(\mathbf1_L(x)\in\{0,1\}\). Put \(n=|x|\), allowing \(n=0\). Computation uses finite multitape Turing-machine programs over fixed finite tape alphabets. Each ordinary tape transition costs one step. A randomized transition may read at most one fresh independent unbiased bit. There is no oracle, advice, quantum operation, input distribution or promise excluding some inputs.

The condition \(L\in\mathrm{BPP}\) means that there exist one randomized program \(R\) and fixed positive integers \(C,d\) such that, with \(p(n)=C(n+1)^d\), both of the following hold for every \(x\):
\[\begin{gathered}
 R(x)\text{ halts within }p(n)\text{ steps on every random tape and outputs a bit},\\
 \Pr[R(x)=\mathbf1_L(x)]\ge 2/3.
\end{gathered}\]
The probability is only over the internal fair bits. An exact finite interpretation is to supply a uniformly distributed string \(z\in\{0,1\}^{p(n)}\), ignoring its unused suffix. The probability condition is then the integer inequality
\[3\bigl|\{z\in\{0,1\}^{p(n)}:R(x;z)=\mathbf1_L(x)\}\bigr|\ \ge\ 2\cdot 2^{p(n)}.\]
The time bound is worst case over both the input and every random tape, rather than an expectation. The error bound is pointwise: success on almost all inputs of a length does not suffice. The same constants apply at every length; an input-dependent exponent is not polynomial time in this definition.

The condition \(L\in\mathrm P\) means that there exist one deterministic program \(A\) and fixed positive integers \(C',d'\) such that for every binary string \(x\), the program halts within \(C'(|x|+1)^{d'}\) steps and outputs \(\mathbf1_L(x)\). Reading, writing, arithmetic and tape access all count toward time. The deterministic program and its constants may depend on the language and its randomized decider, but not on the particular input or its length.

The requested deterministic computation may use a different algorithm and a different polynomial exponent. The target does not require an effective compiler taking descriptions of randomized machines to deterministic ones. It asks for existence of a polynomial-time deterministic decider for each language in the class. Deterministic programs are also randomized programs that ignore their coins, so \(\mathrm P\subseteq\mathrm{BPP}\) holds directly. Sampling a distribution, returning a valid witness, and answering only promised inputs are different tasks from deciding this total membership bit.
cards.answer_criterion:
Give a complete, mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of the stated inclusion, or of its logical negation
\[\exists L\subseteq\{0,1\}^{*},\qquad L\in\mathrm{BPP}\ \land\ L\notin\mathrm P.\]
A positive proof must establish existence, correctness and a uniform polynomial time bound for a deterministic decider of every language satisfying the randomized definition. A negative proof must give one fixed language with a single randomized decider meeting the full pointwise error and worst-case polynomial time guarantees, and prove that no deterministic program with any fixed polynomial time bound decides that language.

A result conditional on an unproved hardness assumption, a nonuniform circuit simulation, an oracle separation, a promise-problem separation, or a simulation valid only at some lengths does not settle the target. A lower bound for one simulation rule or one generator family does not exclude every deterministic decider. The probability threshold is exact; this is a yes/no question with no numerical approximation tolerance.
cards.why: This asks whether independent random bits increase the set of total decision problems solvable efficiently. An equality would identify deterministic and randomized polynomial-time decision power; a separation would exhibit an inherent benefit of randomness even when a different deterministic algorithm is allowed.

context_blocks.text: A randomized answer is allowed to be wrong with probability at most one third on any specified input. For example, correctness on 99% of all strings of each length would still fail this definition if a remaining string were always answered incorrectly. The uncertainty belongs to the machine’s internal choices, not to which inputs the user may supply.

Adleman’s theorem gives \(\mathrm{BPP}\subseteq\mathrm{P}/\mathrm{poly}\). Here \(\mathrm{P}/\mathrm{poly}\) allows a separate polynomial-size Boolean circuit at each input length, without requiring one efficient procedure that constructs these circuits. This is a nonuniform existence statement; the target requires one finite deterministic program for all lengths.

Impagliazzo and Wigderson prove a conditional equality: if a Boolean function computable in deterministic time \(2^{O(n)}\) has worst-case circuit complexity at least \(2^{\varepsilon n}\), for some fixed \(\varepsilon>0\) and all sufficiently large \(n\), then \(\mathrm P=\mathrm{BPP}\). Circuit complexity here counts gates of unrestricted nonuniform Boolean circuits over a fixed complete finite basis that compute the function correctly on every input of that length. The exponential lower-bound hypothesis is part of the theorem; this is not an unconditional equality or a theorem assuming only \(\mathrm P\ne\mathrm{NP}\).

Doron, Moshkovitz, Oh and Zuckerman’s May 2026 preprint obtains finer conditional derandomization bounds for algorithms with a specified insensitivity property. For each fixed input, changing one uniformly chosen coin coordinate of a correct tape must rarely make the answer incorrect. Their two-sided version additionally constrains incorrect tapes that have a correct neighbor. Theorem 9.10 retains explicit circuit-hardness, insensitivity and error assumptions; these structural conditions are not properties required of every BPP program. The paper distinguishes hitting-set and pseudoentropy generators from general pseudorandom generators.

Tianrong Lin’s July 2026 revision states a direct claim of \(\mathrm P\subsetneq\mathrm{BPP}\) in Theorem 1.1, with additional claimed separations. That would answer this card negatively if its proof were valid. This review read the claimed theorem and checked its version history, but has not certified its proof or located independent primary validation in the bounded searches. It is therefore recorded as an unverified claim, and the card retains uncertain status.

cards.title: Optimal explicit pseudorandom generators for read-once branching programs
cards.formal:
Does there exist one deterministic finite-program algorithm \(A\) and absolute integers \(C,D\ge1\) with the following property? For every \(n,w\ge2\) and \(p\ge1\), all integers, the algorithm specifies an integer seed length \(s=s(n,w,p)\ge0\) and a function
\[G_{n,w,p}:\{0,1\}^{s}\longrightarrow\{0,1\}^{n}\]
with \(s\le Cq\), where \(q=\lceil\log _2 n\rceil+\lceil\log _2 w\rceil+p\), such that every length-\(n\), width-at-most-\(w\) ordered binary read-once branching program \(B\) satisfies
\[\left|\Pr_{u\sim U_s}[B(G_{n,w,p}(u))=1]-\Pr_{z\sim U_n}[B(z)=1]\right|\le 2^{-p}?\]
Here \(U_k\) is the uniform distribution on the \(2^k\) binary strings of length \(k\). Require \(A\) to compute both \(s(n,w,p)\) and any requested bit \(G_{n,w,p}(u)_i\), \(1\le i\le n\), in at most \(Dq\) work bits and \((nw2^p)^D\) steps per call, in the model below. The same algorithm, constants and generator family must work for every parameter triple and every permitted program.
cards.definitions:
A length-\(n\), width-at-most-\(w\) ordered binary read-once branching program consists of nonempty finite layers \(V_0,\ldots,V_n\), each of size at most \(w\), a start state in \(V_0\), an accepting subset of \(V_n\), and functions \(\delta_{i,b}:V_{i-1}\to V_i\) for \(1\le i\le n\), \(b\in\{0,1\}\). On input \(z\), the state is updated by \(\delta_{i,z_i}\) at step \(i\); \(B(z)=1\) exactly when the final state is accepting. The bit order is \(z_1,\ldots,z_n\). Transitions may merge states, including two equally labeled edges from distinct states; no regularity or permutation promise is imposed. The transition tables, start state and accepting subset are arbitrary finite, possibly nonuniform data. The generator receives none of them.

The algorithm is a deterministic multitape Turing machine with a fixed finite program and a mode flag. In the seed-length mode its input is \((n,w,p)\) and its output is \(s(n,w,p)\) in binary. In the bit mode its input is \((n,w,p,u,i)\) and it outputs exactly one bit before halting. Integer parameters use canonical binary notation with separators; the seed is its full binary string, with leading zeroes retained. Inputs occupy read-only tapes whose heads are bounded by endmarkers. There is a fixed finite number of initially blank, semi-infinite work tapes over \(\{0,1,\square\}\), with heads moving by at most one cell per transition. Each distinct work-tape cell visited is charged two work bits, including blank cells. This fixed encoding of tape symbols only fixes a constant in the space bound. All counters, arithmetic, stored history and preprocessing are charged; output is write-only and cannot serve as storage. There is no advice, oracle, external clock or other uncounted memory. Each transition costs one time step. The required bounds hold on every valid call, for every seed and requested index. Only the requested bit must be output in bit mode; there is no requirement to store the whole length-\(n\) string.

Probabilities are exact uniform finite averages. In particular, a seed always has weight \(2^{-s}\), even if several seeds produce the same string; signed weights and externally assigned coefficients are not permitted. The parameter \(p\) controls additive error, not failure probability of a randomized construction: \(A\) itself is deterministic. With \(\varepsilon=2^{-p}\), the target is \(O(\log n+\log w+\log(1/\varepsilon))\) seed length and work space. Ceiling conventions change only constants. Arbitrary \(0<\varepsilon<1\) can be covered by a dyadic tolerance no larger than \(\varepsilon\). No compression requirement \(s<n\) is imposed in parameter regimes where the displayed allowance is already at least \(n\).
cards.answer_criterion: Supply a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of the existential proposition above or its full logical negation. An affirmative proof must specify a single finite program and universal constants, formalize its seed-length and bit computations, establish the stated worst-case resource bounds, and prove the additive-error inequality for every permitted program and every parameter triple. A negative proof must rule out every such uniform program and choice of constants; a limitation of one construction, one analysis or one restricted generator class is insufficient. The theorem must use the stated ordinary uniform-seed distribution and arbitrary merging transitions. A result solely for weighted generators, hitting sets or a restricted branching-program subclass does not meet this target.
cards.why: A solution would give a uniform optimal-seed pseudorandom distribution for arbitrary small-memory computations and imply L = BPL. It would close the central gap between the existence of short seeds and their computation in small space, beyond the structural restrictions and weighted approximations covered by current results.

context_blocks.text: A branching program models a stream computation that remembers only its current state. Its width \(w\) permits roughly \(\log_2 w\) memory bits, while its length \(n\) counts inspected input bits. The quantifiers require one distribution that works simultaneously for every allowed transition table. Computing a favorable distribution after seeing a particular table would answer a different question.

Short-seed distributions exist nonconstructively; in particular, seed length \(O(\log(n/\varepsilon))\) is known for width-\(n\), length-\(n\) programs. The unresolved issue is explicit computation with the required space bound. An optimal ordinary generator of the kind requested here would imply \(\mathrm L=\mathrm{BPL}\), the equality of deterministic and bounded-error randomized logarithmic-space decision classes. The card does not assert the converse implication.

The classical general bound is \(O(\log n\cdot\log(nw/\varepsilon))\) seed bits. For polynomial width and constant error, this becomes \(O(\log^2 n)\), whereas the requested bound is \(O(\log n)\). The September 2026 RANDOM paper still identifies this general gap, while distinguishing improvements in special width/length regimes.

Weighted generators approximate the acceptance probability by an average \(\mathbb E_u[\rho(u)B(G(u))]\), where \(\rho\) may take negative values. Hoza’s Theorem 1.5 obtains seed length \(O(\log(wn)\log n+\log(1/\varepsilon))\) for this relaxed object. Such weights are useful for deterministic estimates but do not define the ordinary sampled distribution required in this question.

Cheng–Wu’s July 2026 version improves weighted constructions across several parameter regimes. Its optimal-space simulation theorem concerns regular programs in a short-wide regime, not arbitrary programs. A regular program has equal incoming and outgoing degree at each state of each consecutive-layer graph; general transitions in this question can concentrate many incoming edges at one state.

Chen and coauthors improve weighted error reduction and alphabet dependence in the September 2026 proceedings version. Its separate ordinary-generator implication assumes an ordinary PRG with stronger parameter dependence; the weighted theorem does not supply that assumption. The paper credits the earlier Cheng–Hoza result for this connection.

A hitting set guarantees at least one accepting output whenever the uniform acceptance probability exceeds a specified threshold. It need not approximate that probability. Cheng–Hoza prove that a logarithmic-space hitting set for polynomial-width programs would nevertheless imply \(\mathrm L=\mathrm{BPL}\). Their conclusion about class derandomization does not itself produce the ordinary generator required by this card.

For permutation programs, each symbol acts bijectively between consecutive layers of equal size. Cohen–Doron–Goldgraber’s July 2026 theorem gives an ordinary generator with seed \(O((\log w+\log(1/\varepsilon))\log n)\), including arbitrary accepting subsets. The structural promise and remaining product of logarithms distinguish it from the general target.

Krak’s September 2026 preprint states a hitting-set result with seed \(O(\log(n/\varepsilon))\) for ordered width-three programs. The theorem is both a hitting guarantee and a constant-width result; its definition of explicitness requires polynomial time rather than the logarithmic workspace imposed here. This scope review does not independently certify the new proof.

The September 2026 RANDOM paper still identifies this general gap, while distinguishing improvements in special width/length regimes.

Weighted generators approximate the acceptance probability by an average \(\mathbb E_u[\rho(u)B(G(u))]\), where \(\rho\) may take negative values. Hoza’s Theorem 1.5 obtains seed length \(O(\log(wn)\log n+\log(1/\varepsilon))\) for this relaxed object. Such weights are useful for deterministic estimates but do not define the ordinary sampled distribution required in this question.

Cheng–Wu’s July 2026 version improves weighted constructions across several parameter regimes. Its optimal-space simulation theorem concerns regular programs in a short-wide regime, not arbitrary programs. A regular program has equal incoming and outgoing degree at each state of each consecutive-layer graph; general transitions in this question can concentrate many incoming edges at one state.

Chen and coauthors improve weighted error reduction and alphabet dependence in the September 2026 proceedings version. Its separate ordinary-generator implication assumes an ordinary PRG with stronger parameter dependence; the weighted theorem does not supply that assumption. The paper credits the earlier Cheng–Hoza result for this connection.

A hitting set guarantees at least one accepting output whenever the uniform acceptance probability exceeds a specified threshold. It need not approximate that probability. Cheng–Hoza prove that a logarithmic-space hitting set for polynomial-width programs would nevertheless imply \(\mathrm L=\mathrm{BPL}\). Their conclusion about class derandomization does not itself produce the ordinary generator required by this card.

For permutation programs, each symbol acts bijectively between consecutive layers of equal size. Cohen–Doron–Goldgraber’s July 2026 theorem gives an ordinary generator with seed \(O((\log w+\log(1/\varepsilon))\log n)\), including arbitrary accepting subsets. The structural promise and remaining product of logarithms distinguish it from the general target.

Krak’s September 2026 preprint states a hitting-set result with seed \(O(\log(n/\varepsilon))\) for ordered width-three programs. The theorem is both a hitting guarantee and a constant-width result; its definition of explicitness requires polynomial time rather than the logarithmic workspace imposed here. This scope review does not independently certify the new proof.

cards.title: L versus BPL
cards.formal:
Is \(\mathrm L=\mathrm{BPL}\)? Equivalently, is it true that
\[\forall S\subseteq\{0,1\}^{*},\qquad S\in\mathrm{BPL}\ \Longrightarrow\ S\in\mathrm L?\]
Here \(\mathrm{BPL}\) consists of total decision languages recognized with two-sided error at most \(1/3\) by one uniform randomized machine using logarithmic work space and polynomial time on every input and every random tape. The target is a uniform deterministic logarithmic-work-space decider for each such language.
cards.definitions:
A language \(S\) is a set of finite binary strings; put \(n=|x|\), including \(n=0\). A machine has a finite program, one two-way read-only input tape bounded by endmarkers, and a fixed finite number of initially blank work tapes over fixed finite alphabets. The input head cannot move outside the endmarkers. Work tapes are semi-infinite; their heads move by at most one cell per step. Space is the sum of the numbers of distinct work-tape cells visited, including blank cells. The read-only input and finite control are excluded from this count; all stored counters, arithmetic operands, history and auxiliary data are included. Acceptance or rejection is a halting control state, not an additional readable output tape.

A randomized transition can obtain at most one fresh independent fair bit. Past bits cannot be revisited unless retained in counted work space. There is no random-tape address, free clock, oracle, advice, or additional uncounted storage. A deterministic machine has the same tape model and no coin transitions. One ordinary machine transition costs one time step.

Membership \(S\in\mathrm{BPL}\) means that there exist one randomized program \(R\) and positive integers \(K,C,d\) such that for every input \(x\) and every realization of its random choices, \(R\) visits at most
\[K\lceil\log_2(n+2)\rceil\]
work cells and halts with a bit in at most \(T(n)=C(n+2)^d\) steps. In addition, for every \(x\),
\[\Pr[R(x)=\mathbf 1_S(x)]\ge 2/3.\]
The probability is only over internal coins. Exactly, supply a uniform string \(u\in\{0,1\}^{T(n)}\), consuming one bit whenever requested and ignoring the unused suffix; the success requirement is
\[3\bigl|\{u\in\{0,1\}^{T(n)}:R(x;u)=\mathbf1_S(x)\}\bigr|\ge 2\cdot2^{T(n)}.\]
This finite counting formula defines the probability; it is not an extra operation available to the machine. The space and time bounds hold on every random string, not merely in expectation. Success is required separately on every member and nonmember, not only for a typical input distribution. No promise excludes inputs with intermediate acceptance probability: a valid decider for \(S\) must meet the appropriate bound on every binary string.

Membership \(S\in\mathrm L\) means that there exist one deterministic program \(D\) and a positive integer \(K'\) such that for every \(x\), \(D\) halts with \(\mathbf1_S(x)\) and visits at most \(K'\lceil\log_2(n+2)\rceil\) work cells. In this bounded-input-head model there are only polynomially many configurations at a fixed input length. A halting deterministic run cannot repeat a configuration, so a separate polynomial time guarantee follows. The program and its constants may depend on \(S\), but not on the particular input or its length.

The deterministic machine may have a different space constant, time exponent and computation from the randomized decider. Uniformity means a single finite program serves all input lengths, without length-dependent advice. Deterministic machines are a special case of randomized machines, so \(\mathrm L\subseteq\mathrm{BPL}\). The question asks for the reverse inclusion of languages; it does not prescribe a pseudorandom-generator construction or a compiler transforming arbitrary machine descriptions.

context_blocks.text: Logarithmic memory is enough for a constant number of input-position counters but not for storing an arbitrary long random history. Fresh coins can guide the computation without remaining available afterward. Allowing the machine to freely revisit an entire random string changes the resource model, which is why the random-access convention is part of the question.

Saks and Zhou obtained deterministic simulation in \(O((\log n)^{3/2})\) space. Hoza’s Theorem 1.6 improves this to
\[O\!\left(\frac{(\log n)^{3/2}}{\sqrt{\log\log n}}\right)\]
as \(n\to\infty\). This remains larger than \(O(\log n)\). These are space bounds; they do not assert that the improved-space simulation also runs in polynomial time.

A read-once branching program is a finite layered computation: each newly read random symbol selects a transition to the next layer, and a designated final state determines the answer. Its width is the number of states per layer and its length is the number of symbols read. This represents the random part of a bounded-space computation after the ordinary input is fixed. Restricted transition structures or unusually short programs need not capture every BPL computation.

An ordinary pseudorandom generator approximates acceptance probabilities using a genuine distribution generated from a short uniform seed. A weighted generator instead associates possibly negative real weights with seeds and approximates acceptance through a signed weighted average. Such estimates can be useful for derandomization, but they are not themselves sampling probabilities. Improving weighted generators does not automatically supply an ordinary generator with identical parameters.

Chen, Cohen, Doron, Khaskelberg and Ta-Shma’s May 2026 revision improves error reduction into weighted generators, including dependence on the alphabet size. The revision explicitly attributes the relevant earlier arity/error implication to Cheng and Hoza. It retains the general BPL versus L question as open; neither its weighted output nor the conditional implication supplies the equality here.

Cheng and Wu’s July 2026 version gives \(O(\log w)\)-space derandomization for regular branching programs of width \(w\), length at most \(2^{O(\sqrt{\log w})}\), binary alphabet, and inverse-polynomial additive error. Regularity means that every consecutive-layer transition graph has the same incoming and outgoing degree at every vertex. Both regularity and the short-length regime are genuine hypotheses. The result does not cover arbitrary polynomial-length, polynomial-width programs representing general BPL computations.

cards.why: This asks whether randomness adds computational power when an algorithm can remember only logarithmically many bits of an arbitrarily long input. An equality would permit deterministic bounded-memory decision whenever bounded-error randomized decision is possible; a separation would show an inherent memory advantage of randomness.
cards.answer_criterion:
Give a complete, mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of the inclusion in the statement, or of its logical negation
\[\exists S\subseteq\{0,1\}^{*},\qquad S\in\mathrm{BPL}\ \land\ S\notin\mathrm L.\]
A positive proof must establish a uniform deterministic decider with one logarithmic work-space bound for every language satisfying the full randomized definition. A negative proof must establish one fixed total language with a valid bounded-error randomized decider and exclude every deterministic decider with every constant logarithmic space bound for that language.

Extra polylogarithmic space, a rereadable uncounted random tape, advice, an oracle, a promise-problem separation, or correctness only at selected lengths does not meet this target. A failed generator construction or a lower bound for a restricted family of simulations does not rule out all deterministic deciders. Unproved hardness assumptions yield conditional results only. This is a yes/no class-comparison question with an exact probability threshold, not a numerical approximation target.

importance.reason: A central derandomization question with a resource regime and known techniques distinct from P=BPP. Specialist work on space-bounded pseudorandomness, including 2026 weighted-generator results, documents continuing interest. cards.title: Optimal deterministic restricted-isometry matrices
cards.formal: Do there exist universal constants \(C,B,b>0\) and a deterministic algorithm which, for every pair of integers \(N\ge 2\) and \(2\le s\le N\), outputs in at most \(B N^{b}\) bit operations a rational \(m\times N\) matrix A, with \(m\le C s \ln (eN/s)\), such that \((2/3)\Vert x\Vert _{2}^{2}\le \Vert Ax\Vert _{2}^{2}\le (4/3)\Vert x\Vert _{2}^{2}\) for every real vector \(x\in \mathbb{R} ^{N}\) with at most s nonzero coordinates?
cards.definitions: The input consists of N and s in binary. The output is an explicit list of all entries of A, each encoded as a signed integer numerator and positive integer denominator in binary. Its total encoding length must also be at most \(B N^{b}\). Time is ordinary deterministic Turing-machine bit complexity, polynomial in N; randomness, advice and unit-cost exact real arithmetic are unavailable. The row count m is a positive integer chosen by the algorithm. The same constants and algorithm work for all allowed pairs N,s. The norm is Euclidean, and the displayed inequalities concern squared norms. They define restricted isometry of order s and distortion \(\delta =1/3\). The condition must hold simultaneously for every support of size at most s and every real choice of coefficients on that support. No probability over supports or signals is permitted. The natural logarithm and the factor e ensure a nonzero expression when s is close to N. The omitted case \(s=1\) is trivial and can be handled by a single row of ones.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a deterministic algorithm satisfying all the uniform dimension, encoding, time and restricted-isometry requirements, or prove that no such algorithm exists. A negative result conditional on a complexity assumption must state it. An existence proof, a construction using random bits, success for most sparse signals, or a deterministic construction with a larger asymptotic row count does not settle the stated question.
cards.why: A central gap between random existence and efficient explicit construction, with direct consequences for uniform sparse recovery and for how pseudorandomness controls exponentially many spectral constraints.

context_blocks.text: Suppose an unknown vector has N coordinates but only s of them matter. A measurement matrix replaces the vector by m linear measurements. Sparsity allows m to be much smaller than N, but the matrix must preserve every possible sparse direction if the measuring device is to work uniformly. The question asks whether a short, guaranteed measurement design can be computed without random choices.

The restricted-isometry requirement has a concrete spectral interpretation. For every set S of at most s column indices, all eigenvalues of \(A_{S}^{T}A_{S}\) must lie between \(2/3\) and \(4/3\). Thus columns must behave almost orthogonally in every small group. Checking only individual column lengths, only pairs of columns, or a large collection of sampled test vectors leaves many of these simultaneous constraints untested.

This condition supports stable sparse recovery. If a matrix has restricted isometry of order 2t with distortion \(1/3\), then two different t-sparse signals cannot have identical measurements: their difference has at most 2t nonzero coordinates. Standard recovery theorems also give robust reconstruction by \(\ell\)\(_{1}\) minimization. The distinction between order t and order 2t is necessary; injectivity for t-sparse differences alone would not compare arbitrary t-sparse signals.

Random independent Bernoulli or Gaussian matrices attain \(m=O(s \log (eN/s))\) for fixed distortion, and matching row lower bounds make this the optimal order for \(s\ge 2\). Rao’s paper summarizes this benchmark and improves the amount of randomness needed to attain it. The unresolved resource in the card is therefore deterministic construction time, rather than whether matrices with the desired geometric property exist.

Requiring rational output does not destroy the random benchmark. For example, choose the number of rows to be a perfect square \(t^{2}\) within a constant factor of a sufficiently large target value, and use independent entries ±\(1/t\). This keeps the usual normalized Bernoulli construction while giving an exact, short binary description of every entry. The real difficulty is choosing all the signs deterministically with a proof that every sparse direction is preserved.

One basic deterministic analysis bounds the coherence \(\mu\), the largest absolute inner product between two unit columns. Gershgorin’s theorem then gives restricted-isometry constant at most \((s- 1)\mu\). When \(\mu\) is about \(1/\sqrt{m}\), this argument certifies only s on the order of \(\sqrt{m}\). This is a limitation of that sufficient-condition analysis, commonly called the square-root bottleneck, rather than an impossibility theorem for deterministic matrices.

Bourgain, Dilworth, Ford, Konyagin and Kutzarova broke that bottleneck in a restricted parameter regime. Their explicit construction uses additive-combinatorial and exponential-sum estimates to control interactions beyond pairwise coherence. It is a major proof that deterministic analysis can go further, but its small exponent improvement does not reach the optimal \(s \log (eN/s)\) row count uniformly in N and s.

Rao’s construction achieves the optimal row order with \(O(s \log (N/s) \log  s)\) random bits in the sparse parameter regime discussed in the paper. Its proof extends the Hanson–Wright inequality to biased distributions. Reducing the seed length makes progress toward explicit construction, but enumerating all seeds can still take far more than polynomial time, and recognizing a successful seed is a separate issue.

The inherited 2025 paper of Fickus and Lake studies highly symmetric equiangular tight frames, which minimize coherence. It analyzes their minimal dependent column sets through regular simplices and designs. Such structure is informative in both directions: a dependent set of r columns immediately prevents restricted isometry of order r with distortion less than one. Optimal pairwise geometry alone does not guarantee the higher-order property.

For a simple illustration, the \(m+1\) unit vertices of a regular simplex in \(\mathbb{R} ^{m}\) have small and equal pairwise inner products, yet their sum is zero. Their coefficient vector of all ones is therefore a nonzero sparse kernel vector. The example explains why an attractive frame construction must be accompanied by control over all relevant column subsets, not just a calculation of coherence.

The all-parameter formulation also matters. The identity matrix handles s comparable to N, while many explicit algebraic constructions work only along particular dimension sequences or for specified sparsity ranges. A resolution must cover the intermediate sparse regimes with one polynomial-time procedure. Likewise, statistical recovery guarantees and \(\ell\)\(_{1}\)-norm versions of restricted isometry answer different geometric questions.

It is a major proof that deterministic analysis can go further, but its small exponent improvement does not reach the optimal \(s \log (eN/s)\) row count uniformly in N and s.

Rao’s construction achieves the optimal row order with \(O(s \log (N/s) \log  s)\) random bits in the sparse parameter regime discussed in the paper. Its proof extends the Hanson–Wright inequality to biased distributions. Reducing the seed length makes progress toward explicit construction, but enumerating all seeds can still take far more than polynomial time, and recognizing a successful seed is a separate issue.

The inherited 2025 paper of Fickus and Lake studies highly symmetric equiangular tight frames, which minimize coherence. It analyzes their minimal dependent column sets through regular simplices and designs. Such structure is informative in both directions: a dependent set of r columns immediately prevents restricted isometry of order r with distortion less than one. Optimal pairwise geometry alone does not guarantee the higher-order property.

For a simple illustration, the \(m+1\) unit vertices of a regular simplex in \(\mathbb{R} ^{m}\) have small and equal pairwise inner products, yet their sum is zero. Their coefficient vector of all ones is therefore a nonzero sparse kernel vector. The example explains why an attractive frame construction must be accompanied by control over all relevant column subsets, not just a calculation of coherence.

The all-parameter formulation also matters. The identity matrix handles s comparable to N, while many explicit algebraic constructions work only along particular dimension sequences or for specified sparsity ranges. A resolution must cover the intermediate sparse regimes with one polynomial-time procedure. Likewise, statistical recovery guarantees and \(\ell\)\(_{1}\)-norm versions of restricted isometry answer different geometric questions.

cards.title: Uniform PRGs from exponential-time hardness
cards.formal: Does \(\mathrm{EXP}\not\subseteq\mathrm{BPSUBEXP}\) imply the following generator statement? There are integers \(C,k,a\ge1\), a constant \(A\ge1\), and a single deterministic generator algorithm which, for every \(m\ge2\), maps \(d(m)=C\lceil\log_2m\rceil^k\) seed bits to \(m\) output bits in time at most \(A(m+2^{d(m)})^a\), and has this security property: for every fixed uniform probabilistic distinguisher \(T\) running in time \(O(m)\), there are infinitely many \(m\) such that \[\left|\Pr[T(G_m(U_{d(m)}))=1]-\Pr[T(U_m)=1]\right|\le \frac1m.\] The generator is independent of \(T\), and the infinitely many successful lengths may depend on \(T\).
cards.why: Hardness against algorithms is a weaker kind of premise than hardness against arbitrary circuits. A generator with only polylogarithmically many seed bits would turn strong uniform hardness into correspondingly fast average-case derandomization. The remaining gap tests how much of the familiar nonuniform hardness-versus-randomness tradeoff survives with uniform assumptions.
