sentences: The hypothesis says that some exponential-time language resists randomized subexponential-time algorithms.
The question asks whether this uniform hardness yields a single generator with only polylogarithmically many seed bits.
Its output must fool each fixed linear-time probabilistic distinguisher on infinitely many output lengths.
The generator may take quasipolynomial time, but it must be uniform and independent of the distinguisher.
Known low-end and more structured high-end results leave this general hardness-to-randomness implication distinct.

cards.definitions: All machines are multitape Turing machines with a fixed finite program and no advice. Time counts every transition, including input and output processing. Randomized machines use independent fair bits and have their time bound on every random tape. For a time function \(t\), \(\mathrm{DTIME}(t(n))\) consists of languages decided on every input of length \(n\) by a deterministic machine in \(O(t(n))\) time, and \(\mathrm{BPTIME}(t(n))\) uses a randomized machine that is correct on each input with probability at least \(2/3\). Define \(\mathrm{EXP}=\bigcup_{j\ge1}\mathrm{DTIME}(2^{n^j})\) and \(\mathrm{BPSUBEXP}=\bigcap_{j\ge1}\mathrm{BPTIME}(2^{n^{1/j}})\). The intersection permits different algorithms for different \(j\), but each must solve the language on all input lengths. Noncontainment means that some language in the union is absent from that intersection. The generator receives \(1^m\) and an independent seed \(s\in\{0,1\}^{d(m)}\), and produces exactly \(m\) bits \(G_m(s)\). Its one finite program, constants and seed-length exponent are common to all \(m\) and all distinguishers. Integer powers of \(\lceil\log_2m\rceil\) are a concrete normalization of polylogarithmic seed length; extra seed bits may be ignored. The displayed generator running time is the meaning of mildly explicit and may exceed the distinguishing time. A distinguisher \(T\) receives only an \(m\)-bit string, returns one bit, and has a constant \(K_T\) with running time at most \(K_Tm\) on every input and random tape. It receives no input-dependent advice, seed, hard-language oracle or additional auxiliary input. Here \(U_j\) is the uniform distribution on \(\{0,1\}^j\); in each displayed probability the seed or uniform input is independent of the distinguisher’s internal fair random bits. The security quantifiers are \(\forall T\,\forall M\ge2\,\exists m\ge M\) satisfying the inequality. They neither require security at all sufficiently large lengths nor a single length at which every possible finite program is fooled.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct Lean proof of the stated implication, with a uniform generator and all seed-length, construction-time and distinguishing guarantees under its hypothesis, or a complete Lean proof of its logical negation. A result assuming nonuniform circuit hardness, hardness only for a smaller complexity class, nonuniform advice for the generator, or a different exceptional-length quantifier does not by itself prove this implication. A limitation on a restricted kind of reduction alone is not a refutation of the implication.

context_blocks.text: This is Open Problem 8.7 with its polylogarithmic-seed, mildly explicit and infinitely-often conventions made explicit. The printed phrase about the generator’s “input” being pseudorandom is read as referring to its output distribution, consistently with the surrounding generator definitions. The inverse-linear advantage is a stated conventional security normalization; the seed is not revealed to the distinguisher.

Trevisan and Vadhan define uniform distinguishing success at all sufficiently large lengths, so failure of every such distinguisher means that each fixed program is fooled infinitely often. Their paper also studies a stronger seed-visible convention; this card does not add that stronger requirement to the textbook’s output-only question.

The textbook distinguishes its known low-end uniform tradeoff from the open high-end implication. It records the corresponding stronger-assumption result when EXP is replaced by PSPACE; that replacement is not the hypothesis asked for here.

Chen, Rothblum and Tell obtain stronger uniform tradeoffs for hard functions with additional uniform-circuit depth structure. Their high-end theorem also uses advice for its BPP simulation. These are material differences from a single advice-free generator derived solely from the EXP noncontainment in this card.

Sdroievski’s 2024 dissertation still describes the high-end uniform equivalence as open. This is a later primary discussion of the gap, rather than a claim that every subsequent manuscript has been exhaustively checked.

cards.title: Two-source extraction at log n plus constant entropy
cards.formal:
Does there exist an integer \(C\ge0\) and one uniform deterministic polynomial-time algorithm \(A\) defining functions
\[
E_n:\{0,1\}^n\times\{0,1\}^n\longrightarrow\{0,1\}\qquad(n\ge1)
\]
such that, for every \(n\) and every two independent probability distributions \(X,Y\) on \(\{0,1\}^n\) with
\[
H_\infty(X),H_\infty(Y)\ge\log_2 n+C,
\]
we have
\[
\left|\Pr[E_n(X,Y)=1]-\frac12\right|\le\frac1{100}?
\]
The algorithm receives only \(n\) and the two strings. The same additive constant, finite program and polynomial running-time bound must work for all lengths and all eligible distributions.
cards.definitions:
Write \(S_n=\{0,1\}^n\) for all binary strings of length \(n\). A probability distribution on this finite set is any function \(p:S_n\to[0,1]\) with real values and \(\sum_xp(x)=1\). Its min-entropy is
\[
H_\infty(p)=-\log_2\!\left(\max_{x\in S_n}p(x)\right).
\]
Thus the required entropy condition means \(p(x)\le 1/(2^C n)\) for every string \(x\). Distributions need not be uniform on their support, rational, computable or efficiently samplable. Independence means that the joint distribution is \(\Pr[X=x,Y=y]=p(x)q(y)\). The output probability in the question is the finite sum
\[
\Pr[E_n(X,Y)=1]=\sum_{x,y\in S_n}p(x)q(y)\,\mathbf1_{\{E_n(x,y)=1\}}.
\]
The indicator is one when its subscripted condition holds and zero otherwise. For a single output bit, the displayed bias is its statistical distance from the uniform bit, where statistical distance between distributions \(r,s\) on a finite set is \(\frac12\sum_z|r(z)-s(z)|\). There is no conditioning on either source in this guarantee.

Computation uses a deterministic multitape Turing machine with a fixed finite program and fixed finite tape alphabet. Its read-only input is \(1^n\#x\#y\), where \(|x|=|y|=n\), and its work tapes initially contain blanks. One transition reads and writes at most one symbol on each tape and moves each tape head by at most one cell, costing one step. There are no random coins, oracle calls, auxiliary seed, advice or length-dependent precomputed tables. The machine must halt and output exactly one bit on every such input. There must be integers \(K,d\ge1\) such that this takes at most \(K(n+1)^d\) transitions for all \(n,x,y\), including inputs at lengths with no eligible sources. The input contains no distribution description or samples other than \(x,y\); \(C,K,d\) and the machine are fixed existential choices, independent of both distributions and of \(n\). Let \(\mathcal A\) be the class of all machines meeting this total polynomial-time evaluation condition, and write \(E^A_n\) for the function computed by a member \(A\).

Only the probability bound concerns the random choice of the two input strings; the evaluator itself is deterministic. When \(\log_2n+C>n\), no eligible distribution exists, so the extraction requirement at that length is vacuous. Using a nonnegative integer for the existential additive constant fixes a harmless convention: any fixed real constant can be increased to such an integer. The task has one output bit and fixed error \(1/100\); it does not demand arbitrarily small error, more output bits or resilience to tampering.

context_blocks.text: Li’s introduction and concluding open questions explicitly distinguish the optimal additive threshold \(\log_2n+O(1)\) from the achieved asymptotic order \(O(\log n)\). This card retains its existing one-bit, error-\(1/100\), uniform polynomial-time version of that question; it does not interpret the paper’s title as claiming the additive threshold.

The source records nonconstructive existence at \(\log_2n+O(1)\). Its Theorem 1.6 gives polynomial-time extraction for every fixed positive constant error when each source has at least \(c\log_2n\) entropy for a suitable fixed \(c>1\), even when the two sources’ bits are interleaved. The remaining distinction is the coefficient of the logarithm.

Extraction from arbitrary independent sources is stronger than merely requiring a function to take both values on every sufficiently large Cartesian product. The latter property is a two-source disperser and yields a bipartite Ramsey graph. The fixed small-bias guarantee here requires approximate balance, not only nonconstancy.

Li and Zhong’s 2024 construction adds resistance to separate tampering of the sources. Its constant-error, one-bit theorem still has an entropy requirement \(c\log n\), with a constant \(c>1\); it does not assert the additive threshold.

Oh and Shaltiel’s July 2026 revision constructs extractors under a computational hardness assumption for distributions generated by small circuits. It concerns a restricted source class and a conditional result, whereas the present target is unconditional and covers arbitrary independent distributions.

cards.why: The additive threshold asks whether polynomial-time evaluation can match the entropy scale available without an efficiency restriction, including its leading coefficient. It is a basic question about converting two independent imperfect sources into a nearly unbiased bit and has consequences for explicit Ramsey constructions.
cards.answer_criterion:
Give a complete mathematically correct Lean proof of the existence proposition, including one finite machine, its uniform polynomial-time bound and the probability guarantee for all eligible distributions. Alternatively, give a complete Lean proof of its logical negation: for every integer \(C\ge0\) and every \(A\in\mathcal A\), there exist \(n\ge1\) and distributions \(p,q\) on \(S_n\), each having min-entropy at least \(\log_2n+C\), for which
\[
\left|\sum_{x,y\in S_n}p(x)q(y)\mathbf1_{\{E^A_n(x,y)=1\}}-\frac12\right|>\frac1{100}.
\]
In this negation the length and distributions may depend on the machine and additive constant. A construction requiring \(c\log_2n\) entropy for an unspecified constant \(c>1\), nonuniform existence alone, or a conditional implication does not establish the displayed unconditional target.

cards.title: Unconditional subexponential simulation of BPP
cards.formal:
Is \(\mathrm{BPP}\subseteq\mathrm{SUBEXP}\) unconditionally? Here the subexponential class is the intersection
\[\mathrm{SUBEXP}=\bigcap_{k\ge1}\mathrm{DTIME}\!\left(2^{n^{1/k}}\right).\]
Thus, for every language \(L\subseteq\{0,1\}^{*}\) decidable with two-sided bounded error in randomized polynomial time, and for every integer \(k\ge1\), must there exist a deterministic algorithm deciding \(L\) on every input in time \(O(2^{n^{1/k}})\)? The algorithm and the constant in its time bound may depend on \(L,k\). The target selects the subexponential question in the source's Open Problem 3.4; its separate quasipolynomial-time question is stronger.
cards.why: This asks whether randomness can provide a much larger speedup than the usual derandomization conjectures predict, even after allowing deterministic time far beyond polynomial. An unconditional simulation would move the general worst-case upper bound into the source’s much smaller subexponential class. A counterexample would establish a major separation between randomized and deterministic computation.
cards.status_note: Open Problem 3.4 and Definition 3.1 of Vadhan were read directly on 2026-09-14. A bounded later-literature search found conditional and restricted derandomization results but no unconditional all-input containment of BPP in the source’s SUBEXP class.

sentences: BPP contains decision problems solved efficiently using random bits with bounded error on every input.
The question asks whether all of them have exact deterministic simulations in the class SUBEXP.
Here SUBEXP requires a simulation in time two to the n-to-epsilon power for every fixed positive epsilon.
The simulator may depend on the chosen exponent, but it must work on every input without advice or assumptions.
Known general brute-force simulations take larger exponential time, while stronger derandomization theorems rely on unproved hardness.

cards.definitions:
A language is a set of finite binary strings. An algorithm decides \(L\) if it halts and outputs one exactly on inputs in \(L\), and zero on all other inputs. Use uniform multitape Turing machines with finite descriptions independent of input length. One transition costs one time unit. A randomized machine may additionally request independent unbiased bits, at unit cost per bit. It has no advice, oracle or preprocessing that depends on input length without being computed by the machine.

Membership in \(\mathrm{BPP}\) means that there are such a randomized machine \(M\) and constants \(a,C\ge1\) with worst-case runtime at most \(C(n+1)^a\) on every length-\(n\) input and every random tape, and with
\[x\in L\Rightarrow\Pr[M(x)=1]\ge2/3,\qquad x\notin L\Rightarrow\Pr[M(x)=1]\le1/3.\]
This is a class of total decision problems. The acceptance-probability gap holds on every input; it is not a promise that an external user must supply.

The notation \(L\in\mathrm{DTIME}(2^{n^{1/k}})\) means that a deterministic machine decides \(L\) and has worst-case runtime at most \(C_k\lceil2^{n^{1/k}}\rceil\) for all sufficiently large \(n\), for some fixed \(C_k\). All finitely many smaller inputs must also be decided correctly and with termination. Requiring every integer \(k\) is equivalent to requiring time \(O(2^{n^\varepsilon})\) for every fixed real \(\varepsilon>0\). The machine is allowed to change with the exponent; an effective compiler taking \(M,k\) and producing the simulator is not an additional requirement.

This definition of SUBEXP is the source's intersection of subpower-exponential time classes. A single \(2^{o(n)}\)-time bound, such as \(2^{n/\log n}\), need not meet it. Likewise, correctness only on most inputs, or on infinitely many input lengths, is insufficient. The simulator must decide the same language exactly on all strings.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct Lean-checked proof of the inclusion or its negation. A positive proof must cover every BPP language and every fixed exponent \(1/k\), without a hardness assumption, oracle or advice. A negative proof must establish a language in BPP that is outside one of the deterministic time classes in the displayed intersection. A conditional simulation, a simulation for a particular randomized problem, or a heuristic correct on almost all inputs does not settle the question.

context_blocks.text: Enumerating every random tape gives a deterministic simulation in \(2^{\mathrm{poly}(n)}\) time. A polynomial-time randomized algorithm can use polynomially many random bits, so this direct simulation gives EXP rather than the displayed SUBEXP target.
If \(\mathrm{BPP}=\mathrm P\), the desired inclusion follows. The converse is not asserted: a subexponential simulator may still take much more than polynomial time.

Known hardness-versus-randomness theorems yield much stronger derandomization under suitable circuit lower-bound assumptions. For example, the Impagliazzo–Wigderson theorem derives BPP = P from exponential circuit hardness for a language computable in single-exponential time. Those hardness hypotheses are part of the conditional theorem and cannot be removed by citing it.

Fixing a good random tape separately for each length gives a nonuniform object. Uniformity requires a finite deterministic algorithm that computes its behavior; a sequence of good tapes supplied for free does not meet the target.

cards.title: Does arithmetic formula hardness derandomize identity testing?
cards.formal: Does \(H_{\mathrm{form}}\Rightarrow D_{\mathrm{form}}\) hold over \(\mathbb Q\)? Here \(H_{\mathrm{form}}\) asserts that there exists an explicit family \(f_m\in\mathbb Q[x_1,\ldots,x_m]\) of multilinear polynomials with \(L_{\mathrm{form}}(f_m)=m^{\omega(1)}\), in the precise sense below. The assertion \(D_{\mathrm{form}}\) is that, for every real \(\varepsilon>0\), polynomial identity testing for unrestricted arithmetic formulas has a uniform deterministic algorithm taking time \(2^{O(N^{\varepsilon})}\), where \(N\) is the input's bit length. This card selects the hardness-to-derandomization branch of the source's two-direction question; it asks for subexponential time, without requiring polynomial time.

source_formulation.text: For example, does super-polynomial lower bounds for arithmetic formulas imply non-trivial deterministic algorithms for PIT for arithmetic formulas, and vice-versa?
source_formulation.caption: Complete selected source sentence; PDF p. 3

cards.why: This asks whether hardness against arithmetic computation without shared subexpressions already suffices to remove randomness from identity testing in that same fundamental model. A resolution would clarify whether the central circuit hardness–randomness principle survives the restriction to formulas, connecting algebraic lower bounds with deterministic symbolic computation.
cards.status_note: The selected forward branch is explicitly motivated by the 2018 source and repeated in its 2019 journal version; a 2019 survey also poses a stronger polynomial-time version. A bounded primary-source review through 16 September 2026 found no verified resolution of the stated unrestricted-formula implication. The checked 2025 uniform-network and border-determinant results, and the 2026 read-4 algorithm, have materially different hypotheses or models. This records bounded review, not an exhaustive certification of current openness. The source quotation retains its original two-direction wording; the formal target explicitly selects the forward subexponential branch.

progress.text: Kabanets and Impagliazzo prove the general-circuit forward tradeoff and a Boolean-or-algebraic lower-bound consequence of derandomizing formula PIT.
Chou, Kumar and Solomon state the unrestricted-formula question while proving a conditional PIT result for bounded-depth circuits using a low-degree hardness hypothesis.
The expanded journal paper repeats the formula question and gives the exact coefficient-list explicitness definition used here.
Andrews, Kush and Tell give a polynomial-time PIT equivalence for uniform arithmetic networks under a different, almost-all-inputs hardness condition.
Andrews constructs a generator for polynomial-size formulas under a specific border-formula lower bound for the determinant.
Kaplan and Shpilka obtain polynomial-time white-box and quasipolynomial-time black-box PIT for read-4 formulas, a restricted subclass of the target model.

importance.reason: A central structural question joining algebraic formula lower bounds to derandomization in the same computation model. It probes the scope of a foundational hardness–randomness principle and has consequences for deterministic polynomial identity testing beyond a narrow circuit subclass. The score reflects this broad conceptual reach, not the venue or the former provisional midpoint.

sentences: An arithmetic formula is a tree of additions and multiplications with rational constants and commuting variables.
Assume a coefficient-explicit multilinear polynomial family eventually requires formulas larger than every fixed polynomial in its variable count.
Must there then be deterministic identity testers for every unrestricted formula in time 2^{O(N^epsilon)} for every epsilon > 0?
The selected target is the forward, subexponential branch of the original two-direction question.
Known later results change the hardness assumption or restrict the formula model; the bounded review found no verified resolution of this implication.

cards.definitions:
An arithmetic formula over \(\mathbb Q\) is a finite rooted binary tree. Each leaf is labeled by a rational constant or a variable, and each internal node by addition or multiplication. It computes its polynomial in commuting variables by the indicated operations; there are no division or exponentiation gates and no shared internal subcomputations. Negative rational constants are allowed. Its size is its number of edges. Let \(L_{\mathrm{form}}(f)\) be the minimum size among formulas computing exactly \(f\). Rational constants of arbitrary bit length are permitted in this minimum, and their bit lengths are not charged to this algebraic size. The lower bound is against every formula, with no depth, read-count, homogeneity or intermediate multilinearity restriction. A polynomial is multilinear when each variable has exponent at most one in every monomial. Explicitness of \((f_m)_{m\ge1}\) means that there are positive integers \(a,b,C\) and one deterministic Turing machine which, on unary input \(1^m\), outputs the ordered list of all \(2^m\) rational coefficients of \(f_m\) in time at most \(2^{a m+C}\), and every coefficient has numerator/denominator bit length at most \(C(m+1)^b\). The order is lexicographic on exponent vectors in \(\{0,1\}^m\); zero coefficients are included. Coefficients are written as a signed binary numerator and positive binary denominator in reduced form. The assertion \(L_{\mathrm{form}}(f_m)=m^{\omega(1)}\) means \(\forall k\in\mathbb N_{\ge1}\ \exists m_0\ \forall m\ge m_0:\ L_{\mathrm{form}}(f_m)>m^k\). Thus the hard family is uniform in its coefficient generation, while the competing formulas are nonuniform. For PIT the input is an arbitrary formula, with its tree and gate labels explicitly supplied, variable indices in binary, and rational constants in binary numerator/denominator form. Use the following prefix encoding. For a nonnegative integer \(r\), let \(\ell\) be the bit length of \(r+1\) and write \(\ell\) one-bits, one zero-bit and the \(\ell\)-bit binary representation of \(r+1\). A signed integer \(p\) is represented by this code for \(2p\) when \(p\ge0\), and for \(-2p-1\) otherwise. A rational is its signed-numerator code followed by its positive-denominator code, with numerator and denominator coprime. The four two-bit formula tags are 00 for a rational leaf (followed by that rational code), 01 for a variable leaf (followed by its positive integer index), 10 for addition and 11 for multiplication. Each internal-node tag is followed recursively by the encodings of its left and right children. No trailing bits are permitted. Let \(N\) be the total encoding length. The hard-family coefficient list uses the same rational encoding, concatenated in the specified order. The required output is whether the computed formal polynomial has every coefficient zero. The tester may examine the formula description (white-box access); a black-box hitting-set construction is not required. There is no promise that the input computes a multilinear polynomial. Time is measured in bit operations of a deterministic Turing machine, including reading constants, and the tester uses neither randomness nor advice nor an oracle. More precisely, for every \(\varepsilon>0\) there must be a machine \(A_\varepsilon\), constants \(c_\varepsilon,C_\varepsilon>0\), and a threshold \(N_\varepsilon\) such that it is correct on every valid formula and takes at most \(C_\varepsilon 2^{c_\varepsilon N^\varepsilon}\) steps on every formula of length \(N\ge N_\varepsilon\). Machines and constants may depend on \(\varepsilon\), but not on the input. The implication concerns existence of these algorithms; it does not additionally require a uniform compiler from descriptions of hard families to testers.

For the stated bit costs, a deterministic multitape Turing machine has one read-only input tape, finitely many initially blank work tapes, fixed finite control and alphabet, and one head on each tape. One transition reads the symbols under the heads, changes state, writes at most one symbol on each work tape and moves each head by at most one cell; it may append at most one output bit. Each transition costs one. Tape cells are indexed by nonnegative integers and a left move at zero stays there. The program and tape count are independent of input length. Malformed encodings may be rejected; correctness and the displayed clocks are required on every valid encoded instance.
cards.answer_criterion:
Give a mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of the full implication \(H_{\mathrm{form}}\Rightarrow D_{\mathrm{form}}\), or a Lean-checked refutation establishing \(H_{\mathrm{form}}\land\neg D_{\mathrm{form}}\) under exactly the definitions above. A positive answer must cover unrestricted rational arithmetic formulas and every \(\varepsilon>0\). A result assuming lower bounds against general circuits, exponential formula hardness, a particular stronger border-complexity hypothesis, or hardness only for an additionally constrained polynomial family does not by itself prove this implication. A restricted-depth, bounded-read or noncommutative PIT algorithm alone is insufficient. This is a logical implication; proving the hard-family hypothesis unconditionally is not required for a positive answer.

Equivalently, failure of \(D_{\mathrm{form}}\) means there is an \(\varepsilon>0\) such that, for every uniform deterministic machine \(A\) that halts with the correct PIT answer on every valid formula, all positive constants \(c,C\), and every length threshold \(N_0\), there is a valid formula \(F\) of encoding length \(N\ge N_0\) on which \(A\) takes more than \(C2^{cN^\varepsilon}\) transitions. A refutation must establish this failure together with the hard-family hypothesis.

context_blocks.text: The 2018 source asks about both directions between formula lower bounds and nontrivial deterministic PIT. The chosen branch tests whether the usual superpolynomial hardness-to-subexponential-time principle for circuits also holds for formulas. The source's formal coefficient-list definition supplies the explicitness condition used here.

For general arithmetic circuits, Kabanets and Impagliazzo establish the corresponding forward tradeoff: superpolynomial hardness of an explicit multilinear family gives deterministic PIT in time with arbitrarily small positive powers in the exponent. A stronger hardness assumption gives quasipolynomial time. Circuit hardness is a stronger hypothesis than formula hardness.

The reverse direction depends on how the tester accesses its input. A black-box hitting set is a finite set of evaluation points on which every nonzero polynomial in the specified formula class is nonzero somewhere. Such constructions imply algebraic lower bounds. An arbitrary white-box tester need not provide a hitting set. The known white-box formula-PIT consequence in Kabanets–Impagliazzo is a disjunction: either a nondeterministic exponential-time language has no polynomial-size Boolean circuits, or the permanent has no polynomial-size division-free integer arithmetic formulas. It is not stated as the converse of this card's single explicit-family hypothesis.
The 2019 survey explicitly poses a stronger forward formula question with a polynomial-time conclusion. The present target retains the weaker subexponential conclusion from the 2018 question.

The 2025 polynomial-time PIT equivalence uses hardness against uniform arithmetic networks with PIT gates on almost all individual inputs. Its model and hardness condition differ from the nonuniform formula-size hypothesis here.

Another 2025 theorem gives a hitting-set generator for formulas assuming a stronger, specific lower bound: superpolynomial border-formula complexity of the determinant. Border complexity permits polynomials arising as limits of computations, and its lower bound is not supplied merely by the hypothesis in this card.
The 2026 read-4 result supplies deterministic PIT algorithms when each variable occurs at most four times in a formula. The target here permits an unbounded number of occurrences and arbitrary depth.

checked_sources: The source's unrestricted-formula sentence is different from its numbered Question 1 about bounded-depth circuits. Theorem 3 does not answer the general formula question. Retain ordinary commutative rational formulas of unrestricted depth and variable reuse; do not silently move to multilinear formulas, bounded-read formulas, ABPs, noncommutative formulas or a general circuit lower-bound hypothesis.

Quantifier recovery: CCC 2018 p. 13:2 footnote 3 explicitly points to subexponential versus quasipolynomial time depending on hardness. Its referenced KI 2004 Theorem 7.7, visually checked on pp. 36–37, states s_p(m) in m^{omega(1)} and time 2^{n^epsilon} for every epsilon > 0; the stronger 2^{m^{Omega(1)}} hardness gives quasipolynomial time. Thus the proposed formula analogue uses almost-everywhere superpolynomial growth, not merely an infinitely-often failure of membership in a polynomial-size class. This is an explicit recovery of the cited tradeoff, not a claim that the informal 2018 sentence itself writes all these quantifiers.

Explicitness follows CCC 2018 Definition 10 (p. 13:8), confirmed by journal 2019 Definition 4.7 (p. 12): all coefficient bit lengths are polynomial, and all 2^m coefficients are listed in 2^{O(m)} time. Do not replace this with the stronger per-coefficient polynomial-time condition suggested by an informal journal introduction footnote. Restricting to Q follows the paper's setup; no extension to every field is demanded. Multilinearity applies to the hypothetical hard polynomial family only, not to the circuits that are lower-bounded or the PIT inputs.

Algebraic hardness size counts wires and permits arbitrary rational constants without charging their bit lengths, matching the source's circuit convention. Binary fan-in is a harmless normalization: each unbounded-fan-in formula gate can be replaced by a binary tree with only linear size change. Rational signs can be represented by constants. There is no division or compressed power operation. PIT is a conventional white-box decision problem on the full finite formula description; its bit cost includes constants. Its bit length and reasonable alternative prefix encodings are polynomially related, which leaves membership in the intersection over all epsilon > 0 of DTIME(2^{N^epsilon}) invariant.

The source's displayed bounded-depth runtime is expressed in variables, size and degree. For an explicitly supplied formula, degree and number of distinct variables are at most linear in its tree size, while all input coefficient bits are part of N. The proposed total-bit-length SUBEXP formulation is the ordinary decision-language version of the selected nontrivial runtime regime. It does not demand subexponential complexity independently of arbitrarily large input coefficient encodings or a polynomial-time algorithm. Each epsilon may have a different uniform deterministic machine; no input-length advice, oracle or random coins are allowed.

The existence implication deliberately does not add an effective uniform compiler accepting the generator of any hard family or a proof of its lower bound. The mathematical family is uniform through its coefficient-list algorithm; its lower bound applies to nonuniform formulas. A positive proof is conditional on H and need not construct an unconditional superpolynomial lower bound. A negative proof must establish H and failure of the full D, not merely failure of a particular generator construction.

The saved 'vice-versa' cannot automatically be read as D iff exactly H. KI 2004 Theorem 4.9, visually inspected on p. 25, excludes simultaneous NEXP subset P/poly, polynomial-size division-free integer formulas for permanent, and infinitely-often nondeterministic SUBEXP AFIT. It gives a Boolean-or-arithmetic disjunction, not H alone. Black-box hitting sets give algebraic hardness by a different theorem; a general white-box tester need not output a hitting set. The 2019 survey distinguishes these issues in Sections 3.1–3.2, PDF pp. 7–9. The forward selection preserves a genuine explicitly sourced branch without silently asserting a stronger equivalence.

Kumar–Saptharishi 2019 Question 4.14 (PDF p. 21, repeated pp. 29–30) asks the stronger polynomial-time forward question. It corroborates the significance of the formula branch but does not authorize replacing this card's original nontrivial/subexponential target by polynomial time. That survey is used as a primary source for its own open-question formulation, not as a substitute for checking the newer theorem statements.

Bounded later review: actual 2025 TR25-042 Theorems 1.2–1.3, printed p. 3/PDF p. 5, use strongly uniform circuits and uniform arithmetic networks with PIT gates, together with hardness on every sufficiently late individual input. This is materially different from H. Actual CCC 2025 Theorem 1.2, p. 15:7, assumes superpolynomial border-formula complexity specifically of determinant; p. 15:8 emphasizes this distinction. No PIT runtime is inferred just from a generator's existence or a small stretch. Actual TR26-076 abstract and Section 1.1 concern read-4 only. A bounded ECCC PIT-index check and targeted primary searches through the review date found no matching full theorem; this is not exhaustive status certification.

The KI PDF has corrupted extracted character encodings. Cache its original PDF, retain its raw .txt with this caveat, and rely on the visually verified pp. 25 and 36–37 for the cited statements. Other cached PDF/text pairs use prefix formula-hvr-. Source metadata for the journal version were verified on its publisher page: revised 30 January 2019, published 1 November 2019. CCC 2025 publication was 29 July, not the arXiv submission date; ECCC read-4 report date and publication timestamp differ by one day and both are recorded.

Importance was genuinely unassessed at 50. Recommend 90 independently for the forward branch: it asks whether a foundational correspondence survives the difference between circuits and formulas, coupling two major themes with broad implications for symbolic computation. Preserve the existing category. This is a yes/no conditional implication, so numerical 1/100 acceptance and asymptotic-curve approximation do not apply.

User scope decision received on 2026-09-16: select the precisely supported forward implication from formula lower bounds to deterministic subexponential PIT. The saved two-direction quotation is preserved, and the chosen branch is disclosed in formal, context and status. The user confirmed this choice before canonical completion.

Root added an exact prefix encoding and multitape bit-step model so no representation choice remains. The coefficient generator receives unary m and writes the same rational code. These polynomially related encodings preserve the all-epsilon SUBEXP convention. The expanded negative criterion is H together with a fixed epsilon that defeats every correct total deterministic PIT machine under every exponential coefficient and length threshold.

cards.title: Explicit near-optimal vertex expanders
cards.formal: Is the following proposition true? For every rational \(\delta>0\), there exists an integer \(d_0\ge3\) such that, for every integer \(d\ge d_0\), there exist a rational \(\eta\in(0,1/2)\), real \(K>0\), integer \(a\ge1\), and one deterministic multitape Turing machine \(A\) which, for every integer \(j\ge1\) supplied in unary, outputs a finite simple undirected \(d\)-regular graph \(G_j\) within \(K(j+1)^a\) bit operations, with strictly increasing vertex counts \(n_j=|V(G_j)|\), and such that \[|\Gamma_{G_j}(S)\setminus S|\ \ge\ (d-2-\delta)|S|\qquad\text{for every }S\subseteq V(G_j)\text{ with }1\le |S|\le\eta n_j?\]
cards.why: Random regular graphs have almost the largest possible external neighborhood for every small set. Matching that additive guarantee by deterministic constructions would sharpen a central benchmark for expanders, with consequences for combinatorial structures underlying coding, routing and pseudorandomness.
cards.status_note: Uncertain after individual review on 2026-09-16. The original Open Problem 10.8 states the sharp additive external-neighbor bound d-2-delta. The 2025 lossless-expander paper cites that historical problem while its displayed main theorem establishes arbitrarily small fixed relative loss at sufficiently large degree. The review did not verify a theorem meeting the literal additive target and quantifier order. This card therefore neither claims the target resolved nor certifies its continued openness.

cards.definitions:
A finite simple undirected graph has no loops or multiple edges. It is \(d\)-regular if each vertex has exactly \(d\) distinct neighbors. Its labeled vertex set is \([n_j]=\{1,\ldots,n_j\}\). For \(S\subseteq[n_j]\), define
\[
\Gamma_{G_j}(S)=\{v\in[n_j]:\ \exists u\in S,\ \{u,v\}\in E(G_j)\}.
\]
The left side in the target counts distinct neighbors outside \(S\), not edges leaving \(S\), not neighbors counted with multiplicity, and not neighbors inside \(S\). The cutoff \(\eta n_j\) is a real number; the condition is imposed on every integer set size satisfying the displayed inequality. Empty sets impose no requirement. The same positive \(\eta\) works for the entire family at the fixed values of \(\delta,d\).

The output of \(A\) is \(n_j\) in binary followed by an explicit list of the edges, each an unordered pair of distinct binary vertex labels, with delimiters. Isolated vertices would still be specified by \(n_j\), although none occur for \(d\ge3\). Reading the unary index, all computation and every output bit count in the bound. The machine has a finite program, no random bits, advice, oracle or uncharged preprocessing. It must work on every \(1^j\), not merely on infinitely many selected indices. The integers \(n_j\) must increase strictly, so the construction gives arbitrarily large graphs; an allowed family need not contain every admissible vertex count.

The degree threshold \(d_0\) may depend on \(\delta\). After \(d\) is fixed, the machine \(A\) and constants \(\eta,K,a\) may depend on both \(\delta,d\), but not on \(j\) or \(S\). No algorithm uniform in \(\delta,d\) is required. The construction requirement is the survey's mild explicitness convention, polynomial time in the family index, with full output charged. It does not additionally require computing one neighbor in time polynomial in \(\log n_j\). Restricting positive \(\delta\) and the small-set fraction to rationals loses no expansion guarantee: a smaller positive rational tolerance or fraction can be chosen when needed.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct Lean proof of the entire proposition, including the explicit algorithm families, their cost bounds and the expansion inequality for all indicated sets, or a complete Lean proof of its negation. Random existence alone is insufficient. A construction with a relative loss tending to zero as degree grows does not meet this additive-loss target without a proof of the displayed bound with the stated quantifier order. A result for one degree or a one-sided bipartite expansion promise does not by itself establish the proposition.

context_blocks.text: The saved survey explicitly asks for \(d-2-\delta\) external vertex expansion for every sufficiently large degree, with a positive small-set fraction depending on \(d,\delta\). Definitions 2.3 and 4.6 supply the mild explicitness and external-neighborhood conventions; it does not replace the question by a relative \((1-\varepsilon)d\) target.

Theorem 4.16 shows that random regular graphs have the displayed small-set expansion asymptotically. This establishes the combinatorial feasibility of the bound, not a deterministic polynomial-time family.

Hsieh, Lubotzky, Mohanty, Reiner and Zhang give explicit lossless expanders: for every fixed \(\varepsilon>0\), all sufficiently large degrees admit a \((1-\varepsilon)d\) distinct-neighbor guarantee. Their introduction cites the survey question as a longstanding problem addressed by their construction.

The two quantitative formulations are not identical. A degree threshold depending on \(\varepsilon\) does not by itself justify taking \(\varepsilon\) proportional to \(1/d\) at the same degree. Moreover, counting all distinct neighbors and counting only external neighbors differ. The review therefore does not infer the exact additive \(d-2-\delta\) proposition from the stated relative-loss theorem.

The retained status is uncertain because the limited review has not established the present status of this sharper literal survey formulation after the lossless-expander breakthrough. The formulation is precise, and the original source question is preserved; the uncertainty concerns current resolution, not a license to claim the broader historical problem remains unsolved.

cards.title: Pseudorandom generators from hitting-set generators
cards.formal:
Does the existence of a polynomial-time hitting-set generator secure against all polynomial-size Boolean circuits imply the existence of a polynomial-time pseudorandom generator secure against all such circuits, in the cryptographic regime defined below? In symbols, decide
\[
\bigl(\exists H\;\operatorname{HSG}(H)\bigr)
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
\bigl(\exists G\;\operatorname{PRG}(G)\bigr).
\]
Both generators must be uniform, have a seed shorter than their output, and meet their respective security conditions with negligible error. Their seed lengths, negligible functions and polynomial running-time bounds may differ. This is an implication between existence statements; it does not require an algorithm that compiles a given hitting-set generator into a pseudorandom generator.

source_formulation.text: There are proof techniques that enable derandomizing two-sided-error randomized algorithms using a hitting set generator [12]; however, it is unknown if a hitting set generator […]
source_formulation.caption: Truncated source excerpt (at most 25 words); PDF p. 2

cards.why: This asks whether hitting dense sets and reproducing acceptance probabilities have the same existential power when a uniform efficient generator must withstand arbitrarily stronger polynomial-size tests. Pseudorandom generators are foundational cryptographic objects connected to one-way functions, while the weaker hitting guarantee arises naturally from errorless average-case hardness. A resolution would clarify whether these two notions represent distinct assumptions about computational randomness, rather than merely improve the parameters of one construction.
cards.status_note: The selected cryptographic question is explicitly open in Santhanam 2020 and is highlighted again in the 2022 source. The 2022 positive theorem has seed-prefix and NC1/poly restrictions. The checked 2023 conditional equivalence and 2024–2026 results use different assumptions, adversaries or targets. Individual primary-source reading and a bounded later-work search completed on 16 September 2026 found no resolution of the stated existence implication. This supports a dated source-open classification, not a claim of exhaustive current verification.

progress.text: Santhanam explicitly asks whether HSGs and PRGs are equivalent in the cryptographic regime. Section 2.2 fixes the default security error to negligible, the generator time to a fixed polynomial in output length, and the tests to arbitrary polynomial-size circuits.

Hirahara and Santhanam revisit the question and prove Theorem 28 for seed-extending generators against \(\mathrm{NC}^{1}/\mathrm{poly}\), meaning nonuniform polynomial-size Boolean circuits of logarithmic depth. That special case is distinct from the unrestricted polynomial-size test class of this card.

Under the Meta-Complexity Padding Conjecture, Hirahara proves related equivalences involving HSGs, PRGs and one-way functions against uniform randomized polynomial-time algorithms with infinitely-often security. The conditional hypothesis, adversary model and length quantifiers differ from the present target.

cards.definitions:
For an integer \(m\ge 0\), let \(U_m\) denote the uniform distribution on the \(2^m\) binary strings of length \(m\). Output lengths are integers \(N\ge 2\). An admissible generator family \(F=(F_N)_{N\ge 2}\) has a seed-length function \(s:\{2,3,\ldots\}\to\mathbb N\) with \(1\le s(N)<N\) and maps \(F_N:\{0,1\}^{s(N)}\to\{0,1\}^{N}\). One deterministic multitape Turing machine computes \(s(N)\) from \(1^N\), and another computes \(F_N(z)\) from \((1^N,z)\) for every seed \(z\). Here \(1^N\) is the unary encoding of \(N\). There are constants \(A,b\ge 1\), depending only on the family, such that each computation takes at most \(A(N+1)^b\) steps. In particular, time is polynomial in the output length. A machine has finite control, one read-only input tape and a fixed finite number of initially blank work tapes with a fixed finite alphabet. In one step each head reads and may move by at most one cell, each work head may write one symbol, and at most one output bit may be appended. All tapes start at their first cell and are indexed by nonnegative integers; a left move at zero stays at zero. The generator input is the literal string \(1^N\#z\), and the seed-length output is the binary encoding of \(s(N)\). The machine programs and tape counts are independent of \(N\). These machines receive no advice, oracle or randomness. The output need not contain the seed, and different seeds may have the same output.

A test at length \(N\) is an arbitrary deterministic Boolean circuit \(C:\{0,1\}^{N}\to\{0,1\}\), with AND and OR gates of fan-in two, NOT gates of fan-in one, constant gates, unrestricted fan-out and unrestricted depth. Its size is its number of gates, excluding the input nodes. There is no uniformity requirement on tests at different lengths. Security against polynomial-size circuits means the quantifier \(\forall c\in\mathbb N_{\ge 1}\) followed by a threshold length that may depend on \(c\), and then a guarantee for every circuit of size at most \(N^c\) at every larger length.

A function \(\nu:\{2,3,\ldots\}\to(0,1]\) is negligible if for every integer \(a\ge 1\) there is an integer \(N_a\) such that \(\nu(N)\le N^{-a}\) for all \(N\ge N_a\). No computability assumption is imposed on a security-bound function.

For an admissible family \(H\) with seed length \(s\), the property \(\operatorname{HSG}(H)\) means that there exists a negligible function \(\varepsilon\) such that
\[
\forall c\in\mathbb N_{\ge 1}\ \exists N_c\ge 2\ \forall N\ge N_c\ \forall C\text{ of size at most }N^c,
\]
\[
\Pr_{x\sim U_N}[C(x)=1]\ge\varepsilon(N)
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
\exists z\in\{0,1\}^{s(N)}\; C(H_N(z))=1.
\]
The hit is an existence guarantee; it need not occur with any specified fraction of seeds.

For an admissible family \(G\) with its own seed length \(t\), the property \(\operatorname{PRG}(G)\) means that there exists a negligible function \(\eta\) such that
\[
\forall c\in\mathbb N_{\ge 1}\ \exists M_c\ge 2\ \forall N\ge M_c\ \forall C\text{ of size at most }N^c,
\]
\[
\left|\Pr_{z\sim U_{t(N)}}[C(G_N(z))=1]
-\Pr_{x\sim U_N}[C(x)=1]\right|\le\eta(N).
\]
Thus generated outputs are sampled by a uniform seed, with multiplicity when seeds collide. The same generator and the same negligible function must serve every circuit-size exponent. In the implication, all generator, seed-length, time-bound and security-bound witnesses are existentially quantified separately on the two sides.
cards.answer_criterion: An accepted answer is a complete, mathematically correct Lean proof of the stated existence implication or of its negation. A positive answer must establish the existence of a generator satisfying the full PRG definition whenever a generator satisfying the HSG definition exists. A negative answer must establish that an HSG as defined exists while no PRG as defined exists, in the stated ordinary model. A theorem restricted to a smaller test class, additional hardness assumptions, infinitely many lengths, or the impossibility of a particular conversion method does not decide this implication.

context_blocks.text: A hitting-set generator guarantees that every sufficiently dense efficiently recognizable set contains at least one generated string. A pseudorandom generator controls each test's acceptance probability under a uniformly selected seed. The question asks whether the first kind of efficiently generated object already entails the existence of the second.

The 2022 source raises a broad conversion question in its introduction and footnote 2. This card explicitly selects the cryptographic existence question stated earlier as Question 6 in Santhanam's 2020 paper, which the 2022 discussion cites. The defaults in Section 2.2 of that paper specify polynomial time in output length, arbitrary polynomial-size circuit tests and negligible error. The seed may have any nontrivial length; neither a prescribed stretch nor preservation of parameters is part of the target. Unary output-length input and polynomial-time computation of the seed length make the uniform-family convention explicit.

The 2022 paper proves a different positive result for seed-extending generators tested by polynomial-size circuits of logarithmic depth. Seed-extending means that the seed is a prefix of the output. The restrictions on both generator form and test class are part of that theorem. It does not settle the cryptographic implication above.

cards.title: Linear-seed hardness-to-randomness sampling
cards.formal:
Does there exist one explicit family of point samplers
\[H_{\ell,s}:\{0,1\}^{d(\ell,s)}\to(\{0,1\}^{\ell})^{m(\ell,s)}\]
and absolute constants \(C\ge1\) and rational \(\beta\in(0,1)\) with the following property for every pair of integers \(\ell\ge1\), \(s\ge2\)? The lengths obey
\[d(\ell,s)\le C\ell,\qquad \max\{1,\lfloor s^{\beta}\rfloor\}\le m(\ell,s)\le s.\]
For every Boolean function \(f:\{0,1\}^{\ell}\to\{0,1\}\) satisfying
\[\forall B\text{ of size at most }s,\quad\Pr_{x\sim U_{\ell}}[B(x)=f(x)]\le\tfrac12+\tfrac1s,\]
form the \(m\)-bit generator
\[G_f(z)=f(H_{\ell,s}(z)_1)\,f(H_{\ell,s}(z)_2)\cdots f(H_{\ell,s}(z)_m).\]
Must it then satisfy
\[\forall D\text{ of size at most }m,\quad\bigl|\Pr_{z\sim U_d}[D(G_f(z))=1]-\Pr_{u\sim U_m}[D(u)=1]\bigr|\le1/m?\]
The circuits, explicitness and probability spaces are defined below. The sampler is chosen independently of \(f\); each output bit of \(G_f\) is exactly one evaluation of \(f\) at the corresponding sampled point.
cards.why: This asks whether strong average-case hardness can be converted into many pseudorandom bits while using a seed only a constant factor longer than one input to the hard function, and preserving an especially simple evaluation form. Such a result would make the hardness-to-randomness connection more modular and usable across different computational classes. The restriction concerns the structure of the transformation, not merely the final existence of a short-seed generator.

A bounded later-literature search and comparison with the 2022 nearly optimal generator theorem found no resolution of the exact sampled-evaluation transformation under ordinary average-case circuit hardness. This is a dated source-open target with a bounded later check.

sentences: A hard Boolean function can provide pseudorandom bits by being evaluated at carefully correlated inputs.
The question asks for a uniform sampler using only a constant multiple of one input length as its random seed.
It must produce polynomially many bits in the hardness parameter, each from exactly one evaluation of the original function.
Every function with the specified average-case circuit hardness must yield a generator fooling the stated circuits to inverse-output-length error.
General short-seed transformations and newer results under stronger hardness assumptions do not automatically preserve this required evaluation form.

cards.definitions:
\(U_t\) denotes the uniform distribution on \(t\)-bit strings. The probabilities in the premise and conclusion use fresh independent uniform strings of the indicated lengths. They are computational distinguishability guarantees, not statistical closeness against unbounded tests.

A Boolean circuit is a finite acyclic graph with input wires, free Boolean constants, fan-in-two AND and OR gates, unary NOT gates, and one output wire. Size counts computation gates, including NOT gates, but not input wires or constants. The circuits \(B\) and \(D\) are deterministic and completely nonuniform; \(B\) has \(\ell\) inputs and \(D\) has \(m\). Their choices may depend on all parameters and on \(f\). They have no oracle access to \(f\). Allowing additional independent random input wires does not change these guarantees, because fixing the random bits gives a deterministic circuit of no greater size and averaging preserves the displayed inequalities. The premise means that even the best size-\(s\) predictor has advantage at most \(1/s\) over a fair guess.

Explicitness is uniform deterministic polynomial-time computation of the sampler. There are fixed multitape Turing machines and integers \(K,q\ge1\) such that the parameter machine on \((1^{\ell},s)\), with \(s\) binary, outputs integer lengths \(d,m\), and the evaluation machine on \((1^{\ell},s,z)\) writes the ordered list of all \(m\) sampled \(\ell\)-bit strings. Each runs in at most \(K(\ell+s+1)^q\) steps on valid inputs. Equivalently the time can be polynomial in \(\ell+m\), because of the polynomial relationship between \(s\) and \(m\). All preprocessing and output writing are counted. There is no advice, oracle, hard-function description or hard-function truth table available to these machines.

The constants and the machines precede the parameters, and \(H_{\ell,s}\) precedes the universal quantifier over \(f\). The family must be computed even for parameter pairs at which no function satisfies the hardness premise; its implication is then vacuous. No algorithm recognizing hard functions is required. The function \(f\) need not itself be efficiently computable: this is a transformation guarantee conditional on its finite-length circuit hardness, not a claim that such hard functions have been constructed. When \(f\) is also computable within a suitable exponential-time bound, the transformation has the usual derandomization applications.

The normalization \(m\le s\) and the lower bound using \(\lfloor s^{\beta}\rfloor\) express the source's polynomially many output bits. A larger qualifying output can be truncated, and fixed multiplicative factors in a polynomial lower bound can be absorbed by reducing \(\beta\) and handling finitely many small hardness parameters. The single-evaluation requirement excludes encoding or otherwise transforming the truth table of \(f\) before producing the output bits.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct Lean-checked proof or refutation of the stated sampler-family claim. A positive proof must supply the uniform sampler and constants and establish the implication for every promised \(f\), including the linear seed bound, polynomial output length and size-\(m\), error-\(1/m\) guarantee. A negative proof must rule out all such families, not merely one combinatorial-design construction or one kind of security reduction. A general hardness-to-randomness generator that encodes the hard function or combines several evaluations per output bit does not answer this sampling question.

context_blocks.text: The Nisan–Wigderson construction evaluates the hard function at correlated points determined by a combinatorial design. The source obtains a seed bound of order \(\ell^2/\log s\) while keeping polynomially many output bits. This is linear in \(\ell\) when \(s\) is exponential in \(\ell\), but not throughout the lower-hardness range.

General hardness-to-randomness constructions already improve the seed dependence to linear in the relevant hard-function input length. Vadhan explains that their output bits can depend on an encoding of the entire hard function. Open Problem 7.25 asks for the more restrictive point-evaluation form written here, so those results do not directly settle it.

The 2022 Doron–Moshkovitz–Oh–Zuckerman theorem refines quantitative derandomization under hardness for randomized single-valued nondeterministic circuits. It uses pseudoentropy and extraction and assumes a different, stronger type of circuit hardness. Its nearly optimal parameters are not a theorem for every ordinary average-case-hard function under the one-evaluation-per-bit requirement.

A lower bound for one construction or for a specified reconstructive proof technique would not refute the semantic existence statement. Conversely, merely assuming that a hard function exists is not the desired answer: the question requires one uniform sampler with the stated implication for every function meeting the premise.

cards.title: Seeded extraction with constant total entropy loss
cards.formal:
Do there exist an explicit family of ordinary seeded extractors and absolute constants \(C,\Delta\in\mathbb N\) such that, for every integer \(n\ge2\) and \(0\le k\le n\), the family supplies a function
\[\operatorname{Ext}_{n,k}:\{0,1\}^{n}\times\{0,1\}^{d(n,k)}\longrightarrow\{0,1\}^{m(n,k)}\]
with
\[d(n,k)\le C\lceil\log_2 n\rceil,\qquad 0\le k+d(n,k)-m(n,k)\le\Delta,\]
and, for every distribution \(X\) on \(\{0,1\}^{n}\) with min-entropy at least \(k\),
\[\operatorname{TV}\bigl(\operatorname{Ext}_{n,k}(X,U_{d(n,k)}),U_{m(n,k)}\bigr)\le1/100?\]
The seed is uniform and independent of \(X\). Explicitness means uniform deterministic evaluation in time polynomial in \(n\), with the same algorithm and polynomial for all \(n,k\). This is the constant-total-entropy-loss question in Vadhan's Open Problem 6.41.
cards.why: This asks whether an efficient general randomness purifier can preserve all but a constant number of the available random bits while using only a logarithmic seed. In applications that enumerate seeds or pay exponentially for entropy loss, the additive loss determines a multiplicative cost. Resolving the question would distinguish information-theoretic feasibility from the achievable efficiency of explicit extraction.
cards.status_note: Open Problem 6.41 and the surrounding parameter table were read directly on 2026-09-14. A bounded later-literature search and inspection of Doron–Ribeiro version 2 (9 February 2026) found no matching uniform logarithmic-seed, constant-total-loss construction or impossibility theorem. This is source-open with a bounded update, not an exhaustive certification of current openness.

sentences: A seeded extractor combines an arbitrary weak random source with a short independent uniform seed.
This question asks for logarithmic seed length and an output losing at most a constant number of the combined available entropy bits.
The statistical error is fixed at one hundredth for every source meeting the min-entropy bound.
The entire family must be evaluated by one deterministic polynomial-time algorithm, including any preprocessing.
Nonconstructive existence and recent faster constant-fraction extractors leave this specific combination of parameters unsettled in the checked sources.

cards.definitions:
All lengths \(n,k,d,m\) are integers measured in bits, with \(d,m\ge0\), and logarithms have base two. For a finite random variable \(X\),
\[H_{\infty}(X)=-\log_2\max_x\Pr[X=x].\]
Thus the source promise is \(\Pr[X=x]\le2^{-k}\) for every \(n\)-bit string \(x\). The source may have arbitrary dependencies between its coordinates and need not be samplable by an efficient algorithm. The extractor receives a sample string, not a description of its distribution. \(U_t\) denotes the uniform distribution on all \(t\)-bit strings, including the unique empty string when \(t=0\). For distributions \(P,Q\) on the same finite set,
\[\operatorname{TV}(P,Q)=\tfrac12\sum_z|P(z)-Q(z)|.\]
The condition is statistical and quantifies over every promised source, with no computational restriction on a test of the output.

A family is explicit if there are two fixed deterministic multitape Turing machines and integers \(K,q\ge1\): a parameter machine on \((1^n,k)\), with \(k\) in binary, outputs \(d(n,k),m(n,k)\) in binary; an evaluation machine on \((1^n,k,x,y)\) outputs the entire \(m(n,k)\)-bit string. Both halt within \(K(n+1)^q\) steps on all valid inputs. All preprocessing and output writing are counted. There is no advice, oracle, randomized construction or length-dependent table supplied for free. The machines, \(C,\Delta,K,q\) are chosen before \(n,k\) and before the source distribution.

Total entropy loss means \(k+d-m\): it counts the source's guaranteed entropy together with all perfect seed bits consumed. This ordinary extractor requirement concerns the output distribution alone. It does not require that the output remain uniform when the seed is separately disclosed. A strong extractor, whose output is uniform jointly with a disclosed seed, may be converted to an ordinary one by including its seed in the total output, but those seed bits must then be counted in \(m\). The convention \(m\le k+d\) is harmless output truncation for this error level. Integer entropy thresholds suffice for the stated additive-constant target; rounding down a real threshold changes the loss by less than one bit.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct Lean-checked proof or refutation of the displayed uniform construction claim. A positive answer must specify the algorithms and universal constants and prove the extraction guarantee, logarithmic seed bound, constant total loss and polynomial evaluation time throughout the parameter domain. A negative answer must rule out every such uniform family. An existence proof without efficient evaluation, a loss growing with \(n\) or \(k\), or an output bound that ignores consumed seed entropy does not meet the criterion.

context_blocks.text: The probabilistic existence bounds in the source permit logarithmic seed length and constant total entropy loss at fixed error. The obstacle in this question is a single efficiently evaluable construction, rather than the existence of a suitable finite table for each pair of parameters.

Vadhan contrasts logarithmic-seed constructions that extract a constant fraction of the source entropy with constructions extracting all but a constant number of source bits using a polylogarithmic seed. Neither parameter guarantee by itself gives \(m\ge k+d-O(1)\) with \(d=O(\log n)\).

The 2026 revised Doron–Ribeiro paper improves evaluation time for short-seed strong extractors. Its Theorem 1 gives \(m\ge(1-\eta)k\) and \(d=O(\log(n/\varepsilon))\) for fixed \(\eta>0\), with stated entropy and preprocessing conditions. Even after counting the seed as part of an ordinary output, the theorem allows a loss proportional to \(k\); it does not establish the constant-loss target.

The adjacent seed-length question TCS-1016 instead fixes the leading coefficient of the logarithm and allows only a constant fraction of source entropy as output. These two additive-precision questions have different required guarantees.

cards.title: Extraction with log n plus constant seed length
cards.formal:
Is there an explicit family of ordinary seeded extractors with error at most \(1/100\), a rational constant \(\gamma\in(0,1]\) and an integer constant \(C\ge0\) such that, for all integers \(n\ge2\) and \(0\le k\le n\),
\[\operatorname{Ext}_{n,k}:\{0,1\}^{n}\times\{0,1\}^{d(n,k)}\to\{0,1\}^{m(n,k)},\qquad d(n,k)\le\lceil\log_2 n\rceil+C,\qquad m(n,k)\ge\lfloor\gamma k\rfloor?\]
For every distribution \(X\) on \(n\)-bit strings satisfying \(H_{\infty}(X)\ge k\), and a uniform seed independent of \(X\), the required guarantee is
\[\operatorname{TV}\bigl(\operatorname{Ext}_{n,k}(X,U_{d(n,k)}),U_{m(n,k)}\bigr)\le1/100.\]
The family, \(C\), \(\gamma\) and its polynomial evaluation bound must be uniform across \(n,k\). This selects the main \(m=\Omega(k)\) target in Vadhan's Open Problem 6.42, retaining its weaker polynomial-output alternative as context.
cards.why: A logarithmic seed is often enumerated over all possibilities. Fixing its leading coefficient at one makes that enumeration linear in the source length up to a constant factor, instead of an unspecified polynomial. Achieving substantial output at that seed length for arbitrary min-entropy would sharpen a central resource bound in explicit randomness extraction.
cards.status_note: Open Problem 6.42 was read directly on 2026-09-14. A bounded later-work search and inspection of the 2022 short-seed theorem and February 2026 Doron–Ribeiro revision found no matching construction or refutation for coefficient-one seed length and constant-fraction output across every entropy threshold. Current openness is source-based, not an exhaustive literature certification.

progress.text: Open Problem 6.42 asks for seed length log n plus an additive constant at error 0.01, with a constant fraction of k output bits as the main target.

The JACM paper Nearly Optimal Pseudorandomness from Hardness includes a finer short-seed extractor in a restricted entropy regime, with a coefficient above one and the output tradeoff stated in Theorem 1.7.
The Doron–Ribeiro revision gives faster evaluation with an order-optimal logarithmic seed, rather than the additive-optimal seed bound required here.

sentences: This question asks how close an efficiently computable extractor can get to the minimum useful seed length.
It requires at most the base-two logarithm of the source length plus a constant number of seed bits.
The output must contain a fixed positive fraction of the source entropy and have statistical error at most one hundredth.
One deterministic polynomial-time family must meet these guarantees for every source length and entropy threshold.
Known constructions in the checked sources optimize related parameters but do not supply this full combination.

cards.definitions:
The parameters \(n,k,d,m\) are nonnegative integer bit lengths, with the domain restrictions in the statement and \(m\le n+d\). The latter is a harmless output-length normalization. All logarithms have base two. Min-entropy is \(H_{\infty}(X)=-\log_2\max_x\Pr[X=x]\), so the source promise bounds every point mass by \(2^{-k}\). No efficient sampling assumption, independence between source coordinates or extra side-information promise is imposed. The extractor gets \(x,y\), not a source distribution or its support. The seed distribution \(U_d\) assigns equal probability to each \(d\)-bit string and is independent of the source. \(U_0\) is the point mass at the empty string. Statistical distance is \(\operatorname{TV}(P,Q)=\frac12\sum_z|P(z)-Q(z)|\).

Explicitness means that two fixed deterministic multitape Turing machines, using no advice or oracle, compute the parameters on \((1^n,k)\) and the full output on \((1^n,k,x,y)\), respectively. Here \(k\) is binary, \(|x|=n\), and \(|y|=d(n,k)\). There are fixed integers \(K,q\ge1\) such that each computation, including preprocessing and writing its output, halts within \(K(n+1)^q\) steps for every valid input. The parameters must be computed by the family; they cannot depend on the unknown source. Correctness is statistical for every promised distribution, even one with no efficient sampler.

The extractor is ordinary: the output alone must be close to uniform. Uniformity conditional on a separately disclosed seed is not an additional requirement. The seed may contribute bits to the ordinary output, which is why a nontrivial source-output condition is expressed uniformly over all \(k\). The fixed coefficient one in \(\lceil\log_2 n\rceil+C\) is essential: a bound \(A\log n\) with unspecified \(A>1\) need not qualify. Rounding changes the seed length and minimum output by at most one bit and does not alter the additive-constant and constant-fraction target.
cards.answer_criterion: Supply a complete mathematically correct Lean-checked proof of existence or nonexistence of the specified uniform family. Existence requires algorithms and universal constants proving the seed bound with logarithmic coefficient one, output at least \(\lfloor\gamma k\rfloor\), statistical error at most \(1/100\) for every promised source, and polynomial evaluation time for all \(n,k\). A refutation must rule out every such choice. A construction for a restricted entropy range, a seed bound \((1+\delta)\log_2 n+O(1)\) with fixed \(\delta>0\), or merely \(k^{\beta}\) output for fixed \(\beta<1\), is insufficient for this selected main target.

context_blocks.text: The source explicitly separates two improvements over constant-factor-optimal extraction: constant total entropy loss, and a seed of \(\log_2 n+O(1)\) bits. This card concerns the latter and does not require constant loss.

Open Problem 6.42 presents \(\Omega(k)\) output as its main target and also asks about the weaker possibility of \(k^{\Omega(1)}\) output. The card makes the constant-fraction target precise; it does not treat the two as equivalent.

Doron, Moshkovitz, Oh and Zuckerman obtain short seeds in a substantial entropy regime. Their Theorem 1.7 gives seed length \((1+c\alpha)\log n+c\log(1/\varepsilon)\) and output of order \(n^{1-2\alpha}\) for entropy at least \(n^{1-\alpha}\), under the stated parameter conditions. This is a finer seed bound than unspecified \(O(\log n)\), but for fixed positive \(\alpha\) it does not meet coefficient one or constant-fraction output throughout the card’s domain.

The 2026 revised Doron–Ribeiro theorem improves the running time of constructions with \(O(\log(n/\varepsilon))\) seed length and a constant fraction of the entropy as output, with entropy and preprocessing qualifications. Its asymptotic seed bound leaves the leading constant unspecified.

cards.title: Universal determinant evaluations for bipartite matching
cards.formal:
Can one construct, in uniform deterministic NC, an integer table
\[\alpha^{(m)}=(\alpha_{i,j}^{(m)})_{i,j\in[m]}\in\{0,1,\ldots,m2^{m^2}\}^{m^2}\]
for each integer \(m\ge1\), such that the same table works for every simple bipartite graph \(G\) with labeled vertex classes \([m]\) and \([m]\)? Precisely, define the integer matrix
\[A_G(\alpha)_{i,j}=\begin{cases}\alpha_{i,j}&\text{if }(i,j)\in E(G),\\0&\text{otherwise.}\end{cases}\]
The requirement is
\[\forall G,\qquad \det A_G(\alpha^{(m)})\ne0\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad G\text{ has a perfect matching}.\]
The construction receives only \(1^m\), not \(G\). This card selects the NC construction explicitly proposed in Vadhan's Open Problem 3.7; its more permissive request for an efficient or even subexponential sequential construction is not an equivalent target.
cards.why: A universal evaluation table would give a reusable deterministic replacement for all random entries in the classical determinant test for bipartite matching. The same polynomial-size data would preserve every matching-existence test at a given graph size. The source uses NC construction as a particularly strong form of explicitness, connecting this algebraic derandomization object to efficient parallel computation.

The newer algorithmic claim is recorded separately and has not been independently proof-verified.

cards.definitions:
The notation \([m]\) means \(\{1,\ldots,m\}\). A simple bipartite graph in the statement is an arbitrary subset \(E\subseteq[m]\times[m]\), with no multiple edges. A perfect matching is a permutation \(\pi\) of \([m]\) for which \((i,\pi(i))\in E\) for all \(i\). The determinant is over the integers:
\[\det B=\sum_{\pi\in S_m}\operatorname{sgn}(\pi)\prod_{i=1}^{m}B_{i,\pi(i)},\]
where \(S_m\) is the set of all permutations and \(\operatorname{sgn}(\pi)\) is their parity sign. Nonzero means exact integer nonzero, not a floating-point test or a residue modulo an unspecified prime.

Encode each entry of \(\alpha^{(m)}\) as a nonnegative binary integer padded to
\[L_m=\lceil\log_2(m2^{m^2}+1)\rceil\]
bits, and list entries in row-major order. The output contains exactly \(m^2L_m\) bits. Exponentially large entry values thus have polynomially many bits; their entire encoding is counted.

Uniform deterministic NC here means a logspace-uniform Boolean circuit family computing this full output from \(1^m\). There are fixed positive integers \(K,a,b\) such that the circuit for length \(m\) has at most \(K(m+1)^a\) gates and depth at most \(K\lceil\log_2(m+1)\rceil^b\). Gates are fan-in-two AND and OR, unary NOT, input bits and Boolean constants. A single deterministic Turing machine, on \(1^m\), writes the circuit and its output-wire list using \(O(\log(m+1))\) work space and polynomial time. Its output tape is write-only and is not free readable memory. No random bits, advice, oracle or table depending on \(m\) is supplied. The constants, circuit-generation machine and computation family precede the universal quantifiers over \(m,G\). Arbitrary unit-cost operations on integers are not part of this Boolean model.

The graph can be represented by its \(m^2\)-bit incidence table when stating correctness, but it is not an input to the constructor. An assignment chosen separately for each graph, or an algorithm deciding matching using another matrix, does not by itself provide a universal scalar table in the specified range.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct Lean-checked proof or refutation of this NC construction claim. A positive proof must specify the uniform circuit construction, its polynomial-size and polylogarithmic-depth bounds, the entry range, and the determinant equivalence simultaneously for every graph. A negative proof must rule out every such uniform NC family. Nonconstructive existence of the tables, graph-dependent substitutions, or an NC matching algorithm without the required universal tables is insufficient.

context_blocks.text: The determinant polynomial of the symbolic bipartite adjacency matrix is nonzero exactly when a perfect matching exists. Distinct perfect matchings contribute distinct monomials before evaluation; cancellation between their evaluated integer contributions is the obstacle the table must avoid.

The source proves that a suitable table exists for each \(m\). There are \(2^{m^2}\) graphs, and a uniformly chosen table from the specified range makes the determinant vanish incorrectly for any fixed matching-containing graph with probability at most \(m/(m2^{m^2}+1)\). The resulting simultaneous-existence bound does not supply an efficient uniform constructor.

The 2016 Fenner–Gurjar–Thierauf result gives uniform circuits of quasipolynomial size and polylogarithmic depth for bipartite perfect matching. Quasipolynomial size exceeds the polynomial-size NC requirement in this card.

The July 2026 Chatterjee–Ghosh–Gurjar–Raj–Thierauf preprint claims NC algorithms for bipartite matching, including weighted and search versions. Its decision algorithm tests the rank of a larger block matrix built from the input graph. The checked construction is a different algebraic test and does not supply one scalar substitution into the original adjacency matrix for all graphs. This card therefore retains the universal-table question, while recording that its historical algorithmic motivation has a separate new claimed resolution.

cards.title: Promise-BPP derandomization implying EXP circuit hardness
cards.formal: Does complete deterministic derandomization of bounded-error polynomial-time promise problems force a deterministic exponential-time language to require superpolynomial Boolean circuits? Precisely, is the implication \[\mathrm{prBPP}=\mathrm{prP}\quad\Longrightarrow\quad\mathrm{EXP}\not\subseteq\mathrm{P/poly}\] true?
cards.why: Determine whether full promise-problem derandomization necessarily yields deterministic exponential-time circuit hardness, closing a central gap between efficient algorithms and nonuniform lower bounds.
