sentences: Derandomization replaces efficient bounded-error randomized algorithms by deterministic ones.
The question assumes this replacement for promise problems and asks whether it forces an exponential-time language to lack polynomial-size Boolean circuits.
Known implications involving nondeterministic exponential time do not establish the deterministic-class target.
The issue is a converse to hardness-based pseudorandomness constructions.
The project seeks to explain whether eliminating randomness necessarily reveals an explicit source of circuit hardness at the corresponding deterministic computational scale.

cards.definitions: All languages and promise inputs are binary strings. A promise problem is a pair \((Y,N)\) of disjoint subsets of \(\{0,1\}^*\); only inputs in \(Y\cup N\) require a correct answer. It is in \(\mathrm{prBPP}\) if a uniform randomized multitape Turing machine halts in \(C(n+1)^a\) steps on every input of length \(n\) and every random tape, for constants \(C,a\) depending on the machine, accepts every input in \(Y\) with probability at least \(2/3\), and accepts every input in \(N\) with probability at most \(1/3\). Random bits are independent and fair. The class \(\mathrm{prP}\) has the same total polynomial clock and promise requirement with a deterministic machine and exact correctness. The hypothesis quantifies over all promise pairs, with a potentially different deterministic machine and polynomial for each pair; it does not require a single effective transformation of programs. There is no correctness requirement off the promise. Define \(\mathrm{EXP}=\bigcup_{a\ge1}\mathrm{DTIME}(2^{n^a})\), with standard constant-factor time bounds, and \(\mathrm E=\mathrm{DTIME}(2^{O(n)})\). A Boolean circuit has \(n\) input bits, fan-in-two AND and OR gates, unary NOT gates, constants, unrestricted fan-out and one output bit. Its size is its number of non-input gates, including constant gates. Let \(s_L(n)\) be the minimum circuit size computing the characteristic function of \(L\) on every length-\(n\) input. A language belongs to \(\mathrm{P/poly}\) when \(s_L(n)\le C(n+1)^k\) for all \(n\), for some constants \(C,k\); its circuits need not be generated uniformly. Thus the conclusion requires one fixed language \(L\in\mathrm{EXP}\) such that, for every integers \(k\ge1\), \(C\ge1\) and \(N_0\ge1\), some \(n\ge N_0\) satisfies \(s_L(n)>C(n+1)^k\). Hardness at infinitely many lengths is sufficient; hardness at all sufficiently large lengths is not part of the target.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of the stated implication or its logical negation, using these promise, uniformity and circuit-size definitions. A negative answer must establish \(\mathrm{prBPP}=\mathrm{prP}\) together with \(\mathrm{EXP}\subseteq\mathrm{P/poly}\); a relativized counterexample only proves a relativization limitation. A lower bound in a nondeterministic class, a different hard language for each polynomial exponent, or a theorem with an additional unproved hypothesis does not establish the requested implication.

context_blocks.text: A promise separates the inputs on which an algorithm must answer correctly from those on which either answer is acceptable. This permits randomized decision procedures whose acceptance probability is guaranteed to avoid an intermediate interval only on valid inputs. The hypothesis derandomizes every such promise problem, and is stronger than merely identifying the classes of total decision languages.

Uniform algorithms use one finite program at every input length. A nonuniform circuit family may contain unrelated circuits at different lengths. The conclusion says that some language with a deterministic exponential-time algorithm still defeats every polynomial size bound in this more permissive computational model.

Vadhan states the question as Open Problem 8.8 for E and notes its equivalence to the EXP formulation. The distinction matters in stronger exponential lower bounds, but it does not change the polynomial-circuit separation requested here.

The surrounding source discussion records a consequence for NEXP, the nondeterministic exponential-time class. It also records a consequence giving, for each fixed circuit exponent, a hard language in NP. Neither statement supplies the single deterministic exponential-time language required by this card.

Lu, Oliveira, Ren and Santhanam still describe the necessity of nonuniform circuit hardness for derandomization as an open issue in their 2024 paper. Their Heavy Avoid results include uniform and infinitely-often characterizations; these have distinct quantifiers and do not assert the present implication.

A positive answer would show that fully eliminating bounded-error randomness necessarily entails a circuit lower bound at a deterministic exponential-time scale. This is a necessity question about derandomization: proving that some particular hardness assumption suffices for derandomization answers a different direction.

cards.title: Lossless condensers with constant output overhead
cards.formal:
Is there an explicit family of functions
\[\operatorname{Con}_{n,k}:\{0,1\}^{n}\times\{0,1\}^{d(n,k)}\to\{0,1\}^{m(n,k)}\]
and absolute integer constants \(C,\Delta\ge1\) such that, for every integer \(n\ge2\) and \(0\le k\le n\),
\[d(n,k)\le C\lceil\log_2 n\rceil,\qquad k+d(n,k)\le m(n,k)\le k+d(n,k)+\Delta,\]
and for every distribution \(X\) on \(n\)-bit strings with \(H_{\infty}(X)\ge k\), there is a distribution \(Y_X\) on \(m(n,k)\)-bit strings satisfying

cards.why: A lossless condenser compresses an arbitrary weak source while preserving its available randomness. Constant output overhead would leave that randomness concentrated in a string only a constant number of bits longer than its entropy, using a short seed. In graph terms it asks for nearly collision-free expansion with an almost minimal number of right vertices, a useful resource in extraction and data structures.

sentences: A lossless condenser compresses a weak random source while preserving its guaranteed entropy together with the seed entropy.
This question asks for a logarithmic seed and an output only a constant number of bits longer than that preserved entropy.
The output may be nonuniform, but it must be within one hundredth in statistical distance of a distribution with the required min-entropy.
The equivalent graph target has nearly lossless expansion and only a constant factor more right vertices than the number of outgoing edges from a source set.
Recent multiplicity-code and two-sided-expansion results improve related structure without meeting this constant-overhead target.

cards.definitions:
All lengths are integers in bits and all logarithms have base two. The min-entropy of a finite distribution is \(H_{\infty}(X)=-\log_2\max_x\Pr[X=x]\). The input promise therefore says that every point has probability at most \(2^{-k}\). Input distributions may be arbitrary; their coordinates need not be independent, and they need not have efficient samplers. The input to the condenser is a sample string and a seed, not a distribution description. \(U_t\) is uniform on all \(t\)-bit strings, with the single empty string when \(t=0\). Statistical distance is
\[\operatorname{TV}(P,Q)=\tfrac12\sum_z|P(z)-Q(z)|.\]
The comparison distribution \(Y_X\) may depend on the entire source distribution. Its existence is a mathematical guarantee; no algorithm for producing or sampling it is required.

Explicitness means that two fixed deterministic multitape Turing machines compute the lengths from \((1^n,k)\) and the full output from \((1^n,k,x,y)\), respectively. The entropy parameter is binary, \(|x|=n\), and \(|y|=d(n,k)\). For some fixed positive integers \(K,q\), each computation uses at most \(K(n+1)^q\) transitions, including preprocessing and output writing. No advice, oracle, randomized choice of construction or free length-dependent table is allowed. The machines and constants are fixed before \(n,k,X\); the comparison distribution is quantified after \(X\).

Lossless means that the comparison distribution preserves all \(k+d\) guaranteed input-and-seed entropy bits. The bounded quantity \(m-(k+d)\) is the output entropy gap, or output overhead, not lost entropy. The condenser is not required to output an almost-uniform string: it only has to be close to a distribution with the specified min-entropy. Uniformity conditional on a separately disclosed seed is not imposed.

There is an equivalent graph view for these parameters. Let \(N=2^n\), \(D=2^d\), \(M=2^m\), and \(K_0=2^k\). Treat the condenser as a neighbor function \([N]\times[D]\to[M]\), identifying integers with fixed-length binary strings. It defines a left-regular bipartite multigraph; seeds label edges, and repeated neighbors are permitted. The lossless condition is equivalent to requiring at least \((99/100)DK_0\) distinct neighbors for every set of exactly \(K_0\) left vertices. The size bounds become \(D\le(2n)^C\) and \(DK_0\le M\le2^{\Delta}DK_0\). Only this source-equivalent one-sided expansion is required; neither right-regularity nor right-to-left expansion is an additional condition.
cards.answer_criterion: Provide a complete mathematically correct Lean-checked proof or refutation of the displayed uniform condenser-family claim. A construction must specify its algorithms and constants and establish all length, time, distance and entropy requirements over the entire domain. An equivalent graph construction qualifies with a proved translation to these guarantees. A negative answer must rule out every such family. A constant fraction of output entropy gap, a superlogarithmic seed, or a construction only for a restricted entropy regime does not meet the target.

context_blocks.text: Open Problem 5.36 asks for degree polynomial in \(\log N\), expansion \(0.99D\), and only \(O(K_0D)\) right vertices. Proposition 6.33 translates the powers-of-two case into lossless condensation. The card fixes the binary representation and the exact fixed-error condenser formulation of Open Problem 6.35.

The 2022 Kalev–Ta-Shma construction gives a different lossless condenser with logarithmic seed length. Its Theorem 2 allows an output entropy gap proportional to the source entropy, with parameter restrictions; it does not establish an absolute constant gap. The paper explicitly distinguishes entropy loss from entropy gap and describes small-gap extraction as an outstanding challenge.

The September 2026 paper proves that the Kalev–Ta-Shma graph also expands losslessly in the reverse direction and characterizes its expansion. This additional two-sided property concerns a different resource. Its stated right-side size still has a power loss relative to the source set size in the checked parameters, so it does not give the constant output overhead requested here.

The source relates a positive answer to improved extraction with constant total entropy loss, the separate target TCS-1015. A condenser is allowed a nonzero output entropy gap; an extractor instead asks that the output itself be close to uniform. The card preserves that distinction.

cards.title: FPT versus \(\mathrm{W}[1]\)
cards.formal: Does there exist one deterministic algorithm A, a total computable function \(f:\mathbb N\to\mathbb N_{\ge1}\), and an integer \(c\ge0\), such that A decides whether G contains a k-clique and uses at most \(f(k)(N+2)^c\) steps for every encoded pair (G,k) of total bit length N? The exponent c is independent of both k and G. Equivalently, is \(\mathrm{FPT}=\mathrm{W}[1]\) under parameterized many-one reductions?
cards.definitions: A graph G is finite, simple and undirected, with vertex set \([n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}\), including n=0. A k-clique is a subset of exactly k vertices with an edge between each pair of distinct vertices. The empty subset is a 0-clique; no k-clique exists when k>n. For a fixed binary encoding, write \(1^n0\), then the n by n adjacency matrix in row order, then the ordinary binary representation of the nonnegative integer k (0 is written as 0, and otherwise there are no leading zeroes). A valid matrix is symmetric with zero diagonal, and the entire remaining suffix is the representation of k. N counts all bits, including k. A rejects any malformed string in time polynomial in its bit length. The bound in the statement applies to every valid pair, including k>n. The parameter is k alone; there is no promise on density, degree, clique number or any other graph property. A is one uniform deterministic multitape Turing machine with a finite program and fixed finite tape alphabets, a read-only input and initially blank work tapes; each transition reads or writes only at the heads and moves each head by at most one cell. The runtime includes parsing, input access and all internal work. Correctness is exact, and no advice, randomness, oracle or quantum operations are supplied. The same A, f and c work for every pair; f must be computable by a machine that halts on every nonnegative integer input, but its growth and the time needed to compute it have no prescribed bound. Constant multiplicative overhead can be absorbed into f. Using full input length rather than n gives the usual FPT question: for k at most n the two lengths are polynomially related, and k>n is rejected after parsing. For completeness, a parameterized language is a set of pairs \((x,k)\in\{0,1\}^*\times\mathbb N\), with both components explicitly encoded. It belongs to FPT if one uniform deterministic machine decides it within \(h(k)(M+2)^a\) steps for a total computable positive h, a fixed nonnegative integer a and complete encoding length M. A parameterized many-one reduction computes a single output pair \((y,k^{\prime})\) in such a time bound, preserves yes versus no membership, and satisfies \(k^{\prime}\le g(k)\) for a total computable function g; writing the output counts toward its runtime. The class W[1] can equivalently be defined as all parameterized languages admitting such a reduction to the Clique problem just specified. This characterization fixes the reduction convention without a change of target. It includes FPT, and Clique belongs to it, so FPT membership of Clique is equivalent to equality of the two classes.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof of the existence of the single algorithm, computable multiplier and constant exponent in the statement, or prove their joint nonexistence. In the affirmative case, prove correctness and the uniform worst-case bound on all pairs, together with the malformed-input convention. In the negative case, exclude every such algorithm, computable f and exponent c; a conditional lower bound, a bound for a restricted algorithm model, or failure at one proposed multiplier and exponent does not settle this target. An algorithm whose polynomial exponent depends on k also does not satisfy the displayed quantifiers.
cards.why: This is the principal boundary question for algorithms whose exponential difficulty is confined to a small parameter. It determines the force of thousands of parameterized hardness reductions and separates efficient small-solution search from algorithms whose input-size exponent grows with the solution size.

importance.reason: The defining unresolved tractability separation of parameterized complexity, with Clique as a precise and widely used complete problem.

progress.text: The textbook specifies parameterized reductions and proves the completeness framework for Clique, via its complement relation with Independent Set. Theorem 14.21 derives the stronger exclusion of \(f(k)n^{o(k)}\) Clique algorithms assuming ETH.

Bottesch identifies the FPT-versus-W[1] separation as the central conjecture, explains its known implications relative to P versus NP and ETH, and proves structural results with explicitly specified oracle conventions. These do not prove the unrelativized separation.
Lin gives a gap reduction showing that a constant-factor FPT approximation of Clique would imply an exact FPT algorithm. The consequence remains conditional on FPT differing from W[1].

Chen, Feng, Laekhanukit and Liu give a combinatorial proof of the \(k^{o(1)}\) parameterized inapproximability consequence under W[1]-hardness. The checked August 2024 revision precedes the SOSA 2025 publication.

Abboud, Fischer and Shechter improve combinatorial fixed-k Clique bounds by logarithmic factors. Their August 2024 author revision retains a polynomial exponent depending on k; the institutional record lists the Algorithmica publication on 22 May 2026.

cards.status_note: The textbook and Bottesch explicitly state the unresolved separation, and the later approximation papers retain it as an assumption. The checked fixed-k algorithm paper and its 2026 publication metadata provide no FPT algorithm. A bounded primary-source search on 14 September 2026 found no verified resolution; the review does not independently reprove the cited results.

context_blocks.text: For each fixed k, exhaustive search over vertex subsets decides Clique in polynomial time. The exponent grows with k, so this observation gives a different kind of tractability: increasing the target clique size can increase the power of n in the running time. The question asks whether all dependence on k can instead be moved into one multiplicative function. For example, \(2^{2^{k}}n^{3}\) meets the requested form, while \(n^{k/10}\) does not.

The unrestricted Clique problem is NP-complete, but this alone cannot rule out fixed-parameter tractability. The permitted function f can grow much faster than any polynomial when k grows with n. If \(\mathrm{P}=\mathrm{NP}\) then Clique is certainly FPT; the converse implication is not known. Thus \(\mathrm{FPT}\ne \mathrm{W}[1]\) is a stronger separation conjecture than \(\mathrm{P}\ne \mathrm{NP}\) in the direction currently proved.

Parameterized reductions keep the output parameter controlled solely by the original parameter. Since Clique is complete under these reductions, an FPT Clique algorithm would solve every \(\mathrm{W}[1]\) problem in FPT time. This is why a \(\mathrm{W}[1]\)-hardness proof is useful evidence against a parameterized algorithm for another problem. The evidence is conditional on the separation being true, even when the reduction theorem itself is unconditional.

The Exponential Time Hypothesis supplies a stronger quantitative barrier: it rules out \(f(k)n^{o(k)}\) algorithms for Clique. That conclusion excludes FPT, but uses an assumption that is itself open. Matrix-multiplication methods and improved combinatorial methods accelerate Clique for fixed k while leaving an exponent that grows with the parameter. Their progress does not eliminate the central gap.

Approximation has become another way to measure the reach of the conjecture. Lin proves that even fixed-factor parameterized approximation of Clique is \(\mathrm{W}[1]\)-hard. Later constructions strengthen the factor and simplify the reductions. These results enlarge the consequences of a separation; they do not prove \(\mathrm{FPT}\ne \mathrm{W}[1]\).

Uniformity is essential: one finite program must handle every k. Neither a separately chosen algorithm for each fixed k nor a bound with an exponent that increases with k establishes FPT. Conversely, the allowed computable multiplier can be enormous; this is a structural tractability question and does not assert that an affirmative algorithm would be practical.

cards.title: Exponential Time Hypothesis
cards.formal: Is \(s_3>0\) in the deterministic bit model defined below? Equivalently, does there exist one real \(c>0\) such that no 3-SAT decider A has a runtime bound \(t_A(F)\le C\,2^{c n(F)}(L(F)+1)^d\) on every valid 3-CNF formula F for any fixed integers \(C\ge1,d\ge0\)? The same positive c must exclude all such algorithms. This is the deterministic Exponential Time Hypothesis.
cards.definitions: Fix an integer clause-width bound \(q\ge 3\). A q-CNF formula is a finite list of clauses, each a finite list of at most q literals. A literal is a variable \(x_i\) or its negation \(\neg x_i\), with \(1\le i\le n\). The variables that occur are exactly \(x_1,\ldots,x_n\), so n counts distinct variables, not clauses or input bits. Repeated literals, repeated clauses and clauses containing both signs of a variable are allowed. A Boolean assignment satisfies the formula if every clause has at least one true literal. An empty clause is false; the empty conjunction is true and has n=0. For a completely specified binary encoding, let \(\operatorname{code}(a)\), for a nonnegative integer a, be \(1^b0\) followed by the b-bit binary expansion of a+1, where \(b=\lfloor\log_2(a+1)\rfloor+1\). Encode n and the number m of clauses with this code, then each clause by its coded length followed by its literals. Each literal is a sign bit (0 for positive, 1 for negated) and the code of its variable index. All indicated lists must be fully present, with no trailing bits, valid indices and every declared variable occurring. Let L be the complete bit length. Ill-formed strings, including clauses wider than q, are rejected. No density, satisfiability-count, occurrence or input-distribution promise is imposed. A q-SAT decider A is one uniform deterministic multitape Turing machine with a finite program and fixed finite tape alphabets, a read-only input tape and initially blank work tapes. Each transition reads or writes only the cells at the heads and moves each head by at most one cell. The total transition count includes parsing, input access and all internal work. A must halt on all inputs, decide satisfiability exactly on valid q-CNF formulas, and reject malformed strings in polynomial time in their length. It receives no advice, random bits, quantum operations, oracle or precomputed instance information. The machine may depend on the fixed q. For a valid formula F, let \(t_A(F)\) be its runtime and \(n(F),L(F)\) its variable count and bit length. An exponent \(\alpha\ge 0\) is attainable at width q if there exist such a decider A and fixed integers \(C\ge1,d\ge0\) with \(t_A(F)\le C\,2^{\alpha n(F)}(L(F)+1)^d\) for every valid q-CNF formula F. The constants are independent of F. Define \(s_q\) as the infimum of all attainable exponents. This set is nonempty because exhaustive assignment testing gives an attainable exponent 1, so \(0\le s_q\le1\). The infimum need not itself be attainable. Polynomial factors in L remain explicit, including when clauses are repeated many times. The chosen explicit syntax and malformed-input normalization do not impose a new satisfiability promise; they fix the bit model for the source’s exponential-rate question. This card specializes q to 3. Its negation, \(s_3=0\), means that for every real \(\varepsilon>0\) there is a 3-SAT decider \(A_\varepsilon\) with fixed constants \(C_\varepsilon,d_\varepsilon\) satisfying \(t_{A_\varepsilon}(F)\le C_\varepsilon 2^{\varepsilon n(F)}(L(F)+1)^{d_\varepsilon}\) on every valid formula. cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof of \(s_3>0\) or of \(s_3=0\) for the explicitly defined rate. A positive answer requires a positive constant excluding every valid deterministic decider at that exponential rate, with any polynomial input factor. A negative answer must establish arbitrarily small attainable positive exponents with the stated quantifiers. A fixed improved positive exponent, a bound for a restricted algorithm class, or a conditional lower bound does not settle this question. No numerical estimate of \(s_3\) is requested: the target is its strict positivity.

context_blocks.text: NP-completeness describes the possibility of polynomial-time algorithms and does not itself impose a positive exponential rate. Even if P differs from NP, a running time such as \(2^{\sqrt{n}}\) remains possible for 3-SAT. ETH asks for a stronger obstruction: some fixed amount of exponential work must remain unavoidable when complexity is measured by the number of Boolean choices.

That parameter must be preserved carefully by a reduction. An ordinary polynomial-time reduction may turn an n-variable formula into an instance of size \(n^{3}\), which can destroy a claimed exponential lower bound in the new parameter. Sparsification supplies a controlled disjunction of bounded-density formulas, allowing variables and clauses to be related without an arbitrary polynomial blowup. This is a main reason ETH can support sharp bounds across many problems.

The infimum over all algorithms matters. Excluding one \(2^{o(n)}\) algorithm is the common informal wording, but the textbook explicitly keeps the stronger positive-infimum statement because the converse is unclear. ETH would be false if arbitrarily small constant exponents were attainable, even if the known algorithms depended on the desired exponent. A card that omitted this distinction would change the quantified question.

Liu’s deterministic algorithm has runtime \(O(1.32793^n)\) up to polynomial input factors. It therefore supplies an upper bound on \(s_3\); it establishes neither a positive lower bound nor the value of \(s_3\). The existence of one algorithm with a positive exponential rate does not rule out a much faster algorithm. Empirical solver success and promises on the formula are also distinct from this all-input infimum.

ETH is weaker than SETH, whose optimal rates approach one as the fixed clause width grows. It also differs from randomized ETH and from Gap-ETH, which asks for hardness of distinguishing fully satisfiable formulas from formulas with a constant unsatisfied fraction. Recent lattice reductions illustrate the value of tracking these distinctions: some approximation hardness can be obtained from deterministic ETH, while other results use randomized ETH. They extend the consequences of assumptions without proving the assumptions.

A single fixed exponent in ETH must obstruct every algorithm. Refuting one proposed lower-bound constant does not suffice, because another smaller positive constant could still work. Conversely, a refutation may use a different finite algorithm for each desired exponent; no effective procedure generating those algorithms is added to the target.

cards.title: Breaking the \(2^{n}\) barrier for weighted TSP
cards.formal:
Does exact symmetric weighted travelling salesman admit a classical algorithm with a fixed exponential base below two, allowing bounded-error randomization and polynomial dependence on the input bit length?

Precisely, do there exist a real constant \(0<\varepsilon<1\), positive integers \(K,c,B\) with \(B\ge2\), and one uniform classical randomized word-RAM algorithm \(\mathcal A\) such that, for every \(n\ge3\) and every complete undirected graph on vertices \(\{1,\ldots,n\}\) with nonnegative integer edge weights encoded as below, both of the following hold?
\[\Pr[\mathcal A\text{ outputs a minimum-weight Hamiltonian cycle}]\ge\frac23,\]
\[\text{number of charged operations on every random execution}\ \le\ K(2-\varepsilon)^n(n+L)^c.\]
Here \(L\) is the total bit length of the explicit input, and the machine model is fixed below using \(B\). All constants and the algorithm precede the quantifiers over the graph, its weights and its encoding length. A deterministic algorithm qualifies as a special case.
cards.definitions:
Instance and encoding. There is one weight \(a_{ij}=a_{ji}\in\mathbb Z_{\ge0}\) for each unordered pair \(1\le i<j\le n\), and no loops. Weights are exact integers of arbitrary finite bit length. Let \(b(t)\) be the ordinary binary representation of a nonnegative integer \(t\), without leading zeros, with \(b(0)=0\). Define the self-delimiting code
\[U(t)=1^{|b(t)|}0b(t).\]
The input is \(U(n)\) followed by \(U(a_{ij})\) in lexicographic order of \((i,j)\), for all \(1\le i<j\le n\). Its length in bits is \(L\). No matrix entry is supplied implicitly by an oracle or by a succinct circuit.

Objective and output. A tour is any permutation \(\pi\) of \(\{1,\ldots,n\}\), interpreted cyclically. Set \(\pi(n+1)=\pi(1)\). Its cost and the optimum are
\[\operatorname{cost}_a(\pi)=\sum_{i=1}^n a_{\pi(i),\pi(i+1)},\qquad \operatorname{OPT}(a)=\min_{\pi\in S_n}\operatorname{cost}_a(\pi),\]
where \(S_n\) is the finite set of all such permutations. The graph is complete, so a tour always exists and the minimum is attained. The output is the explicit list of its \(n\) vertex labels, each in \(\lceil\log_2(n+1)\rceil\) bits. Any minimum-cost tour is accepted, including any rotation or reversal of one; no uniqueness is required. An invalid list, an explicit failure output, or a suboptimal tour counts as failure. Returning only the optimum value, a bound or an approximate tour is not the required output.

Machine and charges. Use a word RAM whose word length on this input is
\[w=B\left\lceil n+\log_2(L+2)\right\rceil\text{ bits}.\]
The algorithm has one finite program independent of \(n,L\) and all weights. A word is an unsigned integer in \(\{0,\ldots,2^w-1\}\); a memory address is one word. The input bits are packed in order into consecutive read-only words, padding the last word with zeros and exposing the true input length. Working memory is initially zero and contains no advice or precomputed tables. Reading or writing one addressed word, copying a word, comparing two words, branching, bitwise Boolean operations, and a left or right shift by a word-specified amount each cost one operation. A shift by at least \(w\) gives zero. Addition, subtraction and multiplication are modulo \(2^w\) and cost one operation; integer quotient and remainder by a nonzero word also cost one operation. Division by zero is not permitted. A fresh independent fair random bit costs one operation. Outputting a word, including the final partial word, costs one operation.

Integers longer than one word must be represented and processed using multiple charged operations; there is no unit-cost arithmetic on unbounded integers or exact real numbers. Reading and decoding the input, constructing tables, generating random bits, preprocessing, arithmetic and writing the entire tour are included in the clock. Addressing exponential-size subset tables is allowed by the linear-in-\(n\) word length. There is no separate polynomial-space restriction, and no quantum memory, quantum query, advice string or ideal oracle. The fixed polynomial overhead permitted in \(n+L\) accommodates the bit cost of operations on these finite-width words; this does not assert that sequential simulation of arbitrary random memory access has only polynomial overhead.

Probability and uniformity. For each fixed input the probability is over the machine’s independent fair coin stream. The same success guarantee holds on every input, not just on average over a distribution of weights. The running-time bound holds for every possible coin stream, including unsuccessful executions, so it is a worst-case clock rather than an expected-time bound. The constants \(\varepsilon,K,c,B\) cannot depend on the weights, their range or any property of the instance.

Scope. There is no triangle inequality, Euclidean geometry, bounded-weight, small-doubling or other structural promise. Polynomial dependence on \(L\) is allowed; polynomial dependence on the numerical maximum or sum of the weights is not automatically allowed. The fixed saving \(\varepsilon>0\) cannot tend to zero with \(n\).
cards.answer_criterion: Provide a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of the algorithm-existence proposition or its full logical negation. A positive proof must specify one uniform classical algorithm and fixed constants, prove the worst-case clock including input and output costs, and prove per-instance success probability at least \(2/3\) for an exactly optimal tour. A negative proof must exclude every such algorithm and every permitted choice of constants in the stated randomized word-RAM model. A conditional lower bound settles only that conditional assertion. A restriction on one dynamic-programming framework, a local-search rule or a polynomial-space algorithm does not exclude all allowed algorithms. Faster Hamiltonicity detection, pseudo-polynomial dependence on weight magnitudes, a restricted weight class, approximate optimization or a quantum algorithm does not meet the full positive target.
cards.why: Exact weighted TSP is a basic test of whether optimization over all orders of a set fundamentally requires base-two exponential time. A fixed reduction of that base would save an exponential factor for every sufficiently large instance, even when costs have arbitrary binary representations. Understanding this boundary would distinguish the difficulty of selecting an optimal tour from the already faster task of merely detecting a tour.

context_blocks.text: In a complete graph the existence of a Hamiltonian cycle is automatic. The difficulty is selecting the cheapest one among the possible orders. Two tours with almost identical edges can have very different costs, and there is no restriction tying those costs to a geometric distance. The card therefore concerns exact optimization rather than finding any spanning cycle.

The Bellman and Held–Karp algorithms from 1962 give the familiar \(O(2^n n^2)\) arithmetic-operation bound. Stoian’s 2024 result improves this to deterministic time \(2^n n^2/2^{\Omega(\sqrt{\log n})}\) in its stated model. This is a real improvement to the long-standing bound, but its exponent is still \(n-o(n)\). It does not give a fixed constant \(\varepsilon>0\) in \((2-\varepsilon)^n\). Arbitrary-length costs still require the bit-length accounting stated in this card.

Björklund gives a Monte Carlo \(O^*(1.657^n)\) algorithm for undirected Hamiltonicity. The weighted extension in Theorem 3 has running time \(O^*(W1.657^n)\), where \(W\) is the sum of the positive integer edge weights. A value \(2^b\) needs only \(b+1\) binary digits, so a factor polynomial in \(W\) can be exponential in the number of input bits used for weights. That extension does not establish the arbitrary-binary-weight target.

The input-bit distinction is not a demand for strongly polynomial arithmetic complexity. A polynomial factor in the total binary encoding length is expressly allowed. What is excluded is hiding dependence on enormous numerical weights inside that factor. Likewise, randomized success must hold on each fixed instance, and every execution must obey the clock. A favorable average over sampled instances is a different guarantee.

The STACS 2026 small-doubling result goes beyond numerically small weights. If \(A\) is the set of distinct input weights and \(A+A=\{a+b:a,b\in A\}\), its promise is \(|A+A|\le C|A|\) for a fixed constant \(C\). Under that additional structure, the stated TSP time matches the unweighted exponential scale, with factors depending on \(C\). Arbitrary weight sets need not have a bounded doubling constant; allowing \(C\) to grow with the input does not give this card’s fixed uniform bound.

Time and memory are separate resources. Dallant and Kozma’s April 2026 paper improves interior time-space tradeoffs: it studies running time \(T^{n+o(n)}\) and space \(S^{n+o(n)}\) for \(2<T<4\), obtaining a product \(ST<3.572\) at one point. An improvement in the product does not assert \(T<2\). The paper explicitly retains the base-two running-time question as open.

The July 2026 follow-up improves the achievable time-space product to roughly \(3.1819\) in the relevant set-system framework. Its lower bound of more than \(3.1818\) is a limitation of that framework, whose parameters describe families of subsets and their chains. It is not a lower bound against arbitrary randomized TSP algorithms. The introduction still identifies \(O^*(2^n)\) as the best known unrestricted classical time scale.

Quantum algorithms form a different comparison. Dallant’s July 2026 theorem assumes quantum computation and quantum random-access memory. The saving from quantum search cannot be treated as an implementation on a classical RAM with independent random bits. The selected target permits classical randomization but supplies no quantum operations.

The ESA paper published on 25 August 2026 similarly reports a time base of 1.859 with a QRAM space base of 1.315. The inspected official abstract makes the quantum resource explicit. Those sub-two numbers therefore do not constitute a classical solution to this card; the full theorem was not independently audited in this review.

The SODA 2026 paper on \(k\)-opt proves that prescribed local-improvement processes can take exponentially many iterations even with an optimal choice of improving move. Its conclusion concerns those processes, including particular three- and four-edge neighborhoods. The card allows all uniform algorithms, and asks for a global optimum, so that lower bound is not the logical negation of the target.

The question also imposes no polynomial-space requirement. An exponential-space algorithm with a fixed time base below two would qualify. Limits on a specific time-space curve, a subset recurrence or a local search rule do not establish an unrestricted impossibility theorem. The reviewed sources distinguish this open algorithmic question from a conjectured hardness assumption for another problem.

Arbitrary-length costs still require the bit-length accounting stated in this card.

Björklund gives a Monte Carlo \(O^*(1.657^n)\) algorithm for undirected Hamiltonicity. The weighted extension in Theorem 3 has running time \(O^*(W1.657^n)\), where \(W\) is the sum of the positive integer edge weights. A value \(2^b\) needs only \(b+1\) binary digits, so a factor polynomial in \(W\) can be exponential in the number of input bits used for weights. That extension does not establish the arbitrary-binary-weight target.

The input-bit distinction is not a demand for strongly polynomial arithmetic complexity. A polynomial factor in the total binary encoding length is expressly allowed. What is excluded is hiding dependence on enormous numerical weights inside that factor. Likewise, randomized success must hold on each fixed instance, and every execution must obey the clock. A favorable average over sampled instances is a different guarantee.

The STACS 2026 small-doubling result goes beyond numerically small weights. If \(A\) is the set of distinct input weights and \(A+A=\{a+b:a,b\in A\}\), its promise is \(|A+A|\le C|A|\) for a fixed constant \(C\). Under that additional structure, the stated TSP time matches the unweighted exponential scale, with factors depending on \(C\). Arbitrary weight sets need not have a bounded doubling constant; allowing \(C\) to grow with the input does not give this card’s fixed uniform bound.

Time and memory are separate resources. Dallant and Kozma’s April 2026 paper improves interior time-space tradeoffs: it studies running time \(T^{n+o(n)}\) and space \(S^{n+o(n)}\) for \(2<T<4\), obtaining a product \(ST<3.572\) at one point. An improvement in the product does not assert \(T<2\). The paper explicitly retains the base-two running-time question as open.

The July 2026 follow-up improves the achievable time-space product to roughly \(3.1819\) in the relevant set-system framework. Its lower bound of more than \(3.1818\) is a limitation of that framework, whose parameters describe families of subsets and their chains. It is not a lower bound against arbitrary randomized TSP algorithms. The introduction still identifies \(O^*(2^n)\) as the best known unrestricted classical time scale.

Quantum algorithms form a different comparison. Dallant’s July 2026 theorem assumes quantum computation and quantum random-access memory. The saving from quantum search cannot be treated as an implementation on a classical RAM with independent random bits. The selected target permits classical randomization but supplies no quantum operations.

The ESA paper published on 25 August 2026 similarly reports a time base of 1.859 with a QRAM space base of 1.315. The inspected official abstract makes the quantum resource explicit. Those sub-two numbers therefore do not constitute a classical solution to this card; the full theorem was not independently audited in this review.

The SODA 2026 paper on \(k\)-opt proves that prescribed local-improvement processes can take exponentially many iterations even with an optimal choice of improving move. Its conclusion concerns those processes, including particular three- and four-edge neighborhoods. The card allows all uniform algorithms, and asks for a global optimum, so that lower bound is not the logical negation of the target.

The question also imposes no polynomial-space requirement. An exponential-space algorithm with a fixed time base below two would qualify. Limits on a specific time-space curve, a subset recurrence or a local search rule do not establish an unrestricted impossibility theorem. The reviewed sources distinguish this open algorithmic question from a conjectured hardness assumption for another problem.

cards.title: Set Cover conjecture
cards.formal:
Is the Set Cover conjecture true? For every \(\varepsilon\in(0,1)\), does there exist a fixed integer \(d\ge1\) such that no uniform randomized bounded-error algorithm solves \(\le d\)-Set Cover on an \(n\)-element universe in worst-case time
\[O\!\left((2-\varepsilon)^n(n+1)^r\right)\]
for any fixed exponent \(r\)? An instance supplies a family \(\mathcal F\subseteq2^{[n]}\) with \(|S|\le d\) for every \(S\in\mathcal F\), and an integer \(t\in\{0,\ldots,n\}\). The task is to decide whether some subfamily \(\mathcal H\subseteq\mathcal F\) of at most \(t\) sets satisfies \(\bigcup_{S\in\mathcal H}S=[n]\). Sets chosen for the cover may overlap. The randomized interpretation is explicit in the later primary sources.
cards.why: Set Cover is a central example of an exact algorithm whose natural dynamic-programming base remains two. The conjecture provides barriers for other exponential-time problems and is not merely a restatement of the familiar SAT hypotheses. Its incompatibility with the asymptotic rank conjecture links this algorithmic barrier to fundamental questions in algebraic complexity.

sentences: Set Cover asks whether a few supplied sets can cover a given universe.
The conjecture concerns exact algorithms when each available set has a fixed maximum size.
It says that no constant improvement over exponential base two works across all such size bounds.
The target allows bounded-error randomization and polynomial factors that depend on the fixed bound.
Recent results show that a major conjecture about tensor rank would refute SCC, but neither side is settled unconditionally.

cards.definitions:
Let \([n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}\), with \(n\ge1\). Each set is represented by its sorted list of distinct element indices in binary; the family is an explicitly supplied list without duplicate sets. Empty sets and an empty family are allowed. Write \(m=|\mathcal F|\). For fixed \(d\),
\[m\le\sum_{j=0}^{\min(d,n)}\binom nj\le(n+1)^d,\]
so the entire valid input has length polynomial in \(n\), with its degree allowed to depend on \(d\). The threshold can be capped at \(n\), since any cover contains a subcover of at most \(n\) sets. The question counts the universe size, not the number of available sets or selected sets, in the exponential part of the time bound.

Use a uniform random-access machine with finite program, binary words of length \(w=\lceil4(n+\log_2(m+2)+1)\rceil\), and word-addressed memory. This allows the usual exponential-size dynamic-programming tables while keeping each word polynomially many bits long. Unit-cost instructions are word reads/writes, copies, branches, comparisons, addition/subtraction/multiplication modulo \(2^w\), integer division with remainder by a nonzero divisor, bitwise Boolean operations, shifts, and obtaining a uniformly random independent word. Shifts by at least \(w\) and division by zero may return zero. Initially memory holds only the input and otherwise zeroes. Every table construction and preprocessing operation is counted. The machine has no oracle or nonuniform advice, and no operation acts on an exponentially long bit string as one word. Charging polynomial bit cost for scalar word operations only alters the allowed polynomial factor.

A randomized algorithm must return the correct decision with probability at least \(2/3\) on every valid input and halt within its asserted time bound on every random tape. The bound means that for a fixed \(d,\varepsilon\), there are constants \(K,r,n_0\) for which runtime is at most \(K(2-\varepsilon)^n(n+1)^r\) whenever \(n\ge n_0\). All finite smaller valid instances must also be correctly decided. These constants and the program may depend on \(d,\varepsilon\), but not on \(n,\mathcal F,t\).

The negation is a single \(\varepsilon>0\) that works for every fixed \(d\), allowing a different algorithm and polynomial factor for each \(d\). An improved base for one particular set-size bound does not refute the conjecture. The decision version used here and the source's minimum-cover optimization version have the same exponential base: searching thresholds and recovering a cover uses only polynomially many calls for fixed \(d\).
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct Lean-checked proof of the conjecture or its negation in the stated randomized computational model. A refutation must give a uniform positive improvement of the exponential base across every fixed maximum set size. Proving a lower bound assuming SETH or another conjecture, restricting to deterministic algorithms, improving one bounded-size case, or counting only arithmetic operations on unbounded-size objects does not settle this target.

context_blocks.text: A subset dynamic program solves the problem in \(2^n\operatorname{poly}(n,m)\) time. The target asks whether the base two can be reduced by a constant independent of the maximum allowed set size. Polynomial factors are explicitly permitted and may grow with that fixed size bound.

The family is given explicitly and each set has at most d elements. This is distinct from requiring exactly d elements, requiring a partition into disjoint sets, or bounding how many sets contain each element. The 2024 source studies reductions between such variants, but the card fixes the at-most-d covering version.

Cygan and coauthors use the Set Cover assumption for tight conditional bounds on several exact algorithms. Their work does not prove that the ordinary Strong Exponential Time Hypothesis implies this Set Cover conjecture.

Björklund and Kaski prove that Strassen’s asymptotic rank conjecture would yield a randomized sub-two-base algorithm and hence refute SCC. Pratt strengthens the conditional algorithm. These are incompatibility and conditional-algorithm theorems, not unconditional resolutions of either conjecture.

cards.title: FPT approximation of twin-width
cards.formal: Do there exist total computable functions \(f,g:N\to N\) and a constant \(c\ge 1\), and one deterministic Turing machine A, such that for every finite nonempty simple graph G on n vertices and integer \(k\ge 0, A\) halts within \(f(k)(n+1)^{c}\) bit operations and either correctly reports \(tww(G)>k\) or outputs a contraction sequence of G of width at most \(g(k)\)? No order, decomposition or contraction sequence is supplied with G.
cards.definitions: The input gives n, the \(n\times n\) adjacency matrix of G, and k in binary. A contraction sequence is a sequence of partitions of \(V(G)\), starting with the singleton partition and ending with \(\{V(G)\}\), each obtained from its predecessor by merging two parts. For distinct parts X,Y, their pair is mixed if there exist both an adjacent pair \(x\in X,y\in Y\) and a nonadjacent pair \(x' \in X,y' \in Y\) in the original graph. The red degree of a part is the number of other parts with which it has a mixed pair. The sequence width is the maximum red degree over every part of every partition. Twin-width \(tww(G)\) is the minimum sequence width; a one-vertex graph has twin-width zero. The output lists the \(n- 1\) merges using integer part labels. Both f and g depend only on k, whereas c is independent of k and G. If \(tww(G)\le k\), rejection is forbidden. If \(tww(G)>k\), either a correct rejection or the stated bounded-width sequence is allowed.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove the proposition in the problem statement or its logical negation with the stated model, hypotheses and quantifier order. The proof must settle the entire target. A result conditional on an additional assumption settles only that conditional version. Benchmark acceptance requires a complete proof checked by a proof assistant and matching this statement.

cards.title: Polynomial kernel for Edge Multiway Cut
cards.formal:
Does undirected Edge Multiway Cut, parameterized only by the allowed number \(k\) of edge deletions, admit a randomized polynomial kernel? Specifically, do there exist a uniform randomized algorithm \(R\) and positive integers \(C,a,b\) such that for every explicitly encoded instance \(I=(G,T,k)\) of length \(N\), on every random tape \(R\) halts within \(C(N+1)^a\) steps and outputs a well-formed instance \(I'=(G',T',k')\) of the same problem with
\[|I'|\le C(k+1)^b,\qquad k'\le C(k+1)^b,\]
and
\[\Pr_R[I\text{ is a yes-instance}\ \Longleftrightarrow\ I'\text{ is a yes-instance}]\ge2/3?\]
A yes-instance has a set of at most \(k\) edges whose removal leaves no connected component containing two terminals. The number of terminals is unbounded and is not an extra parameter. The constants, including the exponent \(b\), must be independent of \(|T|\).
cards.why: Kernelization asks whether the information relevant to a small cut budget can be compressed before solving the remaining hard instance. Edge Multiway Cut is a central test of that principle because it combines many terminal-separation requirements while parameterizing only the number of removed edges. A polynomial kernel would replace arbitrarily large graphs by uniformly small equivalent instances without fixing the number of terminals.

The question asks whether polynomial-time preprocessing can reduce any instance to an equivalent instance of size polynomial in the deletion budget alone.

cards.definitions:
An input graph is a finite undirected unweighted loopless multigraph \(G=(V,E)\). Vertices are labeled \(1,\ldots,n\); edges are an explicitly listed sequence of unordered pairs of distinct vertices. Parallel edges are distinct listed objects, each costing one deletion. The terminal set \(T\subseteq V\) consists of distinct designated vertices. The budget \(k\ge0\) is an integer in binary. Encode \(n\) in unary, the edge-list length and endpoints in a self-delimiting binary format, the terminal set as an \(n\)-bit membership vector, and \(k\) in self-delimiting binary. The total encoding length \(N\) includes every listed edge, vertex and terminal and the budget. The output uses the same format; succinct circuits, binary edge multiplicities and binary weights are not allowed.

A cut is a subset \(F\subseteq E\) of edge identities with \(|F|\le k\). The graph \(G-F\) retains every vertex and terminal. It must contain no path between any two distinct terminals. Terminals cannot be deleted, and terminal labels carry no further pairing data: every terminal must be separated from every other. Disconnected graphs, empty graphs, zero budgets and fewer than two terminals are included. The kernel need only preserve the decision answer, not the optimum cut value or every terminal-partition cut. It may relabel vertices and change the terminal set and budget.

The multigraph convention permits the contractions used in kernelization. It does not change polynomial-kernel existence relative to explicit simple graphs: replacing every edge by its own two-edge path through a fresh nonterminal gives a simple graph of polynomial encoding size with the same minimum number of edge deletions needed to separate terminals. Either part of such a path can be deleted at unit cost, while deleting both never helps beyond deleting one.

Use a uniform multitape probabilistic Turing machine with independent fair random bits and one transition per time unit, charging for writing the output. There is no advice, oracle or separately provided preprocessing. Runtime, output-format and size guarantees hold on every random tape. The probability of preserving equivalence is at least \(2/3\) for each fixed input, with two-sided error permitted. This explicitly fixes the saved card's allowance of randomized preprocessing; deterministic or one-sided-error polynomial kernels also qualify. The failure probability is not averaged over a distribution of graphs.

A polynomial kernel has size bounded solely by a fixed polynomial in \(k\), even when the original graph and terminal set are much larger. A bound such as \(k^{|T|+1}\) does not satisfy this condition, since its exponent changes with the input. A size bound \(k^{\log^{O(1)}k}\) is quasipolynomial and is likewise insufficient. Both bounds use the full encoding length, not just the number of vertices while ignoring labels, edges or weights.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct Lean-checked proof or refutation of the randomized polynomial-kernel claim. A positive proof must provide the preprocessing algorithm and verify the all-tape polynomial runtime, output size and parameter bounds, and per-instance equivalence probability for arbitrary terminal sets. A negative proof must rule out every algorithm in this model. A kernel for a fixed number of terminals, a reduction to a different decision language, quasipolynomial preprocessing or output size, or a conditional exclusion relying on an unproved complexity assumption does not by itself settle the stated unconditional claim.

context_blocks.text: The source contrasts polynomial kernels for each fixed terminal count with the open case of arbitrary terminal sets. For a bound \(|T|\le s\), the earlier kernel has a size exponent depending on \(s\); that dependence is exactly what the present question must avoid.

Wahlström proves a randomized quasipolynomial kernel for Edge Multiway Cut in the revised 2021 manuscript, with size \(k^{O(\log^3 k)}\) in the displayed bounds. The same work distinguishes a smaller nonconstructive mimicking-network bound from the network size achievable by randomized polynomial-time preprocessing.

The source’s mimicking networks preserve a richer family of terminal cut values. The benchmark asks only for an equivalent Edge Multiway Cut decision instance, so a solution does not need to construct such a stronger universal network.

The 2025 MFCS paper obtains deterministic kernels using quasipolynomial-time preprocessing for several problems whose randomized polynomial kernels were already known. It explicitly treats Multiway Cut with deletable terminals and separately mentions quasipolynomial-size Edge Multiway Cut kernels. Neither changing the deletion model nor allowing more preprocessing time resolves this card.

cards.definitions: The input is \(n\ge1\), a target \(t\ge0\), and an explicitly listed multiset \(x_{1},\ldots,x_{n}\) of positive integers, all in binary with delimiters; \(L\) is the bit length of that full encoding. Accept if and only if there is \(I\subseteq[n]\) with \(\sum_{i\in I}x_{i}=t\). Each index is used at most once, repetitions of values are permitted, and the empty subset is allowed. Use a uniform random-access machine with \(w=d(n+\lceil\log_{2}(L+2)\rceil)\)-bit words for fixed \(d\ge1\), large enough to address exponential memory. Unit-cost instructions are word read/write, copy, addition, subtraction and multiplication modulo \(2^{w}\), integer quotient and remainder with nonzero divisor, comparisons, Boolean operations and shifts; shifts by at least \(w\) return zero. Multiword integers are handled through charged component operations. Input packing, preprocessing and memory initialization are charged. Random words are independent and uniform and cost one instruction each. A fixed finite program receives no advice or tables. It answers correctly with probability at least \(2/3\) on every input and the time bound holds on every random execution. Constants are independent of all input values and \(n,L\). Quantum operations and random-instance promises are absent.

context_blocks.text: Subset Sum asks whether some selection of the supplied indices adds to the target exactly. For values \((3,3,5)\), target \(6\) is attainable by taking both occurrences of \(3\); an occurrence cannot be used twice. Target zero is always attainable by the empty subset. The input multiplicities and the exact integer comparison are part of the problem.

The classical meet-in-the-middle benchmark is \(2^{n/2}\) times polynomial factors. The question asks for a smaller fixed exponential rate on every input, not an improvement in one polynomial factor. A bound such as \(2^{n/2}/n^{100}\) would still leave the requested exponent saving unresolved.

Pseudopolynomial algorithms depend on the numerical target rather than just the number of bits needed to write it. They can be excellent when the target is small, but binary input values can be exponentially large relative to their descriptions. Chan’s 2026 work improves this separate regime while explicitly retaining the worst-case exponential question.

An August 2026 preprint claims a quantum \(O^{\ast}(2^{2n/7})\) algorithm and still identifies the classical half-exponent benchmark. The star notation hides polynomial factors. The use of quantum computation is decisive: this does not supply the classical algorithm quantified over here. The new preprint proof was not independently checked.

Random instances, uniqueness promises and restrictions on the magnitude or density of the numbers can also alter exponential complexity. This target has none of those input promises and permits bounded-error classical randomness on every instance. Exponential memory is allowed and addressable in the specified RAM; a polynomial-space restriction would ask a different question.

cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof that one uniform classical randomized algorithm, constants \(0<\varepsilon<1/2\), \(c\ge1\), and a constant multiplier meet the stated \(2^{(1/2-\varepsilon)n}L^c\) time bound on every random execution and success probability at least \(2/3\) on every input, or prove in Lean that no such choices exist. The theorem must allow unrestricted binary magnitudes, repeated positive values, all targets, and the full permitted RAM model.

cards.title: Single-exponential Directed Feedback Vertex Set
cards.formal: Do there exist a uniform deterministic algorithm and constants \(A,c>0\), \(d\in\mathbb N\), which decide Directed Feedback Vertex Set on every \(n\)-vertex directed graph and deletion budget \(0\le k\le n\) within \(A\,2^{ck}(n+1)^d\) bit-computation steps? The answer must be YES exactly when deleting at most \(k\) vertices makes the graph acyclic. The exponential dependence is solely on the solution-size budget, and the polynomial exponent is independent of \(k\).
cards.why: Deleting a small number of vertices to destroy every directed cycle is a basic model of repairing cyclic dependencies. Fixed-parameter algorithms make small deletion budgets tractable in principle, but the known factorial dependence is much larger than a fixed exponential base. The target asks whether directed cycle structure inherently causes that additional parameter cost.
cards.status_note: The checked 2025 primary papers retain the general single-exponential parameter question or the stronger unresolved subfactorial improvement. The SOSA 2025 bound retains k! and does not settle the target. Bounded subsequent-result checks through 2026-09-16 verified no general resolution; this is not an exhaustive certification of current openness.
cards.review_note: Completed individual review against P versus NP on 2026-09-16; see research/card-completion-20260913/reviews.jsonl.

importance.reason: Directed Feedback Vertex Set is a central cycle-deletion problem whose fixed-parameter tractability is established but whose factorial-versus-single-exponential parameter dependence remains unresolved. sentences: A directed feedback vertex set meets every directed cycle by deleting its vertices.
The question asks for an exact deterministic algorithm with a fixed exponential base in the allowed number of deletions.
The remaining dependence on graph size must be polynomial with an exponent independent of the deletion budget.
Known fixed-parameter algorithms retain a factorial-scale parameter cost, including the checked SOSA 2025 improvement.
This card targets arbitrary digraphs, while the survey’s planar restriction and structural-parameter results remain distinct.

cards.definitions: The input digraph is \(D=([n],E)\), \(n\ge1\), with \(E\subseteq[n]\times[n]\). Self-loops and opposite arcs are allowed; repeated copies of an arc are not represented and have no effect. A directed cycle is a sequence of distinct vertices \(v_1,\ldots,v_t\), \(t\ge1\), with arcs \((v_j,v_{j+1})\) for \(j<t\) and \((v_t,v_1)\). Thus self-loops are cycles of length one, and opposite arcs give a cycle of length two. For \(S\subseteq[n]\), the remaining graph is the induced digraph \(D[[n]\setminus S]\). A feedback vertex set is a set \(S\) for which this remaining digraph contains no directed cycle. Its cost is the cardinality \(|S|\); no vertex weights are present. There are no promises of planarity, bounded degree, bounded treewidth, a supplied solution or bounds on cycle length. Use a deterministic multitape Turing machine with one finite program for all \(n,k,D\), no advice and no random bits. A valid input consists of the prefix \(1^n0\), followed by the \(n^2\) adjacency bits in row-major order, followed by exactly \(\ell=\lceil\log_2(n+1)\rceil\) bits encoding \(k\in\{0,\ldots,n\}\) in most-significant-bit-first binary. The machine must halt and return the correct decision on every valid input. Each Turing-machine transition costs one step, including all input processing and preprocessing. No running-time condition on malformed strings is part of the target. The fixed encoding has length polynomial in \(n\), so ordinary polynomial-time changes of explicit graph encoding only alter the permitted polynomial factor. The quantified constants \(A,c,d\) are independent of \(n,k,D\). The target is worst-case exact decision, including NO instances; it requires neither an optimal deletion set nor enumeration of all solutions.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct Lean-checked construction of the specified deterministic algorithm with its correctness and \(A2^{ck}(n+1)^d\) worst-case bound, or a complete Lean-checked proof that no such algorithm and constants exist. A \(2^{O(k\log k)}n^{O(1)}\) algorithm, an exponent depending on \(k\) in the polynomial input-size factor, an approximation, or a result for restricted graph classes is insufficient for the affirmative answer. A lower bound conditional on an additional unproved hypothesis establishes only that conditional version of the negative statement.

context_blocks.text: Open Problem 3.3 groups the general vertex-deletion and arc-deletion questions and separately asks about planar vertex deletion. This card selects the unrestricted vertex-deletion question and makes the deterministic algorithm convention explicit. A positive answer also covers planar digraphs; a negative answer for unrestricted inputs alone would not settle that subclass.

The general unweighted vertex and arc versions have parameter-preserving polynomial reductions between them, so their single-exponential fixed-parameter existence questions are equivalent. Planarity is an additional restriction and is not presumed to be preserved by those general reductions.

The survey records the established \(k^{O(k)}n^{O(1)}\) parameterized running time and asks whether it can become \(2^{O(k)}n^{O(1)}\). Both are fixed-parameter bounds, but the exponent \(k\log k\) in the former is not bounded by a constant times \(k\).

Xiong and Xiao’s SOSA 2025 result improves the bound to \(O(k!\,2^{o(k)}(n+m))\), where \(m\) is the number of arcs. The factorial term remains, so this result is not a single-exponential algorithm in the deletion budget.

The June 2025 Acta Informatica paper still calls improving the general \(2^{O(k\log k)}\) dependence to \(2^{o(k\log k)}\) a major open problem. Its positive results exploit additional graph structure, and bounds exponential in a treewidth or cycle-length parameter are not bounds exponential only in the deletion budget.

cards.title: Exact recognition of bounded clique-width
cards.formal: For every fixed integer \(k\ge 1\), do there exist a deterministic Turing machine \(A_{k}\) and constants \(C_{k},c_{k}\ge 1\) such that \(A_{k}\) decides whether \(\operatorname{cw}(G)\le k\) for every finite simple undirected graph G in at most \(C_{k}(N+1)^{c_{k}}\) steps, where N is the bit length of G’s adjacency-matrix encoding?
cards.why: Tests whether a major dense-graph width parameter admits efficient exact recognition at every fixed value.

cards.definitions: A k-expression is a finite expression building a labeled graph using labels from \(\{1,\ldots ,k\}\). It can create one isolated vertex with a chosen label; take the disjoint union of two previously constructed labeled graphs; add all edges between the vertices labeled i and those labeled j for distinct i,j; or change every label i to j. Edge insertion leaves existing edges in place without duplicating them. Relabeling changes no edges. The two operands of a disjoint union may both be arbitrary expressions, so this is ordinary clique-width, not linear clique-width. For a nonempty graph \(G, \operatorname{cw}(G)\) is the least k for which some k-expression produces a graph isomorphic to G after labels are erased. Set \(\operatorname{cw}(\varnothing )=0\). The input contains \(n\ge 0\) and the \(n\times n\) symmetric zero-diagonal \(0/1\) adjacency matrix for the graph on \(\{1,\ldots ,n\}\). It contains no construction expression or promise about its width. \(A_{k}\) outputs YES exactly when \(\operatorname{cw}(G)\le k\) and NO otherwise, always halting with the stated worst-case bit bound. The quantifier order is \(\forall k \exists A_{k},C_{k},c_{k} \forall G: k\) is fixed for each machine, and the polynomial exponent may depend on it. Each \(A_{k}\) is a single finite program with no advice depending on graph size; the statement imposes no effective map from k to its program and no uniform exponent.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove polynomial-time exact recognition for every fixed threshold k in the model stated, or prove that for at least one fixed k the language \(\{G:\operatorname{cw}(G)\le k\}\) has no deterministic polynomial-time decider. An expression with more than k labels does not establish a YES answer; failure of one construction does not establish NO. Variable-k NP-hardness, or fixed-k hardness under an unproved assumption, does not alone unconditionally refute this proposition.

context_blocks.title: A width that permits dense graphs
context_blocks.text: Clique-width counts reusable labels in a construction, not the size of a largest clique. Every nonempty edgeless graph has width 1. Complete graphs with at least two vertices have width 2, regardless of their size. Thus even very dense graphs can have small clique-width; the parameter captures how uniformly groups of vertices can be assembled.

context_blocks.title: Fixed thresholds versus the general optimization problem
context_blocks.text: Fellows and coauthors prove NP-completeness when both G and k are input. The present statement allows a different polynomial bound for each fixed k. For example, a hypothetical bound \(N^{k+2}\) would be polynomial for each such threshold, while not giving a polynomial bound when k grows with N. The source lists fixed-threshold recognition separately from the stronger FPT question, which asks for one algorithm with runtime \(f(k)N^{c}\) and c independent of k.

context_blocks.title: Small thresholds are understood
context_blocks.text: Polynomial-time recognition is known through \(k=3\), with the full three-label algorithm published by Corneil and coauthors in 2012. The cited sources retain \(k=4\) as the first unresolved threshold. A solution only for four labels would still leave the card’s quantification over every fixed k.

context_blocks.title: Approximate or supplied decompositions serve a different purpose
context_blocks.text: A procedure that returns an expression with \(f(k)>k\) labels for graphs of width at most k can enable other graph algorithms, yet leave the exact threshold undecided. Likewise, the July 2026 feedback-vertex-set result assumes a k-expression is already supplied. These results explain the usefulness of clique-width without providing the recognizer requested here.

cards.title: Independent set algorithms from tropical circuit size
cards.formal: Do there exist one deterministic multitape Turing machine \(A\), a real constant \(K>0\) and an integer \(a\ge1\) such that, for every finite simple graph \(G\) on \(n\ge1\) labeled vertices and every nonnegative integer weight vector \(w\), the machine outputs the exact value \(\operatorname{MWIS}(G,w)\) within \(K(\tau(G)+n+L+1)^a\) bit operations? Here \(L\) is the total encoded length of the weights and \(\tau(G)\) is the minimum tropical-circuit size defined below. The input contains only \(G,w\), without a circuit, a decomposition or the value of \(\tau(G)\).
cards.definitions:
The vertex set is \([n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}\). The graph is supplied as \(n\) in binary and its explicit \(n\times n\) symmetric zero-diagonal binary adjacency matrix. The weights \(w_1,\ldots,w_n\in\mathbb Z_{\ge0}\) are listed in binary with delimiters, including one zero bit for a zero weight. Let \(L\) include all those weight bits and delimiters. A set \(I\subseteq[n]\) is independent if no two distinct vertices of \(I\) are adjacent. For every real vector \(x\in\mathbb R^n\), define
\[
\operatorname{MWIS}(G,x)=\max_{\substack{I\subseteq[n]\\ I\text{ independent}}}\ \sum_{v\in I}x_v.
\]
The empty set is allowed and has weight zero. The required output of \(A\) is the nonnegative integer \(\operatorname{MWIS}(G,w)\), in ordinary binary notation.

A tropical circuit on variables \(x_1,\ldots,x_n\) is a finite directed acyclic graph with one designated output gate. Each input gate has no incoming wires and is labeled by one variable or by the constant \(0\). Every other gate has two input wires and is labeled either \(\max\) or \(+\), interpreted as ordinary maximum or addition of real numbers. Input wires may carry the same previously computed value; fan-out is unrestricted. No other constants, comparisons with branching, multiplication, subtraction or oracle gates are allowed. Size is the total number of gates, including input and constant gates. A circuit for \(G\) is valid if its output equals \(\operatorname{MWIS}(G,x)\) for every \(x\in\mathbb R_{\ge0}^n\). Its topology and labels depend on \(G\) alone, not on the weight assignment. Define \(\tau(G)\) as the minimum size of such a valid circuit. This finite integer exists for every graph.

The machine \(A\) may perform arbitrary deterministic Turing-machine computation; it is not restricted to the operations allowed in the circuits that define \(\tau\). Its program and the constants \(K,a\) are independent of \(G,w,n\). All graph reads, arithmetic on binary weights, preprocessing and output writing are charged. The \(n\) term in a fixed polynomial also accounts for the \(n^2\)-bit adjacency matrix. There are no random bits, nonuniform advice or uncharged preprocessing. The guarantee is a worst-case bound for each valid input. Only the optimum value is requested, not a witnessing independent set or a tropical circuit.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct Lean proof of a uniform algorithm and fixed constants meeting the exact computational task and bound for all graphs and weights, or a complete Lean proof of their nonexistence. A quasipolynomial dependence on the circuit-size parameter, a construction that is supplied a circuit, or an algorithm restricted to a graph class does not establish the stated polynomial target. A conditional lower bound retains its condition and alone does not give an unconditional negative answer.
cards.why: A compact circuit can express a dynamic program for every weight assignment to one graph without explaining how to discover it. This question asks whether the existence of that compact representation always yields an effective uniform algorithm, connecting nonuniform computation with exact graph optimization.

cards.title: Fixed-parameter tractability of graph isomorphism by rank-width
cards.formal: Do there exist one deterministic multitape Turing machine \(A\), a total computable function \(f:\mathbb N\to\mathbb N_{\ge1}\), and an integer \(c\ge1\) such that, for every pair of finite simple undirected graphs \(G,H\), \(A\) decides whether \(G\cong H\) within \[f(k)(|V(G)|+|V(H)|+2)^c\] bit operations, where \(k=\max\{\operatorname{rw}(G),\operatorname{rw}(H)\}\)? Graphs are supplied by their explicitly encoded adjacency matrices; neither a rank decomposition nor a width bound is supplied.
cards.definitions:
A graph of order \(n\ge0\) has vertex set \([n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}\), with \([0]=\varnothing\), and an \(n\times n\) symmetric zero-one adjacency matrix with zero diagonal. Thus there are no loops, parallel edges, colors or vertex labels that an isomorphism must preserve. For graphs of orders \(n,m\), the assertion \(G\cong H\) means that there is a bijection \(\pi:[n]\to[m]\) satisfying
\[
\{u,v\}\in E(G)\ \Longleftrightarrow\
\{\pi(u),\pi(v)\}\in E(H)
\quad\text{for every }u,v\in[n].
\]
The required output is one decision bit; an isomorphism, canonical labeling or canonical graph is not required.

For \(X\subseteq V(G)\), let \(M_G(X)\) be the adjacency submatrix whose rows are indexed by \(X\) and columns by \(V(G)\setminus X\). Define the cut-rank
\[
\rho_G(X)=\operatorname{rank}_{\mathbb F_2}M_G(X),
\]
where \(\mathbb F_2=\{0,1\}\) has addition and multiplication modulo two, and rank is the dimension of the row space over this field. A matrix with no rows or no columns has rank zero.

For \(n\ge2\), a rank decomposition consists of a finite tree \(T\) of maximum degree at most three and a bijection between its leaves and \(V(G)\). Removing any edge \(e\) partitions the leaves into two sets; write \(X_e\subseteq V(G)\) for either side. The width of the decomposition is \(\max_{e\in E(T)}\rho_G(X_e)\). This is independent of the chosen side because the two cut matrices are transposes. The rank-width \(\operatorname{rw}(G)\) is the minimum width over all such trees and leaf bijections. For \(n\le1\), set \(\operatorname{rw}(G)=0\). The unrooted decomposition convention here gives the same width as a rooted binary decomposition whose nodes represent the descendant leaf sets.

For a concrete input encoding, let \(\mathrm{bin}(n)\) be the ordinary binary expansion of \(n\), with \(\mathrm{bin}(0)=0\), and set \(b=|\mathrm{bin}(n)|\). Encode \(n\) by \(1^b0\,\mathrm{bin}(n)\), followed by the \(n^2\) adjacency bits in row-major order. Concatenate the two graph encodings. The machine must reject malformed strings; the displayed parameterized bound is required on valid graph pairs. The model charges every input access, tape move, arithmetic operation as its bit-level implementation, preprocessing step and output bit. No decomposition, parameter value, advice, oracle, randomness or uncharged preprocessing is available.

The program \(A\) and exponent \(c\) are fixed for all graph sizes and widths. The function \(f\) must be computable by an ordinary halting algorithm on every nonnegative integer, although it need not be polynomial, elementary or explicitly evaluated by \(A\). It may grow arbitrarily rapidly with the parameter. An algorithm with exponent depending on \(k\), or a separate nonuniform algorithm for each width without the stated common computable bound, is not the claimed fixed-parameter algorithm.

context_blocks.text: Question 6.2 contains two separate targets: fixed-parameter tractability and a smaller parameter-dependent polynomial exponent. This card retains the first branch. Grohe and Neuen give a polynomial-time isomorphism algorithm at every fixed rank-width, with running time \(O(n^{3k+5}\log n)\) for the stated bounded-width setting. The exponent still grows with \(k\). The revised paper corrects a proof issue in its earlier version; the cited revision is the July 2022 version.

The parallel canonization result gives small-depth circuits for each fixed rank-width, but their size has an exponent depending on the width. It does not supply the fixed exponent required by this card.

The 2026 connectivity-function result improves computation of rank-width and its decomposition. This is a different task from determining whether two graphs are isomorphic. The card charges any decomposition work done by its algorithm and does not assume one is given.

The survey also discusses isomorphism parameterized by rank-depth, which restricts the depth as well as the cut structure. Its cited fixed-parameter result is nonuniform and concerns the more restrictive parameter; it does not establish this rank-width target.

cards.why: Rank-width captures dense graphs with structured adjacency cuts, extending the reach of graph decomposition beyond sparse settings. A uniform fixed-parameter isomorphism test would make the polynomial exponent independent of this structural complexity and settle a central boundary in parameterized graph isomorphism.

cards.title: Polynomial compression versus polynomial kernelization
cards.formal: Does there exist a fixed parameterized language \(Q\subseteq\{0,1\}^*\times\mathbb N\) such that its unary-parameter encoding \(\widetilde Q\) is NP-complete and \[\operatorname{PC}(Q)\ \land\ \bigl(\operatorname{PK}(Q)\ \Longrightarrow\ \mathrm{NP}\subseteq\mathrm{coNP}/\mathrm{poly}\bigr)?\] Here \(\operatorname{PC}\) means deterministic polynomial compression to an arbitrary fixed language, and \(\operatorname{PK}\) means deterministic polynomial kernelization back to \(Q\), with the exact definitions below. Thus the requested compression is unconditional, while its separation from kernels uses the explicitly stated hypothesis \(\mathrm{NP}\nsubseteq\mathrm{coNP}/\mathrm{poly}\).
cards.why: Kernelization asks whether small equivalent instances can remain in the original problem language, while compression permits a different representation. A separation would expose a fundamental limit of preprocessing back into the same NP-complete problem even when short decision-equivalent information is computable.

sentences: A polynomial compression replaces an instance by a short string for a possibly different decision language.
A polynomial kernel must instead return a short equivalent instance of the original parameterized problem.
The selected question asks for an NP-complete unary source language with deterministic polynomial compression but a conditional obstruction to polynomial kernels.
