cards.title: Polylogarithmic approximation for Directed Steiner Tree
cards.area: Approximation algorithms and hardness of approximation
cards.formal:
Do there exist positive integers \(a,C,K,q\) and one uniform randomized classical algorithm \(A\) such that, for every feasible Directed Steiner Tree instance \(I\) of encoding length \(N\) with \(k\ge1\) terminals, every execution halts within \(K(N+1)^q\) bit steps and outputs a feasible arc subset \(F\), and
\[\Pr\!\left[c(F)\le a\bigl(\log_2(k+2)\bigr)^C\operatorname{OPT}(I)\right]\ge\frac23?\]
The probability is over the algorithm’s internal randomness, separately for each input. The graph is arbitrary and directed, with exactly represented nonnegative rational arc costs. All four constants and the program must be independent of the instance.
cards.definitions:
Instance. The vertex set is \(V=[n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}\), where \(n\ge2\). A finite list of \(m\) indexed arcs specifies their tails and heads in \(V\); different indices denote different arcs even when their endpoints coincide. Loops and parallel arcs are allowed. The root is \(r\in V\), and the terminal set is \(T\subseteq V\setminus\{r\}\), with \(k=|T|\ge1\). Every arc \(e\) has cost \(c_e=u_e/v_e\), where \(u_e\) is a nonnegative integer and \(v_e\) a positive integer, both supplied in binary. Zero costs and arbitrarily long cost descriptions are allowed. There is no planarity, acyclicity, degree, treewidth, depth or metric promise.

Reachability and feasibility. A directed path follows arc orientations from its first vertex to its last; it may be taken without repeated vertices. The input is promised feasible: every terminal is reachable from \(r\). A feasible output is a subset \(F\subseteq E\) of arc indices such that the subgraph \((V,F)\) has a directed \(r\)-to-\(t\) path for every \(t\in T\). Nonterminal vertices may be used freely as intermediate vertices. Arc cost is paid once, regardless of how many terminal paths use it:
\[c(F)=\sum_{e\in F}c_e,\qquad\operatorname{OPT}(I)=\min\{c(F):F\subseteq E\text{ is feasible}\}.\]
The minimum exists because there are finitely many subsets and at least one is feasible. It may equal zero. The name “tree” does not impose an additional output-syntax condition: a feasible directed subgraph qualifies. Nonnegative costs also permit deletion of redundant arcs to obtain a rooted outward branching without increasing cost. Terminals are not required to be leaves.

Encoding and size. The graph, root, terminal list and every arc cost are explicit. One fixed encoding lists \(n,m,r,k\), all vertex labels \(1,\ldots,n\), the \(k\) distinct terminal labels in increasing order, and, for each indexed arc in order, its tail, head, numerator and denominator. Encode each nonnegative integer by its binary expansion preceded by its length in unary and a zero delimiter; the expansion of zero is the single bit zero. Let \(N\) be the total bit length. In particular \(N\ge n\), and every bit of every cost contributes to \(N\). Output identifies the selected arc indices, or equivalently their \(m\)-bit indicator vector.

Computation and randomness. Use an ordinary uniform multitape Turing machine with a finite program, read-only input, initially blank work tapes and a write-only output tape. A step reads and updates a constant number of tape symbols and moves each head by at most one cell; a random step additionally supplies one independent fair bit. Reading the input, writing the entire solution, exact rational arithmetic and all preprocessing count in the bit time. No nonuniform advice, free optimization oracle, supplied fractional solution or unit-cost exact-real operation is available. The required bound holds for every random bit sequence, not just on average.

Guarantee. On each feasible input, every execution must return a feasible subset; on an event of probability at least \(2/3\), its cost must also satisfy the displayed ratio. On other executions the cost may be larger but feasibility is still required. When \(\operatorname{OPT}=0\), the successful output must have cost zero; an additive positive error is not allowed. The \(k+2\) convention makes the factor defined and positive also at one terminal. Choosing positive integer constants rather than arbitrary real constants at least one does not change existence, since the logarithm is greater than one and rounding constants upward only relaxes the bound. No behavior is prescribed on malformed encodings; infeasible well-formed instances may be detected and reported in polynomial time before applying the feasible-instance algorithm.
cards.answer_criterion:
Give a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of the existence claim or its negation. For a positive answer, specify an algorithm and fixed constants, and prove its bit running time on every execution, feasibility of every output, and the per-instance probability and cost bound throughout the full class. The proof must account for binary rational costs and zero optimum. A procedure with a variable time exponent depending on \(k\), or with uncharged access to a special fractional solution, does not meet the statement.

A negative answer must rule out every fixed power \(C\) of \(\log_2(k+2)\), every factor \(a\), every polynomial time bound and every permitted randomized program. For example, for every uniformly polynomial-time program that always returns feasible outputs and for every \(a,C\), it suffices to prove the existence of a feasible instance on which the probability of the requested ratio is less than \(2/3\). A lower bound for deterministic programs alone is insufficient. A conditional hardness theorem must identify its unproved assumptions and does not by itself give an unconditional negative answer.

A polylogarithmic ratio in quasipolynomial time, an \(O(k^{\varepsilon})\) ratio for each separately fixed \(\varepsilon>0\), a theorem for planar graphs, or an integrality gap for one chosen relaxation is partial progress. Hardness below a particular logarithmic power leaves larger fixed powers possible. Expected-time or expected-cost analyses must be converted into the stated execution-time and success guarantees in the checked proof; they cannot simply replace those requirements.

context_blocks.text: The problem asks how cheaply a root can reach many destinations through one shared directed network. Buying a common initial segment can save cost across many root-to-terminal paths, but the directions restrict which branching structures are usable. With one terminal the problem is shortest path. With many terminals, selecting where the paths should share infrastructure becomes the central optimization challenge.

A simple reduction explains why ordinary reachability is insufficient. For a set-cover instance, create a vertex for each set and each element, an arc of cost one from the root to every set vertex, and zero-cost arcs from each set to its elements. Make all element vertices terminals. A feasible network must buy a collection of set arcs covering all elements, and its cost equals the number of chosen sets. The directed graph can thus encode a nontrivial covering problem even with only two layers after the root.

The familiar polynomial-time approximation frontier is \(O(k^{\varepsilon})\) for every fixed \(\varepsilon >0\), from the classical directed Steiner algorithms. The running-time exponent depends on the chosen accuracy parameter. Setting \(\varepsilon\) to a quantity that shrinks with k is not a free improvement: it changes that dependence and can produce quasipolynomial time. A power of k, however small and fixed, eventually exceeds every fixed power of log k.

Grandoni, Laekhanukit and Li prove a randomized \(O(\log^2 k/\log\log k)\) approximation with running time \(n^{O(\log^5 k)}\), in the asymptotic range where this expression is used. This is quasipolynomial: its exponent grows with the input parameter. The target here permits a larger fixed power of the logarithm, but requires one polynomial time exponent for every instance. The old classical paper’s original quasipolynomial \(O(\log^2 k)\) claim was corrected to \(O(\log^3 k)\) because of a height-reduction lemma; the 2019 paper explicitly records that correction.

The same work gives near-matching quasipolynomial-time hardness under additional complexity assumptions, including the Projection Games Conjecture. This does not show that every polynomial-time polylogarithmic approximation is impossible: a larger fixed logarithmic power is allowed in this card. The issue is a gap between what can currently be computed in polynomial time and what is known with more time, rather than the already settled hardness of exact optimization.

A natural flow relaxation buys a fractional capacity \(x_{e}\) for each arc and, separately for each terminal, sends a unit flow from the root using at most \(x_{e}\) on that arc. Different terminals may reuse the same purchased capacity because a network edge is bought once. In general graphs this relaxation has polynomial-size integrality gaps, including \(\Omega (\sqrt{k})\) examples. Those examples explain why a straightforward LP-rounding strategy cannot guarantee a polylogarithmic factor against that relaxation on every instance. They do not rule out stronger relaxations or a different algorithm.

The December 2024 general approximation claim was withdrawn in version 2. Version 3, submitted in October 2025, calls itself a rectification and assumes access to a relatively integral solution of a strengthened relaxation: for each terminal and arc, its flow is either zero or the whole purchased capacity. Theorem 1 states an expected-polynomial-time rounding result under this extra hypothesis. This is neither an algorithm that supplies the needed solution on every ordinary input nor a proof for arbitrary standard flow-LP optima. The live record still carries the reachability-proof withdrawal comment. The restricted result is recorded as a reported claim, not an independently verified general approximation.

Planarity changes the picture substantially. Friggstad and Mousavi give a polynomial-time \(O(\log  k)\)-approximation for planar directed graphs, using shortest-path separators. Later work extends the structural approach to other rooted planar network-design problems and bounds a natural planar LP gap by \(O(\log ^{2} k)\). These theorems show that directedness alone does not preclude the requested factor, but their separator arguments do not apply to arbitrary directed graphs.

Chekuri and Jain’s length-constrained work appeared on arXiv in July and was published on 9 September 2026. The published introduction still explicitly identifies the general polynomial-time polylogarithmic DST question as open. For planar graphs, Theorem 2 gives logarithmic cost approximation with logarithmic length slack, while Theorem 3 gives a log-squared bound against a fractional relaxation with the same length slack. Removing the path-length constraint does not remove their planarity assumption. The related directed-forest theorem has multiple source–sink demands, a different target from one-root DST.

The old classical paper’s original quasipolynomial \(O(\log^2 k)\) claim was corrected to \(O(\log^3 k)\) because of a height-reduction lemma; the 2019 paper explicitly records that correction.

The same work gives near-matching quasipolynomial-time hardness under additional complexity assumptions, including the Projection Games Conjecture. This does not show that every polynomial-time polylogarithmic approximation is impossible: a larger fixed logarithmic power is allowed in this card. The issue is a gap between what can currently be computed in polynomial time and what is known with more time, rather than the already settled hardness of exact optimization.

A natural flow relaxation buys a fractional capacity \(x_{e}\) for each arc and, separately for each terminal, sends a unit flow from the root using at most \(x_{e}\) on that arc. Different terminals may reuse the same purchased capacity because a network edge is bought once. In general graphs this relaxation has polynomial-size integrality gaps, including \(\Omega (\sqrt{k})\) examples. Those examples explain why a straightforward LP-rounding strategy cannot guarantee a polylogarithmic factor against that relaxation on every instance. They do not rule out stronger relaxations or a different algorithm.

The December 2024 general approximation claim was withdrawn in version 2. Version 3, submitted in October 2025, calls itself a rectification and assumes access to a relatively integral solution of a strengthened relaxation: for each terminal and arc, its flow is either zero or the whole purchased capacity. Theorem 1 states an expected-polynomial-time rounding result under this extra hypothesis. This is neither an algorithm that supplies the needed solution on every ordinary input nor a proof for arbitrary standard flow-LP optima. The live record still carries the reachability-proof withdrawal comment. The restricted result is recorded as a reported claim, not an independently verified general approximation.

Planarity changes the picture substantially. Friggstad and Mousavi give a polynomial-time \(O(\log  k)\)-approximation for planar directed graphs, using shortest-path separators. Later work extends the structural approach to other rooted planar network-design problems and bounds a natural planar LP gap by \(O(\log ^{2} k)\). These theorems show that directedness alone does not preclude the requested factor, but their separator arguments do not apply to arbitrary directed graphs.

Chekuri and Jain’s length-constrained work appeared on arXiv in July and was published on 9 September 2026. The published introduction still explicitly identifies the general polynomial-time polylogarithmic DST question as open. For planar graphs, Theorem 2 gives logarithmic cost approximation with logarithmic length slack, while Theorem 3 gives a log-squared bound against a fractional relaxation with the same length slack. Removing the path-length constraint does not remove their planarity assumption. The related directed-forest theorem has multiple source–sink demands, a different target from one-root DST.

cards.title: Small-Set Expansion Hypothesis
cards.area: Approximation algorithms and hardness of approximation
cards.formal: For every rational constant \(\eta \in (0,1/2)\), is there a rational constant \(\delta \in (0,1/2)\) such that the following promise problem is NP-hard under deterministic polynomial-time many-one reductions? Given a regular graph G on n vertices with \(\delta n\) an integer, distinguish YES: some \(S\subseteq V(G)\) with |\(S|=\delta n\) has \(\Phi _{G}(S)\le \eta\), from NO: every \(S\subseteq V(G)\) with |\(S|=\delta n\) has \(\Phi _{G}(S)\ge 1- \eta\).

cards.definitions: Use finite simple undirected d-regular graphs \(G=([n],E), n\ge 2\) and \(d\ge 1\), given explicitly by their adjacency matrices. Regular means that every vertex has exactly d neighbours; d is not a fixed constant or an extra promise. For nonempty \(S, \partial _{G} S\) is the set of edges with exactly one endpoint in S, and \(\Phi _{G}(S)=|\partial _{G} S|/(d|S|)\). Internal edges contribute twice to d|S| and zero to the boundary. This is normalized edge expansion, not the number of outside neighbours. The graph has no promised connectivity, geometry or spectral gap. The constants \(\eta ,\delta\) are chosen before the input; they are not parameters tending to zero with n. For \(\delta =a/b\) in lowest terms, inputs have n a positive multiple of b, so exact set size has no rounding ambiguity. The YES and NO cases are disjoint since \(\eta <1/2\); inputs meeting neither case have no required decision answer. NP-hardness means that for every language L with polynomially checkable witnesses, a deterministic polynomial-time map sends each \(x\in \mathrm{L}\) to a YES graph and each \(x\notin \mathrm{L}\) to a NO graph. Equivalently, it suffices to supply such a reduction from Boolean satisfiability. Reduction constants and the polynomial exponent may depend on \(\eta\) and its chosen \(\delta\). The card fixes the unweighted regular-graph, exact-cardinality version of the imported question; weighted-volume, randomized-hardness and size-interval versions must be identified when cited.
cards.answer_criterion: A positive resolution proves the stated NP-hardness for every \(\eta\) by choosing \(\delta\) and giving a valid promise-preserving reduction. A negative resolution refutes this quantified hardness statement for some fixed \(\eta\). Polynomial-time algorithms for every fixed \(\delta\) at that \(\eta\) would refute the hardness claim under \(\mathrm{P}\ne \mathrm{NP}\); an algorithm alone must not be called an unconditional disproof of NP-hardness. Results restricted to special graph classes or allowing a different output set size do not automatically settle this formulation.

context_blocks.title: What expansion measures
context_blocks.text: Choose a vertex uniformly from S, then choose one of its neighbours uniformly. The probability of leaving S is exactly \(\Phi _{G}(S)\). A set with expansion near zero is a group whose connections mostly remain inside it. Expansion near one means that almost every connection goes out. The promise asks whether one unusually insulated set exists at the specified size, or whether every set of that size is almost completely exposed.

context_blocks.title: Small means a fixed fraction
context_blocks.text: If \(\delta =1/1000\), the target has one thousand vertices in a million-vertex graph and one million vertices in a billion-vertex graph. Its size still grows linearly with n. Enumerating all sets of a fixed number of vertices therefore does not give a polynomial-time algorithm for the question. The order of constants also matters: \(\delta\) may depend on the desired expansion gap \(\eta\), and an algorithm for one convenient pair of constants would not refute the full hypothesis.

context_blocks.title: A sparse large cut can miss the issue
context_blocks.text: Take the disjoint union of two complete graphs on 50 vertices. Either whole component has expansion zero. Yet a two-vertex set contained in one component has expansion \(48/49\), and a two-vertex set split between the components has expansion one. Thus every set of the specified small size expands very well even though a larger zero-expansion cut exists. Optimizing over all sets up to half the graph can answer a different question from the exact small-size promise.

context_blocks.title: Why a large gap remains difficult
context_blocks.text: For a proposed set, its size and edge boundary are easy to count. The universal NO condition ranges over all sets of that size. The hypothesis asserts hardness even though YES and NO graphs are separated by a wide gap, with many intermediate graphs excluded by the promise. A graph expansion construction, a bound on one spectral parameter, or an algorithm with an uncontrolled change in set size is not automatically a distinguisher for this promise.

context_blocks.title: Connections and current boundary
context_blocks.text: Raghavendra and Steurer reduce small-set expansion to Unique Games, making this hypothesis a sufficient foundation for Unique Games hardness. Raghavendra, Steurer and Tulsiani relate it to a version of Unique Games with an additional expansion requirement and derive conditional hardness for graph partitioning and arrangement problems. This does not establish equivalence to unrestricted Unique Games in both directions. In August 2026, Lin, Mirrokni and Woodruff use a randomized, weighted, exact-volume variant to prove a sparse least-squares hardness result. Such an application assumes an SSE statement; it does not prove the statement itself, and its modeling conventions should not be silently transferred to this card. The checked sources leave the hypothesis unresolved.

sentences: Is it NP-hard to distinguish one poorly expanding small set from uniformly strong expansion at the same set size?
The target set occupies a fixed fraction \(\delta\) of the graph, with \(\delta\) chosen after the gap parameter \(\eta\).
Expansion is the fraction of incident edges that leave the set.
A sparse cut of a larger size does not necessarily reveal any poorly expanding set of the target size.
Known reductions connect the hypothesis to Unique Games and conditional hardness without resolving it.

cards.title: Subtour-LP integrality gap for metric TSP
cards.area: Approximation algorithms and hardness of approximation
cards.formal: Determine \(\Gamma =\sup _{n\ge 3,c} \operatorname{OPT}_{\mathrm{TSP}}(c)/\operatorname{OPT}_{\mathrm{LP}}(c)\), where c ranges over every metric on n labeled points and \(\operatorname{OPT}_{\mathrm{LP}}\) is the symmetric subtour relaxation defined below.
cards.definitions: For \(V=\{1,\ldots ,n\}\) and \(E=\{\{u,v\}:u\ne v\}, a\) metric has \(c_{uu}=0, c_{uv}=c_{vu}>0\) for \(u\ne v\), and \(c_{uv}\le c_{uw}+c_{wv}\). Costs are arbitrary real numbers; no Euclidean embedding is assumed. \(\operatorname{OPT}_{\mathrm{TSP}}\) is the minimum sum of edge costs on a Hamiltonian cycle of the complete undirected graph. For \(S\subseteq V, \delta (S)\) contains edges with exactly one endpoint in S, and \(x(F)=\sum_{e\in F}x_{e}\). Define \(\operatorname{OPT}_{\mathrm{LP}}=\min  \sum_{e} c_{e} x_{e}\) subject to \(x(\delta (\{v\}))=2\) for every \(v, x(\delta (S))\ge 2\) for every nonempty proper \(S\subsetneq V\), and \(0\le x_{e}\le 1\) for every e. The LP is feasible and has positive optimum. The supremum ranges over every finite size, not one fixed n. This is the symmetric metric subtour-LP integrality gap, not an approximation ratio measured only against \(\operatorname{OPT}_{\mathrm{TSP}}\), an asymmetric TSP relaxation, or a restricted geometric metric.
cards.answer_criterion: Supply a specified real number a and prove in Lean that |\(a- \Gamma |\le 1/100\). The proof must certify both a lower and an upper bound for the unrestricted quantity in this card. Equivalently, certified bounds \(\ell\)\(\le u\) of width at most \(1/50\) qualify by taking \(a=(\ell +u)/2\). An exact value with proof of equality also qualifies. An unevaluated copy of the defining extremum, a one-sided improvement, or a numerical estimate without a proved error bound does not meet this criterion. The \(1/100\) tolerance is benchmark acceptance; it does not prove an associated exact threshold conjecture.
cards.why: The exact strength of the principal relaxation for a canonical optimization problem, joining polyhedral structure, probabilistic rounding and approximation. A resolution would explain a longstanding gap between fractional connectivity and integral tours.

cards.status_note: The general \(4/3\) equality remains open through the primary-source review of 11 September 2026. The established explicit upper bound recorded here is \(3/2- 2.18\cdot 10^{- 34}; a\) September 2 preprint claims a further small improvement, clearly separated from verified literature. Restricted-class theorems and finite-size verification do not resolve the universal conjecture. The 12 September 2026 edit adopts absolute 0.01 benchmark acceptance; the saved open-status evidence concerns the underlying exact question and does not independently certify openness at that tolerance.

context_blocks.text: The target is the value of the universal integrality gap. The classical \(4/3\) conjecture proposes \(\Gamma =4/3; a\) larger determined value is also an answer to this quantitative question.

The relaxation allows fractional edge purchases while retaining two elementary properties of every tour: each vertex has degree two, and every nontrivial cut is crossed at least twice. It therefore knows much more than a disconnected cycle-cover relaxation, but its feasible points need not be convex combinations of Hamiltonian cycles. The conjecture asks for the exact worst loss caused by that remaining freedom.

For example, a feasible fractional vector may put positive weight on several alternative connections at one vertex without choosing a single predecessor and successor. The cut inequalities ensure aggregate connectivity, yet they do not force these local choices to assemble into one integral cycle. The proposed factor \(4/3\) says that, in a metric, repairing all such inconsistencies never costs more than one third of the fractional optimum.

The metric assumption is what makes shortcutting possible. If a connected Eulerian multigraph visits a vertex several times, replacing a detour by the direct edge between its endpoints does not increase cost. One can consequently search for a suitably cheap Eulerian structure rather than construct a Hamiltonian cycle at every intermediate step. This observation explains why spanning trees and parity correction recur in approximation algorithms for the problem.

A minimum spanning tree followed by a minimum-cost matching on its odd-degree vertices yields the classical \(3/2\) guarantee. Wolsey’s analysis measures both components against the LP: the tree costs at most the fractional optimum, and the matching at most half that value. The inherited July 2026 paper recalls this argument before studying a particular randomized refinement.

An algorithmic ratio and an integrality-gap ratio must use the correct denominator. A guarantee cost\(\le \alpha \cdot \operatorname{OPT}_{\mathrm{TSP}}\) does not establish \(\operatorname{OPT}_{\mathrm{TSP}}\le \alpha \cdot \operatorname{OPT}_{\mathrm{LP}}\), since the fractional optimum can be smaller. Karlin–Klein–Oveis Gharan’s FOCS 2022 result explicitly supplies an LP-relative guarantee below \(3/2\), extending the earlier approximation breakthrough. It is this later theorem that directly improves the general gap bound.

The modern approach samples a spanning tree from a distribution constrained by fractional edge marginals, then corrects its parity. Tree cost and parity-repair cost interact, so treating the two separately can lose the desired saving. Gurvits–Klein–Leake strengthen probability estimates using capacities of real stable polynomials. Their Lemma 4.5 is explicitly LP-relative and yields the certified bound \(\Gamma \le 3/2- 2.18\cdot 10^{- 34}\). The small constant reflects a worst-case proof, not a claim that practical tours are that close to \(3/2\).

A class can have a better integrality gap than the worst ratio of a particular algorithm on it. Jin–Klein–Williamson prove the \(4/3\) bound for half-integral cycle-cut instances using a specialized construction. Half-integral means that nonzero fractional coordinates are \(1/2\) or 1, with an additional restriction on the hierarchy of tight cuts. This result does not cover every half-integral instance, still less every subtour solution.

Their July 2026 paper, which supplied the inherited reference, proves a \(10/7\) guarantee for the maximum-entropy algorithm on that same restricted class. Since \(10/7\) exceeds \(4/3\), it improves understanding of the chosen algorithm rather than improving the already-known class gap. The authors also identify examples giving a lower bound of \(11/8\) on the algorithm’s performance. Such an algorithm-specific obstruction cannot refute the conjecture about the cheapest possible tour.

Two complementary approaches restrict the fractional solution in other ways. Villa–Vercesi–Barta–Mastrolilli prove the \(4/3\) bound when an optimal solution has at most \(n+6\) nonzero components, combining structural reasoning and computation. This is a support-size condition, not a theorem for every instance on at most \(n+6\) vertices. Larger support remains outside its stated guarantee.

Cook–Hougardy–Petrich’s September 8, 2026 revision reports exact verification for all metric instances through \(n=16\) and for half-integral extreme points through \(n=18\). It also repairs omissions in earlier extreme-point lists. This is stronger evidence than sampling finitely many random metrics, because the computation organizes the relevant polyhedral cases. It still leaves unbounded n, and the catalogue has not rerun that enumeration.

A September 2 preprint by Zhao Song claims a larger universal saving, \(\varepsilon\)★>\(2.05522\cdot 10^{- 30}\), through a refined maximum-entropy analysis. Its main theorem is explicitly relative to \(\operatorname{OPT}_{\mathrm{LP}}\). The statement was checked, but the lengthy proof and numerical certificate were not independently verified here, so the value is recorded as a recent claim rather than silently replacing the established bound. Even if confirmed, it would remain far above the conjectured ratio \(4/3\).

A September 2 preprint by Zhao Song claims a larger universal saving, \(\varepsilon\)★>\(2.05522\cdot 10^{- 30}\), through a refined maximum-entropy analysis. Its main theorem is explicitly relative to \(\operatorname{OPT}_{\mathrm{LP}}\). The statement was checked, but the lengthy proof and numerical certificate were not independently verified here, so the value is recorded as a recent claim rather than silently replacing the established bound. Even if confirmed, it would remain far above the conjectured ratio \(4/3\).

cards.title: Optimal polynomial-time approximation ratio for metric k-Median
cards.area: Approximation algorithms and hardness of approximation
cards.formal: Determine \(\rho _{\mathrm{med}}=\inf\){\(r\ge 1: a\) uniform randomized polynomial-time algorithm always opens at most k facilities and has cost at most \(r\cdot\)OPT with probability at least \(2/3\) on every metric k-Median instance}, in the model below.
cards.definitions: An input consists of a finite set V, a full table of nonnegative rational distances d on V encoded in binary, nonempty subsets \(C,F\subseteq V\) of clients and allowable facilities with \(C\cup F=V\), and an integer \(1\le k\le |F|\). The table is promised to satisfy \(d(u,v)=d(v,u), d(u,v)=0\) exactly when \(u=v\), and the triangle inequality. Each client has unit demand. For nonempty \(S\subseteq F\) define \(\operatorname{cost}(S)=\sum_{c\in C}\min _{s\in S}d(c,s)\), and OPT=\(\min \{\operatorname{cost}(S):S\subseteq F,1\le |S|\le k\}\). L is the total bit length of the input. For each fixed guarantee r in the infimum, require one uniform classical randomized algorithm \(A_{r}\), with constants \(K_{r},d_{r}\) such that every execution takes at most \(K_{r} \mathrm{L}^{d_{r}}\) bit operations. It always returns an explicit nonempty \(S\subseteq F\) with |\(S|\le k\), and on each input \(\Pr [\operatorname{cost}(S)\le r\cdot \operatorname{OPT}]\ge 2/3\). Here e is the base of the natural logarithm. The algorithm and constants may depend on r but not on k, |C|, |F| or distance precision. No Euclidean, low-dimensional, stability, capacity or input-distribution promise is made. Candidate facilities are part of the input and cannot be enlarged. The guarantee also covers OPT=0. The infimum need not be attained by one algorithm. An exact value \(\rho\) means that feasible guarantees approach \(\rho\) from above and no algorithm in the stated class guarantees a factor smaller than \(\rho\).
cards.answer_criterion: Supply a specified real number a and prove in Lean that |\(a- \rho _{\mathrm{med}}|\le 1/100\). The proof must certify both a lower and an upper bound for the unrestricted quantity in this card. Equivalently, certified bounds \(\ell\)\(\le u\) of width at most \(1/50\) qualify by taking \(a=(\ell +u)/2\). An exact value with proof of equality also qualifies. An unevaluated copy of the defining extremum, a one-sided improvement, or a numerical estimate without a proved error bound does not meet this criterion. The \(1/100\) tolerance is benchmark acceptance; it does not prove an associated exact threshold conjecture. Any additional complexity assumption must be explicit; a conditional hardness theorem proves only the corresponding conditional value or bound.

context_blocks.text: The target is the optimal approximation ratio itself, with the exact facility budget and randomized polynomial-time model fixed. The previously selected \(1+2/e\) threshold is a candidate value motivated by the hardness evidence described below.

Metric k-Median selects a limited number of service locations and minimizes total distance to the nearest selected location. The number of clients and the number of candidate facilities may differ, and the distance table need not come from a Euclidean embedding. The same formulation models representative selection for clustering and placement of facilities. Its simplicity makes the unresolved approximation threshold a central benchmark for algorithm design.

The two endpoint numbers are approximately 1.73576 and 2. The lower endpoint is the classical hardness threshold \(1+2/e\); the best general feasible guarantee in the checked literature is \(2+\varepsilon\). The inherited STOC 2025 paper explicitly asks for a tight approximation result after obtaining that upper bound. Asking for \(1+2/e+\varepsilon\) for every fixed \(\varepsilon\) avoids requiring that an infimum approximation ratio be achieved exactly.

The coverage origin of the lower endpoint can be seen directly. Represent each set as a candidate facility and each universe element as a client. Give a client–facility pair distance one when the set contains the element and distance three otherwise, and give distinct pairs on the same side distance two. These distances satisfy the triangle inequality. A collection of k sets covering a fraction p of the elements then has clustering cost \((3- 2p)\) times the universe size.

Feige’s Max k-Cover gap distinguishes complete coverage from coverage of at most \(1- 1/e+\eta\), for any fixed \(\eta >0\). Under the preceding metric construction this becomes a gap between cost one per client and cost at least \(1+2/e- 2\eta\) per client. This is why the constant is not an arbitrary numerical target. A randomized algorithm beating that gap on every input would yield randomized algorithms for the underlying NP-hard decision problem; the appropriate exclusion is \(\mathrm{NP}\ne \mathrm{RP}\) for this card’s success convention.

Jain–Mahdian–Saberi’s 2002 paper gives the classical metric k-Median lower bound through a reduction to approximating Set Cover. Its historical statement uses the then-known slightly-superpolynomial-time assumption for Set Cover hardness. The coverage reduction above explains the stronger ordinary NP-hardness formulation without silently changing the assumption in the original theorem. Neither lower-bound route excludes approximation from just above \(1+2/e\).

The 2025 algorithm combines two components. One permits a logarithmic number of extra centers while retaining a \(2+\varepsilon\) cost bound; another handles instances where deleting one optimal center increases the optimum substantially. Combining them returns a feasible solution opening at most k centers. The full paper’s May 2026 revision retains this result. It is therefore incorrect to describe the headline \(2+\varepsilon\) theorem as only a bicriteria approximation.

The usual linear relaxation has a separate barrier near two. It uses fractional openings \(y_{s}\), assignments \(x_{c,s}\le y_{s}\), unit total assignment for each client, and \(\sum_{s} y_{s}\le k\). For a star with \(q\ge 3\) leaves, all vertices available as facilities, clients at the leaves and \(k=q- 1\), every integral optimum has cost two. Set the central opening to \(1/(q- 1)\), each leaf opening to \((q- 2)/(q- 1)\), and assign each client’s remaining fraction to the center. This feasible LP solution costs \(q/(q- 1)\), giving an integrality gap approaching two.

That explicit example limits a guarantee measured against this relaxation, not every polynomial algorithm measured against OPT. A sharper algorithm might use additional constraints, a different relaxation, or another method. Likewise, a lower bound for one rounding framework is not a computational impossibility theorem for the original optimization problem. The card’s target is deliberately stated using the true integral optimum.

There is already a matching-threshold algorithm in a different runtime regime. Cohen-Addad–Gupta–Kumar–Lee–Li’s ICALP 2019 work achieves \(1+2/e+\varepsilon\) in fixed-parameter time with respect to k. The potentially large dependence on the number of opened facilities is permitted there. This does not supply a polynomial-time algorithm when k grows as part of the input, but it shows that the target ratio has meaningful algorithmic support.

A 2026 development concerns geometric input. Cohen-Addad and coauthors improve approximation-scheme runtimes in low-dimensional Euclidean spaces, where additional structure is available. Such a scheme does not apply to arbitrary distance tables.

Anand and coauthors’ July 2026 spectral dual-fitting paper improves k-Means guarantees, including in general metrics. That objective sums squared distances; squaring changes both the analysis and the hardness constants. It does not establish the stated k-Median ratio.

Determining the optimal ratio would locate the computational price of general metric clustering. A value at the coverage threshold would match the known obstruction, whereas a larger value would require a different limiting obstruction. The exact facility budget is essential to either conclusion: averaging an excessive number of facilities over random choices changes the feasible problem.

cards.title: Vertex Cover approximation below factor two
cards.area: Approximation algorithms and hardness of approximation
cards.formal:
Do there exist a rational constant \(\varepsilon\in(0,1)\), a uniform deterministic algorithm \(A\), and integers \(B,k\ge1\) such that, on every explicitly encoded finite simple undirected graph \(G\) of input bit length \(L\), the algorithm halts within \(B(L+1)^k\) Turing-machine steps and returns a vertex cover \(S\) satisfying
\[|S|\le(2-\varepsilon)\tau(G),\qquad
\tau(G)=\min\{|T|:T\subseteq V(G),\ T\text{ is a vertex cover of }G\}?\]
The same positive improvement \(\varepsilon\) and the same algorithm must work for graphs of all sizes, with no structural promise. Vertices have unit cost. The question asks for an unconditional algorithm-existence theorem or its unconditional negation.
cards.definitions:
Graphs and objective. Let \(n\in\mathbb N\), \(V=[n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}\), and \(E\subseteq\{\{u,v\}:u,v\in V,\ u\ne v\}\). For \(n=0\), the vertex set and edge set are empty. Edges are unordered pairs, with no loops or multiplicities. A set \(S\subseteq V\) is a vertex cover if every \(\{u,v\}\in E\) has \(u\in S\) or \(v\in S\). The quantity \(\tau(G)\) is the minimum cardinality of such a set; the minimum exists because the finite set \(V\) itself covers every edge. All vertices have weight one, so the cost is the number selected. If \(E=\varnothing\), then \(\tau(G)=0\), and the approximation inequality requires the output \(S=\varnothing\). Isolated vertices are allowed. The class includes disconnected, bipartite, nonbipartite, sparse and dense graphs without imposing any of those promises.

Input and output. The input is the full \(n\)-by-\(n\) binary adjacency matrix, preceded by a self-delimiting binary encoding of \(n\). One fixed encoding is \(1^b0\) followed by the \(b\)-bit binary expansion of \(n+1\), where \(b=\lfloor\log_2(n+1)\rfloor+1\), followed by the matrix entries in row order. A valid input has a symmetric matrix with zero diagonal, and entry \((u,v)\) equals one exactly when \(\{u,v\}\in E\). Its bit length is \(L=n^2+2b+1\). This explicitly includes all vertices, including isolated ones; there is no succinct matrix generator or graph oracle. The output is an \(n\)-bit indicator vector, with entry one exactly at selected vertices. Reading the input and writing this output count toward time. No guarantee is required on malformed encodings. Every labeling of the vertices by \([n]\) is a valid input order on which the guarantees must hold.

Computation. The algorithm is one deterministic Turing-machine program with a fixed finite alphabet and a fixed finite number of tapes. Each step reads and writes one symbol on each tape, changes finite control and moves each head by at most one position. Work tapes are initially blank. No randomness, oracle, nonuniform advice or uncharged preprocessing is allowed. Integer or rational arithmetic, if used internally, is performed on finite binary representations with all bit operations charged. The time bound is worst-case over every valid input, rather than expected or amortized time. The constant \(\varepsilon\) is chosen once with the algorithm, not supplied as a graph-dependent accuracy parameter.

Quantifiers and accuracy. The order is
\[\exists\varepsilon\in\mathbb Q\cap(0,1)\ \exists A\ \exists B,k\in\mathbb N_{>0}\ \forall G.\]
The time constants may depend on this chosen algorithm and improvement but not on the input graph. Requiring a rational improvement does not change the original real-constant question: any positive real improvement implies a smaller positive rational one. The objective inequality is multiplicative, with no additive error, asymptotic slack or exceptional small graphs. A guarantee strictly below two separately on each finite graph, such as \(2-1/n\), does not give one improvement valid for all sizes. The numerical benchmark tolerance of 0.01 is not an additive tolerance on this approximation-ratio existence question.

context_blocks.text: A cover chooses vertices so that every edge is touched. A star with many leaves has optimum one, while a triangle has optimum two. The complement of a vertex cover is an independent set, but the identity between their optimum sizes does not preserve multiplicative approximation factors. This card uses unit vertex costs, retaining the unweighted target selected at admission.

The original seminar source discusses weighted Vertex Cover, its factor-two approximation, and its role in the primal-dual framework. The event was on 11 December 2000, and the online account is a summary by Claire Kenyon. It motivates the approximation barrier; it does not supply a contemporary status check or specify the full deterministic bit model used here.

Polynomial-time approximation bounds of the form \(2-\Theta(1/\sqrt{\log n})\) improve on two at each sufficiently large fixed size. The improvement nevertheless tends to zero as \(n\) grows. Karakostas’s result therefore does not answer whether one fixed \(\varepsilon>0\) works on all inputs. The present deterministic target also requires the stated worst-case bit-time and output guarantees.

The 2-to-2 Games line of work proves NP-hardness of approximation within \(\sqrt2-\eta\) for every fixed \(\eta>0\). The 2025 Khot–Minzer–Safra journal account explains how later work proved the combinatorial hypotheses in its original reduction. This hardness gives an algorithmic impossibility consequence under \(\mathrm P\ne\mathrm{NP}\), but leaves a gap up to two and does not unconditionally rule out the algorithms quantified here.

Khot and Regev prove NP-hardness below every fixed factor \(2-\varepsilon\), assuming the Unique Games Conjecture. Thus UGC together with \(\mathrm P\ne\mathrm{NP}\) would imply a negative answer to this card. Conversely, a deterministic improvement would contradict that conjunction; it would not by itself unconditionally refute UGC. If \(\mathrm P=\mathrm{NP}\), an exact polynomial-time cover algorithm would give a positive answer.

Claimed improvements require version and quantifier checks. The latest Salvador preprint, version 3 posted 6 July 2026, labels its universal \(7/4\) ratio as Conjecture 1, supported by finite experiments. The earlier version’s asserted \(7/5\) theorem is not the current conclusion. The latest version therefore supplies no proved fixed improvement for every graph.

The inspected March 2026 Hallelujah preprint states \(|S|<2\tau(G)\) for each finite nonempty graph, not a graph-independent positive gap. Its explicit lexicographic selection rule also has a direct limiting example: on \(K_{r,r}\) with the two parts labeled by alternating odd and even numbers, all degrees tie and the selected union has \(2r-1\) vertices while the optimum is \(r\). Its ratio is therefore \(2-1/r\). This observation concerns that preprint’s stated rule; the separately published version was accessible only through its abstract. Neither this pointwise claim nor its stated UGC interpretation certifies the target here.

The 6 September 2026 Karthik–Minzer preprint reports stronger NP-hardness for vertex cover in hypergraphs: factor \(1+\sqrt2-\eta\) for three-element edges, and \(k-\eta\) for fixed edge size \(k\ge4\). Ordinary graphs have two-element edges and are outside those new parameter ranges. The recent perfect-completeness four-to-one-games result likewise continues to list \(\sqrt2\) as the graph Vertex Cover hardness frontier in its introduction.

cards.why: Vertex Cover is a basic covering problem with a long-standing gap between its factor-two algorithmic benchmark and known unconditional hardness thresholds. A fixed improvement would distinguish the true computational limit from a barrier shared by many methods. Ruling out every such algorithm would require an unconditional complexity separation, so the logical strength of the chosen question must remain explicit.
cards.answer_criterion: Supply a complete, mathematically correct Lean-checked proof of the formal statement or its logical negation. A positive answer must specify a fixed \(\varepsilon>0\), one deterministic program and common polynomial time constants, and prove termination, valid-cover output and \(|S|\le(2-\varepsilon)\tau(G)\) on every valid adjacency-matrix input, including empty and edgeless graphs. A negative answer must prove that for every rational \(\varepsilon\in(0,1)\) and every deterministic program having a polynomial running-time bound on all valid inputs, some graph produces an invalid cover encoding, an uncovered edge, or a cover larger than \((2-\varepsilon)\tau(G)\). It must rule out all such algorithms, not merely one rounding scheme or restricted family. A conditional result under UGC, \(\mathrm P\ne\mathrm{NP}\), ETH or another unproved hypothesis does not establish this unconditional negation. A vanishing improvement, experiments, an estimate of the optimum without a cover, or an algorithm restricted to a graph class does not meet the stated universal guarantee.

cards.context:
A cover chooses vertices so that every edge is touched. A star with many leaves has optimum one, while a triangle has optimum two. The complement of a vertex cover is an independent set, but the identity between their optimum sizes does not preserve multiplicative approximation factors. This card uses unit vertex costs, retaining the unweighted target selected at admission.

The original seminar source discusses weighted Vertex Cover, its factor-two approximation, and its role in the primal-dual framework. The event was on 11 December 2000, and the online account is a summary by Claire Kenyon. It motivates the approximation barrier; it does not supply a contemporary status check or specify the full deterministic bit model used here.

Polynomial-time approximation bounds of the form \(2-\Theta(1/\sqrt{\log n})\) improve on two at each sufficiently large fixed size. The improvement nevertheless tends to zero as \(n\) grows. Karakostas’s result therefore does not answer whether one fixed \(\varepsilon>0\) works on all inputs. The present deterministic target also requires the stated worst-case bit-time and output guarantees.

The 2-to-2 Games line of work proves NP-hardness of approximation within \(\sqrt2-\eta\) for every fixed \(\eta>0\). The 2025 Khot–Minzer–Safra journal account explains how later work proved the combinatorial hypotheses in its original reduction. This hardness gives an algorithmic impossibility consequence under \(\mathrm P\ne\mathrm{NP}\), but leaves a gap up to two and does not unconditionally rule out the algorithms quantified here.

Khot and Regev prove NP-hardness below every fixed factor \(2-\varepsilon\), assuming the Unique Games Conjecture. Thus UGC together with \(\mathrm P\ne\mathrm{NP}\) would imply a negative answer to this card. Conversely, a deterministic improvement would contradict that conjunction; it would not by itself unconditionally refute UGC. If \(\mathrm P=\mathrm{NP}\), an exact polynomial-time cover algorithm would give a positive answer.

Claimed improvements require version and quantifier checks. The latest Salvador preprint, version 3 posted 6 July 2026, labels its universal \(7/4\) ratio as Conjecture 1, supported by finite experiments. The earlier version’s asserted \(7/5\) theorem is not the current conclusion. The latest version therefore supplies no proved fixed improvement for every graph.

The inspected March 2026 Hallelujah preprint states \(|S|<2\tau(G)\) for each finite nonempty graph, not a graph-independent positive gap. Its explicit lexicographic selection rule also has a direct limiting example: on \(K_{r,r}\) with the two parts labeled by alternating odd and even numbers, all degrees tie and the selected union has \(2r-1\) vertices while the optimum is \(r\). Its ratio is therefore \(2-1/r\). This observation concerns that preprint’s stated rule; the separately published version was accessible only through its abstract. Neither this pointwise claim nor its stated UGC interpretation certifies the target here.

The 6 September 2026 Karthik–Minzer preprint reports stronger NP-hardness for vertex cover in hypergraphs: factor \(1+\sqrt2-\eta\) for three-element edges, and \(k-\eta\) for fixed edge size \(k\ge4\). Ordinary graphs have two-element edges and are outside those new parameter ranges. The recent perfect-completeness four-to-one-games result likewise continues to list \(\sqrt2\) as the graph Vertex Cover hardness frontier in its introduction.

cards.title: Does a fixed d-to-1 Games conjecture imply Unique Games?
cards.area: Approximation algorithms and hardness of approximation
cards.formal:
Is the following implication true for the classical constraint games and deterministic polynomial reductions defined below?
\[\bigl(\exists\,d\in\mathbb N,\ d\ge2\text{ and }D_d\bigr)\ \Longrightarrow\ \mathrm{UGC}.\]
Here \(D_d\) is the perfect-completeness \(d\)-to-one Games conjecture with \(d\) fixed independently of the soundness parameter; \(\mathrm{UGC}\) is the full near-perfect-completeness Unique Games conjecture. Equivalently, for every fixed \(d\ge2\), does \(D_d\) imply \(\mathrm{UGC}\)? The card retains the forward implication singled out in the saved source excerpt.

sentences: The question asks whether perfect-completeness d-to-one hardness for any fixed d implies the full Unique Games conjecture.
Every game is an explicit finite classical constraint system, and hardness means deterministic polynomial reductions from Boolean satisfiability.
Known direct conversion gives a fixed positive Unique Games completeness rather than a value arbitrarily close to one.
A September 2026 preprint claims perfect-completeness four-to-one hardness, which would establish the antecedent if correct.
The implication remains a separate target and, conditional on that theorem, is equivalent to proving full UGC.

cards.definitions:
A constraint game has two finite disjoint vertex sets \(U,V\) and a nonempty finite list of edges \(e=(u_e,v_e)\in U\times V\). Repeated edges, with their own constraints, are allowed and count separately. Every edge has equal weight in the list. No regularity or bounded-degree promise is imposed. All vertices, edges and constraint tables are explicitly encoded with binary integers; there is no succinct representation or compressed multiplicity.

For integers \(d\ge2\) and \(r\ge1\), a \(d\)-to-one game gives left vertices labels in \([dr]\), right vertices labels in \([r]\), and every edge a surjective map \(\pi_e:[dr]\to[r]\) with exactly \(d\) preimages of every right label. Here \([m]=\{1,\ldots,m\}\). An assignment is a pair of maps \(\alpha:U\to[dr]\) and \(\beta:V\to[r]\); it satisfies edge \(e\) when \(\pi_e(\alpha(u_e))=\beta(v_e)\). Its value is the fraction of list entries it satisfies. The optimum \(\operatorname{val}(G)\) is the maximum of this fraction over all assignments. It lies in \([0,1]\) and is a finite rational maximum. Perfect completeness means the YES instance has optimum exactly one.

A Unique Game has the same bipartite constraint format, a common alphabet \([k]\) on both sides, and a permutation \(\pi_e:[k]\to[k]\) on each edge. Assignment, satisfaction and optimum are defined by the same equality. This is a classical combinatorial optimum; no entangled, interactive, nonsignalling or quantum strategy is used.

For a promised pair of disjoint YES and NO sets of such instances, NP-hard means that Boolean 3-SAT has a deterministic polynomial-time many-one reduction to that pair. Specifically, a single finite Turing program maps every explicitly encoded Boolean formula in conjunctive normal form with at most three literals per clause to a valid game. It maps satisfiable formulas into YES and unsatisfiable formulas into NO and uses at most \(K(L+1)^c\) bit steps on every length-\(L\) input, for fixed constants \(K,c\). Literal indices, signs, clauses, vertex names and table entries use ordinary explicit binary encodings. An algorithm for the promised game need have no specified behaviour outside YES and NO. NP-hardness here asserts the existence of a reduction; it does not assume \(\mathrm P\ne\mathrm{NP}\).

For a fixed integer \(d\ge2\), define \(D_d\) to mean:
\[\forall\gamma\in\mathbb Q\cap(0,1),\ \exists r\ge1:
\quad \operatorname{GapD}_{d,r}(1,\gamma)\text{ is NP-hard},\]
where the YES condition is \(\operatorname{val}(G)=1\) and the NO condition is \(\operatorname{val}(G)\le\gamma\). The integer \(d\) is outside the quantifier over \(\gamma\). The alphabet size \(r\), reduction program and its polynomial constants may depend on \(d,\gamma\), but not on the formula length. Allowing \(d\) to increase as \(\gamma\) decreases would be a different antecedent.

Define full \(\mathrm{UGC}\) by
\[\forall\eta,\gamma\in\mathbb Q\cap(0,1/4),\ \exists k\ge1:
\quad \operatorname{GapUG}_{k}(1-\eta,\gamma)\text{ is NP-hard}.\]
Its YES condition is \(\operatorname{val}(G)\ge1-\eta\) and its NO condition is \(\operatorname{val}(G)\le\gamma\). The constants \(k\) and the polynomial reduction may depend on both gap parameters. The rational, small-gap convention gives disjoint promises and is equivalent to requesting all arbitrarily small positive gaps: smaller rational gaps imply the less stringent real gaps. There is no demand for one alphabet or one polynomial degree working for all gap choices, or for a uniform algorithm generating all the reductions from their parameters.

The target is the implication between these mathematical hardness propositions. It is not a question about formal unprovability in a separately chosen axiom system, nor is it limited to one specified family of gadget or oracle reductions. The reverse implication from UGC to perfect-completeness \(d\)-to-one hardness is a separate question mentioned in the source, not an additional requirement on this card.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof or refutation of the displayed implication. An affirmative answer must establish full UGC from the assumption that \(D_d\) holds for some fixed \(d\ge2\), respecting the gap quantifiers and the deterministic polynomial reductions. An unconditional proof of UGC would also establish the implication. A negative answer must prove the conjunction \((\exists d\ge2\ D_d)\land\neg\mathrm{UGC}\); showing only that a particular reduction loses completeness, or that some restricted reduction class cannot work, does not refute the implication. Hardness of Unique Games with a fixed YES value such as \(1/d\) or \(1/2\) is not the required near-one YES value for every \(\eta>0\). Exact asymptotic proof is required; the numerical approximation tolerance does not alter these logical statements.

context_blocks.text: Both games ask for globally consistent labels subject to local compatibility rules. Unique Games has one allowed right label for each left label and also one allowed left label for each right label. A d-to-one constraint keeps the first property but permits d compatible left labels for a given right label. This additional freedom changes which perfect-completeness gaps are possible.

The source already proves a weaker implication: its Appendix B gives one-sided Unique Games hardness with completeness 1/d. This is one fixed positive completeness constant. Full UGC instead requires a YES value arbitrarily close to one while keeping soundness arbitrarily close to zero. The weaker implication therefore does not answer the source question.

Perfectly satisfiable Unique Games can be checked efficiently by trying a starting label in each connected component and propagating the forced labels. The conjecture deliberately permits a small positive fraction of unsatisfied constraints in the YES case. Substituting exact satisfiability for near-satisfiability would change the problem.

The 2025 journal account explains the sequence that proved almost-perfect-completeness two-to-one hardness. It retains exact perfect completeness as a separate conjecture and states full UGC separately. These distinctions matter even though all the parameters may be described informally as almost satisfiable games.

Fei, Minzer and Wang’s 14 September 2026 preprint claims perfect-completeness four-to-one hardness for every positive soundness constant. If correct, its Theorem 1.6 establishes D₄ and hence the antecedent of this card. Under that theorem, the forward implication is equivalent to UGC itself: an implication proof would give UGC, while UGC immediately implies the implication. This is a logical consequence of the claimed theorem, not a claim that UGC has been proved. The new full proof has not been independently audited here.

This connection would turn a hardness theorem with several compatible labels into the general Unique Games hypothesis underlying many sharp approximation thresholds. Keeping alphabet size, constraint multiplicity, completeness and soundness explicit prevents a useful weaker hardness theorem from being mistaken for that conclusion.

cards.definitions:
A directed metric is a function \(c:V	imes V	o R\ge 0\) with \(c(i,i)=0\) and \(c(i,k)\le c(i,j)+c(j,k)\) for all i,j,k. Symmetry is not required, and distinct vertices may have zero distance. The complete directed graph has one arc \((i,j)\) for each \(i
e j\) and no loops. A Hamiltonian cycle visits every vertex once before returning to its start; its cost is the sum of its n arc costs. \(\operatorname{OPT}_{\mathrm{ATSP}}(c)\) is the minimum over all such cycles. For \(S\subseteq V, \delta ^{+}(S)=\{(i,j):i\in S,j
otin S\}\) and \(\delta ^{-}(S)=\{(i,j):i
otin S,j\in S\}\); for a set of arcs F write \(x(F)=\sum_{(i,j)\in F} x_{ij}\). \(\mathrm{LP}_{\mathrm{ATSP}}(c)\) minimizes \(\sum_{i
e j} c(i,j)x_{ij}\) over real variables \(x_{ij}\ge 0\) subject to \(x(\delta ^{+}(\{v\}))=x(\delta ^{-}(\{v\}))=1\) for every v, and \(x(\delta ^{+}(S))\ge 1\) for every nonempty proper \(S\subsetneq V\). The degree equalities imply \(x(\delta ^{+}(S))=x(\delta ^{-}(S))\), so an additional incoming-cut inequality would be redundant. No integrality restriction is placed on x. The feasible set is nonempty and compact; both optima are attained. Zero-LP instances are excluded from the ratio; they also have zero tour optimum. Indeed, the positive support of a zero-cost feasible solution is strongly connected by the cut constraints, and directed triangle inequalities then give zero distance between every ordered pair. For positive LP value, the integrality ratio is \(\operatorname{OPT}_{\mathrm{ATSP}}(c)/\mathrm{LP}_{\mathrm{ATSP}}(c)\), and the overall gap is its supremum over all n and directed metrics. The question is a universal comparison of optimum values, without a running-time restriction on finding the tour. It concerns closed tours, not a prescribed-start/end path. The supremum is over every finite size and is not required to be attained. The usual factor-two conjecture asserts \(\Gamma _{\mathrm{ATSP}}=2\), taking account of known approaching lower-bound families.
cards.answer_criterion: Supply a specified real number a and prove in Lean that |\(a- \Gamma _{\mathrm{ATSP}}|\le 1/100\). The proof must certify both a lower and an upper bound for the unrestricted quantity in this card. Equivalently, certified bounds \(\ell\)\(\le u\) of width at most \(1/50\) qualify by taking \(a=(\ell +u)/2\). An exact value with proof of equality also qualifies. An unevaluated copy of the defining extremum, a one-sided improvement, or a numerical estimate without a proved error bound does not meet this criterion. The \(1/100\) tolerance is benchmark acceptance; it does not prove an associated exact threshold conjecture.

context_blocks.text: This card determines the universal subtour-LP integrality gap. The factor-two conjecture is a proposed exact answer; refuting that factor alone would not determine a larger gap.

context_blocks.title: Buying fractions of directed arcs
context_blocks.text: A tour buys each used arc completely. The relaxation permits fractional amounts of several arcs, while requiring one unit to enter and leave every city and at least one unit to leave every proper group of cities. Every tour is feasible for the LP, so the LP gives a lower bound on the tour cost. The quantity measures the largest possible multiplicative loss when converting fractional cost into an actual tour; the classical conjecture sets that loss at two. A fractional solution need not be a probability distribution over whole tours.

context_blocks.title: Why subtour constraints matter
context_blocks.text: Suppose six cities form two groups of three, with travel cost 1 within a group and 10 between groups. Two separate three-city directed cycles satisfy every degree condition and cost only 6, but do not form a tour visiting all cities. The cut inequality for either group rules out this disconnected solution. These inequalities therefore add a global requirement to the local degree constraints; whether that requirement is strong enough to keep the full gap at two is the unresolved issue.

context_blocks.title: The current general gap
context_blocks.text: Families of directed instances have ratios tending to 2, so no smaller universal factor can work. Traub and Vygen’s 2022 article establishes an upper bound of 22. Their 2024 book improves the proved bound to 17 and explicitly retains the factor-2 question. Its circulation LP has the same optimum as the degree-constrained LP on directed metrics, so the model matches this card. The book also notes room for a small further numerical improvement; 17 is a stated theorem, not a claim that no refinement exists.

context_blocks.title: Finite computations and half-integral vertices
context_blocks.text: Vercesi and coauthors construct improved lower-bound instances at particular sizes. The June 2026 revision by Sosso, Bernardelli and Gualandi computes the gaps for all half-integral extreme points through twelve vertices, where half-integral means coordinates in \(\{0,1/2,1\}\). An extreme point is a feasible LP solution that cannot be written as a nontrivial convex combination of two distinct feasible solutions. Other denominators and arbitrarily large instances remain outside that enumeration. These computations add evidence without proving the universal conjecture.

context_blocks.title: What a resolution would establish
context_blocks.text: The comparison measures the strength of this specific relaxation. A polynomial-time method achieving cost at most twice the LP optimum would settle the inequality and give an approximation guarantee, but the existence inequality itself does not promise an efficient construction. The symmetric metric TSP has a different classical \(4/3\) conjecture; its constants and finite verifications do not transfer to the larger family in which travel costs can depend on direction.

cards.context:
This card determines the universal subtour-LP integrality gap. The factor-two conjecture is a proposed exact answer; refuting that factor alone would not determine a larger gap.

A tour buys each used arc completely. The relaxation permits fractional amounts of several arcs, while requiring one unit to enter and leave every city and at least one unit to leave every proper group of cities. Every tour is feasible for the LP, so the LP gives a lower bound on the tour cost. The quantity measures the largest possible multiplicative loss when converting fractional cost into an actual tour; the classical conjecture sets that loss at two. A fractional solution need not be a probability distribution over whole tours.

Suppose six cities form two groups of three, with travel cost 1 within a group and 10 between groups. Two separate three-city directed cycles satisfy every degree condition and cost only 6, but do not form a tour visiting all cities. The cut inequality for either group rules out this disconnected solution. These inequalities therefore add a global requirement to the local degree constraints; whether that requirement is strong enough to keep the full gap at two is the unresolved issue.

Families of directed instances have ratios tending to 2, so no smaller universal factor can work. Traub and Vygen’s 2022 article establishes an upper bound of 22. Their 2024 book improves the proved bound to 17 and explicitly retains the factor-2 question. Its circulation LP has the same optimum as the degree-constrained LP on directed metrics, so the model matches this card. The book also notes room for a small further numerical improvement; 17 is a stated theorem, not a claim that no refinement exists.

Vercesi and coauthors construct improved lower-bound instances at particular sizes. The June 2026 revision by Sosso, Bernardelli and Gualandi computes the gaps for all half-integral extreme points through twelve vertices, where half-integral means coordinates in \(\{0,1/2,1\}\). An extreme point is a feasible LP solution that cannot be written as a nontrivial convex combination of two distinct feasible solutions. Other denominators and arbitrarily large instances remain outside that enumeration. These computations add evidence without proving the universal conjecture.

The comparison measures the strength of this specific relaxation. A polynomial-time method achieving cost at most twice the LP optimum would settle the inequality and give an approximation guarantee, but the existence inequality itself does not promise an efficient construction. The symmetric metric TSP has a different classical \(4/3\) conjecture; its constants and finite verifications do not transfer to the larger family in which travel costs can depend on direction.

cards.title: Constant-factor approximation for uniform Sparsest Cut
cards.area: Approximation algorithms and hardness of approximation
cards.formal: Do a universal \(C\ge 1\) and a randomized polynomial-time algorithm exist which, on every finite simple undirected graph G on \(n\ge 2\) vertices, output a nonempty proper set S with \(\varphi _{G}(S)\le C \min _{\varnothing \ne T\subsetneq V} \varphi _{G}(T)\), with probability at least \(2/3\)?
cards.definitions: Here \(\varphi _{G}(S)=|E(S,V\setminus S)|/(|S|\cdot |V\setminus S|)\), where \(E(S,V\setminus S)\) is the set of edges having exactly one endpoint in S. The graph is supplied explicitly by an adjacency matrix. Polynomial time is measured in bit operations on every random tape; the same algorithm and constant must work for all graphs. The zero-optimum disconnected case requires returning a zero cut. Uniform refers to equal demand for each pair of vertices, not regularity of the graph.

context_blocks.text: Uniform Sparsest Cut balances a cut’s edge boundary against the number of separated pairs. It is a basic measure of the decomposability of a graph and a major test case for approximation algorithms.

The ARV result gives an \(O(\sqrt{\log  n})\) approximation, with a bound growing with the graph size. A constant factor would cross the remaining qualitative approximation barrier. Nonuniform pair demands, conductance normalized by volumes, and Small-Set Expansion have different targets and are not silently substituted here.

cards.title: Unconditional NP-hardness at the Goemans–Williamson Max-Cut threshold
cards.area: Approximation algorithms and hardness of approximation
cards.formal: For every rational \(\varepsilon\) with \(0<\varepsilon <1- \alpha _{\mathrm{GW}}\), do rationals \(0<b<a\le 1\) with \(b/a<\alpha _{\mathrm{GW}}+\varepsilon\) exist such that distinguishing Max-Cut value at least a from value at most b is NP-hard under deterministic polynomial-time many-one reductions?
cards.definitions: For a finite simple undirected graph with at least one edge, its Max-Cut value is the maximum fraction of edges crossing a bipartition. Let \(\alpha _{\mathrm{GW}}=\min _{0<\theta \le \pi} 2\theta /(\pi (1- \cos  \theta ))\). NP-hardness means there is a polynomial-time map from 3-CNF formulas to graphs mapping satisfiable formulas to the at-least-a case and unsatisfiable formulas to the at-most-b case. The reduction and constants may depend on \(\varepsilon\). No Unique Games or other hardness conjecture is assumed.

context_blocks.text: The Goemans–Williamson approximation ratio is a landmark in semidefinite optimization. Matching hardness from ordinary NP-hardness would identify that ratio as an intrinsic computational threshold under \(\mathrm{P}\ne \mathrm{NP}\).

Known optimal hardness follows from Unique Games; it is not an unconditional NP-hardness theorem. The target deliberately concerns the reduction itself, so a conditional implication from UGC does not count as a solution. This separates the problem from the Unique Games conjecture and from improving a particular rounding algorithm.

cards.title: Optimal polynomial-time approximation ratio for metric TSP
cards.area: Approximation algorithms and hardness of approximation
cards.formal: Determine \(\rho_{\mathrm{TSP}}\), the infimum of achievable expected polynomial-time approximation ratios for the symmetric metric traveling salesman problem.
cards.definitions: An instance is an integer \(n\ge3\) and an explicitly listed symmetric rational distance matrix \(d\in\mathbb Q_{\ge0}^{n\times n}\), with \(d(i,i)=0\), \(d(i,j)>0\) for i unequal to j, and \(d(i,k)\le d(i,j)+d(j,k)\) for all triples. A feasible tour is a permutation \(\pi\) of \(\{1,\ldots,n\}\), of cost \(\sum_{i=1}^{n}d(\pi(i),\pi(i+1))\), where \(\pi(n+1)=\pi(1)\). OPT is the minimum over these tours. The metric is arbitrary, without Euclidean or graph-family restrictions. An algorithm is a uniform randomized Turing machine with independent fair random bits. Its worst-case running time, over all random tapes, is polynomial in the binary input length. It always returns a feasible solution, and its expected cost is measured over its coins. A real number \(r\ge1\) is achievable if one such algorithm satisfies \(\mathbb E[\operatorname{cost}(A(I))]\le r\operatorname{OPT}(I)\) for every valid instance I. The target is the infimum of achievable r; the polynomial and algorithm may depend on r. An infimum need not be attained. All integers and rational input data use explicit binary encodings, with numerator and positive denominator for each rational; their full lengths count toward the input size. No complexity assumption is built into the definition.

cards.title: Optimal polynomial-time approximation ratio for asymmetric TSP
cards.area: Approximation algorithms and hardness of approximation
cards.formal:
Determine the real constant \(\rho_{\mathrm{ATSP}}\), the infimum of achievable expected-cost approximation ratios for the asymmetric metric traveling salesman problem, under worst-case polynomial running time. Let \(\mathcal I\) be the set of valid rational distance-matrix instances and \(\mathcal A\) the class of uniform randomized, always-feasible algorithms defined below. Put
\[
\mathcal R=
\left\{r\in\mathbb R:\ r\ge1\ \land\ \exists A\in\mathcal A\ \forall I\in\mathcal I,
\quad\mathbb E_{\omega}\bigl[\operatorname{cost}_I(A(I;\omega))\bigr]
\le r\operatorname{OPT}(I)\right\},
\qquad
\rho_{\mathrm{ATSP}}=\inf\mathcal R.
\]
Supply a real value \(a\) with a complete Lean proof that
\[
\left|a-\rho_{\mathrm{ATSP}}\right|\le\frac1{100}.
\]
The algorithm and its polynomial time bound may depend on the achievable ratio \(r\), but must work for every valid instance. No complexity assumption is included in the target. The requested accuracy is additive error in the dimensionless approximation ratio.
cards.definitions:
For an integer \(n\ge3\), write \([n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}\). A valid instance \(I=(n,d)\) consists of the complete matrix \(d\in\mathbb Q_{\ge0}^{n\times n}\), satisfying
\[
d(i,i)=0,\qquad d(i,j)>0\ (i\ne j),\qquad
d(i,k)\le d(i,j)+d(j,k)\quad(i,j,k\in[n]).
\]
No symmetry condition is imposed. Every directed distance is finite and explicitly given; the input is not an oracle for distances or a succinctly represented graph. A feasible tour is a permutation \(\pi:[n]\to[n]\), represented by the ordered list \(\pi(1),\ldots,\pi(n)\). With \(\pi(n+1)=\pi(1)\), define
\[
\operatorname{cost}_I(\pi)=\sum_{i=1}^{n}d\bigl(\pi(i),\pi(i+1)\bigr),
\qquad
\operatorname{OPT}(I)=\min_{\pi\text{ a permutation of }[n]}\operatorname{cost}_I(\pi).
\]
This is a closed directed Hamiltonian tour, with no prescribed start vertex or pair of distinct endpoints. Strictly positive off-diagonal distances ensure \(\operatorname{OPT}(I)>0\).

The encoding fixes the full bit cost. Let \(b(t)\) be the ordinary binary representation of a nonnegative integer \(t\), with no leading zeros and with \(b(0)=0\). Express every entry uniquely as \(d(i,j)=p_{ij}/q_{ij}\), where \(p_{ij}\ge0\), \(q_{ij}\ge1\), and \(\gcd(p_{ij},q_{ij})=1\). Form the list consisting of \(n\), then \(p_{11},q_{11},p_{12},q_{12},\ldots,p_{nn},q_{nn}\), with matrix entries in row order. Write each list element as \(b(t)\), place one separator \(\#\) between consecutive elements, and encode each resulting symbol by \(0\mapsto00\), \(1\mapsto01\), \(\#\mapsto10\). There is no trailing separator. Let \(L(I)\) be the number of bits in this string. The output list of vertex labels uses the same integer and separator encoding. All numerator and denominator bits count; arithmetic and comparison are not unit-cost operations on arbitrary rational numbers.

An algorithm is a single probabilistic multitape Turing machine with a finite program, a fixed finite tape alphabet, a read-only input tape, finitely many initially blank work tapes and a sequential output tape. Input is between end markers, and each tape head moves by at most one cell per transition. A transition may read at most one fresh independent fair random bit; it otherwise performs the machine's finite transition rule, and counts as one step. The number of tapes and the program do not depend on the input length. There is no advice, oracle, real-number instruction, or uncharged preprocessing. Deterministic algorithms are included by ignoring random bits.

The class \(\mathcal A\) consists of precisely those machines \(A\) for which there exist integers \(C,k\ge1\) such that, on every binary input string \(z\) and every infinite random-bit sequence \(\omega\in\{0,1\}^{\mathbb N}\), the machine halts within \(C(|z|+1)^k\) transitions, and on every valid instance and every such sequence it outputs a feasible tour. On invalid encodings it may output any finite string within that same time bound. Constants \(C,k\) may depend on \(A\) but not on the instance or its random sequence. Time is bounded on every execution, not only in expectation. Output cost is averaged over the independent fair coins; there is no distribution on the input instances and no allowed probability of infeasibility. Since the runtime is bounded, the expectation is a finite average over sufficiently long random-bit prefixes.

Every \(r\in\mathcal R\) bounds expected tour cost on every instance, with no additive error term or exception for small instances. The set \(\mathcal R\) is nonempty because constant-factor polynomial-time approximation algorithms are known, and it is bounded below by \(1\). Its infimum is therefore a finite real number. An algorithm achieving exactly \(\rho_{\mathrm{ATSP}}\) need not exist. In particular, \(\rho_{\mathrm{ATSP}}=1\) means that for each \(\varepsilon>0\) some eligible algorithm has ratio at most \(1+\varepsilon\), without requiring a ratio-one algorithm or one program taking \(\varepsilon\) as input.

For the conditional hardness statements in the context, \(\mathrm{NP}\) denotes the languages with polynomial-length certificates checked deterministically in polynomial time, and \(\mathrm{RP}\) denotes the languages decided by uniform randomized polynomial-time machines that never accept a no-instance and accept every yes-instance with probability at least \(1/2\). Neither a separation nor an equality of these classes is assumed in the definition of \(\rho_{\mathrm{ATSP}}\).

context_blocks.text: The first constant-factor approximation for general asymmetric TSP established that directed routing admits a uniform constant guarantee, despite the long gap between known algorithms and hardness results.

This card retains the explicit numerical interpretation of the optimal-approximation question: rational positive directed metrics, worst-case polynomial time, always-feasible outputs and a ratio measured by expected cost over the algorithm’s coins.
Vygen’s March 2026 preprint proves a ratio \(12+2\sqrt2+\varepsilon\) for every fixed \(\varepsilon>0\), and a subsequent remark reports a further improvement below \(14.7\).

Karpinski, Lampis and Schmied prove NP-hardness of approximation below \(75/74\); for the randomized expected-cost model here, the corresponding exclusion is conditional on \(\mathrm{NP}\ne\mathrm{RP}\), rather than an unconditional lower bound.

The separate subtour-relaxation question concerns the strength of a specified linear program, whereas this constant ranges over all eligible algorithms and the known bounds do not determine it within the benchmark’s absolute tolerance \(1/100\).

cards.why: Asymmetric TSP is a central model of directed routing, where travel costs can depend on direction. Determining its efficient approximation threshold would measure how much optimality must be sacrificed for polynomial computation, beyond the breakthrough establishing that some constant factor is possible.
