progress.text: Karpinski, Lampis and Schmied establish NP-hardness of approximation within every constant strictly below \(75/74\). In this card’s randomized, always-feasible expected-cost model, the reduction gives \(\rho_{\mathrm{ATSP}}\ge75/74\) assuming \(\mathrm{NP}\ne\mathrm{RP}\). This conditional inference does not supply an unconditional bound above one.

The full Svensson–Tarnawski–Végh version gives a deterministic polynomial-time algorithm with ratio \(506\), establishing a finite upper bound on the optimal constant. Its main theorem compares the produced tour to the standard relaxation, and therefore also to the minimum tour cost.

Vygen’s Theorem 1 gives an approximation ratio \(12+2\sqrt2+\varepsilon\) for each fixed \(\varepsilon>0\), which yields an upper bound \(12+2\sqrt2\) on the infimum without asserting attainment. The remark after the main proof reports a further guarantee below \(14.7\), using additional results from the Traub–Vygen book. These are reported preprint bounds, not a determination of the optimal ratio.

cards.answer_criterion:
An accepted answer supplies an unambiguous real value \(a\) and a complete, mathematically correct Lean proof of \(|a-\rho_{\mathrm{ATSP}}|\le1/100\) for the specified instance class and algorithm model. A certified interval \([\ell,u]\) with \(\ell\le\rho_{\mathrm{ATSP}}\le u\) and \(u-\ell\le1/50\) qualifies via its midpoint. The supplied value need not be rational or a decimal expansion, and exact equality is welcome but not required.

Bounds must concern the infimum with its correct endpoint convention: an upper bound \(\rho_{\mathrm{ATSP}}\le u\) permits achievable ratios approaching \(u\) from above and need not provide an algorithm attaining \(u\); a lower bound must apply to every eligible algorithm. A lower bound under an unproved complexity assumption establishes only that conditional statement and does not by itself certify this unconditional constant. A gap for one linear-programming relaxation, a lower bound for one chosen algorithm, or results only on finitely many input sizes do not determine the target. Merely renaming the defining infimum is not a determination.

cards.title: Optimal polynomial-time approximation ratio for Euclidean k-means
cards.area: Approximation algorithms and hardness of approximation
cards.formal: Determine \(\rho_{\mathrm{EucKM}}\), the infimum of achievable expected approximation ratios for Euclidean k-means with an unrestricted number of clusters and unrestricted dimension.
cards.definitions: An instance consists of integers \(n,d\ge1\), \(1\le k\le n\), and a list of rational points \(x_1,\ldots,x_n\in\mathbb Q^d\), allowing repetitions. A solution is a list of exactly k centers \(c_1,\ldots,c_k\in\mathbb Q^d\), allowing repeated centers, of cost \(\sum_{i=1}^{n}\min_{j\in\{1,\ldots,k\}}\|x_i-c_j\|_2^2\). OPT is the minimum over k centers in \(\mathbb R^d\); an optimum has rational centers because each nonempty cluster can use its mean. Neither k nor d is fixed. Centers may be anywhere in the space and are not required to be input points. An algorithm is a uniform randomized Turing machine with independent fair random bits. Its worst-case running time, over all random tapes, is polynomial in the binary input length. It always returns a feasible solution, and its expected cost is measured over its coins. A real number \(r\ge1\) is achievable if one such algorithm satisfies \(\mathbb E[\operatorname{cost}(A(I))]\le r\operatorname{OPT}(I)\) for every valid instance I. The target is the infimum of achievable r; the polynomial and algorithm may depend on r. An infimum need not be attained. All integers and rational input data use explicit binary encodings, with numerator and positive denominator for each rational; their full lengths count toward the input size. No complexity assumption is built into the definition.

context_blocks.text: The problem minimizes squared distances with a strict center budget. Fixed-dimensional schemes and algorithms whose time is exponential in k do not determine the unrestricted polynomial-time ratio.
The STOC 2026 bound is followed by a July preprint reporting a ratio approaching 3 + ln 2. The introduction explicitly treats unrestricted Euclidean centers, which is the model used here.

cards.title: Optimal approximation for nonmonotone submodular maximization over a matroid
cards.area: Approximation algorithms and hardness of approximation
cards.formal:
Determine the optimal expected approximation ratio for maximizing a nonnegative, not necessarily monotone submodular set function subject to one matroid independence constraint, in the polynomial-time oracle model specified below.

For an instance \(J=(n,f,\mathcal I)\), write
\[
\operatorname{OPT}(J)=\max\{f(S):S\in\mathcal I\}.
\]
Let \(\mathscr A\) be the class of uniform randomized oracle algorithms defined below: each always outputs an independent set and has a polynomial bound on its total number of elementary operations, on every valid instance and every random tape. Define
\[
\mathcal R=\left\{\alpha\in[0,1]:
 \exists A\in\mathscr A\ \forall J\
 \mathbb E_{\omega}\!\left[f\!\left(A^{f,\mathcal I}(n;\omega)\right)\right]
 \ge \alpha\,\operatorname{OPT}(J)\right\},
\qquad
\rho_{\mathrm{mat}}=\sup\mathcal R.
\]
The universal quantifier ranges over every finite ground-set size, every nonnegative submodular function on that ground set, and every matroid on it. The approximation constant and algorithm are chosen before the instance. The target is the real number \(\rho_{\mathrm{mat}}\); it is not assumed that an algorithm attains the supremum. Supply a real answer \(a\) with a Lean-checked proof that
\[
|a-\rho_{\mathrm{mat}}|\le \frac{1}{100}.
\]

cards.why: This is a central approximation question for a general combinatorial optimization model, rather than a guarantee for one application or a running-time refinement. Matroids include cardinality, partition and linear-independence constraints, and submodularity encompasses many cut, coverage and information objectives. Determining the optimal guarantee would identify the inherent cost of combining diminishing returns, potentially harmful additions and independence constraints. Unlike several neighboring monotone or unconstrained models, the known algorithmic and information-theoretic bounds still leave a substantial gap.
cards.status_note: Open in the 2022 source, with a bounded later-source review through 16 September 2026. Chen and coauthors' March 2026 preprint explicitly describes the remaining gap as open. The September 2026 online continuous result does not claim optimality and is a different model. No verified resolution or interval meeting the card's 1/100 answer tolerance was found. The review inspected model definitions, theorem statements and limited supporting arguments; it is not an exhaustive literature review, a full proof audit or a Lean verification.

cards.definitions:
For \(n\in\mathbb N_{0}\), the ground set is \([n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}\), with \([0]=\varnothing\), and \(2^{[n]}\) denotes its power set. The objective is a function \(f:2^{[n]}\to\mathbb R_{\ge0}\) satisfying
\[
f(S)+f(T)\ge f(S\cup T)+f(S\cap T)
\quad\text{for all }S,T\subseteq[n].
\]
This is submodularity. Monotonicity would additionally require \(f(S)\le f(T)\) whenever \(S\subseteq T\); no such requirement is imposed. Nonnegativity applies to every subset, including infeasible ones. No normalization \(f(\varnothing)=0\) is required.

A matroid independence family \(\mathcal I\subseteq2^{[n]}\) satisfies three axioms: \(\varnothing\in\mathcal I\); every subset of an element of \(\mathcal I\) belongs to \(\mathcal I\); and if \(S,T\in\mathcal I\) with \(|S|<|T|\), then some \(t\in T\setminus S\) satisfies \(S\cup\{t\}\in\mathcal I\). An output is any set in \(\mathcal I\), and need not be maximal. The rank, defined as \(\max_{S\in\mathcal I}|S|\), is unrestricted. A cardinality constraint is the special case \(\mathcal I=\{S:|S|\le k\}\).

The input explicitly supplies the integer \(n\) in binary, with zero represented by the single bit zero. Sets supplied to or returned by an oracle are represented by their \(n\)-bit incidence vectors. Two exact oracles are available: a value oracle returns the real number \(f(S)\), and an independence oracle returns the bit indicating whether \(S\in\mathcal I\). The oracles remain fixed throughout a run. Neither the full table of \(f\) nor a list of all independent sets is supplied, and there is no oracle for a continuous extension, its derivatives, or an optimum.

Fix the following exact-real oracle computation convention. An algorithm is one finite program with finite control, finitely many ordinary bit tapes and finitely many tapes of exact real cells. It may contain finitely many rational constants, each specified by a signed integer numerator and a positive integer denominator. Initially work tapes are blank or zero. Elementary instructions are ordinary bit-tape read/write and one-cell head moves; one-cell real-tape head moves; copying or loading a real cell; addition, subtraction, multiplication or division of a fixed finite number of currently addressed real cells; exact comparison of two such cells; obtaining one independent fair random bit; or one of the two oracle calls. Each instruction costs one operation. Division must have a nonzero divisor on every valid run. The query incidence vector must already have been written on the query tape; reading and writing its bits are charged by the bit-tape instructions. An oracle answer is deposited in a designated real cell or bit cell in one operation. Outputting the final incidence vector is also charged. Real cells have no instruction for inspecting a binary expansion or converting an arbitrary real directly into an integer.

This is a unit-cost exact-arithmetic oracle model: the size parameter is \(n\), and real answers are not charged by a bit length. All computation between queries is counted. Programs have no advice depending on \(n\) or the instance, no arbitrary real constants, and no other oracles. This explicit convention completes the source's polynomial-time/value-oracle formulation; it does not assert equivalence to a bit-complexity model for rational objectives.

Formally, \(A\in\mathscr A\) means that there are integers \(C\ge1\) and \(q\ge0\), fixed for that program, such that for every valid \(J=(n,f,\mathcal I)\) and every random tape \(\omega\), the program makes only valid operations and queries, halts within \(C(n+1)^q\) elementary operations, and outputs an \(n\)-bit vector encoding a member of \(\mathcal I\). Thus both its number of oracle queries and its other work are polynomially bounded. No feasibility error is allowed. The expectation in the guarantee concerns objective value, not feasibility or running time.

The random tape consists of independent fair bits, so each specified prefix of length \(r\) has probability \(2^{-r}\). For a program with the above clock, at most \(C(n+1)^q\) bits are read; its expected value is consequently a finite average over that many fair bits, with unused bits ignored. If \(\operatorname{OPT}(J)=0\), the multiplicative guarantee is automatically satisfied; no quotient by zero is used. Always returning the empty set guarantees factor zero, so \(\mathcal R\) is nonempty and its supremum is well-defined in \([0,1]\).
cards.answer_criterion:
Supply a specified real number \(a\), or an unambiguous expression defining it, and a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of
\[
|a-\rho_{\mathrm{mat}}|\le \frac{1}{100}
\]
for exactly the instance class and algorithm class above. Merely restating the supremum that defines \(\rho_{\mathrm{mat}}\) is not a determination.

A certified interval is sufficient: give \(l,u\in[0,1]\), prove
\[
l\le\rho_{\mathrm{mat}}\le u,\qquad u-l\le\frac{1}{50},
\]
and use \(a=(l+u)/2\). To make explicit what both sides mean, the lower bound can be certified by proving
\[
\forall\varepsilon>0\ \exists A\in\mathscr A\
\forall J\
\mathbb E_{\omega}[f(A^{f,\mathcal I}(n;\omega))]
\ge(l-\varepsilon)\operatorname{OPT}(J).
\]
The upper bound can be certified by proving
\[
\forall\varepsilon>0\ \forall A\in\mathscr A\
\exists J\
\mathbb E_{\omega}[f(A^{f,\mathcal I}(n;\omega))]
<(u+\varepsilon)\operatorname{OPT}(J).
\]
Membership in \(\mathscr A\) includes the full program, uniform polynomial clock and unconditional feasibility requirements from the definitions. In the lower statement the program and its polynomial constants may depend on \(\varepsilon\), but not on \(J\); the upper statement ranges over every such program and all possible polynomial degrees. This permits approaching a supremum without attaining it.

Exact determination is welcome but is not mandatory. A guarantee for a subclass of matroids or objectives, for deterministic algorithms alone, or for polynomially many queries with unrestricted computation does not by itself determine this target. Nor does an upper bound assuming an unproved complexity separation constitute the unconditional upper certificate above.

context_blocks.text: Qi's original question concerns general constrained submodular maximization: a single nonnegative submodular objective over independent sets of one matroid. Although the paper mainly studies a sum with a linear function, that linear term is absent from the extracted open question. The source measures approximation in expectation and running time polynomially in ground-set size.

The 2022 source records a \(0.385\) approximation and a \(0.478\) oracle inapproximability threshold. Qi also proves the latter threshold already for the cardinality-constrained special case. The upper bound therefore applies to algorithms for all matroids, but does not make the special case and general case identical problems.

Buchbinder and Feldman's STOC 2024 result improves the approximation guarantee to \(0.401\) for a matroid constraint. Their Corollary 1.3 is stated directly for the discrete set-function problem; the result is not merely a guarantee for a continuous objective with stronger oracle access.

The checked results give the conservative bracket \(401/1000\le\rho_{\mathrm{mat}}\le239/500\). Its width is \(77/1000\), larger than the benchmark's sufficient interval width \(1/50\). These bounds therefore do not already meet this card's numerical acceptance criterion.

A March 2026 preprint explicitly describes the remaining \(0.401\)-versus-\(0.478\) gap as open while improving a deterministic guarantee to \(0.385-\varepsilon\). A September 2026 online continuous-optimization preprint explicitly says its \(0.401\) result does not claim optimality. Neither supplies the requested determination in this card's offline randomized model.

The source does not prescribe machine instructions, numeric bit encodings, a random-tape distribution or how the matroid is accessed at the bit level. The draft explicitly completes these with exact-real arithmetic, a membership oracle for independence, binary set queries, independent fair random bits, finite rational program constants and total polynomial operation cost. The exact-real model counts both oracle calls and all intervening work, so it does not silently weaken polynomial time to polynomial query count with unlimited computation. Matroid rank is unrestricted, feasible output is required on every random tape, and the polynomial clock is uniform over objectives and matroids. Because the ratio is a supremum, arbitrarily close guarantees may use distinct finite programs and polynomial degrees; no algorithm attaining the endpoint is demanded.

Its 0.478 result is for matroid independent sets; a separate 0.394 result concerns bases and must not be applied to this card. The complete hardness proof was not independently audited. The direct later Qi theorem supplies an additional checked primary statement of the same obstruction under the cardinality special case.

Read Buchbinder–Feldman arXiv:2311.01129v1, 2 November 2023, Theorem 1.2 and Corollary 1.3 p. 3. The latter directly states a polynomial-time 0.401 approximation for nonnegative submodular set functions under a matroid constraint. Appendix A pp. 38–39 explains access through the discrete value oracle, sampling error and the strict numerical slack beyond 0.401; this is not merely an exact-gradient-oracle theorem. Section 6 p. 31 still identifies a gap to 0.478, and also notes a tiny fourth-decimal improvement, so the card calls [0.401,0.478] a conservative bracket rather than claiming those decimals are exact frontier endpoints. The PDF typeset date is 17 March 2026, but the arXiv revision date is 16 March.

It matches the constructive 0.401 factor in an online continuous DR-submodular model and explicitly disclaims claiming optimality. Its online feedback, continuous objective and convex-feasibility assumptions are different from this card's discrete offline value/independence-oracle model. No theorem from that paper is used to alter the target or to establish a new discrete lower bound.

Bounded later searches through 16 September 2026 included general nonmonotone submodular matroid approximation, 0.401, 0.478, 2025/2026 and post-August-2026 queries. Surfaced deterministic, dynamic, streaming, symmetric, curvature-restricted and online results were distinguished from the general target. No matching ratio or sufficiently narrow two-sided interval was found. The current conservative interval has width 77/1000, exceeding 1/50, so the default numerical benchmark tolerance does not already render the card solved.

The Lean criterion uses a real answer with absolute error at most 1/100. Optional lower and upper certificates quantify over every valid input and every admissible algorithm, respectively; their epsilon quantifiers accommodate a nonattained supremum. cards.context:
Qi's original question concerns general constrained submodular maximization: a single nonnegative submodular objective over independent sets of one matroid. Although the paper mainly studies a sum with a linear function, that linear term is absent from the extracted open question. The source measures approximation in expectation and running time polynomially in ground-set size.

The 2022 source records a \(0.385\) approximation and a \(0.478\) oracle inapproximability threshold. Qi also proves the latter threshold already for the cardinality-constrained special case. The upper bound therefore applies to algorithms for all matroids, but does not make the special case and general case identical problems.

Buchbinder and Feldman's STOC 2024 result improves the approximation guarantee to \(0.401\) for a matroid constraint. Their Corollary 1.3 is stated directly for the discrete set-function problem; the result is not merely a guarantee for a continuous objective with stronger oracle access.

The checked results give the conservative bracket \(401/1000\le\rho_{\mathrm{mat}}\le239/500\). Its width is \(77/1000\), larger than the benchmark's sufficient interval width \(1/50\). These bounds therefore do not already meet this card's numerical acceptance criterion.

A March 2026 preprint explicitly describes the remaining \(0.401\)-versus-\(0.478\) gap as open while improving a deterministic guarantee to \(0.385-\varepsilon\). A September 2026 online continuous-optimization preprint explicitly says its \(0.401\) result does not claim optimality. Neither supplies the requested determination in this card's offline randomized model.

cards.title: Optimal polynomial-time approximation ratio for Steiner Tree
cards.area: Approximation algorithms and hardness of approximation
cards.formal:
Determine the real constant \(\rho_{\mathrm{ST}}\), the infimum of achievable expected-cost approximation ratios for undirected weighted Steiner Tree under worst-case polynomial running time. For the valid instances \(\mathcal I\) and the uniform randomized, always-feasible algorithms \(\mathcal A\) defined below, put
\[
\mathcal R_{\mathrm{ST}}=
\left\{r\in\mathbb R:
r\ge1\ \land\
\exists A\in\mathcal A\ \forall I\in\mathcal I,\
\mathbb E_{\omega}\!\left[\operatorname{cost}_I(A(I;\omega))\right]
\le r\,\operatorname{OPT}(I)\right\},
\qquad
\rho_{\mathrm{ST}}=\inf\mathcal R_{\mathrm{ST}}.
\]
Supply an unambiguous real value \(a\) and a complete Lean proof that
\[
\left|a-\rho_{\mathrm{ST}}\right|\le\frac1{100}.
\]
The algorithm and its polynomial time bound may depend on \(r\), but must work for every valid instance. The expectation concerns output cost, not running time. No complexity assumption is part of the definition. The requested error is additive in this dimensionless approximation ratio.
cards.definitions:
For an integer \(n\ge2\), let \([n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}\). A valid instance \(I=(n,E,R,w)\) consists of a connected simple undirected graph \(G=([n],E)\), a set of terminals \(R\subseteq[n]\) with \(2\le |R|\le n\), and nonnegative rational weights \(w:E\to\mathbb Q_{\ge0}\). An edge is an unordered pair of distinct vertices; each pair occurs at most once. Connected means every two vertices are joined by a finite path. The whole graph, terminal list and all weights are explicitly given. There is no restriction on the topology, number of terminals, weight magnitudes, or ratio between positive weights.

A feasible solution is an edge set \(F\subseteq E\) such that the graph on vertex set
\[
W=R\cup\bigcup_{\{u,v\}\in F}\{u,v\}
\]
with edge set \(F\) is connected and has no cycle. Thus the output is one tree containing all terminals; its other vertices may be any subset of the available nonterminals. Its cost and the optimum are
\[
\operatorname{cost}_I(F)=\sum_{e\in F}w(e),
\qquad
\operatorname{OPT}(I)=
\min\{\operatorname{cost}_I(F):F\text{ is a feasible solution of }I\}.
\]
Every valid instance has a feasible solution, so the minimum is over a nonempty finite set and is attained. Output edges must be original input edges. Neither new Steiner points outside \([n]\), a separate cost for selected vertices, a set of pairwise connection demands, nor directed edges are part of this problem.

The following encoding fixes the full bit cost. Write each weight uniquely as \(p_e/q_e\), where \(p_e\ge0\), \(q_e\ge1\), and the integers are relatively prime, so a zero weight is encoded as \(0/1\). Order edges lexicographically by their endpoints \(u<v\), obtaining \(e_1,\ldots,e_m\), and order terminal labels increasingly, obtaining \(r_1,\ldots,r_h\). Form one list of integers consisting of \(n\), the explicit vertex list \(1,\ldots,n\), \(m\), the four entries \(u,v,p_{e_j},q_{e_j}\) for each edge \(e_j=\{u,v\}\) in order, then \(h,r_1,\ldots,r_h\). Encode each integer in ordinary binary without leading zeros, with \(0\) represented by one zero. Put a separator \(\#\) between consecutive integers and no trailing separator. Finally encode the three symbols by \(0\mapsto00\), \(1\mapsto01\), \(\#\mapsto10\). The length of the resulting binary string is \(L(I)\). A valid output is the list consisting of \(|F|\) followed by the strictly increasing indices of the selected edges in \(e_1,\ldots,e_m\), using the same integer, separator and binary-symbol encoding. All numerator, denominator, endpoint and output bits count; arithmetic on rational numbers is not a unit-cost operation.

An algorithm is a single probabilistic multitape Turing machine with a finite program, a fixed finite tape alphabet, a read-only input tape, a fixed finite number of initially blank work tapes, and a sequential output tape. The input is delimited by end markers. Each transition reads the scanned symbols, can write one symbol per writable tape, and moves each head by at most one cell; it counts as one step. A transition may additionally read at most one fresh independent fair random bit. The program and tape count do not depend on the input length. There is no advice, oracle, real-arithmetic instruction or uncharged preprocessing. A deterministic algorithm is included by ignoring the random bits.

The set \(\mathcal A\) contains exactly the machines \(A\) for which there exist integers \(C,k\ge1\) such that, on every binary input \(z\) and every random sequence \(\omega\in\{0,1\}^{\mathbb N}\), the machine halts within \(C(|z|+1)^k\) steps, and on every valid instance and every such sequence its output encodes a feasible solution. Invalid inputs may receive any output within that same bound. The constants \(C,k\) may depend on \(A\), but not on the instance or the random bits. This is a bound on every execution, not merely an expected-time bound.

The random sequence \(\omega\) has the product distribution of independent fair bits; there is no probability distribution on inputs. Since at most \(C(L(I)+1)^k\) bits can be read, the expected cost is the finite average over all bit strings of that length, each with equal probability, disregarding unused bits. Infeasibility has no permitted error probability. The multiplicative bound must hold on every valid instance, with no additive cost term or exception for small inputs. Instances with \(\operatorname{OPT}(I)=0\) are included: their expected output cost must be zero. As every finite random execution has positive probability and costs are nonnegative, this requires zero output cost on every execution of such an instance.

Known polynomial-time approximations make \(\mathcal R_{\mathrm{ST}}\) nonempty; it is bounded below by \(1\), so its infimum is a finite real number. An algorithm attaining exactly \(\rho_{\mathrm{ST}}\) need not exist. In particular, \(\rho_{\mathrm{ST}}=1\) would mean that for every \(\varepsilon>0\) some eligible algorithm achieves ratio at most \(1+\varepsilon\), without requiring an exact algorithm or one program that takes \(\varepsilon\) as an additional input.

For the conditional results in the context, \(\mathrm P\) is the class of languages decidable by deterministic polynomial-time Turing machines. The class \(\mathrm{NP}\) consists of languages with polynomial-length binary certificates checked by a deterministic polynomial-time verifier. The class \(\mathrm{RP}\) consists of languages decided by randomized machines with polynomial running time on every random tape that never accept a no-instance and accept every yes-instance with probability at least \(1/2\). No equality or separation among these classes is assumed in \(\rho_{\mathrm{ST}}\).

context_blocks.text: The source model is an undirected weighted graph with a terminal subset; passing to shortest-path distances preserves the approximation problem. This card retains the canonical graph input with nonnegative rational weights, explicit binary encoding, worst-case polynomial time and expected feasible-output cost. These machine and encoding conventions make the inherited numerical target precise.

Byrka, Grandoni, Rothvoß and Sanità obtain a polynomial-time \((\ln 4+\varepsilon)\)-approximation for every fixed \(\varepsilon>0\), and their full account derandomizes the algorithm. Consequently the infimum satisfies the unconditional bounds \(1\le\rho_{\mathrm{ST}}\le\ln 4\), without an assertion that the upper endpoint is attained.

Traub and Zenklusen obtain the same limiting guarantee by a combinatorial algorithm, first presented in their 2021 preprint and SODA 2022 paper and incorporated into their 2025 journal article. Their model discussion explicitly explains the compatibility of positive and nonnegative edge weights.

Chlebík and Chlebíková prove NP-hardness of achieving factors below \(96/95\). For the always-feasible randomized expected-cost model of this card, their gap reduction excludes those factors assuming \(\mathrm{NP}\ne\mathrm{RP}\); that randomized-model consequence is an editorial inference, not an unconditional lower bound.
The 2024 result bounding the bidirected cut relaxation's integrality gap by \(1.9988\) settles a different question about a specified relaxation.

A July 2026 primary paper still reports \(\ln 4+\varepsilon\) as the best known general Steiner Tree approximation guarantee. The checked bounds do not determine \(\rho_{\mathrm{ST}}\) within absolute error \(1/100\).

cards.why: Steiner Tree is a basic network-design problem and a recurring subproblem in more general connectivity objectives. Determining its efficient approximation threshold would establish how closely polynomial-time algorithms can approach optimal connection cost in unrestricted weighted graphs. The target compares all algorithms, making it broader than the accuracy of one method or the strength of one relaxation.

cards.answer_criterion:
An accepted answer supplies an unambiguous real value \(a\) and a complete, mathematically correct Lean proof of
\[
\left|a-\rho_{\mathrm{ST}}\right|\le\frac1{100}
\]
for precisely the instance class and machine model above. A certified interval \([\ell,u]\) with
\[
\ell\le\rho_{\mathrm{ST}}\le u,\qquad u-\ell\le\frac1{50}
\]
qualifies through \(a=(\ell+u)/2\). The value need not be an integer, rational number or decimal expansion; exact determination is welcome but is not required. Merely renaming the defining infimum does not specify an answer.

The proof must respect the infimum's endpoint convention. To establish an upper bound \(\rho_{\mathrm{ST}}\le u\), achievable ratios approaching \(u\) from above suffice; an algorithm achieving \(u\) itself is not required. Equivalently, one may prove that for every \(\varepsilon>0\) there is an eligible algorithm whose expected cost on every instance is at most \((u+\varepsilon)\operatorname{OPT}\). A lower bound \(\ell\le\rho_{\mathrm{ST}}\) must exclude every eligible algorithm from achieving each ratio \(r\) with \(1\le r<\ell\). For every such \(r\) and algorithm, this requires some valid instance with expected cost strictly greater than \(r\operatorname{OPT}\).

A hardness bound under an unproved complexity assumption proves only the corresponding conditional statement. It does not by itself certify the unconditional constant requested here. A gap for a particular linear-programming relaxation, the worst case of one selected algorithm, a guarantee only for a restricted graph family, or computations on finitely many input sizes do not determine this infimum over all eligible algorithms and all valid instances.
cards.status_note: The inspected primary results give ratios approaching the natural logarithm of four and conditional inapproximability, leaving the optimal numerical constant undetermined. cards.title: Optimal polynomial-time approximation ratio for metric k-means
cards.area: Approximation algorithms and hardness of approximation
cards.formal: Determine \(\rho_{\mathrm{MetKM}}\), the infimum of achievable expected approximation ratios for metric k-means with an explicit set of possible centers.
cards.definitions: An instance consists of a finite labeled set U with its entire rational distance matrix \(d:U\times U\to\mathbb Q_{\ge0}\), nonempty subsets D,F of U with \(D\subseteq F\), and an integer \(1\le k\le|F|\). Require \(d(u,v)=0\) exactly when u=v, symmetry, and the triangle inequality. D is the unweighted client set and F the possible centers. A solution is a subset \(S\subseteq F\) of cardinality k, of cost \(\sum_{x\in D}\min_{s\in S}d(x,s)^2\). OPT is the minimum of this cost over all such S. The squared cost itself need not satisfy the triangle inequality. The metric is unrestricted and fully listed; neither a Euclidean promise nor a distance oracle is provided. An algorithm is a uniform randomized Turing machine with independent fair random bits. Its worst-case running time, over all random tapes, is polynomial in the binary input length. It always returns a feasible solution, and its expected cost is measured over its coins. A real number \(r\ge1\) is achievable if one such algorithm satisfies \(\mathbb E[\operatorname{cost}(A(I))]\le r\operatorname{OPT}(I)\) for every valid instance I. The target is the infimum of achievable r; the polynomial and algorithm may depend on r. An infimum need not be attained. All integers and rational input data use explicit binary encodings, with numerator and positive denominator for each rational; their full lengths count toward the input size. No complexity assumption is built into the definition.

context_blocks.text: Metric k-means squares the underlying distances, unlike k-median. The admissible center set is explicit, and opening extra centers does not meet the card’s feasibility condition.

The July 2026 paper reports a ratio approaching 4.9 and discusses a much larger known hardness barrier for general metrics than for the Euclidean setting. A bound under a complexity assumption is not an unconditional determination of the algorithmic infimum.

cards.why: Determine the computational limit of squared-distance clustering in arbitrary metrics, a central network and data-clustering approximation problem.

cards.title: Constant-factor approximation for Dasgupta’s hierarchical clustering objective
cards.area: Approximation algorithms and hardness of approximation
cards.formal: Do there exist real constants \(C\ge1\), \(K>0\), an integer \(a\ge1\), and one deterministic multitape Turing machine which, on every explicitly encoded nonnegative rational similarity graph \(G\), outputs a hierarchy \(T\) with \(\operatorname{cost}_G(T)\le C\operatorname{OPT}(G)\) within \(K(N+1)^a\) bit operations, where \(N\) is the total input bit length and the cost and allowed hierarchies are defined below?
cards.definitions:
An input is an integer \(n\ge2\) and a finite simple undirected graph \(G=([n],E,w)\), where \([n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}\), \(E\subseteq\{\{u,v\}:1\le u<v\le n\}\), and \(w:E\to\mathbb Q_{\ge0}\). The encoding explicitly lists all \(n\) vertices, including isolated ones, and all edges with their endpoints and weights. Integers use ordinary binary notation with delimiters; each rational weight is a nonnegative integer numerator and positive integer denominator in binary. The explicit vertex list ensures \(N\ge n\). There are no loops or repeated edges. An absent edge has weight zero. The graph need not be connected and has no metric, clusterability, density or sampling promise.

A hierarchy is a finite rooted full binary tree whose leaves are labeled bijectively by \([n]\); every internal node has exactly two children. For a node \(z\), let \(L_T(z)\subseteq[n]\) be its descendant leaf labels. For distinct leaves \(u,v\), let \(\operatorname{lca}_T(u,v)\) be their least common ancestor. Define
\[
\operatorname{cost}_G(T)=\sum_{\{u,v\}\in E}w(\{u,v\})\,|L_T(\operatorname{lca}_T(u,v))|,
\qquad
\operatorname{OPT}(G)=\min_T\operatorname{cost}_G(T).
\]
Each unordered edge contributes once. The minimum is over all such trees, with no restriction on height or balance. The output explicitly lists the root, child edges and leaf labels of one tree. If all weights are zero, the required cost is zero and any valid hierarchy qualifies.

The same finite machine and constants must work for every \(n\), graph and weight encoding. All input reads, binary arithmetic, preprocessing and output writes count in the worst-case running time. The machine has no random bits, advice, external comparison or cluster-label oracle, or uncharged preprocessing. The factor \(C\) is independent of \(n\), the number of edges and the sizes or ratios of the weights; it is not an input parameter. Only the tree is required as output, and its stated cost guarantee is mathematical, using exact rational weights.

context_blocks.text: The source defines a cost for a complete hierarchy of pairwise similarities. This card retains the previously selected deterministic polynomial-time, constant-factor question. The explicit rational encoding and vertex list fix bit complexity and output size; they do not impose a structural promise.

The general approximation guarantee of Charikar and Chatziafratis is \(O(\sqrt{\log n})\). Their Theorem 3.4 proves Small-Set-Expansion hardness of approximation within every constant factor, already on unweighted graphs. This is a conditional complexity barrier, not an unconditional proof that the requested machine cannot exist.
The ICALP 2025 sublinear result assumes a clusterable graph and access to cluster labels of sampled seeds. Its input model and guarantee do not supply the unrestricted algorithm asked for here.

The July 2026 generalized clustering paper permits a leaf cluster to remain a whole graph from a specified class, such as a tree. Its objective can consequently vanish on inputs for which singleton-leaf hierarchies have positive cost. Those results concern a different stopping rule.

A constant-factor guarantee for the complementary revenue-maximization objective does not, just from that guarantee, give a constant-factor bound for this minimization objective. The target here is the displayed cost itself.

cards.why: A hierarchy must represent similarity at every scale, so optimizing a single flat partition is insufficient. A constant approximation for this canonical objective would give a uniform quality guarantee on arbitrary similarity data and would cross a major graph-partitioning hardness barrier.
cards.answer_criterion: Supply a complete mathematically correct Lean proof of the existence of a machine and fixed constants satisfying every stated guarantee, or a complete Lean proof of their nonexistence. An approximation factor growing with the input size, a result for a promised graph class, or a guarantee with an additional oracle does not settle this target. A conditional hardness result establishes its implication but does not by itself prove the unconditional negative answer.

cards.title: Min-CSP approximation at the SDP integrality gap
cards.area: Approximation algorithms and hardness of approximation
cards.formal:
For every fixed finite domain \(D\), positive arity \(k\), and finite set \(\Lambda\) of nonnegative rational cost functions \(f:D^k\to[0,1]\), is the following true? For every rational \(\varepsilon>0\), there is a randomized polynomial-time algorithm which, on every \(n\)-variable minimization \(\Lambda\)-CSP instance \(I\) with finite \(n\)-variable SDP integrality gap \(\alpha_\Lambda(n)\), returns an assignment \(\sigma\) such that
\[\Pr\bigl[\operatorname{cost}_I(\sigma)\leq (1+\varepsilon)\alpha_\Lambda(n)\operatorname{OPT}(I)\bigr]\geq\tfrac23?\]
The same algorithm handles all \(n\); it also halts and returns an assignment on the sizes where the gap is infinite, but no multiplicative guarantee is imposed there. The gap and the basic SDP are defined below.
cards.why: A universal theorem would extend the general SDP approximation framework to multiplicative minimization guarantees, including instances whose optimum vanishes with input size. It would connect a geometric obstruction of a standard relaxation to actual polynomial-time approximation across all finite cost languages. A counterexample would identify a limit to interpreting integrality gaps as achievable algorithmic benchmarks.
cards.status_note: The 2017 chapter explicitly poses this n-dependent multiplicative question after distinguishing it from the 2009 additive rounding theorem. The February 2026 robust-satisfiability paper supplies results under additional template hypotheses, not the universal statement. A bounded primary-source search checked on 16 September 2026 found no matching resolution; this does not establish that the historical question remains open beyond the checked sources.

importance.reason: A universal bridge between SDP integrality gaps and polynomial-time multiplicative approximation would organize minimization across all finite-domain cost languages, including near-satisfiable instances where the existing additive theory loses its guarantee.
importance.basis: Individual source and scope review of the universal n-dependent gap question; significance is editorial, not a proof-status judgment.

sentences: A minimization CSP assigns finite-domain values to variables to minimize the average of fixed local nonnegative costs.
Its basic SDP can achieve a lower cost using consistent local distributions and vectors than any actual assignment.
The question asks whether a randomized polynomial-time algorithm can match the SDP’s worst gap at each number of variables within every factor 1+ε.
The multiplicative guarantee must also protect zero or very small optimum values, which existing additive universal rounding does not do.
A resolution would clarify whether size-dependent SDP gaps universally predict achievable approximation for minimization CSPs.

cards.definitions:
Fix \(D=\{1,\ldots,q\}\), with \(q\geq1\), and a finite nonempty \(\Lambda\). Its rational cost tables and \(k\geq1\) are fixed, not input. The nonnegative rational convention gives a finite effective version of the source’s generalized nonnegative predicates; negative costs do not define the multiplicative approximation question. An instance has variables \(x_1,\ldots,x_n\), \(n\geq1\), and a finite list of \(m\) constraints \(C=(f_C,(i_1,\ldots,i_k))\). Every \(f_C\in\Lambda\), and each \(i_j\in[n]\). Repeated coordinates and repeated occurrences are allowed, with each occurrence having unit weight. There are no hard constraints, infinite costs, extra unary pins or input-dependent predicates. For an assignment \(\sigma:[n]\to D\), set
\[\operatorname{cost}_I(\sigma)=\frac1m\sum_C f_C(\sigma(i_1),\ldots,\sigma(i_k)),\qquad \operatorname{OPT}(I)=\min_\sigma\operatorname{cost}_I(\sigma).\]
For \(m=0\), cost and optimum are zero. A zero-one cost table records violation by value one and satisfaction by value zero. Different arities can be represented by a common maximum arity with unused arguments; the question is not restricted to Boolean predicates.

Define the basic semidefinite relaxation as follows. Choose real vectors \(v_0,u_{i,a}\in\mathbb R^{1+nq}\), for \(i\in[n],a\in D\), satisfying
\[\langle v_0,v_0\rangle=1,\qquad \sum_{a\in D}u_{i,a}=v_0,\qquad \langle u_{i,a},u_{i,b}\rangle=0\quad(a\ne b).\]
For each constraint occurrence \(C\), let \(S_C\) be its set of distinct variables and choose a local distribution \(\mu_C:D^{S_C}\to\mathbb R_{\geq0}\) with total mass one. Impose
\[\sum_{z:z(i)=a}\mu_C(z)=\langle u_{i,a},u_{i,a}\rangle\quad(i\in S_C),\]
\[\sum_{z:z(i)=a,\ z(j)=b}\mu_C(z)=\langle u_{i,a},u_{j,b}\rangle\quad(i,j\in S_C,\ i\ne j).\]
Thus all local one- and two-variable marginals agree with the common vector inner products. Repeated occurrences of a variable in a constraint use the same value \(z(i)\). The SDP value \(\operatorname{SDP}(I)\) is the minimum of
\[\frac1m\sum_C\sum_{z\in D^{S_C}}\mu_C(z)f_C(z(i_1),\ldots,z(i_k)),\]
with value zero when \(m=0\). This is a finite semidefinite program via its Gram matrix; the stated vector dimension suffices for every such matrix. It is feasible and compact in Gram-matrix and distribution coordinates. Every assignment gives a feasible point, so \(0\leq\operatorname{SDP}(I)\leq\operatorname{OPT}(I)\). No higher level of an SDP hierarchy is included.

For a fixed instance define its gap ratio as \(\operatorname{OPT}(I)/\operatorname{SDP}(I)\) if the denominator is positive, as one if both values are zero, and as \(+\infty\) if only the denominator is zero. Let \(\alpha_\Lambda(n)\) be the supremum of these ratios over all lists of constraints on exactly \(n\) labelled variables; unused variables are counted. Then \(1\leq\alpha_\Lambda(n)\leq+\infty\), and the gap may grow with \(n\). The algorithm is not supplied with its value or an oracle for it. This is an instance-size gap, not a single constant supremum over every size.

Encode \(n,m\) in unary and each constraint by its fixed-table index and its \(k\) variable indices in binary; the total bit length is \(L\). The algorithm is a finite probabilistic multitape Turing machine using independent fair coin bits. For each fixed \(D,k,\Lambda,\varepsilon\), one program has worst-case running time \(C(L+1)^c\) on every input and every coin sequence; \(C,c\) may depend on these fixed parameters. Malformed strings may be rejected. The output explicitly gives all \(n\) labels. No polynomial dependence on \(1/\varepsilon\), common exponent across languages or effective algorithm for finding the program from \(\Lambda\) is required. The probability convention is the explicit bounded-error interpretation of the source’s randomized approximation framework.

The guarantee is multiplicative, relative to the actual optimum. When that optimum is zero and the size-dependent gap is finite, the algorithm must find a zero-cost assignment with probability at least \(2/3\). There is no additive error term, and no assertion that it must round a supplied SDP point or achieve the stronger bound with \(\operatorname{SDP}(I)\) in place of \(\operatorname{OPT}(I)\).
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of the universal algorithmic assertion, or of its logical negation. A positive proof must establish one polynomial-time machine for every fixed language and positive accuracy, working at all input sizes with the stated success probability, size-dependent gap and zero-optimum convention. A negative proof must establish a fixed finite language and positive accuracy for which no such machine exists. A constant additive guarantee for normalized cost, an algorithm restricted to one predicate family, or a conditional obstruction to one rounding scheme does not settle the universal statement. An unproved complexity assumption may support partial progress but is not part of this unconditional target.

source_formulation.text: If the minimization SDP gap at n variables is α_n, can a polynomial-time algorithm attain approximation factor (1+ε)α_n for every positive ε?
source_formulation.caption: Editorial paraphrase of Chapter 11, §7, Open Problem 4; the n-dependent gap is retained, with finite cost encoding, zero cases and success probability made explicit.

context_blocks.text: The integrality gap measures a relaxation’s worst discrepancy from a genuine assignment. In minimization, the SDP can make local constraints appear cheaper than any global assignment. This question asks whether an efficient algorithm can always match the resulting size-dependent benchmark to arbitrarily small relative slack; it does not ask to compute the gap itself.

The source distinguishes maximization and minimization with nonnegative predicates. For maximization, a random assignment provides a positive baseline for each nonzero fixed predicate, allowing additive approximation losses to become relative losses. For minimization, satisfiable or nearly satisfiable instances can have optimum zero or arbitrarily close to zero, so the same argument fails.

Raghavendra and Steurer’s universal rounding theorem obtains the integrality-gap curve with an additive error in both its argument and its returned objective. Its running-time dependence on that additive accuracy can be very large. Taking the accuracy to shrink with the instance size therefore does not yield the polynomial-time multiplicative guarantee asked here.

The source explicitly permits α_n to depend on n. Replacing it by one global constant would discard major minimization examples, while a generic additive approximation to a normalized objective would leave zero and very small costs unprotected. These are essential parts of the question, not presentation choices.

The 2026 robust-satisfiability work obtains quantitative guarantees for specified majority and plurality preservation classes, along with separate conditional hardness for a particular promise problem. Those results concern selected families and loss curves. They do not assert a universal algorithm matching the exact n-variable multiplicative SDP gap for every finite nonnegative cost language.

cards.title: Deterministic competitiveness of k-server
cards.formal:
For every integer \(k\ge1\), determine the universal deterministic competitive-ratio infimum
\[R_{\mathrm{det}}(k)=\inf\mathcal R_k,\]
where
\[\mathcal R_k=\Bigl\{r\in[1,\infty):\ \forall(M,d)\in\mathcal M_k\ \forall C_0\in M^k\ \exists A\ \exists\beta\in\mathbb R_{\ge0}\ \forall\sigma\in M^{<\omega},\quad
\operatorname{cost}_{A}(\sigma;C_0)\le r\operatorname{OPT}(\sigma;C_0)+\beta\Bigr\}.\]
Here \(\mathcal M_k\) consists of all finite or infinite metric spaces having at least \(k+1\) points, \(A\) is a deterministic online rule in the serving model below, and \(M^{<\omega}\) is the set of all finite request sequences, including the empty sequence. Give a real-valued function \(g\) and a complete Lean proof that
\[\forall k\in\mathbb N_{\ge1},\qquad |g(k)-R_{\mathrm{det}}(k)|\le\frac1{100}.\]
The tolerance is absolute in the competitive ratio and is the same for every \(k\).
cards.definitions:
A metric space here consists of a set \(M\) and a function \(d:M\times M\to\mathbb R_{\ge0}\) with finite values, satisfying \(d(x,y)=0\) exactly when \(x=y\), symmetry, and \(d(x,z)\le d(x,y)+d(y,z)\). The space is known to the rule. It need not be finite, bounded, discrete, complete, compact, or given by computable distances. The quantifier ranges over ordinary set-based metric spaces.

There are exactly \(k\) servers with equal movement costs. For precise bookkeeping label them by \([k]=\{1,\ldots,k\}\) and write a configuration as a tuple \(C=(x_1,\ldots,x_k)\in M^k\). Several servers may occupy the same point. Labels only identify which server moves and confer no different costs or service capabilities; the physical configuration is a multiset. The initial tuple \(C_0\) is specified before the first request and is identical for the online rule and the offline comparator.

For a request sequence \(\sigma=(q_1,\ldots,q_T)\), request \(q_t\) must be served before \(q_{t+1}\) is revealed. If a server already occupies \(q_t\), all servers stay put and the cost of that step is zero. Otherwise the rule chooses one index \(i_t\in[k]\), moves that server from its current position \(x_{i_t,t-1}\) to \(q_t\), and pays \(d(x_{i_t,t-1},q_t)\). All other positions remain unchanged. Let \(\delta_t\) denote this step cost. The total cost is \(\sum_{t=1}^{T}\delta_t\). These are lazy moves; for the ordinary sum-of-movement-distances objective, the classical laziness lemma shows that this restriction does not worsen the attainable competitive guarantees.

A deterministic online rule is a function assigning a legal next move to each nonempty revealed request prefix, with the current configuration determined recursively from earlier moves. On two sequences with the same prefix it must make the same decisions through that prefix. It may use the known metric, \(k\), the initial tuple, and the whole revealed history. No random bits, future-dependent advice, request horizon or next request are provided. All finite sequences are included, of arbitrary length; the definition also covers requests chosen adaptively from the rule's past moves. Covered requests may remain in the remembered history.

This is a question about existence of online decision rules, without any time, space, computability, finite-program or finite-precision restriction. In particular, a rule on a specified real metric is an abstract function; no unmentioned representation of all real distances is required. The ratio \(r\) depends only on \(k\). The chosen rule and finite constant \(\beta\) may depend on \(k,r,(M,d),C_0\), but neither may be chosen after seeing the future sequence. The same \(A,\beta\) must satisfy the inequality for all sequence lengths and contents on that metric and initial placement.

The quantity \(\operatorname{OPT}(\sigma;C_0)\) is the minimum total cost of all legal lazy move sequences serving \(\sigma\) from \(C_0\), with all requests known in advance. There are at most \(k^T\) choices of server indices, so the minimum is attained and finite even when \(M\) is infinite. Both costs are zero for the empty sequence. There is no final return requirement and no prescribed terminal configuration. The competitive inequality is used directly, including when \(\operatorname{OPT}=0\); it is not a quotient by a possibly zero cost.

Movement costs and \(\beta\) have the same distance units, while \(r\) and \(R_{\mathrm{det}}(k)\) are dimensionless. Multiplying all distances by a positive constant rescales costs and the allowed additive constant, but does not change the competitive ratio. No normalization of metric diameter is imposed.

The known universal upper bound gives \(2k-1\in\mathcal R_k\), so this set is nonempty and its real infimum exists; the deterministic lower bound gives \(k\le R_{\mathrm{det}}(k)\le2k-1\). The infimum need not be attained. For \(u\ge1\), an upper bound \(R_{\mathrm{det}}(k)\le u\) means that for every \(\eta>0\), the ratio \(u+\eta\) belongs to \(\mathcal R_k\). The selected rules and additive constants may depend on \(\eta\). A lower bound \(\ell\ge1\) means that for every \(r\in[1,\ell)\) there exist a metric and initial placement such that every online rule and every finite additive constant fail the competitive inequality on some finite sequence. The obstructing metric may depend on \(r\); no single metric witnessing attainment of a supremum is required.
cards.answer_criterion:
Specify an unambiguous function \(g:\mathbb N_{\ge1}\to\mathbb R\) and give a complete, mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of
\[\forall k\ge1,\quad |g(k)-R_{\mathrm{det}}(k)|\le1/100.\]
Both sides of the error interval must be proved with the metric, rule, additive-constant and sequence quantifiers above. In particular, certified functions \(\ell,u\) satisfying \(\ell(k)\le R_{\mathrm{det}}(k)\le u(k)\) and \(u(k)-\ell(k)\le1/50\) for every positive integer \(k\) qualify through their midpoint. Exact determination also qualifies. An upper bound on an infimum must not silently be replaced by existence of a rule attaining its endpoint.

The absolute error must remain at most \(1/100\) as \(k\) grows; relative error \(k/100\), a constant-factor asymptotic estimate, or finitely many solved server counts does not meet it. A rule for a particular metric family or one named algorithm establishes only the corresponding restricted guarantee. A lower bound must rule out all allowed deterministic rules on its witnessing metric, rather than only one proposed algorithm or proof certificate. No unproved additional hypothesis is part of the target. There is no fixed formula grammar or polynomial evaluation requirement for \(g\), but repeating the defining infimum without determining its value is not an answer. The benchmark precision does not assert the classical exact equality \(R_{\mathrm{det}}(k)=k\) or endpoint attainment.
cards.why: The k-server problem measures the movement cost of responding to demand without knowing future requests. It includes paging and serves as a basic problem in competitive analysis, with the same number of resources available to the online rule and the offline optimum.

importance.reason: A foundational conjecture about online decision-making, with an optimal lower bound, one broadly applicable candidate algorithm, and a persistent gap on general metrics despite many resolved special cases.

progress.text: Manasse–McGeoch–Sleator establish the deterministic lower bound \(k\), the two-server case and the \((k+1)\)-point case.
Chrobak–Larmore obtain \(k\)-competitiveness on tree metrics.
Koutsoupias–Papadimitriou establish the general \(2k-1\) deterministic upper bound. The inspected author-hosted manuscript is dated 22 May 1995.
Huang–Zhang prove the three-server circle theorem; their canonical-certificate limitation has a separate restricted scope.
Bubeck–Coester–Rabani's preprint, published at STOC 2023, disproves the randomized logarithmic conjecture with a squared-logarithmic lower bound.
ISAAC publishes a \(2k-1\) lower bound for the time-optimal variant. Its maximum-movement objective differs from the classical sum-of-distances objective.
The potential-discovery benchmark retains the general deterministic conjecture and records the limits of its finite experiments.
ICALP publishes polynomial-time randomized algorithms and a separate advice-assisted consequence, retaining their additional randomness or input.

A new preprint claims that the work-function algorithm is \(k\)-competitive on every metric, with an explicit sequence-independent additive term. If correct, its Theorem 1.2 and the classical lower bound determine \(R_{\mathrm{det}}(k)=k\) exactly. The claim is not independently verified here.

context_blocks.text: On the uniform metric, where every two different points have distance one, the covered points represent pages currently in a cache. A request at an uncovered point incurs a page replacement. General metrics permit different movement costs between different demand locations. The comparison here always gives exactly \(k\) servers to both parties.

Manasse, McGeoch and Sleator prove the deterministic lower bound \(k\) and a matching algorithm for two servers. Their original paper also handles metrics with exactly \(k+1\) points. The lower-bound argument permits an offline starting-position change at a finite additive cost, so requiring the same initial placement does not remove the asymptotic obstruction. Together with the direct one-server case, the established initial values are \(R_{\mathrm{det}}(1)=1\) and \(R_{\mathrm{det}}(2)=2\).

Koutsoupias and Papadimitriou establish a universal \((2k-1)\)-competitive deterministic rule, the work-function algorithm. Their manuscript explicitly allows infinite metrics and repeated server locations. As the classical bound before the September 2026 claim, this yields \(k\le R_{\mathrm{det}}(k)\le2k-1\). The result concerns competitive movement cost; it does not supply a polynomial running-time guarantee, and the present target does not require one.

The classical conjecture predicts an actual \(k\)-competitive rule for every metric, which would imply \(R_{\mathrm{det}}(k)=k\). Knowing only the infimum value need not imply endpoint attainment. The new preprint claims the stronger actual competitiveness statement, so its stated theorem would also determine this card's function exactly, rather than merely approximate it within \(1/100\).

Chrobak and Larmore obtain the optimal factor \(k\) on tree metrics, whose distances are the lengths of unique connecting paths in an edge-weighted tree. This covers the line as a special case. It is a guarantee for that geometry rather than for every metric.

Huang and Zhang prove that the work-function algorithm is 3-competitive on a circle. For circumference \(L>0\), this metric is \([0,L)\) with \(d(x,y)=\min\{|x-y|,L-|x-y|\}\). Their separate computer-assisted limitation concerns a precisely defined family of potential certificates under a specified universal condition. It does not disprove 3-competitiveness of all online rules or exclude every proof for the work-function algorithm. The inspected text is the 2022 preprint; the journal article appeared in 2024.

Bubeck, Coester and Rabani give metrics on \(k+1\) points with randomized competitive ratio \(\Omega(\log^2 k)\). This refutes the randomized \(O(\log k)\) conjecture. Their ratio compares expected movement cost to the offline optimum with a sequence-independent additive constant. It neither refutes the deterministic factor \(k\) nor determines the deterministic infimum function.

Frei and coauthors' ISAAC 2025 result has a deterministic lower bound \(2k-1\) for a different objective: each request costs the maximum simultaneous server movement, rather than the sum of movements. That time objective can reward moving several servers at once, so the lazy distance model in this card is not an interchangeable formulation. The new lower bound is not a matching lower bound for \(R_{\mathrm{det}}\).

The April 2026 k-server-bench preprint evaluates candidate proof certificates on finite instances, including four-server circle instances. It explicitly distinguishes passing those finite checks from a proof covering all configurations and request sequences. Its reported experiments do not resolve the remaining general case.

Coester and Cosson's ICALP 2026 theorem gives a polynomial-time randomized \(O(\log n\log^2 k)\)-competitive algorithm on \(n\)-point metrics. Its reduction uses few random bits, but does not eliminate randomness. A separate deterministic consequence supplies advice that depends on the instance. Neither extra input nor randomization is present in this card, so these computational improvements do not determine its universal deterministic ratio.

Coester, Koutsoupias and Zbysiński's preprint submitted on 14 September 2026 states in Theorem 1.2 that, for every metric and every finite request sequence,
\[\operatorname{WFA}_{C_0}(\sigma)\le k\operatorname{OPT}_{C_0}(\sigma)+\sum_{1\le i<j\le k}d(s_i,s_j).\]
Here \(s_1,\ldots,s_k\) are the initial server locations. The additive term is finite and depends only on the initial placement, as permitted here. The paper explicitly handles coincident positions with distinct location labels and a pseudometric, and states the theorem for any metric space. Its lazy implementation agrees with the serving convention of this card. The matching claim changes the current status to uncertain pending verification; this review has not independently certified the whole proof.

cards.title: Optimal approximation ratio for unrelated-machine makespan
cards.formal:
For offline makespan minimization on unrelated parallel machines, determine the real number
\[\rho_{\mathrm{unrel}}=\inf\mathcal R,\qquad \mathcal R=\Bigl\{r\in[1,\infty):\exists A\ \exists c,k\in\mathbb N_{\ge1}\ \forall I\in\mathcal I,\ \begin{array}{l} A(I)\text{ halts in at most }c(L(I)+2)^k\text{ bit steps,}\\ A(I)\text{ outputs a feasible schedule }\sigma_I,\\ C_{\max}(\sigma_I)\le r\operatorname{OPT}(I)\end{array}\Bigr\}.\]
Here \(\mathcal I\) is the full class of finite rational processing-time matrices defined below, \(L(I)\) is the full binary input length, and \(A\) ranges over finite deterministic Turing-machine programs. Approximate \(\rho_{\mathrm{unrel}}\) within absolute error \(1/100\), with a complete Lean proof. No complexity hypothesis is included in the definition of this number.
cards.definitions:
An instance has integers \(m\ge1\), \(n\ge0\), machine set \([m]=\{1,\ldots,m\}\), job set \([n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}\), and a fully listed matrix \(p\in(\mathbb Q_{\ge0}\cup\{\infty\})^{m\times n}\). Set \([0]=\varnothing\). Each job has at least one finite entry. The symbol \(\infty\) forbids that machine–job assignment; it is not an arithmetic input with finite cost. Entries may differ arbitrarily between both machines and jobs. All processing times use the same time unit.

A feasible schedule is a function \(\sigma:[n]\to[m]\) such that \(p_{\sigma(j),j}<\infty\) for every job. Its load on machine \(i\) is \(\sum_{j:\sigma(j)=i}p_{ij}\), with an empty sum equal to zero. Define
\[C_{\max}(\sigma)=\max_{i\in[m]}\sum_{j:\sigma(j)=i}p_{ij},\qquad \operatorname{OPT}(I)=\min_{\sigma\text{ feasible}}C_{\max}(\sigma).\]
This minimum is finite and attained because the feasible set is finite and nonempty. Jobs are independent, available at time zero and indivisible. A machine executes its assigned jobs consecutively, one at a time, without preemption; their order does not affect the objective. There are no release dates, precedence constraints, setup times, communication costs or additional scheduling promises. For \(n=0\), the unique empty assignment has makespan zero.

Fix the following concrete binary encoding. For an integer \(u\ge0\), let \(b(u)\) be its binary expansion without leading zeros, with \(b(0)=0\), and put \(E(u)=1^{|b(u)|}0b(u)\), where juxtaposition denotes concatenation. A finite entry \(a/b\) is represented in lowest terms with \(a\ge0\), \(b\ge1\), as the tag bit \(0\) followed by \(E(a)E(b)\); \(\infty\) is the single tag bit \(1\). The input is \(E(m)E(n)\) followed by the \(mn\) entry encodings in row order. Its total bit length is \(L(I)\). The output is \(E(\sigma(1))\cdots E(\sigma(n))\) in job order; the empty schedule has an empty output. Equivalent ordinary encodings with polynomial-time translations give the same approximation-ratio infimum.

A program is a deterministic multitape Turing machine with no advice, random bits, optimization oracle or noncomputable constants. Input reading, work-tape computation and writing the full output count toward its bit running time. Arithmetic on the encoded rationals must be performed within that bound; an arbitrary-precision arithmetic operation is not a unit-cost primitive. Guarantees are required on every valid instance; invalid strings are outside \(\mathcal I\). The algorithm receives the complete matrix in advance, regardless of the category’s historical online-algorithms label.

For each fixed achieved ratio \(r\), the same program and constants \(c,k\) must work for all \(m,n,p\). They may depend on \(r\), but \(r\) is not additional advice or an input to the program. A different program for each input length is not allowed. The set \(\mathcal R\) concerns an absolute multiplicative guarantee on each instance, with no additive slack and no asymptotic or average-case exception. If \(\operatorname{OPT}(I)=0\), the output must also have makespan zero; no quotient by zero is used. All these conventions include empty instances.

The ratio is dimensionless. The established factor-two algorithm gives \(2\in\mathcal R\), so \(\mathcal R\) is nonempty and \(1\le\rho_{\mathrm{unrel}}\le2\). The infimum need not be attained: \(\rho_{\mathrm{unrel}}\le u\), for \(u\ge1\), means that for every \(\eta>0\) some program achieves a ratio at most \(u+\eta\), without requiring one program to attain \(u\) or one uniform procedure generating all these programs. A lower bound \(\ell\ge1\) means that no program achieves any fixed \(r\in[1,\ell)\) on every instance. The numerical tolerance applies to this infimum, not to the feasibility or objective guarantee of a proposed schedule.
cards.answer_criterion:

context_blocks.text: The original source question asks whether some fixed \(\varepsilon>0\), independent of the instance, permits a polynomial-time \((2-\varepsilon)\)-approximation. The user-authorized quantitative reformulation of 12 September 2026 instead asks for the full infimum of achievable ratios with absolute \(1/100\) benchmark precision. This broader quantity retains the original scheduling model. An approximation to that quantity can satisfy the benchmark while leaving the exact below-two threshold unanswered.

Unrelated machines need not have any common ranking by speed. A job can be fast on one machine and slow on another, while a second job has the reverse pattern. The makespan measures when all work has finished, so a schedule must balance indivisible loads rather than minimize their sum. Eligibility restrictions are included by forbidding selected assignments.

Lenstra, Shmoys and Tardos prove a polynomial-time factor-two approximation and show that every fixed ratio below \(3/2\) would imply \(\mathrm P=\mathrm{NP}\). Their hardness already uses a finite positive-integer subcase. Thus the unconditional bounds here are \(1\le\rho_{\mathrm{unrel}}\le2\); assuming \(\mathrm P\ne\mathrm{NP}\), they become \(3/2\le\rho_{\mathrm{unrel}}\le2\). If \(\mathrm P=\mathrm{NP}\), the finite rational scheduling optimization admits exact polynomial-time search and \(\rho_{\mathrm{unrel}}=1\). The hardness assumption cannot be omitted from the lower endpoint.

Shchepin and Vakhania achieve ratio \(2-1/m\) for \(m\) machines. The same formula is below two for each finite \(m\), but its supremum over all machine counts is two. It therefore gives no fixed universal improvement. Likewise, the polynomial approximation scheme of Lenstra, Shmoys and Tardos fixes the number of machines in advance; its running-time dependence is different from the single polynomial required for unbounded \(m\).

For a target time \(T\), the configuration linear program has one nonnegative variable \(y_{i,S}\) for each machine and each job subset \(S\) whose total processing time on that machine is at most \(T\). It requires \(\sum_S y_{i,S}=1\) for each machine and total fractional coverage one for every job. Verschae and Wiese show that the supremum of the integral optimum divided by the least feasible relaxation time is two, even when each job has at most two eligible machines with potentially different processing times. This is a statement about that relaxation, not an impossibility result for every polynomial-time algorithm.

Restricted assignment requires a job to have the same processing time on every eligible machine. The SODA 2024 work of Bamas and coauthors gives a \((7/4+\delta)\)-approximation for its two-size subcase. For general two-value matrices with entries in \(\{u,w,\infty\}\), it gives \(2-1/n^{\delta}\) for every fixed \(\delta>0\), where \(n\) is the number of jobs. The exponent is on \(n\), not on the whole ratio. These guarantees preserve their restrictions and instance-size dependence.

The same paper proves that a polynomial-time \((2-1/\alpha)\)-approximation for unrestricted makespan, for any fixed \(\alpha\ge2\), yields a polynomial-time \((\alpha+\delta)\)-approximation for general Santa Claus allocation for every fixed \(\delta>0\). In that problem indivisible items have nonnegative player-dependent values, and the objective is to maximize the minimum total value received by a player. The reduction preserves the algorithmic significance of any fixed improvement here; the paper’s converse equivalence is confined to the two-value variants.

Baba, Bampis and Mitropoulos’ June 2026 preprint supplies an additional predicted partial job assignment. Its guarantee improves when prediction errors relative to an optimum are small and retains a worst-case factor two. The stated running time has a factor \((mn)^K\), so the search budget \(K\) must remain fixed for its polynomial-time claim. The inspected model uses positive processing times; neither good predictions nor a growing budget are supplied by the classical target.

The \(3/2\) result in Proportionally Fair Makespan Approximation concerns a mechanism’s fairness guarantee using an optimal initial allocation. The June 2026 revision explicitly states that its transformation is polynomial time given an allocation, while obtaining an optimal initial allocation is NP-hard. Consequently this existence result does not establish \(\rho_{\mathrm{unrel}}\le3/2\). Fairness or incentive constraints and their separate existence bounds must be distinguished from computing a schedule with the complete polynomial-time guarantee in this card.

cards.title: Optimal approximation ratio for precedence-constrained makespan
cards.formal:
Determine the infimum approximation ratio achievable in deterministic polynomial time for nonpreemptive precedence-constrained makespan minimization on an input number of identical machines:
\[\rho_{\mathrm{prec}}=\inf\mathcal R,\]
where \(\mathcal R\) consists of all real \(r\ge1\) for which there exist one uniform deterministic algorithm \(A\) and constants \(K>0\), \(d\in\mathbb N\) such that for every valid instance \(I\) of bit length \(L\), the algorithm outputs a feasible schedule \(S_A(I)\) in at most \(K(L+1)^d\) steps and
\[C_{\max}(S_A(I))\le r\,\operatorname{OPT}(I).\]
The algorithm receives the entire instance before producing its schedule. The numerical answer must determine \(\rho_{\mathrm{prec}}\) to absolute error at most \(1/100\), with the proof requirement stated below. The infimum need not be attained by a single algorithm.
cards.definitions:
Instance. There are jobs \(J=\{1,\ldots,n\}\), with \(n\ge1\), positive integer processing times \(p_j\), a positive integer machine count \(m\), and a directed acyclic graph \(D=(J,F)\). An arc \((i,j)\in F\) requires job \(i\) to finish before job \(j\) starts. Every arc is a requirement; its transitive consequences also hold. There is no promise on the shape or depth of the directed acyclic graph, and the machine count is not fixed in advance. Every job may run on every machine, and every machine takes exactly \(p_j\) units of time to process job \(j\).

Schedule and feasibility. A schedule specifies for each job a machine \(a_j\in\{1,\ldots,m\}\) and a nonnegative start time \(s_j\). The job occupies precisely the half-open interval \([s_j,s_j+p_j)\) on that machine. Intervals on the same machine must be pairwise disjoint, and
\[s_j\ge s_i+p_i\quad\text{for every }(i,j)\in F.\]
Execution is continuous and uninterrupted: no job may be split, preempted or migrated. Finishing one job and starting another at the same instant is allowed. All jobs are available initially subject to their precedences. There are no release dates, deadlines, communication delays, setup times, machine eligibility restrictions or other resource constraints. The schedule uses the same number of unit-speed machines as the optimum; extra machines or speed are not allowed.

Objective. The makespan is the latest completion time,
\[C_{\max}(S)=\max_{j\in J}(s_j+p_j),\qquad
\operatorname{OPT}(I)=\min_{S\text{ feasible}}C_{\max}(S).\]
This is elapsed time from zero, not the sum or average of completion times. The optimum is positive and at most \(W=\sum_j p_j\). It is unchanged if start times are restricted to nonnegative integers: for any feasible schedule, retain its machine assignments and within-machine job orders and start each job as early as those orders and the precedences allow. Positive integer durations give an acyclic augmented order and integral earliest starts without increasing the makespan. Thus an optimal integer schedule exists. Having more than \(n\) machines offers no advantage, although the full encoded value of \(m\) is counted in the input length.

Encoding. For an integer \(i\ge0\), let \(\ell\) be the bit length of \(i+1\) and set \(U(i)=1^\ell0\operatorname{bin}(i+1)\), with exactly \(\ell\) bits in the last part. Encode an instance as \(U(n)U(m)U(p_1)\cdots U(p_n)\) followed by the \(n^2\) adjacency bits of \(D\) in row-major order. Valid inputs have the stated positivity and acyclicity properties. Encode an output schedule as the list \(U(a_1)U(s_1)\cdots U(a_n)U(s_n)\), with integer starts. These are explicit binary data, not succinct circuits or value oracles. All output bits and arithmetic costs count.

Algorithms and ratios. Computation uses a finite deterministic multitape Turing machine with a fixed finite alphabet, no advice, oracle or random bits. Polynomial time is measured in the full bit length \(L\), including all durations and the machine count, not in the numeric sum of processing times. Invalid encodings may be rejected. Each algorithm defining membership in \(\mathcal R\) must halt within its fixed polynomial bound on all valid inputs and always output a feasible schedule. Its factor \(r\) must hold simultaneously for every job count, machine count, positive duration vector and precedence graph. The program and polynomial may depend on the fixed factor \(r\), but cannot be chosen separately for each instance size. No accuracy parameter is supplied to that program in this definition.

The infimum. Graham’s polynomial-time list-scheduling guarantee implies \(2\in\mathcal R\), while feasibility forces all ratios to be at least one. Hence \(1\le\rho_{\mathrm{prec}}\le2\). The real infimum is defined even if no algorithm attains it. In particular, proving \(\rho_{\mathrm{prec}}\le u\) may establish algorithms with ratios arbitrarily close to \(u\) from above; it need not exhibit an algorithm with ratio exactly \(u\).
cards.answer_criterion:
Specify a real number \(a\) and give a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean that
\[|a-\rho_{\mathrm{prec}}|\le\frac1{100}.\]
Equivalently, supply certified bounds \(\ell\le\rho_{\mathrm{prec}}\le u\) with \(u-\ell\le1/50\), and use their midpoint. An exact value with a proof of equality also qualifies. The answer may be an unambiguous mathematical expression or a certified evaluation rule; a decimal expansion is not mandatory.

Both bound directions must concern the full stated algorithm class and every permitted instance. An upper bound at a possibly unattained infimum may be justified by polynomial-time algorithms with guarantee at most \(u+\varepsilon\) for every fixed \(\varepsilon>0\); do not assume attainment. A lower bound must exclude every uniform deterministic polynomial-time guarantee strictly below \(\ell\), not only a specific heuristic or relaxation. Known bounds, a one-sided improvement, numerical experiments, or an unevaluated restatement of the defining optimization do not suffice unless they certify the required error.

The target is unconditional. Any complexity assumption used for a lower bound must remain explicit; a conditional interval alone does not certify this unconditional numerical answer unless the additional assumption is also proved. The tolerance is benchmark acceptance and does not by itself settle whether the exact threshold equals two.
cards.why: Precedence constraints make scheduling depend on both how much work can run in parallel and which completions unlock later jobs. The optimal approximation ratio measures the algorithmic cost of coordinating these two effects. Pinning it down would settle a central scheduling approximation boundary whose basic factor-two guarantee dates to the 1960s.

cards.status_note: Checked on 16 September 2026. The inspected sources give the unconditional bound \(1\le\rho_{\mathrm{prec}}\le2\), with the classical lower bound \(4/3\) requiring P≠NP. Svensson’s factor-two hardness uses the specific Bansal–Khot variant; together with P≠NP it gives only a conditional value. No inspected result certifies the unconditional threshold to absolute 1/100. Fixed-machine quasipolynomial schemes, exact unit-job algorithms and July 2026 unique-machine hardness have different computational or input scope.
