context_blocks.text: The input is an entire task graph, not a stream of arrivals. A scheduler may inspect all durations and dependencies before choosing assignments and start times. It must place every job, keep each job uninterrupted, and minimize the last completion time. Changing to an online rule, preemption, machine-dependent durations or total completion time changes the problem.

Total work \(W=\sum_j p_j\) gives the lower bound \(W/m\) on any feasible makespan. The total duration \(D\) of a longest directed path in the precedence graph gives another lower bound, since that chain runs sequentially. The difficulty is that filling machines now and finishing jobs that unlock future work can call for different priorities.

Graham’s list scheduling starts available jobs according to a priority order when machines become free. A job is available after all its predecessors finish. The established bound is \(C_{\max}\le W/m+(1-1/m)D\le(2-1/m)\operatorname{OPT}\). Although this is below two for each finite \(m\), its supremum over input machine counts is two. It therefore gives the universal bound \(\rho_{\mathrm{prec}}\le2\), not a fixed improvement below two.

A priority example separates a poor list from algorithmic impossibility. For \(m\ge2\), take \(m(m-1)\) independent unit jobs and one independent job of length \(m\). Listing the long job last gives makespan \(2m-1\), whereas starting it immediately and distributing the units over the other machines gives makespan \(m\), which also equals the work lower bound. This shows tightness for that list order; it has no precedence edges and does not prove hardness for every algorithm.

Classical NP-hardness excludes every factor strictly below \(4/3\) unless \(\mathrm P=\mathrm{NP}\). Consequently \(\mathrm P\ne\mathrm{NP}\) implies \(4/3\le\rho_{\mathrm{prec}}\le2\). The word “unless” is essential: NP-hardness is not an unconditional proof that a polynomial-time algorithm cannot exist.

If \(\mathrm P=\mathrm{NP}\), feasible integer schedules of polynomial bit length can be found optimally in polynomial time, so \(\rho_{\mathrm{prec}}=1\). Here all optimum starts lie at most at total processing time, whose binary length is polynomial in the input length. Thus an unconditional lower bound strictly above one would in particular separate P from NP. This implication explains why the numerical target must keep its assumptions visible.

Svensson proves a transfer from the approximability of a different objective: total weighted completion time on a single machine with precedences. Hardness arbitrarily close to two for that problem transfers to makespan on identical parallel machines, even with unit jobs. The transferred loss tends to zero, but the two scheduling objectives and their approximation parameters are not identical.

His Corollary 1 uses the Bansal–Khot Unique Games variant in Appendix Hypothesis 1. It requires a satisfiable large bipartite portion in the completeness case and an extra expansion condition in the soundness case. The paper explicitly distinguishes it from ordinary UGC and does not establish their equivalence. Together with P different from NP, this hypothesis gives inapproximability for every fixed factor below two and hence the conditional value two.

The infimum asks which ratios can be approached by finite uniform algorithms. It need not have a minimizing algorithm: \(\rho_{\mathrm{prec}}=1\), for example, would not by its definition alone assert an exact polynomial-time optimizer. Similarly, an upper bound on the infimum can be witnessed by algorithms approaching that bound. The prescribed \(1/100\) accuracy concerns the real threshold, not the approximation error of one submitted scheduling algorithm.

For unit jobs on a fixed number of machines, approximation schemes with quasipolynomial running time represent substantial progress. Das and Wiese give a simpler such scheme at ESA 2022, following earlier results. Its runtime is still not polynomial in the sense required here, and the fixed-machine, unit-duration promises do not cover all inputs in this card.

Nederlof, Swennenhuis and Węgrzycki give an exact unit-job algorithm running in \((1+n/m)^{O(\sqrt{nm})}\) time; this is subexponential when \(m=o(n)\). They also improve the exponential base in the regime \(m=\Theta(n)\). The work appeared at SODA 2025 and online in TALG in January 2026. Faster exact exponential-time algorithms do not supply a polynomial-time universal approximation ratio.

The July 2026 unique-machine preprint proves NP-hardness of every constant approximation factor for unit jobs when each job has one predetermined eligible machine. This removes assignment flexibility and is an additional input restriction on allowable schedules, absent from the present model. Its stronger hardness therefore does not contradict the factor-two algorithm for freely assignable identical machines.

The checked evidence does not locate the unconditional threshold within an interval of width \(1/50\). The known factor-two upper bound, the classical conditional lower bound and the stronger hypothesis-based value address different logical conclusions. A small improvement below two could be a major advance while still leaving the numerical acceptance target unresolved.

cards.title: Constant additive error for one-dimensional bin packing
cards.formal: Do a universal integer \(C\ge 0\) and a randomized polynomial-time algorithm exist that pack every explicitly listed one-dimensional bin-packing instance into at most OPT+C unit-capacity bins with probability at least \(2/3\)?
cards.definitions: The input is a list of \(n\ge 1\) rational item sizes \(s_{1},\ldots ,s_{n}\in\)(0,1], each encoded as a binary numerator and positive binary denominator; L is the total encoding length. A feasible packing is a map \(b:[n]\to [k]\) with \(\sum_{i:b(i)=j}s_{i}\le 1\) for every bin j. OPT is the minimum feasible integer k. The algorithm is uniform and classical, has access to the entire input before assigning items, and must output an explicit feasible packing. For absolute constants K,d, every execution must take at most \(KL^{d}\) bit operations. Its output is always feasible, and on each fixed input it uses at most OPT+C bins with probability at least \(2/3\) over its private random bits. C,K,d are independent of n, the number of distinct sizes, OPT and coefficient precision. No capacity augmentation, splitting of items, cardinality constraint or promise on the input distribution is allowed. Repeated items are explicitly listed rather than represented by binary multiplicities. Randomization is expressly allowed; a deterministic algorithm would also resolve the question. In this statement, “explicitly given/encoded/listed” means the entire finite list, table or syntax tree described above is part of the input or output, with its full encoding counted; it does not mean a circuit, oracle or program generating a larger object.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove the proposition in the problem statement or prove its logical negation, using exactly the definitions, hypotheses and quantifier order stated here. The proof must cover the complete target.
cards.why: A basic boundary between asymptotic approximation and almost exact combinatorial optimization: can efficient packing lose only a fixed number of bins on every instance?

importance.reason: A longstanding central problem in approximation algorithms, with connections to configuration LPs, discrepancy and the computational effect of input encoding.

cards.status_note: Reviewed through 11 September 2026. No universal constant-additive polynomial-time algorithm or general impossibility result was found in the checked primary sources. context_blocks.text: The objective is to minimize the number of identical containers needed to hold indivisible items. Each bin has a single numerical capacity constraint, so the model contains no geometric placement issue. Nevertheless, many different combinations of small and large items can fit exactly or almost exactly, and choices that look locally efficient can leave unusable capacity elsewhere. The inherited invited survey explicitly asks for an OPT+\(O(1)\) guarantee.

Additive and multiplicative errors behave differently as the optimum grows. A one-percent excess can mean thousands of unnecessary bins on a large instance; an additive constant remains fixed. Conversely, this card allows any universal constant, even a very large one. It does not ask for an additive-one algorithm or for exact optimization on small instances.

The elementary hardness example is distinguishing instances needing two bins from those needing three, through Partition. This rules out exact polynomial optimization under the usual complexity assumptions, but it does not settle constant additive approximation. With allowance \(C=1, a\) valid three-bin answer is permitted in both cases. A stronger hardness argument would need a gap that survives the particular additive allowance.

Asymptotic approximation schemes achieve a ratio approaching one, with additional losses depending on their accuracy parameter. This does not automatically give OPT+C. Choosing \(\varepsilon\) on the order of 1/OPT makes \(\varepsilon \cdot\)OPT small, but the additive term and the running time may worsen as \(\varepsilon\) shrinks. The dependence on every parameter must be controlled simultaneously; the existence of a scheme alone does not establish the desired fixed loss.

Several published bounds use the Gilmore–Gomory configuration LP. A configuration specifies a multiset of item types that fits in one bin. The LP permits fractional numbers of such bins while covering all required items. Its optimum \(\operatorname{OPT}_{f}\) is a lower bound on the integral optimum. Karmarkar–Karp obtain a polynomial-time packing with \(O(\log ^{2} \operatorname{OPT})\) additive loss by combining approximate LP optimization with repeated rounding.

Hoberg–Rothvoss improve the guarantee to \(\operatorname{OPT}_{f}+O(\log  \operatorname{OPT}_{f})\), and hence OPT+\(O(\log  \operatorname{OPT})\). Their Theorem 2 gives randomized expected polynomial time in the number of explicitly represented items, with the usual accounting for encoded numerical data. Packing first into intermediate containers, and then into bins, improves how rounding errors accumulate. This is the logarithmic-additive general algorithmic benchmark found in the checked literature.

A constant additive LP integrality gap is a related mathematical conjecture, but it is not identical to this card. An efficiently constructible packing within a constant of \(\operatorname{OPT}_{f}\) would suffice. A nonconstructive proof of a small gap would still need an algorithmic rounding step. Conversely, an unbounded gap for this LP would not rule out a different algorithm whose guarantee is measured against the true integral optimum.

Discrepancy results explain why several familiar approaches encounter barriers. Eisenbrand–Pálvölgyi–Rothvoß connect a restricted bin-packing relaxation to discrepancy of three permutations. Their revised paper also proves limitations for a class of algorithms based on rounding item sizes upward. Those limitations concern specified techniques, rather than all algorithms for the original packing problem.

Newman–Nikolov disprove the conjecture that three permutations always have constant discrepancy, constructing examples requiring \(\Omega (\log  n)\). This eliminates one proposed route to a constant additive bound. It does not itself provide numerical item sizes with a growing bin-packing integrality gap, and it does not show that every polynomial-time packing algorithm must lose logarithmically many bins.

Recent work also settles nearby structural questions. Jansen–Pirotton–Tutas’s ESA 2025 paper constructs bin-packing instances requiring exponentially many distinct configurations as a function of the number of item types. Its discussion records an OPT+1 algorithm whose runtime depends heavily on that parameter. Exponential support in the number of types does not contradict a polynomial algorithm in an explicit list of all items, and a parameter-dependent additive-one algorithm is not uniformly polynomial as the number of types grows.

The ICALP 2026 work of Jansen–Ohnesorge–Pirotton proves a tight ETH-based lower bound for the dependence on the number of types in a high-multiplicity exact algorithmic regime. Binary multiplicities can encode far more items than the input length. Both the compressed input model and exact optimization differ from the constant-additive, explicitly listed target here. The result should therefore not be reported as a negative answer to this question.

This problem isolates how close efficient approximation can come to an integral packing optimum. A constant-additive algorithm would show that all unavoidable combinatorial inefficiency can be confined to a bounded number of extra bins, regardless of instance size. A general impossibility theorem would establish a meaningful approximation barrier beyond the standard two-versus-three-bin hardness example.

cards.title: Optimal competitive ratio for convex body chasing
cards.formal:
Determine, up to universal constant factors as a function of \(d\), the optimal deterministic competitive ratio \(\mathcal C(d)\) for general convex body chasing in Euclidean space \(\mathbb R^d\). The domain is every integer \(d\ge1\).

An online strategy starts at \(x_0=0\), sees a nonempty compact convex set \(K_t\subseteq\mathbb R^d\) at round \(t\), and must immediately choose \(x_t\in K_t\) using only \(K_1,\ldots,K_t\). Its cost on a finite request sequence is \(\sum_{t=1}^{T}\|x_t-x_{t-1}\|_2\). Let
\[\operatorname{OPT}(K_1,\ldots,K_T)=\min_{y_t\in K_t,\ y_0=0}\sum_{t=1}^{T}\|y_t-y_{t-1}\|_2\]
and define
\[\mathcal C(d)=\inf\left\{c\ge1:\ \exists A\ \forall T\ge1\ \forall K_1,\ldots,K_T,\quad\operatorname{cost}_A(K_1,\ldots,K_T)\le c\,\operatorname{OPT}(K_1,\ldots,K_T)\right\}.\]
The strategy may depend on \(d\), but must serve all horizons and request sequences in that dimension. The target is the asymptotic order of this dimension-dependent ratio, resolving the source's gap between order \(\sqrt d\) and order \(d\).
cards.why: Convex body chasing isolates the movement cost of maintaining feasibility when constraints arrive without advance notice. The optimal dependence on dimension measures how much geometric complexity alone can penalize online decisions, independently of computational efficiency. Matching bounds would resolve a central quantitative gap between what convexity permits offline and what an online strategy can guarantee.

sentences: Convex body chasing requires an online player to move into each newly revealed convex set.
The player pays Euclidean movement while an offline comparator knows all future requests.
This question asks for the optimal deterministic competitive ratio as dimension grows, up to universal constant factors.
The strategy must work for arbitrary finite request sequences without knowing the horizon.
The checked sources leave a gap between square-root and linear dimension dependence for general requests, with stronger results only in restricted settings.

cards.definitions:
The Euclidean norm is \(\|v\|_2=(\sum_{j=1}^{d}v_j^2)^{1/2}\). A request set is nonempty, compact and convex: it is closed and bounded, and contains \((1-\lambda)u+\lambda v\) whenever \(u,v\) lie in it and \(0\le\lambda\le1\). Lower-dimensional sets, including points and faces of polytopes, are allowed. There is no common diameter bound, containment relation or promise that consecutive requests intersect. In particular, the sequence need not be nested.

A deterministic online strategy is a sequence of maps \(A_t\), one for every positive integer \(t\), taking every length-\(t\) request history to a point in its final set. These maps jointly specify one causal strategy: two request sequences with the same prefix have the same choices on that prefix, irrespective of their eventual lengths or later requests. Its own previous locations are determined by that history. The full current set is available before choosing the current point; no future set, horizon, forecast, advice or random choice is supplied.

This is the information-theoretic model of competitive analysis used in the sources. Strategies are mathematical maps on convex sets, with unrestricted computation; a finite input encoding, polynomial-time evaluator or bounded number of membership queries is not an extra requirement. An answer must specify its strategy well enough to prove feasibility and cost, but the benchmark measures movement, not computational time.

The offline comparator starts at the same origin, knows the whole finite sequence, and may choose a different feasible point at every round. Compactness makes its displayed minimum attainable. There is no required return to the origin and no additional service cost or cost for reading a request. Competitiveness is a purely multiplicative guarantee on every finite sequence, with no additive constant. If OPT is zero, the online strategy must also incur zero cost; the definition uses an inequality to avoid division by zero. Requests may be selected adversarially after previous moves, since the guarantee covers every finite request history for a deterministic strategy.

The infimum is over all qualifying ratios and strategies in each dimension; it need not be attained. Its value is finite by the known dimension-dependent upper bound. Determination up to universal factors means providing a noncircular positive function \(h\) on the positive integers and constants \(a,b>0\), independent of dimension, such that \(a h(d)\le\mathcal C(d)\le b h(d)\) for every \(d\ge1\). Equivalent eventually valid asymptotic bounds may be extended over the finitely many smaller dimensions by adjusting constants. The question does not require an exact ratio or an additive \(1/100\) estimate of that ratio.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct Lean-checked determination of the asymptotic growth of \(\mathcal C(d)\), with matching upper and lower bounds up to universal constant factors. The upper bound must cover arbitrary finite, possibly non-nested request sequences with one horizon-independent deterministic strategy in each dimension. The lower bound must apply to every permitted strategy. A nonattained infimum may be handled by arbitrarily approaching bounds. Merely renaming the optimization defining \(\mathcal C\), proving a bound for nested requests, allowing the ratio to grow with the horizon, or establishing a lower bound in another norm does not meet the criterion.

context_blocks.text: The 2025 source lists an \(O(d)\) upper bound for general convex body chasing and an \(\Omega(\sqrt d)\) lower bound in Euclidean space. It separately lists the stronger upper bound for nested requests; the saved card concerns the unrestricted sequence problem.

Sellke proves a competitive ratio of \(d\) for convex body chasing in an arbitrary \(d\)-dimensional normed space. That dependence is tight for the maximum-coordinate norm, but the corresponding general Euclidean lower bound is only of order \(\sqrt d\). A worst-case norm cannot be substituted for the fixed Euclidean norm here.

For Euclidean requests of horizon \(T\), Sellke also proves an \(O(\sqrt{d\log T})\) guarantee. Combining it with the dimension-only bound helps at shorter horizons, but it does not yield a sublinear-in-d bound uniformly over arbitrary \(T\).

The nested problem adds \(K_{t+1}\subseteq K_t\). Its \(O(\sqrt{d\log d})\) Euclidean upper bound is nearly the square-root lower bound, but that extra containment hypothesis is not available in this card. Recent applications to shrinking feasible regions therefore do not by themselves close the general chasing gap.

cards.title: Minimax dimension dependence in bandit convex optimization
cards.formal: Determine, up to universal constant factors jointly in dimension d and horizon T, the information-theoretic minimax expected regret \(R*(d,T)\) for one-point adversarial bandit convex optimization with losses in \([0,1]\). Use the oblivious-adversary, exact-feedback model and worst-case normalized convex body defined below; logarithmic dependence is part of the requested rate.
cards.why: Determines the price of limited feedback in a basic model of online convex optimization.
cards.status_note: The March 2026 primary book explicitly lists the minimax dimension dependence as open. Searches through 11 September 2026 found no established matching rate for the specified unrestricted one-point model. Recent smooth-loss and two-point results do not settle it.
cards.review_note: Recovered the oblivious exact-observation model from the same author’s 2020 primary formulation; the imported proposal mentioned only one function value per round. Fixed loss range, affine domain normalization, expected minimax quantifiers and a fixed hindsight comparator. Kept the full joint rate question rather than choosing a conjectured exponent, and separated the book’s noisy and stochastic variants.

cards.definitions: Let \(d,T\ge 1\) be integers and \(B_{2}^{d}=\{x\in R^{d}:\sum_{i} x_{i}^{2}\le 1\}\). A permitted constraint set K is a compact convex subset of \(R^{d}\) satisfying \(B_{2}^{d}\subseteq K\subseteq dB_{2}^{d}\); the learner knows K,d,T in advance. This is an affine normalization of general full-dimensional convex bodies, not a smoothness condition on losses. Write \(F(K)\) for the Borel-measurable convex functions \(f:K\to [0,1]\), where convexity means \(f(\lambda x+(1- \lambda )y)\le \lambda f(x)+(1- \lambda )f(y)\) for \(x,y\in K\) and \(\lambda \in [0,1]\). No common Lipschitz, differentiability, strong-convexity or curvature bound is imposed. Before any play, an oblivious adversary fixes \(f_{1},\ldots ,f_{T}\in F(K)\), possibly using knowledge of the learner’s policy but not its realized random choices. At round t the learner chooses \(X_{t}\in K\), incurs \(f_{t}(X_{t})\), and observes exactly that one real value. It receives no noise, gradient, second evaluation, whole function or future loss. A policy is a sequence of Borel probability kernels assigning a distribution on K to each observed history \((X_{1},f_{1}(X_{1}),\ldots ,X_{t- 1},f_{t- 1}(X_{t- 1}))\). This permits arbitrary randomized decision rules; computation, representation and sampling time are unrestricted, so the target is statistical rather than polynomial-time optimization. For fixed K, define \(R_{K}(T)=\inf _{\pi} \sup _{f_{1},\ldots ,f_{T}} E_{\pi}[\sum_{t} f_{t}(X_{t})- \inf _{x\in K}\sum_{t} f_{t}(x)]\), with the supremum over fixed legal loss sequences and expectation only over policy randomness. Finally \(R*(d,T)=\sup _{K} R_{K}(T)\), over the normalized bodies above. The comparator is one fixed point for all rounds, chosen in hindsight. Using an infimum avoids assuming a minimizer on the boundary. Joint constant-factor precision means a stated function \(g(d,T)\) and universal constants \(a,b>0\) with a \(g(d,T)\le R*(d,T)\le b g(d,T)\) for all \(d,T\ge 1\). Constants cannot depend on the shape of K. The Borel convention ensures the displayed expectations are defined.
cards.answer_criterion: Identify a joint rate \(g(d,T)\) and prove upper and lower bounds within universal constant factors for the defined minimax value. The upper bound must hold for every allowed convex body and loss sequence with some admissible policy for that known body; the matching lower bound must hold against every policy on suitable allowed instances. Bounds for a fixed dimension with unspecified dimension-dependent constants, or bounds that hide an unresolved polynomial or logarithmic factor, do not give the full requested rate. Efficient implementation is not an additional acceptance condition.

context_blocks.title: One value does not reveal a direction
context_blocks.text: On the interval \([- 1,1]\), the convex losses \(f(x)=(1+x)/2\) and \(h(x)=(1- x)/2\) both equal \(1/2\) at \(x=0\), but their minimizing endpoints are opposite. Observing one loss value therefore need not reveal which way to move. Across rounds the loss may also change, so a value observed yesterday is not a second evaluation of today’s function.

context_blocks.title: The benchmark is one fixed decision in hindsight
context_blocks.text: Regret compares accumulated loss with the best single point that could have been used throughout the sequence. It does not compare with a different minimizer on every round. This distinction makes learning possible even when the environment changes. Randomization protects the learner against a sequence chosen before its random actions, while the adversary may still choose that sequence with knowledge of the policy.

context_blocks.title: Dimension remains a major gap
context_blocks.text: Lattimore’s 2020 theorem gives an upper bound of order \(d^{5/2}\sqrt{T}\), apart from a logarithmic factor, for exact one-point feedback. In the regime where T is sufficiently large relative to d, known lower bounds grow as \(d\sqrt{T}\). The March 2026 book explicitly retains the dimension gap. For smaller horizons, regret is always at most T because each loss lies in \([0,1]\); an asymptotic expression must respect this saturation.

context_blocks.title: Normalization and computational cost
context_blocks.text: Bounded loss values fix the scale of regret. Restricting K to a rounded affine position prevents an arbitrary choice of coordinates from introducing an extra geometric parameter. This still permits general convex losses and many domain shapes. The information-theoretic question asks what is attainable by decision rules with no computation limit. A practical algorithm can be a major advance while still having a worse dimension dependence than the best existence bound.

context_blocks.title: Which newer results change the assumptions
context_blocks.text: The July 2026 revision of Ye’s paper uses two evaluations per loss and assumes strong convexity, with carefully stated comparator guarantees. Cheng, Hatano and Takimoto’s June 2026 result allows globally budgeted perturbations but assumes a smooth convex underlying loss even when the perturbations vanish. These assumptions differ from arbitrary bounded convex functions with one exact observation. Neither establishes the minimax rate requested here.

cards.title: Matroid secretary conjecture
cards.formal:
Does there exist a finite universal real constant \(C\ge1\) such that, for every finite matroid \(M=(E,\mathcal I)\), there is a randomized online selection strategy \(\mathcal A_M\) satisfying
\[\forall w:E\to\mathbb R_{\ge0},\qquad
\mathbb E_{\pi,U}\!\left[\sum_{e\in S_{\mathcal A_M}(w,\pi,U)}w(e)\right]
\ge\frac1C\max_{I\in\mathcal I}\sum_{e\in I}w(e)?\]
The element weights are fixed adversarially before a uniformly random arrival permutation \(\pi\) and the strategy's independent randomness \(U\) are chosen. Each acceptance decision is irrevocable and must preserve independence. The same \(C\) must work for all matroids and all weights.
cards.definitions:
A finite matroid consists of a finite ground set \(E\) and a nonempty family \(\mathcal I\subseteq2^E\) of independent sets with two properties. First, \(B\subseteq A\in\mathcal I\) implies \(B\in\mathcal I\). Second, if \(A,B\in\mathcal I\) and \(|A|<|B|\), some \(e\in B\setminus A\) satisfies \(A\cup\{e\}\in\mathcal I\). In particular, \(\varnothing\in\mathcal I\). Loops, zero weights, ties and the empty ground set are allowed. The matroid rank is \(\max_{I\in\mathcal I}|I|\).

The strategy knows \(E\) and \(\mathcal I\) in advance, including all element identities and \(n=|E|\), but has no information about the weights of unarrived elements. At step \(t\), it sees the identity \(\pi(t)\) and its finite real weight \(w(\pi(t))\). Before the next arrival, it chooses to accept or reject that element. Its decision may use only the known matroid, the revealed prefix, its previous decisions and its random seed. An accepted element cannot subsequently be discarded, and a rejected element cannot subsequently be accepted. Every accepted prefix must belong to \(\mathcal I\), for every input, arrival order and seed. The notation \(S_{\mathcal A_M}(w,\pi,U)\) denotes the final accepted set.

A randomized strategy is a measurable nonanticipating decision rule; one may model its private randomness by \(U\) uniform on \([0,1]\), independent of \(\pi\). The permutation is uniform among the \(n!\) permutations of \(E\) and independent of the fixed weight assignment. Expectations include these two sources of randomness. For every fixed assignment the optimum is finite, so the expected reward is well-defined and finite. If all feasible weights are zero, the inequality still applies with a zero right-hand side.

The quantifier order is \(\exists C\;\forall M\;\exists\mathcal A_M\;\forall w\). A strategy cannot be selected after seeing the weight assignment. The guarantee has no additive loss, no dependence of \(C\) on size or rank, and no high-probability requirement beyond the stated expectation. There is no restriction on computation, preprocessing or independence queries. This is the competitive-existence question in the known-matroid model, with arbitrary nonnegative real weights; no finite encoding or polynomial running time is appended.

context_blocks.text: The classical secretary task chooses one item whose unknown value is revealed on arrival. Matroids extend the feasibility rule to collections of items. For example, a uniform matroid permits any set up to a prescribed size, while a graphic matroid permits sets of edges containing no cycle. The offline optimum knows every weight; the online strategy sees only a random prefix at each decision.

Random arrival order and random assignment of weights are distinct sources of information. In the random-assignment variant, a multiset of weights is distributed uniformly among ground-set elements. Santiago, Sergeev and Zenklusen obtain a constant guarantee for that variant even without advance knowledge of the matroid. Their May 2023 preprint explicitly leaves the adversarial-assignment conjecture open. Its theorem cannot by itself justify the general claim here.

Before the new September claim, the cited general guarantee was \(O(\log\log r)\), with the small-rank cases treated separately, where \(r\) is the matroid rank. A growing rank-dependent factor differs from a universal constant, even though many particular matroid classes already admit constant guarantees.

Dughmi proves that a competitive secretary algorithm implies random-order contention resolution for arbitrarily correlated active sets, losing only the same multiplicative factor relative to the best offline guarantee. The later equivalence theorem establishes the converse at the level of universal constants. This connection concerns a known probability distribution and an information-theoretic guarantee; it does not require the distribution to be a product law.

Singla's preprint submitted on 13 September 2026 states in Theorem 3.1 that each element of a canonical offline optimum is accepted with probability at least \(1/4\), while the selected set is always independent. This would imply the displayed target with \(C=4\). The stated theorem allows fixed nonnegative values and needs only the ground-set size and independence queries on already arrived elements. Those assumptions are compatible with, and more restrictive than, this card's advance matroid knowledge.

The fresh preprint is recorded as a matching solution claim, pending independent verification. Its full PDF and theorem scope were inspected, but this review does not certify the complete proof. Section 4 separately announces extensions and defers their detailed proofs; those announcements are not treated as already established results. The paper also distinguishes the original constant-factor conjecture from the stronger proposed factor \(e\), where \(e\) is the base of the natural logarithm.

cards.why: This is a central question about the power of random arrival order in online selection under general independence constraints. A universal bound would apply across all matroids and is equivalent, through established reductions, to a general random-order contention-resolution guarantee.
cards.answer_criterion: Supply a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of the displayed constant-competitiveness proposition, or of its full logical negation. A positive proof must give a finite universal constant and admissible strategies with the expected guarantee for every matroid and weight assignment. A negative proof must show that for every proposed finite constant some matroid defeats every admissible strategy on some fixed nonnegative weight assignment. A result for a restricted matroid family, randomly assigned weights, or a constant depending on rank does not settle this target. A newly posted proof claim is not itself a Lean-checked answer.

A growing rank-dependent factor differs from a universal constant, even though many particular matroid classes already admit constant guarantees.

Dughmi proves that a competitive secretary algorithm implies random-order contention resolution for arbitrarily correlated active sets, losing only the same multiplicative factor relative to the best offline guarantee. The later equivalence theorem establishes the converse at the level of universal constants. This connection concerns a known probability distribution and an information-theoretic guarantee; it does not require the distribution to be a product law.

Singla's preprint submitted on 13 September 2026 states in Theorem 3.1 that each element of a canonical offline optimum is accepted with probability at least \(1/4\), while the selected set is always independent. This would imply the displayed target with \(C=4\). The stated theorem allows fixed nonnegative values and needs only the ground-set size and independence queries on already arrived elements. Those assumptions are compatible with, and more restrictive than, this card's advance matroid knowledge.

The fresh preprint is recorded as a matching solution claim, pending independent verification. Its full PDF and theorem scope were inspected, but this review does not certify the complete proof. Section 4 separately announces extensions and defers their detailed proofs; those announcements are not treated as already established results. The paper also distinguishes the original constant-factor conjecture from the stronger proposed factor \(e\), where \(e\) is the base of the natural logarithm.

cards.title: Randomized competitiveness of k-server
cards.formal:
Determine the growth, up to universal multiplicative constants, of the optimal randomized competitive ratio for \(k\)-server on all finite metrics against an oblivious adversary. For each integer \(k\ge2\), define
\[R_{\mathrm{rand}}(k)=\inf\mathcal R_k,\]
where \(\mathcal R_k\) is the set of real \(r\ge1\) such that
\[\forall (X,d)\in\mathcal M_k\;\forall C_0\in X^k\;\exists\mathcal A\;\exists\beta\in\mathbb R_{\ge0}\;\forall\sigma\in X^{<\omega},\qquad
\mathbb E_U[\operatorname{cost}_{\mathcal A}(\sigma;C_0,U)]
\le r\operatorname{OPT}(\sigma;C_0)+\beta.\]
Here \(\mathcal M_k\) consists of all finite metric spaces with at least \(k+1\) points, and \(\mathcal A\) is an online randomized strategy as defined below. Give an unambiguous positive function \(h\) on the integers \(k\ge2\) and fixed real constants \(0<a\le b<\infty\) such that
\[a h(k)\le R_{\mathrm{rand}}(k)\le b h(k)\qquad\text{for all integers }k\ge2.\]
The requested precision is matching asymptotic bounds, including any logarithmic dependence.
cards.definitions:
A metric on a finite set \(X\) is a finite-valued function \(d:X\times X\to\mathbb R_{\ge0}\) with \(d(x,y)=0\) exactly when \(x=y\), symmetry and the triangle inequality. The number \(n=|X|\) is unbounded relative to \(k\). The strategy knows the full metric and initial configuration before any request. Distances may be arbitrary real numbers: no rational encoding, finite-precision cost or computability restriction is imposed on this information-theoretic question.

Exactly \(k\) identical servers serve the requests. For bookkeeping write a configuration as a tuple \((x_1,\ldots,x_k)\in X^k\); repeated locations are allowed and the labels confer no different costs. A finite sequence \(\sigma=(q_1,\ldots,q_T)\) is revealed one request at a time. If a server already occupies \(q_t\), all servers stay and this step costs zero. Otherwise the strategy chooses one server, moves it from its current position \(x_i\) to \(q_t\), and pays \(d(x_i,q_t)\). All other servers stay. The total cost is the sum over the \(T\) steps. This lazy convention has the same attainable competitive guarantees as the ordinary sum-of-movement-distances model. It is not a simultaneous maximum-movement objective.

An online strategy is a measurable rule whose move depends on the known metric, \(k,C_0\), the revealed request prefix, its past choices and its private randomness. One may model the randomness by a uniform seed \(U\in[0,1]\). It must make a legal move for every prefix and seed, and serve the current request before observing the next. No future request, request horizon, prediction or advice depending on the sequence is supplied. There is no time, space, number-of-random-bits or finite-program bound. The same seed law and nonanticipating rule serve all finite sequences on the chosen instance.

The adversary is oblivious: each sequence \(\sigma\) in the guarantee is fixed independently of \(U\). It may know the strategy and its distribution, but may not choose the next request from observed random moves. Expectation is over \(U\), for that fixed sequence. Every finite-sequence cost is bounded by \(T\) times the finite metric diameter, so the expectation is finite. The offline comparator starts at the identical tuple \(C_0\), knows all of \(\sigma\), and minimizes total movement under the same serving convention. This minimum exists because there are finitely many possible server choices for a finite sequence. The empty sequence has online and offline cost zero.

For fixed \(k,r\), the strategy and finite additive term \(\beta\) may depend on the metric and initial tuple, but neither may depend on the future sequence or its length. The ratio \(r\), and ultimately the comparison constants \(a,b\), cannot depend on \(n\), distances or initial placement. The same chosen strategy and \(\beta\) must satisfy the inequality for all lengths and contents. Classical deterministic bounds imply \(1\le R_{\mathrm{rand}}(k)\le2k-1\), so the infimum is a finite dimensionless number. No strategy attaining the infimum is presumed to exist.

An upper bound on this infimum need not give an algorithm attaining its endpoint: for every positive slack, strategies with ratios at most the proposed upper bound plus that slack suffice on every metric and initial placement. A lower bound must exclude every smaller universal ratio; for such a smaller ratio some metric and initial placement must defeat every eligible strategy and every fixed additive constant on a sequence independent of the realized seed. The unknown function \(h\) must specify the asymptotic scale, rather than merely rename the defining infimum.

context_blocks.text: On the uniform metric, all distances between distinct points equal one, and the server positions represent pages held in a cache. General metrics give different costs for replacing one location by another. Randomization can protect an online strategy from a fixed request sequence, but the comparator sees the whole sequence and has the same number of servers.

The old randomized conjecture proposed an \(O(\log k)\) ratio on every metric. Bubeck, Coester and Rabani refute it with \((k+1)\)-point metrics requiring \(\Omega(\log^2 k)\) randomized competitiveness. Their definition permits an arbitrary fixed additive constant and compares expected online cost to offline cost, matching the relevant convention here. The obstruction still leaves possible larger polylogarithmic ratios.

The \((k+1)\)-point special case has order \(\Theta(\log^2 k)\) through its connection with metrical service and task systems. This does not determine the card's function, which takes the worst case over every finite number of metric points. Allowing \(n\) much larger than \(k\) is an essential part of the remaining target.

Coester and Cosson's ICALP 2026 paper gives a polynomial-time randomized \(O(\log^2 k)\)-competitive algorithm on hierarchically separated trees. These are a structured class of leaf metrics of weighted rooted trees whose edge scales decrease geometrically by a fixed factor along root-to-leaf paths. Theorem 1 also bounds the amount of randomness independently of request-sequence length. The geometry restriction matters to the competitive guarantee.

Their Corollary 2 gives \(O(\log n\log^2 k)\) competitiveness on arbitrary \(n\)-point metrics. This is a computational improvement, but the factor \(\log n\) cannot be hidden in a universal function of \(k\). The same paper explicitly states that even an \(o(k)\) ratio on arbitrary metrics remains open. Its separate advice-assisted consequence has additional future-dependent information and is not the oblivious randomized model here.

The classical deterministic \(2k-1\) guarantee is also a randomized upper bound, because a randomized strategy may ignore its coins. Together with the squared-logarithmic lower bound, it leaves a gap between \(\Omega(\log^2 k)\) and \(O(k)\). The quantitative question is to determine the entire asymptotic scale within this gap, not just to improve one endpoint.

The September 2026 preprint by Coester, Koutsoupias and Zbysiński claims that the deterministic work-function algorithm attains ratio \(k\) on every metric. If correct, it also gives \(R_{\mathrm{rand}}(k)\le k\); it does not supply a randomized lower bound of \(k\), or improve the order \(O(k)\). Its theorem therefore does not settle this card's matching-asymptotics target. The new proof has not been independently certified in this review.

cards.answer_criterion: Provide a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of both displayed inequalities for some unambiguous \(h\) and universal \(a,b\). This is the retained constant-factor asymptotic-complexity target, not an additive numerical approximation requirement. Upper bounds must cover all finite metrics, all initial placements and all obliviously chosen finite request sequences with the permitted additive term. Lower bounds must cover every eligible randomized strategy on suitable metrics and cannot rely on an adversary observing its random outcomes. Respect possible nonattainment of the infimum. A one-sided improvement, a bound depending on \(|X|\), or a determination restricted to one metric family does not establish the full scale.

cards.title: Constant-factor online contention resolution for matroids
cards.formal:
Is there a finite universal real constant \(C\ge1\) such that the following holds? For every finite matroid \(M=(E,\mathcal I)\), every real \(\alpha\ge1\), and every probability distribution \(D\) on \(2^E\) that admits an offline \(\alpha\)-competitive contention-resolution map, there exists a randomized online random-order strategy \(\mathcal A\) which always returns an independent subset \(S\subseteq R\) and satisfies
\[\forall e\in E,\qquad \Pr[e\in S]\ge\frac{\Pr_{R\sim D}[e\in R]}{C\alpha}.\]
Here \(R\sim D\) is the active set, the elements of \(E\) arrive in an independent uniformly random order, and the strategy learns whether an element is active only when it arrives. The strategy knows \(M,D,\alpha\) in advance; \(C\) is independent of all of them. The target is unconditional existence, without assuming the matroid secretary conjecture.

source_formulation.text: Dughmi’s ICALP 2020 §6 asks whether the unconditional conclusion of Theorem 4.1 holds: a universal online contention-resolution scheme losing a constant factor compared with offline balance. The complete target here uses the definitions in §3 and the random-order model of §4. Full knowledge of the prior and no computation restriction are retained. This replaces the previously truncated source excerpt with a fully specified statement, without turning it into a prior-independent or efficient-oracle question.

cards.why: This question isolates the additional cost of making feasible selections online when the active set can have arbitrary correlations. Comparing with the best available offline balance avoids charging the online algorithm for distributional obstructions that already exist offline. Its constant-factor form is equivalent to the matroid secretary conjecture.
cards.status_note: Current status checked on 16 September 2026. Singla’s arXiv:2609.14555v1, submitted 13 September, claims the general factor-four matroid secretary theorem. Through Dughmi’s published ICALP 2020 Theorem 4.1 it would imply this entire known-prior correlated contention-resolution target with C=4. The theorem/model match was checked, but the complete new proof has not been independently certified or Lean-checked here. The record is uncertain pending verification rather than source_open. The 2022 equivalence and 2025 journal abstract corroborate the relationship; efficient and prior-independent variants are separate.

sentences: A random set of active elements is drawn from an arbitrary known distribution on a finite matroid.
An offline map can inspect the whole active set before selecting an independent subset while preserving each element’s probability up to a factor alpha.
The question asks whether an irrevocable strategy seeing activity in uniformly random arrival order can always match that balance within one universal extra constant.
This known-prior correlated model is equivalent at the constant-factor level to the matroid secretary conjecture.
A September 2026 secretary proof claim would settle the target with extra factor four, so its current status awaits independent verification.

cards.definitions:
The ground set \(E\) is finite, and \(\mathcal I\subseteq2^E\) contains \(\varnothing\), is closed under taking subsets, and satisfies augmentation: if \(I,J\in\mathcal I\) and \(|I|<|J|\), some \(e\in J\setminus I\) has \(I\cup\{e\}\in\mathcal I\). These are the matroid axioms. Elements, including loops that belong to no nonempty independent set, have fixed identities known to the strategy. Empty ground sets are allowed.

An arbitrary distribution \(D\) specifies probabilities \(D(R)\ge0\) for every \(R\subseteq E\), summing to one. Activations may be correlated in any way. An offline contention-resolution map \(\phi\) chooses a random independent subset \(\phi(R)\subseteq R\), after seeing the entire active set. Formally, it is a probability kernel from the finite set \(2^E\) to \(\mathcal I\), supported on subsets of its input. It is \(\alpha\)-competitive for \(D\) when
\[\forall e\in E,\quad \Pr_{R\sim D,\phi}[e\in\phi(R)]\ge\frac1\alpha\Pr_{R\sim D}[e\in R].\]
The premise requires the existence of such a map; the online strategy is not given its realized output or the realized set \(R\). This premise is called \(\alpha\)-uncontentiousness in the source.

First draw \(R\sim D\), a permutation \(\pi\) uniform among all permutations of \(E\), and private randomness \(U\), independently. One may represent \(U\) by a uniform seed on \([0,1]\) with measurable decisions. At step \(t\), the strategy sees only \(\pi(t)\) and the bit indicating whether \(\pi(t)\in R\), in addition to its revealed history. It must decide before the next arrival whether to select this element. Inactive elements cannot be selected. Every selected prefix must be independent, and neither acceptance nor rejection can later be reversed. The full stream contains inactive as well as active elements. The same strategy, selected from \(M,D,\alpha\), must work over all possible realized sets, orders and seeds, and may not use their future contents.

The target probability includes the active set, arrival order and private randomness. For an element with positive activation probability it is equivalently a conditional acceptance probability at least \(1/(C\alpha)\) given that the element is active; zero activation probabilities make the displayed inequality automatic. One strategy must meet the guarantee simultaneously for every element, rather than choosing a different strategy for each element. Universal means a family of strategies for all known distributions with one loss factor \(C\), not a single strategy ignorant of the prior. The model imposes no running-time, representation, sampling or oracle restriction. Exact distributional knowledge is part of the mathematical instance, and arbitrary preprocessing is permitted.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of the universal constant-factor proposition or its full logical negation. A positive answer must establish one finite \(C\) and admissible online strategies for every promised matroid, distribution and \(\alpha\). A negative answer must show that every finite \(C\) fails on some such instance despite the existence of the stated offline map. The guarantee must hold for all elements simultaneously and all possibly correlated distributions. A theorem conditional on an unproved secretary conjecture, or a guarantee only for product distributions, does not alone establish the unconditional target. A fresh preprint claim is not itself a checked benchmark answer.

context_blocks.text: Contention resolution takes a random active subset of a ground set and retains a feasible subset while protecting the inclusion probability of every element. In a matroid, feasibility means independence. The balance guarantee is per element, so a scheme that obtains a large total cardinality while systematically discarding one active element may still fail the requirement.

The offline benchmark matters when activations are correlated. For a rank-one matroid on \(n\) elements, let \(R=E\) with probability \(1/n\) and \(R=\varnothing\) otherwise. Every element has marginal activation probability \(1/n\), but at most one element can be selected on the rare nonempty event. Even offline, simultaneous balance requires \(\alpha\ge n\). The target asks for only a constant additional loss relative to this intrinsic offline obstruction.

For product distributions, all activation indicators are independent, and classical contention-resolution results provide constant guarantees under suitable marginal feasibility. The source studies a larger class characterized by the existence of a balanced offline map, including distributions with positive correlations. Neither independent activation nor a marginal feasibility condition alone is the definition of the premise here.

Dughmi's ICALP 2020 Theorem 4.1 proves that a \(\gamma\)-competitive secretary algorithm for a matroid gives an online \(\gamma\alpha\)-competitive map for every \(\alpha\)-uncontentious distribution on that matroid. The theorem assumes the distribution is known. The paper separately discusses the difficulties of removing that knowledge and of obtaining efficient implementations; those are different questions.

The ITCS 2022 sequel proves the converse at the level of universal constants: known-prior random-order contention resolution matching offline balance up to a constant would establish the matroid secretary conjecture. Thus the unconditional target is an equivalent formulation of that conjecture, rather than merely a special case for independent random activations.

Singla's September 2026 preprint claims a secretary algorithm with factor 4 for every matroid. Combined with the published 2020 implication, this would establish this card's target with \(C=4\). This consequence uses the claimed main secretary theorem, not the separate single-sample and matroid-intersection extensions whose detailed proofs are deferred in that preprint. The current status is uncertain because this review has not independently certified the complete new proof.

The source studies a larger class characterized by the existence of a balanced offline map, including distributions with positive correlations. Neither independent activation nor a marginal feasibility condition alone is the definition of the premise here.

Dughmi's ICALP 2020 Theorem 4.1 proves that a \(\gamma\)-competitive secretary algorithm for a matroid gives an online \(\gamma\alpha\)-competitive map for every \(\alpha\)-uncontentious distribution on that matroid. The theorem assumes the distribution is known. The paper separately discusses the difficulties of removing that knowledge and of obtaining efficient implementations; those are different questions.

The ITCS 2022 sequel proves the converse at the level of universal constants: known-prior random-order contention resolution matching offline balance up to a constant would establish the matroid secretary conjecture. Thus the unconditional target is an equivalent formulation of that conjecture, rather than merely a special case for independent random activations.

Singla's September 2026 preprint claims a secretary algorithm with factor 4 for every matroid. Combined with the published 2020 implication, this would establish this card's target with \(C=4\). This consequence uses the claimed main secretary theorem, not the separate single-sample and matroid-intersection extensions whose detailed proofs are deferred in that preprint. The current status is uncertain because this review has not independently certified the complete new proof.

cards.title: Constant-factor related-machine precedence scheduling
cards.formal: Does nonpreemptive precedence-constrained makespan minimization on uniformly related parallel machines admit a deterministic polynomial-time approximation with a universal constant factor? Precisely, do there exist one algorithm \(A\), constants \(K\ge1,C>0\), and an integer \(b\ge1\), such that for every instance of binary encoding length \(L\) specified below, \(A\) returns a feasible schedule of makespan at most \(K\,\mathrm{OPT}\) in at most \(C(L+1)^b\) Turing-machine steps? All constants are independent of the numbers of jobs and machines, processing requirements, machine speeds and precedence graph.
cards.why: Identical machines already allow nontrivial parallelism constrained by a dependency graph, and different speeds add a global allocation choice. A universal constant approximation would show that this extra heterogeneity can be handled with bounded worst-case loss. A negative resolution would identify a basic source of approximation difficulty even though every job can run on every machine and execution times have the simple requirement-divided-by-speed form.
cards.status_note: Explicitly highlighted in the 2011 book. The checked later upper bound is Li’s nonconstant approximation, and the checked 2022 inapproximability result for this exact model depends on additional unproved assumptions. The 2023 communication-aware result and bounded 2025–2026 searches through 2026-09-15 did not yield a constant approximation or an unconditional refutation of its existence. This review does not certify an exhaustive literature search.

category_assignment.reason: Topic of the imported textbook or survey question

importance.reason: A central long-standing approximation question at the boundary between identical and arbitrary machine environments. It asks whether speed heterogeneity and precedence alone force a growing loss, connecting a canonical scheduling model to substantial structural inapproximability conjectures rather than tuning an isolated ratio.

sentences: The problem asks for a polynomial-time constant-factor approximation to the makespan of precedence-constrained jobs on machines with different speeds.
Every job may use every machine, and its uninterrupted execution time is its processing requirement divided by the selected machine’s speed.
The approximation factor must remain fixed as the number of machines and the range of speeds grow.
The checked general upper bound grows logarithmically divided by an iterated logarithm, while known stronger hardness uses extra unproved hypotheses.
A solution must cover arbitrary finite rational inputs in the explicitly stated deterministic bit model.

cards.definitions: An instance consists of integers \(n,m\ge1\), jobs \(J=[n]\), machines \(M=[m]\), positive rational job requirements \(p_j\), positive rational machine speeds \(s_i\), and a directed acyclic graph \(D=(J,E)\) of precedence requirements. Write \([q]=\{1,\ldots,q\}\). A job \(j\) assigned to machine \(a(j)\in M\) occupies one uninterrupted interval \([t_j,t_j+p_j/s_{a(j)})\), with start \(t_j\ge0\). Two intervals on the same machine must be disjoint, and every edge \((j,\ell)\in E\) imposes \(t_\ell\ge t_j+p_j/s_{a(j)}\). Every job executes exactly once on exactly one machine; it cannot be split, migrated or duplicated. Every job is eligible on every machine, and all jobs and the entire precedence graph are supplied before scheduling. There are no communication delays, release times, job weights or additional restrictions. The makespan is \(C_{\max}(a,t)=\max_{j\in J}(t_j+p_j/s_{a(j)})\). Define \(\mathrm{OPT}\) as the infimum of this makespan over all feasible assignments and nonnegative real start times; it is finite and positive. The input explicitly lists \(n,m\), the graph’s edge pairs, and each positive rational as a binary positive numerator and denominator in lowest terms. Counts and edge endpoints are binary integers with fixed separators; \(L\) is the total bit length of this list. No bound on numerical magnitudes or speed ratios is imposed beyond this finite encoding. The output explicitly lists each machine assignment and a nonnegative rational start time, again in binary rational form. The algorithm is one finite deterministic program with ordinary work tapes, and its time includes parsing, exact arithmetic and writing the complete output. Polynomial dependence on the numerical values rather than their bit lengths does not qualify. Randomized or expected-only guarantees are outside this stated deterministic target.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean that the stated universal constant-factor polynomial-time algorithm exists, or prove the negation of that existence statement. An affirmative answer must specify a uniform algorithm and prove feasibility, the multiplicative makespan guarantee and the polynomial bit-complexity bound for every input. A negative answer must exclude every finite universal factor and every deterministic polynomial-time algorithm. A theorem conditional on an additional unproved scheduling or complexity hypothesis does not establish that unconditional negation. Bounds growing with \(m\), algorithms restricted to a fixed number of machines or speed values, and results for a different scheduling objective do not meet the target.

context_blocks.text: Williamson and Shmoys list this as Problem 8 among the book’s highlighted open approximation questions. The surrounding discussion contrasts the constant guarantee for identical machines with the then-known logarithmic guarantee when speeds vary. The target remains existence of a constant approximation, with the ordinary deterministic finite-input model made explicit.

Shi Li’s Theorem 1.3 improves the general upper bound to \(O(\log m/\log\log m)\) as \(m\) grows; the guarantee can be written \(O(1+\log(m+2)/\log\log(m+3))\) to include small \(m\). Although the paper title emphasizes total weighted completion time, its theorem explicitly covers makespan as well. The 2011 book’s logarithmic bound is therefore historical rather than the latest checked upper bound.

Bazzi and Norouzi-Fard obtain nonconstant hardness under an additional structural hypothesis about multipartite graphs. Davies and coauthors subsequently derive a growing lower bound for related-machine precedence scheduling from their Unique Machine Precedence Scheduling conjecture together with the exclusion of quasipolynomial algorithms for NP. Those assumptions remain part of the cited results.

The unconditional reduction in the latter work is often encountered under a title about communication delays. Its main communication-delay hardness result concerns a different model; its consequence for the delay-free related-machine problem here still requires the additional scheduling conjecture. Neither consequence is recorded as an unconditional resolution of this card.

Su, Ren, Vardi and Wierman study related machines with machine-dependent communication effects. Their bound also refers to a communication-free optimum, and specializes to a nonconstant approximation when the extra communication contribution vanishes. It does not supply a universal constant for arbitrary speed ratios.

cards.title: Minimax rate of sequential binary calibration
cards.formal: Determine \(C(T)=\inf _{A} \sup _{B} E[\sum _{p\in \mathrm{P}_{A}}|\sum _{t:p_{t}=p}(y_{t}- p)|]\) up to universal multiplicative constants as the integer horizon T tends to infinity, in the finite-forecast sequential game below. The requested rate includes logarithmic factors.
cards.definitions: Before play, forecaster A selects a finite set \(\mathrm{P}_{A}\subseteq [0,1]\), which may depend on T. Both players know this set and T. At each time t, A selects \(p_{t}\in \mathrm{P}_{A}\) and adversary B selects \(y_{t}\in \{0,1\}\) simultaneously; neither sees the other’s current selection. Each may randomize using independent coins and the full history \((p_{s},y_{s})_{s<t}\), and after the round both selections become public. The infimum is over every such finite set and randomized forecaster, and the supremum is over all randomized adaptive adversaries. There is no computational restriction. The displayed sum measures unnormalized \(\ell\)\(_{1}\) calibration error and is finite; groups are defined by exact equality of predictions. Expectation is over both players’ coins.

context_blocks.text: Calibration asks whether forecasts agree with empirical frequencies on the rounds when each probability was announced. The minimax rate measures the unavoidable error in this requirement against an adaptive sequence of binary events.

The long-standing \(T^{2/3}\) upper bound has already been improved by a constant in the exponent. A lower bound strictly above \(\sqrt{T}\) is also known. Thus neither the old two-thirds barrier nor a square-root target is an appropriate new open question. The remaining problem is the optimal rate itself.

cards.why: A fundamental quantitative problem in sequential prediction, with consequences for calibrated learning and decision making.
cards.answer_criterion: Determine the stated minimax quantity up to universal multiplicative constants, including all logarithmic factors, with matching upper and lower bounds. Benchmark acceptance requires a complete proof-assistant-checked proof of the full target.

sentences: Weighted k-server assigns a separate movement-cost multiplier to each server.
All distinct locations are at unit distance, isolating uncertainty about which weight to move.
The target is the optimal randomized competitive ratio as a function of the number of servers.
It takes the worst case over finite metric sizes and arbitrary positive weights against oblivious requests.
The recent \(\exp (O(k^{2}))\) upper bound removes the old doubly-exponential barrier but leaves a substantial gap above exponential lower bounds.

cards.definitions: For \(k\ge 1\) an instance environment consists of a finite set X with |\(X|\ge k+1\), uniform distance \(d(x,y)=1\) if \(x\ne y\) and 0 otherwise, positive real weights \(w_{1},\ldots ,w_{k}\), and an initial location \(c_{i}\in X\) for each labeled server i. Co-location is permitted. These data are known to the online algorithm. A finite request sequence \(\sigma \in X\)* is revealed one request at a time. Before proceeding, at least one server must occupy the requested location. Moving server i from x to y costs \(w_{i} d(x,y)\); all movements count. The algorithm may use arbitrary computation but cannot inspect future requests. \(\operatorname{OPT}(\sigma )\) is the minimum cost of an offline execution with the same weights and initial locations. A real \(c\ge 1\) is universally achievable for k if, for every environment, there are a randomized online strategy A and \(b\ge 0\) such that for every finite \(\sigma , E[\operatorname{cost}_{A}(\sigma )]\le c \operatorname{OPT}(\sigma )+b\). The strategy and b may depend on the environment; b may not depend on \(\sigma\) or its length. The sequence is fixed independently of the algorithm’s private random choices, and expectation is over those choices. Define \(R_{w}(k)\) as the infimum of universally achievable c. It is finite by known upper bounds and need not be attained. Metric size and the ratios between server weights are unbounded independently of k. No running-time bound or bit encoding of the real weights is imposed; the target measures online movement cost.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a positive function \(g(k)\) and constants \(a,A>0,k_{0}\) such that a \(g(k)\le R_{w}(k)\le A g(k)\) for every integer \(k\ge k_{0}\), proving both bounds in the specified randomized model. Constants must not depend on metric size or weights. An improvement for one algorithm, fixed weight ratios or a bounded number of locations does not by itself determine this worst-case function. Precision is multiplicative constant factors in \(R_{w}\), not additive 0.01 and not merely constant factors in its logarithm.

cards.title: Sublinear-in-q prophet inequalities for q-matroid intersection
cards.formal: Is there a function \(g:\mathbb N_{\ge1}\to[1,\infty)\) with \(\lim_{q\to\infty}g(q)/q=0\) such that, for every sequence of independent nonnegative random values and every feasibility constraint given by the intersection of \(q\) matroids, some online irrevocable selection strategy obtains expected reward at least \(1/g(q)\) times the expected offline optimum? The arrival order is fixed in advance, all value distributions and constraints are known to the strategy, and the guarantee is independent of the number of elements.

source_formulation.text: Are there asymptotically better algorithms for the matroid intersection prophet inequality?

cards.why: A prophet knows all random values before choosing a feasible set, while an online selector must commit before later values arrive. Matroid intersections capture many simultaneous resource constraints. Determining whether the approximation loss can grow sublinearly in their number would distinguish a limitation imposed by lack of future information from the performance of existing selection guarantees.

importance.reason: This asks whether intersecting many independent feasibility constraints forces an essentially linear loss from sequential decisions even with full distributional knowledge and unlimited computation. sentences: Independent random element values arrive one at a time in a fixed known order.
The selector must irrevocably choose a set that is independent in each of q given matroids.
It knows the value distributions, while the offline comparator sees all realized values before making its choice.
The question asks whether the ratio of their expected rewards can always be bounded by a function growing sublinearly in q.
The checked source improves a square-root lower obstruction but corrects an earlier erroneous linear lower-bound claim and leaves the gap open.

cards.definitions: Fix integers \(q,n\ge1\). The ground set is \([n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}\), with elements arriving in the known order \(1,\ldots,n\). For each \(j\in[q]\), a matroid independence family \(\mathcal I_j\subseteq2^{[n]}\) contains \(\varnothing\), is hereditary, and satisfies augmentation: whenever \(A,B\in\mathcal I_j\) and \(|A|<|B|\), some \(b\in B\setminus A\) has \(A\cup\{b\}\in\mathcal I_j\). The feasible sets are \(\mathcal I=\bigcap_{j=1}^q\mathcal I_j\); repetitions among the matroids are allowed. For each \(t\), let \(D_t\) be an arbitrary Borel probability distribution on \([0,\infty)\) with finite first moment, and draw \(X_1,\ldots,X_n\) independently with laws \(D_1,\ldots,D_n\). The offline optimum is \(\operatorname{OPT}(X)=\max_{S\in\mathcal I}\sum_{t\in S}X_t\), after all values have been revealed. An online strategy knows \(q,n,\mathcal I_1,\ldots,\mathcal I_q,D_1,\ldots,D_n\) in advance. Upon seeing \(X_t\), it accepts or rejects element \(t\) irrevocably. Its decision is a measurable function of \(t\), the observed prefix \(X_1,\ldots,X_t\), previous decisions and an internal random seed \(U\) uniform on \([0,1]\) and independent of all \(X_t\). Deterministic strategies may ignore \(U\). Every accepted prefix must be feasible, for every value sequence and seed, and previously accepted elements cannot be removed. Let \(S_{\mathcal A}(X,U)\) be the final accepted set and \(\operatorname{ALG}_{\mathcal A}(X,U)=\sum_{t\in S_{\mathcal A}(X,U)}X_t\). No bound on computation, distribution access or preprocessing is imposed; this is the information-theoretic online model. Exact distributions are part of the mathematical instance, not an implicit finite encoding or a sampling oracle. The target quantifiers are \(\exists g\;\forall q\ge1\;\forall n\ge1\;\forall(\mathcal I_j)_{j=1}^q\;\forall(D_t)_{t=1}^n\;\exists\mathcal A\) such that \(\mathbb E[\operatorname{ALG}_{\mathcal A}]\ge\mathbb E[\operatorname{OPT}]/g(q)\). Expectations include both the independent values and the independent internal seed. The first-moment assumption makes both expectations finite. The inequality also applies when the offline expectation is zero. The limit requirement means that for every \(\eta>0\), some \(q_0\) satisfies \(g(q)\le\eta q\) for all \(q\ge q_0\). The fixed arrival order represents any adversarially chosen order known before the random values are drawn; the order cannot adapt to their realizations.

cards.title: Sublogarithmic competitiveness for online metric TSP
cards.formal: Does there exist one deterministic online insertion algorithm \(A\), in the unrestricted-space model below, and a function \(\rho:\{2,3,\ldots\}\to[1,\infty)\) such that \(\lim_{n\to\infty}\rho(n)/\log_2 n=0\) and \(\operatorname{cost}_A(D)\le\rho(n)\operatorname{OPT}(D)\) for every \(n\ge2\) and every valid sequence of \(n\) metric arrivals? The algorithm knows \(n\), but receives distances only as points arrive and does not know the final offline optimum. Earlier relative-order decisions are irrevocable.
cards.why: An online tour can insert new points between old ones while keeping the old relative order. The question asks how costly that one irreversible choice is when future distances are unknown. Its resolution would identify whether the logarithmic guarantee reflects an inherent online limitation or a limitation of known ordering rules.
cards.status_note: Explicitly open in ICALP 2026 Section 4 and the checked 7 August 2026 full version. The capacity-dependent lower bounds do not settle the unrestricted insertion model. Bounded later checks through 2026-09-16 verified no resolution.

progress.text: The ESA paper specifies online ordering through the distances between consecutive array entries, with repeated points allowed. Its fixed-capacity results concern a stricter insertion model.

The ICALP paper improves the upper bound with a small amount of extra array capacity and proves a capacity-dependent deterministic lower bound. Section 4 explicitly leaves improving logarithmic competitiveness with unlimited space open.
The full arXiv version repeats the unlimited-space open question and the distinction between known and unknown offline optimum.

sentences: Points arrive with distances to earlier points and must immediately be inserted into an evolving order.
Each insertion preserves the relative order of all previous arrivals, but there is no fixed array capacity or computational resource bound.
The final cost is the sum of distances between consecutive points, compared with the best offline ordering.
The question asks whether a deterministic algorithm can guarantee a competitive ratio smaller than logarithmic by an asymptotic factor on every metric input.
This would isolate how much performance is lost through irreversible ordering alone, beyond the additional losses caused by limited storage.

cards.definitions:
An instance of length \(n\) is a real symmetric matrix \(D=(d_{ij})_{1\le i,j\le n}\) with \(d_{ii}=0\), \(d_{ij}\ge0\), and \(d_{ij}\le d_{ik}+d_{kj}\) for all \(i,j,k\). Distinct arrival indices may have distance zero, representing repeated occurrences of the same point. Equivalently, this is a sequence of points in an arbitrary metric space, with repetitions permitted. There is no bound on the number of distinct points, metric dimension, nonzero distance ratios or magnitude of distances. Arrival indices carry no information beyond their order.

The integer \(n\) is given initially. At step \(t\), the algorithm receives exactly the vector \((d_{t1},\ldots,d_{t,t-1})\), in addition to the prefix information and its stored state. It must then choose a position for the new index \(t\) in its current ordered list. If \(\pi_{t-1}\) is the list before this step, \(\pi_t\) must be obtained by inserting \(t\) in one of its \(t\) gaps, including before its first and after its last element. The order of all earlier indices is preserved. The algorithm must finish this choice before receiving step \(t+1\). It has no access to distances involving future arrivals, a description of the ambient metric, future points, the final optimum, predictions or advice. There is no limit on the number of available insertion positions imposed by a fixed array, and no memory bound.

For a permutation \(\pi\) of \([n]\), define
\[
\ell_D(\pi)=\sum_{j=1}^{n-1}d_{\pi(j),\pi(j+1)}.
\]
The final cost is \(\operatorname{cost}_A(D)=\ell_D(\pi_n)\), and \(\operatorname{OPT}(D)=\min_{\pi\in S_n}\ell_D(\pi)\), where \(S_n\) is the set of all permutations of \([n]\). Endpoints are free, and no return edge is charged; this follows the online-ordering source’s path-length convention. Costs at intermediate stages are not separately accumulated. There is no additive allowance in the competitive guarantee. When all arrivals coincide, \(\operatorname{OPT}=0\) and the multiplicative inequality still applies.

For explicit uniformity, an algorithm is a single finite deterministic program with ordinary binary integer control and exact real registers. It may copy real values, use \(0,1\), addition, subtraction, multiplication, division by a nonzero value, and order or equality comparisons; its integer control may perform arbitrary finite bit computation. The revealed distances are exact real input values, rather than numerical approximations. Arbitrary real constants, advice indexed by \(n\), an oracle for unreceived distances and random instructions are unavailable. Each insertion decision must halt after finitely many operations on every valid prefix, but there is no running-time or storage bound. The quantity being compared is solely the length of the final ordering. This fixes an ideal exact-distance model; it does not impose polynomial-time optimization between arrivals.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct Lean proof of such a uniform deterministic algorithm and a sublogarithmic competitive bound for every valid input, or a complete Lean proof that no such algorithm exists. The proof must cover unrestricted metrics and all arrival orders, with a common \(\rho(n)=o(\log n)\). A constant-factor improvement to an \(O(\log n)\) bound, a lower bound for one particular insertion rule, or a lower bound requiring a restricted array capacity does not settle this target. No \(1/100\) additive tolerance is attached to this asymptotic resource comparison.

context_blocks.text: The selected sentence concerns improving the \(O(\log n)\) guarantee even with unlimited space. This card makes the deterministic branch in the surrounding paragraph explicit and interprets “improving” asymptotically as \(o(\log n)\). It does not require constant competitiveness or a near-linear array.

The model is online construction of an ordering. It is different from a traveling server that moves while new requests are released: here there are no release times, movement before the final ordering, deadlines or service constraints.

The ESA 2024 definition charges distances between consecutive occupied positions and allows repeated points. With arbitrary insertions and no fixed array capacity, only the relative order of previous arrivals is committed. Closing the path into a tour changes costs by at most a factor two in a metric, so that endpoint convention does not change the sublogarithmic existence question.

The 2026 source reports the classical \(O(\log n)\) guarantee for unrestricted insertion. Its new lower bound requires an array of limited size and therefore does not establish a logarithmic lower bound in the unrestricted-space model.

For \(m=(1+\varepsilon)n\), the 2026 paper gives a deterministic \(O(\log^3 n/\varepsilon)\) guarantee in its stated parameter range. This is progress on the space tradeoff, while the unlimited-space sublogarithmic question remains explicitly open in its closing remarks.
