cards.context:
A minimum spanning tree connects a graph as cheaply as possible without redundant cycles. It is a basic optimization problem used in network design and clustering. The optimum can already be found in polynomial time; the unsettled issue is whether its exact deterministic computational cost can be only a constant multiple of the \(n\) vertex records and \(m\) edge records in the input.

Sorting every edge is sufficient for classical algorithms, but produces more information than the requested output. If the input graph is already a tree, every edge belongs to the answer regardless of the weight order. For a triangle, omitting any largest-weight edge gives a minimum tree. The comparison lower bound for sorting all keys therefore does not automatically give a superlinear lower bound for this graph problem.

The optimum edge set can be identified using the order of the weights, even though its correctness is defined by a sum. The classical cut and cycle characterizations explain why numeric weight arithmetic is unnecessary. With ties there may be several minimum trees, all acceptable here. Distinct edge identifiers allow algorithms to impose a consistent order among equal keys, without imposing distinctness as an input promise.

Karger, Klein and Tarjan combine random sampling with linear-time MST verification to obtain a Las Vegas algorithm with expected \(O(m+n)\) running time. It always returns a correct tree; randomness controls the work spent on recursive filtering. The target here is a deterministic guarantee for every input, so fixing an arbitrary random seed does not inherit the expected-time theorem.

Chazelle's deterministic comparison algorithm runs in \(O(m\alpha(m,n))\) time, apart from the trivial one-vertex case, where \(\alpha\) is an inverse-Ackermann function. It can be implemented on a pointer machine and assumes no numerical representation of the weights. Although its extra factor grows extremely slowly, the worst-case factor is unbounded asymptotically. The question asks for a constant overhead over input size, rather than a bound that is effectively small on practical instances.

Pettie and Ramachandran relate total deterministic computational cost to the optimal worst-case edge-comparison decision-tree complexity of the minimum spanning forest problem. Their construction is uniform: the cost of building and using small optimal decision trees is part of the analysis. For the present connected-graph problem, input reading and explicit output also remain charged. The resulting optimality theorem does not determine whether the worst-case bound is linear or slightly superlinear.

Eisenstat and coauthors distinguish two different girth restrictions. Girth is the length of a shortest cycle, with acyclic graphs assigned infinite girth. Their conditional reductions show equivalence of the unrestricted linear-time question with its restriction to any fixed lower bound on girth, and also with a suitably sparse family having at most \(3n/2\) edges. Their actual linear-time theorem assumes a girth threshold that grows with \(n\), according to an inverse-Ackermann variant. That size-dependent restriction leaves the general question unresolved.

Changing the access model can remove the obstacle. Fredman and Willard give a deterministic linear-time algorithm using integer-word operations on the weights. That theorem can exploit their binary representation, which the real-key comparison model deliberately withholds. Similarly, an algorithm that is fast for a random graph topology has an average-instance guarantee, even if the algorithm itself is deterministic; it does not bound the work on every graph.

Pettie and Ramachandran also give randomized linear-time algorithms consuming far fewer random bits than the original sampling method. Reducing the number of random choices while preserving an expected time bound does not provide one deterministic program with a linear worst-case guarantee.

Doron and coauthors use minimum spanning tree as a motivating example in their May 2026 work on pseudorandomness for insensitive algorithms. Section 10.1 explicitly says that the existing deterministic near-linear MST algorithms are more efficient than the derandomizations expected from their results. The paper therefore supplies recent context on randomness reduction, not a new deterministic linear-time MST theorem.

benchmark_focus.reason: A foundational graph-algorithm question about the necessity of randomness and the relationship between comparison complexity and actual computation.

cards.title: Erdős–Hajnal conjecture
cards.formal: For each integer \(h\ge 2\) and each undirected simple graph \(H\) on \([h]\), is there a real constant \(c_H>0\) such that, for every integer \(n\ge 1\) and every undirected simple graph \(G\) on \([n]\) containing no induced copy of \(H\), \[\max\{\alpha(G),\omega(G)\}\ge n^{c_H}?\] The exponent is chosen after the entire forbidden graph \(H\) and before the host graph \(G\); the assertion must hold for all such \(H\).
cards.definitions: Write \([m]=\{0,1,\ldots,m-1\}\). A simple undirected graph on \([m]\) is a symmetric irreflexive adjacency relation on this set; it has no loops or multiple edges. An induced copy of \(H\) in \(G\) is an injection \(f:[h]\to[n]\) such that \(u\) and \(v\) are adjacent in \(H\) if and only if \(f(u)\) and \(f(v)\) are adjacent in \(G\), for every distinct \(u,v\in[h]\). Both edges and nonedges must be preserved. A clique is a vertex subset in which every distinct pair is adjacent, and an independent or stable set is one in which every distinct pair is nonadjacent. The integers \(\omega(G)\) and \(\alpha(G)\) are their respective maximum cardinalities; a homogeneous set in this card means a clique or an independent set. The right side \(n^{c_H}\) is an ordinary positive-real power, and the integer on the left is compared as a real number. The constant \(c_H\) may depend on all of \(H\), but not on \(G\) or \(n\). There is no additional degree, density, dimension or algorithmic promise. All positive host sizes, including \(n<h\), are included. This is an existence statement, with no required algorithm for computing \(c_H\) or finding the homogeneous set. A hereditary graph class is closed under isomorphism and induced subgraphs; a proper such class omits some finite graph.
cards.answer_criterion: Supply a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of the displayed proposition or its logical negation. A positive answer proves existence of a positive exponent for every finite forbidden graph and the homogeneous-set guarantee for every permitted host graph. A negative answer proves that there is one fixed graph \(H\) with \(|V(H)|\ge2\) such that, for every real \(c>0\), some positive integer \(n\) and some \(H\)-free graph \(G\) on \([n]\) satisfy \(\max\{\alpha(G),\omega(G)\}<n^c\). The witness host graph may depend on \(c\), but the forbidden graph must be the same for all \(c\). Failure of one proposed exponent or verification of finitely many host sizes does not establish this negation. No numerical approximation to an optimal exponent is being requested.
cards.why: This central conjecture asks whether every proper hereditary restriction forces a polynomial-size clique or independent set, far beyond the logarithmic scale possible in arbitrary graphs. It would provide a common structural guarantee across all forbidden-induced-subgraph classes and clarify the relation between local exclusions, large nearly uniform vertex sets and neighborhood complexity. These are basic objects in structural and algorithmic graph theory; the assertion itself is an existence theorem, not an efficient clique or independent-set algorithm.

importance.reason: A major unifying conjecture for hereditary graph classes, with a sharp qualitative gap between general bounds and the target and substantial recent progress on special cases.

context_blocks.text: Ramsey theory guarantees homogeneous sets on the logarithmic scale in arbitrary graphs, and random graphs show that a polynomial guarantee is impossible without restrictions. The Erdős–Hajnal conjecture asks whether excluding any one fixed induced pattern always changes that scale to \(n^{c_H}\) for some positive constant. A proper hereditary class omits a graph \(H\) and hence every induced copy of it, so the conjecture is equivalently a polynomial homogeneous-set guarantee for every proper hereditary class.

The conjecture is traced to 1977 in the checked modern primary papers, and Erdős and Hajnal developed it in their 1989 Ramsey-type paper. Their general bound is \(2^{a_H\sqrt{\log_2 n}}\) for a suitable positive constant. Bucić, Nguyen, Scott and Seymour improved this to \(2^{b_H\sqrt{\log_2 n\,\log_2\log_2 n}}\) for all \(n\ge2\). Their journal article appeared online on 6 May 2024. This still has a sublinear exponent in \(\log_2 n\) and does not yield a fixed positive power of \(n\).

Nguyen, Scott and Seymour proved the conjecture for the five-vertex path \(P_5\), whose only edges join consecutive vertices of a path. The preprint began in December 2023; the checked accepted revision is from 23 February 2026, and the journal publication is dated 23 March 2026. Together with the earlier bull and five-cycle cases and the known preservation properties, it completes all forbidden graphs on at most five vertices. The theorem concerns every \(P_5\)-free graph, with one positive exponent independent of its size.

The separate all-path theorem gives the following weaker guarantee: for every fixed path \(P\) and every real \(d\) with \(0<d<1\), there is \(a_{P,d}>0\) such that every \(P\)-free graph with \(n\ge2\) vertices has a homogeneous set of size at least \(2^{a_{P,d}(\log_2 n)^d}\). The constant can depend on both the path and \(d\). This explains the source notation \(2^{(\log n)^{1-o(1)}}\); its assertion for all fixed \(d<1\) does not include the required fixed-power case \(d=1\).

The 31 August 2026 revision by Huang, Ju and Zhou reports two further six-vertex cases. Both can be specified using the path \(a-b-c-d-e\) and a sixth vertex \(f\): the E-graph adds only \(cf\), while the Bird adds only \(bf\) and \(cf\). These definitions match Figures 4 and 5 of that revision. Each forbidden graph contains an induced \(P_5\), so its exclusion allows a larger host class than excluding \(P_5\). Theorems 1.10 and 1.11 concern these particular patterns, not every six-vertex graph.

Tran and Nguyen posted a further case on 28 August 2026. Their forbidden graph has vertex set \(\{a,b,c,d,e,f\}\) and exactly the edges \(\{ab,bc,cd,de,af,bf,df\}\); Theorem 1.1 states its Erdős–Hajnal property. It is distinct from both the E-graph and the Bird. The checked introduction still describes the general conjecture as open. The complete proofs of this preprint and the two cases in the preceding paragraph were not independently verified in this review.

Bucić, Fox and Pham prove, for each fixed forbidden graph, equivalence with two polynomial quantitative properties. The polynomial Rödl property requires that for every \(0<\varepsilon\le1/2\), an \(H\)-free graph on \(n\) vertices contain at least \(\varepsilon^{C_H}n\) vertices inducing edge density at most \(\varepsilon\) or at least \(1-\varepsilon\), for a fixed positive \(C_H\). The polynomial Nikiforov property permits a polynomially small proportion of induced copies of \(H\) instead of none. Their Theorem 4 proves the equivalence of these properties with Erdős–Hajnal; it does not establish any of them for every graph.

A July 2026 preprint of Sun, Wang and Zeng sharpens a result under an extra neighborhood restriction. For a graph \(G\), the open-neighborhood family is \(\{N_G(v):v\in V(G)\}\). It shatters \(S\subseteq V(G)\) if every \(A\subseteq S\) equals \(N_G(v)\cap S\) for some vertex \(v\); VC-dimension is the maximum size of a shattered set. Theorem 1.2 reports an absolute \(C\ge1\) such that dimension at most an integer \(d\ge1\) ensures a homogeneous set of size at least \(n^{(Cd)^{-d}}\). This improves the exponent in a previously proved bounded-dimension theorem. General \(H\)-free hosts in this card have no such dimension bound. The new proof was checked for scope, not independently certified.

Sági claims the full conjecture in Theorem 3.20 of the revision listed as arXiv v3, submitted 18 August 2017. The arXiv history records withdrawal of the earlier proof on 24 July 2017, and the author explicitly acknowledges a serious error in the 2012 version while offering different technical details in the revision. The withdrawal therefore cannot itself be treated as a refutation of v3. The revised full proof has not been verified here, while the checked 2026 primary literature continues to treat the general conjecture as open. This card is marked uncertain to record that unresolved proof claim accurately.

cards.title: Reed’s conjecture
cards.formal: Does every nonempty finite simple undirected graph \(G\) satisfy \[\chi(G)\leq\left\lceil\frac{\Delta(G)+1+\omega(G)}{2}\right\rceil?\] The quantification is over every number of vertices and every edge set, with no restriction on maximum degree or graph class.
cards.definitions: For an integer \(n\geq1\), let \(V=\{1,\ldots,n\}\), and let \(E\) be any set of two-element subsets of \(V\). Thus \(G=(V,E)\) has no loops or parallel edges, and an edge has no direction. Vertices \(u,v\) are adjacent exactly when \(\{u,v\}\in E\). A proper \(k\)-colouring, for an integer \(k\geq1\), is a function \(c:V\to\{1,\ldots,k\}\) with \(c(u)\ne c(v)\) for every edge; colours need not all be used. The chromatic number \(\chi(G)\) is the least such \(k\), which exists since \(k=n\) always suffices. Write \(d_G(v)=|\{u\in V:\{u,v\}\in E\}|\) and \(\Delta(G)=\max_{v\in V}d_G(v)\). A clique is a subset \(S\subseteq V\) whose distinct vertices are pairwise adjacent, and \(\omega(G)=\max\{|S|:S\text{ is a clique}\}\). Both maxima are over finite sets, and a singleton is a clique. The ceiling \(\lceil x\rceil\) is the least integer at least the real number \(x\); the division by two in the displayed bound is real division before rounding. Disconnected graphs, isolated vertices and all nonempty edgeless graphs are included; the latter have \(\chi=\omega=1\) and \(\Delta=0\). Labelling the vertices imposes no structural restriction. One may also include the empty graph with \(\chi=\omega=\Delta=0\), for which the inequality is immediate. This is an existence question about one ordinary proper colouring per graph, with no input algorithm, running-time, randomness, list assignment or recolouring requirement.
cards.answer_criterion: Supply a complete, mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of the universal displayed inequality, or a complete Lean-checked refutation: a specified integer \(n\geq1\), a specified finite simple graph \(G\) on \(\{1,\ldots,n\}\), and a proof that \(\chi(G)>\lceil(\Delta(G)+1+\omega(G))/2\rceil\). cards.why: A defining question about how a local degree constraint and a global clique obstruction jointly control ordinary graph colouring. Its significance is structural even without an efficient algorithm for finding the guaranteed colouring.

context_blocks.text: The basic bounds are \(\omega(G)\leq\chi(G)\leq\Delta(G)+1\): a clique requires different colours at all its vertices, while the upper bound follows from the usual greedy-colouring theorem. Reed asks whether the rounded average of these two scales is always an upper bound. The conjecture concerns the global partition into independent sets, meaning vertex sets containing no edge, rather than a separate choice of colours within each neighbourhood.

The ceiling matters. A five-cycle has \(\Delta=\omega=2\) and \(\chi=3\), whereas the unrounded average is \(5/2\). Complete graphs attain the proposed rounded bound as well. These examples distinguish the exact statement from an asymptotic estimate with an unspecified additive constant.

The coefficient \(1/2\) cannot be increased in a universal interpolation \(\lceil(1-\varepsilon)(\Delta+1)+\varepsilon\omega\rceil\). Replace each vertex of a five-cycle by a clique of size \(t\geq1\), and put all edges between two replacement cliques exactly when their original cycle vertices are adjacent. This graph has \(5t\) vertices, \(\Delta=3t-1\), \(\omega=2t\), and no independent set larger than two vertices, hence \(\chi\geq\lceil5t/2\rceil\). For any fixed \(\varepsilon>1/2\), the proposed interpolation would be smaller than this lower bound for sufficiently large \(t\). This explicitly defined clique blowup is the example intended in the source; its description there as a Cartesian product is inaccurate.

Reed proved that some universal \(\varepsilon>0\) does give the weaker bound \(\chi(G)\leq\lceil(1-\varepsilon)(\Delta(G)+1)+\varepsilon\omega(G)\rceil\) for every graph. Thus a saving proportional to the gap between degree plus one and clique number is known; the unresolved target is the sharp half-average. The September 2026 digraph paper restates the original conjecture and this result as Conjecture 1.1 and Theorem 1.2, respectively.

Hurley, de Joannis de Verclos and Kang give \(\chi(G)\leq\lceil0.881(\Delta(G)+1)+0.119\omega(G)\rceil\) when \(\Delta(G)\geq\Delta_0\) for a universal threshold \(\Delta_0\). Their published 2022 Remark 3.1 explicitly says that an ingredient attributed to Delcourt and Postle had not then completed peer review; it also records an alternative published ingredient giving coefficients \(0.887\) and \(0.113\). This is a dated qualification about the 2022 argument, not a claim about the present review status of that ingredient. Neither variant provides coefficient \(1/2\), and the stated large-degree restriction must be retained.

Bonamy, Kelly, Nelson and Postle prove a different kind of improvement, \(\chi(G)=O(\Delta\sqrt{\ln\omega/\ln\Delta})\), for graphs of maximum degree at most \(\Delta\) and clique number at most \(\omega\), in the large-\(\Delta\) regime with \(\omega\geq2\). The implicit constant is universal. This becomes substantially smaller than the degree bound when \(\ln\omega/\ln\Delta\) is small; it does not give the exact half-average for every parameter range. The theorem in the 2018 author preprint also bounds the list-chromatic number, where every vertex has its own list of allowed colours.

A Kempe change swaps two colours on one connected component of the subgraph induced by those colours. The 2025 recolouring paper studies whether every pair of proper \(k\)-colourings is connected by a sequence of such changes. Its general conjectured clique coefficient is \(1/3\), due to obstructions to moving between colourings; this is a separate property from the existence of one colouring. For odd-hole-free graphs, meaning graphs with no induced odd cycle of length at least five, Theorem 4 guarantees recolourability above a local threshold, and in particular for \(k>\lceil(\omega+\Delta+1)/2\rceil\). The strict inequality leaves the equality case open in that recolouring question.

The September 2026 revision of Kawarabayashi and Picasarri-Arrieta replaces undirected colour classes by acyclic colour classes in a digraph, where acyclic means containing no directed cycle, including no two-cycle of opposite arcs. In the symmetric digraph obtained by replacing each edge by both opposite arcs, this is exactly ordinary proper colouring. Their proposed directed half-average bound therefore implies Reed’s conjecture, but their proved general interpolation has only some positive coefficient. Conjecture 1.1 of this revision still lists the full undirected half-average as open.

cards.title: Graph isomorphism in polynomial time
cards.formal: Does there exist a uniform deterministic Turing machine M and fixed positive integers C,k such that on every binary input x, M halts within \(C(|x|+1)^k\) transitions and accepts exactly when x encodes two isomorphic finite simple undirected graphs? Equivalently, is the language \(\mathrm{GI}\) defined below in deterministic polynomial time?
cards.definitions: For \(n\ge 0\), write \([n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}\), with \([0]\) empty. A finite simple undirected graph G on \([n]\) has an adjacency matrix \(A_G\in\{0,1\}^{n\times n}\) that is symmetric with zero diagonal. Its vertices are labeled; its edges are unordered pairs of distinct vertices. Encode a pair G,H by \(1^n0\), followed by the full row-major matrix of G, followed by \(1^m0\) and the full row-major matrix of H. The total binary length is \(N=n^2+m^2+n+m+2\). Extra trailing bits, missing entries, or nonsymmetric or nonzero-diagonal matrices make an encoding malformed. Graphs G,H are isomorphic, written \(G\cong H\), if there is a bijection \(\pi:[n]\to[m]\) such that \(A_G(i,j)=A_H(\pi(i),\pi(j))\) for every \(i,j\in[n]\). If \(n\ne m\), no such bijection exists; the two empty graphs are isomorphic. All valid graph pairs are in the domain, without degree, connectivity, automorphism, sparsity or random-input promises. Computation receives the entire binary string, rather than an oracle or succinctly generated adjacency matrix. The computation model is one uniform classical multitape Turing machine with a finite program, finite tape alphabets, a read-only input tape and initially blank work tapes. In one transition each tape head moves at most one cell. Time counts all transitions, including input access and internal computation. Polynomial time means a bound \(C(N+1)^k\) for fixed positive integers C,k, independent of the input and of the graph sizes. There is no advice, prover, witness supplied with the input, graph-isomorphism oracle or uncounted preprocessing. The machine is deterministic and must always answer correctly. The language \(\mathrm{GI}\) contains exactly the valid encodings with \(G\cong H\); malformed encodings are rejected. P is the class of all binary languages decided under these uniform deterministic polynomial-time conventions. Ordinary vertex-permutation isomorphism is the equivalence relation in the target.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof that the specified language \(\mathrm{GI}\) belongs to P, or that \(\mathrm{GI}\notin\mathrm P\). A positive answer must establish one deterministic machine, fixed polynomial bounds and correctness on every input, including rejection of malformed strings. A negative answer must exclude every such polynomial-time machine; a lower bound for only one algorithm, invariant or representation does not suffice. No isomorphism witness or canonical representative must be output: the target is decision.
cards.why: Tests whether the central equivalence problem for finite combinatorial structures can be recognized in deterministic polynomial time after the quasipolynomial barrier was broken.

context_blocks.text: The same graph can appear under many vertex names. For example, renumbering a cycle leaves its adjacency relations unchanged as an unlabeled structure. Isomorphism asks whether this explains the entire difference between two inputs. A proposed bijection can be checked efficiently, but a negative instance requires ruling out all bijections. This places the decision problem in NP, the class with polynomially bounded certificates verifiable in polynomial time.

Simple summaries can agree on different graphs: a six-cycle and two disjoint triangles both have six vertices and every vertex has degree two. They are not isomorphic because one is connected and the other is disconnected. Any complete decision procedure must distinguish every nonisomorphic pair, including pairs with much stronger coincident invariants.

Babai’s general upper bound has the form \(\exp((\log(n+2))^{O(1)})\). This is a quasipolynomial upper bound, whose permitted exponents go beyond the fixed polynomial bound requested here. It does not prove a superpolynomial lower bound on the problem or on every implementation of that method.

Efficient algorithms on restricted graph classes provide substantial structure without settling the unrestricted target. In particular, a runtime with a degree or width parameter in the exponent is polynomial when that parameter is fixed, but it need not be polynomial when the parameter grows with the input. The 2026 survey explicitly separates these parameterized bounds from the general open problem.

A randomized polynomial-time algorithm with bounded error for ordinary isomorphism would settle the neighboring BPP question. It would not by itself provide the deterministic algorithm asked for here. A quantum algorithm deciding the same ordinary relation is another computational variant; the distinct relation called quantum graph isomorphism is a different mathematical target.

The two consolidated MFCS 2021 sources independently restate the general polynomial-time question. Butti and Dalmau discuss it beside fractional homomorphisms and linear-programming relaxations. Dawar and Vagnozzi discuss its equivalence to computing automorphism-orbit partitions and compare algebraic relaxations. These source contexts are preserved without substituting a conjecture about one relaxation for general graph isomorphism.

cards.title: Tutte’s 5-flow conjecture
cards.formal: Does every finite loopless bridgeless undirected multigraph \(G=(V,E)\) admit an orientation \(D\) of all its edges and a function \(f:E\to\{1,2,3,4\}\) such that, at every vertex \(v\in V\), \[\sum_{e\in E:\,\operatorname{head}_D(e)=v}f(e)=\sum_{e\in E:\,\operatorname{tail}_D(e)=v}f(e)\] as an equality of integers?
cards.definitions: A finite loopless undirected multigraph has a finite vertex set \(V\) and a finite set \(E\) of distinct edge identities, each assigned an unordered pair of two distinct vertices. Multiple edges with the same pair of endpoints are allowed and counted separately in every sum. Two vertices lie in the same connected component when a finite sequence of incident edges joins them; a vertex is joined to itself by the empty sequence. A bridge is an edge whose deletion, with the vertex set retained, increases the number of connected components. Bridgeless means that no edge has this property. Disconnected graphs, isolated vertices and the graph with no vertices are allowed. An orientation chooses, for each edge, one endpoint as its tail and the other as its head. The orientation and all values are chosen together for the whole graph; conservation must hold at all vertices simultaneously. Empty sums equal zero. For an integer \(k\ge2\), a nowhere-zero \(k\)-flow in this convention has the same conservation law and values in \(\{1,\ldots,k-1\}\). Thus a 5-flow uses four possible positive integer values; it may use any subset of them. Equivalently, after fixing an arbitrary reference orientation, signed integer values \(z(e)\) with \(1\le|z(e)|\le4\) may be used: a negative value is represented by reversing that edge and taking its absolute value. Values are scalar integers, not vectors, and conservation is exact, not merely a congruence. There are no sources, sinks, externally prescribed demands, capacities, embedding, degree restrictions or construction-time requirements. The proposition is universal over finite graphs, with the orientation and values allowed to depend on the graph.
cards.answer_criterion: Supply a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of this universal existence proposition, or a Lean-checked proof of its logical negation: there exists a finite loopless bridgeless undirected multigraph \(G\) such that for every orientation \(D\) and every assignment \(f:E(G)\to\{1,2,3,4\}\), at least one vertex violates the integer conservation equality. A negative answer must prove both the graph hypotheses and the nonexistence of every permitted flow; failure of one orientation, one search method or a finite collection of trial assignments is insufficient unless it establishes that universal nonexistence. A positive answer must cover every size and all allowed parallel edges and components. A 6-flow, an assertion only for graphs with an additional restriction, or a statement conditional on an unproved conjecture does not settle this target. An alternative formulation can qualify only with a Lean-checked implication establishing the exact proposition or its negation. No efficient procedure for constructing the witness is required.

context_blocks.text: Flow conservation models circulation with no accumulation at any vertex. If an edge is a bridge, summing conservation on one side of that bridge would force its value to be zero. Bridgelessness is therefore necessary. The issue is whether it is sufficient with the fixed range \(1,2,3,4\), independently of graph size. Components can be treated separately, and edgeless components satisfy conservation with the empty assignment. This extends the connected formulation in Conjecture 3 without changing the mathematical target.

Seymour’s 1981 6-flow theorem supplies values in \(\{1,2,3,4,5\}\) for every bridgeless graph. Younger’s 1983 work gives a polynomial-time construction, as recalled in Theorem 5 of the 2025 paper. The missing assertion is the universal reduction of the maximum value from five to four. The construction-time improvement in the known theorem is additional to the existence requirement on this card.

Tutte’s integer/group-flow theorem equates existence of a nowhere-zero integer 5-flow with existence of a flow over \(\mathbb Z/5\mathbb Z\), the residues modulo five, using nonzero values and conservation in that group. This equivalence is an existence theorem; simply interpreting the same residues as positive integers need not preserve integer conservation. Theorem 2.3 in the 2026 reconfiguration paper recalls the lifting statement.

For a connected bridgeless graph drawn in the plane without crossings, the dual graph has a vertex for each face and an edge crossing each original edge between its incident faces. Tutte’s duality identifies existence of an integer \(k\)-flow with a proper \(k\)-coloring of that dual: adjacent dual vertices receive different colors. This explains why flow questions extend coloring phenomena beyond graphs with a planar embedding.

A directed cut consists of all arcs crossing a nontrivial vertex partition when every crossing arc points in the same direction; a dijoin is a set of arcs meeting every such cut. Cornuéjols, Liu and Ravi’s Theorem 3 implies that, when the underlying graph admits a 5-flow, a digraph with finite minimum directed-cut size \(\tau\ge2\) contains \(\lfloor\tau/5\rfloor\) pairwise arc-disjoint dijoins. The established 6-flow theorem yields \(\lfloor\tau/6\rfloor\). The 5-flow conjecture would improve this guarantee without asserting Woodall’s full packing equality.

Li and Su’s 2025 publisher abstract reports a 5-flow for every bridgeless graph of Euler genus at most 20. Euler genus is the least surface parameter admitting a crossing-free drawing: twice the number of handles for an orientable closed surface, or the number of crosscaps for a nonorientable one. This is a restricted graph class; no uniform bound on genus is assumed here. The present review inspected that abstract, not the full proof.

Esperet and coauthors’ July 2026 revision gives a graph with existing nowhere-zero 5-flows that cannot all be connected by steps changing a flow only along a cycle, while keeping every intermediate flow nowhere zero. Their Theorem 3.4 refutes this reconfiguration property in both the integer and modulo-five settings. It does not refute existence of a 5-flow; their introduction retains Tutte’s conjecture and the 6-flow theorem as the general benchmark.

Li, Li, Luo and Su’s January 2026 paper defines flows with vector values in several real dimensions and proves bounds on their norms. Its Conjecture 1.3 separately states the ordinary one-dimensional 5-flow question. A higher-dimensional flow has additional freedom and does not itself supply the scalar integer assignment required here.

cards.title: Almost-linear-time exact maximum matching in general graphs
cards.formal:
Does there exist one uniform randomized sequential word-RAM algorithm that, on every explicitly represented finite simple undirected graph \(G\), terminates almost surely, always outputs a valid matching when it terminates, and outputs a maximum-cardinality matching with probability at least \(2/3\), with expected running time
\[(n+m+2)^{1+o(1)}?\]
Here \(n=|V(G)|\), \(m=|E(G)|\), and the precise machine, input, probability and asymptotic conventions are below. In particular, the same program must meet every positive exponent slack; an algorithm chosen separately for each fixed slack is not the stated target.
cards.definitions:
Graph and optimum. Let \(n\in\mathbb N_{\ge0}\), \(V=\{1,\ldots,n\}\), and let \(E\) be a set of distinct unordered pairs of distinct vertices. Disconnected graphs, isolated vertices, odd cycles, the empty graph and the edgeless graph are included. Put \(m=|E|\) and \(N=n+m+2\). A matching is a subset \(M\subseteq E\) such that no vertex belongs to two selected edges. Its cardinality is \(|M|\), and
\[\nu(G)=\max\{|M|:M\subseteq E\text{ is a matching}\}.\]
The empty matching is allowed, so this finite maximum exists on every input. The problem is unweighted. The algorithm must return the selected edges, not only the number \(\nu(G)\), a fractional solution, or a certificate that a perfect matching exists. Any maximum matching is acceptable.

Explicit representation. Use an edge list with headers \(n,m\), the vertex list \(1,\ldots,n\), and then \(m\) indexed pairs \((u_j,v_j)\) with \(1\le u_j<v_j\le n\) and no repeated pair. Edge indices are \(j=1,\ldots,m\); their order is arbitrary. Each integer occupies one machine word, so the entire input has \(2+n+2m\) words. Isolated vertices count in \(n\). The graph is a full list, not a succinct circuit or query oracle. The output consists of its cardinality \(t\) and a list of \(t\) distinct valid edge indices, in any order. Ordinary explicit adjacency lists can be converted to this form in \(O(n+m)\) word operations, preserving the target time scale. No guarantee is required on malformed inputs.

Machine. The algorithm fixes an integer \(b\ge2\) and, on inputs of size parameter \(N\), uses words of exactly
\[w=b\lceil\log_2N\rceil\]
bits. A word represents an unsigned integer in \(\{0,\ldots,2^w-1\}\). The machine has a fixed finite program, a constant number of word registers and random-access work memory addressed by one word, initially all zero. The input is read-only and the output is a sequential list of words. Each instruction operates on a constant number of words. Reading or writing an addressed word, copying, comparing, branching, bitwise AND/OR/XOR/NOT, and arithmetic addition, subtraction and multiplication modulo \(2^w\) cost one operation. Integer quotient and remainder with a nonzero divisor also cost one operation. A left or right shift by fewer than \(w\) positions discards bits outside the word and fills with zeros; a shift by at least \(w\) returns zero. Larger exact integers use multiple words, and their processing is charged. A random instruction supplies one fresh uniform \(w\)-bit word, independent of all previous random words. There are no exact-real primitives, oracle calls, nonuniform advice, or precomputed tables supplied at no cost. The program may use \(w\) as the machine word length. Preprocessing, input access, initialization it performs and writing every output word are included in time.

Randomness and correctness. For a fixed valid input, the probability space is the infinite sequence of independent uniform random words used by the machine. Let \(T_A(G,R)\) count its operations, with value \(+\infty\) on a nonterminating execution. For every input, termination must have probability one. On every terminating execution, including those outside the success event, the output indices must represent a matching. On each input separately,
\[\Pr_R[\text{the output matching has cardinality }\nu(G)]\ge2/3.\]
The output may be suboptimal on other executions, but it must remain feasible. No distribution over input graphs is assumed, and success is not merely an expectation bound on matching size. A single program is used for every graph and edge-list order.

Almost-linear expected time. The expectation is over the algorithm's random words, with the input fixed. The notation in the question means that this same algorithm and word constant satisfy
\[\forall\varepsilon>0\ \exists C_\varepsilon>0\ \exists N_\varepsilon\in\mathbb N_{>0}\ \forall G\text{ with }N\ge N_\varepsilon:\quad \mathbb E_R[T_A(G,R)]\le C_\varepsilon N^{1+\varepsilon}.\]
Constants and the threshold may depend on \(\varepsilon\) and on the fixed algorithm, but not on the graph, its density, its edge order or its random choices. The slack \(\varepsilon\) is not an input selecting a different program. This is a worst-case-over-inputs bound on expected time, not a bound on every individual random execution. The claim covers sparse and dense graphs simultaneously and allows subpolynomial overhead beyond polylogarithmic factors.
cards.answer_criterion:
Give a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of the existence statement or its logical negation. An affirmative proof must specify a uniform finite program and a fixed word constant, prove almost-sure termination and feasibility on every terminating execution, prove per-input success probability at least \(2/3\), and establish the displayed expected-time bound for every positive exponent slack. All preprocessing, arithmetic and explicit output costs must fit that proof. A deterministic exact algorithm meeting the time bound is also a positive answer.

A negative answer must rule out all algorithms in the allowed randomized model. Equivalently, for every fixed word constant and program satisfying the termination, feasibility and success requirements, prove that there is some \(\varepsilon>0\) such that, for every \(C>0\) and every size threshold \(N_0\), there is a valid graph encoding with \(N\ge N_0\) and \(\mathbb E[T_A]>C N^{1+\varepsilon}\). The exponent slack may depend on the program. A conditional running-time lower bound must name its unproved assumptions and does not alone establish this unconditional negation.

Algorithms only for bipartite graphs, a near-linear maximal matching, a fixed-accuracy approximation, the optimum size without an output matching, and average performance on random input graphs do not meet the full target. Bounds for pointer machines, parallel rounds, catalytic space or restricted algorithmic techniques must not be substituted for the permitted word-RAM expected time. No additive numerical tolerance applies to either exact optimality or the asymptotic exponent.
cards.why: A major remaining exact graph-optimization problem beyond the almost-linear flow framework. It asks whether odd-cycle and blossom structure impose a real asymptotic cost, even when randomization is allowed.

importance.reason: A core combinatorial optimization primitive with a large gap between general graphs and the fast bipartite case, connecting augmenting paths, polyhedral methods and algebraic algorithms.

cards.status_note: Checked through 16 September 2026. No valid almost-linear exact general-graph algorithm was found in the bounded primary-source search. The June catalytic result gives a different polynomial-time/space guarantee; almost-linear flow applies to the bipartite consequence, and fixed-accuracy matching is weaker than exact optimality. The old Glauber-dynamics O(m log² n) claim is expressly invalidated by the authors in the current arXiv record. The retained target allows bounded-error randomization and expected word-RAM time; external proofs were not independently certified.

context_blocks.text: Maximum matching is a basic model of pairing compatible objects while using each object at most once. General graphs allow compatibility patterns that cannot be separated into two sides. Edmonds’ blossom method established that this optimization is polynomial-time solvable. The remaining question is how close its exact computational cost can come to the size of the graph that must be read.

Maximum and maximal have different meanings. A maximal matching merely cannot be extended by adding a single edge. On a four-vertex path, the middle edge alone is maximal, while the two outside edges form a maximum matching of size two. A greedy linear-time procedure can therefore solve maximal matching and still fail the exact task on a tiny input. The card requires the global optimum, with no allowed loss of even one matched pair.

Classical exact algorithms use alternating paths to increase the size of a matching and blossoms to represent the odd-cycle structure of general graphs. Micali and Vazirani's 1980 algorithm has an \(O(m\sqrt n)\) RAM bound on its matching computation, or \(O(n+m\sqrt n)\) when reading all listed isolated vertices is included. Vazirani's later proof distinguishes this from an additional inverse-Ackermann factor in the pointer model. The historical bound is not evidence that such an overhead is necessary for every algorithm.

Bipartite maximum matching reduces to integral unit-capacity maximum flow with \(O(n+m)\) vertices and edges. Chen and coauthors explicitly obtain an almost-linear bipartite matching consequence from their exact flow theorem. Integrality in that setting yields an actual optimum matching. The reduction does not establish the same result on arbitrary undirected graphs, where no bipartition is available and odd-set constraints matter.

A triangle illustrates the integrality issue. Assigning value \(1/2\) to each edge respects a unit bound on the sum incident to every vertex, but has total value \(3/2\), whereas an integral matching has size at most one. For every odd vertex set \(S\), an integral matching contains at most \((|S|-1)/2\) edges entirely inside \(S\). These additional inequalities distinguish the general matching polytope from the simpler bipartite constraints.

Mucha and Sankowski construct maximum matchings by randomized algebraic computation in \(O(n^\omega)\) time for an available matrix-multiplication exponent \(\omega>2\); their Remark 1.1 records an extra logarithmic factor if the exponent is exactly two. Their finite-field arithmetic uses polynomially sized fields. This improves the classical bound on dense graphs, but even a quadratic-in-vertices bound does not approach the explicit input size on sparse graphs.

Duan, Pettie and Su prove a \((1-\delta)\)-approximation for maximum weight matching in \(O(m\delta^{-1}\log\delta^{-1})\) time, so the graph-processing time is linear for fixed \(\delta\). Unit edge weights give the cardinality case, with an additional \(O(n)\) cost for the explicit vertex list. Fixed positive relative error can still allow the loss of many matching edges as \(n\) grows. Making the allowed loss less than one when the optimum is proportional to \(n\) requires inverse-linear accuracy, for which that running-time expression is no longer almost linear.

Ansaripour, Danaei and Mehlhorn’s 2024 implementation study is useful for interpreting experiments: the observed behaviour on random graphs can be close to linear, while specially constructed inputs expose substantial differences between algorithms. Empirical speed and average graph behaviour therefore cannot establish the bound quantified over every input here. Their paper also keeps the distinction between the faster bipartite results and general matching explicit.

A June 2026 revision by Chakraborty and coauthors places construction of a general maximum matching in polynomial-time catalytic logspace. This model permits a large auxiliary tape with arbitrary initial contents, provided those contents are restored. It is progress on space and reversible use of auxiliary memory. The polynomial-time statement is not an almost-linear running-time theorem, so it does not resolve this card.

A 2011 preprint by Jindal, Kochar and Pal has an abstract claiming \(O(m\log^2 n)\) maximum matching via Glauber dynamics. Its current official arXiv record also contains the authors' correction: the coupling has incorrect marginals, so the mixing-time bound and the main result do not hold. The retained abstract must not be treated as a valid resolution of this target.

Known almost-linear bipartite algorithms, approximation schemes and catalytic-space results do not settle the general exact target, and the older Glauber-dynamics claim has an acknowledged error.

cards.context:
Maximum matching is a basic model of pairing compatible objects while using each object at most once. General graphs allow compatibility patterns that cannot be separated into two sides. Edmonds’ blossom method established that this optimization is polynomial-time solvable. The remaining question is how close its exact computational cost can come to the size of the graph that must be read.

Maximum and maximal have different meanings. A maximal matching merely cannot be extended by adding a single edge. On a four-vertex path, the middle edge alone is maximal, while the two outside edges form a maximum matching of size two. A greedy linear-time procedure can therefore solve maximal matching and still fail the exact task on a tiny input. The card requires the global optimum, with no allowed loss of even one matched pair.

Classical exact algorithms use alternating paths to increase the size of a matching and blossoms to represent the odd-cycle structure of general graphs. Micali and Vazirani's 1980 algorithm has an \(O(m\sqrt n)\) RAM bound on its matching computation, or \(O(n+m\sqrt n)\) when reading all listed isolated vertices is included. Vazirani's later proof distinguishes this from an additional inverse-Ackermann factor in the pointer model. The historical bound is not evidence that such an overhead is necessary for every algorithm.

Bipartite maximum matching reduces to integral unit-capacity maximum flow with \(O(n+m)\) vertices and edges. Chen and coauthors explicitly obtain an almost-linear bipartite matching consequence from their exact flow theorem. Integrality in that setting yields an actual optimum matching. The reduction does not establish the same result on arbitrary undirected graphs, where no bipartition is available and odd-set constraints matter.

A triangle illustrates the integrality issue. Assigning value \(1/2\) to each edge respects a unit bound on the sum incident to every vertex, but has total value \(3/2\), whereas an integral matching has size at most one. For every odd vertex set \(S\), an integral matching contains at most \((|S|-1)/2\) edges entirely inside \(S\). These additional inequalities distinguish the general matching polytope from the simpler bipartite constraints.

Mucha and Sankowski construct maximum matchings by randomized algebraic computation in \(O(n^\omega)\) time for an available matrix-multiplication exponent \(\omega>2\); their Remark 1.1 records an extra logarithmic factor if the exponent is exactly two. Their finite-field arithmetic uses polynomially sized fields. This improves the classical bound on dense graphs, but even a quadratic-in-vertices bound does not approach the explicit input size on sparse graphs.

Duan, Pettie and Su prove a \((1-\delta)\)-approximation for maximum weight matching in \(O(m\delta^{-1}\log\delta^{-1})\) time, so the graph-processing time is linear for fixed \(\delta\). Unit edge weights give the cardinality case, with an additional \(O(n)\) cost for the explicit vertex list. Fixed positive relative error can still allow the loss of many matching edges as \(n\) grows. Making the allowed loss less than one when the optimum is proportional to \(n\) requires inverse-linear accuracy, for which that running-time expression is no longer almost linear.

Ansaripour, Danaei and Mehlhorn’s 2024 implementation study is useful for interpreting experiments: the observed behaviour on random graphs can be close to linear, while specially constructed inputs expose substantial differences between algorithms. Empirical speed and average graph behaviour therefore cannot establish the bound quantified over every input here. Their paper also keeps the distinction between the faster bipartite results and general matching explicit.

A June 2026 revision by Chakraborty and coauthors places construction of a general maximum matching in polynomial-time catalytic logspace. This model permits a large auxiliary tape with arbitrary initial contents, provided those contents are restored. It is progress on space and reversible use of auxiliary memory. The polynomial-time statement is not an almost-linear running-time theorem, so it does not resolve this card.

A 2011 preprint by Jindal, Kochar and Pal has an abstract claiming \(O(m\log^2 n)\) maximum matching via Glauber dynamics. Its current official arXiv record also contains the authors' correction: the coupling has incorrect marginals, so the mixing-time bound and the main result do not hold. The retained abstract must not be treated as a valid resolution of this target.

cards.title: Gyárfás–Sumner conjecture
cards.formal:
Is the following proposition true? For every finite nonempty tree \(T\) and every integer \(r\ge1\), there exists an integer \(B\ge0\) such that every finite simple undirected graph \(G\) satisfies
\[\bigl(\omega(G)\le r\ \land\ G\text{ has no induced copy of }T\bigr)
\ \Longrightarrow\ \chi(G)\le B.\]
The quantifier order is \(\forall T\,\forall r\,\exists B\,\forall G\). The bound may depend on the entire tree \(T\) and on \(r\), but must be independent of the number of vertices and every other parameter of \(G\). No rate of growth or computational requirement on \(B\) is prescribed.
cards.definitions:
Graphs and trees. A finite simple undirected graph \(G=(V,E)\) consists of a finite vertex set and a set of unordered pairs of distinct vertices. There are no loops or multiple edges. A path has distinct vertices, with adjacent consecutive vertices; a cycle has at least three distinct vertices with consecutive and last-to-first adjacency. A tree is a nonempty connected graph containing no cycle. Connected means that each pair of vertices is joined by a path. The one-vertex tree is allowed. Host graphs need not be connected and may have no vertices. Equivalently, one may quantify over graphs with vertex set \([n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}\) for every integer \(n\ge0\), with \([0]=\varnothing\); labels have no mathematical significance.

Induced exclusion. For \(S\subseteq V(G)\), the graph \(G[S]\) has vertex set \(S\) and exactly the edges of \(G\) with both ends in \(S\). An induced copy of \(T\) is an injective map \(\varphi:V(T)\to V(G)\) such that for all distinct \(u,v\in V(T)\),
\[\{u,v\}\in E(T)\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
\{\varphi(u),\varphi(v)\}\in E(G).\]
A graph is \(T\)-free when no such map exists. The requirement preserves nonedges as well as edges. It is different from excluding an ordinary subgraph, a minor or a subdivision of \(T\). Edges from the image to vertices outside it are unrestricted.

Clique and chromatic numbers. A clique is a vertex subset whose distinct vertices are pairwise adjacent. Its maximum possible size is \(\omega(G)\). A proper \(k\)-colouring is a map \(c:V(G)\to[k]\) with \(c(u)\ne c(v)\) for every edge \(\{u,v\}\). The least nonnegative integer \(k\) admitting such a map is \(\chi(G)\). Thus both parameters are zero for the empty graph, and every nonempty edgeless graph has both equal to one. The bound \(\omega(G)\le r\) is equivalent to excluding a clique on \(r+1\) vertices. Colour classes are independent sets, meaning subsets with no adjacent pair. Colouring here is ordinary vertex colouring, without lists, weights, fractional assignments or edge orientations.

Scope of the bound. Both the tree and the clique bound are fixed before the host graph varies. There is no maximum-degree, girth, geometric-representation, size or other promise on the host. The integer \(B=B(T,r)\) may grow arbitrarily quickly with its two allowed parameters. The target asks for existence of a finite bound, not its minimum value, a polynomial in \(r\), a computable function, or a procedure finding a colouring. There is consequently no input encoding, algorithmic running time or random-error parameter in the proposition.

Equivalent terminology. A class of graphs is hereditary if it is closed under taking induced subgraphs. The \(T\)-free graphs form such a class. Saying it is \(\chi\)-bounded means that there is a function \(f_T:\mathbb N\to\mathbb N\) such that \(\chi(G)\le f_T(\omega(G))\) for every graph in the class. The conjecture asserts this for every nonempty tree; there is no requirement that the same function work for all trees. A negative answer means there are one fixed tree \(T\) and one fixed integer \(r\ge1\) for which chromatic numbers of the permitted hosts have no finite upper bound.
cards.answer_criterion:
Give a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of the proposition or its negation. A positive answer must establish a finite \(B(T,r)\) for every permitted pair and prove the bound for every finite host graph. A nonconstructive existence proof is sufficient; neither a sharp formula nor an efficient colouring algorithm is required.

A negative answer must specify a single finite tree \(T\) and a single integer \(r\ge1\) and prove
\[\forall k\ge1\ \exists G:\quad G\text{ is finite and }T\text{-free},\qquad
\omega(G)\le r,\qquad\chi(G)\ge k.\]
Equivalently, supply such a family \((G_k)_{k\ge1}\) with verified unbounded chromatic number. Changing the excluded tree or clique bound as \(k\) grows does not refute the proposition. One finite example can invalidate a proposed numerical bound but cannot rule out a larger bound.

Bounds depending on host size, special tree families, additional host promises, path-induced copies, or a different colouring parameter do not resolve the full statement. Nor does disproving only a polynomial or computable strengthening refute the unrestricted finite-bound target.
cards.why: Would characterize induced forests as the single forbidden patterns capable of bounding ordinary chromatic number in terms of clique number, clarifying a central structural obstruction to graph colouring and large independent sets.

importance.reason: A central organizing conjecture for hereditary graph colouring and forbidden induced subgraphs, defining the proposed forest boundary for χ-boundedness.

context_blocks.text: A large clique forces many colours, but it is not the only obstruction: triangle-free graphs can also require arbitrarily many colours. The conjecture says that each fixed induced tree must eventually appear in every sufficiently high-chromatic graph with a fixed clique bound. Its force lies in independence from graph size; adding vertices cannot keep increasing the required palette while avoiding the same tree.

Ordinary and induced copies encode different restrictions. A triangle contains a three-vertex path as an ordinary subgraph, but does not induce that path because its endpoints are adjacent. More generally, a complete graph contains every tree on at most its number of vertices as an ordinary subgraph, but no induced tree on three or more vertices. The clique restriction alone does not solve the issue: the conjecture must hold for every fixed clique bound, including triangle-free hosts.

The forest boundary has a precise reason. Graphs can have arbitrarily high chromatic number and girth, where girth is the length of a shortest cycle. If an excluded graph contains a cycle, sufficiently large girth avoids that graph while still allowing unbounded chromatic number and no triangles. The nonempty-forest version of the conjecture is equivalent to the all-trees version: every finite forest is an induced subgraph of some finite tree.

Important tree families are known. Kierstead and Penrice proved the radius-at-most-two case in 1994; radius at most two means that some vertex has distance at most two from every other vertex. Scott and Seymour’s later Theorem 1.6 controls chromatic number polynomially in the part size of an excluded complete multipartite ordinary subgraph, for a fixed number of parts and a fixed radius-two tree. Its polynomial statement in that parameter is not a proof of polynomial dependence on clique number for every tree.

The inherited Nguyen–Scott–Seymour paper proves a weaker embedding theorem for every rooted tree: sufficiently high chromatic number at fixed clique bound forces a path-induced copy. Each root-to-vertex path has no extra edge among its own vertices. Edges between separate branches remain possible, so the entire image need not be an induced tree. Its main theorem therefore does not prove the conjecture stated here.

Their near-linear-stable-set theorem applies to every fixed forest and clique bound: an \(n\)-vertex permitted graph has an independent set of size \(n^{1-o(1)}\) and chromatic number \(n^{o(1)}\). In particular, for every fixed \(\varepsilon>0\), the chromatic bound is eventually at most \(n^\varepsilon\). This is much smaller than any fixed positive power, but can still diverge; \(\log n\) illustrates that distinction.

The same paper bounds fractional chromatic number for multibrooms, obtained by identifying the roots of paths with extra leaves at their far ends. Fractional colouring permits weighted independent sets covering every vertex to total weight at least one; ordinary colouring requires an actual partition. General multibrooms remain an open case of the latter statement in that source.

Davies and Yuditsky’s April 2026 journal theorem treats intersection graphs of axis-aligned boxes in \(\mathbb R^d\), for each fixed dimension \(d\). Vertices represent boxes and adjacency means nonempty intersection. Excluding a fixed induced forest then gives a polynomial bound in clique number, but the polynomial may depend on both the forest and \(d\). This extra dimension parameter prevents the theorem from giving the unrestricted bound in the card.

The conjecture concerns existence of colourings and has consequences for independent-set size, because one colour class must contain at least the number of vertices divided by the number of colours. It does not automatically provide an efficient algorithm for finding either object. Separating the structural assertion from its possible computational refinements keeps the benchmark focused on the established conjecture.
A September 2026 paper studies a tournament analogue using directed clique and chromatic parameters. These differ from the ordinary undirected parameters in this card.
A June 2026 paper instead studies domatic number, which partitions vertices into dominating sets. The shared conjecture name does not make that parameter ordinary chromatic number.

cards.title: Optimal bounds in the Excluded Grid Theorem
cards.formal:
For every integer \(r\ge2\), define
\[f(r)=\min\{t\in\mathbb Z_{\ge0}:\ \forall\text{ finite simple undirected graphs }G,\ \operatorname{tw}(G)\ge t\ \Longrightarrow\ Q_r\text{ is a minor of }G\},\]
where \(Q_r\) is the square grid of side length \(r\). Determine the asymptotic order of \(f(r)\) up to universal constant factors, including all logarithmic or other unbounded factors. In particular, supply an independently specified positive function \(h\) and prove
\[\exists a,b>0\ \exists r_0\ge2\ \forall r\in\mathbb Z_{\ge r_0}:\quad a\,h(r)\le f(r)\le b\,h(r).\]
The constants and the threshold \(r_0\) are independent of the host graph and of \(r\). The problem asks for the actual asymptotic order; it does not assume a quadratic or cubic conjectured answer.
cards.definitions:
Graphs and grids. A finite simple undirected graph \(G=(V,E)\) has a finite vertex set and an edge set consisting of unordered pairs of distinct vertices; there are no loops or parallel edges. The vertex set of \(Q_r\) is \(\{1,\ldots,r\}^2\), and two vertices \((i,j)\) and \((i',j')\) are adjacent exactly when
\[|i-i'|+|j-j'|=1.\]
Thus \(r\) counts the side length, while the grid has \(r^2\) vertices. Host graphs may be disconnected and have arbitrary order, degree and genus.

Minor containment. A graph \(H\) is a minor of \(G\) if there are nonempty vertex subsets \((B_v)_{v\in V(H)}\) of \(V(G)\) such that they are pairwise disjoint, each induced graph \(G[B_v]\) is connected, and for every edge \(uv\in E(H)\) an edge of \(G\) joins \(B_u\) to \(B_v\). These subsets are called branch sets. Extra edges inside or between branch sets are allowed. Equivalently, one may delete vertices and edges and contract edges, then remove loops and merge parallel edges. This is ordinary minor containment, with no prescribed roots, induced-subgraph condition or topological-minor requirement.

Treewidth. A tree decomposition of \(G\) consists of a finite nonempty tree \(T\) and bags \(X_t\subseteq V(G)\) for its nodes such that every vertex lies in a bag, both endpoints of every edge lie together in a bag, and for each vertex the nodes whose bags contain it form a nonempty connected subtree of \(T\). A tree is a connected acyclic undirected graph. The decomposition width is \(\max_{t\in V(T)}|X_t|-1\). The treewidth \(\operatorname{tw}(G)\) is the minimum width over all such decompositions. In particular, the empty graph has treewidth \(-1\) under this convention and has no effect on thresholds \(t\ge0\).

Extremal threshold. The qualitative Grid-Minor Theorem ensures that the defining set of thresholds is nonempty. Since treewidth is integer valued,
\[f(r)=1+\max\{\operatorname{tw}(G):G\text{ is a finite simple undirected graph with no }Q_r\text{ minor}\}.\]
This maximum exists: its set of integer values is nonempty and bounded above by the qualitative theorem. It is a maximum of widths, not a bound on the number of vertices of a grid-excluding graph. Arbitrarily large trees, for example, do not contain \(Q_r\) for \(r\ge2\).

Asymptotic convention. The domain of \(h\) is the integers \(r\ge2\), with values in \(\mathbb R_{>0}\). Bounds must hold at every sufficiently large integer side length. Write \(\log r=\log_2 r\); another fixed logarithm base only changes constant factors. The notation \(\operatorname{polylog}r\) in known bounds denotes \((\log r)^c\) for some fixed nonnegative constant \(c\). It may be suppressed when stating historical progress, but not when claiming matching bounds for this target. This is an extremal existence question, with no algorithm, input encoding, grid-finding time or random-error guarantee imposed on an answer.
cards.answer_criterion:
Give an explicit asymptotic description \(h\) and complete mathematically correct proofs checked in Lean that there are constants \(a,b>0\) and an integer \(r_0\ge2\) for which \(a h(r)\le f(r)\le b h(r)\) at every integer \(r\ge r_0\). The upper bound must apply to all finite simple undirected host graphs; the lower bound must establish grid-excluding graphs with sufficiently large treewidth to give the matching order. No efficient construction of these graphs or of grid models is required.

The description must determine the growth rate rather than rename the defining minimum or maximum. A residual factor that tends to infinity, even a logarithm, fails the constant-factor criterion. Improving only the polynomial exponent, proving a bound with unspecified logarithmic loss, obtaining the result only on planar or fixed-minor-free host graphs, or replacing ordinary minors by another containment relation is insufficient. cards.why: The Grid-Minor Theorem connects an abstract measure of graph connectivity with a concrete planar pattern. Its quantitative loss controls the strength of many structural and parameterized-algorithm results. Determining the optimal loss would identify how much treewidth is inherently needed to force a grid in unrestricted graphs, including whether the remaining logarithmic obstruction captures the whole difficulty.

context_blocks.text: Treewidth records the smallest possible largest bag in a tree decomposition, minus one. Many graph algorithms can process small bags efficiently even when the whole graph is large. A grid is a canonical obstruction to small treewidth. The qualitative theorem says that sufficiently large treewidth forces any fixed grid as a minor; the unresolved issue is the optimal dependence on grid size.

The grid \(Q_r\) itself has treewidth \(r\), but this does not imply a linear threshold for arbitrary host graphs. The complete graph on \(r^2-1\) vertices has treewidth \(r^2-2\), yet cannot contain a minor with \(r^2\) vertices. Thus \(f(r)\ge r^2-1\). Branch sets can contract large parts of a host, but they must remain pairwise disjoint and nonempty.

The established lower bound is stronger: \(f(r)=\Omega(r^2\log r)\). The cited work attributes it to Robertson, Seymour and Thomas using constant-degree expanders of logarithmic girth. Such graphs combine treewidth proportional to their order with long shortest cycles; a large grid minor forces many disjoint cycles in the host. The extra logarithmic obstruction survives even for sparse graphs.

Chekuri and Chuzhoy first made the relationship polynomial. Their theorem is stated in the reverse direction: treewidth \(k\) guarantees grid side length at least a constant times \(k^{1/98}\) divided by a fixed power of \(\log k\). Equivalently, it gives an upper bound \(f(r)=O(r^{98}\operatorname{polylog}r)\). Confusing side length with vertex count, or the threshold with this inverse guarantee, changes the exponents.

That first polynomial result is constructive and gives a randomized polynomial-time procedure for finding a grid model at its guaranteed scale. The present question asks for the best existence threshold. An improved structural bound would answer the mathematical upper-bound side even without a matching grid-finding algorithm; algorithmic guarantees must be assessed separately.

Chuzhoy and Tan prove \(f(r)\le C r^9(\log r)^c\) for absolute constants \(C,c>0\). The 2026 revised product-structure paper and the SODA 2026 fixed-minor paper still cite this general quantitative result. It remains far above the quadratic-logarithmic lower bound. Knowing the leading polynomial exponent alone would also leave the card unfinished if an unbounded logarithmic gap remained.

The literature records different predictions. Robertson, Seymour and Thomas conjectured that the \(r^2\log r\) lower bound is tight, whereas Demaine and coauthors conjectured cubic growth. The target here is the true asymptotic order. Even an upper bound of the form \(r^2\) times an unspecified power of \(\log r\) would not by itself establish the required matching constant-factor characterization.

The Grid-Minor Theorem Revisited gives a finer structural description: graphs excluding a fixed planar graph embed as subgraphs of clique blow-ups of graphs of controlled treewidth. A clique blow-up replaces each vertex by a fixed-size complete graph and every original edge by all edges between the corresponding cliques. The factor controlling the clique size may depend on the excluded graph, so the theorem does not determine this card’s optimal numerical dependence on grid side length.

Catching Rats in H-minor-free Graphs proves that excluding both a fixed graph \(H\) and \(Q_r\) gives treewidth \(O(g_H r+t^{2304})\), where \(t=|V(H)|\) and \(g_H\) is the Euler genus of \(H\). Euler genus is the minimum value \(2-\chi\) of a closed connected surface admitting an embedding, with \(\chi\) its Euler characteristic. Since \(g_H=O(t^2)\), the paper also gives \(O(t^2r+t^{2304})\). For fixed \(H\), the dependence on \(r\) is linear.

The additional exclusion in that theorem matters. General host graphs do not avoid a common fixed \(H\). Choosing \(H=Q_r\) is allowed for a grid-excluding graph, but then \(H\) varies with \(r\) and \(t=r^2\); it cannot yield a linear universal threshold. This distinction prevents a sharp special-class result from being mistaken for a solution of the all-graphs problem.

The ICALP 2026 paper studies a designated set of vertices and grid models whose every branch set meets that set. It obtains polynomial bounds for the corresponding structural decomposition. Those bounds concern an annotated generalization and are not a matching estimate of the ordinary threshold defined here. Additional structure in a decomposition and an optimal numerical treewidth bound are different conclusions.

The May 2026 disjoint-paths preprint sharpens bounds for vital linkages and for vertices whose deletion preserves bounded-size rooted-minor information. Its parameters include the number of terminals and the size of a grid rooted on an annotated set. Despite the phrase “Optimal Bounds” in the title, its theorems do not claim a constant-factor characterization of the unrestricted excluded-grid threshold.

Sharper general grid bounds affect the quantitative consequences of routing, packing-versus-covering results and parameterized algorithms. Their role is to turn sufficiently large treewidth into a usable grid, or to bound treewidth when such a grid is absent. Matching lower bounds would also identify an unavoidable limitation of that structural implication.

cards.title: Caccetta–Häggkvist conjecture
cards.formal:
For every integer \(n\ge2\), every integer \(r\) with \(1\le r\le n-1\), and every simple loopless digraph \(D=(V,A)\) on \(n\) vertices, does
\[\bigl(\forall v\in V:\ d_D^+(v)\ge r\bigr)\quad\Longrightarrow\quad\bigl(\exists\text{ a directed cycle of length }\ell\le\lceil n/r\rceil\bigr)\]
hold? Opposite arcs are allowed, and a pair of opposite arcs counts as a directed cycle of length two. The bound is exact, for every permitted pair \((n,r)\), with no additive error.
cards.definitions:
A simple loopless digraph consists of a finite set \(V\), with \(|V|=n\), and an arc set
\[A\subseteq\{(u,v)\in V\times V:u\ne v\}.\]
There is at most one copy of each ordered pair; both \((u,v)\) and \((v,u)\) may occur. Relabeling the vertices by \(\{1,\ldots,n\}\) changes no requirement. The out-neighborhood and outdegree of a vertex are
\[N_D^+(v)=\{w\in V:(v,w)\in A\},\qquad d_D^+(v)=|N_D^+(v)|.\]
The minimum outdegree is \(\delta^+(D)=\min_{v\in V}d_D^+(v)\). Every vertex must meet the lower bound; an average-degree bound or a condition on only some vertices is not the hypothesis.

A directed cycle of length \(\ell\) is a sequence of pairwise distinct vertices \(v_0,\ldots,v_{\ell-1}\), where \(2\le\ell\le n\), such that \((v_i,v_{i+1})\in A\) for \(0\le i<\ell-1\) and \((v_{\ell-1},v_0)\in A\). It need not be induced: additional arcs among these vertices are allowed. Length counts arcs, equivalently the number of distinct vertices on the cycle. The closing return to \(v_0\) is not counted as an additional vertex. A repeated-vertex closed walk is not the cycle witness specified here.

The directed girth \(g(D)\) is the minimum length of a directed cycle, with value \(+\infty\) if there is none. Under the positive minimum-outdegree hypothesis it is finite. The ceiling is the least integer at least the real quotient \(n/r\); equivalently, \(\lceil n/r\rceil=\lfloor(n+r-1)/r\rfloor\) for the positive integers used here. Thus the target can also be written
\[g(D)\le\lceil n/r\rceil,\quad\text{or equivalently}\quad n\ge r(g(D)-1)+1.\]
It does not assert \(g(D)\le n/r\) without rounding.

No lower bound on indegree is imposed. In particular, a graph need not be regular, strongly connected, vertex-transitive, planar or randomly generated. An oriented graph is the restricted case with no opposite pair of arcs. The target includes oriented graphs and all the other simple loopless digraphs above. This is a finite extremal existence statement, with no construction, search-algorithm, encoding or computational resource requirement.
cards.answer_criterion: Provide a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of the universal proposition or its logical negation. A positive answer must cover all integers \(n,r\) in the stated ranges and all eligible digraphs, producing a cycle with the exact ceiling bound. A negative answer may specify finite \(n,r\) and a finite arc set, but must prove in Lean both the minimum-outdegree condition and the absence of every directed cycle of lengths \(2,\ldots,\lceil n/r\rceil\). A proof of the full logical negation without an explicitly listed counterexample also qualifies. An asymptotic estimate, an additive-constant relaxation, a special degree value, or an extra regularity, indegree or forbidden-subgraph hypothesis settles only a restricted statement.
cards.why: The conjecture asks whether a lower bound on every vertex’s number of outgoing neighbors forces a cycle at the sharp possible length. It would determine the exact universal relation between a local directed-degree condition and global cyclic structure. Even the dense regime that should force a directed triangle remains a major unresolved case, despite broad approximate bounds and results for symmetric graph classes.

context_blocks.text: Positive minimum outdegree already guarantees that some directed cycle exists. The content of the conjecture is its exact length guarantee as the degree grows. Requiring the bound at every vertex matters: many arcs in total can coexist with acyclicity if vertices near the end of a directed ordering have small outdegree. There is no corresponding escape from the positive minimum-degree assumption.

The ceiling is essential, and the conjectured bound is sharp for every allowed \((n,r)\). The standard extremal digraph has vertices modulo \(n\), with arcs from \(i\) to \(i+1,\ldots,i+r\), using residues modulo \(n\). Its outdegree is \(r\) and its directed girth is exactly \(\lceil n/r\rceil\). These are existing extremal examples, rather than evidence that all digraphs obey the bound.

Two uses of the parameter must be distinguished. The fixed-degree case \(r=3\) is known, but the triangle-forcing regime \(r\ge n/3\) is not thereby settled. In the latter regime the degree grows with the number of vertices. For an oriented graph the conjecture predicts a directed triangle at minimum outdegree at least \(n/3\); in the more general model of this card a directed two-cycle is also an acceptable outcome.

Hladký, Král’ and Norin establish a directed triangle at minimum outdegree at least \(0.3465n\) in an oriented graph. Their paper explicitly forbids opposite arcs in its definition of “digraph.” This is a published advance toward the \(n/3\) threshold, rather than the threshold itself. The April 2026 paper still cites it as the best known partial result for this regime.

The conjecture is known for fixed minimum-degree thresholds \(r=1,2,3,4,5\), and for vertex-transitive digraphs, where an arc-preserving permutation can send any chosen vertex to any other. These successes cover substantial families but do not impose the required conclusion on an arbitrary nonsymmetric digraph. A regular graph, whose indegrees and outdegrees are all the same, need not be vertex-transitive.

Approximate girth estimates also leave a genuine exact question. Hompe and Huynh recall Shen’s universal bound \(\lceil n/r\rceil+73\). Their own 2025 article proves an additive-constant result for the stronger rainbow-cycle setting, with an error depending on the fixed color-class size. Neither additive relaxation supplies the exact ceiling required here.

A rainbow cycle has no repeated edge color. Aharoni’s conjecture asks for a short rainbow cycle in an edge-colored graph with as many color classes as vertices and sufficiently many edges in each class; the general rainbow conjecture would imply the directed conjecture. The implication is not an equivalence assertion, and a theorem for a restricted family of color classes does not establish the universal directed result.

Guo’s 2026 journal article obtains logarithmic rainbow girth when a positive fraction of the color classes have specified non-star structure, under its size conditions. An edge set is a star when all its edges meet at one vertex. Such extra structure excludes the all-star configurations relevant to the extremal directed examples. The paper explicitly retains both the directed and general rainbow conjectures as open.

Steiner’s April 2026 preprint proves a different conjecture about regular digraphs: the number of directed cycles through a common vertex, disjoint away from that vertex, must grow at least linearly with the common degree. It also proves a directed tree-width result. The introduction separately states that the exact degree–girth conjecture remains open even for regular digraphs. Counting many overlapping cycles does not itself give the sharp shortest-cycle length in this card.

The 28 July 2026 revision of the DeVos and coauthors paper retains the exact rainbow theorem for color classes of size at least two. The arXiv revision note concerns a correction in a later matroid theorem. It should not be mistaken for a newly proved all-degree Caccetta–Häggkvist theorem merely because the paper reappeared among recent revisions.

A 2008 preprint claims a complete proof, but its stated labeling lemma does not establish the required universal path bound: a small digraph passing its degree and labeling conditions violates that bound. The review records the explicit check. The later primary papers inspected here continue to state the general conjecture as open; the historical proof claim is not treated as a verified resolution.

For n vertices and minimum outdegree at least r, it predicts a cycle of length at most the ceiling of n divided by r.
The graph may contain opposite arcs, which form a two-cycle, but has no loops or repeated arcs.
The target is an exact theorem for every graph and degree threshold, with no extra regularity or indegree assumption.
Sharp examples and many partial results are known, while the recent rainbow and regular-digraph results do not resolve the general statement.
