cards.title: Almost-linear triangle detection
cards.formal: Does there exist one uniform randomized word-RAM algorithm that, on every finite simple undirected graph with n vertices and m edges given by adjacency lists, decides whether a triangle exists with success probability at least \(2/3\) and worst-case running time \((n+m+2)^{1+o(1)}\)?
cards.definitions: A triangle is a set of three distinct vertices u,v,w for which all three unordered edges \(\{u,v\},\{v,w\},\{w,u\}\) are present. The input gives labelled vertices \(1,\ldots ,n\) and explicit adjacency lists; it is promised to describe a simple undirected graph, and can be disconnected or contain isolated vertices. The RAM has words of \(w=\lceil 4 \log _{2}(n+2)\rceil\) bits, random-access memory, and unit-cost word reads/writes, comparisons, Boolean operations, shifts, addition, subtraction and multiplication modulo 2ʷ, and integer division by a nonzero word. Independent random words may be generated at unit cost. Input reading and all preprocessing count toward time. The running-time bound holds for every graph and every random tape, while correctness probability is over the algorithm’s internal randomness. The \(o(1)\) is a function tending to zero as \(n+m\) tends to infinity, for this one fixed algorithm; equivalently, for every \(\varepsilon >0\) the same algorithm eventually uses at most \((n+m+2)^{1+\varepsilon}\) operations. There is no promise on density, degree, arboricity or triangle count. Matrix multiplication and other algebraic techniques are allowed if their implementation fits this machine model. Only one yes/no answer is required.
cards.answer_criterion: Construct and analyze an algorithm meeting the stated all-input time and probability guarantees, or prove that no such algorithm exists. A deterministic \(O(n+m)\) algorithm would be an even stronger positive answer. A fixed exponent above one, an \(O(n^{2})\) bound that is only input-linear on dense graphs, output-sensitive listing, or an algorithm restricted to bounded-arboricity graphs does not settle the question. The target fixes the original draft’s “linear or at least almost-linear” alternative at the precise almost-linear threshold.
cards.why: Determine whether detecting the simplest cyclic graph pattern requires a superlinear amount of computation beyond reading the input.

importance.reason: A fundamental graph primitive and fine-grained hardness assumption with consequences for dynamic data structures, joins and string matching.

progress.text: Chiba–Nishizeki give \(O(m\cdot a(G))\) triangle listing, yielding linear time for bounded-arboricity families.

context_blocks.text: Triangle detection is among the smallest nontrivial pattern-finding tasks in a graph. The pattern has only three vertices, but a graph may contain an enormous number of possible triples. The question asks whether all the relevant combinations can be handled in essentially the time required to read the graph. It must also handle triangle-free instances, where an algorithm cannot stop upon finding a convenient local witness.

Detection is different from listing. A complete graph has \(\Theta (n^{2})\) input edges and \(\Theta (n^{3})\) triangles, so explicitly listing every triangle cannot take linear time in the input size. A yes/no answer has constant output size and faces no such output-size obstruction. Likewise, approximate counting or finding triangles in a distribution of random inputs does not supply an exact decision guarantee on every adversarial graph.

Chiba and Nishizeki give triangle listing in \(O(m\cdot a(G))\) time, apart from reading isolated vertices, where arboricity \(a(G)\) is the minimum number of forests needed to cover the graph’s edges. This gives linear time on any family of bounded arboricity, including planar graphs. General graphs can have arboricity of order \(\sqrt{m}\), so this approach has a superlinear worst-case cost. A sparse graph can still contain a dense, difficult region.

Alon, Yuster and Zwick improve the general sparse-graph bound using a degree threshold. Handle triangles touching a low-degree vertex by local enumeration, and use matrix multiplication on the smaller set of high-degree vertices. For an available square matrix-multiplication exponent \(\tau\), the resulting standard bound is \(O(n+m^{2\tau /(\tau +1)})\), roughly \(O(n+m^{1.407})\) at familiar current exponents. The optimization balances the cost of the two parts.

Even setting the matrix-multiplication exponent to two in this particular reduction leaves exponent \(4/3\) in m. Thus faster dense multiplication alone, inserted into the same degree-splitting argument, would not make the sparse algorithm almost linear. This is an observation about the upper-bound method, not a proof that a different graph algorithm cannot do better.

Abboud and Vassilevska Williams formulate a no-almost-linear triangle hypothesis and use it to derive conditional lower bounds for dynamic problems. The conjecture concerns general algorithms on logarithmic-word RAMs. Their separate combinatorial Boolean-matrix-multiplication conjecture restricts the kinds of techniques used; it should not be substituted for the unrestricted question here. Reductions transfer assumed hardness, rather than establish an unconditional superlinear lower bound.

The distinction remains useful in current work. Kumabe and Uezato’s ICALP 2026 paper reduces triangle detection to matching certain fixed regular expressions with two backreference uses. Consequently, an almost-linear algorithm for that matching task would also give an almost-linear triangle algorithm. This illustrates why a small graph pattern can govern complexity in a seemingly unrelated setting.

Search results require source checks. Dumitrescu’s March 2024 claim of faster combinatorial triangle algorithms was withdrawn three days after posting; the author states that the algorithm may fail and identifies an invalid case analysis. It is not an established improvement.

I also checked the parent-edge rule in Vega’s August 2025 linear-time proposal. Consider the path 0–1–2–3–4–5–6 plus edges 0–3, 3–6 and 0–6. A legal DFS follows the whole path. Its unique triangle is \(\{0,3,6\}\), consisting entirely of back edges. No test restricted to a DFS parent, its child and a common neighbour can find it. A local simulation and exhaustive triple check confirm this counterexample to the stated rule; this is not a test of later replacement implementations.

A separate September 2026 Aegypti revision claims \(O(n^{2})\) time via bucket reduction. That claimed bound is not almost linear for every sparse input, even if its correctness were established. I have not adjudicated its different proof. An all-density statement must keep both n and m visible: a dense-case breakthrough and an input-linear sparse algorithm are distinct achievements.

A resolution would identify whether a basic three-way adjacency condition inherently requires substantial work beyond scanning an explicit graph. A positive algorithm would affect graph-pattern routines and invalidate hardness assumptions used by many reductions. A negative result would provide a major unconditional lower bound for a simple polynomial-time graph problem on a strong, standard machine model.

cards.title: Seese’s conjecture
cards.formal: For every isomorphism-closed class C of finite simple undirected graphs, does decidability of its MSO\(_{1}\) satisfiability problem imply that some constant k bounds the clique-width of every graph in C?
cards.definitions: An MSO\(_{1}\) sentence is built from vertex equality, adjacency \(E(x,y)\), membership \(x\in X\) in vertex sets, Boolean connectives, and quantification over individual vertices and subsets of the vertex set. There is no built-in vertex order, edge-set quantification, parity predicate or other counting extension. For a fixed class \(C, Sat_{MSO_{1}}(C)\) consists of all finite encoded MSO\(_{1}\) sentences \(\varphi\) for which some \(G\in C\) satisfies \(\varphi\). Decidable means that one Turing machine, allowed to depend on C, halts and answers correctly for every input sentence. C itself is not an input to that machine; no complexity bound is required. By negating sentences this is equivalent to deciding the theory \(Th_{MSO_{1}}(C)\)={\(\varphi\): every \(G\in C\) satisfies \(\varphi\)}. A k-expression builds a labeled graph from single vertices with labels in \([k]\), disjoint union, relabeling every vertex of one label to another, and adding all edges between two distinct labels. The clique-width \(\operatorname{cw}(G)\) is the smallest k permitting such an expression after labels are forgotten; set \(\operatorname{cw}(\varnothing )=0\). The conclusion is \(\exists k\forall G\in C \operatorname{cw}(G)\le k\), with k depending on C. No hereditary, minor-closed, bounded-degree or finite-forbidden-subgraph assumption is imposed.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove the implication for every such graph class, or give one class of unbounded clique-width together with a correct terminating algorithm for its entire MSO\(_{1}\) satisfiability problem. A single finite graph cannot refute a uniform width bound for a class. Model checking on a supplied graph, or decidability with a promise about sentence size, is not the premise. Results requiring parity predicates or restricted graph classes do not prove the full statement.
cards.why: A major proposed structural necessity for logical decidability, connecting graph decompositions, finite model theory and algorithms over infinite families of finite inputs.

importance.reason: A foundational conjecture asking whether bounded clique-width is unavoidable whenever an entire graph class has decidable vertex-set monadic logic.

progress.text: Seese establishes foundational connections between decidable monadic graph theories and bounded structural width, and formulates the conjectural MSO\(_{1}\) boundary.
Courcelle–Oum prove that decidable MSO\(_{1}\) with parity predicates implies bounded clique-width.
Dawar–Sankaran develop the antichain/minimal-hereditary-class reduction for the stronger grid-interpretation conjecture; preprint 2020, CSL 2022, journal volume 2025.
Mählmann characterizes bounded shrub-depth through logical expressiveness and records a stronger MSO-dependence conjecture that would imply Seese’s.
Duron–Mählmann–Toruńczyk prove bounded clique-width for hereditary 2-WQO classes; the hypothesis differs from decidability of MSO\(_{1}\) satisfiability.

cards.status_note: Reviewed through 11 September 2026. Seese’s MSO\(_{1}\) decidability implication remains unresolved in the checked primary literature. The parity extension, the shrub-depth expressiveness characterization and the July 2026 2-WQO result have distinct hypotheses or conclusions.

context_blocks.text: An MSO\(_{1}\) sentence can describe a graph property by quantifying over sets of vertices. Three-colorability, for example, can be expressed by choosing three sets that partition the vertices and requiring each set to be independent. Checking such a sentence on one finite graph is always decidable by exhaustive search. The premise here is much stronger: from a sentence alone, decide whether it holds in at least one member of an entire, potentially infinite graph class.

Clique-width measures how many vertex labels are needed to construct a graph using a small repertoire of operations. Labels identify groups of vertices that receive the same future edge additions. Dense graphs can have small clique-width: a complete graph can be built with two labels by inserting one vertex, joining it to all previous vertices, and merging its label. Thus the conjectured structural restriction is not a sparsity condition.

The classical treewidth theorem provides the motivation. Seese proves structural restrictions from decidability of monadic theories, and the version allowing quantification over edge sets forces bounded treewidth. Grid-minor machinery supports that argument. The MSO\(_{1}\) conjecture replaces edge-set quantification by vertex-set quantification and asks for bounded clique-width instead. Transferring the proof requires a logical way of recovering the appropriate obstruction.

Bounded-width descriptions support decidability because graph properties can be translated into properties of construction trees. In particular, for each fixed k the full class of graphs of clique-width at most k has decidable MSO\(_{1}\) satisfiability. But the conjecture is only a necessary-condition statement for an arbitrary class C. One cannot infer that every subclass of a bounded-width class has decidable theory.

For a simple reason, such a converse would be false. Choose an undecidable set S of positive integers, and let C contain exactly the edgeless graphs whose numbers of vertices belong to S. All those graphs have clique-width one. A sentence specifying exactly n vertices would decide whether \(n\in S\) if satisfiability over C were decidable. Restricting which sizes occur can encode undecidability even when each individual graph has trivial structure.

Courcelle–Oum prove the implication after extending MSO\(_{1}\) with the predicate \(Even(X)\), saying that a vertex set has even cardinality. Their vertex-minor and isotropic-system machinery establishes bounded clique-width from decidability of this stronger logic. This strengthens the premise: a decision procedure for ordinary MSO\(_{1}\) sentences need not handle parity sentences. Therefore their theorem supplies substantial progress while leaving the exact statement here open.

Hereditary classes, which are closed under taking induced subgraphs, are a useful focus even though the card quantifies over all classes. If satisfiability is decidable on C, it is also decidable on its hereditary closure: ask whether some vertex subset induces a graph satisfying the input sentence, using a relativized MSO\(_{1}\) formula. Unbounded clique-width is preserved on passing to that larger class. Thus a proof covering all hereditary classes would suffice.

Dawar–Sankaran develop a stronger route through interpreting arbitrarily large grids. Their Theorem 3.2 reduces that stronger assertion to two settings: antichains of unbounded clique-width under induced-subgraph containment, and minimal hereditary classes of unbounded clique-width. They verify the grid interpretation for the known minimal families studied in their paper. This is a research program and collection of cases, not a completed classification of all such families.

The inherited ICALP 2025 paper by Mählmann settles a different boundary: on hereditary classes, bounded shrub-depth characterizes coincidence of first-order and monadic second-order expressive power. Its conclusion formulates a stronger conjectural relationship between clique-width and MSO dependence, explaining how parts of that conjecture would imply Seese’s. Shrub-depth and clique-width are distinct parameters, and a theorem about expressive power does not by itself decide satisfiability.

Duron–Mählmann–Toruńczyk’s July 2026 preprint proves that every hereditary 2-WQO class has bounded clique-width. Here 2-WQO means that every infinite sequence of graphs with two possible vertex labels contains an earlier graph embedding as a label-preserving induced subgraph of a later one. This resolves a related structural conjecture, but it starts from a well-quasi-ordering hypothesis. It does not turn an arbitrary MSO\(_{1}\) decision procedure into such an ordering property.

The unresolved implication asks whether decidable graph theories always have bounded constructional complexity. A proof would show that broad logical decidability cannot arise from some entirely different mechanism on classes of unbounded clique-width. A counterexample would reveal precisely such a mechanism. Either outcome would change how structural graph theory explains the limits of automated reasoning over whole families of finite structures.

cards.title: Exact directed maximum flow in \(O((m+n) \operatorname{polylog} n)\) time
cards.formal: For every fixed integer \(a\ge 1\), do there exist a constant \(k\ge 0\) and a uniform classical randomized algorithm \(A_{a}\) that, on every directed graph with \(n\ge 2\) vertices, m arcs, distinguished distinct vertices s,t and integer capacities in \(\{0,\ldots ,n^{a}\}\), outputs an exact maximum s–t flow with probability at least \(2/3\) in worst-case time \(O((m+n)(\log (n+2))^{k})\)?
cards.definitions: The graph is explicitly given by its labelled vertex set \(\{1,\ldots ,n\}\) and an arc list, with no loops and at most one arc per ordered vertex pair; opposite arcs are allowed. A flow assigns an integer \(f_{e}\) to each arc, with \(0\le f_{e}\le u_{e}\) and equal incoming and outgoing sums at every vertex other than s,t. Its value is the outgoing sum at s minus the incoming sum at s; maximum refers to the largest such value. Output the m flow values, not only an approximate value. Use a word RAM with word length \(B_{a}\lceil \log _{2}(n+2)\rceil\) for a fixed integer \(B_{a}\) large enough to store capacities, total flow and memory addresses. Unit-cost operations are random-access word reads/writes, comparisons, Boolean operations, shifts, addition, subtraction, multiplication modulo \(2^{w}\) and integer division of nonzero divisors. Multiword computations are charged for their component operations. Independent fair random bits are allowed, with each generated word charged. All preprocessing and output are included, and the time bound holds on every random execution. There are no oracles or input-dependent advice. \(A_{a}, k, B_{a}\) and the hidden constant may depend on a, but not on the graph. The \(m+n\) convention includes explicitly listed isolated vertices.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove the proposition in the problem statement or its logical negation, with all definitions, promises, resource bounds and quantifiers as stated. A conditional result establishes only the explicitly conditional claim. Benchmark acceptance requires a complete proof-assistant-verified proof of the full target.

context_blocks.text: Maximum flow is a basic model for routing through capacity constraints. A feasible solution must obey conservation at intermediate vertices, and optimality measures the largest transferable amount between two terminals. Even a graph with small integer capacities can require globally coordinated changes to a feasible routing. The question asks whether finding the exact optimum can cost only a polylogarithmic factor more than reading the graph.

Almost-linear algorithms already represent a major qualitative advance. Chen and coauthors obtained exact maximum flow and minimum-cost flow in \(m^{1+o(1)}\) time for polynomially bounded integral data. Li and Wice’s August 2026 preprint obtains an almost-linear maximum-flow bound through a different framework. Neither stated asymptotic guarantee is \(O(m \operatorname{polylog} n)\).

The distinction concerns the remaining overhead. For example, \(\exp (\sqrt{\log  n})\) is subpolynomial in n but exceeds every fixed power of log n. A running time containing that factor can be almost linear without satisfying this card. Removing the residual gap would identify a sharper computational cost for a central graph optimization primitive.

Exactness is also a substantive part of the target. A flow whose value is within a fixed relative error of optimum does not determine the optimum integer value when that value is large. Conversely, restricting capacities to polynomial magnitude means their binary encodings occupy logarithmically many bits each. The question is therefore not asking an algorithm to read arbitrarily long capacities in a graph-size-only time bound.

The primary topic is a static graph algorithm, so the current catalogue places the question in Structural graph theory and graph algorithms. Dynamic maintenance, parallel computation and strong polynomiality for unbounded-bit linear programming impose different requirements. No existing maximum-matching or dynamic-connectivity card represents this flow target.

cards.title: Vertex reconstruction conjecture
cards.formal: For every integer \(n\ge 3\) and every pair of finite simple undirected graphs G,H on n vertices, does equality \(D(G)=D(H)\) of their vertex decks imply that G and H are isomorphic?
cards.why: The conjecture asks whether all overlapping one-vertex views determine an entire graph. It tests how much structural information survives deletion and loss of labels, and connects graph structure to reconstruction and isomorphism problems.

Heinrich and coauthors’ revised preprint proves every interval graph of order at least three reconstructible, with a polynomial-time reconstruction consequence.

cards.definitions: A finite simple undirected graph \(G=(V,E)\) has a finite vertex set V and an edge set E consisting of unordered two-element subsets of V; there are no loops or parallel edges. An isomorphism from G to H is a bijection \(f:V(G)\to V(H)\) such that \(\{u,v\}\) is an edge of G if and only if \(\{f(u),f(v)\}\) is an edge of H. Write \([G]\) for its isomorphism class. For \(v\in V(G), G- v\) is the induced graph on \(V(G)\setminus \{v\}\): remove v and exactly the edges incident with v. Define \(D(G)\) to be the multiset \(\{[G- v]:v\in V(G)\}\), with one entry for every deleted vertex. Thus \(D(G)=D(H)\) means that for each isomorphism class K of graphs on \(n- 1\) vertices, the number of vertices v with \([G- v]=K\) equals the corresponding number for H. Each entry forgets all original vertex labels, including the identity of the deleted vertex; repeated isomorphism classes retain their multiplicities. All graphs, including disconnected graphs and graphs with isolated vertices, are included. The question is a structural uniqueness statement and imposes no running-time requirement on an algorithm.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove that equal vertex decks imply isomorphism for every \(n\ge 3\), or refute the conjecture by exhibiting two nonisomorphic finite simple undirected graphs with \(n\ge 3\) and identical decks, with proofs of those properties.

context_blocks.text: Imagine receiving every graph obtained by deleting one vertex from an unknown graph, with the vertex labels erased in each view. Different deletions can yield identical-looking graphs, and their number of occurrences remains part of the data. The conjecture says this complete collection determines the original graph uniquely up to relabeling.

For a path on three vertices, deleting either endpoint leaves a single edge, while deleting the middle vertex leaves two isolated vertices. Its deck therefore consists of two copies of the edge and one edgeless two-vertex graph. The triangle instead has three copies of the edge. The lower limit of three vertices is necessary: an edge and an edgeless graph on two vertices both have a deck of two isolated single vertices.

Some global information survives deletion automatically. If \(n\ge 3\), every original edge appears in exactly \(n- 2\) members of the deck, so the total number of edges is the sum of the edge counts in the deck divided by \(n- 2\). Comparing each member’s edge count with that total also recovers the multiset of vertex degrees. These counts do not specify how all vertices fit together; that missing arrangement is the substance of the question.

Uniqueness has a different meaning from efficient recovery. There are finitely many graphs of a fixed order, so one can always enumerate those whose decks match the input. The conjecture says there is just one matching isomorphism class whenever the input is the deck of a graph with at least three vertices. It does not require that this enumeration be replaced by a polynomial-time algorithm.

McKay reports exhaustive verification through 13 vertices, and the 2026 revision by Heinrich and coauthors proves reconstruction for every interval graph with at least three vertices. Neither a finite range nor this particular graph class covers all finite graphs. The computations and proofs were not independently reproduced in this review.

A 2026 AI-assisted result concerns a structured bipartite incidence-deletion analogue: it retains the deleted vertex as an isolated vertex, preserves a given bipartition in isomorphisms, and assumes 2-connectivity and pairwise distinct vertex types. Its theorem is not the unrestricted vertex reconstruction conjecture.

The status record also preserves a 2024 general proof claim by O’Shea and Wilkins. Its publisher abstract was checked, but the full argument was inaccessible and is not validated here. Later specialist sources still formulate the general conjecture as open, so this review does not label it resolved.

cards.title: Berge–Fulkerson conjecture
cards.formal: Does every finite loopless bridgeless cubic multigraph G have an ordered list \((M_{1},\ldots ,M_{6})\) of perfect matchings such that for every edge \(e\in E(G), |\{i\in \{1,\ldots ,6\}:e\in M_{i}\}|=2\)?
cards.definitions: Edges of a multigraph have distinct identities and may share their unordered pair of endpoints; loops are forbidden. Cubic means every vertex has degree three, counting incident edge identities with multiplicity. A bridge is an edge whose deletion increases the number of connected components, and bridgeless graphs have none. Disconnected graphs are allowed. A matching is a subset of edges no two of which share an endpoint. It is perfect if every vertex is incident with exactly one of its edges. The six matchings may repeat; membership counts positions in the list, not just distinct subsets. cards.title: Barnette’s conjecture
cards.formal: Is every finite simple undirected graph that is 3-connected, cubic, bipartite and planar Hamiltonian?
cards.definitions: A simple graph has neither loops nor parallel edges. It is 3-connected if it has at least four vertices and deleting any set of at most two vertices leaves a connected graph. Cubic means every vertex has degree exactly three. Bipartite means its vertices admit a partition into two sets with no edge having both endpoints in the same set. Planar means it has a drawing in the plane whose edge interiors do not intersect and contain no vertices; different edges may meet only at shared endpoints. A Hamiltonian cycle is a cyclic ordering \(v_{1},\ldots ,v_{n}\) of all vertices, each appearing exactly once, such that \(\{v_{i},v_{i+1}\}\) is an edge for every i, with \(v_{n+1}=v_{1}\). The cycle must use only edges already present in the graph. No algorithmic running-time guarantee is requested.

cards.title: Seymour’s second-neighborhood conjecture
cards.formal: Does every finite nonempty oriented graph D contain a vertex v for which |\(N^{++}(v)|\ge |N^{+}(v)|\), where \(N^{+}(v)\) consists of vertices at directed distance one from v and \(N^{++}(v)\) consists of vertices at directed distance exactly two?
cards.definitions: An oriented graph is a finite vertex set V and an arc set \(A\subseteq V\times V\) with no loops and with at most one of \((u,v),(v,u)\) present for each distinct pair. Arc multiplicities are not allowed. \(N^{+}(v)=\{u:(v,u)\in A\}\). \(N^{++}(v)\)={\(w\in V\setminus (N^{+}(v)\cup \{v\})\): there exists u with \((v,u)\in A\) and \((u,w)\in A\)}. Thus a vertex already in the first neighborhood is not counted in the second, even if it is also reachable by a length-two walk. Cardinalities count vertices rather than paths or arcs. A sink has both sets empty and satisfies the inequality. No lower bound on outdegree, connectivity or planarity is imposed.

cards.title: Strongly polynomial near-linear negative-weight shortest paths
cards.formal: Do there exist a uniform randomized comparison-addition algorithm and constants \(C>0\), \(k\ge0\) that compute all exact distances from one specified source in every directed graph with arbitrary real arc lengths and no negative directed cycle, using at most \(C(m+n)(\log(n+2))^{k}\) operations and succeeding with probability at least \(2/3\)?
cards.definitions: The graph is given by its vertex set \([n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}\), with \(n\ge2\), and an explicit list of \(m\) arcs. It has no loops and at most one arc per ordered pair; opposite arcs are allowed. Arc lengths may be positive, zero or negative. A path length is the sum of its arc lengths; the empty path has length zero. Output the minimum source-to-vertex path length for every vertex, or an infinity marker if unreachable. The promise excludes negative cycles anywhere in the graph. Use a uniform comparison-addition RAM. Real cells contain exact real numbers and support copying, addition, subtraction and comparison at unit cost; fixed rational program constants are allowed. Real multiplication, division, floor, bit extraction and conversion of an input-dependent real to an integer are not primitives. Integer control and address words have \(d\lceil\log_{2}(n+2)\rceil\) bits for a fixed constant \(d\), with unit-cost Boolean operations, shifts, comparison and arithmetic on words. Integer operations cannot inspect real encodings. A fixed finite program receives no advice or free tables. Memory accesses, control, preprocessing and output all count. Bounds are uniform over all real edge values. Randomness consists of independent uniform random words, each generated at unit cost. On every input, the whole output must be correct with probability at least \(2/3\). The time bound holds for every random execution, including unsuccessful ones. The operation bound is independent of all magnitudes and numerical encoding lengths. On rational inputs, intermediate values must have bit length polynomial in the total binary input length; this is the usual additional encoding condition for strong polynomiality.

context_blocks.text: Negative lengths allow shortest paths to express costs, credits and difference constraints. They make the numerical model essential: a graph-size bound uniform over real weights is stronger than a bound depending on the number of bits in integer weights.

Bernstein, Nanongkai and Wulff-Nilsen obtained near-linear integer-weight shortest paths with a \(\log W\) dependence. Bringmann, Cassis and Fischer improve the logarithmic factors and explicitly ask whether strong polynomiality can remove that dependence.

The February 2026 preprint by Li, Li and Zhang gives \(n^{2+o(1)}\) time for real weights. This is almost linear for dense graphs, but it neither has polylogarithmic overhead nor gives the requested sparse-graph bound.
Mareš supplies the shortest-path background; the endpoint and status distinctions here come from the later research papers.

cards.title: Strongly polynomial maximum flow below the \(mn\) barrier
cards.formal: Do there exist a constant \(\varepsilon\in(0,1/2)\) and a uniform randomized strongly polynomial algorithm that computes an exact maximum flow in every directed network with arbitrary nonnegative rational capacities, \(n\ge2\) vertices and \(m\ge n-1\) arcs, in \(O((mn)^{1-\varepsilon})\) worst-case arithmetic-RAM operations with success probability at least \(2/3\)?
cards.definitions: The graph is given by its vertex set \([n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}\), with \(n\ge2\), and an explicit list of \(m\) arcs. It has no loops and at most one arc per ordered pair; opposite arcs are allowed. A feasible flow assigns a value \(f_{e}\) to every arc with \(0\le f_{e}\le u_{e}\) and equal incoming and outgoing total flow at each vertex except the distinct specified source \(s\) and sink \(t\). Its value is outgoing minus incoming flow at \(s\). The required output is a feasible flow attaining the largest possible value, including every arc value. Capacities and output values are finite rationals. Use exact rational cells with unit-cost copying, addition, subtraction, multiplication, division by a nonzero rational and comparison. Integer control and addresses use \(O(\log(n+m+2))\)-bit words with unit-cost arithmetic, Boolean operations and shifts; they cannot inspect rational encodings or apply floor to rationals. Fixed rational constants and a fixed finite program are allowed, with no advice or free tables. Charge all arithmetic, control, memory access, random-word generation and output operations, treating each rational input or output as one cell. The count is independent of capacity magnitudes and binary lengths. For input bit length \(L\), every intermediate numerator and denominator and the total used bit space must be polynomially bounded in \(L\), including on unsuccessful executions. Independent fair random words are allowed. The bound holds on every execution; the entire flow must be correct with probability at least \(2/3\). Constants and the polynomial bit-space bound are uniform over all instances.

cards.title: Dynamic optimality conjecture
cards.formal: Fix n ordered keys and an access sequence X. In the root-BST model, an access is served by rotations until its key is at the root; its cost is one plus the number of rotations. Let \(\operatorname{OPT}(X)\) minimize total cost over offline executions, allowing an optimal initial tree. Is there a universal constant C such that, for every initial splay tree \(T_{0}\) and every X, \(\mathrm{cost}_{\mathrm{splay}}(X;T_0)\le C(\mathrm{OPT}(X)+n)\)? The additive term allows an arbitrary initial configuration.

context_blocks.text: A balanced search tree guarantees logarithmic time per access, but that worst-case guarantee ignores the sequence. Repeatedly accessing one key, or scanning nearby keys, can be much cheaper if the tree adapts. Dynamic optimality asks for one online rule that exploits every such pattern without being told which pattern will occur.

The benchmark is itself allowed to rotate its tree and knows all future requests. Competing with the best fixed tree only captures access frequencies; competing with a changing tree also captures temporal structure. Splaying uses only local zig, zig-zig, and zig-zag rotations after each access, with no explicit prediction of the future.

For a concrete example, consider a chain on n keys with the requested key at its bottom. The first splay can cost \(\Theta (n)\), whereas an offline comparator can put that key at the root initially. The additive n allowance accounts for this starting discrepancy. Repeating the same request then costs one per access in both trees. A large cost for one badly initialized access therefore does not refute the statement.

The July 2026 preprint bounds splay cost by \(O((\operatorname{OPT}(X)+n) \log  \log  n \cdot  \log ^{2} \log  \log  n)\). Its competitive factor depends only on the number of keys, so the result covers every access pattern; that factor nevertheless grows without bound. A constant bound would be strictly stronger. The theorem is stated asymptotically, with the finitely many small values of n absorbed into constants.

Competitiveness concerns the total cost of a sequence. It does not require every individual access to be cheap, and it does not compare against an arbitrary RAM program with a hash table. Both executions must maintain binary search trees and pay for the specified rotations. Within those rules the offline execution can depend on the complete sequence, while the splay rule reacts only to the current request and tree.

context_blocks.title: Additional source and scope
context_blocks.text: Sublogarithmic competitiveness of splay trees is a weaker quantitative milestone on the way to constant competitiveness. It is preserved as context and is not claimed to imply dynamic optimality.

cards.why: It asks whether a simple local adjustment rule can match every legal strategy with complete knowledge of the future. The issue is fundamental to instance-sensitive data structures: success would replace a growing competitive penalty by a constant for all access patterns. A counterexample would identify a limitation of splaying that its many separate locality guarantees fail to reveal.
cards.definitions: Keys are \([n]=\{1,\ldots ,n\}, n\ge 1\), ordered by their integer values. A binary search tree has one node per key, every key in a left subtree smaller than its root and every key in a right subtree larger. A rotation on a parent-child edge exchanges those two nodes while reattaching the intermediate subtree so that the order is preserved. To splay a requested key x, repeatedly apply the following bottom-up rule until x is root. If its parent is root, rotate the edge from x to its parent (zig). Otherwise let p be its parent and g its grandparent. If x and p are both left children or both right children, first rotate p above g and then x above p (zig-zig). Otherwise rotate x above p and then x above g (zig-zag). Each access costs one plus its number of rotations. The tree after the access is the initial tree for the next access. For a finite sequence \(X\in [n]*, \operatorname{cost}_{\mathrm{splay}}(X;T_{0})\) is the sum of these costs starting from \(T_{0}\). A comparator execution may start with any tree, knows X in full, and serves each request by any finite sequence of parent-child rotations anywhere in the current tree whose final root is the requested key. Its cost is the same one-plus-rotations sum. \(\operatorname{OPT}(X)\) is the minimum cost over all such initial trees and executions; it is zero for the empty sequence. There are no insertions, deletions or additional node operations. This root-BST cost convention is the one used in the saved source, with the additive n term accounting for the initial tree.

The preprint proves \(O((\mathrm{OPT}(X)+n)\log\log n\,\log^2\log\log n)\) total splay cost. Theorem 1 includes the initialization term explicitly. Constant competitiveness remains the target.

cards.context:
A balanced search tree guarantees logarithmic time per access, but that worst-case guarantee ignores the sequence. Repeatedly accessing one key, or scanning nearby keys, can be much cheaper if the tree adapts. Dynamic optimality asks for one online rule that exploits every such pattern without being told which pattern will occur.

The benchmark is itself allowed to rotate its tree and knows all future requests. Competing with the best fixed tree only captures access frequencies; competing with a changing tree also captures temporal structure. Splaying uses only local zig, zig-zig, and zig-zag rotations after each access, with no explicit prediction of the future.

For a concrete example, consider a chain on n keys with the requested key at its bottom. The first splay can cost \(\Theta (n)\), whereas an offline comparator can put that key at the root initially. The additive n allowance accounts for this starting discrepancy. Repeating the same request then costs one per access in both trees. A large cost for one badly initialized access therefore does not refute the statement.

The July 2026 preprint bounds splay cost by \(O((\operatorname{OPT}(X)+n) \log  \log  n \cdot  \log ^{2} \log  \log  n)\). Its competitive factor depends only on the number of keys, so the result covers every access pattern; that factor nevertheless grows without bound. A constant bound would be strictly stronger. The theorem is stated asymptotically, with the finitely many small values of n absorbed into constants.

Competitiveness concerns the total cost of a sequence. It does not require every individual access to be cheap, and it does not compare against an arbitrary RAM program with a hash table. Both executions must maintain binary search trees and pay for the specified rotations. Within those rules the offline execution can depend on the complete sequence, while the splay rule reacts only to the current request and tree.

Sublogarithmic competitiveness of splay trees is a weaker quantitative milestone on the way to constant competitiveness. It is preserved as context and is not claimed to imply dynamic optimality.

cards.title: Superlogarithmic static cell-probe lower bounds
cards.formal: Does there exist a fixed integer \(k\ge 2\) and a uniformly polynomial-time computable family of Boolean functions \(F_{n}\) on an n-word database and a \(k\lceil \log _{2} n\rceil\)-bit query such that its optimal deterministic static cell-probe query complexity \(t*F(n)\), with word size \(\lceil 4\log _{2} n\rceil\) bits and \(n\lceil \log _{2} n\rceil ^{2}\) memory cells, satisfies \(t*F(n)/\log _{2} n\to \infty\) as \(n\to \infty\)?
cards.definitions: For each integer \(n\ge 2\) put \(w=\lceil 4\log _{2} n\rceil\) and \(s=n\lceil \log _{2} n\rceil ^{2}\). A database is \(D\in (\{0,1\}^{w})^{n}, a\) query is \(q\in \{0,1\}^{k\lceil \log _{2} n\rceil}\), and \(F_{n}(D,q)\in \{0,1\}\). Explicit means that a single deterministic Turing machine computes \(F_{n}(D,q)\), given \((1^{n},D,q)\), in time polynomial in n; no advice is allowed in this definition. A data structure may preprocess D by any map \(E_{n}\) into s cells of w bits each. Preprocessing time is unrestricted, and this encoding may be nonlinear and nonuniform. For each query, a deterministic adaptive decision tree reads cells, choosing the next address from the query and previously read contents, and must output \(F_{n}(D,q)\) exactly for every database. Computation between probes is free. The trees may depend on n, F and the query, but their only access to D is through \(E_{n}(D)\). Each query starts without free database-dependent private information; memory is static and read-only. Define \(t*F(n)\) as the minimum, over all such encodings and trees, of the maximum number of probes over all D and q. All memory cells count toward s. This card fixes a near-linear-space, short-query, one-bit-answer specialization of the broader static lower-bound challenge; it does not assert equivalence to every space or word-size variant.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove that some fixed k and admissible uniform family F satisfy: for every real \(B>0\) there is N such that \(t*F(n)>B \log _{2} n\) for every \(n\ge N\). Alternatively, prove the exact negation: for every fixed k and every admissible family F, there is a finite \(B>0\) such that \(t*F(n)\le B \log _{2} n\) for arbitrarily large n. In particular, the negative answer need not establish an \(O(\log  n)\) bound for all sufficiently large n.

The STOC 2026 paper retains the broader static barrier as Open Problem 1.1. context_blocks.text: A static data structure pays an initial cost to organize a database and then answers queries against that fixed information. In the cell-probe model, only the number of memory cells read during a query matters. The query algorithm has unlimited computational power between reads. Consequently, a lower bound must identify information that cannot be made locally accessible even by an ingenious encoding; showing that a particular search procedure or arithmetic computation is slow is insufficient.

The space allowance is central. With enough space, preprocessing could store every answer in a table, giving constant-probe queries. Here there are at least \(n^{2}\) possible queries, while the stored representation has only \(O(n \log ^{3} n)\) bits. Conversely, the database itself fits in n cells, so reading all n cells always suffices. The target therefore lies strictly between two elementary strategies: an unrestricted table with one entry for every possible query exceeds the budget, but the problem is always solvable without a computational-time obstruction.

The one-bit answer avoids obtaining a large probe bound merely because the output contains many independent bits. The query length is \(O(\log  n)\), with a fixed constant k. Increasing the query length to n bits can create communication lower bounds of an entirely different magnitude. Likewise, allowing only linear combinations in preprocessing or forbidding adaptive reads changes the collection of encodings and algorithms that a lower bound must defeat.

Koucký, Loff, Molli and Saks formulate the broad static challenge explicitly as Open Problem 1.1. Away from storage that is extremely close to the information-theoretic minimum, familiar general lower-bound approaches have not exceeded the logarithm of the number of queries. The present card turns this challenge into one yes/no proposition by fixing the word size, storage overhead, output alphabet and uniform meaning of an explicit problem. Its stricter conventions should be kept in mind when transferring results from a survey.

Korten, Pitassi and Impagliazzo obtain stronger tradeoffs through local pseudorandom generators. Their improvements are especially informative when the number of probes is small and the cells contain few bits. Their general bound includes an explicit dependence on word size. A gain proved for one-bit cells therefore cannot simply be carried over unchanged to \(\Theta (\log  n)\)-bit words. These results advance the tradeoff frontier without proving the superlogarithmic lower bound at the parameters fixed here.

Ko’s 2025 result illustrates another important parameter distinction. For random linear operators with m possible row queries, the lower bound is \(\Omega (\min \{\log (m/s), n/\log  s\})\) in a bit-cell formulation. It can exceed log n when the number m of queries grows sufficiently rapidly. With only polynomially many queries, the first term is at most \(O(\log  n)\). The random choice of an operator also does not by itself supply the uniformly polynomial-time explicit family required in this card.

The STOC 2026 natural-proofs paper supplies conditional obstacles to a broad class of proof methods. Such a proof recognizes a sufficiently large, efficiently testable property of function tables that implies data-structure hardness; conjectured local pseudorandom functions would obstruct that recognition. This is not an unconditional impossibility theorem for stronger lower bounds. The authors’ errata also flag a new sampling method whose coverage had not been checked and explain why a previously cited rigidity consequence no longer constitutes an unachieved barrier.

Static and dynamic memory have different sources of hardness. Larsen, Weinstein and Yu crossed the logarithmic barrier for dynamic Boolean problems, where updates limit how information can be reorganized. Ko’s March 2026 preprint claims a further \(\Omega ((\log  n/\log  \log  n)^{2})\) bound for a dynamic multiphase problem. Those update constraints are absent here: the whole database may be preprocessed without a time bound before any query arrives. Neither dynamic result automatically gives the requested static lower bound.

A positive solution would identify a uniformly computable query whose information cannot be recovered with only logarithmically many reads, even after unrestricted preprocessing. This separates a memory-access bottleneck from the running time of known implementations. The limit in the statement is stronger than an arbitrarily large ratio on an infinite subsequence: the ratio must eventually exceed each fixed constant and remain above it. That distinction also affects the exact negative answer.

cards.title: Deterministic linear-time static dictionaries
cards.formal: Is the following proposition true? For every fixed integer \(d\ge 1\) there are uniform deterministic construction and query programs \(A_{d},Q_{d}\) and a constant \(C_{d}\ge 1\) such that, for every \(n\ge 2\), every word length \(\lceil \log _{2}(n+1)\rceil \le w\le d\lceil \log _{2}(n+1)\rceil\), and every n-record input with distinct w-bit integer keys and w-bit values, \(A_{d}\) builds a static dictionary in at most \(C_{d} n\) operations and \(C_{d} n\) words of total space, and \(Q_{d}\) answers every membership-and-value query in at most \(C_{d}\) operations.
cards.why: Exact constant-time lookup is a basic component of many larger data structures. The unresolved cost is obtaining the representation deterministically in optimal time, so a resolution would settle whether randomness is essential to this combination of construction, storage and lookup guarantees.

cards.definitions: The universe is \(U_{w}\)={\(0,\ldots ,2\)ʷ−1}. An input is a list of n pairs \((x_{i},v_{i})\in U_{w}\times U_{w}\) with pairwise distinct \(x_{i}\) and arbitrary \(v_{i}\); the input order is unrestricted. On query \(q\in U_{w}\) the output is \((1,v_{i})\) if \(q=x_{i}\) and \((0,0)\) if q is absent. The stored set and values do not change after construction. The machine is a sequential word RAM with w-bit registers and cells. The primitive unit-cost instructions are memory reads and writes, copies, comparisons, conditional branches, addition and subtraction modulo 2ʷ, multiplication returning the full product in two words, integer quotient and remainder of two words with nonzero divisor, bitwise Boolean operations, and logical shifts. A shift by at least w returns zero; otherwise shifted-out bits are discarded. Addresses may occupy a fixed number of words, and all operations computing them are charged. Programs have finitely many instructions and constants, may receive n and w, and contain no input-size or word-size advice, random instruction, free table or special hashing primitive. Every table, parameter computation, memory initialization and output write performed by construction counts toward its time; input storage, the resulting dictionary and temporary storage count toward its space. Query reads the constructed representation and may use temporary workspace, with every operation charged; all retained information about the input is in the counted representation. The query must be correct on every q, including absent keys. Programs and constants may depend on d but not on n, w, the input or query. This spells out the saved \(w=\Theta (\log  n)\) convention as a claim for every fixed polynomial-size universe; Pagh’s broader arbitrary-word-length formulation is not asserted equivalent here.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove the proposition with deterministic algorithms meeting all three bounds for every fixed d, or disprove it for at least one fixed d. The negation says that no pair of admissible correct programs has simultaneously linear worst-case construction time, linear total space and constant worst-case query time for all inputs in that word-length range. Failure of a particular hash family, an average-input lower bound, or a lower bound in a comparison-only model is not that negation.

context_blocks.text: A dictionary is an exact lookup table for a sparse set of keys. For example, records \((12,5), (47,9)\) and \((103,2)\) require the answers 9 on key 47 and absent on key 48. The values need not be unique. The problem is to prepare a representation in time proportional to the number of records and then answer every lookup in a bounded number of machine steps, regardless of whether the key is present.

Direct addressing uses the key itself as an array index. This achieves constant lookup time, but an array for a universe of \(n^{2}\) possible keys occupies \(n^{2}\) cells even if only n keys are present. Such space is outside the target. At the opposite extreme, keeping the keys in sorted order uses linear space but ordinary binary search needs logarithmically many comparisons. These examples show why construction, storage and query time must be required simultaneously.

Randomized perfect hashing already gives linear expected construction time, linear storage and constant worst-case lookup time. The randomness concerns finding a suitable representation during construction; once a valid dictionary has been built, lookup can be exact and have a worst-case bound. Thus the open issue is not whether every query can avoid probabilistic errors, but whether the construction time can be bounded linearly without any random choices.

Pagh obtained deterministic \(O(n \log  n)\) construction for logarithmic-size words. Ružić subsequently related construction cost to integer sorting with only a log log n overhead. The latter is a much smaller overhead, but it still grows with n. The source question asks for its complete removal while retaining the other two guarantees. A representation whose existence is known but whose parameters take longer to find does not meet the construction requirement.

The dependence on word length matters even when keys occupy one machine word. Here a fixed polynomial-size universe is intended: the constant relating w to log n is fixed before the inputs vary. Constants in the guarantees may depend on that fixed bound. This is the logarithmic-word version already selected for this card; it does not silently claim a solution for word lengths growing faster than log n.

Uniformity also matters. Earlier dictionary results sometimes supplied word-size-dependent constants at no construction cost. The present formulation charges for computing every table and parameter that is not part of a fixed program. A one-time computation on a particular physical machine cannot disappear from an asymptotic bound that covers arbitrarily large inputs.

The dependency remains visible in modern applications. The 2024 internal-pattern-matching paper uses constant-time deterministic dictionaries with a general \(O(m(\log  \log  m)^{2})\) construction bound for a dictionary of size m, and treats very small dictionaries separately. The surrounding text length can be much larger than m, so that application must not be read as fixing word length to \(\Theta (\log  m)\). Kosolobov’s 2026 compressed index likewise records a slowdown when dictionary randomness is removed.

These applications explain the scientific stakes: a basic lookup operation can determine whether a larger construction remains deterministic within its intended time bound. The 2026 index is evidence that the issue remains useful, rather than a theorem resolving this static linear-construction question.

The randomness concerns finding a suitable representation during construction; once a valid dictionary has been built, lookup can be exact and have a worst-case bound. Thus the open issue is not whether every query can avoid probabilistic errors, but whether the construction time can be bounded linearly without any random choices.

Pagh obtained deterministic \(O(n \log  n)\) construction for logarithmic-size words. Ružić subsequently related construction cost to integer sorting with only a log log n overhead. The latter is a much smaller overhead, but it still grows with n. The source question asks for its complete removal while retaining the other two guarantees. A representation whose existence is known but whose parameters take longer to find does not meet the construction requirement.

The dependence on word length matters even when keys occupy one machine word. Here a fixed polynomial-size universe is intended: the constant relating w to log n is fixed before the inputs vary. Constants in the guarantees may depend on that fixed bound. This is the logarithmic-word version already selected for this card; it does not silently claim a solution for word lengths growing faster than log n.

Uniformity also matters. Earlier dictionary results sometimes supplied word-size-dependent constants at no construction cost. The present formulation charges for computing every table and parameter that is not part of a fixed program. A one-time computation on a particular physical machine cannot disappear from an asymptotic bound that covers arbitrarily large inputs.

The dependency remains visible in modern applications. The 2024 internal-pattern-matching paper uses constant-time deterministic dictionaries with a general \(O(m(\log  \log  m)^{2})\) construction bound for a dictionary of size m, and treats very small dictionaries separately. The surrounding text length can be much larger than m, so that application must not be read as fixing word length to \(\Theta (\log  m)\). Kosolobov’s 2026 compressed index likewise records a slowdown when dictionary randomness is removed.

These applications explain the scientific stakes: a basic lookup operation can determine whether a larger construction remains deterministic within its intended time bound. The 2026 index is evidence that the issue remains useful, rather than a theorem resolving this static linear-construction question.

cards.title: Constant-time deterministic dynamic dictionaries
cards.formal: For every fixed integer \(c\ge2\), does there exist a uniform deterministic word-RAM dictionary with capacity \(N\), word size \(w=\lceil c\log_2(N+2)\rceil\), \(O(N)\) words of space, \(O(1)\) worst-case lookup time and \(O(1)\) amortized insertion and deletion time? The guarantees must hold for every valid online sequence on \(w\)-bit keys and values, starting empty, after \(O(N)\) initialization.
cards.definitions: A uniform sequential word RAM has a fixed finite program, word-sized registers and addressed memory cells. Unit-cost instructions are reads and writes, comparisons, branching, addition, subtraction, multiplication, integer division with nonzero divisor, Boolean bit operations and logical shifts. Arithmetic stored in one word is modulo \(2^w\); shifts by at least \(w\) yield zero. Addresses must fit the available word size. All table construction and input-dependent auxiliary memory count; there is no free advice or input-dependent oracle. Randomized programs may generate independent uniform random words. The program receives \(N\ge2\) and \(w\). Insert supplies a new key and a value, Delete names a present key, and Lookup returns its value or an absent marker. At most \(N\) keys are simultaneously stored. No random instruction is allowed in this deterministic target. For each fixed \(c\), constants may depend on \(c\) but not on \(N\), input keys or sequence length. The joint amortized bound is total cost \(O(N+q+u)\) for \(q\) queries and \(u\) updates, while every query individually costs \(O(1)\). All retained input information, including any direct-address table, counts toward the \(O(N)\) space bound. This logarithmic-word, fixed-capacity formulation asks already for constant amortized updates; it does not demand constant worst-case updates.

cards.title: Multiphase conjecture
cards.formal: Do there exist constants \(\gamma>1\) and \(\delta>0\) such that every always-correct Las Vegas word-RAM solution of the following three-phase problem has overhead \(\tau(n)=\Omega(n^\delta)\) for \(k=\lceil n^\gamma\rceil\)? Phase I preprocesses \(S_1,\ldots,S_k\subseteq[n]\) in expected \(O(kn\tau(n))\) time; Phase II receives \(T\subseteq[n]\) and takes expected \(O(n\tau(n))\) time; Phase III receives \(i\in[k]\) and decides whether \(S_i\cap T=\varnothing\) in expected \(O(\tau(n))\) time.
cards.definitions: A uniform sequential word RAM has a fixed finite program, word-sized registers and addressed memory cells. Unit-cost instructions are reads and writes, comparisons, branching, addition, subtraction, multiplication, integer division with nonzero divisor, Boolean bit operations and logical shifts. Arithmetic stored in one word is modulo \(2^w\); shifts by at least \(w\) yield zero. Addresses must fit the available word size. All table construction and input-dependent auxiliary memory count; there is no free advice or input-dependent oracle. Randomized programs may generate independent uniform random words. A candidate program chooses a fixed integer \(a\ge2\) and uses words of \(w=\lceil a\log_2(n+k+2)\rceil\) bits. All its addresses must fit in one word, so the available address space is polynomial; the lower-bound claim quantifies over every such fixed \(a\). Sets may be given as incidence vectors, so their input lengths are \(kn\) and \(n\) bits. One uniform finite program for each phase must work for all \(n\) in the selected \(k=\lceil n^\gamma\rceil\) regime. The program may retain its computed memory between phases; all computation, initialization and copying are charged to the phase performing them. Phase I does not know \(T\) or \(i\), Phase II does not know \(i\), and Phase III receives only the index plus the retained state. Inputs are fixed independently of the random bits. Answers are always correct and each phase terminates almost surely; expected bounds hold for every fixed complete input. Define overhead as the maximum of 1 and the three worst-input expected phase costs divided respectively by \(kn,n,1\). A constant-factor asymptotic lower bound is required for all sufficiently large \(n\); a conditional hardness proof is not an unconditional resolution.

cards.title: Superlinear cell-probe lower bounds for succinct Boolean matrix-vector products
cards.formal:
For every family of deterministic exact static cell-probe data structures representing arbitrary matrices \(M\in\{0,1\}^{n\times n}\) in \(n^2+o(n^2)\) bits, with word length
\[w_n=\left\lceil\log_2(n^2+1)\right\rceil,\]
must its worst-case number \(T(n)\) of word probes for answering a Boolean matrix-vector query satisfy
\[T(n)=\omega(n)?\]
The representation may encode the whole matrix arbitrarily; it need not retain the original matrix as a separately readable array. Computation between probes and preprocessing time are uncharged, as specified below.
cards.why: A superlinear lower bound with almost no storage overhead would go beyond the standard static-data-structure barriers for this central problem. It would isolate an information-access obstruction independently of how much computation is performed between memory reads.
cards.status_note: Source-open for the explicitly stated general succinct deterministic cell-probe model. The complete 2017 problem page and the original upper-bound theorem were checked; the 2018 paper’s main results explicitly concern systematic representations, with the stated lower theorem counting original matrix entries. Its unrestricted-redundancy word-probe conversion and representation restriction do not establish this exact target. Bounded later-work searches through 16 September 2026 found no matching general resolution. This is a source/formulation and theorem-scope review, not independent verification or Lean formalization of every cited proof.

cards.definitions:
For \(M\in\{0,1\}^{n\times n}\) and a query \(v\in\{0,1\}^n\), the required answer is the entire vector \(y=Mv\in\{0,1\}^n\) over the Boolean semiring:
\[y_i=\bigvee_{j=1}^n(M_{ij}\wedge v_j),\qquad i\in[n].\]
Here \(\wedge\) and \(\vee\) are logical AND and OR. This is not multiplication over the two-element field, where addition would instead be parity. Every matrix and every query vector is allowed.

For each integer \(n\ge2\), choose an integer number of memory cells \(S_n\), with \(1\le S_n\le2^{w_n}\), and an encoding map
\[E_n:\{0,1\}^{n\times n}\longrightarrow(\{0,1\}^{w_n})^{S_n}.\]
The stored memory on input \(M\) is exactly \(E_n(M)\). All persistent matrix-dependent information must be in these cells. The space bound includes padding to complete words: define \(r_n=S_nw_n-n^2\), and require \(r_n\ge0\) and \(r_n/n^2\to0\). This is the meaning of succinct storage. No particular rate such as \(r_n=n^{7/4}\), and no smaller fixed redundancy budget, is imposed.

The query gets \(n\) and \(v\) for free, plus access to the stored cells at addresses \(0,\ldots,S_n-1\). One probe reads one entire \(w_n\)-bit word. The next address may depend on the query and all words previously read. Arbitrary finite computation and temporary workspace between probes cost nothing; reading the query vector and producing the output vector also cost nothing. Temporary state starts empty apart from the query and public size parameters, so there is no free matrix-dependent advice. The representation is static and read-only, and each query starts afresh; no state left by earlier queries is available.

Equivalently, for each \(n\) and query \(v\), the query rule is a finite decision tree whose internal nodes specify cell addresses, whose outgoing edges are indexed by possible word contents, and whose leaves specify an output vector. Its leaves must give the correct \(Mv\) on every stored encoding. The trees and their computations may depend on \(n\) and \(v\), but not on \(M\) except through the probed words. There is no restriction on their description size or on the encoding's preprocessing time. Thus the lower bound is in the usual permissive, nonuniform cell-probe model; restricting the query computation to an efficient word-RAM program would be a different target. The formulation fixes the deterministic exact version: no random coins or error probability are allowed in the data structures quantified over here.

For one such family \(\mathcal D\), let
\[T_{\mathcal D}(n)=\max_{M\in\{0,1\}^{n\times n},\ v\in\{0,1\}^n}
\#\{\text{word probes on query }v\text{ after storing }M\}.\]
Repeated reads count repeatedly. The assertion means that for every eligible family \(\mathcal D\) and every real \(C>0\), some \(n_0\) satisfies \(T_{\mathcal D}(n)>Cn\) for every \(n\ge n_0\). The threshold may depend on the family and \(C\). The fixed choice \(w_n=\Theta(\log n)\) makes words large enough for cell addresses without allowing one word to hold the whole matrix.

A systematic representation stores the unchanged matrix and separate redundant bits. That is a restriction on \(E_n\), not part of this general succinct target. The source page does not require that restriction; its example upper bound happens to have it. The distinction matters for applying later lower bounds.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof or refutation of the universal superlinear lower bound. An affirmative answer must cover every deterministic exact representation and adaptive query family with the stated \(n^2+o(n^2)\) total storage. A negative answer must exhibit an eligible family, a constant \(C>0\), and arbitrarily large \(n\) with \(T(n)\le Cn\); a bound holding at all sufficiently large sizes is sufficient but not necessary to negate the displayed limit. A lower bound only for systematic encodings, nonadaptive queries, smaller redundancy, individual matrix-entry probes, or charged word-RAM computation does not establish this statement without the needed conversion. This is exact asymptotic yes/no acceptance, not an approximation of a finite running time.

source_formulation.text: The source asks whether succinct data structures for Boolean matrix-vector multiplication must use more than a linear number of cell probes per query.
source_formulation.caption: Editorial paraphrase of Problem 75; general succinct encoding, exact deterministic queries and logarithmic word size are made explicit

context_blocks.text: The matrix contains n² independent bits, but one query asks only for n Boolean answers. Preprocessing can reorganize the information before any query arrives. The question asks whether nearly minimal storage still forces substantially more than n memory accesses on a worst-case query, even when all arithmetic and logical work is free.

The source contrasts this model with the online matrix-vector conjecture for ordinary computation. A time lower bound in a word-RAM model charges operations that the cell-probe model ignores. The online conjecture therefore cannot simply be substituted for an unconditional memory-access lower bound.

Larsen and Williams give a deterministic cell-probe structure using \(O(n^{7/4}/\sqrt w)\) probes per query and only \(O(n^{7/4}\sqrt w)\) bits beyond the stored matrix. With logarithmic words this is succinct and polynomially faster in probe count than scanning all matrix entries. It remains superlinear and hence does not refute the proposed lower bound.

The 2018 paper proves a much stronger tradeoff for systematic representations. Its Theorem 1.2 gives \(t_{\rm bit}r=\Omega(n^3)\) when \(n\le r\le n^2/4\), even for queries correct with probability at least \(1-1/n\), and permits reading all redundant bits. Here \(t_{\rm bit}\) counts original matrix entries, not words. A word-probe consequence loses a factor of \(w\), yielding \(\Omega(n^3/(rw))\) in that restricted representation model.

Two qualifications prevent that theorem from settling this card as stated. It retains the matrix in its original layout, whereas a general succinct representation may encode every bit differently. Moreover, even its word-probe consequence is superlinear only for suitably smaller redundancy; arbitrary o(n²) redundancy need not be o(n²/w). The title of a succinct-data-structure theorem alone does not establish the general claim.

The same paper improves the systematic upper bound to roughly n³ᐟ² probes and redundant bits, up to logarithmic factors at logarithmic word size, using randomized queries. This is useful progress on the tradeoff, while the exact deterministic lower-bound question here remains a separately specified target.

category_assignment.reason: Maintains ordered labels in a bounded array and charges relocations, a general representation primitive.

importance.reason: The problem measures the unavoidable movement needed to maintain a sorted array with spare capacity, a primitive used throughout ordered storage and indexing.

sentences: An ordered list is stored using a fixed range of numerical labels.
Insertions and deletions must preserve label order while keeping spare labels available.
The cost counts how many existing items receive a different label.
Randomization achieves nearly logarithmic expected amortized cost in the cited result.
The remaining task is to determine the optimal asymptotic rate for constant slack.

cards.definitions: Fix a capacity \(n\ge2\) and start with an empty ordered list. An insertion specifies the rank at which a new distinct item enters the list; a deletion names a live item. The list never contains more than \(n\) items. After each update the algorithm assigns distinct labels from \(\{1,\ldots,2n\}\) to the live items, in strictly increasing list order. Cost is one for the update plus the total number of relabelings of surviving items during it; assigning a label to the new item costs at most one additional unit. The input sequence is fixed independently of all random choices. Only relabelings are charged: local computation, rank search and auxiliary metadata are free, so this is a movement-cost model, not a word-RAM running-time target. An upper rate \(f\ge1\) means a uniform online algorithm and a constant \(C\) satisfy expected total cost at most \(C(n+M f(n))\) for every capacity and every finite valid sequence of \(M\) updates. For tightness, every algorithm and every rate \(g\) permitting such a bound must have \(g(n)=\Omega(f(n))\). Constants are independent of the sequence and capacity. The array has fixed constant slack; other label-universe regimes are outside this card. The algorithm is a fixed finite computable program taking the capacity as input, without advice or an oracle, and may use independent fair random bits. It receives updates sequentially, has no access to future updates, and must finish each operation almost surely with a valid ordered labeling. Its finite local computation and auxiliary storage are not charged by the movement objective. An oblivious sequence may depend on the algorithm and the capacity but not on the sampled random bits or observed random labels. The expectation is over the algorithm’s random choices for that fixed full sequence. A surviving item changed more than once during an update is counted for each relabeling; labels of live items must be valid at the end of the update. Here \(f(n)\) and competing rates \(g(n)\) concern integer capacities \(n\ge2\), and the asymptotic lower comparison is as \(n\to\infty\).

context_blocks.text: List labeling represents order by positions in an array with empty slots. An insertion supplies a new position in the logical order, but an empty array slot need not already be available between its neighbors. Other items may have to move. Deletions create space without prescribing where future insertions will occur.

The capacity is fixed and the array has twice that many slots. This gives a constant fraction of spare space even at maximum occupancy. A nearly full array or a polynomially larger label universe can have different bounds, so neither can silently replace this regime.

Movement and computation are separate resources here. A program can spend arbitrary finite effort deciding which labels to change; the objective counts the changes themselves. Similarly, expected amortized cost allows occasional expensive updates provided every fixed full sequence has the required expected total cost. It does not assert a worst-case time bound for each individual call.

The See-Saw theorem gives \(O(\log n(\log\log n)^3)\) amortized expected cost at any fixed positive constant slack. Its stated slack parameter may be fixed below one and its smaller array embedded in \([2n]\), giving the upper bound for this card. The paper records a general randomized lower bound of \(\Omega(\log n)\). Removing the remaining growing factor is the unresolved tight-bound issue.

Lower bounds for deterministic, history-independent, or other restricted labeling algorithms do not automatically apply to all randomized online algorithms. The adversary here commits to the whole sequence without observing random labels; adaptive choices based on those labels would change the game.

The original seminar question concerned randomized online labeling broadly. The retained benchmark selects constant slack, both insertions and deletions, and an oblivious adversary, matching the subsequently specified researcher-linked variant. The answer requires a tight asymptotic rate, rather than just the analysis of one named algorithm.

cards.answer_criterion: Supply an unambiguously defined rate \(f:\mathbb Z_{\ge2}\to\mathbb R_{\ge1}\) and complete Lean-checked upper and matching lower bounds up to constant factors in the stated expected amortized movement model. The upper bound must provide one uniform online algorithm with expected total cost \(O(n+Mf(n))\) for every capacity and oblivious valid sequence. The lower bound must establish the stated \(g(n)=\Omega(f(n))\) requirement for every competing permitted algorithm and achievable rate. cards.context:
List labeling represents order by positions in an array with empty slots. An insertion supplies a new position in the logical order, but an empty array slot need not already be available between its neighbors. Other items may have to move. Deletions create space without prescribing where future insertions will occur.

The capacity is fixed and the array has twice that many slots. This gives a constant fraction of spare space even at maximum occupancy. A nearly full array or a polynomially larger label universe can have different bounds, so neither can silently replace this regime.

Movement and computation are separate resources here. A program can spend arbitrary finite effort deciding which labels to change; the objective counts the changes themselves. Similarly, expected amortized cost allows occasional expensive updates provided every fixed full sequence has the required expected total cost. It does not assert a worst-case time bound for each individual call.

The See-Saw theorem gives \(O(\log n(\log\log n)^3)\) amortized expected cost at any fixed positive constant slack. Its stated slack parameter may be fixed below one and its smaller array embedded in \([2n]\), giving the upper bound for this card. The paper records a general randomized lower bound of \(\Omega(\log n)\). Removing the remaining growing factor is the unresolved tight-bound issue.

Lower bounds for deterministic, history-independent, or other restricted labeling algorithms do not automatically apply to all randomized online algorithms. The adversary here commits to the whole sequence without observing random labels; adaptive choices based on those labels would change the game.

The original seminar question concerned randomized online labeling broadly. The retained benchmark selects constant slack, both insertions and deletions, and an oblivious adversary, matching the subsequently specified researcher-linked variant. The answer requires a tight asymptotic rate, rather than just the analysis of one named algorithm.

cards.title: Amortized decrease-key complexity of standard pairing heaps
cards.formal: Determine, up to constant factors, the amortized decrease-key bound \(d(N)\) of the standard two-pass pairing heap, while insert, meld and find-min are charged \(O(1)\) and delete-min is charged \(O(\log(2+N))\). The bound is required for every finite sequence starting from empty heaps with at most \(N\) live items in all heaps combined.
cards.definitions: A heap is a rooted heap-ordered tree. Link compares two roots and makes the larger root the new leftmost child of the smaller. Insert links a singleton to the root; meld links the two roots. Decrease-key receives a handle, reduces its key and, if it is not a root, cuts its whole subtree and links it to the root. Delete-min removes the root, links consecutive children from left to right in disjoint pairs, leaving an unpaired last child unchanged, then combines the resulting roots from right to left by successive links. Find-min reads the root. Keys are opaque ordered values; ties follow a fixed identity order. Constant-size nodes have enough sibling and parent pointers for a cut in constant time. Charge comparisons, links, cuts and pointer work. An admissible upper bound is a function \(d\ge1\) for which a universal \(C\) bounds total cost by \(C(a+b\log(2+N)+c d(N))\), where \(a\) counts the constant-cost operations, \(b\) delete-min operations and \(c\) decreases. A tight answer must also prove that every admissible charge function dominates the supplied rate within a universal constant for sufficiently large \(N\); the constants cannot depend on the sequence. Variants changing either pass, rank metadata or the linking discipline are different algorithms.
cards.why: A tight analysis would resolve the central complexity uncertainty for one of the simplest and most widely studied self-adjusting priority queues.
