cards.title: Space-query exponent curve of 3SUM indexing
cards.formal: Determine \(\tau_{\mathrm{3SI}}(s)\) for every real \(s\in[1,2]\), where \(\tau_{\mathrm{3SI}}(s)\) is the infimum of real \(t\ge0\) for which, for every rational \(\eta>0\), a uniform randomized 3SUM index uses \(O(n^{s+\eta})\) words and answers queries in \(O(n^{t+\eta})\) worst-case time.
cards.definitions: The input is two sets \(A,B\subseteq\{0,\ldots,n^4-1\}\), each of size \(n\ge2\), supplied explicitly. A query \(z\in\{0,\ldots,2n^4-2\}\) asks whether \(z=a+b\) for some \(a\in A,b\in B\), using ordinary addition. Set \(L=n\) and fix \(d=10\) in the word-RAM model below. Use a uniform sequential word RAM with word length \(w=d\lceil\log_2(L+2)\rceil\), for a fixed integer \(d\ge 8\) chosen with the algorithm. A fixed finite program must handle every input size; there is no advice, precomputed lookup table or input-dependent oracle. Unit-cost operations are reads, writes, copying, comparisons, branching, Boolean operations, logical shifts, addition, subtraction and multiplication modulo \(2^w\), and integer quotient and remainder for a nonzero divisor. Shifts by at least \(w\) return zero. Addresses and stored values fit words; multiword operations pay for their constituent instructions. Randomized algorithms, when explicitly permitted, may generate independent uniform random words. All initialization, preprocessing, tables and output writes are charged. A static query starts without input-dependent private state, and every retained copy of the input or auxiliary information counts toward index space. Preprocessing may take arbitrary time but must terminate almost surely; this preserves the preexisting card’s space-hardness convention. Every retained input, table and random seed is counted. Each fixed input/query is answered correctly with probability at least \(2/3\) over preprocessing and query randomness, and space and query time bounds hold on every random outcome. Queries cannot communicate input-dependent state for free. For each chosen \(s,t,\eta\), one finite program pair and constants handle every \(n\); there is no per-size choice of advice. Parameters select programs and are not real-number computational inputs. The infimum need not be attained. The quantity is a dimensionless query exponent, and it ignores subpolynomial factors only through the displayed quantifiers.
cards.why: The curve asks how much information about a quadratic family of sums must be stored to support reusable membership queries, a general representation barrier underlying several string indexes.

context_blocks.text: An index is built once for all future sum-membership queries. Storing every potential sum and scanning one input set occupy very different points of the space-query frontier.
The original framework separates different 3SUM-indexing hardness hypotheses; its strongest old tradeoff should not be treated as a theorem.
The revised 2026 paper improves intermediate space regimes without determining the entire frontier.

The previous card asked specifically for genuinely subquadratic space with polylogarithmic queries. The present curve broadens the target; a query exponent of zero or a numerical approximation to it does not by itself establish a polylogarithmic bound.

cards.title: Strong SetDisjointness conjecture
cards.formal: Is the following statement true? For every admissible uniform static word-RAM data structure for SetDisjointness, with worst-case retained space \(S(N)\) words and worst-case query time \(T(N)\) steps, there exist constants \(c>0\), \(b\in\mathbb N\), and \(N_0\ge2\) such that \(S(N)T(N)^2\ge cN^2/(\log_2(N+2))^b\) for every integer \(N\ge N_0\). For every integer \(N\ge2\), the input is a list \(A_1,\ldots,A_m\) of nonempty subsets of \([N]=\{1,\ldots,N\}\), with \(1\le m\le N\) and total size \(N=\sum_{i=1}^m|A_i|\). A query supplies indices \(i,j\in[m]\) and must return whether \(A_i\cap A_j=\varnothing\).
cards.definitions:
The input gives \(N\), \(m\), the lengths of the sets, and each set's elements explicitly as words, without repetitions within a set. Different listed sets may be equal. The indices of two stored sets are the whole query; there is no new query set. The case \(i=j\) is allowed. Each admissible data structure is a fixed pair of finite programs, one for preprocessing and one for queries, working for every input size. The word length is \(w=\lceil10\log_2(N+2)\rceil\). The sequential word RAM has word-sized registers and addressed memory cells; each read, write, comparison, branch, addition, subtraction, multiplication, division by a nonzero integer, Boolean bit operation, or logical shift costs one step. Arithmetic stored in a word is modulo \(2^w\), and a shift by at least \(w\) returns zero. Addresses fit in one word. Outputting the answer and all memory operations are charged.

Preprocessing must halt on every valid input and random execution, but its finite running time is unrestricted. Only the resulting stored representation is accessible to a query; the original input is not available for free. The representation includes all retained input-dependent tables, seeds, pointers and metadata. A query begins with its two indices, the input-size metadata and that representation, with no input-dependent private state inherited from earlier queries. It leaves the representation unchanged. Temporary query storage starts empty; accessing or filling it costs time. There is no advice, oracle, input-specific code, or uncharged precomputed table.

The two programs may generate independent uniformly random words in one step. For every fixed input and fixed valid query, the probability of the correct empty/nonempty answer, over preprocessing randomness and independent query randomness, is at least \(2/3\). The query bound holds for every random outcome, including erroneous ones. Let \(s(N)\) be the maximum retained word count over all valid inputs of total size exactly \(N\) and preprocessing outcomes, and let \(T(N)\ge1\) be the maximum query step count over those inputs, their produced representations, all valid queries and all query outcomes. These maxima are required to be finite. Use the saved card's space normalization \(S(N)=\max\{N,s(N)\}\), and restrict to structures with \(S(N)\le N^2\). Unused cells may be padded. All constants in the asserted bound may depend on the fixed programs, but not on \(N\), the input family, or the query. The displayed bound is the precise meaning of \(S(N)T(N)^2=\widetilde\Omega(N^2)\); it suppresses only fixed powers of a logarithm, not an arbitrary \(N^{o(1)}\) factor.
cards.why: This conjecture underlies many space-query conditional lower bounds for text indexes, graph oracles and set systems.

context_blocks.text: Goldstein, Kopelowitz, Lewenstein and Porat formulate the Strong SetDisjointness conjecture as \(S=\widetilde\Omega(N^2/T^2)\). Their \(N\) is total set incidence count, not the number of sets. The source explicitly uses the tilde notation to suppress polylogarithmic factors.

A matching upper tradeoff has retained space \(O(N+N^2/t^2)\) words and query time \(O(t)\), in particular \(S T^2=O(N^2)\) in the relevant range \(1\le t\le\sqrt N\). This upper bound does not establish the conjectured universal lower bound.

The 2020 algorithms of Kopelowitz and Vassilevska Williams improve the tradeoff between preprocessing time and query time. Their analysis measures preprocessing time separately from retained storage, so its improved preprocessing bound does not refute this space-query conjecture.

Huang, Tao and Wang use the same space-query conjecture in their 2026 work on join sampling, in a word-RAM with logarithmic word length. Their Lemma 21 relates an expected-query-time formulation for exact answers to the formulation with deterministic query time. They assume the conjecture rather than prove its lower bound.

This review retains the card's explicitly chosen uniform, bounded-error word-RAM convention and normalized space range. The 2017 conjecture itself does not spell out these machine, uniformity and error details. Relabelling the elements of the union into \([N]\) preserves every intersection; empty sets and self-pair queries are trivial.

The Strong 3SUM-Indexing conjecture mentioned alongside SetDisjointness in the original paper was subsequently refuted. The 2019 bounded-universe paper explicitly distinguishes that development and continues to assume Strong SetDisjointness for its conditional results.

cards.context:
Goldstein, Kopelowitz, Lewenstein and Porat formulate the Strong SetDisjointness conjecture as \(S=\widetilde\Omega(N^2/T^2)\). Their \(N\) is total set incidence count, not the number of sets. The source explicitly uses the tilde notation to suppress polylogarithmic factors.

A matching upper tradeoff has retained space \(O(N+N^2/t^2)\) words and query time \(O(t)\), in particular \(S T^2=O(N^2)\) in the relevant range \(1\le t\le\sqrt N\). This upper bound does not establish the conjectured universal lower bound.

The 2020 algorithms of Kopelowitz and Vassilevska Williams improve the tradeoff between preprocessing time and query time. Their analysis measures preprocessing time separately from retained storage, so its improved preprocessing bound does not refute this space-query conjecture.

Huang, Tao and Wang use the same space-query conjecture in their 2026 work on join sampling, in a word-RAM with logarithmic word length. Their Lemma 21 relates an expected-query-time formulation for exact answers to the formulation with deterministic query time. They assume the conjecture rather than prove its lower bound.

This review retains the card's explicitly chosen uniform, bounded-error word-RAM convention and normalized space range. The 2017 conjecture itself does not spell out these machine, uniformity and error details. Relabelling the elements of the union into \([N]\) preserves every intersection; empty sets and self-pair queries are trivial.

The Strong 3SUM-Indexing conjecture mentioned alongside SetDisjointness in the original paper was subsequently refuted. The 2019 bounded-universe paper explicitly distinguishes that development and continues to assume Strong SetDisjointness for its conditional results.

cards.title: Unified bound for binary search trees
cards.formal:
Does there exist one uniform deterministic online binary-search-tree program \(A\) in the model below and one integer \(C\ge1\) such that, for every integer \(n\ge1\), every integer \(m\ge0\), and every request sequence \(X=(x_1,\ldots,x_m)\in[n]^m\), the program correctly completes all requests and
\[
T_A(n,X)\le C\bigl(n\log_2(n+2)+U_n(X)\bigr),
\qquad
U_n(X)=\sum_{t=1}^{m}\log_2\!\left(2+\min\left\{n,\min_{1\le s<t}(t-s+|x_t-x_s|)\right\}\right)?
\]
Here \([n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}\), an empty minimum is \(+\infty\), an empty sum is zero, and \(T_A\) includes initialization and all computation. The same program, its fixed storage constants, and \(C\) must work for all \(n,m,X\). The guarantee is total amortized cost for every finite sequence, including every finite prefix, with no worst-case bound on an individual request.
cards.definitions:
There is exactly one node for each key in \([n]\). Each node has an immutable key and parent, left-child and right-child pointers, any of which may be null. At all times these pointers describe one rooted binary tree in symmetric order: every key in a left subtree is smaller than its root key and every key in a right subtree is larger. An access to \(x\) must visit its node with the cursor and signal completion before the next request is revealed. The cursor starts at the current root for each access. There are no key insertions or deletions during the request sequence.

The program has finite control and fixed positive integers \(c,d,r\). A word has exactly \(w=d\lceil\log_2(n+2)\rceil\) bits. Each node has \(c\) additional mutable words; outside the tree there are at most \(r\) word registers, a root pointer and one cursor. The constants and program are independent of \(n,m,X\). The input supplies \(n\) and then one key at a time; it supplies neither \(m\) nor a free time counter. Registers may retain data between accesses. Earlier requests are accessible only through this charged state. There are no other memory records, random bits, advice, or oracles.

The following instructions each cost one unit: copy a word or a program constant into a register; compare two unsigned words; add, subtract or multiply words modulo \(2^w\); unsigned integer quotient or remainder, returning zero when the divisor is zero; bitwise Boolean operations; logical shifts, with a shift by at least \(w\) giving zero; and conditional or unconditional branching. Each instruction has only a fixed finite number of operands. Reading the current node's key or one of its additional words, writing one of its additional words, and testing one of its three pointers for null each cost one unit. The finite instruction set is fixed; there is no instruction for arbitrary functions of a word. Root and cursor pointers cannot be converted to words, ordered or computed arithmetically. A numerical key or a number stored in metadata cannot be used as a memory address.

Moving the cursor along one parent or child edge costs one unit. A rotation between the current node and its nonnull parent costs one unit, updates the usual constant number of structural pointers, preserves symmetric order, and leaves the cursor at the same key. These are the only changes to the tree during accesses. Reading another node's key or metadata requires moving the cursor there; rotations do not provide free access to that metadata. There are no auxiliary pointer fields, persistent fingers, arbitrary node jumps or cursor resets during an access. At the start of each access, receiving its key and placing the cursor at the root is one charged instruction; acknowledging successful completion is another. A null-edge move, invalid rotation, premature acknowledgement, or broken tree invariant is an incorrect execution.

Initialization precedes all requests, sees only \(n\), and counts toward \(T_A\), also when \(m=0\). It starts with no nodes and zeroed registers except the input \(n\). Only during this phase, a unit-cost allocation instruction may create a zeroed node with a supplied key as the root of an empty tree or as a null left or right child of the current node, placing the cursor at the new node. Each allocation must preserve symmetric order; at most \(n\) nodes may be allocated, and no nodes are reclaimed. The other instructions and storage restrictions remain as above. Initialization must terminate with all keys present in the canonical balanced tree \(B_n\): for an interval \([a,b]\), its root is \(\lfloor(a+b)/2\rfloor\), its left subtree recursively represents \([a,\lfloor(a+b)/2\rfloor-1]\), and its right subtree represents \([\lfloor(a+b)/2\rfloor+1,b]\); an empty interval has no node. Any initialized metadata and registers must be computed by the same program at charged cost. Thus neither constructing the initial tree nor preprocessing is free.

The bound uses elapsed access indices \(t-s\), exactly as in Definition 2 of the 2024 source. It does not substitute the number of distinct intervening keys. For \(t\ge2\), taking \(s=t-1\) shows that the inner minimum is at most \(n\), so the cap has no effect. When \(m\ge1\), the \(t=1\) term is \(\log_2(n+2)\); the source omits that term, which is absorbed by the initialization allowance. Logarithms and indices in the displayed bound are mathematical quantities, not free machine operations.

This fixes the existing card's bounded-storage BST interpretation as a real-world BST with all local computation charged. The classical geometric BST cost counts touched nodes or cursor moves and rotations, and can leave the computation choosing those operations uncharged; its bounds are not automatically full-runtime bounds in the model fixed here.
cards.why: The unified bound asks one search tree to exploit temporal and rank locality together, beyond separate working-set and dynamic-finger guarantees. Resolving whether that combined access bound is achievable would clarify a central limit of adaptive binary search trees.

context_blocks.text: The 2024 paper states the elapsed-access version of the unified bound and reports \(O(U_n(X)+m\log\log n)\) BST access bounds, apart from initialization. Its conclusion explicitly retains the question of removing the extra per-access term.

The real-world BST definition uses a constant number of logarithmic-bit registers and logarithmic extra bits per node. The card makes this storage convention and the cost of local computation explicit; it does not transfer a geometric access-cost theorem to full runtime without an implementation proof.

Derryberry's thesis claimed a BST achieving the unified bound. Iacono's 2013 survey describes that claim as potentially faulty, and the 2024 paper again calls it questioned. The 2011 workshop abstract itself claims success; it is not a published correction or an independently verified resolution.

A preprint dated 14 April 2026 introduces a different unified bound for heaps and still says that no BST achieving the search-tree unified bound is known. Its positive tree result permits arbitrary internal remodeling and leaves outside sorted order, so it does not meet this card's BST model. The preprint's proofs were not independently verified.

cards.title: Superconstant word-RAM time for prefix-\(U_1\)
cards.formal:
Is it impossible to maintain a length-\(n\) bit sequence under substitutions and answer prefix-AND queries using a deterministic uniform word-RAM data structure with \(O(n)\) preprocessing and \(O(1)\) worst-case time for each update and each query?

An update \(\operatorname{set}(i,b)\) replaces the bit at position \(i\in\{1,\ldots,n\}\) by \(b\in\{0,1\}\). A query at \(k\in\{0,\ldots,n\}\) must return
\[\operatorname{prefix}(k)=\bigwedge_{i=1}^{k}b_i,\qquad\operatorname{prefix}(0)=1.\]
The word length is \(w=\lceil c\log_2(n+2)\rceil\) for a fixed integer constant \(c\ge1\). The impossibility is to hold for every such fixed constant and every correct data structure in the model below.

This retains the source's worst-case time convention. The target is absence of any constant bound, not a prescribed logarithmic lower-bound rate or the stronger exclusion of amortized constant time.

source_formulation.text: There is no structure for prefix-U1 with complexity \(O(1)\).

cards.why: This small dynamic problem isolates whether maintaining even threshold information about a changing minimum requires more than a constant number of actual word operations. Its hardness would complete conditional classifications of dynamic regular-language membership, and newer work extends that connection to tree languages. The challenge concerns computation inside the machine as well as memory access, making it a foundational word-RAM question.

cards.definitions:
The sequence length \(n\ge1\) remains fixed for the lifetime of the structure. Its initial bits are supplied explicitly, one per input cell. Preprocessing receives \(n\) and that sequence and must run in at most \(K(n+1)\) word operations for one fixed constant \(K\). It builds the state from which all subsequent operations are served. The two-element monoid \(U_1=\{0,1\}\) has multiplication Boolean AND, with identity one and absorbing element zero. Hence a nonempty prefix has product zero exactly when it contains a zero.

Equivalently, the zero positions form a changing subset \(S\subseteq\{1,\ldots,n\}\). Substitution adds or removes a supplied position, and the complemented prefix answer says whether \(S\cap\{1,\ldots,k\}\) is nonempty. Repeating a substitution with the present value is allowed and must also meet the cost bound. Queries do not ask for the minimum element itself or a predecessor of the query position. No insertion or deletion of sequence positions, change of \(n\), or restriction on which positions may change is included.

Use a finite-program unit-cost random-access machine whose cells and addresses are unsigned \(w\)-bit words. One operation can read or write one addressed cell, copy a word, compare two words or branch, apply word addition, subtraction or multiplication, apply unsigned integer division or remainder by a nonzero word, apply bitwise AND, OR, XOR or NOT, or shift a word left or right by a supplied integer amount. Arithmetic results are reduced modulo \(2^w\), except that division and remainder have their usual unsigned integer meanings; left shifts discard overflowing bits, right shifts insert zeros, and shifts by at least \(w\) give zero. Division by zero must be avoided or handled as an error, not an extra operation. Constant literals are fixed by the finite program. The program can use \(n\) and \(w\); both are supplied at initialization. Each listed operation has unit cost. No other arbitrary word function or input-dependent instruction is provided.

There are at most \(2^w\) addressable cells, all initially zero except the supplied input. Every read, write and table construction counts; no nonuniform precomputed table or advice depending on \(n\) is supplied free of charge. There is no additional linear-space requirement: the machine may use its polynomially many addressable cells, even if many were populated by previous updates. The fixed program, positive integer \(c\) and preprocessing constant \(K\) may depend on the data structure, but never on the input length, initial bits or future history. These explicit word operations instantiate the source's unit-cost arithmetic RAM convention, with only logarithmically many bits per word.

Updates and queries arrive one at a time. The answer to each query must be exactly correct for the state after all earlier updates, before a later operation is revealed. Every finite operation history is allowed, including histories selected using earlier answers and histories much longer than \(n\). All operation invocations must terminate. The structure is deterministic, with no error probability and no random or expected-time convention.

A constant-time structure would have one constant \(T\) bounding the work of every individual update and query, for every initial sequence, every length and every history. The work done by one operation cannot be charged to earlier or later operations. Allowing an onset \(n_0\) rather than all lengths gives the same existence question, since the finitely many smaller lengths can be handled separately. Consequently a positive impossibility result can be expressed as follows: for every correct linear-preprocessing structure, every proposed bound \(B\) and every onset \(N\), there is a length \(n\ge N\), an initial sequence and a finite operation history in which an individual operation takes more than \(B\) steps. No particular function tending to infinity is prescribed in advance.

The cell-probe model, mentioned in the context, charges only memory accesses and allows arbitrary computation on values already read at no cost. It is more permissive than the word-operation model just defined; a counting argument that ignores all such computation cannot automatically establish the requested word-RAM barrier.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct Lean-checked proof or refutation of the claimed nonexistence. A proof must exclude every correct deterministic uniform structure with linear preprocessing and fixed logarithmic word-length constant from having a common constant worst-case bound for both operations. It may give a quantitative lower bound, but must justify that it excludes all constants in this model. A refutation must give a single finite-program structure, some fixed word-length constant, linear preprocessing and exact constant worst-case bounds for both updates and queries on every history. An amortized or expected constant upper bound alone does not refute the specified worst-case conjecture. A lower bound for a stronger query task, larger monoid, smaller instruction set or stricter space limit does not alone prove it.

context_blocks.text: Section 2 explicitly uses worst-case operation cost and linear preprocessing. The question concerns the two-element AND monoid. The separately discussed three-element monoid has a stronger predecessor-type task and a different known lower bound.

The source records an \(O(\log\log n)\) deterministic upper bound and a better expected bound when randomness is allowed. It emphasizes that this does not provide the superconstant lower bound and distinguishes the word-RAM problem from unrestricted local computation in the cell-probe model.

The 2022 string-data-structure paper formulates a stronger amortized constant-time hardness conjecture. Its conditional consequences are evidence of the primitive’s relevance, but this card retains the original worst-case question rather than silently changing the cost convention.

The 2025 tree-language paper still states prefix-U-one hardness as a conjectural premise. Under that premise it classifies constant-time maintainability for its specified class of regular tree languages with a neutral letter; it does not prove the premise.

cards.title: Logarithmic fully retroactive priority queues
cards.formal:
Does there exist one deterministic comparison pointer-machine program \(A\), with fixed constants \(C_t,C_s>0\), that implements the fully retroactive priority queue defined below on every valid finite sequence of commands? Starting with an empty history, it must insert and remove historical insertion or extract-min records, and return the minimum item immediately after any queried historical time. Write \(m_j\) for the number of historical records after command \(j\), \(m_0=0\), and \(M_j=\max\{m_{j-1},m_j\}\). For every \(q\ge0\), require
\[
T_A(q)\le C_t\left(1+\sum_{j=1}^{q}\log_2(2+M_j)\right),
\]
where \(T_A(q)\) counts initialization and all steps through the first \(q\) commands. During command \(j\), at most \(C_s(1+M_j)\) records may be allocated and not yet reclaimed; after it finishes, at most \(C_s(1+m_j)\) may remain. Initialization uses at most \(C_s\) records. Thus time is amortized over all edits and queries, while space is linear in the currently maintained history, including working storage.
cards.definitions:
Fix three opaque totally ordered domains: priorities, item identities and historical times. The same program and constants must work for every choice of these domains and every valid input sequence. An item is a pair \((p,\iota)\) of priority and identity, ordered lexicographically: compare priorities first and use identities to break ties. Identities of items whose insertion records are currently in the history are distinct. Atoms in each domain can be copied and compared in constant time, with no access to their representation.

The history is a finite set of records with pairwise distinct timestamps. A record is either \(\operatorname{InsertItem}(t,p,\iota)\) or \(\operatorname{ExtractMin}(t)\). Its meaning is obtained by sorting the records by time and replaying them from an empty queue. An insertion adds its item; an extraction removes the least surviving item in the lexicographic order. The history after every edit is promised valid: no extraction is encountered with an empty queue. There is no monotonicity promise on priorities. The data structure need not detect invalid commands or histories.

An input command has one of four forms. \(\operatorname{AddInsert}(t,p,\iota)\) adds an insertion record at an unused timestamp. \(\operatorname{AddExtract}(t)\) adds an extraction record at an unused timestamp. Either addition returns a constant-size stable handle for the new historical record. \(\operatorname{Remove}(h)\) removes the existing historical record named by its valid handle; a handle becomes invalid after that removal. \(\operatorname{Minimum}(t)\) returns the identity and priority of the least item after replaying all current records with timestamp at most \(t\), or a distinguished empty marker. The supplied query time may coincide with a record, lie between records, or precede or follow all records. Thus an insertion at \(t\) is already effective at \(t\), and an extraction at \(t\) has already removed its item. Edits change the interpretation of all subsequent historical records. An extraction record is not a request to remove a named item, and a removal command deletes a historical operation rather than executing an extra queue extraction.

The computation is online: each command arrives only after the preceding response, and its response must be completed before the next command is seen. Commands may depend on earlier responses. Input atoms and a removal handle occupy only constantly many input registers; earlier inputs remain available to the program only if it stores them in its charged memory. The client may retain returned handles, but gives the program only the handle named by the current command, with no auxiliary stored computation.

A program has finite control and a fixed finite number of registers. Memory consists of records with a fixed finite number of pointer fields and data fields. A pointer is null or the address of an allocated record. A data field contains one input atom or a symbol from a fixed finite alphabet. Each step may read or write a fixed field of a record reached by a register, copy a register or field, follow a stored pointer, compare two pointers for equality, compare two atoms from the same ordered domain, test a finite-alphabet symbol, branch, allocate or reclaim one record, or emit one output field. Each such primitive costs one step. Allocation supplies a fresh available address; addresses cannot be ordered, converted to data, used in arithmetic, or used for computed array access. Pointer access starts from the fixed registers or follows stored pointers. Unbounded integers and bit strings, if needed, must be represented by charged records and manipulated through these primitives; there is no unit-cost arithmetic on counters. There are no random bits, advice, oracle operations or uncharged preprocessing.

Every allocated record counts toward space until reclaimed, including historical records, handle records, indexes, temporary storage and unreachable garbage. Rebuilding and reclamation count toward time. The parameters \(m_j,M_j\) are used to state the guarantee and are not free machine inputs or unit-cost counters. A query does not change \(m_j\), and an edit changes it by exactly one. The bounds hold for every finite prefix, including arbitrarily long sequences that repeatedly add and remove records while keeping the current history small. They do not use the cumulative number of commands as a replacement for history size. The record format, register count, program and resource constants are fixed independently of all inputs.
cards.why: A single change to the past can alter which items many later extractions remove. Matching ordinary priority-queue costs despite this dependence would show that unrestricted historical access can be maintained without an asymptotic time or space penalty in the stated model.

context_blocks.text: The original retroactive model distinguishes edits to a history from queries about its states and promises that edited histories remain consistent. Its partially retroactive priority queue has logarithmic update time, but queries concern only the present.

cards.title: Optimal randomized memory-reallocation overhead
cards.formal: Determine, up to absolute constant factors as \(\varepsilon\to0\), the optimal worst-case expected reallocation overhead \(F(\varepsilon)\) for online allocators with load at most \(1-\varepsilon\). The allocator stores objects in contiguous intervals of a fixed array and may relocate live objects after each insertion or deletion.
cards.definitions: For every fixed real \(0<\varepsilon\le1/2\) and integer array length \(M\ge1\), a request inserts a fresh object of positive integer size \(s\), or deletes a named live object. Valid finite sequences start empty and have total live size at most \((1-\varepsilon)M\) after every request. At each operation boundary, every live object occupies one contiguous interval of its size in \(\{0,\ldots,M-1\}\), and these intervals are disjoint. On an update involving an object \(x\), cost is \(1+\sum_y s(y)/s(x)\), where the sum is over objects live both before and after the update whose starting addresses change. This counts allocation changes at operation boundaries; local computation and allocation metadata are uncharged. The online rule may know \(M,\varepsilon\) but no future requests, and may use private randomness. A sequence is fixed independently of that randomness; allocations must always be valid. For a family of rules covering all \(M\), its overhead is the supremum, over all capacities, valid finite request sequences and individual update indices, of expected update cost. \(F(\varepsilon)\) is the infimum of those overheads over all such families. No history-independence or resizability constraint is imposed. The target measures each update’s expectation, rather than expected amortized cost or a high-probability bound.
cards.why: A tight result would establish the intrinsic price of fragmentation when a general-purpose allocator operates close to full capacity.

context_blocks.text: The 2024 work studies low-overhead memory reallocation and its relationship with stronger resizability and history-independence guarantees. Those extra guarantees are not required for the target here.

Jin’s February 2026 paper gives an upper bound \(O((\log(1/\varepsilon))^4(\log\log(1/\varepsilon))^2)\) and a lower bound \(\Omega(\log(1/\varepsilon))\) for general allocators. The new general lower bound improves the scope of earlier bounds restricted to resizable allocators.

cards.title: Deque conjecture
cards.formal: Start from an arbitrary binary search tree containing \(n\) ordered keys, and perform \(m\) legal double-ended queue operations. Insert-min creates a new minimum as the root with the old tree as its right child; insert-max is symmetric. Delete-min splays the minimum to the root, removes it, and keeps its right subtree; delete-max is symmetric. Is the total number of primitive pointer operations and rotations always \(O(n+m)\), with a universal constant? This is Tarjan’s deque conjecture for the specified splay implementation.
cards.why: I include this because it tests whether one general-purpose adaptive representation can recognize a workload whose optimal cost is linear. The remaining gap is tiny numerically but significant mathematically: a proof would explain why expensive local restructuring cannot accumulate across arbitrary alternations of the two ends.
cards.definitions: Splaying uses the standard zig, zig-zig, and zig-zag rules. Deletions are allowed only on a nonempty tree, and an inserted key must be outside the current key range at the specified end. Amortized cost is a bound on the total sequence, not a worst-case guarantee for each deletion. The initial tree may have any shape.

progress.text: Pettie proves \(O((n+m)\alpha^*(n+m))\) total cost, where \(\alpha^*\) counts how many iterations of the inverse-Ackermann function reduce the argument to a constant.
Levy and Tarjan connect the deque conjecture to a subsequence property sufficient for dynamic optimality. This provides a structural route to a proof, not the required linear bound itself.
The new analysis of splay competitiveness still describes the deque guarantee as nearly constant per operation. Its general search bound does not supply constant amortized deque cost.

context_blocks.text: A deque allows insertion and deletion at either end of a sequence. A linked representation can implement this abstract interface in constant time per operation. The conjecture concerns what happens when the same interface is implemented by a self-adjusting search tree: it asks whether the tree automatically achieves the linear total cost available for this restricted workload.

Deleting the minimum of a long left spine can require many rotations in a single operation. That does not disprove the conjecture, because the initial tree contributes an additive budget proportional to its size. The real difficulty is to understand whether alternating insertions and deletions at opposite ends can repeatedly rebuild expensive configurations.

For a concrete contrast, deleting keys in increasing order is a sequential-access pattern. A deque workload can switch ends after every operation and introduce new extreme keys between deletions. A bound for one monotone scan therefore does not immediately control this more flexible sequence.

The known total bound has an iterated inverse-Ackermann factor, which grows extraordinarily slowly but is asymptotically unbounded. Removing it would answer a structural question about how rotations reuse earlier work. This is a focused subproblem of the broader study of splaying, with updates included explicitly rather than only searches.

cards.title: Constant-update working-set heaps on pointer machines
cards.formal: Does there exist a deterministic online priority queue in the pointer-machine model below and an absolute constant C such that every legal sequence of M operations, starting from an empty queue, has total cost at most \(C(M+\sum_{x\ \mathrm{extracted}}\log \Gamma(x))\)? The operations are insert, find-min, decrease-key, and extract-min. For an extracted item x, define \(\Gamma(x)=1+\) the number of insertions strictly after x was inserted and before it was extracted, including inserted items that have already been removed. An insertion creates a distinct item and returns its handle; decrease-key receives that handle and its new key. Require exact answers for all sequences; melding is not required.
cards.definitions: Keys are opaque values in a totally ordered set and can only be compared; ties are broken by a fixed order on item identities. Find-min returns the minimum live item; extract-min also removes it. Decrease-key changes the key of an existing item to a no-larger value and does not reset its insertion time. A pointer machine has records containing O(1) pointers and O(1) auxiliary bits, together with the supplied key records. A fixed program operates through O(1) pointer registers. Charge one step for a key comparison, a pointer traversal or change, a constant-bit operation, or allocation of one constant-size record. It cannot perform address arithmetic or unit-cost operations on an unbounded auxiliary integer; larger counters must be explicitly represented and manipulated. All work between requests is charged. Amortization is over every finite sequence, including sequences leaving items in the queue.
cards.why: This is a basic test of whether temporal adaptivity and cheap priority changes can coexist without word-level machine tricks. A solution would clarify a model distinction in a fundamental graph-algorithm primitive. The small remaining factor makes it a sharper structural question than simply asking for a faster heap.

context_blocks.text: The usual priority-queue guarantee charges for extraction according to the number of stored items. A working-set guarantee instead takes account of how recently the extracted item entered the queue. For example, keep a large collection of expensive items present, repeatedly insert one smaller item, and immediately extract it. Each of these recent items has Gamma equal to one, so the proposed budget charges only a constant per such pair of requests. This illustrates the adaptive behavior that the question asks the implementation to exploit.

Fast decreases matter independently of these insertion times. A graph algorithm can discover a better tentative distance for an item that has been waiting for a long time. The interface gives the algorithm a handle to that item, but the queue still has to update the organization used to find its next minimum. Efficient extraction alone therefore does not settle the requested operation sequence bound.

The pointer restriction isolates the contribution of machine operations to this adaptivity. The July 2026 revision of van der Hoog and coauthors gives constant amortized insertion and working-set extraction, with inverse-Ackermann amortized decrease-key. That remaining factor is very slowly growing, but is asymptotically different from a constant.

A separate July 2026 construction achieves constant decrease-key with a stronger, stack-like extraction guarantee, while charging an iterated-log-star overhead to insertion. Its different trade-off is useful progress, but the joint constant-update target here still requires another argument. This card fixes the insertion-count definition of the working set and expresses the amortized question as a single total-cost inequality.

cards.context:
The usual priority-queue guarantee charges for extraction according to the number of stored items. A working-set guarantee instead takes account of how recently the extracted item entered the queue. For example, keep a large collection of expensive items present, repeatedly insert one smaller item, and immediately extract it. Each of these recent items has Gamma equal to one, so the proposed budget charges only a constant per such pair of requests. This illustrates the adaptive behavior that the question asks the implementation to exploit.

Fast decreases matter independently of these insertion times. A graph algorithm can discover a better tentative distance for an item that has been waiting for a long time. The interface gives the algorithm a handle to that item, but the queue still has to update the organization used to find its next minimum. Efficient extraction alone therefore does not settle the requested operation sequence bound.

The pointer restriction isolates the contribution of machine operations to this adaptivity. The July 2026 revision of van der Hoog and coauthors gives constant amortized insertion and working-set extraction, with inverse-Ackermann amortized decrease-key. That remaining factor is very slowly growing, but is asymptotically different from a constant.

A separate July 2026 construction achieves constant decrease-key with a stronger, stack-like extraction guarantee, while charging an iterated-log-star overhead to insertion. Its different trade-off is useful progress, but the joint constant-update target here still requires another argument. This card fixes the insertion-count definition of the working set and expresses the amortized question as a single total-cost inequality.

cards.title: Buffered fully persistent search trees
cards.formal:
For every fixed real \(0<\varepsilon<1\), does there exist one uniform deterministic comparison-based external-memory data structure and a constant \(c\ge1\) that maintain the fully persistent ordered-set interface below, for every integer block size \(B\ge2\), internal-memory capacity \(M\ge2B\), and every online operation history? Require correctness and termination, worst-case at most \(c\) I/Os for each explicit \(\operatorname{Clone}\), and the following joint amortized bound on every finite history \(H\):
\[
\operatorname{IO}(H)\le c\!\left(1+C_H+\sum_{j\in\mathcal U_H}B^{\varepsilon-1}L_j+\sum_{j\in\mathcal Q_H}L_j+\sum_{j\in\mathcal R_H}\frac{K_j}{B}\right),
\qquad L_j=1+\log_B(2+N_j).
\]
Here \(\mathcal U_H\) indexes insertions and deletions, \(\mathcal Q_H\) indexes successor and range queries, \(\mathcal R_H\subseteq\mathcal Q_H\) indexes range queries, \(C_H\) counts explicit clones, \(N_j\) is the size of the version accessed by operation \(j\), and \(K_j\) is that range query’s output size. At every point require at most
\[
c\!\left(1+\frac{U+C}{B}\right)
\]
external-memory blocks, including metadata and temporary storage, where \(U,C\) count update and clone operations begun by that point. The constants and program may depend on \(\varepsilon\), but not on the block parameters, history, keys or version sizes. This retains the card’s stated simultaneous quantitative sharpening of the source’s broader question about buffered full persistence and efficient cloning.
cards.definitions:
Keys are indivisible atoms from an arbitrary totally ordered set. A version stores a finite set of keys, without multiplicities. Initially version \(0\) is empty. Each insertion, deletion and explicit clone creates a distinct new immutable version, assigned the next unused nonnegative integer handle. Every existing version remains available indefinitely. Operations are:

\(\operatorname{Insert}(v,x)\) returns a new handle \(w\) with \(S_w=S_v\cup\{x\}\). It creates a version even if \(x\in S_v\).

\(\operatorname{Delete}(v,x)\) returns a new handle \(w\) with \(S_w=S_v\setminus\{x\}\). It creates a version even if \(x\notin S_v\).

\(\operatorname{Clone}(v)\) returns a new handle \(w\) with \(S_w=S_v\).

\(\operatorname{Search}(v,x)\) returns \(\min\{y\in S_v:x\le y\}\), or a distinguished empty marker when that set is empty.

\(\operatorname{Range}(v,a,b)\), for \(a\le b\), reports every key in \(S_v\cap[a,b]\) once, in increasing order. An empty result is permitted.

In every operation, \(v\) can be any previously returned handle, including an ancestor or a version used many times before. The sizes \(N_j=|S_v|\) are measured before the operation. No version is overwritten or merged with another. In particular, an update already preserves its parent and must meet its update charge without an additional explicit clone charge. An explicit clone is a separate requested operation. Every operation must finish and return its full answer before the next is received. Later requests may depend on earlier answers; no future operations or length of the history are known to the data structure.

The I/O model has at most \(M\) internal cells and an initially blank external array partitioned into blocks of \(B\) consecutive cells. A cell holds one key atom or one metadata word. Data can be inspected or changed only in internal memory. One I/O transfers one entire block between internal and external memory and costs one. Reads and writes both count, including all preprocessing, rebuilding, buffer flushing and version metadata access. Computation on resident data is free for the I/O measure but must terminate. Keys may only be copied, stored, output or compared for order/equality; their bit representation cannot be inspected, arithmetically manipulated, packed with other keys into one cell or used as an address. Metadata words encode integers, addresses, handles and finite tags; each contains at most \(d\lceil\log_2(t+M+B+2)\rceil\) bits during the \(t\)-th operation, for one fixed integer \(d\ge1\) chosen with the program. All program work storage and persistent metadata count toward the stated memories. Fixed finite control is not a source of growing storage. Apart from the supplied current operation, the program cannot read past inputs, old outputs or the caller’s collection of handles without having stored the needed information itself.

The program knows \(B,M\), so cache obliviousness is not required. It is a finite deterministic algorithm, with no advice, randomness, oracle or input-dependent precomputed tables. For each fixed \(\varepsilon\) there must be a single such program for all \(B,M\); no algorithm taking an arbitrary real \(\varepsilon\) as input is requested. There is no separate internal computation-time bound or prescribed B-tree layout.

Operation arguments and a constant-size returned handle/key are presented through the interface without an extra compulsory I/O. A range answer is written to an output-only stream in blocks; each flushed full or final partial output block counts as an I/O. The stream is unavailable for later reads and is excluded from retained data-structure space. Internal output buffering counts toward \(M\). Allocated external storage, including partially filled blocks, is charged; freed blocks cease to count. The space bound holds throughout an operation using the number of updates/clones already begun, and at every completed prefix. No deletion of historical versions or garbage collection of their logical contents is allowed.

\(\operatorname{IO}(H)\) counts all transfers from initialization through completion of \(H\). The displayed single inequality defines amortization jointly across operation types and every prefix. Its additive constant covers initialization and rounding; it does not add one to the charge of each update. The clone bound is additionally a per-operation worst-case bound. The space bound concerns the whole retained history, not the sum of the sizes of its sets, and is independent of the number of queries.
cards.why: Buffering reduces storage transfers for updates, while full persistence permits new branches from historical states. Combining them with queries measured by the accessed version’s size and space measured by the update history would provide both capabilities in one comparison-based storage index.

context_blocks.text: The ESA 2025 paper permits queries at every old version while allowing updates only at the newest version. Its Theorem 1 proves buffered update cost \(O(B^{\varepsilon-1}\log_B N_v)\), successor-query cost \(O(\log_B N_v)\), range-reporting cost \(O(\log_B N_v+K/B)\), and space linear in the update history for fixed \(\varepsilon\). Its model needs only \(M\ge2B\).

The source’s Section 4 explicitly leaves efficient cloning with buffered full persistence open. It does not conjecture the entire numerical combination on this card. The retained editorial target adds the exact per-version bounds, worst-case constant cloning, immutable versions after every update and linear total history space. In particular, it does not hide a constant clone charge inside each subconstant amortized update.

The STOC 2023 result provides full persistence with \(O(1)\) worst-case cloning, \(O(\log_BN_v)\) amortized updates and \(O(\log_BN_v+K/B)\) worst-case range reporting. It has no buffering factor in its update bound. Its interface uses mutable leaves and explicit cloning to preserve a version before modifying it.

Svenning’s dissertation, dated 4 October 2025, includes the buffered partial-persistence work and repeats the open question about efficient cloning. This is a later copy of the same research question rather than an independent proof of the combined target.

A July 2026 paper on a retroactive buffer tree describes batched edits to a temporal history using partial persistence. Its inspected publisher abstract does not claim the immutable branching interface and simultaneous bounds required here. Retroactivity changes later states along a history, whereas this card preserves every existing version.

cards.title: Combined depth and size bounds for confluently persistent tries
cards.formal: For every fixed integer \(k\ge2\), does there exist a deterministic uniform functional trie representation and a constant \(C_k>0\) that supports the version, finger-navigation and subtree-copy interface below, with worst-case navigation time \(C_k\log_2(2+\Delta)\), no new permanent records from navigation, and both worst-case modification time and newly permanent record count at most \(C_k[1+\min\{D\log_2(2+\Delta),\log_2(2+N)\}]\) for every valid operation sequence?
cards.definitions:
A logical trie is a finite rooted tree, including its root, with distinct totally ordered labels on the outgoing edges of each node and one constant-size data atom per node. Logical occurrences are counted separately even when their physical representations share records. For each fixed integer \(k\ge2\), every stored version has \(k\) finger positions, possibly coincident. Selecting a version restores those positions in at most \(C_k\) operations; navigation changes a working copy of them. Reading a node’s data also costs at most \(C_k\) operations. These calls do not permit uncharged preprocessing. It can reset a finger to the root, move it to its parent, follow a child with a supplied label, or read the data at a finger. A failed parent or child move reports failure and leaves the finger unchanged. A modification creates a new stored version and leaves every previous version usable. It can change data at a finger, add a new leaf with an unused child label, remove the non-root subtree at a finger, or copy the subtree at a finger of any source version as a child with an unused label at a destination finger. The source and destination versions may coincide. The copy is a logical duplicate, so later changes to either occurrence do not change the other. Surviving destination fingers keep their logical positions; fingers in a removed subtree reset to the root. A copy may replace any specified subset of the resulting finger slots by counterparts of source fingers inside the copied subtree. Thus at most \(k\) fingers are stored in the resulting version. All parameters are supplied through version handles, finger indices and constant-size atoms; arbitrary logical nodes cannot be addressed directly.

Use a deterministic uniform pointer program with a fixed number of fields per record. A field holds a pointer, an opaque label or data atom, or an integer counter. Reading a field, comparing or copying atoms or pointers, comparing labels, and adding, subtracting or comparing counters cost one operation. New records may be initialized, but a previously initialized record is never overwritten. There is no pointer arithmetic, address-indexed array lookup, arithmetic on labels, random choice, oracle or nonuniform table. Counters have magnitude polynomial in the largest logical version size and operation count so far; costs count record operations, not their bit implementation. The program and field count are independent of all versions and operation sequences; constants may depend on the fixed finger bound \(k\). The initial version is a single root and costs \(O(k)\) operations and records.

For a modification, let \(N\) be the sum of the logical node counts of its participating input versions and its output version, counting a shared input only once. Let \(\Delta\ge2\) be the maximum of two and all node outdegrees in those versions. Let \(D=1+\sum_f\operatorname{depth}(f)\), summing the depths of the \(k\) stored or working fingers in each participating input version; root depth is zero. Define \(B=1+\min\{D\log_2(2+\Delta),\log_2(2+N)\}\). For navigation, \(\Delta\) is instead the maximum of two and the outdegrees in the selected logical version. Navigation must cost at most \(C_k\log_2(2+\Delta)\) operations, and a modification at most \(C_kB\) operations, in the worst case for every individual call in every finite valid sequence.

A record is permanent when reachable from any stored version handle, including that version’s stored finger representation. All stored versions remain available. Navigation may allocate temporary records but must leave the set of permanent records unchanged. A modification is charged every record newly made permanent by its result, including records allocated during earlier navigation; this count must be at most \(C_kB\). Existing permanent records shared by the new version are not charged again. Temporary allocation time is always charged to the call performing it; the permanent-space guarantee is not a bound on peak temporary storage. All logarithms and bounds use logical version sizes, not the number of previously allocated physical records.
cards.why: The question concerns whether persistent hierarchical data can exploit shallow or local changes while also protecting users against arbitrarily deep versions.

context_blocks.text: Version control must preserve old directory trees while allowing a whole directory to be copied between branches. A logical subtree copy can contain very many nodes, yet a representation can initially share their unchanged contents. Confluent persistence requires both source versions and all older versions to remain usable after this operation.

The source gives two functional representations. One exploits locality of finger operations with \(O(\log\Delta)\) time and allocation per call; navigation records can later become permanent. The other uses \(O(\log n)\) time and permanent space per modification, with \(O(\log\Delta)\) navigation time and no permanent navigation space. These are different guarantees because navigation may be followed by either another query or a modification.

An arbitrarily long path illustrates the size/depth distinction. A change near its root has small root depth even when the version is enormous, whereas a change near the bottom has large depth. The requested minimum would retain a shallow-update bound and also cap deep-update costs logarithmically in logical size. The question concerns one representation with simultaneous guarantees, not choosing a separate representation after seeing the next operation.

Charging only the records allocated inside the final update would conceal part of the first representation’s cost. Records produced by earlier finger moves count against the update if the new stored version retains them. Conversely, a navigation-only sequence produces no new stored versions, so discarded temporary work does not count as permanent history.

Editorial specification: Section 6 states the combined depth/size goal but leaves the multi-finger parameters implicit. This benchmark uses the sum of participating finger depths, a maximum degree over participating versions, and the sum of input/output logical sizes. With a fixed number of fingers these specify a single bound for copies and deletions; a one-finger point modification retains the root-depth scale \(1+d\). They are explicit conventions for the combined variant, not definitions quoted verbatim from the authors.

The source’s constant-time comparison of labels and functional pointer-record model are retained. This is not a claim about the cost of comparing arbitrary file-name strings, storing file contents, or implementing large counters in a bit machine. The documented temporary/permanent distinction is part of the target, rather than an unrecorded memory exemption.

cards.context:
Version control must preserve old directory trees while allowing a whole directory to be copied between branches. A logical subtree copy can contain very many nodes, yet a representation can initially share their unchanged contents. Confluent persistence requires both source versions and all older versions to remain usable after this operation.

The source gives two functional representations. One exploits locality of finger operations with \(O(\log\Delta)\) time and allocation per call; navigation records can later become permanent. The other uses \(O(\log n)\) time and permanent space per modification, with \(O(\log\Delta)\) navigation time and no permanent navigation space. These are different guarantees because navigation may be followed by either another query or a modification.

An arbitrarily long path illustrates the size/depth distinction. A change near its root has small root depth even when the version is enormous, whereas a change near the bottom has large depth. The requested minimum would retain a shallow-update bound and also cap deep-update costs logarithmically in logical size. The question concerns one representation with simultaneous guarantees, not choosing a separate representation after seeing the next operation.

Charging only the records allocated inside the final update would conceal part of the first representation’s cost. Records produced by earlier finger moves count against the update if the new stored version retains them. Conversely, a navigation-only sequence produces no new stored versions, so discarded temporary work does not count as permanent history.

Editorial specification: Section 6 states the combined depth/size goal but leaves the multi-finger parameters implicit. This benchmark uses the sum of participating finger depths, a maximum degree over participating versions, and the sum of input/output logical sizes. With a fixed number of fingers these specify a single bound for copies and deletions; a one-finger point modification retains the root-depth scale \(1+d\). They are explicit conventions for the combined variant, not definitions quoted verbatim from the authors.

The source’s constant-time comparison of labels and functional pointer-record model are retained. This is not a claim about the cost of comparing arbitrary file-name strings, storing file contents, or implementing large counters in a bit machine. The documented temporary/permanent distinction is part of the target, rather than an unrecorded memory exemption.

cards.title: Deterministic fully dynamic connectivity with polylogarithmic worst-case updates
cards.formal:
Does there exist a finite deterministic word-RAM program \(A\), with fixed positive integer constants \(C,c,d,a\), such that for every integer \(n\ge2\) it maintains an initially empty simple undirected graph on \([n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}\) under every finite valid online sequence of edge insertions, edge deletions and pairwise connectivity queries, with all the following guarantees?
\[\begin{aligned}
 \text{initialization time}&\le Cn^d,\\
 \text{total stored words at every time}&\le Cn^d,\\
 \text{time of each individual operation}&\le C(\log_2 n)^c.
\end{aligned}\]
Every query must return the exact connectivity bit. Initialization receives only \(n\); the word size is \(w=\lceil a\log_2 n\rceil\), and computation uses the machine conventions below. All constants and the same finite program are chosen before \(n\) or the operation sequence. Give a complete Lean proof of this existence proposition or its logical negation.
cards.definitions:
A graph state is a set \(E\subseteq\{\{u,v\}:u,v\in[n],\ u\ne v\}\), initially empty. An operation has a tag and two vertex labels, each supplied as one word. A valid \(\operatorname{insert}(u,v)\) requires distinct endpoints and an absent edge, and adds that edge. A valid \(\operatorname{delete}(u,v)\) requires a present edge and removes it. A query \(\operatorname{connected}(u,v)\) is valid for any \(u,v\in[n]\) and outputs one bit. Its answer is one exactly when there is a finite sequence \(u=x_0,x_1,\ldots,x_k=v\), with \(k\ge0\), whose consecutive pairs are edges of the current graph. In particular, a vertex is connected to itself. The graph has no additional promise on density, planarity, degree or expansion.

The machine must finish the current operation before the next is supplied. No operation count, future sequence, or complete input graph is available during initialization. The guarantee applies to every finite valid sequence of arbitrary length, including sequences selected using all previously observable states and answers. Persistent memory is bounded in terms of \(n\) alone, independently of the elapsed number of operations. Past output is write-only and cannot serve as free external storage.

Fix a word RAM with a finite instruction list and a fixed finite number of word registers. Words are unsigned integers in \(\{0,\ldots,2^w-1\}\); memory addresses are also words. Each indirect load or store, register copy, comparison, conditional branch, Boolean bitwise operation, shift, and arithmetic operation on at most two words costs one step. Arithmetic primitives are addition, subtraction, multiplication, integer quotient and remainder. Addition, subtraction and multiplication return their result modulo \(2^w\); quotient and remainder use unsigned integer division and a zero divisor causes failure. A left shift discards bits outside the word; a right shift fills with zeros; either returns zero when the shift amount is at least \(w\). Reading an input word and writing the query bit also cost one step. The finite program can contain fixed integer constants, interpreted modulo \(2^w\), but has no oracle, random instruction, advice string or input-size-dependent instruction table. Any longer arithmetic computation pays for all constituent instructions.

Mutable registers and allocated memory, including every table and representation of the graph, count toward the stated space bound. Initially they contain only zeros except for the input \(n\); data-dependent initialization, allocation and zeroing of allocated words are charged. Every addressed location must be allocated and have a representable address. The fixed coefficient \(a\) may be chosen sufficiently large for the program's polynomial space; it cannot depend on \(n\) or sequence length. Polynomial preprocessing may depend only on \(n\), and all its computation and stored output count toward the initialization and space bounds. The program and its fixed finite control are independent of \(n\).

Time includes all graph maintenance, rebuilding, memory management, query computation and response output performed during that operation. No background work between operations is free. The operation bound is a worst-case bound for each individual call, not an average over a sequence or an expectation. Using positive integer constants is a normalization of the original polynomial-space and polylogarithmic-time bounds: enlarging constants or exponents absorbs fixed factors and small input sizes. It imposes no graph restriction.
cards.answer_criterion:
Give a complete, mathematically correct Lean proof of either
\[\exists A\ \exists C,c,d,a\in\mathbb N_{\ge1}\ \forall n\ge2\ \forall s\in\mathcal S_n,\quad \operatorname{Guarantees}(A,C,c,d,a,n,s),\]
or its logical negation. Here \(A\) ranges over the finite deterministic programs just defined, \(\mathcal S_n\) is the set of all finite valid operation sequences, and \(\operatorname{Guarantees}\) includes initialization, termination, exact answers, memory use and the per-operation bounds in the statement. A positive answer must establish all guarantees for one program and constants that work for every \(n,s\). A negative answer must rule out every such program and every constant choice, equivalently show that each candidate fails a required guarantee for some size and finite valid sequence, with the empty sequence also testing initialization. Failure to terminate is a failure of the applicable time bound.

All memory and running-time statements must refer to the specified machine semantics. A lower bound for a restricted family of implementations, a single counterexample to one proposed algorithm, or a theorem requiring an unproved complexity assumption does not negate the full proposition. An amortized, randomized, expected-time, restricted-graph or offline guarantee does not prove it. This is an existence question, with no numerical tolerance or weaker intermediate target.
cards.why: Exact dynamic connectivity is a basic test of whether a graph data structure can guarantee uniformly low latency without randomness. The question separates efficient processing of a long sequence from a fast response after every individual change, and is relevant to graph algorithms that call connectivity as a subroutine.

The inspected October 2025 preprint, published at SODA 2026, explicitly leaves the deterministic polylogarithmic worst-case target open and proves an expected randomized bound plus a conditional deterministic theorem. However, the official FOCS 2026 accepted list and an author page now announce a closely matching new paper by Meierhans, Probst Gutenberg and Yeh. context_blocks.text: Connectivity asks whether two vertices lie in the same component, not for a shortest path or an explicit list of all vertices in that component. Deleting an edge can change this answer for many pairs simultaneously. The required output is still only the queried bit; the target concerns how much work must be charged to each operation.

Holm, de Lichtenberg and Thorup give a deterministic structure with \(O(\log^2 n)\) amortized update time and \(O(\log n/\log\log n)\) connectivity query time. Their guarantee controls the total work over a sequence, while permitting an expensive individual update. It does not establish the per-operation guarantee asked here.

Kapron, King and Mountjoy give worst-case bounds \(O(\log^4 n)\) for insertion, \(O(\log^5 n)\) for deletion and \(O(\log n/\log\log n)\) for queries. Their randomized structure has one-sided error: a reported connection is valid, but a reported disconnection can be wrong with small probability. This does not give the exact deterministic guarantee.

Chuzhoy and coauthors establish deterministic \(n^{o(1)}\) worst-case update time. This notation permits functions growing more quickly than every fixed power of \(\log n\), for example \(\exp(\sqrt{\log n})\). Consequently a subpolynomial bound alone leaves a gap to the fixed polylogarithm in this card.

Meierhans and Probst Gutenberg’s SODA 2026 Theorem 1.1 is Las Vegas: it maintains a correct spanning forest with polylogarithmic expected worst-case update time. Its guarantee even allows an adaptive adversary observing the internal state and random bits. The expectation is over the algorithm’s randomness for an operation, rather than amortization over operations; it remains different from a deterministic bound on every execution. Theorem 1.3 gives a conditional deterministic result, not an unconditional resolution of this card.

Pătraşcu and Demaine prove \(\max\{t_u,t_q\}=\Omega(\log n)\), together with update–query tradeoffs, in the cell-probe model with \(O(\log n)\)-bit cells. Here \(t_u\) and \(t_q\) measure update and query cost. The bound applies even to disjoint paths and permits amortization and randomization. Cell probes count memory accesses while allowing free computation, so a bound there also constrains a word RAM. A logarithmic lower bound is compatible with the requested polylogarithmic upper bound.

As checked on 15 September 2026, the official FOCS 2026 accepted-paper list includes Dynamic Connectivity, Minimum Spanning Tree, and 2-Edge Connectivity with Polylogarithmic Worst-Case Update Time, by Simon Meierhans, Maximilian Probst Gutenberg and Yu-Cheng Yeh. The inspected entry provides a title and authors, with no theorem or manuscript link. It does not specify whether the guarantee is deterministic. The current status is therefore recorded as uncertain; this announcement is neither treated as a verified matching solution nor ignored in favor of an older open-problem statement.

Probst Gutenberg’s publication page independently lists the same FOCS 2026 title and coauthors, again without a manuscript link in that entry. The conference is scheduled for November 2026; its acceptance announcement is distinct from an inspected proceedings paper. A complete statement is needed to decide whether the result meets this exact deterministic target.

cards.title: Fully dynamic near-optimal matching with polylogarithmic updates
cards.formal: For every fixed rational \(\varepsilon \in (0,1)\), is there a randomized fully dynamic algorithm that maintains an explicit matching M with |\(M|\ge \nu (G)/(1+\varepsilon )\) in every current general graph G using polylogarithmic expected amortized update time against an oblivious adversary?
cards.definitions: The graph is simple, undirected and unweighted, on the fixed vertex set \([n], n\ge 2; \nu (G)\) is its maximum matching cardinality. It starts empty. An update inserts one absent edge or deletes one present edge. Updates arrive online, but the entire valid sequence is fixed independently of the algorithm’s random bits and is not revealed in advance. More precisely, for every fixed \(\varepsilon\) and constant \(a\ge 1\), require constants K,d,B and a uniform randomized word-RAM algorithm \(A_{\varepsilon ,a}\) such that every sequence of \(T\le n^{a}\) updates has expected total initialization-plus-update cost at most \(K[n+T(\log _{2}(n+2))^{d}]\). Words have \(B\lceil \log _{2}(n+2)\rceil\) bits; standard word operations, memory access and retained random bits are charged. With probability at least \(1- n^{- 3}\), after every update in the sequence an explicit mate array represents a valid matching satisfying the approximation bound. Reading a vertex’s mate or the matching cardinality takes \(O(1)\) time; enumerating all matching edges costs \(O(n)\) and need not occur after every update. Changes to the mate array count toward update cost. Constants may depend on \(\varepsilon\) and a, but not on n, T or the sequence. No polynomial dependence on \(1/\varepsilon\), adaptive-adversary guarantee or worst-case per-update bound is required. The word instructions are random-access reads/writes, comparisons, conditional branches, addition, subtraction and multiplication modulo \(2^{w}\), integer quotient/remainder with nonzero divisor, bitwise Boolean operations, and shifts of a w-bit word; shifts by at least w yield zero. The constant in word length \(w=\Theta (\log  n)\) (or \(\Theta (\log  N)\) when N is the stated input size) is fixed with the algorithm. Address arithmetic has the same cost, larger integers occupy multiple words, and no instruction performs arbitrary-precision arithmetic in one step. When randomization is allowed, a fresh independent uniform w-bit word costs one operation. In this statement, “explicitly given/encoded/listed” means the entire finite list, table or syntax tree described above is part of the input or output, with its full encoding counted; it does not mean a circuit, oracle or program generating a larger object.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove the proposition in the problem statement or prove its logical negation, using exactly the definitions, hypotheses and quantifier order stated here. The proof must cover the complete target.
cards.why: The principal update-time frontier for maintaining actual near-optimal matchings under arbitrary edge insertions and deletions, beyond maximality and matching-size estimation.

cards.status_note: Reviewed through 11 September 2026. No polylogarithmic-update algorithm meeting the fixed-accuracy, explicit-matching target was found. Matching-size estimators, ordered-RS-dependent bounds and the 2026 maximal-matching improvement do not resolve it.

context_blocks.text: A maximum matching allocates the largest possible number of disjoint pairs. When an edge changes, recomputing it from scratch ignores the substantial information retained from the preceding graph. The dynamic problem asks how much of that information can be reused while keeping a solution within an arbitrarily small fixed relative loss of optimum. Both insertions and deletions are allowed, so previously useful structure can disappear.

The graph’s optimum changes by at most one after a single edge update, but a particular solution may require coordinated replacements. On a long alternating path, gaining one additional matched edge can involve changing many pairs. Approximation creates room to postpone or distribute some repairs. The difficulty is to do so without accumulating a large loss or spending too much time discovering the repairs that are needed.

An explicit solution is part of the target. A number close to \(\nu (G)\) need not identify even one edge that can safely be used with the others. A mate array makes this distinction observable: a query at a vertex must return its current partner or report that it is unmatched. Requiring the whole array to be printed after every update would impose an artificial linear output cost, so the formulation instead charges only actual changes and queries.

Maximality is also weaker than near-optimality. In a four-vertex path, selecting only the middle edge gives a maximal matching of size one, while the two outside edges give a maximum matching of size two. Randomized maximal-matching algorithms already achieve very small update times against oblivious sequences. Chuzhoy–Khanna–Song’s STOC 2026 result improves deterministic maximal matching to \(n^{1/2+o(1)}\) amortized time; its guarantee still concerns maximality.

A separate sequence of breakthroughs beats the factor-two barrier for estimating matching size in polylogarithmic update time. Azarmehr–Behnezhad–Roghani’s SODA 2024 result obtains an estimate corresponding to a \(2- \sqrt{2}- \eta\) fraction of optimum in general graphs, for fixed \(\eta >0\). The paper explicitly studies size estimation. Its title alone can therefore suggest a stronger maintenance result than the theorem actually supplies.

For maintaining actual near-optimal matchings, Assadi–Khanna–Kiss’s SODA 2025 work develops a connection to ordered Ruzsa–Szemerédi graphs. Such a graph has its edges partitioned into matchings, with each matching induced in the union of itself and later matchings. Dense examples quantify how often certain expensive matching searches can recur. Their update bound is expressed through this extremal quantity and works even against adaptive adversaries.

cards.context:
A maximum matching allocates the largest possible number of disjoint pairs. When an edge changes, recomputing it from scratch ignores the substantial information retained from the preceding graph. Both insertions and deletions are allowed, so previously useful structure can disappear.

The graph’s optimum changes by at most one after a single edge update, but a particular solution may require coordinated replacements. On a long alternating path, gaining one additional matched edge can involve changing many pairs. Approximation creates room to postpone or distribute some repairs. The difficulty is to do so without accumulating a large loss or spending too much time discovering the repairs that are needed.

An explicit solution is part of the target. A number close to \(\nu (G)\) need not identify even one edge that can safely be used with the others.
