cards.title: Polylogarithmic worst-case updates for exact dynamic minimum spanning forests
cards.formal:
For every fixed pair of integers \(a,b\ge1\), does there exist a uniform randomized data structure that maintains the exact canonical minimum spanning forest of the graph below, with polynomial preprocessing and space and polylogarithmic worst-case time for each edge insertion or deletion? For every valid update sequence \(\sigma\) of length \(T\le n^a\) fixed independently of its randomness, require
\[\Pr_R\bigl[\widehat F_t=F(G_t)\text{ for every }0\le t\le T\bigr]\ge1-n^{-b}.\]
The event also requires every edge-change report to be valid as defined below. Here \(G_t\) is the graph after update \(t\), \(F(G_t)\) is its specified exact forest, and \(\widehat F_t\) is reconstructed from the reported edge changes. Each update must finish within its time bound on every execution, including executions on which the answer is wrong. The data structure receives no future updates in advance.
cards.definitions:
Graph and updates. Fix an integer \(n\ge2\), with labelled vertices \([n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}\). The graph is simple and undirected: no loops or parallel edges. Initially \(G_0\) has no edges. An insertion supplies distinct endpoints \(u,v\) of an absent edge and an integer weight \(w\in\{1,\ldots,n^4\}\); a deletion supplies the endpoints of a present edge. A weight stays fixed until its edge is deleted. Reinsertion may assign a different weight. A valid sequence respects these rules at every prefix; disconnected graphs, isolated vertices and repeated insertions after deletions are allowed. Vertices are never inserted or deleted. The exponent four is the retained concrete choice of polynomial weight range.

Exact target and ties. A spanning forest has one spanning tree in each connected component, with an isolated vertex contributing no edges. Its cost is the sum of its edge weights, and a minimum spanning forest minimizes that sum. To specify one answer when several forests have the same cost, order edges by the triple \((w,\min(u,v),\max(u,v))\), in increasing lexicographic order. Define \(F(G)\) by starting with no edges, scanning the present edges in this order, and retaining an edge exactly when adding it does not create a cycle. This is the canonical minimum spanning forest; the scan defines the target and is not a required implementation. In particular \(F(G_0)=\varnothing\).

Required output. After each update, before receiving the next one, report a list \(D_t\) of forest edges removed and a list \(A_t\) of forest edges added, using unordered endpoint pairs represented with their smaller endpoint first. Starting from \(\widehat F_0=\varnothing\), the reported forest is \(\widehat F_t=(\widehat F_{t-1}\setminus D_t)\cup A_t\). On a correct execution these lists must be exactly \(F(G_{t-1})\setminus F(G_t)\) and \(F(G_t)\setminus F(G_{t-1})\), respectively. Each contains at most one edge for a single valid update. Printing all current tree edges is not required. Duplicate or invalid reports count as a correctness failure; they never excuse exceeding the time or space bound. No later query or background computation may postpone completing the report.

Machine and costs. Use a classical sequential word RAM, with word length \(w_n=\lambda\lceil\log_2(n+2)\rceil\) for some fixed positive integer \(\lambda\) chosen with the data structure. Unit-cost operations are direct or indirect word reads and writes; word comparisons, branches and copies; addition, subtraction and multiplication modulo \(2^{w_n}\); integer quotient and remainder with nonzero divisor; bitwise Boolean operations; and shifts with zero fill and truncation to one word. A shift by at least the word length produces zero. One instruction may generate one independent uniformly random word. Larger integers require multiple words and their actual operations are charged. Endpoints and allowed weights occupy a constant number of words. Addressable memory cells contain words and have word-sized addresses. Input reading, output writing, random generation, memory access and all computation count. There is no rank oracle, free query to another graph algorithm, arbitrary-precision unit-cost arithmetic, parallel computation or uncharged lookup table.

Uniformity and resource bounds. For each fixed \(a,b\), choose one finite program, constants \(K\ge1\), integers \(C,D\ge1\), and \(\lambda\). These choices are independent of \(n\) and of the sequence. On input \(n\), initialization of the empty graph finishes within \(Kn^D\) steps and uses at most \(Kn^D\) words; all later memory use has the same bound. Initialized tables must be computed within this preprocessing budget. There is no advice or precomputed table varying with \(n\). For every valid sequence in the stated horizon and every realization of all random choices, update \(t\) finishes in at most
\[K\bigl(\log_2(n+2)\bigr)^C\]
steps, including its report. Choose the word-length constant large enough to address the permitted memory. Randomness may be used in preprocessing and updates. The parameters \(a,b\) tune the allowable polynomial horizon and failure probability; the program and constants may depend on them. No uniform bound on that dependence is requested.

Probability convention. The entire input sequence is fixed before the data structure draws any random bits, so it is an oblivious sequence. The probability is over all random words \(R\), including initialization, and covers simultaneous correctness of every report throughout the sequence. Separate per-update probability bounds without a simultaneous bound are insufficient. The time and memory bounds themselves have no exceptional random outcomes. This is the retained Monte Carlo formulation: a small probability of a wrong answer is permitted, whereas an always-correct deterministic data structure would be a stronger positive answer.
cards.answer_criterion:
Give a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of the quantified existence claim or its negation. For a positive answer, specify the programs for every fixed \(a,b\), their resource constants and randomization. Prove initialization, exact canonical forest maintenance, online reporting, worst-case time and space on every random execution, and the simultaneous probability bound for every valid oblivious sequence of length at most \(n^a\).

A negative answer must refute the stated quantified claim: for some fixed \(a,b\), no allowed uniform program and constants meet all requirements. It must cover randomized data structures with polynomial preprocessing and space in this word-RAM model. Failure of one technique or one logarithmic exponent, a deterministic-only lower bound, or an impossibility limited to a more restrictive access model does not suffice. A conditional lower bound must retain its assumptions and does not by itself refute this unconditional proposition.

Amortized polylogarithmic time, subpolynomial worst-case time, an expected-time bound alone, an approximate forest or a deferred expensive query does not meet the criterion. A result with probabilistic time bounds needs an explicit conversion satisfying the stated hard time cap and simultaneous correctness guarantee. A rank-query count or parallel span is not the sequential running time specified here.
cards.why: A basic dynamic optimization problem with very small changes to its answer but potentially expensive global replacement searches. It tests whether amortized efficiency can be made reliable for every update.

importance.reason: One of the main unresolved worst-case update barriers in dynamic graph algorithms, closely connecting connectivity, weighted optimization, sparsification and expander maintenance.

progress.text: Holm–de Lichtenberg–Thorup establish deterministic \(O(\log ^{4} n)\) amortized minimum-spanning-forest updates.
Holm–Rotenberg–Wulff-Nilsen improve amortized bounds; the \(O(\log ^{4} n/\log  \log  n)\) option uses randomized priority queues in the stated RAM model.
Nanongkai–Saranurak–Wulff-Nilsen give Las Vegas subpolynomial worst-case update time with high probability.
Chuzhoy and coauthors obtain deterministic \(n^{o(1)}\) worst-case updates via deterministic expander decomposition.

Meierhans–Probst Gutenberg’s SODA paper gives expected polylogarithmic worst-case connectivity maintenance; its weighted extension is \((1+\varepsilon )\)-approximate with inverse-\(\varepsilon\) overhead.
De Vos–Grilnberger give logarithmically many rank queries per dynamic minimum-weight-base update, without a corresponding RAM update-time guarantee.

cards.status_note: Checked on 16 September 2026. Inspected primary sources retain the gap between exact polylogarithmic amortized updates and exact subpolynomial worst-case updates. The SODA 2026 weighted extension is approximate, and ESA 2026 minimum-weight-base maintenance counts rank queries without bounding their implementation time. No matching exact polylogarithmic worst-case RAM resolution was found in the bounded source search; cited proofs were not independently formalized.

context_blocks.text: One edge update can force a global search even though the optimal forest changes by very little. Deleting a tree edge splits one tree into two parts; the algorithm must find the cheapest surviving edge crossing that cut, if one exists. There may be many candidate edges dispersed throughout the graph. Inserting an edge is easier to understand: it creates a cycle if its endpoints are already connected, and it replaces the largest edge on that cycle when this improves the ordered forest.

The reporting convention makes the maintained answer observable without requiring the algorithm to print all \(n- 1\) tree edges after every update. With fixed tie-breaking, the forest changes by at most one insertion and one deletion. Holm, Rotenberg and Wulff-Nilsen use this explicit update model in their formulation. The difficulty is finding those few changes quickly, rather than paying for a large unavoidable output.

Polylogarithmic amortized maintenance is already established. Holm, de Lichtenberg and Thorup give a deterministic \(O(\log^4 n)\) amortized update bound. Amortization bounds the total cost across a sequence and permits individual updates to be much slower. The present target requires the current answer within the same polylogarithmic time budget after every single update, including a deletion chosen to expose a difficult replacement search.

Later amortized refinements improve the logarithmic factors. The 2015 work of Holm, Rotenberg and Wulff-Nilsen obtains \(O(\log ^{4} n/\log  \log  n)\) using the randomized priority-queue option in its table of RAM implementations. Its deterministic implementation has a different bound. None of these variants supplies the worst-case per-update guarantee requested here.

The worst-case frontier crossed a major threshold in 2017. Nanongkai, Saranurak and Wulff-Nilsen obtain a Las Vegas algorithm: its answers are always correct, while each update has subpolynomial time in expectation and with high probability. These probability guarantees concern time. This card instead places a hard limit on time and allows a small probability of an incorrect forest. The two conventions must be distinguished even before comparing their asymptotic bounds.

Chuzhoy and coauthors subsequently obtain deterministic \(n^{o(1)}\) worst-case time for exact dynamic MSF. Subpolynomial remains weaker than polylogarithmic: \(\exp(\sqrt{\log n})\), for example, grows more slowly than every fixed positive power of \(n\) but faster than every fixed power of \(\log n\). Thus the deterministic theorem is a major improvement without meeting this card’s sharper running-time target.

The SODA 2026 connectivity result of Meierhans and Probst Gutenberg achieves expected polylogarithmic worst-case updates for maintaining an unweighted spanning forest, and also discusses conversion to high-probability time bounds. It extends to a \((1+\varepsilon )\)-approximate weighted minimum spanning forest with overhead proportional to \(\log (U)/\varepsilon\) for weights in \([1,U]\). The approximation parameter is essential; this is not an exact weighted minimum-forest theorem.

The dependence on \(\varepsilon\) prevents reading the approximate theorem as an exact polylogarithmic-time result. Integer forest costs differ by at least one, but a forest may have total weight as large as \((n-1)n^4\). Requiring multiplicative error small enough to certify exact cost in every instance introduces a polynomial, rather than polylogarithmic, overhead in the displayed guarantee. Exact cost would also still have to respect this card’s fixed choice among tied optima.

The ESA 2026 paper on dynamic matroids gives a deterministic algorithm maintaining a minimum-weight base with \(O(\log N)\) rank queries per update, where \(N\) is the matroid ground-set size. A rank query asks for the maximum size of an independent subset of an arbitrary supplied set. For a graph this requires determining the largest forest inside that edge set. The paper expressly distinguishes its oracle-query count from update time: it does not bound the cost of implementing these rank queries on a concrete matroid. Its proposition therefore does not settle the ordinary RAM problem here.

The oblivious-adversary convention means the update sequence is chosen without reacting to the data structure’s random outcomes. A solution robust to an adaptive adversary would be stronger. Even this stated convention would remove a longstanding delay barrier for a central dynamic optimization primitive, with uses in algorithms that repeatedly maintain weighted spanning structures.

cards.title: Polylogarithmic maintenance of the exact global minimum cut
cards.formal: Can a fully dynamic simple, unweighted, undirected n-vertex graph maintain its exact global minimum-cut value with expected \(\operatorname{polylog}(n)\) amortized update time, worst-case \(\operatorname{polylog}(n)\) query time and polynomial space, with high probability over every polynomial-length oblivious operation sequence?
cards.definitions: Fix vertices \([n], n\ge 2\). Start from the empty graph. A legal update inserts one absent unordered edge or deletes one present edge; there are no loops, parallel edges, weights or vertex updates. A query returns the integer \(\lambda (G)=\min \{|\{uv\in E:u\in S,v\notin S\}| : \varnothing \ne S\subsetneq [n]\}\). In particular \(\lambda (G)=0\) for a disconnected graph; no distinguished terminals are supplied. Only the value is required, not a list of vertices or edges realizing the cut. Use a uniform randomized word-RAM with \(\Theta (\log (n+2))\)-bit words, ordinary arithmetic, bit operations and random access, and count all maintenance and query work. Precisely, ask for fixed exponents b,c and an algorithm accepting any fixed constant \(a\ge 1\) as a confidence parameter. For every legal sequence with U updates and Q queries, \(U+Q\le n^{a}\), fixed independently of its random bits, it uses \(O_{a}(n^{b})\) words on every execution; expected total initialization and update work is \(O_{a}(n^{b}+U \log ^{c}(n+2))\); each query takes \(O_{a}(\log ^{c}(n+2))\) worst-case time; and all query answers are simultaneously correct with probability at least \(1- n^{- 3}\). Initial preprocessing may take \(O_{a}(n^{b})\) time, accounting for the additive term. Each operation must finish before the next is revealed. The exponents are independent of \(\lambda (G), n\) and a. This fixes an expected-amortized Monte Carlo convention explicitly; it does not demand correctness against updates chosen from the random internal state.
cards.answer_criterion: Construct a data structure satisfying the complete specification for unrestricted cut values, or prove that no such data structure exists in the stated model. Conditional lower bounds must state their assumptions. Algorithms for insertion-only sequences, approximate cut values, bounded connectivity or subpolynomial but superpolylogarithmic update time are partial progress. Hardness for weighted cuts or fixed-terminal s–t cuts alone is not a negative resolution.

cards.status_note: Reviewed through 11 September 2026. No exact fully dynamic algorithm meeting the polylogarithmic bounds at unrestricted connectivity was found in the checked primary sources. The 2026 exact \(n^{o(1)}\) result has a cut-size restriction, and the unrestricted 2026 tree-packing bound remains polynomial rather than polylogarithmic.

context_blocks.text: The global minimum cut measures the weakest separation anywhere in a network: how many edges must fail before some nonempty part separates from the rest. Maintaining this number as individual links appear and disappear is a natural extension of dynamic connectivity. Connectivity only distinguishes \(\lambda =0\) from \(\lambda \ge 1\); the present question requires the exact integer throughout its full range from zero to \(n- 1\).

A small update need not make the identity of the best cut easy to maintain. For example, two dense clusters joined by a few edges have a global cut determined by their interface, although every individual vertex can have high degree. As the interface changes, an unrelated part of the graph can become the weakest separation. Tracking vertex degrees alone therefore does not identify the optimum.

The value changes by at most one after a single edge insertion or deletion: each individual cut changes by at most one, and taking the minimum preserves that bound. This simple stability is useful, but it does not tell an algorithm whether the answer actually changed. Certifying that no alternative cut is smaller is the difficult global part of an update.

The card requests a number, allowing a polylogarithmic query bound without an output-size obstruction. Listing the edges of a large minimum cut or all vertices on one side can require linear time merely to write the answer. It also uses the ordinary global convention \(\lambda =0\) for disconnected graphs. The inherited 2026 algorithm uses minimum proper, nonzero cuts internally; those intermediate objects are not the definition of this card’s output.

Henzinger, Krinninger, Nanongkai and Saranurak’s OMv paper explicitly identifies dynamic minimum cut as an unresolved frontier for polylogarithmic updates. Its many conditional lower bounds do not automatically transfer to this task. A minimum s–t cut must separate prescribed terminals, whereas a global minimum cut may isolate a completely different region. A reduction has to preserve that freedom, not silently introduce terminal constraints.

The update model is also decisive. Goranci, Henzinger and Thorup obtained deterministic polylogarithmic amortized update time and constant query time for exact incremental minimum cut. In that setting edges are only inserted. Deletions can invalidate the compressed structural information retained during a monotone growth process, so this theorem does not settle fully dynamic maintenance.

For unrestricted cut values in simple graphs, Goranci and coauthors obtained exact fully dynamic algorithms with roughly linear-in-n randomized worst-case update time and sublinear-in-m deterministic amortized update time. Their 2024 revision corrects a runtime in the expander-decomposition analysis. This establishes substantial reuse across updates without reaching a polylogarithmic bound.

De Vos and Christiansen improve the deterministic amortized bound to \(\widetilde{O}\)\((m^{11/12})\); their final 2026 theorem gives the more detailed minimum of \(m^{11/12}, m^{11/13}n^{1/13}\), and \(n^{3/2}\), up to logarithmic factors. Their analysis uses greedy tree packings: either a packed tree crosses a minimum cut only once, or a suitable contraction exposes a minimum cut around one vertex. Both structural outcomes help reduce the candidate cuts that must be maintained.

The inherited SODA 2026 paper of El-Hayek, Henzinger and Li reaches \(n^{o(1)}\) deterministic amortized update time for exact cuts of size up to \(2^{\Theta ((\log  n)^{3/4- \eta})}\), for fixed \(0<\eta <3/4\) in the stated parameter regime. This greatly expands the previous small-cut range. It still restricts the minimum-cut value, and \(n^{o(1)}\) does not itself mean a fixed power of log n.

The same paper explains the accuracy barrier behind this restriction. Its recursive procedure controls a very small multiplicative approximation error, allowing exact recovery while the integral cut value stays below the inverse error. Making that error much smaller increases the work propagated between recursive levels. Thus simply substituting a large cut value into the theorem does not preserve its running time.

Approximation has progressed separately. El-Hayek, Henzinger and Li’s SODA 2025 algorithm maintains a \((1+o(1))\)-approximate global cut in subpolynomial amortized time without a small-cut promise. For an integer optimum \(\lambda\), rounding a multiplicative estimate to an exact answer generally needs additive error below one, hence relative error on the order of \(1/\lambda\). A fixed approximation guarantee cannot supply this for arbitrary connectivity.

The remaining question isolates two bottlenecks at once: exactness for unrestricted connectivity and polylogarithmic update cost. Randomization and amortization are allowed to make it a broad algorithmic target. A positive result would put a numerical global resilience measure close to the cost of maintaining basic connectivity, while a suitable lower bound would explain why this more detailed information requires fundamentally more work.

cards.title: Logarithmic Las Vegas dynamic connectivity
cards.formal: Does an always-correct Las Vegas word-RAM data structure maintain connectivity of an initially empty undirected simple graph on \([n]\) with \(O(\log(2+n))\) amortized expected time per edge update and \(O(\log(2+n))\) worst-case time per query, using \(O((n+m)\log^c(2+n))\) words for some fixed \(c\), where \(m\) is the current number of edges?
cards.definitions: A uniform sequential word RAM has a fixed finite program, word-sized registers and addressed memory cells. Unit-cost instructions are reads and writes, comparisons, branching, addition, subtraction, multiplication, integer division with nonzero divisor, Boolean bit operations and logical shifts. Arithmetic stored in one word is modulo \(2^w\); shifts by at least \(w\) yield zero. Addresses must fit the available word size. All table construction and input-dependent auxiliary memory count; there is no free advice or input-dependent oracle. Randomized programs may generate independent uniform random words. Here \(w=\lceil a\log_2(n+2)\rceil\) for a fixed constant \(a\) sufficient to address the allowed space. Insert adds a missing edge; Delete removes a present edge; Connected(u,v) returns whether a path joins the two supplied vertices. Valid operations form any finite sequence fixed independently of the random bits. The expected total cost is \(O(n\log^c(2+n)+(u+q)\log(2+n))\) for \(u\) updates and \(q\) queries; the first term includes initialization from the empty graph. Every individual query must meet its worst-case bound. Every answer is correct, and all operations terminate almost surely. This asks for amortized expected updates against an oblivious adversary, not deterministic or worst-case update guarantees. The algorithm has no advance access to future updates.
cards.why: Closing the remaining iterated-logarithm gap would pin down a central dynamic graph primitive near its information-theoretic lower bounds.

context_blocks.text: The 2023 Las Vegas structure has \(O(\log n(\log\log n)^2)\) amortized expected update time and \(O(\log n/\log\log\log n)\) worst-case queries.
Polylogarithmic worst-case connectivity is a separate research direction: a larger polylogarithm per operation does not provide logarithmic amortized update time.

cards.title: Dynamic APSP with edge-linear updates
cards.formal: For every fixed positive integer c, do there exist a deterministic data structure and constants \(a,d \ge  1\) such that the following holds for all \(n \ge  2\) and $n\le m\le n^2$? Maintain a directed simple graph on a fixed set of n vertices, with at most m edges at every time and integer edge weights in \(\{1,\ldots ,n^{c}\}\), under single-edge insertions, deletions, and weight changes. Return the exact current distance from any queried vertex s to any queried vertex t in $O(\log^a n)$ worst-case time. After $O(n^d)$ preprocessing, require $O(m\log^a n)$ amortized time per update and polynomial space. Constants may depend on c, but not on n, m, the initial graph, or the operation sequence.
cards.definitions: The capacity m is supplied in advance and bounds the maximum number of live edges throughout the sequence; it is not a count of all updates. Each ordered vertex pair has at most one edge and there are no self-loops. An insertion adds an absent edge, a deletion removes a present edge, and a weight change replaces the weight of one present edge by another permitted weight. A distance query returns the minimum sum of edge weights on a directed s-to-t path, zero for \(s=t\), and a distinguished infinity value if no path exists. Only the distance is requested, not every path or the whole distance matrix. All answers must be exact for any interleaving of updates and queries. Use a word RAM with \(Theta(\log  n)\)-bit words, with a sufficiently large constant for the fixed weight exponent and polynomially bounded addresses; comparisons, arithmetic, Boolean operations, shifts, and random access cost one step. Amortization means that after preprocessing any U updates and Q queries together cost $O(U m\log^a n+Q\log^a n)$; the query bound must also hold for each query individually.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a data structure with these guarantees for every fixed polynomial weight bound, or prove that the quantified proposition is false. A conditional lower bound must state its assumption. A near-quadratic-in-n update bound only meets the target for dense graphs; a subpolynomial approximation ratio or a guarantee only for insertions does not meet the exact fully dynamic specification.
cards.why: This asks whether exact shortest-path information can be maintained at a cost reflecting the number of input edges, rather than all possible vertex pairs. It is a central dynamic-graph trade-off between update work, sparse structure, and immediate exact access to global information.

importance.reason: A broad exact dynamic-graph frontier with a major sparse-versus-dense gap. It tests whether global metric information can be maintained at input-scale update cost while preserving fast queries.

progress.text: Demetrescu and Italiano give deterministic \(O(n^{2} \log ^{3} n)\) amortized updates and constant worst-case distance queries for general directed nonnegative-weight graphs.

Henzinger asks for fully dynamic APSP with edge-linear update cost and constant query cost, both allowing polylogarithmic factors. The fixed weight, edge-update, and amortization conventions here make that direction precise.
Mao’s revised paper gives a Monte Carlo algorithm with tilde-\(O(n^{5/2})\) worst-case vertex-update time and near-quadratic space. This addresses a different update guarantee.

Kyng, Meierhans, and Zöcklein use sparsification for near-linear total processing of a bounded-length update sequence with polylogarithmic queries, but their returned distances have a subpolynomial approximation factor.

cards.status_note: The edge-sensitive target is open in the 2021 source. Searches through 10 September 2026 did not locate an exact algorithm with the stated sparse update and query bounds. This is a deterministic bounded-integer-weight specialization; approximate and worst-case vertex-update results are recorded with their different guarantees.

context_blocks.text: Recomputing distances from every source after each change is expensive, while postponing the work until a query can make a single query expensive. A dynamic distance oracle tries to divide this work so that both kinds of operation remain useful. The requested update budget is roughly the size of the current graph representation, even when that graph is sparse.

A single changed edge can alter distances for quadratically many vertex pairs. That observation does not by itself rule out a fast oracle: the representation may store those changes implicitly, and the interface only asks for one pair at a time. Proving a lower bound therefore requires more than counting changed entries in a materialized distance matrix.

The classical Demetrescu–Italiano algorithm achieves \(O(n^{2} \log ^{3} n)\) amortized update time and constant distance-query time for nonnegative weights. This is already close to the proposed bound when m is quadratic in n. The substantial gap is the sparse regime, where the desired amortized update cost can be nearly a factor n smaller.

Several nearby frontiers have different guarantees. Mao’s revised 2024 result targets worst-case vertex-update time and gives a randomized bound at the \(n^{5/2}\) scale. ESA 2025 sparsification gives extremely fast dynamic approximate distances, with a growing approximation factor. Neither result establishes the exact, edge-sensitive, amortized target on this card. Fixing those distinctions is necessary when assessing progress.

cards.title: Worst-case logarithmic dynamic planar convex hulls
cards.formal: Does there exist a deterministic data structure maintaining a finite set \(P\subset\mathbb R^2\) under point insertion and deletion, using \(O(1+|P|)\) space, with \(O(\log(2+n))\) worst-case time for every update and every extreme-point query? Here \(n\) is the larger set size immediately before and after the operation. An extreme-point query supplies \(u\in\mathbb R^2\setminus\{0\}\) and returns a point maximizing \(\langle u,p\rangle\) over \(p\in P\), or an empty marker.
cards.definitions: The set is initially empty. Insertions supply distinct points; deletions name a present point by a stable handle returned at insertion. Ties may be resolved by any fixed deterministic rule. Use an algebraic real RAM: exact real addition, subtraction, multiplication, division by a nonzero value and comparisons each cost one step, as do constant-size record and pointer operations; no floor, bit extraction from reals or arbitrary-precision encoding operation is supplied. A point, pointer or scalar occupies one cell. One finite program must handle every finite valid online sequence, without advance knowledge, with universal constants in the bounds. Only a maximizing point is returned, not an explicit list of all hull vertices.
cards.why: This asks whether optimal dynamic geometric query performance can be guaranteed for individual updates rather than only averaged over a sequence.

For each \(n\ge2\), vertices are \([n]\), no parallel edges or loops are inserted, and the complete finite insertion/query sequence is fixed independently of the algorithm’s random bits. Word length is \(\lceil a\log_2(n+2)\rceil\), for a fixed algorithm-chosen constant \(a\) large enough for its storage addresses. After every insertion there must be a total order of all vertices with every edge directed forward. A query on \((u,v)\) returns whether \(u\) precedes \(v\) in that maintained order, with all queries between insertions referring to the same order. It is not a reachability query, and printing a fresh list of all vertices after every insertion is not required. Answers are always correct, and operations terminate almost surely. The update bound means that for every constant \(\eta>0\) there is a constant \(C_\eta\) such that expected initialization plus update time is at most \(C_\eta(n+m)^{1+\eta}\) for every prefix; \(q\) order queries add \(O(q)\) time. No predictions, special graph family or advance edge information are supplied. The target allows the full stated RAM, without an undefined restriction to combinatorial algorithms.

cards.title: Polylogarithmic dynamic maximal matching against adaptive updates
cards.formal:
Does there exist a uniform randomized algorithm that explicitly maintains a maximal matching in a fully dynamic \(n\)-vertex simple graph against an adaptive adversary, with polylogarithmic expected amortized update time? More precisely, are there an algorithm and constants \(C,c>0\) such that, for every \(n\ge2\), every horizon \(T\ge1\), and every valid adaptive update strategy, the algorithm is always correct and its expected total update work is at most
\[C T(\log_2(n+2))^c,\]
after initialization in at most \(C n(\log_2(n+2))^c\) expected time? The graph starts empty and each update inserts or deletes one edge. The model and adversary are defined below. A deterministic algorithm is permitted as a special case.

This card selects the polylogarithmic question expressly included in the 2022 source. Its earlier sublinear-time question has since received positive answers; that weaker threshold is retained as dated progress rather than presented as open.
cards.why: Maximal matching is a basic dynamic graph primitive whose current answer can influence the next change to the graph. This problem asks whether the cost of responding to that feedback can be reduced to a polylogarithm. It would clarify a major difference between algorithms that assume an independently chosen update sequence and algorithms whose guarantees survive interaction.

The selected polylogarithmic target is expressly asked in the source and is not established by these results. A bounded later-work search found no matching general adaptive polylogarithmic algorithm or impossibility theorem. cards.definitions:
The fixed vertex set is \([n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}\). The graph is undirected, loopless and simple, with no sparsity, degree or bipartiteness promise. An insertion gives two distinct vertex labels whose edge is currently absent; a deletion specifies a currently present edge. Both kinds may occur in any order, and the next update is unavailable until the current one is finished.

A matching \(M\subseteq E\) has no two edges sharing an endpoint. It is maximal if no edge of \(E\setminus M\) can be added while preserving this condition; equivalently, every edge of the graph has at least one endpoint incident to \(M\). The requirement is inclusion-wise maximality after every update. No maximum-cardinality optimality requirement is imposed.

Explicit maintenance means retaining an array \(\mathrm{mate}[1..n]\) with value zero for an unmatched vertex and value \(v\) at \(u\) when \(\{u,v\}\in M\). Array changes are charged to update time; reading one mate entry takes constant time. The whole matching need not be printed after each update.

Use a word-RAM with words of \(w=\lceil c_w\log_2(n+2)\rceil\) bits for a fixed constant \(c_w\) chosen with the algorithm, polynomially many addressable words of persistent memory, and unit-cost word reads, writes, comparisons, branches, Boolean operations, shifts, addition, subtraction and multiplication modulo \(2^w\), and integer quotient/remainder by a nonzero word. Each independent uniform random word also costs one operation. All preprocessing, memory management and changes to the maintained matching are charged. The algorithm has one finite program for all \(n\), with no graph-dependent advice or uncharged table depending on the input. Its memory bound and word-size constant are fixed independently of the update horizon.

Before selecting update \(t+1\), the adversary may inspect the complete current matching, all previous updates and all observed update runtimes. It has unbounded computation and may use its own independent randomness. It does not see hidden algorithm state, past unexposed random choices or future random bits. Correctness and expected cost must hold for every such adaptive strategy, with the horizon \(T\) fixed before the experiment. The expectation includes randomness of both parties. Allowing the adversary to inspect the matching is an observation convention, not a requirement to print the array at every step.

Always correct means that every completed update returns a valid maximal matching, and every finite valid adaptive experiment terminates with probability one. Randomness may affect running time and which maximal matching is chosen, but may never permit an incorrect answer. This is a Las Vegas guarantee. The total-time inequality is amortized: a single update may cost more than a polylogarithm, provided every finite prefix obeys the stated expected total bound. All constants are independent of \(n,T\), the graph and the adversary.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct Lean-checked proof of existence or nonexistence of an algorithm with these guarantees. A positive answer must maintain an explicit maximal matching for all valid adaptive insertion/deletion sequences, with the stated uniformity, always-correct behavior and expected prefix-total bounds. A bound only against an oblivious adversary, a maintained estimate of maximum matching size, or a matching that is approximately maximum but not maximal is insufficient. A merely sublinear polynomial update bound does not reach the polylogarithmic target. A negative answer must rule out randomized algorithms in this model, not just one deterministic implementation.

context_blocks.text: The original problem paragraph asks several related questions. This review takes its explicit polylogarithmic target and fixes the permissive expected-amortized, always-correct randomized setting against an adversary observing the matching. It does not combine the separate lower-bound question into the answer criterion.

The 2026 paper reports earlier oblivious-adversary algorithms with constant amortized update time and polylogarithmic worst-case update time. Those guarantees assume that the update sequence cannot adapt to the maintained matching.

Bernstein, Bhattacharya, Kiss and Saranurak’s STOC 2025 results, summarized in the 2026 introduction, achieve \(\widetilde O(n^{3/4})\) randomized adaptive update time and \(\widetilde O(n^{8/9})\) deterministic update time, both amortized. Thus the source’s basic sublinear threshold is no longer the open target.

Chuzhoy, Khanna and Song’s Theorem 1.1 gives a deterministic fully dynamic algorithm with amortized update time \(n^{1/2+o(1)}\). This also tolerates adaptive updates, but its guarantee does not supply polylogarithmic update time. Here \(\widetilde O\) suppresses polylogarithmic factors, and \(o(1)\) in the exponent tends to zero as \(n\) grows.

cards.title: Dynamic spanning trees with polylogarithmic average stretch
cards.formal:
Is there a uniform randomized fully dynamic algorithm that maintains a spanning forest \(F_t\) of an unweighted simple graph \(G_t\) with polylogarithmic expected average stretch and sublinear expected amortized update time? Precisely, do there exist such an algorithm, constants \(C,a,c>0\), and a function \(u:\mathbb N_{\ge2}\to\mathbb R_{\ge0}\) with
\[\lim_{n\to\infty}\frac{u(n)}n=0,\]
such that for every \(n\ge2\) and every finite oblivious sequence of \(T\) edge insertions and deletions starting from the empty \(n\)-vertex graph,
\[\mathbb E[\operatorname{avstr}_{F_t}(G_t)]\le C(\log_2(n+2))^c\quad(0\le t\le T),\]
and the expected total work for the updates is at most \(T u(n)\), after at most \(C n^a\) expected initialization work? The maintained object must always be an actual spanning forest using current graph edges.

For a connected graph, a spanning forest is a spanning tree. The componentwise convention below makes the target meaningful when a deletion disconnects the graph, as in the original dynamic low-stretch algorithm. This card chooses the first question in the workshop source, with the expectation and amortization conventions of that prior work; it does not also require resistance to adaptive updates.
cards.why: Low-stretch spanning trees replace a graph by a particularly simple subgraph while controlling average detours. They underpin graph optimization and linear-system algorithms. The question asks whether a polylogarithmic quality guarantee can survive repeated edge changes without spending a linear amount of work per update; it isolates the cost of requiring the approximation to remain a genuine subgraph.
cards.status_note: The November 2022 Section 4.3, Forster–Goranci’s full author manuscript (Theorem 1.1 and Corollary 1.2), and Forster–Goranci–Henzinger arXiv:2004.10319v2 introduction were read on 2026-09-14. The Chechik–Zhang 2020 bound is recorded through the checked workshop report rather than a claimed full reading of that paper. A bounded later-work search through this review date found no matching all-graph fully dynamic spanning-forest result with the selected quality and update bounds. Related probabilistic tree embeddings and dynamic spanners do not meet the subgraph-forest requirement. Status remains source-open with these limits.

sentences: A changing unweighted graph must retain a spanning tree in each connected component.
The quality measure is the average tree-path length between the endpoints of graph edges.
The question asks for polylogarithmic expected quality with sublinear expected amortized work per edge insertion or deletion.
The update sequence is fixed independently of the algorithm’s randomness, and disconnected intermediate graphs are covered.
Existing subpolynomial-stretch forests and polylogarithmic-stretch metric embeddings leave different parts of this target unresolved.

cards.definitions:
The graph \(G_t=([n],E_t)\) is finite, undirected, loopless and simple, with unit edge lengths. Its vertex set remains fixed. An insertion specifies an absent edge between two distinct labels, and a deletion specifies a present edge. No maximum-degree or sparsity promise is imposed, and components may split or merge. A valid spanning forest \(F_t=([n],E_t^F)\) has \(E_t^F\subseteq E_t\), is acyclic, and connects every pair of vertices that lie in the same connected component of \(G_t\). Thus it contains one spanning tree for each nontrivial component and all isolated vertices.

For \(\{v,w\}\in E_t\), let \(d_{F_t}(v,w)\) be the number of edges on the unique path between its endpoints in \(F_t\). Put
\[\operatorname{avstr}_{F_t}(G_t)=\begin{cases}|E_t|^{-1}\displaystyle\sum_{\{v,w\}\in E_t}d_{F_t}(v,w),&|E_t|>0,\\0,&|E_t|=0.\end{cases}\]
All current edges participate in the average, including forest edges, whose distance is one. The target bounds this absolute stretch quantity, not its ratio to the best possible forest. The expectation is over the algorithm's internal randomness at each fixed time, after averaging over the graph edges; a bound for every individual edge is not required.

The update sequence is fixed independently of the algorithm's random choices and is revealed one operation at a time. The algorithm is not given future updates. Its guarantee covers every finite sequence length, and hence every finite prefix of any fixed infinite valid sequence. The same constants and function \(u\) work for all graphs, edge counts, times and sequences.

Use a word-RAM with \(w=\lceil c_w\log_2(n+2)\rceil\)-bit words for a fixed constant \(c_w\) large enough to address the algorithm's polynomially many persistent words. Unit-cost operations are word reads/writes, comparisons, branches, Boolean operations, shifts, modular addition/subtraction/multiplication, integer quotient/remainder by a nonzero word, and independent uniform random words. The algorithm has one finite program for all \(n\); no input-dependent advice or uncharged precomputed table is allowed. Initialization starts with no graph edges and is charged separately as specified.

The forest is maintained explicitly as its edge set: a linked list or equivalent enumerable collection of its current edge records is stored, and each current graph edge record indicates whether it belongs to the forest. Given an existing edge-record handle, this flag is readable in constant time, and all forest edges can be enumerated in time proportional to their number plus one. Finding graph-edge records from endpoint labels, changing forest membership, random choices, rebuilds and memory management are included in update work. No full forest printout or rooted-parent array is required after every update.

Every completed update must produce a valid spanning forest, and each finite execution must terminate with probability one. Only the quality and runtime guarantees are in expectation. Amortized expected time bounds the sum of update costs; it imposes no worst-case per-update bound. The source's word 'sublinear' is made precise as \(o(n)\), without additionally requiring a fixed polynomial saving \(n^{1-\delta}\).
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct Lean-checked proof of existence or nonexistence under the stated model. A positive result must simultaneously achieve the expected polylogarithmic average-stretch bound and an expected amortized update bound \(u(n)=o(n)\) on all valid fully dynamic graph sequences. A spanning forest with only \(n^{o(1)}\) stretch, a decremental-only algorithm, or a bound on an unrelated tree metric does not meet the target. The maintained forest must consist of graph edges; introducing auxiliary weighted tree edges or Steiner vertices is not allowed. A negative answer must apply to the stated randomized expected guarantees, not only to deterministic or worst-case variants.

context_blocks.text: The workshop source records static spanning trees of average stretch \(O(\log n\log\log n)\), and dynamic algorithms with subpolynomial stretch and update time. Its first open question asks to improve the stretch guarantee to a polylogarithm while keeping updates sublinear.

Forster and Goranci formulate the dynamic object as a spanning forest and analyze expected average stretch against an oblivious adversary. Their Corollary 1.2 gives \(n^{o(1)}\) expected average stretch and \(n^{1/2+o(1)}\) expected amortized update time.
The workshop reports Chechik–Zhang’s SODA 2020 improvement to \(n^{o(1)}\) expected amortized update time while retaining subpolynomial average stretch.

A subpolynomial function grows more slowly than every fixed positive power of its argument, but need not be bounded by a fixed power of its logarithm. Consequently, the recorded subpolynomial-stretch algorithms do not automatically meet the polylogarithmic quality target.

Forster, Goranci and Henzinger obtain dynamic probabilistic metric-tree embeddings with polylogarithmic expected stretch at suitable update-time tradeoffs. Such an embedding may use a tree that is not a subgraph of the changing graph. Their introduction explicitly distinguishes this result from maintaining low-average-stretch spanning trees.

The source separately asks for algorithms tolerating adaptive adversaries. That requirement is not combined with the first question here: the requested improvement already concerns sequences chosen independently of the random choices.

cards.title: Dynamic edge coloring with sublinear additive slack
cards.formal:
Does there exist a uniform randomized fully dynamic edge-coloring algorithm and fixed constants \(\gamma\in(0,1)\), \(C\ge1\), and \(a,b\ge0\), such that for every \(n\ge2\), every fixed degree bound \(1\le\Delta\le n-1\), and every valid oblivious sequence of edge insertions and deletions, it explicitly maintains a proper coloring with at most
\[K(n,\Delta)=\Delta+\left\lceil C\Delta^{1-\gamma}(\log_2(n+2))^a\right\rceil\]
colors in expected amortized update time at most \(C(\log_2(n+2))^b\)? The algorithm must always return a valid coloring. The bound must hold uniformly in both \(n\) and \(\Delta\), with the same constants, not only at each fixed \(\Delta\).

This is the update-time question in the workshop report, with the polylogarithmic factors and probability/cost convention made explicit. The author's separate, weaker recourse-only question is context rather than the main target.
cards.why: The question asks whether a changing graph can stay close to the optimal edge-color bound while each update costs only a polylogarithm. Its central issue is the joint dependence on graph size and degree: bounds that are fast for fixed relative error can become slow when the allowed extra colors shrink by a power of the degree. A resolution would sharpen the resource tradeoff for dynamic conflict-free scheduling represented by edge coloring.
cards.status_note: The November 2024 report, Costa’s undated expanded primary note, Sadeh–Kaplan arXiv:2602.09497v2 (Theorems 2.5 and 2.8 and Section 3), and the publisher abstract for Christiansen’s SODA 2026 paper were checked on 2026-09-14. The recourse results retain restrictions on the palette or arboricity, and the deterministic result has a subpolynomial update bound rather than the requested polylogarithmic guarantee. A bounded search through the review date located no matching all-graph resolution. Source-open status records these verification limits, not an independent proof check of every cited result.

sentences: A changing graph must keep a proper integer color on every edge.
The target allows only a power-sublinear additive number of colors above the maximum-degree bound, up to logarithmic factors.
One uniform algorithm should maintain that coloring in polylogarithmic expected amortized time over all degree scales.
The question remains meaningful even when updates are chosen independently of the algorithm’s randomness.
Small recoloring counts and recent restricted-graph or subpolynomial-time results do not by themselves meet the stated total-work guarantee.

cards.definitions:
The graph is undirected, simple and unweighted, on a fixed vertex set \([n]\), and starts without edges. Every insertion adds a currently absent edge between distinct vertices, and every deletion removes a currently present edge. The sequence may contain both operations in arbitrary order, always respecting maximum degree at most the input bound \(\Delta\). This is a fixed upper bound for the whole sequence, rather than the current degree recomputed after each update. Disconnected graphs are allowed; no sparsity or bipartiteness promise is imposed.

A proper edge coloring is a map \(\chi:E\to[K(n,\Delta)]\) in which distinct incident edges have distinct colors. The palette consists of fixed integer labels throughout the execution. Explicit maintenance requires storing the current integer color with every existing edge; each change to such a stored label is charged. Given a handle to an existing edge record, its color is available in constant time. Updates use endpoint labels, and locating or creating the record is part of their cost. The algorithm need not print all edge colors after each update.

Use a word-RAM with \(w=\lceil c_w\log_2(n+2)\rceil\)-bit words for a fixed algorithm-dependent constant \(c_w\), large enough for its polynomial space addresses and color labels. Charge one step for a word read/write, comparison, branch, Boolean operation, shift, modular addition/subtraction/multiplication, quotient/remainder by a nonzero word, or independent uniform random word. Only polynomially many persistent words are allowed, with one fixed exponent independent of the update horizon. The algorithm has a single finite program for all \(n,\Delta\); there is no uncharged input-dependent advice or table.

Initialization on the empty graph takes at most \(C n(\log_2(n+2))^b\) expected time. For every finite valid update sequence of length \(T\), the expected sum of all update work must be at most \(C T(\log_2(n+2))^b\). This includes writing colors, recolorings, lookup, memory management and any rebuilds. The sequence is fixed independently of the algorithm's random choices and is not revealed in advance. It may be arbitrarily long. Expectations are over the internal randomness; the constants are independent of \(n,\Delta,T\) and the sequence. Larger constants may absorb finite exceptional small instances.

Always-correct randomized behavior means that every completed update gives a proper coloring in the stated palette, and every finite valid execution terminates with probability one. No failure probability for an invalid coloring is allowed. Amortization permits expensive individual updates subject to every-prefix expected total bounds. Deterministic algorithms also qualify. The recourse is the number of existing edges whose colors change while processing an update; it is a lower bound on explicit update work, but bounding recourse does not bound the computation needed to select those changes.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct Lean-checked proof of existence or nonexistence of such an algorithm and fixed constants. Any fixed positive \(\gamma<1\) suffices for a positive answer; an exponent that tends to zero with \(n\) does not. The time bound must be independent of polynomial factors in \(\Delta\), and every permitted graph and degree scale must be covered. A guarantee only on the number of recolorings, only on forests or bounded-arboricity graphs, or only for constant maximum degree is insufficient. A lower bound for repairing one adversarially prescribed starting coloring alone is insufficient to rule out an algorithm that controls the colorings it maintains.

context_blocks.text: The workshop report asks for a power saving in the additive number of colors together with polylogarithmic update time. The constants in the displayed target spell out its two suppressed polylogarithmic factors.

Costa’s expanded note explicitly separates recoloring cost from computation and says that even its recourse-only version is open against an oblivious adversary with amortization. This card retains the report’s stronger total-update-work target while choosing that permissive adversary and amortization setting.

Known algorithms use \((1+\varepsilon)\Delta\) colors with update bounds polynomial in \(1/\varepsilon\), up to polylogarithmic factors. Substituting an inverse-polynomial-in-degree relative slack can therefore introduce a polynomial degree dependence in time, which the target forbids.

The May 2026 Sadeh–Kaplan revision gives recourse improvements for large palettes and for graphs of low arboricity, where arboricity is the minimum number of forests covering all edges. Those restrictions and the distinction between recourse and running time remain essential; they do not establish the all-graph update-time target.

The SODA 2026 deterministic algorithm uses a relative-error palette and achieves subpolynomial update time in its stated accuracy range. Subpolynomial time is a larger class of bounds than polylogarithmic time, so this result does not itself provide the required guarantee.

cards.title: Low-loss deterministic reduction from weighted to unweighted dynamic matching
cards.formal:
Is there a uniform deterministic black-box transformation that converts every explicit fully dynamic \(\alpha\)-approximate maximum-cardinality matching algorithm into a fully dynamic \(\alpha(1-1/q)\)-approximate maximum-weight matching algorithm on general graphs, for every fixed \(\alpha\in(0,1]\) and integer \(q\ge2\), with only an accuracy-dependent polylogarithmic overhead in update time and with preservation of worst-case as well as amortized bounds?

The precise overhead and interfaces are specified below. The transformation must work at the original approximation ratio \(\alpha\); it may not demand a stronger unweighted algorithm with approximation approaching one as \(q\) grows. This card selects the deterministic, fully dynamic version of the source’s broader feature-preserving conversion question. Randomized and partially dynamic extensions are not part of this chosen statement.
cards.why: A low-loss conversion would transfer a broad range of dynamic matching improvements from counting matched edges to optimizing their weights. The central unresolved scope includes algorithms with fixed approximation ratios such as one half or two thirds, not only near-optimal algorithms. Preserving determinism and time guarantees would make the conversion useful across existing algorithmic tradeoffs without redesigning each algorithm.
cards.status_note: The 2022 workshop question, the full 2021 framework PDF (Theorem 3.1 and Remark 3.2), and Bernstein–Chen arXiv:2510.19049v1 (Theorem 6.5 and Section 1.1 limitations) were checked on 2026-09-14; the SIAM publisher confirms the latter’s SODA 2026 publication. The recent reduction is for near-optimal ratios and does not establish the source’s arbitrary-ratio goal or the selected deterministic guarantee. A bounded later-work search found no matching general all-ratio deterministic reduction. The detailed source-grounded variant is complete editorially; its source-open status retains these search and proof-verification limits.

sentences: The question asks for a reusable conversion from dynamic unweighted matching to dynamic weighted matching on general graphs.
An input algorithm with approximation ratio alpha should yield one with ratio alpha times one minus the chosen accuracy.
The selected variant preserves determinism and transfers both worst-case and amortized update guarantees when the input algorithm provides them.
The overhead may depend on accuracy but should be only polylogarithmic in graph size and weight range, apart from the stated auxiliary graph enlargement.
A recent general-graph conversion works for near-optimal input algorithms, leaving the arbitrary-ratio target unresolved.

cards.definitions:
All graphs are finite, undirected, loopless and simple. A matching is a set of edges with pairwise disjoint endpoints. For an unweighted graph \(H\), let \(\nu(H)\) be the maximum number of edges in a matching. An \(\alpha\)-approximation returns a matching \(M\) with \(|M|\ge\alpha\nu(H)\). For a positively weighted graph \(G\), let \(\operatorname{OPT}_w(G)=\max_M\sum_{e\in M}w(e)\). The weighted output must satisfy
\[\sum_{e\in M}w(e)\ge\alpha(1-1/q)\operatorname{OPT}_w(G).\]
The empty graph has optimum zero.

Both problems start with an empty graph on a fixed labelled vertex set. Updates insert an absent edge or delete a present edge, in any order. Weighted insertions additionally specify an integer weight in \([W]\), for a supplied integer \(W\ge1\). A weight change can be expressed as deletion followed by insertion. No bipartiteness or sparsity promise is imposed. Updates are revealed sequentially and may depend on earlier outputs, since the chosen algorithms are deterministic. Weights, vertex labels, \(W\) and \(q\) are represented in binary.

The input subroutine \(A\) has a uniform finite program, initializes an empty unweighted graph, and supports edge insertion and deletion. It stores an explicit current matching: a mate lookup is constant-time and its edge list can be enumerated in time proportional to its length plus one. Each update supplies the list of matching edges inserted or removed during that update, and the cost of producing that list is included in \(A\)'s update time. Thus changes of output are charged, as required by the recourse condition in the 2021 source. The transformation can create independent instances of \(A\), call their operations and inspect their reported matchings; it cannot inspect their implementation or hidden state. Only their \(\alpha\)-approximation promise may be used, so the guarantee must survive every valid choice of approximate matching by the subroutine. The transformed algorithm also maintains its weighted matching explicitly and charges every output change.

Here is the required overhead. There must be one transformation, one total computable function \(F:\mathbb N_{\ge2}\to\mathbb N_{\ge1}\), and one fixed exponent \(b\ge0\), independent of \(\alpha\) and \(A\). For a weighted sequence on \(n\ge2\) vertices with at most \(m\) edges present at any time, put
\[N=\lceil F(q)n\rceil,\quad D=\min\{\binom{N}{2},\lceil F(q)(m+n)\rceil\},\quad L=F(q)(1+\log_2(n+2)+\log_2(W+1))^b.\]
Let \(I_A(N)\ge N\) be any nondecreasing upper bound on empty-graph initialization time of \(A\). Let \(U_A(N,D)\ge1\) be any upper bound, nondecreasing in both arguments, on its update time for sequences with at most \(N\) vertices and \(D\) edges. The weighted algorithm must initialize within \(L(I_A(N)+n)\) operations and have update bound
\[L\bigl(U_A(N,D)+1\bigr).\]
If \(U_A\) is a worst-case per-update bound, this must be a worst-case weighted bound. If it is only an amortized bound, every weighted prefix of \(T\) updates must cost at most \(TL(U_A(N,D)+1)\), excluding the separately charged initialization. These are implications for each applicable bound, not a requirement to turn an amortized input guarantee into a worst-case output guarantee. Multiplicative constants may be absorbed into \(F\). No polynomial dependence on \(q\) is required: it is an accuracy parameter, and the source’s bipartite blueprint already allows a larger dependence.

Use a word-RAM with \(\Theta(\log_2(nWF(q)+2))\)-bit words, with a fixed sufficiently large constant multiplier. Word memory accesses, comparisons, branches, Boolean operations, shifts, modular addition/subtraction/multiplication and quotient/remainder by a nonzero word have unit cost. Both subroutine calls and all surrounding work are charged; the subroutine is evaluated in the same word model. The transformation may use at most \(\lceil L\rceil\) simultaneous instances, each on at most \(N\) vertices and \(D\) edges, and auxiliary memory bounded by \(F(q)(n+\log_2(W+1)+2)^d\) words for one fixed exponent \(d\). Its state has no uncharged graph-dependent advice. The bound is uniform over every finite update sequence and over the given \(W\); using unit-weight graphs as oracle instances does not give their answers for free.

The explicit overhead formalizes an accuracy-dependent enlargement of the auxiliary graph and a polylogarithmic factor in size and weight range. Allowing \(m+n\) in the edge bound accommodates auxiliary vertices and edges; it does not promise exact preservation of sparse graph size. These bookkeeping choices and the deterministic restriction are editorial specifications of the source’s requested type of transformation.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct Lean-checked proof or refutation of the existence of this uniform transformation and overhead parameters. A positive proof must cover every admissible approximation factor and subroutine, preserve its deterministic correctness, and establish the stated transfer of both kinds of time guarantee when applicable. A result requiring \(\alpha\) to approach one with \(q\), a constant multiplicative loss bounded away from one, or a conversion only for bipartite weighted graphs is insufficient. A weighted algorithm unrelated to the supplied subroutine does not establish the black-box theorem merely because it is polynomial-time. Failure of one particular transformation is not a refutation of the existence claim.

context_blocks.text: The source asks for a general-graph analogue of the bipartite reduction, with little loss in approximation and update complexity. Its broader discussion also includes randomized and partially dynamic settings. This card isolates the deterministic fully dynamic feature-preserving statement and records its explicit interface and overhead.

Theorem 3.1 of Bernstein–Dudeja–Langley gives the desired \(\alpha\mapsto(1-\varepsilon)\alpha\) conversion on bipartite graphs, with accuracy-dependent graph enlargement and logarithmic weight-range dependence. Remark 3.2 explains why explicit matching output provides the recourse bound required by the conversion.

Bernstein and Chen’s SODA 2026 result gives a low-loss conversion for general weighted graphs when the unweighted algorithm already has approximation \(1-\varepsilon_0\), where \(\varepsilon_0\) must be polynomially smaller than the desired error. Theorem 6.5 is randomized and amortized.

The later paper’s limitations discussion explicitly says that its result cannot transfer arbitrary fixed approximation ratios with small loss, and retains that more general conversion as the desired goal. Thus its title and near-optimal result do not resolve the all-ratio deterministic statement selected here.

cards.title: Logarithmic fully dynamic planar nearest neighbors
cards.formal: Does a uniform Las Vegas data structure maintain a finite set of planar points under insertions and deletions, answer exact Euclidean nearest-neighbor queries in \(O(\log(n+2))\) worst-case time, and support updates in expected amortized \(O(\log(n+2))\) time, using \(O((n+1)\log^c(n+2))\) space for some fixed constant \(c\)?
cards.why: A logarithmic fully dynamic structure would establish the natural two-dimensional counterpart of a basic ordered-search interface.
cards.status_note: Rechecked on 13 September 2026. The 2025 incremental theorem has optimal logarithmic queries but a growing insertion overhead and no general deletion interface. A bounded later-work search did not locate a result meeting this explicit fully dynamic Las Vegas variant. Approximate high-dimensional indexing results do not meet its exact planar model; source proofs were not independently verified.

progress.text: Iacono–Nekrich give \(O(\log n)\) queries and \(O(\log^{1+\eta}n)\) insertions for fixed \(\eta>0\) in an incremental structure.

cards.definitions: The structure initializes the empty set in constant time and space. An insertion supplies a real point not currently present and returns a stable handle. A deletion supplies the handle of a present point. A query supplies \(q\in\mathbb R^2\) and returns any present \(p\) minimizing \((p_x-q_x)^2+(p_y-q_y)^2\), or an empty marker. Ties may be resolved arbitrarily but correctly. At any instant \(n\) is the number of stored points. Use an algebraic real RAM with exact real addition, subtraction, multiplication, division by a nonzero real, and comparisons, each at unit cost. A point coordinate, scalar, pointer or fixed-size record field occupies one cell. Reading, writing and following pointers cost one step; no floor, bit extraction from reals, or packing unbounded discrete information into a real is an available operation. The program is uniform and finite; there is no advice or free table construction. Each independently generated fair random bit costs one operation; sampling an arbitrary exact real number is not a primitive. All answers are exact on every terminating execution and the structure terminates almost surely. For every fixed finite legal operation sequence chosen independently of its random bits, with \(u\) updates and maximum set size \(M\), the expected total update time is \(O(u\log(M+2))\); each query separately has worst-case \(O(\log(n+2))\) time on every execution. Space holds on every execution, including retained points and temporary work. All constants are universal. This states the amortization convention using the maximum size of the sequence, without an adaptive-adversary guarantee. The space exponent \(c\) may be any fixed nonnegative integer. All logarithms are base two. The sequence and its real coordinates may depend on the program but are fixed before its random bits are sampled; the bounds impose no adaptive-adversary guarantee.

context_blocks.text: A nearest-neighbor query asks for an actual stored point minimizing Euclidean distance to the query. On a line, ordered search can inspect the predecessor and successor. In the plane, closeness depends on two coordinates together, and a nearby point in one coordinate can be far away in the other.

Deletion is a substantive operation. Removing the previously closest point can expose a different answer at many query locations, while the data structure must still answer whichever query arrives next. The target retains every allowed insertion and deletion sequence instead of assuming that the stored point set only grows.

The 2025 incremental result achieves \(O(\log n)\) queries and \(O(\log^{1+\eta}n)\) insertion time for fixed positive \(\eta\). Its query bound meets this target, but its insertion bound still has a growing factor over logarithmic time and the incremental interface does not include arbitrary deletions.

Randomness is permitted to affect work, not geometric correctness: every returned point must really minimize the squared distance, with any exact minimizer acceptable in a tie. Updates are bounded in expected total time over each fixed sequence, whereas a query must meet its time bound on every execution. These are separate promises.

The original source asks for logarithmic costs in the fully dynamic planar problem. The retained benchmark states an explicit Las Vegas variant with expected amortized updates, worst-case queries and near-linear space. Its real-arithmetic cost model does not claim a logarithmic bit complexity for arbitrary real coordinates.

Approximate-neighbor libraries, empirical query throughput and high-dimensional vector indexes address related applications but do not imply this exact two-dimensional worst-case interface. The space guarantee also counts temporary work and must hold for the current number of points.

cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof of a single uniform Las Vegas representation and constants satisfying all stated guarantees: exact answers, worst-case logarithmic query time, expected total update time \(O(u\log(M+2))\) for every oblivious finite sequence, and \(O((n+1)\log^c(n+2))\) space on every execution. Alternatively prove in Lean that no such representation and constants exist in the specified model. An insertion-only structure, approximate answers or a time bound retaining an unbounded extra logarithmic factor does not meet the full target.

cards.title: DynFO maintenance of red-predecessor parity
cards.formal: Does there exist a DynFO program that maintains the Boolean query |\(\{y\in D:\exists x\in D (R(x)\land E(x,y))\}|\equiv 1\) mod 2 under arbitrary single-tuple insertions and deletions in a directed edge relation \(E\subseteq D^{2}\) and a red-vertex relation \(R\subseteq D\)? Use one fixed finite auxiliary relational vocabulary and fixed first-order update formulas for every finite domain D. All input and auxiliary relations are empty initially, and there are no built-in order or arithmetic relations. The program must be correct after every finite sequence of updates, with no bound on the length of that sequence.

cards.definitions: The domain D is a fixed finite set throughout a run; updates do not create or delete vertices. An element y is covered when at least one red predecessor x has an arc \(x\to y\). A covered vertex is counted once, regardless of how many red predecessors it has, and it need not itself be red. E is a binary relation, so loops are allowed; R is unary. The four update types are \(ins_{E}(u,v), del_{E}(u,v), ins_{R}(u)\), and \(del_{R}(u)\). Insertions of present tuples and deletions of absent tuples leave the input relation unchanged and are also allowed. A program chooses finitely many auxiliary relation symbols S, each of a fixed finite arity, including a distinguished zero-ary answer bit Ans. For each S and update type \(\delta\) it supplies a first-order formula \(\varphi _{S,\delta}(\bar\{p\};\bar\{z\})\), where p̄ are the changed tuple’s parameters and z̄ has the arity of S. The formula may use equality, the current input and auxiliary relations, Boolean connectives, and quantification over individual domain elements. It has no parity/counting quantifier, quantification over sets, function symbol or built-in numeric relation. After update \(\delta (\bar\{a\})\), each auxiliary relation becomes \(\{\bar\{b\}:(I,A)\models \varphi _{S,\delta}(\bar\{a\};\bar\{b\})\}\), evaluated on the old input I and old auxiliary state A. All auxiliary updates occur simultaneously, alongside the specified input change. Empty initialization makes Ans false, correctly answering the empty covered set. The program’s formulas and arities are independent of |D| and of the update history. The number and arities of auxiliary relations are unrestricted finite constants chosen by the program; thus it may use polynomially many auxiliary bits, with its own fixed polynomial exponent. DynFO measures expressibility of these updates, rather than sequential constant-time execution of a formula on a Turing machine.
cards.answer_criterion: A positive answer is a finite collection of first-order update formulas and a proof of correctness from empty initialization for every finite domain and every finite update sequence. A negative answer must show that every such program, allowing arbitrary fixed auxiliary arities, fails on some domain and sequence. A lower bound only for quantifier-free formulas or a fixed arity, a program requiring unrestricted initial advice, or an algorithm for a bounded-degree variant does not settle the stated DynFO question.

cards.definitions: The vertex set is \([n]\), with \(n\ge2\), and the source \(s\in[n]\) is fixed at initialization. Graphs are simple and undirected. Every present edge has an integer weight in \(\{1,\ldots,n^3\}\). An update inserts an absent edge with its weight, deletes a present edge, or changes the weight of a present edge. A query supplies \(v\in[n]\) and must return exactly the minimum sum of edge weights along an \(s\)-to-\(v\) path in the current graph, or a special infinity symbol if no path exists; the distance to \(s\) is zero. Each operation must finish before the next is supplied. The sequence may be arbitrarily long and chosen using all previous outputs; the data structure receives no future operations. It must work at every density. The subquadratic bound is in the vertex count, so it expresses a saving over rebuilding for dense graphs, not a promised saving relative to the edge count of every sparse graph. The uniform machine is a word-RAM with word length \(w=c\lceil\log_2(n+2)\rceil\), for one fixed integer \(c\ge5\) chosen with the algorithm. Unit-cost instructions are indirect read/write of an addressed word, comparison, branching, unsigned addition, subtraction and multiplication modulo \(2^w\), bitwise Boolean operations, shifts by fewer than \(w\) places, and integer quotient/remainder by a nonzero word. Larger integers require multiple words and charged operations. Initial input is an explicit adjacency/weight table. For fixed constants \(K,C\), initialization takes at most \(Cn^K\) operations and at most \(Cn^K\) words are stored at any time, with addresses fitting the word length. Each individual update takes at most \(Cn^{2-\delta}\) operations and each query at most \(C\), after enlarging constants for small \(n\). The program, constants and \(\delta\) are independent of \(n\), weights and the operation sequence. The machine has no randomization, nonuniform advice or unit-cost unbounded-precision arithmetic. A path certificate is not required.
