cards.title: Worst-case sample complexity of trace reconstruction
cards.formal: For every fixed deletion probability \(\delta\in(0,1)\), determine the worst-case sample-complexity function \(N_\delta(n)\) up to multiplicative constant factors as \(n\to\infty\). This is the least number of independent deletion traces from which one estimator can reconstruct every unknown \(n\)-bit string exactly with probability at least \(2/3\). Computation is unrestricted, the original length and deletion probability are known, and constants may depend on \(\delta\).
cards.definitions:
Observation space. Fix \(n\in\mathbb N\) with \(n\ge2\), and a real \(\delta\in(0,1)\). An arbitrary fixed string \(x=(x_1,\ldots,x_n)\in\{0,1\}^n\) is unknown. A deletion trace independently keeps each input bit with probability \(p=1-\delta\) and concatenates the surviving bits in their original order. The output lies in the finite set
\[\mathcal Y_n=\bigcup_{k=0}^{n}\{0,1\}^k,\]
where \(\{0,1\}^0\) consists of the empty string. The length of each received trace is observable. Its original retained indices and deletion mask are not supplied. There are no substitutions, insertions, reversals, cyclic shifts or alignment labels.

Trace law. For \(y\in\{0,1\}^k\), let \(e_x(y)\) be the number of increasing index tuples \(1\le i_1<\cdots<i_k\le n\) with \(x_{i_j}=y_j\) for all \(j\). Define \(e_x(\varnothing)=1\). The trace distribution is
\[\mu_{x,\delta}(y)=e_x(y)(1-\delta)^k\delta^{n-k}.\]
Different deletion masks producing the same observed string all contribute to this probability. For example, for \(x=00\), the one-bit trace \(0\) has probability \(2(1-\delta)\delta\). All \(m\) observations use independent masks on the same original \(x\), so their joint distribution is \(\mu_{x,\delta}^{\otimes m}\).

Estimators. A randomized estimator for fixed \(n,\delta,m\) is a stochastic kernel \(K\) assigning every observed tuple \(\mathbf y\in\mathcal Y_n^m\) a probability distribution on \(\{0,1\}^n\). Thus \(K(\mathbf y,z)\ge0\) and \(\sum_zK(\mathbf y,z)=1\). The kernel may depend on \(n,\delta,m\), but not on the unknown string. It describes all permitted internal randomization; a deterministic estimator assigns probability one to a single output. Its success probability on \(x\) is
\[s_{x,\delta}(K)=\sum_{\mathbf y\in\mathcal Y_n^m}\left(\prod_{j=1}^{m}\mu_{x,\delta}(y_j)\right)K(\mathbf y,x).\]
The output must equal the whole original string, with its original linear order. Small edit distance, a list containing the string, or recovery of only some coordinates does not count as success. There is no prior distribution on \(x\); the success inequality must hold separately for every string.

Sample complexity. With \(\mathbb N_0=\{0,1,2,\ldots\}\), set
\[N_\delta(n)=\min\left\{m\in\mathbb N_0:\exists K\ \forall x\in\{0,1\}^n,\ s_{x,\delta}(K)\ge\frac23\right\}.\]
For \(m=0\), the observation tuple is empty and the product is one. The minimum is finite: a single trace has length \(n\) with probability \((1-\delta)^n>0\), and any such trace equals \(x\). Consequently the probability of receiving at least one complete trace tends to one with the number of independent samples. The cost is the fixed total number of traces, including empty or repeated traces, not their total bit length. Allowing a procedure to use at most \(m\) traces gives the same convention by ignoring unused samples; a bound only on the expected number of observations is not the definition.

Information-theoretic scope. There is no limit on running time, storage, description length or processing between observations, and no computability or uniformity restriction on the kernel family. The real deletion probability is a known mathematical parameter, so no finite encoding or estimation of \(\delta\) is required. These conventions make the question purely statistical. The input string has no codebook, sparsity, separation, random-generation or other promise. The asymptotic limit varies \(n\) while keeping \(\delta\) fixed; a simultaneous guarantee for \(\delta\) depending on \(n\), or uniform constants as \(\delta\) approaches an endpoint, is not required.
cards.answer_criterion:
Supply a positive function \(f_\delta(n)\) and a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean that, for every fixed \(\delta\in(0,1)\), there exist \(0<c_\delta\le C_\delta<\infty\) and an integer \(n_\delta\ge2\) such that
\[c_\delta f_\delta(n)\le N_\delta(n)\le C_\delta f_\delta(n)\qquad(n\ge n_\delta).\]
Finite exceptional lengths may equivalently be absorbed into constants for a positive finite representative \(f_\delta\). Give an informative mathematical description of the growth rate, rather than restating the defining minimum or assigning \(f_\delta=N_\delta\) without determining it.

The upper bound must establish estimators with the stated sample budget and success probability for every string. The lower bound must cover all randomized kernels allowed above, not only a named algorithm, local statistics, efficient computation or a restricted family of observations. Worst-case hard strings may depend on the estimator and sample budget; no single string must defeat every estimator.

The requested constant factors multiply the number of traces itself. Matching only the order of \(\log N_\delta(n)\), a polynomial exponent with an unspecified growing factor, or a polynomial-versus-superpolynomial classification is insufficient unless it yields the displayed bounds. This asymptotic criterion has no additive \(1/100\) tolerance. Average-case strings, approximate recovery, circular traces, a chosen codebook, or one special deletion probability do not determine the full target.

cards.status_note: Checked on 16 September 2026. The inspected July 2026 preprint gives quasipolynomial sample complexity for every fixed retention probability, while the unrestricted lower bound cited by it and the September graph-trace preprint remains polynomial. Neither determines N_delta(n) up to constant factors. Circular, local-SQ, separated-string and graph-trace results have different promises or observation models. No matching resolution was found in the bounded primary-source search; source proofs were not independently formalized.

context_blocks.text: The target asks how the optimal number of observations grows, including its exponent and any unbounded logarithmic factors. Whether some polynomial number of traces suffices is an important unresolved qualitative question within this more precise target.

The input is one unknown string, observed repeatedly through independent losses of symbols. A surviving output bit carries its value but loses its original index. Repetition gives more evidence about the same underlying string, so the question is how many damaged copies contain enough information for exact recovery in the worst case.

A deletion does not mark its former position. Two different deletion masks can produce the same observed string, even when the original input is fixed. Trace lengths are visible, and an undeleted trace would reveal the entire input, but its probability \((1-\delta)^n\) decays exponentially for a fixed nonzero deletion rate. The definition therefore has a finite elementary upper bound while still leaving room for vastly better sample complexity.

Chase proves a worst-case lower bound of \(\Omega(n^{3/2}/\log^7 n)\) for every fixed deletion probability and constant success threshold. The proof exhibits pairs of strings whose trace laws are hard to distinguish. This is an information-theoretic obstruction, not a running-time hypothesis or a limitation of one reconstruction procedure. It rules out near-linear sample complexity, but is consistent with a larger polynomial bound.

Chase’s earlier general upper bound uses \(\exp (\widetilde{O} (n^{1/5}))\) traces. This substantially improved previous subexponential bounds, but left a large gap above the polynomial lower bound. The saved ICALP 2025 source accurately described that frontier at publication; it is no longer the latest general sample upper bound.

Burudgunte, Valiant and Wang’s July 2026 preprint gives a quasipolynomial sample upper bound for every fixed positive retention probability. Its Theorem 43 bounds the number of traces by \(\exp(p^{-7/3}(\log_2 n)^c)\) for an absolute constant \(c\), where \(p=1-\delta\). This considerably narrows the earlier gap, but neither proves polynomial sample complexity nor gives matching lower bounds. In particular, it does not determine the multiplicative-constant growth rate requested here.

The same paper explicitly separates samples from running time. It gives quasipolynomial sample complexity for reconstructing an arbitrary unknown string and quasipolynomial time for distinguishing two supplied candidates. It leaves a quasipolynomial-time general reconstruction algorithm unresolved. Since this card permits unrestricted processing, its upper-bound progress remains relevant even without that further algorithmic guarantee.

A local statistical-query procedure receives approximate expectations of functions inspecting a short consecutive block of trace positions. Chen and coauthors prove strong accuracy requirements for that restricted model, nearly matching the earlier subexponential sample bound. Their theorem does not apply to arbitrary processing of individual traces. The later general upper bound is therefore compatible with the local-query lower bound.

Structural promises can also make the problem easier. Aamand, Liu and Narayanan show that \(O(n \log  n)\) traces suffice, with polynomial processing time, when successive ones are separated by sufficiently many zeros and the deletion probability is a sufficiently small constant. Their definition requires polylogarithmic separation. The theorem cannot be applied to arbitrary dense strings or to every constant deletion probability without additional arguments.

Circular trace reconstruction adds an unknown cyclic shift to each observation and asks for recovery up to rotation. The 2026 circular lower bound of roughly \(n^{5}\) is consequently a theorem for a different observation model. It should not replace the linear-model lower bound in this card. Likewise, deletion-channel coding permits a chosen codebook, while the worst-case reconstruction requirement here must cover every binary string.

A September 2026 preprint studies reconstruction of graph degree sequences from vertex-deleted subgraphs. Its introduction separately cites the quasipolynomial upper bound and polynomial lower bound for binary strings. Its new graph theorems do not supply a matching bound for the linear string observation model of this card.

cards.context:
The target asks how the optimal number of observations grows, including its exponent and any unbounded logarithmic factors. Whether some polynomial number of traces suffices is an important unresolved qualitative question within this more precise target.

The input is one unknown string, observed repeatedly through independent losses of symbols. A surviving output bit carries its value but loses its original index. Repetition gives more evidence about the same underlying string, so the question is how many damaged copies contain enough information for exact recovery in the worst case.

A deletion does not mark its former position. Two different deletion masks can produce the same observed string, even when the original input is fixed. Trace lengths are visible, and an undeleted trace would reveal the entire input, but its probability \((1-\delta)^n\) decays exponentially for a fixed nonzero deletion rate. The definition therefore has a finite elementary upper bound while still leaving room for vastly better sample complexity.

Chase proves a worst-case lower bound of \(\Omega(n^{3/2}/\log^7 n)\) for every fixed deletion probability and constant success threshold. The proof exhibits pairs of strings whose trace laws are hard to distinguish. This is an information-theoretic obstruction, not a running-time hypothesis or a limitation of one reconstruction procedure. It rules out near-linear sample complexity, but is consistent with a larger polynomial bound.

Chase’s earlier general upper bound uses \(\exp (\widetilde{O} (n^{1/5}))\) traces. This substantially improved previous subexponential bounds, but left a large gap above the polynomial lower bound. The saved ICALP 2025 source accurately described that frontier at publication; it is no longer the latest general sample upper bound.

Burudgunte, Valiant and Wang’s July 2026 preprint gives a quasipolynomial sample upper bound for every fixed positive retention probability. Its Theorem 43 bounds the number of traces by \(\exp(p^{-7/3}(\log_2 n)^c)\) for an absolute constant \(c\), where \(p=1-\delta\). This considerably narrows the earlier gap, but neither proves polynomial sample complexity nor gives matching lower bounds. In particular, it does not determine the multiplicative-constant growth rate requested here.

The same paper explicitly separates samples from running time. It gives quasipolynomial sample complexity for reconstructing an arbitrary unknown string and quasipolynomial time for distinguishing two supplied candidates. It leaves a quasipolynomial-time general reconstruction algorithm unresolved. Since this card permits unrestricted processing, its upper-bound progress remains relevant even without that further algorithmic guarantee.

A local statistical-query procedure receives approximate expectations of functions inspecting a short consecutive block of trace positions. Chen and coauthors prove strong accuracy requirements for that restricted model, nearly matching the earlier subexponential sample bound. Their theorem does not apply to arbitrary processing of individual traces. The later general upper bound is therefore compatible with the local-query lower bound.

Structural promises can also make the problem easier. Aamand, Liu and Narayanan show that \(O(n \log  n)\) traces suffice, with polynomial processing time, when successive ones are separated by sufficiently many zeros and the deletion probability is a sufficiently small constant. Their definition requires polylogarithmic separation. The theorem cannot be applied to arbitrary dense strings or to every constant deletion probability without additional arguments.

Circular trace reconstruction adds an unknown cyclic shift to each observation and asks for recovery up to rotation. The 2026 circular lower bound of roughly \(n^{5}\) is consequently a theorem for a different observation model. It should not replace the linear-model lower bound in this card. Likewise, deletion-channel coding permits a chosen codebook, while the worst-case reconstruction requirement here must cover every binary string.

A September 2026 preprint studies reconstruction of graph degree sequences from vertex-deleted subgraphs. Its introduction separately cites the quasipolynomial upper bound and polynomial lower bound for binary strings. Its new graph theorems do not supply a matching bound for the linear string observation model of this card.

cards.title: Constant-factor edit-distance approximation in \(O(n\operatorname{polylog} n)\) time
cards.formal:
Do there exist absolute real constants \(C\geq1\), \(K>0\), \(d\geq0\), an integer word-size constant \(B\geq3\), and one uniform classical randomized algorithm \(A\) such that for every integer \(n\geq1\) and all explicitly given \(x,y\in\{0,1,\ldots,n^2+1\}^n\), every execution uses at most
\[Kn\bigl(\log_2(n+2)\bigr)^d\]
word-RAM instructions and its integer output \(D\) satisfies
\[\Pr\bigl[\operatorname{ED}(x,y)\leq D\leq C\operatorname{ED}(x,y)\bigr]\geq\frac23?\]
The constants and program are chosen once for all input lengths and all pairs. The distance is unit-cost Levenshtein distance; the probability is over the algorithm’s internal randomness on that fixed pair.
cards.definitions:
Write \(\Sigma_n=\{0,1,\ldots,n^2+1\}\). The input is \(n\geq1\) followed by two arrays of \(n\) symbols from \(\Sigma_n\), stored in consecutive memory cells with one symbol per word. Binary strings and strings over any fixed alphabet are included after relabeling. The arrays are explicitly present; there is no compressed representation, access oracle, preprocessed database or promised input distribution.

The distance \(\operatorname{ED}(x,y)\) is the minimum number of single-symbol insertions, deletions and substitutions that transform \(x\) into \(y\). Inserted and substituted symbols belong to \(\Sigma_n\), and intermediate strings may have any finite length. Each operation has cost one; leaving an equal symbol unchanged has cost zero. No transpositions, block moves, variable symbol weights or affine gap penalties are allowed. A substitution costs one, not two. The optimum is an integer between zero and \(n\).

The word length is \(w=B\lceil\log_2(n+2)\rceil\) bits, with one fixed integer \(B\geq3\) for the algorithm. A word represents an unsigned integer from \(0\) to \(2^w-1\); memory addresses are words and all cells outside the given input are initially zero. The machine has a fixed finite instruction sequence and fixed integer constants, independent of \(n,x,y\). The unit-cost instructions are random-access reads or writes of one word, comparisons, conditional branches, bitwise Boolean operations, logical shifts, addition, subtraction and multiplication modulo \(2^w\), and integer quotient or remainder with a nonzero word divisor. Shifts fill with zeros and discard overflow; a shift amount at least \(w\) gives zero. Address calculations obey the same costs. Larger integers occupy several words and require several charged instructions. No arbitrary-precision arithmetic, advice, oracle or quantum instruction is available.

One fresh independent uniform \(w\)-bit random word costs one instruction; its individual bits are independent fair bits, and different draws are independent. All preprocessing, memory operations, random draws and output writing count toward the bound. The output is an integer in signed binary notation. Only its value is requested, not a sequence of edits. Every execution must terminate within the stated bound, including those that produce an incorrect estimate. An incorrect execution may return an integer outside the interval. The success guarantee is separate for every pair, not an average over an input distribution.

The quantifier order is \(\exists C,K,d,B,A\;\forall n,x,y\), followed by the displayed probability and all-execution time requirements. Neither the approximation factor nor the logarithmic exponent may grow with \(n\). There is no promise that the distance is large or positive. In particular, when \(x=y\), successful output must be zero. There is no additive error. The shorthand \(O(n\operatorname{polylog}n)\) refers exactly to one bound of the displayed form with fixed \(K,d\), not to \(n^{1+\eta}\) for each fixed \(\eta>0\) or to an arbitrary \(n^{1+o(1)}\) overhead.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete, mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of the existence of one algorithm and fixed constants meeting both requirements on all input pairs, or of its logical negation. A negative answer must rule out every finite approximation constant, every fixed logarithmic exponent and every permitted randomized algorithm and word-size constant; failure at one chosen factor or for deterministic algorithms alone is insufficient. A conditional lower bound gives only a conditional conclusion unless its hypothesis is also proved. An \(n^{1+\eta}\)-time algorithm for a fixed positive \(\eta\), an approximation factor growing with input length, an additive-error guarantee, an expected-time bound alone, or a theorem only for distant pairs does not settle the question. A large but fixed approximation constant is acceptable. This is an existence question, with no additional numerical approximation tolerance on its answer.
cards.why: This asks whether allowing one universal constant loss of alignment accuracy reduces worst-case sequence comparison to the cost of reading the input, apart from a fixed polylogarithmic overhead. The result would locate a basic computational boundary that remains beyond the known fast constant-factor algorithms. Even a large universal factor would resolve this existence question.

importance.reason: A central remaining precision–runtime boundary for edit distance, distinct from the established n^{1+ε} constant-factor algorithms and from exact-computation hardness.

context_blocks.text: Alignment matters because insertions and deletions shift later positions. For \(x=(01)^r\) and \(y=(10)^r\), with \(r\geq1\), every corresponding position differs, while \(\operatorname{ED}(x,y)=2\). Thus Hamming distance, which counts unequal corresponding positions, is \(2r\) and is not a universal constant-factor estimate for edit distance. The task concerns the optimum over all alignments.

The multiplicative guarantee includes nearby pairs. Equal strings require successful output zero, and distance-one pairs require an estimate at most the same universal constant used at all lengths. An additive error that grows with length cannot be absorbed into that bound. Reading both complete inputs is allowed; this is a total-runtime question rather than a sublinear-query question.

Andoni and Onak’s early theorem already gives a subpolynomial approximation factor in \(n^{1+o(1)}\) time, including for binary strings. Here subpolynomial means bounded by \(n^\eta\) eventually for every fixed \(\eta>0\). Such a bound still permits a factor that grows without bound, and an arbitrary subpolynomial runtime overhead need not be a fixed power of a logarithm. Their result therefore does not supply either fixed quantity required on this card.

Koucký and Saks prove a guarantee \(\operatorname{ED}(x,y)\leq U\leq R(\operatorname{ED}(x,y)+n^{1-\zeta})\) with high probability, for constants \(R,\zeta>0\) depending on a fixed runtime parameter. Their full Theorem 1.1 uses time \(\widetilde O(n^{1+1/T})\), with fixed \(T\geq1\); the tilde hides logarithmic factors. This gives a constant factor on sufficiently distant pairs, but the additive term prevents that conclusion uniformly for all distances.

Andoni and Nosatzki remove the distance restriction: for each fixed \(\eta>0\), their algorithm has time \(O(n^{1+\eta})\) and factor \(f(1/\eta)\). Theorem 1.1 of the full manuscript and its following paragraph specify dependence on the runtime slack, described as doubly exponential. Their journal article was published online on August 17, 2026. The publication does not change the fixed-slack theorem into a fixed-polylogarithmic-overhead theorem.

For every fixed \(\eta>0\), the factor \(n^\eta\) eventually exceeds every fixed power of \(\log n\). Making \(\eta\) depend on \(n\) also changes the theorem’s approximation factor and hidden constants. Thus the existing family does not automatically supply one algorithm with fixed \(C,K,d\). The open question is this remaining simultaneous control of approximation and overhead, rather than the already established existence of a strongly subquadratic constant-factor algorithm.

Mao and Rubinstein’s STOC 2026 theorem gives a different tradeoff: \((1+\varepsilon)\)-approximation for each fixed \(\varepsilon>0\), with stated time \(n^2/2^{\log^{\Omega(1)}n}\). It achieves near-exact accuracy, but its stated runtime does not meet this card’s much smaller overhead. Their separate LCS theorem is not substituted for the ordinary edit-distance theorem.

Backurs and Indyk’s conditional exact-computation result relates a fixed exponent saving for edit distance to a fixed exponential saving for CNF satisfiability. It does not rule out the coarse approximation required here. The known fast constant-factor algorithms already show that approximation must be distinguished from exact computation.

TCS-7220 asks for every fixed \((1+\varepsilon)\) accuracy with some positive fixed saving from exponent two, and TCS-7235 asks for the same accuracy in \(n^{1+o(1)}\) time. Neither stated guarantee alone supplies this card’s fixed polylogarithmic overhead. Conversely, one unspecified fixed factor here does not imply arbitrary near-exact accuracy. These user-approved targets remain distinct. Weighted or tree edit distances, codeword promises, quantum algorithms and data structures with separate preprocessing have different models.

cards.title: Almost-linear-time \((1+\varepsilon)\)-approximation of edit distance
cards.formal:
For every fixed rational \(\varepsilon\in(0,1)\), does there exist one uniform classical randomized algorithm \(A_\varepsilon\) which, on every pair of explicitly given strings \(x,y\) of total length \(n=|x|+|y|\geq2\), outputs an integer \(D\) such that
\[\Pr\bigl[\operatorname{ED}(x,y)\leq D\leq(1+\varepsilon)\operatorname{ED}(x,y)\bigr]\geq\frac23,\]
and has worst-case running time \(n^{1+o(1)}\) in the word-RAM model below? Here \(\operatorname{ED}\) is unit-cost Levenshtein distance, the probability is only over the algorithm’s independent random bits, and the time bound must hold on every execution. For each fixed accuracy, the same algorithm must satisfy every positive fixed exponent slack.
cards.definitions:
For total length \(n\), let \(\Sigma_n=\{0,1,\ldots,n^2+1\}\). The input consists of two lengths \(p,q\geq0\) with \(p+q=n\geq2\), and arrays \(x\in\Sigma_n^p\), \(y\in\Sigma_n^q\), one symbol per word. Either string may be empty. The lengths and all \(n\) symbols are given explicitly in consecutive input cells, not by a compressed representation or an oracle.

The distance \(\operatorname{ED}(x,y)\) is the minimum length of a finite sequence of edits transforming \(x\) into \(y\). An edit inserts one alphabet symbol at any position, deletes one symbol, or replaces one symbol by another. Each edit costs one; leaving a matching symbol unchanged costs zero. All intermediate strings use \(\Sigma_n\). Insertions and deletions can shift later positions. There are no block moves, transpositions, symbol-dependent weights or affine gap costs. In particular, this is not the distance that forbids substitutions and charges two for a replacement. The minimum is a nonnegative integer and at most \(n\).

For each fixed \(\varepsilon\), the machine may choose an integer \(B_\varepsilon\geq3\); its word length on total length \(n\) is
\[w=B_\varepsilon\lceil\log_2(n+2)\rceil.\]
A word is an unsigned integer from \(0\) to \(2^w-1\). Memory addresses are words, input cells contain the explicit lengths and arrays, and the remaining memory is initially zero. The program is one finite instruction sequence independent of \(n\), with a fixed finite list of integer constants. Unit-cost instructions are a word read or write at a word address, a comparison, conditional branch, a bitwise Boolean operation, a logical shift, addition, subtraction or multiplication modulo \(2^w\), or integer quotient or remainder with a nonzero word divisor. A logical shift fills with zeros, discards overflow, and returns zero when its shift amount is at least \(w\). Address calculations are charged under the same rules. Larger integers occupy multiple words and require multiple charged instructions. There is no arbitrary-precision arithmetic or precomputed input-dependent table at unit cost. Each draw of one independent fair random bit costs one instruction. Runtime includes all preprocessing, random draws and output writing. No advice, oracle, preprocessed database or quantum operations are provided.

The output is an integer in signed binary notation, with every written word charged. Only its numerical value is required; an edit script is not. On a failed random execution it may be outside the specified interval. Success must have probability at least \(2/3\) separately for every fixed input pair, regardless of its distance. Thus equal strings require output zero on successful executions, and no additive error depending on \(n\) is permitted.

Let \(T_{A_\varepsilon}(n)\) be the maximum number of instructions over all valid pairs of total length \(n\) and all random-bit sequences. It must be finite for every \(n\geq2\). The asymptotic requirement is
\[\forall\eta\in\mathbb Q_{>0}\;\exists C_{\varepsilon,\eta}>0\;\exists N_{\varepsilon,\eta}\geq2\;\forall n\geq N_{\varepsilon,\eta}:\quad
T_{A_\varepsilon}(n)\leq C_{\varepsilon,\eta}n^{1+\eta}.\]
Here the threshold is an integer. The choice of program and \(B_\varepsilon\) comes before \(\eta\). They may depend on the fixed accuracy but not on an exponent slack later used to describe their runtime. The accuracy is not an additional varying input. Andoni and Nosatzki obtain, for each fixed runtime slack \(\eta>0\), a randomized \(O(n^{1+\eta})\)-time approximation with factor \(f(1/\eta)\). cards.title: Truly subquadratic \((1+\varepsilon)\)-approximation of edit distance
cards.formal:
For every fixed rational \(\varepsilon\in(0,1)\), do there exist real constants \(\delta_\varepsilon\in(0,1)\), \(K_\varepsilon>0\) and one uniform classical randomized algorithm \(A_\varepsilon\) such that, for every integer \(n\geq1\) and every pair of length-\(n\) strings \(x,y\), every execution uses at most \(K_\varepsilon(n+2)^{2-\delta_\varepsilon}\) word-RAM instructions and its integer output \(D\) satisfies
\[\Pr\bigl[\operatorname{ED}(x,y)\leq D\leq(1+\varepsilon)\operatorname{ED}(x,y)\bigr]\geq\frac23?\]
The distance is unit-cost Levenshtein distance, the alphabet and computational model are specified below, and probability is over independent internal random bits for each fixed input pair.
cards.definitions:
The input consists of \(n\geq1\) and two explicit arrays \(x,y\in\Sigma_n^n\), where \(\Sigma_n=\{0,1,\ldots,n^2+1\}\). Each symbol occupies one word. The arrays and length are stored in consecutive input cells. Binary and any fixed alphabet are included, after relabeling the symbols. No compressed representation, access oracle, prior preprocessing or input distribution is supplied.

The distance \(\operatorname{ED}(x,y)\) is the minimum number of edits in a sequence transforming \(x\) into \(y\), where one edit inserts one symbol of \(\Sigma_n\), deletes one symbol, or substitutes one symbol for another. Each costs one, and an equal-symbol match costs zero. Intermediate strings may have different lengths. There are no block edits, transpositions, symbol weights or affine gap penalties. In particular, a substitution costs one rather than an insertion plus a deletion. The minimum is an integer between zero and \(n\).

For each fixed accuracy, the algorithm may choose a fixed integer \(B_\varepsilon\geq3\) and uses words of
\[w=B_\varepsilon\lceil\log_2(n+2)\rceil\]
bits. Words represent unsigned integers modulo \(2^w\); memory is addressed by words, and all non-input cells start at zero. The program is a finite list of instructions and integer constants independent of \(n,x,y\). One instruction can read or write one word, compare words, branch, perform a bitwise Boolean operation, shift a word, add, subtract or multiply modulo \(2^w\), or compute an integer quotient or remainder with a nonzero divisor. Shifts discard overflow and fill with zeros; a shift by at least \(w\) returns zero. Address arithmetic has the same cost. Larger integers require several words and several charged instructions. A fresh independent fair random bit costs one instruction. All preprocessing, random draws and output writing are charged; no arbitrary-precision, oracle, advice or quantum instruction is available. The bound in the statement holds on every random-bit sequence, including executions with an incorrect answer, and forces termination.

The output is an integer written in signed binary notation. A successful execution must satisfy the displayed interval; a failed execution may output an integer outside it. Only the estimate is required, not a sequence of edits. Success must hold separately on every input pair, including identical strings and pairs at distance one. No additive error term is allowed.

The accuracy \(\varepsilon\) is fixed before choosing the algorithm, the word-size constant, the exponent saving and the runtime constant. They may all depend on \(\varepsilon\), but never on \(n\) or the strings. Thus the order is \(\forall\varepsilon\;\exists A_\varepsilon,B_\varepsilon,\delta_\varepsilon,K_\varepsilon\;\forall n,x,y\). No one positive exponent saving must work for all accuracies. The accuracy is not a varying input to a common algorithm, and no effective procedure generating these algorithms, or bound polynomial in \(1/\varepsilon\), is required. The term truly subquadratic means the positive saving \(\delta_\varepsilon\) remains fixed as \(n\) grows; savings such as a fixed power of \(\log n\) do not suffice.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete, mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of the full existence statement for every fixed rational accuracy, or of its logical negation. A negative answer must prove that for some fixed rational \(\varepsilon\in(0,1)\), no permitted randomized algorithm and word-size constant achieve the per-input multiplicative guarantee with any positive fixed exponent saving and any fixed runtime constant. A deterministic lower bound alone does not rule out the stated randomized algorithms. A conditional lower bound settles only the corresponding conditional claim unless its hypothesis is also proved. One fixed coarse approximation factor, a bound with only a subpolynomial saving from quadratic time, an expected-time guarantee alone, or a theorem for restricted input pairs is insufficient. This is an algorithm-existence target with the stated relative accuracy, not a numerical target with a separate additive tolerance.

context_blocks.text: Rubinstein explicitly posed this in Open question 2 of his July 2018 exposition, with near-linear time as a further possibility. His May 2020 update resolves the separate constant-factor question, not the arbitrary-accuracy question. The present card keeps the truly subquadratic branch, with accuracy chosen before the positive exponent saving.

For example, fixing \(\varepsilon=1/100\) asks for a one-percent relative estimate and some positive exponent saving that remains fixed at all lengths. The saving may become smaller at other, more demanding accuracies. Therefore the claim does not require a fixed subquadratic algorithm for exact distance. Choosing an accuracy below \(1/n\) to force exactness instead makes the accuracy depend on the input length, which the theorem does not allow.

Mao and Rubinstein’s 2026 theorem gives \((1+\varepsilon)\)-approximation for each fixed \(\varepsilon>0\) in stated time \(n^2/2^{\log^{\Omega(1)}n}\). Theorem 6.1 and footnote 21 give success at least \(1-1/n\) when \(n\) denotes total string length. This is a substantial improvement beyond fixed logarithmic savings, but its stated guarantee does not establish a fixed positive saving in the quadratic exponent. The result is for unit-cost edit distance; its separate LCS guarantee concerns another objective.

Andoni and Nosatzki obtain a constant approximation factor in \(O(n^{1+\eta})\) time for each fixed \(\eta>0\). Their Theorem 1.1 permits the approximation factor to depend on \(\eta\); the following paragraph describes it as doubly exponential in \(1/\eta\). It is not a guarantee of \(1+\varepsilon\) for a prescribed small \(\varepsilon\). The paper’s August 2026 journal publication retains this different accuracy–time tradeoff.

Backurs and Indyk show that a fixed exponent saving for exact edit distance would yield a fixed exponential saving for CNF satisfiability. Their reduction provides conditional evidence against fast exact computation. It does not itself yield a fixed multiplicative-accuracy lower bound or an unconditional impossibility theorem for this card.

The retained TCS-6624 asks for any fixed constant factor in \(O(n(\log(n+2))^d)\) time with fixed \(d\). A positive answer here would not supply that runtime, while such a coarse fast estimate would not supply arbitrary \(1+\varepsilon\) accuracy. TCS-7235 asks for the stronger near-exact bound \(n^{1+o(1)}\). Its positive answer would imply the target here, but a fixed saving from exponent two does not imply an exponent approaching one. These approved targets remain separate.

Purely multiplicative accuracy constrains small distances as well. If \(\operatorname{ED}=0\), the successful output is zero. If \(\operatorname{ED}=1\) and \(\varepsilon<1\), its integer output must be one. Thus a growing additive error or a guarantee only for distant pairs does not meet the question. Weighted edits, tree structures, codeword promises and random-input models likewise have different hypotheses.

cards.why: This asks whether any fixed tolerance for a relative alignment error permits a fixed polynomial saving from the quadratic time scale on arbitrary sequences. Exact edit distance has strong conditional hardness evidence, while fast coarse approximations already exist. The question isolates whether near-exact approximation can cross the fixed-exponent boundary for every desired fixed accuracy.

importance.reason: A longstanding central accuracy–runtime question for edit distance, explicitly posed before the constant-factor breakthroughs and sharpened by the 2026 approximation scheme. Retained alongside TCS-6624 because one target asks for near-exact accuracy and the other for nearly linear overhead; their stated algorithmic guarantees do not imply one another.

Purely multiplicative accuracy constrains small distances as well. If \(\operatorname{ED}=0\), the successful output is zero. If \(\operatorname{ED}=1\) and \(\varepsilon<1\), its integer output must be one. Thus a growing additive error or a guarantee only for distant pairs does not meet the question. Weighted edits, tree structures, codeword promises and random-input models likewise have different hypotheses.

cards.definitions: An instance gives \(k\ge2\) explicit strings over a finite alphabet \(\Sigma\), and a table \(d:(\Sigma\cup\{-\})^2\to\mathbb Q_{\ge0}\) encoded by binary numerators and denominators. The distinguished gap symbol \(-\) is not an input-string symbol. Promise \(d(a,b)=d(b,a)\), \(d(a,b)=0\) exactly when \(a=b\), and the triangle inequality for all alphabet and gap symbols. An alignment is a \(k\)-row array of equal-length strings over \(\Sigma\cup\{-\}\) such that erasing gaps from each row returns its input string, and no column consists entirely of gaps. The cost is \(\sum_{1\le i<j\le k}\sum_c d(A_{i,c},A_{j,c})\). The minimum is over all such alignments. Empty input strings are allowed, and the all-empty instance has the empty alignment and zero optimum. The output is an explicit feasible alignment with cost at most \((2-\varepsilon)\) times optimum. Time is measured on a deterministic finite-tape Turing machine in the total bit length of the explicit strings and metric table. The constant, finite program and polynomial are independent of \(k\), the alphabet, lengths and costs. The metric promise is part of the input domain; the algorithm must halt within one fixed polynomial on all input strings, with output correctness required on well-formed promised instances. Ordinary length-delimited encodings list all alphabet symbols, all strings, and all metric-table entries; empty strings still have explicit list entries. If \(N\) is the total number of input symbols, every feasible alignment has at most \(N\) columns because each column contains at least one non-gap symbol. Hence the feasible set is finite and nonempty, and the stated minimum is attained. A zero optimum requires a zero-cost output. Gap costs are charged separately per column and pair; no additional gap-opening or run-length penalty is present.

context_blocks.text: An alignment adds gaps to put all strings into common columns while preserving the order of the original symbols. The sum-of-pairs objective charges every unordered pair of rows in every column. For example, a column containing a, a and a gap contributes twice the cost of comparing a with a gap, rather than one consensus-column penalty.

Pairwise comparison and multiple alignment are different optimization tasks. Pairwise alignments chosen independently need not be realizable simultaneously in one common table of columns. The target optimizes over globally feasible tables for all supplied strings, with the number of rows part of the input.

The classical metric guarantee is \(2-2/k\) for \(k\) strings. It is below two for every fixed \(k\), but the improvement \(2/k\) tends to zero as the number of strings grows. The conjectured algorithm must improve the factor by one fixed positive amount independent of \(k\).

The supplied survey also records extensions whose improvement depends on a fixed auxiliary parameter divided by the number of strings. Such guarantees do not by themselves supply one uniform polynomial-time constant improvement for arbitrary row counts. The source distinguishes the sum-of-pairs objective from evolutionary-tree alignment.

The metric includes the gap symbol and obeys symmetry and the triangle inequality. Nonmetric scores, negative rewards, affine gap penalties, structural-contact objectives and maximization of a similarity score can have different algorithms and hardness results. They are not substituted for this minimum-cost metric problem.

Exact optimization is already difficult, but NP-hardness of exact optimization alone does not rule out a constant-factor approximation. A negative answer to the present question needs the quantified impossibility of every permitted polynomial-time algorithm; an approximation-hardness theorem conditional on a complexity assumption must retain that assumption.

cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof of one rational \(0<\varepsilon<1\), one uniform deterministic algorithm and one polynomial bit-time bound that always return a feasible alignment of cost at most \((2-\varepsilon)\operatorname{OPT}\) for every promised instance, including zero-optimum cases. Alternatively prove in Lean that no such choices exist. The improvement and polynomial must be independent of the number of strings, alphabet, lengths and rational metric entries; a fixed-number-of-strings guarantee or a conditional lower bound alone does not decide the full proposition.

cards.title: Almost-linear constant-factor approximation of LCS
cards.formal: Do there exist a universal constant \(C\ge1\) and a uniform randomized algorithm which, for every pair of explicit strings of total length \(n\ge2\) over \([0..n^2)\), returns a common subsequence of length at least \(\operatorname{LCS}(A,B)/C\) with probability at least \(2/3\), in \(n^{1+o(1)}\) worst-case time?
cards.definitions: A subsequence is obtained by deleting zero or more symbols without changing the remaining order; \(\operatorname{LCS}(A,B)\) is the maximum possible length common to both strings. Empty strings are permitted. The algorithm outputs the subsequence explicitly and must always output a valid common subsequence; only the approximation guarantee may fail. Set \(L=n\). Use a uniform sequential word RAM with word length \(w=d\lceil\log_2(L+2)\rceil\), for a fixed integer \(d\ge 8\) chosen with the algorithm. A fixed finite program must handle every input size; there is no advice, precomputed lookup table or input-dependent oracle. Unit-cost operations are reads, writes, copying, comparisons, branching, Boolean operations, logical shifts, addition, subtraction and multiplication modulo \(2^w\), and integer quotient and remainder for a nonzero divisor. Shifts by at least \(w\) return zero. Addresses and stored values fit words; multiword operations pay for their constituent instructions. Randomized algorithms, when explicitly permitted, may generate independent uniform random words. All initialization, preprocessing, tables and output writes are charged. A static query starts without input-dependent private state, and every retained copy of the input or auxiliary information counts toward index space. The same finite algorithm and approximation constant work for every input size. The runtime convention means that for every real \(\eta>0\) there exist \(K_\eta,n_\eta\) such that every random execution takes at most \(K_\eta n^{1+\eta}\) steps for every \(n\ge n_\eta\). The probability is over internal randomness on each fixed input. The alphabet grows with input length; a guarantee depending on alphabet size is not a universal constant approximation.

cards.title: Space-query exponent curve of gapped string indexing
cards.formal:
Determine the dimensionless space exponent \(s_{\mathrm{gap}}(\delta)\) for every real \(\delta\in[0,1]\). For each such \(\delta\), let
\[
s_{\mathrm{gap}}(\delta)=\inf\{s\in[1,\infty):\ \forall\eta\in\mathbb Q_{>0}\ \exists\mathcal D,K,C_0,h,d\text{ satisfying the bounds below}\}.
\]
Here \(\mathcal D=(P,Q)\) is a uniform randomized static indexing scheme in the stated word-RAM model, \(K,C_0\ge1\) are constants, and \(h\ge1,d\ge8\) are integers. For every \(n\ge2\), every length-\(n\) text, and every valid query, preprocessing takes at most \(C_0(n+2)^h\) steps; the index together with query workspace uses at most \(Kn^{s+\eta}\) words; and the query takes at most
\[
K\bigl(m_1+m_2+n^{\delta+\eta}(1+\mathrm{occ})\bigr)
\]
steps. Each bound holds for every outcome of the random choices. For each fixed text and query, the complete output is correct with probability at least \(2/3\), over preprocessing and query randomness. The chosen programs and constants may depend on \(\delta,s,\eta\), but not on the text, its length, or a query. The requested answer is a real-valued function \(g\) on \([0,1]\), certified to satisfy \(\lvert g(\delta)-s_{\mathrm{gap}}(\delta)\rvert\le1/100\) at every point.
cards.definitions:
The input text is an explicit array \(T[0],\ldots,T[n-1]\), with each entry in \(\{0,\ldots,n-1\}\). A query consists of two explicit nonempty arrays \(P_1,P_2\) over the same alphabet, their lengths \(1\le m_1,m_2\le n\), and integers \(0\le a\le b<n\). A start \(i\) for \(P_1\) is valid when \(0\le i\le n-m_1\) and \(T[i+u]=P_1[u]\) for every \(0\le u<m_1\); define starts \(j\) for \(P_2\) analogously. The answer is the set of all ordered pairs \((i,j)\) of valid starts with \(a\le j-i\le b\). Each pair must be written exactly once, in any order, followed by termination. Overlapping occurrences and \(i=j\) are allowed when they satisfy the conditions. The true cardinality of this set is \(\mathrm{occ}\), even when evaluating the time bound on an unsuccessful random outcome. The gap measures start-to-start distance, not the number of characters between two nonoverlapping occurrences. Both gap endpoints arrive with the query.

Preprocessing \(P\) receives \(n\) and the explicit text and produces a finite stored index. Query program \(Q\) receives \(n\), that index, and the explicit query. The text is available during a query only to the extent it was retained in charged index memory. The index is static and read-only during a query. Each query starts with empty working memory and no input-dependent private state from earlier queries. Random words used at different steps are independent and uniform; retained preprocessing randomness is accessible only through the stored index. Success is required separately for every fixed text/query pair; a single preprocessing outcome need not answer all possible queries simultaneously, and no guarantee against queries selected after inspecting private random choices is imposed. Time and space bounds are worst-case, not expected or amortized.

The machine is a sequential word RAM with word length \(w=d\lceil\log_2(n+2)\rceil\). Its programs have finite descriptions and a fixed finite number of registers and instructions. Input integers and symbols are supplied as ordinary words; \(n,m_1,m_2,a,b\) are included. Unit-cost instructions are reading or writing one addressed word, copying, comparison, branching, Boolean operations, logical shifts, addition, subtraction and multiplication modulo \(2^w\), and integer quotient or remainder with a nonzero divisor. Logical shifts by at least \(w\) return zero. Generating one independent uniform \(w\)-bit word costs one instruction. Addresses and individual stored values must fit a word. Computations on larger integers pay for all constituent instructions. There is no advice, input-dependent oracle, free random function, or uncharged table.

All initialization, reads, writes, random generation, table construction, and output writes count toward the time of the phase in which they occur. Preprocessing workspace is charged to preprocessing time and is therefore polynomially bounded; it need not satisfy the smaller retained-space bound. Every retained word counts toward index space, including stored text, metadata, tables, seeds and registers retained between phases. During a query, that space bound additionally counts all registers and working memory. Only the read-only current query and the streamed output are excluded from storage, and writing the output is charged to query time. Finite control is part of the fixed program, not a source of size-dependent advice. The constants, register count and polynomial preprocessing degree are fixed once \(\delta,s,\eta\) are chosen.

The quantifiers allow different finite programs for different parameter choices and different positive rational slack values. They do not require a computable procedure that takes an arbitrary real \(\delta\) or \(s\) and constructs a program, and those real numbers are never supplied to a machine. The slack defines exponents rather than hidden fixed logarithmic factors. The infimum is finite and need not be attained; the target does not demand a scheme at exactly the optimal exponent without slack. The normalization \(s\ge1\), full domain \([0,1]\), polynomial preprocessing and inclusion of query workspace retain the card's selected convention.

context_blocks.text: The original paper asks whether simultaneous subquadratic storage and sublinear query overhead are possible and answers that question affirmatively. The present card retains the user-approved editorial extension to the optimal exponent curve; it is not a restatement of that already answered binary question.

Theorem 1 reports space \(\widetilde O(n^{2-\delta/3})\) or \(\widetilde O(n^{3-2\delta})\), with query time \(\widetilde O(m_1+m_2+n^\delta(1+\mathrm{occ}))\). cards.title: Almost-quadratic unweighted tree edit distance
cards.formal: Is there a uniform deterministic algorithm computing the exact unit-cost edit distance between two rooted ordered labeled trees with a total of \(n\ge2\) vertices in \(n^{2+o(1)}\) worst-case time?
cards.definitions: Trees are supplied by explicit ordered child lists and vertex labels in \([0..n^2)\). A fixed unlabelled super-root is attached above each input root; it may not be deleted or relabelled and is not counted in \(n\). Intermediate objects may be ordered forests below this super-root. Deleting a vertex replaces it in its parent’s ordered child list by its own ordered children. Inserting a vertex is the inverse operation, grouping a consecutive block of children, possibly empty, under one new vertex. Relabelling changes one ordinary vertex label. Each of these three operations costs one. The distance is the minimum total cost of a sequence transforming the first ordered labeled object into the second. The output is this single integer, not an edit script. Set \(L=n\). Use a uniform sequential word RAM with word length \(w=d\lceil\log_2(L+2)\rceil\), for a fixed integer \(d\ge 8\) chosen with the algorithm. A fixed finite program must handle every input size; there is no advice, precomputed lookup table or input-dependent oracle. Unit-cost operations are reads, writes, copying, comparisons, branching, Boolean operations, logical shifts, addition, subtraction and multiplication modulo \(2^w\), and integer quotient and remainder for a nonzero divisor. Shifts by at least \(w\) return zero. Addresses and stored values fit words; multiword operations pay for their constituent instructions. Randomized algorithms, when explicitly permitted, may generate independent uniform random words. All initialization, preprocessing, tables and output writes are charged. A static query starts without input-dependent private state, and every retained copy of the input or auxiliary information counts toward index space. The same algorithm works for all inputs. The time condition means that for every \(\eta>0\), some constants \(K_\eta,n_\eta\) bound its time by \(K_\eta n^{2+\eta}\) whenever \(n\ge n_\eta\). All preprocessing is charged, and no randomness is permitted.

cards.title: Constant-factor approximation of the smallest grammar
cards.formal: Do there exist an absolute constant C and a deterministic polynomial-time algorithm that, for every explicit nonempty string s, outputs an acyclic context-free grammar generating exactly s whose size is at most $C g^*(s)$? There is one production per nonterminal, one designated start nonterminal, and every right-hand side is a nonempty string of terminals and nonterminals. The dependency graph on nonterminals must be acyclic. Grammar size is the sum of all right-hand-side lengths, and $g^*(s)$ is the minimum such size. The alphabet is part of the input, encoded by integer symbols in {1,...,|s|}.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove existence of one polynomial-time algorithm with some fixed approximation constant valid for all strings, or prove that no such algorithm exists. A hardness theorem conditional on \(\mathrm{P} \ne  \mathrm{NP}\) should be reported with that assumption. Exact optimization and ratios tending to one are stronger targets than the constant-factor question.
cards.definitions: Expanding a nonterminal means repeatedly replacing it by its unique right-hand side. Acyclicity guarantees termination, and the start expansion must equal the input string with no extra strings generated. Each terminal or nonterminal occurrence on a right-hand side contributes one unit to size. Runtime is measured in the ordinary binary encoding of the explicit input, not the compressed output length. Constant C cannot depend on the alphabet size, string length, or optimal grammar size. Arbitrarily long right-hand sides are permitted; the size convention is not just the number of productions.
cards.why: This is a fundamental compression-versus-optimization question: can an efficient procedure recover a representation within a fixed factor of the best hierarchical description? It also supplies a benchmark for compressed-data algorithms, whose costs often depend on grammar size rather than on the original string length.

progress.text: Charikar and coauthors give an \(O(1+\log (|s|/g*(s)))\) approximation and rule out approximation ratios below \(8569/8568\) unless \(\mathrm{P} = \mathrm{NP}\).
Casel and coauthors establish hardness over fixed alphabets of size at least 17 and retain constant-factor approximation as Open Problem 2. The hardness result does not rule out every constant.

context_blocks.text: A grammar can share repeated pieces of a string and then share larger pieces assembled from them. For example, a sequence of doubling rules represents an exponentially long run using only a linear number of rules. This makes grammar size a useful concrete measure of repetitive structure, with a finite optimum that can in principle be found by exhaustive search.

The problem is to choose the shared pieces. Two useful repeated substrings may overlap, and a locally attractive substitution can prevent a better organization at a larger scale. A method that compresses some families extremely well can therefore still have an unbounded ratio to the best grammar on other families. The proposed guarantee must cover every input, not only average compression performance.

Known approximation guarantees depend logarithmically on the ratio between the explicit string length and its optimal grammar size. Hardness rules out sufficiently accurate approximation under \(\mathrm{P} \ne  \mathrm{NP}\), but this does not exclude a coarser universal constant. The space between these two conclusions is the question on this card.

The size measure is essential. Counting productions, binary concatenations, or all right-hand-side symbols gives related but different optimization problems. Stating the measure explicitly also avoids confusing exact binary-alphabet hardness questions with the unrestricted constant-factor approximation target.

cards.title: Optimal \(\ell_{1}\) distortion of binary edit distance
cards.formal: For each integer \(n\ge2\), let \(X_n=\{0,1\}^{n}\) and define \[D_{\mathrm{ED}}(n)=\inf\bigl\{D\in[1,\infty):\ \exists m\in\mathbb N_{\ge1},\ \exists f:X_n\to\mathbb R^m,\ \exists a>0,\ \forall x,y\in X_n,\ a\,\mathrm{ED}(x,y)\le\|f(x)-f(y)\|_1\le D a\,\mathrm{ED}(x,y)\bigr\}.\] Determine the asymptotic growth of \(D_{\mathrm{ED}}(n)\) up to universal multiplicative constants as \(n\to\infty\).
cards.definitions: The integer \(n\) is the length of each string; the metric space \(X_n\) contains \(2^n\) strings. The distance \(\mathrm{ED}(x,y)\) is the minimum number of single-character insertions, deletions and substitutions needed to transform \(x\) into \(y\), each at cost one. Inserted and substituted characters are binary, and intermediate strings may have any finite length. For \(v\in\mathbb R^m\), \(\|v\|_1=\sum_{i=1}^{m}|v_i|\). The dimension \(m\) is any finite positive integer, coordinates are arbitrary real numbers, and the map need not have an efficient or computable description. There is no bound on dimension or construction/evaluation time, and no requirement for a uniform algorithm across different \(n\). The same map \(f\) and positive scale \(a\) must satisfy both inequalities simultaneously for all pairs in \(X_n\); \(f,m,a\) may depend on \(n\). The infimum ranges over all such choices. Every finite metric space has a finite-distortion embedding into some finite-dimensional \(\ell_1\), so \(1\le D_{\mathrm{ED}}(n)<\infty\).

context_blocks.text: The card retains the quantitative growth question adopted in its earlier review. This is an editorial broadening of asking only whether a polylogarithmic-distortion embedding exists: a matching asymptotic determination can settle either growth regime. It is not attributed to the source as an identically worded conjecture.

Ostrovsky and Rabani prove \(D_{\mathrm{ED}}(n)\le 2^{O(\sqrt{(\log n)(\log\log n)})}\). This is a subpolynomial upper bound whose displayed growth exceeds every fixed power of \(\log n\). Their geometric theorem places no algorithmic constraint on the embedding. Here and in the asymptotic bounds, logarithms may be taken to base two and the displayed formulas concern sufficiently large \(n\).

Krauthgamer and Rabani prove \(D_{\mathrm{ED}}(n)=\Omega(\log n)\). Together with the upper bound, this leaves a gap between logarithmic and subpolynomial distortion. Both of these papers explicitly include unit-cost substitutions, matching this card's distance.

The earlier Khot–Naor lower bound is \((\log n)^{1/2-o(1)}\), rather than logarithmic. That paper permits only insertions and deletions. If \(\mathrm{ED}_{\mathrm{indel}}\) denotes this convention, then \(\mathrm{ED}\le\mathrm{ED}_{\mathrm{indel}}\le2\mathrm{ED}\), so the two optimal distortion functions agree within a factor of two; they need not agree pointwise.

Near-linear-time constant-factor approximation of the distance between two supplied strings concerns a different mathematical guarantee. It does not give a single map of the entire binary-string metric into ordinary \(\ell_1\) with constant distortion.

The FOCS 2025 work develops average embeddings into similarity measures and obtains polylogarithmic approximation for edit-distance nearest-neighbor search. The primary abstract states this different target; it does not claim the all-pairs ordinary-l1 embedding required here.

cards.why: Determining this distortion would explain how closely the geometry of binary sequence editing can be represented by sums of coordinate differences, closing a longstanding gap between metric embeddings and their obstructions.
cards.answer_criterion: Specify a positive function \(h:\mathbb N_{\ge2}\to\mathbb R_{>0}\) describing the asymptotic growth, and give a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean that there are absolute constants \(0<c\le C<\infty\) with \(c\,h(n)\le D_{\mathrm{ED}}(n)\le C\,h(n)\) for every integer \(n\ge2\). The proof must establish matching upper and lower bounds for the unrestricted embeddings and edit operations specified above. Merely repeating the defining infimum, computing a finite table, or giving unmatched upper and lower bounds does not determine the asymptotic order. A polylogarithmic upper bound alone need not meet this criterion. The required precision is multiplicative constant factors, as appropriate for the retained asymptotic-complexity question.

cards.context:
The card retains the quantitative growth question adopted in its earlier review. This is an editorial broadening of asking only whether a polylogarithmic-distortion embedding exists: a matching asymptotic determination can settle either growth regime. It is not attributed to the source as an identically worded conjecture.

Ostrovsky and Rabani prove \(D_{\mathrm{ED}}(n)\le 2^{O(\sqrt{(\log n)(\log\log n)})}\). This is a subpolynomial upper bound whose displayed growth exceeds every fixed power of \(\log n\). Their geometric theorem places no algorithmic constraint on the embedding. Here and in the asymptotic bounds, logarithms may be taken to base two and the displayed formulas concern sufficiently large \(n\).

Krauthgamer and Rabani prove \(D_{\mathrm{ED}}(n)=\Omega(\log n)\). Together with the upper bound, this leaves a gap between logarithmic and subpolynomial distortion. Both of these papers explicitly include unit-cost substitutions, matching this card's distance.

The earlier Khot–Naor lower bound is \((\log n)^{1/2-o(1)}\), rather than logarithmic. That paper permits only insertions and deletions. If \(\mathrm{ED}_{\mathrm{indel}}\) denotes this convention, then \(\mathrm{ED}\le\mathrm{ED}_{\mathrm{indel}}\le2\mathrm{ED}\), so the two optimal distortion functions agree within a factor of two; they need not agree pointwise.

Near-linear-time constant-factor approximation of the distance between two supplied strings concerns a different mathematical guarantee. It does not give a single map of the entire binary-string metric into ordinary \(\ell_1\) with constant distortion.

The FOCS 2025 work develops average embeddings into similarity measures and obtains polylogarithmic approximation for edit-distance nearest-neighbor search. The primary abstract states this different target; it does not claim the all-pairs ordinary-l1 embedding required here.

cards.title: Optimal top-k document retrieval in compact space
cards.formal: Does a uniform deterministic static index exist for every collection \(D_1,\ldots,D_d\) of nonempty strings of total length \(n\ge2\) over \([0..\sigma)\), where \(2\le\sigma\le n\), using \(O(n\log\sigma)\) bits and answering top-\(k\) queries in \(O(1+m/\log_\sigma n+k)\) worst-case time?
cards.definitions: A query gives \(1\le k\le d\) and a nonempty packed pattern \(P\) of length \(m\le n\). The frequency of \(P\) in a document is its number of starting positions, counting overlapping occurrences. Return the identifiers of the \(\min(k,h)\) highest-frequency documents among the \(h\) documents containing \(P\), in decreasing frequency, breaking ties by increasing identifier. No occurrence crosses a document boundary. Documents are identified by their input order. The alphabet symbols occupy \(\lceil\log_2\sigma\rceil\) bits each in the packed query. Set \(L=n\). Use a uniform sequential word RAM with word length \(w=d\lceil\log_2(L+2)\rceil\), for a fixed integer \(d\ge 8\) chosen with the algorithm. A fixed finite program must handle every input size; there is no advice, precomputed lookup table or input-dependent oracle. Unit-cost operations are reads, writes, copying, comparisons, branching, Boolean operations, logical shifts, addition, subtraction and multiplication modulo \(2^w\), and integer quotient and remainder for a nonzero divisor. Shifts by at least \(w\) return zero. Addresses and stored values fit words; multiword operations pay for their constituent instructions. Randomized algorithms, when explicitly permitted, may generate independent uniform random words. All initialization, preprocessing, tables and output writes are charged. A static query starts without input-dependent private state, and every retained copy of the input or auxiliary information counts toward index space. Preprocessing takes polynomial time in \(n\). Space includes document boundaries, identifiers, retained text and every persistent auxiliary structure. Query working memory, excluding the supplied pattern and streamed output, also fits the stated bit bound. All constants are uniform in \(n,d,\sigma,m,k\).

context_blocks.text: A collection-level search query often needs the most relevant documents rather than every individual occurrence of a pattern.

On small alphabets that additional storage is asymptotically larger than the text. Sorting results by frequency and counting all stored boundaries are part of the target.

cards.why: This joins ranked retrieval with compact text indexing, a basic requirement for searchable document and genome collections whose auxiliary indexes should not dominate their input.

cards.title: General-alphabet Hamming oracles with optimal preprocessing
cards.formal: Is there a uniform deterministic data structure which, for every pair of strings of lengths \(n,m\ge1\) and every integer \(1\le x\le\min(n,m)\), uses \(\widetilde O(nm/x)\) preprocessing time and stored words and answers exact substring Hamming-distance queries in \(O(x)\) worst-case time?
cards.definitions: The strings \(A\) and \(B\) are supplied explicitly over \([0..(n+m)^2)\). A query \((i,j,\ell)\) satisfies \(0\le i\le n\), \(0\le j\le m\), and \(0\le\ell\le\min(n-i,m-j)\). It returns \(|\{t:0\le t<\ell,\ A[i+t]\ne B[j+t]\}|\). Positions are zero-based; a length-zero query returns zero. Set \(L=n+m\). Use a uniform sequential word RAM with word length \(w=d\lceil\log_2(L+2)\rceil\), for a fixed integer \(d\ge 8\) chosen with the algorithm. A fixed finite program must handle every input size; there is no advice, precomputed lookup table or input-dependent oracle. Unit-cost operations are reads, writes, copying, comparisons, branching, Boolean operations, logical shifts, addition, subtraction and multiplication modulo \(2^w\), and integer quotient and remainder for a nonzero divisor. Shifts by at least \(w\) return zero. Addresses and stored values fit words; multiword operations pay for their constituent instructions. All initialization, preprocessing, tables and output writes are charged. A static query starts without input-dependent private state, and every retained copy of the input or auxiliary information counts toward index space. The soft-O means multiplication by \((\log(L+2))^c\) for one fixed constant \(c\), independent of \(x,n,m\). One fixed algorithm receives \(x\) during preprocessing and handles all admissible parameters. The stored space includes both strings, if retained, and all auxiliary information. Query space is included; no offline knowledge of future queries is supplied. More explicitly, there must be constants \(C\ge1\), \(c\ge0\) and \(d\ge8\), independent of all input parameters, such that preprocessing uses at most \(C(nm/x)(\log_2(L+2))^c\) operations, total stored and query workspace uses at most that many words, and every query takes at most \(Cx\) operations. The constants can absorb the finitely many smallest inputs. No randomness or error is allowed.

context_blocks.text: Hamming distance counts mismatched positions in two equal-length strings. Here the input is a fixed pair of longer strings, but each query chooses its own pair of starting positions and common length. The output is a single exact integer, so the query need not list the mismatches.

For example, with \(A=(1,2,1,3)\) and \(B=(1,3,1,2)\), the query \((0,0,4)\) returns two, while \((1,1,2)\) returns one. The starting positions may differ, and neither interval must be a prefix. Symbols are arbitrary integers in the specified range; their numerical differences have no role.

The parameter \(x\) specifies a family of preprocessing–query compromises for the same task. When \(n=m\), the target includes nearly quadratic preprocessing with constant query time at \(x=1\), and nearly linear preprocessing with linear query time at \(x=n\). Every intermediate value must be handled by the same uniform algorithm.

Boneh and coauthors obtain \(\widetilde O(nm/x)\) preprocessing and \(O(x)\) exact query time for constant alphabets. Their general polynomial-integer-alphabet bound is \(\widetilde O(nm/\sqrt{x})\) preprocessing with the same query time. The card retains the previously selected deterministic question of removing this preprocessing gap.

The paper also gives approximate randomized oracles. Their guarantees allow an error in the reported distance and therefore concern a different output requirement. The present proposition requires exact answers on every query and has no probabilistic success qualification.

The source lower bound assumes a hypothesis about combinatorial matrix multiplication and applies to combinatorial oracles. The target here allows all operations in the stated word RAM. That restricted conditional result therefore does not establish an unconditional optimum or refute the proposed general-alphabet bound.

cards.title: Optimal approximation ratio for shortest common superstring
cards.formal: Determine \(\rho _{\mathrm{SCS}}=\inf\){\(r\ge 1: a\) uniform deterministic polynomial-time algorithm returns a feasible solution of objective value at most \(r\cdot\)OPT on every shortest common superstring instance}, in the input and output model below.
cards.definitions: Symbols are integers from \(\{1,\ldots ,\sigma\}\), encoded in binary; \(\sigma\) and all strings are input. Running time is measured on a deterministic Turing machine in the total bit length of this explicit representation. String length counts symbols. Repeated and empty input strings are allowed. For an empty collection, OPT is zero. The output is an explicit string over the input alphabet, and containment means ordinary forward contiguous occurrence without reversal, reverse complementation or cyclic wraparound. All preprocessing is charged. For each fixed ratio r in the defining set, one finite deterministic algorithm and one time polynomial must work on every instance; both may depend on r. The infimum is over these globally uniform guarantees and need not be attained. There is no per-input-size choice of algorithm, advice or free optimization oracle.

context_blocks.text: The target is the infimum polynomial-time approximation ratio. The factor-two algorithmic question discussed in the saved history selects one threshold in this larger numerical target.
Shortest common superstring formalizes assembly of overlapping sequences. The unresolved factor two is an approximation barrier for the problem itself, regardless of the algorithm used.

An August 2026 preprint gives a \(7/3\) approximation. A separate September preprint claims a counterexample to the factor-two guarantee for maximum-overlap greedy. Even if that claim is correct, it concerns a particular algorithm and does not answer the general existence question here.

cards.why: A long-standing approximation threshold for a basic string-assembly problem with direct algorithmic genomics and compression motivation.
cards.answer_criterion: Supply a specified real number a and prove in Lean that |\(a- \rho _{\mathrm{SCS}}|\le 1/100\). The proof must certify both a lower and an upper bound for the unrestricted quantity in this card. Equivalently, certified bounds \(\ell\)\(\le u\) of width at most \(1/50\) qualify by taking \(a=(\ell +u)/2\). An exact value with proof of equality also qualifies. An unevaluated copy of the defining extremum, a one-sided improvement, or a numerical estimate without a proved error bound does not meet this criterion. The \(1/100\) tolerance is benchmark acceptance; it does not prove an associated exact threshold conjecture. Any hardness assumption must be stated explicitly; a conditional lower bound establishes only its conditional conclusion.

cards.title: Polyloglogarithmic suffix-array access in compact space
cards.formal:
Do there exist two deterministic finite word-RAM programs \(P,Q\), integers \(a,c\ge1\) and \(d\ge8\), and constants \(C,K>0\), such that the following holds simultaneously for every integer \(n\ge2\), every binary string \(T\in\{0,1\}^{n}\), and every rank \(i\in\{0,\ldots,n-1\}\)?
The preprocessing program \(P\), given \(n\) and the packed bits of \(T\), constructs a static index \(I_T\) in at most \(K(n+2)^a\) operations. Given only \(n,i,I_T\), the query program \(Q\) returns the exact value \(\operatorname{SA}_T[i]\) in at most
\[
K\bigl(1+\log_2\log_2(n+2)\bigr)^c
\]
operations. At every point of a query, the index and all query working storage together use at most \(Cn\) bits in the model below. The same programs and constants must work for every input length; all bounds are worst-case.
cards.definitions:
The string \(T\) has positions \(0,\ldots,n-1\). Its nonempty suffix at position \(j\) is \(T[j]T[j+1]\cdots T[n-1]\). Lexicographic order compares the first unequal symbols using \(0<1\); when one string is a proper prefix of the other, the shorter string is smaller. The suffix array \(\operatorname{SA}_T\) is the unique permutation of the positions such that these suffixes, in that order, are lexicographically increasing. There is no empty suffix in the array and no sentinel symbol in the input. A suffix-array query translates a rank into the corresponding starting position. It is not the inverse query that translates a position into its rank.

Use a uniform sequential word RAM with word length \(w=d\lceil\log_2(n+2)\rceil\). The preprocessing input gives \(n\) in one word and the bits of \(T\) packed consecutively into \(\lceil n/w\rceil\) words, with unused final bits zero. The programs have finite code independent of \(n\) and the input, using finitely many fixed integer constants. Word reads, writes, copies, comparisons, branches, bitwise Boolean operations, logical shifts, addition, subtraction and multiplication modulo \(2^w\), and integer quotient and remainder with a nonzero divisor cost one operation each. A shift by at least \(w\) returns zero. Addresses and values fit in words; operations on multiple words pay for their constituent instructions. There are no random operations, nonuniform advice strings, free lookup tables or input-dependent oracles.

The output index is a finite bit string stored in consecutive words with zero padding. Its length and any metadata, pointers, retained text copies, generated tables and other stored information are part of the index-space charge. A query may read the index but cannot change it. Its separate workspace and registers start without information from earlier queries, and all storage used by the query counts toward the same \(Cn\)-bit bound. Word padding counts as stored bits. The externally provided \(n\) and \(i\), and the returned answer, occupy only a constant number of words; they do not contain any other input-dependent information. The original text is unavailable to \(Q\) unless its representation is included in \(I_T\).

All preprocessing operations, including producing tables and writing the index, count toward the polynomial construction bound. Preprocessing can use temporary storage beyond \(Cn\) bits, subject to the word-RAM address space; this temporary storage is discarded and unavailable during queries. All query computation and writing of its answer count toward its time bound. There is no restriction to repetitive texts, a small set of queries or an average over input strings. The exponent \(c\) is a single constant chosen with the programs, not a function of \(n\); the same applies to \(a,d,C,K\).

context_blocks.text: The retained threshold \(O((1+\log\log(n+2))^c)\), binary alphabet and polynomial deterministic preprocessing are editorial specifications of the compact suffix-array frontier. They are not a verbatim question from Thankachan. His September 2026 revision discusses barriers to \(\log^{o(1)}n\) forward-query time; the card selects a particular stronger upper-bound target within that regime.

The 2026 construction paper reports compact suffix-array representations with \(O(n)\) bits and \(O(\log^\varepsilon n)\) query time for each fixed \(\varepsilon>0\), for binary texts. Selecting a smaller fixed \(\varepsilon\) is different from obtaining one fixed power of \(\log\log n\).

The separate August 2026 lower-bound preprint states that deterministic suffix-array structures for binary strings of length at most \(N\), with \(O(N)\) bits and \(\Theta(\log N)\)-bit cells, require \(\Omega(\log\log N/\log\log\log N)\) worst-case probes. This excludes constant time in that model, but remains compatible with the polyloglogarithmic target. The detailed theorem, rather than just its simplified introduction, explicitly specifies determinism.

The companion August 2026 preprint claims \(O(1)\)-time inverse suffix-array queries in \(O(n)\) bits for binary texts. Its forward suffix-array tradeoffs have different space and query-time factors. The inverse-access result does not provide the requested rank-to-position access. These recent preprint statements were checked for scope; their complete proofs were not independently certified in this review.

The June 2020 paper gives a compact text index with sublinear deterministic construction time and pattern-occurrence queries. Construction speed and pattern searching provide relevant history, but are different guarantees from the forward-access threshold fixed here.

Thankachan’s final question in Section 7 concerns reducing auxiliary suffix-tree/array space while retaining polylogarithmic query times. This card does not attribute its particular polyloglogarithmic threshold to that concluding question.

cards.why: A text contains enough information to determine the full suffix order, but explicitly storing every starting position costs an extra logarithmic factor in bits. This question asks whether that factor can be removed while each rank-to-position lookup takes only a fixed polynomial in the double logarithm of the text length.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct Lean proof that the programs and constants specified above exist, or a complete Lean proof of the logical negation of that proposition. An upper bound with superlinear bit space, a result only for inverse suffix-array access, an expected-time bound, or a lower bound that only rules out constant query time does not settle this exact target.
