cards.definitions: An instance has \(n\ge 1\) agents, \(m\ge 0\) indivisible chores, and finite real costs \(c_{i},g\ge 0\). Agent i assigns a bundle \(S\subseteq [m]\) the additive cost \(c_{i}(S)=\sum _{g\in S}c_{i},g\); lower cost is better. Let \(\Pi _{n}([m])\) be the finite set of ordered partitions of \([m]\) into n disjoint bundles, allowing empty bundles. Define \(\mu _{i}=\min _{(\mathrm{P}_{1},\ldots ,\mathrm{P}_{n})\in \Pi _{n}([m])} \max _{1\le j\le n} c_{i}(\mathrm{P}_{j})\). All bundles in this minimum are evaluated using the same agent i’s costs. A complete allocation belongs to \(\Pi _{n}([m])\): each chore has exactly one owner, with no splitting, disposal or payments. The allocation must satisfy all agents’ inequalities simultaneously, although their benchmark partitions can differ. The inequalities also apply when \(\mu _{i}=0\), without dividing by zero; in that case every chore has zero cost to i. There is no computation-time requirement or fixed bound on n or m. The smallest universal factor exists: for each finite instance its feasible factors form a closed upper interval, and the known universal upper bound makes the intersection of these intervals nonempty.
cards.answer_criterion: Supply a specified real number a and prove in Lean that |\(a- \alpha *|\le 1/100\). The proof must certify both a lower and an upper bound for the unrestricted quantity in this card. Equivalently, certified bounds \(\ell\)\(\le u\) of width at most \(1/50\) qualify by taking \(a=(\ell +u)/2\). An exact value with proof of equality also qualifies. An unevaluated copy of the defining extremum, a one-sided improvement, or a numerical estimate without a proved error bound does not meet this criterion. The \(1/100\) tolerance is benchmark acceptance; it does not prove an associated exact threshold conjecture.

context_blocks.title: The burden an agent can guarantee herself
context_blocks.text: Imagine partitioning all chores into n bundles before receiving the most costly bundle. The minimax share is the smallest worst burden that the agent can arrange. With two bundles and chore costs 4, 3 and 3, this benchmark is 6, achieved by {4} and \(\{3,3\}\); the proportional cost is only 5. Indivisibility is why the two benchmarks differ.

context_blocks.title: Exact fairness can fail
context_blocks.text: Different agents can disagree about which chores are difficult, so their individually optimal partitions need not fit together. Feige, Sapir and Tauber give a three-agent, nine-chore example in which every agent’s minimax share is 43 but every complete allocation gives someone cost at least 44. Thus \(\alpha *\ge 44/43>1\).

context_blocks.title: The universal gap
context_blocks.text: Huang and Segal-Halevi prove that factor \(13/11\) always suffices. Together with the negative example, the checked bounds are \(44/43\le \alpha *\le 13/11\), approximately 1.0233 to 1.1818. The upper bound is an existence statement at the exact factor; finding such an allocation within a specified running time is an additional question.

context_blocks.title: What newer guarantees cover
context_blocks.text: The 2025 bin-packing paper gives a \(15/13\) multiplicative guarantee for personalized bivalued costs and improves a different, ordinal MMS benchmark in general. These do not replace the general multiplicative bound here. The September 2026 comparison-query preprint still uses \(13/11\) as the general frontier and studies how little preference information an algorithm needs.

context_blocks.title: Why this optimum matters
context_blocks.text: The factor measures the unavoidable loss caused by allocating whole burdens while respecting everyone’s own costs. A factor closer to 1 means that every agent can be kept closer to her personal benchmark. The easy/difficult-chores source gives exact fairness in special cost models, illustrating why those models must be distinguished from unrestricted additive costs.

cards.title: Optimal universal approximation factor for EFX
cards.area: Algorithmic game theory, mechanism design and fair division
cards.formal:
Determine the universal additive-goods EFX approximation constant
\[\alpha_* = \sup\{\alpha\in[0,1]:\ \forall n\ge1\ \forall m\ge0\ \forall v\in\mathbb R_{\ge0}^{n\times m}\ \exists A\in\mathcal A_{n,m},\ A\text{ is }\alpha\text{-EFX for }v\}.\]
Here \(n,m\) are integers, \(\mathcal A_{n,m}\) is the set of complete allocations of \(m\) goods to \(n\) agents, and \(\alpha\)-EFX uses the positive-good convention defined below. The requested benchmark precision is absolute error at most \(1/100\): supply a real number \(a\) and prove \(|a-\alpha_*|\le1/100\). This is an existence constant with unrestricted allocation computation, not a polynomial-time approximation threshold.
cards.why: This constant measures how much of the demanding EFX fairness comparison can always be guaranteed when all indivisible goods must be assigned. It gives a quantitative target even if exact EFX existence is unresolved. Its scope is every number of agents and every additive valuation profile, so improvements for special structures do not alone determine the universal guarantee.
cards.status_note: The source survey v2, Amanatidis–Markakis–Ntokos v2 Theorem 4.4, the frontier paper v3 dated 29 July 2026, and Filos-Ratsikas–Kalantzis–Wang v1 Section 1.1 and Definition 2.1 were read on 2026-09-14. The checked recent work retains a distinction between unrestricted additive EFX, restricted agent classes, and removal of multiple goods. A bounded search through this date found no determination of the universal constant to the requested tolerance or exact all-agent additive EFX resolution. The source-open status is limited by this literature check, and does not assert independent verification of the cited algorithmic proofs.

Every good must be allocated, and the comparison removes any good that the potentially envious agent values positively.
There is no bound on the number of agents and no computational-time restriction on choosing the allocation.

cards.definitions:
Write \([k]=\{1,\ldots,k\}\) for integers \(k\ge0\), with \([0]=\varnothing\). Each entry \(v_{ig}\) is a finite nonnegative real number giving agent \(i\)'s value for good \(g\). For a bundle \(S\subseteq[m]\), its value is \(v_i(S)=\sum_{g\in S}v_{ig}\). No normalization, strict positivity, integrality, rationality, number-of-types or agreement-on-ordering assumption is imposed on values.

A complete allocation \(A=(A_1,\ldots,A_n)\) is an ordered partition of \([m]\): the bundles are pairwise disjoint and their union is all of \([m]\). Empty bundles are allowed. There are no payments, negative-valued chores, fractional goods, discarded goods or additional efficiency constraints.

For \(\alpha\in[0,1]\), the allocation is \(\alpha\)-EFX if
\[\forall i,j\in[n]\ \forall g\in A_j:\quad v_{ig}>0\ \Longrightarrow\ v_i(A_i)\ge\alpha\,v_i(A_j\setminus\{g\}).\]
Both the test of whether the removed good has positive value and the bundle comparison use the potentially envious agent \(i\)'s values. If every good of \(A_j\) has value zero to \(i\), there is no constraint for that pair. If the remaining bundle has value zero, the inequality is automatically satisfied. This is Definition 6 of the source survey. The stronger per-allocation convention often called EFX-zero tests also removed goods of zero value; the card does not silently substitute that convention.

The universally feasible set in the supremum is nonempty, because it includes zero, and is bounded above by one by definition. The constant is dimensionless. Its quantifier order allows a different allocation for each valuation matrix; no single common partition must serve all profiles. Neither an efficient algorithm nor any oracle-access restriction is part of the existence guarantee.

For a fixed finite instance \(v\), one can equivalently define \(\beta(v)\) as the largest \(\alpha\in[0,1]\) for which some complete allocation is \(\alpha\)-EFX. This maximum exists: there are finitely many allocations, and each has a closed interval of feasible factors. Then \(\alpha_*\) is the infimum of these \(\beta(v)\) over all permitted instance sizes and profiles. There need not be one instance attaining this infimum. This equivalent definition makes the universal lower-bound and worst-instance upper-bound meanings explicit.

Exact equality \(\alpha_*=1\) is equivalent to existence of a complete EFX allocation for every additive instance: for each fixed instance, finitely many allocations and closed inequalities prevent loss of the endpoint. A numerical answer within \(1/100\) need not decide that exact equality. The present acceptance tolerance measures the numerical constant and does not relax the definition of \(\alpha\)-EFX itself.
cards.answer_criterion: Supply a specified real number \(a\) and a complete mathematically correct Lean-checked proof that \(|a-\alpha_*|\le1/100\). A certified interval of width at most \(1/50\) containing \(\alpha_*\) qualifies via its midpoint; an exact value also qualifies. Bounds must concern all finite nonnegative additive instances and complete allocations under the stated positive-good convention. A universal construction proves only a lower bound on the constant unless accompanied by sufficient upper information. An upper bound may be established without a worst instance attaining the infimum. Restricted numbers of agents, partial allocations, nonadditive counterexamples, or guarantees allowing removal of multiple goods do not by themselves determine this constant. A simulation or an unproved decimal estimate is insufficient.

context_blocks.text: Open Problem 3 asks for the best factor guaranteeing existence. The survey separately asks about efficient computation, and this card retains the existence interpretation. The related exact EFX card asks whether the endpoint one is universally attainable.

Amanatidis, Markakis and Ntokos prove a universal factor \((\sqrt5-1)/2\), approximately \(0.618\), in Theorem 4.4. Their definition tests every removed good, including zero-valued goods, so their guarantee also implies the positive-good condition here. This supplies a lower bound on \(\alpha_*\), not its proved optimal value.

The EC 2024 work establishes \(2/3\)-EFX under restrictions including at most seven agents or at most three common value levels. Its July 2026 revision still identifies the golden-ratio bound as the general all-agent additive guarantee. Those restricted \(2/3\) theorems do not establish \(\alpha_*\ge2/3\).

The May 2026 paper extends the \(2/3\)-EFX guarantee to eight agents. It also gives all-agent results for EFkX with \(k\ge2\), where the comparison permits removing a set of \(k\) goods; it expressly states that this general theorem does not apply when \(k=1\). These are distinct from the universal single-good constant.
The numerical tolerance belongs to benchmark acceptance. It allows a certified approximation of the constant without claiming that the exact EFX existence question has been decided.

cards.context:
Open Problem 3 asks for the best factor guaranteeing existence. The survey separately asks about efficient computation, and this card retains the existence interpretation. The related exact EFX card asks whether the endpoint one is universally attainable.

Amanatidis, Markakis and Ntokos prove a universal factor \((\sqrt5-1)/2\), approximately \(0.618\), in Theorem 4.4. Their definition tests every removed good, including zero-valued goods, so their guarantee also implies the positive-good condition here. This supplies a lower bound on \(\alpha_*\), not its proved optimal value.

The EC 2024 work establishes \(2/3\)-EFX under restrictions including at most seven agents or at most three common value levels. Its July 2026 revision still identifies the golden-ratio bound as the general all-agent additive guarantee. Those restricted \(2/3\) theorems do not establish \(\alpha_*\ge2/3\).

The May 2026 paper extends the \(2/3\)-EFX guarantee to eight agents. It also gives all-agent results for EFkX with \(k\ge2\), where the comparison permits removing a set of \(k\) goods; it expressly states that this general theorem does not apply when \(k=1\). These are distinct from the universal single-good constant.

The numerical tolerance belongs to benchmark acceptance. It allows a certified approximation of the constant without claiming that the exact EFX existence question has been decided.

cards.definitions: The cake is \([0,1]\). Each of n agents has a nonatomic Borel probability measure \(\mu _{i}\): values are nonnegative and countably additive, \(\mu _{i}([0,1])=1\), and every point has value zero. A bundle is a finite union of intervals. Its value need not equal its length. The protocol accesses valuations only by exact Robertson–Webb queries: \(Eval(i,x,y)\) returns \(\mu _{i}([x,y]); Cut(i,x,a)\), for \(0\le a\le \mu _{i}([x,1])\), returns \(y\ge x\) with \(\mu _{i}([x,y])=a\). Query endpoints are 0, 1 and earlier cut marks; additivity allows combining known interval values. If a cut has multiple valid answers, correctness must hold for every answer. Finite exact computation on the transcript is allowed without a bit-time bound. The output uses known marks as endpoints. Endpoints themselves may be assigned arbitrarily because they have value zero. Envy-freeness means \(\mu _{i}(A_{i})\ge \mu _{i}(A_{j})\) for every ordered pair i,j. Proportionality means \(\mu _{i}(A_{i})\ge 1/n\) for every i, measured against the whole original cake. There is no approximation, randomness, density bound or promise that agents agree. In this question each \(A_{i}\) must be one interval, up to ownership of its endpoints. The intervals may have gaps between them, and the residue \([0,1]\setminus \bigcup _{i}A_{i}\) may be discarded. Envy is compared with other agents’ assigned intervals, not with the residue. Count every Eval and Cut call as one query. The bound \(B_{n}\) depends only on the fixed n and its protocol, never on the valuation profile or oracle responses. The statement permits a separate finite protocol for each n; it does not require \(B_{n}\) to be polynomial, and does not add an algorithm that generates all \(\mathrm{P}_{n}\).
cards.answer_criterion: Prove the existence of such a bounded protocol for every fixed \(n\ge 4\), or prove that for at least one fixed \(n\ge 4\) no deterministic protocol and finite bound satisfy the stated guarantees. Existence of a suitable division alone, a procedure that merely converges to one, approximate proportionality, or allowing an agent several intervals does not meet this target.

context_blocks.title: Fairness with one usable piece
context_blocks.text: A connected share is a single interval, as in a continuous appointment slot or one tract of land. Envy-freeness says each person prefers her own assigned interval to anyone else’s. Proportionality additionally protects the amount she receives: at least one n-th of her value for the whole resource.

context_blocks.title: Why disposal changes the question
context_blocks.text: With disposal, giving everyone nothing is envy-free. For example, agents with identical uniform values can each receive an interval of length \(1/(2n)\), leaving half the cake unused; none envies another, but all receive less than their proportional share. The exact \(1/n\) requirement excludes such wasteful outcomes.

context_blocks.title: The connected impossibility has a specific scope
context_blocks.text: Stromquist proves that no finite protocol can always allocate the entire cake envy-freely with one interval per agent once \(n\ge 3\). This assumes complete allocation. Allowing residue is the change studied here, so that theorem does not refute this question.

context_blocks.title: Known partial-allocation guarantees
context_blocks.text: Waste Makes Haste gives a bounded connected envy-free proportional protocol for three agents in its density model. For four agents its connected guarantee is \(1/7\) instead of the required \(1/4\). Aziz and Mackenzie give a bounded connected partial allocation with a \(1/(3n)\) value guarantee in general. These results motivate the question but do not supply exact proportionality for all \(n\ge 4\).

context_blocks.title: Later progress allows fragmented shares
context_blocks.text: The September 2026 Ye–Bai preprint reports a single-exponential query bound for complete envy-free allocation. Complete envy-freeness implies proportionality, but the output may contain multiple intervals per agent. It therefore does not answer this connected-piece question.

sentences: The cake is a divisible interval valued differently by each agent.

Unallocated cake is allowed, but it cannot reduce that proportionality guarantee.
Known connected partial protocols provide weaker guarantees for larger numbers of agents, while recent complete protocols allow fragmented shares.
The question is whether a fixed finite query bound can achieve all the requested properties for every fixed \(n\ge 4\).

cards.title: Universal maximin-share approximation for additive goods
cards.area: Algorithmic game theory, mechanism design and fair division
cards.formal: Determine the universal maximin-share approximation constant for additive indivisible goods, \[\alpha_{\mathrm{MMS}}=\sup\bigl\{\alpha\in[0,1]:\ \forall n\ge1\ \forall m\ge0\ \forall v\in\mathbb R_{\ge0}^{n\times m}\ \exists(A_1,\ldots,A_n)\in\Pi_n([m])\ \forall i\in[n],\ v_i(A_i)\ge\alpha\,\mu_i(v)\bigr\}.\] Here \(n,m\) range over integers, \(v_i(S)=\sum_{g\in S}v_{ig}\), and \(\mu_i(v)=\max_{(P_1,\ldots,P_n)\in\Pi_n([m])}\min_{j\in[n]}v_i(P_j)\). The benchmark asks for this one dimensionless constant with absolute error at most \(1/100\), together with a complete Lean-checked proof of the error bound.
cards.why: Maximin share gives each agent a fairness benchmark determined by their own values, independent of how the other agents evaluate the goods. These personal guarantees can conflict when objects are indivisible. The universal constant measures the unavoidable loss from satisfying all agents simultaneously, separating a limitation of fairness itself from a limitation of available algorithms. It is a central quantitative threshold for additive fair division, with significance across instances and arbitrary numbers of participants.
cards.status_note: The January 2026 source explicitly poses this constant. Checked primary statements through 14 September 2026 give the published upper bound 39/40 and a revised-preprint lower-bound claim of 7/9, still far apart at benchmark precision. The 7 September 2026 revision reports a corrected bug; this review verifies its stated scope, not every step of its proof. No matching determination was found in the bounded search.

progress.text: Feige, Sapir and Tauber, Theorem 1, prove the universal upper bound \(\alpha_{\mathrm{MMS}}\le39/40\) using three agents and nine goods. Their Theorem 3 is tight only within that restricted instance size.

Heidari et al., Theorem 3.1, establish the \(10/13\) additive-goods guarantee. This is the value stated in their own manuscript, rather than the \(7/9\) value grouped with the citation on the problem-list page.
The TCS Open Problems entry asks for the best universal maximin-share approximation and links the additive-goods literature.

Huang and Zhou’s arXiv version 2 states a \(7/9\) guarantee through Theorem 3.1 and the general-instance correspondence in Lemma 2.4; Theorem 10.4 concerns \((7/9-\varepsilon)\)-MMS computation. The revision notice reports a corrected bug. The claimed interval still does not determine the benchmark constant within \(1/100\).

sentences: Each agent’s maximin share is the best value they can secure by partitioning the goods and receiving a least-valued bundle.
The target is the largest fraction of those personal shares that can always be met simultaneously for nonnegative additive valuations.
It ranges over all finite numbers of agents and indivisible goods, with equal entitlements and no sharing.
Determining this constant would quantify the inherent loss of fairness caused by indivisibility, independently of computational efficiency.
The card requires a Lean-certified absolute error of at most one hundredth and records the precise versions and limits of the known bounds.

cards.definitions: Write \([m]=\{1,\ldots,m\}\), with \([0]=\varnothing\). The set \(\Pi_n([m])\) consists of ordered \(n\)-tuples of pairwise disjoint subsets whose union is all of \([m]\); empty bundles are allowed. Each item belongs to exactly one agent, with no splitting, sharing, disposal, payments or externalities. Each entry \(v_{ig}\) is an arbitrary finite nonnegative real value, and values of bundles are additive. Every agent has the same entitlement; the number of agents determining each maximin share is the original \(n\). The partition maximizing \(\mu_i(v)\) is chosen separately for each agent using that agent’s valuations. Its maximum exists because there are finitely many partitions. If \(\mu_i(v)=0\), the corresponding approximation requirement is simply \(v_i(A_i)\ge0\); no ratio with a zero denominator is taken. Valuations need not be identical, normalized, strictly positive or drawn from a finite value set. The allocation may depend on the entire instance. No runtime bound, incentive condition, randomness model or finite encoding of the real entries is imposed, because the target concerns mathematical existence rather than efficient computation. The supremum is well-defined in \([0,1]\), since the feasible set contains zero. The question covers all finite agent and item counts simultaneously, rather than the best guarantee for any one fixed \(n\).
cards.answer_criterion: Supply a real number \(a\), or an unambiguous mathematical specification of one, and a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean that \(|a-\alpha_{\mathrm{MMS}}|\le1/100\), using exactly the universal domain and maximin-share definition above. A proved interval \([L,U]\) containing \(\alpha_{\mathrm{MMS}}\) with \(U-L\le1/50\) qualifies via its midpoint. One-sided guarantees, counterexamples without a matching sufficiently close lower bound, empirical searches, or results only for a fixed number of agents do not meet the criterion. Determination of the exact supremum is welcome but not required; the submitted approximation need not itself be a universally attainable allocation ratio. The existing gap between \(7/9\) and \(39/40\) is wider than the permitted interval.

context_blocks.text: An agent can imagine partitioning the goods into as many bundles as there are participants and then receiving a least-valued bundle. Optimizing that personal partition defines the maximin share. Actual allocation must respect all agents at once, although their best partitions and their rankings of the goods can be different.

The source asks for the best universal approximation and points to results for additive goods. Those linked papers fix the intended valuation class and distinguish it from chores or more general set valuations. The card makes this source-supported interpretation explicit and retains an existence target, without adding a demand for an efficient allocation algorithm.

Feige, Sapir and Tauber give a three-agent, nine-good instance in which every allocation leaves someone with at most \(39/40\) of their maximin share. This bounds the universal constant from above even though its definition includes arbitrarily large instances. Their tight result for that particular pair of agent and item counts is not a tight universal guarantee.

Heidari, Kaviani, Seddighin and Shahrezaei prove a \(10/13\) guarantee. Huang and Zhou’s revised September 2026 manuscript states a \(7/9\) existence guarantee and a fully polynomial approximation scheme for slightly smaller ratios. These are distinct results: the problem-list entry groups their citations under \(7/9\), but the Heidari et al. paper itself states \(10/13\).

The Huang–Zhou revision explicitly reports correction of a bug and substantial rewriting of the proof. Its version and theorem scope are recorded here, without certifying the full proof independently. Computational approximation schemes and stronger results under restrictions on the number of agents remain different from determining the unrestricted existence constant.

cards.title: EF1 and Pareto optimality for additive mixed items
cards.area: Algorithmic game theory, mechanism design and fair division
cards.formal: Does every finite instance of indivisible mixed-item allocation with \(n\ge3\) agents and arbitrary real additive utilities admit a complete allocation that is both envy-free up to one item (EF1) and Pareto optimal (PO)? The item removed to eliminate an agent’s envy may come from the envied bundle or from the envious agent’s own bundle, with at most one item removed in total.
cards.why: Fairness and efficiency can conflict when an indivisible item benefits one participant and burdens another. This question asks whether one standard minimal relaxation of envy is always compatible with the absence of a Pareto improvement. Resolving it would determine whether a central fairness–efficiency guarantee survives unrestricted mixed valuations beyond the now-understood pure-goods and pure-chores existence settings.
cards.status_note: The January 2026 Barman–Verma revision explicitly leaves standard EF1 together with PO open for unrestricted additive mixed manna. The checked September 2026 weighted-fairness results and November 2025 pure-chores theorem do not settle this target. The search through 2026-09-15 was bounded and does not certify that no later resolution exists.

progress.text: The survey’s Open Question 2 asks whether EF1 and PO allocations always exist for additive mixed items and at least three agents.
Mahara’s revised preprint states general additive-chores existence in Theorems 1.1–1.2, including the stronger fractional Pareto requirement. These theorems concern the pure-chores subcase.
Barman and Verma’s v3 establishes introspective EF1 with PO for mixed manna while explicitly identifying standard EF1 with PO as open.
Teh’s v2 gives weighted EF1 existence for arbitrary mixed additive values and separate efficiency results under restricted magnitudes; the checked results do not close the general joint guarantee.

sentences: Each participant may value an indivisible item positively, negatively or at zero.
Every item must be assigned, and the participants have additive utilities and equal entitlements.
EF1 permits eliminating each envy comparison by removing at most one item from one of the two bundles.
The question is whether an allocation with this fairness guarantee can always also be Pareto optimal for at least three agents.
Recent results settle pure chores and some alternative mixed-item fairness guarantees, but the checked 2026 sources do not resolve the unrestricted combination.

cards.definitions: The agents are \([n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}\), and the items are \([m]\) for any integer \(m\ge0\). Each agent \(i\) has values \(v_{i,g}\in\mathbb R\), with no restrictions on their signs or magnitudes, and \(u_i(S)=\sum_{g\in S}v_{i,g}\) for every \(S\subseteq[m]\). The same item may have positive, zero or negative value to different agents. Agents have equal entitlements; no normalization of utility totals is imposed. An allocation \(A=(A_1,\ldots,A_n)\) is a partition of all items into pairwise disjoint bundles, which may be empty. Every item must be assigned exactly once. No disposal, monetary transfers or fractional assignment is permitted. Allocation \(A\) is EF1 if for every ordered pair of distinct agents \(i,j\), at least one of the following holds: \(u_i(A_i)\ge u_i(A_j)\); there exists \(g\in A_j\) such that \(u_i(A_i)\ge u_i(A_j\setminus\{g\})\); or there exists \(g\in A_i\) such that \(u_i(A_i\setminus\{g\})\ge u_i(A_j)\). These alternatives remove at most one item from one of the two bundles for this comparison only; they do not change the allocation. In particular, removing one item from each bundle is not allowed. Allocation \(A\) is PO if no other complete integral allocation \(B\) satisfies \(u_i(B_i)\ge u_i(A_i)\) for every \(i\) and \(u_j(B_j)>u_j(A_j)\) for at least one \(j\). The quantifiers are \(\forall n\ge3\;\forall m\ge0\;\forall v\in\mathbb R^{n\times m}\;\exists A\), with both properties required of the same \(A\). The target is existence; there is no polynomial-time computation or representation requirement for an allocation-selection rule.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct Lean-checked proof of the universal existence statement, or a complete Lean-checked refutation. A refutation may specify a finite real-valued instance and prove that none of its complete integral allocations satisfies both defined properties. An existence theorem confined to pure goods, pure chores, two agents, restricted value magnitudes or a different envy relaxation does not prove the general statement. A computation-time bound is not additionally required.

context_blocks.text: Open Question 2 of the August 2024 survey asks for existence of an EF1 and PO allocation for at least three agents with additive utilities. Its subsequent question about polynomial-time computation is a separate issue. This card selects the stated existence question and uses the survey’s mixed-item EF1 convention.

The survey defines mixed-item EF1 by allowing deletion of at most one item either from the envied bundle or from the envious agent’s own bundle. All utility comparisons use the envious agent’s valuation. For purely nonnegative values the useful deletion is from the other bundle; for purely nonpositive values it is from the agent’s own bundle.

Mahara’s November 2025 revision establishes EF1 together with PO, and also fractional PO, for arbitrary additive chores. Consequently, the survey’s 2024 observation that even the chores case was unresolved is no longer an appropriate current-status description.

Barman and Verma’s January 2026 revision explicitly retains the general mixed-manna EF1-and-PO question. It proves PO together with introspective EF1, a different condition that modifies an agent’s own bundle. That result does not assert standard mixed-item EF1 together with PO.

Teh’s September 2026 revision establishes complete weighted EF1 existence for unrestricted additive mixed manna. Its joint fractional-efficiency guarantee applies to restricted value magnitudes, so the results checked there do not establish the unrestricted EF1-and-PO statement.

cards.title: EF1 existence for arbitrary mixed-item utilities
cards.area: Algorithmic game theory, mechanism design and fair division
cards.formal: For every integer \(n\ge 3\), every finite item set M and every profile of utility functions \(u_{i}:2^{M}\to \mathbb{R}\) with \(u_{i}(\varnothing )=0\), does there exist a complete allocation \(A=(A_{1},\ldots ,A_{n})\) such that for every ordered pair of agents i,j there is a set \(X\subseteq A_{i}\cup A_{j}\) with |\(X|\le 1\) satisfying \(u_{i}(A_{i}\setminus X)\ge u_{i}(A_{j}\setminus X)\)?
cards.why: Tests whether one-item envy relief remains possible when item values have unrestricted interactions and may change sign across bundles. A positive answer would extend a basic fairness guarantee far beyond additive goods and chores; a negative answer would identify a limit of that guarantee itself.
cards.status_note: Survey v4 question and definitions checked, with subsequent-work searches through 11 September 2026. No resolution of the general EF1 existence question was located; no exhaustive literature or independent proof audit is claimed.

cards.definitions: The n agents are indexed by \(\{1,\ldots ,n\}\). Each utility is an arbitrary real-valued function on all subsets of the finite set M, normalized only at the empty set; no additivity, monotonicity, submodularity, common ranking or identical-utilities assumption is imposed. A complete allocation is an ordered partition of M into n pairwise disjoint bundles, with empty bundles allowed. An agent i envies j when \(u_{i}(A_{i})<u_{i}(A_{j})\). The displayed condition is envy-freeness up to one item \((\mathrm{EF}1)\) for mixed items. If there is no envy, \(X=\varnothing\) works. Otherwise one may hypothetically remove one item from i’s bundle or one item from j’s bundle, and compare both remaining bundles using i’s utility. Removing one item from both bundles simultaneously is not permitted. The choice of X may depend on i,j and the whole allocation. These removals only define the fairness comparison; no item is discarded or transferred from the complete allocation. Items have no required permanent designation as goods or chores, since an item’s marginal utility may depend on the surrounding bundle. The question concerns existence and imposes no input encoding, value-query bound or running-time requirement.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove EF1 existence for every \(n\ge 3\) and every normalized arbitrary utility profile on a finite item set, or give a finite profile and prove that every complete allocation violates the displayed inequality for some ordered pair, for every allowed one-item removal. An impossibility result for a stronger fairness notion does not refute EF1, and an existence theorem permitting two removed items does not establish it.

context_blocks.title: Why either bundle can supply the removed item
context_blocks.text: With desirable goods, envy can disappear after ignoring a valuable item held by someone else. With burdens, it can disappear after ignoring a costly item in the envious agent’s own bundle. For example, if i values her bundle at −4 and j’s at 2, and deleting one item from her own bundle raises its value to 2, that comparison satisfies EF1.

context_blocks.title: One item can change character
context_blocks.text: An arbitrary utility can satisfy \(u(\{a\})=u(\{b\})=1\) but \(u(\{a,b\})=- 3\). Each item is beneficial when received alone and harmful when added to the other. This is allowed by the question, so a fixed classification of every item as a good or chore would restrict the model.

context_blocks.title: What was known in the survey
context_blocks.text: The survey records EF1 existence for two agents with arbitrary utilities and for any number of agents under additive or doubly-monotonic utilities. Doubly-monotonic means that, for each agent, every item has a fixed nonnegative or nonpositive marginal effect in every bundle. Open Question 1 removes that restriction for three or more agents.

context_blocks.title: One removal versus two
context_blocks.text: The AAAI 2026 paper proves related existence statements for a relaxation allowing one removal from each compared bundle, for nonnegative or nonpositive valuations. That may remove two items in a comparison. The present target allows at most one item in total and permits arbitrary real utility values.

cards.title: Polynomial-time mixed equilibria in coordination polymatrix games
cards.area: Algorithmic game theory, mechanism design and fair division
cards.formal: Is there a uniform deterministic algorithm that, for every finite rational coordination-only polymatrix game, outputs an exact mixed Nash equilibrium in time polynomial in the complete binary input length?
cards.why: Locate the tractability boundary for exact mixed equilibrium when every pairwise interaction has common payoffs, distinguishing the complexity of network coordination from general games and from pure local-search equilibria.
cards.status_note: The exact coordination-only tractability question is open in the checked primary sources. A bounded later-work search on 14 September 2026 found no matching resolution. Pure-equilibrium hardness and the 2025 two-team result concern different tasks; they are not treated as a refutation or an unconditional lower bound for this proposition.

progress.text: Cai–Daskalakis establish pure-equilibrium PLS-completeness and mixed-equilibrium membership in PLS and PPAD, leaving polynomial-time mixed-equilibrium tractability open.
Savani poses the coordination-only mixed-equilibrium complexity question in the Dagstuhl report.
The two-team hardness result allows zero-sum interactions between teams and hence does not settle this coordination-only restriction.

sentences: Each player uses one action across several pairwise interactions in a graph.
The two endpoints of each edge receive equal payoffs from that interaction.
The target is a deterministic polynomial-time algorithm returning any exact mixed Nash equilibrium.
Pure equilibria are permitted outputs, but an algorithm may also use genuinely mixed profiles.
Known pure-equilibrium and adversarial two-team hardness results do not settle this coordination-only mixed search task.

cards.definitions: An instance is a finite simple undirected graph \(G=(V,E)\), with \(V=\{1,\ldots,r\}\), and for each player \(i\) a nonempty explicitly enumerated action set \(A_i=\{1,\ldots,k_i\}\). Each edge \(\{i,j\}\), with \(i<j\), carries an explicitly listed matrix \(M_{ij}\in\mathbb Q^{k_i\times k_j}\). If its endpoints choose \(a\in A_i\) and \(b\in A_j\), both receive the same edge payoff \(M_{ij}(a,b)\). Set \(M_{ji}(b,a)=M_{ij}(a,b)\) for reverse orientation. Each player selects one action for all its incident edges and receives the sum of those edge payoffs; nonedges contribute zero. A mixed profile \(p=(p_i)_{i\in V}\) uses independent probability vectors \(p_i\) on \(A_i\). For a pure deviation \(a\in A_i\), write \[v_i(a,p_{-i})=\sum_{j:\{i,j\}\in E}\sum_{b\in A_j}p_j(b)M_{ij}(a,b),\qquad u_i(p)=\sum_{a\in A_i}p_i(a)v_i(a,p_{-i}).\] It is an exact Nash equilibrium when \(v_i(a,p_{-i})\le u_i(p)\) for every player \(i\) and every action \(a\). The required output explicitly lists nonnegative rational probabilities summing to one for each player. A pure profile is allowed as a degenerate mixed profile; neither full support nor a genuinely randomizing player is required. Vertices, edges and all actions are listed, and each payoff is encoded by a signed binary numerator and positive binary denominator with delimiters. Thus the input length \(N\) includes the action lists, graph and every payoff bit; no succinct payoff circuit is allowed. Use a uniform deterministic multitape Turing machine with a fixed finite program, no advice or oracles, and a bound \(C(N+1)^d\) on all valid inputs for constants \(C,d\) independent of the instance. Charge every bit operation and output bit. The target is exact equilibrium, with no approximation parameter or promise on payoff magnitudes, graph degree or action counts.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of the existence of the stated uniform polynomial-time algorithm, including termination, the full bit bound and exact equilibrium correctness, or of its logical negation. A hardness reduction under an unproved separation establishes only a conditional conclusion. A polynomial bound in numerical payoff magnitudes, a fixed graph or action-count special case, or an approximate-equilibrium algorithm without an exact guarantee does not meet the target.

context_blocks.text: Coordination is imposed locally: the two endpoints agree on the payoff of their shared interaction. A player with several neighbors must nevertheless choose one action that participates in all those interactions. Equal payoffs on each edge therefore do not mean that every player has the same total payoff on every full profile.

For example, on a three-vertex path, the middle player receives the sum from both edges, while each endpoint receives only its single edge payoff. The middle player can face conflicting preferences from its two interactions even though each separate interaction gives identical rewards to its two participants.

The 2014 Dagstuhl report attributes the network-coordination question to Rahul Savani and explicitly imposes equality in each edge’s payoff pair. The present card makes polynomial-time tractability the binary target of that broader complexity question; Cai and Daskalakis already explicitly ask whether this search problem is in P.

Cai and Daskalakis show that finding a pure equilibrium is complete for polynomial local search, abbreviated PLS, while finding any mixed equilibrium belongs to both PLS and the parity-based total-search class PPAD. Permitting mixed output changes the search task even though pure equilibria exist: hardness of finding a pure equilibrium alone does not classify the task that may return any mixed one.

The same primary source records that rational polymatrix games have mixed equilibria with rational probabilities and polynomial description length. Exact output is consequently meaningful in the bit model and is not obstructed by a need to print arbitrary irrational numbers.

Hollender, Maystre and Nagarajan prove hardness for two-team polymatrix games with coordination inside teams and zero-sum interactions between teams. Their result allows adversarial edges absent from this card, and therefore does not classify coordination-only games. Likewise, an equilibrium constrained to be symmetric is a different output requirement.

The question tests whether permitting players to randomize makes arbitrary networks of local common-interest interactions computationally tractable. The input restriction and the freedom to return any equilibrium both matter; neither general-game hardness nor the ease of a single two-player coordination game settles this network case.

cards.definitions: The input explicitly lists vertices \(V=[n]\), \(n\ge0\), distinct nonempty hyperedges \(E=\{e_1,\ldots,e_m\}\subseteq2^V\), and, for each vertex, a permutation of its incident edge indices from most to least preferred. Vertex and edge indices are binary encoded with ordinary length-delimited list syntax; the input length \(L\) counts every listed vertex, incidence and preference entry. The incidence matrix is \(A_{v,j}=1\) for \(v\in e_j\) and zero otherwise. The promise is total unimodularity: every square submatrix has determinant in \(\{-1,0,1\}\). A matching \(M\subseteq E\) consists of pairwise disjoint edges. Every vertex prefers any incident edge to remaining unmatched. An edge \(e\notin M\) blocks \(M\) if every \(v\in e\) is unmatched or strictly prefers \(e\) to the unique edge of \(M\) containing \(v\). Stability means no edge blocks. There are no ties, capacities above one, edge-size bounds or optimization objective. Use one deterministic multitape Turing machine, without advice, randomness or an oracle, running within \(C(L+1)^k\) steps for fixed \(C>0\) and integer \(k\ge1\) on every input string. It must return a list of edge indices forming a stable matching on every well-formed promised instance; its answer outside that promise is unrestricted.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof of a uniform polynomial-time algorithm satisfying the stated search specification on all promised instances, or prove in Lean that no such algorithm exists. A conditional complexity lower bound establishes only its conditional conclusion. Fractional existence, finding a stable solution in a proper subclass, and optimizing the weight of a stable solution are distinct targets.

context_blocks.title: Coalitions rather than pairs
context_blocks.text: A hyperedge represents a group that could cooperate. Selected groups cannot share members. Stability forbids an unselected group whose members would all prefer forming it to their current situation. The input includes each participant’s ranking, so merely finding disjoint groups is insufficient.

context_blocks.title: Existence and computation
context_blocks.text: The source explains why total unimodularity together with a classical stable-fractional existence theorem guarantees an integral stable matching. It does not give a general polynomial running-time bound. Hardness of maximizing weight among stable matchings is a different question from finding any stable one.

context_blocks.title: A newer special-case result
context_blocks.text: An August 2026 preprint gives a polynomial-time algorithm for network hypergraphs. In that class the ground elements are arcs of an oriented tree and each hyperedge is a directed tree path. Network hypergraphs are a subclass of unimodular hypergraphs, so this narrows the open frontier without resolving the general target.

Without a structural promise, stability can fail even for groups of size two. On three vertices with possible pairs ab, bc and ca, let a prefer ab to ca, b prefer bc to ab, and c prefer ca to bc. Every chosen pair is blocked by another pair, and the empty matching is blocked as well. The incidence matrix of this triangle has a square determinant of magnitude two, so it is outside the totally unimodular domain.

The objective is to return any stable matching. Different vertices may favor different stable outcomes, but the card imposes no social-welfare, maximum-cardinality, or weighted objective. This distinction matters because optimizing over stable outcomes can be hard even in a class where finding one outcome is efficient.

references.authors: Bouyer, Patricia; Markey, Nicolas; Stan, Daniel

cards.definitions:
A game has a finite nonempty state set \(S\), a specified initial state \(s_0\), and two players \(i\in\{1,2\}\). At each state \(s\), player \(i\) has a finite nonempty action set \(A_i(s)\). Both players choose actions simultaneously. A deterministic transition function maps \((s,a_1,a_2)\) to the next state. There is no additional random transition mechanism.

Terminal states are absorbing: every legal action pair leaves their state unchanged. Each terminal state \(f\) has a fixed finite real reward \(r_i(f)\geq0\) for each player. A play that first reaches \(f\) gives player \(i\) the one-time payoff \(r_i(f)\). A play that never reaches a terminal state gives zero. There are no intermediate rewards, discounting or repeated payments after absorption. No promise of almost-sure termination is imposed.

A strategy \(\sigma_i\) assigns a probability distribution on \(A_i(s_t)\) to every finite visited-state history \(s_0s_1\cdots s_t\). At each round, actions are drawn independently for the two players according to these distributions. The strategy has access to state history, not the history of either player's chosen actions. This is the source's action-insensitive behavioral model, called “mixed strategies” there. It permits arbitrary history dependence and real probabilities; neither finite memory nor computability is required.

The transition rule and strategies induce a probability distribution on infinite plays. Let \(u_i(\sigma_1,\sigma_2;s_0)\) be the expected one-time payoff, including zero on nontermination. Rewards are bounded because the game is finite, so this expectation is well defined. A profile is an exact Nash equilibrium from \(s_0\) if
\[
u_i(\tau_i,\sigma_{-i};s_0)\leq u_i(\sigma_i,\sigma_{-i};s_0)
\]
for both players and every alternative strategy \(\tau_i\) in the same state-history model. The other player's strategy stays fixed.

The question quantifies over every such finite game and initial state. It asks for an equilibrium against all permitted deviations, not merely stationary deviations, and does not require an equilibrium after every possible history as subgame perfection would. No payoff threshold, welfare guarantee or algorithm for constructing the profile is part of the target. Positive scaling of a player's rewards preserves the question, but adding a constant only at terminals need not: infinite plays still receive zero.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove that an exact equilibrium exists for every game and initial state in the specified two-player, nonnegative, state-history model, or give a finite game in that model and prove that no permitted strategy profile is an exact equilibrium from its initial state. A failure of stationary or finite-memory equilibria alone is insufficient. Approximate equilibria and equilibria under imprecise deviations do not meet the exact criterion.

cards.title: Matrix multiplication exponent
cards.formal: Determine, with the absolute \(1/100\) acceptance precision below, the matrix multiplication exponent \(\omega=\inf\{\tau\in\mathbb R:\exists C>0\ \forall n\in\mathbb N,\ n\ge2\Rightarrow s(n)\le Cn^\tau\}\). Here s(n) is the minimum number of arithmetic gates in a circuit computing all entries of the product of two arbitrary n by n complex matrices exactly, in the model below.
cards.definitions: For each integer \(n\ge2\), the inputs are the \(2n^2\) independent complex variables \(a_{ij},b_{ij}\), with \(1\le i,j\le n\). The required n squared outputs are the polynomials \(c_{ij}=\sum_{t=1}^n a_{it}b_{tj}\). A circuit is a finite directed acyclic graph whose source nodes are input variables or constants from \(\mathbb C\), and whose other nodes have two ordered inputs and apply addition, subtraction or multiplication. Multiple uses of a previously computed value are allowed. Each ordered output position (i,j) designates a node whose polynomial is exactly c_ij, so one circuit must be correct on every pair of complex matrices. Circuit topology and constants may depend on n, but not on the matrix entries. Size is the number of arithmetic gates, including gates operating on constants; source nodes and output designations have zero cost. No division, comparison, branching, randomness, approximation or test of the input values is permitted. This is a nonuniform algebraic model: a separate finite circuit may be chosen for each n, with no required algorithm generating the circuits or their constants. Scalar arithmetic is exact, and costs of representing complex numbers in bits are outside the model. The number of gates differs only by a constant factor from the source’s binary-circuit wire measure, and allowing an explicit subtraction gate also changes size by at most a constant factor; neither changes the exponent. Define s(n) as the least size among correct circuits. This minimum exists because the elementary multiplication formula gives a circuit, and sizes are nonnegative integers. The n squared output polynomials are distinct and none is a source polynomial, so each needs a distinct arithmetic gate and \(s(n)\ge n^2\). The elementary upper bound \(s(n)\le2n^3\) makes the exponent set nonempty and gives \(2\le\omega\le3\). The infimum need not be attained. Specifically, \(\omega\le u\) means that for every real \(\varepsilon>0\) there is a real \(C_\varepsilon>0\) such that \(s(n)\le C_\varepsilon n^{u+\varepsilon}\) for every integer n at least two. A lower bound \(\omega\ge\ell\) means that for every real \(\tau<\ell\) and C>0 there is an integer n at least two with \(s(n)>Cn^\tau\). These quantified bounds do not demand a circuit family attaining the endpoint exponent or a pointwise lower bound at that endpoint. The source’s conjecture \(\omega=2\) is one possible value of the numerical target selected for this card.
cards.answer_criterion: Specify a real number a by an unambiguous mathematical description and give a complete Lean-checked proof that \(|a-\omega|\le1/100\) for the unrestricted circuit quantity above. Equivalently, certify bounds \(\ell\le\omega\le u\) with \(u-\ell\le1/50\) and take \(a=(\ell+u)/2\). A proved exact value also qualifies. The proof must justify both sides of the error interval, with the infimum and nonattainment conventions in the definitions. Merely copying or renaming the defining infimum, reporting an optimized upper bound, or giving a bound only for a restricted tensor method does not meet the requirement. This tolerance concerns the value of the exponent and does not assert a proof of the exact conjecture that omega equals two.
cards.why: This exponent measures the asymptotic arithmetic cost of a fundamental operation and governs many other algebraic and graph algorithms. Determining its value would locate the limit of savings from shared computation.

importance.reason: One of the main questions in algebraic algorithms, governing a widely used primitive and many dependent complexity bounds. Both faster constructions and a superquadratic lower bound would have broad consequences.

progress.text: Strassen gives matrix multiplication in \(O(n^{\log_2 7})\) arithmetic operations, establishing a strictly subcubic exponent.
Alman’s revised universal-method paper proves that its application to any Coppersmith–Winograd tensor cannot give an exponent below 2.16805. This is a method-specific barrier.
The SODA publication of More Asymmetry Yields Faster Matrix Multiplication states \(\omega<2.371339\).

Dupont and coauthors report \(\omega<2.371177\). Section 4 describes rational certification and says the verification repository is being prepared; that certificate has not been replayed in this review.
The third arXiv revision of More Asymmetry incorporates the later optimization while distinguishing it from the original published bound. It does not establish a matching general lower bound.

cards.status_note: The checked source states the exponent-two conjecture, and the August 2026 papers report improved upper bounds without determining omega. The known interval displayed here remains wider than the requested numerical tolerance. A bounded primary-source search on 14 September 2026 found no verified determination at that precision. The optimization certificate was not independently replayed, and its repository was still described as in preparation in the checked version.

context_blocks.text: The usual algorithm computes \(n^{2}\) inner products of length n, spending cubic arithmetic work. That computation treats the outputs separately even though they share their input matrices. Strassen’s construction shows that this shared structure can save an asymptotic factor: seven block multiplications replace eight in a two-by-two block product, and recursive use gives exponent \(\log _{2}7\).

The scientific target is the value of the exponent, whether it equals two or is larger. The familiar \(\omega =2\) conjecture specifies one possible answer. Because \(\omega\) is an infimum, an upper bound may approach it with a different circuit family and constant for every positive slack in the exponent. Exact scalar arithmetic over a fixed field separates this quantity from approximate numerical multiplication and hardware throughput.

Modern upper bounds encode multiplication in tensors and exploit savings across large tensor powers. A substantial part of their analysis can be expressed as an optimization over parameters. The August 2026 improvement expands that optimization and uses new search procedures to find better parameters; the paper then describes rational verification of the resulting inequalities. That is an arithmetic exponent result, not an empirical speed comparison.

Alman proves a lower bound of 2.16805 for exponents achievable by applying the universal method to Coppersmith–Winograd tensors. That bound quantifies over a specified tensor framework. It does not imply \(\omega\ge2.16805\), because the quantity in this card permits every arithmetic circuit over the complex numbers.

An improvement in an upper bound and a determination of the exponent are different achievements. Even the reported upper bound 2.371177, together with the elementary lower bound 2, leaves an interval much wider than the required 0.02. A certified value within 0.01 would locate the optimum more closely, while still not necessarily deciding the exact conjecture \(\omega=2\).

cards.context:
The usual algorithm computes \(n^{2}\) inner products of length n, spending cubic arithmetic work. That computation treats the outputs separately even though they share their input matrices. Strassen’s construction shows that this shared structure can save an asymptotic factor: seven block multiplications replace eight in a two-by-two block product, and recursive use gives exponent \(\log _{2}7\).

The scientific target is the value of the exponent, whether it equals two or is larger. The familiar \(\omega =2\) conjecture specifies one possible answer. Because \(\omega\) is an infimum, an upper bound may approach it with a different circuit family and constant for every positive slack in the exponent. Exact scalar arithmetic over a fixed field separates this quantity from approximate numerical multiplication and hardware throughput.

Modern upper bounds encode multiplication in tensors and exploit savings across large tensor powers. A substantial part of their analysis can be expressed as an optimization over parameters. The August 2026 improvement expands that optimization and uses new search procedures to find better parameters; the paper then describes rational verification of the resulting inequalities. That is an arithmetic exponent result, not an empirical speed comparison.

Alman proves a lower bound of 2.16805 for exponents achievable by applying the universal method to Coppersmith–Winograd tensors. That bound quantifies over a specified tensor framework. It does not imply \(\omega\ge2.16805\), because the quantity in this card permits every arithmetic circuit over the complex numbers.

An improvement in an upper bound and a determination of the exponent are different achievements. Even the reported upper bound 2.371177, together with the elementary lower bound 2, leaves an interval much wider than the required 0.02. A certified value within 0.01 would locate the optimum more closely, while still not necessarily deciding the exact conjecture \(\omega=2\).

cards.title: Permanent versus determinant
cards.formal: Over \(\mathbb C\), is the determinantal complexity of the permanent not bounded above by any polynomial? Precisely, writing \(d_n=\operatorname{dc}_{\mathbb C}(\operatorname{perm}_n)\) as defined below, is it true that for every triple of integers \(B,k,N\ge1\) there is an integer \(n\ge N\) with \(d_n>B(n+1)^k\)? The matrices in the definition are unrestricted exact affine-linear representations over \(\mathbb C\).
cards.definitions: For an integer \(n\ge1\), let \(X=(x_{ij})_{1\le i,j\le n}\) consist of \(n^2\) algebraically independent commuting variables over \(\mathbb C\). Let \(S_n\) be the set of all permutations of \(\{1,\ldots,n\}\), and set \(\operatorname{perm}_n(X)=\sum_{\sigma\in S_n}\prod_{i=1}^n x_{i,\sigma(i)}\). For any \(m\times m\) matrix \(M\) over a commutative ring, \(\det(M)=\sum_{\pi\in S_m}\operatorname{sgn}(\pi)\prod_{a=1}^m M_{a,\pi(a)}\), where \(\operatorname{sgn}(\pi)=(-1)^{|\{(a,b):a<b,\ \pi(a)>\pi(b)\}|}\). Define \(d_n\) to be the least integer \(m\ge1\) for which there exist constant matrices \(A_0,A_{ij}\in\mathbb C^{m\times m}\), one \(A_{ij}\) for each input variable, such that \[\operatorname{perm}_n(X)=\det\!\left(A_0+\sum_{i=1}^n\sum_{j=1}^n x_{ij}A_{ij}\right)\] as an identity in \(\mathbb C[x_{ij}:1\le i,j\le n]\). Thus every entry is a constant plus an arbitrary complex linear combination of all input variables. Equality means equality of every coefficient, equivalently equality for every complex assignment, not just Boolean assignments. Finite representations exist, so the minimum is defined; for example the known bound \(d_n\le2^n-1\) suffices. The resource is the matrix dimension \(m\), not its number of entries, coefficient bit lengths or time to find the matrices. Constants can be arbitrary complex numbers, independently for each \(n\), with no computability or uniform construction requirement. Variables may be reused in any number of entries. No symmetry, sparsity, rank condition on \(A_0\), sign restriction, read-once property or restriction on cancellation is imposed. A limit of determinants is not an exact representation unless some permitted matrix already has determinant equal to the permanent. Since every \(d_n\) is finite, the formal assertion is equivalent to nonexistence of integers \(B,k\ge1\) satisfying \(d_n\le B(n+1)^k\) for all \(n\ge1\): finitely many exceptions to an upper bound can be absorbed into \(B\). The stated lower-bound quantifiers require arbitrarily large violating indices for every proposed polynomial, not eventual domination of that polynomial at every sufficiently large index.
cards.answer_criterion: Supply a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of the quantified lower-bound proposition, or of its logical negation: there exist integers \(B,k\ge1\) such that for every \(n\ge1\) there exist an integer \(1\le m\le B(n+1)^k\) and complex matrices \(A_0,A_{ij}\) satisfying the exact polynomial identity above. A negative answer may prove existence of this nonuniform family without an algorithm to generate its constants. A positive answer must exclude all allowed affine-linear matrices for the relevant \(n,m\), including those that break the permanent’s symmetries. A fixed-degree polynomial lower bound, a bound restricted to real coefficients or a restricted matrix class, or a lower bound for a different polynomial does not prove the proposition. A polynomial-size limiting representation alone does not refute this exact target.
cards.why: The permanent and determinant have almost identical permutation formulas, but the determinant is a basic efficiently computable polynomial whereas the permanent encodes algebraic counting. This conjecture asks whether enlarging the matrix and changing all its entries to affine forms can bridge that difference at polynomial cost. A superpolynomial lower bound would exclude an entire central model of algebraic computation, including polynomial-size algebraic branching programs and formulas.

progress.text: Valiant’s framework supplies finite determinantal representations, efficient simulation of formulas and branching programs, and completeness of the permanent for algebraic counting; the inspected 2021 source explains the distinction from unrestricted VP lower bounds.
Mignon and Ressayre’s Theorem 2 gives the characteristic-zero lower bound \(d_n\ge n^2/2\). The author manuscript’s statement and definitions were visually inspected.

Grenet’s exponential-size construction is recorded and shown optimal under left permutation/diagonal symmetry in Landsberg and Ressayre’s Theorem 2.8. The inspected preprint is from August 2015; the journal publication is from 2017.
Kumar and Volk’s Theorem 1 improves the lower bound for the different polynomial \(\sum_i x_i^n\), while their introduction retains the permanent’s quadratic-versus-exponential gap.

The Algebraic Cost of a Boolean Sum separates the permanent and determinant under a uniform fixed additive cost for simple projections after shared-bit summation. This does not establish a general superpolynomial determinantal lower bound.

Bogart and Valero’s journal article studies two generalized permanent families; its introduction continues to identify the unrestricted ordinary-permanent question as open. The available publisher text and full 2022 preprint introduction were checked.

Sheshadri’s preprint claims a quadratic border bound for diagonal power sums. The inspected Theorem 1 concerns a different family, and its proof was not independently checked. Version 1 remains the sole arXiv version on 14 September.

context_blocks.text: The determinant attaches a permutation sign to each product that the permanent sums without signs. Simply changing signs on the original \(n\times n\) matrix is a very special representation; this card permits arbitrarily larger matrices and arbitrary affine entries. Its size parameter is \(n\), while the number of independent input variables is \(n^2\). Polynomial boundedness in either parameter is equivalent, but the distinction matters when describing a quadratic lower bound.

An algebraic branching program is a finite directed acyclic graph with a source and sink, whose edges carry affine-linear forms; it computes the sum, over source-to-sink paths, of the products of their edge labels. Polynomial-size branching programs and polynomial-size determinantal representations simulate each other with polynomial overhead. General arithmetic circuits are directed acyclic computations using addition and multiplication and may reuse earlier results more freely. The algebraic class \(\mathrm{VP}\) permits polynomial-size circuits for families with polynomially bounded degree and number of variables; \(\mathrm{VNP}\) additionally permits summation over polynomially many Boolean variables. The permanent is complete for \(\mathrm{VNP}\). A polynomial-size determinant family for it would imply \(\mathrm{VP}=\mathrm{VNP}\), but the requested superpolynomial determinant lower bound by itself is not a separation from every unrestricted arithmetic circuit.

Mignon and Ressayre’s characteristic-zero theorem gives \(d_n\ge n^2/2\), while Grenet’s construction gives \(d_n\le2^n-1\). The quadratic lower bound is only linear in the permanent’s \(n^2\) variables and falls short of excluding every polynomial. The 2026 Bogart–Valero introduction still presents a quadratic-versus-exponential gap for the ordinary permanent; its new bounds concern generalized permanent families. Historical or recent bounds for another polynomial are not automatically permanent bounds.

Landsberg and Ressayre’s Theorem 2.8 proves the \(2^n-1\) lower bound for \(n\ge3\) when a representation respects the action of left multiplication by permutation and invertible diagonal matrices, and Grenet’s construction meets it. This theorem restricts how symmetries of the input polynomial lift to the representation. It imposes more than the exact identity defining \(d_n\). No symmetry requirement of this kind is part of the question.

Orzel and coauthors define a Boolean sum by first identifying all selected variable positions with one new variable \(y\), then adding the results for \(y=0\) and \(y=1\). This is a two-term sum, even when two positions are selected. Their Theorem 6 proves that for at most two selected positions the permanent can absorb this operation through a simple projection with dimension increased by at most three, while no fixed additive dimension increase works uniformly for the determinant. A simple projection substitutes constants or individual variables and uses each surviving variable at most once, allowing a nonzero overall scalar. This restricted, constant-additive-cost distinction leaves the unrestricted polynomial-size affine representations in this card open.

Border determinantal complexity also admits coefficientwise limits of fixed-dimension determinant representations; their matrix coefficients may vary and become unbounded along the limit. It is at most exact determinantal complexity. Thus a border lower bound implies the same exact lower bound, while an exact lower bound does not automatically exclude limiting representations. Changing the coefficient field also changes the model: allowing \(\mathbb C\) can reduce complexity compared with \(\mathbb R\), and in characteristic two the permanent equals the determinant. These variants cannot silently replace the fixed complex-field target.

Sheshadri’s June 2026 preprint claims a quadratic border lower bound for the diagonal power sum \(\sum_{i=1}^n z_i^n\). That polynomial has \(n\) variables and is not the \(n\times n\) permanent. The inspected theorem therefore does not close this card’s gap, regardless of its stronger dependence on the number of variables. The preprint proof has not been independently verified here.

cards.title: Shub–Smale \(\tau\)-conjecture
cards.formal: Does there exist an integer \(C\geq1\), independent of the polynomial, such that every nonzero \(f\in\mathbb Z[x]\) satisfies \[z_{\mathbb Z}(f)\leq(1+\tau(f))^C,\] where \(z_{\mathbb Z}(f)\) is the number of distinct integer roots and \(\tau(f)\) is the minimum number of additions, subtractions and multiplications needed to construct \(f\) from only \(1\) and \(x\)?
cards.definitions:
The ring \(\mathbb Z[x]\) consists of formal univariate polynomials with integer coefficients. A straight-line program of length \(s\in\mathbb N=\{0,1,2,\ldots\}\) starts with registers \(g_0=1\) and \(g_1=x\). For each \(i=2,\ldots,s+1\), it chooses \(j_i,k_i<i\) and one operation from \(\{+,-,\times\}\), and sets \(g_i=g_{j_i}\mathbin{\circ_i}g_{k_i}\). Operands may coincide, and an earlier register may be used arbitrarily many times. One register is designated as output. The program computes \(f\) if this output equals \(f\) as a formal polynomial. Define \(\tau(f)\) to be the least possible \(s\) among such programs. Every integer polynomial can be constructed in finitely many operations, so this minimum exists. When \(s=0\), only \(1\) or \(x\) can be output.

Every new arithmetic register costs one operation, including operations used to build integer constants. In particular \(2\), \(0\) and \(-1\) are not additional free inputs. There is no division, primitive exponentiation, comparison, conditional branch or access to a supplied coefficient list. The finite program may be chosen separately for each polynomial; there is no uniformity requirement on these choices. Intermediate degrees, coefficient sizes and integer magnitudes are unrestricted. Cost measures arithmetic operations, not the number of bits in coefficients, a formula without shared registers or the bit length of the program encoding.

For \(f\ne0\), define \(z_{\mathbb Z}(f)=|\{a\in\mathbb Z:f(a)=0\}|\), counting negative roots, zero and positive roots once each, regardless of multiplicity. This cardinality is finite because a nonzero univariate polynomial has at most its degree many roots; a nonzero constant has no roots. The zero polynomial is excluded. The exponent \(C\) must be one constant for all \(f\), without dependence on degree, coefficients, root sizes or the choice of an optimal program. The question asks only for a bound, not for an efficient root-counting or root-finding algorithm.
cards.answer_criterion: Provide a complete Lean-verified proof of the universal bound or its logical negation, \(\forall C\in\mathbb Z_{\geq1}\ \exists f\in\mathbb Z[x]\setminus\{0\}:z_{\mathbb Z}(f)>(1+\tau(f))^C\). A positive answer may use any one absolute exponent; a negative answer must exclude all such exponents. No computable rule for choosing the counterexample polynomials is required. A counterexample to just one proposed exponent, bounds for a restricted program class, multiplicity counts, or results only about real or complex roots do not settle this full target. Conditional consequences of the conjecture are not proofs of it.
cards.why: The conjecture asks whether a polynomial compressed into a short arithmetic computation can nevertheless have very many distinct integer zeros. Its elementary statement links arithmetic structure to fundamental lower bounds in algebraic computation. A proof would imply separation of polynomial-time nondeterministic and deterministic computation over the complex numbers, as well as important constant-free circuit separations; neither consequence is presently supplied by the conjecture itself.

importance.reason: A central arithmetic complexity conjecture with a very elementary statement and strong consequences for algebraic P versus NP and constant-free circuit lower bounds.

progress.text: Shub and Smale connect the complexity of integer computations to infeasibility testing over the complex numbers. Smale’s later Problem 4 explicitly records the distinct-integer-root conjecture and its complex P versus NP consequence.

Rojas’s second arXiv version states the full root conjecture, proves the fixed-prime residue-class implication, and bounds rational roots using additive complexity. The latter bound is not polynomial in \(\tau\).
The SIAM paper on semialgebraic proofs publishes conditional IPS lower bounds from the root conjecture over rational functions and from a distinct factorial-multiple hypothesis over the rationals.
A Zenodo preprint reports a finite census through eight operations with free constants -1,0,1. Its computation is unverified here and its finite scope does not resolve a universal exponent.

context_blocks.text: After \(s\) squarings, the program for \(x^{2^s}\) has only \(s\) operations but exponential degree. In general \(\deg f\leq2^{\tau(f)}\), giving only \(z_{\mathbb Z}(f)\leq2^{\tau(f)}\). The example has just one distinct integer root, although that root has multiplicity \(2^s\). This is why both the arithmetic compression and the word “distinct” matter.

The corresponding unrestricted real-root assertion is false. Let \(q_0(x)=x\) and \(q_{j+1}(x)=q_j(x)^2-2\). Building 2 once and using two operations per iteration gives \(\tau(q_j)\leq2j+1\). cards.title: VP versus VBP over the complex numbers
cards.formal: Is \(\mathrm{VP}_{\mathbb C}=\mathrm{VBP}_{\mathbb C}\)? More explicitly, let \((m_n,f_n)_{n\ge1}\) be any family with integers \(m_n\ge0\) and commutative polynomials \(f_n\in\mathbb C[x_1,\ldots,x_{m_n}]\). Suppose that some positive integer \(a\) satisfies \[m_n\le(n+2)^a,\qquad \deg f_n\le(n+2)^a,\qquad c(f_n)\le(n+2)^a\quad\text{for all }n\ge1,\] where \(c\) is minimum arithmetic-circuit size in the model below. Must there exist a positive integer \(b\), depending on the whole family, such that \[\operatorname{abp}(f_n)\le(n+2)^b\quad\text{for all }n\ge1?\] Computation is exact and nonuniform over the complex field, and the competing branching programs are unrestricted.
cards.definitions:
A polynomial is a finite complex linear combination of commutative monomials in the listed variables. Its total degree is the maximum sum of exponents among nonzero monomials, with degree zero assigned to the zero polynomial. An arithmetic circuit is a finite acyclic graph with one designated output. Input gates are labelled by one listed variable or one arbitrary complex constant. Every other gate has two ordered input ports and is labelled by addition or multiplication in the polynomial ring; both ports may refer to the same predecessor, and any predecessor may be reused. There are no division gates. Size is the number of gates plus the number of wires, counting each input port’s wire separately; constant and variable input gates each have unit cost. Intermediate degrees are not separately bounded: the degree hypothesis is on the output polynomial after cancellations. The minimum of this size among circuits computing \(f\) is \(c(f)\).

An algebraic branching program (ABP) is a finite directed acyclic multigraph with distinct designated vertices \(s,t\), no edges entering \(s\), and no edges leaving \(t\). Each edge \(e\) is labelled by an affine form \(\lambda_e=\alpha_{e,0}+\sum_{j=1}^{m}\alpha_{e,j}x_j\), with arbitrary complex coefficients. It computes \(\sum_{\pi:s\leadsto t}\prod_{e\in\pi}\lambda_e\), where distinct paths include their edge choices and an empty sum is zero. Its size is \[|V|+|E|+\sum_{e\in E}\left(\mathbf1_{\alpha_{e,0}\ne0}+2\bigl|\{j\in[m]:\alpha_{e,j}\ne0\}\bigr|\right).\] Here \([m]=\{1,\ldots,m\}\), including the empty set if \(m=0\), and \(\mathbf1_P\) is one when \(P\) holds and zero otherwise. Thus every nonzero scalar coefficient and its variable occurrence are charged; labels are not arbitrary polynomial oracles. There is no width, layering, variable-order, read-once, syntactic multilinearity, symmetry, homogeneity or monotonicity requirement. The minimum size computing \(f\) is \(\operatorname{abp}(f)\).

Both minima concern formal polynomial identities, not agreement on finitely many inputs or convergence of coefficients. Sizes count algebraic objects and field elements, not bits encoding complex numbers; coefficients need not have bounded or computable bit descriptions. No algorithm generating a family’s circuits, programs or constants is required. Every polynomial has finite representations in both models. Positive integer exponents in \((n+2)^a\) absorb multiplicative constants and finitely many initial values of any polynomial bound. The families meeting the circuit hypotheses define \(\mathrm{VP}_{\mathbb C}\); polynomially many variables and a polynomial ABP bound define \(\mathrm{VBP}_{\mathbb C}\). ABP size already bounds output degree, and ABPs have polynomial-size circuit simulations, so only the displayed converse inclusion is at issue.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of the displayed inclusion or its negation, with the specified field, polynomial identities, resource accounting and quantifiers. A positive proof establishes a polynomial ABP bound for every family satisfying the circuit and degree hypotheses; it need not produce an efficient uniform converter. A negative proof establishes one family \((m_n,f_n)\) and one fixed positive integer \(a\) satisfying all three circuit-side bounds, but such that \[\forall b\ge1\ \forall N\ge1\ \exists n\ge N,\quad \operatorname{abp}(f_n)>(n+2)^b.\] The lower bound must cover every permitted ABP over \(\mathbb C\), including arbitrary constants, reuse of variables and cancellations. There is no required effective generator for a separating family. A lower bound in a restricted ABP model, a family of exponential output degree, or a border-complexity separation does not meet this criterion.
cards.why: The question compares unrestricted arithmetic circuits with path-sum computation inside the class of efficiently representable polynomials. Equality would make polynomial-size determinants of affine matrices sufficient to express every polynomial-degree circuit family. Inequality would establish a fundamental separation within efficient algebraic computation, isolating power supplied by general multiplication together with reuse of intermediate results.

importance.reason: A basic class equality linking general arithmetic circuits, algebraic branching programs and determinant universality; current symmetry and multilinearity results remain model-specific.
