cards.title: Strassen’s asymptotic rank conjecture
cards.formal:
Work over the complex field \(\mathbb C\). Is the following general cubic formulation of the asymptotic rank conjecture true?
\[\forall n\in\mathbb N_{>0}\ \forall T\in\mathbb C^n\otimes\mathbb C^n\otimes\mathbb C^n:\quad \bigl(\operatorname{rank}F_1(T)=\operatorname{rank}F_2(T)=\operatorname{rank}F_3(T)=n\bigr)\ \Longrightarrow\ \widetilde R(T)=n,\]
where \(F_i(T)\) are the three matrix flattenings and
\[\widetilde R(T)=\lim_{k\to\infty}R(T^{\boxtimes k})^{1/k}=\inf_{k\ge1}R(T^{\boxtimes k})^{1/k}?\]
Here \(R\) is exact tensor rank, and \(\boxtimes\) groups corresponding factors of tensor products. The tensor \(T\) and its dimension \(n\) are fixed while \(k\) tends to infinity. The quantifier covers all complex tensors satisfying the flattening condition; no additional symmetry, support or computational promise is imposed.
cards.definitions:
Tensors and flattenings. For a positive integer \(d\), let \([d]=\{1,\ldots,d\}\) and let \(e_1,\ldots,e_d\) be the standard basis of \(\mathbb C^d\). A tensor \(T\) in three factors of dimensions \(a,b,c\) is the coefficient array \((t_{ij\ell})_{(i,j,\ell)\in[a]\times[b]\times[c]}\), interpreted as \(\sum_{i,j,\ell}t_{ij\ell}e_i\otimes e_j\otimes e_\ell\). For the cubic format \(a=b=c=n\), define three \(n\)-by-\(n^2\) matrices by
\[(F_1(T))_{i,(j,\ell)}=t_{ij\ell},\qquad(F_2(T))_{j,(i,\ell)}=t_{ij\ell},\qquad(F_3(T))_{\ell,(i,j)}=t_{ij\ell}.\]
Pairs are ordered lexicographically; the ordering does not affect matrix rank. Matrix rank is the dimension of the column span over \(\mathbb C\). A tensor is concise in this format when all three matrix ranks are \(n\). This excludes zero tensors and tensors that effectively use a smaller subspace in some factor. For \(n=1\), it just means a nonzero scalar.

Exact rank. For any positive dimensions \(a,b,c\), define
\[R(S)=\min\left\{r\in\mathbb N:\ S=\sum_{s=1}^{r}u_s\otimes v_s\otimes w_s,\quad u_s\in\mathbb C^a,\ v_s\in\mathbb C^b,\ w_s\in\mathbb C^c\right\}.\]
The empty sum is zero. A pure tensor has coefficients \((u_i v_j w_\ell)\); equality in a decomposition is exact coefficientwise equality. Finite decompositions always exist, so the minimum is well-defined. The three vectors in a summand are independent choices: there is no symmetric-rank restriction. Their complex entries are unrestricted, including noncomputable numbers; the question does not ask for a finite input encoding or an algorithm to find the decomposition.

Grouped powers. For \(k\ge1\), the tensor \(T^{\boxtimes k}\) has exactly three factors, each with coordinates indexed by \([n]^k\), and hence each of dimension \(n^k\). Its entries are
\[(T^{\boxtimes k})_{(i_1,\ldots,i_k),(j_1,\ldots,j_k),(\ell_1,\ldots,\ell_k)}=\prod_{h=1}^{k}t_{i_h j_h\ell_h}.\]
Its rank is taken after this grouping. A vector in a rank decomposition may be any element of \(\mathbb C^{n^k}\); it need not itself split into \(k\) vectors of dimension \(n\). Thus ranks of grouped powers need not equal \(R(T)^k\).

Asymptotic value. Tensoring decompositions gives
\[R(T^{\boxtimes(k+\ell)})\le R(T^{\boxtimes k})R(T^{\boxtimes\ell}).\]
For a concise tensor the elementary flattening lower bound and a slice decomposition give
\[n^k\le R(T^{\boxtimes k})\le n^{2k}.\]
Subadditivity of the logarithms therefore proves existence of the positive real limit in the question and its equality with the displayed infimum. In particular \(n\le\widetilde R(T)\le n^2\). The proposed equality is equivalently
\[\forall n\ \forall T\text{ concise}\ \forall\varepsilon\in\mathbb R_{>0}\ \exists K\ge1\ \forall k\ge K:\quad R(T^{\boxtimes k})\le(n+\varepsilon)^k.\]
Here \(K\) may depend on \(n,T,\varepsilon\), with no uniform or effective rate required. The actual decompositions may depend on \(k\) as well. Neither attainment of the infimum at a finite power nor rank \(n^k\) for any finite power is asserted.

Related ranks. Border rank of \(S\) is the least integer \(r\) such that \(S\) is a Euclidean limit of tensors of exact rank at most \(r\) in its fixed complex coefficient space. The defining ranks in this card are exact ranks. A finite-power border-rank result or a finite-power exact-rank lower bound must be connected to the quantified asymptotic statement before it can settle this question.

context_blocks.text: A rank decomposition expresses a three-factor tensor as a sum of elementary products. Allowing many copies to be processed jointly can save products because vectors in each grouped factor can correlate different copies. The conjecture says that these savings eventually leave no exponential overhead above the flattening lower bound. For the diagonal tensor \(\Delta_n=\sum_{i=1}^n e_i\otimes e_i\otimes e_i\), the elementary decomposition and flattening bound already match at every power.

The matrix multiplication tensor \(M_m=\sum_{i,j,\ell=1}^{m}e_{ij}\otimes e_{j\ell}\otimes e_{\ell i}\) is concise in three factors of dimension \(m^2\). In particular \(\widetilde R(M_2)=2^\omega\), where \(\omega\) is the infimum of exponents for arithmetic matrix multiplication over \(\mathbb C\). The proposed equality for this tensor would give \(\omega=2\). The implication in the reverse direction is not known from this example; the card quantifies over far more than matrix multiplication tensors.

The literature uses both general and restricted formulations. The retained target is the general cubic concise formulation discussed in the primary source and in the April 2026 spectrum paper. Lee’s January 2026 Conjecture 1 additionally assumes tightness: after suitable basis choices, injective integer weights on each factor sum to zero on every nonzero coefficient. That extra support condition is absent here. The numerical census supplies data for upper bounds, not a proof of this universal equality.

The June 2026 revision of the primary paper proves that each asymptotic-rank sublevel set is defined by vanishing of finitely many polynomials, and that a nonincreasing sequence of attainable asymptotic ranks eventually stabilizes. Its threshold-decision theorem applies over computable fields and is nonuniform in the threshold. These structural results do not identify all values with the flattening bound or supply an effective solution for arbitrary complex coefficients.

Alman, Li and Pratt’s April 2026 paper characterizes one part of the asymptotic tensor spectrum and gives algorithms for its edge support functionals. The spectrum is a collection of normalized, additive, multiplicative and restriction-monotone tensor parameters; its full maximum describes asymptotic rank. Characterizing selected members does not prove that they exhaust the spectrum. The paper explicitly separates its edge results from the full rank conjecture.

Two September 2026 papers give new lower bounds for individual tensors. Yang treats exact rank of rectangular matrix multiplication; Mańdziuk determines border ranks for specified direct sums and products. Neither inspected theorem supplies a single concise cubic tensor with a positive asymptotic gap above its dimension. Such finite-tensor lower bounds are compatible with the conjecture.

Holtrup and Zuiddam’s 15 September 2026 preprint settles a different extremal question: it bounds and classifies the largest stabilizer dimension of concise cubic tensors. A stabilizer consists of invertible changes of basis that preserve the tensor. Maximizing that group dimension does not determine the rank growth of all tensor powers, so this new result is not a resolution of the card.

cards.why: The conjecture asks whether every bilinear operation attains, in the exponential growth rate of jointly processed copies, the elementary lower bound already visible from matrices. A positive answer would force matrix multiplication exponent two and impose a simple common asymptotic law on all concise tensors. A negative answer would exhibit an obstruction that survives arbitrarily many grouped copies, beyond the familiar difficulty of decomposing a single tensor.
cards.answer_criterion:
Provide a complete, mathematically correct Lean-checked proof of the proposition or its logical negation, including the stated limit convention. An affirmative proof must cover every positive dimension and every concise complex tensor, with arbitrarily small positive \(\varepsilon\) in the equivalent power bound. A negative proof must establish the existence of a positive integer \(n\), a concise \(T\) in the specified cubic format, and a real \(\eta>0\) such that
\[\forall k\in\mathbb N_{>0}:\quad R(T^{\boxtimes k})\ge(n+\eta)^k.\]
This is equivalent to a counterexample with \(\widetilde R(T)>n\); no explicitness or computability condition is added to the counterexample. A large rank at one power is insufficient. A result only for a restricted class of tensors, only over another field, or conditional on an unproved complexity assumption does not settle the universal complex-field target. This is an exact yes/no conjecture, so a fixed additive tolerance such as \(1/100\) does not replace the equality.

progress.text: The original primary preprint establishes structural results for asymptotic tensor rank; its June 2026 revision gives the current statements used here.
Lee reports a numerical census improving upper-bound data in five computationally accessible formats and states the tight concise conjecture. The experiments do not certify the unrestricted equality.
Alman, Li and Pratt establish edge support functionals over arbitrary fields and characterize them using matrix multiplication. Their result does not characterize the full spectrum.
The revised primary source gives Zariski-closed sublevel sets, threshold-specific decision algorithms over computable fields and discreteness from above, while retaining the rank conjecture.
Mańdziuk gives new border-rank lower bounds for specific direct sums and products; the checked results do not provide an asymptotic counterexample.
Yang proves lower bounds for exact rank of rectangular matrix multiplication. The power-uniform exponential gap required here is a different guarantee.
Holtrup and Zuiddam determine the maximum stabilizer dimension for all concise cubic tensors, resolving that separate symmetry question.

sentences: A three-factor tensor can be decomposed into elementary products, and its rank is the least number of those products.
The question asks whether every concise complex tensor of equal factor dimension has asymptotic rank exactly that dimension when corresponding factors of many copies are grouped.
The dimension and tensor stay fixed during the limit, and no tightness, symmetry, computability or uniform convergence promise is imposed.
A complete Lean proof must establish the equality for all such tensors or a counterexample whose grouped powers all require a strictly larger exponential base.
The inspected 2026 structural, numerical, finite-rank and symmetry results do not settle this general asymptotic equality.

cards.context:
A rank decomposition expresses a three-factor tensor as a sum of elementary products. Allowing many copies to be processed jointly can save products because vectors in each grouped factor can correlate different copies. The conjecture says that these savings eventually leave no exponential overhead above the flattening lower bound. For the diagonal tensor \(\Delta_n=\sum_{i=1}^n e_i\otimes e_i\otimes e_i\), the elementary decomposition and flattening bound already match at every power.

The matrix multiplication tensor \(M_m=\sum_{i,j,\ell=1}^{m}e_{ij}\otimes e_{j\ell}\otimes e_{\ell i}\) is concise in three factors of dimension \(m^2\). In particular \(\widetilde R(M_2)=2^\omega\), where \(\omega\) is the infimum of exponents for arithmetic matrix multiplication over \(\mathbb C\). The proposed equality for this tensor would give \(\omega=2\). The implication in the reverse direction is not known from this example; the card quantifies over far more than matrix multiplication tensors.

The literature uses both general and restricted formulations. The retained target is the general cubic concise formulation discussed in the primary source and in the April 2026 spectrum paper. Lee’s January 2026 Conjecture 1 additionally assumes tightness: after suitable basis choices, injective integer weights on each factor sum to zero on every nonzero coefficient. That extra support condition is absent here. The numerical census supplies data for upper bounds, not a proof of this universal equality.

The June 2026 revision of the primary paper proves that each asymptotic-rank sublevel set is defined by vanishing of finitely many polynomials, and that a nonincreasing sequence of attainable asymptotic ranks eventually stabilizes. Its threshold-decision theorem applies over computable fields and is nonuniform in the threshold. These structural results do not identify all values with the flattening bound or supply an effective solution for arbitrary complex coefficients.

Alman, Li and Pratt’s April 2026 paper characterizes one part of the asymptotic tensor spectrum and gives algorithms for its edge support functionals. The spectrum is a collection of normalized, additive, multiplicative and restriction-monotone tensor parameters; its full maximum describes asymptotic rank. Characterizing selected members does not prove that they exhaust the spectrum. The paper explicitly separates its edge results from the full rank conjecture.

Two September 2026 papers give new lower bounds for individual tensors. Yang treats exact rank of rectangular matrix multiplication; Mańdziuk determines border ranks for specified direct sums and products. Neither inspected theorem supplies a single concise cubic tensor with a positive asymptotic gap above its dimension. Such finite-tensor lower bounds are compatible with the conjecture.

Holtrup and Zuiddam’s 15 September 2026 preprint settles a different extremal question: it bounds and classifies the largest stabilizer dimension of concise cubic tensors. A stabilizer consists of invertible changes of basis that preserve the tensor. Maximizing that group dimension does not determine the rank growth of all tensor powers, so this new result is not a resolution of the card.

cards.title: Explicit three-dimensional tensors of superlinear rank
cards.formal: Do there exist one deterministic multitape Turing machine \(A\), a real constant \(K>0\) and an integer \(a\ge1\) such that, for every \(n\ge1\), on input \(1^n\) it outputs all entries of a rational tensor \(T_n\in\mathbb Q^{n\times n\times n}\) within \(K(n+1)^a\) bit operations, and \[\forall B\in\mathbb R_{>0}\ \exists N\ge1\ \forall n\ge N:\quad \operatorname{rank}_{\mathbb C}(T_n)\ge Bn?\] Here rank is ordinary tensor rank over the complex numbers. Thus the required ratio \(\operatorname{rank}_{\mathbb C}(T_n)/n\) tends to infinity, with no prescribed rate.
cards.why: Tensor rank measures the number of independent bilinear products needed to express a computation. Explicit superlinear-rank families would turn generic hardness into concrete examples and yield lower bounds for the corresponding constant-degree arithmetic computations.

importance.reason: A central explicit lower-bound challenge for tensor rank and arithmetic computation: the gap between generic quadratic rank and explicit linear lower bounds persists even for three-way tensors and relates directly to unrestricted arithmetic circuit barriers.

sentences: A three-way tensor is a cubic array, and its ordinary rank is the fewest rank-one arrays whose sum equals it.
The selected branch asks for rational entries written by one deterministic algorithm in polynomial time in the dimension.
Rank is measured over the complex numbers, and its ratio to the side length must tend to infinity.
The algorithm must produce every dimension without advice, symbolic number-field entries or uncharged output bits.
Known explicit linear border-rank bounds and recent semi-explicit high-rank constructions do not meet this superlinear rational-output target.

cards.definitions:
A tensor \(T\in\mathbb Q^{n\times n\times n}\) is the array \((T_{ijk})_{1\le i,j,k\le n}\), regarded as an element of \(\mathbb C^n\otimes\mathbb C^n\otimes\mathbb C^n\) through the usual inclusion of the rationals into the complex numbers. Its ordinary rank is the smallest integer \(r\ge0\) for which there are vectors \(u^{(s)},v^{(s)},w^{(s)}\in\mathbb C^n\), for \(1\le s\le r\), satisfying
\[
T_{ijk}=\sum_{s=1}^{r}u^{(s)}_i\,v^{(s)}_j\,w^{(s)}_k
\quad\text{for every }1\le i,j,k\le n.
\]
An empty sum is the zero tensor. The factors in a rank decomposition may be arbitrary complex vectors, although the constructed tensor entries are rational. No symmetry is required. The target is not matrix rank of an array rearrangement, slice rank, border rank, or an asymptotic tensor-power rank.

The machine outputs the \(n^3\) entries in lexicographic order of \((i,j,k)\). Each entry is an explicitly written signed binary integer numerator and positive binary integer denominator, with delimiters. All bits are charged, so their total length and each individual entry's bit length are polynomially bounded in \(n\). A symbolic power, root-of-unity description, unevaluated arithmetic expression or arbitrary real constant is not a rational-entry output under this convention. All input reading, integer arithmetic, preprocessing and output writing count. The finite program and \(K,a\) are independent of \(n\); there is no advice, oracle, randomness or uncharged preprocessing.

The algorithm is required on every positive integer dimension, and the rank guarantee holds for all sufficiently large dimensions for each \(B\). The integer threshold \(N\) may depend on \(B\) and the fixed family; it is not required to be computed. No rank decomposition, rank value or lower-bound certificate is an output requirement for \(A\); the rank-growth guarantee must instead be established by the submitted proof. Explicitness here means polynomial time in the dimension to write the whole tensor, not a separate polylogarithmic-time entry-query requirement.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct Lean proof of the existence of such a finite construction algorithm, its uniform polynomial bit-cost bound and the entire eventual superlinear rank guarantee, or a complete Lean proof that no such algorithm exists. An existence proof without the construction cost, a fixed constant multiple of the dimension, growth only along an unspecified subsequence, or a conditional lower bound alone does not meet this target. Any growth rate tending to infinity in the displayed normalized rank suffices; a fixed positive power improvement is not required.

context_blocks.text: Open Problem 15 asks for explicit three-dimensional tensors of superlinear rank after explaining their connection to arithmetic circuits. The survey writes the ground field generically and leaves representation details implicit. This card selects the characteristic-zero branch with rationally encoded entries and rank over the complex numbers; it does not claim equivalence to every possible field or algebraic-number encoding.

The full-output polynomial-time convention follows the explicitness discussion in Definition 1.1 of Landsberg and Michałek. Their construction uses integer coordinates, and their border-rank lower bound grows linearly with the dimension. Such a result is meaningful progress but does not make the rank-to-dimension ratio tend to infinity.

The July 2026 sumset-expansion paper explicitly distinguishes efficiently constructible tensor entries from short algebraic descriptions. Its high-border-rank tensors use number-field coordinates and are described as semi-explicit; they do not constitute the rational bit-output construction fixed here. Its Remark 5 still states the explicit superlinear-rank challenge.

The target asks for ordinary rank. A superlinear lower bound on border rank would be sufficient, but proving that stronger property is not required. Conversely, improved linear bounds for either notion do not settle the superlinear target.

cards.title: Derandomizing black-box depth-four PIT
cards.formal: Does there exist one deterministic uniform polynomial-time construction of hitting sets for all size-\(s\), \(n\)-variable \(\Sigma\Pi\Sigma\Pi\) arithmetic circuits, in the field-operation model specified below? Precisely, one algorithm and constants \(C>0,b\in\mathbb N\) must work for every \(n,s\ge1\), every working field \(K\), and every supplied list \(T\) of \(2s^2+1\) distinct elements of \(K\). In at most \(C(n+s+1)^b\) operations it must output a list \(H\subseteq K^n\) such that every nonzero formal polynomial computed by any allowed circuit over \(K\) has a nonzero evaluation at some point of \(H\). The algorithm receives no circuit description, coefficients, or evaluation oracle for a particular polynomial.
cards.why: Identity testing asks whether a compact arithmetic computation represents the zero polynomial. A uniform collection of evaluations would remove randomness without inspecting the computation itself. The depth-four case is especially consequential because of its established relationship to much more general arithmetic circuits, and its unrestricted fan-ins distinguish it from several recent positive results.
cards.status_note: The unrestricted problem is posed in the 2010 survey. The checked 2021 and 2026 primary results give restricted-family algorithms and do not cover the target’s unrestricted fan-ins and arbitrary working fields. Bounded searches through 2026-09-15 found no general resolution. This records the scope of sources checked, not an independent certification of every later proof.

importance.reason: A central derandomization target in algebraic complexity. Depth four already captures a decisive barrier connected by depth reduction to general arithmetic identity testing, while black-box uniformity requires explicit evaluation sets rather than access to circuit syntax. Recent progress on restricted depth-four families leaves the unrestricted challenge substantial.

sentences: The question asks for a deterministic polynomial-time construction of evaluation points that detect every nonzero polynomial computed by a size-bounded depth-four arithmetic circuit.
The same generated set must work for every circuit of the given size without seeing its coefficients or gates.
The model charges field operations and output length, and explicitly permits a sufficiently large working field.
There is no constant bound on the top fan-in or bottom degree and no homogeneity or multilinearity assumption.
Recent polynomial-time results impose fixed fan-in, quadratic factors or powering restrictions, while the general target remains unresolved in the checked literature.

cards.definitions: An allowed circuit is a finite directed acyclic arithmetic circuit with one output, four alternating layers of unbounded-fan-in arithmetic gates, and input leaves labeled by variables \(x_1,\ldots,x_n\) or arbitrary constants of \(K\). From output to inputs the operations are sum, product, sum, product. Fan-in-one gates may pad smaller depth. Gates and subexpressions may be shared; the size is the total number of wires, including wires from input leaves and with repeated uses counted separately. There are at most \(s\) wires. Addition and multiplication are the only polynomial operations; division gates, exponentiation gates with compressed exponents, and tests inside the hidden circuit are excluded. In expression form the output is a sum of products of sparse polynomials, with no fixed bound on the top fan-in or on the bottom monomial degrees beyond the wire budget. The total degree is at most \(s^2\), since each bottom product has degree at most \(s\) and each upper product has at most \(s\) factors. Homogeneity, multilinearity, and bounded variable occurrence are not assumed. A nonzero polynomial means one with at least one nonzero coefficient, not merely a function that is nonzero somewhere on the original base field. The construction uses one finite program with ordinary discrete control and registers holding opaque elements of \(K\). A field addition, subtraction, multiplication, division by a tested nonzero element, equality test, copy, or access to a supplied field element costs one operation; discrete control is charged by its ordinary bit operations. The only initial field values are zero, one and the entries of \(T\). Field representations carry no readable extra advice. The constants \(C,b\) are independent of characteristic, field, \(T,n,s\) and all circuit coefficients. The cost includes writing every coordinate of every output point; existence of a small set without an efficient construction does not qualify. No randomness, parameter-dependent advice, or uncharged preprocessing is allowed. The input list \(T\) makes the source’s sufficiently-large-field convention explicit. For a smaller base field \(F\), evaluations may instead take place in a supplied extension \(K\supseteq F\) with such a list; the circuit is then viewed over \(K\). Constructing or encoding that extension is outside this field-operation target. This is not a claim about bit complexity over arbitrary field presentations or an algorithm confined to evaluations inside a too-small field.
cards.answer_criterion: Provide a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of the uniform hitting-set construction and its polynomial resource bound, or prove that no such construction exists in the stated model. A positive proof must handle every allowed coefficient assignment, every working field with the supplied distinct elements, and every size and variable count. It must establish that evaluating on all of \(H\) distinguishes the zero polynomial from every nonzero polynomial in the class. A negative proof must rule out every finite uniform algorithm and polynomial bound; failure of one candidate hitting set is insufficient. A white-box algorithm, a nonconstructive existence proof, a construction with superpolynomial running time, or a construction restricted to bounded top fan-in or bottom degree does not meet this target.

context_blocks.text: Open Problem 18 explicitly asks to derandomize black-box depth-four PIT. Definition 1.1 counts wires and permits unbounded fan-in at bounded depth; Remark 1.1 uses arbitrary fields by default. Section 4 permits extension-field evaluations, while Section 4.1 defines hitting sets. These conventions are made explicit in the field-operation target here.

Theorem 4.9, attributed to Agrawal and Vinay, relates polynomial-time explicit hitting sets for depth-four circuits to quasipolynomial-size explicit hitting sets for general arithmetic circuits. This is a stated consequence of solving the restricted-depth target; the card does not add a general-circuit result to the required answer.

Dutta, Dwivedi and Saxena’s 2021 Theorem 2 gives quasipolynomial-time black-box testing for bounded-top-fan-in depth-four circuits with either sums of univariates or bounded-degree bottom polynomials. Their polynomial-time theorem is white-box and for the sums-of-univariates subclass.

Garg, Oliveira, Sengupta, Shalmon and Shpilka’s 2026 Corollary 1.4 gives polynomial-time black-box PIT in characteristic zero when top fan-in is fixed and bottom degree is at most two. Its polynomial dependence is for each fixed top fan-in; it is not a polynomial-time guarantee uniform in unrestricted fan-in.

Shpilka and Tal’s February 2026 preprint gives explicit hitting sets for sums of \(r\) powers of sparse polynomials when the common power \(d\) satisfies \(d>r^2\), over characteristic zero or sufficiently large characteristic. Upper product gates in the present card may multiply unrelated factors, so the powering result covers a different restricted family.

cards.formal: Let \(S(n)\) be the minimum size of a complex arithmetic straight-line program that computes all n coordinates of the discrete Fourier transform (DFT) exactly, in the model below. cards.definitions: For \(n\ge 1\) set \(\omega _{n}=\exp (- 2\pi i/n)\), and define \(DFT_{n}(x)_{j}=\sum_{k=0}^{n- 1}\omega _{n}^{jk}x_{k}\) for \(j=0,\ldots ,n- 1\) and \(x\in \mathbb{C} ^{n}\). This is the unnormalized cyclic DFT. A straight-line program is a finite acyclic list of scalar instructions. Each instruction either adds, subtracts or multiplies two previously available values, or multiplies one value by a fixed complex scalar. Input coordinates and any fixed complex constants are available initially. Values may be reused without limit, and all n required output coordinates must occur among the computed values. Size is the number of instructions; each complex scalar operation costs one, regardless of operand magnitude. The sequence and all constants may depend on n but not on x. Constants need not be efficiently generated or have a bounded bit representation. There is no restriction on circuit depth, reuse, storage, intermediate magnitudes or numerical conditioning. Operations are exact and must compute the required polynomial identities for every complex input. This is the standard division-free arithmetic-circuit formulation used to make the imported model precise; subtraction and multiplication by any reciprocal constant are allowed. No comparison, branching, floor, bit extraction, approximation or quantum operation is present. For this linear output map, allowing products of input-dependent intermediate values changes minimum size by at most a constant factor compared with linear circuits using only addition, subtraction and scalar multiplication, as stated in the cited circuit reference. Counting a two-input linear combination as one instruction instead of at most three also changes cost only by a constant factor.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove the uniform lower bound for every sufficiently large power-of-two length and every program in the stated model, or refute it. Precisely, a refutation must show that for every \(c>0\) and every threshold N there is a power of two \(n\ge N\) and a program of size less than \(c n \log _{2}n\). A family using \(o(n \log  n)\) operations would suffice, but the full logical negation does not require a uniformly generated family or such a bound at every length. A lower bound requiring bounded coefficients, unitary gates, limited storage or numerical stability does not establish the target.

context_blocks.title: A fast transform reuses intermediate values
context_blocks.text: For four inputs, form \(a=x_{0}+x_{2}, b=x_{1}+x_{3}, c=x_{0}- x_{2}\) and \(d=x_{1}- x_{3}\). The four Fourier outputs are \(a+b, c- id, a- b\) and \(c+id\). Shared sums let the same work serve several output coordinates. The classical FFT extends this reuse to obtain \(O(n \log  n)\) operations; the question is whether a different unrestricted program can do asymptotically better.

context_blocks.title: Normalization should not decide this question
context_blocks.text: Dividing all outputs by \(\sqrt{n}\) gives the normalized DFT. In the unbounded-scalar model, converting either normalization to the other costs at most n extra operations, so the conjectured asymptotic lower bound is equivalent for the two. A lower-bound argument tied to one normalization may nevertheless fail for the other when its coefficients are restricted.

context_blocks.title: What the classical lower bound assumes
context_blocks.text: Morgenstern’s lower bound, recalled in both full sources, gives order n log n for the unnormalized transform when scalar magnitudes have a fixed bound. The determinant magnitude of that transform is \(n^{n/2}\), whereas the normalized matrix has determinant magnitude one. Arbitrarily large scalars invalidate the bounded per-operation growth used by that result. Thus the known theorem does not already settle this card.

context_blocks.title: Unitary and well-conditioned models
context_blocks.text: Ailon proves an n log n bound for normalized Fourier computation with two-coordinate unitary gates and no extra storage. Subsequent results relate possible speedup to numerical ill-conditioning. These are meaningful restrictions on computations; the present model permits general arithmetic, arbitrary reuse and large intermediate values, so those lower bounds have a narrower scope.

context_blocks.title: Related tasks use different cost measures
context_blocks.text: The 2026 source studies necessary divisions in Toom-Cook interpolation at integer evaluation points and division-aware costs. It does not give an unrestricted DFT operation lower bound. Counting only multiplications, approximating Fourier outputs at fixed precision, or applying a quantum Fourier transform to state amplitudes also asks a different question from computing this entire classical complex output vector.

cards.title: Uniform exact permanent circuits below base two
cards.formal:
Does there exist a rational \(\varepsilon\in(0,1)\), an integer \(C\ge1\), and one deterministic circuit generator \(G\) such that, for every integer \(n\ge1\), \(G(1^{n})\) outputs a division-free rational arithmetic circuit \(\mathcal C_{n}\) with at most \(C(2-\varepsilon)^{n}\) nodes, within at most \(C(2-\varepsilon)^{n}\) Turing-machine steps, and
\[\forall K\text{ of characteristic zero}\ \forall A\in K^{n\times n},\qquad \mathcal C_{n}(A)=\operatorname{per}(A)=\sum_{\pi\in S_{n}}\prod_{i=0}^{n-1}A_{i,\pi(i)}?\]
Here \(S_{n}\) is the set of permutations of \(\{0,\ldots,n-1\}\), and every rational circuit constant is interpreted through the canonical embedding \(\mathbb Q\to K\). This fixes the uniform rational-circuit version of the saved characteristic-zero arithmetic-operation question.

sentences: The permanent is the unsigned sum of permutation products of a square matrix.
This card asks whether exact division-free rational circuits can beat exponential base two while being generated uniformly within the same exponential bound.
The generated polynomial must work for every matrix over every characteristic-zero field, with bit costs for circuit construction separated from field-operation costs for evaluation.
Checked recent results give conditional circuit improvements, finite-ring algorithms, bounded-entry bit-time savings or lower bounds for restricted formula classes.
A complete Lean proof must establish the specified uniform circuit family with a fixed positive base saving or rule out every family meeting these conventions.

cards.definitions:
A field \(K\) has characteristic zero when the sum of any positive number of copies of its multiplicative identity is nonzero; this gives a unique injective field homomorphism \(\mathbb Q\to K\). The domain contains every square matrix over every such field, including rational, real and complex matrices, with no sign, magnitude, sparsity, rank, symmetry or integrality promise. The permanent is the unsigned permutation sum above; it is not the determinant. All evaluations must be exact.

An arithmetic circuit is a finite list of nodes in topological order, with the last node the output. Each node is either an input variable \(x_{i,j}\) with \(0\le i,j<n\), a rational constant, or a binary \(+\), \(-\), or \(\times\) gate whose two ordered parent indices refer to earlier nodes. Repeated use of the same parent is allowed, so shared intermediate values and squaring are permitted. Unused nodes may be omitted. The size counts all nodes, including constants and variable nodes. On a matrix \(A\), an input node evaluates to its entry, constants are embedded in \(K\), and internal gates perform the indicated field operations. Each internal gate costs one arithmetic operation, independently of the sizes of field elements; a rational constant is a permitted circuit input. There is no division by an input-dependent value, branching on an input entry, rounding, bit extraction, transcendental gate, oracle gate, or limit computation. Subtraction is equivalently addition using the constant \(-1\), so it does not introduce an extra algebraic operation type beyond the source circuit convention.

The generator is one finite deterministic multitape Turing machine over fixed finite alphabets, given only \(1^{n}\). It receives neither matrix entries nor a description of the field. Its program and clock constants are fixed independently of \(n\). For definiteness, for a nonnegative integer \(t\), let \(b(t)\) be its ordinary binary expansion with \(b(0)=0\), and encode \(t\) by \(E(t)=1^{|b(t)|}0b(t)\). The output begins with the encoded positive node count. Each node then has a three-bit tag: 000 for a variable followed by \(E(i)E(j)\); 001 for a constant followed by a sign bit and \(E(u)E(v)\), representing \((-1)^{s}u/v\), with \(u\ge0,v\ge1\) in lowest terms and zero having sign zero; 010, 011 or 100 for addition, subtraction or multiplication followed by the two encoded parent indices. Indices start at zero, and the output must be a well-formed list with no trailing bits. Every generator transition, including writing every constant and index bit, is charged. Thus a separate unbounded search or arbitrary nonuniform circuit choice is not hidden outside the construction bound.

Circuit generation and field evaluation are different costs: the first is bounded binary computation on the dimension, while the second counts exact field operations on abstract entries. There is no claim of a bit-time bound independent of entry length when evaluating on encoded integers or rationals. The same generated rational polynomial must work in all characteristic-zero fields; no field-dependent or noncomputable constants are allowed. This is a specified uniform circuit model, not an assertion that all branching arithmetic algorithms or all field-specific circuit models are equivalent to it. The fixed base saving is uniform in dimension. Polynomial prefactors may be absorbed by a smaller positive base saving, but \(2^{n-o(n)}\) alone does not meet the target. This is an exact complexity-existence question, so absolute numerical tolerance does not apply.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete, mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of the proposition or its logical negation. A positive answer must specify the finite generator, rational \(\varepsilon\), integer \(C\), valid output circuits and their two bounds for every dimension, and prove their exact evaluation identity for every matrix over every characteristic-zero field. A polynomial identity proof over \(\mathbb Q\), together with its transfer under the canonical field embedding, can establish the required universal identity. A negative answer must exclude every permitted generator and every fixed positive base saving, rather than one construction, bounded circuit depth or coefficient pattern. It need not be a single finite counterexample matrix. A conditional implication is only conditional unless its hypotheses are also proved. Approximate permanent values, algorithms only for bounded integer entries or finite rings, a sublinear saving in the exponent, and small circuits with no generator meeting the bound do not suffice. A negative result for this precise circuit model is not automatically a lower bound for every stronger arithmetic model.

context_blocks.text: Ryser’s classical upper bound uses \(O(n2^{n})\) field operations to compute the permanent. A fixed improvement from exponential base two would change the scale of exact algebraic counting, while still allowing exponential running time. Exact #P-completeness on zero–one integer matrices explains the absence of an expected polynomial-time counting algorithm, but it does not rule out a fixed exponential-base improvement in this arithmetic model.

For a \(2\times2\) matrix with rows \((a,b)\) and \((c,d)\), the permanent is \(ad+bc\), whereas the determinant is \(ad-bc\). Removing alternating signs changes the algebraic complexity substantially. On nonnegative entries the permanent also counts weighted bipartite perfect matchings, but this card allows every field entry and asks for exact evaluation. The randomized or deterministic relative approximations in the neighboring cards do not give this circuit family.

The proposal cited the uniform-circuit results of Björklund, Kaski, Koana and Nederlof. Their Section 2.2 uses division-free arithmetic circuits, and Theorem 1.3 bounds both construction time and circuit size. This card makes the previously unstated coefficient and uniformity conventions concrete by choosing a finite generator of rational circuits that works throughout characteristic zero. This portable rational model and the fixed exponential-base target are explicit editorial choices; they are not presented as identical to every possible reading of Knuth’s broader arithmetic-operation question quoted in that source.

The ICALP 2026 paper proves that a sufficiently low rank growth rate for a sequence of balanced tripartitioning tensors yields a uniform permanent circuit construction with a fixed exponential improvement. It relates the needed rank bounds to Strassen’s asymptotic rank conjecture. A tensor rank here is the least number of products of three linear forms needed to express the associated trilinear form. These are conditional upper bounds with a specified underlying field; the paper does not establish the required rank hypothesis unconditionally or identify every coefficient model. Its result is relevant evidence about the barrier, not a completed positive answer.

Björklund and Williams give a deterministic \(2^{n-\Omega(n/r)}\)-time permanent algorithm over a finite ring with \(r\le n\) elements. For fixed \(r\) this is a fixed base improvement, but a finite field has positive characteristic and is outside this card’s domain. They also obtain faster exact counting on regular zero–one matrices, where the saving depends on the degree. Those input restrictions must be retained when comparing the theorem to an unrestricted characteristic-zero circuit family.

Baitian Li’s revised paper of 3 May 2026, published at ICALP 2026, gives \(2^{n-\Omega(\sqrt n)}\)-type bit-time bounds for integer permanents, with polynomial dependence on the bit bound for entries. Its hafnian formulation uses a \(2n\times2n\) symmetric matrix; a permanent of order \(n\) is a special case at that size. The theorem is a significant exact speedup, but its sublinear exponent saving is not a fixed \((2-\varepsilon)^{n}\) guarantee, and its numerical operations are not this input-oblivious characteristic-zero circuit model. The revised title and more general hafnian scope replace the older title in the proposal’s reference trail.

Fonollosa’s July 2026 preprint compares Ryser, Glynn and Fourier evaluation formulas at the same \(\Theta(n2^{n})\) arithmetic scale. Its revised Corollary 1 gives a lower bound on the number of evaluations for the particular row-product evaluation schemes considered in that paper. That restricted-formula bound does not rule out general arithmetic circuits with reused intermediate values and unrestricted depth. The new proof was not independently verified in full during this review.

The fixed base, the dimension, the field, the coefficient representation and uniform construction all matter. A finite-ring computation, an experiment on structured matrices, a smaller constant number of exponential terms or a better approximate count may be useful without answering this question. A resolution would clarify the exact algebraic cost of one of the central counting polynomials.

The proposal cited the uniform-circuit results of Björklund, Kaski, Koana and Nederlof. Their Section 2.2 uses division-free arithmetic circuits, and Theorem 1.3 bounds both construction time and circuit size. This card makes the previously unstated coefficient and uniformity conventions concrete by choosing a finite generator of rational circuits that works throughout characteristic zero. This portable rational model and the fixed exponential-base target are explicit editorial choices; they are not presented as identical to every possible reading of Knuth’s broader arithmetic-operation question quoted in that source.

The ICALP 2026 paper proves that a sufficiently low rank growth rate for a sequence of balanced tripartitioning tensors yields a uniform permanent circuit construction with a fixed exponential improvement. It relates the needed rank bounds to Strassen’s asymptotic rank conjecture. A tensor rank here is the least number of products of three linear forms needed to express the associated trilinear form. These are conditional upper bounds with a specified underlying field; the paper does not establish the required rank hypothesis unconditionally or identify every coefficient model. Its result is relevant evidence about the barrier, not a completed positive answer.

Björklund and Williams give a deterministic \(2^{n-\Omega(n/r)}\)-time permanent algorithm over a finite ring with \(r\le n\) elements. For fixed \(r\) this is a fixed base improvement, but a finite field has positive characteristic and is outside this card’s domain. They also obtain faster exact counting on regular zero–one matrices, where the saving depends on the degree. Those input restrictions must be retained when comparing the theorem to an unrestricted characteristic-zero circuit family.

Baitian Li’s revised paper of 3 May 2026, published at ICALP 2026, gives \(2^{n-\Omega(\sqrt n)}\)-type bit-time bounds for integer permanents, with polynomial dependence on the bit bound for entries. Its hafnian formulation uses a \(2n\times2n\) symmetric matrix; a permanent of order \(n\) is a special case at that size. The theorem is a significant exact speedup, but its sublinear exponent saving is not a fixed \((2-\varepsilon)^{n}\) guarantee, and its numerical operations are not this input-oblivious characteristic-zero circuit model. The revised title and more general hafnian scope replace the older title in the proposal’s reference trail.

Fonollosa’s July 2026 preprint compares Ryser, Glynn and Fourier evaluation formulas at the same \(\Theta(n2^{n})\) arithmetic scale. Its revised Corollary 1 gives a lower bound on the number of evaluations for the particular row-product evaluation schemes considered in that paper. That restricted-formula bound does not rule out general arithmetic circuits with reused intermediate values and unrestricted depth. The new proof was not independently verified in full during this review.

The fixed base, the dimension, the field, the coefficient representation and uniform construction all matter. A finite-ring computation, an experiment on structured matrices, a smaller constant number of exponential terms or a better approximate count may be useful without answering this question. A resolution would clarify the exact algebraic cost of one of the central counting polynomials.

cards.title: NP-hardness of PosSLP
cards.formal: Is \(\mathrm{PosSLP}\) NP-hard under deterministic polynomial-time many-one reductions? Concretely, does there exist one deterministic Turing-computable map \(g\) and constants \(C>0,d\in\mathbb N\) such that \(g\) runs in time at most \(C(N+1)^d\) on every input of bit length \(N\), outputs a valid integer straight-line program, and for every encoded 3-CNF formula \(F\), \[F\text{ is satisfiable}\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad \operatorname{value}(g(F))>0?\] The reduction must be unconditionally correct on all inputs, with no algebraic conjecture, randomness, oracle or advice. Malformed input encodings are treated as no-instances and must also map to nonpositive outputs.

source_formulation.text: And finally, can we prove unconditional hardness results for PosSLP?
source_formulation.caption: Complete selected source sentence; PDF p. 14

cards.why: A short sequence of elementary integer operations can represent numbers whose binary expansions are enormous. PosSLP isolates the task of deciding the sign of such a number. Its connections to numerical computation make a conventional hardness classification consequential well beyond the particular instruction format.
cards.status_note: The checked 2024 primary papers leave unconditional PosSLP hardness open, and Miltzow’s March 2026 discussion still describes the NP-hardness evidence as conditional. Bounded later-work checks through 2026-09-15 found no proof or refutation of the specified deterministic many-one NP-hardness target. The source’s broader hardness direction is preserved separately and is not claimed equivalent to this concrete specialization.

progress.text: Bürgisser and Jindal publish their conditional randomized hardness implication and explicitly ask for unconditional NP-hardness in Section 6.

Bläser, Dörfler and Jindal publish results connecting integer sign testing to sums of squares, establish hardness for a polynomial variant, and retain unconditional PosSLP hardness as their final open question.
Miltzow posts an introduction to computation over the reals whose straight-line-program discussion still treats the NP-hardness evidence for PosSLP as conditional.

category_assignment.reason: The object is the exact sign of a succinctly computed integer.

importance.reason: PosSLP is a central bridge between exact arithmetic computation and discrete complexity, yet no general NP-hardness result is established in the checked literature. An unconditional reduction would materially clarify the computational strength of succinct integer sign testing and the interpretation of many PosSLP-hard numerical tasks.

sentences: The target is unconditional NP-hardness of deciding whether a succinctly represented integer is positive.
The integer is produced by a straight-line program starting from one and using only addition, subtraction and multiplication.
The required reduction must deterministically convert each 3-SAT instance to one such program in polynomial bit time.
Known conditional consequences for randomized algorithms and unconditional hardness of polynomial variants do not supply this reduction.
A complete answer would clarify the discrete complexity of exact sign testing without also requiring a proof that P and NP differ.

cards.definitions: An integer straight-line program consists of an implicit initial value \(b_0=1\) and a finite sequence of \(m\ge0\) instructions. Instruction \(i\), for \(1\le i\le m\), is a triple \((j_i,k_i,\circ_i)\), where \(0\le j_i,k_i<i\) and \(\circ_i\in\{+,-,\times\}\); it defines \(b_i=b_{j_i}\circ_i b_{k_i}\). The output value is the exact integer \(b_m\), with output one when \(m=0\). Values may be negative or zero, and previous values may be reused arbitrarily. The program contains no input variables, divisions, roots, sign tests, branches, loops, separately supplied integer constants or compressed repetition instructions. The program is encoded by a self-delimited binary encoding of \(m\), followed in order by binary predecessor indices and an operation symbol for each instruction. All delimiters use a fixed finite alphabet; standard binary encodings of that alphabet are equivalent within constant factors. The PosSLP language accepts exactly valid encodings with positive output, and rejects valid zero or negative outputs and malformed programs. There is no promise on the sign or magnitude. A 3-CNF input is an explicit finite list of clauses, each containing at most three signed positive binary variable indices, with delimiters; repeated occurrences are allowed. Satisfiability means that some Boolean assignment to all occurring variables makes at least one literal in every clause true. An empty clause is false, and a conjunction with no clauses is true. The source input size \(N\) is its full encoded bit length. The reduction is one finite deterministic program on ordinary finite-alphabet Turing tapes; all reading, writing and index manipulation are charged by ordinary bit steps. Its time bound includes writing the entire straight-line program. It need not output the exponentially long binary expansion of the integer represented by that program. A many-one reduction makes one output instance with the displayed exact equivalence; it is not an adaptive oracle computation or a randomized transformation. Since 3-SAT is NP-complete under these reductions, this specific reduction is equivalent to NP-hardness, meaning that every language accepted by a polynomial-time nondeterministic Turing machine has a polynomial-time many-one reduction to PosSLP.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean that such a deterministic polynomial-time many-one reduction exists, or prove that none exists. A positive answer must specify one reduction and prove its polynomial bit complexity, output validity and exact preservation of both satisfiable and unsatisfiable inputs. It must discharge every assumption needed for correctness. A negative answer must rule out all reductions of this form; failure of one construction does not suffice. NP-hardness is a relationship between decision problems and by itself does not establish \(\mathrm P\ne\mathrm{NP}\), membership in NP, or NP-completeness of PosSLP. A conditional implication about randomized algorithms, an oracle reduction with no conversion to many-one form, or hardness for a polynomial-positivity variant does not meet this specified target.

context_blocks.text: The imported FSTTCS 2024 conclusion asks broadly for unconditional hardness results for PosSLP. To make that direction a single reviewable target, this card selects the concrete NP-hardness question explicitly posed in Bürgisser and Jindal’s earlier SODA 2024 conclusion, and fixes deterministic many-one reductions. It does not equate every possible hardness advance in the source direction with this particular target.

Bürgisser and Jindal show that a randomized polynomial-time algorithm for PosSLP would yield randomized polynomial-time algorithms for all NP languages, assuming an unproved constructive univariate-radical conjecture. This is a conditional complexity consequence and does not itself provide the unconditional deterministic reduction asked for here.

Bläser, Dörfler and Jindal prove unconditional coNP-hardness for a variant whose input represents a univariate polynomial and whose question is positivity at every real point. The quantification over real points changes the problem from testing the sign of one fixed integer. Their conclusion retains unconditional hardness of PosSLP as an open direction.

Miltzow’s March 2026 introduction to real computation again defines PosSLP by constant-one integer straight-line programs and describes the known NP-hardness results as conditional on assumptions that are far from resolved. Its informal discussion is used as a later status check; the complete input and reduction conventions here are stated independently.

cards.title: Hilbert’s tenth problem over the rationals
cards.formal: Does there exist one deterministic Turing machine \(A\) that, on every input encoding a polynomial \(f\in\mathbb Z[X_1,\ldots,X_m]\) with \(m\geq1\), halts and outputs YES exactly when \[\exists(q_1,\ldots,q_m)\in\mathbb Q^m\quad f(q_1,\ldots,q_m)=0,\] and outputs NO otherwise? The number of variables, degree and coefficients are unrestricted finite input data, and there is no time or space efficiency requirement.
cards.definitions:
The field \(\mathbb Q\) consists of exact fractions \(a/b\), with \(a\in\mathbb Z\) and \(b\in\mathbb Z_{>0}\), identifying fractions of the same value; addition and multiplication are the usual exact field operations. A polynomial input describes \(f=\sum_{j=1}^{r}a_j\prod_{i=1}^{m}X_i^{e_{ji}}\), with \(r\geq0\), \(a_j\in\mathbb Z\) and \(e_{ji}\in\mathbb N=\{0,1,2,\ldots\}\). Repeated monomials and zero coefficients are allowed. The empty sum is the zero polynomial and \(X_i^0=1\), including when evaluating at zero. Constants are represented with all exponents zero. A rational zero is any tuple in \(\mathbb Q^m\) giving exact value zero; there is no bound on its numerators or denominators and no integrality restriction.

Use the following explicit effective binary encoding. For \(u\geq0\), let \(\operatorname{code}(u)=1^b0\operatorname{bin}(u+1)\), where the binary expansion has \(b\) bits and no leading zeroes. Encode an integer \(a\) by a sign bit followed by \(\operatorname{code}(|a|)\), with 0 denoting a nonnegative integer and 1 a negative integer; negative zero is invalid. A complete input is \(\operatorname{code}(m)\operatorname{code}(r)\), followed for each \(j=1,\ldots,r\) by the signed code of \(a_j\) and \(\operatorname{code}(e_{j1}),\ldots,\operatorname{code}(e_{jm})\), with no trailing bits. Require \(m\geq1\). The machine halts and outputs NO on every malformed encoding.

The algorithm is a single finite deterministic multitape Turing-machine program with a finite tape alphabet, ordinary discrete transitions and unbounded work tapes, without advice or an oracle. On every input it must halt after finitely many transitions; its running time need not satisfy a polynomial, elementary or other prescribed bound. Its program is independent of \(m,r\), all degrees and all coefficients. The input supplies only the polynomial, without additional height-comparison predicates or a promise of solvability. The question concerns decision of existence; a YES output need not itself contain a rational tuple.
cards.answer_criterion: Provide a complete Lean-verified proof of the existence proposition or its logical negation. A positive answer must specify one effective algorithm and prove termination and exact correctness on every polynomial in the stated domain, together with rejection of invalid input. A negative answer must prove that no such total correct Turing machine exists. Recognizing only polynomials that have a rational zero, excluding polynomial-time algorithms, or proving undecidability for equations with integer-constrained unknowns or added predicates does not establish the required negation. Any conditional result must be identified as conditional and does not alone settle this unconditional question.
cards.why: This asks whether exact rational polynomial constraints admit any general terminating solver. It connects the computability of arithmetic, logical definability and the existence of rational points on algebraic varieties. The unresolved boundary persists despite undecidability over the integers and decidability of polynomial feasibility over the reals and algebraically closed fields; allowing fractions fundamentally changes the permitted witnesses.

importance.reason: A central unsolved decidability problem for an elementary, pervasive constraint language. A resolution would locate the computability boundary for rational polynomial feasibility.

progress.text: The Davis–Putnam–Robinson–Matiyasevich theorem settles the integer-solution problem negatively; rational solvability remains a different decision problem.

Anscombe and coauthors explicitly record Hilbert’s tenth problem over \(\mathbb Q\) as open and review its relation to existential definability.

The height-comparison undecidability paper appears in Journal of Number Theory after its 2023 preprint. It settles an expansion by height predicates, while retaining the ordinary rational question as open.

Poonen’s account reviews the rings-of-integers breakthrough and gives an alternative proof of the relevant Diophantine-definability implication. Its domain restriction remains essential.

cards.status_note: Explicitly open over Q in the cited rational-solvability sources. A bounded primary-source check through 14 September 2026 located no resolution of this exact question. Checked recent results prove undecidability over rings of integers or after adjoining height-comparison predicates; neither settles existence of an unrestricted total rational-solvability decider. This is a formulation and source-scope audit, not an independent verification of every cited proof.

context_blocks.text: Rational tuples can be effectively enumerated and tested by exact substitution, so every YES-instance is eventually recognizable. Such a search does not halt on a NO-instance. The target requires termination in both cases, irrespective of efficiency. A solver for all instances would also allow a rational zero to be found when one exists.

The Davis–Putnam–Robinson–Matiyasevich theorem proves that no general algorithm decides integer solvability. It does not automatically decide the rational problem: \(2X-1=0\) has a rational zero but no integer zero. A rational solver cannot simply be applied to the unchanged integer equation.

Allowing rational coefficients gives the same decision problem, because their denominators can be cleared effectively. Finite systems of equations are also equivalent to a single equation: over \(\mathbb Q\), \(f_1=\cdots=f_r=0\) holds exactly when \(\sum_i f_i^2=0\). More generally, disequalities can be encoded using inverse variables and disjunctions using products. These equivalences identify the problem with decidability of the existential first-order theory of \(\mathbb Q\) in the language of rings.

An existential definition of \(\mathbb Z\) in \(\mathbb Q\) would transfer integer undecidability to this problem. Koenigsmann’s Theorem 1 instead defines \(\mathbb Z\) by a universal formula; its Corollary 3 establishes undecidability for universal-existential sentences. Quantifier alternation is essential to that conclusion: the full first-order theory and the universal-existential fragment are already undecidable, while neither fact settles the purely existential target.

Alpöge, Bhargava, Ho and Shnidman prove undecidability over the ring of integers \(\mathcal O_K\) of every number field \(K\). Here a number field is a finite extension of \(\mathbb Q\), and \(\mathcal O_K\) consists of elements satisfying a monic polynomial with integer coefficients. This restricts the solution domain; in particular \(\mathcal O_{\mathbb Q}=\mathbb Z\), whereas the present question permits every rational number.

Poonen’s account dated 3 July 2026 reviews the recent proof of undecidability for these rings and supplies an alternative definability argument from rank stability. Its Theorem 4.2 concerns definitions over rings of integers. This account does not extend the negative answer to the whole field \(\mathbb Q\).

Garcia-Fritz, Pasten and Vidaux prove undecidability when rational equations are supplemented with finitely many height-comparison conditions. For a rational tuple \(q\), their logarithmic height is \(h(q)=\log\max\{d,|dq_1|,\ldots,|dq_m|\}\), where \(d\geq1\) is its least common denominator, and the added predicates compare heights of tuples. These extra constraints are absent from the target. Their ordinary rational-solvability question remains explicitly open.

cards.title: Polynomial-time, polynomial-factor approximation of Euclidean SVP
cards.formal:
Do there exist a real constant \(C>0\), a real constant \(K>0\), an integer \(k\geq1\), and one uniform classical randomized algorithm \(A\) such that for every pair of integers \(d\geq n\geq1\) and every explicitly encoded \(B\in\mathbb Q^{d\times n}\) with linearly independent columns, every run halts in at most \(K(N+1)^k\) bit operations and returns a nonzero \(z\in\mathbb Z^n\), with
\[\Pr\!\left[\|Bz\|_2\leq n^C\lambda_1(L(B))\right]\geq\frac23?\]
The input length \(N\) includes all matrix entries. The lattice is \(L(B)=\{Bz:z\in\mathbb Z^n\}\), and \(\lambda_1\) is its shortest nonzero Euclidean length. Randomness consists of independent fair bits on that fixed input. The program and all constants are chosen once, before any input.
cards.definitions:
The input contains \(d,n\) and all \(dn\) rational entries in row-major order. To fix a binary encoding, let \(b(t)\) be the ordinary binary expansion of a nonnegative integer \(t\), using the one-bit string \(0\) for zero, and put \(E(t)=1^{|b(t)|}0b(t)\). Dimensions use \(E(d),E(n)\). A rational number is encoded by a sign bit followed by \(E(|a|)E(q)\), where it equals \(a/q\), \(q>0\), and \(\gcd(|a|,q)=1\); zero has positive sign and denominator one. There are exactly \(dn\) entries and no trailing bits. Valid inputs satisfy \(d\geq n\geq1\) and column independence over \(\mathbb Q\). The total number of encoded bits is \(N\). The polynomial clock applies on every binary input; behavior and output on malformed or dependent-basis inputs are otherwise unrestricted.

The Euclidean norm of \(v\in\mathbb R^d\) is \(\|v\|_2=(\sum_{i=1}^d v_i^2)^{1/2}\). The lattice consists of all integer combinations of the columns, with its usual embedding in \(\mathbb R^d\). Independence makes \(z\mapsto Bz\) injective and makes \(L(B)\) discrete in its real span. Thus
\[\lambda_1(L(B))=\min_{z\in\mathbb Z^n\setminus\{0\}}\|Bz\|_2>0\]
is attained. No uniqueness of the shortest vector up to sign is assumed. The algorithm returns the coefficient vector: its \(n\) signed integer coordinates use a sign bit and \(E\) of the absolute value, with positive sign for zero. It must return a valid nonzero vector on every run on a valid input. An unsuccessful run may exceed the norm bound, but may not output zero, fail to halt or omit the vector. The squared norm can equivalently be used in the displayed guarantee with squared factor \(n^{2C}\).

Use one probabilistic multitape Turing machine with a finite description independent of all input parameters. Its tapes have a fixed finite alphabet encoding bits. Each transition can read and write only a fixed number of cells and move each head by at most one cell. An additional instruction obtains one fresh independent fair bit at unit cost. This describes ordinary uniform classical bit computation, with no advice, oracle, quantum operations, uncharged preprocessing or unit-cost arithmetic on unbounded integers. All reading, writing, arithmetic, memory manipulation and random-bit generation count toward the bound. The output uses the integer encoding specified above, and every bit written is charged.

For a given valid input, randomness is the product measure of independent uniform bits on an infinite random tape; the polynomial clock ensures that only finitely many are read. The success event is the displayed norm inequality, separately for every input. All runs, including those outside that event, must return a valid nonzero integer vector within the same clock. A deterministic algorithm is allowed as the special case that uses no random bits. Expected polynomial time alone is not the stated requirement.

The quantifier order is \(\exists C,K,k,A\;\forall d,n,B\), with both the probability guarantee and the all-run clock imposed after choosing the input. In particular, \(C\) may be large but must be fixed. The factor is \(n^C\), determined by lattice rank; it is not a polynomial in the ambient dimension, the coefficient magnitude or the input bit length. In rank one it is exactly one. There is no input-distribution, shortest-vector uniqueness, ideal-lattice, conditioning, modular or basis-quality promise. The problem concerns arbitrary finite rational bases, including ones with very large coefficients.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete, mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of the existence of one algorithm and constants meeting every requirement, or of the logical negation of that existence statement. A negative answer must rule out every fixed exponent \(C>0\) and every permitted randomized polynomial-time algorithm, rather than only a deterministic algorithm or a selected small approximation factor. A positive answer must establish the actual nonzero-vector output, success on each basis and all-run bit clock, including coefficient and output lengths. A conditional complexity lower bound gives only a conditional conclusion unless its assumption is proved. A gap-decision certificate, a factor depending without a rank bound on the input basis, a uniqueness-promised result, an oracle-call bound excluding subroutine time, or a quantum algorithm alone does not settle this classical search target. No additional numerical tolerance weakens this exact existence proposition.
cards.why: This asks whether efficient classical computation can find short vectors in every Euclidean lattice with a loss bounded by one fixed power of rank. The gap between known general algorithms and this regime is a basic obstacle in lattice complexity. Resolving it would clarify the relation between lattice geometry, efficient approximation and worst-case hardness assumptions used in cryptography; its consequences for particular schemes still depend on the exact problem and parameters.

progress.text: LLL establishes polynomial-time reduction with an exponential-in-rank short-vector guarantee.
Aharonov–Regev give polynomial certificates on both sides of the specified square-root-rank gap-decision problem.
Haviv–Regev obtain nearly polynomial approximation hardness under explicitly randomized complexity assumptions.
Bennett’s survey separates general polynomial-time approximation, search-to-decision questions and cryptographic parameter regimes.
Shenoy’s article is published with a basis-dependent approximation expression; the checked theorem does not supply a uniform rank-polynomial bound.
The checked Hair–Sahai revision gives deterministic subexponential reductions and a subpolynomial approximation gap under its stated hardness assumption.

Wan’s major revision replaces a false premise in its first version and retains fixed-factor claims while dropping the earlier dimension-dependent claims.

cards.status_note: Checked on 14 September 2026. The survey’s unrestricted classical polynomial-factor search gap remains the saved target. The checked Shenoy expression is basis-dependent, PotBKZ counts costly enumeration calls, and the 2026 hardness results concern smaller factors, explicit assumptions or a different oracle model. Wan’s 8 September revision expressly withdraws its first version’s dimension-dependent claims. context_blocks.text: For integer \(M\geq1\), the basis columns \((M,1)\) and \((M+1,1)\) are both long but their lattice contains \((1,0)\). Thus input column lengths alone do not determine the shortest lattice length. More generally, the same lattice has many bases, and the guarantee must be relative to its intrinsic minimum on every supplied basis.

With its standard parameter, LLL gives a nonzero vector of length at most \(2^{(n-1)/2}\lambda_1\) in polynomial bit time. The original paper separately controls the number of arithmetic operations and the binary lengths of their operands. Its approximation factor is exponential in rank even though the running time is polynomial; a runtime statement alone does not specify the quality of the vector.

Bennett’s 2023 survey summarizes improved general polynomial-time guarantees with factor \(2^{O(n\log\log n/\log n)}\). This established upper guarantee is still much larger than any fixed polynomial in rank. It does not prove that every algorithm must lose that much: whether the guarantee can be improved to some \(n^C\) is the existence question on this card.

Haviv and Regev prove hardness at factors \(2^{(\log n)^{1-\varepsilon}}\), for fixed \(0<\varepsilon<1\), unless NP has one-sided-error randomized quasipolynomial-time algorithms. Under the stronger randomized subexponential-time assumption they obtain \(n^{c/\log\log n}\) for some fixed \(c>0\). Both factors are subpolynomial: for every fixed \(C>0\), they eventually lie below \(n^C\). Their theorem therefore does not rule out the looser approximation asked for here. The randomness assumptions are part of the result.

For \(\gamma\geq1\), GapSVP asks whether \(\lambda_1\leq r\) or \(\lambda_1>\gamma r\), promised one of those alternatives and given \(r>0\). Aharonov and Regev place this decision problem, for some factor \(\gamma=c\sqrt n\), in \(\mathrm{NP}\cap\mathrm{coNP}\): each promised answer has a polynomial-length certificate verifiable in polynomial time. This is not a polynomial-time method of finding the requested vector. Their full Corollary 1.2 specifies a constant \(c\); it does not assert the result for every smaller factor hidden in big-O notation.

Bennett’s separate search-to-decision question underscores that approximate search SVP, gap decision, unique-SVP and shortest-independent-vectors problems must be distinguished. Cryptographic worst-case-to-average-case reductions concern specified variants at specified approximation and noise parameters. An algorithm here would change the search-SVP landscape; a security reduction alone does not make every cryptographic problem equivalent to it.

Shenoy’s 2024 article advertises an approximation expressed through \(1/(1-\delta)\). In the checked accepted manuscript, Theorem IV.2 defines \(\delta\) from the actual basis, and Corollary IV.3 retains that dependence in a squared-length bound. Merely knowing \(0\leq\delta<1\) supplies no fixed rank-polynomial upper bound on the factor. The manuscript is not counted as a solution of this card; its general convergence claim was not independently verified.

Sato and Yasuda’s May 2026 theorem bounds the number of calls to PotENUM by a quantity polynomial in rank and input coefficient bit length for a fixed reduction parameter. The full Theorem 2 and Remark 2 separately retain an exponential-in-blocksize enumeration factor and the cost of processing each enumeration node. A polynomial number of calls is therefore not a polynomial total bit-time guarantee with arbitrary blocksize.

Hair and Sahai’s April 2026 revision gives a deterministic subexponential-time reduction from satisfiability to Euclidean GapSVP with a subpolynomial approximation gap. Its deterministic hardness conclusion assumes that NP is not contained in the intersection of deterministic time classes \(\operatorname{DTIME}(\exp(m^\eta))\) over all fixed \(\eta>0\), where \(m\) is the source input length. A deterministic reduction does not remove the stated complexity assumption, nor automatically exclude bounded-error randomized algorithms under that same deterministic assumption.

Hirahara and Ogitsuka’s paper, published at RANDOM on September 9, 2026, obtains deterministic constant-factor Euclidean hardness under an explicit lower-bound assumption against nondeterministic circuits. Its parameterized results use another resource measure. Wan’s September 8 revision separately claims unconditional deterministic reductions for every fixed constant factor, but explicitly removes its first version’s dimension-dependent claims after identifying a false tensor-product premise. Neither statement gives unconditional impossibility for all randomized algorithms and all polynomial factors. The new proofs were not independently verified.

The September Wan revision is the version used here: its Theorem 1.2 concerns fixed constant factors, and its introduction expressly withdraws the earlier dimension-dependent consequences. An older abstract or first-version summary must not be used to restore those withdrawn consequences.

Joglekar, Shinde and Agarkar’s September 9 revision concerns a generic metric supplied through a black-box distance oracle, for small constant approximation factors. Its adversary is permitted to perturb the metric. That is distinct from the explicit rational basis and fixed Euclidean norm on this card, and is not an unconditional lower bound for this target.

A classical algorithm satisfying this card also qualifies for the quantum approximation target TCS-7234. The converse is not automatic. Exact quantum search is separately retained as TCS-7169. The present target permits any fixed approximation exponent, rather than asking to optimize that exponent or requiring exact shortest-vector recovery.

This card asks whether one uniform classical randomized algorithm can approximate that length within some fixed power of the rank on every basis.

Known general upper guarantees, conditional hardness at smaller factors and basis-dependent approximation expressions do not settle this target.
The September 2026 review retains the distinctions between search and decision, classical and quantum computation, and current theorems and withdrawn claims.
