cards.title: Integer factorization in randomized polynomial time
cards.formal: Do there exist integers \(C\ge1,c\ge0\) and one uniform classical randomized algorithm A such that, for every positive integer N in binary, A outputs the complete prime factorization of N with probability at least \(2/3\), and for every random-bit sequence halts within \(C(n+1)^c\) bit steps, where \(n=\lfloor\log_2 N\rfloor+1\)? The same A, C and c must work for all N.
cards.definitions: The input is the ordinary base-two representation of N, with no leading zeroes; its length n counts bits, not the numerical value of N. The one-character string 1 represents N=1. The empty string and all strings beginning with 0 are invalid and must be rejected on every random-bit sequence within the same polynomial bound in their length. For \(N\ge2\), the unique correct factorization is the finite list \((p_1,e_1),\ldots,(p_r,e_r)\), where \(p_1<\cdots<p_r\) are primes, each \(e_i\) is a positive integer, and \(N=\prod_{i=1}^r p_i^{e_i}\). A prime is an integer at least 2 whose only positive divisors are 1 and itself. The correct list for N=1 is empty. To fix a binary output format, encode a nonnegative integer a by \(\operatorname{code}(a)=1^b0\) followed by the b-bit binary representation of a+1, where \(b=\lfloor\log_2(a+1)\rfloor+1\). A successful output is 1 followed by code(r) and then code(p_i), code(e_i) for i in increasing order, with no other bits; the single bit 0 is the failure or invalid-input symbol. A is a probabilistic multitape Turing machine with one finite program, a fixed finite number of tapes and fixed finite alphabets. It has a read-only input tape and initially blank work and output tapes; a transition accesses only cells at the heads and moves each head by at most one cell. It may request one new independent fair bit at a transition. The probability space is \(\{0,1\}^{\mathbb N}\) with independent uniform coordinates, and the probability guarantee is separate for every fixed input N. The runtime is the total transition count, including all input access, random-bit requests, arithmetic and output writing. Every random-bit sequence obeys the clock; thus only finitely many random bits affect each run. A malformed factor list, an incorrect list and the failure symbol all count as failure on a positive input. The algorithm receives no promise that N is semiprime or belongs to a particular distribution, no advice or precomputed factors, no order-finding or factoring oracle, and no quantum or unit-cost operations on unbounded integers. The task is full factorization, not merely deciding whether N is prime.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof that one algorithm and constants satisfy the all-input success guarantee and the all-random-sequences polynomial clock, or prove that no such algorithm and constants exist. A negative proof must exclude arbitrary uniform classical randomized algorithms with arbitrary fixed polynomial exponents; excluding deterministic algorithms alone does not suffice. For the affirmative answer, correctness includes every prime base, multiplicity, ordering and product in the complete output. A heuristic complexity estimate, a guarantee for sampled or restricted inputs, or a quantum algorithm does not meet the stated classical worst-case target.
cards.why: Integer factorization is a basic inverse problem in arithmetic and a central test case for the potential power of quantum computation. Its classical complexity has direct consequences for factoring-based cryptography and for algorithms that currently require access to a factoring subroutine.

importance.reason: A defining open problem of computational number theory, with broad consequences for cryptography, arithmetic algorithms, and classical-versus-quantum computation.

progress.text: Shor establishes polynomial-time quantum factorization. The full paper’s January 1996 revision explicitly uses quantum computation, which is outside the classical randomized machine model of this card.
Agrawal, Kayal and Saxena publish deterministic polynomial-time primality testing. This makes prime-factor lists efficiently checkable but does not provide their discovery.

Harvey and Hittmeir prove complete deterministic factorization in \(O(N^{1/5}(\log N)^{16/5}/(\log\log N)^{3/5})\) bit operations as N tends to infinity. The 2022 journal result improves a logarithmic factor while retaining an exponential dependence on binary input length.

Harvey and Hittmeir’s revision removes the previous power-of-N lower restriction on the large-order threshold and slightly improves its runtime factor. Theorem 1.1 may return a large-order element instead of a divisor, and Section 1.1 still explicitly identifies polynomial-time factoring as unknown.

cards.status_note: The undated source survey explicitly asks for randomized polynomial-time factoring, and Harvey–Hittmeir Section 1.1 in the 5 June 2026 revision confirms the absence of a known polynomial-time factoring algorithm even with probabilistic methods. Bounded later-work searches on 14 September 2026 found no verified resolution. The cited heuristic estimate and quantum result are not certified as solutions in this classical model, and new proof claims were not independently verified.

context_blocks.text: Multiplying the prime factors is easy, and the factors themselves fit in a polynomial-size output. Discovering them is the unresolved step. Trial division up to \(\sqrt{N}\) is polynomial in the number’s value but exponential in its binary input length. The distinction between N and log N is essential even when a newer algorithm improves the power of N substantially.

Primality testing and factorization are different tasks. The Agrawal–Kayal–Saxena algorithm decides in deterministic polynomial time whether a number is prime, without necessarily exhibiting a divisor when the answer is composite. It also makes a proposed full factorization efficiently checkable: verify that every listed base is prime and that the product is N.

Efficient verification makes the two common randomized formulations equivalent in existence: bounded-error polynomial worst-case time, and always-correct polynomial expected time with possible nontermination only on a probability-zero set of random tapes. This equivalence uses an all-input expected bound and fresh independent randomness, and the expected-time formulation alone does not give a worst-case clock on each run. The card chooses the bounded-clock formulation to state the success event without any runtime averaging.

The general number field sieve has the familiar heuristic expected-time estimate \(\exp (((64/9)^{1/3}+o(1))(\ln  N)^{1/3}(\ln  \ln  N)^{2/3})\). This is subexponential but still superpolynomial in the bit length. Rigorous deterministic bounds of \(N^{1/5+o(1)}\) make a different tradeoff and remain exponential in that length. Neither bound is a proof that faster classical factoring is impossible.
Shor’s quantum algorithm factors in polynomial time, using quantum order finding. It provides an upper bound in the quantum model and does not establish a classical lower bound.

The newer deterministic large-order theorem has a different output contract: it may produce a certified high-order group element instead of a divisor. Even when the requested order threshold is small and the subroutine is fast, that output alternative does not amount to a complete factorization. Its usefulness within factoring algorithms must not be mistaken for a solution of the entire factoring problem.

A classical polynomial-time factoring algorithm would undermine the corresponding cryptographic hardness assumptions. Neither the efficiency of multiplication nor a conjectured separation \(\mathrm P\ne\mathrm{NP}\) provides a proved classical factoring lower bound. Factoring and inverting RSA are also distinct problems; the historical source explains that the reverse general reduction is unknown.

cards.title: Prime-field discrete logarithms in randomized polynomial time
cards.formal: Does there exist one uniform classical probabilistic multitape Turing machine \(A\), and integers \(C,c\ge1\), such that \(A\) halts within \(C(L+1)^c\) steps on every binary input of length \(L\) and every sequence of its random bits, and has the following correctness property? For every prime \(p\), every generator \(g\) of the multiplicative group \(\mathbb F_p^{\times}\), and every \(h\in\mathbb F_p^{\times}\), given the binary encoding of \((p,g,h)\) specified below, it outputs the unique integer \(x\in\{0,\ldots,p-2\}\) satisfying \(g^x\equiv h\pmod p\) with probability at least \(2/3\).
cards.definitions: The field \(\mathbb F_p\) consists of residues \(\{0,\ldots,p-1\}\) with addition and multiplication modulo the prime \(p\). Its multiplicative group \(\mathbb F_p^{\times}\) is \(\{1,\ldots,p-1\}\) with multiplication modulo \(p\). The promise that \(g\) is a generator means that \(g^0,g^1,\ldots,g^{p-2}\), reduced modulo \(p\), list these \(p-1\) residues without repetition; hence the requested exponent exists and is unique. Each input integer is represented by its ordinary base-two expansion \(\operatorname{bin}(a)\), without leading zeros and with \(\operatorname{bin}(0)=0\). Writing \(\ell(a)=|\operatorname{bin}(a)|\), set \(\operatorname{code}(a)=1^{\ell(a)}0\operatorname{bin}(a)\). The complete input is \(\operatorname{code}(p)\operatorname{code}(g)\operatorname{code}(h)\), with \(p\) prime and \(1\le g,h<p\). Its length \(L=2(\ell(p)+\ell(g)+\ell(h))+3\) is \(\Theta(\log_2 p)\) on promised inputs. A successful output is exactly \(\operatorname{bin}(x)\); any different output or a designated failure symbol is unsuccessful. For \(p=2\), the sole promised pair is \(g=h=1\) and the answer is \(x=0\). The machine has a fixed finite program, fixed finite alphabets, a read-only input tape, finitely many work tapes and an output tape; each transition costs one step, and any random transition reads one fresh independent fair bit. The time bound includes input processing, bit arithmetic, random-bit generation, output and all preprocessing. The same \(A,C,c\) work for every input, with no advice, oracle, precomputed table or supplied factorization of \(p-1\). Arbitrary classical computations on the concrete binary residues are permitted, not just generic group operations. Malformed encodings may be rejected as failure; on well-formed triples outside the mathematical promise, only the global time bound is required. The success guarantee is separately for each promised triple, over the machine’s coins, not over a distribution of primes or targets. The question concerns the multiplicative group of a prime field; additive groups, extension fields and elliptic-curve groups are different models.
cards.answer_criterion: Supply a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of existence of \(A,C,c\) with both the all-input, all-random-sequence time bound and the per-promised-input success guarantee, or a Lean-checked proof that no such triple exists. Equivalently, a negative answer must prove that every machine obeying some global polynomial clock has a promised input on which its probability of outputting the required exponent is less than \(2/3\). Failure of a particular algorithm, an average-case conjecture for a selected prime distribution, or a lower bound restricted to generic group operations does not establish this negation. A quantum algorithm, success only for selected prime families, or a bound polynomial in \(p\) rather than its bit length does not meet the positive target.
cards.why: Discrete logarithms expose a basic gap between efficient modular exponentiation and our ability to invert it. A uniform classical polynomial-time solver would defeat the corresponding finite-field discrete-logarithm assumptions and solve computational Diffie–Hellman in this setting. An unrestricted impossibility proof would establish a fundamental classical lower bound for a concrete arithmetic problem already solvable in quantum polynomial time.

importance.reason: One of the principal unresolved number-theoretic algorithmic problems, with direct connections to cryptography, index calculus, and quantum speedups.

progress.text: Prime-field NFS methods achieve heuristic subexponential estimates, described precisely in the cited 2008 survey. Those historical estimates are distinct from proven expected-time bounds and from a lower bound against arbitrary algorithms.
Shor supplies a quantum polynomial-time discrete-logarithm algorithm; §6 of the inspected manuscript uses the same prime-field and supplied-generator mathematical problem.
Shoup’s Theorem 1 proves a generic-encoding lower bound parameterized by the largest prime divisor of the group order. It does not apply to unrestricted computation on concrete residues.

Kleinjung and Wesolowski’s fixed-characteristic theorem appears in the inspected 18 November 2019 version and the 2022 JAMS article. The expected-time bound and extension-degree parameter do not give a prime-field polynomial-bit algorithm.

Discrete Logarithm Factory analyzes shared preprocessing for a constant proportion of fields of a given approximate size and degree, with individual-target costs separated. Its publisher abstract and full introduction were checked.

Lido’s Finite Fields and Their Applications article concerns small characteristic. The inspected preprint’s Theorem 1.1 requires \(d>p\), so its quasipolynomial guarantee does not settle the prime-field question.

Wu and coauthors explicitly assume worst-case classical hardness of prime-field DLP in a new quantum-complexity preprint. Version 1 remains the sole version on 14 September; its conditional reduction is not a resolution of the assumption.

cards.status_note: The original number-theory survey leaves the classical prime-field problem open. The same generator-input problem is explicitly assumed classically hard in Wu et al., arXiv:2608.15545v1 of 16 August 2026, still its sole version on 14 September. The reviewed 2026 small-characteristic publication and quantum results do not resolve this target. A bounded later-work search found no matching classical polynomial-time solution or unrestricted impossibility proof; source proofs and new conditional reductions were not independently certified.

context_blocks.text: For a supplied \(g\) and exponent \(x\), modular exponentiation takes time polynomial in their bit lengths. Inverting this operation would reveal the shared value \(g^{ab}\) from \(g,g^a,g^b\) in the corresponding Diffie–Hellman setting. This implication does not identify discrete-logarithm hardness with every Diffie–Hellman or encryption-security assumption. The card asks a worst-case algorithmic question; a negative answer alone does not prove average-case hardness for a cryptographic parameter distribution.

Candidate answers are efficiently verifiable by checking \(0\le x\le p-2\) and \(g^x\equiv h\pmod p\). Thus, as an elementary consequence of verification, existence of the stated bounded-error algorithm is equivalent to existence of a Las Vegas solver that is never wrong and has a uniform polynomial expected running-time bound on every promised input. Independent verified repetition has bounded expected cost in one direction; truncation at three times an expected-time bound gives success at least \(2/3\) by Markov’s inequality in the other. This does not require every run of a Las Vegas solver to terminate, only probability-one termination and finite expected cost.

Schirokauer’s survey gives a conjectured expected-time NFS bound of the form \(\exp(O((\ln p)^{1/3}(\ln\ln p)^{2/3}))\) in the prime-field regime. This is a heuristic complexity analysis, not an unconditional polynomial-time theorem or an unrestricted lower bound. The displayed scale grows faster than every fixed power of \(\log p\). The 2024 Discrete Logarithm Factory paper separately studies costs shared across fields and targets; any such preprocessing must still fit this card’s complete single-input budget.

Shoup’s lower bound concerns randomly encoded group elements. If \(q\) is the largest prime divisor of a cyclic group’s order, constant success requires \(\Omega(\sqrt q)\) generic group operations in that model. His parameter \(q\) is not the field characteristic \(p\); for this card the group order is \(p-1\). The theorem averages over the random encoding, exponent and algorithm coins. It does not exclude algorithms that use the actual integer residues and their arithmetic structure.

Kleinjung and Wesolowski’s Theorem 1.1 gives expected time \((p d)^{2\log_2 d+O(1)}\) for the multiplicative group of \(\mathbb F_{p^d}\). For fixed \(p\) and growing extension degree \(d\), this is quasipolynomial in the input size. Substituting \(d=1\) supplies at most a polynomial-in-\(p\) guarantee, not the requested polynomial in \(\log p\). The occurrence of the product \(p d\) in their bound must not be confused with the field order \(p^d\).

Lido’s paper, published in March 2026, also proves a quasipolynomial expected-time theorem in small characteristic. In the inspected version its hypothesis is explicitly \(d>p\) for a field of size \(p^d\), excluding the growing prime-field family with \(d=1\). The source’s field-regime restriction remains part of the theorem even though all these problems share the name discrete logarithm.

Shor’s polynomial-time algorithm uses quantum computation. Wu and coauthors’ August 2026 preprint uses the same prime-field generator-input problem as an explicit classical-hardness assumption for a claim about estimating outputs of adaptive shallow quantum circuits. That assumption is not a proved classical lower bound; the reduction and its quantum resource claims were not independently verified in this review.

cards.title: Quantum polynomial-factor approximation of Euclidean SVP
cards.formal:
Do there exist a real constant \(C>0\), an integer \(k\geq1\), a real constant \(K>0\), and one uniform quantum algorithm \(A\) with the following property? For every pair of integers \(d\geq n\geq1\) and every explicitly given matrix \(B\in\mathbb Q^{d\times n}\) with linearly independent columns, the algorithm terminates within \(K(N+1)^k\) charged operations on every execution and outputs a nonzero integer vector \(z\in\mathbb Z^n\), with
\[\Pr\!\left[\|Bz\|_2\leq n^C\lambda_1(L(B))\right]\geq\frac23.\]
Here \(N\) is the full binary input length, \(L(B)=\{Bz:z\in\mathbb Z^n\}\), and \(\lambda_1(L(B))\) is the length of its shortest nonzero vector. The probability is over the computation’s measurement outcomes on this fixed classical input. All constants and the program are chosen before the input; the approximation exponent depends on neither rank nor coefficient size.
cards.definitions:
The input contains \(d,n\) and all \(dn\) rational entries in row-major order. To fix a binary encoding, let \(b(t)\) be the ordinary binary expansion of a nonnegative integer \(t\), using the one-bit string \(0\) for zero, and put \(E(t)=1^{|b(t)|}0b(t)\). Dimensions use \(E(d),E(n)\). A rational number is encoded by a sign bit followed by \(E(|a|)E(q)\), where it equals \(a/q\), \(q>0\), and \(\gcd(|a|,q)=1\); zero has positive sign and denominator one. There are exactly \(dn\) entries and no trailing bits. Valid inputs satisfy \(d\geq n\geq1\) and column independence over \(\mathbb Q\). The total number of encoded bits is \(N\). The polynomial clock applies on every binary input; behavior and output on malformed or dependent-basis inputs are otherwise unrestricted.

The Euclidean norm of \(v\in\mathbb R^d\) is \(\|v\|_2=(\sum_{i=1}^d v_i^2)^{1/2}\). The lattice consists of all integer combinations of the columns, with its usual embedding in \(\mathbb R^d\). Independence makes \(z\mapsto Bz\) injective and makes \(L(B)\) discrete in its real span. Thus
\[\lambda_1(L(B))=\min_{z\in\mathbb Z^n\setminus\{0\}}\|Bz\|_2>0\]
is attained. No uniqueness of the shortest vector up to sign is assumed. The algorithm returns the coefficient vector: its \(n\) signed integer coordinates use a sign bit and \(E\) of the absolute value, with positive sign for zero. It must return a valid nonzero vector on every execution on a valid input. An unsuccessful execution may exceed the norm bound, but may not output zero, fail to halt or omit the vector. The squared norm can equivalently be used in the displayed guarantee with squared factor \(n^{2C}\).

A uniform quantum algorithm means one finite deterministic multitape Turing-machine controller with classical input, work and output tapes and a collection of initially zero qubits. In addition to ordinary bit-machine steps, it may apply a gate from \(\{H,T,\mathrm{CNOT}\}\) to explicitly addressed qubits, or measure an addressed qubit in the computational basis and receive its classical result. Qubit indices are written in binary on control tapes; writing and processing them take ordinary charged steps. Initializing a fresh zero qubit is charged, so the number of qubits is also polynomially bounded. The input is supplied as classical bits, not as a quantum state-preparation oracle. Classical input bits may be transferred to qubits through charged computation.

For computational basis states \(|0\rangle,|1\rangle\), the gates are
\[H=\frac1{\sqrt2}\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\1&-1\end{pmatrix},\qquad
T=\operatorname{diag}(1,e^{i\pi/4}),\qquad
\mathrm{CNOT}|a,b\rangle=|a,a\mathbin\oplus b\rangle,\]
where \(a,b\in\{0,1\}\) and \(\oplus\) is addition modulo two. A register of \(q\) qubits has state a unit vector in \((\mathbb C^2)^{\otimes q}\). A gate acts on its addressed factors and as the identity elsewhere. Measurement outcome \(a\) has probability equal to the squared norm of the projection onto the subspace whose measured bit is \(a\), after which the state is that normalized projection. Classical control may depend on all earlier outcomes. Probabilities of complete executions are defined by these conditional Born probabilities. Fair classical random bits can be generated by a Hadamard gate followed by measurement; their cost is included.

Each classical Turing-machine step, gate, initialization, measurement and output-bit write costs one operation; any fixed overlap in bookkeeping changes only the constant \(K\). The stated bound holds on every possible measurement branch, including unsuccessful branches. There is no quantum advice, computational oracle, free input oracle, postselection on rare outcomes or arbitrary-precision unit-cost arithmetic. The program is independent of input length and of the particular basis. All classical control, including input parsing and generation of the quantum operations, contributes to the same bound.

The approximation parameter is the rank \(n\), not the ambient dimension \(d\) or the bit length \(N\). In rank one the factor is exactly one. Coefficients may have arbitrary binary length, subject only to being part of the input. There is no promised gap between successive vector lengths, random input distribution, special ring structure, modular form or bound on the basis conditioning. Success is required separately on every valid basis, not on average over bases.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete, mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of the existence of one algorithm and fixed constants \(C,K,k\) satisfying the entire statement, or of its logical negation. A negative answer must rule out every constant polynomial approximation factor and every uniform quantum algorithm with any fixed polynomial clock in the full bit length; an impossibility for one exponent, one circuit family, one oracle model or classical algorithms alone is insufficient. A valid positive answer must prove the actual nonzero-vector output and success probability on all valid inputs, with every-execution cost including classical processing. A decision algorithm for a length threshold, an algorithm assuming a unique shortest direction, a conditional cryptanalytic reduction, or a numerical experiment is not by itself an answer. Conditional results establish only their conditional conclusions unless the additional assumptions are proved. This is an exact existence proposition; the benchmark’s numerical tolerance does not weaken its approximation or probability requirements.
cards.why: This isolates whether quantum computation changes the polynomial-time approximation boundary for unrestricted Euclidean lattice search. A positive answer would improve the guarantee from a superpolynomial loss to one fixed power of rank on every lattice. A negative answer would establish an unconditional limitation on general quantum computation, far beyond the failure of any particular quantum lattice algorithm. Its cryptographic implications depend on the exact lattice task and approximation exponent.

context_blocks.text: Long basis vectors need not imply a large lattice minimum. The two columns \((M,1)\) and \((M+1,1)\), with integer \(M\geq1\), generate a lattice containing \((1,0)\), although both input columns are long. The objective concerns all nonzero integer combinations. It differs from finding the shortest input column and from minimizing over real coefficients, where arbitrarily small nonzero combinations exist.

Bennett’s survey defines approximate search SVP by the same multiplicative comparison with \(\lambda_1\). It records the classical polynomial-time LLL guarantee \(2^{O(n)}\). The factor \(n^C\) requested here is a much stronger bound for every fixed \(C\), while allowing any such constant is a substantial relaxation of exact shortest-vector search. Small-dimensional experiments or guarantees for a particular basis family do not cover this quantifier order.

The decision problem \(\gamma\)-GapSVP is given a basis and a threshold \(r>0\), with a promise of either \(\lambda_1\leq r\) or \(\lambda_1>\gamma r\), and asks which case holds. It does not output a vector. Bennett’s §4.2 explicitly records the unresolved general search-to-decision connection with polynomially controlled approximation. This card does not silently identify those two tasks. Likewise, unique-SVP assumes that every vector linearly independent of a shortest vector is longer by a promised factor; unrestricted SVP has no such promise.

Regev’s original worst-case-to-average-case theorem says that an efficient solver for specified Learning With Errors parameters yields quantum algorithms for the stated GapSVP and shortest-independent-vectors tasks. Learning With Errors supplies random linear equations with a controlled noise distribution; it is not the classical arbitrary-basis input specified here. The direction, task and parameter losses of a reduction matter. In particular, this theorem is not an unrestricted equivalence between polynomial-factor search SVP and every LWE family.

The Brakerski–Kirshanova–Stehlé–Wen paper explicitly describes Regev’s dihedral-coset reduction as a reduction for unique-SVP, then establishes an LWE connection with extrapolated dihedral cosets under parameter losses. Such coset problems supply particular quantum samples as input. Their efficient solution is a separate claim whose consequences for an arbitrary classical basis require a proved reduction with the appropriate target.

The April 2024 Chen manuscript initially claimed new polynomial-time quantum lattice and LWE algorithms. Its archive entry includes an explicit April 18 author correction: a bug in Step 9 invalidates the stated polynomial-modulus LWE claim, with no repair then known. The surviving old abstract is therefore not evidence of a verified breakthrough.

Zhang’s May 14, 2026 revision analyzes a conditional replacement for part of that procedure. Its current statement requires additional front-end conditions and access to a run-dependent offset residue; the introduction explicitly says the resulting LWE conclusion is conditional. These assumptions do not form a complete arbitrary-basis algorithm in the model of this card. Earlier stronger-looking descriptions are not substituted for the latest revision.

Simon’s ePrint 2026/1591, first posted August 3 and last revised August 17, explicitly advertises a polynomial-time dihedral-coset algorithm and polynomial-factor SVP consequences. The archive also records a correction to the first draft’s Lemma 3 and the author’s acknowledgment of a subsequent refutation. The available abstract alone does not verify the asserted unrestricted search consequence or its bit-complexity conventions. The claim is recorded as disputed, not as a resolution.

Gupte, Ragavan and Zhandry’s response, revised September 1, states that Simon’s August 11 algorithm cannot recover even the secret’s least-significant bit with nonnegligible advantage. They provide accompanying Lean 4 code. The repository describes precise rounding and register conventions, and a theorem about the specified bit-output procedure and controllers of its coarse outcomes; it explicitly distinguishes this from a formalization of the full-secret recursion. This audit read those scope declarations but did not build or independently verify the proofs, and could not retrieve either ePrint PDF. The rebuttal is evidence against that proposed algorithm, not a lower bound against all algorithms on this card.

The accompanying repository explicitly states that its full-secret solver recursion is not formalized and that its controller theorem observes prescribed restart/bit outcomes rather than every internal measurement record. Those declared limits must be retained when describing what has been machine checked by its authors.

A classical solution of TCS-6667 with the matching factor would also solve this quantum existence target, and an exact quantum solution of TCS-7169 would supply the stronger approximation guarantee. Neither implication reverses automatically. An algorithm here would be a major lattice-complexity advance, but declaring a particular cryptosystem broken would require checking its problem variant, parameters and reductions.

cards.title: Exact Euclidean SVP in single-exponential time and polynomial space
cards.formal: Do absolute constants \(C,d>0\) and a randomized classical algorithm exist that, given any rational rank-n lattice basis B of bit length L, find a shortest nonzero Euclidean lattice vector with probability at least \(2/3\) using at most \(2^{Cn}\mathrm{L}^{d}\) bit operations and \(\mathrm{L}^{d}\) bits of working space?
cards.definitions: The input is \(B\in Q^{m\times n}\), with \(m\ge n\ge 1\) and linearly independent columns; each rational entry is encoded by a signed binary numerator and a positive binary denominator. L includes the matrix dimensions and all entry encodings. The lattice is \(\Lambda (B)=\{Bz:z\in Z^{n}\}\), and \(\lambda _{1}(\Lambda )=\min\)_{\(z\in Z^{n}\)\{0}}\(\Vert Bz\Vert _{2}\), with the ordinary Euclidean norm in \(R^{m}\). Output a nonzero integer coordinate vector z satisfying \(\Vert Bz\Vert _{2}=\lambda _{1}(\Lambda )\); any minimizer is acceptable. The algorithm is a uniform probabilistic Turing machine with read-only input, write-only output and a stream of independent random bits. Every stored bit, including retained randomness and intermediate lattice vectors, counts toward space; external writable storage and preprocessing oracles are unavailable. The time and space limits must hold on every execution, and the success probability must hold separately for every valid input. The exponent n is lattice rank, not ambient dimension or coefficient precision. All preprocessing and precision management count. There is no promise of a unique shortest vector, a random lattice, a reduced input basis or approximation slack.
cards.answer_criterion: An affirmative answer gives an algorithm satisfying both bounds simultaneously with a proof of exact success on every lattice. A negative answer proves that every randomized polynomial-space algorithm fails some single-exponential-time requirement, or establishes an appropriate time-space lower bound excluding the stated constants. An example defeating one enumeration or sieving method is not enough. Exponential-space algorithms and polynomial-space algorithms taking \(2^{\Theta (n \log  n)}\) time leave the question open.
cards.why: A canonical time-space tradeoff question in exact algorithms: can the single-exponential speed of lattice sieving and Voronoi methods be achieved with only polynomial memory?

importance.reason: A longstanding resource boundary for exact lattice algorithms, central to enumeration versus sieving and increasingly relevant to lattice time-space hardness assumptions.

Ajtai–Kumar–Sivakumar obtain randomized single-exponential-time SVP with exponential space, as described in the inherited paper.
Hanrot–Stehlé sharpen the enumeration analysis to \(n^{n/(2e)+o(n)}\) for SVP, retaining polynomial space.
Micciancio–Voulgaris establish deterministic Voronoi-cell algorithms; the March 2012 revision gives roughly \(2^{2n}\) time and \(2^{n}\) space, followed by the SIAM journal publication.

Koyuncu–Linker–Ozel discuss a coarse-grained polynomial-memory sieving regime; a general exact-success and single-exponential-time guarantee for that regime is not established in the inspected analysis.
Albrecht–Lai–Postlethwaite connect hinted-ISIS algorithms to polynomial-memory single-exponential algorithms for broader lattice tasks, relying on rather than proving time-space hardness.

cards.status_note: Open for exact Euclidean SVP with the simultaneous worst-case time and space bounds stated here, following primary literature checked through 11 September 2026. The 2026 sheaf-based proposal discusses a memory-saving regime but does not establish the required uniform exact-success and runtime theorem. Cryptographic time-space hardness is an assumption, not an unconditional negative resolution.

context_blocks.text: The familiar exact algorithms offer two different resource profiles. Enumeration explores candidate lattice vectors while retaining a relatively small search state, but its proved worst-case time is \(n^{O(n)}\). Sieving and Voronoi methods achieve \(2^{O(n)}\) time by retaining exponentially many vectors or geometric constraints. The question asks whether one can obtain the faster asymptotic time without the exponential memory.

These time scales differ by more than a constant in the exponent: \(n^{cn}=2^{cn \log _{2}n}\). For any fixed C, the factor \(\log _{2}n\) eventually makes \(n^{cn}\) exceed \(2^{Cn}\). Conversely, this card permits a large constant C. A polynomial-memory algorithm with time \(2^{100n}\) would resolve the existence question affirmatively even if it were unusable in practice and slower than current exponential-memory algorithms at moderate ranks.

The output is exact, and the zero vector is excluded. Returning a vector whose length is within a fixed or polynomial factor of optimum solves a different task. Ties create no ambiguity: if several shortest vectors exist, any one is valid. Rational input also allows exact comparison of squared lengths, so the definition does not rely on floating-point tolerance or an unspecified geometric oracle.

The standard basis illustrates why practical performance alone says little about the general bound. For \(B=I, a\) shortest vector is immediately visible. A basis with long, strongly correlated columns may describe a lattice with much shorter integer combinations. Preprocessing can improve the basis substantially, but its own running time and memory must be charged. Supplying an already ideal basis would remove part of the problem.

Kannan’s enumeration method uses recursive preprocessing to control the search region. Hanrot–Stehlé’s analysis gives the more precise \(n^{n/(2e)+o(n)}\) time benchmark, up to polynomial input-size factors, and later work reduces preprocessing overhead. This refines the constant multiplying n log n; it does not change that scale to \(O(n)\). The bound is about the method, not an unconditional lower bound on every polynomial-space algorithm.

The inherited Micciancio–Voulgaris paper proves a different landmark: deterministic single-exponential algorithms using Voronoi-cell computations. Its March 2012 revision improves the bound to roughly \(2^{2n}\) time and \(2^{n}\) space, suppressing polynomial factors. The paper explicitly leaves single-exponential time with polynomial space as an open direction. Reading only the phrase deterministic single exponential in its title would miss the resource that remains unresolved.

Exponential memory can encode reusable relationships among many short vectors. Recomputing a discarded value may save space, but repeated recomputation can increase the running time beyond the allowed bound. A valid positive solution must control this global cost as well as the size of each local calculation. Streaming a large list through a small buffer is not sufficient if later steps require repeatedly reconstructing most of the list.

Theoretical and heuristic guarantees also need separation. Pruning an enumeration tree or keeping a smaller sieve pool may work well on tested lattices. A proof for the present question must additionally show that the retained search process reaches an exact minimizer with probability at least \(2/3\) on every input within the stated time. Successful benchmark instances cannot supply that universal guarantee.

A January 2026 paper by Koyuncu–Linker–Ozel proposes a sheaf-based sieving framework and discusses polynomial memory under coarse graining. Its §4 initially gives storage \(O((M+K)n)\) for M initial vectors and K iterations, then suggests reducing memory when most new vectors replace old ones. It does not provide a uniform proof that this replacement regime retains the exact-success guarantee and a \(2^{O(n)}\) iteration bound on every lattice. It is therefore recorded as a related proposal rather than a resolution of this precise question.

The resource gap is also used in current cryptographic research. Albrecht–Lai–Postlethwaite’s CRYPTO 2026 work derives consequences from hypothetical algorithms for hinted inhomogeneous short-integer solutions, connecting them to single-exponential algorithms with polynomial memory for broader worst-case lattice tasks. Its hardness conclusions rely on a time-space assumption; they do not prove that such algorithms are impossible.

The importance of the problem is that it isolates memory as a potential source of exponential speedups in exact geometry. A solution could change the theoretical basis for choosing between enumeration and large-pool methods. Its cryptographic consequences would still have to be assessed through the relevant reductions and concrete parameters; the existence of some \(2^{Cn}\)-time exact solver is not itself a polynomial-time attack.

A polynomial-memory algorithm with time \(2^{100n}\) would resolve the existence question affirmatively even if it were unusable in practice and slower than current exponential-memory algorithms at moderate ranks.

The output is exact, and the zero vector is excluded. Returning a vector whose length is within a fixed or polynomial factor of optimum solves a different task. Ties create no ambiguity: if several shortest vectors exist, any one is valid. Rational input also allows exact comparison of squared lengths, so the definition does not rely on floating-point tolerance or an unspecified geometric oracle.

The standard basis illustrates why practical performance alone says little about the general bound. For \(B=I, a\) shortest vector is immediately visible. A basis with long, strongly correlated columns may describe a lattice with much shorter integer combinations. Preprocessing can improve the basis substantially, but its own running time and memory must be charged. Supplying an already ideal basis would remove part of the problem.

Kannan’s enumeration method uses recursive preprocessing to control the search region. Hanrot–Stehlé’s analysis gives the more precise \(n^{n/(2e)+o(n)}\) time benchmark, up to polynomial input-size factors, and later work reduces preprocessing overhead. This refines the constant multiplying n log n; it does not change that scale to \(O(n)\). The bound is about the method, not an unconditional lower bound on every polynomial-space algorithm.

The inherited Micciancio–Voulgaris paper proves a different landmark: deterministic single-exponential algorithms using Voronoi-cell computations. Its March 2012 revision improves the bound to roughly \(2^{2n}\) time and \(2^{n}\) space, suppressing polynomial factors. The paper explicitly leaves single-exponential time with polynomial space as an open direction. Reading only the phrase deterministic single exponential in its title would miss the resource that remains unresolved.

Exponential memory can encode reusable relationships among many short vectors. Recomputing a discarded value may save space, but repeated recomputation can increase the running time beyond the allowed bound. A valid positive solution must control this global cost as well as the size of each local calculation. Streaming a large list through a small buffer is not sufficient if later steps require repeatedly reconstructing most of the list.

Theoretical and heuristic guarantees also need separation. Pruning an enumeration tree or keeping a smaller sieve pool may work well on tested lattices. A proof for the present question must additionally show that the retained search process reaches an exact minimizer with probability at least \(2/3\) on every input within the stated time. Successful benchmark instances cannot supply that universal guarantee.

A January 2026 paper by Koyuncu–Linker–Ozel proposes a sheaf-based sieving framework and discusses polynomial memory under coarse graining. Its §4 initially gives storage \(O((M+K)n)\) for M initial vectors and K iterations, then suggests reducing memory when most new vectors replace old ones. It does not provide a uniform proof that this replacement regime retains the exact-success guarantee and a \(2^{O(n)}\) iteration bound on every lattice. It is therefore recorded as a related proposal rather than a resolution of this precise question.

The resource gap is also used in current cryptographic research. Albrecht–Lai–Postlethwaite’s CRYPTO 2026 work derives consequences from hypothetical algorithms for hinted inhomogeneous short-integer solutions, connecting them to single-exponential algorithms with polynomial memory for broader worst-case lattice tasks. Its hardness conclusions rely on a time-space assumption; they do not prove that such algorithms are impossible.

The importance of the problem is that it isolates memory as a potential source of exponential speedups in exact geometry. A solution could change the theoretical basis for choosing between enumeration and large-pool methods. Its cryptographic consequences would still have to be assessed through the relevant reductions and concrete parameters; the existence of some \(2^{Cn}\)-time exact solver is not itself a polynomial-time attack.

cards.title: Vinogradov’s least quadratic nonresidue conjecture
cards.formal:
For an odd prime \(p\), let \(n(p)\) be the least positive quadratic nonresidue modulo \(p\), defined below. Is it true, unconditionally, that
\[\forall\varepsilon\in\mathbb R_{>0}\ \exists P_\varepsilon\in\mathbb N\ \forall p\ge P_\varepsilon\text{ odd prime},\qquad n(p)\le p^{\varepsilon}?\]
Equivalently, is \(n(p)=p^{o(1)}\) as \(p\) tends to infinity through the odd primes? The threshold may depend on \(\varepsilon\), but not on the prime. No unproved analytic hypothesis is assumed.
cards.why: A small quadratic nonresidue is a basic witness used in finite-field arithmetic, and its size measures how long the initial integers can all behave like squares modulo a prime. The conjecture asks for uniform cancellation strong enough to beat every fixed power of the modulus. It would cross a long-standing barrier in character sums and bound the range of deterministic searches for such witnesses; subpolynomial size in the modulus is not the same claim as polynomial size in its bit length.
cards.status_note: Tao’s Conjecture 1.1 and Theorem 1.3 and Quesada-Herrera’s June 2025 slides 14–15 were checked on 2026-09-14. The latter retains the unconditional Burgess bound and explicitly labels its stronger recent bound as conditional on GRH. A bounded search including 2026 work found no matching unconditional all-primes resolution. This is source-open status with those limits.

cards.definitions:
For integers \(a,b\) and a positive integer \(p\), the congruence \(a\equiv b\pmod p\) means that \(p\) divides \(a-b\). An integer \(a\in\{1,\ldots,p-1\}\) is a quadratic residue modulo \(p\) if there exists \(x\in\{0,\ldots,p-1\}\) with \(x^2\equiv a\pmod p\); otherwise it is a quadratic nonresidue. Define
\[n(p)=\min\{a\in\{1,\ldots,p-1\}:\forall x\in\{0,\ldots,p-1\},\ x^2\not\equiv a\pmod p\}.\]
For an odd prime, exactly half of its nonzero residue classes are squares, so the set is nonempty. Representatives are ordered as ordinary positive integers; this is not the least absolute value among positive and negative representatives. Multiples of \(p\) are not counted as nonresidues.

The domain is all odd primes, not composite moduli, almost all primes, or one prescribed congruence class. The prime \(2\) is omitted because every nonzero residue modulo \(2\) is a square. Real powers have the convention \(p^\varepsilon=\exp(\varepsilon\log p)\), where \(\log\) is the natural logarithm.

The statement can equivalently be expressed using only integer powers:
\[\forall k\in\mathbb N_{\ge1}\ \exists P_k\in\mathbb N\ \forall p\ge P_k\text{ odd prime},\qquad n(p)^k\le p.\]
Likewise, the subpolynomial notation means \(\lim_{p\to\infty,\ p\ \mathrm{prime}}\log n(p)/\log p=0\). The source writes \(n(p)=O_\varepsilon(p^\varepsilon)\); since its claim quantifies over every positive exponent, the implicit constant can be absorbed by using a smaller exponent and increasing the threshold. The unit-leading-constant formulation above is therefore equivalent. The conjecture asks for existence of the thresholds, without an extra requirement to compute them effectively.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct Lean-checked proof of the displayed universal statement, or a Lean-checked refutation. A refutation must establish a fixed \(\varepsilon_0>0\) and arbitrarily large odd primes \(p\) with \(n(p)>p^{\varepsilon_0}\). A finite numerical exception cannot refute an eventual bound. A result for almost all primes, a bound with one fixed positive exponent, or a theorem assuming GRH or Elliott–Halberstam is insufficient without also proving the necessary hypothesis.

cards.definitions: The lattice generated by B is \(\Lambda (B)=\{Bz:z\in \mathbb{Z} ^{d}\}; d\) is its rank and m its ambient dimension. Its first minimum \(\lambda _{1}(\Lambda )\) is the minimum Euclidean length of a nonzero lattice vector. Full column rank makes this minimum positive and attained. The output is the signed binary coefficient vector z, so lattice membership and the corresponding integer vector Bz can be recovered without a real-number encoding. Any shortest vector is acceptable, with no uniqueness promise; the zero vector is excluded. Exactness means squared length equals \(\lambda _{1}^{2}\), rather than being within a multiplicative factor greater than one. Use the standard uniform quantum circuit model: a classical polynomial-time machine generates, from \(1^{\mathrm{L}}, a\) circuit on an L-bit input register, zero-initialized ancillary qubits and output qubits, using the fixed universal gates H, T and CNOT, followed by computational-basis measurement and polynomial-time classical decoding. H is the Hadamard gate, \(T=diag(1,\exp (i\pi /4))\), and CNOT maps |\(a,b\rangle\) to |\(a,a\oplus b\rangle\). Circuit size, qubit count, input processing and output writing are polynomial in L. No advice, oracle, pre-supplied quantum state or unit-cost access to an exponentially large memory is provided. Failure is allowed on at most one third of runs for each valid input; it is not an average over randomly chosen lattices. Malformed encodings and rank-deficient matrices can be rejected classically. Integer bases are the imported target; clearing rational denominators preserves shortest vectors up to a common scale and increases encoding length only polynomially.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove existence of the algorithm with the stated worst-case polynomial cost and exact-search success on every valid basis, or prove that no such algorithm exists. Classical NP-hardness alone does not establish the negative answer for quantum computation. A polynomial-factor approximation, an algorithm for a promised special family, or an exponential-time speedup does not establish the positive answer.

context_blocks.title: The basis can hide a short vector
context_blocks.text: The vectors \((100,1)\) and \((101,1)\) are both long, but their difference is \((1,0)\). Since every nonzero integer vector has length at least one, this difference is shortest in their lattice. SVP searches all integer combinations of the supplied basis, rather than choosing its shortest column.

context_blocks.title: Exactness is a separate demand from probability
context_blocks.text: A successful run must output a genuinely shortest vector. Bounded error permits some runs to fail; it does not permit every run to return a slightly longer vector. Similarly, a quantum state encoding many candidate vectors is not the requested classical answer until a shortest coefficient vector can be extracted with the required probability.

context_blocks.title: Why classical hardness does not settle the quantum question
context_blocks.text: Micciancio proves randomized NP-hardness even for some constant-factor Euclidean approximations, hence also for exact search. A polynomial-time quantum exact solver would therefore put all NP decision problems in BQP, the class with bounded-error polynomial-time quantum algorithms. This is a complexity consequence of the reduction, not a proved impossibility: \(\mathrm{NP}\subseteq \mathrm{BQP}\) is not known to be false.

context_blocks.title: Faster exponential algorithms still leave the target open
context_blocks.text: The 2025 paper gives exact quantum algorithms with exponential dependence on rank and explicitly separates QRAM access. Hhan’s August 2026 preprint states expected classical time about \(2^{0.6039d}\) and quantum time about \(2^{0.5411d}\), up to lower-order exponential and polynomial factors; the quantum bound uses exponentially large QRAM. Kim’s concurrent sampling preprint also gives an exponential exact-SVP consequence. These recent claims were checked for scope, not independently proved. None gives polynomial time in L.

Gupte, Ragavan and Zhandry’s response, revised on 1 September, claims a direct impossibility result for that proposed algorithm. The claim and response therefore do not supply a resolution of the exact-search problem on this card.

cards.title: Quantum-ETH hardness of cryptographic-factor GapSVP
cards.formal:
Does the quantum Exponential Time Hypothesis defined below imply that, for some fixed integer \(k\ge1\), there is no bounded-error uniform quantum polynomial-time algorithm for Euclidean
\[\operatorname{GapSVP}_{\gamma_k},\qquad \gamma_k(n)=n^{3/2+1/k}?\]
Equivalently, the target is the conditional assertion
\[\mathrm{QETH}\ \Longrightarrow\ \exists k\in\mathbb N_{\ge1}:\operatorname{GapSVP}_{\gamma_k}\notin\mathrm{PromiseBQP}.\]
The source asks for hardness at \(n^{3/2+\varepsilon}\) for some constant \(\varepsilon>0\) under a standard complexity assumption, without selecting that assumption. This card explicitly selects quantum ETH for classical 3-SAT; it is an editorial variant of that research direction, not a claim that the source stated this particular implication.
cards.why: This question asks whether a familiar quantum satisfiability assumption can support hardness of lattice approximation at a scale relevant to worst-case-to-average-case cryptographic reductions. That scale is much larger than constant-factor approximation, and hardness at a small factor does not automatically persist as the promise gap grows. A proof would connect lattice-based security foundations to a separate complexity assumption while addressing quantum algorithms explicitly.

The recent results concern other norms or constant factors, and the Euclidean preprint proof was not independently verified. A bounded later-work search found no matching hardness theorem or algorithm for the selected cryptographic-factor implication. Quantum ETH is an explicitly chosen assumption variant of the source’s broader question; current source-open status does not assert that this particular implication was posed verbatim by Bennett.

cards.definitions:
An instance consists of an integer \(n\ge1\), a nonsingular rational matrix \(B\in\mathbb Q^{n\times n}\), and a positive rational threshold \(r\). The columns of \(B\) form a full-rank lattice basis. Its lattice and shortest-vector length are
\[\mathcal L(B)=\{Bz:z\in\mathbb Z^n\},\qquad \lambda_1(B)=\min_{z\in\mathbb Z^n\setminus\{0\}}\|Bz\|_2,\]
where \(\|x\|_2=(\sum_{i=1}^n x_i^2)^{1/2}\). The minimum exists and is positive for a nonsingular basis. No ideal-lattice, module-lattice, random-lattice or special-basis promise is imposed.

The promise problem has YES instances with \(\lambda_1(B)\le r\) and NO instances with \(\lambda_1(B)>\gamma_k(n)r\). Either condition is promised. For \(r<\lambda_1(B)\le\gamma_k(n)r\), either answer is allowed. This preserves the source’s strict inequality on the NO side. The task is deciding the promise, not outputting a short vector. The dimension in the approximation factor is \(n\), not the bit length of the matrix entries.

Use a binary encoding of \(n\), the matrix entries and \(r\), each rational represented by its signed reduced numerator and positive denominator, with self-delimiting lengths. Let \(L\) denote the total input bit length. A quantum polynomial-time solver is one finite uniform quantum algorithm, for the fixed chosen \(k\), which uses at most \(C(L+1)^a\) elementary operations for constants \(C,a\) on every branch, and returns the correct promise answer with probability at least \(2/3\) on every YES and every NO instance. It must halt on all inputs within the time bound; malformed encodings, singular matrices and inputs outside the promise require no particular answer. This is the meaning of \(\mathrm{PromiseBQP}\) here. The program and polynomial may depend on \(k\), which is not an instance parameter.

For definiteness, uniform quantum computation uses a classical Turing controller, qubits initially in computational-basis states, gates \(H,T,\mathrm{CNOT}\), and computational-basis measurements with the Born probabilities. On one qubit, \(H|b\rangle=(|0\rangle+(-1)^b|1\rangle)/\sqrt2\) for \(b\in\{0,1\}\), and \(T=\operatorname{diag}(1,e^{i\pi/4})\). The controlled-not gate maps \(|a,b\rangle\) to \(|a,a\mathbin{\oplus}b\rangle\), where \(\oplus\) is addition modulo two. Classical tape work, input reading, generation of gate instructions, gate applications and measurements are charged. The algorithm has no advice, external oracle, uncharged quantum state or postselection. Adaptive classical control and classical randomization obtained by measurement are allowed.

Quantum ETH in this card is a statement about classical Boolean satisfiability. A 3-CNF formula is a conjunction of clauses, each a disjunction of at most three signed Boolean variables. It is satisfiable if some assignment makes every clause true. Let \(N\) be its number of variables and \(s\) its binary encoding length. The assumption asserts that there exists \(\delta>0\) for which no uniform quantum algorithm decides satisfiability on every such formula, with error at most \(1/3\), in time \(C2^{\delta N}(s+1)^a\) for any fixed constants \(C,a\). Time is worst-case over inputs and measurement outcomes, in the same uniform quantum model. This uses the positive exponential-rate formulation of Definition 4.25 in the cited quantum complexity paper; it is not a hypothesis about the quantum satisfiability or local-Hamiltonian problem.

The exponent increment is fixed before instances or candidate solvers are considered. Writing it as \(1/k\) loses no existence case from an arbitrary constant \(\varepsilon>0\): choosing \(1/k\le\varepsilon\) only reduces the approximation factor, and a solver for the smaller factor also solves the larger-factor promise. The source’s alternative LWE target is not bundled into this card. No lattice-hardness or cryptographic-security assumption is available in addition to the stated quantum ETH premise.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct Lean-checked proof or refutation of the displayed conditional assertion with these encodings, norm, approximation factor and uniform quantum model. A positive answer may assume quantum ETH as defined but must establish the claimed exclusion of polynomial-time algorithms, rather than assume hardness of GapSVP or LWE. It must obtain a fixed positive exponent increment and cover all promised rational-basis inputs. A lower bound only for classical algorithms, a constant-factor approximation problem, another norm, or exact SVP alone does not establish this target. Refuting the conditional assertion requires more than showing that one proposed reduction fails; likewise, refuting quantum ETH alone would make the implication vacuously true rather than false.

context_blocks.text: Open Problem 4.11 distinguishes cryptographic approximation factors \(n^{3/2+\varepsilon}\) from smaller powers of the dimension and explicitly includes quantum algorithms. The named assumption is left open by the author; selecting the quantum 3-SAT hypothesis makes this card’s proof obligation concrete.

The cited quantum complexity paper defines a positive-exponential-rate quantum ETH for classical 3-SAT. Its assumption provides the premise used here, rather than an already known reduction to lattice problems.

The source surveys worst-case-to-average-case reductions connecting sufficiently large-factor Euclidean GapSVP hardness to appropriate Learning with Errors parameters. The direction relevant here is that an efficient LWE algorithm would give an efficient worst-case lattice algorithm; these reductions do not themselves derive lattice hardness from SAT hardness.

The source also describes certificate-based obstacles to ordinary NP-hardness at large approximation factors. This helps explain why a standard-assumption hardness theorem in the cryptographic range remains a distinct question from constant-factor NP-hardness.

Hecht and Safra’s STOC 2026 deterministic hardness results assume norms strictly above two. Their displayed factors and norm hypotheses do not establish the Euclidean, cryptographic-factor, quantum conclusion.

Wan’s July 2026 preprint claims deterministic Euclidean hardness within constant factors below \(\sqrt2\), as a special case of its Theorem 1.8. Even if that claim is verified, its approximation scale does not yield hardness for \(n^{3/2+1/k}\). It is recorded as a preprint claim, not as an independently verified resolution of the target.

cards.title: Polynomial-factor approximation of cyclotomic ideal SVP
cards.formal:
Is there a uniform classical randomized polynomial-time algorithm that finds a polynomial-factor approximate shortest nonzero vector in every ideal of every power-of-two cyclotomic ring?

More precisely, do there exist one probabilistic multitape Turing machine \(A\) and fixed positive integers \(c,C,d\) such that, for every \(n=2^k\) with integer \(k\ge1\), and every nonsingular matrix \(B\in\mathbb Z^{n\times n}\) whose column lattice \(I_B=B\mathbb Z^n\) is an ideal of \(R_n=\mathbb Z[X]/(X^n+1)\), the following holds? On the explicit binary input \((n,B)\) of length \(L\), every run of \(A\) halts within \(C(L+1)^d\) bit steps, and
\[\Pr\!\left[A(n,B)\text{ outputs }v\in I_B\setminus\{0\}\text{ with }\|v\|_2\le n^c\lambda_1(I_B)\right]\ge\frac23,\qquad
\lambda_1(I_B)=\min_{z\in\mathbb Z^n\setminus\{0\}}\|Bz\|_2.\]
The constants and program are chosen before the dimension and ideal. The approximation factor depends on dimension, not on coefficient bit lengths. The output must be the full integer coefficient vector \(v\).
cards.why: The central issue is whether the algebraic structure used to make lattice cryptography compact also makes a core worst-case search problem efficiently solvable at polynomial approximation. The selected family is a standard cyclotomic family with growing dimension, not a collection of hand-picked easy ideals. Resolving the question would clarify the computational strength of these structured hardness assumptions. An efficient ideal-SVP algorithm would not, merely by reversing a known security reduction, constitute an attack on every ring-LWE or ring-SIS distribution.

sentences: An ideal in a power-of-two cyclotomic ring is a full integer lattice closed under multiplication by the ring.
The selected question asks for a classical randomized polynomial-time algorithm returning an actual nonzero vector within a fixed polynomial factor of the shortest length.
One program and fixed exponents must work for every dimension and every explicitly supplied ideal basis, with all preprocessing and output charged.

cards.definitions:
Identify \(R_n\) with the integer polynomials of degree less than \(n\), with addition and multiplication reduced modulo \(X^n+1\). Coordinates are ordered as the coefficients of \(1,X,\ldots,X^{n-1}\). The coefficient Euclidean norm is \(\|a\|_2=(\sum_{j=0}^{n-1}a_j^2)^{1/2}\). For these dimensions, \(X^n+1\) is the cyclotomic polynomial of conductor \(2n\), so \(R_n\) is the full ring of integers of \(\mathbb Q(\zeta_{2n})\). The dimension varies without an upper bound.

An integral ideal is an additive subgroup closed under multiplication by every ring element. In the supplied coordinates, the input promise is exactly that \(B\) is nonsingular over \(\mathbb Q\) and \(S(B\mathbb Z^n)\subseteq B\mathbb Z^n\), where
\[S(a_0,\ldots,a_{n-1})=(-a_{n-1},a_0,\ldots,a_{n-2}).\]
Closure under \(S\) and under integer linear combinations gives closure under every ring element. Equivalently, all entries of \(B^{-1}SB\) are integers. Every nonzero integral ideal has a full additive basis of this form. The basis need not be reduced, canonical, circulant or generated by one ring element. Arbitrary prime and composite ideals are included, and no factorization, short generator or special distribution of ideals is promised. Nonsingularity makes \(I_B\) a discrete full-rank lattice, so its positive shortest length is attained.

The input is a dense, explicitly written integer matrix. To fix a binary convention, encode a nonnegative integer \(a\) by \(U(a)=1^\ell 0b\), where \(b\) is the usual binary expansion of \(a\), without leading zeros, and \(\ell\) is its length; use \(b=0\) for zero. Encode a signed integer by a sign bit followed by \(U(|a|)\), with sign zero for zero. Write \(U(n)\) followed by the signed entries of \(B\) in row-major order. Their total length is \(L\). No omitted zeros, succinct matrix circuits or unit-cost large integers are available. Valid outputs list the \(n\) signed coordinates in the same integer encoding; writing every output bit is charged.

The machine has a fixed finite program, alphabet and number of tapes. Each transition reads and writes finitely many tape symbols and moves each head by at most one cell; an independent fair random bit can be drawn at a charged transition. Time includes reading, arithmetic, any preparation depending on \(n\), and writing the output. The time bound holds on all input strings of length \(L\) and all coin sequences. Mathematical success is required only on promised inputs. Outside the promise, any output is permitted. On a promised input, a failure marker, malformed vector or vector violating the displayed conditions counts as failure. Success probability is over the independent coins for each fixed input, not over a distribution of bases.

No quantum computation, oracle, nonuniform advice, precomputed table depending on the field, unit-group basis or ideal factorization is supplied for free. Such information may be computed only within the stated classical time bound. Polynomial exponents may be large but must be universal. Allowing a fixed multiplicative constant in the approximation would be equivalent after increasing \(c\), since \(n\ge2\).

The norm is fixed explicitly to avoid an embedding ambiguity. For \(\zeta_{2n}=\exp(\pi i/n)\), the canonical embedding lists the \(n\) values \(a(\zeta_{2n}^{2j+1})\), \(0\le j<n\). Its squared Euclidean norm is \(n\sum_j a_j^2\). Thus, in this selected family, canonical and coefficient norms differ by the common factor \(\sqrt n\), which cancels in the relative approximation guarantee. This statement does not identify the two norms in arbitrary number rings.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of the displayed existence statement or its full negation. A positive answer must specify one finite classical program and universal constants, with a proved bound on every execution and at least \(2/3\) success on each promised basis. A negative answer must rule out every program and every choice of polynomial approximation and time bounds in this model. In particular, for each machine with a global polynomial clock and each fixed exponent \(c\), some promised input must have success probability below \(2/3\). A conditional consequence under an unproved complexity assumption is not an unconditional negative answer. Algorithms for selected ideals, quantum algorithms, superpolynomial approximation factors, or uncharged field preprocessing do not establish this target. Producing or estimating only the shortest length does not satisfy the required search output.

source_formulation.text: Peikert's 2016 Question 3 asks broadly whether ideal-lattice algorithms, possibly quantum, can substantially outperform general-lattice algorithms, and whether such advances extend to ring-SIS/LWE. It does not choose a field family, approximation scale or running time. Following the user's instruction to replace broad directions by concrete variants, this card selects the standard search-SVP problem with polynomial approximation and classical randomized polynomial time on power-of-two cyclotomic ideals. This is a documented editorial specialization, not a quotation or equivalent restatement of all of Question 3. It does not ask for a proved separation from every general-lattice algorithm or for a direct cryptographic attack. Existing conditional quantum speedups at larger approximation factors answer other parts of the historical direction without deciding this target.

context_blocks.text: The 2016 survey frames the question as a tradeoff between the efficiency gained from ring structure and possible additional algorithmic weaknesses. Its search problem asks for an actual short vector. This distinction is essential: the same survey explains that certain polynomial-gap decision versions on ideals can be easy even when finding an adequately short vector is not known to be efficient.

Multiplication by \(X\) gives a signed rotation of every coefficient vector in the selected ideal. For example, \(q\mathbb Z^n\) is an allowed ideal with shortest length \(|q|\) for each nonzero integer \(q\). Such easy instances do not determine the worst-case question, which also includes ideals without a short generator supplied in the input. A change of additive basis describes the same ideal; the guarantee must hold for every explicit basis and charges its actual bit length.

General lattice algorithms already give polynomial-time approximations whose factors are much larger than polynomials in dimension. Peikert's §2.2.2 records that historical time–approximation landscape. Restricting to ideal lattices is useful here only if the output quality and full running time meet both polynomial requirements. The earlier broad phrasing “outperform general lattices” is replaced by this testable threshold, without claiming a lower bound for all generic algorithms.

Cramer, Ducas and Wesolowski give a quantum algorithm with approximation factor \(\exp(\widetilde O(\sqrt m))\) for cyclotomic conductor \(m\). Their Theorem 5.1 assumes GRH and a class-group generation hypothesis, and its running time also depends polynomially on the real-subfield class number. Polynomial boundedness of that class number is an additional hypothesis used for the advertised polynomial-time consequence. This important advance has a different computation model and a superpolynomial approximation guarantee.

Pan, Xu, Wadleigh and Cheng prove classical polynomial-time exact SVP for prime ideals above rational primes \(p\equiv3,5\pmod8\) in the power-of-two family, and for a specified class of products of such primes. Their introduction stresses that the proportion of easy instances depends on how ideals are sampled. The result does not cover every ideal, and the paper explicitly distinguishes these algorithms from a break of ring-LWE.

The CRYPTO 2022 work of Boudgoust, Gachon and Pellet-Mary extends the easy-instance analysis using ideals preserved by many field automorphisms. Its cryptographic application concerns particular partial Vandermonde knapsack instances. The publisher/ePrint abstract was checked for this scope; it is not evidence of a general polynomial-time algorithm for every ideal.

Cui, Li and Zhuang's January 2026 revision studies further prime-ideal classes. In particular, its Theorem 2 describes shortest lengths above primes \(p\equiv7,9\pmod{16}\). Its hypotheses still restrict the ideals, and a formula for a shortest length is distinct from the full uniform search guarantee. No claim that this preprint resolves the all-ideals target is made here.

Martin’s September 2026 preprint claims a dimension-preserving reduction from generic lattices to ideals in varying totally real monogenic number rings. Theorem 1.1 does not force a chosen cyclotomic field; the surrounding discussion explicitly preserves the possible advantage of field-specific methods. Its separate full-ring-of-integers extension has additional conjectural qualifications. This new hardness claim is not a hardness theorem for the fixed cyclotomic family selected here.

Wan’s September 2026 preprint claims exact Euclidean SVP hardness for ideals of \(\mathbb Z[X]/(X^N-1)\), with \(N=q-1\) for varying odd primes \(q\). That quotient has a different rational algebra from \(\mathbb Q[X]/(X^n+1)\). The paper explicitly makes neither a fixed-factor approximation claim nor a cryptographic key-distribution claim. Even if its proof is correct, the stated exact cyclic result does not determine this polynomial-factor cyclotomic search question.

A worst-case-to-average-case security reduction has a direction: an algorithm for the average-case cryptographic problem would solve an associated worst-case lattice problem with stated parameters. An algorithm for the worst-case lattice problem does not automatically run that implication backwards. The historical second question about direct ring-SIS/LWE attacks therefore remains separate from this card’s selected algorithmic target.

cards.title: Deterministic polynomial-time construction of a prime of a given bit length
cards.formal: Is there a deterministic algorithm and constants \(C,c>0\) which, on input \(1^{n}\) for every \(n\ge 2\), output a prime p with \(2^{n- 1}\le p<2^{n}\) in at most \(Cn^{c}\) bit operations?
cards.definitions: Use uniform classical deterministic Turing computation, with no advice or oracle. Integers and rational numerators and denominators are encoded in binary; L denotes the total input bit length. A polynomial bound has constants independent of the input. The unary input parameter requests an n-bit output. A prime is an integer greater than one with no positive divisors other than one and itself. Correctness and the bound must hold for every \(n\ge 2\); neither randomization, an oracle, a prime table supplied as advice, nor an unproved number-theoretic hypothesis is allowed.

cards.title: NP-hardness of Euclidean covering radius
cards.formal: Is exact Euclidean lattice covering radius NP-hard under deterministic polynomial-time many-one reductions? Equivalently, does there exist one deterministic polynomial-time map sending each Boolean 3-CNF formula \(\varphi\) to a rational full-column-rank matrix \(B\) and a positive rational threshold \(r\), such that \[\varphi\text{ is satisfiable}\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad\mu_2(L(B))\le r?\] Unsatisfiable formulas must map to instances with \(\mu_2(L(B))>r\). This is the exact decision problem, with approximation factor one and no promised gap between the two cases.

source_formulation.text: In particular, we reiterate that the problem of showing NP-hardness of exact GapCRP in the l2 norm (the most important special case) remains open.
source_formulation.caption: Complete selected source sentence; PDF p. 7

cards.why: The covering radius measures how far a point can be from its nearest lattice point. It is a central lattice invariant with connections to integer programming and to worst-case lattice problems used in cryptography. Establishing even exact Euclidean NP-hardness would close a basic gap in the complexity classification of lattice problems, without requiring the stronger approximation-hardness results known in other norms.

cards.definitions: The input basis is a matrix \(B=(b_1,\ldots,b_n)\in\mathbb Q^{m\times n}\), where \(m\ge n\ge1\) and the \(n\) columns are linearly independent over \(\mathbb R\). Its lattice is \(L(B)=\{Bz:z\in\mathbb Z^n\}\). For \(v\in\mathbb R^m\), the Euclidean norm is \(\|v\|_2=(\sum_{j=1}^m v_j^2)^{1/2}\). Define \[\mu_2(L(B))=\sup_{t\in\operatorname{span}_{\mathbb R}(B)}\inf_{z\in\mathbb Z^n}\|t-Bz\|_2=\max_{w\in[0,1]^n}\min_{z\in\mathbb Z^n}\|B(w-z)\|_2.\] The points \(t\) range over the real linear span of the lattice, not the whole ambient space when \(n<m\). The compact fundamental parallelepiped \(B[0,1]^n\) gives the equivalent finite-radius maximum. The minimum ranges over all integer combinations, including coefficients outside \(\{0,1\}\). The exact decision language contains precisely valid pairs \((B,r)\) with \(r\in\mathbb Q_{>0}\) and \(\mu_2(L(B))\le r\); equality is a YES instance and any strict excess is a NO instance. Encode dimensions and signed rational numerators and positive denominators in binary, with explicit delimiters and all matrix entries listed. Complexity is measured in total encoding length, including entry precision and the threshold, not just dimension. A 3-CNF formula is a conjunction of clauses, each a disjunction of at most three Boolean variables or their negations, with variable indices encoded in binary; it is satisfiable when some Boolean assignment makes every clause true. The requested reduction is one finite deterministic Turing-machine program with a fixed polynomial bit-time bound. It must output a valid instance on every valid formula, and the equivalence must hold for all formulas. All output bits and exact rational arithmetic costs count. No oracle, advice, randomness, real-number oracle or unbounded-precision unit-cost arithmetic is available. NP-hardness here is deterministic many-one hardness for every language with a polynomial-time verifier and polynomial-length witnesses, equivalently hardness for the specified 3-SAT language.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct Lean-checked proof that such a reduction exists, including polynomial bit complexity, valid output bases and both directions of the satisfiability equivalence, or a complete Lean-checked proof of the logical negation. A proof of a polynomial-time algorithm would refute NP-hardness only with an appropriate complexity separation; it is not by itself a negative answer. Hardness in another norm, hardness of linear discrepancy or of coding-theoretic covering radius, randomized reductions alone, and a reduction that reverses YES and NO do not establish this target. The task does not require NP membership or a quantitative approximation gap.

context_blocks.text: Bennett and Ly explicitly single out NP-hardness of exact \(\ell_2\) covering radius in Section 1.4 of their September 2026 proceedings paper. Definition 4 specifies the decision orientation: small covering radius is YES, while radius strictly above the threshold is NO.

Their new hardness theorem applies for fixed \(p>p_0\), where \(p_0\approx35.31\), in the norm \(\|v\|_p=(\sum_j|v_j|^p)^{1/p}\). It gives approximation hardness with factors greater than one for suitable parameters. The Euclidean value \(p=2\) lies outside that theorem.

The paper distinguishes covering radius from linear discrepancy, \(\max_{w\in[0,1]^n}\min_{z\in\{0,1\}^n}\|B(w-z)\|_p\). Restricting the nearest point to binary combinations can change the value, even when the generated lattice is unchanged. The present question uses all lattice points.

The introduction relates approximate covering radius to worst-case lattice problems and integer programming. These connections motivate the complexity question but do not supply a hardness proof for the exact Euclidean decision language.
