cards.definitions: A composite integer is an integer \(n>1\) with a divisor strictly between 1 and n. Even integers greater than 2 and perfect squares are rejected; thus a candidate here is odd and nonsquare. Write \(n- 1=2^{s} d\) with d odd. The strong base-2 test accepts if \(2^{d}\equiv 1\) (mod n), or \(2^{2^{r} d}\equiv - 1\) (mod n) for some integer \(0\le r<s\). For the Lucas test, examine \(D=5,- 7,9,- 11,13,- 15,\ldots\) in that order, namely \(D_{k}=(- 1)^{k}(2k+5)\) for \(k\ge 0\). At each step reject if \(1<\gcd (|D|,n)<n\); otherwise stop at the first D with Jacobi symbol \((D/n)=- 1\). For odd \(n=\prod p_{j}^{e_{j}}\), the Jacobi symbol \((a/n)\) is \(\prod (a/p_{j})^{e}_{j}\), where \((a/p)\) is 0 if p divides a, +1 if a is a nonzero square modulo p, and −1 otherwise. This defines the symbol without requiring factorization as an implementation. Squares were excluded because their Jacobi symbols cannot be −1; for odd nonsquares the search terminates. Set \(\mathrm{P}=1\) and \(Q=(1- D)/4\). Define integer sequences \(U_{0}=0, U_{1}=1, V_{0}=2, V_{1}=\mathrm{P}\) and, for \(j\ge 0, U_{j+2}=\mathrm{P} U_{j+1}- Q U_{j}\) and \(V_{j+2}=\mathrm{P} V_{j+1}- Q V_{j}\). Write \(n+1=2^{t} u\) with u odd. The strong Lucas test accepts if \(U_{u}\equiv 0\) (mod n), or \(V_{2^{r} u}\equiv 0\) (mod n) for some integer \(0\le r<t\). Passing means surviving the parameter search and satisfying both strong tests, with exact integer congruences. The number 2 is accepted separately but cannot answer this composite-existence question. No extra trial-division cutoff, random bases or additional congruence checks are part of the specified variant.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a composite n together with a proof of compositeness and exact verification of the parameter search and both acceptance conditions, or prove that no composite integer passes this specified variant. A finite search bound, a heuristic count of expected counterexamples or a counterexample to only one component does not settle the question.

context_blocks.title: Why combine two tests
context_blocks.text: A composite can imitate some arithmetic properties of primes. For example, \(2047=23\cdot 89\) passes the strong base-2 test because \(2^{1023}\equiv 1\) modulo 2047. It fails the strong Lucas test with \(D=5\). The question is whether a composite can evade both parts together, however large it is.

context_blocks.title: The exact variant matters
context_blocks.text: Selfridge’s Method A fixes \(\mathrm{P}=1\) and \(Q=(1- D)/4\). The main source also describes Method A*, which changes P and Q to 5 when \(D=5\), and proves equivalence of the strong Lucas outcomes for integers coprime to 10. Its proposed strengthened test adds further congruences. This card keeps the imported strong base-2 plus strong Lucas target and spells out Method A.

cards.definitions: For a positive integer m, an addition chain of length r is a finite strictly increasing sequence of positive integers \(1=a_{0}<a_{1}<\cdots <a_{r}=m\) such that, for each \(i\in \{1,\ldots ,r\}\), there exist \(j,k\in \{0,\ldots ,i- 1\}\) with \(a_{i}=a_{j}+a_{k}\). The indices j and k may coincide, and any previously produced value may be reused any number of times. The length counts the r additions, excluding the initial 1. Define \(\ell\)\((m)\) as the minimum such r; this minimum exists because \(1,2,\ldots ,m\) is an allowed chain, and \(\ell\)\((1)=0\). Only additions of two previously available numbers are allowed: subtraction, division, arbitrary preloaded constants and sums of three or more terms in one step are excluded. All additions have cost one, regardless of operand size; this is an operation-count question, not a bit-running-time bound. A star chain, also called a Brauer chain, additionally requires each step to have a representation \(a_{i}=a_{i- 1}+a_{j}\) with \(j<i\). Write \(\ell\)*\((m)\) for its minimum length. Thus \(\ell\)\((m)\le \ell *(m)\); the conjecture uses the unrestricted \(\ell\) on both sides. The integer \(2^{n}- 1\) has n ones in binary, and the quantifier includes \(n=1\).
cards.answer_criterion: Prove the inequality for every positive integer n, or give an integer n together with rigorous bounds on the two minimum lengths showing \(\ell\)\((2^{n}- 1)>n- 1+\ell (n)\). A positive proof may establish existence of the required chains without an efficient algorithm for finding a shortest chain. Equality is not required. Restricted-chain results, a finite verification range, and validity for a density-one set of integers are weaker than the universal assertion.

context_blocks.text: An addition chain is a plan for reusing intermediate powers. Once \(x^{a}\) and \(x^{b}\) have been computed, one multiplication produces \(x^{a+b}\). Starting from x, a chain for m therefore specifies a multiplication-only computation of \(x^{m}\) with one multiplication per chain step. This correspondence explains the interest in short chains; it does not include algorithms that use division or other algebraic operations.

For \(n=5\), the chain 1,2,4,5 has length three and is shortest, since two additions can reach at most four. The conjectured upper bound for \(2^{5}- 1=31\) is therefore \(5- 1+3=7\). The chain 1,2,3,6,12,24,30,31 attains that upper bound: its last two additions are \(24+6\) and \(30+1\). Exhibiting it checks this instance without claiming that every n admits an analogous optimal pattern.

The target compares the cost of building an integer n with the cost of building a much larger integer whose binary expansion is entirely ones. Its dominant term is \(n- 1\), with only \(\ell\)\((n)\) further additions allowed. Merely finding a chain of order n steps would leave the exact additive allowance unresolved.

Brauer’s theorem gives \(\ell\)*\((2^{n}- 1)\le n- 1+\ell *(n)\). In a star chain, every step must use the immediately preceding value. This proves the desired inequality whenever n has a shortest unrestricted chain that is also a star chain. In general, replacing \(\ell\)*\((n)\) by the potentially smaller \(\ell\)\((n)\) is precisely the distinction that the restricted result does not settle.

Tall’s 2024 paper proves the conjecture for an explicit infinite family of integers with seven ones in binary and \(\ell\)\((2n)=\ell (n)\), and also for their doubles. An infinite family need not cover all possible exponents; its role here is a proved special case, rather than a resolution of the universal target.

A May 2026 preprint claims that the proportion of \(n\le N\) satisfying the conjecture tends to one as N tends to infinity. Its introduction expressly distinguishes this claim from a proof for all n. Even a valid density-one theorem can leave exceptions, and this preprint’s proof has not been independently verified in this review.

There is no contradiction in a chain for \(2^{n}- 1\) being shorter than the displayed bound: the conjecture is an upper bound. Nor must a positive solution provide a fast procedure for computing \(\ell\)\((n)\). These distinctions keep an existence inequality separate from exact-length formulas and shortest-chain optimization.

The analogous theorem for star chains and known infinite families leave the unrestricted universal inequality open in the checked sources.
Resolving it would explain how efficiently optimal exponentiation plans can control the cost of all-ones binary exponents.

sentences: Factoring is a central arithmetic search problem whose complete output is a unique prime-power decomposition.

cards.definitions: The input is the ordinary base-two expansion of N without leading zeroes, and \(n=\lfloor \log _{2}N\rfloor +1\). The output is the list of distinct increasing primes \(q_{1}<\cdots <q_{r}\) and positive integer exponents \(e_{i}\), all in binary, with \(N=\prod _{i} q_{i}^{e_{i}}\). A prime input has the single pair \((N,1)\). The oracle returns the same unique prime-factorization representation on M. Queries may be adaptive but must all satisfy \(\lfloor \log _{2}M\rfloor +1<n\) relative to the original input length. Merely requiring \(M<N\) would be weaker and is not the target. The ordinary Turing-machine cost includes writing queries, reading answers and writing the output; supplying a correct oracle answer is the sole oracle operation. The output length of prime factorization is polynomial in n. There is no randomness, advice or nonuniform family of reducers. The reduction must work for every input, with one polynomial bound independent of its factorization.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove existence of the uniform polynomial-time reduction or its logical negation. Factoring using smaller numerical values of the same bit length, arbitrary smaller circuits for a factoring relation, or an exponential-time recursion does not meet the stated definition. The output need not be a decimal expansion of the input; its prime-power representation is explicit.

cards.title: Dimension-preserving search-to-decision reductions for SVP
cards.formal: Does there exist a uniform classical randomized polynomial-time oracle reduction that, using only \(\gamma\)-GapSVP queries on lattices of the same dimension \(n\), solves SVP with approximation factor polynomial in \(n\) and \(\gamma\)? Concretely, do there exist absolute positive integers \(C,a,b\) and one randomized oracle machine \(R\) such that for every \(n\ge1\), every nonsingular \(B\in\mathbb Q^{n\times n}\), every rational \(\gamma\ge1\), and every admissible oracle \(O_\gamma\) below, \(R^{O_\gamma}(B,\gamma)\) runs in at most \(C(N+2)^b\) steps and outputs \(z\in\mathbb Z^n\setminus\{0\}\) with \[ \Pr\!\left[\|Bz\|_2\le C(n\gamma)^a\lambda_1(L(B))\right]\ge2/3? \] Here \(N\) is the bit length of the encoded input, and the probability is over the reduction’s random bits.
cards.why: Search returns a short lattice vector, whereas a decision oracle only certifies which side of a length gap the lattice lies on. Bridging these versions with polynomial approximation loss and no dimension increase would sharpen a basic computational relationship at the center of lattice algorithms and worst-case hardness assumptions in cryptography.
cards.status_note: The target is explicitly open in Bennett’s 24 January 2023 source. The near-exact 2016 theorem and the older reduction-map convention were checked directly, as were the dated June 2022 workshop questions. Bounded later searches through 14 September 2026 located no verified matching same-dimension classical reduction with polynomial loss. Recent LWE/LPN search-to-decision results concern different average-case problems and were not treated as resolutions. This is a limited source review, not exhaustive current-status or Lean proof certification.

sentences: The input is a rational lattice basis, and the search task is to produce a nonzero vector whose length approximates the shortest possible length.
The available oracle only distinguishes short-vector lengths across a multiplicative gap.
The question asks for a classical polynomial-time reduction that keeps every query in the original dimension and loses only a polynomial in dimension and approximation factor.

A resolution would clarify whether approximate lattice decision algorithms can be converted efficiently into search algorithms without an exponential dimensional penalty.

cards.definitions:
The input lattice is \(L(B)=\{Bz:z\in\mathbb Z^n\}\subseteq\mathbb R^n\), with a rational full-rank square basis whose columns generate it. The Euclidean norm is \(\|x\|_2=(\sum_i x_i^2)^{1/2}\), and \(\lambda_1(L)=\min\{\|v\|_2:v\in L,\ v\ne0\}\). The output is an exact integer coefficient vector \(z\), so its nonzero lattice vector is unambiguously represented even when coordinates are rational. There is no norm other than \(\ell_2\), target point, uniqueness promise, preprocessing of a fixed lattice, or ideal-lattice restriction.

An oracle query is \((\widetilde B,r)\), where \(\widetilde B\in\mathbb Q^{n\times n}\) is nonsingular and \(r\in\mathbb Q_{>0}\). An admissible \(O_\gamma\) is any total Boolean function on these valid queries satisfying \[ \lambda_1(L(\widetilde B))\le r\implies O_\gamma(\widetilde B,r)=1,\qquad \lambda_1(L(\widetilde B))>\gamma r\implies O_\gamma(\widetilde B,r)=0.\] When \(r<\lambda_1(L(\widetilde B))\le\gamma r\), its answer can be either bit. The reduction must succeed for every such total completion of the promise problem, including completions with no computability assumption. Repeated identical queries have the same answer because the oracle is a function. The same input value \(\gamma\) applies to every query. At \(\gamma=1\) there is no gap.

Dimension preservation means every oracle lattice has exactly the original dimension \(n\), including its ambient dimension and rank. Queries may use different bases and thresholds, but cannot increase dimension even by an additive constant. This follows the explicit same-\(n\) statement of Open Problem 4.5. Adaptively chosen queries are allowed; this is a Cook (oracle Turing) reduction, not a requirement of one nonadaptive query.

Integers, rational numerators and positive denominators are encoded in binary with signs and delimiters; \(N\) includes the entire basis and \(\gamma\). Use a probabilistic multitape oracle Turing machine with independent unbiased coin flips, a read-only input tape, work tapes and a query tape. Writing a query and reading its one-bit answer are charged; the oracle itself returns that bit in one oracle step. All arithmetic is implemented on binary tapes and pays its full bit cost. The displayed polynomial bounds total time on every random tape and every admissible oracle, and therefore bounds the number and bit lengths of queries and output. Only valid full-rank rational queries are allowed. There is no additional oracle, advice, quantum computation, or free real arithmetic.

The constants and the finite program are fixed before \(n,B,\gamma\) and the oracle are chosen. A bound \(C(n\gamma)^a\) expresses an unspecified polynomial loss uniformly over the domain \(n,\gamma\ge1\); replacing it by any fixed polynomial in these two parameters gives the same polynomial-loss existence target after increasing \(C,a\). The chosen reduction is allowed bounded-error randomness. This makes explicit the classical randomized reduction convention used by the cited near-exact results, rather than adding a deterministic-only requirement.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean that such a reduction and uniform polynomial bounds exist, with correctness against every admissible completion of the promise oracle, or prove their nonexistence. A positive result must bound the output norm, bit complexity, and dimension of every query. Preserving dimension only up to an unbounded factor, obtaining an approximation loss exponential in \(n\), assuming special lattices, or giving only a quantum reduction does not meet the target. The known exact case or approximation factors approaching one alone do not establish the quantified statement.

context_blocks.text: The source asks for polynomial loss in the approximation factor, not exact preservation of that factor. It also explicitly retains dimension. This matters for lattice algorithms whose costs depend exponentially on dimension, and for distinguishing an algorithm that recognizes short vectors from one that actually finds them.

The search and decision versions are known to be equivalent under dimension-preserving reductions in the exact case \(\gamma=1\). The 2016 randomized reduction has search loss \(\gamma^{n/s}\) and running time \(2^{O(s)}\gamma^{O(n)}\), for \(s\ge\log(n+1)\), with input-bit polynomial factors suppressed in that summary. Choosing \(s\) logarithmic gives an efficient useful guarantee when \(\gamma\) is very close to one; it does not give a polynomial-loss polynomial-time reduction for all approximation factors.

Bennett’s 2023 problem is phrased using rational square bases and Euclidean length. The older reduction map uses a relaxed convention that permits an additive constant in dimension, while the card follows the later explicit same-dimension wording. The distinction is recorded so that a looser reduction is not silently counted as satisfying the target.

The source relates a solution at polynomial approximation factors to worst-case search-SVP foundations for lattice cryptography. The Simons list also discusses search-to-decision questions for closest vectors and independent short vectors, including quantum variants. Those questions have different outputs, oracles or computational models and do not settle the reduction here.

cards.title: Capacity of the two-user Gaussian interference channel
cards.formal:
Determine the weighted capacity function
\[F(a,b,P_{1},P_{2},\lambda)=\sup_{(R_{1},R_{2})\in C(a,b,P_{1},P_{2})}\bigl(\lambda R_{1}+(1-\lambda)R_{2}\bigr)\]
for all \(a,b\in\mathbb R\), \(P_{1},P_{2}\in\mathbb R_{\ge0}\), and \(\lambda\in[0,1]\). The real memoryless channel is
\[Y_{1,t}=X_{1,t}+aX_{2,t}+Z_{1,t},\qquad Y_{2,t}=bX_{1,t}+X_{2,t}+Z_{2,t}.\]
The region \(C\) uses two independent private messages, deterministic separate encoders, average power over messages and time, no feedback or cooperation, and vanishing joint average decoding error, as defined below. The required absolute accuracy is \(1/100\) bit per real channel use everywhere on this domain.
cards.definitions:
All five parameters are finite real numbers and remain fixed as block length grows. Negative, zero, and positive gains are included; powers may be zero or arbitrarily large. The two direct gains and the noise variances are normalized to one. For every \(i\in\{1,2\}\) and time \(t\), the noise \(Z_{i,t}\) has density \((2\pi)^{-1/2}\exp(-z^{2}/2)\) on \(\mathbb R\). All these noises are mutually independent and independent of both messages. There is no fading, channel state, or additional channel memory. Channel parameters and both codebooks are known to all terminals.

For a positive integer \(K\), let \([K]=\{0,\ldots,K-1\}\). An \((n,K_{1},K_{2})\) code has \(n,K_{1},K_{2}\ge1\), two independent uniform messages \(M_{i}\in[K_{i}]\), deterministic encoders \(f_{i}:[K_{i}]\to\mathbb R^{n}\), and Borel-measurable decoders \(d_{i}:\mathbb R^{n}\to[K_{i}]\). Transmitter \(i\) sends \(X_{i}^{n}=f_{i}(M_{i})\), and receiver \(i\) estimates only its own message using \(d_{i}(Y_{i}^{n})\). Each code must satisfy
\[\frac{1}{nK_{i}}\sum_{m\in[K_{i}]}\sum_{t=1}^{n}f_{i}(m)_{t}^{2}\le P_{i},\qquad i=1,2.\]
This is a separate power budget for each transmitter, averaged over messages and time. It is not a bound on every symbol or every individual codeword, and power cannot be transferred between transmitters. The error is
\[P_{e}=\Pr\bigl[d_{1}(Y_{1}^{n})\ne M_{1}\ \text{or}\ d_{2}(Y_{2}^{n})\ne M_{2}\bigr],\]
averaged over the independent uniform messages and all Gaussian noise. There is no maximal-error-over-messages requirement. The encoders may depend arbitrarily on time and their own messages, with arbitrary real codeword entries and no computation bound. They have no shared random seed, common message, feedback, or communication link; neither encoder knows the other message. The receivers cannot communicate. Predetermined time sharing, unequal powers in different phases, and arbitrary temporal dependence within each codeword are allowed subject to the displayed average budgets. There is no secrecy or prescribed signaling-distribution constraint.

All rate logarithms have base two. A nonnegative rate pair \((R_{1},R_{2})\) is achievable if there is a code for each integer block length \(n\ge1\), with message sizes \(K_{i,n}\), such that \(P_{e,n}\to0\) and
\[\liminf_{n\to\infty}\frac{\log_{2}K_{i,n}}{n}\ge R_{i},\qquad i=1,2.\]
The region \(C(a,b,P_{1},P_{2})\) is the Euclidean closure of all achievable pairs. It is a nonempty compact convex downward-closed subset of \([0,c_{1}]\times[0,c_{2}]\), where \(c_{i}=\tfrac12\log_{2}(1+P_{i})\); hence \(F\) is finite. These are bits per one real scalar channel use, not per complex channel use. No finite block code must attain a boundary rate. The weights include both endpoints, and the exact supporting function determines the closed region. The task has real mathematical parameters; it does not silently restrict them or the codebooks to rational encodings.
cards.answer_criterion:
Supply one unambiguous real-valued function \(g\) on \(\mathbb R^{2}\times\mathbb R_{\ge0}^{2}\times[0,1]\) and a complete, mathematically correct proof checked in Lean that, for every tuple in this domain,
\[|g(a,b,P_{1},P_{2},\lambda)-F(a,b,P_{1},P_{2},\lambda)|\le\frac1{100}.\]
The proof must justify both sides of this error against the operational code definition, using its average-power and average-error conventions and bits per real use. Certified lower and upper bounds of width at most \(1/50\) qualify by their midpoint. An exact function also qualifies. A formula or another unambiguous mathematical description may be used; no single-letter syntax, fixed number of auxiliary variables, polynomial evaluation bound, or finite encoding of arbitrary real inputs is required. Any proposed evaluation rule must have a proved meaning and the stated guarantee on the full real domain. An unevaluated restatement of the capacity optimization or its limiting code definition, a sampled plot, and bounds with an unclosed gap do not determine the answer. Sum capacity alone, a restricted signaling optimum, a special interference regime, or an asymptotic high-power approximation is insufficient. The fixed tolerance does not assert an exact capacity theorem.
cards.why: A defining problem in network information theory: even two interfering sender–receiver pairs expose limits of our ability to characterize optimal communication. An exact solution would distinguish which forms of message splitting, interference decoding and power allocation are fundamentally necessary.

importance.reason: A foundational multi-user capacity frontier with a simple channel model, strong approximate results and unresolved exact tradeoffs. Recent disputed claims make the precise formulation and status record especially valuable.

context_blocks.text: Two separately informed transmitters use the same medium, so each receiver observes its desired signal plus interference and Gaussian noise. The point-to-point rate \(c_{i}=\tfrac12\log_{2}(1+P_{i})\) is an individual upper bound, but the two upper bounds generally cannot be reached together. The target describes every tradeoff between the independent conversations; knowing only their best total rate leaves other supporting weights undetermined.

The general two-user model is a foundational network information theory problem. Han–Kobayashi regions are established achievable inner bounds, and several structured parameter regimes have exact capacity or exact sum-capacity results. Shang and Chen’s monograph explicitly distinguishes these two kinds of conclusions. An optimal value within one specified signaling family is also different from a converse bounding every permitted code.

For strong interference, \(|a|\ge1\) and \(|b|\ge1\), the known capacity region is given by \(0\le R_{i}\le c_{i}\) and
\[R_{1}+R_{2}\le\min\!\left\{\tfrac12\log_{2}(1+P_{1}+a^{2}P_{2}),\ \tfrac12\log_{2}(1+b^{2}P_{1}+P_{2})\right\}.\]
These are the two Gaussian multiple-access sum bounds in this card’s real normalization. With \(a=b=0\), capacity is the rectangle \([0,c_{1}]\times[0,c_{2}]\). The solved cases explain why an answer must retain both gains and both powers, rather than assume symmetry or a single interference-strength ordering.

Etkin, Tse and Wang establish the celebrated universal one-bit approximation using achievable and outer regions. The checked preprint’s formal model is complex-valued, and its error notion is an additive coordinate gap, not a bound on the error of a plotted sum-rate curve. That constant-gap theorem is a major approximate characterization, but it is not a certificate at this card’s much smaller tolerance in bits per real use. Its units and power convention must be accounted for in any precise transfer to this model.

Nair and Ng prove that allowing temporally correlated vector Gaussian inputs in the multiletter Han–Kobayashi region gives the same region as scalar Gaussian inputs when the comparison includes time sharing and its power allocation. This is an invariance theorem within a signaling class. It does not rule out other input distributions or establish full capacity. Huleihel and Merhav’s older preprint claiming an improvement from Gaussian memory was withdrawn in April 2018; its original abstract must not be counted as a valid advance.

Nair and Zhao’s ISIT 2025 work settles a structural conjecture about the Gaussian-signaling region for the one-sided, or Z, channel. Under its explicit parameter condition, multiplexing is unnecessary for the optimum of that inner region. The theorem does not assert that the inner region equals capacity for all Z channels.

Their January 2026 manuscript gives parameters where non-Gaussian distributions outperform Gaussian ones in a restricted single-phase superposition region without power control. Its Conjecture 1 still concerns the full Gaussian Han–Kobayashi region including power allocation over time. Section II.D explains that the new counterexample regime is disjoint from the regime in which the previous no-multiplexing theorem applies. Thus these results do not jointly yield a counterexample to the full capacity conjecture. Remark 2 also records the authors’ inability to verify parts of an earlier Khandani proof claim.

Gohari, Nair and Zhao’s February 2026 manuscript combines converse bounds through auxiliary receivers. The full Gaussian discussion in Section II.C restricts its matching corner, sum-rate and slope conclusions to the stated very-weak-interference regime and corresponding one-sided specializations. These conclusions must not be expanded to arbitrary weak interference merely from the broader abstract wording. The paper supplies an outer bound, not the general capacity function.

Khandani’s current v12, posted on 7 September 2026, claims that Gaussian Han–Kobayashi signaling attains weak-interference capacity with at most two time-sharing phases. Its equations use nonnegative squared cross-gain parameters under square roots; those symbols are not this card’s possibly signed amplitude gains. The claim covers a major subdomain and is recorded under uncertain status, without asserting a solution over all real gains.

cards.title: Optimal asymptotic binary rate–distance tradeoff
cards.formal:
Determine the optimal asymptotic binary rate–distance function
\[R_2(\delta)=\limsup_{n\to\infty}\frac{\log_2 A_2(n,\lceil\delta n\rceil)}{n},\qquad 0<\delta<\frac12,\]
where \(A_2(n,d)\) is the largest cardinality of any nonempty binary code of length \(n\) whose distinct codewords have Hamming distance at least \(d\). Supply an unambiguous real-valued approximation \(g:(0,1/2)\to\mathbb R\), with a complete Lean proof that
\[\forall\delta\in(0,1/2),\qquad |g(\delta)-R_2(\delta)|\le\frac1{100}.\]
The error is absolute rate error in information bits per transmitted bit. Codes may be nonlinear and have no construction, encoding or decoding efficiency requirement. The same error bound must hold on the entire real domain.
cards.definitions:
Finite codes. For integers \(n\ge1\) and \(0\le d\le n\), a binary length-\(n\) code is a nonempty subset \(C\subseteq\{0,1\}^n\). Its elements are codewords. For \(x,y\in\{0,1\}^n\), define their Hamming distance by
\[d_H(x,y)=|\{i\in\{1,\ldots,n\}:x_i\ne y_i\}|.\]
The distance requirement means \(d_H(x,y)\ge d\) for every distinct pair \(x,y\in C\). A singleton satisfies it vacuously; no minimum over an empty set needs to be chosen. Define
\[A_2(n,d)=\max\{|C|:\varnothing\ne C\subseteq\{0,1\}^n,\ \forall x,y\in C,\ x\ne y\Rightarrow d_H(x,y)\ge d\}.\]
This is a finite maximum over a nonempty collection, and \(1\le A_2(n,d)\le2^n\). The rate of \(C\) is \(r(C)=\log_2|C|/n\). The distance parameter \(d/n\) is a required relative separation, not the fraction of independent random channel errors. All logarithms are base two.

Asymptotic convention. Fix the real parameter \(\delta\) before taking the block length to infinity. The integer \(\lceil\delta n\rceil\) is the smallest integer at least \(\delta n\). For \(0\le\delta\le1\), write \(a_n(\delta)=\log_2 A_2(n,\lceil\delta n\rceil)/n\). Explicitly,
\[R_2(\delta)=\inf_{N\in\mathbb N_{>0}}\ \sup_{n\in\mathbb N,\ n\ge N} a_n(\delta).\]
Every term is in \([0,1]\), so the tail suprema and infimum are well-defined finite real numbers. The limsup allows a favorable infinite subsequence of block lengths and does not assert that the ordinary limit exists. The optimum ranges over all codes, without linearity or a single effective code-family generator. The requested domain is exactly \((0,1/2)\); the same definition outside it gives the known regimes \(R_2(0)=1\) and \(R_2(\delta)=0\) for \(1/2\le\delta\le1\).

Conventions for bounds. A lower curve \(L\) satisfies \(L(\delta)\le R_2(\delta)\) precisely when, for each fixed \(\delta\in(0,1/2)\), every \(\varepsilon>0\) and every integer \(N\ge1\), there are an integer \(n\ge N\) and a valid code of length \(n\), distance at least \(\lceil\delta n\rceil\), and rate at least \(L(\delta)-\varepsilon\). An upper curve \(U\) satisfies \(R_2(\delta)\le U(\delta)\) precisely when, for each fixed \(\delta\in(0,1/2)\) and every \(\varepsilon>0\), some integer \(N\ge1\) has the following property: for every \(n\ge N\), every valid code at that distance has rate at most \(U(\delta)+\varepsilon\). Block length thresholds may depend on \(\delta\) and \(\varepsilon\); a common threshold for all real distances is not required. These existence bounds do not impose polynomial-time code construction.

For the background bounds, the binary entropy is \(h_2(t)=-t\log_2t-(1-t)\log_2(1-t)\) on \([0,1]\), with each endpoint term \(0\log_2 0\) interpreted as zero.
cards.answer_criterion: Supply a specified function \(g:(0,1/2)\to\mathbb R\) and a complete, mathematically correct Lean-checked proof of \(|g(\delta)-R_2(\delta)|\le1/100\) for every real \(\delta\) in that domain, using the finite-code maximum, rounding, limsup and normalization above. This requires both \(g(\delta)-1/100\le R_2(\delta)\) and \(R_2(\delta)\le g(\delta)+1/100\); the preceding quantified code statements specify the corresponding lower and upper guarantees. Alternatively, certified curves \(L,U\) satisfying \(L(\delta)\le R_2(\delta)\le U(\delta)\) and \(U(\delta)-L(\delta)\le1/50\) everywhere qualify through their midpoint. A formula, certified evaluation rule or another unambiguous mathematical description may specify the answer; no predetermined formula grammar or evaluation-time bound is imposed. Merely renaming the defining optimization or limsup does not supply the requested determination. An exact determination qualifies, but exact equality to the Gilbert–Varshamov curve is not required. Finitely many samples, an uncertified numerical plot, a bound on only one side, or a result restricted to linear codes or to some distances does not establish the stated whole-domain guarantee.
cards.why: This function is the intrinsic packing limit for binary information protected against worst-case substitutions. Determining it to a certified rate accuracy would quantify the necessary redundancy independently of how a code is represented, constructed or decoded. Exact determination would settle a foundational coding-theory question; the selected tolerance is a distinct, weaker benchmark target.

importance.reason: A foundational coding-theory limit with a precise extremal target, a large gap between existence and converse bounds, and connections to combinatorics, information theory and quantum methods.

context_blocks.text: A code represents messages by selected bit strings. More codewords carry more information per transmitted bit, while greater pairwise separation permits correction of more adversarial errors. This question asks for the best possible asymptotic compromise over every binary code, independently of algorithmic restrictions.

The repetition code \(\{000,111\}\) has rate \(1/3\) and distance three, and corrects one arbitrary flipped bit. The complete set of three-bit strings has rate one and distance one, and cannot correct even one arbitrary flip. In general, correction of every pattern of at most \(t\) substitutions requires and is guaranteed by pairwise distance at least \(2t+1\), for an integer \(t\ge0\).

The Gilbert–Varshamov existence bound gives \(R_2(\delta)\ge1-h_2(\delta)\), whereas the elementary Hamming bound gives \(R_2(\delta)\le1-h_2(\delta/2)\). Vadhan’s Open Problem 5.9 asks for the largest asymptotically attainable binary rate at a fixed relative distance. Its infinite-family formulation is represented here by the explicit limsup and subsequence convention.

The 1977 McEliece–Rodemich–Rumsey–Welch bounds sharpen the upper side. The first gives \(R_2(\delta)\le h_2(1/2-\sqrt{\delta(1-\delta)})\); the second is never weaker. These were the long-standing general upper bounds, but the August 2026 preprints report strict improvements, so the 1977 frontier must not be described as current.

Alrabiah and Guruswami’s 10 August 2026 preprint reports strict improvements to the first and second MRRW bounds at every \(0<\delta<1/2\). The theorems concern arbitrary classical binary codes, including nonlinear ones; quantum states occur in the analysis and do not change the code alphabet. The introduction still identifies the GV curve as the best general asymptotic lower bound.

The requested tolerance needs a separate check from exact openness. At relative distance one quarter, the GV rate is approximately 0.18872, while Table 2 of the August preprint reports a numerical upper-bound estimate near 0.35038. The authors explicitly label the table as floating-point evaluations, not certified global optima. These reported values illustrate the remaining difference between the displayed lower and upper estimates; they are not a certified interval or a proof that no different approximation theorem exists. The checked sources do not supply the requested error of 0.01 throughout the domain.

Barg’s 1 September 2026 note compares the new channel bound with the concurrent Delsarte-certificate result. Its Section 2 identifies the coinciding variational formulas for the improvement of the first MRRW bound. The note provides a mathematical relation between those results, rather than a determination of the full rate–distance function.

Finite-length improvements can leave the limiting rate unchanged. Jiang and Vardy obtain a factor of order \(n\) over the binary Gilbert bound for each fixed \(0<\delta\le0.499\). Such a multiplicative factor contributes only \(O(\log n/n)\) after taking the logarithm and dividing by block length. It does not constitute an increase in the asymptotic rate exponent.

Yuan and Zhu’s January 2026 preprint gives a probabilistic proof of a square-root block-length improvement for linear codes and an extension to quantum codes. The paper acknowledges the earlier classical square-root improvement. These polynomial factors do not by themselves alter \(R_2\), and the quantum-code statement has different objects and constraints.

Capacity under independent random bit flips, list decoding, and codes over larger alphabets have different targets. This card asks for worst-case pairwise separation over the binary alphabet. A construction above the GV curve at even one distance would address the separate beyond-GV question, while this card requires two-sided accuracy over the entire distance interval.

cards.title: Capacity of the general broadcast channel
cards.formal:
Determine the function
\[F(W,\lambda)=\sup_{(R_{1},R_{2})\in C(W)}\bigl(\lambda R_{1}+(1-\lambda)R_{2}\bigr)\]
for every finite discrete memoryless broadcast channel \(W\) with a rational transition table and every \(\lambda\in\mathbb{Q}\cap[0,1]\). Here \(C(W)\) is the capacity region for two independent private messages, deterministic codes, vanishing joint average decoding error, and no feedback, as defined below. The required accuracy is absolute \(1/100\) bit per channel use throughout this entire domain.
cards.definitions:
For a positive integer \(m\), write \([m]=\{0,\ldots,m-1\}\). The domain contains all positive integers \(a,b,c\), alphabets \(\mathcal X=[a]\), \(\mathcal Y=[b]\), \(\mathcal Z=[c]\), and arrays \(W(y,z\mid x)\in\mathbb Q_{\ge0}\) such that \(\sum_{y\in\mathcal Y,z\in\mathcal Z}W(y,z\mid x)=1\) for every \(x\). Alphabet sizes are unbounded, and zero transition probabilities are allowed. There is no conditional-independence requirement on the two outputs in a single use. For each block length \(n\ge1\), the channel law is
\[\Pr(Y^{n}=y^{n},Z^{n}=z^{n}\mid X^{n}=x^{n})=\prod_{t=1}^{n}W(y_{t},z_{t}\mid x_{t}).\]
The table specifies the whole channel; it has no additional state or memory.

An \((n,K_{1},K_{2})\) code, with positive integer message sizes, consists of maps \(f:[K_{1}]\times[K_{2}]\to\mathcal X^{n}\), \(d_{1}:\mathcal Y^{n}\to[K_{1}]\), and \(d_{2}:\mathcal Z^{n}\to[K_{2}]\). The messages \(M_{1},M_{2}\) are independent and uniform, the encoder transmits \(f(M_{1},M_{2})\), and the receivers output \(d_{1}(Y^{n})\) and \(d_{2}(Z^{n})\). Its joint average error is
\[P_{e}=\Pr\bigl[d_{1}(Y^{n})\ne M_{1}\ \text{or}\ d_{2}(Z^{n})\ne M_{2}\bigr],\]
where the probability averages over both messages and the specified channel randomness. No worst-case-over-messages error requirement is imposed. The encoder knows both messages; each decoder observes only its own output block. There is no common message, feedback, receiver communication, shared randomness, secrecy condition, or input-cost constraint. Codes are arbitrary deterministic maps with no uniform construction or complexity bound. Dependence among the transmitted symbols and deterministic time sharing are allowed.

All logarithms defining rates have base two; rates and the target function are measured in bits per channel use. A pair \((R_{1},R_{2})\in\mathbb R_{\ge0}^{2}\) is achievable if there is a sequence of such codes, indexed by \(j\ge1\), with \(n_{j}\to\infty\), \(P_{e,j}\to0\), and \(\liminf_{j\to\infty}\log_{2}(K_{i,j})/n_{j}\ge R_{i}\) for both \(i=1,2\). Define \(C(W)\) as the Euclidean closure of the achievable pairs. It is a nonempty compact convex downward-closed subset of \([0,\log_{2}b]\times[0,\log_{2}c]\); these properties and the endpoint weights make \(F\) a finite real function, including when an alphabet has size one. A supremum in the definition does not require a finite code attaining a boundary rate. Its exact values at all rational weights determine the closed region; the benchmark below requires only their stated approximation.

If an answer is given as an algorithm, its finite input is the three alphabet sizes followed by the full table in lexicographic order and the weight, with integers in binary and rational numbers as reduced numerator/positive-denominator pairs separated by delimiters. All valid inputs in this encoding are included. No time bound or fixed grammar for a mathematical answer is imposed.
cards.answer_criterion:
Supply one unambiguous real-valued function \(g\) on the entire domain above and a complete, mathematically correct proof checked in Lean that
\[\forall W\ \forall\lambda\in\mathbb Q\cap[0,1],\qquad |g(W,\lambda)-F(W,\lambda)|\le\frac1{100}.\]
The proof must match the code model, average error, limiting convention, units, and unbounded range of alphabet sizes. It must justify both sides of the error guarantee against the operational capacity definition. Certified bounds \(L(W,\lambda)\le F(W,\lambda)\le U(W,\lambda)\) with \(U-L\le1/50\) qualify through their midpoint. An exact determination also qualifies. Any submitted evaluation algorithm must terminate for every valid input and certify its returned value; a mathematical expression is not required to have a prescribed computational complexity. Sampled agreement, an uncertified numerical optimizer, a one-sided achievable or converse bound, and a renaming of the defining supremum or an unevaluated limiting characterization do not suffice. Resolving whether one particular inner bound is exact is not by itself the requested function, and an impossibility result for a different evaluation task does not replace this answer.
cards.why: One of the smallest communication networks whose full capacity region is unknown. It asks for the basic law governing simultaneous transmission of independent information to different receivers, with consequences for coding methods and converse techniques throughout network information theory.

importance.reason: A central multiuser capacity problem with a precisely defined rate region, decades of partial characterizations and recent challenges to the longstanding candidate inner bound.

progress.text: Marton gives a general achievable region for independent private messages and identifies special capacity cases.

The checked v3 of Gohari–Anantharam gives auxiliary-cardinality bounds, closedness and computability of the inner region, and a mismatch with a known outer region; the journal publication followed in 2012.
Geng and coauthors obtain capacity for new product-channel classes and show that the UV outer bound can be loose.
Dou and coauthors publish numerical bound-evaluation algorithms with convergence guarantees under specified concavity and initialization conditions.
The checked Gohari–Liu–Nair full manuscript gives stronger outer bounds and example improvements; it still describes general capacity as unknown.

Huang–Liu–Liu v1 claims a finite unconstrained counterexample to full one-letter Marton optimality, including an explicit rational enlarged channel. This narrower claim is not an independently verified capacity solution.

cards.status_note: Individually checked on 14 September 2026. The checked primary literature, including the January 2026 outer-bound manuscript and Huang–Liu–Liu’s 20 August 2026 v1, describes the general exact capacity characterization as open. The latter claims only strict suboptimality of the full one-letter Marton inner bound, with an explicit rational enlarged channel, and would not supply the requested capacity function even if correct. Its proof and numerical certificates have not been independently verified. The 2024 numerical convergence results have explicit hypotheses and concern bounds. Bounded later-work and rational-channel evaluation searches found no matching full solution; historical exact-question openness does not independently certify the fixed 1/100 benchmark as unsolved. Retained as source_open with these limits.

context_blocks.text: One transmitter must convey two independent messages through a single stream of inputs. Each receiver sees its own noisy observations, so the possible pairs of reliable rates form a tradeoff region. Unlike an interference channel, there are no separately informed transmitters. This is a central network information theory question because even the general two-receiver case lacks a known evaluable capacity characterization in the checked sources.

The two individual capacities do not determine the joint region. If the same noiseless input bit reaches both receivers, either receiver alone can receive one bit per use, but the private rates satisfy \(R_{1}+R_{2}\le1\). If the input is instead a pair of bits and each receiver receives its designated bit, the region is \([0,1]^{2}\), although both individual capacities are still one. These examples distinguish the shared resource in the question from two independent point-to-point capacity calculations.

Marton’s 1979 region is a general achievable inner bound, and the original paper identifies channel classes for which capacity is known. Its two independent private messages match this card. The original separate average-error requirements and this card’s vanishing probability that either decoder fails are equivalent by elementary probability bounds; neither is the maximal-message error criterion.

Gohari and Anantharam establish finite bounds on the auxiliary alphabet sizes in Marton’s inner region, making that region closed and computable. Their formulation permits a common message; setting its rate to zero gives the private-message slice relevant here. They also establish that this inner region and the Nair–El Gamal outer region can differ. This gap alone does not identify which bound is loose, and computability of an inner region does not establish its equality with capacity.

Geng and coauthors determine capacity for certain product-channel classes and prove that the UV outer bound is not always tight. Their full version also explains the multiletter sum-rate characterization: normalized Marton sum rates on successively longer repeated channels recover the operational sum capacity in the limit. This limiting equality supplies no general finite stopping guarantee for the numerical answer requested here. Nonadditivity of Marton’s inner bound must not be confused with a failure of the usual rate normalization for repeated uses of the channel itself.

Dou and coauthors give numerical methods for evaluating several inner and outer bounds. Their Theorems 5–7 prove convergence under explicit hypotheses: the initial distribution and a global maximizer must lie in a suitable connected superlevel set, and the objective must be concave there. These are conditional convergence results, not an unconditional global capacity evaluator. Even exact optimization of a bound would still leave the issue of its tightness. Their numerical conventions use natural logarithms unless otherwise specified; this card fixes bits throughout.

Gohari, Liu and Nair’s 2026 manuscript strengthens sum-rate outer bounds through two auxiliary receivers, with a full-region version in its appendix and numerical improvements for skew-symmetric examples. The auxiliary receivers are proof variables, not extra terminals available to a code. The reported improvements still leave inner/outer gaps and do not give the general function.

Huang, Liu and Liu’s preprint of 20 August 2026 claims strict suboptimality of the complete one-letter Marton region. A fixed-input-distribution example has ternary input; their separate constraint-removal theorem and explicit construction produce an unconstrained channel on a much larger finite alphabet. Section III.D specifies rational mixing probabilities and a rational joint channel, so that example is within this card’s domain. It should not be described as an unconstrained ternary-input counterexample. The claim concerns a gap from an inner bound, not a matching capacity evaluation. Its full proof and interval-arithmetic certificates were not independently verified or rerun in this review.

The rational-table domain is the saved editorial specialization of the general capacity question. The absolute \(1/100\) acceptance rule follows the user-approved numerical formulation of 12 September 2026 and is retained here. It is not an assertion of exact equality with any proposed capacity curve. The checked literature discusses the underlying exact characterization; this review does not infer that a historical open-status statement alone proves that the fixed-tolerance benchmark remains unsolved.

cards.context:
One transmitter must convey two independent messages through a single stream of inputs. Each receiver sees its own noisy observations, so the possible pairs of reliable rates form a tradeoff region. Unlike an interference channel, there are no separately informed transmitters. This is a central network information theory question because even the general two-receiver case lacks a known evaluable capacity characterization in the checked sources.

The two individual capacities do not determine the joint region. If the same noiseless input bit reaches both receivers, either receiver alone can receive one bit per use, but the private rates satisfy \(R_{1}+R_{2}\le1\). If the input is instead a pair of bits and each receiver receives its designated bit, the region is \([0,1]^{2}\), although both individual capacities are still one. These examples distinguish the shared resource in the question from two independent point-to-point capacity calculations.

Marton’s 1979 region is a general achievable inner bound, and the original paper identifies channel classes for which capacity is known. Its two independent private messages match this card. The original separate average-error requirements and this card’s vanishing probability that either decoder fails are equivalent by elementary probability bounds; neither is the maximal-message error criterion.

Gohari and Anantharam establish finite bounds on the auxiliary alphabet sizes in Marton’s inner region, making that region closed and computable. Their formulation permits a common message; setting its rate to zero gives the private-message slice relevant here. They also establish that this inner region and the Nair–El Gamal outer region can differ. This gap alone does not identify which bound is loose, and computability of an inner region does not establish its equality with capacity.

Geng and coauthors determine capacity for certain product-channel classes and prove that the UV outer bound is not always tight. Their full version also explains the multiletter sum-rate characterization: normalized Marton sum rates on successively longer repeated channels recover the operational sum capacity in the limit. This limiting equality supplies no general finite stopping guarantee for the numerical answer requested here. Nonadditivity of Marton’s inner bound must not be confused with a failure of the usual rate normalization for repeated uses of the channel itself.

Dou and coauthors give numerical methods for evaluating several inner and outer bounds. Their Theorems 5–7 prove convergence under explicit hypotheses: the initial distribution and a global maximizer must lie in a suitable connected superlevel set, and the objective must be concave there. These are conditional convergence results, not an unconditional global capacity evaluator. Even exact optimization of a bound would still leave the issue of its tightness. Their numerical conventions use natural logarithms unless otherwise specified; this card fixes bits throughout.

Gohari, Liu and Nair’s 2026 manuscript strengthens sum-rate outer bounds through two auxiliary receivers, with a full-region version in its appendix and numerical improvements for skew-symmetric examples. The auxiliary receivers are proof variables, not extra terminals available to a code. The reported improvements still leave inner/outer gaps and do not give the general function.

Huang, Liu and Liu’s preprint of 20 August 2026 claims strict suboptimality of the complete one-letter Marton region. A fixed-input-distribution example has ternary input; their separate constraint-removal theorem and explicit construction produce an unconstrained channel on a much larger finite alphabet. Section III.D specifies rational mixing probabilities and a rational joint channel, so that example is within this card’s domain. It should not be described as an unconstrained ternary-input counterexample. The claim concerns a gap from an inner bound, not a matching capacity evaluation. Its full proof and interval-arithmetic certificates were not independently verified or rerun in this review.

The rational-table domain is the saved editorial specialization of the general capacity question. The absolute \(1/100\) acceptance rule follows the user-approved numerical formulation of 12 September 2026 and is retained here. It is not an assertion of exact equality with any proposed capacity curve. The checked literature discusses the underlying exact characterization; this review does not infer that a historical open-status statement alone proves that the fixed-tolerance benchmark remains unsolved.

cards.title: Li–Li conjecture
cards.formal:
For every network instance \(I\) defined below, is
\[\mathcal C(I)=\mathcal R(I)?\]
Here \(\mathcal C(I)\) is the closure of the rate vectors supported by finite deterministic causal zero-error network codes, with an entropy capacity shared between the two directions of every undirected edge. The region \(\mathcal R(I)\) consists of all rates supported by fractional multicommodity routing. The quantification includes every finite network size, every positive rational capacity vector, every finite list of independent unicast sessions, every finite message and symbol alphabet, every causal schedule and every nonlinear local encoding function.
cards.definitions:
Network and sessions. An instance is \(I=(G,c,((s_i,t_i))_{i=1}^k)\). The supply graph \(G=(V,E)\) is finite, connected, simple and undirected, with at least two vertices; an edge is an unordered pair of distinct vertices. Each edge \(e\) has a capacity \(c_e\in\mathbb Q_{>0}\). The number of sessions \(k\) is a positive integer, and \(s_i,t_i\in V\) with \(s_i\ne t_i\). Different sessions may share either endpoint, have opposite directions, or have the same ordered endpoint pair. Such sessions still carry independent messages, each required at its own single destination.

Messages and initial knowledge. Choose a nonempty finite alphabet \(A_i\) for each session. The random variables \(M_i\) are independent and uniformly distributed on \(A_i\); singleton alphabets are allowed. Initially, a vertex \(v\) knows exactly the tuple of messages with \(s_i=v\), along with the fixed instance and code. Thus a destination can also know messages of other sessions for which it is itself a source. There is no additional message-dependent initial information and no private or shared random seed. Local computation and storage have no resource bound.

Causal finite code. Before messages are sampled, fix a nonnegative integer \(L\), a schedule \((u_\ell,v_\ell)_{\ell=1}^L\) with \(\{u_\ell,v_\ell\}\in E\), and nonempty finite transmitted-symbol alphabets \(\Sigma_\ell\). At step \(\ell\), the sender \(u_\ell\) sends \(Z_\ell\in\Sigma_\ell\) to \(v_\ell\). Its encoding function is an arbitrary deterministic function of all messages initially at \(u_\ell\) and the tuple of symbols received there at steps strictly less than \(\ell\). Previously sent symbols are already functions of that information. The schedule and alphabets do not depend on the messages; timing and unrecorded silence carry no extra information. For each \(i\), a deterministic decoder at \(t_i\), applied to its initially known messages and all symbols received there, must output \(M_i\) for every tuple in \(\prod_{j=1}^k A_j\). This is exact recovery with zero error. Linear encoding is not required.

Entropy and supported rates. All probabilities come from the uniform product distribution of the messages. For a finite random variable \(Z\), write
\[H(Z)=-\sum_{z:\Pr[Z=z]>0}\Pr[Z=z]\log_2\Pr[Z=z].\]
Entropy is measured in bits, so \(H(M_i)=\log_2|A_i|\). For each orientation \(u\to v\) of an edge, let \(X_{u\to v}\) be the ordered tuple of all symbols sent in that direction during the whole schedule; the empty tuple has entropy zero. For a real scale \(b>0\), a code supports \(r\in\mathbb R_{\ge0}^k\) if
\[H(M_i)\ge b r_i\quad(1\le i\le k),\qquad H(X_{u\to v})+H(X_{v\to u})\le b c_{\{u,v\}}\quad(\{u,v\}\in E).\]
Each directional transcript is measured jointly across its uses, and the two directional entropies are then added. This is not the entropy of their combined bidirectional tuple, nor a separate full-capacity allowance in each direction. The positive scale normalizes messages and edge budgets together. It may depend on the code and need not be an integer. No bound on the schedule length or on the alphabets is imposed in terms of this scale.

Coding region. Let \(\mathcal C_0(I)\) be the set of supported rate vectors over all such finite codes, alphabets and positive scales, and let \(\mathcal C(I)=\overline{\mathcal C_0(I)}\) in the ordinary topology of \(\mathbb R^k\). Explicitly, \(r\in\mathcal C(I)\) means \(r\in\mathbb R_{\ge0}^k\) and, for every \(\varepsilon>0\), there is \(r'\in\mathcal C_0(I)\) with \(\max_i|r_i-r'_i|<\varepsilon\). The closure allows limiting rates; it does not allow decoding errors. This card fixes the inherited entropy-capacity model. Equivalence with a fixed-length bit-budget or vanishing-error definition is not assumed.

Routing region. Let \(\mathcal P_i\) be the finite set of simple paths from \(s_i\) to \(t_i\) in \(G\). A vector \(r\in\mathbb R_{\ge0}^k\) belongs to \(\mathcal R(I)\) exactly when there are real numbers \(f_{i,P}\ge0\), one for every \(i\) and \(P\in\mathcal P_i\), such that
\[\sum_{P\in\mathcal P_i}f_{i,P}\ge r_i\quad(1\le i\le k),\qquad \sum_{i=1}^k\sum_{\substack{P\in\mathcal P_i\\e\in P}}f_{i,P}\le c_e\quad(e\in E).\]
A unit of flow consumes one unit of capacity on every edge of its path, regardless of the traversal direction. Each commodity may split among arbitrarily many of these paths. Flows need not be integral. The region is a closed bounded polytope, since the graph, path lists and capacities are finite and every source differs from its destination. Multicast delivery of one common message to several receivers and recovery of functions instead of messages are different tasks.
cards.answer_criterion:
Give a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of the universal equality or its negation. An affirmative proof must cover all the specified instances, independent finite messages, deterministic causal nonlinear codes and positive scales, and must justify passage to the closure. The familiar inclusion \(\mathcal R(I)\subseteq\mathcal C(I)\) is also part of the checked equality; the substantive conjecture is the reverse inclusion.

A negative answer may give one finite instance, a finite code, a positive scale and a supported rate vector outside \(\mathcal R(I)\). The checked proof must establish every encoder's causality, exact decoding on every message tuple, the transcript-entropy capacity inequalities, and infeasibility of the fractional routing constraints at that rate. This finite-code form loses no possible counterexample: a point of the coding closure outside the closed routing region has a neighborhood disjoint from that region and hence contains a supported finite-code rate.

Beating a particular routing algorithm, integral paths, or a cut bound does not establish a separation from the optimal fractional region. A result for directed edges, correlated messages or multicast does not refute this statement. An impossibility result only for linear encoders does not prove it. Any use of a different error or capacity convention requires a checked implication to the model above. There is no additive numerical tolerance on this exact yes-or-no equality.
cards.why: Asks whether computation inside an undirected network can increase the throughput of independent unicast messages, with direct connections to multicommodity flow and major computational lower bounds.

importance.reason: A central capacity conjecture whose resolution would clarify the power of network coding and influence circuit and data-structure lower bounds.

progress.text: Li and Li formulate the undirected no-coding-advantage conjecture, as recorded in the subsequent primary literature.
Jain and coauthors prove that the four-session \(K_{3,2}\) example has coding rate equal to routing rate \(3/4\).
Braverman–Garg–Schvartzman show that any constant strict advantage amplifies to a polylogarithmically growing gap.
Afshani and coauthors derive conditional multiplication-circuit lower bounds from the conjecture.
Vamsi–Thakor analyze specified asymmetric demands in layered networks.
Braverman–He give superconstant undirected multicast gaps; the unicast conjecture is explicitly left open.
Liu–Que–Li–Li report metric-based proofs for further network classes, including at most five terminal locations.

A separate session-interaction framework reduces the conjecture to a property of all irreducible cores; it does not establish that property universally. Its manuscript corrects a quantifier in the conference definition to require one common witnessing solution.

cards.status_note: Checked through 16 September 2026. The August 2026 primary manuscripts explicitly retain the general multiple-unicast conjecture. Their restricted topology theorems and session-interaction characterization do not establish it universally; multicast separations have a different demand model. The card retains its precise causal zero-error directional-entropy formulation. No matching general resolution was found in the bounded primary-source search, and external proofs were not independently certified.

context_blocks.text: Routing treats each message as a separate commodity that consumes capacity along paths. Network coding lets an intermediate node combine messages before forwarding them. If a node knows bits \(x\) and \(y\), it may send \(x\oplus y\); a receiver that already knows \(y\) can recover \(x\). Whether the necessary side information can be supplied cheaply enough to improve total throughput depends on the entire network. The conjecture says that undirected edges always let fractional routing match coding for independent one-destination messages.

Fractional routing is essential to the comparison. A message may be split among many paths, and different commodities may share an edge up to its total capacity. This is more flexible than requiring one path per message or requiring edge-disjoint paths. The rate region is described by a linear program, so an apparent coding improvement over a greedy routing choice does not establish a gap. One must beat the optimum over all fractional routings.

The capacity convention also matters. An undirected edge of capacity one has one combined budget for both directions, rather than a separate budget of one in each direction. The formal statement follows the cited entropy-based definition: the entropy of each complete directional transcript is counted, and decoding is exact. Taking the closure permits limiting rates. This states precisely which capacity notion is being compared instead of assuming that all zero-error, fixed-length and vanishing-error conventions are interchangeable.

Cut constraints provide necessary information bounds, but meeting all of them need not make multiple demands fractionally routable. In the unit-capacity \(K_{3,2}\) example, put vertices \(a,b,c\) on one side and \(d,e\) on the other, and use sessions \((a,b),(b,c),(c,a),(d,e)\) at one common rate. The sparsity bound is one, while the maximum concurrent routing rate is \(3/4\). Jain, Vazirani, Yeung and Yuval prove that coding also cannot exceed \(3/4\). Thus a cut–flow gap alone is not a coding advantage.

Braverman, Garg and Schvartzman show that any fixed coding advantage greater than one can be amplified into a family whose gap grows as a positive power of \(\log |V|\). General cut–flow bounds give a logarithmic upper bound. Consequently a single strict separation would imply unbounded asymptotic improvements, rather than merely an isolated constant-factor gain.

Afshani, Freksen, Kamma and Larsen show that the conjecture implies an \(\Omega(n\log n)\) lower bound for Boolean circuits multiplying two \(n\)-bit integers when both fan-in and fan-out are bounded by a constant. Their theorem is conditional on the network-coding conjecture; a multiplication lower bound has not already been obtained from ordinary cut constraints. The bounded-degree circuit model matters to the stated consequence.

Recent positive results remain sensitive to the session arrangement. Vamsi and Thakor’s ISIT 2025 work handles specified asymmetric demands in layered networks, including partition-symmetric demands in their Type-I bipartite family. It also studies gaps between routing constructions and information-theoretic bounds for three-layer cases. Such a gap is a reason to examine an instance more closely; it is not itself a demonstrated coding scheme outside the routing region.

An August 2026 preprint by Liu, Que, Li and Li reports new cases via graph metrics, including networks with at most five terminal locations and certain planar instances supported on at most three designated face boundaries. In the planar case, each session has both endpoints on one of those faces. Five terminal locations is not the same restriction as five sessions or five total graph vertices. The general conjecture remains explicitly open in that paper.

The strongest recent undirected separation located in this review changes the demand model. Braverman and He obtain a superconstant multicast coding advantage using locally decodable codes. Each source message there must reach a set of receivers, and the routing comparison is a Steiner-tree packing problem. Replacing those copies by independent unicast messages removes exactly the shared-message structure used by the construction, so the result does not disprove Li–Li.

The other August 2026 manuscript reports a session-interaction characterization: universal validity is equivalent to an independence property of every irreducible core. It does not establish this property for every core. Its Definition 3.1 footnote corrects the conference wording so that one common optimal coding solution witnesses all the independence requirements, rather than allowing a separately chosen solution for each pair. The characterization and its restricted cases are recorded as reported progress, with that quantifier correction.

category_assignment.reason: The Li-Li conjecture compares network-coding capacity with routing capacity, an information-theoretic rate-region question rather than algorithmic round complexity.

sentences: An undirected network carries independent messages, each from one source to one destination, with a common capacity budget for both directions of every edge.
The Li–Li conjecture asks whether arbitrary causal zero-error network coding has exactly the same closed rate region as optimal fractional multicommodity routing.
The card fixes independent finite uniform messages, deterministic encoding, exact decoding and the sum of the two whole-transcript entropies on each edge.
A complete Lean proof must establish the universal equality or certify a finite coding instance whose supported rate is outside the fractional routing region.

Recent restricted topology results and a corrected session-interaction framework leave the general question open, while undirected multicast separations rely on shared messages with multiple receivers.

cards.title: Capacity of the binary deletion channel
cards.formal:
Supply a function \(g:[0,1]\to\mathbb R\) and prove
\[\forall\delta\in[0,1],\quad |g(\delta)-C(\delta)|\le\frac1{100},\]
where \(C(\delta)\) is the operational capacity of the binary independent deletion channel, measured in bits per input bit. The probability \(\delta\) is fixed as the block length tends to infinity. This retained benchmark is a formalization task at the stated accuracy: an unrestricted finite approximation scheme is already known. It does not require a new exact capacity formula.
cards.definitions:
Channel. For each positive integer \(n\), an input is a binary string \(x\in\{0,1\}^n\). Independently at each of its \(n\) positions, the channel deletes the bit with probability \(\delta\) and retains it with probability \(1-\delta\). It outputs the retained bits in their original order. The output alphabet is the disjoint union \(\mathcal Y_n=\bigcup_{k=0}^n\{0,1\}^k\), including the empty string. The receiver observes the string and its length, but neither terminal observes the deletion positions. There are no erasure markers, insertions, substitutions, feedback or additional communication channels. Both terminals know \(n\) and the real parameter \(\delta\).

Transition probabilities. For \(y\in\{0,1\}^k\) with \(0\le k\le n\), let \(e_x(y)\) be the number of increasing tuples \(1\le i_1<\cdots<i_k\le n\) such that \(x_{i_j}=y_j\) for all \(j\). The empty tuple has count one. Then
\[\mu_{n,\delta}(y\mid x)=e_x(y)(1-\delta)^k\delta^{n-k}.\]
Use \(0^0=1\) in this finite probability formula, so it also defines both endpoints. Distinct deletion patterns producing the same string contribute separately; repeated symbols do not identify their original positions.

Codes and error. A length-\(n\) code has a positive integer message count \(M_n\) and deterministic maps
\[\operatorname{Enc}_n:[M_n]\to\{0,1\}^n,\qquad \operatorname{Dec}_n:\mathcal Y_n\to[M_n],\]
where \([M]=\{1,\ldots,M\}\). A uniformly distributed message is encoded once and sent through the channel. Average error is
\[P_{e,n}=\frac1{M_n}\sum_{m=1}^{M_n}\sum_{y\in\mathcal Y_n}\mu_{n,\delta}(y\mid\operatorname{Enc}_n(m))\,\mathbf1\{\operatorname{Dec}_n(y)\ne m\}.\]
The encoder need not be injective by definition; the reliability condition still applies to every message in this average. Any repetition, redundancy or markers inserted by the encoder are part of its \(n\) transmitted bits and are charged in the rate. There is no shared randomness or state supplied outside this code. Encoding and decoding have no time or storage bounds. Their maps may depend arbitrarily on \(n\) and the known \(\delta\); a uniform algorithm producing the family is not required.

Achievable rate and capacity. For a fixed \(\delta\), a real rate \(R\ge0\) is achievable if codes exist for every positive integer \(n\) with
\[P_{e,n}\longrightarrow0,\qquad \liminf_{n\to\infty}\frac{\log_2 M_n}{n}\ge R.\]
Define \(C(\delta)\) as the supremum of all achievable nonnegative rates. It is not assumed that a code family attains this supremum. The denominator is the number of input bits, not the random number of surviving bits. The noiseless and completely deleted endpoints give \(C(0)=1\) and \(C(1)=0\), and \(0\le C(\delta)\le1-\delta\) throughout the domain.

Finite-block information. For a probability distribution \(P\) on a finite set, write \(H(P)=-\sum_{z:P(z)>0}P(z)\log_2 P(z)\). If \(p\) is a distribution on \(\{0,1\}^n\), let \(q(y)=\sum_x p(x)\mu_{n,\delta}(y\mid x)\) and define
\[I_p(X;Y)=H(q)-\sum_x p(x)H(\mu_{n,\delta}(\,\cdot\mid x)),\qquad C_n(\delta)=\frac1n\max_p I_p(X;Y).\]
The maximum ranges over all probability distributions on the finite input alphabet, including correlated input bits, and exists by compactness and continuity. The coding theorem identifies \(C(\delta)=\lim_{n\to\infty}C_n(\delta)\). These \(C_n\) are normalized per input bit; some references instead use the same symbol for the unnormalized maximum.
cards.answer_criterion:
Give an unambiguous real-valued function on the entire real interval \([0,1]\) and a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of the stated absolute-error inequality, with the operational capacity and channel defined above. A formula, a certified evaluation rule or another mathematical description may specify the answer. No polynomial evaluation-time bound, prescribed expression grammar, numerical table size or new scientific theorem is required. An exact determination also qualifies.

A pair of functions \(L,U\) with proved inequalities \(L(\delta)\le C(\delta)\le U(\delta)\) and \(U(\delta)-L(\delta)\le1/50\) for every \(\delta\) qualifies through its midpoint. The proof must establish the full real-parameter domain and both coding and converse sides needed for the certificate. If it uses an information-theoretic characterization instead of the operational definition, their equivalence must be part of the checked justification. Merely renaming the defining capacity, restating an unevaluated asymptotic limit without a proved error bound, giving an uncertified plot, or checking finitely many parameter values is insufficient.

This is deliberately a formalization benchmark for a known approximation guarantee. A rigorous finite-block description with a proved uniform error bound can qualify even if its practical evaluation is prohibitive. It need not improve known numerical bounds or settle the separate exact-capacity question.

The retained absolute 1/100 approximation guarantee is already available in principle from the classical uniform finite-block bound; the user explicitly retains it as a Lean formalization task, not a claim of unresolved approximate capacity. context_blocks.text: A deletion removes a bit and also hides where it belonged. For example, receiving 00 after sending three bits is compatible with several input strings and deletion patterns. The output length reveals how many symbols survived, but it does not reveal their positions. This uncertainty couples the interpretation of consecutive output symbols even though the deletion decisions themselves are independent.

If the receiver were additionally given the deletion locations, the channel would become the binary erasure channel with capacity \(1- \delta\). Revealing information cannot make decoding harder, so \(C(\delta )\le 1- \delta\) is an immediate upper bound. The challenge is to quantify the further loss caused by missing alignment. Counting surviving bits alone therefore does not determine the answer.

The approximation guarantee is already a classical result. Dalai’s Lemma 1 states, for every \(n\ge1\) and every \(\delta\in[0,1]\),
\[C_n(\delta)-\frac{\log_2(n+1)}n\le C(\delta)\le C_n(\delta).\]
The error bound is independent of the deletion probability and tends to zero. It therefore yields fixed-accuracy determination in principle, despite the \(2^n\)-element input alphabet. There is no unresolved existence of an unrestricted approximation scheme at the retained tolerance. The user explicitly chose to keep its complete Lean formalization as this card’s benchmark.

The input bits in a code need not be independent, and restricting the optimizing distributions would change the capacity problem. Rubinstein and Con prove \(C(\delta)>0.1221(1-\delta)\) for every \(0<\delta<1\). Their result establishes a positive constant fraction of the surviving-bit rate throughout the open interval. It is a lower bound on the unrestricted capacity, not an equality or a requirement that every optimal code use their particular input process.

Near the noiseless endpoint, a much sharper asymptotic description is available. Kanoria and Montanari prove \(C(\delta )=1+\delta  \log _{2} \delta - A_{1}\delta +A_{2}\delta ^{2}+O(\delta ^{3- \varepsilon})\) for every fixed \(\varepsilon >0\) as \(\delta\) tends to zero, with explicit constants \(A_{1}\approx 1.15416377\) and \(A_{2}\approx 1.67814594\). They also identify input distributions achieving this order. This determines several leading terms, but its remainder does not vanish identically at a fixed nonzero deletion probability.

Numerical converse bounds use finite channels in which the input and output lengths are bounded and the transition matrix is explicit. Blahut–Arimoto optimization can bound their capacities, which in turn upper-bound the unsegmented deletion channel. Pinto and Ribeiro’s 2026 implementation handles larger instances, including selected input lengths of 31, and reports \(C(\delta )\le 0.3578(1- \delta )\) for \(\delta \ge 0.64\). These are computer-assisted bounds reported by the authors; this review has not rerun their large computations.

Published numerical estimates still leave a substantial practical gap at half deletion: the 2023 table gives an achievable rate above 0.104075, and the April 2026 upper-bound table reports 0.1896. These particular computations do not certify the full curve to absolute error 0.01. This practical gap is consistent with the classical finite approximation theorem: the latter imposes no feasible computation limit and may require an enormous finite optimization.

An August 2026 preprint by Chen claims a further half-deletion lower bound above 0.11032415, using joint information from several output runs and a rational certificate. Its asserted slightly sharper upper number is conditional on a precision assumption about a previously published table. This card records the new lower bound as a preprint claim whose certificate has not been independently reproduced here, and does not present the conditional upper number as a separately established converse. Even if the new lower bound is confirmed, a substantial gap remains.

A September 2026 preprint by Soysal claims
\[C(\delta)\le\frac{1-\delta}{4}\qquad\text{for }\frac{13}{20}\le\delta<1,\]
together with finite-block information and decoding-error bounds. The paper supplies a Lean development and exact finite certificate. Its repository reports separate fresh replay of the components followed by checking final theorems over those verified imports. This review inspected the theorem statements, verification description and author’s machine-readable record; it did not rerun the large proof. The claim concerns a one-sided bound on only part of the domain, and does not determine the exact curve or supply the entire accuracy certificate in this card.

This is a transmission problem: the sender may select a codebook designed for the channel. Trace reconstruction instead starts with an arbitrary unknown string and observes repeated independently deleted copies of that same string. Adversarial deletion codes also use a different error model. Progress in either neighboring subject can be informative without giving the capacity curve with the certified accuracy required here.
