cards.title: Polynomial testability versus distance estimation
cards.formal: Is every polynomially testable property of finite simple graphs also polynomially estimable in the dense graph model? Precisely, for every graph property \(\mathcal P=(\mathcal P_n)_{n\ge1}\) satisfying the definitions below, does existence of a uniform randomized tester and integers \(C,a\ge1\) with worst-case adjacency-query bound \(Ct^a\) imply existence of a uniform randomized distance estimator and integers \(D,b\ge1\) with bound \(Dt^b\)? The guarantees must hold for every graph order \(n\), every integer \(t\ge2\), and every input graph, with proximity and additive accuracy \(\varepsilon=1/t\). Programs and polynomial constants may depend on \(\mathcal P\), but not on \(n,t\) or the input graph.
cards.definitions: A finite simple graph on \([n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}\) is an undirected graph whose edges are unordered pairs of distinct vertices. For each integer \(n\ge1\), \(\mathcal P_n\) is a nonempty collection of these graphs invariant under every permutation of \([n]\). No closure under vertex or edge deletion is assumed. For \(n\ge2\), define \[d(G,\mathcal P_n)=\frac{1}{\binom n2}\min_{H\in\mathcal P_n}|E(G)\mathbin{\triangle}E(H)|.\] Here \(E(G)\) is the edge set and symmetric difference \(\triangle\) counts each added or deleted edge once. Set \(d(G,\mathcal P_1)=0\). The minimum exists because \(\mathcal P_n\) is nonempty and finite. Distance lies in \([0,1]\); it is normalized by all possible unordered pairs, not by the number of present edges. A tester receives \(n,t\) in binary and can query whether any chosen pair of distinct vertices is an edge. Queries may depend on previous answers and independent fair random bits. It accepts each \(G\in\mathcal P_n\) with probability at least \(2/3\) and rejects each \(G\) with \(d(G,\mathcal P_n)\ge1/t\) with probability at least \(2/3\). Either answer is permitted when \(0<d(G,\mathcal P_n)<1/t\). An estimator has the same input and oracle access and outputs a binary-encoded rational number \(z\) such that \[\Pr\bigl[|z-d(G,\mathcal P_n)|\le1/t\bigr]\ge2/3\] on every graph, with no distance promise. Each algorithm is one finite probabilistic Turing oracle program with no advice or additional oracle. It must terminate on every execution. Local computation, storage and output length have no quantitative bound; the charged resource is the total number of adjacency queries, bounded on every input and every random execution. Each probability is over the program's random bits for the fixed input graph. The algorithm does not receive a description of \(\mathcal P\): its fixed program may depend on that property. The implication asks for existence of the estimator, not a uniform meta-algorithm taking a tester's code as input. Accuracy is required at every reciprocal integer; this discretization fixes the parameter encoding without imposing a graph-size-dependent bound.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof of the stated universal implication or of its logical negation. An affirmative proof must provide the full estimator guarantees whenever the tester hypothesis holds. A negative proof must establish a property with a polynomial-query tester for which every uniform estimator fails every fixed polynomial query bound under the same model. A separation between particular algorithms, or a conversion with exponential rather than polynomial query overhead, is insufficient. This is a yes/no question about algorithms at arbitrarily small accuracy, not a request for one distance estimate at the numerical benchmark tolerance.
cards.why: A decision tester recognizes only a large violation, whereas a distance estimator measures the minimum repair needed at every distance scale. A general polynomial implication would transfer efficient sampling guarantees to quantitative assessment across the dense-graph model. A separating property would establish an information-cost distinction between these two basic tasks even when unlimited local computation is allowed.

context_blocks.text: A tester can answer arbitrarily on inputs that are close to a property but do not satisfy it. A distance estimator must still provide an accurate number there. For example, its output must distinguish small, moderate and large repair costs on the same scale, rather than merely certify a sufficiently large violation.

The input contains \(\binom n2\) potential edge bits. A polynomial-in-\(t\) query bound is independent of \(n\), so for large graphs the algorithm reads only a small part of the adjacency relation. This is an information constraint; difficult computation on the observed sample is not excluded.

The existing card explicitly selected the polynomial implication from the stronger quantitative question in the source. Problem 5.4 asks for a conversion preserving an arbitrary testing complexity after polynomial rescaling of accuracy. Such a conversion would imply this card, but a proof of this card would not by itself establish that stronger relationship for nonpolynomial testing functions. The present review preserves this previously recorded target.

The source defines estimation through tolerance thresholds. Returning an additive-distance estimate, as used here and by Fiat–Ron, captures the polynomial-query regime as well: a polynomial number of threshold comparisons at finer accuracy, with amplified success probabilities, suffices to obtain a distance estimate. The factor between pair-count and squared-order normalization is bounded for every order at least two.

The general Fischer–Newman theorem establishes qualitative tester-to-estimator conversion. Its original quantitative loss is of tower type. This does not yield a polynomial estimator from a polynomial tester.

The later conversion improves that loss to double exponential for general properties and to single exponential for hereditary properties. Hereditary means closed under taking induced subgraphs; the universal target here has no such restriction.

Polynomial estimators are known for several particular graph classes, including the stated induced-path and chordal examples. They show that the stronger task can be efficient, but do not settle its cost for every polynomially testable graph property.

cards.title: Sublinear testing of bounded-degree graph isomorphism
cards.formal:
Can isomorphism between two arbitrary bounded-degree graphs be tested with a sublinear number of adjacency-list queries? Precisely, does there exist a uniform randomized tester \(A\), with explicit inputs \(n\ge1\), a degree bound \(d\ge1\), and an integer \(q\ge2\), satisfying the following guarantees for every pair of allowed \(n\)-vertex input graphs \(G_1,G_2\)?
\[G_1\cong G_2\ \Longrightarrow\ \Pr[A\text{ accepts}]\ge2/3,\]
\[\operatorname{dist}_{\mathrm{iso}}(G_1,G_2)\ge1/q\ \Longrightarrow\ \Pr[A\text{ rejects}]\ge2/3.\]
For each fixed \(d,q\), its worst-case query bound \(Q(n,d,q)\) must satisfy
\[\lim_{n\to\infty}\frac{Q(n,d,q)}n=0.\]
Both graphs are given only through oracles. The graph model, distance and query accounting are specified below. The target retains the sublinear-existence question in the saved card, which is one part of the source’s broader request to determine the full query complexity.
cards.why: The problem asks whether two large sparse structures can be compared without reading a linear fraction of their neighborhoods. It isolates the information needed to recognize structural similarity when both objects are unknown. A resolution would locate a basic boundary of sublinear access and explain whether large connected components create an obstruction beyond the known distribution-like examples.

cards.definitions:
The graphs \(G_i=([n],E_i)\), where \([n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}\), are undirected and simple, with maximum degree at most \(d\). Disconnected graphs and isolated vertices are allowed. There is no expansion, hyperfiniteness, component-size or randomness promise on their structure.

Graph \(G_i\) is represented by an incidence oracle \(g_i:[n]\times[d]\to[n]\cup\{\bot\}\). Its first \(\deg_{G_i}(v)\) entries at vertex \(v\) list the distinct neighbors of \(v\) in an arbitrary fixed order, and the remaining entries are \(\bot\). The oracles are promised consistent with undirected simple graphs. One adjacency query chooses \(i\in\{1,2\}\), \(v\in[n]\), and \(j\in[d]\), and receives \(g_i(v,j)\). Queries may depend on earlier answers. Correctness must hold for every permitted neighbor ordering.

For a permutation \(\sigma\) of \([n]\), put \(\sigma(E_2)=\{\{\sigma(u),\sigma(v)\}:\{u,v\}\in E_2\}\). Define
\[\operatorname{dist}_{\mathrm{iso}}(G_1,G_2)=\frac1{dn}\min_{\sigma\in S_n}|E_1\mathbin{\triangle}\sigma(E_2)|,\]
where \(S_n\) is the set of all permutations and \(\triangle\) denotes symmetric difference. Each deleted or added undirected edge counts once. Thus distance zero means graph isomorphism, and the rejection promise means at least \(dn/q\) edge edits are needed after the best vertex relabelling. Neighbor-list positions do not affect this distance. For nonisomorphic pairs at distance strictly below \(1/q\), either output is allowed.

The tester is a probabilistic oracle Turing algorithm given binary \(n,d,q\), access to both incidence oracles, independent fair random bits and a primitive returning an independent uniformly sampled vertex label in \([n]\). Count every incidence-oracle call and every such vertex-sampling call as one query. All other finite local computation is unrestricted, and the tester must halt. The bound \(Q(n,d,q)\) holds on every allowed pair, every representation and every sequence of random outcomes. Success probabilities include all internal randomness and vertex samples. No graph-dependent advice or full description of either graph is provided; any preprocessing uses only \(n,d,q\).

The degree and reciprocal proximity are fixed when taking the sublinear limit. There is no requirement for one bound uniform in growing \(d\) or \(q\), and no polynomial runtime requirement beyond the query guarantee. Using reciprocal integer accuracies covers all fixed positive proximities by choosing a smaller reciprocal threshold. The edge-edit normalization follows the saved card; the source also uses a convention with a factor of two in the edge threshold. That constant rescaling does not change the all-fixed-proximities existence question.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct Lean-checked proof of existence of a tester with the stated correctness, access and sublinear-query guarantees, or a Lean-checked refutation of that existence statement. A positive answer must cover every pair of bounded-degree input graphs and every fixed proximity, with two-sided error at most \(1/3\). A near-linear bound that is not \(o(n)\), a guarantee for almost all graphs, a known-target tester, or a result only for small connected components is insufficient. A lower bound of order \(n^{2/3}\) up to logarithmic factors alone does not rule out sublinear testing.

context_blocks.text: Open Problem 2.4 explicitly separates testing against a known fixed graph from testing a pair of oracle inputs. This card chooses the latter, as in its saved formulation, and retains two-sided error.

Goldreich proves upper and lower query bounds of order \(n^{2/3}\), up to polylogarithmic factors and proximity dependence, when connected components have polylogarithmic size. The lower bound also applies to general inputs, but the upper bound retains its component-size restriction.

Goldreich and Tauber obtain a \(\widetilde O(\sqrt n)\) tester for almost all fixed regular target graphs, with a matching lower bound up to logarithmic factors. Their model supplies the target graph in advance; it neither supplies both graphs only by oracle nor covers every possible target.

The relevant resource here is query complexity. A tester may perform extensive finite computation on its observations. Therefore a fast algorithm for explicit graph isomorphism does not, by itself, meet the oracle-query target, and a query bound does not by itself assert fast total runtime.

cards.title: Polynomial testing of induced four-cycle freeness
cards.formal: Do there exist integers \(C,a\ge1\) such that the canonical sampling test below, with sample size \[s(\varepsilon)=\lceil C\varepsilon^{-a}\rceil,\] rejects every finite simple graph that is \(\varepsilon\)-far from having no induced four-cycle with probability at least \(2/3\), for every rational \(\varepsilon\in(0,1)\)? The constants must be independent of the graph order and of \(\varepsilon\). The test always accepts graphs with no induced four-cycle, so this asks for polynomial-query one-sided testing in the dense graph model.
cards.why: This is the unresolved concrete case, up to complementation, in the classification of polynomial testing for a single forbidden induced graph. An induced four-cycle has its four cycle edges and neither diagonal, and repairing the graph permits both edge additions and deletions.

cards.definitions: A finite simple graph is an undirected graph \(G=([n],E)\), where \(n\ge1\), \([n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}\), and \(E\) is a set of unordered pairs of distinct vertices. An induced four-cycle consists of four distinct vertices \(v_1,v_2,v_3,v_4\) whose edges among those vertices are exactly \(\{v_1,v_2\},\{v_2,v_3\},\{v_3,v_4\},\{v_4,v_1\}\); the two diagonals are absent. Let \(\mathcal P_n\) be the graphs on \([n]\) with no such induced subgraph. Define \[d(G,\mathcal P_n)=\frac{1}{n^{2}}\min_{([n],E')\in\mathcal P_n}|E\mathbin{\triangle}E'|.\] Here \(\triangle\) is symmetric difference, so both edge additions and deletions are allowed and each undirected edit is counted once. The minimum exists because \(\mathcal P_n\) is nonempty and finite. The graph is \(\varepsilon\)-far when \(d(G,\mathcal P_n)>\varepsilon\), with strict inequality. This uses the edge-count-over-\(n^{2}\) convention of the selected survey; it is half the adjacency-matrix-entry distance in the original Goldreich question. The tester is given \(n\) and rational \(\varepsilon\), and has oracle access to the adjacency bit of any unordered vertex pair. For a positive integer \(s\), the canonical test chooses a uniformly random subset \(S\subseteq[n]\) of cardinality \(\min\{n,s\}\), queries every unordered pair in \(S\), and rejects exactly when \(G[S]\) contains an induced four-cycle. All \(\binom{\min\{n,s\}}{2}\) adjacency queries count; the property check on the finite sampled graph has no additional query cost, and no running-time bound is requested. Uniform subset sampling is the stated finite probability distribution, with sampling and local computation not charged as adjacency queries. If \(n\le s\), the entire graph is inspected. In particular, orders below four are always accepted and never far. No behavior is required for nonsatisfying graphs at distance at most \(\varepsilon\). Every host graph is allowed; no degree, density, chordality or other promise is imposed. The deterministic sampling-size formula and rejection rule specify a single uniform family of tests once \(C,a\) are fixed.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove the formal proposition or its logical negation with a complete Lean-checked proof. A positive answer must exhibit fixed polynomial constants and establish rejection probability at least \(2/3\) for every far input and every permitted proximity parameter. A negative answer must show that for every choice of \(C,a\) there are a proximity parameter and a graph at the stated distance for which that sampling test rejects with probability less than \(2/3\). A merely exponential sample bound, a result for ordinary four-cycle freeness, or a tester with an additional host-graph promise does not meet the target.

context_blocks.text: An induced four-cycle is a cycle without either diagonal. A complete graph on four vertices contains ordinary four-cycles, but no induced four-cycle. This distinction changes both the set of valid graphs and the repair task: adding a diagonal can destroy an induced cycle, while adding edges cannot eliminate an ordinary subgraph copy.

The tester does not try to find every violation or to reconstruct a repaired graph. It distinguishes graphs satisfying the property from graphs requiring more than \(\varepsilon n^{2}\) edits. A polynomial sample bound would mean that the number of queried adjacencies remains polynomial in reciprocal proximity even when the host graph is arbitrarily large.

The induced removal lemma relates edit distance to the number of forbidden induced copies. For a fixed pattern, polynomial bounds on that density and polynomial bounds for canonical one-sided sampling are equivalent up to changes in polynomial exponents. The known four-cycle removal bound is exponential in a power of reciprocal distance, which is far larger than the polynomial dependence conjectured here.

Alon and Shapira classified the polynomial and superpolynomial cases for single forbidden induced graphs apart from a few small patterns. Alon and Fox settled the four-vertex-path case, leaving the induced four-cycle and its complement as the remaining case. Complementing all adjacencies preserves edit distance and transfers the sampling question between those two patterns.

Goldreich's Open Problem 8.26 concerns all dense-graph properties, permits two-sided error, and asks for a characterization; it is strictly broader in scope and is not asserted equivalent to this testability conjecture. The separate active finite-family classification card also remains a different target.

The 2026 container characterization connects one-sided tester complexity to quantitative combinatorial parameters. It supplies an equivalence, rather than polynomial values of those parameters for every particular property. Consequently, the existence of that characterization does not itself settle the induced-four-cycle bound.

cards.title: Planar graphs from local neighborhoods
cards.formal: For every real \(\varepsilon>0\), does there exist a positive integer \(D=D(\varepsilon)\) such that, for every integer \(n\ge1\) and every pair of finite simple planar graphs \(G,H\) on \(n\) vertices, equality of their multisets of rooted radius-\(D\) neighborhoods implies \[\min_{\phi:V(G)\cong V(H)}\left|\phi(E(G))\mathbin{\triangle}E(H)\right|\le\varepsilon n?\] The minimum is over all vertex bijections, and \(\triangle\) denotes symmetric difference of edge sets. There is no maximum-degree bound; the radius may depend only on \(\varepsilon\).
cards.why: This asks whether local structure determines approximate global structure throughout the planar family, even around vertices of very high degree. It isolates a structural obstruction behind extending sparse-graph testing beyond bounded-degree and outerplanar settings.

sentences: The question compares two planar graphs through the rooted neighborhoods around all their vertices.
It asks whether a radius depending only on the allowed error makes identical neighborhood multisets imply closeness under edge edits and vertex relabeling.
No maximum-degree bound is imposed, so even a small-radius neighborhood may be large.

cards.definitions:
A finite simple undirected graph is a finite vertex set \(V\) and a set \(E\) of unordered pairs of distinct vertices. Thus loops and multiple edges are excluded. A planar graph admits a drawing in the plane with distinct points for vertices and curves for edges whose interiors neither intersect one another nor meet a vertex. A drawing is not part of the data, and it is not used to compare neighborhoods. Graphs need not be connected. Their order is \(n=|V|\), and the two graphs in the question have the same order.

The graph distance \(\operatorname{dist}_G(u,v)\) is the minimum number of edges in a path from \(u\) to \(v\), with distance infinity when no path exists. The rooted radius-\(D\) neighborhood \(B_G(v,D)\) is the subgraph induced by \(\{u\in V(G):\operatorname{dist}_G(u,v)\le D\}\), together with the distinguished root \(v\). An induced subgraph retains every edge whose two endpoints belong to that set. Rooted graphs are isomorphic when a bijection of their vertices preserves edges and sends one root to the other. Vertex labels, the planar drawing, any ordering of neighbors, and edges leaving the neighborhood are not part of its rooted isomorphism type.

The multiset of radius-\(D\) neighborhoods records each rooted isomorphism type with its multiplicity among the \(n\) possible roots. Equality means that, for every finite rooted graph \(F\), the number of vertices \(v\) for which \(B_G(v,D)\) is isomorphic to \(F\) equals the corresponding number in \(H\). Thus multiplicities matter. Although corresponding roots can be paired, their individual neighborhood isomorphisms need not agree on overlapping vertices. In particular, such a pairing is not already a global graph isomorphism. Even a radius-one neighborhood may contain arbitrarily many vertices, because degrees are unrestricted.

For a vertex bijection \(\phi:V(G)\to V(H)\), define \(\phi(E(G))=\{\{\phi(u),\phi(v)\}:\{u,v\}\in E(G)\}\). The symmetric difference consists of edges in exactly one of its two arguments. Its cardinality counts edge deletions plus edge additions, each at unit cost, after a free relabeling of vertices. Taking the minimum over bijections gives the edit distance to isomorphism. There are no vertex edits or isolated-vertex padding in this equal-order question. Intermediate graphs during edge editing are not required to be planar. The permitted number of edits is at most \(\varepsilon n\), normalized by vertex count rather than by the number of possible edges or by a degree bound. For \(n=1\) the conclusion is automatic. No algorithm for finding the bijection, a computable bound on \(D\), or property-testing oracle is requested; this is a structural existence statement.

source_formulation.text: Do identical sufficiently large rooted local-neighborhood multisets force two planar graphs of the same order to be close to isomorphic under edge edits?

context_blocks.text: The broad imported question asked for a classification of graph properties testable with sublinear query complexity. This card now adopts the separate, concrete planar local-neighborhood question from the same source. The change of scope was explicitly selected on 16 September 2026; it does not claim to complete the original general classification programme.

The structural issue is whether sufficiently large local views determine a sparse planar graph up to a small linear number of edge edits. The neighborhoods carry no consistent global labels. Matching their multiplicities therefore supplies statistical local information, not a ready-made global correspondence.

For planar graphs with a fixed maximum degree, earlier local-to-global results provide a radius depending on both the error tolerance and that degree bound. The selected question asks whether the degree dependence can be removed completely. Planarity bounds average degree, but permits individual degrees growing with the graph order.

Babu, Khoury and Newman prove the required local-view implication for outerplanar graphs, with no maximum-degree bound. Outerplanar means that the graph has a plane drawing with every vertex incident to the exterior face. Their Theorem 4.4 states the same qualitative radius-versus-edge-distance conclusion for that subclass.

The source extends its methods to graphs with a fixed number of edge-removal outer layers. It distinguishes this from removing exterior vertices layer by layer, and explicitly retains the ordinary 2-outerplanar case as open at publication. Those positive results therefore must not be read as covering every planar graph.

The paper also obtains polylogarithmic-query property testers for its unbounded-degree subclasses, using ordered-neighbor and degree access. These algorithmic results explain the motivation for the structural question, but the selected target itself asks only for the stated finite-graph implication.

Basu, Kumar and Seshadhri sharpen the dependence on proximity for testing properties of bounded-degree planar graphs and show matching exponential behavior for isomorphism testing. Their results retain a maximum-degree bound and therefore do not settle the unbounded-degree local-view question.

cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof of the displayed universal statement, or a complete Lean-checked proof of its logical negation: there exists a fixed \(\varepsilon_0>0\) such that for every positive integer \(D\), there are some \(n\ge1\) and simple planar \(n\)-vertex graphs \(G,H\) with identical radius-\(D\) neighborhood multisets but edit distance strictly greater than \(\varepsilon_0 n\). A proof restricted to bounded maximum degree or to outerplanar graphs does not establish the assertion for all planar graphs. Equality of the set of neighborhood types without multiplicities is a different hypothesis. A radius growing with \(n\) or maximum degree is insufficient. This is an exact yes/no implication, not a numerical approximation problem.

cards.title: Sharp graph-removal bounds for fixed patterns
cards.formal: Determine the asymptotic order of the extremal copy-count function \(M_H(\varepsilon,n)\) defined below, for every fixed connected finite simple graph \(H\) with at least two edges. Both the proximity parameter \(\varepsilon\) and the graph order \(n\) vary. The requested precision is matching upper and lower bounds up to multiplicative constants depending only on \(H\), uniformly over all feasible pairs \((\varepsilon,n)\). Thus the answer must specify bounds \(B_H(\varepsilon,n)>0\) and prove that, for each such \(H\), there are constants \(0<c_H\le C_H<\infty\) such that \[c_H B_H(\varepsilon,n)\le M_H(\varepsilon,n)\le C_H B_H(\varepsilon,n)\] for every feasible pair. The copies are ordinary subgraphs, with extra edges allowed.
cards.why: Removal bounds quantify how visible a forbidden configuration must become once a graph is globally far from avoiding it. Their dependence on the distance parameter controls the sampling cost of detecting violations and connects dense-graph testing to extremal and additive combinatorics. Distinguishing polynomial from superpolynomial dependence identifies a broad boundary, but does not determine the rate on either side of it.
cards.status_note: The source poses this quantitative target in 2017. The source definitions, Fox’s logarithmic-height tower bound, the minimum-degree restriction in Fox–Wigderson, the 2025 survey and the 2025 hypergraph classification were checked on 15 September 2026. A bounded search of later work did not identify matching general bounds; this is not an exhaustive certification of openness or an independent verification of the cited proofs. Constant-factor precision, the subset-copy convention and the feasible-domain treatment are recorded editorial specifications.

progress.text: The graph-removal theorem supplies a positive density guarantee, while the ordinary subgraph-freeness dichotomy distinguishes bipartite patterns, which have polynomial bounds, from nonbipartite patterns, which do not. This is a classification of the broad rate regime, not matching bounds for every pattern.

Fox's Theorem 1 improves the general removal guarantee to an inverse tower of twos whose height is \(O_H(\log(1/\varepsilon))\), after translating distance and copy conventions. This is an upper bound on the required reciprocal density; it is not a matching construction showing that tower growth is necessary.
Goldreich poses the connected-pattern copy-count question as Open Problem 8.17 and summarizes available bounds in Theorem 8.18; footnote 41 records the logarithmic-height tower improvement.

Fox–Wigderson prove linear clique-removal bounds under a minimum degree greater than \((2r-5)n/(2r-3)\) by a fixed positive fraction of \(n\), for the pattern \(K_r\). Below that threshold they recover superpolynomial behavior. The additional minimum-degree hypothesis is absent from the general target.

Gishboliner–Shapira settle the higher-uniformity analogue of the polynomial-removal classification: ordinary hypergraph removal has polynomial bounds precisely for partite patterns. That result does not give matching growth bounds for the nonbipartite graph cases here.

The Polynomial Property Testing survey retains the polynomial/nonpolynomial dichotomy in Section 3.1. A bounded later-work search on 15 September 2026 did not identify matching general bounds for the full copy-count target.

sentences: For each fixed connected graph pattern, the question asks how few ordinary copies a graph can contain while still being far from avoiding that pattern.
Distance is the fraction of adjacency-matrix entries that must change, and each vertex subset supporting the pattern is counted once.
The target is matching constant-factor bounds in both the graph order and the proximity parameter, with constants allowed to depend on the pattern.
The removal lemma guarantees positive density at every fixed distance, but the general quantitative bounds remain widely separated.
Sharp bounds would quantify the worst-case visibility of local violations and the sampling cost of detecting them.

cards.definitions: Write \([n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}\), and let \(t=|V(H)|\). All graphs are undirected and have neither loops nor multiple edges. A graph is \(H\)-free if there is no injective map \(\phi:V(H)\to V(G)\) taking every edge of \(H\) to an edge of \(G\); nonedges of \(H\) impose no restriction. Let \(r_H(G)\) be the least number of edges that must be deleted from \(G\) to make it \(H\)-free. Allowing edge additions as well cannot decrease this minimum. Use the source's adjacency-matrix distance \(d_H(G)=2r_H(G)/n^{2}\): each changed undirected edge changes two matrix entries. Say that \(G\) is \(\varepsilon\)-far when \(d_H(G)>\varepsilon\), with a strict inequality. Define \(N_H(G)\) to be the number of \(t\)-element subsets \(S\subseteq[n]\) for which \(G[S]\) contains an ordinary copy of \(H\), counting each such subset once even if it supports several embeddings. This fixes the copy convention suggested by the source's random-subset test; counting injective labelled embeddings instead changes the count by factors between one and \(t!\). A feasible pair is a rational \(\varepsilon\in(0,1)\) and an integer \(n\ge t\) for which at least one graph on \([n]\) has \(d_H(G)>\varepsilon\). On precisely this domain, set \[M_H(\varepsilon,n)=\min\{N_H(G):V(G)=[n],\ d_H(G)>\varepsilon\}.\] The minimum is over a nonempty finite set, so it is a positive integer. No value is requested for an infeasible pair. The constants in the matching bounds may depend on the whole fixed pattern \(H\), but not on \(n\) or \(\varepsilon\); in particular, \(\varepsilon\) may decrease with \(n\). The target is the growth of this extremal function, not the running time of enumerating graphs. No extra minimum-degree, regularity, randomness or sparsity promise is imposed on \(G\).
cards.answer_criterion: Supply the matching asymptotic bounds in the formal statement and a complete Lean-checked proof of both inequalities for every permitted pattern and feasible parameter pair. The lower inequality must hold for every graph at the stated distance, and the upper inequality must establish existence of graphs with the claimed copy count. Merely restating the defining minimization, tabulating finitely many values, giving one-sided bounds, or establishing only that some positive removal bound exists does not meet this growth target. The precision here is a multiplicative constant factor depending only on the pattern, not additive \(1/100\) accuracy on a normalized copy density.

context_blocks.text: For a fixed pattern on \(t\) vertices, a random \(t\)-vertex subset detects a violation with probability exactly \(N_H(G)/\binom{n}{t}\). The extremal function asks how small that probability can be while repairing the whole graph still requires changing a positive fraction of its adjacency matrix. This connects a global repair requirement to the frequency of small observable witnesses.

Ordinary and induced removal are different questions. An ordinary copy only requires the pattern's edges to be present; an induced copy also requires its nonedges to remain absent. For example, three mutually adjacent vertices contain a three-vertex path as an ordinary subgraph, but not as an induced path. This card retains ordinary copies from Definition 8.16 and the connected-pattern scope of Open Problem 8.17.

The classical removal lemma ensures a positive copy density for every fixed positive distance, uniformly over graph order. Its quantitative content can nevertheless be extremely weak: the known general lower guarantee involves an inverse tower of exponentials, while nonbipartite examples exclude every fixed polynomial dependence on distance. A positive constant for each fixed distance therefore says much less than a sharp answer as the distance tends to zero.

The source asks for relatively tight bounds on a function of both distance and graph order. This card makes that precision explicit as constant-factor matching bounds with pattern-dependent constants, retaining both parameters and specifying the feasible domain. It does not silently replace the question by the triangle-only case, by a large-graph limit, or by the already known polynomial/nonpolynomial classification. The matrix normalization differs by a factor of two from the edge-count-over-\(n^{2}\) convention in several later papers.

The dependence on the host graph matters. A sufficiently large minimum degree can give linear removal bounds for cliques, whereas unrestricted hosts admit much smaller copy densities. Such a theorem clarifies a special regime and cannot supply a bound for every graph in the domain of this card.

cards.title: Polynomial-time density learning of Gaussian mixtures
cards.formal: Does there exist a uniform randomized algorithm that properly learns every mixture of at most \(k\) nondegenerate Gaussian distributions on \(\mathbb R^d\), to any fixed total-variation accuracy, in time polynomial jointly in \(k\) and \(d\)? Precisely, is there one algorithm \(A\) in the arithmetic model below such that, for every integer \(t\ge3\), there are integers \(C_t,a_t\ge1\) for which the following holds for all integers \(k,d\ge1\) and all \(P\in\mathcal G_{k,d}\)? Given \(k,d,t\) and independent samples from \(P\), the algorithm uses at most \(C_t(k+d)^{a_t}\) operations and outputs a description of \(\widehat P\in\mathcal G_{k,d}\) satisfying \[\Pr[d_{\mathrm{TV}}(P,\widehat P)\le1/t]\ge2/3.\] The time bound holds on every execution and includes sampling and writing the output. Its constants are uniform over all mixture parameters. No polynomial dependence on \(t\) is required: this card asks the source's joint polynomial dependence on the number of components and dimension at each fixed accuracy.

source_formulation.text: Can Gaussian mixtures be learned in running time polynomial in both the number of components and the ambient dimension, even without privacy?
source_formulation.caption: Editorial paraphrase of the source question on page 6

cards.why: Gaussian mixtures are a basic example where enough observations can be available but extracting a useful distribution from them may remain computationally difficult. Joint dependence on dimension and component count distinguishes scalable learning from methods efficient only for a small fixed mixture. Resolving this target would clarify that statistical–computational gap in the absence of separation or conditioning assumptions.
cards.status_note: Source-open in ALT 2024 for joint polynomial dependence on component count and dimension. On 16 September 2026 the full source definitions and question, the 2017 and 2022 hardness manuscripts, the November 2024 score-matching theorem, and the April 2025/August 2026 primary abstracts were checked. A bounded later-work search found no unconditional resolution of the stated target. Proper output follows the source definition; fixed-accuracy quantifiers and exact-real primitives are explicit editorial computational conventions, not a claimed bit-complexity theorem. Conditional hardness and restricted-model lower bounds remain qualified. Cited proofs were not independently verified or formalized in Lean.

sentences: The learner receives independent observations from a mixture of at most k nondegenerate Gaussians in d dimensions.
It must output another such mixture whose whole distribution is close in total variation, without reconstructing the original components.
The question asks for a uniform algorithm with time polynomial jointly in k and d for each fixed accuracy, using explicitly specified exact-real arithmetic.
Polynomial sample sufficiency coexists with statistical-query lower bounds and conditional computational hardness, neither of which is silently treated as an unconditional resolution.
Newer positive results with bounded parameters, fixed component counts or growing dimension exponents do not establish the full target.

cards.definitions: For a positive integer \(d\), a nondegenerate Gaussian distribution \(N(\mu,\Sigma)\) has mean \(\mu\in\mathbb R^d\) and a symmetric positive-definite matrix \(\Sigma\in\mathbb R^{d\times d}\). Positive definite means \(v^{\mathsf T}\Sigma v>0\) for every nonzero \(v\in\mathbb R^d\). Its density at \(x\in\mathbb R^d\) is \[(2\pi)^{-d/2}(\det\Sigma)^{-1/2}\exp\!\left(-\tfrac12(x-\mu)^{\mathsf T}\Sigma^{-1}(x-\mu)\right).\] The class \(\mathcal G_{k,d}\) consists of all distributions \(P=\sum_{i=1}^k w_iN(\mu_i,\Sigma_i)\), where \(w_i\ge0\), \(\sum_iw_i=1\), and each component satisfies the preceding conditions. Zero weights allow fewer than \(k\) components; repeated components are allowed. Means, covariance eigenvalues and component separation have no upper or lower promises beyond positive definiteness, and positive weights have no prescribed minimum. If \(p,q\) are the densities of \(P,Q\), their total variation distance is \[d_{\mathrm{TV}}(P,Q)=\tfrac12\int_{\mathbb R^d}|p(x)-q(x)|\,dx,\] where integration is with respect to Lebesgue measure. The learner has no access to the hidden component label or parameters. Each sampling request returns a fresh independent vector drawn from \(P\). The output consists of \(k\) weights, \(k\) means and \(k\) positive-definite covariance matrices, describing a valid member of the same class on every execution. This requirement is called proper learning. No correspondence between true and output components is required. The success probability is over all sampled vectors and the algorithm's independent fair random bits. Computational convention: \(A\) is one finite program, with rational constants and no nonuniform advice, using exact real registers together with a Turing work tape. Allowed real operations are copying, addition, subtraction, multiplication, division by a nonzero value, square root of a nonnegative value, and order or equality comparisons; each costs one operation. Reading or writing a real register costs one operation; a sample vector costs \(d\) operations. Each fair random bit and each ordinary tape step costs one operation. Integer inputs use binary encoding. Undefined arithmetic operations are forbidden. Each output scalar must be written and charged. No integration, optimization, density-evaluation or arbitrary-function oracle is available. The density formula defines the mathematical distribution, not an extra primitive of the program. This explicit arithmetic convention measures computation on real observations; it does not claim polynomial bit complexity for an unspecified finite-precision encoding.
cards.answer_criterion: Provide a complete Lean-checked proof of the algorithm-existence statement or of its logical negation in the stated model. An affirmative proof must establish validity of the proper output, total execution bound and uniform total-variation guarantee for every allowed mixture and every accuracy parameter. A negative proof must rule out all algorithms in the specified arithmetic model, rather than only statistical-query algorithms or one proposed method. A conditional hardness theorem must be identified with its additional hypothesis and does not by itself settle this unconditional yes/no target. Learning with a fixed number of components, recovering component parameters under separation assumptions, or returning only an arbitrary sampler does not establish the requested statement. The reciprocal-accuracy parameter belongs to the learning guarantee; it is not a single numerical answer to be approximated at the benchmark's default tolerance.

context_blocks.text: A mixture combines several Gaussian populations without telling the learner which population generated an observation. Density learning asks for a distribution that predicts the whole population well. Two different lists of components can describe the same, or nearly the same, distribution; therefore success does not require reconstructing the original list.

The source defines proper PAC learning and unbounded positive-definite Gaussian components. Its highlighted computational question appears in a paper about private learning, but explicitly remains a question even when privacy is removed. The present target has no privacy requirement.

Section 9.3 recalls near-optimal nonprivate sample complexity \(\widetilde\Theta(kd^2/\alpha^2)\) at accuracy \(\alpha\), with logarithmic factors suppressed. A statistical existence bound does not make the search for a suitable mixture polynomial-time. The private construction also uses a nonconstructive cover, a separate obstacle discussed on page 6.

The statement fixes proper output, exact arithmetic primitives and the order of quantifiers explicitly. The source says polynomial in the two structural parameters and does not specify a bit model in its open-question sentence. Allowing the exponent to depend on fixed accuracy avoids silently strengthening that sentence to a fully polynomial accuracy guarantee.

Statistical-query lower bounds restrict algorithms that obtain information through approximate expectations of bounded test functions. They explain an obstruction for a broad family of learning methods, but alone do not exclude every algorithm with direct sample access.

There is also conditional evidence beyond statistical queries. Gupte–Vafa–Vaikuntanathan derive hardness of Gaussian-mixture density estimation from Learning with Errors assumptions. Those assumptions concern the difficulty of recovering or distinguishing hidden linear structure from noisy modular observations. The reductions and computational assumptions belong to their stated model; the card does not promote them to an unconditional theorem for its exact-real machine.

The score-matching theorem assumes a bounded conditioning/size parameter \(\tau\) and minimum positive weight at least inverse-polynomial in \(k\). It uses \(d^{\operatorname{poly}(k\tau/\alpha)}\) samples, runs in time polynomial in that sample count, and returns a sampler. The dimension exponent grows with the number of components, so this guarantee does not supply the joint polynomial bound sought here.

The 2025 parallel-pancake work studies shared-covariance structure and gives statistical-query limitations even with uniform weights, alongside a quasipolynomial testing guarantee. Its restrictions and model remain explicit.

The August 2026 manuscript concerns unit covariances, bounded means and a fixed component count. Its claimed sharp polynomial-time risk bound for that family does not settle arbitrary covariances or joint polynomial dependence. The card records the claim and its scope without asserting independent verification of the manuscript.

cards.title: Query complexity of Max-CSP testing
cards.formal: Determine, up to constant factors as \(n\to\infty\), the randomized query complexity \(q_{D,\Gamma,d,\alpha,c,s}(n)\) of distinguishing bounded-degree constraint instances with optimum satisfied fraction at least \(c\) from those with optimum at most \(s\). The target ranges over every fixed finite predicate template \((D,\Gamma)\), degree bound \(d\), density lower bound \(\alpha\), and gap \(0\le s<c\le1\), under the variable-query model defined below. Taking \(\alpha=0\) includes unrestricted bounded-degree inputs; positive \(\alpha\) includes the source’s density-bounded model.

source_formulation.text: Determine the query complexity of \(MaxCSP(\Gamma )[c, s]\) in the bounded-degree model, for all predicate families \(\Gamma\) and parameters c and s.
source_formulation.caption: Complete selected source sentence; PDF p. 6

cards.why: This asks for a general account of how much of a sparse constraint system must be inspected to distinguish high from low optimum value. It covers different predicates, value gaps and densities in one query model, and could identify broad structural boundaries between local testing and essentially complete inspection. Its complexity bounds are information-based and need not assume computational hardness conjectures.

cards.definitions: The domain \(D\) is a nonempty finite set, and \(\Gamma\) is a finite collection of predicates \(R:D^{k_R}\to\{0,1\}\), with positive integer arities \(k_R\). A predicate is specified by its full finite table and ordered coordinates; these tables are fixed parameters known to the tester. For an integer \(n\ge1\), an instance has variable set \([n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}\) and a finite multiset \(\mathcal C\) of \(m\) constraint occurrences. An occurrence consists of a predicate \(R\in\Gamma\) and an ordered tuple of \(k_R\) distinct variable labels. Identical occurrences may be repeated and each copy is counted separately. The degree of a variable is the number of occurrences containing it. Fix an integer \(d\ge0\) and a real \(\alpha\in[0,d]\); admissible instances have maximum degree at most \(d\) and \(m\ge\alpha n\). Thus \(\alpha=0\) permits empty or very sparse instances, while \(\alpha>0\) enforces a linear number of constraints. For an assignment \(\tau:[n]\to D\), an occurrence \((R,(v_1,\ldots,v_{k_R}))\) is satisfied when \(R(\tau(v_1),\ldots,\tau(v_{k_R}))=1\). If \(m>0\), define \[\operatorname{val}(I)=\frac{1}{m}\max_{\tau:[n]\to D}\sum_{(R,\mathbf v)\in\mathcal C}R(\tau(v_1),\ldots,\tau(v_{k_R})).\] Put \(\operatorname{val}(I)=1\) when \(m=0\). Fix real constants \(0\le s<c\le1\). YES instances have \(\operatorname{val}(I)\ge c\), NO instances have \(\operatorname{val}(I)\le s\), and no correctness condition is imposed between the two thresholds. The tester knows \(n,D,\Gamma,d,\alpha,c,s\), but receives neither the constraint list nor its actual length \(m\). A query specifies a variable \(v\in[n]\). If an as-yet-unrevealed constraint occurrence involving \(v\) exists, the oracle reveals one such occurrence, giving its predicate and full ordered variable tuple. Otherwise it returns \(\bot\). Revealing an occurrence marks that copy as seen globally, including at its other variables. Distinct identical copies remain distinct possible future responses. Which available occurrence is returned may be chosen adversarially as a function of past queries and replies, subject to one fixed input instance; the oracle cannot depend on unrevealed future random choices. Every oracle call, including one returning \(\bot\), costs one query. Arbitrary variable labels may be queried without first being discovered. Local computation, storage and private random choices are free; there is no direct uniform-constraint sampling oracle, no degree oracle and no free inspection of \(m\). Query complexity is defined by finite randomized adaptive decision trees: finite probability distributions over deterministic query-and-answer trees, with rational probabilities, whose leaves output accept or reject. Each deterministic tree can choose its next variable from the preceding transcript. No time, space or tree-size bound is imposed. A tester is valid if it accepts every YES instance and rejects every NO instance with probability at least \(2/3\), for every valid oracle response policy. Its cost is the maximum number of queries on any branch. Let \(q_{D,\Gamma,d,\alpha,c,s}(n)\) be the minimum integer cost of a valid tester. If one promise side is empty, including when no admissible instance exists, this minimum can be zero. All parameters in the subscript are held fixed as \(n\) grows; they are not growing input-length parameters. A matching asymptotic classification must retain their effects on which growth regime occurs.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct characterization checked in Lean of the asymptotic query growth for all fixed parameter tuples in the definition. In particular, specify nonnegative comparison functions \(f_{D,\Gamma,d,\alpha,c,s}(n)\), with corresponding upper and lower bounds, such that for each fixed tuple some constants \(A,B>0\) and \(n_0\) satisfy \[A f_{D,\Gamma,d,\alpha,c,s}(n)\le q_{D,\Gamma,d,\alpha,c,s}(n)\le B f_{D,\Gamma,d,\alpha,c,s}(n)\qquad(n\ge n_0).\] Constants may depend on the fixed tuple, but not on \(n\), the instance or the oracle order. Zero-query cases must be correctly included. The classification need not consist of a prescribed finite list of cases, but it must establish growth rates rather than merely rename or repeat the defining decision-tree optimization. Polylogarithmic gaps between upper and lower bounds do not meet the requested constant-factor precision. Results only for perfect completeness \(c=1\), one template, a special gap, or a positive-density subclass do not cover the full target. A streaming-space or polynomial-time approximation classification is not a query classification.

context_blocks.text: A Max-CSP instance asks for an assignment satisfying as many local predicates as possible. A query tester is allowed to inspect only selected incident constraints and must distinguish two separated ranges of the optimum value, even though it has unlimited ability to process what it has seen.

The fraction satisfied is normalized by the actual number of constraint occurrences. This differs from ordinary bounded-degree property-testing distance, which counts edits relative to the degree bound times the number of variables. The difference matters when most variables are isolated.

Fei therefore introduces \(\mathrm{BD}^{*}(d,\alpha,n)\), requiring at least \(\alpha n\) constraints for fixed positive \(\alpha\). The present density parameter includes both that model and \(\alpha=0\), the original bounded-degree regime. It keeps the sparse-instance issue visible rather than silently assuming linear density.

Question 13 asks for the complexity of all predicate families and completeness–soundness pairs. This card makes the degree, density and oracle conventions explicit and chooses constant-factor matching bounds as its asymptotic acceptance precision. No claim is made that a previously proved dichotomy already supplies those bounds.

Even the perfect-completeness satisfiability setting displays several behaviors. The source surveys constant-query languages, square-root lower bounds with nearly matching upper bounds for graph bipartiteness, and linear lower bounds for graph 3-colorability. These examples do not classify every imperfect-completeness gap.

Fei’s Theorem 8 proves a linear lower bound at some fixed gap, degree and positive density for every unbounded-width template. Here bounded width means that some fixed level of local consistency suffices to decide satisfiability for all instances; unbounded width means that no such fixed level suffices. The theorem does not determine the optimal hardness gap or the growth at all other parameter choices.

Fei, Minzer and Wang’s April 2026 preprint strengthens related streaming lower bounds and extends the unbounded-width obstruction to that model. Its Section 1.4 explicitly still refers to the full query-complexity question as unresolved. The streaming results therefore provide relevant progress without completing the requested query classification.

Reading the entire bounded-degree instance gives a linear-query upper bound for fixed degree, irrespective of local computation time. The substantive issue is which templates and value gaps allow substantially less inspection and what the precise intermediate rates are.

cards.title: Sample complexity of symmetric Markov-chain identity testing
cards.formal: Determine the minimax trajectory-length complexity \(M(n,\varepsilon)\) of identity testing for symmetric Markov chains in the model below, up to universal multiplicative constants. Both the state-space size \(n\) and reciprocal proximity \(1/\varepsilon\) vary. Give an explicit positive comparison function \(B(n,\varepsilon)\), a uniform tester attaining its upper bound, and constants \(c,C>0\) and \(n_0\ge2\) such that \[cB(n,\varepsilon)\le M(n,\varepsilon)\le CB(n,\varepsilon)\] for every integer \(n\ge n_0\) and rational \(\varepsilon\in(0,1/4]\). Constants must be independent of the reference chain, the starting state, \(n\) and \(\varepsilon\); logarithmic factors in these parameters may not be suppressed. If the complexity is infinite on part of this domain, identify that part and prove infinitude there instead of assigning it a finite bound.
cards.why: This asks how much dependent data is needed to validate an entire stochastic transition rule when the experiment cannot be restarted or directed toward unvisited states. Sharp bounds would separate the intrinsic information cost of testing dynamics from the cost of fully exploring the reference chain, extending the foundations of distribution testing beyond independent samples.
cards.status_note: Source-open as the optimal trajectory-complexity question in COLT 2018 Section 6. On 15 September 2026, the full original model and bounds, the 2019 irreducibility convention and theorem, and the 2022/2023 reversible extensions were checked. A bounded later-work search did not identify matching joint bounds for the retained full symmetric model. The minimax precision and exact-real computational primitives are explicitly recorded model specifications, not proof certification. Cited proofs were not independently verified or formalized in Lean.

progress.text: The COLT paper defines the single-trajectory spectral-discrepancy model, proves a hitting-time-dependent upper bound and an \(\Omega(n/\varepsilon)\) lower bound, and proposes \(\Theta(n/\varepsilon)\) in its first open question.

Cherapanamjeri–Bartlett Theorem 10 gives a \(\widetilde O(n/\varepsilon^4)\) tester under the irreducible symmetric setting stated in Section 2.1; the conclusion retains the optimal reciprocal-distance dependence as an open question.
Fried–Wolfer extend testing to irreducible reversible chains under a stationary-distribution proximity promise. Their symmetric specialization recovers the \(\widetilde O(n/\varepsilon^4)\) scale.
Wolfer–Watanabe give a geometric reduction under additional conditions, explicitly separating this discrepancy-based problem from testing under the matrix infinity norm.

importance.reason: A foundational dependent-data testing problem with a single uncontrolled trajectory, a carefully motivated spectral discrepancy and a substantial unresolved joint parameter gap. It probes whether validation needs global exploration and connects information-theoretic testing with Markov dynamics.

sentences: The tester observes one trajectory from an unknown symmetric Markov chain and receives a complete known reference transition matrix.
It must distinguish equality from positive spectral discrepancy for every uncontrolled starting state, without resets or chosen-state sampling.
The target is matching joint dependence of the worst-case required trajectory length on the number of states and the proximity parameter.
Later testing results remove hitting-time dependence under their stated irreducibility assumptions, but the checked bounds still leave a reciprocal-distance gap.
The card preserves the full original symmetric model and distinguishes its transition discrepancy from stationary-distribution or matrix-norm testing.

cards.definitions: A chain on \([n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}\) has a transition matrix \(P\in[0,1]^{n\times n}\) with \(\sum_jP_{ij}=1\) for each \(i\). Symmetry means \(P_{ij}=P_{ji}\). Probabilities may be arbitrary real numbers, and zeros, holding probabilities and disconnected state spaces are allowed. For two such matrices set \[R(P,Q)_{ij}=\sqrt{P_{ij}Q_{ij}},\qquad \Delta(P,Q)=1-\rho(R(P,Q)),\] where \(\rho\) is the spectral radius, the maximum absolute value of an eigenvalue. The square root is entrywise; it is not a matrix square root. The resulting discrepancy lies in \([0,1]\), but it need not be a metric. The tester receives \(n\), rational \(\varepsilon\), the complete reference matrix \(Q\), and observations from one trajectory of an unknown symmetric matrix \(P\). For every initial state \(x\in[n]\), \(X_0=x\) and \[\Pr[X_{t+1}=j\mid X_0,\ldots,X_t]=P_{X_t,j}.\] The tester sees \(X_0\) without a transition cost; each subsequent observed transition costs one. It cannot choose the initial state, reset the chain, request a transition from an arbitrary state, or inspect entries of \(P\). It may stop early, but it must stop within the claimed worst-case number of transitions. It accepts with probability at least \(2/3\) if \(P=Q\), and rejects with probability at least \(2/3\) if \(\Delta(P,Q)>\varepsilon\), for every starting state. No guarantee is imposed for other unequal pairs. Probabilities include both the Markov trajectory and independent internal fair random bits. Correctness for every fixed starting state also covers every starting distribution. The tester is one finite uniform program across all \(n,\varepsilon,Q\), with integer and bit-string work storage and exact real registers holding the supplied entries of \(Q\). It has rational constants, exact arithmetic \(+,-,\times,\div\) with division by zero forbidden, nonnegative square root, and exact order/equality comparisons; it has no advice or other oracle. The integer and rational parameters use binary encodings. These conventions specify exact numerical access; no bit-time guarantee for arbitrary real input is being requested. Local computation, memory and access to the explicitly supplied \(Q\) are uncharged, but every execution terminates. For each \(n,\varepsilon\), let \(M(n,\varepsilon)\) be the least integer \(m\) attained as a worst-case transition bound by a uniform tester correct for every permitted parameter value, reference and unknown chain. The worst case includes every \(Q,P\), starting state and execution. Set \(M=+\infty\) if no finite bound exists. This is a worst-reference minimax quantity, rather than a reference-dependent hitting-time or mixing-time complexity. The full symmetric class in the original boxed problem is retained; irreducibility, aperiodicity and stationary initialization are not extra promises.
cards.answer_criterion: Supply the comparison function and a complete Lean-checked proof of the matching bounds, including correctness and trajectory cost of one uniform upper-bound tester and a lower bound against every tester in the stated model. Any asserted infinite values require a Lean proof that no finite uniform bound exists there. Merely repeating the defining minimization, suppressing unbounded logarithmic factors, or proving a bound only for fast-mixing or irreducible inputs does not meet the full target. The source's proposed \(\Theta(n/\varepsilon)\) answer is a conjectured value of this complexity, not an assumption that an accepted answer must confirm.

source_formulation.text: Determine the optimal sample complexity for identity testing of symmetric Markov chains; the source proposes order n/epsilon and asks whether explicit hitting-time dependence can be removed.
source_formulation.caption: Editorial paraphrase of Section 6, item 1

context_blocks.text: Independent distribution samples can be collected from scratch. Here the next observation is constrained by the current state, so revisiting an uninformative region may consume many observations. The reference matrix is fully known; only the transition rule that generated the trajectory is unknown.

A worst-case start makes some unequal chains indistinguishable: they may share a closed component with identical transitions, and the trajectory may never leave it. The source chooses a spectral discrepancy that vanishes in such cases. Replacing it with a maximum row distance would impose rejection obligations that a single trajectory might never be able to meet.

The square-root overlap matrix compares both transition rules on the same labeled state space. Its leading spectral behavior measures how quickly the distributions of long trajectories can separate. Testing equality of stationary distributions alone would not test this object; in particular, symmetric chains all admit the uniform stationary distribution.

The original sample complexity is trajectory length in observed states. This card counts transitions after the initial state, a difference of one. It retains the original strict farness inequality and asks for matching joint dependence on state count and proximity, with constants and the minimax reference convention made explicit.

The original upper bound includes a reference hitting-time term, and its lower bound is \(\Omega(n/\varepsilon)\). The hitting time is the largest expected time to reach a specified state from another state; it may be very large or infinite. Section 6 conjectures that a matching order-\(n/\varepsilon\) bound should avoid that dependence.

The 2019 paper removes hitting-time dependence in its stated irreducible symmetric setting, with bound \(\widetilde O(n/\varepsilon^4)\). Its Section 5 still asks whether the reciprocal-distance gap can be closed. This review records the irreducibility assumption from Section 2.1 rather than silently treating that theorem as an unrestricted statement about every reducible input.

Later work extends this line to reversible chains with additional stationary-distribution conditions, and develops a geometric reduction. Those extensions address broader types of transition matrix under promises; the checked results do not establish matching joint bounds for the full original symmetric problem.

Bounds in a matrix norm, experiments with a controlled restart interface, or results stated after assuming stationary initialization solve distinct testing problems. The source also asks other questions about its discrepancy and more general chains; those directions are not additional targets of this card.

cards.title: Polylogarithmic-query pattern-freeness testing
cards.formal: For every integer \(k\ge2\) and every permutation \(\pi\) of \([k]\), is there a uniform randomized one-sided-error value-query tester \(A_\pi\) such that, for each fixed rational \(\varepsilon\in(0,1)\), there are integers \(C_{\pi,\varepsilon},a_{\pi,\varepsilon}\ge1\) for which the tester uses at most \[C_{\pi,\varepsilon}\bigl(1+\lceil\log_2(n+1)\rceil\bigr)^{a_{\pi,\varepsilon}}\] queries on every execution for every \(n\ge1\)? On input \(n,\varepsilon\) and access to any \(f:[n]\to\mathbb R\), it must accept with probability one if \(f\) is \(\pi\)-free, and reject with probability at least \(2/3\) if the normalized Hamming distance to \(\pi\)-freeness is at least \(\varepsilon\). No polynomial dependence on \(k\) or \(1/\varepsilon\) is required; those parameters are fixed when measuring the growth in \(n\).

source_formulation.text: We conjecture, however, that the query complexity is \(\operatorname{polylog} n\) for all constant \(k\).
source_formulation.caption: Selected source sentence; ICALP 2022 p. 98:5, mathematical typography normalized

cards.why: A fixed order pattern is a basic obstruction in sequences and generalizes monotonicity. The conjecture asks whether adaptive access makes every such obstruction testable from only a polylogarithmic number of values, despite large lower bounds for predetermined queries. Its resolution would clarify the reach of adaptivity in ordered property testing and its connection with sublinear sequence analysis.

The latter explicitly retains the one-dimensional conjecture and separates it from its higher-dimensional obstruction. A bounded later-work search did not verify a resolution. The exact-real computation convention is an explicit model specification; cited proofs were not independently verified or formalized in Lean.

progress.text: ICALP publishes the general one-sided adaptive bound \(\widetilde O_{k,\varepsilon}(n^{O(1/\log\log\log n)})\) in Theorem 1.1, with the asymptotic understood for sufficiently large \(n\). Its open-question passage explicitly conjectures polylogarithmic complexity.
The final TheoretiCS paper retains the general subpolynomial upper bound and the explicit polylogarithmic conjecture on pp. 7–8.

The SODA hypergrid work distinguishes the unresolved conjecture for the line from a false analogous conjecture in dimension two. Its Introduction still identifies the Newman–Varma subpolynomial tester as the best general one-dimensional upper bound.

importance.reason: A uniform structural question over all fixed permutation patterns, with a major adaptive versus nonadaptive gap and links to monotonicity and sequence estimation. The first difficult nonmonotone patterns already have length four; the target goes beyond optimizing one tester.

sentences: A permutation pattern specifies the strict relative order of values at increasing positions of a real-valued sequence.
The question asks whether every fixed pattern has an adaptive one-sided tester using only a polylogarithmic number of queries in the sequence length.
Distance is the fraction of entries that must change to remove all occurrences, and the query bound may depend arbitrarily on the fixed pattern and proximity.
The checked general adaptive upper bound is subpolynomial but not polylogarithmic, while newer lower bounds on hypergrids concern a different domain.
Resolving the conjecture would clarify how much adaptive observations can improve the testing of ordered obstructions.

cards.definitions: For a positive integer \(m\), write \([m]=\{1,\ldots,m\}\). A permutation \(\pi:[k]\to[k]\) is a bijection. A \(\pi\)-appearance in \(f:[n]\to\mathbb R\) consists of indices \(1\le i_1<\cdots<i_k\le n\) satisfying \[f(i_s)<f(i_t)\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad\pi(s)<\pi(t)\qquad(s,t\in[k]).\] The comparisons are strict, so all values in an appearance are distinct. The function is \(\pi\)-free if it has no such appearance. Inputs may have repeated values, and there is no monotonicity, bounded-range, integrality or permutation promise on \(f\). Let \(\mathcal F_{\pi,n}\) be all \(\pi\)-free real-valued functions on \([n]\), and define \[d_0(f,\mathcal F_{\pi,n})=\frac1n\min_{g\in\mathcal F_{\pi,n}}|\{i\in[n]:f(i)\ne g(i)\}|.\] For \(k\ge2\), the class is nonempty because a constant function is free, and a minimum exists among finitely many possible disagreement counts. When \(n<k\), every input is free. A query chooses an index \(i\) and returns the exact value \(f(i)\); every such call costs one. Queries may adapt to all earlier returned values and random bits. The tester is one finite program for the fixed \(\pi\), receiving \(n\) in binary and \(\varepsilon\) as a ratio of positive binary integers. Its work storage consists of integers, bit strings and exact real registers, with rational constants, copying, addition, subtraction, multiplication, division by nonzero values, and exact equality and order comparisons. It uses independent fair random bits, has no real advice or other oracle, and must terminate on every execution. There is no cost bound on local computation or storage. This specifies the exact-value oracle model, not a bit-time or noisy-value model. The stated query bound is a worst-case bound over input functions and all random executions. Probabilities are over the program's random bits for a fixed function. Behavior at positive distance below \(\varepsilon\) is unrestricted. The program may depend on \(\pi\), and both the multiplicative constant and logarithmic exponent may also depend on the fixed \(\varepsilon\); neither may depend on \(n\) or \(f\).
cards.answer_criterion: Prove the proposition or its logical negation with a complete Lean-checked proof. A positive answer must work for every fixed permutation pattern, arbitrary real-valued input functions and every positive rational proximity parameter, with one tester per pattern and the stated polylogarithmic-in-\(n\) worst-case query bound. A negative answer must rule out this guarantee for at least one pattern. A bound of \(n^{o(1)}\), a lower bound restricted to nonadaptive algorithms, or a result on a higher-dimensional domain does not settle this proposition.

context_blocks.text: A pattern specifies relative ranks rather than prescribed values. For example, \(\pi=(1,3,2)\) occurs at increasing positions when the first value is smallest, the second largest and the third between them. Equal values cannot form this occurrence. Avoiding \((2,1)\) is exactly being nondecreasing.

The repair distance counts how many entries must be changed, independently of how far their numerical values move. It is different from distances on permutations that charge the movement of points or inversions. Restricting the input itself to be a permutation would also change the model.

The source studies fixed pattern length and fixed proximity. This card therefore allows arbitrary dependence on those parameters and asks only for a polylogarithmic bound in sequence length. The one-sided convention follows the source algorithms and its separate discussion of whether two-sided error can help.

An adaptive tester can use values already seen to decide which positions to inspect next. A nonadaptive tester must select all query positions without their answers. The paper’s strongly sublinear adaptive bound and the much larger known worst-pattern nonadaptive bounds expose the importance of this distinction.

The best general bound in the checked source is \(\widetilde O_{k,\varepsilon}(n^{o(1)})\). A subpolynomial function of \(n\) can still grow faster than every fixed power of \(\log n\), so this does not establish the conjecture. The source separately records polylogarithmic bounds for patterns of length at most three and stronger bounds for monotone patterns.

The SODA 2026 hypergrid paper explicitly restates the one-dimensional conjecture. Its new polynomial lower bound concerns nonmonotone patterns on a two-dimensional partially ordered domain, where positions are not all comparable. It does not refute the conjecture on the line considered here.

cards.title: Polynomial-query submodularity testing
cards.formal: Is there a uniform randomized one-sided-error tester for submodularity of arbitrary real-valued set functions using a number of value queries polynomial in the dimension and reciprocal distance? Precisely, do there exist one tester \(A\) in the model below and integers \(C,k\ge1\) such that, for every integer \(n\ge1\), every rational \(\varepsilon\in(0,1)\), and every function \(f:2^{[n]}\to\mathbb R\), the algorithm \(A^{f}(n,\varepsilon)\) halts and makes at most \(C((n+1)/\varepsilon)^{k}\) value queries on every execution, accepts with probability one if \(f\) is submodular, and rejects with probability at least \(2/3\) if \(d_0(f,\mathcal S_n)\ge\varepsilon\)? The constants and program must work simultaneously for all parameters and functions.
cards.why: Submodularity formalizes diminishing returns and underlies many optimization and valuation models. Its value table has exponentially many entries, while algorithms using a submodular value oracle typically see only a small part of it. Polynomial-query testing would determine whether global consistency with that structural assumption can be checked from comparably limited information, with rejection guaranteed for functions requiring widespread changes.
cards.status_note: Source-open under the explicitly recorded one-sided Hamming-distance interpretation. On 15 September 2026, the foundational journal definitions and bounds, Hatami–Vondrák’s manuscript theorem, Blais–Bommireddi’s ITCS 2017 result and Haris–Palit’s published 9 September 2026 work were checked. The later work still records the ordinary-submodularity gap. The original problem page was recovered from its saved full text when live requests failed. This is a bounded status review, not an independent verification of the cited proofs or a Lean formalization.

progress.text: Seshadhri's Bertinoro problem explicitly asks whether \(\operatorname{poly}(n/\varepsilon)\) queries suffice. The listed matroid-rank and coverage directions are separate special questions, not promises imposed on the general target.

Seshadhri–Vondrák give a one-sided tester with query complexity \((1/\varepsilon)^{O(\sqrt n\log n)}\) in the small-distance regime. Their Theorem 1.4 also gives examples with few violated squares; that obstruction to this particular local test is not a superpolynomial lower bound for all testers.

Hatami–Vondrák's author manuscript proves an \(\Omega(n^{2}/\log n)\) query lower bound for constant distance in Theorem 1.2. This is still compatible with a polynomial-query tester of larger degree. No later publication venue is inferred for this manuscript.

Blais–Bommireddi prove dimension-independent query bounds for testing \(f:\{0,1\}^{n}\to[0,1]\) under \(\ell_p\) distance for each fixed finite \(p\ge1\) and fixed positive proximity parameter. Theorem 1.1 uses a different distance metric from this card.

Haris–Palit's published k-submodularity paper records the remaining gap for ordinary submodularity. Its constant-query theorem concerns bounded functions in \(\ell_p\) distance; its Hamming-distance results test separate component properties with subexponential bounds. These results do not supply the polynomial Hamming tester asked for here.

sentences: Submodularity expresses diminishing returns for a real-valued function on all subsets of a finite ground set.
The question asks whether a polynomial number of exact value queries can test this property with one-sided error.
Distance is the fraction of table entries that must change to obtain a submodular function, regardless of change magnitude.
Known general upper and lower bounds leave the polynomial-query question unresolved, and constant-query norm-distance results concern a different task.
A resolution would determine how efficiently an oracle’s global diminishing-returns structure can be checked from limited access.

cards.definitions: Here \([n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}\), and \(2^{[n]}\) is its set of all subsets, represented by their \(n\)-bit indicator vectors. The class \(\mathcal S_n\) consists of all functions \(g:2^{[n]}\to\mathbb R\) satisfying \[g(S)+g(T)\ge g(S\cap T)+g(S\cup T)\qquad(S,T\subseteq[n]).\] The distance is normalized Hamming distance on the full domain: \[d_0(f,\mathcal S_n)=\min_{g\in\mathcal S_n}2^{-n}\bigl|\{S\subseteq[n]:f(S)\ne g(S)\}\bigr|.\] This minimum exists because attainable disagreement counts form a nonempty subset of the finite set \(\{0,\ldots,2^n\}\). It measures how many table entries change, regardless of the magnitudes of the changes. There is no promise of monotonicity, nonnegativity, bounded range, integrality or normalization at the empty set. The input supplies \(n\) in binary and \(\varepsilon\) as a ratio of positive binary integers; the full value table is accessible only through queries. One value query chooses a subset \(S\) and returns the exact real number \(f(S)\), at cost one. Queries may depend on earlier answers and random bits. To specify computation on these exact values, use a finite program with integer and bit-string work storage, real registers initialized by rational constants, exact real addition, subtraction, multiplication and division by nonzero values, and exact order/equality comparisons. Division by zero is forbidden. The program can request independent fair random bits and can copy queried real values into registers. There is no real-valued advice, noncomputable primitive or other oracle. Only value queries are charged; intervening computation and storage have no quantitative bound, but every execution must terminate after finitely many steps. Acceptance probabilities are over the independent random bits, for each fixed input function. Behavior is unrestricted when \(0<d_0(f,\mathcal S_n)<\varepsilon\).
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof of the existence of a tester with every guarantee in the formal statement, or a complete Lean-checked proof of its logical negation. A positive answer must cover arbitrary real-valued functions and all dimensions and proximity parameters with one finite program and fixed polynomial constants. A negative answer must exclude every such program and every fixed choice of polynomial constants, not only a particular local tester. A result for average value error, a restricted value range, a monotonicity promise, or a constant-dimensional grid does not settle this target.

context_blocks.text: A set function assigns a value to each possible subset of a ground set. Submodularity says that adding an element cannot become more valuable merely because the receiving set has grown. Equivalently, it satisfies the union/intersection inequality in the definitions. With \(n\) elements there are \(2^{n}\) values, so inspecting a polynomial number of them is a small fraction of the complete object.

Testing allows an unresolved band of nearby nonsubmodular inputs. The tester must accept genuinely submodular functions and reject functions that disagree with every submodular function on at least an \(\varepsilon\)-fraction of subsets. It is not required to reconstruct the closest submodular function or to decide exact membership for every oracle.

Hamming distance treats any changed entry as one disagreement. In contrast, an \(\ell_p\) distance for finite \(p\) averages the magnitudes of changes. Many tiny discrepancies can therefore contribute little to that norm while affecting a large fraction of the table. The published constant-query result for bounded functions in an \(\ell_p\) metric does not imply polynomial-query testing in the Hamming metric used here.

The saved problem asks both for optimal query complexity and, specifically, whether polynomially many queries suffice. This card selects that explicitly posed polynomial threshold as its single yes/no target. The one-sided-error convention is taken from Definition 1.2 of the cited foundational paper. The finite-program exact-real convention makes the value-oracle interpretation explicit; it is not a claim about bit complexity or noisy measurements.

The existing upper and lower bounds leave a substantial gap: known general testing uses a subexponential number of queries for fixed distance, while a nearly quadratic lower bound rules out much smaller sample budgets. Neither result decides whether some fixed polynomial suffices. Bounds on the frequency of a particular kind of local violation also have a narrower scope than a lower bound against every adaptive tester.
