cards.title: Deterministic polynomial-time equivalence testing for d-DNNFs
cards.formal:
Is there a deterministic polynomial-time algorithm that, given two d-DNNF circuits \(C,D\), returns yes exactly when
\[\forall a:X\to\{0,1\},\qquad f_C(a)=f_D(a),\]
where \(X\) is the union of the variables appearing in the two inputs?

The algorithm must work for all promised pairs, without any requirement that their internal decompositions or variable trees agree. It must give the exact yes/no answer in worst-case time polynomial in their total binary encoding length. The two circuits are supplied explicitly; no truth table, equivalence certificate, common compiled representation or source formula is supplied.
cards.why: Equivalence testing checks whether two compiled representations express the same Boolean knowledge despite different decompositions. A deterministic polynomial-time test would support exact comparison and verification of representation changes without a probabilistic failure event. The gap between known randomized testing and the deterministic target also links this concrete compilation task to broader derandomization questions.

cards.definitions:
A negation-normal-form Boolean circuit is a finite directed acyclic graph with a designated output gate. A leaf is a constant \(0\) or \(1\), or a literal \(x\) or \(\neg x\) for a variable in a finite set \(X\). Each internal gate is AND or OR with a finite nonempty input list. Arbitrary fan-in and sharing of subcircuits are allowed, and every input occurrence counts as an edge. Evaluation on an assignment \(a:X\to\{0,1\}\) uses the ordinary Boolean operations. There are no other negation gates. Constants suffice when \(X\) is empty.

For a gate \(g\), let \(\operatorname{var}(g)\) be the variables appearing in the literals reachable by following its input edges. Decomposability requires that the input subcircuits of each AND gate have pairwise disjoint such variable sets. Determinism requires that, for every OR gate, no assignment to \(X\) makes two distinct input occurrences true simultaneously. A d-DNNF satisfies both conditions at every gate. Determinism is a semantic mutual-exclusion property; it is not a restriction to gates that branch on a single variable.

Write \(f_C(a)\) for the output of circuit \(C\) and \(s(C)=|V(C)|+|E(C)|\) for its size, including leaves and all wires. Unused variables in \(X\) do not affect evaluation. Smoothness, which would require all inputs of an OR gate to mention the same variables, is not assumed. There is also no common tree organizing the variable splits of all conjunction gates. Thus the target uses general d-DNNFs, not only the smaller class of structured d-DNNFs. When two circuits are compared, their variable names denote the same coordinates of a common assignment; a missing coordinate is simply ignored by that circuit.

For computational tasks, encode a circuit as a topologically ordered list of gate records, with gate kinds, signed variable indices at literal leaves, input-list lengths and binary indices of earlier input gates. Include the output index. Variables occurring in the input circuit, or jointly in the two input circuits for a comparison, are consistently renamed to \(1,\ldots,n\); the number \(n\) is at most the total number of input literal occurrences. The input length \(b\) is the total number of bits of these records and delimiters. Gate-and-wire size and bit length are polynomially related with this convention.

An algorithm is one deterministic multitape Turing machine with no oracle, advice or randomness. Polynomial time means at most \(K(b+1)^d\) bit steps for fixed constants \(K,d\) independent of the circuits and number of variables. The inputs are promised to be d-DNNFs. The machine must satisfy the time bound on every input encoding, but its output may be arbitrary when the promise fails; it is not required to recognize the semantic determinism promise. All input reading and output writing count toward the bound.

Equivalence concerns the same assignment in the two circuits; it does not allow renaming variables separately to obtain isomorphism. The inputs may have different numbers of gates and may mention different subsets of \(X\). Logical nonequivalence means that at least one assignment makes their outputs differ. Equal numbers of satisfying assignments do not by themselves establish equivalence. The only required output is the decision bit; construction of a distinguishing assignment is not an additional task.

For comparison with the known randomized result, a one-sided randomized equivalence test can always accept equivalent circuits while rejecting each nonequivalent pair with probability at least \(2/3\), in polynomial time using independent random bits. The target here removes randomness entirely. A probabilistic test, even with arbitrarily small failure probability, does not meet its guarantee.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct Lean-checked proof or refutation of the deterministic polynomial-time existence claim in the stated promise model. A positive answer must give one uniform algorithm, prove exact equivalence decisions on all promised pairs, and establish a polynomial worst-case bit-time bound. A negative answer must exclude every such algorithm; it need not produce a single pair that defeats every algorithm. A randomized algorithm, a procedure requiring a common variable tree, or a hardness result for arbitrary DNNFs without determinism does not by itself settle this problem. Neither does hardness of verifying a proposed conjunction of two circuits, which is a different input-output relation.

context_blocks.text: The 2026 source explicitly leaves equivalence across different variable trees open even for structured representations. This card retains the broader general d-DNNF question, independently stated in the knowledge-compilation map; it does not attribute that broader formulation solely to the structured-circuit paper.

Darwiche and Huang give a one-sided randomized polynomial-time equivalence test for general d-DNNFs. Their analysis includes a polynomial bound on the bit length of arithmetic values; the algorithmic claim is stronger than merely bounding the number of unit-cost arithmetic operations.

The knowledge-compilation map distinguishes exact model counting, equivalence and entailment. Efficient counting does not automatically decide whether two represented sets of assignments coincide, and a common variable order or compatible structured decomposition is an additional restriction.

The 2026 paper establishes efficiently checkable restricted restructuring steps while leaving the one-shot comparison across arbitrary trees open. Its hardness discussion for checking a conjunction relation concerns three representations and does not establish hardness of the two-circuit equivalence problem.

cards.title: Greedy CDCL without restarts versus resolution
cards.formal: Does greedy CDCL without restarts p-simulate resolution in the asserting-learning model below? Precisely, do there exist a deterministic Turing machine \(M\), a constant \(C>0\) and \(k\in\mathbb N\) such that for every finite CNF formula \(F\) and every valid resolution refutation \(\pi\) of \(F\), on the explicit binary input \((F,\pi)\) of length \(L\), \(M\) halts within \(C(L+1)^k\) steps and outputs a legal greedy CDCL refutation of the same \(F\), without restarts, of at most \(C(L+1)^k\) bits? The single program and polynomial must work for all formulas and supplied proofs.
cards.definitions:
Literals are \(x_{i}\) or \(\neg x_{i}\) for \(i\in \{1,\ldots ,n\}\); clauses are sets of literals and F is a finite set of clauses. A resolution inference derives \((C\setminus \{x\})\cup (D\setminus \{\neg x\})\) from clauses C containing x and D containing \(\neg x\). A refutation is a finite sequence ending in the empty clause, each entry being an input clause or an inference from earlier entries, with parent indices and pivot recorded. Variable indices and pointers use binary notation. Clause and formula encodings explicitly list their literals.

A CDCL state consists of a database D containing F and an ordered trail of assignments to distinct variables of F. Each assignment is marked either as a decision or with its reason clause in D. Its decision level is the number of decisions up to that assignment. Initially \(D=F\) and the trail is empty. A clause is falsified if all its literals are false on the trail; it is unit if exactly one literal is unassigned and all others are false. The following priority of actions is mandatory.

If D has a falsified clause, a conflict must be processed before any other action. At decision level zero the run ends with UNSAT. Otherwise choose a falsified clause K and a trivial resolution analysis: start with K and repeatedly resolve the current clause with a reason clause recorded on the current trail, using a distinct pivot at each step. Every intermediate clause must be falsified by the current trail. Stop at a nonempty asserting clause C, meaning that exactly one of its variables has the current highest decision level. The trace records the full analysis. Add C to D and erase the suffix of the trail whose decision levels exceed a, where a is the maximum level of the other literals of C, or zero if there are none. Then perform one legal unit propagation and return to the conflict-first priority check.

If there is no conflict but a unit clause exists, choose such a clause, assign its unassigned literal to true, record that clause as the reason, and repeat the priority check. Only when neither conflicts nor units exist may a new decision assign either value to an unassigned variable. At such a stable state the run may first delete any subset of learned clauses, retaining all input clauses and all reasons appearing on the current trail, and must then make a decision. A satisfying complete trail ends with SAT, not a refutation. There is no independent operation clearing or shortening the trail: backjumping is allowed only after a conflict and only to the assertion level.

All choices of decisions, unit reasons, conflict clauses, trivial asserting analyses and permitted deletions are free components of the output trace. No fixed branching heuristic or first-UIP policy is imposed. No new variables, preprocessed replacement formula, unrecorded learned axioms or restarts are permitted. The only learned clauses are those derived by the recorded conflict analyses. The trace length counts all clauses, literals, assignments, analysis steps and pointers in an explicit binary encoding, so expensive analysis cannot be hidden in one step. This is the restart-free instantiation of the Vinyals model with arbitrary trivial asserting learning. The requested p-simulation is a uniform translation supplied with \(\pi\); mere existence of a short trace, or finding one from F alone, is a different claim.

The input promise is that the explicitly recorded resolution derivation is a valid refutation of the supplied formula; correctness is required for every promised input, including a formula already containing the empty clause. Invalid encodings or derivations may be rejected. All computation and output costs use ordinary sequential bit time. Choices made by the translator are deterministic and fully recorded, with exact clause and Boolean semantics; no randomness, numerical approximation, oracle or nonuniform advice is available. The model permits a conflict-justified backjump to level zero, which does not count as an independent restart.

context_blocks.text: Clause learning stores consequences of encountered conflicts and reuses them during a SAT search. General resolution permits arbitrary reuse of earlier clauses, without requiring that they arise along a current partial assignment. This question asks whether the constraints of a greedy search, even with freely chosen decisions and learning, impose a superpolynomial cost when restarting is unavailable.

The operational model matters. Exhaustive unit propagation and immediate conflict processing constrain which trails are reachable. A restart discards the current trail while retaining learned information, whereas a backjump must be justified by the newly learned asserting clause. The statement specifies those actions separately rather than treating every return to decision level zero as a prohibited restart.

Vinyals gives an execution-trace proof system with explicit propagation reasons, conflict-analysis derivations, deletion rules and cost measures. The present card selects its no-restart policy and allows arbitrary trivial asserting analyses. This avoids making the question depend on a particular solver implementation, while retaining actual greedy search restrictions.

The supplied resolution proof is part of the translator’s input. An affirmative answer therefore would not give a polynomial-time SAT solver or a practical heuristic that discovers short proofs unaided. A theorem guaranteeing only polynomial-size traces, without a polynomial-time translation, would establish the corresponding size-simulation statement rather than the full p-simulation asked here.

Vinyals’ 2022 exposition distinguishes no-restart simulations using non-greedy propagation or preprocessing from the greedy comparison. Such changes alter which search traces are legal, so those positive results do not satisfy the transitions written here.

Buss–Thapen construct formulas with short resolution proofs whose height must nevertheless be large. They discuss these as candidates for separating pool resolution from general resolution, explicitly state that they cannot prove that separation, and give polynomial-size pool proofs for a simpler variant. This is related progress, not a checked identification of pool resolution with every operational CDCL model.

The SAT 2026 graph-backtracking paper proves correctness and termination of a generalized solver and shows how suitable weights reproduce chronological and nonchronological backtracking. Its more general repair operation can retain assignments outside the ordinary retained prefix. These are simulations between backtracking policies; they do not supply the requested translation of arbitrary resolution proofs into the unchanged greedy no-restart model.

The bounded search through 16 September 2026 found no checked proof of the stated p-simulation or its negation. The dated specialist open discussion and subsequent related papers support retaining the target; this search is not an exhaustive proof of current openness.

cards.why: Restarts are a central operation in modern clause-learning SAT solvers. This target isolates whether their removal causes an unavoidable loss in proof generation even when the solver may choose decisions, propagation order and learned asserting clauses with full knowledge of a supplied resolution proof. A resolution would connect an exact operational restriction of search with the polynomial simulation structure studied in proof complexity.
cards.answer_criterion: Provide a complete Lean proof of the displayed uniform p-simulation or its logical negation. A positive answer must formalize the finite clause encoding and resolution proof checker, the stated CDCL state and transition system, and a computable translator with a polynomial bit-time bound, proving that every valid input proof yields a trace on the original formula ending in the permitted UNSAT state. The trace must obey conflict and propagation priority, trivial asserting analysis, assertion-level backjumps, deletion restrictions and the absence of restarts. A negative answer must rule out all such uniform polynomial-time translators; a lower bound for one fixed heuristic or a different backtracking policy is insufficient. Existence of polynomial-size traces alone does not supply the required efficient translator. Conditional theorems settle only their stated conditional variants unless their premises are also proved. No proof-assistant verification of either answer is claimed by this editorial review.

importance.reason: A concrete bridge between SAT solving and proof complexity: it isolates the computational role of restarts while allowing helpful search choices. The significance comes from the unresolved comparison with general resolution and explicit specialist discussion, not from an unspecified explanation of solver performance.

cards.title: Decidability of termination for one-rule string rewriting
cards.formal: Is global termination of a one-rule string rewriting system decidable? The input is a finite alphabet \(\Sigma\) and two explicitly written words \(\ell,r\in\Sigma^{*}\). Define \(u\to v\) when \(u=x\ell y\) and \(v=xry\) for some \(x,y\in\Sigma^{*}\). Decide whether there exists no infinite sequence \(w_0\to w_1\to w_2\to\cdots\) of finite words. The quantifier includes every starting word and every choice of replacement position.
cards.why: A single literal replacement is among the simplest possible descriptions of an unbounded computation. Settling its global termination problem would locate a sharp limit on automatic reasoning about repeated symbolic transformations, without relying on a large instruction set or richer term syntax.
cards.status_note: The 2002 primary paper and the August 2026 authored note present arbitrary one-rule termination as unresolved. A bounded check on 13 September 2026 found no later resolution. The note and historical proofs have not been independently verified; source-open status is not an exhaustive certification.

Known decision procedures cover special rule families, while an August 2026 note still lists the arbitrary one-rule question as open.
The answer must prove decidability or undecidability in Lean for global termination, rather than only termination from one supplied word.

definitions: The alphabet is a finite nonempty set listed by distinct binary symbol indices. Both sides of the rule are explicit finite sequences of these symbols, including possibly the empty word \(\varepsilon\). No variables, compressed word descriptions, contexts supplied as inputs, or additional rewrite rules occur.

One rewrite step chooses one contiguous occurrence of \(\ell\) and replaces it with \(r\), preserving the prefix \(x\) and suffix \(y\). If \(\ell=\varepsilon\), any boundary in a word, including its ends, is an occurrence. A rule application counts as a step even when the resulting word is identical to the original word. Thus \(\ell=r\) admits a constant infinite reduction sequence from \(\ell\).

Global termination means that for every \(w_0\in\Sigma^{*}\) there is no function \(w:\mathbb{N}\to\Sigma^{*}\) with first value \(w_0\) and \(w_i\to w_{i+1}\) for all \(i\geq0\). There is no fixed leftmost or rightmost evaluation strategy. Requiring only that each word has some terminating sequence would be a different property.

Decidability asks for a single deterministic Turing machine that halts on every valid finite description and outputs yes exactly for globally terminating systems. No running-time bound is imposed. Malformed descriptions can be rejected. The rule itself varies across instances; neither its length nor the alphabet size is a fixed constant.
cards.answer_criterion: A complete Lean-checked proof of a total decision algorithm for all one-rule systems in this model, or a Lean-checked proof that no such algorithm exists. Deciding termination from one supplied start word, analyzing one strategy, or handling a restricted family of rules alone is insufficient.

cards.title: Singly exponential shortest solutions of word equations
cards.formal:
Do positive integers \(c,k\) exist such that every satisfiable word equation \(u=v\), over every finite alphabet \(\Sigma\) of constant letters and a disjoint finite set \(\mathcal X\) of variables, has a solution \(h\) satisfying
\[\max_{x\in\mathcal X}|h(x)|\le 2^{c(n+1)^k},\qquad n=|u|+|v|?\]
Here \(\mathcal X\) consists exactly of the variables occurring in the equation, each occurrence contributes one to \(n\), and the maximum over no variables is zero. A solution replaces each variable consistently by a finite word over \(\Sigma\), possibly empty, fixes the constant letters and makes the two expanded words identical.

The same constants \(c,k\) must work independently of the equation, the alphabet and the number of variables. This is the polynomial-exponent meaning of singly exponential. A linear exponent is welcome but is not required.
cards.why: Very short equations can describe solutions whose expanded words are enormous. A universal singly exponential shortest-solution bound would constrain this hidden growth and, by the source’s compression theorem, imply NP membership of general word-equation satisfiability. This links a basic combinatorial question about strings to the unresolved complexity of exact string constraints.

cards.definitions:
For a finite alphabet \(\Sigma\), the free monoid \(\Sigma^*\) consists of all finite sequences of its letters, including the empty word \(\varepsilon\). Multiplication is concatenation, and \(\varepsilon\) is its identity. The length \(|w|\) is the number of letters in the sequence \(w\), with \(|\varepsilon|=0\). Distinct constant letters are distinct symbols, not variables or numbers. The alphabet may have any finite cardinality; if it is empty, its only word is \(\varepsilon\).

An equation is a pair of explicitly written words \(u,v\in(\Sigma\cup\mathcal X)^*\). Each variable and each constant occurrence counts as one symbol in the equation size \(n\). No compressed input, binary-encoded repeat operator, regular-language membership condition, length constraint, inequality, involution or cancellation operation is supplied. Exponent notation in an example of an equation is only shorthand for its fully expanded string, and its expanded length is charged. Variables may occur arbitrarily many times and may appear on either or both sides.

A solution is a monoid morphism \(h:(\Sigma\cup\mathcal X)^*\to\Sigma^*\) that fixes every \(a\in\Sigma\) and satisfies \(h(u)=h(v)\). Equivalently, choose one word \(h(x)\in\Sigma^*\) for each variable, substitute the same word at every occurrence, and concatenate in the original order. Empty substitutions are allowed, and no letter outside \(\Sigma\) may occur in a substitution. This is solving an equation in a free monoid, not in a free group or a semigroup with mandatory nonempty substitutions.

For a satisfiable equation, define
\[m(u,v)=\min_{h:\,h(u)=h(v)}\ \max_{x\in\mathcal X}|h(x)|.\]
The minimum exists because the feasible lengths form a nonempty subset of the nonnegative integers. The claim is \(m(u,v)\le2^{c(n+1)^k}\) for all satisfiable equations. It asks for at least one bounded solution to each equation, not for a bound on every solution. An equation can have infinitely many solutions with unbounded lengths and still satisfy the proposed shortest-solution bound.

The source also measures a solution by the length of the common expanded word \(h(u)=h(v)\). For each solution with \(M=\max_x|h(x)|\), every occurring variable image is a factor of that common word, and
\[M\le |h(u)|\le n\max(1,M).\]
These inequalities also cover the no-variable case using \(M=0\). Thus existence of a singly exponential bound on the shortest common-word length and the displayed variable-image bound are equivalent after changing the universal polynomial in the exponent. The card does not assert equality of these two minimum-length quantities.

The negative answer is the quantified assertion that for every pair of positive integers \(c,k\), some satisfiable equation has no solution meeting \(\max_x|h(x)|\le2^{c(n+1)^k}\). It is not enough to exhibit an exponential-length solution when a shorter one exists, or to beat one chosen polynomial exponent. No efficient construction of a solution or of a counterexample family is part of this nonconstructive length question.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct Lean-checked proof or refutation of the existence of the universal singly exponential bound. A proof must provide fixed positive integers \(c,k\) and prove the bound for all satisfiable equations under the free-monoid and explicit-symbol conventions. A refutation must prove that every such polynomial-exponent bound fails. cards.title: Decidability of fifth-order \(\beta\)-matching
cards.formal: Is fifth-order \(\beta\)-matching decidable in the source's closed range formulation? Given finite simple types \(\sigma,\tau\) and closed simply typed lambda terms \(F:\sigma\to\tau\) and \(N:\tau\), with \(\operatorname{ord}(\sigma)\le5\), decide whether \[\exists M\;\bigl(\varnothing\vdash M:\sigma\ \land\ F\,M=_\beta N\bigr).\] The unknown \(M\) is a finite closed term. One deterministic Turing machine must halt and decide this predicate for every such input, with no time bound. Type order starts at one, exactly as in the source.
cards.why: Matching is a central restricted form of higher-order unification, with uses in rewriting and symbolic reasoning. The fifth-order boundary asks exactly how much higher-order functional structure is needed for beta-only matching to encode undecidable behavior. It also exposes the substantive effect of extensional eta equality: a change in the equality relation, rather than just the input size, changes the general decidability result.

cards.definitions:
Simple types are the finite trees \(A::=\iota\mid A\to A\), over one fixed ground atom \(\iota\); arrows associate to the right. Their order is \(\operatorname{ord}(\iota)=1\) and \(\operatorname{ord}(A\to B)=\max(\operatorname{ord}(A)+1,\operatorname{ord}(B))\). Thus \(\iota\to\iota\) has order two. The bound five applies to the type \(\sigma\) of the term to be instantiated, rather than to \(\sigma\to\tau\) or to every type in the input derivations; \(\tau\) has no independent order bound. This is the convention made explicit for the order-six construction in the August 2026 source. A convention starting at zero shifts all these order numbers down by one.

Terms are finite expressions \(t::=x\mid(t\,t)\mid\lambda x.t\), up to consistent renaming of bound variables. There are no constants, recursion operators, polymorphic types, additional rewrite rules or extensional equations. A typing context \(\Gamma\) assigns simple types to finitely many distinct variables. Typing has exactly the variable rule \(x:A\in\Gamma\Rightarrow\Gamma\vdash x:A\), application \(\Gamma\vdash t:A\to B,\ \Gamma\vdash u:A\Rightarrow\Gamma\vdash tu:B\), and abstraction \(\Gamma,x:A\vdash t:B\Rightarrow\Gamma\vdash\lambda x.t:A\to B\). Closed means no free variables, as witnessed by the empty context. The input includes finite type trees, term trees and typing derivations for \(F\) and \(N\); the finite encodings use binary variable/de Bruijn indices and explicit trees. A purported input failing typing, closedness or the order bound may be rejected. These syntactic conditions are decidable.

A beta step replaces \((\lambda x.t)u\) by the capture-avoiding substitution \(t[x:=u]\) in any subterm, including underneath lambda abstractions. The relation \(=_\beta\) is the reflexive, symmetric, transitive closure of these steps, modulo bound-variable renaming. The eta equation \(\lambda x.f x=f\), where \(x\) is not free in \(f\), is not an allowed additional equation. The known equivalence of beta convertibility with equality of beta normal forms does not require candidate terms to be eta-expanded. The substitution occurs only at the unknown argument of \(F\); the closed target \(N\) is fixed. The same machine handles all allowed types and all finite term sizes, including types with no closed inhabitant. It returns exact YES/NO answers, with no oracle, random error or numerical tolerance.
cards.answer_criterion: An accepted answer is a complete Lean proof of existence of a total computable decider for the displayed predicate or a proof that none exists. A positive answer must formalize the pure simply typed syntax, typing, the order-one ground convention, capture-avoiding beta conversion and the algorithm's termination and correctness for every allowed instance. A negative answer must prove noncomputability while keeping \(\operatorname{ord}(\sigma)\le5\); undecidability using order-six candidate types does not qualify. Neither a beta-eta decision theorem nor a restriction to eta-long candidates answers the beta-only question. This review does not claim to port or rerun the cited Rocq/Coq development in Lean.

cards.title: Polynomial-time equivalence of free binary decision diagrams
cards.formal: Does there exist a deterministic polynomial-time algorithm for equivalence of two explicitly given free binary decision diagrams? In full quantifiers, are there a deterministic Turing machine \(M\), constants \(C>0\) and \(k\in\mathbb N\) such that for every valid pair \((B_1,B_2)\), of total binary encoding length \(L\), the machine halts within \(C(L+1)^k\) steps and returns YES exactly when \[\forall a:X\to\{0,1\},\qquad f_{B_1}(a)=f_{B_2}(a),\] where \(X\) is the union of the variable labels appearing in the two inputs? No shared variable order is promised.
cards.why: FBDDs allow different branches to choose different variable orders and can be much more compact than ordered diagrams. Reliable equivalence testing is needed to compare independently compiled representations or optimized versions of a Boolean function. The question asks whether that representational flexibility can coexist with deterministic exact polynomial-time comparison, beyond the known randomized guarantee.
cards.status_note: Darwiche–Marquis 2002 mark FBDD equivalence as unknown; the checked Darwiche–Huang theorem supplies a randomized one-sided polynomial-time test. The 2026 proof-system discussion concerns stronger join verification and different structured formats, not a checked resolution of two-FBDD deterministic equivalence. A bounded primary-source search through 16 September 2026 found no matching resolution; source-open records the dated question, not exhaustive present-status certification.

cards.definitions:
A free binary decision diagram (FBDD) is a finite rooted directed acyclic graph. Each nonterminal vertex is labelled by a Boolean variable and has exactly two outgoing edges, one marked 0 and one marked 1; their targets may coincide. A terminal vertex has no outgoing edge and is labelled by the output bit 0 or 1. All vertices can be taken reachable from the root. On every directed root-to-terminal path, each variable occurs at most once. Different paths, and the two different input diagrams, may inspect variables in different orders. In particular no fixed global linear order or common graph ordering is part of the input. Redundant tests and shared subgraphs are permitted; the diagrams need not be reduced or isomorphic.

For an assignment \(a:X\to\{0,1\}\), start at the root and at a vertex labelled \(x\) follow its edge marked \(a(x)\); acyclicity leads to a terminal, whose label is \(f_B(a)\). Variables absent from a diagram do not affect its value. Constant diagrams consisting of one terminal and the case \(X=\varnothing\) are included. The input is an explicit finite vertex table giving the root, each node's type and label, and its two successor indices when present. Identifiers, labels and indices are binary encoded, and \(L\) counts all bits in both tables. Inputs are promised to meet the graph and path conditions. All arithmetic, preprocessing and reading costs belong to the ordinary sequential deterministic bit-time bound; no unit-cost manipulation of unbounded integers, oracle, random coins or nonuniform advice is allowed. One program and one polynomial work for all pairs. Correctness is exact on every assignment, not agreement on most assignments or numerical approximation. Only the YES/NO equivalence answer is required; canonicalization or construction of a combined diagram is not an additional output.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean proof that such a uniform polynomial-time equivalence decider exists, including the graph semantics, input encoding, runtime and both correctness directions, or prove the negation of the displayed quantified claim. The negative target rules out every deterministic polynomial-time machine on the promised FBDD input class; failure of one graph comparison or one representation-conversion method is insufficient. A randomized polynomial-time test or a deterministic test requiring a common ordering does not meet the full target. A conditional lower bound settles only its conditional version unless its premise is proved. This review supplies no Lean proof of either answer.

source_formulation.text: Does the FBDD representation support polynomial-time equivalence testing?
source_formulation.caption: Editorial paraphrase of the unresolved EQ entry in the knowledge-compilation map

context_blocks.text: An FBDD records a branching computation that tests a variable at most once on each path. It generalizes an ordered binary decision diagram by allowing the order to vary between branches. Shared subgraphs make its explicit representation potentially much smaller than the full truth table.

Darwiche–Marquis Table 5 marks equivalence for FBDDs as unknown. This is distinct from entailment between diagrams and from constructing their conjunction; the map treats these as separate operations. The card retains equivalence alone.

Darwiche–Huang give randomized polynomial-time equivalence testing for FBDDs and even for general d-DNNFs. For every fixed equivalent pair the test accepts with certainty; for every fixed inequivalent pair it incorrectly accepts with probability at most one half. This is the one-sided-error class coRP, and their bit-length analysis makes the polynomial-time claim an ordinary finite-arithmetic claim.

That error statement is conditioned on the fixed input, not a posterior probability that the input is equivalent after a positive answer. The source’s informal confidence wording is therefore expressed here as the precise one-sided algorithmic guarantee. The requested deterministic answer admits no such error.

The 2026 structured-circuit paper discusses hardness of verifying a join rule for FBDDs: testing whether a third represented function equals the conjunction of two others. That is a different, three-diagram operation. Its hardness is not presented as a lower bound for the two-diagram equivalence question.

Every FBDD has a polynomial-size translation into deterministic decomposable negation normal form. Thus a deterministic general d-DNNF equivalence algorithm would also solve this card; an FBDD-only algorithm would not by itself settle that broader question. The related cards retain those different targets.

The September 2026 bounded search checked the foundational map, the randomized theorem and the newer proof-system discussion, without finding a matching deterministic solution or impossibility theorem. The dated unknown table cell is not an exhaustive certificate of present openness.

Darwiche–Huang give randomized polynomial-time equivalence testing for FBDDs and even for general d-DNNFs. For every fixed equivalent pair the test accepts with certainty; for every fixed inequivalent pair it incorrectly accepts with probability at most one half. This is the one-sided-error class coRP, and their bit-length analysis makes the polynomial-time claim an ordinary finite-arithmetic claim.

That error statement is conditioned on the fixed input, not a posterior probability that the input is equivalent after a positive answer. The source’s informal confidence wording is therefore expressed here as the precise one-sided algorithmic guarantee. The requested deterministic answer admits no such error.

The 2026 structured-circuit paper discusses hardness of verifying a join rule for FBDDs: testing whether a third represented function equals the conjunction of two others. That is a different, three-diagram operation. Its hardness is not presented as a lower bound for the two-diagram equivalence question.

Every FBDD has a polynomial-size translation into deterministic decomposable negation normal form. Thus a deterministic general d-DNNF equivalence algorithm would also solve this card; an FBDD-only algorithm would not by itself settle that broader question. The related cards retain those different targets.

The September 2026 bounded search checked the foundational map, the randomized theorem and the newer proof-system discussion, without finding a matching deterministic solution or impossibility theorem. The dated unknown table cell is not an exhaustive certificate of present openness.

cards.title: Two-sided distributive unification with a unit
cards.formal: Let \(E\) be exactly the four identities \[x\cdot(y+z)=(x\cdot y)+(x\cdot z),\qquad (x+y)\cdot z=(x\cdot z)+(y\cdot z),\qquad x\cdot1=x,\qquad1\cdot x=x.\] Is general first-order \(E\)-unification decidable? Namely, does one deterministic Turing machine halt on every finite signature and finite list of equations \(s_i\doteq t_i\), under the conventions below, and return YES exactly when a single finite-term substitution \(\sigma\) satisfies \(s_i\sigma=_E t_i\sigma\) for every \(i\)?
cards.why: Distributivity couples two operations, so the standard decomposition methods for disjoint equational theories do not immediately apply. The multiplicative unit creates additional identifications between expanded and unexpanded expressions. Determining decidability for exactly this small axiom set would clarify a longstanding boundary in symbolic constraint solving, between known distributive fragments and stronger theories with undecidable unification.
cards.status_note: The 2001 handbook explicitly lists this question as open. Checked the exact axiom sets in the two distinct 1996 positive results, the 1987 associative-extension negative result and the 2010 one-sided algorithm correction. A bounded primary-source search on 16 September 2026 found no verified resolution of the general four-identity target. Because no recent explicit status confirmation was found, scientific status remains uncertain.

sentences: Unification asks whether a common substitution can make every pair of supplied expressions equal under specified algebraic identities.
Here the identities are both distributive laws together with a two-sided multiplicative unit.
The expressions may also use uninterpreted symbols, and neither operation is assumed associative or commutative.

cards.definitions:
The fixed theory signature consists of binary symbols \(+\) and \(\cdot\) and a constant \(1\). An input signature \(F\) is any finite extension by uninterpreted function symbols of specified finite arities, including extra constants; these free symbols have no further equations. This uses the handbook's general-unification convention from §3.1 and §3.2.2 and includes elementary problems and problems with free constants as subcases. A term is a finite ordered rooted tree: a leaf is a variable or a constant, and a node labelled by a symbol of arity \(r\) has exactly \(r\) children. Variables come from a countable set of identifiers; only finitely many occur in an input. The equations form an explicitly written finite list, possibly empty. Signature declarations, arities, identifiers and complete term trees have finite binary encodings; no succinct circuits or infinite rational trees are inputs. A substitution assigns finite terms over \(F\) and variables to the finitely many input variables, fixes the other variables, and extends homomorphically through each function symbol. The same substitution applies to every equation. It is an ordinary simultaneous substitution, not an instruction to unfold terms indefinitely. Additional variables in its range are allowed. A unifier need not be most general, and the decision machine need not output one.

The relation \(=_E\) is the least equivalence relation on terms closed under application of every function symbol and substitutions, and containing every instance of the four displayed identities. Equivalently, equality has a finite equational derivation from exactly these identities, using reflexivity, symmetry, transitivity, congruence and substitution. Parentheses and operand order therefore remain meaningful except where those identities identify them. Neither operation is assumed associative or commutative; no idempotence, additive zero, annihilation, additive inverse or cancellation law is included. The unit is two-sided and belongs to multiplication only. The notation resembles arithmetic, but the target is equality in the presented equational theory, not equality under a chosen integer or semiring interpretation. The same uniform machine must handle every finite input signature, variable count and equation list, halt on both YES and NO inputs, and use no oracle or random error. No time or memory bound is imposed, and no numerical tolerance applies.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean proof that this precisely defined general-unification language is computable, or that it is not. A positive proof must represent finite signatures, terms, substitutions and the generated equational congruence, prove termination of one uniform algorithm on every well-formed input, and show that its YES output is equivalent to existence of a common unifier. A negative proof must establish noncomputability using only the four identities and the permitted free symbols. A result for a different axiom set, a matching problem with variables on only one side, or a nonterminating search for unifiers does not settle the card. The Lean proof must justify the exact signature convention it uses; a constants-only procedure does not automatically prove the general result. This source review is not a completed formal proof.

source_formulation.text: Is unification modulo both distributive laws and a two-sided multiplicative unit decidable?
source_formulation.caption: Editorial paraphrase of the handbook question; general finite-signature unification convention stated explicitly

context_blocks.text: The handbook defines the two distributive theories separately, their union D, and the two-sided unit theory U. It then explicitly leaves D combined with U open. This is not an ordinary semiring problem because the associative, commutative and zero axioms of a semiring are absent.

Schmidt-Schauß’s 1996 distributive-unification theorem concerns the two distributive identities without the unit. Its publisher abstract lists those identities explicitly. The mention of unit-bearing auxiliary theories in that algorithm must not be mistaken for a multiplicative-unit axiom in its input theory.

A different 1996 result handles one-sided distributivity with a multiplicative unit. Having an algorithm after omitting either the second distributive law or the unit does not decide their combination.

Adding associativity of addition changes the situation: Tidén and Arnborg obtain undecidability for a theory with one-sided distributivity, associativity of addition and a one-sided multiplicative unit. That theorem does not settle the four-identity target, which lacks associativity.

The handbook separately distinguishes elementary unification, unification with extra constants and general unification with arbitrary free function symbols. The present card keeps the general first-order setting rather than silently restricting the problem to closed arithmetic-shaped terms.

The 2001 discussion repeats an early polynomial-time claim for the original one-sided algorithm. Narendran, Marshall and Mahapatra later give inputs requiring exponentially many steps for that algorithm. This correction concerns a neighboring algorithm’s running time, not a resolution of two-sided unification with a unit.

The September 2026 search checked these primary statements and later work indexed under distributivity and unification, without verifying a resolution of this exact theory. The old open statement is retained as historical evidence; its age and search absence are not proof of current openness.

cards.title: Decidability of subsequence constraints with regular domains
cards.formal: For each fixed finite alphabet \(A\), consider the following decision problem. An input consists of a finite set \(X\) of variables, one regular expression \(r_x\) over \(A\) for every \(x\in X\), and a finite list \(C\) of constraints \(x\preceq y_1\cdots y_k\), where \(x,y_i\in X\) and \(k\ge0\). Does there exist, for every fixed \(A\), a deterministic Turing machine that halts on every such input and decides whether there is an assignment \(h:X\to A^*\) satisfying \[h(x)\in L(r_x)\quad(x\in X),\qquad h(x)\preceq h(y_1)\cdots h(y_k)\quad((x\preceq y_1\cdots y_k)\in C)?\] The same variable may occur repeatedly, and the directed dependencies between variables may contain arbitrary cycles.
cards.why: This question isolates the effect of cyclic reuse of unknown strings in a small constraint language. Regular domains and ordered concatenation are basic operations in string analysis, while subsequence constraints model loss of letters. A resolution would identify whether these ingredients alone retain effective satisfiability testing, clarifying a boundary obscured by undecidability results for richer interfaces.
cards.status_note: Source-open in the checked July 2024 problem statement and March 2024 primary paper. On 15 September 2026 a bounded later-work search found no matching resolution. Acyclic algorithms and richer-model undecidability do not settle this exact syntax; paper proofs were not independently verified.

progress.text: The published STACS paper gives an NEXPTIME decision bound for acyclic regular constraints even in its richer model. Its §6.2 leaves decidability open when regular constraints use only concatenation and arbitrary cycles are allowed; the undecidability constructions discussed there require operations absent here.
Automata Exchange records the exact question with one variable on each left side, a word of variables on each right side, and regular-expression domains.

The original problem page and the precise open passage in STACS 2024 were rechecked. A bounded search of subsequent work did not locate a resolution matching these constraints. This is a dated source-status report, not an independent proof that the question remains open.

sentences: Each variable denotes one finite word constrained to a specified regular language.
A relational constraint requires that word to occur as a scattered subsequence of a concatenation of other assigned words.
The question asks for total decidability over every fixed finite alphabet, allowing repeated variables and arbitrary dependency cycles.
Known algorithms for acyclic systems and undecidability results with shuffle or transducers concern different input classes.
A resolution would locate the decidability boundary of a basic language for relating incomplete and concatenated strings.

cards.definitions: A word over \(A\) is a finite sequence of its letters; \(A^*\) contains the empty word \(\varepsilon\). Concatenation appends sequences in their given order. For words \(u=u_1\cdots u_m\) and \(v=v_1\cdots v_n\), \(u\preceq v\) means that there exist indices \(1\le i_1<\cdots<i_m\le n\) with \(u_j=v_{i_j}\) for every \(j\). Thus it is the scattered-subsequence relation, including \(\varepsilon\preceq v\). For \(k=0\), the right-hand side evaluates to \(\varepsilon\). Every occurrence of a variable receives the same assigned word. A regular expression is a finite syntax tree generated by letters of \(A\), \(\varnothing\), \(\varepsilon\), binary union, concatenation and Kleene star; its language is defined by these operations, with star allowing any finite number of repetitions, including zero. Variables may receive empty words exactly when their domain expressions permit them. The input explicitly lists the expression trees and variable occurrences, using binary integer indices and delimiters; no compressed strings, numeric length predicates or additional relation symbols occur. A dependency edge \(x\to y\) is present if \(y\) occurs on the right of a constraint whose left side is \(x\). No acyclicity promise is imposed. Up to renaming, the alphabet can be written \(A=\{0,\ldots,a-1\}\) for \(a\in\mathbb N\). The quantifier order is \(\forall a\,\exists M_a\,\forall I\): one finite machine for every instance over that fixed alphabet. This preserves the source's fixed-alphabet convention; it does not demand an effective construction of \(M_a\) from \(a\). Machines must terminate with the exact answer on both satisfiable and unsatisfiable inputs. No time or space bound is requested.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof of the quantified decidability statement or its negation. A positive result must provide total, correct decision procedures covering every finite system over every fixed finite alphabet with exactly the syntax above. A negative result must prove that for at least one fixed finite alphabet no such total computable decision procedure exists. Deciding only systems with acyclic dependencies, or proving undecidability after adding shuffle, transducers, concatenations on the left, or nonregular domain languages, does not settle this statement.

context_blocks.text: A domain expression describes the possible complete value of one variable. A constraint such as \(x\preceq yz\) asks that this value survive as a subsequence after the values of \(y\) and \(z\) are joined. The assignment is shared across the whole system, so different constraints cannot choose independent values for the same variable.

The left side is always one variable, whereas the right side may repeat and concatenate variables. This syntactic asymmetry matters: the card does not ask for arbitrary pairs of concatenated terms related by subsequence. The open question also permits dependencies that return to an earlier variable; results requiring acyclicity cover only part of this domain.

The STACS paper studies a broader language that can interleave strings by shuffle and transform them by finite-state transducers. Its acyclic regular fragment is decidable, while general cyclic fragments of that richer language are undecidable. Section 6.2 explicitly separates the present concatenation-only, transducer-free case as unresolved. Those neighboring theorems therefore do not justify retiring this card.

cards.title: Polynomial-time complementation of d-DNNFs
cards.formal:
Is there a deterministic polynomial-time algorithm that, given any d-DNNF circuit \(C\), outputs a d-DNNF circuit \(D\) over the same variables such that
\[\forall a:X\to\{0,1\},\qquad f_D(a)=1-f_C(a)?\]
The runtime is measured in the explicit binary input encoding and includes writing the entire output. The output may use different decompositions and share subcircuits arbitrarily, subject to the same d-DNNF conditions. It may omit irrelevant input variables, but may not introduce new variables, quantifiers or negation gates above leaves.

One uniform algorithm and one polynomial bound must work for all input sizes and all promised circuits. This is a construction question, distinct from the nonconstructive polynomial-size closure question.
cards.why: Complementation is a basic operation needed to reuse a compiled Boolean representation for exceptions, exclusions and opposite events. General d-DNNFs support useful counting and reasoning tasks, but it is unknown whether this logical transformation can always preserve their computational advantages with polynomial overhead. Resolving the construction question would clarify which operations can be performed directly on this succinct representation.
cards.status_note: Checked on 2026-09-14: the source question, Darwiche–Marquis Sections 2, 4–5, Vinall-Smeeth Theorem 2 and conclusion, and STACS 2026 Section 7. These sources keep arbitrary d-DNNF complementation distinct from the resolved structured-output restriction. A bounded later-work search found no matching general deterministic polynomial-time construction or refutation; openness is not exhaustively certified.

cards.definitions:
A negation-normal-form Boolean circuit is a finite directed acyclic graph with a designated output gate. A leaf is a constant \(0\) or \(1\), or a literal \(x\) or \(\neg x\) for a variable in a finite set \(X\). Each internal gate is AND or OR with a finite nonempty input list. Arbitrary fan-in and sharing of subcircuits are allowed, and every input occurrence counts as an edge. Evaluation on an assignment \(a:X\to\{0,1\}\) uses the ordinary Boolean operations. There are no other negation gates. Constants suffice when \(X\) is empty.

For a gate \(g\), let \(\operatorname{var}(g)\) be the variables appearing in the literals reachable by following its input edges. Decomposability requires that the input subcircuits of each AND gate have pairwise disjoint such variable sets. Determinism requires that, for every OR gate, no assignment to \(X\) makes two distinct input occurrences true simultaneously. A d-DNNF satisfies both conditions at every gate. Determinism is a semantic mutual-exclusion property; it is not a restriction to gates that branch on a single variable.

Write \(f_C(a)\) for the output of circuit \(C\) and \(s(C)=|V(C)|+|E(C)|\) for its size, including leaves and all wires. Unused variables in \(X\) do not affect evaluation. Smoothness, which would require all inputs of an OR gate to mention the same variables, is not assumed. There is also no common tree organizing the variable splits of all conjunction gates. Thus the target uses general d-DNNFs, not only the smaller class of structured d-DNNFs. When two circuits are compared, their variable names denote the same coordinates of a common assignment; a missing coordinate is simply ignored by that circuit.

For computational tasks, encode a circuit as a topologically ordered list of gate records, with gate kinds, signed variable indices at literal leaves, input-list lengths and binary indices of earlier input gates. Include the output index. Variables occurring in the input circuit, or jointly in the two input circuits for a comparison, are consistently renamed to \(1,\ldots,n\); the number \(n\) is at most the total number of input literal occurrences. The input length \(b\) is the total number of bits of these records and delimiters. Gate-and-wire size and bit length are polynomially related with this convention.

An algorithm is one deterministic multitape Turing machine with no oracle, advice or randomness. Polynomial time means at most \(K(b+1)^d\) bit steps for fixed constants \(K,d\) independent of the circuits and number of variables. The inputs are promised to be d-DNNFs. The machine must satisfy the time bound on every input encoding, but its output may be arbitrary when the promise fails; it is not required to recognize the semantic determinism promise. All input reading and output writing count toward the bound.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct Lean-checked proof or refutation of the existence of such a uniform polynomial-time complementing algorithm. A positive answer must prove the output d-DNNF properties, equality to the complement on every assignment and the full bit-time bound. A negative answer must exclude all deterministic polynomial-time algorithms meeting this promise specification, not merely one construction or one output structure. A polynomial-size existence theorem without an efficient construction does not prove the claim. A conditional lower bound establishes only its stated conditional implication unless the needed assumption is also proved.

cards.definitions:
A finite algebra \(\mathbf A=(A;f_{1},\ldots,f_{m})\) has a nonempty explicitly listed finite universe and a finite signature. Each basic operation \(f_{j}:A^{r_{j}}\to A\) is supplied by its complete table, with its arity. Nullary operations, when present, specify distinguished constants. The universe size, number of operations and arities may vary with the input. Let \(L\) be the total binary length of this description. A large-arity operation is not given by a succinct circuit or program.

A term is an expression made from variables and the given operation symbols; interpreting it on \(\mathbf A\) gives a term operation. Constants not in the given signature are not automatically available as term symbols.

The Taylor promise means that there are an arity \(r\geq2\) and a term operation \(t:A^{r}\to A\) such that \(t(a,\ldots,a)=a\) for every \(a\in A\), and for every coordinate \(i\in\{1,\ldots,r\}\) there are two tuples \(\mathbf u_{i},\mathbf v_{i}\in\{x,y\}^{r}\) with \((\mathbf u_{i})_{i}=x\), \((\mathbf v_{i})_{i}=y\), satisfying
\[t(\mathbf u_{i}(a,b))=t(\mathbf v_{i}(a,b))\qquad\text{for every }a,b\in A.\]
The choices of \(r,t\) and identities may depend on the algebra. This is what the source means by membership in a Taylor variety. A witnessing term or operation table is not supplied, and recognizing whether the promise holds is not part of the task.

An endomorphism of \(\mathbf A\) is a map \(h:A\to A\) preserving every basic operation:
\[h(f_{j}(a_{1},\ldots,a_{r_{j}}))=f_{j}(h(a_{1}),\ldots,h(a_{r_{j}})).\]
It must also fix the interpretation of every nullary symbol. Its image is a subalgebra. A core is an endomorphic image minimal under inclusion among such images, equipped with the restricted operations. For finite algebras these cores are unique up to isomorphism; equivalently, every endomorphism of the core is an automorphism.

Abelianness here is the universal-algebraic term-condition property. A concrete definition uses the algebra of \(2\times2\) matrices over a finite algebra \(\mathbf B\), with each basic operation applied entrywise. Let \(M_{\mathbf B}\) be the smallest subset of \(B^{2\times2}\) closed under these operations and containing all matrices
\[\begin{pmatrix}a&a\\ b&b\end{pmatrix},\qquad
\begin{pmatrix}c&d\\ c&d\end{pmatrix}\qquad(a,b,c,d\in B).\]
Then \(\mathbf B\) is abelian if every matrix \(\begin{pmatrix}x&y\\ z&w\end{pmatrix}\in M_{\mathbf B}\) satisfies \(x=y\Rightarrow z=w\). This is the source’s condition \([1_{\mathbf B},1_{\mathbf B}]=0_{\mathbf B}\). It is not a requirement that each basic operation be commutative.

One uniform deterministic algorithm must run in \(O(L^{k})\) bit operations for a fixed constant \(k\), with a fixed multiplicative constant, on all inputs. It must answer correctly for every well-formed algebra satisfying the Taylor promise. On other inputs the answer is unrestricted, but the polynomial time bound still applies. The requested output is only YES or NO; no particular representative of the core has to be chosen.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a deterministic algorithm with a uniform polynomial bound in the full table encoding length that recognizes abelian cores on every promised input, or prove that none exists. A conditional lower bound must identify its assumption. The source also asks for faster construction of the core and its Mal’cev operation in positive cases; those are additional output tasks and are not silently asserted equivalent to the selected decision question.

cards.title: FO model checking on hereditary monadically dependent graph classes
cards.area: Database theory and finite model theory
cards.formal:
For every hereditary effectively monadically dependent class \(\mathcal C\) of finite simple undirected graphs, is first-order model checking fixed-parameter tractable with a computable parameter dependence?

Precisely, does every such \(\mathcal C\) admit a single deterministic algorithm \(A_{\mathcal C}\), a total computable function \(f_{\mathcal C}:\mathbb N\to\mathbb N_{\ge1}\), and a constant integer \(d_{\mathcal C}\ge0\) such that, for every \(G\in\mathcal C\) and every first-order graph sentence \(\varphi\), the algorithm outputs whether \(G\models\varphi\) within
\[f_{\mathcal C}(|\varphi|)\,(|V(G)|+1)^{d_{\mathcal C}}\]
steps? The algorithm receives only the graph and the sentence, in the encodings below, and must halt on every input. The exponent may depend on the class but not on the sentence. The effective structural hypothesis is the computable powerset-obstruction bound defined below.
cards.definitions:
Graph class and promise. A finite simple undirected graph has a finite vertex set and a symmetric irreflexive adjacency relation \(E\); the empty graph is permitted. A class \(\mathcal C\) is closed under graph isomorphism. It is hereditary if \(G[S]\in\mathcal C\) for every \(G\in\mathcal C\) and every \(S\subseteq V(G)\), where \(G[S]\) retains exactly the edges with both endpoints in \(S\). The class is fixed before the algorithm is chosen, not given as part of an instance. No decision procedure for membership in the class is assumed. Correctness and the displayed time bound are required only when the input graph belongs to the class. On other inputs the algorithm may return either answer, but must halt.

First-order syntax and truth. The graph signature has equality and a binary adjacency symbol, with variables \(x_i\) indexed by \(i\in\mathbb N\). Formulas are built from atoms \(x_i=x_j\), \(E(x_i,x_j)\), negation, binary conjunction, and existential quantification \(\exists x_i\); other connectives and universal quantification are abbreviations expanded into this syntax. A sentence has no free variables. Atoms are interpreted using actual equality and graph adjacency; Boolean operations have their usual truth tables, and quantifiers range over all vertices. On the empty graph an existential statement is false and a universal statement is true. The query language has no unary predicates, vertex order, arithmetic, function symbols or set quantification. Write \(G\models\varphi\) for truth of the sentence.

Encoding and computation. For a nonnegative integer \(i\), let \(\ell\) be the binary length of \(i+1\), and encode it as \(U(i)=1^\ell0\operatorname{bin}(i+1)\), where the last part has exactly \(\ell\) bits. Encode \(G\) with labeled vertex set \(\{0,\ldots,n-1\}\) as \(U(n)\) followed by its upper-triangular adjacency bits, in lexicographic order of pairs \(i<j\). All these bits are supplied explicitly. Formulas use prefix syntax: tags 000, 001, 010, 011, 100 respectively stand for equality, adjacency, negation, conjunction and existential quantification. An atom tag is followed by \(U(i)U(j)\), negation by one encoded subformula, conjunction by two in order, and the existential tag by \(U(i)\) and one subformula. The parameter \(|\varphi|\) is this binary length, including variable indices. A valid input concatenates the graph code and one sentence code; invalid inputs may be rejected. An algorithm is a finite deterministic multitape Turing machine with a fixed finite tape alphabet and no oracle, advice or randomness; time counts its transitions. Polynomial simulation overhead between the usual explicit graph representations and finite-word computational models can be absorbed in the class-dependent exponent and parameter function.

Unary expansions for the structural condition. For this purpose only, allow additional unary symbols \(P_j\), \(j\in\mathbb N\), with atom \(P_j(x_i)\) encoded by tag 101 followed by \(U(j)U(i)\). Each formula uses finitely many such symbols. They are interpreted independently as arbitrary vertex subsets; they may overlap. Their names and variable indices are included in formula length. There are no additional parameters or constant symbols.

Transduction. Let \(\theta(x_0,x_1)\) be any formula in this expanded syntax whose only possible free variables are \(x_0,x_1\). Given \(G\), choose arbitrary interpretations of all unary symbols used in \(\theta\). On the same vertex set, form an undirected graph by putting an edge between distinct \(u,v\) exactly when \(\theta(u,v)\lor\theta(v,u)\) holds in that expansion of \(G\). Finally keep any subset of vertices and take the induced graph on it. Denote by \(T_\theta(G)\) the set of all graphs obtainable in this way, up to isomorphism. Colors are discarded in the output. There is no copying of vertices or tuple-valued output domain in this definition.

Monadic dependence and its effective version. A class is monadically dependent when no single formula \(\theta\) produces every finite simple graph among the outputs \(T_\theta(G)\) as \(G\) ranges over the class. To state the quantitative promise, for an integer \(s\ge1\) let \(P_s\) be the bipartite powerset graph with disjoint vertex sets \(\{a_1,\ldots,a_s\}\) and \(\{b_S:S\subseteq\{1,\ldots,s\}\}\), and edges exactly \(a_i b_S\) with \(i\in S\). It has \(s+2^s\) vertices and no edges within either part.

The class \(\mathcal C\) is effectively monadically dependent if there is a total computable function \(b:\mathbb N\to\mathbb N_{\ge1}\) such that
\[\forall\theta\ \forall G\in\mathcal C:\quad P_{b(|\theta|)}\notin T_\theta(G).\]
Absence means that no choice of unary predicates and retained vertex subset yields a graph isomorphic to that powerset graph. The bound is uniform over all formulas of the given length, all graphs in the class, and all their colorings. It is the effective dependence-function convention of Mählmann’s Definition 12.24, which in particular implies monadic dependence. The finite program computing \(b\) may depend on \(\mathcal C\).

Uniformity of the requested algorithm. For each class, one finite program \(A_{\mathcal C}\) must handle all input sentence lengths. It may depend on the class and its effective dependence witness, but receives neither a class-membership certificate nor a graph decomposition on an instance. The quantifiers are class-wise existence of the algorithm, computable function and exponent; no single procedure that accepts arbitrary descriptions of classes and constructs their algorithms is required. There is no prescribed growth rate for \(f_{\mathcal C}\), beyond total computability.
cards.answer_criterion:
Provide a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of the stated proposition or its logical negation. A positive answer must establish, for every class satisfying the hereditary and effective-dependence promises, one total deterministic algorithm and one computable parameter bound with a sentence-independent polynomial exponent, for the specified graph-and-sentence input model.

A negative answer must establish a particular hereditary effectively monadically dependent class for which no such algorithm, computable parameter function and fixed exponent work. In particular, every candidate total deterministic algorithm and bound must fail on some graph in that class and some sentence, either in correctness or in running time. An obstruction applying only to one proposed algorithm, an ineffective class, or a restricted decomposition method is insufficient. A conditional hardness result alone does not refute this unconditional target unless its additional assumption is also proved. Structural existence theorems, a different algorithm for each sentence length, randomized algorithms, or algorithms supplied with extra decompositions do not by themselves meet the criterion.
cards.why: First-order formulas express a broad family of graph queries, but direct evaluation lets the graph-size exponent grow with the query. The proposed structural condition aims to explain when that dependence can be confined to a computable function of the query alone, even on dense graph classes. Settling this tractability direction would complement the established hardness of hereditary classes that can logically encode arbitrary graphs.

cards.status_note: Checked on 16 September 2026. The July 2026 primary paper explicitly keeps the full dependent-class tractability direction open. Its almost linear neighborhood complexity and polynomial-time radius-one construction do not give the stated deterministic, decomposition-free algorithm with computable parameter dependence. The effective hypothesis is the dissertation’s precise powerset-obstruction convention, retained from the saved target. No general resolution was found in bounded later searches; the review checked theorem statements and computational scope rather than independently verifying every long proof.

context_blocks.text: First-order model checking asks whether a finite graph satisfies an input sentence. Clique, independent-set and dominating-set queries of a specified size are basic examples. Trying all assignments of vertices to variables gives polynomial time for each fixed sentence, but its exponent depends on the sentence. Fixed-parameter tractability requires one exponent for all sentences on the chosen class.

For example, a sentence can assert the existence of a fixed number of vertices such that every other vertex is adjacent to at least one of them. Increasing that number increases the sentence length and the direct enumeration cost. The target permits an arbitrarily large computable cost depending on sentence length, while keeping a fixed polynomial dependence on the graph size. It is a uniform guarantee across the whole query language.

The hereditary condition is closure under deleting vertices, keeping all remaining edges. It allows sparse and dense classes alike. Complete graphs illustrate why edge density is not itself the barrier: a dense class may still have tightly controlled logical behavior. The conjectured boundary uses what a fixed formula can encode after arbitrary unary marking, rather than an edge-count bound.

A transduction changes the edge relation according to a formula, after vertices have been marked by finitely many unary predicates, and may discard vertices. The formula is fixed while graph size grows. Monadic independence means that one such fixed scheme can yield every finite graph. Dependence excludes this unrestricted encoding, while allowing richer structure than monadic stability.

Computability is a genuine qualification in the saved target. A class can have a finite obstruction bound at each formula length without any computable function dominating those bounds. The dissertation illustrates this distinction with graph classes indexed by Busy Beaver growth. That example shows why a proof with arbitrary class-dependent constants cannot automatically be advertised as a computable FPT bound; it is not itself an unconditional counterexample to the present effective conjecture.

The structural witness and the query algorithm play different roles. The function b bounds powerset graphs obtainable by all short colored formulas; it does not recognize which graphs belong to the class. The requested algorithm receives a promised member of the class and an uncolored sentence. Neither a membership test nor a decomposition oracle is included in the input.

Dreier, Mählmann and Toruńczyk prove that model checking is \(\mathrm{AW}[*]\)-hard on every hereditary monadically independent class. Their stronger interpretation theorem produces uncolored instances efficiently, so this is not merely a hardness statement with extra vertex colors supplied. Under the standard assumption \(\mathrm{FPT}\ne\mathrm{AW}[*]\), the independent side cannot have FPT model checking. That conditional intractability does not prove the positive dependent side.

Monadic stability is the stronger condition excluding arbitrarily large half-graphs under transductions: a half-graph of order \(s\) has two disjoint parts \(a_1,\ldots,a_s\) and \(b_1,\ldots,b_s\), with edge \(a_i b_j\) exactly when \(i\le j\). The stable-class model-checking theorem gives a major positive case. The dissertation makes its parameter function computable under effective stability bounds; ordinary stability alone should not silently be substituted for that effective hypothesis.

Merge-width measures graph construction sequences that merge vertex groups and resolve pairs as edges or nonedges. At radius r, the width bounds how many current groups a vertex can reach using at most r resolved pairs. The existing bounded-merge-width model-checking theorem assumes that a witnessing sequence is supplied. Existence of a useful sequence alone does not meet the card’s input model.

The July 2026 paper proves almost linear neighborhood complexity for every monadically dependent class. Writing \(N_G(v)\) for the neighbors of \(v\), for every \(\eta>0\) there is a constant \(c_{\mathcal C,\eta}\) such that for all \(G\in\mathcal C\) and all nonempty \(S\subseteq V(G)\), the number of distinct sets \(N_G(v)\cap S\) is at most \(c_{\mathcal C,\eta}|S|^{1+\eta}\). The nonempty-set qualification avoids the zero-size edge case.

The same paper constructs radius-one merge-width sequences in \(O(n^5)\) time, with width \(n^{o(1)}\) on every monadically dependent class. Here \(n^{o(1)}\) means that for every fixed positive exponent the width is eventually at most a constant times that power of \(n\), with constants depending on the class. This is meaningful algorithmic progress, but gives neither a constant width bound nor corresponding control at all larger radii.

Dreier and Kuske’s February 2026 work speeds up low-crossing orders and neighborhood covers, with a faster model-checking application for monadically stable classes. Its ordering and cover subroutines use randomness. A faster theorem on that already understood subclass does not establish the deterministic guarantee for every effectively monadically dependent class.

The July 2026 paper explicitly retains the general tractability direction as open. A positive answer here would establish the effective algorithmic direction of the proposed classification. A negative answer would require an effective hereditary class that defeats every single uniform algorithm with computable parameter dependence, not merely a class whose currently known decomposition bounds are ineffective.

cards.context:
First-order model checking asks whether a finite graph satisfies an input sentence. Clique, independent-set and dominating-set queries of a specified size are basic examples. Trying all assignments of vertices to variables gives polynomial time for each fixed sentence, but its exponent depends on the sentence. Fixed-parameter tractability requires one exponent for all sentences on the chosen class.

For example, a sentence can assert the existence of a fixed number of vertices such that every other vertex is adjacent to at least one of them. Increasing that number increases the sentence length and the direct enumeration cost. The target permits an arbitrarily large computable cost depending on sentence length, while keeping a fixed polynomial dependence on the graph size. It is a uniform guarantee across the whole query language.

The hereditary condition is closure under deleting vertices, keeping all remaining edges. It allows sparse and dense classes alike. Complete graphs illustrate why edge density is not itself the barrier: a dense class may still have tightly controlled logical behavior. The conjectured boundary uses what a fixed formula can encode after arbitrary unary marking, rather than an edge-count bound.

A transduction changes the edge relation according to a formula, after vertices have been marked by finitely many unary predicates, and may discard vertices. The formula is fixed while graph size grows. Monadic independence means that one such fixed scheme can yield every finite graph. Dependence excludes this unrestricted encoding, while allowing richer structure than monadic stability.

Computability is a genuine qualification in the saved target. A class can have a finite obstruction bound at each formula length without any computable function dominating those bounds. The dissertation illustrates this distinction with graph classes indexed by Busy Beaver growth. That example shows why a proof with arbitrary class-dependent constants cannot automatically be advertised as a computable FPT bound; it is not itself an unconditional counterexample to the present effective conjecture.

The structural witness and the query algorithm play different roles. The function b bounds powerset graphs obtainable by all short colored formulas; it does not recognize which graphs belong to the class. The requested algorithm receives a promised member of the class and an uncolored sentence. Neither a membership test nor a decomposition oracle is included in the input.

Dreier, Mählmann and Toruńczyk prove that model checking is \(\mathrm{AW}[*]\)-hard on every hereditary monadically independent class. Their stronger interpretation theorem produces uncolored instances efficiently, so this is not merely a hardness statement with extra vertex colors supplied. Under the standard assumption \(\mathrm{FPT}\ne\mathrm{AW}[*]\), the independent side cannot have FPT model checking. That conditional intractability does not prove the positive dependent side.

Monadic stability is the stronger condition excluding arbitrarily large half-graphs under transductions: a half-graph of order \(s\) has two disjoint parts \(a_1,\ldots,a_s\) and \(b_1,\ldots,b_s\), with edge \(a_i b_j\) exactly when \(i\le j\). The stable-class model-checking theorem gives a major positive case. The dissertation makes its parameter function computable under effective stability bounds; ordinary stability alone should not silently be substituted for that effective hypothesis.

Merge-width measures graph construction sequences that merge vertex groups and resolve pairs as edges or nonedges. At radius r, the width bounds how many current groups a vertex can reach using at most r resolved pairs. The existing bounded-merge-width model-checking theorem assumes that a witnessing sequence is supplied. Existence of a useful sequence alone does not meet the card’s input model.

The July 2026 paper proves almost linear neighborhood complexity for every monadically dependent class. Writing \(N_G(v)\) for the neighbors of \(v\), for every \(\eta>0\) there is a constant \(c_{\mathcal C,\eta}\) such that for all \(G\in\mathcal C\) and all nonempty \(S\subseteq V(G)\), the number of distinct sets \(N_G(v)\cap S\) is at most \(c_{\mathcal C,\eta}|S|^{1+\eta}\). The nonempty-set qualification avoids the zero-size edge case.

The same paper constructs radius-one merge-width sequences in \(O(n^5)\) time, with width \(n^{o(1)}\) on every monadically dependent class. Here \(n^{o(1)}\) means that for every fixed positive exponent the width is eventually at most a constant times that power of \(n\), with constants depending on the class. This is meaningful algorithmic progress, but gives neither a constant width bound nor corresponding control at all larger radii.

Dreier and Kuske’s February 2026 work speeds up low-crossing orders and neighborhood covers, with a faster model-checking application for monadically stable classes. Its ordering and cover subroutines use randomness. A faster theorem on that already understood subclass does not establish the deterministic guarantee for every effectively monadically dependent class.

The July 2026 paper explicitly retains the general tractability direction as open. A positive answer here would establish the effective algorithmic direction of the proposed classification. A negative answer would require an effective hereditary class that defeats every single uniform algorithm with computable parameter dependence, not merely a class whose currently known decomposition bounds are ineffective.
