cards.title: Constant-delay conjunctive-query classification
cards.area: Database theory and finite model theory
cards.formal: Is there a total algorithm that, given any conjunctive query q with self-joins allowed, decides whether q admits enumeration of all distinct answers with \(O_{q}(N)\) preprocessing and \(O_{q}(1)\) worst-case delay on every database of size N?
cards.definitions: A query is a finite formula \(q(\bar\{x\})=\exists \bar\{y\} \land _{i} R_{i}(\bar\{z\}_{i})\), with no constants, negation, disequalities or aggregation. The head x̄ lists distinct variables; every variable occurs in a relational atom. Relation symbols have fixed positive finite arities within q and may occur repeatedly; repeated variables within atoms are allowed. Boolean queries have an empty head. A database D explicitly lists finite set-valued relations over a domain \([n]; N=1+n\)+the total number of tuple entries in these lists. Each domain identifier fits in \(O(\log (N+2))\) bits. \(q(D)\) is the set of head tuples extendible to an assignment satisfying all atoms. Fix the deterministic word-RAM convention with addition, multiplication, comparison, Boolean word operations and indirect access costing one step, words of \(O_{q}(\log (N+2))\) bits, and a polynomial address universe of initially zero cells. Accessed cells and operations are charged; no linear-space or constant-extra-space restriction is imposed. This allows direct tuple-membership tables without charging for touching every unused address. Membership in the target class means that for this fixed q there are an enumerator and constants \(C_{q},B_{q}\) whose preprocessing takes at most \(C_{q} N\) steps, whose word length is at most \(B_{q} \log _{2}(N+2)\), and whose time to the first answer, between consecutive answers, and from the last answer to termination is at most \(C_{q}\) after preprocessing. Empty output must be reported within the same delay bound. Output order is arbitrary and each tuple appears exactly once. The classifier takes q, not D, as input and must halt on every query; it has no prescribed runtime bound and need not output the enumerator. This is an explicit effective yes/no formulation of the source’s broader request for a complete tractability classification. The word instructions are random-access reads/writes, comparisons, conditional branches, addition, subtraction and multiplication modulo \(2^{w}\), integer quotient/remainder with nonzero divisor, bitwise Boolean operations, and shifts of a w-bit word; shifts by at least w yield zero. The constant in word length \(w=\Theta (\log  n)\) (or \(\Theta (\log  N)\) when N is the stated input size) is fixed with the algorithm. Address arithmetic has the same cost, larger integers occupy multiple words, and no instruction performs arbitrary-precision arithmetic in one step. When randomization is allowed, a fresh independent uniform w-bit word costs one operation. In this statement, “explicitly given/encoded/listed” means the entire finite list, table or syntax tree described above is part of the input or output, with its full encoding counted; it does not mean a circuit, oracle or program generating a larger object.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove the proposition in the problem statement or prove its logical negation, using exactly the definitions, hypotheses and quantifier order stated here. The proof must cover the complete target.

cards.status_note: Reviewed through 11 September 2026. The checked primary sources leave the general self-join classification unresolved. The exact target is an editorial effective formulation, with a specified RAM and permissive polynomial memory. Known negative classifications use stated fine-grained hypotheses; newer projected-query and dynamic results do not cover the whole class.

context_blocks.text: A conjunctive query combines relational lookups with shared variables, then projects away variables that are not requested in the output. For example, \(q(x,z)=\exists y R(x,y)\land S(y,z)\) asks for all endpoint pairs connected through an intermediate value. It may have many witnesses y for one answer \((x,z)\), but under the set semantics here that answer must be printed only once. A self-join occurs when several atoms use the same relation symbol.

This is data complexity: q is fixed while the database grows. Even a fixed query can produce quadratically or cubically many answers, so linear total running time is often impossible just because of output size. Linear preprocessing followed by constant delay is a more appropriate ideal. It permits total time proportional to input plus output while also controlling the wait for each answer, including the first one and the final termination signal.

The classical positive condition is free-connex acyclicity. Form the query hypergraph with a vertex for each variable and one edge for the variables of each atom. It is acyclic when its edges admit a join tree: the edges containing any particular variable form a connected subtree. Free-connex additionally requires acyclicity after adding one edge containing all output variables. Bagan–Durand–Grandjean develop constant-delay enumeration for this structure.

For the example \(\exists y R(x,y)\land S(y,z)\), the two atom edges form a path, but adding the output edge \(\{x,z\}\) creates a cycle. Its answers are exactly the nonzero entries in the Boolean product of the two relation matrices. This explains why projection is tied to matrix multiplication. Classical hardness for acyclic self-join-free queries relies on a Boolean-matrix-multiplication assumption, rather than an unconditional superlinear lower bound.

Carmeli–Segoufin show that the self-join-free classification does not extend merely by ignoring repeated relation names. Some cyclic queries with self-joins allow constant-delay enumeration. Their paper gives positive and negative conditions, a classification for queries with at most two output variables under stated hyperclique assumptions, and further results for queries whose Boolean cores are cyclic. A general classification remains outside these theorems.

A particularly instructive example is the full query \(R(x,y)\land R(y,z)\land R(x,t)\land R(t,z)\). A two-step path from x to z already yields an answer with \(t=y\). When another middle vertex becomes available for those endpoints, it can be paired with previously stored middle vertices to produce further answers. The paper generalizes this symmetry through mirror queries. Its algorithms may store information proportional to the output, which is why this card explicitly allows growing memory.

Adding a predicate on only one of the two middle vertices can break that symmetry. More generally, assignments can identify several query variables with one database element. This is allowed by the syntax; injective matching would be another task. Such identifications generate extra answers that can invalidate a hardness reduction designed for independent relations. Any complete criterion has to account for the interaction between repeated symbols, variable identifications and the chosen output variables.

Rouvroy’s May 2025 research report studies acyclic queries with self-joins and projections, focusing on atoms of arity at most two. It develops a sufficient condition through a construction called patching, alongside necessary conditions and examples not captured by either side. The report explicitly says it is not yet polished. These are useful additional tractability results, but the report does not claim the full classification; relation arity at most two also differs from having at most two output variables.

The source question asks for a structural classification. To make this card a definite yes/no problem, the formal target asks whether membership in the tractable class is decidable from query syntax. This does not demand a fast classifier, nor one uniform enumerator with constants independent of q. It does demand termination for every query. A finite list of sufficient patterns is progress only if there is also a justified answer for every remaining query.

Recent dichotomies for incremental view maintenance concern another resource tradeoff. Chmielewski–Draghici–Olteanu–Zhang’s June 2026 preprint studies insertions into semiring-annotated databases and classifies a self-join-free setting using acyclicity and p-hierarchy. There the update cost and the semiring affect tractability. Such a dynamic, annotated classification does not resolve static distinct-answer enumeration with arbitrary self-joins.

A solution would explain exactly when a query can be compiled into an output stream with predictable response time after one linear scan of its data. The significance reaches beyond one faster join implementation: it would provide a general language-level boundary for a basic form of relational computation. The explicit memory, projection and duplicate conventions make proposed classifications comparable instead of allowing the target to change between examples.

cards.definitions: A finite relational vocabulary \(\tau\) lists finitely many relation symbols with fixed positive arities. A finite \(\tau\)-structure A has a nonempty finite domain and interprets each r-ary symbol as a subset of \(A^{r}\). An isomorphism is a bijection between domains that preserves and reflects every relation. For computation, label the n domain elements by \([n]\) and encode the domain explicitly together with all relation tables in binary. Different labelings of the same abstract structure are permitted; the input supplies no distinguished order relation. A Boolean property is an isomorphism-closed class of structures of one vocabulary. It is in PTIME when one deterministic Turing machine decides membership for every encoding in time polynomial in its length. The logic has a decidable set of finite binary sentence encodings with their vocabularies. Each sentence \(\varphi\) has a truth value \(A\models \varphi\) invariant under isomorphism. One total computable compiler, given a valid \((\tau ,\varphi )\), outputs a deterministic machine \(M_{\varphi}\) and integers \(C_{\varphi},k_{\varphi}\ge 1\) such that \(M_{\varphi}\) decides \(A\models \varphi\) in at most \(C_{\varphi}(N+1)^{k_{\varphi}}\) steps on every valid input structure encoding of length N. Finally, for every finite \(\tau\) and every PTIME Boolean property Q of \(\tau\)-structures, some fixed \(\tau\)-sentence \(\varphi\) satisfies \(A\models \varphi\) exactly when \(A\in Q\) for all finite A. Neither sentence construction from an arbitrary machine nor polynomial-time compilation is required. The exponent may depend on the sentence. No uniform polynomial bound for the combined input \((\varphi ,A)\) is imposed. The same syntax and compiler must work across vocabularies; no oracle, advice or externally chosen ordering is supplied to the semantics.
cards.answer_criterion: A positive resolution gives a formalism satisfying decidable syntax, invariant semantics, effective polynomial-time compilation and expressive completeness for every finite relational vocabulary. A negative resolution proves that no formalism can satisfy all these requirements. Failure of one named logic, capture on a restricted class of structures, or capture with an additional input order does not decide general existence.

context_blocks.title: Properties should survive renaming
context_blocks.text: A graph with vertices called 1, 2 and 3 has the same abstract edges after a consistent permutation of those names. The property “the graph is connected” is unchanged; the property “vertex 1 has a neighbour named 2” can change. A logic for structures must express the first kind of property. An ordinary algorithm still receives a labeled encoding and may use its order internally, but its final Boolean answer must depend only on the structure being represented.

context_blocks.title: Why an effective syntax matters
context_blocks.text: One could assign a symbol to each polynomial-time property and declare that the symbol names that property. This supplies no way to evaluate the symbols. The compiler requirement makes the connection operational: from a sentence, one must obtain an actual algorithm and its polynomial clock. Similarly, listing all clocked machines does not ensure that every listed machine gives the same answer after relabeling its input. The task is to combine effective enumeration with invariance and full expressive power.

context_blocks.title: The known ordered theorem
context_blocks.text: The Immerman–Vardi theorem captures polynomial time by fixed-point logic on structures equipped with a linear order. Fixed-point operators express iterative constructions such as repeatedly extending a reachability relation until no new pairs appear. The order allows the logic to organize elements and simulate an ordinary computation. In the present question the order is absent from the mathematical input. Adding one to every structure changes what the sentence is permitted to access, so the ordered theorem does not directly settle the unordered case.

context_blocks.title: Capturing is not one universal time bound
context_blocks.text: One sentence may compile to a quadratic algorithm and another to an algorithm taking the tenth power of the input size. Both are permitted. The sentence is fixed when its data complexity is measured. Conversely, expressive completeness asks for a single sentence for an entire property on all finite input sizes. Writing a separate sentence for each graph, or a different sentence for each domain size, would not supply the required description.

context_blocks.title: The remaining gap
context_blocks.text: Known extensions of fixed-point logic add counting, linear algebra or symmetry-preserving computation, but ruling out a particular candidate is not a proof that no logic exists. Lichter and Schweitzer’s witnessed symmetric choice extends a candidate logic and yields capturing results on classes where isomorphism is definable; the premise is not known for all structures. Dahan’s August 2026 paper explicitly retains the general question. Its obstruction to choosing small symmetric generating sets concerns a structured output task, rather than proving that no logic can express every PTIME Boolean property. Finally, if \(\mathrm{P}=\mathrm{NP}\), existential second-order logic would capture P by Fagin’s theorem and would have effective polynomial-time evaluation. cards.context:
A graph with vertices called 1, 2 and 3 has the same abstract edges after a consistent permutation of those names. The property “the graph is connected” is unchanged; the property “vertex 1 has a neighbour named 2” can change. A logic for structures must express the first kind of property. An ordinary algorithm still receives a labeled encoding and may use its order internally, but its final Boolean answer must depend only on the structure being represented.

One could assign a symbol to each polynomial-time property and declare that the symbol names that property. This supplies no way to evaluate the symbols. The compiler requirement makes the connection operational: from a sentence, one must obtain an actual algorithm and its polynomial clock. Similarly, listing all clocked machines does not ensure that every listed machine gives the same answer after relabeling its input. The task is to combine effective enumeration with invariance and full expressive power.

The Immerman–Vardi theorem captures polynomial time by fixed-point logic on structures equipped with a linear order. Fixed-point operators express iterative constructions such as repeatedly extending a reachability relation until no new pairs appear. The order allows the logic to organize elements and simulate an ordinary computation. In the present question the order is absent from the mathematical input. Adding one to every structure changes what the sentence is permitted to access, so the ordered theorem does not directly settle the unordered case.

One sentence may compile to a quadratic algorithm and another to an algorithm taking the tenth power of the input size. Both are permitted. The sentence is fixed when its data complexity is measured. Conversely, expressive completeness asks for a single sentence for an entire property on all finite input sizes. Writing a separate sentence for each graph, or a different sentence for each domain size, would not supply the required description.

Known extensions of fixed-point logic add counting, linear algebra or symmetry-preserving computation, but ruling out a particular candidate is not a proof that no logic exists. Lichter and Schweitzer’s witnessed symmetric choice extends a candidate logic and yields capturing results on classes where isomorphism is definable; the premise is not known for all structures. Dahan’s August 2026 paper explicitly retains the general question. Its obstruction to choosing small symmetric generating sets concerns a structured output task, rather than proving that no logic can express every PTIME Boolean property. Finally, if \(\mathrm{P}=\mathrm{NP}\), existential second-order logic would capture P by Fagin’s theorem and would have effective polynomial-time evaluation. Thus a proof that no such logic exists would also separate P from NP.

cards.title: Asser’s problem
cards.area: Database theory and finite model theory
cards.formal:
Is the class of finite first-order spectra closed under complement within the positive integers?

For every finite relational vocabulary \(\tau\) and every first-order sentence \(\varphi\) over \(\tau\), does there exist a finite relational vocabulary \(\sigma\) and a first-order sentence \(\psi\) over \(\sigma\) such that
\[\forall n\in\mathbb Z_{>0}:\quad \bigl(\exists\text{ an }n\text{-element }\sigma\text{-structure satisfying }\psi\bigr)\ \Longleftrightarrow\ \neg\bigl(\exists\text{ an }n\text{-element }\tau\text{-structure satisfying }\varphi\bigr)?\]
The vocabulary and sentence \((\sigma,\psi)\) may depend on \((\tau,\varphi)\), but must work simultaneously for every positive size \(n\). They need not use the original vocabulary. No effective procedure for obtaining \(\psi\), or bound on its length, is required.
cards.definitions:
Vocabulary and syntax. A finite relational vocabulary is a finite, possibly empty list \(R_1,\ldots,R_m\) of distinct relation symbols with specified positive integer arities \(a_1,\ldots,a_m\). There are no function or constant symbols. Equality is a logical symbol and is always available. Variables are drawn from a countable supply. Formulas are finite expressions built from equality atoms \(x=y\), relation atoms \(R_i(x_1,\ldots,x_{a_i})\), negation, conjunction, and first-order existential quantification; other Boolean connectives and universal quantification have their usual equivalent definitions. Variables in an atom may repeat. A sentence has no free variables. Neither the number of symbols, their arities, the number of variables nor quantifier depth has a fixed global bound.

Structures and semantics. A structure over \(\tau\) consists of a nonempty finite domain \(A\) and, for each symbol \(R_i\), an arbitrary interpretation \(R_i^A\subseteq A^{a_i}\). Equality is actual equality of elements. A relation atom holds under a variable assignment exactly when the assigned tuple belongs to its interpreted relation; equality, Boolean operations and existential quantification are evaluated in the usual way, with quantified variables ranging over elements of \(A\). Write \(\mathcal A\models\varphi\) when a sentence is true in this structure. There is no built-in order, arithmetic, graph condition or fixed interpretation of a relation. A sentence may itself require such properties.

Spectrum. Define
\[\operatorname{Spec}(\varphi)=\{n\in\mathbb Z_{>0}:\exists\mathcal A,\ |A|=n\text{ and }\mathcal A\models\varphi\}.\]
The existence quantifier ranges over all interpretations of all symbols at that size. One may fix the domain to \(\{1,\ldots,n\}\), since relabeling does not affect truth. The target is
\[\operatorname{Spec}(\psi)=\mathbb Z_{>0}\setminus\operatorname{Spec}(\varphi).\]
Only cardinalities are retained; the spectrum does not count how many models or isomorphism types exist at a size. Empty and infinite structures are outside this definition, and the complement does not include zero.

Scope. The restriction to relational vocabularies preserves the ordinary class of first-order spectra: finite-arity functions and constants can instead be represented by relations, together with first-order conditions enforcing their graph or unique-value interpretation on the same domain. No second-order quantifiers over relations or arbitrary external numerical predicates are added to the representing sentence. The target is an existence statement about finite formulas and their entire sets of model sizes. It imposes no computational model, sentence-construction resource bound or model-search algorithm requirement.
cards.answer_criterion: Provide a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of the displayed universal complement-closure statement or its full logical negation. A positive proof must establish a single representing first-order sentence for the whole positive-integer complement of each input spectrum; the new vocabulary is unrestricted except for finiteness and the stated relational syntax. A negative proof must establish a first-order spectrum whose complement is not the spectrum of any first-order sentence over any permitted finite vocabulary. Equivalently, for that input sentence, every candidate representing sentence must fail at some positive size, which may depend on the candidate. Checking finitely many sizes, ruling out a fixed vocabulary or variable bound, or showing that literal sentence negation fails is insufficient. The theorem must be unconditional unless it also proves every additional assumption used.
cards.why: A first-order sentence can describe rich finite structures, while its spectrum keeps only the possible domain sizes. Asser’s question asks whether the sizes excluded by one such description can always be the sizes admitted by another. Its equivalence with closure of nondeterministic exponential time under complement makes this a fundamental meeting point of finite model theory and computational complexity.

importance.reason: A classical foundational question of finite model theory and descriptive complexity, explicitly surveyed as an unresolved central spectrum problem. Its complement target is distinct from PTIME capture, query containment and ordinary finite satisfiability.

context_blocks.text: Scholz asked in 1952 how to characterize the sets of finite sizes admitted by first-order sentences. Asser’s 1955 complement question asks for a particular closure property of that class. Characterizing the class in another language does not by itself settle its closure under complement; the historical survey treats these as distinct questions.

The quantifier over structures is essential. For example, over a unary predicate \(P\), the sentence \((\exists x\,P(x))\land(\exists y\,\neg P(y))\) has a model exactly at sizes at least two. Its logical negation has a model at every positive size, since \(P\) can be empty. The complement of the original spectrum is just \(\{1\}\). Thus truth of a negated sentence in some structure is different from absence of every model of the original sentence at that size.

A spectrum forgets which structures realize a size. It can be empty, finite, cofinite or infinite with large gaps. The survey records closure under finite unions and intersections, with relation vocabularies allowed to vary. Complement is the missing general Boolean closure operation. Requiring a representative in the original vocabulary would impose an additional condition not present in Asser’s question.

The computational characterization uses binary representations of sizes. If \(m\) is the number of bits in \(n\), the class \(\mathrm{NE}\) consists of languages accepted by a nondeterministic Turing machine in time \(O(2^{cm})\) for some fixed constant \(c\). Jones and Selman, and independently Fagin, identify first-order spectra with the sets whose canonical binary representations belong to this class. Here a canonical positive representation begins with a one and has no leading zeros.

Consequently, general spectrum complement closure is equivalent to \(\mathrm{NE}=\mathrm{coNE}\), where the latter class contains complements of languages in \(\mathrm{NE}\). The input-size convention matters: unary encoding has length \(n\), whereas binary encoding has length proportional to \(\log n\). The relevant complexity class is single-exponential nondeterministic time in that binary length, not polynomial time in an explicitly supplied structure.

A negative answer would also imply \(\mathrm{NP}\ne\mathrm{coNP}\), and therefore \(\mathrm P\ne\mathrm{NP}\), as noted in the two-variable paper. The converse is not asserted. This is a precise one-way connection to those complexity questions, not an identification of Asser’s problem with P versus NP.

For two-variable logic with counting, denoted \(C^2\), Kopczyński and Tan prove a complete answer: its spectra are exactly the semilinear sets and are closed under complement even within \(C^2\). This logic reuses only two variable names, with quantifiers asserting that at least a fixed number of elements satisfy a formula. In one dimension, semilinear sets are ultimately periodic: beyond a finite threshold, membership depends only on the residue modulo some positive period.

The variable-hierarchy paper shows that allowing more variables genuinely increases spectrum expressibility along an infinite hierarchy. Nevertheless, its complement problem reduces to input sentences with only three variables and binary relations. These are different claims: a reduction of the complement question does not say that every spectrum itself has a three-variable description. The complement representative in that reduction may use arbitrarily many variables.

The 2018 paper sharpens the reduction further to input sentences using three variables and one symmetric binary relation, all of whose models are undirected bipartite graphs. Its encoding changes model sizes by a fixed affine transformation. The resulting equivalence still asks whether each restricted input spectrum’s complement is some first-order spectrum; it does not require a three-variable bipartite representative for that complement.

The 2024 paper extends the two-variable spectrum analysis to ultimately periodic counting conditions. Its Theorem 9.1 effectively describes finite model sizes by a formula of Presburger arithmetic, the first-order arithmetic of addition and order. That is substantive progress for an expressive restricted logic. It does not remove the two-variable restriction or settle complement closure for arbitrary first-order sentences.

Finite satisfiability asks whether a sentence has any finite model at all; Asser’s problem asks about the entire set of its possible finite sizes. The known undecidability of the former does not refute the latter’s non-effective existence claim. Likewise, a positive answer here would not, by itself, provide a decision procedure for finite satisfiability.

cards.title: Decidability of conjunctive-query entailment in SROIQ
cards.area: Database theory and finite model theory
cards.formal: Does one total algorithm decide, for every finite SROIQ knowledge base K and every Boolean conjunctive query q, whether \(K\models q\) under the standard semantics over all finite or infinite models?
cards.definitions: Fix classical SROIQ without datatypes, using the syntax of Horrocks–Kutz–Sattler (2006), Definitions 1–6. Concept names denote subsets of a nonempty domain; nominal concept names denote singletons; individual names denote elements, without a unique-name assumption. Role names denote binary relations, inverse roles reverse their arguments, and U denotes the universal relation. Concepts are built from names, ⊤, ⊥, Boolean operations, \(\exists r\).C and \(\forall r\).C, qualified number restrictions \(\ge k s\).C and \(\le k s\).C, and \(\exists s\).Self. The last three require a simple role s. They mean, respectively, at least or at most k distinct s-successors satisfying C, and an s-edge from an element to itself. The nonnegative integer k is encoded in binary. K consists of concept inclusions C⊑D, individual assertions \(C(a), r(a,b), \neg r(a,b), a\ne b\), and a legal role box. Role inclusions have form w⊑R, with R a non-universal role name and w a nonempty string of non-universal roles, interpreted by relational composition. Regularity requires a strict partial order ≺ on roles satisfying S≺R iff \(Inv(S)\)≺R, such that each inclusion has \(w=RR, w=Inv(R)\), or \(w=S_{1}\ldots S_{t}, RS_{1}\ldots S_{t}\), or \(S_{1}\ldots S_{t}R\) with every \(S_{i}\)≺R. Equivalent roles can first be identified. Transitivity and symmetry are represented by RR⊑R and \(Inv(R)\)⊑R. A role is non-simple if a composition of length at least two is included in it, or in one of its subroles, closing under inverse; all other roles are simple. Reflexivity assertions are allowed; irreflexivity, strict asymmetry and role-disjointness assertions require simple roles. U cannot occur in role-box assertions. These are the standard global regularity and simplicity restrictions, not unrestricted role-chain rules. The query is \(q=\exists x_{1}\ldots x_{t} \land _{j}\alpha _{j}\), where each atom is \(A(u)\) or \(r(u,v), A\) is a concept name, r is a role name, and terms are variables or individual names. Query roles may be non-simple. Query atoms have no negation, inequality or regular-path operators; variables may receive the same value. A model satisfies q when some assignment makes every atom true. \(K\models q\) means every model of K satisfies q, including infinite models; an inconsistent K entails every query. Both K and q are input, and the sought algorithm must halt on every legal pair, with no prescribed complexity bound.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove the proposition in the problem statement or prove its logical negation, using exactly the definitions, hypotheses and quantifier order stated here. The proof must cover the complete target.
cards.why: A basic decidability boundary for querying expressive ontologies: the logic has decidable consistency, but unrestricted conjunctive-query entailment still lacks a general resolution.

importance.reason: A longstanding foundational question connecting description logics, database queries and infinite-model reasoning, with sharply different outcomes for nearby restrictions.

context_blocks.text: A knowledge base describes incomplete information about a world. Its assertions name some objects, while its general axioms can require additional unnamed objects in every possible world. A Boolean query asks whether a finite relational pattern must exist. The problem is to decide whether the pattern follows from the whole specification, rather than whether it can be found among explicitly stored facts.

For example, let K assert \(Person(a)\) and Person⊑\(\exists\)knows.Person. Every model then contains a person who knows a person, so K entails \(\exists x\exists y\)(\(Person(x)\land knows(x,y)\land Person(y)\)). No named witness for y is needed. The same individual may serve as both variables when the model permits it. More complicated queries reuse variables across several edges, requiring a single assignment that satisfies all joins simultaneously.

SROIQ combines concept negation, existential and universal restrictions, singleton concepts, inverse roles, counting and regular role chains. This expressive combination underlies the logical core of OWL 2 DL. The role restrictions in the definitions are substantive: removing regularity or allowing arbitrary counting over composite roles produces different logics. The original SROIQ paper supplies a decision procedure for consistency, but that alone does not answer arbitrary conjunctive queries.

The conjunction of K with \(\neg q\) is inconsistent exactly when K entails q, but the negation of an arbitrary joined relational pattern need not be expressible as a SROIQ knowledge base. Likewise, a finite graph built by a consistency tableau is usually a compact representation of models, not an ordinary database on which evaluating q automatically gives the right answer. Unfolding repeated nodes can change whether a query cycle exists.

Rudolph and Glimm resolved a major part of the surrounding question in 2010. They handle nominals, inverse roles and counting together, and obtain decidability for SROIQ when all binary query predicates are simple roles. Thus the mere presence of those three constructors is not the remaining obstacle. The full question on this card also allows the query to inspect roles affected by transitivity and more general role compositions.

A different positive frontier comes from Horn restrictions. Ortiz, Rudolph and Šimkus show decidability even for a stronger path-query language over Horn-SROIQ, with doubly exponential combined complexity. Horn knowledge bases exclude forms of disjunctive choice that full SROIQ permits. Their result is therefore highly relevant progress, while leaving the unrestricted combination of knowledge-base features and query joins unresolved.

The distinction between all models and finite models is particularly consequential. Rudolph proves undecidability of finite conjunctive-query entailment already in a fragment of SROIQ. This is not an undecidability proof for the semantics chosen here: the sets of countermodels differ, and the distinction can affect the answer even on a small example.

To see the difference directly, require every domain element to have exactly one r-successor and at most one r-predecessor, and require a named element a to have no predecessor. The role r can be simple. Such a knowledge base has an infinite model, the natural-number successor chain, but no finite model: on a finite set, an injective total successor function would be surjective. A fresh predicate A may be empty in the infinite model, so \(\exists x A(x)\) is not entailed over all models. Over finite models it is vacuously entailed, because there are none.

Steigmiller and Glimm’s 2019 absorption method addresses practical entailment checking in very expressive logics and is implemented in Konclude. Its termination argument depends on a bounded supply of newly generated nominals in the difficult feature combination. Useful empirical behavior and termination on substantial fragments do not establish a total procedure for every SROIQ input. This conditional termination is exactly why the inherited source continues to present full decidability as open.

There is relevant progress as recently as 2026, but on a different slice of the language. Ibáñez-García, Jung, Michielini and Murlak show that conjunctive-query entailment for S, which adds transitive roles to ALC, is 2ExpTime-complete; hardness already uses two transitive roles and a Boolean conjunctive query. Their May 2026 full version also treats restrictions giving smaller upper bounds. This settles a complexity question for S, not the decidability of full SROIQ.

A positive solution would establish that general finite query patterns can always be answered against this expressive ontology language in principle. A negative solution would identify a sharp gap between consistency checking and pattern entailment inside a standard logical framework. Either outcome would clarify which expressive features can be combined while retaining an algorithmic foundation for querying incomplete knowledge.

cards.title: Conjunctive-query containment under bag semantics
cards.area: Database theory and finite model theory
cards.formal: Does a Turing machine exist that halts on every pair of finite conjunctive queries \(q_{1}\) and \(q_{2}\) with the same output arity and decides whether $q_1(D)(a)\le q_2(D)(a)$ for every finite bag database D over their common relational signature and every output tuple a? A query $q(x)\!:\!-A_1,\ldots,A_m$ is evaluated by $q(D)(a)=\sum_{h:h(x)=a}\prod_{j=1}^{m}D(A_j[h])$, where h ranges over assignments of its variables to the finite database domain and \(D(A_{j}[h])\) is the nonnegative integer multiplicity of the instantiated tuple. Both input relations and query answers retain multiplicities.
cards.definitions: A relational signature lists finitely many relation names and their arities. A finite bag database supplies a finite domain U and, for each relation symbol of arity r, a function \(U^{r}\) to the nonnegative integers. Zero means the tuple is absent. A query body is a finite list of positive relational atoms with variables or named constants as arguments; constants denote distinct fixed elements of U. Every variable, including every output variable, must occur in a body atom. Repeated occurrences of relation names, variables, or entire atoms are allowed and are interpreted by the displayed sum-product rule. Assignments fix constants. No disjunction, negation, inequality, comparison predicate, aggregation operator, or recursion is permitted. The output tuple lists the values of the head variables in order. Boolean queries have an empty head and return the multiplicity of the single empty tuple. The question is about deciding containment from the queries alone, with no database supplied and no size or multiplicity bound on databases.
cards.answer_criterion: Construct a total algorithm deciding exactly this universal multiplicity inequality, or prove that no such algorithm exists. Enumerating counterexample databases only semidecides noncontainment. A procedure for set-valued databases, query equivalence, or a proper subclass of queries is insufficient; undecidability for unions, inequalities, or a modified numerical comparison is insufficient unless reduced to the stated plain-CQ problem.
cards.why: Bag semantics captures duplicate-sensitive query behavior, and containment is a basic correctness test for query optimization. Its unknown decidability marks a fundamental gap between simple positive query syntax and unbounded counting over finite structures. The problem also connects database theory with homomorphism inequalities and arithmetic decision problems.

importance.reason: A longstanding central decidability question for the most basic duplicate-sensitive query language. It has broad consequences for query rewriting and connects finite-model counting with undecidability boundaries.

progress.text: Chaudhuri and Vardi raise the bag-containment decidability question; the 2025 seminar traces the problem to their PODS paper.

Marcinkowski and Orda prove undecidability for nearby generalizations, including comparison after a supplied linear transformation of a Boolean query’s count. This is not the unmodified containment predicate.
Konstantinidis and Mogavero prove decidability when the left query is join-on-free and the right query is a general CQ. This extends the earlier projection-free decidable case.
The revised Marcinkowski–Ostropolski-Nalewaja paper develops techniques connecting CQ and UCQ containment, while explicitly leaving ordinary CQ-versus-CQ bag-containment decidability open.
Amarilli’s maintained question list continues to list bag-containment decidability. Current searches did not locate a resolution of the plain two-CQ formulation.

context_blocks.text: Containment asks whether one query can ever produce more of some answer than another. Under set semantics only presence matters. Under bag semantics, a join multiplies available copies and projection adds contributions from different witnesses. The multiplicities can therefore change even when the two queries return exactly the same set of answers.

For a minimal example, let \(q(x)\) have body \(R(x)\), and let \(r(x)\) have body \(R(x),R(x)\). If \(R(a)\) has multiplicity m, then q returns m copies of a and r returns \(m^{2}\). Their answer sets always coincide, but the reverse bag-containment r contained in q fails as soon as \(m=2\). This demonstrates why duplicate-insensitive rewrites need a different correctness argument.

For one fixed finite database, both values can be computed by enumerating assignments. The challenge is the quantifier over every database of every size and every choice of multiplicities. Noncontainment has a finite witness that can eventually be found by exhaustive enumeration. A decision procedure also needs to halt when no witness exists; a counterexample search by itself does not solve that side.

The 2025 seminar still identifies this as a longstanding unresolved boundary. Recent work establishes decidability for a restricted left-hand query in which existential variables do not participate in joins, while related work proves undecidability after extending the query language or numerical comparison. These results make the precise boundary especially significant: small changes around the basic formulation have known answers, but do not settle two unrestricted plain conjunctive queries.

cards.formal: Does there exist one effective logic \(\mathcal L\), in the precise sense below, whose sentences define exactly all deterministic logarithmic-space Boolean properties of finite unordered relational structures, for every finite relational vocabulary?

importance.reason: A broad descriptive-complexity existence question for a central resource class, with consequences for the expressive limits of order-independent database queries. It is distinct from improving one proposed recursion operator.

sentences: The input is a finite relational structure with no distinguished ordering of its elements.
The question asks for an effective logic expressing exactly all isomorphism-invariant Boolean queries decidable in deterministic logarithmic space.
Each sentence must compile to a halting evaluation algorithm with a certified logarithmic workspace bound.
The proposed CLogspace logic is known to miss some such queries, while ordered structures and strings admit stronger capturing results.
A solution would settle a broad descriptive-complexity question linking small-memory computation to the expressive power of logical queries.

cards.definitions:
A vocabulary \(\tau\) is a finite list of relation symbols, each with a fixed positive integer arity. A \(\tau\)-structure \(A\) has a finite nonempty domain and, for each \(r\)-ary symbol, an \(r\)-ary relation on that domain. An isomorphism is a bijection preserving and reflecting every relation. A Boolean property of \(\tau\)-structures is a class closed under isomorphism. The mathematical input supplies no distinguished ordering of its elements.

For computation, label the domain by \([n]=\{0,\ldots,n-1\}\). Encode \(n\) in unary followed by all relation truth tables in the vocabulary order and lexicographic tuple order, using one bit per tuple. Write \(N\) for the full encoding length. All labelings of a structure are valid encodings. A property is in deterministic logarithmic space, denoted \(\mathrm L\), if a fixed deterministic Turing machine halts and decides it correctly on every such encoding using at most \(C\lceil\log_2(N+2)\rceil\) work-tape cells for some fixed positive integer \(C\). Machines have a read-only two-way input tape, a finite control, and a fixed finite number of work tapes over fixed finite alphabets. Work space counts all cells visited on the work tapes; the input tape is not writable. They have no oracle, advice, auxiliary input, or random bits. A machine may use the encoding order internally, but its answer must be the same on all isomorphic inputs.

The proposed logic has a decidable set of finite binary encodings of pairs \((\tau,\varphi)\), where \(\varphi\) is a sentence over \(\tau\). Each valid sentence has a Boolean satisfaction relation \(A\models\varphi\) on all finite nonempty \(\tau\)-structures, invariant under isomorphism. There must be one total computable compiler that, on a valid pair, outputs a deterministic Turing machine \(M_\varphi\) and a positive integer \(C_\varphi\). For every valid encoding of every \(\tau\)-structure, \(M_\varphi\) must halt, return its satisfaction value, and use at most \(C_\varphi\lceil\log_2(N+2)\rceil\) work cells. On invalid sentence encodings the compiler may return a fixed error symbol. Syntax checking and compilation are not required to run in logarithmic space or polynomial time.

Expressive completeness requires that for every finite \(\tau\) and every isomorphism-invariant \(\mathrm L\) property \(Q\) of its structures, there is one fixed \(\tau\)-sentence \(\varphi\) such that \[ \forall A:\quad A\models\varphi\iff A\in Q.\] The sentence and its space constant may depend on \(Q\) and \(\tau\), but not on \(A\). The same syntax and compiler work across all vocabularies. No computable translation from arbitrary invariant machines to sentences is required. There is no uniform logarithmic-space requirement when the sentence is part of the evaluation input. A relational query with a fixed tuple of distinguished elements can be represented as a Boolean property in a vocabulary expanded by singleton unary relations marking those elements; the target uses the Boolean convention throughout.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean that such a logic exists, including decidable syntax, invariant semantics, effective evaluation with certified per-sentence space constants, and expressive completeness; or prove that no logic meets all those conditions. The formalism and its semantics must be specified, rather than merely assigning an uninterpreted name to each logarithmic-space property. A result for one candidate logic or for a restricted family of input structures does not settle this general existence question.

context_blocks.text: The source motivation is computation on large relational inputs with very little working memory. A representation necessarily labels the elements, but a query about the abstract structure must not change when those labels are permuted. Capturing asks for both expressive completeness and an effective resource-bounded evaluation of every sentence.

The 2019 paper constructs CLogspace as a logic for computations that preserve input symmetries. Its objects are finite sets built from input elements and further finite sets, equipped with size annotations and restricted recursion. Theorem 27 proves that this particular logic is strictly weaker than logarithmic space. That negative result concerns a candidate, not the existence of any capturing logic.

The saved passage asks whether ideas from CLogspace can yield a stronger logic. It specifies no formal class of permitted extensions. This card makes explicit the general logic-existence objective discussed in the same paper’s introduction and Section 5; it does not require a particular extension grammar or claim that CLogspace itself captures the class. The effective-syntax and compiler requirements follow the standard capturing convention, with the space bound stated separately here.

An externally supplied order changes the descriptive problem. The 2019 source recalls that deterministic transitive-closure logic captures logarithmic space on ordered structures. More recently, Bell, Day and Freydenberger obtain LOGSPACE-capturing fragments for string queries; the June 2026 abstract concerns strings, not arbitrary unordered relational inputs.

cards.title: Computability of entropic query-size bounds
cards.area: Database theory and finite model theory
cards.formal:
Is the logarithmic entropic query-size bound uniformly computable? More precisely, does a single deterministic Turing machine, given any finite set of degree constraints \(\mathcal D=\{(X_i,Y_i,b_i):1\leq i\leq k\}\) on \([n]\) with nonnegative rational logarithmic budgets, and any \(m\in\mathbb N\), halt and output either \(+\infty\) when \(E(\mathcal D)=+\infty\), or a rational \(q\) satisfying \(|q-E(\mathcal D)|\leq 2^{-m}\) when
\[E(\mathcal D)=\sup\{h([n]):h\in\overline{\Gamma_n^*},\ h(Y_i)-h(X_i)\leq b_i\ (1\leq i\leq k)\}<+\infty?\]
Here \(\overline{\Gamma_n^*}\) is the closure of the discrete entropy region defined below; \(n\) is part of the input.
cards.why: The strongest information-theoretic query estimates are useful algorithmically only if their numerical values can be obtained effectively. A computability theorem would make this extremal use of arbitrary discrete distributions accessible to uniform algorithms; a noncomputability theorem would identify a fundamental limit on exact information-theoretic database estimation, even with unlimited running time.
cards.status_note: The 2022 seminar asks Question 7.1. Mengel–Romashchenko v1, 27 August 2026, abstract and introduction explicitly say that general entropic-bound computability is not known. A bounded primary-source check on 16 September 2026 found no matching resolution; cited results were read for their statements and scope, not independently proved.

progress.text: Hung Ngo poses computability of the entropic bound as Question 7.1 at Seminar 22301; the report appears in February 2023.

Suciu’s expanded paper gives the cone and duality framework; Theorem 9.7 identifies the entropic upper value with optimization over the almost-entropic closure. It does not provide a general computation procedure.
Im, Moseley, Ngo and Pruhs give a polynomial-size formulation for simple degree constraints, providing a tractable case of the coincident bounds.
Mengel and Romashchenko explicitly retain general entropic-bound computability as unknown while obtaining new results for acyclic constraints and projections.

sentences: Entropy bounds limit the number of tuples returned by a database join from constraints on conditional degrees.
The entropic bound optimizes total entropy over the closure of all finite discrete entropy vectors.
The question asks for one terminating algorithm that computes this value to every requested absolute accuracy in arbitrary dimension.
Simple constraints admit effective special cases, while the general polymatroid relaxation can overestimate the desired value.
Resolving computability would determine whether the strongest information-theoretic estimate is accessible to algorithms at all.

cards.definitions:
Let \(n\geq1\), \([n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}\), and \(2^{[n]}\) be its set of subsets. Given jointly distributed discrete random variables \(Z_1,\ldots,Z_n\), each with a finite alphabet, their entropy vector is the real set function
\[h(S)=H(Z_S)=-\sum_z\Pr[Z_S=z]\log_2\Pr[Z_S=z],\qquad h(\varnothing)=0,\]
where \(Z_S\) is the tuple with indices in \(S\), and \(0\log_2 0=0\). Alphabets and real joint probabilities are unrestricted. The set of all such vectors is \(\Gamma_n^*\). Its closure \(\overline{\Gamma_n^*}\) in the finite-dimensional Euclidean space of subset coordinates consists of all limits of sequences of entropy vectors and is the almost-entropic cone. Neither alphabet sizes nor convergence rates are input bounds. Continuous differential entropy is not used.

A degree constraint is a triple \((X,Y,b)\), where \(X\subseteq Y\subseteq[n]\) and \(b\in\mathbb Q_{\geq0}\). It bounds the conditional entropy \(h(Y)-h(X)\). The case \(X=\varnothing\) gives a cardinality-type constraint, and \(b=0\) gives a functional dependency. Equal sets, repeated triples and an empty list are permitted. The all-zero entropy vector is always feasible, so the supremum is in \([0,+\infty]\). The optimization is over the closed almost-entropic cone, not just the nonclosed set of entropy vectors satisfying the constraints exactly; this distinction matters on faces defined by zero budgets.

For a database interpretation, a full conjunctive query returns the natural join of finite relations: an output tuple assigns all variables and its projection onto each relation's columns is present in that relation. There are no duplicate output tuples and no existentially projected variables. A bound of \(N\) on the number of extensions from columns \(X\) to columns \(Y\) gives the entropy budget \(b=\log_2 N\). Drawing a join tuple uniformly makes its full entropy the logarithm of the join size. The quantity \(2^{E(\mathcal D)}\) is the information-theoretic upper bound; the question asks to compute its logarithm, rather than to enumerate joins or compute the exact maximum size of a finite database instance.

The finite encoding used here writes \(n\) and the list length in unary, every subset as an \(n\)-bit mask, and each rational budget as a nonnegative binary numerator and a positive binary denominator, with delimiters. The precision \(m\) is given in unary. This is an explicit rational logarithmic-budget version of the source's numerical problem, with no real-number oracle. At the level of computability it also covers positive integer degree bounds supplied as \(N\): cone homogeneity handles rational budgets by scaling them to integer logarithms, while positive values \(\log_2 N\) can be bracketed multiplicatively by rational numbers, keeping zero budgets exactly zero. This equivalence concerns computability, not polynomial-time equivalence of the two encodings.

Unbounded inputs are included. They can be recognized by starting with \(S=\varnothing\) and repeatedly adjoining \(Y_i\) whenever \(X_i\subseteq S\). The optimum is finite exactly when the resulting closure is \([n]\). In that case conditional-entropy inequalities and subadditivity supply an explicit finite upper bound. If some variables remain outside, let them all share an arbitrarily high-entropy random variable and make the other variables constant; every constraint is satisfied while the objective is unbounded. Thus recognizing infinity is not the unknown part of the problem.

The machine must halt on every valid input, with a finite binary rational output in the bounded case; malformed strings may be rejected. There is no time or space bound, no advice, oracle, fixed dimension or randomness. Accuracy is absolute in base-two entropy units. In particular the machine must achieve error at most \(1/100\), by taking \(m=7\), and also every finer requested accuracy. A one-sided sequence of estimates without a computable error guarantee does not suffice.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean that the displayed uniform machine exists, or that it does not. An affirmative proof must provide an effective procedure and prove termination and the requested two-sided absolute error for every finite dimension, rational degree-constraint list and precision, including zero budgets and the stated infinity convention. A negative proof must establish noncomputability of this particular functional, not merely undecidability of a different entropy-region membership or information-inequality problem. An exact symbolic formula is unnecessary, while a computable value for each separately fixed input without one uniform procedure is insufficient. There are no unproved complexity assumptions in the target.

source_formulation.text: Does an algorithm compute the entropic bound on query output size from the supplied constraints?
source_formulation.caption: Editorial paraphrase of Question 7.1; entropy closure, numerical representation and accuracy are made explicit in this card.

context_blocks.text: The seminar groups several algorithmic questions about information-theoretic database bounds. Question 7.1 asks for computability of the entropic bound; Question 7.2 separately asks about the complexity of its polymatroid relaxation. The first issue is whether any terminating numerical algorithm exists, before asking whether one is efficient.

Entropy inequalities constrain correlations among columns in a join. Using every valid inequality gives a potentially sharper bound than the familiar Shannon inequalities alone. Suciu formulates the entropic upper bound by such inequalities and identifies its value with optimization over the closed almost-entropic cone. This closure specifies which limiting entropy vectors belong to the target.

Replacing the almost-entropic cone by normalized monotone submodular set functions gives a finite linear program, with exponentially many subset coordinates. This yields a computable upper relaxation, but a gap between that relaxation and the entropic optimum prevents it from settling the question. Restricting alphabet sizes also changes the feasible region unless a sufficient effective approximation theorem is proved.

For simple degree constraints, where every conditioning set has size at most one, the entropic and polymatroid bounds coincide and a polynomial-size linear program is available. This tractable subclass does not cover arbitrary conditioning sets or all zero-budget functional dependencies.

Mengel and Romashchenko still describe general computability as unresolved in August 2026. Their new work examines acyclic dependencies and shows that allowing projected variables can create gaps between entropy and polymatroid bounds. That result concerns the comparison of bounds in a richer query setting, not an algorithm or impossibility proof for the full general numerical target here.

cards.title: Linear-round convergence over stable semirings
cards.area: Database theory and finite model theory
cards.formal: Is there a universal constant C such that the following holds for every integer \(p\ge 0\), every \(n\ge 1\), every commutative p-stable semiring S, and every polynomial map \(F:S^{n} -> S^{n}\) with coefficients in S? Starting with \(x^{0}=(0,\ldots ,0)\), perform synchronous iteration \(x^{t+1}=F(x^{t})\). There must exist an integer \(t\le C(p+1)n\) with \(x^{t+1}=x^{t}\). Here p-stability means $1\oplus a\oplus\cdots\oplus a^p=1\oplus a\oplus\cdots\oplus a^{p+1}$ for every a in S. The constant C is independent of the semiring, coefficients, number of monomials, and polynomial degrees. This is the grounded polynomial-system formulation of the source’s proposed linear convergence bound.
cards.definitions: A commutative semiring has associative, commutative addition op-plus with identity 0 and associative, commutative multiplication op-times with identity 1. Multiplication distributes over addition, and 0 times \(a=0\). No additive inverses are assumed. Powers use semiring multiplication and \(a^{0}=1\). Every component of F is a finite sum of finite products of coefficients and variables; repeated variables and constant terms are allowed. S need not be finite. One round evaluates all components using only the previous vector, not partially updated coordinates. Equality means exact equality of semiring elements. The cost measure is the number of rounds, irrespective of the work needed to evaluate a component or represent an element. In a grounded Datalog program, coordinates represent individual derived facts and their values are annotations; using all n coordinates also includes any that remain zero.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove the universal bound, or refute it by constructing systems whose first fixed-point time divided by \((p+1)n\) is unbounded. A fixed example exceeding n rounds does not refute an unspecified constant C. A bound with a growing factor depending on degrees, coefficients, or n does not establish this target. A faster evaluation algorithm with a different update rule does not by itself bound the number of synchronous naive iterations.
cards.why: The problem asks whether local algebraic stability imposes a sharp global limit on recursive evaluation. A universal linear bound would explain why a broad class of annotated recursive computations needs only an output-scale number of rounds, while a separation would expose a fundamental cost of nonlinear interactions.

importance.reason: A foundational convergence question for semiring-valued recursion, with implications beyond one query language. Its historical significance is high, but a newly announced directly relevant paper makes current open status uncertain.

progress.text: Work on convergence of Datalog over pre-semirings establishes stable-semiring convergence and an exponential upper bound in the number of grounded coordinates; the later polynomial paper reviews this starting point.
Im, Moseley, Ngo, and Pruhs establish polynomial convergence for nonlinear programs. The inspected arXiv v2 states the additional sigma and lambda dependencies explicitly.
Ngo records the gap between the polynomial upper bound and \(Omega((p+1)n)\), and proposes a matching linear upper bound.

Author publication pages list Optimal Convergence of Iterative Methods for Datalogo, with a forthcoming PODS 2027 label on Ngo’s page. No theorem text was obtained for that entry. Its relationship to this exact target requires verification.

context_blocks.text: In ordinary Boolean Datalog, a derived fact switches from absent to present at most once. A nonstationary round must add a fact, so the number of possible facts bounds the number of rounds. Annotated recursion can improve the value attached to an already known fact many times. Counting how many coordinates exist therefore ceases to give an immediate termination bound.

The stability assumption controls repeated use of a single semiring element. It says that a sufficiently long truncated geometric sum absorbs the next power. The question asks whether a system of n interacting recurrences can multiply the resulting delay by only \(O(n)\), even when the equations are nonlinear. This is a structural claim about composition of recursive dependencies, not a bound on the time taken by one database join.

The examined Im–Moseley–Ngo–Pruhs preprint proves a polynomial convergence bound, with explicit dependence on sigma, the number of distinct coefficients referenced, and lambda, the maximum number of multiplicands. Its bound is O(sigma \(p n^{2}\) (\(n^{2} \log\)(lambda+1)+log(sigma+1))) for positive p; the 0-stable case has a separate linear bound. Suppressing sigma and lambda would conceal part of the remaining challenge.

The 2025 seminar asks for \(O((p+1)n)\), matching the order of its stated lower bound. A newer paper titled Optimal Convergence of Iterative Methods for Datalogo is now listed by its authors. The inspected listings supply no theorem or accessible manuscript for that entry. This card therefore preserves the precise historical question with an uncertain current status; the title alone does not identify which convergence bound, iteration scheme, or semiring hypotheses it settles.

cards.title: Complexity of polymatroid query-size bounds
cards.area: Database theory and finite model theory
cards.formal:
Is computing the general polymatroid query-size bound NP-hard? Use the following exact comparison formulation and deterministic polynomial-time Turing reductions. Given \(n\geq1\), a finite list \(\mathcal D=\{(X_i,Y_i,b_i):1\leq i\leq k\}\) of rational logarithmic degree constraints and a rational threshold \(t\), let
\[P(\mathcal D)=\sup\{h([n]):h\in\Gamma_n,\ h(Y_i)-h(X_i)\leq b_i\text{ for all }i\},\]
where \(\Gamma_n\) is the cone of normalized monotone submodular set functions on \([n]\). Is the language
\[\mathrm{POLYBOUND}=\{\langle n,\mathcal D,t\rangle:P(\mathcal D)\geq t\}\]
NP-hard under the reduction convention below, when dimension and all constraints are part of the input?
cards.why: A general polynomial-time procedure would make a broad information-theoretic relaxation available for query planning without enumerating exponentially many subset entropies. A hardness theorem would explain why the known algorithms require special dependency structure. Determining which conclusion is justified separates a useful compact optimization method from a bound whose direct formulation is mainly an existential certificate.
cards.status_note: The 2022 source explicitly asks whether computing the general polymatroid bound is NP-hard. Im–Moseley–Ngo–Pruhs, 3 April 2025, still describe general polynomial-time computability as open and distinguish their normal-function hardness theorem from the unrestricted cone. A bounded primary-source search checked on 16 September 2026 found no matching general resolution; the exact rational-threshold and Turing-reduction conventions are stated editorial choices, and absence of a located resolution is not a proof of openness.

progress.text: The seminar records Hung Ngo’s question about the general complexity and possible NP-hardness of the polymatroid bound.
The Optimizing Polymatroid Functions preprint reports polynomial-time optimization for simple constraints and NP-hardness for the distinct normal-function optimization.

Theorem 1.1 supplies a polynomial-size LP for simple constraints; Theorem 1.3 gives general-to-restricted reductions, and Theorem 1.4 proves hardness only for normal functions. The introduction and conclusion still leave general polynomial-time computability open.

importance.basis: Saved question, title, and category scope; importance review only, not a fresh proof or open-status review.

sentences: Polymatroid query bounds maximize a normalized monotone submodular function subject to supplied degree constraints.
The obvious linear program has exponentially many coordinates even when its input constraint list is short.
The source explicitly asks whether computing this general bound is NP-hard, formalized here through exact rational threshold comparisons.
Simple constraints admit polynomial-time algorithms, while hardness for the smaller cone of normal functions leaves the general question unresolved.
An answer would clarify whether this broad database estimation framework can be computed efficiently from compact dependency descriptions.

cards.definitions:
For \([n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}\), a polymatroid function is a real-valued function \(h:2^{[n]}\to\mathbb R\) such that
\[h(\varnothing)=0,\qquad h(S)\leq h(T)\quad(S\subseteq T),\]
\[h(S)+h(T)\geq h(S\cup T)+h(S\cap T)\quad(S,T\subseteq[n]).\]
These conditions imply \(h(S)\geq0\). Their cone is \(\Gamma_n\). Coordinates may be arbitrary real numbers; functions need not be integer-valued matroid ranks or entropy vectors. A constraint \((X,Y,b)\) has \(X\subseteq Y\subseteq[n]\) and \(b\in\mathbb Q_{\geq0}\), and means \(h(Y)-h(X)\leq b\). An empty list, zero budgets, equal sets and repeated constraints are allowed. The zero function is feasible. Set \(P(\mathcal D)=+\infty\) for an unbounded objective; in that case every finite threshold is accepted. Otherwise the finite rational linear program attains a rational optimum, and equality with the threshold counts as yes.

The input explicitly lists the constraints, not the \(2^n\) values of a candidate function. Write \(n\) and the list length in unary, each subset as an \(n\)-bit mask, and every rational as a binary integer numerator and a positive binary denominator with delimiters; the threshold numerator may be negative. Let \(L\) be the total number of bits. Invalid strings are rejected. This card fixes the usual rational logarithmic-budget bit model for the source's optimization question: numbers \(b_i\), rather than potentially enormous degree counts \(2^{b_i}\), are supplied. It does not assume unit-cost exact arithmetic on arbitrary real inputs. Comparison is exact, with no numerical tolerance, promise gap, fixed dimension or fixed constraint arity.

The database meaning is as follows. A full conjunctive query joins finite relations by matching common columns and returns all variable columns, with set semantics. A degree bound \(N\) limits how many distinct \(Y\)-tuples extend each fixed \(X\)-tuple. For a uniform random output tuple, conditional entropy is at most \(\log_2 N\), while the entropy of the complete tuple is the logarithm of the result size. Every entropy vector satisfies the displayed polymatroid inequalities, so maximizing over polymatroids yields a valid logarithmic upper estimate. The source's linear-program framework is formalized here with rational logarithmic budgets. No database instance is an input to POLYBOUND, and maximizing the actual finite join size is a different optimization problem.

A language lies in NP when yes instances have binary certificates of polynomially bounded length verified by a deterministic polynomial-time Turing machine. NP-hardness here means that every such language can be decided by a deterministic oracle Turing machine with access to exact POLYBOUND membership and worst-case running time \(C(L+1)^c\), for some constants depending only on the reduced language. An oracle query returns one membership bit; writing the query and all other bit operations count toward the time bound. Equivalently, it suffices to give such a reduction from satisfiability of Boolean formulas in conjunctive normal form with at most three literals per clause. Clauses are disjunctions of variables or their negations, and the formula is the conjunction of its clauses. This explicitly chosen Turing-reduction convention avoids changing hardness when the complementary threshold convention is used. No randomized reduction, advice or entropy oracle is allowed.

The full optimization has \(2^n\) subset variables and exponentially many monotonicity and submodularity inequalities, so explicit rational linear programming gives a terminating algorithm taking time at most exponential in a polynomial of \(L\). That upper bound does not establish NP-hardness. The issue is the cost in the compact input length; with \(n\) fixed the linear program has fixed dimension.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean that POLYBOUND is NP-hard under the stated deterministic polynomial-time Turing reductions, or a proof of the logical negation of that assertion. A positive proof must preserve the general polymatroid feasible cone and the finite input encoding, and establish correctness for every source instance. Hardness of a restriction on the admissible functions, such as the cone of normal functions, does not imply this claim unless a valid reduction to POLYBOUND is proved. A polynomial-time algorithm would settle the principal algorithmic side of the source's broader complexity question, but by itself proves the negation of NP-hardness only together with a proved separation of P from NP; an unproved separation must be stated as a conditional result. Neither an exponential-size LP formulation nor difficulty computing a different entropic bound is a negative algorithmic result for this problem.

source_formulation.text: Determine the complexity of computing the polymatroid bound; in particular, is the general computation NP-hard?
source_formulation.caption: Editorial paraphrase of Question 7.2. The card retains its explicit NP-hardness question and fixes rational logarithmic inputs, exact comparison and polynomial-time Turing reductions.

context_blocks.text: The source asks both for the complexity of the polymatroid bound and, explicitly, whether it is NP-hard. The displayed yes/no target is this stated hardness question for the entire degree-constraint class. The companion entropic question concerns existence of any computation procedure; the polymatroid bound is already computable by finite linear programming.

Unlike minimizing one supplied submodular function, this problem optimizes over the values of an unknown submodular function. The constraint list is compact but a direct feasible function has exponentially many subset coordinates. Standard polynomial-time solvability of explicit linear programs therefore leaves the desired compact-input complexity unresolved.

A degree constraint is simple when its conditioning set has at most one variable. For this class, Im and coauthors give a linear program with O(k n²) variables and O(k n) constraints, and an efficiently obtainable derivation of the bound using Shannon inequalities. The 2022 preprint already reports the tractability breakthrough; the 2025 paper supplies the formulation and theorem locators used here.

Theorem 1.3 of the 2025 paper reduces the general problem to several apparently restricted degree languages, including constraints with conditioning sets of size at most two and total sets of size at most three. Its statement that these cases are as hard as the general case is a reduction result, not a proof that any of them is NP-hard.

The same paper does prove NP-hardness after restricting feasible polymatroids to normal functions. Such functions have the form h(S)=Σ_T w_T·1[S∩T≠∅], with nonnegative weights indexed by nonempty variable subsets T. This is a smaller cone; its constrained maximum can change when arbitrary polymatroids are permitted. The hardness therefore does not settle Question 7.2.

This is a smaller cone; its constrained maximum can change when arbitrary polymatroids are permitted. The hardness therefore does not settle Question 7.2.

cards.title: BDD/FC conjecture
cards.area: Database theory and finite model theory
cards.formal: Is every finite set \(R\) of existential tuple-generating dependencies with bounded derivation depth finitely controllable? Use the precise query-rewriting definition of bounded derivation depth below. The required conclusion is that for every finite database \(I\) and every Boolean conjunctive query \(q\), \[(I,R)\models q\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad(I,R)\models_{\mathrm{fin}}q.\] The left side quantifies over all models extending \(I\) and satisfying \(R\); the right side quantifies only over finite such models. The conjecture quantifies over every finite relational signature of arbitrary finite arities, and permits conjunctions of several atoms in rule heads.
cards.why: Bounded derivation depth permits queries under existential rules to be answered through finite positive rewritings on the original database. Finite controllability asks whether considering only finite possible worlds changes those answers. Connecting the two would clarify when this useful query-processing property also supports finite-model semantics, across arbitrary relational arities.
cards.status_note: The general conjecture is explicitly open in the checked PODS 2025 paper, which was posted to arXiv in March 2026. Its structural theorem does not imply full finite controllability, and the original binary-signature theorem assumes single-head rules. Bounded later-work checks through 2026-09-15 found no resolution of the unrestricted target; the review is not an exhaustive proof or literature certification.

importance.basis: Saved question, title, and category scope; importance review only, not a fresh proof or open-status review.

sentences: The BDD/FC conjecture asks whether every finite existential rule set with bounded derivation depth is finitely controllable.
Bounded derivation depth is expressed by a finite positive rewriting for each conjunctive query that works on every database.
Finite controllability means that a query failing in some unrestricted model also fails in a finite model.
The question allows arbitrary finite relational arities and several atoms in a rule head.
The known binary theorem requires single-head rules, and the checked PODS 2025 result posted in 2026 leaves the general conjecture open.

cards.definitions: A relational signature is a finite collection of relation symbols, each with a fixed nonnegative integer arity. An atom has the form \(P(t_1,\ldots,t_a)\), with repeated arguments allowed. In rules and queries the arguments are variables; there are no function symbols, built-in equality or inequality, negation, or interpreted order. A rule is the sentence \(\forall\bar x\,\forall\bar y\,(B(\bar x,\bar y)\to\exists\bar z\,H(\bar y,\bar z))\), where \(B,H\) are finite nonempty conjunctions of atoms, each universal variable occurs in \(B\), and the only universal variables in \(H\) come from \(\bar y\). The tuples of universal and existential variables are disjoint. The existential tuple may be empty, so ordinary positive Datalog rules are included. A rule set is finite, and rule heads may contain several atoms. A database \(I\) is a finite set of relational facts on finitely many named distinct elements; its active domain is the set of elements appearing in these facts. Empty active domains and nullary facts are allowed. A model extending \(I\) has a nonempty domain containing its named elements and includes every fact of \(I\); it may add elements and facts, including new facts on old elements. It satisfies \(R\) with ordinary first-order semantics, and must preserve the identities of the named database elements. “Finite model” means a finite domain, with no prescribed cardinality bound. A conjunctive query \(q(\bar u)=\exists\bar v\,A(\bar u,\bar v)\) uses a finite nonempty conjunction of relational atoms, with every displayed free variable occurring in an atom. A Boolean query has no free variables. A union of conjunctive queries is a finite disjunction of such queries with the same free variables; the empty disjunction denotes false. Query evaluation on a database means a variable assignment into its active domain satisfying all required facts, and for a union means satisfaction of at least one disjunct. For an answer tuple \(\bar a\) from the active domain, \((I,R)\models q(\bar a)\) means that every model extending \(I\) and satisfying \(R\) satisfies this instantiated query. Define \(R\) to have bounded derivation depth if for every conjunctive query \(q(\bar u)\) there is a finite union of conjunctive queries \(Q(\bar u)\) over the same signature such that, for every finite database \(I\) and every compatible answer tuple \(\bar a\), \((I,R)\models q(\bar a)\) if and only if \(I\models Q(\bar a)\). The rewriting \(Q\) may depend on \(R,q\) but not on the database or answer tuple. This is the source’s equivalent positive query-rewriting formulation of bounded derivation depth; it does not require one depth bound for all queries. Finite controllability is the displayed unrestricted-versus-finite equivalence for every \(I,q\). There is no syntactic guardedness, stickiness, binary-arity or single-head restriction on \(R\), and no time bound for constructing a rewriting or countermodel.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of the implication for every finite signature and rule set, or refute it. A positive answer must show that whenever a Boolean conjunctive query fails in some possibly infinite model of \(I,R\), it also fails in some finite model of the same database and rules, assuming only the stated bounded derivation depth property. A negative answer must provide one finite signature and rule set \(R\), prove its rewriting property for every conjunctive query, and provide a finite database \(I\) and Boolean conjunctive query \(q\) such that every finite model of \(I,R\) satisfies \(q\) but some infinite model does not. Showing bounded behavior for a single query does not establish the premise on \(R\). A counterexample whose rules lack bounded derivation depth, or a theorem for binary single-head rules alone, does not settle this target.
